Ut prius Aposto- lus docuit verum DEI dilectionem à falsa discerne- re, & affirmavit cum non diligere Deum, qui fra- trem non diligat: ita nunc etiam veram charita- tem proximi à falsa discernit, & ostendit eum non diligere fratrem, qui Deum non diligit, & man- data ejus non servat, sed in gratiam hominis sibi dilecti facit, quod cum verbo & mandato Dei pu- gnat. Sic non diligunt proximum suum, qui ad falsa dogmata connivent, quæ verbo Dei repugnant. Neque illi diligunt fratres, qui scelera, quæ ratione vocationis suæ debebant punire, inulta esse sinunt. Nec illi dilectionem proximi habent, qui alios in peccando adjuvant, & solicitantibus ad impurita- tem aut injustitiam morem gerunt. Hoc non est diligere proximum, sed est diligere nequitiam. Ve- ra enim proximi dilectio ad normam mandatorum Dei regulata & formata esse debet. Et Deum ante omnia diligere debemus, ut ipsius mandata in nul- lius hominis gratiam violemus, uti hæc explicat Osiander.

## 5:3
Verse 3.

For this is the love of God, that we keep his commandments.] 'That' here is explanatory, and in the word 'love' there is a metonymy. For it signifies the manifestation of that love by which we are moved toward God. See Exodus XX, 6; Deuteronomy V, 10, where 'that' is explanatory.

And his commandments are not grievous.] 'And' for a relative, as if he were saying, which commandments of his are not grievous, namely on account of divine aid.

Nothing is to be despaired of with Christ as leader and Christ as patron. Consider what we said on Matthew XI, verse 30, and what will now follow.

The commandments are not grievous partly with respect to the faith apprehending the obedience of Christ, who for us fulfilled the law unto righteousness for every believer, Romans X, v. 4, provided that this is a matter of faith, and the Apostle testifies that we overcome the world through faith, and that for this reason Jesus willed to come by water and blood, and also by his Spirit, so that through them, regenerated by faith, we might both overcome the world and fulfill his commandments: partly with respect to the obedience of the reborn proceeding from faith, which although it is only begun, is nevertheless sincere and not hypocritical, and to God, even if imperfect, it is pleasing through faith covering that imperfection. St. John does not say that his commandments can be perfectly fulfilled; but he says they are not grievous and burdensome, because they do not aggravate, or press upon the reborn like a burdensome weight, for the law is not laid down for the just, 1 Timothy I, verse 9. The blessed Hunnius explains the sense thus: As if he were saying, God does not demand from his reborn and beloved children that absolute perfection of charity which Moses demands: but he prescribes such commandments as are not grievous to the regenerated by the power of the Holy Spirit, since they act both by a spontaneous Spirit toward the obedience of God, and GOD is delighted by their begun obedience, while he supplies the remaining defect with the fullness and dignity of the obedience of his Son. Which is more fully explained by Flacius: The commandments of GOD are called light in Christ for many reasons: 1. Because God freely imputes to us the fulfillment of the whole law made by the Son. 2. Because regenerating us through the Son, he creates us for good works, and inscribes his law and his work upon our heart, so that we now delight in it from the soul. 3. Because he pardons all those things which we do not perform. 4. Because he transferred its curse and the punishment of the unperformed commandments onto his Son. 5. Because he imputes our mere endeavor of zealously obeying in Christ as full obedience, or takes it in good part: just as a most kind Father values even the smallest duties of a Son more than the hardest and most perfect works of a servant. 6. Finally, because he himself everywhere promptly succors us, giving the will, the power, and the performance according to his good pleasure. Otherwise, concerning the true and full observation of the law, it is most rightly argued by Paul that no one, not even the reborn, fully satisfies it, so that it now does and effects nothing more properly in us than to denounce to us our supreme injustice and the wrath of God and eternal punishments, and to condemn us. Therefore, the Papists and Schwenckfeldists wickedly abuse this testimony to amplify human powers and to obscure the law and the severity of the justice of God, and even the very remission of sins, or the assiduous absolution of our filth made by the blood of CHRIST.

Guilhelmus Estius, although he argues from this passage that because the commandments of GOD are not grievous to a justified man, they are much less impossible for him: yet he twists himself greatly in his explanation of it. For at one moment he says they are light in themselves, because nothing is easier than to love that which is supremely lovable: at another he compares himself to the state in which the first parents were created: and he acknowledges that as far as nature corrupted by sin is concerned, they are grievous and difficult: at another he thinks that a distinction must still be made, and that one must speak differently of a man not yet reborn, and differently of the reborn: he confesses that to the former the commandments of GOD are grievous, and in a certain sense impossible, but not so to the latter: at another he acknowledges that even for a man reborn and justified, he still suffers difficulty in the way of the commandments of God on account of the rebellion of the flesh against the Spirit, so that for this reason he must say with Paul: I am carnal, sold under sin. Why then does he still boast that the commandments of the law are possible to fulfill, and not difficult? He finally answers: But because he has a will absolutely conformed to the will of GOD, so that he can say with the same Apostle in the same place: I consent to the divine law, because it is good. And again: I delight in the law of God according to the inner man, Rom. VIII, it follows that to such a one the commandments of God are light, easy, and delightful. But indeed, he who consents to the law of God, that it is good, yet does not do what he wills, he indeed delights in the law of God according to the inner man; but he sees another law in his members warring against the law of his mind, and taking him captive under the law of sin, which is in his members; his will is not absolutely conformed to the will of God, but only as regards the inner man, and to him, because of the rebellion of the flesh against the Spirit, the commandments of God are not light, easy, and delightful, much less can they be fully fulfilled without any defect. Moreover, this rebellion and repugnance and the operation of those things which he does not will is ἁμαρτία, and therefore ἀνομία, 1 John III, verse 4; but where there is ἀνομία or deviation from the law, there is not a full fulfillment of the law.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

Αὕτη γάρ ἐστιν ἡ ἀγάπη τῦ Θεῦ, ἵνα τὰς ἐντολὰς αὐτῦ τη- ρῶμεν.] Ἱνα hic est εἰδικὸν, & in ἀγάπης voce est metonymia. Significatur enim ostensio ejus dilectionis, qua in Deum fe- rimur. Vide Exod. XX, 6. Deut V, 10. ubi ἥ est ἐξηγητικόν.

Καὶ αἱ ἐντολαὶ αὐτῦ βαρεῖαι ὐκ εἰσίν.] Καὶ pro relativo, quasi diceret, quæ præcepta ejus gravia non sunt, nempe propter opem divinam.

Nil desperandum Christo Duce & Auspice Christo. Considera quæ diximus Matth. XI. vers. 30. & quæ jam se- quentur.

Mandata gravia non sunt partim respectu fi- dei apprehendentis obedientiam Christi, qui pro nobis legem implevit ad justitiam omni credenti, Roman. X. v. 4. siquidem hic de fide agatur, & per fidem mundum nos vincere testetur Aposto- lus, atque ideo Jesus venire voluerit aqua & san- guine, nec non Spiritu suo, ut per ea regeniti fide cum mundum superemus, tum mandata ejus im- pleamus: partim respectu obedientiæ renatorum ex fide profectæ, quæ licet inchoata tantum sit, sincera tamen est, & non hypocritica, Deoque et- iamsi imperfecta, qua fidem tegentem illam im- perfectionem, grata. Non dicit S. Johannes man- data ejus perfecte impleri posse; sed dicit ea non esse gravia & onerosa, quia non aggravant, aut instar molis onerosæ premunt renatum, justo enim lex ὐ κεῖται, 1. Timoth. I. vers. 9. Sensum ita exponit B. Hunnius: Quasi dicat, Deus à renatis & dilectis filiis suis non exigit illam absolutam perfectionem charitatis, quam Moses exigit: sed talia præcepta præscribit, quæ regeneratis virtute Spiritus Sancti gravia non sunt, cum & spontaneo agantur Spiritu ad Dei obsequia, & DEUS inchoata illorum obe- dientia delectetur, residuum vero defectum pleni- tudine & dignitate obedientiæ Filii sui suppleat. Quod plenius explicatur à Flacio: Mandata DEI in Christo dicuntur multis de causis levia 1. Quia Deus nobis totius legis impletionem à Filio factam gratis imputat. 2. Quia nos per Filium regene- rans condit ad bona opera, nobisque legem suam ac opus ejus cordi inscribit, ut jam delectemur ea ex animo. 3. Quia condonat omnia ea, quæ non præ- stamus. 4. Quia maledictionem ejus pœnamque non præstitorum mandatorum in Filium suum transtu- lit. 5. Quia conatum tantum nostrum sedulo obe- diendi in Christo pro plena obedientia imputat seu boni consulit: sicut benignissimus Pater etiam mi- nima officia Filii pluris facit, quam durissima & perfectissima opera servi. 6. Denique quia ipse ubique nobis prompte succurrit, dans velle, posse, ac perficere pro suo beneplacito. Alioqui de vera plenaque observatione legis rectissime à Paulo dispu- tatur, adeo ei neminem nec regeneratum quidem plene satisfacere, ut ea nunc nihil magis proprie agat & efficiat in nobis, quam ut nobis nostram summam injustitiam & iram Dei pœnasque æter- nas denunciet nosque condemnet. Nefarie ergo Pa- pistæ & Schwenckfeldistæ abutuntur hoc testimo- nio, ad amplificandas vires humanas, & obscuran- dam legem ac severitatem justitiæ Dei, ipsamque et- iam remissionem peccatorum, aut assiduam abso- lutionem sordium nostrarum sanguine CHRISTI factam.

Guilhelmus Estius, etsi ex hoc loco arguat, quia mandata DEI homini justificato gravia non sunt, multo minus ei impossibilia esse: torquet ta- men valde sese in ejus explicatione. Nam modo levia dicit esse in seipsis, quia nihil facilius sit, quam diligere id, quod est summe diligibile: mo- do confert se ad statum, in quo sunt conditi primi parentes: & agnoscit quoad naturam peccato vi- tiatam gravia esse atque difficilia: modo subdi- stinguendum adhuc censet, aliterque loquendum de homine nondum renato, aliter de renato: Illi gravia esse DEI præcepta, & quodam sensu im- possibilia fatetur, huic, non item: modo de ho- mine renato & justificato etiam agnoscit, pati & illum adhuc difficultatem in via mandatorum Dei propter rebellionem carnis adversus Spiritum, ut hac ratione cum Paulo dicere debeat: Ego carnalis sum, venundatus sub peccato. Quid ergo jactitat adhuc præcepta legis possibilia esse im- pletu, nec difficilia? Respondet denique: Sed quia voluntatem habet absolute conformem DEI voluntati, ut cum eodem Apostolo ibidem dicere possit: Consentio legi divinæ, quia bona est. Et iterum: Condelector lege Dei secundum interiorem hominem, Rom. VIII. consequens est, illi tali levia, facilia & delectabilia esse Dei mandata. Verum enimvero qui legi Dei quidem consentit, quod bona est, non tamen quod vult, facit, condele- ctatur quidem legi Dei secundum interiorem ho- minem; videt autem aliam legem in membris suis repugnantem legi mentis suæ, & captivantem se sub legem peccati, quæ est in membris suis, ejus voluntas non est absolute conformis voluntati Dei, sed tantum quoad interiorem hominem, illique ob rebellionem carnis adversus Spiritum levia, facilia, & delectabilia Dei mandata non sunt, nedum plene impleri possunt sine ullo de- fectu. Ista autem rebellio & repugnantia & ope- ratio eorum, quæ non vult, ἁμαρτία est, adeo- que ἀνομία, 1. Joh. III. vers. 4. ubi autem ἀνομία vel exorbitatio à lege est, ibi non est plena legis impletio.

## 5:4
Vers. 4.

Ὄτι πᾶν τὸ γεγεννημένον ἐκ τῶ̃ Θεῶ̃ νικᾷ τὸν κόσμον.) Certainly, for us there is a struggle with the world, that is, with the allurements, evil examples, dangers, and evils encroaching from the world. But he who has the word of God and His eternal promises implanted in himself has a victory over the world prepared. See above c. III, v. 9, c. IV, 7, 1 Cor. XV, 57.

This is the second fruit of faith, the overcoming of the world, by which name can be understood both the men in the world, who although they are often superior to us and oppress us, yet in the end we carry off a glorious victory, Apoc. XI, & XII; and those things which are proper to worldly people, such as those which are recounted in chapter III, 16, the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life; and the Prince of the world, the devil, John XII, v. 31. The means, however, by which these are overcome, is faith. The argument, which the particle ὅτι implies, stands thus: Whoever overcomes the world through faith, to him the commandments of God are not grievous. But everyone who is born of God overcomes the world through faith. Therefore, to no one who is born of God are the commandments of God grievous. Concerning the world, see John XVI, v. last. Concerning which Flacius: That we overcome the world by faith, that is, Satan, the ungodly, seducers, and our own flesh, and whatever at all it is that tries to lead us away from God and his law under the yoke of Satan or sin; just as also in the preceding chapter IV, v. 4, all our victory against the ungodly is derived from rebirth and the strength supplied by God, and in Heb. XI, the conquest of the ages and empires of the world is attributed to faith, 1. because it obtains then a new heart, and all good strengths, and also every counsel and success from God. 2. because it follows from the gift of God, a mouth and wisdom, which the ungodly cannot resist. 3. And finally, it also obtains from GOD the desired conquest of the ungodly themselves, whether men or devils. But the chief thing in this cause is that faith apprehends Christ, who overcame sin and Satan by his death: for by his merit we obtain the victory. Cf. 1 John IV, 4. Apoc. XII, 13. Phil. IV, 13. That the Apostle says, everything that is born of God, not everyone, Cornelius observes that it has emphasis, and signifies the universality of all nations, as John VI, 37. chapter XVII, 12. Thomas Anglicus says it is used so that it may be signified that in spiritual generation there is no distinction of sex, Gal. III, v. 28.

Grotius does not place the reason for the victory in regeneration, nor in the apprehension of Christ through faith: but in the promise of eternal life, as if that alone were of such value that it makes us victors of the world, which, although there is no doubt that it works by morally persuading and impelling us so that we are excited to the pursuit of piety: yet more is required for the victory of the world and the Prince of the world than the pursuit of piety; indeed, that we may be freed from sin and condemnation, and overcome those most grievous temptations and spiritual enemies; that must happen not by the virtue of our piety, but by the merit and satisfaction of Christ, who alone crushes the head of the serpent and destroys the works of the devil, and thus by faith in Christ. He is ὁ μείζων ἐν ἡμῖν, ἢ ὁ ἐν κόσμῳ, by whose virtue we overcome, 1. John IV, v. 4, by his blood the faithful overcome τὸν κατήγορον, Apocal. XII, v. 11, by his virtue all things are possible through faith, just as he professes of himself in Phil. IV, 13: Πάντα ἰχύω ἐν τῷ ἐνδυναμ῱ντί με Χριστῷ. We also cut the nerve of that Socinian comment, that the mere knowledge of eternal life suffices for the victory of the world and the observation of the precepts of GOD: which was devised solely for the purpose of crushing the force of the satisfaction and merit of Christ and constructing a new method of salvation, namely through the observation of divine precepts, and is diametrically opposed to the whole of Holy Scripture.

And this is the victory that has overcome the world, our faith.) νικήσασα is an aorist for all time, as the Syrian and Latin have accepted it. And there is a metonymy in the word νίκη of the effect for the efficient cause. The cause of the victory is the word, but concocted and digested by faith. See Heb. IV, 2. Understand, however, not just any faith, but an efficacious one, as above at the beginning of this chapter.

The Apostle does not treat of the Word, which is the medium on the part of God, but of faith, which is the medium on our part. The word and faith are related. Nor is there any doubt that the word is the cause of victory when apprehended by faith; but they are nevertheless distinct, not to be confounded. And one must distinguish between the Evangelical word and the word of the Law. For the law does not contribute to this, which works only wrath and condemnation, Rom. IV, 2 Cor. III, but the Gospel, which is the power of GOD unto salvation to everyone who believes, Rom. I, 16. Nor do we obtain the victory as the word is concocted and digested by faith, but as we apprehend Christ Jesus and his merit in the word, and primarily through faith. That concoction and digestion contributes to knowledge and assent, but not indeed to trust, which is the chief part of justifying and saving faith. Moreover, since Grotius does not understand by the word the Gospel announcing the victory of Christ acquired for the human race against Satan and the world, by whose fiducial apprehension Christ's victory becomes our victory, 1 Cor. XV, v. 37, but the precepts and the Mosaic law enriched by Christ, and explains efficacious faith in the Socinian manner, concerning the knowledge and assent of the promises of eternal life, and also the observation of those precepts, it is in the open that the whole of Theology is thus most wickedly perverted. Faith is called victory, that is, the cause of victory, for no other reason than that it apprehends the victory of Christ, who alone and by himself overcame sin, the devil, and death, and freed us by his victory from those enemies, so that those who believe in him may enjoy that victory and liberation, Hos. XIII, 14, 1 Cor. XV, 54, Coloss. II, 15, Heb. II, 14.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

Ὄτι πᾶν τὸ γεγεννημένον ἐκ τῶ̃ Θεῶ̃ νικᾷ τὸν κόσμον.) Cer- tamen nobis quidem est cum mundo, id est, cum illece- bris, malis exemplis, periculis & malis è mundo ingruen- tibus. Sed qui verbum Dei & promissa ejus æterna sibi ha- bet insita, paratam habet de mundo victoriam. Vide supra c. III. v. 9. c. IV, 7. 1. Cor. XV, 57.

Alter hic fructus est fidei mundi devictio, quo nomine tum homines in mundo intelligi possunt, qui etsi sæpe nobis superiores sunt, nosque depri- mant, tandem tamen nos victoriam reportamus gloriosam, Apoc. XI, & XII. tum ea, quæ munda- norum propria sunt, qualia sunt, quæ cap. III, 16. recensentur concupiscentia carnis, concupiscentia oculorum & superbia vitæ; tum mundi Princeps diabolus, Johan. XII. v. 31. Medium autem, quo vincuntur illa, fides est. Argumentum, quod par- ticula ὅτι innuit, sic habet: Qui mundum vincit per fidem, ei mandata Dei gravia non sunt. At omnis, qui genitus est ex Deo, mundum vincit per fidem. Nulli ergo qui ex Deo genitus, gravia sunt mandata Dei. De mundo vid. Johan. XVI. v. ult. Quo de Flacius: Quod fide vincamus mundum, hoc est Satanam, impios, seductores, & propriam carnem, ac quicquid omnino est, quod nos à Deo ac lege ejus abducere conatur sub jugum satanæ aut peccati; quemadmodum & præcedenti cap. IV. v. 4. omnis nostra victoria contra impios ex renascentia & viribus à Deo suppeditatis derivetur, & Ebr. XI. seculorum & imperiorum mundi expugnatio fi- dei tribuatur, 1. quia tum novum cor, omnesque bonas vires, tum & omne consilium ac successum à Deo impetrat. 2. quia consequitur ex dono Dei os & sapientiam, cui impii resistere non possint. 3. Et denique etiam ipsorum impiorum sive hominum sive diabolorum optatam expugnationem à DEO conse- quitur. Præcipuum vero in hac causa est, quod fides apprehendat Christum, qui peccatum & sa- tanam superavit morte sua: Ejus enim merito vi- ctoriam consequimur. Conf. 1. Joh. IV, 4. Apoc. XII, 13. Phil. IV, 13. Quod Apostolus dicit, omne quod natum est ex Deo, non omnis, emphasin ha- bere observat Cornelius, & significare universita- tem omnium gentium, ut Joh. VI, 37. cap. XVII, 12. Thomas Anglicus id adhiberi ait, ut significetur, in generatione spirituali esse nullam distinctionem sexus Gal. III. v. 28.

Grotius non in regeneratione, nec in apprehen- sione Christi per fidem rationem victoriæ collocat: sed in promissione vitæ æternæ, quasi ea sola tanti sit, ut nos victores mundi faciat, quam etsi mora- liter suadendo & impellendo operari, ut excite- mur ad studium pietatis, dubium nullum sit: Plus tamen ad victoriam mundi, & Principis mundi re- quiritur, quam pietatis studium, imo ut à peccato & condemnatione liberemur, & tentationes illas gravissimas hostesque spirituales vincamus; id non nostræ pietatis, sed meriti & satisfactionis Christi virtute, qui solus caput serpentis conterit, & opera diaboli destruit, adeoque fide in Chri- stum fieri oportet. Ille est ὁ μείζων ἐν ἡμῖν, ἢ ὁ ἐν κόσμῳ, cujus virtute vincimus, 1. Joh. IV. v. 4. hu- jus sanguine vincunt fideles τὸν κατήγορον, Apocal. XII. v. 11. hujus virtute omnia per fidem possunt, sicut Phil. IV, 13. de se profitetur: Πάντα ἰχύω ἐν τῷ ἐνδυναμ῱ντί με Χριστῷ. Commento etiam illi Sociniano, quod sola notitia vitæ æternæ ad victo- riam mundi & observationem præceptorum DEI sufficiat, alias nervum incidimus: quod ad vim sa- tisfactionis & meriti Christi elidendam & novam salutis rationem per observationem nempe præce- ptorum divinorum adstruendam unice excogita- tum est, totique Scripturæ sacræ καθδιάμετρον oppositum.

Καὶ αὕτη ἐσὶν ἡ νίκη ἡ νικήσασα τὸν κόσμον, ἡ πίσις ἡμῶν.) Νικήσασα est aoristus pro omni tempore, quomodo accepere Syrus & Latinus. Et μετωνυμία est in voce νίκη effecti pro efficiente. Causa victoriæ est verbum, sed fide concoctum atque digestum. Vide Ebr. IV, 2. Intellige autem fidem non qualemcunque, sed efficacem, ut supra initio hujus capitis.

Non agit Apostolus de Verbo, quod medium est ex parte Dei, sed de fide, quæ est medium ex parte nostri. Relata sunt verbum & fides. Neque du- bium causam victoriæ verbum esse fide apprehen- sum; sed distincta tamen illa sunt, non confunden- da. Et distinguendum est verbum Evangelicum, & verbum Legis. Non enim huc facit lex, quæ iram tantum operatur & condemnationem, Rom. IV. 2. Cor. III. sed Evangelium, quod est potentia DEI ad salutem omni credenti, Rom. I, 16. Neque qua ver- bum fide concoquitur ac digeritur, sed qua verbum fide, & in verbo imprimis Christum Jesum ejus- que meritum apprehendimus, victoriam conse- quimur. Illa concoctio & digestio facit ad noti- tiam & assensum, non vero ad fiduciam, quæ præ- cipua pars est fidei justificæ & salvificæ. Cæterum quum Grotius per verbum non intelligat Evange- lium victoriam Christi contra satanam & mun- dum generi humano acquisitam annuncians, cu- jus fiduciali apprehensione Christi victoria nostra fit victoria, 1. Cor. XV. v. 37. sed præcepta legem- que Mosaicam à Christo locupletatam, & fidem efficacem more Sociniano, de notitia & assensu pro- missionum vitæ æternæ, nec non observatione isto- rum præceptorum explicat, universam Theolo- giam sic pessime perverti in aprico est. Dicitur autem fides victoria, hoc est, causa victoriæ non alia ratione, quam quia victoriam Christi appre- hendit, qui unus & solus peccatum, diabolum & mortem superavit, nosque victoria sua ab istis ho- stibus liberavit, ut qui in ipsum credunt, ea victo- ria & liberatione frui possint, Ose. XIII, 14. 1. Cor. XV, 54. Coloss. II, 15, Ebr. II, 14.

## 5:5
Verse 5.

Who is he who overcomes the world, if not he who believes that Jesus is the Son of God?] An interrogation vehemently affirming, such as above II, 22. It is the same to believe that Jesus is the Christ as it is to be the Son of God, namely in the most eminent way. See what we have said at Matt. 14, 33, c. 26, 63, Luke 22, 66.

The proper object of the faith that overcomes the world is Jesus the Son of God. For the only-begotten and eternal Son of God himself, and ὁμοούσιος to God the Father, willed to become Man, that he might be Jesus our Savior, and might deliver us from the power of sin, Satan, and death, Matt. 1:20, Heb. 2:14. For he, as Flacius rightly says, when he was warring with Satan, the world, sin, death, and the flesh, or the old Adam, and indeed had already overcome them, did so not for himself, but for us: He bids us to be confident as if of our own victory, because he himself has overcome and vanquished the Prince of the world for us, and having despoiled him of his arms, has cast him out beyond his fortress, and thus has even subjugated the whole world. He therefore still fights through us who believe in him by his word, power, and prayers, and by every other spiritual efficacy and weapons from the mouth of infants and sucklings he perfects power and victory, and finally powerfully crushes Satan himself and that old serpent under our feet, and we through and on account of him obtain from God every necessary aid. Although indeed that Jesus is the Christ and is the Son of God are materially the same: yet that they are different is clear even from this, that he is the Son of God by eternal generation from the Father, Ps. 2:7, but Christ by temporal anointing to his office, Ps. 45:7. That name belongs to the divine nature in the concrete, but this one is appropriate to the human nature, which was anointed with the gifts of the Holy Spirit not ἐκ μέτρου, John 3:34, even though the offices to which he is anointed belong to Christ according to both natures. It is also said ambiguously that Christ is the Son of GOD in the most eminent way. For if, with the Socinians, degrees of τῆς υἱότητος are admitted, which even the Son of God by grace, but in a more eminent way, is a most destructive heresy, because Christ is the Son of God by nature, and his υἱότης does not differ from ours by degree only, but by the whole kind: That is eternal and substantial, rendering the Son ὁμοούσιον to the Father; this is temporal and accidental, rendering a son according to υἱοθεσίαν, because we are sons of God not by nature, but by grace.

Moreover, Zanchius notes in de trib. Eloh. col. 4, that all who have written on this passage agree regarding the Apostle's purpose. Namely, that he wishes to prove that Jesus is the one in whom our faith ought to rest exclusively, as the true Son of God and Savior, from whom our whole salvation and victory against the world depends. Regarding which, the blessed Gerhard, disput. I. ad v. 7. 1. Johan. V. th. 33, teaches that the Apostle shows we can and ought to believe firmly that Jesus is the Christ, v. 1, the Son of God, v. 5, because this doctrine concerning Christ is established and confirmed by divine testimony. To believe, it is added, that Jesus is the Christ or Messiah promised in the Old Testament and exhibited in the New, comprises three things primarily: 1. To believe that Jesus, born of the Virgin Mary and preached by the Apostles, is the true Son of God. 2. To believe that Jesus, the Son of God begotten from eternity by the Father and born in time from the virgin, is also true man. 3. To believe that that Jesus, true God and true man, is also our Mediator, Redeemer, and Savior, who by his most holy obedience and most full satisfaction has acquired for us perfect righteousness and eternal life.

Latin:

Vers. 5.

Τίς ἐσιν ὁ νικῶν τὸν κόσμον, εἰ μὴ ὁ πιςεύων, ὅτι Ἰησοῦς ἐσιν ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ Θεοῦ;] Interrogatio vehementer affirmans, qualis su- pra II, 22. Idem est credere Jesum esse Christum, quod esse Filium Dei, nempe modo eminentissimo. Vide quæ diximus ad Matth. 14, 33. c. 26, 63. Luc. 22, 66.

Objectum fidei mundum vincentis proprium est Jesus Filius Dei. Nam ipse Filius Dei unigeni- tus & æternus Deoque Patri ὁμοούσιος fieri voluit Homo, ut Jesus Salvator noster esset, nosque à po- testate peccati, satanæ & mortis liberaret, Matth. I, 20. Ebr II, 20. Is enim, ut recte Flacius, cum bel- ligeretur cum satana, mundo, peccato, morte & car- ne, aut vetere Adamo, imo jam etiam devicisset ipsos non sibi, sed nobis: Jubet nos tanquam de nostra propria victoria confidere, quia ipse nobis Princi- pem mundi devicerit debellaritque, & spoliatum suis armis foras extra suam arcem ejecerit, atque adeo et- iam totum mundum subjugavit. Ipse igitur per nos credentes in eum etiamnum pugnat verbo, virtute & precibus omnique alia spirituali efficacia & armis ex ore infantium & lactentium virtutem victoriam- que perficit, & denique satanam ipsum veteremque illum serpentem potenter sub pedibus nostris conterit, & nos per ac propter eum à Deo omnem necessariam opem impetramus. Quanquam vero Jesum esse Christum & esse Filium Dei materialiter idem sint: tamen illa diversa esse vel inde liquet, quod Filius Dei sit per æternam à Patre generationem, Psal. II, 7. Christus vero per temporalem ad officium unctio- nem, Psalm. XLV, 7. Illud nomen sit naturæ divinæ in concreto, hoc vero naturæ humanæ conveniat, quæ uncta est donis Spiritus sancti non ἐκ μέτρου, Johan. III. v. 34. etsi officia, ad quæ unctus est, Chri- sto conveniant secundum utramque naturam. Ambigue etiam dicitur Christus esse Filius DEI modo eminentissimo. Nam si cum Socinianis admit- tantur gradus τῆς υἱότητος, quod etiam Filius Dei siæ per gratiam, sed eminentiori modo, hæresis est exitiosissima, quia Christus est Filius Dei per na- turam, neque υἱότης ejus à nostra gradu tantum differt, sed toto genere: Illa æterna est & sub- stantialis inferens Filium Patri ὁμοούσιον; hæc tem- poralis est & accidentaria, inferens filium secun- dum υἱοθεσίαν, quia filii Dei sumus non per natu- ram, sed per gratiam.

Cæterum de scopo Apostoli omnes, qui in hunc locum scripserant, convenire, notat Zanchius de trib. Eloh. col. 4. Nimirum eum velle probare, Je- sum esse eum, in quem unicum recumbere debet no- stra fides, utpote verum Dei Filium & Servato- rem, à quo tota nostra pendet salus & victoria con- tra mundum. Quo de B. Gerhardus disput. I. ad v. 7. 1. Johan. V. th. 33. Docet Apostolus firmiter nos credere posse & debere, quod Jesus sit Christus, v. 1. Dei Filius, v. 5. quia divino testimonio hæc doctrina de Christo stabilitur & confirmatur. Credere, ad- ditur, quod Jesus sit Christus sive Messias in Veteri Testamento promissus, in Novo exhibitus, tria po- tissimum complectitur: 1. Credere quod Jesus ex Ma- ria virgine natus & per Apostolos prædicatus sit verus Dei Filius. 2. Credere quod Jesus Dei Filius ab æ- terno a Patre genitus, & ex virgine in tempore na- tus sit etiam verus homo. 3. Credere quod Jesus ille verus Deus & verus homo sit etiam noster Mediator, Redemptor & Salvator, qui sanctissima sua obedien- tia & plenissima satisfactione perfectam justitiam & vitam æternam nobis acquisiverit.

## 5:6
This is he who came by water and blood, Jesus the Christ] He came, that is, he appeared as that which he was, the Son of GOD. By water and blood, that is, by a most pure life, which is accustomed to be signified by water, as in Ezek. XXXVI. v. 25, or by washing, which is the work of water, as in Isa. I. v. 16, Jer. IV. v. 14, concerning which matter we have said more at John III. v. 5. And as a sign of this purity, John the Baptist baptized him, John I. v. 28: See also Eph. V. v. 27, Tit. III. v. 5, Heb. X. 22. Wherefore, since he was most holy in every act, there is no reason to doubt anything concerning the truth of what he said, that he was the Christ or Son of God. Furthermore, the Son of God appeared in that, for the testimony of that profession by which he said he was the Christ or Son of God, he did not refuse a bloody death, John XVIII. 37, 1 Tim. VI. v. 13. See Tertullian on baptism, where he applies to Christians also what is said here about Christ. John, however, joined these two well, because even in the old Law those about to sacrifice would first wash themselves, whence also the Hebrew proverb: Without water there is no sacrifice: Likewise, that the law begins through water and is finished through water. In the Manuscript here is: Δι ὕδατος, καὶ αἵματος, καὶ πνέυματος.

Not in water only, but in water and blood] Some desert in the fear of death what they professed in life. But our Doctor was consistent with himself in life and in death. He shows that there is huge momentum for convincing in the very death of Christ, and indeed such a death. In the Manuscript is: Ἀλλ' ἐν τῷ ὕδατι καὶ πνέυματι.

and the Spirit is that which bears witness] Furthermore, the Spirit of God himself rendered to him a testimony most worthy of faith, that is, by metonymy, his admirable works manifestly proceeding from divine power. For God would not have granted this honor to him if he had falsely called himself the Son of God, that is, if he had been a blasphemer, John X, 36. Christ himself often uses this testimony as invincible, as John V. v. 32, 36, ch. X. v. 25, add Acts II. v. 20.

For the Spirit is the truth] Both the Syrian and the Arab read ἀλήθεια without the article, which is more correct. For ἀλήθεια is put for ἀληθὲς, just as ἀγάπη above ch. IV. v. 8. Ἀληθὲς indeed for that which merits faith, just as we said that word is taken in John V. v. 31, ch. VIII. v. 13. He says that he does not bring forward that testimony from divine works above others in vain, since it is most worthy of faith beyond any controversy.

For the confirmation of the victory not only of Christ, but also of the faithful of Christ, who through faith in him overcome the world, and of the salvation procured by Christ and obtained by the faithful, testimonies beyond all exception are required, which St. John presents with an excellent rationale, both insofar as they were deposited in the days of Christ's flesh, in which the Son of God came to us in the flesh, and as they are deposited in the Church of Christ from then until the consummation of the age for the sake of the glorification of Christ and our salvation. The former are brought in this verse, the latter in the following ones. There are, however, those three: For he came by water, and not only by water, but by water and blood, and the Spirit was added besides, who testified along with them, that the Spirit is the truth. He came ὁ ἐρχόμενος, the one who was to come, which is a name proper to him from Gen. XLIX. v. 10, Ps. XL. v. 8, Isa. XXXV. v. 5, ch. LXII. v. 11, Hag. II. v. 8. Zech. II. v. 10, ch. IX. v. 9, Mal. III. v. 1, Matt. XI, v. 3, John I. v. 15. He came, however, I. by water, which was a document and testimony of the true Messiah, the crusher of the serpent's head. But water of purity of life is not understood in this place, but the water of baptism, such as the advent that was predicted in Ezek. XXXVI. v. 15, Zech. XIII. v. 1, which was a notable and public document of the advent of the Messiah, not only in that his forerunner had to baptize with water, Matt. III. v. 11, Luke III. v. 16, John I. v. 26, from whom Christ himself wished to be baptized not so much for the sake of signifying his own purity, as for the sake of sanctifying the water to be consecrated for our purification, but primarily because he himself instituted the baptism by which we are regenerated and washed from our sins, John III. v. 5, Matt. XXVIII. v. 19, Acts XXII. v. 11, Tit. III. v. 5. and we are instructed by power to overcome the world and Satan, provided that we put on Christ and become children of God through faith, Gal. III. v. 26, 27. Therefore, the water testifies in baptism not only of Christ the victor over Satan, who, had he not come and conquered the devil, the power of this infernal enemy could not be suffocated in the Red Sea of baptism: but also of our liberation and salvation, which we obtain in Christ, because through baptism we are freed from sin and the power of Satan and are transferred into the kingdom of heaven, John III. v. 5. In which manner the Apostle called baptism clean water, Heb. X. 23, as Chrysostom, Theodoret, Theophylact, Oecumenius, and most Latin interpreters explain, which interpretation Estius says is common to both Greeks and Latins, and for that reason clean water is explained by the Fathers in Ezek. XXXVI. v. 25. See Sanctius in the same place. II. He came not only by water, but also by blood; just as in the Old Testament both the Levitical washings and the blood of victims were proofs of divine grace, by which spiritual cleansing and sacrificial atonement, and shadows of things to come, Coloss. II, Heb. IX and X. Thus Christ, in whom we have the very substance and body, came not only by the water of baptism to wash us from sins, but also by the blood, which he also shed for us for the remission of sins, Matt. XXVI. v. 28, because we have been redeemed by the precious λύτρῳ of his blood, 1 Peter I. v. 18, and he offers it to us to drink in the Eucharistic cup, for the application of remission, 1 Cor. X. v. 16, chap. XI. Therefore Bede on this passage says: He came, he says, by water and blood, namely the water of the laver and the blood of his passion. He deigned not only to be baptized for the sake of our cleansing, so that he might consecrate and deliver to us the sacrament of baptism, but he also gave his blood for us, redeeming us by his passion, by whose sacraments we are always refreshed and preserved for salvation. Anselm of Laon in the interlinear gloss: Because he was eternal, he came for salvation and the remission of sins, through the water of baptism and the blood of his passion, and he not only deigned to be baptized for the sake of our cleansing and to consecrate the sacrament of baptism for us, but he also shed his blood for our redemption. And some, both of the ancients and of the moderns, refer to this also, that blood and water flowed from Christ's side, John XIX. v. 34. which some wish to be properly referred to in this place, when Christ is said to have come not only by water, but by water and blood, which is where the explanation of the blessed Hunnius goes. But because St. John puts blood first there, and adds water, whereas in this place he says not by water only, but also by blood, Dorscheus, in his dissertation on the Spirit, water, and blood, page 35, judges that the holy Apostle did not especially refer to this here. Indeed, he says, if the blessed John had first and principally referred in this place to the blood and water flowing from the side of Christ, he would not have said, as if about to commend and inculcate something singular, οὐκ ἐν τῷ ὕδατι μόνον ἀλλ᾽ ἐν τῷ ὕδατι καὶ αἵματι, that is, he would not have commemorated water in the first place, and said that Christ came not only in water, but also in blood. For if you look to that flow of water and blood from the side of Christ, there is not so much a miracle in it, that blood flowed. Indeed, this is more natural than if water flows. But John speaks in such a way as if he places the preternatural quality of the matter in the fact that not only water, but also water and blood flowed out. Since it is more preternatural for water to flow from a corpse with a pierced side than blood. Therefore, the blessed John does not primarily refer to that. Moreover, because the holy Fathers also refer that miracle here, we admit on certain grounds that that testimony, of whose truth the Evangelist testifies so laboriously in chapter XIX, verse 35, also pertains to this. Christ indeed came by those two sacraments, instituting them in life, which he also wished to figure forth in death to seal that institution, when he emitted blood and water separately from his pierced side, and without commixture. In which sense the ancients said that two sacraments flowed from the side of Christ, namely symbolically, because that water figured Baptism, but the blood the holy Eucharist, especially because by the merit of the passion, death, and piercing of Christ's side, that economy of salvation was acquired for us, so that it might be dispensed through the water of baptism for our regeneration, and through the cup, which is the communion of the blood of Christ, for spiritual strengthening in faith, and for drinking and nourishment unto eternal life, 1 Cor. XII. 13.

John VI. v. 54. The blessed Wilhelmus Lyserus in his lectures on the Summary cherished a singular opinion here: namely, that as the blood of Christ is the heavenly thing in the sacrament of the supper, so the water which flowed from the side of Christ is the heavenly thing in the sacrament of baptism. But water is what they call earthly matter in baptism, nor does it seem fitting that the water which flowed from the body of Christ by a supernatural reason should be united with natural elemental water; indeed, baptism is described as being from water and the Spirit, not from common water, and that water miraculously and extraordinarily emitted by Christ is described in John III. v. 5. and in its institution, whence the heavenly thing is to be derived, it is joined not with the water from the side of Christ, but with the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, in which one is to be baptized, Matt. XXVIII. v. 19. Nor did the holy Fathers say that those two sacraments flowed from Christ's side for that reason, that that water which flowed is dispensed in baptism, but that that flow of water was some symbol of holy baptism. Which is evident from the passage of Tertullian, book on baptism, chapter 16: We have indeed also a second baptism, one and the same, namely of blood, of which the Lord said: I have a baptism to be baptized with, when he had already been baptized. For he had come by water and blood, as John wrote, that he might be baptized by water, and glorified by blood. Therefore, that he might make us called by water and chosen by blood, he sent forth these two baptisms from the wound of his pierced side. Because those who believed in his blood would be washed by water, and those who had washed by water would also drink the blood. Gregory of Nyssa in the testimony. Of the Old Testament, translated by Laurentius Sifanus, page 847, has it thus, bringing in also the opinion of Chrysostom on this passage: We are taught by the Gospel that blood and water flowed from the divine and Lordly side, not simply, but first indeed because the legal purifications performed both the sprinklings of blood and the lustrations by water as a figure and shadowing forth of these two. But then also, when the truth came, the sum of our salvation is mystically performed and completed through water and the Spirit; since we believe that we are consecrated and put on divinity both through divine baptism and through the participation and use of the holy blood, just as the divine orator Chrysostom explains in these very expressions and words: He says, blood and water came out, the Scripture showing that such fountains did not flow out simply: but because the Church consists of both of these, and the faithful know and understand this, who are indeed reborn through water, but are nourished through blood and flesh. And hence the mysteries take their beginning, so that when you approach the dreadful cup, you approach as if to drink from the Lordly side itself. Likewise: A few drops of blood reforming and restoring the whole world, and becoming for all men like the rennet of milk, gathering and joining us into one, so that through the opinion of both fathers there are joined not only the power of baptism and the participation of the divine blood, one indeed through water, the other through blood, but also the firm and certain proof of human nature itself. Nor does Jerome seem to have spoken in any other sense to Oceanus, Tom. II. page 322: The side of Christ is struck by a lance, and the sacraments of baptism and martyrdom are poured forth equally. Augustine, tractate XVI on John: The side was struck and immediately blood and water flowed out, which are the twin sacraments of the Church, the water in which the bride is purified, the blood from which she is found to be endowed. Leo the Great in the epistle which the council of Chalcedon. he called the pillar of the true faith: Let him see what kind of nature hung from such fixed nails on the wood of the cross and understands the side of the crucified one opened by the lance of death, from which blood and water flowed out, so that the Church of God might be watered both by the bath and by the cup. Paulinus of Nola in his epistle to Florentius calls Christ the rock, from whose side, pierced by a lance, flowed water and blood, so that it might pour forth for us equally life-giving fountains, the water of grace and the blood of the sacrament. John of Damascus, book IX, On the Orthodox Faith, chapter 5. It gushed forth for us, he says, from the holy and undefiled side of Christ, a fountain of remission, water for regeneration and the washing away of sin and corruption. But the blood is the drink of eternal life. And he gave us precepts to be regenerated through water and the Spirit, with the Holy Spirit coming upon the water through prayer and invocation. To which passage Jodocus Clichtoveus, page 30. That, he says, should not be passed over idly, that the baptismal font had its efficacy, just as its significance, from the gushing of water from the side of our Lord pierced by a lance after death. For that gushing was the fountain of remission and regeneration in Christ, through whom in water and the Spirit we are reborn to God: Just as the blood flowing at the same time from the side of Christ designated his precious blood, left to us for drink and as the cause of eternal life in the most unworthy and, of all sacred things, the most excellent sacrament of the Eucharist. With these agree likewise from the Papists Thomas, part III, question 66, article 3, to 3. From the side of Christ flowed water for washing, blood for redeeming, and therefore blood belongs to the sacrament of the Eucharist, but water to the sacrament of Baptism. Didacus Vanguas in Promptuar. Conc. lib. 1, tract. de Pass. page 405. In this matter we find a great mystery, so that the faithful may know that they have from that side of Christ the water of cleansing and the blood of the saving cup, by which the lovers of God are inebriated at the mystical table. Happy are those who deserve to draw from the very side and fountain of the Lord's breast, and to drink the blood of the wounded one. See also Johan. de Carthagen. book XII, homil. Catholic. in univers. relig. arcana homil page 915. Franciscus Tolet. on John XIX, page 315. Bellarminus lib. II. de effic. sacram. cap. 27. Maldona- tus on cap. XXVII. Matth. confess that almost all the Greeks, indeed all the ancient authors, explain it thus. From the Reformed, Theodorus Beza on this passage says not undeservedly that Augustine said: These two sacraments of the Christian Church flowed as it were from the side of Christ, when blood and water flowed from his pierced side, etc. The interpretations of the water as the tears of Christ by Thomas Anglicus, as the many peoples gathered by Christ, likewise as the wisdom hidden from heaven, which Salmero brought forward, and of the heavenly doctrine by Antonio Bruccioli in his Italian commentary on the scripture, Vol. VI, page 44, are more alien and do not deserve consideration.

III. The testimony of the Spirit is added: And the Spirit testifies, because the Spirit is truth. By the testifying Spirit some understand the Spirit emitted on the altar of the cross, concerning which, and the water and blood emanating from the pierced side, the author of the book on the double martyrdom interprets, which is held among the works of Cyprian, which Pamelius judges to be by a certain modern, and Bellarminus and Rivetus reject. Similarly, Augustine explains it in Vol. VI, against Maximinus, book III, chapter 22. Three things, he says, we know came out of the body of the Lord when he hung on the wood: first the spirit, whence it is written, and bowing his head he handed over the spirit: Then when his side was pierced by a lance, blood and water. Which three, if we look at them by themselves, each one has different substances. Paschasius Radbertus, Abbot of Corbie, book I, on the body and blood of Christ, Vol. IV, Bibl. sanct. Patr. page 180. There are three that give testimony, that Christ is the truth, the Spirit, the blood and the water. Indeed, after he emitted the Spirit from the fountain of his breast, against nature flowed the happy wave of baptism, and the blood of redemption. Strabus Fuldensis in the ordinary gloss. The Spirit is that soul which he emitted in his passion, the water and blood, which flowed from his side, testify to the true nature of his flesh. Innocent II in his epistle to the Bishop of Ferrara, book III, Decret. Gregor. book 41, on the celebration of the Mass. By the fact that at the moment of death, bowing his head, he handed over the Spirit, it is manifestly proven that he himself had a spirit, not only a vital state, but also a rational soul. But by the fact that one of the soldiers opened his side with a lance, and immediately blood and water came out, it is openly proven that Christ had a true body. The same explanation was also made by Gregorius Primatercius in his commentary on this passage. Johannes Mariana, Emanuel Saa, Gvilbelm. Estius, Cornelius à Lapide on this passage, who nevertheless adds, very aptly to the letter and almost literally, that the water, blood, and spirit are considered not only insofar as they were emitted and poured out on the cross, but also insofar as they were resumed in the resurrection, by the proper power of both his humanity and divinity. But this interpretation, whether as handed down by others or as now encrusted by Cornelius, does not agree with the Apostle's words, and the Spirit testifies, ὅτι τὸ πνεῦμά ἐστιν ἡ ἀλήθεια: Oecumenius explains the Spirit as the resurrection, or the Deity, which appeared on the cross and elsewhere. Serarius on this passage, with Catharinus leading the way, understands by the Spirit the spirit of the just, which is the effect of the Holy Spirit, by which they are renewed, anointed, and taught. But this too is alien. For the Spirit is rather the object of the faithful, to whom the testimony is hinted to be made, than the cause of the testimony, which is designated here. Nor does the explanation of Bernard deserve assent, who in sermon I on the octave of Easter understands charity by the Spirit, whom however Petrus Blesensis followed in his sermon on the Trinity. Nor does Ambrosius Catharinus dissent, understanding by the Spirit the internal gift of the Holy Spirit. Antonius Brucciolius wishes divine power and administration to be designated by the Spirit. To which are twin the things that Bullinger had handed down: This is that Jesus Christ coming, or who was to come through water and blood. As if he felt that the divine Spirit had foretold through the Scriptures that a Savior would one day come, who would prove himself to the world through water and blood that he is the Savior. By water, however, we understand heavenly doctrine, and that because of its purity, and because it refreshes and flows. But he also alluded by the name of blood to the sacrifices of the ancients: And without the shedding of blood (says the Apostle) there is no remission. He therefore puts blood for sacrifice, remission, and redemption. Jesus therefore came as Teacher and light of the world, sacrifice and eternal redeemer. For he taught heavenly wisdom, and by his death he vivified us, and with his blood he washed us. By which as infallible arguments he declared to the world that he himself is Christ, that is, that Jesus is the true Messiah, the true Son of God. And on verse 8 he says: By water is signified heavenly doctrine, by blood redemption, and by the Spirit divine power and administration. Nor do the things which Beza has seem different: I think the Spirit is called the power and efficacy, exerting itself through the fruits of faith, that is, charity in all the truly holy. Zanchius on the three. Elohim lib. I. part. 1. cap. 1. p. 6. as by water the doctrine of the Gospel, by blood the quality of the death of Christ: So by the Spirit the power of his Deity, by which he declared who he was through various effects, he understands, recalling these to the prophetic office of Christ, that by water doctrine may be designated, Isa. XI. v. 1. Pontifical by reason of blood & Royal by reason of the Spirit, making this the nerve of the conclusion: He who came first as Prophet by water, bringing namely the doctrine of the Gospel, and spreading it through the whole world, as the Prophet foretold; who came likewise as Pontiff by blood, undergoing namely such a death as the Prophets prophesied the Messiah would undergo, and indeed for the sins of others, as Isaiah had long before predicted in chapter LIII. who finally came as King by the Spirit, that is, by the power by which he might produce such miracles as were predicted concerning the Messiah by the Prophets, and by which he might vanquish enemies, raise himself from death, and subject the world to himself. He, I say, who thus came by water, by blood, by the Spirit, he is the true Christ. But in this way Jesus came. E. Thomas Anglicus wishes the Spirit to be taken essentially for God and Deity, and this to be testified, that Jesus was the truth, that is, true God and man. Augustine, although he understood the Spirit, water, and blood of the soul of Christ, and the water and blood of Christ's side along with others, if we consider those things in themselves, wishes those things which are signified here to be the Father, who is designated by the Spirit, the Son, who is designated by the blood, and the Holy Spirit, who is designated by the water. Clement of Alexandria in this place says: The Spirit is life, water is regeneration and faith, blood is knowledge.

But setting aside those more foreign and purely arbitrary interpretations, most others understand by πνεῦμα τὸ ματυρῦν the Holy Spirit himself. Cyril, On the True Faith to the Queens, book 1: He indeed overcomes the world who believes that Jesus is the Son of God. But who Jesus is, the disciple himself explains to us, saying: This is he who came by water and blood, Jesus Christ. But also in blood and in Spirit: and he says that the three are one. Therefore, the Word indeed was made flesh, but he sanctifies us by the Spirit and purifies by the blood, and washes again with clean water. But there is one Son in every way, whose Spirit and water and blood we also say they are. Thus also with Hesselius, John Lorinus in this place seems to show that John proves the divinity of Christ by a triple testimony. For three things concerning the true Messiah, as Hesselius rightly noted, are preached especially in the Old Testament, of which blessed John makes mention here and hereafter: the first is that he was about to shed his own blood; the second is that men were to be participants in such precious blood through corporal water, that is, through baptism; the third is that Christ was about to send his Spirit into the whole world. John says that Christ came, namely by the incarnation, not only in water by instituting baptism, but also in blood, both by shedding it for us, and by communicating its price and merit in the sacraments, and by proposing it to be drunk in the Eucharist; furthermore in the Spirit, who is given at the same time in baptism and other sacraments, or who was given more abundantly and in a visible manner at Pentecost. Which interpretation, analogous to the interlinear gloss, approaches the mind of St. John more than other expositions of the Papists, if you except the number of the sacraments. Nor does Zwingli, from among the Reformed, deny this, who, although he mixes his tropes with the former, saying: By water we understand the baptism of Christ, and all things which happened to Christ when baptized according to the baptism by virtue of synecdoche; by blood we interpret not only the same [blood] which flowed from the side of Christ who died on the cross when pierced by a lance, but whatever miraculous happened around the cross of Christ. However, he judges that by the name of the Holy Spirit the Holy Spirit himself is rightly designated, although he restricts his testimony too much: Otherwise, he says, by the name of the Holy Spirit [we understand] not only that apparition by which, in the form of a dove, he came from heaven and rested upon the head of Christ when baptized, but also the miracle of Pentecost, etc. Oecumenius, who although he likewise hands down a foreign interpretation concerning water and blood (Demag. 19 in the Epistle of John, page 85), understanding by water the testimony of John the Baptist, and by blood the testimony of the centurion concerning the blood and water flowing from the side of Christ, nevertheless seems to us to agree concerning the Holy Spirit, provided the metonymy were absent, by understanding through the Spirit the testimony of the Apostles, who, having received the Holy Spirit, spoke in various tongues: nay, he even submitted an exegesis of the former that is more convenient: We seem, however, to be admonished here also of the principal sacraments, which were given especially to confirm our consciences, and they cry out, unless we are stupid and faithless toward Christ God. For by sacramental signs faith is helped no less than if Christ were to perform the greatest miracles before our eyes. For in two ways Christ wished his kind will toward us to be undoubted, the symbols of which are named here, namely water and blood, which flowed from the side of the dead Christ not without mystery. Namely, just as once Eve was taken from the side of Adam, so also, while the second Adam was sleeping on the cross, mysteries flowed from his side, by which the Church was born and confirmed. Water is baptism, blood is the communion, which also exhorts us to martyrdom, are commended to us. John Piscator, although he understands by water the legal ablutions, and by blood the expiatory sacrifices of the Old Testament, so that the truth concerning Christ's testimony of legal ablutions and sacrifices might be demonstrated: he nevertheless acknowledges that by the Spirit is understood the Holy Spirit testifying in the hearts of the elect: nor is he consistent with himself in the former explanation. For in the scholia added to the analysis at verse 8, he approaches our exposition: Whether, he says, that water and that blood which flowed from the side of the dead Christ on the cross; or the water of baptism and the cup of the Lord, which is the symbol of his blood itself. Indeed, in the analysis itself he adds: By that water, he says, and blood, which flowed from the side of Christ: insofar as the power and efficacy of the death of Christ, once prefigured by legal ablutions and expiations, was shadowed forth by them. Nor would it be absurd if someone in this place, by antanaklasis, understood by the name of water baptism, and by the name of blood the Lord's Supper. But how much Piscator, not truly Apostolic because of the tropes which the Sacramentarian sect is accustomed to introduce, fluctuates here, not only by metonymy and synecdoche to exclude the presence of the blood of Christ from the sacred supper, but also by a new synecdoche in the word Spirit understood metonymically concerning the Gospel, can teach. For he adds: Provided that the word blood is taken not properly, as if the blood of Christ were already on earth: but metonymically and synecdochically for the holy supper, which is the sacrament of the body and blood of Christ. And further: If anyone, however, should think that water and blood are to be taken here in the same signification as a little before: then it must be said that the testimony of baptism and the Lord's supper is contained by synecdoche in the word Spirit, in that they are appendices of the Gospel, as it were images and seals, applied to declare and seal that more fully. But how does Christ come in water, and not in water only, but in water and blood, if that is understood of legal ablutions and sacrifices? Did he himself employ, or sanction at his coming, those ablutions and sacrifices? Did they not rather cease through his coming, as a figure or shadow, when the body arrived?

The Holy Spirit testifies, however, not only inwardly in the hearts of the faithful, and not only of the elect, but primarily outwardly, to which external testimonies this passage chiefly looks, because the truth of the assertion must first be demonstrated, that Jesus is the Son of God, that is, our Savior, or that Jesus, since the matter comes to the same thing, is that Son of God who came in the flesh, that he might be the Savior of the world, as the promised Messiah or Christ, who was to be anointed with the gifts of the Holy Spirit without measure, that he might be High Priest, Prophet, and King, acquiring salvation for us by his obedience, applying it through the Word and Sacraments, and powerfully preserving us in the same unto eternal life or the kingdom of glory, whoever of us believe in him; then indeed arises the certainty of grace and eternal salvation in our hearts, that is, that we who believe, as born again of God through faith, by which we apprehend Jesus as Savior, not only overcome the world, but also obtain life and eternal salvation in him and through him: to which end this testimony was directed, the Apostle taught with a resonant voice, v. 11. And this is that testimony, that God has given us eternal life, and that this life is in his Son. Since, therefore, God does not confirm us concerning him immediately, as the fanatics wish, but through the Word, that doctrine of the Word concerning Jesus the Son of God, in whom eternal life is had, had to be confirmed most of all, as being that from which that full assurance is to be sought; and through which the Holy Spirit excites and fosters it in our hearts. But how it is confirmed through that which Jesus Christ came by water and blood, and that it is the Spirit who testifies. Those testimonies, certainly, through the water of baptism received from Christ both for our sake and as an institution or means of our regeneration and salvation, and through the blood shed on the cross and ordained in the holy supper for the confirmation of faith and preservation unto eternal life to be drawn by us, are clear, public, and throughout the whole world resounding testimonies, together with the testimony of the Holy Spirit, with whom Christ was anointed, by whose power he taught, and performed miracles, and accomplished the work of redemption, and whom he granted to the Apostles through breathing upon them, John XX. v. 22, and poured out at the feast of Pentecost, so that they might testify of him throughout the world; just as all those things were predicted concerning the Messiah. Which testimonies confirm the doctrine concerning the Son of God, who came into the world for the sake of our salvation, and concerning faith in him, so that we may enjoy that salvation, and they testify of it most effectively: not only as the fulfillment of the Prophetic oracles, but because of the tenor and argument of those testimonies, as also their power and effect. For Christ took upon himself the baptism of water, that he might fulfill all righteousness, Matt. III. v. 15, and might consecrate water as the washing of our regeneration and renewal, Tit. III. v. 5.

When he instituted the sacrament of baptism for the absolution and remission of our sins; did he not demonstrate himself to be the true God, and our Savior, and that Son of God, in whom God the Father was well pleased, Matt. III. v. 17, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit is that one God, whom we all profess in baptism, chap. XXVIII. v. 19. Christ, or that promised Messiah, who came into the world, inaugurated when he was baptized, and to be put on by us through faith, when we are baptized into him as Christ our Savior, Gal. III. 26, 27. But by shedding his blood as the price of our redemption, did he not demonstrate himself to be the true God and man, that unique Mediator of God and men, who gave himself a ransom for all, 1 Tim. II. v. 5, 6. Are we not given to drink of his blood in the holy supper, so that we may have eternal life in him, John VI. v. 54. and the cup, which is the communion of the blood of Christ, is for us the new Testament in his blood, 1 Cor. XI. are we not confirmed by it, that in him, as the God-man, true God and true man, or life manifested in the flesh, we have eternal life, and obtain it through faith in him? Has not the Holy Spirit testified concerning the incarnation of the Son of God, the redemption, and the acquisition of our salvation, and the application and granting of the same, both by word, and by work and deed itself, when by his coming upon her the Son of God was conceived in his mother's womb, he was anointed with his gifts without measure, and instructed by his power, he executed his offices, as that anointed Messiah of the Lord, the Prophetic, Priestly, and

King, Luke I, chap. IV, Acts X, Luke XI. When he himself granted the same Holy Spirit to the Apostles, and instructed them with power from on high: which are not the works of a mere man, but of the God-man, not of some earthly anointed of the Lord, but of that unique promised Messiah and Savior of the world. And we experience the power and effect of all these testimonies, whether of baptism, or of the Eucharist, and of the Holy Spirit, in the very work of our regeneration, justification, renewal, and struggle against the world, and victory, whoever we are who receive Christ with true faith, and do not reject those testimonies, or exclude their power.

St. John adds that the Spirit is the truth. The Latin Vulgate reads: For Christ is the truth; but the Greek and Syriac reading has, for the Spirit is the truth: which reading Pope Leo also has in epistle X, chap. 5, at the end, and St. Augustine on the gift of perseverance, chap. 23. Which, although Estius admits, he nevertheless adds, I would not easily say which reading is to be preferred to the other. But according to the Council of Trent, the Vulgate is undoubtedly to be preferred; but according to the Greek truth, the other reading is entirely to be preferred, which is in truth the only authentic one, confirmed by the authority of all codices. The particle that is explained in two ways. For to some it is determinative, that the Spirit is the truth, and most of these understand by the Spirit, through metonymy, the Gospel of the Spirit, because the words of Christ are spirit and life, John VI. v. 63. But this which is to be proved here, through the testimony of the Spirit, is otherwise in v. 4 and 5, as also afterwards in v. 11. determined by St. John, namely that our victory is faith, and the object of faith, or that which is to be believed, is the Son of God, in whom God has given us eternal life, but the document of proof is taken from the testimony of the Holy Spirit: and then finally in v. 9 the Apostle introduces the truth of the Gospel, that namely it is to be received through faith as confirmed not by human testimony, but by divine and that manifold, therefore with others we prefer to take the particle that in a causal sense, because, or for, so that the testimony of the Spirit may be confirmed, primarily because it is not said and the Spirit testifies that the Spirit is the truth, but and the Spirit is that which testifies, namely concerning this Jesus, that he is the Son of God, in whom God has given us eternal life. For this is that testimony, by the interpretation of John himself, v. 11. Which sense the blessed Gerhard also adopted in his disputation on 1 John 5:7, thesis 38. Ὅτι, because the Spirit is truth, and therefore his testimony is true and certain, so that the particle ὅτι is taken causally, not objectively, for the same reason that (St. John) had said in his Gospel (chap. 19:35), 'he who saw it has borne witness, and his testimony is true,' not only because he is an eyewitness, but also because, with the Holy Spirit as author and mover, he recorded that flow of blood and water from his side. The blessed one judged that this is what is signified in this place, namely that the Spirit testifies to that very thing, consider the water and the blood in the description of the Gospel history; just as Cajetan also interpreted it: 'For it is the Spirit who testifies concerning the blood of Christ offered on the cross and the baptismal water.' But the testimony of the Holy Spirit is not restricted here to that concerning the flow of blood and water, nor does that flow alone come into consideration through that phrase, 'he came by water and blood,' nor is it even primarily signified, even if the aorist ἐλθὼν is explained as a perfect, and that phrase ἐν σαρκὶ from chapter 4:3 is repeated, that Christ came in the flesh, nor is the testimony determined The object of the Spirit in these words comes in water and blood, but they contain other documents of his, concerning which the Spirit himself also testifies, namely that Jesus is that Son of God, and that in his Son sent into the world God has given us life. If indeed for the sake of proving that matter these things are brought forward, both that he came in water and in blood, and that the Spirit himself also testifies, which Spirit is ἡ ἀλήθεια, the truth itself. There is no need, therefore, that we should take the word Spirit metonymically, since a literal sense has a place. That this sense was later preferred by our blessed Gerhard from thesis 39 is clear: The Apostle says that Christ both came to us (by establishing the covenant of grace with us through the institution of the Sacraments) and still comes (by applying to us the benefits of the same through their dispensation in the Church) through water and blood, that is, through baptism, in which there is water, though not alone, and the holy supper, in which there is the blood of Christ, though not alone, the matter of which sacraments flowed forth from his very side on the cross and the ancients testify with unanimous consent. He also explains the use of the sacraments, namely that they testify that Christ has come, has perfected the work of redemption, and has instituted those memorials and means through which God wills to deal with us and to apply to us the remission of sins and eternal life, and he notably adds, not through water only, but also through blood, so that he may show the binary number of the sacraments of the New Testament and through this exaggeration confirm that the blood of Christ is truly exhibited to us present in the supper. He also joins a third witness, namely the Holy Spirit, who not only in the ministry of the Gospel, which is the ministry of the Spirit, John 15:26, 2 Corinthians 3:8, publicly testifies concerning the grace of God promised and offered in Christ, but also privately confirms and seals the promise of grace in the heart of every believer. For if we receive Christ coming to us through those three witnesses through the Word of the Gospel and the Sacraments added to it, then the Holy Spirit testifies inwardly, because the Spirit is the truth, and renders testimony to our spirit that we are the children of God, Romans 8:16, which explanation asserts both the binary number of the sacraments of the New Testament and their principal end, namely the sealing of grace and the benefits of Christ against the Papists, and the true, real, and substantial presence of the blood of Christ in the supper against the Calvinists and Photinians, as was demonstrated in the treatise on the Sacraments § 89, on the cycle and recognition of the Passover § 55, on the Eucharist § 102. Nor does this interpretation conflict with the former one concerning the blood and water flowing from the side of Christ, because, as we also warned before, that flow was not only a testimony of true humanity and death, but also a notable miracle, by which both the true Deity of Christ was demonstrated and a great mystery, by which the two sacraments of the Church, whose matter is blood and water, were designated, which was proven at greater length from Augustine and other ancients in the Harmony of Evangelical History, page 877.

But it is now clear how jejune, how alien to the text is the Grotian commentary, which here followed, as often elsewhere, the Socinians, who in the Racovian Catechism, page 125, handed down the same interpretation, that by the Spirit are noted the miracles of Christ, by water the innocence of life, but by blood death. Which gloss is also Schlichting's in this place. By the name of water he understands the effect of water through a metonymy of the cause, and purity, which, referred to the Spirit and

soul, consists in holiness and innocence. A maximum without argument, that Jesus was truthful. For neither can a liar and impostor have anything in common with such holiness as appeared in Jesus. By blood he understands similarly through metonymy the shedding of blood, because, namely, being most innocent and most holy, he shed his blood for the confirmation of his preaching and that he called himself the Son of God and Christ, never about to do that if he had feigned that he was sent by God. And it is the Spirit that testifies, namely concerning Jesus, that he is that Christ of God: For this is the matter at hand. He adds a third witness greater than the two former by every exception, namely that Spirit by whom Jesus was anointed, who testified concerning Jesus that he was truthful in all things, both by the very fact that he was given to him: for God would not have given that Spirit of his to an impostor, and because he instructed Jesus with plain divine wisdom and most divine works. But thus 1. the object of the testimony is by no means correctly constituted, because it is not that the preaching of Jesus is true, for those who had been converted to the faith of Jesus did not doubt his truth, just as it was not to be demonstrated that Jesus was not an impostor against the Pseudo-Christs, each of whom, while selling himself as the true Christ, had to accuse Jesus of Nazareth of being a mere impostor: For John's business was not against the Pseudo-Christs, but against the Anti-Christs, denying the true Deity or humanity of Jesus, and undermining the office of the one Christ as Savior and Mediator, dreaming of an earthly kingdom of Christ, and undermining his priesthood and propitiatory sacrifice, since they contended that man is justified and saved not through the satisfaction of Christ, but by his own obedience, and thus taking away the certainty of confidence and salvation. These things, therefore, had to be asserted, so that it might be established according to the sense of Scripture that Jesus is the Son of God, the Christ or that promised Messiah, the Savior of the world, in whom he who believes has eternal salvation, and can be certain of it with the undoubted certainty of faith against the world and the prince of the world, and overcome all temptations by true faith. Here the ignorance of Schlichting betrays itself, when he says that others, through ignorance of the Hebrew phraseology, have not observed that the word Christ and the word Son of God signify the same thing; since the word Messiah denotes the anointed; but that the word Son among the Hebrews denotes the anointed is said quite ignorantly. Which error we have also noted before in the Socinianizing Grotius. 2. The proofs which St. John brings forward for this matter are not the purity of life, his bloody death, and the miracles performed through the Spirit, expressed by the words water, blood, and Spirit, which would in no way sufficiently prove it. For any believer can have such purity of life as those men posit, and any martyr shedding blood for the faith thus comes not by water only, but by water and blood, and whoever has the gift of miracles thus also has the testimony of the Holy Spirit. Those things were certainly all common to the Apostles: which the Socinians cannot deny. Shall not, therefore, every one of the Apostles be constituted Christ by that reasoning? For he to whom those proofs apply, by which Christ is demonstrated by St. John, is Christ, according to that explanation. 3. There is no cause or necessity why water should be improperly taken to mean purity of life, nor is the word water taken in that sense anywhere in the Scriptures, nor does it suit it this is the sense: for although the washing may be done by water, and the purification, yet the water is not the purification itself, much less purity itself. The medium of purity is one thing, purity itself is another. 4. There is also no cause or necessity why the word blood should not be taken properly concerning the blood of Christ, just as in these words of Christ: This is the blood of the New Testament, but should signify the bloody death itself in this place, or even, as Schlichting foolishly suggests, that blood should be taken for flesh. The Apostle, he says, uses the word blood for the word flesh used above in chapter IV, verses 2, 3. For it is the same thing for Christ to have come in the flesh and to have come in the blood. But these differ greatly in the Apostolic phrase: for he is said to have come in the flesh because the Son of God performed his office in the assumed flesh: but he came in the blood when he shed his blood for us on the altar of the cross, and offers it to us in the Eucharistic cup for the confirmation of our faith. And how the word blood denotes flesh, through which Schlichting had previously said by metonymy that the shedding of blood was denoted. 5. Although the Spirit also testifies concerning JESUS by the fact that he was given to him and that he instructed him with divine wisdom and most divine works, yet the testimony of the Spirit is not exhausted by these, as he who testifies also through the insufflation, and having been given to the Apostles, indeed he testified descending in a visible form upon Christ, Luke III. Nor do those things testify only that Jesus is not an impostor, but that he is the only-begotten Son of God, and the life which was with the Father from eternity. For unless he were that, surely JESUS of Nazareth could not have received the Holy Spirit οὐκ ἐκ μέτρῳ or without measure, his gifts. Unless, I say, the human nature had been joined to the λόγῳ, it would not have been a participant in the immense fullness of the Deity, which the Apostle teaches dwells in him bodily, Colossians II, verse 9. For infinite and immense gifts could not pass into a mere man, and therefore it was necessary that the eternal Word should be incarnated and become man, so that he might render the assumed flesh a participant of the immense gifts, because communication presupposes union, by which the divine nature of the λόγος communicated itself with all its fullness, and with all the treasures of divine knowledge and wisdom, to the flesh united to it, Colossians I, verse 19, chapter II, verses 3, 9. Which gifts are called the gifts of the Holy Spirit, because the Holy Spirit, who is one with the Father and the Son, 1 John V, verse 7. and the Spirit of the Son of God, Galatians IV, verse 6, both fashioned this personal temple of the body of Christ, Luke I, verse 35, and anointed it with heavenly ointment, and instructed it with his gifts, Psalm XLV, verse 17, Isaiah XL, verse 1, chapter LXI, verse 1. 6.
