The Spirit is called ἡ ἀλήθεια in all the Greek Codices, which the Syriac and Arabic can by no means prejudice, because he is truth itself: as GOD is said to be love; the Son of GOD is said to be wisdom itself, 1 John IV, verse 16, Proverbs VIII, verse 23, not only truthful, much less that he is ἀξιόπιστος, or deserves faith, since it is one thing to signify a formal meaning, namely what a thing is, and another to deserve faith, and therefore those things would not have to be changed here, even if the meaning of the word ἀληθὴς obtained in John V, verse 31, chapter VIII, verse 13, which, however, we are by no means forced to admit. That the Holy Spirit deserves faith when testifying to something was not in doubt, but St. John wished to intimate something further, that the Holy Spirit is the very truth itself, which has testified concerning JESUS, that he is life itself, and that life has been given to us in him.

Latin:

Οὗτός ἐστιν ὁ ἐλθὼν δι' ὕδατος καὶ δι' αἵματος Ἰησοῦς ὁ Χριστὸς] Venit, id est, apparuit id quod erat Filius DEI. Per aquam & sanguinem, id est, per vitam purissimam, quæ per aquam significari solet, ut Ezech. XXXVI. v. 25. sive per lotionem quod aquæ est opus, ut Esa. I. v. 16. Jer. IV. v. 14. qua de re plura diximus ad Johan. III. v. 5. Et in signum hujus pu- ritatis baptizavit eum Johannes Baptista, Joh. I. v. 28: Vide & Ephes. V. v. 27. Tit. III. v. 5. Ebr. X. 22. Quare cum in omni actu sanctissimus fuerit, non est quod de veritate ejus, quod dixit se Christum sive Dei Filium, quicquam dubitetur. Deinde apparuit Dei filius, eo quod in testimonium ejus pro- feffionis, qua se Christum sive Dei Filium dixit, mortem cru- entam non recusavit, Joh. XVIII. 37. 1. Timoth. VI. v. 13. Vide Tertullianum de baptismo, ubi quod hic de Christo di- citur, etiam Christianis applicat. Bene autem hæc duo con- junxit Johannes, quia etiam in veteri Lege sacrificaturi prius se abluebant, unde & proverbium Ebraicum: Sine aqua non esse sacrificium: Item legem incipere per aquam, & finiri per aquam. In Manuscripto hic est: Δι ὕδατος, καὶ αἵματος, καὶ πνέυματος.

Οὐκ ἐν τῷ ὕδατι μόνον, ἀλλ' ἐν τῷ ὕδατι καὶ τῷ αἵματι] Qui- dam quod in vita professi sunt, id mortis metu deserunt. At noster Doctor in vita & in morte sibi constans fuit. Osten- dit ingens ad faciendam fidem esse momentum in ipsaChri sti morte & quidem tali. In Manuscripto est: Ἀλλ' ἐν τῷ ὕδατι καὶ πνέυματι.

καὶ τὸ πνεῦμά ἐστι τὸ μαρτυροῦν] Præterea ei testimonium fide dignissimum reddidit ipse Spiritus Dei, id est, per meto- nymiam admiranda ej9 opera à virtute divina manifeste pro- cedentia. Deus enim hunc honorem ei concessurus non fu- erat, si falso se Filium Dei dixisset, id est si blasphemus fuis- set, Joh. X, 36. Hoc testimonio ut invicto sæpe utiturChri- stus ipse, ut Johan. V. v. 32. 36. cap. X. v. 25. adde Act. II. vers. 20.

Ὅτι τὸ πνεῦμά ἐστιν ἡ ἀλήθεια] Tam Syrus quam Arabs le- gerunt ἀλήθεια fine articulo, quod rectius. Nam ἀλήθεια ponitur pro ἀληθὲς, quomodo ἀγάπη supra c. IV. v. 8. Ἀλη- θὲς vero pro eo, quod fidem meretur, quomodo eam vocem sumi diximus Joh. V. v. 31. cap. VIII. v. 13. Dicit non fru- stra se afferre supra alia illud ex operibus divinis testimoni- um, cum id circa ullam controversiam sit fide dignissi- mum.

Ad confirmationem victoriæ non tantum Christi, sed & fidelium Christi, qui per fidem in ipsum mundum vincunt, & salutis à Christo par- tæ, à fidelibus obtentæ testimonia omni exce- ptione majora requiruntur, quæ S. Johannes ex- cellentissima ratione fistit, tum quatenus in die- bus carnis Christi, qua ad nos in carne Filius Dei venit, ea deposita sunt, tum qua in Ecclesia Christi inde usque ad consummationem seculi glorificationis Christi nostraeque salutis causa deponuntur. Illa hoc commate adducta sunt, haec sequentibus. Sunt autem illa tria: Venit enim per aquam, nec tantum per aquam, sed per aquam & sanguinem, & accessit insuper Spiritus, qui juxta cum illis testificatus est, quod Spiritus est veritas. Venit ὁ ἐρχόμενος, ὁ ἐρχόμενος qui venturus erat, quod nomen ipsi proprium e Gen. XLIX. v. 10. Psal. XL. v. 8. Esa. XXXV. v. 5. cap. LXII. v. 11. Hagg. II. v. 8. Zach. II. v. 10. cap. IX. v. 9. Mal. III. v. 1. Matth. XI, v. 3. Joh. I. v. 15. Ve- nit autem I. per aquam, quod documentum & te- stimonium erat veri Messiae, contritoris capitis serpentini. Non autem aqua puritatis vitae hoc loco intelligitur, sed aqua baptismi, qualis adven- tus praedictus fuit Ezech. XXXVI. v. 15. Zach. XIII. v. 1. quod insigne ac publicum erat documentum adventus Messiae, non tantum qua prodromus ejus aqua baptizare debuit, Matth. III. v. 11. Luc. III. v. 16. Johan. I. v. 26. a quo Christus ipse non tam puritatis suae significandae, quam sanctificatio- nis aquae ad nostram purificationem consecran- dae gratia baptizari voluit, sed imprimis, quia ipse baptismum instituit, quo regeneramur & ablui- mur a peccatis nostris, Joh. III. v. 5. Matth. XXVIII. v. 19. Act. XXII. v. 11. Tit. III. v. 5. & virtute instrui- mur ad superandum mundum, & Satanam, siqui- dem induamus Christum, & Filii Dei evadamus per fidem, Gal. III. v. 26. 27. Testificatur ergo aqua baptismo non de Christo tantum victore Satanae, qui nisi venisset & Diabolum vicisset, hostis hujus infernalis potentia in mari rubro baptismi suffo- cari non posset: sed etiam de liberatione nostri, & salute, quam consequimur in Christo, quia per baptismum a peccato & potestate Satanae libera- mur & in regnum coelorum transferimur, Joh. III. v. 5. Quo pacto baptismum aquam mundam di- xit Apostolus, Ebr. X. 23. ut interpretantur Chry- sostomus, Theodoretus, Theophylactus, Oecumenius, & plerique Latini Interpretes, quam communem tam Graecorum quam Latinorum interpretatio- nem esse Estius ait, eaque ratione aqua munda a Patribus explicatur Ezech. XXXVI. v. 25. Vid. San- ctius ibidem. II. Nec per aquam tantum venit, sed etiam per sanguinem; ut in Veteri Testamen- to tum lotiones Leviticae, tum victimarum sanguis documenta erant gratiae divinae qua spiritualem ablutionem, & sacrificialem expiationem, ac um- brae rerum futurarum, Coloss. II. Ebr. IX. & X. Ita Christus, in quo habemus ipsam substantiam, & corpus, venit non tantum per aquam baptismi ad abluendum nos a peccatis, sed etiam per sangui- nem, quem & effudit pro nobis in remissionem peccatorum, Matth. XXVI. v. 28. quia redempti sumus pretioso λύτρῳ sanguinis, 1. Petri I. vers. 18. & potandum nobis praebet in poculo Eucharistico, ad remissionis applicationem, 1. Cor. X. v. 16. cap. XI. Ideo Beda in h. l. venit, inquit, per aquam, & san- guinem, aquam videlicet lavacri, & sanguinem suae passionis. Non solum baptizari propter nostram ablutionem dignatus est, ut nobis baptismi sacra- mentum consecraret, ac traderet, verum etiam sanguinem suum dedit pro nobis sua passione nos redimens, cujus sacramentis semper refecti con- servemur ad salutem. Anshelmus Laudunensis in glossa interlineari: Quia erat aeternus venit ad sa- lutem, & peccatorum remissionem, per aquam ba- ptismi & sanguinem passionis & non solum dignatus est baptizari propter nostram ablutionem, & ut ba- ptismi sacramentum nobis consecraret, sed & san- guinem pro nostri redemptione fudit. Atque eo referunt etiam nonnulli cum vete- rum, tum recentiorum, quod e Christi latere fluxere sanguis & aqua, Johan. XIX. v. 34. quod nonnulli hoc loco proprie respici volunt, cum Christus venisse dicitur non tantum per aquam, sed per aquam & sanguinem, quo abit B. Hunnii explicatio. Sed quia S. Johannes sanguinem ibi praemittit, aquam subjungit, quum hoc loco di- cat non per aquam tantum, sed & per sanguinem, B. Dorscheus in dissertat. de Spiritu, aqua & san- guine pag. 35. censet eo praecipue hic non respe- xisse sanctum Apostolum. Sane, inquit, si hoc lo- co B. Johannes primo & principaliter respexiffet ad sanguinem & aquam e latere Christi promanan- tem, non dixisset, tanquam singulare quippiam com- mendaturus & inculcaturus, οὐκ ἐν τῷ ὕδατι μόνον ἀλλ᾽ ἐν τῷ ὕδατι καὶ αἵματι, hoc est, non primo lo- co commemorasset aquam, & dixisset, Christum non tantum venisse in aqua, sed & in sanguine. Nam si ad illum fluxum aquae & sanguinis e latere Christi respicias, in eo non est tantum miraculum, quod sanguis fluxerit. Imo hoc naturalius est, quam si aqua fluat. At Johannes ita loquitur, tan- quam praeternaturalitatem rei in eo collocet, quod non aqua tantum, sed & aqua & sanguis efflux- erit. Cum praeternaturalius sit, aquam e cadavere fluere latere perfosso, quam sanguinem. Non ergo primo eo respicit B. Johannes. Caeterum quia san- cti Patres huc etiam referunt illud miraculum, admittimus certa ratione testimonium illud, de cujus veritate tam operose testatur Evangelista cap. XIX. vers. 35. etiam huc facere. Venit nem- pe Christus per duo illa sacramenta, eadem institu- ens in vita, quae ipse in morte ad obsignandum illam institutionem figurare etiam voluit, cum emitte- ret e perfosso latere suo sanguinem & aquam se- orsim, & citra commixtionem. Quo sensu efflu- xisse e latere Christi duo sacramenta veteres di- xere symbolico scilicet, quod aqua illa figurarit Baptismum, sanguis vero sacram Eucharistiam, imprimis quia merito passionis, mortis & perfos- sionis lateris Christi nobis acquisita fuit ista sa lutis οἰκονομία, ut ea dispensaretur per aquam ba- ptismi ad nostri regenerationem, & per calicem, qui est communicatio sanguinis Christi ad confor- tationem in fide spiritualem, & potationem ac nutritionem ad vitam aeternam, 1. Cor. XII. 13.

Joh. VI. v. 54. B. Wilhelmus Lyserus in praelect. in Summarium singularem hic fovit sententiam: nimirum ut sanguis Christi res caelestis est in sacra- mento coenae: Ita aquam, quae e latere Christi fluxit rem caelestem esse in sacramento baptismi. Sed aqua est materia terrena, quam vocant, in bapti- smo, nec conveniens videtur cum aqua elemen- tari naturali unitam esse aquam, quae e corpore Christi effluxit supernaturali ratione; imo bapti- smus ab aqua & Spiritu, non ab aqua communi, & aqua illa miraculose & extraordinarie emissa a Christo describitur Joh. III. v. 5. & in ejus in- stitutione, unde res coelestis derivanda est cum aqua, qua baptizare jubemur, conjungitur non aqua e latere Christi, sed nomen Patris, Filii & Spiritus Sancti, in quo baptizandum est, Matth. XXVIII. v. 19. Neque sancti Patres ea ratione effluxisse dixere duo illa sacramenta e Christi la- tere, quod illa aqua, quae effluxit in baptismo, dis- pensetur, sed quod symbolum aliquod fuerit ille fluxus aquae sacri baptifmatis. Quod e loco Ter- tulliani lib. de baptisin. cap. 16. constat: Est qui- dem nobis etiam secundum lavacrum unum & ipsum sanguinis scilicet, de quo Dominus: Habeo, inquit, baptismo tingi, quum jam tinctus fuisset. Venerat enim per aquam & sanguinem, sicut Jo- hannes scripsit, ut aqua tingeretur, sanguine glo- rificaretur. Proinde ut nos aqua faceret vocatos, sanguine electos, hos duos baptismos de vulnere per- fossi lateris emisit. Quia qui in sanguinem ejus crederent, aqua lavarentur, qui aqua lavissent, etiam sanguinem potarent. Gregorius Nyssinus in testim. Veteris Testamenti Laurentio Sifano In- terprete m. pag. 847. ita habet, adducens etiam Chrysostomi sententiam de hoc loco: Sanguinem & aquam ex divino Dominicoque latere fluxisse ab Evangelio docemur, non simpliciter, sed primum quidem ideo quod purificationes legales ad figuram & adumbrationem horum duorum tum aspersiones sanguinis, tum lustrationes per aquam peragebant. Deinde vero etiam ubi veritas venit, summa no- stra salutis per aquam & Spiritum mystice perfici- tur atque completur; quoniam tum per divinum baptisma, tum per sancti sanguinis participati- nem & usum consecrari nos ac divinitatem indue- re credimus, quemadmodum bis ipsis dictionibus & verbis divinus orator Chrysostomus exponit: Exivit, inquit, sanguis & aqua, ostendente Scri- ptura, quod non simpliciter ejusmodi fontes proflu- erint: sed quoniam ex his ambobus Ecclesia con- stat, atque id cognoscunt & intelligunt fideles, qui per aquam quidem sunt renati, per sangui- nem autem & carnem aluntur. Atque hinc my- steria sumunt initium, ut cum ad horrendum po- culum accedas, tanquam ab ipso Dominico latere bibiturus accedas. Item: Pauca gutta sanguinis totum mundum reformantes & instaurantes, & omnibus hominibus sicuti coagulum lactis evadunt, in unum nos cogentes & conjungentes, ut per u- tramque patrum sententiam conjungantur non so- lum virtus baptismatis & divini sanguinis partici- patio, una quidem per aquam, altera vero per sanguinem, verum etiam ipsa humana naturæ fir- ma certaque probatio. Nec alio sensu Hierony- mus ad Ocean. Tom. II. pag. m. 322. dixisse vide- tur: Latus Christi percutitur lancea, & baptismi atque martyrii pariter sacramenta funduntur. Au- gustinus tract. XVI. in Joh. Percussum est latus & statim emanavit sanguis & aqua, quæ sunt Ec- clesiæ gemina sacramenta, aqua in qua sponsa est purificata, sanguis ex quo invenitur esse dotata. Leo Magnus in epist. quam concil. Chalcedon. rectæ fidei columnam vocavit: Videat quæ natu- ra tam fixa clavis pependerit in crucis ligno & aperto per mortis lanceam latere crucifixi intelli- git, unde sanguis & aqua effluxerint, ut Ecclesia Dei & lavacro rigaretur & poculis. Paulinus Nolanus in epistol. ad Florent. Christum petram nominat, quæ latere lancea perforato aqua fluxit & sanguine, ut pariter salutiferos nobis funderet fontes aquam gratia & sanguinem sacramenti. Johannes Damascenus lib. IX. de orthod. fid. c. 5. Scaturivit nobis, inquit, ex sancto, & incontami- nato latere Christi fons remissionis aqua in regene- rationem & ablutionem peccati & corruptionis. Sanguis vero potus vitæ æternæ causa. Et præcepta nobis dedit per aquam regenerari & Spiritum, Spiritu Sancto per imprecationem & invocationem aquæ supervenienti. Ad quem locum Jodocus Clichtoveus pag. 30. Illud, inquit, otiose non præ- tereundum, fontem baptismalem habuisse efficaciam suam, sicut & significantiam ex scaturigine aquæ de latere Domini nostri lancea post mortem trans- fixo. Fuit enim illa scaturitio fontis remissionis & regenerationis in Christo, per quem in aqua & Spi- ritu renascimur Deo: Sicut & emanans sanguis eodem tempore ex latere Christi designavit suum pretiosum sanguinem, relictum nobis in potum & causam vitæ æternæ indignissimo scilicet & omnium sacrorum excellentissimo Eucharistiæ sacramento. Quibus consonant itidem è Pontificiis Thomas part. III. quæst. 66. artic. 3. ad 3. Ex latere Christi fluxit aqua ad abluendum, sanguis ad redimendum, & ideo sanguis competit sacramento Eucharistiæ, aqua vero sacramento Baptismi. Didacus Vanguas in Promptuar. Conc. lib. 1. tract. de Pass. pag. 405. In hac re invenimus grande mysterium, ut agno- scant fideles, se habere ab illo latere Christi aquam emundationis & sanguinem calicis salutaris, quo in mystica mensa inebriantur amatores Dei. Felices illi, qui ab ipso Dominici pectoris latere & fonte haurire merentur, & bibere vulnerati sanguinem. Cons. & Johan. de Carthagen. libr. XII. homil. Ca- tholic. in univers. relig. arcana homil pag. 915. Franciscus Tolet. in Johan. XIX. pag. 315. Bellar- minus lib. II. de effic. sacram. cap. 27. Maldona- tus in cap. XXVII. Matth. fatentur ita fere Græcos omnes, imo omnes Autores veteres explicare. E Reformatis Theodorus Beza in h. l. non immerito dixisse ait Augustinum: Hæc duo sacramenta Ec- clesiæ Christianæ ex Christi latere velut effluxisse, cum ex ejus perfosso latere proflueret sanguis & aqua, &c. Interpretationes aquæ de lacrymis Chri- sti Thomæ Anglici, de populis multis à Christo con- gregatis, item de sapientia à cælo abscondita, quas attulit Salmero, de doctrina cœlesti Antonii Bruc- cioli in comment. Ital. sup. script. Tom. VI. pag. 44. alieniores sunt, nec calculum merentur.

III. Additur testimonium Spiritus: Et Spiritus testificatur, quod Spiritus sit veritas. Per Spiri- tum testificantem nonnulli intelligunt Spiritum in ara crucis emissum, de quo & aqua & sanguine ex latere effosso emanante, interpretatur Autor li- bri de duplici martyrio, qui habetur inter opera Cypriani, quem vero Neoterici cujusdam esse censet Pamelius, reprobatque Bellarminus & Ri- vetus. Similiter explicat Augustinus Tom. VI. contr. Maximinum lib. III. cap. 22. Tria, inquit, novimus de corpore Domini exiisse, cum penderet èligno: primo spiritum, unde scriptum est, & in- clinato capite tradidit spiritum: Deinde quando latus ejus lancea perforatum est, sanguinem, & aquam. Quæ tria, si per seipsa intuemur, diver- sas habent singula quæque substantias. Paschasius Radbertus Abbas Corbejensis lib. I. de corpore & sangv. Christi Tom. IV. Bibl. sanct. Patr. pag. 180. Tria sunt quæ testimonium dant, quod Christus est veritas, Spiritus, sanguis & aqua. Nimirum post- quam emisit Spiritum de fonte pectoris sui, contra naturam manavit felix unda baptismi, & sanguis redemptionis. Strabus Fuldensis in gloss. ordin. Spiritus is est anima quam emisit in passione, aqua & sanguis, quæ fluxerunt de latere, veram carnis naturam testantur. Innocentius II. in epistol. ad Ferrar. Episcop. lib. III. Decret. Gregor. lib. 41. de celebr. Miss. Per hoc quod in articulo mortis in- clinato capite tradidit Spiritum, manifeste proba- tur, quod ipse Spiritum habebat, non solum statum vitalem, sed etiam animam rationalem. Per hoc autem, quod unus militum lancea latus ejus ape- ruit, & continuo sanguis exivit & aqua, proba- tur aperte, quod Christus verum corpus habebat. Eandem explicationem suam quoque fecere Gregorius Primatercius in comment. ad h. l. Jo- hannes Mariana, Emanuel Saa, Gvilbelm. Estius, Cornelius à Lapide in h. l. qui postremus tamen addit, valde apposite ad literam & pene literaliter, aquam, sanguinem, & spiritum considerari non solum quatenus in cruce emissa & effusa, sed etiam quatenus in resurrectione resumpta, vi propria tam humanitatis quam divinitatis. Sed haec inter- pretatio sive ut ab aliis traditur, seu ut à Cornelio jam incrustatur, non convenit Apostoli verbis, & Spiritus testatur, ὅτι τὸ πνεῦμά ἐστιν ἡ ἀλήθεια: Oecumenius Spiritum explicat de resurrectio- ne, vel Deitate, quae in cruce & alibi apparuit. Serarius in h. l. praeeunte Catharino per Spiritum intelligit Spiritum justorum, qui Spiritus Sancti effectum est, quo renovati uncti & edocti sunt. Sed & hoc alienum est. Nam Spiritus fidelium potius objectum est, cui testificatio fieri innui- tur, quam testificationis causa, quae hic designata. Neque assensum meretur Bernhardi explicatio, qui serm. I. in octav. Pasch. charitatem intelligit per Spiritum, quem tamen sequutus est Petrus Blesensis serm. de Trinit. Nec abnuit Ambro- sius Catharinus per Spiritum intelligens internum Spiritus Sancti donum. Antonius Brucciolius desi- gnari vult virtutem, & administrationem divi- nam per Spiritum. Cui gemina sunt, quae tradi- derat Bullingerus: Hic est ille veniens, aut qui venturus erat per aquam & sanguinem Jesus Chri- stus. Quasi senserit divinum Spiritum per Scri- pturas praenunciasse, aliquando venturum esse Sal- vatorem, qui se mundo probaturus sit per aquam & sanguinem quod sit Salvator. Per aquam vero in- telligimus caelestem doctrinam, idque ob puritatem, & quod reficiat ac fluat. Sed & sanguinis nomine allusit ad veterum sacrificia: Et sine sanguinis ef- fusione (ait Apostolus) non fit remissio. Ponit er- go sanguinem pro hostia, remissione & redemptio- ne. Venit ergo Jesus Doctor & lux mundi, hostia & redemptor aeternus. Nam docuit caelestem sapientiam, & morte sua vivificavit nos, & sanguine suo la- vit. Quibus ceu infallibilibus argumentis mundo declaravit, quod ipse sit Christus, hoc est, quod Jesus verus sit Messias, verus Dei Filius. Et ad vers. 8. ait: Aqua significari caelestem doctrinam, sanguine redemptionem, & Spiritu virtutem & administrationem divinam. Nec diversa viden- tur, quae habet Beza: Spiritum vocari existimo vim & efficacitatem, sese per fidei fructus, id est, charitatem in omnibus vere sanctis exerentem. Zanchius de trib. Elohim lib. I. part. 1. cap. 1. p. 6. ut per aquam doctrinam Evangelii, per sanguinem qualitatem mortis Christi: Ita per Spiritum poten- tiam sua Deitatis, qua se variis effectis, quis esset, declaravit, intelligit, revocans haec ad officium Christi propheticum, quod aqua doctrina defi- gnetur, Esa. XI. v. 1. Pontificium ratione sangui- nis & Regium ratione Spiritus, hunc faciens con- cludendi nervum: Qui venit primo ut Propheta per aquam, doctrinam scilicet Evangelii afferens, & per totum orbem, sicut praedixerunt Propheta spar- gens; qui venit item ut Pontifex per sanguinem, ta- lem scilicet obiens mortem, qualem Propheta vati- cinati sunt obiturum Messiam, & quidem pro alio- rum peccatis, ut Esaias longe ante praedixerat cap. LIII. qui denique venit ut Rex per Spiritum, hoc est, per potentiam, qua talia miracula edat, qualia de Messia praedicta fuerunt per Prophetas, & qua hostes debellet, seipsum à morte excitet, mundum sibi subjiciat. Qui, inquam, ita venit per aquam, per sanguinem, per Spiritum, is verus est Christus. Atqui hoc modo venit Jesus. E. Thomas Anglicus Spiritum vult sumi essentiali- ter pro Deo & Deitate, hancque testificatam, quod Jesus esset veritas, id est, verus Deus & ho- mo. Augustinus etsi Spiritum, aquam & sangui- nem de anima Christi, aqua & sanguine lateris Chri- sti cum aliis acceperit, si illa per seipsa intueamur, vult ea, quæ hic significata sunt, esse Patrem, qui per Spiritum, Filium, qui per sanguinem, & Spiri- tum Sanctum, qui per aquam designetur. Clemens Alexandrinus in h. l. Spiritus, inquit, est vita aqua, regeneratio, & fides, sanguis cognitio.

Sed missis alienioribus istis merèque arbitra- riis interpretationibus allii plerique per πνεῦμα τὸ ματυρῦν ipsummet Spiritum Sanctum intelli- gunt. Cyrillus de recta fide ad Reginas l. 1. Vincit quidem mundum qui credit, quod Jesus est Filius Dei. Quis autem Jesus, ipse discipulus nobis ex- planat, dicens: Hic est, qui venit per aquam & sanguinem, Jesus Christus. Sed & in sanguine & in Spiritu: & tres unum esse dicit. Igitur Verbum quidem caro factum est, sanctificat autem nos Spi- ritu & purificat sanguine, & abluit iterum aqua munda. Unus autem utique omnino Filius, cujus & esse dicimus Spiritum & aquam & sanguinem. Sic & cum Hesselio Johannes Lorinus in h. l. vide- tur Johannes probare Christi divinitatem triplici testimonio. Tria enim de vero Messia, ut rectè annotavit Hesselius, prædicantur potissimum in Ve- teri Testamento, de quibus meminit hic atque dein- ceps B. Johannes: primum est, quod esset sangui- nem proprium effusurus: Secundum est, quod ho- mines participes futuri essent tam pretiosi sanguinis per corporalem aquam, id est, per baptismum. Tertia quod Christus missurus esset Spiritum suum in totum terrarum orbem. Johannes Christum ait venisse nempe per incarnationem non tantum in aqua baptismum instituendo, sed etiam in sanguine, tum illum pro nobis fundendo, tum ejus pretium ac meritum in sacramentis communicando, tum bibendum in Eucharistia proponendo, præterea in Spiritu, qui simul datur in baptismo aliisque sacra- mentis, vel qui largius & visibili modo datus est in Pentecoste. Quæ interpretatio glossæ interlineari analoga præ aliis Papistarum expositionibus, si excipias sacramentorum numerum, accedit ad mentem S. Johannis. Nec abnuit è Reformatis Zvinglius, qui etsi tropos suos prioribus admi- sceat, aqua, inquiens, nos baptismum Christi, atq; omnia quæ Christo baptizato juxta baptismum con- tigere virtute synecdoches intelligimus: per sangui- nem non eundem solum, qui è latere Christi mortui in cruce lancea perfosso effluxit, sed quicquid circa crucem Christi miraculosum evenit, interpreta- mur. Spiritus Sancti nomine tamen recte ipsum- met Spiritum Sanctum designari, censet, licet re- stringat testimonium ejus nimis: Cæterum in- quit, Spiritus Sancti nomine non solum apparitio- nem illam, qua specie columbæ è cælo veniens super caput Christi baptizati consedit, sed & miraculum Pentecostes, &c. Oecumenius, qui etsi pariter alienam interpretationem tradat de aqua & san- guine Demag. 19. in epist. Joh. pag. 85. per aquam intelligens testimonium Johannis Baptistæ, per sanguinem testimonium centurionis de sanguine & aqua è latere Christi profluentibus, de Spiritu Sancto tamen videtur nobis accedere, modo me- tonymia abesset, per Spiritum testimonium Apo- stolorum intelligendo, qui accepto Spiritu Sancto variis loquebantur linguis: quin etiam conveni- entiorem subjecit ἐξήγησιν priorum: Videmur au- tem & hic præcipuorum sacramentorum admoneri, quæ ad confirmandas nostras conscientias potissi- mum data, & clamant, nisi stupidi simus, & per- fidi erga Christum Deum. Etenim sacramentalibus si- gnis non minus fides juvatur, quam si maxima mi- -racula in oculis nostris Christus faceret. Duobus enim modis benignam suam erga nos voluntatem Christus indubitatam esse voluit, quorum symbola hic nominantur, nempe aqua & sanguis, quae ex latere Christi mortui effluxerunt non absque myste- rio. Nempe ut olim Eva ex latere Adae sumpta, ita & dormiente secundo Adam in cruce ex latere ejus profluxerunt mysteria, quibus nata est & confirmata Ecclesia. Aqua baptismus, sanguine synaxis, quae & ad martyrium cohortatur, nobis commendantur. Johannes Piscator, etsi per aquam ablutiones legales intelligat, per sanguinem vero sacrificia expiatoria Veteris Testamenti, ut ita veritas de Christi testimonio legalium ablutionum & sacrificiorum demonstretur: agnoscit tamen per Spiritum intelligi Spiritum Sanctum testificantem in cordibus electorum: nec in priori explicatione sibi constat. Nam in scholiis ἀναλύσει subjunctis ad v. 8. nostrae ἐκθέσει accedit: Sive aqua illa, inquit, & sanguis ille qui effluxit è latere Christi mortui in cruce: sive aqua baptismi & poculum Domini, quod sanguinis ipsius symbolum est. Imo in ipsa ἀναλύσει addit: Per aquam, inquiens, & sanguinem illum, quae fluxerunt ex latere Christi: quatenus iis adumbrata fuit vis & efficacia mortis Christi per ablutiones & expiationes legales olim praefigurata. Nec tamen fuerit absurdum, si quis hoc loco per ἀντανάκλασιν nomine aquae intelligat baptismum, nomine vero sanguinis coenam Dominicam. Sed quantopere Piscator non sane Apostolicus ob tropos, quos gens Sacramentaria invehere consuevit hic fluctuet, non modo metonymia, & synecdoche ad excludendam praesentiam sanguinis Christi è sacra coena, sed etiam nova synecdoche in voce Spiritus metonymice intellecta de Evangelio, docere potest. Addit enim: Dummodo vocabulum sanguinis accipiatur non proprie, quasi sanguis Christi jam sit in terra: sed metonymice & synecdochice pro sacra coena, quae corporis & sanguinis Christi sacramentum est. Et porro: Si quis tamen aquam & sanguinem hic eadem significatione accipienda censeat, qua paulo ante: tum baptismi & coenae Dominicae testimonium per synecdochen contineri dicendum erit vocabulo Spiritus, eo quod Evangelii appendices sint tanquam imagines scilicet & sigilla, ad illud amplius declarandum atque obsignandum adhibita. Sed quomodo venit Christus in aqua, nec in aqua tantum, sed in aqua & sanguine, si id intelligatur de legalibus ablutionibus & sacrificiis? Num ipse adhibuit, aut sancivit in adventu suo ablutiones & sacrificia ista? Annon potius per adventum ejus cessarunt, uti figura vel umbra, cum advenit corpus?

Testificatur autem Spiritus Sanctus non solum κατ' ἔσω in cordibus fidelium nedum electorum solum, sed imprimis κατ' ἔξω, ad quae externa testimonia potissimum hoc loco respicitur, quia demonstranda primum est veritas asserti, quod Filius Dei sit Jesus, hoc est, Salvator noster, vel quod Jesus, quum res eodem recidat, sit Filius ille Dei, qui carne venit, ut Salvator esset mundi, ceu Messias vel Christus promissus, qui ungendus erat donis Spiritus Sancti non ad mensuram, ut esset Pontifex, Propheta, & Rex, salutem nobis obedientia sua acquirens, per Verbum & Sacramenta applicans, nosque in eadem potenter ad vitam aeternam seu regnum gloriae conservans, quicunque in ipsum credimus; tum vero exsurgit certitudo gratiae & salutis aeternae in cordibus nostris, quod scilicet credentes ceu renati ex Deo per fidem, qua apprehendimus Jesum Salvato- rem, non modo mundum vincamus, sed & vi- tam & salutem æternam obtineamus in ipso & per ipsum : quo directam esse hanc μαρτυρίαν Apo- stolus sonora voce docuit, v. 11. Et hoc est illud testimonium, quod vitam æternam nobis dederit Deus, & quod vita illa sit in Filio ejus. Quum er- go Deus de illo nos non confirmet ἀμέσως, ut fa- natici volunt, sed mediante Verbo, ideo doctri- na illa Verbi de Jesu Filio Dei, in quo vita æterna habetur, confirmanda maxime erat, utpote ex qua πληροφορία illa petenda est; & per quam eam exsitat, fovetque Spiritus Sanctus in cordibus nostris. Quomodo autem confirmatur ea per id, quod Jesus Christus venit per aquam & san- guinem, quodque Spiritus est, qui testificatur. Illa certe testimonia per aquam baptismi à Christo & suscepti nostri causa, & instituti ceu medii re- generationis & salutis nostræ, & per sanguinem in cruce effusum & in sacra cœna ad confirmatio- nem fidei & conservationem ad æternam vitam nobis hauriendum sancitum sunt luculenta, pu- blica, & per totum orbem resonantia testimonia, una cum Spiritus Sancti testificatione, quo unctus fuit Christus, cujus virtute docuit, & miracula patravit, & opus redemptionis peregit, quemque concessit Apostolis per insufflationem, Johan. XX. v. 22. & effudit in festo Pentecostes, ut de se per orbem testarentur; quemadmodum de Messia ea omnia prædicta fuere. Quæ testimonia doctri- nam de Filio Dei, qui in mundum salutis nostræ causa venit, deque fide in ipsum, ut salute ista fruamur, confirmant, deque ea testantur effica- cissime : non solum Propheticorum oraculorum complementum, sed ob testimoniorum istorum tenorem & argumentum, ut & δεινότητα vim & effectum. Nam baptismum aquæ Christus susce- pit, ut omnem justitiam impleret, Matth. III. v. 15. & consecraret aquam, ut lavacrum regenerationis & re- novationis nostræ, Tit. III. v. 5.

Cum sacramentum baptismi instituit in abso- lutionem & remissionem peccatorum nostrorum; annon se demonstravit verum Deum, & Salvato- rem nostrum, ac Filius ille Dei, in quo Deus Pa- ter εὐδόκησε, Matth. III. v. 17. qui cum Patre & Spiritu Sancto est unus ille Deus, quem in bapti- smo profitemur omnes, cap. XXVIII. v. 19. Chri- stus, vel Messias ille promissus, qui in mundum venit, inauguratus cum baptizaretur, & à nobis per fidem induendus, cum in ipsum ceu Chri- stum Salvatorem nostrum baptizamur, Gal. III. 26. 27. Sanguinem autem suum profundens in pre- tium redemptionis nostræ annon se demonstra- vit verum Deum & hominem Mediatorem illum Dei & hominum unicum, qui dedit semetipsum ἀντίλυτρον pro omnibus, 1. Timoth. II. v. 5. 6. An- non cum sanguine ejus potamur in sacra cœna, ut in ipso vitam æternam habeamus, Johan. VI. v. 54. & calix, qui est communicatio sanguinis Christi, nobis novum Testamentum est in ejus sanguine 1. Corinth. XI. de ipso confirmamur, quod in ipso, ceu θεανθρώπῳ vero Deo & vero homine vel vita in carne manifestata vitam æternam habeamus, eamque per fidem in ipsum consequamur? Non- ne testificatus est Spiritus Sanctus de Filii Dei in- carnatione, redemptione, & salutis nostræ acquisi- tione, ejusdemque applicatione & concessione, tum verbo, tum opere & facto ipso, quando ejus ἐπε- λεύσει conceptus est in matris utero Filius Dei, ejus donis οὐκ ἐκ μέτρου unctus est, & virtute in- structus exequutus est officia sua, ceu Messias un- ctus ille Domini, Propheticum, Sacerdotale &

Regium, Luc. I. cap. IV. Actor. X. Luc. XI. Quan- do iʒem Spiritum Sanctum concessit ipse Apo- stolis, & virtute ex alto eos instruxit: quæ non sunt ψιλõ ἀνθρώπɤ, sed θεανθρώπɤ, non terreni cujusdam uncti Domini, sed unici illius promissi Messiæ ac Salvatoris mundi. Atque horum o- mnium testimoniorum δεινότητα, vim & effectum sive baptismatis, sive Eucharistiæ, & Spiritus San- cti experimur opere ipso in nostra regeneratione, justificatione, renovatione, & pugna adversus mun- dum, ac victoria, quicunque vera fide Christum suscipimus, non autem testimonia illa reproba- mus, aut eorum vim excludimus.

Addit S. Johannes ὅτι τὸ πνεῦμά ἐστιν ἡ ἀλήθεια. Latina Vulgata legit: Quoniam Christus est veri- tas; sed Græca & Syriaca lectio habet, quoniam Spiritus est veritas: quam lectionem habet etiam Leo Papa epist. X. cap. 5. in fine, & S. Augustinus de dono persever. cap. 23. Quod quum fateatur Estius, addit tamen, haud facilè dixerim, utra lectio alteri sit præferenda? At secundum concilium Tridentinum præferenda sine dubio Vulgata; Se- cundum veritatem Græcam autem omnino præ- ferenda altera lectio, qua revera sola avthentica, omnium codicum autoritate firmata. Particula ὅτι bifariam exponitur. Aliis enim determinativa est, quod Spiritus est veritas, qui plerique per τὸ Πνεῦμα intelligunt per metonymiam Evangelium Spiritus, quia verba Christi Spiritus & vita sunt, Joh. VI. v. 63. Sed hoc quod hic probandum est, per testimonium Spiritus aliter v. 4. & 5. ut & post- ea v. 11. à S. Johanne determinatum est, nempe quod victoria nostra sit fides fideique objectum, vel id quod credendum est, sit Dei Filius, in quo Deus nobis dedit æternam vitam, documentum autem probationis à testificatione Spiritus Sancti desu- mitur: ac deinde demum v. 9. infert Apostolus Evangelii veritatem, quod nempe id ceu testimo- nio non humano, sed divino eoque multiplici confirmatum suscipiendum sit per fidem, idcirco cum aliis malumus accipere particulam ὅτι sensu causali quia, vel quoniam, ut confirmetur Spiritus testificatio, imprimis quia non dicitur & Spiritus testificatur, quod Spiritus sit veritas, sed καὶ τὸ πνεῦμά ἐστι τὸ μαρτυρõν, & Spiritus est qui testifi- catur, scilicet de hoc Jesu, quod sit Filius Dęi, in quo dedit nobis Deus vitam æternam. Nam ἅυτη ἐστὶν ἡ μαρτυρία, hæc est illa testificatio, interprete ipso Johanne v. 11. Quem sensum etiam B. Ger- hardus assumsit in disput. è 1. Joh. V. v. 7. thes. 38. Ὅτι quia Spiritus est veritas, & proinde testimo- nium ejus est verum ac certum, ut particula ὅτι accipiatur causaliter non objective pari ratione, ut (S. Johannes) in Evangelio dixerat (cap. XIX. 35.) qui vidit, testimonium perhibuit, & testimonium ejus verum est, non ideo solum, quia testis est ἀυ- τόπτης, sed etiam quia Spiritu Sancto autore & im- pulsore illum sanguinis & aquæ è latere profluxum annotavit. Quod hoc loco significari censuit ὁ Μακαρίτης, quod nempe Spiritus testificetur, illud ipsum puta de aqua & sanguine in Evangelica sci- licet historiæ descriptione; quemadmodum & Ca- jetanus interpretatus est: Spiritus enim est, qui testificatur de sanguine Christi in cruce oblati & aqua baptismali. Sed Spiritus Sancti testificatio hic non restringitur ad illud de fluxu sanguinis & aquæ, nec flux9 ille solum per illud, venit in aqua & sanguine, imo nec primario significatur, etiamsi aoristus ἐλθὼν pro perfecto explicetur, & illud ἐν σαρκὶ è cap. IV. v. 3 repetatur, quod Christus in carne venerit, nec determinatur testificationis Spiritus objectum istis verbis venit in aqua & sanguine, sed ea continent alia documenta ejus, de quo etiam Spiritus ipse testificatur, nimirum quod Jesus sit Filius ille Dei, & quod in Filio suo in mundum misso nobis vitam dederit Deus. Si- quidem ejus rei probandæ causa hæc adferantur, tum quod venerit in aqua & in sanguine, tum quod testificetur etiam ipse Spiritus, qui Spiritus est ἡ ἀλήθεια ipsa veritas. Non ergo opus est, ut vocem Spiritus metonymice accipiamus, quum proprius sensus locum habeat. Quem sensum postea prætulisse B. Gerhardum nostrum e thes. XXXIX. liquet: Dicit Apostolus Christum ad nos & venisse (per Sacramentorum institutionem fœ- dus gratiæ nobiscum erigendo) & adhuc venire (per eorandem in Ecclesia dispensationem benefi- cia suæ nobis applicando) per aquam & sanguinem, hoc est, per baptismum, in quo est aqua, licet non sola, & sacram cœnam, in qua est sanguis Christi, licet non solus, quorum sacramentorum materia ex ipsius latere in cruce profluxit & veteres una- nimi consensu testantur. Exponit etiam usum sa- cramentorum, quod videlicet testentur Christum venisse, opus redemptionis perfecisse, & illa me- morialia ac media, per quæ Deus nobiscum agere, remissionem peccatorum & vitam æternam nobis applicare velit, instituisse, ac notanter addit, non per aquam solum, sed & per sanguinem, ut binarium sacramentorum Novi Testamenti nume- rum ostendat & per hanc exaggerationem Christi sanguinem vere in cœna præsentem nobis exhiberi confirmet. Conjungit etiam tertium testem, vide- licet Spiritum Sanctum, qui non solum in ministe- rio Evangelii, quod est ministerium Spiritus, Jo- han. XV. v. 26. 2. Corinth. III. vers. 8. publice de gratia Dei in Christo promissa, & oblata testatur, sed etiam privatim in corde cujusvis credentis promissionem gratiæ confirmat & obsignat. Si enim Christum per tres illos testes per Verbum Ev- angelii eique addita Sacramenta ad nos venientem recipimus, tum Spiritus Sanctus interius testatur, quod Spiritus sit veritas, ac testimonium reddit Spiritui nostro, quod simus filii Dei, Roman. VIII. vers. 16. quæ explicatio tum binarium sacramento- rum Novi Testamenti numerum & principalem e- orum finem, obsignationem scilicet gratiæ & benefi- ciorum Christi contra Pontificios, tum veram rea- lem & substantialem sanguinis Christi in cœna præ- sentiam contra Calvinianos & Photinianos asserit, ut in tractat. de Sacrament. §. 89. de circ. & agn. pasch. §. 55. de Eucharist. §. 102. fuit demonstra- tum. Neque pugnat hæc interpretatio cum priore de sanguine & aqua ex latere Christi profluente, quia, ut antea etiam monuimus, profluxus ille non solum fuit veræ humanitatis, & mortis testimoni- um, sed & insigne miraculum, quo & vera Chri- sti Deitas demonstrata & grande mysterium, quo duo Ecclesiæ sacramenta, quorum materia sunt sanguis & aqua, fuerunt designata, id quod ex Au- gustino & aliis veteribus in Harm. Evangel. Histor. pag. 877. pluribus fuit comprobatum.

Patet autem jam quam jejunus, quam alienus a textu sit Grotianus commentarius, qui hic se- quutus est, ut sæpe alias, Socinianos, qui in Ca- tech. Racov. pag. 125. eandem interpretationem tradidere, per Spiritum notari miracula Christi, per aquam vitæ innocentiam, per sanguinem vero mortem. Quæ glossa etiam Schlichtingii est in h. l. Aquæ nomine intelligit aquæ effectum per metony- miam causæ, & puritatem, quæ ad Spiritum &

animam relata confiftit in sanctitate & innocentia. Maximum sine argumento, Jesum fuisse vera- cem. Neque enim mendaci & impostori cum tanta sanctitate, quanta in Jesu apparuit, quicquam com- mune esse potest. Per sanguinem intelligit similiter per metonymiam sanguinis effusionem, quod scilicet innocentissimus & sanctissimus cum esset, pro predi- cationis suæ & quod se diceret Dei Filium & Chri- stum confirmatione sanguinem suum profuderit, nunquam id facturus, si sese à Deo missum esse fin- xiffet. Et Spiritus est qui testatur nempe de Jesu, quod sit Christus ille Dei: Hac enim de re agitur. Addit tertium testem duobus prioribus omni exce- ptione majorem, Spiritum nimirum illum, quo Jesus unctus fuit, qui testabatur de Jesu, quod in omnibus verax esset, tum per idipsum, quod ei da- tus esset: neque enim Deus impostori Spiritum il- lum suum dedisset, tum quod Jesum plane divina sapientia & divinissimis operibus instrueret. Sed ita 1. objectum testificationis nequaquam recte constituitur, quod non est Jesu præconium ve- rum esse, de ejus enim veritate non dubitabant, qui ad fidem Jesu conversi erant, quemadmodum nec id demonstrandum erat, Jesum non fuisse im- postorem adversus Pseudo-Christos, quorum quis- que dum se verum Christum venditabat, Jesum Nazarenum merum impostorem fuisse criminari necesse habebat: Non enim adversus Pseudo- Christos Johanni res erat, sed adversus Anti- Christos, veram Jesu Deitatem aut humanita- tem abnegantes, ac Salvatoris & Mediatoris unius Christi officium labefactantes, regnum Christi terrenum somniantes, & sacerdotium ac sacrifi- cium ejus propitiatorium labefactantes, cum non per satisfactionem Christi, sed propria obedientia hominem justificari, & salvari contenderent, adeoque fiduciæ & salutis certitudinem tollentes. Hæc ergo asserenda erant, ut juxta Scripturæ sensum constaret, quod Jesus sit Dei Filius Chri- stus vel Messias ille promissus, Salvator mundi, in quem qui credit, salutem æternam habet, de- que ea certus esse potest indubitata fidei certitu- dine adversus mundum & mundi principem, o- mnesque tentationes vera fide superare. Tur- pis hic se prodit Schlichtingii inscitia, cum alios è phraseos Ebrææ imperitia non observasse ait, quod vox Christi & vox Filii Dei idem fignificent; quum Messiæ vox unctum notet; Filii autem vo- cem apud Ebræos unctum notare admodum im- perite dicatur. Quem errorem etiam in Socini- zante Grotio antea notavimus. 2. Documen- ta, quæ in hanc rem affert S. Johannes, non sunt puritas vitæ, mors ejus cruenta & miracula per Spiritum patrata, verbis aquæ, sanguinis, & Spi- ritus expressa, quæ id sufficienter minime pro- bassent. Nam puritatem vitæ talem, qualem homines illi statuunt, quivis fidelis habere po- test, & quivis martyr sanguinem pro fide profun- dens, ita venit non per aquam tantum, sed per aquam & sanguinem, & quicunque donum mi- raculorum habet, testimonium ita etiam habet Spiritus Sancti. Communia certe illa omnia fuere Apostolis: Quod negare nequeunt Soci- niani. Num ergo non unusquisque Apostolo- rum ea ratione Christus constituetur? Cui e- nim documenta illa conveniunt, per quæ Chri- stus demonstratur à S. Johanne, is Christus est, juxta istam explicationem. 3. Aqua cur im- proprie accipienda sit de puritate vitæ, nulla cau- sa est vel necessitas, nec uspiam ea ratione ac- cipitur vox aquæ in Scripturis, nec convenit ei hic sensus: nam etsi aqua ablutio fiat, & pu- rificatio, non tamen aqua est ipsa purifica- tio, nedum puritas ipsa. Aliud est medium puritatis, aliud ipsa puritas. 4. Nulla etiam causa vel necessitas est, cur sanguinis vox non proprie de sanguine Christi, quemadmodum in his Christi: Hic est sanguis Novi Testamenti, accipienda sit, sed ipsamet mortem cruentam significare hoc loco debeat, vel etiam ut Schlich- tingius ineptit, sanguis pro carne accipiatur. Sanguinis, inquit ille, vocem ponit Apostolus pro voce carnis superius usurpata cap. IV. vers. 2. 3. Idem enim est Christum venisse in carne: & ve- nisse in sanguine. At hæc maximopere, phra- si Apostolica, distant: nam venisse in carne dicitur, quia Filius Dei in assumpta carne munus suum exequutus est: In sanguine autem venit, cum sanguinem in ara crucis pro nobis effu- dit, & in calice Eucharistico nobis præbet ad fidei nostræ confirmationem. Et quomodo vox sanguinis carnem notat, per quam antea per Metonymiam effusionem sanguinis notari dixe- rat Schlichtingius. 5. Etsi Spiritus etiam per id testetur de JESU, quod ei datus & quod eum instruxerit divina sapientia, & divinissimis o- peribus, non tamen iis exhauritur testificatio Spiritus, utpote qui testatur etiam per insuf- flationem, & effusionem Apostolis datus, imo testatus est descendens visibili specie in Christum Luc. III. neque tantum testantur illa, quod Je- sus non sit impostor, sed quod sit Filius Dei Uni- genitus, & vita quæ ab æterno apud Patrem e- rat. Nisi enim is esset, sane Spiritum San ctum οὐκ ἐκ μέτρῳ seu immensa ejus dona JESUS Nazarenus accipere non potuisset. Nisi inquam λόγῳ copulata fuisset Humana natura, non par- ticeps ea fuisset immensæ plenitudinis Deitatis, quam in ipso corporaliter habitare docet Apo- stolus, Coloss. II. vers. 9. in merum enim homi- nem transire dona infinita & immensa non po- terant, ideoque opus erat, ut æternum Ver- bum incarnaretur & homo fieret, ut partici- pem redderet assumptam carnem donorum im- mensorum, quia communicatio præsupponit unionem, qua divina τοῦ λόγου natura carni sibi unitæ se cum omni sua plenitudine, & cum the- sauris omnibus divinæ cognitionis & sapientiæ communicavit Coloss. I. vers. 19. cap. II. vers. 3. 9. Quæ dona Spiritus Sancti dicuntur, quia Spiri- tus Sanctus, qui unum est cum Patre & Filio 1. Johan. V. vers. 7. & Spiritus Filii Dei Galat. IV. vers. 6. hoc templum personale corporis Chri- sti & elaboravit, Luc. I. vers. 35. & cert unguen- tum cœleste unxit, donisque suis instruxit, Psal. XLV. vers. 17. Ef. XL vers. 1. cap. LXI. v. 1. 6. Spiritus dicitur ἡ ἀλήθεια in omnibus Græcis Codicibus, quibus Syrus & Arabs præjudicare minime potest, quod veritas ipsa sit: ut DEUS charitas; Filius DEI sapientia ipsa esse dicitur, 1. Johan. IV. vers. 16. Proverb. VIII. vers. 23. non tantum verax, nedum quod sit ἀξιόπιστος, seu fidem mereatur, quum aliud formale significa- tum, verum quid esse, aliud fidem mereri, nec ideo ista hic commutanda forent, si maxime Johan. V. vers. 31. cap. VIII. vers. 13. ea vocis ἀλη- θὴς significatio obtineret, quod tamen ut ad- mittamus minime necessum est. Fidem mere- ri Spiritum Sanctum aliquid testificantem du- bium nullum erat, sed amplius quid innuere volebat S. Johannes, Spiritum Sanctum esse ipsammet veritatem, quæ testificata sit de JE- SU, quod sit ipsa vita, nobisque vita in ipso data sit.

## 5:7
Verse 7.

Ὅτι τρεῖς εἰσιν οἱ μαρτυροῦντες ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ ὁ πατὴρ, καὶ ὁ λόγος, καὶ τὸ ἅγιον πνεῦμα, καὶ οἱ τρεῖς εἰς τὸ ἕν εἰσι. Καὶ τρεῖς εἰσιν οἱ μαρτυροῦντες ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς τὸ πνεῦμα, καὶ τὸ ὕδωρ καὶ τὸ αἷμα] I shall not repeat here the many things that learned men have discussed concerning this passage. I will only say that that most ancient Manuscript, whose authority I use most, has nothing here other than ὅτι τρεῖς εἰσιν οἱ μαρτυροῦντες τὸ πνεῦμα καὶ τὸ ὕδωρ καὶ τὸ αἷμα, without the addition of that which both the Syriac and Arabic read: καὶ οἱ τρεῖς ἕν εἶσι. I think this reading, which I have set forth from the Manuscript, and which is confirmed by many other old books, is the true one. Nor were certain words indeed taken away by the Arians, but rather added, from which they might gather that the Father and the SON and the Holy Spirit are not one except by consent, just as the Spirit, water, and blood agree into one testimony. When the Catholics saw this, they indeed took away that which had been inserted concerning the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, but left that the three are one, because it being placed in that way could not harm them. Others, however, having left that passage concerning the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, indeed placed there, They are one; but concerning the Spirit, water, and blood, they are into one, so that another mode of unity might be signified. John here gives the reason why he spoke not only of the Spirit, whose authority is chief in this matter, but also of the water and blood, because in them also the credibility of the testimony is not small, and the ternary number is most perfect in witnesses. Μαρτυροῦντες is used in the Hebrew manner for μάρτυρες. Moreover, the word witness is accustomed to be said even of inanimate things, as in Genesis XXXI, verses 48, 51.

Grotius carps at the Canonical authority of this text with the Socinians, and for their sake, which the Arians once mutilated, who also, as Ambrose is witness in book III of On the Holy Spirit, chapter 11, deleted the words Πνεῦμα ὁ Θεὸς in the Gospel of St. John, chapter VI, verse 24, just as Socrates in book VII of the Ecclesiastical History, chapter 32, and in the Tripartite History, book VII, chapter 4, reports that the ancient Interpreters signified that certain people corrupted that first epistle of John, ῥαδιουργήσαντες τὴν ἐπισολὴν, so that they might separate the man from God in Christ. For Jerome teaches in Psalm CXXXIII that heretics (Arians) possessed all the walls of the churches, whence Athanasius complained in his epistle to those living the solitary life: What church now worships Christ freely? Since it, if it is pious, is subject to dangers. In that oppression of the orthodox Bishops, but in the elevation of the Arians to the Episcopal sees, what did heretical audacity not attempt? It is certainly much more probable that this clause was erased from the codices by the Arians than added by the Catholics, since no one has complained about the frauds of the latter, and they had other testimonies of the ὁμουσίας, and of the Deity of the same Son and Holy Spirit with the Father; but the ancients noted the frauds of the former, as has been shown, just as it is established that the ἀλόγυς or Alogians expunged the whole of John, and a verse could easily fall out by chance, but not be inserted. And Jerome testifies in the Prolegomena to the Canonical Epistles to Eustochium concerning unfaithful translators. These epistles, he says, if they were translated faithfully into the Latin language by the Interpreters just as they were arranged by them (the Greek Codices), they would neither create ambiguity for the readers, nor would the variety of expressions conflict with itself, ESPECIALLY in that place where we read that it is written concerning the unity of the Trinity in the first [epistle] of John, in which also by UNFAITHFUL translators (Latin Interpreters, infected by the Arian plague) we have discovered that there was much error, with those who put only three words, that is, water, blood, and Spirit, in their own edition, and omit the testimony of the Father, the Word, and the Spirit, in which the Catholic faith is especially strengthened, and the one essence of the divinity of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit is proven. In which words of Jerome, B. Gerhard warned that three things in particular should be observed, th. 9. 1. That in the time of Jerome that passage existed in the Greek codices of the Apostolic Epistles, for otherwise he could not accuse the Latin interpreters of infidelity because they omitted it. 2. That at that time it was in all Greek codices, otherwise those interpreters could have objected to Jerome that they did not find it in all codices. 3. That that passage, according to Jerome's opinion, especially strengthens the Catholic faith concerning the one essence of the divinity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. And if at that time the passage had been doubtful, suspected, and controversial, it could not have been attributed such strength and weight. These things are correct. But the Grotian [arguments] consist merely of precarious hypotheses and most empty conjectures. For whence, I ask, will it be taught that certain words were added by the Arians, and the same were in turn removed by the Catholics? While some were nevertheless left or even changed.

Regarding the claim that many old manuscripts agree with the Grotian [manuscript], it had to be taught, not merely asserted. Certainly, more codices have preserved that clause, even if it is missing in some, which were formed according to the Latin translation. For those are more recent than the times of Jerome, in whose age that text was still found in all Greek codices. To which codices of Jerome must be added the most ancient British one, which was of such authority to Erasmus that he did not hesitate to restore it from the same in later editions recognized with the most accurate care. Those codices must be added which the authors of the Complutensian edition of the year 1517 followed, for which it is noted in the preface that the most corrected, in every respect, and most ancient copies were used, as well as the Laurentian codices. Valla, who observed no discrepancy in these codices of his, as also the codices of Hervagius, who published the Greek Bible of the Old and New Testament at Basel in the year 1545, and used various readings from the collation of the best copies, but in this place found no diversity of reading: Likewise the codices of Rob. Stephanus, in seven of which this passage was indeed missing, yet it was found in the remaining nine, whose authority he followed as being better and more ancient: Finally, to pass over others, the Ariemontani codices, for which he also testifies that he used Vatican copies. Nor do the testimonies of the Fathers, who cite the same, confirm that this passage was missing in all Latin [codices]: Which Erasmus acknowledged to have existed in both Constantian copies: It was also cited by Cyprian before the Arians arose, who was crowned with martyrdom around the year of Christ 260, in his book on the simplicity of the prelate or on the unity of the Church, p. 164. The Lord says: I and the Father are one: And again it is written concerning the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, and the three are one. It was cited by Athanasius in the disputation held at the Nicene Synod with Arius or some Arian, and in book I to Theophilus on the united Deity of the Trinity, as also in book VII, and likewise by Idacius Clarus around the year of Christ 380, in book III against Varimundus, Tom. IV of the Library of the Fathers, and likewise in the same century by Phoebadius in book IV against the Arians, ch. 45, by Cyril of Alexandria, on the right faith in GOD to the Queens. In the fifth century by Victor Vitensis, Bishop in Africa, in book II on the persecution of the Vandals. and by Eugenius of Carthage, as he introduces him speaking thus in the confession of the Catholic faith: That we may teach even more clearly than light that the Holy Spirit is of one divinity with the Father and the Son is proven by the testimony of John the Evangelist, for he says, there are three who bear testimony in heaven, the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit, and these three are one. This passage was also cited in the sixth century by Fulgentius of Ruspe, Bishop, in his response to the objections of the Arians, in the Haereseologia of Basilius, year 1554, p. 47, and in the book on the Trinity, edited in Paris by Jac. Sirmond with other works of Fulgentius, and by John II, Roman Pope, in his epistle to Bishop Valerius, Tom. II of the Councils, Bin. p. 403. Nor did the writers of the following centuries doubt it, but held it for the Canonical text, Ambrosius Ansbertus in the year 760, in ch. I of the Apocalypse, Radulphus Ardens on the epistle for the second Sunday after Easter, year 1060. Rupert of Deutz on the works of the Holy Spirit, book III, on wisdom, ch. 2, year 1119. Bernard, year 1130, in two sermons on the three witnesses in heaven and on earth, in the octave of Easter, ch. 139. Hugo of St. Victor, book I on the soul, ch. 20. Alexander III, epistle to the Sultan of Iconium: Innocent III, sermon II on the Feast of Pentecost, concerning which see Coccius in the Thesaurus, Tom. I, book VI, p. 726. The Lateran Council also, at which Greek Archbishops and Patriarchs were also present, Canon II, shows that the Greeks read it thus. What? That in the Western Church on the Sunday of Quasimodogeniti these words have always been publicly read. To which also that of Barthol. Petrus can be added in judgment, to demonstrate that those books are faulty which omit verse 7, I say, because those few books or Ecclesiastical writers who omit it do not agree among themselves in the reading of the eighth verse, while some have 'on earth', others omit it perhaps as idle, after there is nothing to which it is appended for distinction, the preceding sentence having been removed, namely verse 7. The codex which B. Augustine used in the place cited above omitted it. Likewise the codex which S. Leo used, as is likewise clear from the place cited earlier. B. Cyril and Oecumenius omit it in the places alleged. In the text of the Venerable Bede it is not omitted.

Nor is there any doubt that it agrees perfectly with the Johannine phrase, who frequently calls the Son of God the Λόγον, John I. 1. & John I. 1. 2. & Rev. XIX. 13. he testified that this is his name ὁ λόγος τοῦ Θεοῦ, and likewise speaks of the Father & the Son, that they are one, chap. X. 30. and that it agrees most especially with the purpose of John and the present subject matter. For St. John also wished to establish the eternal Deity of Jesus against Cerinthus and Ebion, whence he established the Λόγον as of the same essence with the Father & the Holy Spirit, and introduces these three witnesses testifying about Jesus as heavenly, divine by nature, and superior to every exception; and finally that it squares perfectly with the context of the text. For just as St. John previously taught that Jesus, as he came in water and blood, confirmed this by these very things, and that the Holy Spirit by his testimony as the truth itself approved that which was to be brought against the Anti-Christs, which were testimonies in the very days of the flesh of Jesus concerning the same; so now he rises to the testimonies which perpetually flourish in the Church, and those immediately divine, which witnesses in heaven bear to the divine nature of Jesus Christ, the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit, as well as indirectly divine [witnesses], of witnesses on earth or Ecclesiastical, which are the Spirit, that is the Word of the Spirit, the sacrament of water and the sacrament of the supper designated by the blood of Christ, who is exhibited in the same. For just as John is accustomed to repeat what he has said, or to illustrate or confirm it more fully, so when he had said that Jesus came by water and blood, and that the Holy Spirit moreover testifies concerning that, he now led to proving those things, which the particle ὅτι indicates, because there are three who testify in heaven of a heavenly and divine nature, and thus supreme and unaccountable, and witnesses superior to every exception, the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit, and these three persons of the Divinity do not only testify immediately, but also instituted those means through which they perpetually bear witness concerning Jesus in the Church: the Word, Baptism, and the Eucharist.

Christ himself appeals to the Father's testimony, and, if he were testifying only concerning himself, that is, without the Father, he would not profess his testimony to be true, John 5:31, 32. Therefore he joins the Father to himself as a witness, since truth consists in the mouth of two witnesses. I am not alone, he says, chap. 8:16, but I and the Father who sent me: And it is written in your law: The testimony of two men is true (Deut. 17:6, chap. 19:15). I am he who bears witness concerning myself, and the Father who sent me bears witness concerning me. Concerning which testimony of Jesus, St. John the Baptist [says], John 3:31, he who comes from heaven is above all; and what he has seen and heard, this he testifies. This witness comes from heaven, but is also in heaven, verse 13, the Son of God, whose testimony St. John introduces. Jesus promises the Holy Spirit as a third witness who will likewise testify concerning him, John 15:26, and therefore he speaks in the plural concerning himself and the Holy Spirit, John 3:11, Amen, amen I say to you, because we speak what we know, and we testify what we have seen. Thus the Father testified concerning Jesus, proclaiming twice from heaven: This is my beloved Son in whom I am well pleased, Matt. 3:17 and Matt. 17:5, and concerning the glorification of his name, the voice of the Father heard from heaven, from John 12:28. The Word testified concerning himself and his office and the efficacy of his faith in various sermons, especially in John, such as chap. 3:16, that he is the Only-begotten Son, sent into the world, so that everyone who believes may have eternal life, chap. 4:26, that he is the Messiah, chap. 5:51, the Son of God, the living bread, who descended from heaven, etc., who is also called the faithful witness, Apoc. 1:5, chap. 6, chap. 8, chap. 10, chap. 12, etc. from chap. 5:36, chap. 8:12. He also testified by his works, John 5:36, chap. 10:38, and for that reason he sent out Apostles as witnesses, John 15:ult., and still sends Teachers, Eph. 4:11. Just as the Holy Spirit testified through the visible descent upon Christ, John 1:32, so he had to testify through the preaching of the Apostles and their successors, John 15:26, 27, therefore he was granted to the Apostles, John 20, Acts 2, so that he might testify concerning him, Acts 1:8, chap. 10:42. And he testified not only in the New Testament through the Apostles, but also in the Old Testament through the Prophets, as St. Peter teaches, v. 43, 2 Pet. 1:21. These are the witnesses in heaven: The Father testified from heaven, Matt. 10:27, chap. 17, John 12:18. The Son of God is in the bosom of the Father, John 1:18, and in heaven, chap. 3:13, he came from heaven, and is above all, John 3:31. The Holy Spirit descended from heaven, Matt. 3:16, he was sent from heaven, Acts 2. These witnesses

ARE ONE, of one divine essence. For the Father is the true God. Furthermore, I and the Father are one, says the Son, John 10:30. This is the true God and eternal life, says St. John concerning the Son, 1 Epist. 5:20. The Holy Spirit is God, Acts 5:2, 5. Therefore we are baptized in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, as the one true God, through whom we are regenerated, and to whose faith and worship we are bound by this sacrament, Matt. 28:19.

These are trifles which are retorted here by Schlichting: 1. That there is no coherence with the preceding, which the particle ὅτι requires. For we have already shown it, why should these not cohere? Jesus came by water and blood, and the Holy Spirit is he who testifies: because as there are three witnesses in heaven, who are that one God in essence: the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit: So the witnesses established on earth are subordinate to them, the Word of the Gospel, which is the Spirit according to John, and the water of baptism, through which we are regenerated, and the blood of Christ, through which we are given to drink. 2. The Father's testimony is included in the Spirit's testimony. For the Father bore witness to the Son through the Spirit. Resp. The Father and the Spirit are one in essence, yet they are distinguished in person as one witness and another. And although the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father, yet he is introduced as a distinct witness, because a person is distinguished from the Father, which is clearly seen in the theophany at the Jordan, Matt. 3:16, as the Fathers once said to the Arians; Go to the Jordan and you will see. 3. Since the Father is spoken of with respect to the Son, it would already be taken for granted that Jesus is the Son of God. Resp. It is not to be proved that the Father has a Son, but that Jesus of Nazareth is that Son of God. 4. If heavenly persons are to be named, [he argues] that angels also have testified more than once concerning Jesus. Resp. He wished to bring forward perpetual witnesses in the Church, and those who are in heaven of a heavenly and divine nature, because the Son is of one and the same essence with the Father and the Holy Spirit, and thus one true God, and yet there are three persons who testify in heaven, that is, in heavenly glory, just as our Father is in heaven, whose is the kingdom and the power and the glory forever, Matt. 6:7, 13. Moreover, they testify in heaven, because they are in heaven, and they testify not only to men on earth, but especially to the heavenly beings in heaven. The Trinity, says Salmero, gives testimony in heaven, either by effecting a vision in the blessed concerning the fact that Christ is God and man, or by infusing into men, who are still wayfarers, faith, which is a gift of God. The water, however, and the blood bear witness on earth, because they are of an earthly condition and bound to the earth, they do not pertain to the blessed in heaven, just as Christ distinguishes τὰ ἐπίγεια & ἐπουράνια, John 3:12. Bartholomæus Petri explains that to testify in heaven is by divine authority, and therefore the highest of all: On earth by authority, which is below the divine, comparing Matthew 21:25. To B. Gerhard that exposition seems most simple, that the three witnesses are said to be in heaven because they are heavenly and divine witnesses, whence afterwards in verse 9 their testimony is called the testimony of God. Which also pleased B. Dorschæus in particular l. c. §. 23. The exposition is most simple. The triad of witnesses is said to be in the heavens, because it is not only on earth, but also in heaven, not only in the kingdom of grace, but also in the kingdom of power and glory, because the heaven of heavens does not contain it, because they testify by absolute and divine Majesty, in a word, because those witnesses are divine. What? That Schlichting himself seems to himself to explain them without inconsistency: If these words, he says, of the seventh verse must be received into the context of the Apostles, Father God that one and Most High, who dwells in the heavens, testified concerning Jesus, when he uttered that heavenly voice, both when Christ was baptized at the Jordan and when Christ was transfigured on that holy mountain: This is that my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. The Λόγος who himself is Christ, and now resides in the heavens, testified concerning himself, when Stephen the Protomartyr was pleading his case before the Sanhedrin, at which time he saw the heavens opened and Jesus standing at the right hand of God, for this was undoubtedly the work of Jesus himself. He testified likewise concerning himself in the conversion of Saul and at other times undoubtedly more often. The Holy Spirit, who likewise is in heaven as the source of that Spirit which flows down to men on earth, testifies that Jesus is that Son of God, testifies, I say, through a certain efflux of his, by descending upon Jesus, and upon his disciples in a visible form, and by working admirable effects in them and through them. We can also understand this testimony of those three of the Father and the Λόγος, and the Holy Spirit, (whose source is in God and thus in the heavens) which they performed among men in testimony concerning Jesus, and the truth of his preaching. For all things in which some divinity appeared concerning the preaching of the Gospel are to be attributed to the Father and to the Λόγος and to the Holy Spirit. In which sense in the following verse the word Spirit, for the sake of avoiding tautology, would have to be taken concerning only the gifts and admirable effects of the Holy Spirit. Thus Schlichting. Why therefore does the same man make a tragedy about the inconvenience of this clause? But on the contrary, it would have been altogether inconvenient if, when this matter is being treated by design concerning the witnesses of Jesus, those three witnesses in heaven, who are the highest and principal ones, were omitted altogether, whose testimonies St. John otherwise noted so diligently in the Evangelical history, and to whom Jesus himself appealed. Nor would that particle concerning the witnesses IN EARTH be appropriate, if it did not correspond to those witnesses IN HEAVEN. Since the Socinians understand this, they labor so that those words IN EARTH might also be eliminated, especially Socinus himself in his Commentary on this place. But those existed in the Greek Codices, in the time of Jerome, and before him, nor was there any doubt about them, as is evident from the Prologue to the Canonical Epistles in the British Codex produced by Erasmus in his Annotations, and in the Codices which Cardinal Ximenes had gathered from various and principal European Libraries, in the Codices used by Arias Montanus collected from Spain, Italy and Belgium, in most of the Codices of Robert Stephanus, as also of Laurentius Valla, and of Froben and Hervagius in the Basel edition, and also of Froschover in the Zurich edition, of Beza likewise etc. They are read among the Ancients praised before. Which finally the blessed Dorscheus in his dissertation on the Spirit, Water and Blood §. 8. teaches to require the scope and the very words of John, where he treated at length concerning these three witnesses on earth.

But they are those ἐν τῇ γῇ not only by reason of ὑπάρξεως on account of the institution and gracious oikovoμiαν of the Holy Spirit, since they are witnesses ἐν ὀυρανῷ not on account of the dispensation of a superior principle, but out of supreme perfection and majesty: But also by reason of μαρτυρίας, which they carry out in the Church throughout the whole world, where the victory of the world, and victorious faith reigns, and men are regenerated from God, as also by reason of τρόπυ ὑπάρξεως, because they exist in a certain earthly habit and mode of being: which is evident from the designation of those witnesses.

But who are they? The Spirit, water, and blood: Where by the Spirit some indeed with Augustine, and the ordinary gloss, which most Pontificals follow, understand the soul of Christ: but that Christ has a soul, and that he sent it forth in death, is indeed a testimony of true humanity, but not of divinity, or of the office of Christ, nor does it contribute to the special certainty of our faith and salvation: others wish the Holy Spirit to be designated, who would also be numbered among the witnesses on earth, because he not only testifies immediately, as that one God with the Father and the Word, as a heavenly witness of the divine nature, but also testifies concerning Jesus in the Church through the Word and its preaching, which is proper to the new Testament, insofar as he testifies that what the sacred scriptures handed down concerning the Messiah agrees with this individual Jesus of Nazareth. Concerning which the blessed Gerhard §. 17. from the blessed Hunnius: He is joined to the witnesses in heaven, because he is no less than the Father and the Son a person of the Trinity, by whose eternal counsel and decree the Son willed to be born the Messiah in the world, and because in the baptism of Christ he manifested himself in the bodily form of a dove no less than the Father by an external voice, and descending upon Christ bore immediate testimony concerning him. He is joined to the witnesses on earth, because he is that person who, according to the promise of the Savior, was sent to institute the ministry on earth, for which he instructed and illuminated the Apostles by his gifts, having fallen upon them visibly, and afterwards testified concerning Christ through their preaching, and even now testifies concerning him through the ministry of the Word and Sacraments, and seals that in the hearts of believers, as Dr. Hunnius warns in his commentary on this place. In which opinion he also praises Calvin: We therefore highly approve here those things which the brilliance of truth expressed for Calvin here: Since, he says, the Spirit testifies variously concerning Christ, a double place of testifying is aptly attributed to him. For from the heavens the Father with his eternal Wisdom and Spirit pronounces as if by authority, that Jesus is the Christ. Therefore there only the Majesty of the divinity is to be considered by us. But since the Spirit dwelling in our hearts is an earnest, pledge and seal, for the sealing of that decree, in this way he speaks again on earth through his grace. It is better, however, to understand by the Spirit in this place the Word of the Spirit or the Gospel by Metonymy, which 1. Spirit is spoken of in a phrase accepted by Christ, John VI. 63. the words that I speak, are Spirit and life: nor is it unusual for St. John, Apoc. XIX. 10. which passage Alcazar explains, that the testimony of Jesus is the preaching of the Gospel, and is called the Spirit of prophecy, so that it may be denoted that the Spirit and zeal of preaching the Gospel is a certain most noble Spirit of Prophecy: because the Evangelical doctrine is that great Prophecy, which reveals to men the secret counsels of God and the outcome of good and evil things etc. Therefore, he who is marked by the Spirit of the Evangelical preacher, in him is the Spirit of prophecy. 2. The Gospel is called a testimony, Is. VIII, v. 20. and the Word of God comprised in the sacred scriptures testifies of Christ, John V. 39. concerning which testimony of the Gospel see 1. Cor. I. 6. chap. II. 1. 2. Tim. I. 8. and this 1. John V. 9. 10. 11. Apoc. I. 2. 9. chap. VI. 9. chap. XII. 11. 17. chap. XIX. 10. 3. The Gospel is a perennial and perpetual witness in the Church concerning Jesus, that outside of him there is no salvation, Acts IV. 12. testifying of him throughout the whole world, Rom. X. 8. 17. 18. Coloss. I. 23. 4. It testifies in a distinct manner from water and blood.

By water, however, and blood, as before, we judge that Baptism and the Eucharist are synecdochically designated; because 1. by the name of water baptism is signified, Ezek. XXXVI. v. 25. Heb. X. verse 23. since it was administered in water Matt. III. v. 11. Mark I. v. 9. Luke III. v. 16. John I. v. 26. Acts I. v. 5. chap. VIII. v. 36. chap. X. v. 47. chap. XI. v. 15. And by the name of blood the holy supper is most excellently designated, in which the blessed cup is the communion of the blood of Christ, 1 Corinthians X. v. 16. which the ancients called the sacrament of the cup. See Augustine Vol. III. book 4 on Christian doctrine chap. 21. Paschasius, Abbot of Corbie, on the body and blood of the Lord, who calls the birthday of the cup the day of the Lord's supper. 2. Just as with the Gospel, baptism and the holy supper testify in the most eminent and effective way in the Church concerning Jesus, who therefore as witnesses ought not to be passed over. They are therefore called visible seals of divine things by Augustine on the Catechizing of the Uninstructed, chap. 26. For in baptism there is an infallible assertion of the gracious divine presence of the whole Most Holy Trinity, receiving us in its own name into a most holy covenant in the blood of the Son, and thus testifying to the efficacy of the reconciliation obtained through Christ, Matthew XXVIII. v. 16. whence, when the Apostle had discoursed in Titus III. v. 5, 6 concerning the manifold grace poured out upon us by the Holy Spirit through the washing of regeneration on account of Jesus Christ, it is added in verse 8, πιστὸς ὁ λόγος (the saying is faithful). Add 1 Peter III. v. 21. Damascenus, book IV on the Orthodox Faith, chap. 5, calls baptism σφραγίδα καὶ φυλακτήριον & Φωτισμόν (a seal and a safeguard and illumination). Add Dionysius on the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy, chap. 2. In the sacrament of the supper likewise there is an infallible assertion concerning Jesus Christ, communicating his body and his blood to us in a most singular and most secret way for the remission of sins: as the blessed Dorscheus in the cited place, §. 15. 3. Because these witnesses are proper to the New Testament, in which testimony must be borne concerning Jesus, these sacraments are of the New Testament, most holy and most divine organs, by which the Church of the New Testament is most secure concerning the operation of divine grace. 4. Baptism and the holy supper testify concerning JESUS, in whose name we are baptized, and with whose blood we are given to drink: they testify against the Anti-Christs, that that true and saving life for the world appeared in the world ἔνσαρκος (in the flesh), 1 John I. v. 2. chap. II. v. 18. 5. They testify through all the ages until the end of the world, since the Church ought never to be ἀμάρτυρος (without witness), and it is necessary that the salvation which is in Jesus should perpetually be most certain. 6. Jesus comes to us through the Gospel, baptism, and the Eucharist in a most noble and most eminent way. The most eminent, says the blessed Dorscheus again, th. 18, in his approach to us, Jesus placed a footprint from heaven, communicating his wisdom to us; a second covenant from heaven followed, reconciling us with the Most Holy Trinity in baptism. A third supervened, feeding and giving us to drink from his own substance. 7. The Gospel, Baptism, and the holy Supper testify in a triple and distinct manner, and are therefore deservedly called three witnesses, since the Gospel testifies by voice and letters, baptism presents water to the eyes of men, the holy supper bread and wine: the Gospel promises generally, and exhibits Jesus Christ the God-man, and his benefits, and in them righteousness and salvation to be received by faith: Baptism exhibits a certain peculiar degree of gracious presence, by which the Most Holy Trinity, in view of the merit of Christ, is present in a peculiar way through the medium of water to wash us from sins, and to receive us into the covenant of grace; the holy supper offers to us the blood of Christ peculiarly as the blood of the New Testament, and presents it there under wine in a singular and proper manner. 8. Through water in baptism, the washing of water, and through the blood of Christ in the holy supper, we are not only rendered most certain concerning the person and benefits of Christ the God-man: but God effectively works faith in us, regenerates, and corroborates us unto salvation through these means entrusted to the Church. They are not bare or merely significant testimonies, but practical, operative, and communicative and energetic; in one Spirit we are all baptized into one body (by water) and we are all given to drink into one Spirit in the Eucharist, namely by the blood of Christ, 1 Corinthians XII. v. 13. The very dispensers of this triple testimony on earth are through it effective for regeneration, illumination, conversion, confirmation, and the sealing of faith, Acts XXVI. v. 18. Romans XI. v. 14. 1 Corinthians III. v. 5. 9. chap. IV. v. 15. 2 Corinthians IV. v. 8. Galatians IV. v. 19. Ephesians III. v. 8, and therefore this triple testimony itself will have a much greater divine and excellent efficacy for moving and changing the minds of men. 9. Not a few of the Ancients explain it thus. Tertullian expressly mentions the washing of water and the drinking of blood. St. Cyprian calls them heavenly sacraments, On the Unity of the Church. Ambrose, book III on the Holy Spirit, chap. 11. Hear, he says, how the witness of the Holy Spirit renews the mind; water avails for washing, blood looks to the price. For the Spirit has made us sons of God through adoption, the wave of the sacred font has washed us, the blood of the Lord has redeemed us. Gregory of Nyssa, Oration against the Jews. We believe that we are consecrated and partake of divinity both through divine baptism and through the participation and use of the holy blood. Paulinus of Nola in his epistle to Florentius noted here the water of grace and the blood of the sacrament. Cyril on the True Faith to the Queen. He sanctifies us, he says, by the Spirit, and purifies by blood, and washes again with clean water. Leo the Great, epistle X. The Spirit, he says, of sanctification, and the blood of redemption, and the water of baptism: which three are one and remain inseparable. Bede explains concerning the sacraments of Christ, by which we are always refreshed and nourished unto salvation. Damascenus concerning the water of regeneration and the washing of sin (in baptism) and concerning the drink of the blood (of Christ) (in the holy supper) as the cause of eternal life. More authors have been brought forward to verse 6, who easily agree, even among the Papists and the Reformed.

He speaks, however, of these three witnesses on earth, not as of those in heaven, καὶ ὗτοι οἱ τρεῖς ἕν εἰσι, but κὴ οἱ τρεῖς εἰς τὸ ἕν εἰσι. Franciscus Lucas on this particle in his notes. It is read, he says, as in other Latin books, so also in the remaining Greek copies that we have seen, and furthermore in the Syriac Testaments, and finally by the Fathers, but differently. For Latin codices, with Augustine, Cyril, Leo, and Bede, have 'and these three are one.' But the Greek ones, with Oecumenius and the Syriac ones: 'And these three are to or into one.' Socinus appeals to the Latins: But the Greek text is to be preferred, and one should not depart from it, especially because the codices agree, nor does the Syriac dissent. And how easily the preposition 'to' or 'into' could have been omitted through the carelessness of scribes.
