For we have been taught to listen to a disobedient and gainsaying word, that, saving, save your own soul.' Where Balsamon says: 'Lest you also destroy yourself by communicating with the uncorrected.' Zonaras has similar things. And in the Second Nicene Synod, 'sin unto death' is explained as 'remaining uncorrected.' That 'unto death' is to be understood here by comparison, just as we call a disease or poison 'deadly,' from which there is no hope of recovery, although other diseases and poisons can bring death to a man, and often do.

It is not about the customs and practice of the ancients, whom they received back into communion after a fall, but it must be examined here who are received into grace by God or excluded. For there is no hope of grace left for those for whom it is not permitted to pray, who commit that sin unto death which is being discussed in this place, and thus do not escape death or condemnation. For those for whom God does not admit prayers, as far as their eternal salvation is concerned, no hope of grace and salvation remains for them. Nor does the Shepherd of Hermas deserve to be heard, an author of no faith, and not even approved by the Papists themselves, but rejected by the Spanish Index, p. 149, and the Roman, whose censure see prefixed to the book, XV of the Bibliotheca Patrum, and reprobated by Bellarmine among others for his error concerning repentance, De scriptoribus ecclesiasticis, p. 51. This book was never in the canon of holy and divine books; indeed, it has some harmful things, such as the doctrine of a single repentance according to the errors of the Novatians, which this book seems to favor. The same Cardinal also warned about Tertullian's book on repentance, in the cited book, that erroneous or at least suspicious propositions are found in it, and in book I of De Christo, chapter 9, he says: 'Tertullian has little authority in dogmas, since he is a manifest heretic.' Cornelius a Lapide says that Tertullian's error, which he explains regarding adultery committed after baptism, was condemned in Scripture by the Lateran Council under Innocent III. Regarding Clement of Alexandria, the same censor says that there are not lacking some opinions that smack of error; he says Cyprian is not to be excused from certain errors.

Salmero, Disputation LI on the Epistle to the Romans, Vol. III, p. 474. But Grotius himself also acknowledges that this passage should not be referred to the customs of the Church, and therefore he does not approve the opinion of Ambrose, which Suarez, Vol. IV, p. 87, from book II of De poenitentia, chapters 8 and 9, makes this: that every sin is called 'unto death' in a special way because it is atrocious and enormous, perhaps for the reason that a sin of this kind has a special moral danger of perpetual death, and he compares it with the explanation of Erasmus, that such people were once to be cast out from the fellowship of the Church, and delivered to Satan, and not to be received unless the guilt was wiped away by fasts, tears, and many harsh remedies. Whence Ambrose, book I of De poenitentia, chapter 2, said: 'He who has exaggerated the guilt, also exaggerates the repentance. For greater crimes are washed away by greater weepings.' Which opinion B. Feuerbornius does not entirely disapprove of in his dissertation on the sin against the Holy Spirit, chapter III, p. 24. If indeed one interprets it concerning any most atrocious and most manifest crime, on account of which a sinner is to be excluded for a time from the communion of prayers and sacraments, until he performs penance and is received back, reconciled by the Church: to which view also Brentius, Heerbrandus, and Cardinal Molina subscribe in B. Gerhard, disp. Isag. book XII, ch. V, § 14. However, Cornelius in Turrianus, book IV, for the epistle of the Pontiff, ch. 3, disapproves of that opinion; namely, that it is understood as a sin to which excommunication is annexed, when the excommunicated person is impenitent, and it is not permitted to pray for an excommunicated person by the public prayer of the Church. The reason why he thinks that explanation should not be admitted, he brings forward this: that St. John denies that one should pray for such a person with any prayer, even private. Which reason without doubt also moved Grotius to withdraw his support. And it seems sufficiently firm. For here there is no word concerning the excommunication of the Church, or concerning exclusion from the communion of the Church's prayers, but rather the discourse is about private matters; if anyone, says St. John, sees his brother sinning, likewise, I do not say that he should pray for that, which concerns every private individual. What? That the excommunicated were not excluded from the communion of the Church's prayers. For although those excluded from communion could not pray with others in the Church, yet the Church could, and indeed every person in the Church ought to pray for the same, ἵna τὸ πνεῦμα σωθῇ ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ τῦ Κυρίε, 1 Cor. V, 5.

But does either Cornelius or Grotius bring forward a better interpretation? The latter indeed understands those to be said to sin unto death who, when they have sinned, continue to sin after being warned, or certainly do not wish to submit themselves to the discipline which has been established in the Church. The former wishes in almost the same way for any most grave sin to be indicated, which on account of its enormity or habit, obstinacy and malice, according to the common law through the grace which God is accustomed to give ordinarily, is as it were immediately incorrigible and incurable; but are we not to pray for such, that they may be freed from the snares of the Devil and awake? As to such, 2 Tim. II. 25, 26, repentance and grace are not denied, so neither is prayer to be denied, by the argument of the passage 1 Tim. II. 1, sqq., where we are commanded to pray for all whom God wills to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth. Nor indeed does Cornelius admit that it is absolutely a sin unto death, because he says only AS IF incurable, and that it leads the sinner himself ALMOST certainly and infallibly [to death], unless some distinguished saint and as it were a new Moses obtains extraordinary grace and pardon for him from God. But St. John does not speak of him who is almost, but who is entirely led to death, and of a sin, not which is AS IF, but which is absolutely incurable, if indeed it is unto death and it is in vain to pray for it.

And how will some distinguished saint pray for grace for him, for whom the Apostle strictly forbids praying? Cornelius understands primarily the sin by which a believer has departed from the faith of Christ and the Church, maliciously attacks it, and strives to lead and pervert others from it to his own heresy or idolatry; but he also says of it that it leads AS IF certainly to the death of Gehenna, since the Apostle speaks of that sin which truly CERTAINLY leads to death. The three characteristics of this sin, of which he speaks, teach this: First, that it is absolutely a sin πρὸς θάνατον (unto death). It would not, however, be absolutely ἁμαρτία πρὸς θάνατον (a sin unto death), unless it led certainly to death. Next, that it is distinguished from all other sins and from any injustice whatsoever, which he says are not sins unto death, this one excepted. By the force, therefore, of this opposition, this simply brings death, whereas all the rest, whether of infirmity or of malice, whether venial or mortal, as they call them, are so constituted that, although they bring in themselves the guilt of death and deserve death, which is the wages of every sin (Rom. 6:23), yet repentance can be exercised for them, so that they do not precisely and infallibly lead to death. This, therefore, must be such a sin that it precisely, certainly, and infallibly leads to death. Thirdly, the discourse is about that sin and sinner for whom the Apostle warns that one should simply not pray. How, therefore, would grace extraordinarily reach him for whom God admits no prayers?

But as for the fact that Bartholomæus Petri quibbles that prayers are not simply forbidden here by John, but only that one does not dare to urge any Christian, namely, to pray for such a one with that confidence of obtaining, of which he speaks in v. 14. For St. John says simply: Οὐ περὶ ἐκείνης λέγω, ἵνα ἐρωτήσῃ (I do not say that he should ask for that); as by the prior imperative αἰτήσῃ (he should ask) he was simply urging every Christian, as far as every sin μὴ πρὸς θάνατον (not unto death) is concerned, so he now simply warns that one should not pray for a sin πρὸς θάνατον (unto death), nor does he make a distinction between a great intercessor with a great prayer and any other Christian, which is foisted upon the text by Schlichting, not brought out from the text. Add that Cornelius acknowledges Heb. 6:4 and ch. 10:24 as parallel passages to this one of ours. But there the Apostle does not say that the renewal of such sins is difficult, but that it is ἀδύνατον (impossible) for them to be renewed to repentance, and he testifies that no sacrifice is left for them. Cornelius says that this sin is related and akin to blasphemy against the Holy Spirit (Matt. 12:31), and just as that is forgiven with difficulty, so is this. But Christ teaches that that is clearly not forgiven, neither in this age nor in the age to come. And therefore, neither will the sin which is unto death ever be forgiven. Why, therefore, does Cornelius or Grotius not understand this as the sin or blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, when the characteristics and the comparison of the passages teach that nothing else is to be understood, and the kinship and parallelism of the passages are admitted?

Regarding the sin unto death, Bartholomæus Petri understands the opinion of Bede in this place, that it is that by which, after the knowledge of God which has been given to someone through grace, he himself attacks the brotherhood, and is agitated by the torches of envy against the very grace by which he was reconciled to God, and he says it is taken from Augustine, Book 1, On the Lord's Sermon on the Mount, ch. 22.

In our judgment, however, nothing is truer than that St. John is dealing with the sin against the Holy Spirit, in which we have B. Hunnius as a fellow-voter: John distinguishes between sins, some of which he says are not unto death, and some unto death. For although otherwise outside of Christ all sins are mortal, and especially the reigning sins which are enumerated in Gal. 5, yet in this place the sin unto death and sins not unto death are opposed in a certain other respect, so that the sin not unto death comprehends every sin, except the sin against the Holy Spirit. Since from all other sins a man can repent. But the sin against the Holy Spirit has a most certain hardening and final impenitence attached to it. For this, says John, one should not pray, since such people never return, but are clearly lost and incurable. We also have Flacius agreeing in this place, to whom are added Lucas Osiander and B. Gerhard in his Disputationes Isagogicae. B. Meisner, Anthropologia, decade 1, disputation 10, question 1, thesis 17, and most others of our side, as also from the Reformed, Bullinger, etc.

It is hardly worth the effort to refute the opinions of others, since they can already be disposed of by this list, inasmuch as Jerome on ch. 14 of Jeremiah, Bernard in On the Degrees of Humility, the last chapter, Bonaventure in 2, distinction, thesis, doubt 1, and Thomas in the same place, and Suarez, part 3, Tome 4, disputation 8, section 1, understand a graver sin which God has decreed to punish, as Cornelius brings forward. For who can see or know this, whether someone is committing a sin which God has decreed to punish, since that decree is not expressed in the Holy Scriptures by reason of this or that sinner. Likewise, that Hilary in Psalm 140 judges the sin unto death to be that which is committed deliberately and out of malice, and Ambrose, whom Cornelius brings forward from his book On Repentance, ch. 8 and 9, I understand as any sin which is forgiven with difficulty, and the ordinary gloss judging that any mortal sin is designated. But it has already appeared that the characteristics of the sin πρὸς θάνατον (unto death) do not fit them. John commands us to pray for a mortal sin, so that life may be given to the sinner who is deprived of it on account of a mortal sin, and he teaches that it is not unto death, that it does not certainly and infallibly lead to death, but that forgiveness can be obtained through repentance. Augustine in Retractations, book 1, chapter 19, correcting himself, commands to add: if he should end this life in such a wicked perversity of mind; therefore he explains in chapter 22 of On Corruption and Grace the sin unto death, that it is any mortal sin whatsoever for which repentance is not performed, which is also the opinion of Gregory the Great, book VI of Morals, chapter 31, as also of Gelasius, cited by Cornelius, in the book On Anathema, of Pacian, epistle III, of Bede and Lyra here, of Lombard in 2 Sentences, distinction 43, of Thomas, 3rd part, question 86, article 1, to the 2nd point, of Valentia, Suarez, etc. But which he himself rejects, as does Bartholomaeus Petri, because it cannot be known in which sin anyone will persevere unto death. And although Suarez explains it concerning him who has died in impenitence, and for that reason brings forward those authors already named, for whom one must not pray because he is outside the state of salvation; yet that is irrelevant, because the discourse here is about him whom one sees sinning, and thus about him who is still in this life; nor does it satisfy the doubt, because even concerning those who have ceased to be among the living, it is not certain whether they died in impenitence or not; nor are prayers any longer useful to the dead, and it is so far from the case that Scripture teaches that one must pray for such of the deceased, that nowhere in the Scriptures has anything been handed down that one must pray for the dead. For the fact that Roffensis, article XVII against Luther, proves purgatory from this passage does not deserve a refutation. But the fact that Schlichting says in this passage that it is agreeable to charity to pray for those who have finished their life, because the Judge of the living and the dead has not yet passed a definitive sentence on everyone, or at least has not yet executed it; this is unwritten and contrary to the written word, and contrary to the passages Hebrews 9:27, Ecclesiastes 11:3, John 3:18, 36. The explanation of Bartholomaeus Petri that the sin unto death is any mortal sin of which repentance is not done, as long as and insofar as it is such, is likewise unworthy of assent. For is one not to pray for a sinner persisting in mortal sin, as long as he persists in it, that he may be converted and repent? The passage Jer. ch. XIV, 11 does not apply here: for there it is forbidden to pray for temporal grace to be shown to the Jewish people, namely, for liberation from the Babylonian πανωλεθρίᾳ (total destruction), not for the grace of conversion and eternal salvation, which God has testified by oath that He seriously wills regarding all sinners, Ezech. XVIII and XXXIII. Finally, Schlichting's comment, that the sin unto death is not only blasphemy against the Spirit, but any act whatsoever that is very enormous from a certain vicious and deeply rooted root, the betrayal of a brother, heresy, and other habits of grave sins, as also acts that are too grave and foul, such as parricide, fratricide, and similar ones, etc. which easily renders men desperate and precipitates them into the eternal abyss, may be seen discussed in Exeg. A. Con. art. XII. c. 2.

That which is objected against our explanation concerning the sin against the Holy Spirit, that the sin unto death, of which John speaks, can ALWAYS be known or seen by us, [while] blasphemy against the Holy Spirit cannot always be seen; inasmuch as it is accomplished in the mind, moves us not at all: because neither does St. John speak of the sin unto death in this way, if anyone sees a brother sinning a sin unto death: as [he speaks] of a brother sinning a sin μὴ πρὸς θάνατον, not unto death: Nor does St. John indicate that the sin unto death is always seen, since even the sin μὴ πρὸς θάνατον is not always seen: certainly when it is perpetrated with the mind, it is not seen: But the words are hypothetical, ἐάν τις ἴδῃ (if anyone sees). Furthermore, since the sin against the Holy Spirit involves oral blasphemy, there is no doubt that those who sin in this way can sometimes be recognized. Finally, this manner of speaking of John, ὀυ περὶ ἐκείνης λέγω, ἵνα ἐρωτήσῃ (I do not say that he should ask concerning that), explains only the antecedents, namely, that St. John was not speaking of the sin unto death when he commanded to pray. A bare distinction of sin is therefore handed down, of sin not unto death, and of sin unto death, but it is not taught that the sin unto death can be known by us with certainty, much less that it can ALWAYS be known by others. But it is only said that such a sin is of such a kind that no pardon should be expected by him who commits it.

Αἰτήσει καὶ δώσει ἀυτῷ ζωὴν, τοῖς μὴ ἁμαρτάνουσι πρὸς θάνατον (He shall ask and he will give him life, to those not sinning unto death) In the Manuscript, μὴ ἁμαρτάνουσι ἁμαρτίαν (not sinning a sin). Αἰτήσει here is a future tense used for an Imperative, which the opposite words in this very clause show. That: he will give him life, the Syrian explains as, life will be given to him, so that the Active with its Accusative is taken for a Passive, without the acting person being designated. But you will more correctly understand, God, from the preceding, and because that very αἰτήσει (he will ask) is equivalent to αἰτήσει Θεὸν (he will ask God); God, at the prayers of the faithful, will preserve the faith for that man who does not shun the healing hand of the Church, will give a humbled and contrite heart, and in His own time will render the Holy Spirit, all of which are ways to eternal life, and are not in the hand of man, just as submitting oneself to the Church is. There is, however, here a construction of agreement of the singular with the plural by σύνθεσιν (synthesis), as they say, because that singular does not designate one certain person, but anyone who is a Christian by profession.

Some refer that δώσει (he will give) to the intercessor, or to him who prays for a brother. Thus B. Fœvurbornius on the sin against the Holy Spirit, p. 11. A pious man interceding will give him life by way of asking and obtaining life from GOD through prayers: Just as parents are said to prolong the life of their children, as it is in the Hebrew text, Exod. XX. 12, and pious poor men are said to receive their benefactors into eternal tabernacles, Luke XVI. 9 (and therefore in 1 John V. v. 16 there is no hyperbolic expression, as Marloratus imagines there), that is, into the heavenly dwelling.

Ἔστι ἁμαρτία πρὸς θάνατον, ὀυ περὶ ἐκείνης λέγω, ὅτι ἐρωτήσῃ (There is a sin unto death, I do not say that he should ask concerning that) I do not command that prayers be poured out, so that such great contumacy may be blotted out, because there is no promise upon which such prayers might rely. Here you have the mystical sense of the passage Jer. VII. 16 and Ezech. XIV. 14.

Concerning the sense of the Johannine expression, it has already been spoken of before. Nor can the mystical sense of Jer. VII. 16 and Ezech. XIV. 14 be admitted here. For there it is a matter of the temporal salvation of the people, here of the eternal salvation of a neighbor. Those things are therefore disparate.

Latin:

Vers. 16.

Ἐάν τις ἴδῃ ἀδελφὸν αὑτοῦ ἁμαρτάνοντα) Multum est quod Deus nos non pro nobis tantum, sed & pro aliis, qui Christo nomen dedere, exaudit. Ita enim vox ἀδελ- φὸς hoc loco sumenda ex subjecta materia, eoque magis quia hic additum est αὑτοῦ, ut in re simili Matth. XVIII. 15.

Quod tamen, monente B. Hunnio, non sic ac- cipiendum, quasi vitam impetret aliena precatio alicui, quicquid tandem ille agat, sed si conversio- nis media non violenter a se repellat. Cur vero id non extendendum ad proximum quemcunque? Annon etiam pro conversione & salute infide- lium orat Ecclesia? Et cur oraret si id non fieri secundum voluntatem DEI, aut non exaudiri constaret? Imo pro omnium hominum salute orandum esse docet gentium Doctor 1. Tim. I. vers. 1. seqq. eo quod Deus omnium hominum salutem velit, quodque Christus sese ἀντίλυτρον dederit pro omnibus, idque καλὸν καὶ ἀπόδεκτον di- cit ἐνώπιον τοῦ Σωτῆρος ἡμῶν Θεοῦ. Et orandum hic juxta Evangelistam, pro eo, qui vitam non habet, hoc est, qui non renatus est, adeoque nec frater eo sensu, quo renati & fideles fratres no- stri sunt: nam jubemur tali exorare vitam, & promissio sit, καὶ δώσει αὐτῷ ζωὴν, expers ergo vitae fuit.

Ἁμαρτίαν μὴ πρὸς θάνατον)

Jam pridem multum agitata est haec quaestio, quae sit ἁμαρτία πρὸς θάνατον; Veterum multi intellexere pecca- tum ad mortem esse peccatum ejus, qui baptizatus esset, non tamen omne, quod cum aliqua deliberatione aut spatio ad deliberandum dato fieret, sed aliquod ex illis gravissimis, puta idololatriam, homicidium, adulterium. Talia enim qui admisisset post baptismum plerisque in locis, nunquam recipiebatur ad communionem, ut nec in aliis criminibus, si quis iterum lapsus esset. Non exclu- debantur quidem tales destricte a misericordia Dei, sed ob incertum eventus Ecclesia sponsor esse nolebat. Tertul- liani tempore Episcopus Romanus ad poenitentiam rece- pit semel in adulterium delapsos, eamque sententiam, quanquam multum exagitatam a Tertulliano, non plane novam fuisse Romae ostendit Pastor Hermae. Cypriani tempore de lapsis in idololatriam vel adulterium varia fuit observatio, etiam in Africa. Ideo de lapsis in idololatriam nihil ille constituere voluit, nisi de consensu aliorum ex- tra Africam Episcoporum, & maxime Episcopi Romani. Ac diu expensa, placuit etiam sic lapsos sed post longum tempus recipi. Neque enim credebant hominem subito purgari, sed quo crimen esset gravius, eo tardius & diffi- cilius. Idque probatum in Synodo Nicena magna, quae diu regula fuit Ecclesiastici regiminis; & in idololatriam deli- berato lapsis praescriptum tempus poenitentiae annorum undecim, aliis aliquanto minus pro criminum gravitate. Quod de idololatria, homicidio & adulterio dixi, verum esse apparet ex Tertulliani de pudicitia libro praesertim cap. XIX. & ex Socrate historiae l. 10. ubi hoc ἀσυγγνώ- κατον vocat, quem mordicus tutati sunt Novatiani. Quod vero dixi de aliis criminibus, si repetita essent post bapti- smum, non datam fontibus Ecclesiæ reconciliationem, id docemur a Tertulliano de pœnitentia, cum dicit: Collo- cavit in vestibulo pœnitentiam secundam, quæ pulsanti- bus patefaciat, sed jam semel, quia jam secundo, sed am- plius nunquam, quia proxime frustra. Non enim & hoc semel satis est? Ubi cum dicit pœnitentiam secundam, in- telligit a baptismo, quæ prima pœnitentia est. Sunt & alibi apud eundem similia. Et quidem quod ad mores an- tiquos attinet, res se sic habet. Et ad eos mores hunc lo- cum referunt Ambrosius & alii. Cæterum ego loci hujus sensum eo spectare non arbitror: sed ad mortem dici eos delinquere, qui cum peccaverint, moniti peccare pergunt, aut certe disciplinæ, quæ in Ecclesia constituta est, subji- cere se nolunt. Quæ enim spes sanitatis ei, qui medicum sibi a Deo datum audire non vult? Hermas lib. 6. Quæ- cunque pecora vidisti valde læta & exultantia, ii sunt, qui in perpetuum a Deo discesserunt, & tradiderunt se deside- riis hujus seculi. Iis ergo non est per pœnitentiam regres- sus ad vitam, quoniam quidem adjecerunt ad reliqua de- licta sua, & nomen Domini infandis insectati sunt verbis. Hujusmodi homines morti sunt destinati. Hæ sunt virgæ putridæ apud eundem Hermam III. 8. Nec aliud videtur velle Clemens Alexandrinus, hunc locum citans Strom. II. qui & Strom. VII. eos vocat ἀπηλγηκότας, aitque virum sapientem juste talibus aliqua mala temporalia imprecari. Cyprianus epist. LII. Et idcirco, frater charissime, pœni- tentiam non agentes, nec dolorem delictorum suorum toto corde & manifesta lamentationis suæ professione te- stantes, prohibendos omnino censemus a spe communi- cationis & pacis, si in infirmitate atque in periculo cœpe- rint deprecari: quia rogare illos non delicti pœnitentia, sed mortis urgentis admonitio compellit, nec dignus est in morte accipere solatium, qui se non cogitavit esse moritu- rum. Idem admonitis de peccato & instructis negat posse ignosci epistola LXIII. Basilius ad Amphilochium cap. LXXXIV. πᾶλα δὲ ταῦτα γράφομεν, ὥστε τοὺς καρποὺς ἐκκμά- ζεσθαι τῆς διανοίας. κὶ γὰρ πάντως τῷ χρόνῳ κρίνομεν τὰ τοιαῦτα ἀλλὰ τῷ τρόπῳ τῆς μετανοίας προσέχομεν. Ἐὰν δὲ δυσάποσπά- τως ἔχωσιν τῶν ἰδίων ἐθῶν, καὶ ταῖς ἡδοναῖς τῆς σαρκὸς μᾶλλον δουλεύειν θελήσωσιν, ἢ τῷ Κυρίῳ, καὶ τὴν κατὰ τὸ Εὐαγγέλιον ζωὴν μὴ παραδέχωνται, οὐδεὶς ἡμῖν πρὸς αὐτοὺς κοινὸς λόγος. Ἡμεῖς γὰρ ἐν λόγῳ ἀπειθῆ καὶ ἀντιλέγοντι δεδιδάγμεθα ἀκού- ειν, ὅτι, σώζων σῶζε τὴν ἑαυτοῦ ψυχήν. Ubi Balsamo: Μὴ κἀι σεαυτὸν ἀπολέσῃς ἀδιορθώτοις συγκοινωνῶν Paria habet Zo- naras. Et in Nicæna Synodo II. ἁμαρτία πρὸς θάνατον ex- ponitur ἀδιόρθωτον μένειν. Esse ad mortem hic intelligendum comparare, sicut mortiferum dicimus morbum aut vene- num, unde non fit spes convalescendi, cum & alii morbi & venena homini mortem afferre possint, & sæpe afferant.

Non de veterum moribus & consuetudine, quos receperint post lapsum ad communionem, sed quinam apud Deum recipiantur in gratiam aut excludantur, hic dispiciendum. Nam illis spes gra- tiæ non relinquitur, pro quibus orare non per- mittitur, qui peccatum illud ad mortem, de quo hoc loco agitur, committunt, adeoque mortem vel condemnationem non effugiunt. Pro quibus enim Deus preces non admittit, quantum ad salu- tem eorum æternam, illis spes gratiæ & salutis nulla superest. Neque Pastor Hermæ audiri mere- tur autor nullius fidei, ac nec ipsis Papistis proba- tus, sed rejectus per Indicem expurgat. Hispan. p. 149. & Roman. cujus censuram vide libro præ- fixam XV. Bibl. Patr. & a Bellarmino inter alia ob errorem de pœnitentia reprobatus de script. Ecel. p. 51. Hic liber nunquam fuit in canone sanctorum & divinorum librorum, imo habet aliqua noxia, ut de unica pœnitentia secundum errores Novatia- norum, quibus hic liber favere videtur. De Ter- tulliani etiam libro de pœnitentia monuit idem Cardinalis libr. cit. in eo reperiri propositiones er- roneas vel certe suspectas, & l. I. de Christ. cap. 9. Tertulliani, inquit, in dogmatibus est parva auto- ritas, cum sit manifestus hæreticus. Cornelius a La- pide Tertulliani errorem, qui explicat de mæchia post baptismum commissa, in Scriptura a Concilio Lateranensi sub Innocentio III. damnatum ait. De Clemente Alexandrino idem censor, non deesse ait sententias aliquas, quæ errorem sapiunt; Cypria- num non excusandum a quibusdam erroribus dicit

Salmero disp. LI. in epist. ad Rom. T. III. p. 474. Sed & agnoscit Grotius ipse, ad mores Ecclesiæ hunc locum referendum non esse, ideoque non probat sententiam Ambrosii, quam Suarez T. IV. pag. 87. ex l. II. de pœnit. cap. 8. & 9. hanc facit, omne peccatum speciali modo atrox, & enorme vo- cari ad mortem fortasse ob eam rationem, quia hu- jusmodi peccatum speciale habeat periculum morale perpetuæ mortis, eamque confert cum Erasmi ex- plicatione, quod ejiciendi tales olim fuerint e con- tubernio Ecclesiæ, tradendiq́ Satanæ, nec recipiendi, nisi jejuniis, lacrymis, multisq́ remediis duris dele- ta culpa. Unde Ambrosius l. I. de pœnit. c. 2. di- xerit: Qui culpam exaggeraverit, exaggerat etiam pœnitentiam. Majora enim crimina majoribus ab- luuntur fletibus. Quam sententiam non omnino improbat B. Feuerbornius dissert. de pecc. in Spi- ritum S. c. III. p. 24. Si nempe quis interpretetur de flagitio quovis atrocissimo & manifestissimo, pro- pter quod peccator a communione precum & sacra- mentorum sit tantisper excludendus, donec pœniten- tiam agat, & ab Ecclesia reconciliatus recipiatur: quo etiam abit Brentius, Heerbrandus, & Cardin. Molina apud B. Gerhardum disp. Isag. l. XII. c. V. §. 14. Improbat autem eam sententiam in Tur- riano l. IV. pro epist. Pont. cap. 3. Cornelius; quod nempe intelligatur peccatum, cui annexa est ex- communicatio, quum excommunicatus impœnitens sit, & pro excommunicato publica Ecclesiæ oratione orare non liceat. Causam cur eam explicationem non admittendam censeat, hanc affert, quod S. Jo- hannes neget pro tali orandum oratione qualibet, etiam privata. Quæ ratio sine dubio etiam Gro- tium movit, cur calculum suum subduceret. Et videtur ea satis firma. Nam hic nullo verbo de excommunicatione Ecclesiæ; vel de exclusione a precum Ecclesiæ communione agitur, sed de pri- vatis potius sermo est; si quis, inquit S. Johannes, viderit fratrem suum peccare, item, non de illo di- co ut oret, quæ privatum quemque concernunt. Quid? quod a communione precum Ecclesiæ non exclusi fuerint excommunicati. Etsi enim cum aliis in Ecclesia orare non potuerint a commu- nione exclusi, poterant tamen Ecclesia, imo & de- bebat pro iisdem orare quisque in Ecclesia, ἵna τὸ πνεῦμα σωθῇ ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ τῦ Κυρίε, 1. Cor. V, 5.

Sed num meliorem affert interpretationem vel Cornelius vel Grotius? Hic quidem intelligit, eos iis, qui ad ad mortem delinquere dici, qui cum peccaverint, moniti peccare pergunt, aut certe disciplinæ, quæ in Ecclesia instituta est, se subjicere nolunt. Ille fere eodem modo peccatum quodvis gravissimum in- digitari vult, quod ob sui enormitatem vel con- suetudinem, obstinationem & malitiam juxta le- gem communem per gratiam, quam Deus ordi- narie dare solet, est quasi immediate; incorrigibile, & insanabile; sed num pro talibus non orandum, ut a laqueis Diaboli liberentur ac evigilent. Ut talibus 2. Tim. II. 25. 26. μετάνοια & gratia non denegatur, ita nec oratio deneganda, argumento loci, 1. Tim. II. 1. sqq. quo pro omnibus, quos Deus vult salvos fieri, & ad agnitionem veritatis perve- nire, orare jubemur. Nec vero prorsus id pecca- tum esse πρὸς θάνατον fatetur Cornelius, quia dicit tantum QUASI immedicabile, ipsum peccantem PENE certo & infallibiliter deducere, nisi insignis aliquis sanctus & quasi novus Moses ei extraordi- nariam gratiam & veniam a Deo impetret. At S. Johannes non loquitur de eo, qui pene, sed qui penitus ad mortem deducitur, & de peccato, non quod QUASI, sed quod prorsus est immedicabile, siquidem sit πρὸς θάνατον & frustra pro eo oretur.

Et quomodo insignis aliquis sanctus ei gratiam exorabit, pro quo orare penitus prohibet Apo- stolus. Intelligit Cornelius imprimis peccatum, quo quis fidelis a Christi fide & Ecclesia discessit, illam malitiose impugnat, aliosque ab illa ad suam hæresin vel idololatriam traducere & pervertere satagit, sed & de illo dicit, quod ad mortem gehennæ QUASI certo deducat, quum Apostolus de eo peccato loquatur, quod vere CERTO deducit ad mor- tem. Quod tres characteres illi docent hujusce peccati, de quo loquitur: Primo quod absolute peccatum sit πρὸς θάνατον. Non esset autem abso- lute ἁμαρτία πρὸς θάνατον, nisi certo ad mortem deduceret. Deinde quod ab omnibus aliis pecca- tis & ab injustitia quavis distinguatur, quæ non esse peccata ad mortem hoc uno excepto, ait. Vi ergo hujus oppositionis hoc simpliciter mor- tem infert, quum reliqua omnia sive infirmitatis sive malitiæ, sive venialia, sive mortalia, ut vocant, ita comparata sint, ut quamvis per se reatum mor- tis inferant, & mortem mereantur, quæ omnis peccati stipendium est, Rom. VI. ult. tamen pœni- tentia de illis agi possit, ut præcise & infallibiliter ad mortem non deducant. Hoc ergo tale pecca- tum esse oportet, quod præcise certo ac infallibi- liter adducat ad mortem. Tertio de eo peccato & peccatore sermo est, pro quo simpliciter non esse orandum, monet Apostolus. Quomodo ergo ei extraordinarie gratia obtingeret, pro quo preces nullas admittit Deus.

Quod vero Bartholomæus Petri tricatur, non sim- pliciter hic preces a Johanne prohiberi, sed tantum non audere hortari quemlibet Christianum, ut scilicet pro tali oret cum ea impetrandi fiducia, de qua v. 14. Simpliciter enim S. Johannes: Οὐ περὶ ἐκείνης λέγω, ἵνα ἐρωτήσῃ; ut priori Imperativo αἰτή- σᾀ simpliciter hortabatur quemlibet Christia- num, quautum ad omne peccatum, μὴ πρὸς θά- νατον, ita simpliciter nunc monet, non orandum esse pro peccato πρὸς θάνατον, nec discrimen facit inter magnum intercessorem cum magna prece, & quemlibet alium Christianum, quod a Schlichtingio textui infertur, non e textu effertur. Adde quod pro locis parallelis huic nostro agnoscat Corne- lius Ebr. VI. 4. & cap. X. 24. At ibi non difficilem esse talium peccatorum renovationem dicit Aposto- lus, sed ἀδύνατον impossibile esse eos renovari ad pœnitentiam, nullamque relictam illis esse ho- stiam testatur. Dicit Cornelius agnatum esse hoc peccatum & affine blasphemiæ in Spiritum Sanctum, Matth. XII. 31. & sicut illa difficile remittitur: ita & hoc. At illam plane non remitti Christus do- cet, neque in hoc, neque in futuro seculo. Ideoque nec peccatum, quod ad mortem est, remittetur unquam. Cur ergo non de peccato vel blasphe- mia in Spiritum Sanctum id intelligit Cornelius aut Grotius, quum characteres & collatio loco- rum non aliud intelligendum esse doceant, & co- gnatio ac parallelismus locorum admittatur.

De peccato ad mortem Bartholomæus Petri Bedæ sententiam in h. l. intelligit, quod sit illud, quo post agnitionem Dei, quæ per gratiam cuipiam data est, ipse fraternitatem impugnat, & adversus ipsam gratiam, qua reconciliatus est Deus, inviden- tiæ facibus agitatur, & ex Augustino l. I. de serm. Dom. in monte cap. 22. desumptam dicit.

Nostro vero judicio nihil verius, quam S. Jo- hannem agere de peccato in Spiritum S. in quo ὁμόψηφον habemus B. Hunnium: Distinguit Jo- hannes inter peccata, quorum quædam non ad mor- tem, quædam ad mortem esse dicit. Nam etsi alias extra Christum omnia peccata mortalia sunt, im- primis autem peccata regnantia, quæ Gal. V. enu- merantur, tamen hoc loco peccatum ad mortem, & peccata non ad mortem alio quodam respectu oppo- nuntur, ut peccatum non ad mortem comprehendat omne peccatum, excepto peccato in Spiritum San- ctum. Quandoquidem ex reliquis peccatis omnibus resipiscere potest homo. Peccatum autem in Sp. S. certissimam indurationem & finalem impœniten- tiam adjunctam habet. Pro hoc, dicit Johannes, non orandum, siquidem tales nunquam redeunt, sed sunt plane deplorati & insanabiles. Habemus & Flacium consentientem in h.l. quibus accedunt Lucas Osian- der, B. Gerhardus disp.Isag. B. Meisnerus Anthropol. dec. I. disp. X. q. 1. th. 17. & plerique alii e nostris, ut & e Reformatis Bullingerus &c.

Aliorum sententias confutare vix operæ pre- tium est, quum vel ex hoc elencho jam possint expediri, utpote quod Hieronymus in c. XIV. Jer. Bernhardus de grad. humil. cap. ult. Bonaventura in 2. dist. th. dub. 1. & ibidem Thomas & Suarez p. III. T. IV. disp. 8. s. 1. peccatum gravius, quod Deus punire decrevit, adducente Cornelio, intelli- gunt. Qui enim hoc quis videre vel scire potest, utrum quis peccet peccatum, quod Deus punire decrevit, quum decretum id ratione hujus, vel il- lius peccantis in S. literis expressum non sit. Item quod Hilarius in Psal. CXL. censet peccatum ad mortem esse, quod destinato & ex malitia commit- titur, & Ambrosius, quem e l. c. de pœnit. c. VIII. & IX. adducit Cornelius, quodvis peccatum intelli- go, quod vix remittitur, & glossa ordin. quodvis mortale peccatum designari censens. At illis non convenire characteres peccati πρὸς ϑάνατον jam patuit. Pro peccato mortali orare jubet Johan- nes, ut vita peccanti detur, cujus ob peccatum mortale expers est, idque docet non esse ad mor- tem, non certo & infallibiliter ad mortem ducere, quin per pœnitentiam condonatio haberi possit. Augustinus in Retr. l. 1. c. 19. seipsum emendans addere jubet, si in hac tam scelerata mentis per- versitate finiverit hanc vitam, ideo explicat c. 22. de corrupt. & grat. peccatum ad mortem, quod sit peccatum mortale quodcunque, cujus non agitur pœnitentia, quæ etiam Gregorii M. l. VI. moral. cap. 31. est sententia, ut & Cornelio citante Gelasis l. de anath. Paciani epist. III. Bedæ & Lyrani hic, Lombardi in 2. sent. dist. 43. Thomæ 3. part. q. 86. art. 1. ad 2. Valentia, Suarezii &c. Quam vero ipse reprobat, ut & Bartholomæus Petri, quia sciri non potest, in quo peccato quis ad mortem perseveratu- rus sit. Et quamvis Suarèz de eo, qui decessit in impœnitentia, explicet, eoque autores illos jam no- minatos adducat, pro quo orandum non sit, quia est extra statum salutis; id tamen ἀλλότριον est, quia hic de eo, quem quis videt peccantem, sermo est, adeoque de eo, qui adhuc in hac vita est; nec satis- facit dubio, quia etiam de iis, qui in vivis esse de- fierunt, non constat, an decesserint in impœniten- tia, nec ne? neque mortuis preces amplius utiles sunt, & tantum abest, ut pro qualibus e defunctis orandum sit doceat Scriptura, ut nuspiam pro mortuis orandum esse in Scripturis quicquam tra- ditum sit. Nam quod purgatorium ex hoc loco Roffensis artic. XVII. contra Luth. probat, refuta- tionem non meretur. Quod vero Schlichtingius hoc loco ait pro vita functis orare charitati con- sentaneum esse, quia Judex vivorum & mortuorum necdum sententiam decretoriam de quolibet tulit, saltim nondum eam exequutus est; ἄγραφον est & ἀντίγραφον, locis Ebr. IX. 27. Eccl. XI. 3. Joh. III. v. 18. 36. contrarium. Bartholomæi Petri explicatio peccatum ad mortem esse peccatum quodvis mor- tale, cujus non agitur pœnitentia, quamdiu & qua- tenus tale est, assensu itidem indigna est. Num enim pro peccatore in mortali peccato hærente, quamdiu in eo hæret, orandum non est, ut con- vertatur & resipiscat? Locus Jerem. cap. XIV, 11. huc non facit: nam ibi pro gratia temporali popu- lo Judaico exhibenda, liberationis nempe à Babylo- nica πανωλεθρίᾳ orari prohibetur, non pro gratia conversionis & salutis æternæ, quam Deum serio quoad omnes peccatores velle jurejurando testa- tus ipse est Ezech. XVIII. & XXXIII. Schlichtingii deniq; commentum, quod peccatum ad mortem non tantum sit blasphemia Spiritus, sed actus qui- vis valde enormis è radice quadam vitiosa & altè insita, fratris traditio, hæresis, habitusq; alii pecca- torum gravium, ut & actus nimium graves & fœ- di, parricidium puta, fratricidium & his simi- les &c. quod facile homines desperabundos reddit, & in æternum barathrum præcipitat, discussum videatur Exeg. A. Con. art. XII. c. 2.

Quod objicitur adversus nostram explicatio- nem de peccato in Spiritum Sanctum, quod pec- catum ad mortem, de quo Johannes, SEMPER possit à nobis sciri vel videri, blasphemia in Spiri- tum Sanctum non semper possit videri; utpote cum mente perficitur, nos nihil movet: quia nec S. Jo- hannes de peccato ad mortem ita loquitur, si quis viderit peccantem ad mortem: uti de fratre peccan- te peccatum μὴ πρὸς θάνατον non ad mortem: Nec indicat S. Johannes, peccatum ad mortem semper videri, quum nec peccatum μὴ πρὸς θάνατον sem- per videatur: certe cum animo id perpetratur, non videtur: Sed verba sunt hypothetica, ἐάν τις ἴδῃ. Adhæc quum peccatum in Spiritum S. inferat blasphemiam oralem, agnosci quandoque posse, qui ita peccant, dubium non est. Denique modus iste loquendi Johannes, ὀυ περὶ ἐκείνης λέγω, ἵνα ἐρωτήσῃ, explicat solum antecedentia, S. Johannem scilicet non loquutum esse de peccato ad mortem cum orare jussit. Nuda ergo distinctio peccati traditur, peccati non ad mortem, & peccati ad mor- tem, non vero docetur peccatum ad mortem a no- bis certo sciri, nedum SEMPER sciri posse ab aliis. Sed id dicitur tantum, peccatum illud tale esse, cujus nulla venia expectari debeat ab eo, qui id committit.

Αἰτήσει καὶ δώσει ἀυτῷ ζωὴν, τοῖς μὴ ἁμαρτάνουσι πρὸς θάνατον) In Manuscripto, μὴ ἁμαρτάνουσι ἁμαρτίαν. Αἰτή- σει hic est futurum positum pro Imperativo, quod often- dunt verba opposita in hoc ipso commate. Illud: dabit ei vitam, Syrus exponit, dabitur ei vita, ut Activum cum Ac- cusativo suo sumatur pro Passivo, non designata persona agente. Sed rectius subintelliges, Deus, ex præcedentibus, & quia illud ipsum αἰτήσει valet αἰτήσει Θεὸν Deus ad preces fidelium ei homini, qui Ecclesiæ medicam manum non refugit, servabit fidem, dabit cor humiliatum atque contritum, & suo tempore reddet Spiritum Sanctum, quæ omnia viæ sunt ad vitam æternam, nec in manu sunt ho- minis, sicut est submittere se Ecclesiæ. Est autem hic con- structio convenientiæ singularis cum plurali per σύνθεσιν, ut loquuntur, quia illud singulare non unum certum defi- gnat, sed quemvis professione Christianum.

Illud δώσει referunt nonnulli ad intercessorem, vel qui pro fratre orat. Ita B. Fœvurbornius de pecc. in Spir. S. p. 11. Homo pius intercedens dabit ei vi- tam per modum petendi & a DEO per preces im- petrandi vitam: Quemadmodum parentes dicun- tur prolongare vitam suis liberis, ut est in textu Ebræo, Exod. XX. 12. & pii pauperes perhibentur suos ἐνεργέτας recipere in æterna tabernacula, Luc. XVI. 9. (proindeq; 1. Job. V. v. 16. nulla est hyper- bolica loquutio, quam ibi fingit Marloratus) hoc est in domicilium cœleste.

Ἔστι ἁμαρτία πρὸς θάνατον, ὀυ περὶ ἐκείνης λέγω, ὅτι ἐρω- τήσῃ) Non impero preces fundi, ut tanta contumacia de- leatur, quia nullum est promissum quo tales preces ni- tantur. Hic habes sensum mysticum loci Jerem. VII. 16. & Ezech. XIV. 14.

De sensu loquutionis Johanneæ jam ante di- ctum. Neque hic admitti potest sensus mysticus Jerem. VII. 16. Ezech. XIV. 14. Nam ibi agitur de salute populi temporali, hic de salute proximi æterna. Disparata ergo illa sunt,

## 5:16
v. 16. Rom. X. 13. &c. Finally, what is clearer than that Christ is opposed to idols by himself, 1 Cor. X. 14, 19, 20, 21, whence Socinus himself says doubtfully: You will not find, I think, perhaps ever, that Christ himself is opposed to idols by himself, lib. contra Wujeck. l. c. (3) Finally, that in the present passage Christ is also opposed to idols, from the context, because saving knowledge of the one true God and remaining in that true one, in his Son Jesus Christ (which is a consequence of that, 1 John IV. 15), is obtained in Christ Jesus, by which idols and fictitious gods are fled, is so manifest that even Socinus, forgetful of himself, acknowledges it in his commentary on this passage, p. 522, when he says: I call those false divine cults which are not attributed to God alone and to Christ, etc., which he teaches are designated by the name of idol. Thus, therefore, God and Christ are opposed in this passage to idols according to the mind of Socinus, whence it is easy to invert the argument and turn it back upon Socinus: Since in this passage & God the Father is opposed to idols without any indication of inequality, certainly Christ also, no less than the Father, will be that true God.

To 7. Resp. (1) those words: And we are in that true one, are to be referred to God the Father, and not to Christ, is only said, but it is not proved by any argument: and therefore it is rejected with the same ease with which it is asserted. (2) What Socinus has just now said is clearly probable, he writes thus in his commentary on it, p. 515: It pleases us more (so that that which is less exposed to cavils and reproaches) that the words in the true one, or in that true one, should not be referred to that which immediately precedes, but to that which immediately follows, so that that true one named here in the second place is the Son of God himself, Christ Jesus. (3) The same manner of speaking is here ἐν τῷ υἱῷ αὐτοῦ Ἰησοῦ Χριστῷ, as in the preceding verse, καὶ ἐσμὲν ἐν τῷ ἀληθινῷ, with the prepositive article placed before both. Therefore, just as those pertain to Christ, so also these are without doubt to be referred to him. Add that if those words were referred to the Father, it would be said ὦμεν, just as ἵνα γινώσκομεν precedes. But John expressly distinguishes them, so that we may know that true one: and we are in that true one, in his Son, or Christ: but also an absurd meaning will emerge if all things are referred to the Father: so that we may know that true God (the Father) and we are in that true one (God the Father) in his Son Jesus Christ, this is that true God. Therefore the Vulgate rightly explains it of the Son, and let us be in his true Son. Although in whichever way it is taken, the Son is not to be separated from the Father, since both come to us and make their abode with us, John 14, 23. ἐν τῷ υἱῷ αὐτοῦ ought to be rendered by his Son through a Hebraism, is neither necessary, because the text fits perfectly if that meaning is retained which it has primarily and by itself: nor is it appropriate: because the use of the preposition ἐν is exactly the same in both verses, and it is an apposition pointed out as if by a finger. (4) If it were even granted that those words καὶ ἐσμὲν ἐν τῷ ἀληθινῷ were to be referred to the antecedent, and the words ἐν τῷ υἱῷ were to be rendered BY his Son, it would not yet follow that the relative pronoun οὗτος looks to the Father, not to Christ, partly because οὗτος could still refer to the immediate antecedent, and would not necessarily refer to one somewhat more remote, indeed that it refers to the immediate one has been proved before, partly because that the Father is understood in the antecedent with Christ excluded, not included, is by no means proved by the adversaries, indeed one may argue to the contrary (1) from the complex of the διάνοια. It is a question here of that knowledge of the true God, whose διάνοιαν Christ had given to the Apostles. But that this was also about Christ's passion and resurrection, the marginal passage shows, Luke XXIV. 45, 46, by which he is declared the Son of God, and true God, Rom. I. 4, and the history teaches

Evangelical, that Christ informed the Apostles no less about his own person than about his Father, to which end also all the sermons of the Apostles were directed, Acts II. 38, c. III. 13, seq., c. IV. 11, 12, &c., since eternal life consists no less in his person than in the knowledge of the Father, John XVII. 3, XX. 21. (2) from the effect of the γνώσεως; it is a question of his knowledge, through whose knowledge we are in God, and in Christ. But through Christ, no less than through the knowledge of God the Father, we are in God and in Christ, 1 John IV. 15, Eph. III. 17. Therefore, what is said ἵνα γινώσκωμεν τὸν ἀληθινὸν Θεὸν, is to be taken in such a way that Christ is included under the object of knowledge, not excluded.

To 8. Respond. This is a perpetual Socinian complaint. This or that opinion is inept, ridiculous, contradictory, therefore it is not the opinion of the Holy Spirit, even if the words in their native and genuine meaning import the same. But is this not to bring divine oracles to the tribunal of human reason? Let the wise judge. Indeed, for the pious it is a matter of religion to abandon the manifest letter of Scripture for the sake of the censure of reason, who with simple faith embrace the opinion which the words of the Holy Spirit insert in their simple, native, and genuine meaning, whatever reason may laugh at or contradict. Since therefore the text has taught that the pronoun οὗτος in this passage looks to Christ, not to God, we do not care for the laughter and the ἀντιλογίας of the adversaries. To these (2) we deny that a contradiction is involved when it is said that the Son of God has given us the knowledge of the highest God, and that he himself is the highest God. For what? Can he not be the highest God who has given us the knowledge of the highest God? But Volckelius insists: If Christ himself is the true God, who will be the Son of God, through whom we arrive at the knowledge of the true God? As if the same Christ could not be both the Son of God, through whom we arrive at the knowledge of the true God, and the true God? Indeed, John says both, that the Son of God Christ gave us the διάνοιαν, so that we might know τὸν ἀληθινὸν Θεὸν, and that this very Son of God is ὁ ἀληθινὸς Θεὸς, as has been proven thus far. Wherefore (3) we admit that the Son of God is distinguished from that true God, meanwhile we believe nevertheless that the Son of God is also that true God. But Volckelius plays with that pronoun demonstratively, that, in the words that true God. For he either demonstrates indefinitely that highest God, or definitely God the Father. For when he denies that the Son of God can without contradiction be called that true God whose knowledge He has given us, anyone sees that he understands definitely God the Father, in which way I grant that the Son is not that Father God, but from that it cannot be inferred that the name of the supreme God cannot be predicated indefinitely of the Son of God, or that absolutely the Son of God is not the supreme God. We can therefore answer otherwise: The name of the true God is taken either essentially or personally. If essentially, then both the Father is that true God, that is, the supreme God, and the Son is that true God, or the supreme God, nor is a distinction to be admitted in the name taken essentially, but there is one and undivided essence to the Father and the Son, 1 John V. 7. If personally, we concede a distinction between the true God, if, that is, it denotes the person of the Father, and the Son of the true God, since the person of the Son is not the person of the Father: meanwhile, the only-begotten Son of the Father, the true God (taken hypostatically), is also truly the true God (essentially) or true God by nature. What contradiction is here?

To 9. Resp. (1) This perversity is directly opposed to the preceding. For in that, Socinus had said it was most certain that the pronoun 'this' does not refer to the Son, but to God the Father. Now, however, he says that this is what is most approved by him, that it ought to be referred not only to the Father, but also to the Son. This is the certainty of the Socinian Spirit. (2) It is one thing that the pronoun HIC can have that force, another that it ought to be so understood in this place. The latter, not the former, must be proven. (3) But neither is that proven by the examples which are brought forward. The first, Matt. XIII. 38, τὸ καλὸν σπέρμα, ὗτοί εἰσιν οἱ ὑοὶ τῆς βασιλείας, does not show that the pronoun ὗτος is referred to the whole sentence, and that the masculine is used for the neuter: but only that the pronoun sometimes agrees with the following noun in gender and number, although it refers to the preceding noun (for it refers to what immediately preceded, καλὸν σπέρμα, and provides its ἐξήγησιν), which we do not deny, especially in cases of συνέσει, when, namely, such an idiom and enallage indicates that the discourse is about a person, as Gal. III. 16, Eph. I. 13, 14, etc. But who does not see that this, in the present instance, is entirely ἀπροσδιόνυσον? The latter is taken from John XVII. 3, where the pronoun αὕτη is used absolutely after the manner of the Hebrews for τοῦτο δέ. For since the Hebrews lack a neuter gender, they therefore frequently use the feminine in its place; see Gen. V. 20, Exod. X. 11, John V. 19, Ps. XII. 4, Ps. XXVII. 4, and the same Hebraism occurs in the New Testament at Mark XII. 11. Here, however, a masculine noun is used, nor is there any suspicion of a Hebraism, and therefore that example too is ἀλλότριον. (4) But that the pronoun οὗτος must by all means be taken in this way in this passage is easily proven, first, because the simplest sense is to be granted to a passage wherever it can be granted. Yet who will believe that this sense of Socinus is the simplest, and flowing from the very letter, when it could have occurred to no one before Socinus, whereas on the contrary our explanation is obvious and plain to all, if they insist upon the text:

Latin:

v. 16. Rom. X. 13. &c. Denique quid clarius, quam quod Christus per se idolis opponatur, 1. Cor. X. 14. 19. 20. 21. unde ipse Socinus dubitative: Christum ipsum per se idolis opponi, non invenies, ut arbitror, fortasse unquam, lib. contra Wujeck. l. c. (3) Tan- dem quod in præsenti loco Christus etiam oppo- nitur idolis, ex contextu, quod cognitio salutaris unius veri Dei & permanentia in illo vero, in Filio ejus Jesu Christo, (quæ est illius consequens, 1. Joh. IV. 15.) in Christo Jesu obtingat, quo fugiantur idola, & Dii fictitii, id adeo manifestum est, ut agnoscat etiam Socinus, sui immemor, in coment. super h. l. p. 522. cum inquit: Falsos cultus divi- nos eos appello, qui soli Deo & Christo non tribuuntur &c. quos nomine idoli designari docet. Sic ergo Deus & Christus opponitur h. l. idolis ex mente Socini, unde facile est argumentum invertere, & in Socinum retorquere: Quin h. l. & Deus Pater opponitur idolis absq; ullo inæqualitatis indicio, utique & Christus non minus, quam Pater erit verus ille Deus.

Ad 7. Resp. (1) verba ista: Et sumus in illo vero, referenda esse ad Deum Patrem, & non ad Christum, dicitur tantum, nullo autem argumento proba- tur: ideoque ea facilitate rejicitur, qua adseri- tur. (2) Quod jamjam plane verisimile dixit Soci- nus, de eo comment. p. 515. ita scribit: Verum no- bis magis placet (ut id, quod minus cavillationibus & reprehensionibus est obnoxium) ut verba in vero, sive in illo vero, non ad id, quod proxime præcedit, sed ad id, quod statim sequitur, referantur, ita ut ille verus secundo loco hic nominatus sit ipse Dei Filius, Christus Jesus. (3) Idem loquendi genus hic est ἐν τῷ υἱῷ αὐτοῦ Ἰησοῦ Χριστῷ, quod in præcedenti com- mate, καὶ ἐσμὲν ἐν τῷ ἀληθινῷ, præmisso utrique articulo præpositivo. Proinde sicut illa pertinent ad Christum, ita & hæc dubio procul eo referenda sunt. Adde, quod si verba illa ad Patrem referren- tur, diceretur ὦμεν, sicut præcedit ἵνα γινώσκομεν. At distinguit ea expresse Johannes, ut cognosca- mus verum illum: & sumus in vero illo, in Filio ejus, vel Christo: sed & absona prodibit sententia, si ad Patrem referantur omnia: ut cognoscamus verum illum Deum (Patrem) & sumus in vero illo (Deo Patre) in Filio ejus Jesu Christo, hic est verus ille Deus. Idec recte Vulgata de Filio exponit, & simus in vero Filio ejus. Quamvis utrocunque modo ac- cipiatur, Filius a Patre non sit sejungendus, quum uterque ad nos veniat, & apud nos mansionem fa- ciat, Joh. 14, 23. ἐν τῷ υἱῷ αὐτοῦ reddi debere per Fi- lium ejus per Ebraismum, neque necessum est, quia optime congruit textus, si retineatur significatio ista, quam primo & per se habet: neque conveniens: quia idem prorsus usus est præpositionis ἐν in utroque commate, & quasi digito monstrata appo- sitio. (4) Si daretur etiam verba illa καὶ ἐσμὲν ἐν τῷ ἀληθινῷ referenda esse ad antecedens, & verba ἐν τῷ υἱῷ reddenda esse PER FILIUM ejus, non- dum tamen sequeretur, pronomen relativum οὗτος respicere Patrem, non Christum, partim quia οὗτος adhuc referre possit antecedens proximum, non autem aliquanto remotius necessario referret, imo quod omnino proximum referat, ante probatum, partim quia in antecedenti intelligi Patrem exclu- so Christo, non incluso, haudquaquam probatum est ab adversariis, imo in contrarium licet argu- mentari (1) a διανοίας complexu. De ea veri Dei cognitione hic agitur, cujus διάνοιαν Apostolis de- derat Christus. Hanc autem fuisse de Christi pas- sione quoque & resurrectione, ostendit locus mar- ginalis, Luc. XXIV. 45. 46. qua Filius Dei, & verus Deus declaratus est, Rom. I. 4. & docet historia

Evangelica, quod non minus de persona sua, quam de Patre suo Apostolos Christus informa- rit, quorsum etiam omnes conciones Apostolo- rum directæ fuere, Act. II. 38. c. III. 13. seq. c. IV. 11. 12. &c. quum non minus in persona sua, quam in Patris cognitione vita æterna consistat, Joh. XVII. 3. XX. 21. (2) e γνώσεως effectu; de ejus cogni- tione agitur, per cujus cognitionem in Deo sumus, & in Christo. At per Christum non minus, quam per Dei Patris cognitionem sumus in Deo & in Christo, 1. Joh. IV. 15. Eph. III. 17. Proinde quod dicitur ἵνα γινώσκωμεν τὸν ἀληθινὸν Θεὸν, ita erit accipiendum, ut Christus sub objecto cognitio- nis comprehendatur, non excludatur.

Ad 8. Respond. ἔγκλημα hoc perpetuum est Socinianum. Hæc, vel illa sententia inepta, ridicula, contradictoria est, E. non est Spiritus S. sententia, utut verba in nativa, & genuina significatione eandem importent. Annon autem hoc sit oracu- la divina ad humanæ rationis tribunal sistere? ju- dicent cordati. Sane piis religio est, ob rationis censuram deserere manifestam Scripturæ literam, qui simplici fide amplectuntur sententiam, quam verba Spiritus S. in simplici, nativo, & genuino inserunt significatu, quidquid etiam rideat, vel contradicat ratio. Quum itaque textus docuerit, pronomen ὗτός h. l. Christum respicere, non De- um, nihil moramur risum & ἀντιλογίας adversario- rum. Ad hæc (2) negamus involvi contradictio- nem, quando dicitur, Filium Dei dedisse nobis sum- mi Dei notitiam, eundemq; esse summum Deum. Quid enim? annon summus Deus esse potest, qui summi Dei nobis dedit notitiam? Sed instat Vol- ckelius: Si ipse Christus est verus Deus, quis erit Dei Filius, per quem in notitiam Dei veri perveni- mus? Quasi non possit idem Christus esse & Filius Dei, per quem in notitiam Dei veri pervenimus, & verus Deus? Imo utrumque Johannes dicit, quod Filius Dei Christus dederit nobis διάνοιαν, ut co- gnosceremus τὸν ἀληθινὸν Θεὸν, & quod hic ipse Fi- lius Dei sit ὁ ἀληθινὸς Θεὸς, ut hactenus evictum. Quocirca (3) distingui fatemur Filium Dei a Deo illo vero, interim credimus tamen Filium Dei quoque esse verum illum Deum. Sed Volckelius ludit in pronomine illo δεικτικῶς, ille, in vocibus ve- rus ille Deus. Nam vel demonstrat indefinite De- um illum summum, vel definite Deum Patrem. Quando enim negat, Filium Dei absque contra- dictione posse dici Deum illum verum, cujus noti- tiam nobis dedit, quivis videt, quod intelligat defi- nite Deum Patrem, quo pacto largior, Filium non esse Deum illum Patrem, sed inde nequit inferri, quod nomen summi Dei indefinite de Filio Dei prædicari nequeat, vel quod absolute Filius Dei non sit summus Deus. Ἄλλως itaq; respondere pos- sumus: Nomen Dei veri sumitur vel essentialiter, vel personaliter. Si essentialiter tum & Pater est verus ille Deus, hoc est summus Deus, & Filius est verus ille Deus, vel summus Deus, neque est distin- ctio admittenda in ὀσιωδῶς accepto nomine, sed est una & indivisa Patri & Filio essentia, 1. Joh. V. 7. Si personaliter, distinctionem concedimus, inter τὸν ἀληθινὸν Θεὸν, si sc. personam Patris denotat, & τὲ ἀληθινὲ Θεὲ ὑὸν, cum Filii persona non sit persona Patris: interim Patris, τὲ ἀληθινὲ Θεὲ (ὑποσατικῶς accepti) Filius unigenitus vere quoq; est ὁ ἀληθινὸς Θεὸς (ὀσιωδῶς) vel verus natura Deus. Quæ hic contradictio?

Ad 9. Resp. (1) adversatur hæc ςρεβλότης directe præcedenti. Nam in illa dixerat Socinus certiffi- mum esse pronomen hic non respicere Filium, sed Deum Patrem. Jam vero dicit, hoc potissimum sibi probari, quod non ad Patrem tantum, sed & ad Filium referri debeat. Hæc est Spiritus Sociniani certitudo. (2) Aliud est, pronomen HIC posse eam vim habere, aliud debere hoc loco ita accipi. Hoc, non il- lud probandum. (3) Sed nec illud probatur iis exemplis, quæ adferuntur. Prius Matth. XIII. 38. τὸ καλὸν σπέρμα, ὗτοί εἰσιν οἱ ὑοὶ τῆς βασιλείας, non ostendit pronomen ὗτος referri ad totam orationem, & masculinum poni pro neutro: Sed tan- tum quod pronomen congruat nonnunquam nomini sequenti in genere & numero, licet re- spiciat nomen antecedens (hic enim respicit, quod proxime antecessit καλὸν σπέρμα ejusque tradit ἐξήγησιν) id quod non inficiamur, præsertim in συνέσει, cum scil. talis idiotismus, & enallage indicat, quod de persona sermo sit, ut Gal. III. 16. Eph. I. 13. 14. &c. Sed quis non videt, hoc im- præsentiarium esse prorsus ἀπροσδιόνυσον? Poste- rius est e Joh. XVII. 3. petitum, ubi pronomen αὕτη more Ebræorum absolute ponitur pro τῦ- το δὲ. Nam cum Ebræi destituantur genere neutro, ideo pro eo usurpant crebro fæmininum. vid. Gen. V. 20. Exod. X. 11. Joh. V. 19. Psal. XII. 4. Ps. XXVII. 4. & in Novo Testamento idem Ebraismus occurrit Marc. XII. 11. Hic vero ha- betur nomen masculinum, nec est Ebraismi su- spicio, ideoque & istud exemplum est ἀλλότριον. (4) Quod autem omnino debeat hoc loco ita accipi pronomen ὗτος, facile probatur, tum, quia sensui simplicissimo locus est concedendus, ubicunque concedi potest. Quis autem sensum istum Socini credet simplicissimum, eque litera ipsa fluentem, quum nemini ante Socinum in men- tem venire potuerit, ubi e contra nostra explica- tio omnibus est obvia, & plana, si textui insistant:

## 5:17
V. 17. Πᾶσα ἀδικία ἁμαρτία ἐστὶ (All unrighteousness is sin) He calls unrighteousness not any ignorance or sudden slip, but whatever is sinned either with deliberation, or with time given for deliberation. Such things have in themselves the thought of injury toward God or men, or both this and that. And such is what John calls ἁμαρτίαν (sin) in this epistle, as we have already said several times. See above III. 5.

Καὶ ἔστι ἁμαρτία μὴ πρὸς θάνατον (And there is a sin not unto death) By outcome. Just as also certain diseases of the body, although dangerous, are said not to be unto death, John XI. 4.

The particle καὶ here has an adversative sense according to some: But there is a sin not unto death. But the common sense is more correctly retained in this way: Every iniquity is sin, and there is found a certain sin, which is not unto death. Where the Vulgate rashly omitted the particle of negation; and there is a sin unto death. Schlichtingius makes a sin not unto death to be apostasy through seduction, the denial of the truth, expressed by fear of death and torments, habits of sin not yet fully inveterate. But why should pardon and grace be granted to these alone, and not truly to other apostasies, and other habits of sins, even if inveterate, when the grace of GOD extends to all men, and Christ has been made a propitiation for the sins of the whole world? 1 Tim. II. 4. seqq. 2 Pet. III. 9. 1 John II. verse 1.

PART II. A recapitulation exhibiting the summary of the epistle, and thus of the whole Theology.

Latin:

V. 17. Πᾶσα ἀδικία ἁμαρτία ἐστὶ ) Ἀδικίαν vocat non quamvis ignorantiam aut obreptionem subitam, sed quic- quid peccatur aut cum deliberatione, aut dato ad delibe- randum spatio. Talia in se habent cogitationem injuriæ circa Deum aut homines, aut hos & illum. Et tale est, quod in hac epistola Johannes vocat ἁμαρτίαν, ut jam aliquoties diximus. Vide supra III. 5.

Καὶ ἔστι ἁμαρτία μὴ πρὸς θάνατον ) Eventu. Quomo- do & corporum morbi quidam, quamvis periculosi, dicun- tur ἐκ εἶναι πρὸς θάνατον, Joh. XI. 4.

Particula καὶ hic sensum adversativum juxta nonnullos habet : Sed est peccatum non ad mor- tem. Sed rectius retinetur sensus vulgaris hoc modo: Omnis iniquitas est peccatum, & reperi- tur quoddam peccatum, quod non est ad mortem. Ubi temere Vulgatus particulam negandi omisit; & est peccatum ad mortem. Peccatum non ad mortem Schlichtingius facit apostasiam per sedu- ctionem, veritatis abnegationem, metu mortis & tormentorum expressam, peccatorum habitus non- dum plane inveteratos. Sed cur his solis non vero & aliis apostasiis, aliisque habitibus peccatorum, etsi inveteratis, occupatis, venia & gratia sit con- cedenda, quum gratia DEI se porrigat ad omnes homines, & Christus propitiatio factus sit pro totius mundi peccatis? 1. Tim. II. 4. seqq. 2. Petr. III. 9. 1. Joh. II. vers. 1.

PARS II. Ἀνακεφαλαίωσις summam epistolæ, adeoque totius Theologiæ exhibens.

## 5:18
Verse 18. We know that everyone who is born of God does not sin) One must not here understand 'unto death', but the word 'to sin' is to be taken generally, truly in the sense which we have already stated. And 'born' here, as above in III. 9, denotes a permanent quality; he who is a Son of God, i.e., who preserves the vivid word of God, he does not sin, i.e., he will not do iniquity, Rom. VI. 13. 1 Cor. 13, 6. 2 Tim. II. 19. But he added this deservedly, lest those who might think that they could both be sons of God, and meanwhile commit those sins which are not so unto death. Therefore he admonishes them of his name, so that, mindful of it, they may raise up others who are falling, and not fall by their example.

But he who is born of God) He who perseveres in being a Son of God. Thus both the Syrian and the Arab read, and thus the Manuscript has it, not 'the birth of God'.

He keeps himself) He watches and solicitously guards himself from such sins. Thus 'keep yourself pure', 1 Tim. V. 22. 'to keep oneself unspotted', James I. 27. A similar locution Prov. VII. 5. XVI. 18.

And the wicked one does not touch him) It is a litotes for 'does not wound him', as Gen. XXVI. 29. Ps. CV. 15. Ps. LXIII. 14. & CV. 15. 80. XIX. 21. Is. LIII. 4. He who is such, repels the fiery darts of the Devil with the shield of faith, Eph. VI. 6. He is tempted, but does not fall into temptation. He is delivered from that evil one, as it is in the Lord's Prayer, to which see the things said.

In this recapitulation, as it coheres with the preceding, he repeats 1. what he had taught concerning the regenerate, that they do not sin, but keep themselves, lest they be overcome by the Devil. 2. He applies this to the faithful, that they are certain that they are from God, whereas on the contrary the whole world outside of Christ lies in the wicked one. 3. He teaches that for this reason the Son of God came into the world, and gave us a true understanding, that we might know that true God the Father, and might be (through faith) in that true Son of God Jesus Christ. 4. He asserts that this Son of God Jesus Christ is the true God and eternal life. Finally, he warns them to keep themselves from idolatry, lest they worship and venerate any other than that true God the Father, nor otherwise than in Jesus Christ his Son.

Therefore, the things which he says about the regenerate are two: first, that they do not sin, which is repeated from chapter III. 9, where it is more fully explained, from which the Manichaeans among the ancient heretics, distinguishing men into three orders: the earthy, the intermediate, and the good, wished to deduce these latter, who, created from the matter of light and from a good principle, are not capable of sin, nor can they sin, even if they wish. Jovinian, however, in Jerome, book II against Jovinian, pretended that a man truly baptized cannot sin any longer, and if by chance he sins, he was not dipped, except in water. The Pelagians, moreover, concluded that a man in this life can and ought to live without any sin, as Augustine testifies in book II of 'On the Merits and Remission of Sins', chapter 7, and that only venial sins, which are such by nature, have a place in them (see Bellarmine, book I, 'On the Loss of Grace and the State of Sin', chapter 9); that faith and justice once received cannot be lost, Calvin on John 3:9. The Socinians (to whom Grotius is related) gather that the heart and nature of the reborn is not inclined to sin, and that they themselves can live without sin: finally, the new fanatics dream that through regeneration the substance of the former body is abolished, a new body is given, and the reborn do not have sin in that flesh, nor can it happen that they sin; against whom B. Gerhard dealt with this figment in Disputation I on the new fanatics, and, having overthrown the figment about the substantial abolition of the former body, showed that sin clings to the flesh as long as they live in this life, and that the reborn can fall into sins against conscience, through which they lose faith, the grace of God, the Holy Spirit, and eternal life. But having dismissed those figments of the heretics, which are contrary to the analogy of faith, we noted above that Ambrose explains this passage concerning the state of future glory, which, however, is foreign to the mind of the Apostle, as his scope in 1. John 3:10, which is to distinguish the children of God and the Devil, teaches. Augustine, in book II of 'On the Merits and Remission of Sins', chapter 8, says that this, that they do not sin, is said of the reborn insofar as they are children of God and by reason of renovation, not insofar as they are children of this age, with respect to the oldness of the flesh, which senses are likewise absent from the intention of the Apostle. But Augustine more correctly in Tractate 5 on John, and Jerome in book I against the Pelagians and book II against Jovinian, explain these things concerning mortal sins and those that devastate the conscience, which, in the reborn, insofar as they remain reborn, have no place. What we proved regarding chapter 3:9; and it is sufficiently clear from the following verses in what sense it is said that he who is born of God does not sin, because it is added: we know that we are from God, and the whole world is placed in the evil one, namely that he does not conform himself to the world, does not indulge in sins as worldly men and those not yet reborn are accustomed to do, but fights against the world and overcomes it through faith, which, however, we are taught is not done without the struggle of the flesh and the spirit, Romans 7:14 ff., Galatians 5:14. It therefore means that the reborn, as long as they are reborn, do not sin by purpose against conscience, since the grace of regeneration and a deliberate purpose of sinning cannot stand together.

The other thing, therefore, which the Apostle asserts about the reborn is that those who are born of God keep themselves with all care and zeal, so that they do not fall into sins against conscience, with the promise added that the evil one, that is, not the world, as Didymus and Thomas Aquinas wish, but the Devil, does not touch him, so as to harm him, in the way that 'touch' is taken in Zechariah 8:8 and Psalm 104:15, or does not touch him, namely in such a way as to subject him to himself, when, clothed with Christ who overcame the prince of the world, they overcome the world and Satan by faith that is the victor of the world. Therefore, however much the evil one may solicit the reborn to sin, his darts nevertheless fall in vain, because the reborn, protected by the shield of faith, repels them and resists the Devil through faith, Ephesians 6, 1 Peter 5. Flacius on this passage. The pious man therefore preserves himself, or rather guards himself, as it is in the Greek, because he both takes heed with all zeal that he does not sin, and prays to God that He may preserve him from all temptation and sin, and afterwards, by repenting maturely, seeks forgiveness for the sins committed. That 'the evil one does not touch him' signifies by litotes that he does not wound him lethally, he never entirely brings him into his power: but God both at the beginning drives Satan away from His own, and does not suffer them to be tempted beyond what they can bear, and then afterwards also maturely heals them from the poisonous bites of that serpent.

Latin:

Vers. 18. Οἴδαμεν ὅτι πᾶς ὁ γεγεννημένος ἐκ Θεῦ ἐχ ἁμαρτάνει) Non est hic subintelligendum πρὸς θάνατον, sed vox ἁμαρτάνειν generaliter sumenda, verum eo quo jam diximus sensu. Et γεγεννημένος hic ut supra III. 9. quali- tatem permanentem notat; qui Filius Dei est, i. e. qui ver- bum Dei vividum conservat, is ἐχ ἁμαρτάνει, i. e. ὐ ποιήσει ἀδικίαν, Rom. VI. 13. 1. Cor. 13, 6. 2. Tim. II. 19. Hoc autem merito addidit, ne, qui putarent, se & filios Dei esse posse, & interim illa peccata, quæ non ita sunt ad mortem, com- mittere. Ideo admonet eos sui nominis, ut ejus memo- res alios labentes erigant, non eorum exemplo labantur.

Ἀλλ᾿ ὁ γεννηθεὶς ἐκ τῦ Θεῦ) Qui Dei Filius esse perse- veret. Sic legerunt & Syrus & Arabs, & sic habet Manu- scriptus, non ἡ γέννησις τῦ Θεῦ.

Τηρεῖ ἑαυτὸν) Vigilat atque solicitè sibi cavet a pecca- tis talibus. Sic σεαυτὸν ἁγνὸν τήρει, 1. Tim. V. 22. ἄσπιλον ἑαυτὸν τηρεῖν, Jac. I. 27. Par loquutio Prov. VII. 5. XVI. 18.

Καὶ ὁ πονηρὸς ὐχ ἅπτεται ἀυτῦ) Est λιτότης pro non vulnerat eum, ut Gen. XXVI. 29. Psal. CV. 15. Psal. LXIII. 14. & CV. 15. 80. XIX. 21. Es. LIII. 4. Qui talis est, fidei scuto re- pellit ignita Diaboli tela, Eph. VI. 6. tentatur, sed non incidit in tentationem. Liberatur ab illo maligno, ut est in prece Dominica, ad quam dicta vide.

In hac recapitulatione uti cohæret cum præ- cedentibus, repetit 1. quod docuerat de regenitis, quod non peccent, sed se custodiant, ne a Diabo- lo vincantur. 2. applicat id ad fideles, quod certi sint, se ex Deo esse, quum contra totus mundus ex- tra Christum in maligno jaceat. 3. Docet, ideo venisse Filium Dei in mundum, & dedisse nobis ve- rum intellectum, ut agnosceremus verum illum De- um Patrem, & essemus (per fidem) in vero illo Filio Dei Jesu Christo. 4. Asserit, hunc Dei Filium Jesum Christum esse verum Deum & vitam æter- nam. Tandem monet, ut custodiant semetipsos ab idololatriæ, ne alium, quam illum verum Deum Patrem, nec aliter quam in Jesu Christo Filio ejus colant ac venerentur.

Quæ ergo de regenitis dicit, duo sunt: primum quod non peccent, quod e cap. III. 9. repetitur, ubi plenius id explicatum, e quo e veteribus hæreti- cis Manichæi homines in tres ordines χοικὸς, me- dios, & bonos distinguentes hos postremos dedu- cere volebant, qui ex materia lucis & a bono prin- cipio creati non sint capaces peccati, nec peccare possint, etsi velint. Jovinianus vero apud Hierony- mum l. II. contr. Jovin. hominem vere baptizatum non posse amplius peccare, & si forte peccet, non fuisse tinctum, nisi aqua, fingebat. Pelagiani autem hominem in hac vita sine peccato omni vivere posse & debere Augustino l. II. de peccat. merit. & remiss. c. 7. teste, concludebant, nec nisi venialia, quæ natura talia sunt, in iis locum habere (vid. Bellarm. l. I. de amiss. grat. & stat. pecc. cap. 9.) fidem & justitiam semel acceptam amitti non posse, Cal- vin. in Johan. III. 9. Sociniani (quibus affinis est Grotius) quod renatorum cor & natura non sit inclinata ad peccatum, quodque ipsi vivere possint sine peccato colligunt: Novi denique fanatici per regenerationem abolita corporis prioris substantia novum corpus dari ac renatos in carne illa non habere peccatum, nec fieri posse, ut peccent, so- mniant: contra quos de hoc commento disp. I. de nov. fanat. B. Gerhardus egit, & profligato com- mento de corporis prioris substantiali abolitione peccatum in carne hærere, quamdiu in hac vita degunt, renatosque in peccata contra conscien- tiam prolabi posse, per quæ fidem, gratiam DEI, Sp. S. & vitam æternam amittunt, ostendit. Missis autem illis hæreticorum commentis, analogiæ fidei contrariis, Ambrosium de statu futuræ glo- riæ hunc locum explicare supra notavimus, quod vero alienum esse a mente Apostoli, scopus ejus 1. Joh. III. 10. qui est discernere filios DEI & Dia- boli, docet. Augustinus l. II. de peccat. merit. & remiss. c. 8. de renatis hoc, quod non peccent, dici ait, quatenus filii Dei sunt & ratione renovationis, non quatenus filii hujus seculi sunt, respectu vetu- statis carnis, qui sensus itidem ab intentione Apo- stoli absunt. Rectius autem Augustinus tract. 5. in Joh. & Hieronymus l. I. c. Pelag. & l. II. c. Jovin. de peccatis mortalibus, ac conscientiam vastanti- bus hæc explicant, quæ in renatis, quatenus renati manent, locum non habeant. Quod ad c. III. 9. pro- bavimus; & e seqq. satis luculentum est quo sen- su dicatur, quod qui natus est ex Deo, non pec- cet, quia additur: scimus quoniam ex Deo sumus, & mundus totus in maligno positus est, quod nem- pe non conformet se mundo, non indulgeat pec- catis sicut homines mundani & nondum renati solent, sed contra mundum pugnet, eumque per fidem vincat, quod tamen non sine lucta carnis & spiritus fieri, Rom. VII. 14. seqq. Gal. V. 14. do- cemur. Id ergo vult, quod renati, quamdiu renati sunt, non peccent ex proposito contra conscientiam, siquidem gratia regenerationis, & propositum pec- candi deliberatum simul stare nequeant.

Alterum ergo, quod de renatis asserit Aposto- lus, est, quod, qui ex Deo nati sunt, seipsos omni cura atque studio custodiant, ne in peccata contra consci- entiam labantur, addita promissione, quod mali- gnus, id est, non mundus, ut Didymus & Thomas Anglicus volunt, sed Diabolus, non tangat, ut læ- dat eum, quomodo Zach. VIII. 8. tangere accipi- tur, & Ps. CIV. 15. vel non tangit, ita scilicet, ut sibi subjiciat, quum fide mundi victrice Christum, qui Principem mundi superavit, induti, ejus virtute mundum & Satanam vincant. Utut ergo malignus renatum ad peccandum solicitet, tela tamen illius irrita cadunt, quoniam renatus scuto fidei muni- tus ea repellit, & Diabolo per fidem resistit, Eph. VI. 1. Petr. V. Flacius in h. l. Conservat igitur pius seipsum, vel potius custodit, ut est in Græco, quia & cavet omni studio, nec peccet, & orat Deum, ut se con- servet ab omni tentatione, & peccato, & postea mature resipiscendo petit condonationem peccatorum admisso- rum. Malus ille non tangit significat per liptoten, quod eum non sauciet lethaliter plane, non prorsus eum redigit unquam in suam potestatem: sed tum ini- tio Deus abigit Satanam a suis, nec patitur eos tenta- ri supra quam ferre possint, tum postea etiam mature ipsos a serpentis illius venenatis morsibus sanat.

## 5:19
Verse 19. We know that we are from God) We are conscious to ourselves that we have put on a certain divine character through the Gospel: wherefore it is no wonder if our morals differ from the morals of others.

And the whole world lies in the evil one) That 'in the evil one' can be taken either in the neuter gender or the masculine. But although 'the evil one' excels in the masculine gender, it is better here to be taken in the neuter, with an allusion, however, to that masculine. He, namely the Devil, is evil, and the world is carried toward evils. It is a locution taken from that Exodus 32:22, 'for he is in evil', where the Chaldean says: 'Because he is prone to evil', as if to say: He is wrapped in malice.

He applies to the faithful what the Apostle said, and teaches them to know for certain, and in no way to doubt, that they are from God, which he had taught more fully above; he also describes the state of the world outside of Christ, that it is entirely in the evil one, subject to his power, and through him to every evil, from which it cannot be freed except through regeneration from God and faith in Christ. Therefore he subjoins the remedy which we have in the Son of God. Flacius sets forth this fruit of faith thus: That since we know that all mortals are most unjust, and guilty of eternal destruction, and finally slaves of Satan, we may also know through the same [faith] without doubt that the Son of God came into the world, led us, illuminated through faith and the Word, to the knowledge of the heavenly Father, and made us both His children and His members, and thus by the benefit of this Son, who is also Himself truthful, we have obtained eternal life. Cornelius a Lapide: The whole world is placed in the wicked one, that is, in malice, concupiscence, which solicits to every crime. For because the world, that is, all the men of the world in Adam sinning contracted original sin and concupiscence, hence through it they are driven to every evil, thus Oecumenius, Bede, Lyranus and others. Whence St. Ambrose in Apolog. David. c. 2. The world, he says, is placed in the wicked one, because all men are born under sin, whose very origin is in vice.

Latin:

Vers. 19. Οἴδαμεν ὅτι ἐκ Θεῦ ἐσμεν) Conscii nobis sumus, nos per Evangelium divinam quandam induisse indolem: quare mirum non est, si nostri mores discongruunt ab alio- rum moribus.

Καὶ ὁ κόσμος ὅλος ἐν τῷ πονηρῷ κεῖται) Potest illud ἐν τῷ πονηρῷ sumi aut Neutro genere aut Masculino. At quanquam πονηρὸς in Masculino genere præcellit, satius est hic sumi in Neutro, cum allusione tamen ad Masculi- num illud. Ille, Diabolus scilicet, malus est, & mundus ad mala fertur.
