Est loquutio sumpta ex illo Exod. XXXII. 22. כי ברע הוא, ubi Chaldæus: Quod pronus est ad ma- lum, quasi dicat: Involutus est malitiæ.

Applicat fidelibus quod dixit Apostolus, do- cetque eosdem certo scire, nec ullatenus de eo du- bitare, quod ex Deo sint, quod supra uberius do- cuerat; statum etiam mundi extra Christum de- scribit, quod totus ἐν τῷ πονηρῷ κεῖται in maligno illo, subjectus ejus potestati, & per eum omni malo, a quo non nisi per regenerationem ex Deo, & fidem in Christo liberari potest. Ideo subjun- git remedium, quod in Filio Dei habemus. Hunc fidei fructum ita effert Flacius: Quod cum scia- mus, omnes mortales esse injustissimos, reosq́; æterni exitii, & deniq́; mancipia Satanæ, per eandem etiam indubitanter sciamus, Filium Dei in mundum ve- nisse, nos per fidem ac Verbum illuminatos ad cæle- stis Patris cognitionem perduxisse, nosq́; tum illius filios, tum & sua membra effecisse, sicque nos bene- ficio hujus Filii, qui & ipse est verax, vitam æter- nam consecutos esse. Cornelius a Lapide: Totus mun- dus positus est in maligno, id est in malitia, concu- piscentia, quæ solicitat ad omne scelus. Quia enim mundus, id est, omnes homines mundi in Adamo peccante contraxerunt peccatum originale & con- cupiscentiam, hinc per eam aguntur ad omne ma- lum, ita Oecumenius, Beda, Lyranus & alii. Unde S. Ambrosius in Apolog. David. c. 2. Mundus, ait, in maligno positus est, quia omnes homines sub peccato nascuntur, quorum ipse ortus est in vitio.

## 5:20
Vers. 20. We know that the Son of God is come) After warnings to beware of Anti-Christs and Pseudo-Prophets, he adds in the last place against the Simonians, and those of the falsely-named knowledge, who said that that God, whom Jesus had taught was to be worshipped, was not that supreme God, and furthermore that the gods of the nations could be worshipped without sin. See what we have said in the preface to the Gospel of John and to Matt. XXIV. v. 11. For ἥκει let the Syrian and Arab be seen to have read ἧκε, I think the Latin also. Although the Latin word is ambiguous between the past and the present. But because the past follows immediately, it is more correct to be taken, as I said ἧκε, thus take it as ἐληλυθότα, above IV. vers. 23. ἐλθὼν V. 6. He manifests himself to men by words and deeds.

And he has given us an understanding) he has enlightened the understanding, Eph. I. 18. he opened the mind, Luke XXIV. 45. namely by teaching, and by confirming what he taught with miracles.

That we may know the true God. Thus both the Manuscript and the Latin. The true God, that is, the supreme, eternal, best, the author of all things both visible and invisible. Thus we have ἀληθινὸς Θεὸς also in John XVII. 3. and 1 Thess. 1. 9. The sense is the same in Acts XIV. vers. 15. See what we have said at those places.

And we are in the true one) Supply God from that which precedes and follows. To that true God we have been made most closely joined. For to be in God and to remain he uses for the same thing, as we have said.

In his Son Jesus Christ) In this place it signifies by. That conjunction has been made through the Son of that true God. Jesus Christ is not in the Manuscript, just as it is absent in the Latin.

This is the true God) He namely whom Jesus showed and taught was to be worshipped, not another. This often refers to something preceding not immediately, as Acts 8, 19. c. 10, 6.

Καὶ ζωὴ αἰώνι@) Metonymy. For he wishes to say that He is the first and supreme Author of eternal life. Thus also Christ is called life, John 11:25, ch. 15:6, because He is the proximate cause of that same life from God the Father.

It does not appear that this strikes the Simonians and Gnostics; for if the heretics are considered, it must be believed that this is opposed to those whom we noted before, concerning whom Irenaeus writes in book III, chapter 17, who distinguished Jesus and Christ, asserting that Jesus was the receptacle of Christ, in whose name and power he participated, and that he came so that the Father might be known. These things contain a repetition of the preceding, and the Apostle professes his faith concerning the incarnation of the Son of God, and the cause of the same, so that we may trustfully acknowledge the true God, such as He revealed Himself in His Son, insofar as He gave Him as a propitiation for sins, and as the Savior of the world, and in Him gave us eternal life. Just as St. John asserted this throughout the whole epistle, so now he presents it in summary, and so that no one might separate the Son from the Father, he says not only that we are in the Son, just as in chapter 1, verse 4, he had said that our communion is no less with the Son than with the Father, but with a resonant voice he repeats it again, and in the place of a colophon he inculcates that the Son is the true God, and eternal life. Cornelius a Lapide explains these things thus: as if to say, God for this reason sent His Son into the world and into the flesh, so that through His divine teaching He might give us a sense and knowledge of heavenly things, so that, namely, having abandoned idols as false gods, and having been freed from sin, the Devil, and the world, we might know the true God, and be incorporated into His Son, namely Christ, and into the Church through faith, hope, and charity, and thus be gifted by Him with the life of grace and glory. For He Himself is the true God and He Himself is the true uncreated and eternal life. And to the words: And we may be in His true Son: The Greek, says the Syrian, and Athanasius on this, read God from God, and we may be in Him who is true, namely in His Son Jesus Christ, by which it is signified that the Son is consubstantial with the Father, in that He Himself is true and truth by essence, namely true Deity, just as God the Father is; thus Didymus, St. Jerome in the cited place, St. Athanasius, Cyril, Nazianzen, and all others writing against the Arians. Furthermore, we are in the Son through faith and grace, which we draw from Him, just as a branch is in a tree, from which it draws sap and life, according to that saying of Christ: I am the vine, you are the branches; as a branch cannot bear fruit of itself, unless it has remained in the vine, so neither can you, unless you have remained in me, John 15, 1 and 4. Grotius, choosing the depravation of the worst heretics, the Socinians, over the faith of the Catholics, understands this not of the Son of God, but of God the Father. Since, however, the Deity of the Son of God has been asserted by us against the Socinians from this illustrious passage, it is pleasing to repeat those things here from scattered notes. Our argument stands thus: He who is the true God, He is by nature the eternal God. But Christ is the true God. Therefore, Christ is by nature the eternal God. The major premise is established (1) because He is not the true God, unless He enjoys true Deity, and thus true divine essence: just as He is not a true man, unless He consists of true humanity, that is, true human nature; (2) because the name of the true God is attributed to no one in the Scriptures, except to the supreme God alone; (3) because God with the article, according to the adversaries, is not called anything but the supreme God. The name God with the article always denotes that true God, who is the supreme God, by way of excellence, says Crellius in his book on God and divine attributes, chapter 13; (4) because this true God is here opposed to idols. But to idols, and to those who are not by nature gods, to those who are not gods by nature, He is not opposed as the true God, unless He is God by nature, and thus that one supreme God. (5) Enjedinus himself urges these reasons on page 432, to prove that God the Father (who is without controversy the supreme God) is indicated here by that name, first because elsewhere also God the Father alone is always accustomed to be called the true God, John 17, 3; 1 Thessalonians 1, that you may serve the living and true God, and here (1 John 5) the Father is twice called the true God, etc. Then the Greek article everywhere added to the word true indicates that this concerns God, who is God by way of excellence, and has received divinity from no one. Thirdly, this true God is here opposed to idols, as the last words of John show. But only the Father is accustomed to be opposed to idols in Scripture, 1 Thessalonians 1, 9. These things are from Enjedinus. From which it is permitted to gather that he does not only admit, but also supports with reasons, that proposition, that namely we are and the true God by nature is understood here by the true God. Which the other Socinians likewise acknowledge and confess in their commentaries on this passage, Schmalzius, Crellius, etc.

We confirm the minor premise (1) from the connection of the context, both in this verse: We know that the Son of God has come, and has given us a sense, that we may know the true God, and may be in Him, in the true One, in His Son Jesus Christ: where Christ is also called the true One, and lest He be thought to be different from the Father, or not to be the true God with the Father, it is added that He is that very true God, who is the Father, because as John had said in verse 7, the Father and the Word or Son are one, according to being in essence, and also in the preceding verse 11, God has given us eternal life, and this life is in His Son, chapter 5, 12. He who has the Son, has life, verse 20, whence he now subjoins: this is the true God and eternal life. I argue: He who is that eternal life, the same is that true God. But Christ the Son of God is that eternal life, as is evident from the comparison of verses 11 and 12. Therefore, Christ is that true God. (2) from the nature of the demonstrative pronoun. For the demonstrative pronoun this ordinarily, unless the text evidently requires otherwise, looks to and demonstrates the immediately preceding noun. But here the noun preceding proximately and immediately is the name Jesus Christ. Therefore it looks to that, and not to the more remote name of the Father. (3) from the harmony of other contexts: For St. John, partly in this same epistle near the beginning, chapter 1, 2, calls the Word, the Son of God, the eternal life, which was with the Father, as the eternal God in the beginning of the creation of all things, John 1, 1, and afterwards was manifested to us (which 1 Timothy 3, 6. God is said to have been manifested in the flesh) and furthermore, where he treats again of the equal communion which we have with the Father and the Son v. 3. whom therefore here also, at the end of the Epistle, treating of the same argument, he wished to call true God and eternal life in like manner: partly he taught in the Gospel c. 1. that life was in the λόγῳ and that he himself was life v. 4. whom the same one he also calls God v. 1. and declares and demonstrates to be eternal with a clear voice. Compare also John 11. v. 25. and c. 14, 6. Add that God the Father is nowhere in the N. T. called either ζωὴ or ζωὴ αἰώνιος, but the Son of God, inasmuch as he is the restorer of eternal life, and has led us anew to eternal life. But the same one who is called eternal life is called true God. Socinus himself confesses that Christ is included under this title, but he tears it apart, and refers the former ὁ ἀληθινὸς Θεὸς to the Father, and refers the latter ἡ ζωὴ αἰώνιος to the Son of God l. c. p. 521. But those things cannot be torn apart which St. John has joined and attributed to a single subject, as the manifest words have it: ὗτός ἐστιν ὁ ἀληθινὸς Θεὸς καὶ ἡ ζωὴ αἰώνιος. (3) From the context of the text. For imagine that the more remote pronoun is being pointed to; what will the sense be? That more remote one is ὁ ἀληθινὸς Θεὸς in these words ἵνα γινώσκωμεν τὸν ἀληθινὸν Θεὸν. The Syriac indeed and the Vulgate Greek copies do not read the word Θεὸς, yet in the Complutensian Greek edition, as also in the Latin Vulgate, and likewise in Basil, book 4 against Eunomius, and Cyril, book 3 on the Trinity, it is read entirely, and according to Socinus, loc. cit. pp. 513, 514, it must necessarily be read, whence if the pronoun οὗτος demonstrates not the nearer Christ, but the more remote true God, (the Father of Christ) this will be a proposition plainly identical and inept, οὗτος (the true God) is the true God: or according to the common copies οὗτος the true (understand God) is the true God, so that again a true tautology emerges. Enjedinus indeed objects, as does Goslavius against Keckerm. p. 1. c. 3., that it is familiar to John and the Hebrews to repeat the same thing quite often: But it is one thing to repeat the same proposition, another to have an identical proposition: the former is done without fault, but the latter is inept, and ought not to be attributed to the Holy Writers. Furthermore, Enjedinus denies that it is a tautology, because by this word the Father of Jesus Christ is understood, since Jesus Christ is said to be the Son of that God. But if the Father of Jesus Christ had previously been named simply as the true God in the text, and now he demonstrates him by the pronoun this, then certainly that which was placed in the text must be repeated from the common [antecedent], and that which the adversaries wish the pronoun in the text to demonstrate, that indeed is nothing other than the true God. Thus, therefore, a tautology still remains: This he (which pronoun immediately precedes, and looks back to the more remote name of the true God) is that true God, that true God. Finally, Enjedinus strives to gather the contrary from there: If in the nearest words God the Father is twice named the true God, with what imprudence and inconstancy, he says, would one immediately transfer that title to another? But in this way he does not escape the tautology. Nor indeed is the name true God attributed to the Father twice in the nearest words, but only once, nor is it anything other than divine truth, which the heretic impiously calls inconstancy and imprudence, namely that the Son of God is also the true God and eternal life, whom the Apostle had a little before in verse 7 called one with the true God the Father and the Holy Spirit. (5) From the unanimous opinion of the Church. For thus far it has been confessedly established in the Church, that here the Son of God himself is called the true God because of the evidence of the testimony of the Sun, as it is said, by the ray of the Scripture, so much so that even Arius himself acknowledged this, when Athanasius opposed this saying to him. See the disputation against Arius in the Council of Nicaea, Tom. 3 of his works, p. 201; nay, that some of the more recent Anti-Trinitarians have confessed this, that these words are to be referred to Christ himself, is evident from Socinus, l. c. p. 516. Such is the force and evidence of this testimony, which for that reason the Blessed Athanasius called a written demonstration, l. c.

But Socinus, Enjedinus, the Racovian Catechism, Schmalz, Goslavius, and Volckelius seek various subterfuges to refute the testimony. Enjedinus first denies that Christ would be the eternal God, even if he were called the true God, since it is certain that the true is opposed to the fictitious and imaginary: but those whom God makes gods, they are not shadowy, but true gods, and yet not eternal. (2) Furthermore, Enjedinus denies, and with him the others, that the pronoun this looks to Christ, and they contend that the Father is looked to by it, and so they flee either to a parenthesis, namely that the preceding words ought to be included in a parenthesis and we are in the true, in his Son Jesus Christ, which Socinus establishes as quite probable, appealing to the judgment and consent of all who have not been previously fascinated by the contrary opinion, in his response against Wujeck, p. 320. or they also (3) betake themselves to a peculiar use of the relative, namely that it is referred to the true God, for the reason that relative pronouns, especially in John, are often accustomed not to refer to him who was named immediately before, but to him who was more remote. Thus Socinus, Enjedinus, and others. (4) Especially, however, that in this place the subject is not Christ, but God the Father, (5) and that nowhere else is Christ called that true God, or is such a thing openly affirmed about him. (6) That, moreover, that true God is opposed to idols in the last verse. But Christ is nowhere found to be opposed to idols by himself. (7) That it is clearly likely that those immediately preceding words, and we are in that true one, are to be referred to that same true one, the knowledge of whom the Son of God coming gave to us, so that what immediately follows in his Son may be taken, according to the Hebrew idiom, as if it had been written through his Son. Thus Socinus in Anti-Wujeck, and Enjedinus. (8) That we are said to arrive at the knowledge of the true God through the Son of God, which is said ridiculously and most ineptly, and contradictorily, if those words: This is the true God, pertain to Christ, says Volckelius, l. 5. de ver. Rel. c. 10. p. 424. Finally (9) they say that that pronoun this can here be referred to that whole thing which immediately preceded, in this way, in that which we have said, is that true God, and eternal life, which explanation Socinus says in his Commentary p. 520 is most approved by him, so that thus this is referred not only to the Father, but also to Christ, as he asserts both there and on p. 320 against Wujeck. But that the pronoun, even though it is masculine, can have that force here, he proves, because such pronouns sometimes do not agree in gender and number with the subject, but with the predicate, as Matt. 13:38, John 17:3. Enjedinus adds that we are accustomed to speak thus often, this is, for in this consists, as Apoc. 13:18, this is wisdom, and chap. 17:9, this is the place, etc. p. 432.

Regarding (1) Response. No one is called the true God, except he who is God by nature, just as no one is a true man, except he who has a human nature. Magistrates and Judges, just as they are called gods at least equivocally, so they ought not to be called true gods: since they participate in the name only, not in the truth and essence of the thing. The true is not opposed only to the fictitious, but also to the non-true: since truth is an affection of Being. Furthermore, it is false, according to the Scriptures, that he is called the true God who is made by God: since no one is called the true God in the Scriptures except that one supreme God, John 17:3, 1 Thess. 1:9. But why many words? Since the adversaries themselves acknowledge that no one other than the supreme God is to be understood here by the true God, which Enjedinus also proves with arguments on page 432.

To (2) Response. No trace of that parenthesis appears in any of the most approved codices. It is therefore merely fabricated, and too arbitrary. Furthermore, it is so far from being confirmed by the consensus of all, that it is sufficiently refuted by the very fact that for so many centuries in the Christian world no one has been found who ever even suspected such a parenthesis. And it seems that now to Socinus himself that previously quite probable parenthesis is no longer probable: since in his commentary on this passage, where he repeats the other exceptions from his treatise against Wujeck, he made no mention of it, which certainly should not have been omitted in its proper place, if it is held to be worthy by the judgment and consensus of all.

To (3) Response. It is not a relative, but a demonstrative pronoun ʊ̂τός that occurs here. In vain, therefore, are examples gathered from Scripture concerning the use of the relative pronoun; 2 Thess. 2:9, Heb. 5:17, the relative pronoun ὃς is held, not indeed the demonstrative pronoun ʊ̂τός. (2) When the demonstrative pronoun ʊ̂τός occurs in Scripture, and the substantive verb ἐςιν follows with the article ὁ, as in this place, ʊ̂τός ἐςιν ὁ, not a more remote subject, but the noun immediately preceding, to which it corresponds in gender and number, is understood. See examples Matt. 3:17, ch. 7:12, ch. 21:11, ch. 27:37, Mark 6:2, 3, ch. 7:6, ch. 12:6, 7, John 1:33, ch. 4:29, ch. 6:14, 48, 49, 50, ch. 7:40, 41, 1 John 5:5, 6. And thus the examples in Acts 2:19, ch. 10:6 are dissimilar, inasmuch as in them the substantive verb and the article, ὁ, do not follow, as in this place. (3) But even if we admit that sometimes, although quite rarely also the demonstrative pronoun οὗτος ought to be drawn to a more remote [antecedent], yet that never happens without the context most openly indicating, nay demanding it, as is to be seen in Acts 4:11, 1 John 2:22. Therefore it is never to be referred to a more remote one, unless when the context itself compels that it cannot be referred to the nearest. For the natural use of a demonstrative is to demonstrate the immediately preceding, which is not to be abandoned without necessity, as very many examples of Scripture teach, specifically in D. John ch. 1, 2, 7, 15, 33, 34, ch. 3, 2, ch. 4, 29, ch. 16, 14, 48, 49, 50, 71, ch. 7, 40, 41, ch. 9, 20, ch. 18, 21, 1 John 5, 5, 6, etc. Hence here also it will have to be referred to the nearest, until the Socinians prove from the context that it cannot be referred to it. (4) Socinus says in Antivv., as also in Comment. p. 518, that those pronouns refer to that which is chiefly treated, and then demonstrate that which had been named more remotely. But here the subject is chiefly Christ, not God the Father. It is not to be denied, therefore, that this pronoun demonstrates Christ. (5) We have shown abundantly, and have proven by arguments above, that the pronoun οὗτος ought not to be referred to the more remote God, but to the nearer name of Christ: and therefore there is no reason for us to do the work twice over. (6) What of the fact that Socinus himself, seeing that he could not deflect the force of our arguments by this evasion—that the more remote antecedent is to be looked at—betakes himself elsewhere, and asserts that both the Father and Christ are comprehended by this pronoun, concerning which [see] around the last exception to this place.

To 4. To prove that the subject here is chiefly God the Father exclusively, not Christ; rather the contrary is gathered from these things: (1) the subject here is chiefly he who brought it about that we know that true God, which the whole context indicates, who is certainly Christ. (2) The subject here is chiefly he in whom we are, and through whose communion we have eternal life remaining in us. The former member is evident from this verse 20. The latter from a comparison of verses 11, 12, 13 with this verse. But we are in Christ; as the text has it, in his Son Jesus Christ, and through the communion of Christ we have eternal life, v. 11 and 12, as in ch. 1, 2, 3. Therefore. (3) The subject here is chiefly he whom Christ coming brought it about that we should know, as St. John says. But Christ coming brought it about that we should know no less the Son of God than the Father, which is also manifest from John 17:3, since there the knowledge of the Father and of the Son is joined equally, and eternal life is said to consist in the knowledge of both, and it is evident from the scope of the whole Gospel. See John 20:21. Nay, for the knowledge of the Father, the knowledge of the Son is required, as Scripture testifies, John 8:19, ch. 12:46, ch. 14:7, 9. Therefore it must be admitted by Socinus himself that the subject here is no less chiefly the Son than the Father, and thus his exception will collapse entirely, that the Father alone is the chief subject here. (4) What of the fact that it is manifest as clearly as the sun at noon in the whole of chapter 5 that the chief subject is Jesus, so that he who denies this would deny that the sun shines at this midday. Furthermore, if the chief subject of this place were God the Father, and not Christ (which we entirely deny), yet one could not formally infer from that that the pronoun οὗτος demonstrates God the Father, not Christ, because the mention of Christ preceded, who cannot be excluded from the object just as well, even positing that the subject is only secondarily and incidentally Christ. For it is known that pronouns often look even to that which occurs only secondarily in the text, and is not the primary subject.

To 5. Resp. Even if the Son of God were nowhere else called true God, it would not follow that he is not called true God here either: provided it is not denied elsewhere that he is true God, which will never be proven. Otherwise, by a similar line of reasoning, I would conclude that Christ is not called God blessed over all forever in Rom. 9:5, because, forsooth, these words are nowhere else enunciated concerning Christ. It is equally certain what is said once in the Scriptures as those things which are said more often. (2) But it is false that equivalent things are nowhere predicated of Christ in the Scriptures. Is it anything else to be God blessed over all than to be that true God? Since the name of the only true God is exalted, and he alone is blessed over all, Ps. 72:1, Ps. 147:13, Ps. 136:4, Is. 2:11, 12, Rom. 1:15, etc. Furthermore, Christ is called elsewhere the true one, Apoc. 3:14, ch. 19:11, his name is called the true one and the Word (which Word John 1:1 is said to be God. Conf. ch. 20, Acts 20:28) and King of kings: and Lord of lords (which is a periphrasis of the one true God, 1 Tim. 6:15, as also with the prefixed article the holy one, the true one, Apoc. 3:7. Nor is any other noted in this place by the former words we are in the true one, than the true one, that true one, who is so called by way of excellence, and is the truth itself, or truth itself.

To 6. Resp. (1) That the consequence is made from the undistributed to the distributed. Christ is not otherwise opposed to idols by himself. Therefore not in this place either. (2) Moreover, the antecedent is false. For Gal. 4:3, Christ is opposed to those who are not by nature gods. For the Galatians, having certainly been converted to Christ, were serving the same, and had a saving knowledge of him. Furthermore, I argue from Is. 45:22, 23. To whom all the ends of the earth ought to convert themselves, he is opposed there by himself to idols, which is clearer than the sun from the whole chapter. But all the ends of the earth ought to convert themselves to Christ, so that every knee may bow to him. Conf. v. 23 with Rom. 14:11, Phil. 2:10. Therefore Christ is opposed by himself to idols. See also Ps. 86:10. Likewise from Luke 1:16, 17. Whose forerunner was John, he converted the people of Israel to him. But Christ's forerunner was [he]. E. Furthermore, from Acts 3:19, 22, it is permitted to gather that true conversion is to Christ, that great Prophet: From Acts 2:21, where a huge multitude is said to have believed and to have been converted to Christ the Lord, πισεύσας ἐπέςρεψεν ἐπὶ τὸν Κύριον, that is to say, the Lord, of whom in v. 20, εὐαγγελίζομενοι τὸν Κύριον Ἰησῦν, and from 1 Pet. 2:last, You were like wandering sheep, but now you have been converted to the Shepherd and Bishop of your souls. Add also v. 4 and 9. Furthermore, those passages which Socinus brings forward, that God the Father alone is opposed to idols, do not exclude Christ, especially indeed Acts 17:24, 30 (as the context partly teaches, from which I gather thus: The Apostle preaches that God as the true God, whom the Epicureans and Stoics reckoned among ξένοις δαιμονίοις, v. 18. But he was Jesus, v. same, partly the open passage 1 Cor. 2:2, whom alone Paul says he knew, and 1 Cor. 6:26. (For he, whose temple the faithful are, is here opposed to idols. But the faithful are temples of Christ, as the parallel written in the margin teaches, Eph. 2:17 and 1 Thess. 1:9 and 10. For there it is explained what it is to convert oneself to God through τὸ δυλεύειν θεῷ ζῶντι καὶ ἀληθινῷ, and there is required for conversion no less true faith in Christ the redeemer than true worship of the true and living God.) Furthermore, since Christ, as the σκόπος σκοπιμώτατος of the whole law, Rom. 10:4, Gal. 3:24, indeed the center of the entire Scripture, John 5:39, ch. XX:21, of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms, Luke XXIV:44, has therefore been preached, so that all nations might convert themselves to him, having abandoned all vanities to which they had hitherto clung, Acts XIV:15, who will deny that conversion to Christ is true conversion from idols and all depravities, especially when true conversion is described through faith in Christ, Acts XVI:34, ch. XXVI:15, and the invocation of the name of the Lord Jesus, Acts II:21, ch. 22.

Latin:

Vers. 20. Οἴδαμεν ὅτι ὁ ὑὸς τῦ Θεῦ ἥκει) Post monita ad cavendos Anti-Christos & Pseudo-Prophetas addit ultimo loco contra Simonianos, & τῆς τῆς ψευδωνύμῳ γνώσεως, qui dicebant illum Deum, quem Jesus colendum docuerat, non esse illum summum Deum, ac præterea gentium Deos coli posse sine peccato. Vide quæ diximus in anteloquio ad Evangelium Johannis & ad Matth. XXIV. v. 11. Pro ἥκει videatur Syrus & Arabs legisse ἧκε, puto & Latinus. Quan- quam Latina vox ambigua est inter præteritum & Præsens. Sed quia Præteritum statim sequitur, rectius est accipi, ut dixi ἧκε, sic accipe sicut ἐληλυθότα, supra IV. vers. 23. ἐλθὼν V. 6. Patefaciat se hominibus per verba & facta.

Καὶ δέδωκεν ἡμῖν διάνοιαν) πεφώτικε τὴν διάνοιαν, Eph. I. 18. διήνοιξε τὸν νῦν Luc. XXIV. 45. nempe docendo, & quod do- cebat, miraculis comprobando.

Ἵνα γινώσκωμεν τὸν ἀληθινὸν Θεὸν. Sic & Manuscriptus & Latinus. Verum Deum, id est, summum, æternum, optimum, autorem rerum omnium & visibilium & invisibilium. Sic ἀληθινὸς Θεὸς habemus & Joh. XVII. 31. & 1. Thess. 9. Sensus idem est Act. XIV. vers. 15. Vide quæ ad ea loca diximus.

Καὶ ἐσμὲν ἐν τῷ ἀληθινῷ) Supple Θεῷ ex eo quod præcedit & sequitur. Illi Deo ve- ro facti sumus conjunctissimi. Nam εἶναι ἐν Θεῷ & μένειν pro eodem usurpat ut diximus.

Ἐν τῷ υἱῷ αὐτῦ Ἰησῦ Χριστῷ) Ἐν hoc loco valet per. Ista conjunctio facta est per Filium Dei veri illius. Ἰησῦ Χριστῷ non est in Manuscripto, sicut & abest in Latino.

Οὗτός ἐστιν ὁ ἀληθινὸς Θεὸς) Is nempe quem Jesus mon- stravit colendumque docuit, non alius. Οὗτος sæpe refertur ad aliquid præcedens non ἀμέσως, ut Act 8, 19. c. 10, 6.

Καὶ ζωὴ αἰώνι@) Μετωνυμία. Vult enim dicere, illum Deum esse Autorem primum ac summum vitæ æternæ. Sic & Christus vita dicitur, Joh. 11, 25. c. 15, 6. quia causa est ejusdem vitæ proxima a Deo Patre.

Non apparet hæc Simonianos, & Gnosticos ferire; quia si respiciantur hæretici, illis, quos antea nota- vimus, hæc opponi credendum, de quibus Irenæus l.III.c.17.qui Jesum & Christum discernebant, Jesum receptaculum Christi,de cujus nomine & virtute par- ticiparit, & venerit, ut Pater cognosceretur asseren- tes. Repetitionem autem hæc continent superio- rum, & profitetur Apostolus fidem suam de Filii Dei incarnatione, & causa ejusdem, ut fiducialiter agnoscamus verumDeum,qualem se patefecit in Fi- lio suo, quatenus eum dedit propitiationem pro pecca- tis,& Salvatorem mundi, & in ipso dedit nobis vitam æternam. Quod uti per totam epistolam asseruit S. Johan. Ita nunc ἐπιλογικω̃ς exhibet, ac ne quis separet Filium a Patre, non modo nos esse in Filio dicit,quemadmodum c.I.4. communionem nostram non minus cum Filio, quam cum Patre esse dixerat, sed sonora voce iterum repetit, ac colophonis lo- co inculcat, Filium esse τὸν ἀληθινὸν Θεὸν verum il- lumDeum,καὶ ζωὴν αἰώνιον vitam æternam.Cornelius a Lapide ita hæc explicat: q. d. Deus idcirco misit Filium suum in mundum & carnem, ut per ejus do- &rinam divinam daret nobis sensum & cognitionem rerum cælestium, ut scilicet relictis idolis, quasi falsis Diis, liberati a peccato, Diabolo & mundo, cognosca- mus verum Deum, ejusq́; Filio puta Christo & Eccle- siæ per fidem, spem & charitatem incorporemur, itaq́; ab eo vita gratiæ & gloriæ donemur. Ipse enim est ve- rus Deus ipsaq́; vera vita increata & æterna. Et ad verba: Et simus in vero Filio ejus: Græca, inquit Syrus, & Athanasius in id, Deus de Deo legunt, & si- mus in ipso vero, nempe in Filio ejus Jesu Christo, quo significatur Filium esse ὁμοόύσιον Patri,eo quod ipse sit verus & veritas per essentiam, puta vera Deitas, æque ac est Deus Pater, ita Didymus, S. Hieronymus loco cit. S. Athanasius, Cyrillus, Nazianzenus, & alii omnes scribentes contra Arianos. Porro sumus in Filio per fidem & gratiam, quam nos ab eo sugimus, sicut ramus est in arbore, a qua succum & vitam su- git, juxta illud Christi: Ego sum vitis, vos palmites; sicut palmes non potest ferre fructum a semetipso, nisi manserit in vite, sic nec vos, nisi in me manseri- tis, Joh.15,1.& 4. Grotius hæreticorum pessimorum Socinianorum depravationem præ fide Catholi- corum eligens non de Filio Dei, sed de Deo Patre intelligit. Quum vero ex hoc illustri loco alias Deitas Filii Dei a nobis contra Socinianos asserta sit, placet ea e schedis disjectis hic repetere. Argu- mentum nostrum ita habet: Qui est ὁ ἀληθινὸς Θεὸς verus ille Deus, is natura Deus æternus est. At Christus est ὁ ἀληθινὸς Θεὸς verus ille Deus. E. Christus natura est æternus Deus. Major statu- minatur (1) quia verus Deus non est, nisi qui vera Deitate, adeoque vera divina essentia gaudet: ut verus homo non est, nisi qui vera humanitate, hoc est, vera humana natura constat (2) quia nulli in Scripturis tribuitur nomen veri Dei,nisi soli summo Deo. (3) quia ὁ Θεὸς cum articulo, secundum ad- versarios, non vocatur nisi summus Deus. Nomen Θεꭣ cum articulo semper verum illum Deum, qui est summus Deus,κατ᾽ ἐξοχὴν denotare, ait Crellius lib. de Deo & attrib. div. c.13. (4) Quia opponitur hic verus Deus idolis. At idolis, & τοι̃ς μὴ φύσει ἐσὶ Θεοι̃ς, his qui natura Dii non sunt, non opponitur ut verus Deus, nisi qui τῃ̃ φύσει natura Deus est, adeoque unus ille summus Deus. (5) Urget has ra- tiones ipse Enjedinus p. 432. ut probet Deum Pa- trem, (qui citra controversiam summus Deus est) eo nomine hic indigitari, primo quia alibi etiam semper solus Deus Pater vocari solet verus De- us Joh. 17, 3. 1. Thes. 1. ut serviatis Deo vivo & vero, & hic (1. Joh. 5.) bis Pater vocatur verus Deus, &c. Deinde articulus Graecus ubiq́; voci ἀληθινὸς additus indicat hic agi de Deo, qui κατ᾽ ἐξοχὴν sit Deus, nec ab ullo divinitatem acceperit. Tertio hic verus Deus opponi- tur idolis, ut postrema verba Johannis ostendunt. At solus Pater solet idolis opponi in Script. 1. Thes. 1, 9. Haec Enjedinus. E quibus colligere licet, quod non ad- mittat tantum, sed rationibus etiam suffulciat illam propositionem, quod nempe sumus & verus natu- ra Deus hic intelligatur per τὸν ἀληθινὸν Θεὸν. Quod agnoscunt pariter & fatentur quoque caeteri Socia nus in comment. in h. l. Schmalzius, Crellius, &c.

Minorem confirmamus (1) e contextus συνέ- χειᾳ, tum in hoc versu: Scimus quoniam Filius Dei venit, & dedit nobis sensum, ut cognoscamus τὸν ἀλη- θινὸν Θεὸν verum illum Deum, & simus in illo ἐν τῷ ἀληθινῷ ἐν τῷ ὑἱῷ αὐτῦ Ἰησᾶ Χριστῦ: ubi verus ille di- citur quoq; Christus, & ne putetur esse diversus a Patre, vel non esse cum Patre verus Deus, additur, quod sit ille ipse verus Deus, qui est Pater, quia ut v. 7. dixerat Johannes, Pater & verbum seu Filius ἕν εἰσι unum sunt, secundum τὸ εἶναι τῇ ὀυσιᾳ, vel essen- tia, tum etiam in antecedentibus v. 11. vitam æter- nam dedit nobis Deus, & haec vita est in Filio c. 5, 12. Qui habet Filium, habet vitam, v. 20. unde subjungit jam: hic est verus Deus & vita æterna. Argumentor: Qui est vita illa æterna, idem est ille verus Deus. At Christus Filius Dei est vita illa æterna, ut e col- latione v. 11. & 12. constat. E. Christus est ille verus Deus. (2) e pronominis demonstrativi natura. Pro- nomen enim demonstrativum ὗτος ordinarie, ni- si evidenter textus aliud requirat, immediate an- tecedens nomen respicit ac demonstrat. At hic nomen antecedens proxime & immediate est no- men ἰησῦ χριστῦ. Illud ergo respicit, non vero re- motius Patris nomen. (3) e contextuum aliorum ἁρμονίᾳ: D. Johannes enim partim in hac eadem epistola sub initium c. 1, 2. λόγον Filium Dei vocat τὴν ζωὴν αἰώνιον, quæ apud Patrem erat, ut æternus Deus in principio creationis rerum omnium Joh. 1, 1. & deinde manifestata est nobis (quod 1. Tim. 3,. 6. dicitur Deus manifestatus in carne) ac porro ubi iterum de pari communione agit, quæ nobis est cum Patre & Filio v. 3. quem proinde hic quoque sub finem Epistolæ de eodem argumento agens Deum verum, & vitam æternam similiter appellare vo- luit: partim in Evangelio c. 1. docuit vitam fuisse in λόγῳ & ipsummet fuisse vitam v. 4. quem eundem etiam v. 1. Deum nuncupat & æternum esse λευκάδι φωνῇ perhibet, ac demonstrat. Conf. quoq; Joh. 11. v. 25. & c. 14, 6. Adde quod Deus Pater nuspiam in N. T. vel ζωὴ vocetur, vel ζωὴ αἰώνιος, sed Filius Dei, utpote qui reparator est æternæ vitæ, nosque perduxit denuo ad vitam æternam. Idem autem qui vita æterna dicitur, verus Deus vocatur. Soci- nus fatetur ipse, quod Christus comprehendatur sub hoc elogio, sed discerpit illud, & prius ὁ ἀλη- θινὸς Θεὸς refert ad Patrem, posterius ἡ ζωὴ αἰώ- νιος refert ad Filium Dei l. c. p. 521. Verum discerpi non possunt, quæ conjunxit S. Joh. unique attri- buit subjecto, ut verba manifesta habent: ὗτός ἐστιν ὁ ἀληθινὸς Θεὸς καὶ ἡ ζωὴ αἰώνιος. (3) E textus συ- νεχείᾳ. Nam finge demonstrari pronomen remo- tius, quis erit sensus? Remotius illud est ὁ ἀληθι- νὸς Θεὸς in hisce verbis ἵνα γινώσκωμεν τὸν ἀληθι- νὸν Θεὸν. Syrus quidem & Vulgata exemplaria Græca non legunt vocem Θεὸς, in Complutensi tamen Græca editione, ut & Latina Vulgata, nec non apud Basilium l. 4. contr. Eunom. & Cyrill. l. 3. de Trin. omnino legitur, & secundum Socinum l. c. p. 513. 514. necessario legenda est, unde si prono- men ὗτός demonstret non propinquius Christum, sed remotius Deum verum, (Patrem Christi) haec erit propositio plane identica & inepta, ὗτός (ὁ ἀληθινὸς Θεὸς) ἐστιν ὁ ἀληθινὸς Θεὸς: vel juxta vulgata exemplaria ὗτός ὁ ἀληθινὸς (subintellige Θεὸς) ἐστιν ὁ ἀληθινὸς Θεὸς, ut iterum ταυτολογία vera emergat. Obvertit quidem Enjedin. ut & Goslav. cont. Keckerm. p. 1. c. 3. Johanni & Ebraeis familia- re id esse eadem saepius repetere: Sed aliud est propo- sitionis ejusdem repetitio, aliud identica propositio: illa fit sine vitio, haec vero inepta est, nec S. Scri- ptoribus affingi debet. Deinde negat Enjedinus ταυτολογίαν esse, quia voce hac intelligatur Pater Jesu Christi, cum dicatur ejus Dei esse Filium Jesum Christum. Verum si Pater Jesu Christi prius sim- pliciter in textu verus Deus nominatus fuerat, & nunc per pronomen ὗτός eum demonstrat, utiq; ἀπὸ κοινῶ repetendum erit id quod in textu posi- tum, quodq; demonstrare pronomen in textu vo- lunt adversarii, id vero non est aliud, quam verus Deus. Sic ergo adhuc relinquitur ταυτολογία: Hic αὐτὸς (quod pronomen immediate praecedit, & re- spicit nomen remotius veri Dei) Verus ille Deus est verus ille Deus. Denique contrarium inde colligere fatagit Enjedinus: Si proximis verbis Deus Pater bis nominatus est Deus verus, qua, inquit, esset im- prudentia & inconstantia eum titulum statim ad alium transferre? Sed ita non effugit ταυτολογίαν. Nec vero bis nomen ἀληθινῶ Θεῶ Patri in verbis proximis tributum est, sed semel tantum, nec aliud est, quam divina veritas, quod haereticus impie vocat inconstantiam & imprudentiam, quod nem- pe etiam Filius Dei sit verus Deus & vita aeterna, quem paulo ante vers. 7. Apostolus unum dixerat cum Patre vero Deo & Spiritu S. (5) Ex unanimi Ecclesiae sententia. Hactenus enim ὁμολογημένως ortum fuit in Ecclesia, hic ipsummet Filium Dei vocari verum Deum ob evidentiam testimonii So- lis, quod dicitur, radio Scripti, adeo ut etiam Arius ipse hoc agnoverit, cum ei hoc dictum opponeret Athanasius. Vide disp. contr. Arium in Conc. Nicen. Tom. 3. oper p. 201, quin & nonnullos ex recentioribus Anti-Trinitatis id confessos esse, haec verba ad ipsum Christum referenda esse e Soci- no constat l. c. p. 516. Tanta vis & evidentia est hujus testimonii, quod ideo scriptam demonstratio- nem vocavit B. Athanasius l. c.

Varia autem κρησφύγετα quaerunt Socinus, En- jedinus, Catech. Racov. Schmalz. Goslavius & Volcke- lius, ut testimonium elidant. Enjedinus primum se- qui negat Christum aeternum Deum fore, etiamsi di- ceretur verus Deus, quum certum sit verum fictitio op- poni & imaginario: quos autem Deus facit Deos, illi non sunt umbratitii, sed veri Dii, nec tamen aeterni. (2) Deinde negat Enjedinus, & cum eo caeteri pro- nomen ὗτός respicere Christum, & contendunt Pa- trem eo respici, adeoq; confugiunt vel ad parenthe- sin, includi nempe debere verba praecedentia pa- renthesi κὶ ἐσμεν ἐν τῷ ἀληθινῶ, ἐν τῶ ὑἱῶ αὐτῶ Ἰησῦ Χριστῶ, quod admodum probabile statuit Socinus, provocans ad judicium & consensum omnium, qui contraria opinione prius fascinati non fuerint, in resp. contr. Wujeck. p. 320. vel etiam (3) ad peculiarem relativi usum sese recipiunt, quod nempe refera- tur ad Deum verum, eo quod saepe relativa praeser- tim apud Johannem soleant non eum referre, qui proxime ante nominatus fuit, sed qui remotius. Ita Socinus, Enjedinus & alii. (4) Praeprimis autem quod hoc loco praecipue agatur non de Christo, sed de Deo Patre, (5) quodque nuspiam alibi Christus ve- rus ille Deus nuncupetur, aut tale quid aperte de ipso affirmetur. (6) Quod insuper verus ille Deus opponatur idolis v. ult. Christus autem per se idolis nuspiam inveniatur opponi. (7)Quod plane verisimi- le sit, proxime antecedentia verba illa, & sumus in illo vero, referenda esse ad illum eundem verum, cujus co- gnitionem nobis dedit Filius Dei veniens, ut quæ sta- tim consequuntur in Filio ejus ex Ebræorum idio- tismo sic accipiantur, ac si scriptum fuisset per Fili- um ejus. Ita Socinus in Anti-Wujeck, & Enjedinus. (8) Quod per Filium Dei dicamur pervenire in veri Dei notitiam, quod ridicule & ineptissime, & con- tradictorie dici, si verba illa : Hic est verus Deus, ad Christum pertineant, ait Volckelius l. 5. de ver. Rel. c. 10. p. 424. Deniq; (9) Pronomen illud ʊ̂τός hic re- ferri posse ajunt ad totum illud, quod proxime præ- cessit, hoc modo, in eo, quod diximus, est ille verus Deus, & vita æterna, quam explicationem sibi potis- simum probari ait Socinus in Comm. p. 520. ut ita ʊ̂τός referatur non solum ad Patrem, sed & ad Christum, ut tum ibidem, tum p. 320. contra Wujeck. asserit. Quod autem pronomen, etsi masculinum sit, hic eam vim habere possit, probat, quia ejusmodi pro- nomina interdum non conveniant in genere & nume- ro cum subjecto, sed cum prædicato, ut Matth. 13, 38. Joh. 17, 3. Enjedinus addit, quod ita sæpe loqui solea- mus, hic est, pro in hoc consistit, ut Apoc. 13, 18. hic sapientia est, & cap. 17, 9. hic est locus, &c. p. 432.

Quod ad (1) Resp. Verus Deus non dicitur, ni- si qui natura Deus est, quemadmodum verus ho- mo non est, nisi qui naturam humanam habet. Magistratus & Judices, ut æquivoce saltem dicun- tur Dii, ita veri Dii dici non debent: cum nomen solum, non rei veritatem & essentiam participent. Verum non opponitur tantum fictitio, sed etiam non-vero: quum veritas sit affectio Entis. Adhæc falsum est, juxta Scripturas verum Deum dici, qui factus a Deo sit: cum verus Deus non dicatur in Scripturis nisi unus ille summus Deus, Job. 17, 3. 1. Thes. 1, 9. Sed quid multis? cum ipsimet adversa- rii agnoscant, non alium, quam summum Deum hic per verum Deum intelligendum esse, id quod argumentis etiam probat Enjedinus pag. 432.

Ad (2) Respond. Nullum parentheseos istius vestigium apparet in Codd. quibusvis probatissi- mis. Mere ergo conficta est, nimisq; arbitraria. Quæ porro tantum abest, ut omnium consensu firmetur, ut vel inde satis refellatur, quod tot secu- lis in orbe Christiano nemo repertus sit, qui un- quam vel suspicatus saltem fuerit de tali parenthe- si. Et videtur jam ipsi Socino non amplius proba- bilis esse illa prius admodum probabilis parenthe- sis: Quandoquidem in comment. super h. l. ubi cæteras e tractatu contr. Wujeck. repetit exceptio- nes, nullam ejus mentionem fecerit, quæ certe in propria sede non erat prætermittenda, si omnium judicio, & consensu digna habeatur

Ad(3) Resp. Non Relativum, sed demonstrativum hic occurrit pronomen ʊ̂τός. Frustra ergo exem- pla e Scriptura congeruntur de usu pronominis relativi, 2. Thes. 2, 9. Ebr. 5, 17. habetur pronomen ὃς relativum, non vero pronomen ʊ̂τός demon- strativum. (2) Cum in Scriptura pronomen demon- strativum ʊ̂τός occurrit, & sequitur verbum sub- stantivum ἐςιν cum articulo ὁ, ut hoc loco, ʊ̂τός ἐςιν ὁ, non remotius subjectum, sed nomen proxi- me antecedens, cui genere & numero respondet, intelligitur. Exempla vide Matt. 3, 17. c. 7, 12. c. 21. v. 11. c. 27, 37. Marc. 6, 2. 3. c. 7, 6. c. 12, 6. 7. Job. 1, 33. c. 4, 29. c. 6, 14. 48. 49. 50. c. 7, 40. 41. 1. Joh. 5, 5. 6. Atque ita exempla Actor. 2, 19. cap. 10. vers. 6. dissimilia sunt, utpote in quibus non sequitur verbum sub- stantivum & articulus, ὁ, ut hoc loco. (3) Sed etiamsi admittamus, quandoque, licet admodum raro etiam pronomen demonstrativum ὗτῶ ad re- motius trahi debere, id tamen nuspiam fit, quin a- pertissime contextus id indicet, imo exigat, ut Act. 4, 11. 1. Joh. 2, 22. videre est. Nunquam ergo refe- rendum est ad remotius, nisi quando ad proximum referri non posse ipse contextus cogit. Naturalis enim demonstrativi usus est demonstrare proxime antecedens, qui non est præter necessitatem dese- rendus, quod exempla Scripturæ docent plurima, in specie apud D. Johannem c. 1, 2. 7. 15. 33. 34. c. 3, 2. c. 4, 29. c. 16, 14. 48. 49. 50. 71. c. 7, 40. 41. c. 9, 20. c. 18, 21, 1. Joh. 5, 5. 6. &c. Proinde hic etiam ad pro- ximum id referendum erit, usque dum Sociniani probent e contextu, ad id referri non posse. (4) Pronomina illa id referre, de quo præcipue agitur, & tum ubi id remotius nominatum erat, id demonstrare ait Socin. in Antivv. ut & in Comment. p. 518. At hic præcipue agitur de Christo, non de Deo Patre. Christum ergo demonstrare id pronomen, negan- dum non est. (5) Ostendimus ἐκ περιυσίας, argu- mentisque evicimus supra, pronomen ὗτῶ non referri debere ad remotius Deum, sed ad propin- quius nomen Christi: ideoque non est, quod actum agamus. (6) Quid, quod Socinus ipse videns sese hoc effugio, quod remotius antecedens spectetur, non posse vim argumentorum nostrorum decli- nare, aliorsum se recipiat, & tum Patrem, tum Christum hoc pronomine comprehendi adserat, de quo circa postremam exceptionem ad h. l.

Ad 4. Probandum hic præcipue agi de Deo Pa- tre exclusive, non de Christo; contrarium potius ex hisce colligitur (1) de eo hic agitur præcipue, qui ef- fecit, ut cognoscamus verum illum Deum, quod totus contextus indicat, qui utiq; est Christus. (2) de eo agitur h. l. præcipue, in quo sumus, & per cujus com- munionem habemus vitam æternam in nobis manen- tem. Prius membrum evidens est ex hoc versu 20. Posterius e collatione vers. 11. 12. 13. cum hoc versu. At in Christo sumus; ut habet textus, in Filio ipsius Jesu Christo, & per Christi communionem ha- bemus vitam æternam, v. 11. & 12, ut c. 1. 2. 3. E. (3) de eo hic agitur præcipue, quem ut cognoscere- mus effecit Christus veniens dicente S. Johanne. At Christus veniens effecit, ut cognosceremus non minus Filium Dei, quam Patrem, quod & e Joh. 17, 3. manifestum est, quum ibi conjungatur ex æquo Patris & Filii notitia, & in utriusq; cogni- tione dicatur consistere vita æterna, & e scopo to- tius Evangelii constat. Vid. Joh. 20, 21. imo ad Patris cognitionem requiritur Filii cognitio, teste Scri- ptura, Joh. 8, 19. c. 12, 46. c. 14, 7. 9. Ergo ipsimet So- cino fatendum erit, non minus præcipue de Filio, quam de Patre hic agi, adeooq; corruet prorsus ejus exceptio, quod solus Pater hic præcipuum sit sub- jectum. (4) Quid, quod ὀφθαλμοφανῶς pateat toto capite 5. præcipuum ὑποκείμενον esse Jesum, ut, qui hoc negat, Solem hac meridie lucere neget. Deinde, si maxime ὑποκείμενον præcipuum hujus loci esset Deus Pater, & non Christus (quod pror- sus negamus) inde tamen formaliter haud inferre liceret, pronomen ὗτῶ demonstrare Deum Pa- trem, non Christum, quia præcessit mentio Chri- sti, qui perinde excludi nequit ab objecto, posito etiam, quod secundario & incidenter tantum de Christo agatur. Notum enim est, quod sæpe prono- mina etiam id respiciant, quod secundario tantum in textu occurrit, nec est πρῶτον ὑποκείμενον.

Ad 5. Resp. Etiamsi alias nusquam Filius Dei ve- rus Deus diceretur, non tamen sequeretur, quod neque hic verus Deus dicatur: modo non negetur alibi, quod verus Deus sit, quod nunquam proba- bitur. Alioquin simili ratione colligerem, Chri- stum Rom. 9, 5. non dici Deum super omnia benedi- ctum in secula, quia scil. nullibi alias verba hæcce de Christo enunciantur. Æque certum est, quod se- mel in Scripturis dicitur, atque ea, quæ sæpius di- cuntur. (2) Falsum vero est, quod nuspiam ἰσοδυνα- μῦντα in Scripturis prædicentur de Christo. Nun- quid aliud est Deum benedictum esse super omnia, quam esse verum illum Deum. Quum solius veri Dei nomen excelsum, isque solus sit super omnia benedictus, Ps. 72, 1. Ps. 147, 13. Ps. 136, 4. Es. 2, 11. 12. Rom. 1, 15. &c. Dicitur præterea Christus alibi ἀλη- θινὸς, Apoc. 3, 14. c. 19, 11. nomen ejus vocatur ἀλη- θινὸς & ὁ λόγος (qui λόγος Joh. 1, 1. Deus esse di- citur. Conf. c. 20. Act. 20, 28.) & βασιλεὺς βασιλέων: καὶ κύριος κυρίων (quæ est unius veri Dei περίφρα- σις 1. Tim. 6, 15. ut & cum præposito articulo ὁ ἅγιος, ὁ ἀληθινὸς, Apoc. 3, 7. # 2 John

## 1:1 Introduction
[Abraham Calov, Biblia Novi Testamenti Illustrata (Vol. 2, Part 2). English: machine translation, The Faith Received (Mere Orthodoxy); the original follows each comment.]
NOTE ON THE SECOND EPISTLE

Latin:

ANNOT SECUNDAM EPIST

## 1:1 Introduction: Grotian Preface
GROTIAN PREFACE

That this Epistle and the one which follows are not by John the Apostle, many of the ancients believed long ago, from whom Eusebius and Jerome do not dissent. And there are great arguments for this. For it has always been established that there were two Johns at Ephesus, the Apostle and the Presbyter his disciple, from the sepulchres, one of the former and one of the latter: which sepulchres Jerome saw. Furthermore, this writer does not call himself an Apostle, but a Presbyter, whereas Apostles are not accustomed, even when they write to private individuals, to omit that title by which their writings were most commended. For as to the fact that Peter, addressing the Presbyters, calls himself also κατὰ συγκατάβασιν their συμπρεσβύτερον, that is done outside the inscription out of a certain courtesy, such as that by which Emperors also call themselves fellow-soldiers. Moreover, among many nations these epistles had not been received, indeed not even translated into their language, just as neither was the other which is called Peter’s, nor Jude’s, because they were not held to be Apostolic. Then indeed it is not credible that anyone who wished to be called a Christian could have had such audacity as to oppose the Apostle. In the Constitutions of Clement VII. 45. you have: Κλήμης δὲ μετὰ τὸν Λίνε θάνατον, τῆς ὑπ' ἐμῦ Πέτρε δευτε- ρῶν κεχειροτόνηται, τῆς δὲ Ἐφέσε Τιμόθεος μὲν ὑπὸ Παύλε, Ἰωάννης δὲ ὑπ' Ἰωάννε, which, there is no doubt, comes from ancient tradition.

OBSERVATIONS.

Grotius, in order to undermine the authority of the present epistle and the one that follows, asserts that they did not proceed from St. John the Evangelist and Apostle, but from another of that name called the Presbyter; but this is because the sense of Socinus is utterly ἀσύστατον and inept: for he refers the pronoun οὗτός to the knowledge and possession of God and Christ, when he devises this στρεβλὴν στροφὴν: The knowledge and possession of that true God is the true God, and eternal life: to say nothing of how perversely Socinus makes HOC out of HIC, τῦτο out of οὗτός, and explains τῦτο by in HOC, and interprets τό ἐστι as consistit: namely, in this consists that true God, and eternal life. But if in this manner it is permitted to change, add, subtract, and twist words at will, what in the end could not be obtained? And so much for this testimony.

Verse 21. Keep yourselves from idols

Beware of worshipping false gods, that is to say: which gods were called εἴδωλα by the Greek-speaking Jews, because they were represented by images, and were worshipped in those images. Thus it came about that the word εἰδωλολατρείας succeeded to the place of the Hebrew words עבודה זרה φυλάσσειν ἑαυτὸν, which is also more briefly expressed by the passive for the reciprocal verb φυλάσσεσθαι, Luke XII. 15, meaning to beware of something. The Hebrew שמר is sometimes translated by φυλάττειν, sometimes by προσέχειν. The Syrian here has שרן כפשכון which is from the Greek תרהף. Thus we had above τηρεῖ ἑαυτὸν, 18.

Since he has instructed concerning the true God, he now warns that everyone should beware of idols or false Gods: with the addition of the little word Amen for confirmation and sealing, which Grotius rashly neglected. Moreover, a false God, and an idol of the mind, is whatever is worshipped outside of the Father, and those who are one with Him, the Son and the Holy Spirit, in whose name of the one God we have all been baptized: TO WHICH ONE, ONLY, TRUE GOD BE PRAISE, HONOR AND GLORY FOREVER AND EVER, AMEN!

Latin:

PRÆLOQUIUM GROTIANUM.

HAnc Epistolam & eam quæ sequitur non esse Johannis Apostoli, veterum multi jam olim crediderunt, a quibus non dissen- tiunt Eusebius & Hieronymus. Et magna sunt in id argumenta. Nam duos fuisse Johannes Ephesi, Apostolum ac Presbyterum ejus discipulum, semper constitit ex sepulchris alio hujus, alio illius: quæ sepul- chra vidit Hieronymus. Deinde hic Scriptor non Apo- stolum se vocat, sed Presbyterum, cum non soleant Apo- stoli etiam ubi ad privatos scribunt, omittere eum titulum, quo ipsorum scripta maxime commendabantur. Nam quod Petrus Presbyteros alloquens se quoque κατὰ συγκατάβα- σιν vocat eorum συμπρεσβύτερον, id fit extra inscriptionem ex quadam comitate, quali & Imperatores se commilites vocant. Præterea apud multas gentes hæ epistolæ non fuerant receptæ, imo nec in sermonem earum versæ, ut nec altera Petri quæ dicitur, nec Judæ, quia non habebantur pro Apostolicis. Tum vero credibile non est, quenquam, qui Christianus dici vellet, ea fuisse audacia, ut Apostolo se op- poneret. In Clementis Constitutionibus VII. 45. habes: Κλήμης δὲ μετὰ τὸν Λίνε θάνατον, τῆς ὑπ' ἐμῦ Πέτρε δευτε- ρῶν κεχειροτόνηται, τῆς δὲ Ἐφέσε Τιμόθεος μὲν ὑπὸ Παύλε, Ἰωάννης δὲ ὑπ' Ἰωάννε, quod, quin a veteri fama veniat, dubium non est.

OBSERVATIONES.

AUtoritatem epistolæ præsentis, & quæ se- quitur, ut labefactet Grotius, easdem non a S. Johanne Evangelista & Apostolo, sed ab alio istius nominis Presbytero dicto profectas as- tum quia prorsus ἀσύσατον, & ineptus est sensus Socini : Refert enim ille pronomen οὗτός ad cognitionem & habitum Dei & Christi, quando hancce στρεβλὴν στροφὴν comminiscitur: Cognitio & habitio illius veri Dei est verus Deus, & vita aeterna : ut taceam, quam perverse Socinus ex HIC faciat HOC, ex οὗτός τῦτο, & τῦτο expli- cet per in HOC, & τό ἐςι per consistit interprete- tur: nempe in hoc consistit verus ille Deus, & vita aeterna. Quod si hoc pacto pro lubitu licet verba mutare, addere, detrahere, torquere, quid tandem non obtineri poterit ? Et tantum de hoc testi- monio.

Vers. 21. Φυλάξατε ἑαυτὺς ἀπὸ τῶν εἰδώλων)

Cavete vobis a falsis Diis colendis scilicet : qui Dii a Ju- dæis Græce loquentibus dicebantur εἴδωλα, quia per simu- lacra repræsentabantur, & in illis simulacris colebantur. Ita factum est, ut vox εἰδωλολατρείας succederet in locum vocum Ebræarum עבודה זרה φυλάσσειν ἑαυτὸν, quod & brevius per Passivum pro verbo reciproco φυλάσσεσθαι, Luc. XII. 15. est sibi cavere a re aliqua. Ebræum שמר mo- do vertitur per φυλάττειν, modo per προσέχειν. Syrus hîc שרן כפשכון quod est a Græco תרהף. Sic supra habuimus τηρεῖ ἑαυτὸν, 18.

Quum de vero Deo informarit, nunc ut ab idolis seu falsis Diis sibi quisque caveat, monet: Addita confirmationis & obsignationis vocula Amen, quam temere neglexit Grotius. Falsus autem Deus est, & idolum mentis, quicquid coli- tur extra Patrem, &, qui cum eo unum sunt, Fi- lium & Spiritum Sanctum, in cujus unius Dei no- mine baptizati sumus omnes: CUI UNI, SOLI, VERO DEO SIT LAUS, HONOR ET GLORIA IN SEMPI- TERNA SECULA, AMEN!

## 1:1 Introduction: N. J. Tata on the Whole of St. John
N. J. TATA ON THE WHOLE OF ST. JOHN.

he sows, regarding nothing in that matter the Council of Trent sess. IV, nor even the Council of Carthage b. III. c. XLVII, or the Council of Laodicea c. LIX, nothing the authority of the Ancients S. Tertullian de praescript. c. 33, Athanasius in the Synopsis, Clement of Alexandria in his commentaries, Jerome in his epistle to Paulinus, Augustine b. II. de doctr. Christ. c. 4, Nazianzen in his Poems, Didymus in his commentaries, Damascenus b. IV. de fide cap. 18, Bede & Oecumenius; nothing the consensus of the Church, and not even the Roman Catholic Church, to which he leaned most, inasmuch as by it, along with them, these second and third epistles of St. John the Apostle were entirely held, and defined to be held. Which is also the constant opinion of the Reformers. Among the Papists, Erasmus alone, as far as is known, determined otherwise, and made a Presbyter their Author, distinct from John the Apostle: Cajetan was ambiguous. Nor indeed did so many of the ancients believe that they were not of John the Apostle, and if there were such, why did Grotius not produce them? Eusebius b. III. Eccl. c. ult. relies only on the authority of Papias, a man of no great judgment, and of little authority in the Church on account of the many fabulous things which he handed down: Concerning whom Eusebius himself l. c. Σφόδρα γάρ τοι σμικρὸς ὢν τὸν νῦν: for he was endowed with a very mediocre intellect, as one may conjecture from his writings. Concerning whose earlier fabulous narrations more in the same place.

And it is from the preface of this Papias to his own books that Eusebius uniquely drew that fable about the twin John, one the Apostle, the other the Presbyter, from which it is also likely that the narrative of others, who affirmed that two men of the same name lived in Asia, flowed. When Eusebius reviews the divine Scriptures in book III, chapter 25, he has this to say after mentioning others concerning them: "And these are among the acknowledged, but of the disputed, yet known to the many, is the one called James, and Jude, and the second epistle of Peter, and the so-called second and third of John, whether they happen to be the Evangelist's, or of another of the same name as him." And these indeed are received by the common consent of all. But of those things which are called into doubt, yet which we see mentioned by many, is the epistle which is called James's and that of Jude, and the second of Peter, likewise the second and third of John, whether they were composed by the Evangelist himself in truth, or by another of the same name. Jerome, in his catalogue of ecclesiastical writers, after having said that the first epistle of John is approved by all ecclesiastical and learned men, says at least this, that the remaining two are asserted to be of John the Presbyter, whose other tomb is also shown among the Ephesians: he adds, however, that some think the two later ones are of the same John the Evangelist: concerning which matter he later likewise brought forward Papias, distinguishing John the elder from John the Apostle. But in the Epistle to Evagrius, which is the 81st, the mind of St. Jerome seems to have been different. For thus, he says, concerning St. John the Apostle: "The trumpet of the son of thunder sounds, whom Jesus loved most, who drank the streams of doctrine from the breast of the Savior, the Presbyter to the Elect Lady and her children, whom I love in truth." And in another Epistle, "The Presbyter to Gaius the most beloved, whom I love in truth." Which are taken, without doubt, from the II and III epistles of John: I add epistle 103 of Jerome to Paulinus, where he has it thus: "James, Peter, John, and Jude, the Apostles, published seven epistles as mystical as they are succinct, short in words, long in meanings, so that there is rarely one who does not grow dim-sighted in reading them!"

Then indeed, if we compare the style and subject matter of these Epistles with the first, it sufficiently appears that they proceeded from the same author. Which Baronius taught at the year of Christ 99, no. 9. "Certainly," he says, "if it has ever been permitted to judge sons born of the same parent from the similarity of their faces, anyone will easily be able to understand that those three epistles, bearing before them one and the same image in words, meanings, style, and character, were written by one and the same Author." For in the first place, as regards words and meanings, it has been demonstrated in many instances, as when he says in the first: "I am not writing a new commandment to you, but an old commandment," and in the second likewise: "Not as writing a new commandment to you, but which we had from the beginning." Again in the first: "Everyone who denies the Son does not have the Father; he who confesses the Son also has the Father." and in the second he renders the same meaning clearly in these words: "He who recedes and does not remain in the doctrine of Christ does not have God: he who remains in the doctrine of Christ, this one has both the Father and the Son." What is thus in the first: "Everyone who is born of God does not commit sin," in the third is the same in these words: "He who does good is of God; he who is born of God does not commit sin." And what he has in the first: "That we may love in deed and in truth," he frequently inculcates the same in the second and third concerning loving in truth. While likewise in the first he has these things: "Many false prophets have gone out into the world. In this the Spirit of God is known: Everyone"

Spirit that confesses that Christ has come in the flesh is of God, and everyone who dissolves Jesus is not of God, and this is the Anti-Christ." In the second, rendering the same meaning in almost the same words, he says: "Many seducers have gone out into the world, who do not confess that Jesus has come in the flesh; this is the Seducer and the Anti-Christ." Again in the first: "This is charity, that we keep his commandments." And in the second: "This is charity, that we walk according to his commandments." But the frequent inculcation of charity, love, and truth made in those three epistles clearly declares that in those two epistles the same genuine image of John shines forth, which is in the first, and is clearly seen.

That John calls himself Presbyter, not Apostle, in these epistles, does not teach that John the Evangelist is not the author. The Apostle was sufficiently known to the Elect Lady and Gaius, and as it seems he was commonly called by this name of πρεσβυτέρου, because he had attained a more advanced age than the other Apostles, and was held as it were the Elder of the Christians, both on account of his Apostolic dignity and his venerable gray hair, since he lived as the last of the Apostles and died under the reign of Trajan in the year of Christ 101, according to Jerome and Baronius. An Elder, therefore, who possessed a certain swan-like grace of old age, as Ambrose says in Psalm 36:25. What? That in that age, as Cornelius admits, Presbyter and Bishop were accustomed to be used for the same thing, which Jerome taught in epistle 95 to Evagrius. Whence Oecumenius: John, he says, declares himself to be a Bishop by the name of Presbyter.

That which Grotius says thirdly, that these epistles were not received among many nations, ought to have been proven, not merely asserted. Although some of them were not translated into the language of some, that does not detract from their Apostolic or Canonical authority. For the whole New Testament was not immediately translated into all the languages of those by whom it was received as divine. The reason, according to some, why these epistles were not translated was not that they were simply rejected by the canon or denied to be Apostolic, but that their author was in doubt. But that reason is of no moment at all, which he took fourthly from Diotrephes, who opposed himself to the Apostle. For how was it not credible to him, which is evident from so many examples of Pseudo-Apostles, Hermogenes, Phygellus, Philetus, Alexander, Faber, and others? Finally, the Constitutions of Clement are of no authority, even by the judgment of the Papists themselves, whom Cardinal Bellarmine warned in his book on Ecclesiastical writers, q. 59, have almost no standing in the Latin Church, and are disapproved of even by the later Greeks in the Trullan Council, c. 2, and he himself held them as Apocryphal. Bisciola, however, in the epistles of Baronius, p. 72, affirms that they were relegated among the Apocrypha by all: which Athanasius in the Synopsis rejected as spurious. See Baronius at the year 44, n. 42, and at the year 102, n. 9.

As to the time the epistles of John were written, just as he seems to have written the Gospel before his exile, when he was requested by the Bishops of Asia because of the heresy of Ebion: So Bartholomaeus Petri, at the end of the third epistle, thinks the first and second epistles were written before the Gospel, as being opposed to Basilides, who was earlier than Ebion. Who also thinks the third Epistle was written before the Gospel, but after the death of Peter and Paul, when the care of the Asian Church rested solely upon John among the Apostles. The Apocalypse, however, was written on Patmos, to which he was banished in the 14th year of Domitian, that is, 97 of Christ. But this opinion of Bartholomæus Petri concerning the epistles written long before the exile does not seem to be approved. For even if it be admitted that they were directed against the Basilidians and that their master Basilides existed as a heresiarch not long after the death of Simon Magus his teacher, which death they refer to the year of Christ 68: did not the heresy of the Basilidians endure for many years still, if the Johannine Epistles were written before Ebion, as Petri wishes, how are they opposed to Ebion alongside the Gospel? Nor can we in this regard grant assent to this Bartholomæus, that the Johannine epistles were written long before the Gospel, and even long before he was exiled: although we altogether maintain that he wrote both his Gospel and the epistles before the Apocalypse and the exile of John, and thus we cannot agree with Baronius that they were written in the year of the Lord 99, since he migrated into exile in the fourteenth year of Domitian, which was 97 of the Lord, and arrived at Ephesus upon his being killed in the 1st year of Nerva, 99 of the Lord. The Gospel of St. John seems to have been written first. After that the epistles were written: first the Catholic, then the latter two: most recently the Apocalypse was consigned to the monuments of letters; which most people concede regarding the Apocalypse, nor does Bartholomæus Petri deny it.

Latin:

N. J. TATA IN S. JOHANNIS TOLAM.

serit, nihil ea in re æstimans concilium Tridenti- num sess. IV. ac ne Carthaginense quidem l. III. c. XLVII. aut Laodicenum c. LIX. nihil autorita- tem Veterum S. Tertull. de præscript. c. 33. Atha- nasii in Synopsi, Clementis Alexandrini in com- ment. Hieronymi epist. ad Paulin. Augustini l. II. de doctr. Christ. c. 4. Nazianzeni in Carm. Didy- mi in comment. Damasceni l. IV. de fide cap. 18. Bedæ & Oecumenii; nihil consensum Ecclesiæ, ac ne quidem Romano-Catholicæ, ad quam maxi- me propendebat, utpote a qua cum illis pro epi- stolis S. Johannis Apostoli hæc secunda, & tertia omnino habitæ sunt, atque habendæ definitæ. Quæ etiam Reformatorum constans est sententia. E Pontificiis solus, quod constet, Erasmus aliter statuit, ac Presbyterum earum Autorem fecit, a Jo- hanne Apostolo diversum : Cajetanus ambiguus fuit. Nec vero adeo multi veterum credidere, non esse eas Johannis Apostoli, & si qui tales fuere, cur eos non produxit Grotius? Eusebius l. III. Eccl. c. ult. autoritate tantum nititur Papiæ, viri non magni judicii, & exiguæ autoritatis in Ecclesia propter fabulosa multa, quæ tradidit: De quo Eu- sebius ipse l. c. Σφόδρα γάρ τοι σμικρὸς ὢν τὸν νῦν : fuit enim mediocri admodum ingenio præditus, ut ex scriptis illius conjicere licet. De cujus nar- rationibus fabulosis prioribus ibidem plura.

Et ex hujus Papiæ Procæmio in libros suos unice hausit istam fabulam Eusebius de gemino Johanne, altero Apostolo, altero Presbytero, ex quo etiam aliorum narrationem, qui duos eodem nomine appellatos in Asia vixisse, affirmarunt fluxisse verisimile est. Cum divinas Scripturas recenset Eusebius l. III. c. 25. ita post alias commemoratas de illis habet : Καὶ ταῦτα μὲν ἐν ὁμολογουμένοις, τῶν δὲ ἀντιλεγομένων, γνωρίμων δ' ὂν ὅμως τοῖς πολλοῖς, ἡ λεγομένη ἰακώβου φέρεται, κὴ ἡ ἰούδα, ἥ τε Πέτρου δευτέρα ἐπιστολὴ, καὶ ἡ ὀνομαζομένη δευτέρα κὴ τρίτη ἰωάννου, εἴτε τοῦ Εὐαγγελιστοῦ τυγχάνουσαι, εἴτε καὶ ἑτέρου ὁμωνύμου ἐκείνῳ. Et hæc quidem communi omnium consensu recepta sunt. Ex iis verò quæ in dubium revocantur, a multis vero commemorari videmus, est epistola, quæ dicitur Jacobi & quæ Judæ, & secunda Petri, Johannis item altera & tertia, sive illæ ab ipso revera Evangelista, sive ab altero ejusdem nominis compositæ sunt. Hieronymus in catal. script. Eccl. postquam dixisset primam epistolam Johannis ab universis Ecclesiasticis & eruditis viris probari, id saltim ait, reliquas duas Johannis Presbyteri asseri, cujus & sepulchrum alterum apud Ephesios ostendatur : addit autem nonnullos putare, duas posteriores ejusdem Johannis Evangelistæ esse: In quam rem postea itidem adduxit Papiam, Johannem seniorem a Johanne Apostolo distinguentem. Sed in Epist. ad Evagr. quæ est 81. alia S. Hieronymi mens fuisse videtur. Ita enim, inquit, de S. Johanne Apostolo : Clangit tuba filii tonitru, quem Jesus amavit plurimum, qui de pectore Salvatoris doctrinarum fluenta potavit, Presbyter Electæ Dominæ & filiis ejus, quos diligo in veritate. Et in alia Epistola Presbyter Cajo charissimo, quem ego diligo in veritate. Quæ e II. & III. Johannis epistola, citra dubietatem, desumpta sunt : Addo epist. CIII. Hieronym. ad Paulin. ubi ita habet : Jacobus, Petrus, Johannes, Judas Apostoli septem epistolas ediderunt tam mysticas, quam succinctas, breves in verbis, longas in sententiis, ut rarus sit, qui non in eorum cæcutiat lectione!

Tum vero, si stylum & materiam Epistolarum harum conferamus cum prima, satis apparet ab eodem illas profectas esse autore. Quod Baronius docuit ad ann. Christ. XCIX. n. 9. Certe, inquit, si quando ex facierum similitudine filios eodem parente genitos licuit judicare, tres illas epistolas verbis, sententiis, stylo, charactere unam eandemque præ se ferentes imaginem, ab uno eodemque Autore esse conscriptas, quivis facile poterit intelligere. In primis enim quod ad verba atque sententias spectat, in multis id contigit demonstrari, ut cum ait in prima: Non mandatum novum scribo vobis, sed mandatum vetus, in secunda item : Non tanquam mandatum novum scribens vobis, sed quod habuimus ab initio. Rursum in prima : Omnis, qui negat Filium, nec Patrem habet, qui confitetur Filium, & Patrem habet. & in secunda eandem plane sententiam his verbis reddit: Qui recedit & non permanet in doctrina Christi, Deum non habet: qui permanet in doctrina Christi, hic & Patrem & Filium habet. Quod ita in prima : Omnis, qui ex Deo natus est, peccatum non facit, in tertia idem his verbis : Qui bene facit, ex Deo est, qui ex Deo natus est, peccatum non facit. Et quod in prima habet : Ut diligamus opere & veritate, eadem in secunda & tertia de diligendo in veritate frequenter inculcat. Dum item in prima hæc habet : Multi Pseudo-Prophetæ exierunt in mundum. In hoc cognoscitur Spiritus Dei : Omnis

Spiritus, qui confitetur Christum in carne venisse, ex Deo est, & omnis, qui solvit Jesum, ex Deo non est, & hic Anti-Christus est. In secunda iisdem pene verbis eandem reddens sententiam, ait: Multi seductores exierunt in mundum, qui non confitentur Jesum in carne venisse, hic est Seductor & Anti-Christus. Rursum in prima: Hæc est charitas, ut mandata ejus custodiamus. Et in se- cunda: Hæc est charitas, ut ambulemus secundum mandata ejus. At quæ frequens in tribus illis epistolis facta est charitatis, dilectionis, veritatis inculcatio, plane declarat in illis duabus epistolis eandem, quæ in prima, genuinam elucere, atque per- spicue conspici Johannis imaginem.

Quod vero Presbyterum, non Apostolum se dicit Johannes in his epistolis, non docet, Johan- nem Evangelistam Autorem non esse. Satis no- tus erat Apostolus Electæ & Gajo, & ut videtur communiter hoc πρεσβυτέρου nomine appellaba- tur, quia præ aliis Apostolis provectiorem æta- tem assequutus, ac veluti Christianorum Senior habitus, tum ob Apostolicam dignitatem, tum ob venerabilem canitiem, quum ultimus Apostolo- rum vixerit, & sub Trajani imperio anno Chri- sti CI. diem obierit secundum Hieronymum & Baronium. Senior ergo, cui scilicet cygnea sup- peteret quædam gratia senectutis, dicente Ambro- sio in Psal. XXXVI. 25. Quid? quod illo ævo, fatente Cornelio, Presbyter & Episcopus pro eo- dem usurpari consueverunt, quod Hieronymus docuit epist. XCV. ad Evagr. Unde Oecume- nius: Johannes, inquit, Episcopum se esse nomine Presbyteri declarat.

Quod tertio dicit Grotius, apud multas gentes non receptas fuisse has epistolas, probandum fuis- set, non nude afferendum. Quanquam vero non translatæ fuerint in sermonem nonnullæ earum, id tamen non derogat autoritati earum Apostolicæ, vel Canonicæ. Nam & totum Novum Testamentum non adutum fuit trans- latum in omnium illorum linguas, a quibus re- ceptum id fuit, tanquam divinum. Causa juxta nonnullos fuit, quod non translatæ sint hæ epistolæ, non quod simpliciter reprobatæ a ca- none, aut negatæ Apostolicæ, sed quod dubius fuerit earum Autor. Ea vero ratio nullius prorsus est momenti, quam quarto a Diotrephe, qui se Apostolo opposuit, desumpsit. Quomodo enim non credibile ipsi fuit, quod tot exemplis constat Pseudo-Apostolorum, Hermogenis, Phygel- li, Phileti, Alexandri, Fabri & aliorum? Deni- que Clementis Constitutiones autoritatis nullius sunt, ipsorummet etiam Pontificiorum judicio, quos Cardinalis Bellarminus in Ecclesia Latina nullum fere nomen habere, & ab ipsis etiam Græ- cis posterioribus in Concilio Trullano c. 2. impro- bari libr. de script. Eccles. q. 59. monuit, & pro Apocryphis ipse habuit. Bisciola vero in epist. Baronii p. 72. ab omnibus inter Apocrypha rela- tas affirmat: Quas Athanasius in Synopsi ceu notas reprobavit. Vid. Baronius ad ann. 44. n. 42. & ad ann. 102. n. 9.

Quod ad tempus scriptarum epistolarum Jo- hannis, uti Evangelium ante exilium scripsisse videtur, cum rogaretur ab Episcopis Asiæ ob hæresin Ebionis: Ita Epistolas primam & secun- dam ceu oppositas Basilidi, qui anterior fuit Ebio- ne, ante Evangelium scriptas censet Bartholo- mæus Petri sub finem tertiæ epistolæ. Qui et- iam tertiam Epistolam ante Evangelium scri- ptam putat, sed post obitum Petri & Pauli, quan- do cura Asiaticæ Ecclesiæ soli ex Apostolis Jo- hanni incumbebat. Apocalypsis autem scripta in Pathmo, quo relegatus fuit anno 14. Domitiani, hoc est, 97. Christi. Sed hæc Bartholomæi Petri opinio de epistolis diu ante exilium scriptis pro- banda non videtur. Nam utut admittatur, ad- versus Basilidianos directas esse illorumque Ma- gistrum Basilidem non diu post mortem Simonis Magi Præceptoris sui hæresiarcham extitisse, quam mortem ad ann. Christi 68. referunt : an- non pluribus annis adhuc duravit Basilidianorum hæresis, si ante Ebionem, quod vult Petri, Epi- stolæ Johanneæ scriptæ, quomodo Ebioni oppo- sitæ juxta cum Evangelio? Nec in eo assensum huic Bartholomæo præbere possumus, quod diu ante Evangelium scriptæ sunt Johanneæ episto- læ, multo etiam antequam exularet: etsi omnino statuamus ante Apocalypsin & exilium Johannis tum Evangelium suum, tum epistolas ipsum scri- psisse, adeoque Baronio accedere non possumus, quod scriptæ sint anno Domini 99. siquidem in exi- lium migravit decimo quarto annoDomitiani, qui erat 97. Domini, & adierit Ephesum eo inter- fecto anno 1. Nervæ, Domini 99. Primum S. Jo- hannis scriptum videtur Evangelium. Post epi- stolæ conscriptæ sunt: Primum Catholica, de- hinc posteriores duæ: novissime Apocalypsis litera- rum monumentis consignata est; quod de Apo- calypsi plerique concedunt, nec diffitetur Bartho- lomæus Petri.

## 1:1 Argument
SINGLE CHAPTER. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

The inscription and greeting having been premised, he testifies to his joy concerning the children of the Elect lady walking in the truth, and asks that they, pursuing one another with mutual love, walk according to the commandments of the Lord, and warns that, since many seducers who do not confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh have come into the world, they should watch them, lest the work of the Apostles be in vain, and that they remain in the doctrine of Christ, and not receive him who does not bring it; finally, since he has many things to write, and does not wish to commit them to paper, he promises his arrival, and greets the Elect lady from the children of her Elect sister.

There are two principal parts, if you remove the inscription and the final greeting, I. Exhortation to mutual charity, to v. 6. Exhortation to avoid the heterodoxy of seducers, and to preserve the doctrine of Christ, to v. 13.

PART I. EXHORTATION TO MUTUAL CHARITY.

Vers. 1. The elder.

By that name he was sufficiently known, being ordained by John the Apostle.

Grotius could bring forward nothing certain concerning the diversity of John the Apostle and the Presbyter. For the narrative of the fabulous writer Papias does not deserve belief. Concerning the ordination of the Presbyter performed by the Apostle, he had nothing to praise but the apocryphal writing of Clement. But the confession of Bartholomæus Petri is to be noted concerning the identity of the names of Presbyter and

Bishop against those who contend that a distinction existed in the Apostolic age: It was in use in the first times of the Church that Bishops, even insofar as they are Bishops, were called Presbyters, which Oecumenius notes here, and can be taught from Acts XX, 17, compared then with v. 28 of the same, and from Tit. I, 5, compared with v. 7 of the same.

To the Elect lady.)

We have said that συνεκλεκτὴ in 1 Pet. V, 12 is tacitly referred to the Church. But here one person is altogether indicated, as we see below in 13. And I think Ἐκλεκτὴ was a proper name, in Hebrew בחורה, just as Thomas is Didymus. Such a name is ἴσαντος among the Greeks, Ἀγαθὴ, Ἀγαπητὴ and similar ones made from adjectives into proper names. Just as any men were called Κύριοι, as can be seen in John XX, 15. So women were called Κυρίαι, as can be seen also in the Enchiridion of Epictetus 62, and in Chrysostom against the συνεισάκτους, and elsewhere. This woman, however, seems to have been of the Jewish race, living not in Ephesus, but in another city.

Why should ἐκλεκτῇ not be referred here equally to the Church, as συνεκλεκτὴ in 1 Peter 5:12? Serarius certainly, having followed Oecumenius, which Cornelius à Lapide brings forward, contends to prove by eight conjectures that by Electa is not signified a certain person and matron, but some Church of Asia. For the elect Church is the bride of GOD, according to that in Canticles 6:9, beautiful as the Moon, elect as the Sun.
