Although Cornelius does not approve this, for the reason that letters are to be inscribed to certain persons or Churches, lest they wander into uncertainty, or be carried to strangers to whom they do not pertain: yet that is easily resolved, if the letters are said to be destined to a certain place with a courier or by another occasion. That received opinion being held, other questions are idle, which regard a certain person, whether it is an appellative or a proper name? If an appellative, why and how is she called Electa? If proper, is it merely proper? Concerning which Cornelius inquires in vain, because he finds nothing certain. He wearies the Latin Vulgate, among other things, which does not have Eclecta, as that name, if it were proper, ought to have been retained, but translated it Electa. Whence, having dismissed the proper name, he defines at last that some woman of singular virtue is called Electa, just as she is called Margarita. By what means therefore will he be able to deny the reading of Scripture to the laity, when the Holy Spirit Himself consecrated this epistle to some woman? Κυρία, however, could be called the Church either because of the nobility of the place, or because of the excellence of virtue, or because of a dominant faith. Not to mention that Κυρία may be most choice, gathered in a legitimate manner, which in Acts 19:39 is ἔννομος, as witnessed by Laertius in Zeno, as Serarius and Cornelius explain. Nor do I see why Oecumenius and Serarius deserve to be disapproved here, because they believed that the Asian Church, in which Gaius lived, to whom the third epistle is inscribed, is designated. For St. John does not deny that he wrote to this Church in 3 Epist. verse 9, which seemed to be the case to Cornelius and his epitomizer Tirinus: But he testifies rather that he wrote to the Church: Moreover, no other letters can be named, except those which appeared under the name of John, as his second Epistle.

And to her children.] Educated by the mother in the Christian Religion.

They are fables, which Cornelius trifles here concerning the daughters of Electa promoted to virginity and holiness, or Nuns. For from where will it be taught that such nuns existed at that time? The daughters of Philip are imagined to be such, they cannot be taught from Acts 21:9. But why should we dwell on those trifles? How much simpler it is to understand by children the spiritual sons of the Church begotten through the Gospel.

Whom I love in the truth. Thus Sir. 7, 22. Matth. 22, 16. In Hebrew בֶּאֱמֶת, as Esa. 10, 20. cap. 11, 1. cap. 26, 15. cap. 38, 3. cap. 61, 8. Jerem. 26, 15. cap. 28, 9. cap. 22, 41.

And not I only, but also all who have known the truth. In the Manuscript: And not I only. By truth understand the Gospel, as Ebr. X, 26. 1. Petr. I, 22. And by to know understand, to show knowledge by words and deeds. Thus he describes those who were Christians at Ephesus and in the neighboring places.

Latin:

CAPUT UNICUM. ARGUMENTUM ET PAR- TITIO.

Præmissa inscriptione, & voto, gaudium suum testatur de Electæ liberis in veritate ambu- lantibus, rogatque ut mutuo amore se pro- sequentes ambulent secundum præcepta Domini, ac monet, ut, quum multi sedu- ctores, qui non confitentur, Jesum Christum in carne venisse, in mundum venerint, eos observent, ne opera Apostolorum frustra fuerit, maneantque in doctrina Christi, nec suspiciant illum, qui eum non afferat; denique quum multa habeat scribere, nec charta ea committere velit, adventum suum promittit, & à sororis Electæ liberis Electam salutat.

Partes principales duæ sunt, si inscriptionem & salutationem finalem demas, I. Parænesis ad cha- ritatem mutuam, ad v. 6. Parænesis ad vitandam seductorum heterodoxiam, & servandam Christi doctrinam, ad v. 13.

PARS I. PARÆNESIS AD CHARITATEM MUTUAM.

Vers. 1. ὁ πρεσβύτερος.

Eo nomine satis erat notus, quippe à Johanne Apostolo ordinatus.

De diversitate Johannis Apostoli & Presbyteri nihil certi proferre potuit Grotius. Papiæ enim fabulosi Scriptoris narratio fidem non meretur. De ordinatione Presbyteri ab Apostolo facta non nisi Apocryphum Clementis scriptum laudare habuit. Notanda autem Bartholomæi Petri confessio de identitate nominum Presbyteri &

Episcopi adversus eos, qui discrimen Apostoli- ca ætate locum habuisse contendunt: Fuit primis Ecclesiæ temporibus in usu, ut Episcopi, etiam qua- tenus Episcopi sunt, dicerentur Presbyteri, quod hic monet Oecumenius, & doceri potest ex Act. XX, 17. collato tum vers. 28. ejusdem, & ex Tit. I, 5. collato cum v. 7. ejusdem.

Ἐκλεκτῇ Κυρίᾳ.)

Diximus συνεκλεκτὴ 1. Petr. V, 12. ad Ecclesiam tacite re- ferri. At hic omnino una indicatur persona, ut videmus in- fra 13. Et Ἐκλεκτὴ puto fuisse nomen proprium, Ebraice בחורה sicut Thomas est Didymus. Tale nomen ἴσαντος apud Herm. Ἀγαθὴ, Ἀγαπητὴ & similia ex Adjectivis facta propria. Sicut viri quilibet appellabantur Κύριοι, ut videre est Joh. XX, 15. Ita fœminæ Κυρίαι, ut videre est etiam in En- chiridio Epicteti 62. & apud Chrysostomum contra συνεισά- κτους, & alibi. Videtur autem hæc fœmina fuisse gente Judæa, non Ephesi, sed in alia urbe habitans.

Cur non pariter hic ἐκλεκτῇ ad Ecclesiam refe- ratur, ut συνεκλεκτὴ 1. Petr. V, 12. ? Serarius certe, sequutus Oecumenium, quod affert Cornelius à La- pide, octo conjecturis probare contendit, per Electam non significari certam personam & matronam, sed Ec- clesiam aliquam Asiæ. Ecclesia enim electa est DEI sponsa, juxta illud Cantic. VI, 9. pulchra ut Luna, ele- cta ut Sol. Quod etsi non probet Cornelius, eo, quod literæ certis personis vel Ecclesiis inscribendæ sint, ne in incertum vagentur, vel ad alienos, ad quos non pertinent, perferantur: id tamen facile expeditur, si literæ ad certum locum cum tabel- lario vel alia occasione destinatæ dicantur. Sen- tentia illa recepta, aliæ quæstiones otiosæ sunt, quæ personam certam respiciunt, an sit nomen Appellativum an proprium? Si Appellativum, cur & quomodo Electa dicatur? Si proprium an mere proprium? De quibus Cornelius frustra disquirit, quia nihil certi invenit. Quem inter alia Vulgata Latina, quæ non habet Eclectam, uti nomen il- lud, si proprium foret, retineri debuisset, sed transtulit Electam, fatigat. Unde misso nomine proprio definit tandem, fœminam aliquam singu- laris virtutis vocari Electam, æque ac vocatur Margarita. Quo pacto ergo denegare pote- rit Laicis lectionem Scripturæ, quum ipse Spi- ritus Sanctus alicui mulieri hanc epistolam con- secrarit? Κυρία autem dici poterat Ecclesia sive ob loci nobilitatem, sive ob virtutis præstantiam, sive ob fidem dominatricem. Ne dicam quod Κυρία sit lectissima, legitimo modo congregata, quæ Act. XIX, 39. ἔννομος, teste Laertio in Zenone, ut explicat Serarius & Cornelius. Neque video cur hic improbari mereantur Oecumenius & Sera- rius, quod credidere, Ecclesiam Asianam, in qua degebat Cajus, cui tertia epistola inscripta est, designari. Non enim huic Ecclesiæ se scripsis- se negat S. Johannes 3. Epist. vers. 9. quod visum fuit Cornelio & epitomatori ejus Tirino : Sed testatur potius se scripsisse Ecclesiæ: Nullæ autem aliæ nominari possunt literæ, nisi quæ sub nomi- ne Johannis, ceu secunda ejus Epistola pro- diit.

Καὶ τοῖς τέκνοις αὐτῆς.] Educatis à matre in Religione Christiana.

Fabulæ sunt, quæ de Electæ filiabus ad virgini- tatem & sanctimoniam promotis, vel Nonnis hic Cornelius nugatur. Isto enim tempore moniales ejusmodi extitisse unde docebitur? Philippi filiæ finguntur tales, doceri ex Actor. XXI, 9. non pof- sunt. Sed quid nugis illis immoremur? Quanto simplicius est, per liberos intelligere Ecclesiæ filios spirituales per Evangelium genitos.

Οὓς ἐγὼ ἀγαπῶ ἐν τῇ ἀληθείᾳ.] Quos ego sincere amo. Sic Sir. 7, 22. Matth. 22, 16. Ebrai- ce בֶּאֱמֶת, ut Esa. 10, 20. cap. 11, 1. cap. 26, 15. cap. 38, 3. cap. 61, 8. Jerem. 26, 15. cap. 28, 9. cap. 22, 41.

Καὶ ὐκ ἐγὼ μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ πάντες οἱ ἐγνωκότες τὴν ἀλήθειαν.] In Manuscripto: Οὐκ ἐγὼ δὲ μόνον. Per ἀλήθειαν intel- lige Evangelium, ut Ebr. X, 26. 1. Petr. I, 22. Et per nosse in- tellige, notitiam verbis factisque ostendere. Sic describit eos, qui Ephesi & in vicinis locis erant Christiani.

## 1:2
Vers. 2.

Because of the truth which abides in us. We love you, he says, both I and other Christians with a most just love, because the Gospel is in us, that is, in me and you. A similar locution 1. Joh. II, 14. In the Manuscript for abides is dwelling in the same sense.

And shall be with us forever. And for which in the Hebrew manner. And shall be for let it be, as also in the following verse, for he prays for perseverance for himself and for them.

By the truth some understand Christ, who is the truth, Joh. XIV, 6. Oecumenius [understands] true and firm charity. But it is more correctly understood as the Gospel Joh. XVII, 17.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

Διὰ τὴν ἀλήθειαν τὴν μένεσαν ἐν ἡμῖν.] Amamus vos, inquit, & ego & Christiani alii amore justis- simo, quia Evangelium est in nobis, id est, in me & vobis. Par locutio 1. Joh. II, 14. In Manuscripto pro μένεσαν est οἰκῦ- σαν sensu eodem.

Καὶ μεθ᾽ ἡμῶν ἔσαι εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα.] Καὶ pro quæ more Ebræo. Et ἔσαι pro ἔσω, ut & versu se- quenti, optat enim sibiipsi & illis perseverantiam.

Per veritatem nonnulli Christum intelligunt, qui est veritas, Joh. XIV, 6. Oecumenius veram & firmam charitatem. Sed rectius intelligitur Ev- angelium Joh. XVII, 17.

## 1:3
Vers. 3.

Grace, mercy, peace shall be with you from the Father and from Jesus Christ the Son of the Father. Here the Latin well translated shall be. For often among the Hebrews futures are put for optatives. But in the Manuscript these words shall be with you are missing. The same prayer 1. Tim. I, 2. & 2. Tim. I, 2.

In truth and love. That is, through the knowledge of the true and mutual affection. For through these we provoke, preserve, and increase the benefits of God toward us.

Hugo and Cajetan refer these to the Son, as if to say the Son is loved by the Father in truth and charity. But without doubt it is part of the wish itself. Truth illuminates the mind, charity inflames the will. Furthermore, not only is an Apostolic greeting held here, as is customary for Paul, Peter, Jude, etc., but also against the heresies then beginning to spread, he declares above all things the Divinity of Christ the Lord as the Only-begotten Son and his equality with the Father, and places it as a foundation, as from whom, Christ, no less than from God the Father, salutary gifts are to be expected.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

Ἔσαι μεθ᾽ ὑμῶν χάρις, ἔλεος, εἰρήνη ἀπὸ τῦ Πατρὸς καὶ πα- ρὰ Ἰησοῦ Χρισῦ τῦ ὑιῦ τῦ Πατρός.] Hic ἔσαι Latinus bene ver- tit sit. Sæpe enim Ebræis futura ponuntur pro precativis. At in Manuscripto desunt hæc ἔσαι μεθ᾽ ὑμῶν. Eadem preca- tio 1. Tim. I, 2. & 2. Tim. I, 2.

Ἐν ἀληθείᾳ καὶ ἀγάπῃ.] Id est, per cognitionem veri & di- lectionem mutuam. Nam per hæc in nos Dei beneficia pro- vocamus, conservamus, augemus.

Hugo & Cajetanus hæc ad Filium referunt, q. d. Filius diligitur à Patre in veritate & charitate. Sed sine dubio pars est ipsius voti. Veritas mentem illuminat, charitas voluntatem inflammat. Cæ- terum non tantum salutatio hic habetur Aposto- lica Paulo, Petro, Judæ &c. usitata, sed & adver- sus hæreses tunc grassari incipientes, Christi Do- mini tanquam Unigeniti Filii Divinitatem & cum Patre æqualitatem ante omnia declarat, ac tan- quam fundamentum ponit, utpote à quo, Chri- sto, non minus quam à Deo Patre expectanda sint dona salutaria.

## 1:4
Vers. 4. I rejoiced greatly. .שָׂשְׂתִּי מְאוֹד

That I have found of thy children walking in truth. I have found, that is, I have seen, מָצָאתִי. Certain children of this matron had come to Ephesus, as is credible, for the sake of business. To walk הָלַךְ is to institute a life. In truth sincerely, as we just said.

Καθὼς ἐντολὴν ἐλάβομεν παρὰ τῦ Πατρός.] As we have received a commandment from GOD, namely through Christ. I have known them, he says, to follow the Evangelical precepts from the heart; which is the greatest praise. In the Manuscript it is ἀπὸ τῦ Πατρός. We have seen above at verse 3 that those two prepositions ἀπὸ and παρὰ are used indiscriminately.

He says that he found them from the effects, he does not say he saw them: There is no authority extant concerning the children who may have been reborn at Ephesus. Ἐν ἀληθείᾳ here, just as before, denotes the truth of the Gospel. For there is no reason for changing the meaning and abandoning the propriety of the word.

Latin:

Vers. 4. Ἐχάρην λίαν.] .שָׂשְׂתִּי מְאוֹד

Ὅτι ὕυρηκα ἐκ τῶν τέκνων σε περιπατῦντας ἐν ἀληθείᾳ.] In- veni, id est, vidi, מָצָאתִי. Filii quidam ejus matronæ Ephe- sum, ut credibile est, venerant negotiorum causa. Περιπα- τεῖν הָלַךְ est vitam instituere. Ἐν ἀληθείᾳ sincere, ut modo diximus.

Καθὼς ἐντολὴν ἐλάβομεν παρὰ τῦ Πατρός.] Sicut à DEO præceptum accepimus, nempe per Christum. Cognovi eos ex animo, inquit, sequi præcepta Evangelica; quæ maxima est laus. In Manuscripto est ἀπὸ τῦ Πατρός. Duas istas præ- positiones ἀπὸ & παρὰ promiscue usurpari vidimus supra commate 3.

Invenisse se dicit ex effectis, vidisse non ait: De filiis, qui regeniti Ephesi sint, nulla prostat autori- tas. Ἐν ἀληθείᾳ hic æque ut antea, veritatem Ev- angelii denotat. Nulla enim causa est mutandæ si- gnificationis, & relinquendæ proprietatis vocis.

## 1:5
Vers. 5.

Καὶ νῦν ἐρωτῶ σε, Κυρία.] He used ἐρωτῶ for I pray, in the manner of Greeks imitating the Latins. We spoke about this at John IV, 31.

Οὐχ ὡς ἐντολὴν γράφων σοι καινὴν, ἀλλ᾿ ἣν ἔχομεν ἀπ᾿ ἀρχῆς, ἵνα ἀγαπῶμεν ἀλλήλες.] Ἀπ᾿ ἀρχῆς, that is, we learned it even under the law, although now in a broader and more intense sense: Taken from John's 1st epistle II, 7, where see the things said.

The discourse here is not about the times of the law, but about the beginning of the preached Gospel, as in the prior Johannine epistle. We noted there the Socinian fiction concerning a broader and more intense sense. Those who walk in the Evangelical truth according to the commandment of the Lord, also strive for charity from the heart. For these things are connected, Gal. V, 6. 1 John III, 16.

Latin:

Vers. 5.

Καὶ νῦν ἐρωτῶ σε, Κυρία.] Ἐρωτῶ posuit pro precor, more Græcorum Latinos imitantium. Diximus de eo ad Joh. IV, 31.

Οὐχ ὡς ἐντολὴν γράφων σοι καινὴν, ἀλλ᾿ ἣν ἔχομεν ἀπ᾿ ἀρχῆς, ἵνα ἀγαπῶμεν ἀλλήλες.] Ἀπ᾿ ἀρχῆς, id est, etiam sub lege didici- mus, quanquam nunc latiore & intensiore sensu: Sumptam ex Johanne 1. epistola II, 7. ubi dicta vide.

Non de temporibus legis, sed initio prædicati Evangelii hic, ut in priori Johannea sermo est. Commentum Socinianum de latiori & intensiori sensu ibi notavimus. Qui in veritate Evangelica ambulant secundum præceptum Domini, charita- ti etiam ex animo student. Hæc enim connexa sunt, Gal. V, 6. 1. Joh. III, 16.

## 1:6
Vers. 6.

Καὶ ἄυτη ἐστὶν ἡ ἀγάπη, ἵνα περιπατῶμεν κατὰ τὰς ἐντολὰς ἀυτῦ.

In this appears the love of God, namely that we should order our life according to his precepts. Similar sentiments are at John XIV, 2. and 1st Epistle II, 5. chapter V, 3.

Αὕτη ἐστὶν ἡ ἐντολή, καθὼς ἠκούσατε ἀπ᾿ ἀρχῆς, ἵνα ἐν αὐτῇ περιπατῆτε.]

This is what God has always demanded of us even under the state of the law, that we should love him, not by fulfilling one or another precept, but all his precepts by our deeds, as much as is possible. You have these things joined together in Deut. VI, 5. 6. 7. 8. Add Exodus XV, 26.

That similarity of sentiments, which Baronius also noted before, sufficiently teaches that the same author is St. John the Apostle. Scripture says nothing about the fulfillment of the whole law according to all precepts being possible for us after the fall. It teaches the contrary in Acts XV, 10. Rom. VIII, 11.

PART II.

EXHORTATION TO PRESERVE THE DOCTRINE OF CHRIST AGAINST SEDUCERS.

Latin:

Vers. 6.

Καὶ ἄυτη ἐστὶν ἡ ἀγάπη, ἵνα περιπατῶμεν κατὰ τὰς ἐντολὰς ἀυτῦ.

In eo apparet dilectio Dei, nempe ut vitam instituamus se- cundum præcepta ejus. Similes sententia Joh. XIV, 2. & 1. Epistola II, 5. cap. V, 3.

Αὕτη ἐστὶν ἡ ἐντολή, καθὼς ἠκούσατε ἀπ᾿ ἀρχῆς, ἵνα ἐν αὐτῇ περιπατῆτε.]

Hoc est quod Deus semper exegit a nobis etiam sub statu legis, ut ipsum diligeremus, non unum aut alterum præce- ptum, sed omnia ejus præcepta factis, quantum fieri potest, implendo. Habes hæc conjuncta Deut. VI, 5. 6. 7. 8. Adde Exodi XV, 26.

Similitudo illa sententiarum, quod antea Ba- ronius etiam notavit, satis docet eundem autorem S. Johannem Apostolum. De impletione legis to- tius secundum omnia præcepta nobis post lapsum possibili nihil Scriptura. Contrarium tradit Act. XV, 10. Rom. VIII, 11.

PARS II.

PARÆNESIS AD DOCTRINAM CHRISTI CONTRA SEDUCTORES SER- VANDAM.

## 1:7
Ver. 7.

For many deceivers have entered into the world, who do not confess Jesus Christ coming in the flesh.]

He imitates John the Apostle, his Master, 1 Epist. IV, 2, 3. This new sense begins and coheres with that which follows, βλέπετε ἑαυτούς. He designates both Anti-Christs and Pseudo-Prophets, who did not acknowledge Jesus as the Messiah for the reason that he had come in a humble state, and one subject to many evils. You have the word πλάνοι in Matt. 27, 63. 2 Cor. 6, 8. 1 Tim. 4, 1. מתעים deceivers.

This is the deceiver, and the Antichrist.]

After the plural he introduced the singular, contrary to what the Apostle did in chapter III, 16 of the Epistle, because in such cases either locution is of equal value. The sense is: He who teaches such things, he is an impostor; and if he also calls himself the Messiah or the deliverer of the people, he is the Antichrist. These things seem to have been written a little before the times of Bar Kokhba.

We spoke of those seducers in the former epistle, where we discussed the distinction between the Pseudo-Christ and the Anti-Christ and about Bar Kokhba. There is no need to repeat those things. The same style of St. John, the same argument, what else does it teach than the same Author?

Latin:

Vers. 7.

Ὅτι πολλοὶ πλάνοι εἰσῆλθον εἰς τὸν κόσμον, οἱ μὴ ὁμολογοῦντες Ἰησοῦν Χριστὸν ἐρχόμενον ἐν σαρκί.]

Imitatur Johannem Apostolum Magistrum suum 1. Epist. IV, 2. 3. Hic sensus novus incipit & cohæret cum eo, quod sequitur βλέπετε ἑαυτούς. Designat autem & Anti-Christos & Pseudo-Prophetas, qui Jesum ideo pro Messia non cogno- scebant, quod venisset in statu humili, & multis malis obno- xio. Vocem πλάνοι habes Matth. 27, 63. 2. Cor. 6, 8. 1. Tim. 4, 1. מתעים πλάνοι.

Οὗτός ἐστιν ὁ πλάνος, καὶ ὁ Ἀντίχριστος.]

Post plurale intulit singulare, contra quam Apostolus in E- pistolæ cap. III, 16. quia in talibus idem valet loquutio utra- que Sensus est: Qui talia docet, is est impostor; quod si & semet dicat Messiam aut populi vindicem, is est Antichristus. Videntur hæc scripta paulo ante tempora Barchochebæ.

De illis seductoribus in priori epistola diximus, ubi de discrimine Pseudo-Christi & Anti-Christi & de Barchocheba. Nihil opus est ea repetere. Idem S. Johannis stylus, idem Argumentum quid aliud docet, quam eundem Autorem?

## 1:8
Ver. 8. Look to yourselves.

The same locution is in Mark XIII, 9. Βλέπετε here is the same as φυλάσσετε.

That we may not lose what good things we have wrought, but may receive a full reward.]

In the Manuscript: ἵνα μὴ ἀπολέσητε ἃ εἰργάσασθε, which coheres better with that which preceded. Nor does the Latin read otherwise. To lose works is said metonymically for losing the fruit of good works: that this can happen we are taught both here and in Gal. III, 4. Heb. X, 34, 35. A full reward is the reward of eternal life. For there is also a lesser reward in this life, as in Luke X, 7.

Scripture is rashly changed. The meaning is: Lest the Apostle with his colleagues lose the fruits of the sacred works expended upon them: nor is it a question of the reward of good works, much less is eternal life designated as a reward, about which there is no word here; But he counts as a reward whatever fruit the ecclesiastical labors have brought forth through the Elect lady and her children: about to have a fuller fruit in place of a fuller reward. Cornelius à Lapide explains it thus: The reward of an Apostle and Teacher is full, when he sees the fruit of his works in his disciples, and when he is honored and crowned, receiving remuneration not only in himself, but also in his disciples. Conf. Phil. IV, 1. 1. Thess. II, 10.

Latin:

Vers. 8. Βλέπετε ἑαυτούς.]

Eadem locutio Marc. XIII, 9. Βλέπετε hic idem est, quod φυλάσσετε.

Ἵνα μὴ ἀπολέσωμεν ἃ εἰργασάμεθα καλὰ, ἀλλὰ μισθὸν πλήρη ἀπολάβωμεν.]

In Manuscripto: ἵνα μὴ ἀπολέσητε ἃ εἰργάσασθε, quæ me- lius cohærent cum eo, quod præcessit. Nec aliter legit Lati- nus. Amittere operas est Μετωνυμικῶς dictum pro amittere fructum bonorum operum: quod fieri posse & hic docemur & Gal. III, 4. Ebr. X, 34. 35. Merces plena est merces vitæ æ- ternæ. Nam est & minor merces in hac vita, ut Luc. X, 7.

Temere mutatur Scriptura. Sensus est: Ne amittat Apostolus cum collegis fructus operum sacrorum in ipso impensorum: neque de merce- de bonorum operum agitur, multo minus vita æter- na merces designatur, qua de nullum hic verbum; Sed pro mercede computat, quicquid fructus tu- lerint labores Ecclesiastici per Electam ejusque liberos: Pleniorem fructum plenioris mercedis loco habiturus. Cornelius à Lapide ita exponit: Plena Apostoli & Doctoris est merces, cum operum suorum fructum videt in Discipulis, cumque non tantum in se, sed & in Discipulis suis remuneratio- nem accipiens honoratur & coronatur. Conf. Phil. IV, 1. 1. Thess. II, 10.

## 1:9
Vers. 9. Πᾶς ὁ παραβαίνων καὶ μὴ μένων ἐν τῇ διδαχῇ τοῦ Χρι- στοῦ, Θεὸν οὐκ ἔχει.] To transgress is spoken of in an eminent sense of one who despises the law of God, as we said in Heb. II, 2. But he despises the law of God who does not persist in the Gospel. For here μένειν is used for διαμένειν. He who does that does not have God, that is, does not know Him, as in the Epistle of John II, 23. For God is not known at this time except through the Son, as formerly through Moses.

Ὁ μένων ἐν τῇ διδαχῇ τοῦ Χριστοῦ.] Remaining in words and deeds.

Οὗτος καὶ τὸν πατέρα, καὶ τὸν υἱὸν ἔχει.] He shows that the will of both the Father and the Son is known to him. Thus we have often had 'to know' for 'to show to know,' an expression very familiar to the Hebrews. Παραβαίνειν and μένειν are opposites. St. John loves to express the same thing with equivalent terms, and to explain his meaning both affirmatively and negatively. Here, therefore, we have again a character of Johannine diction. Therefore, one should not resort to the transgression of the law, so that it may finally be inferred that there is a lack of persistence in Evangelical doctrine, since the same thing is handed down synonymously by position and by negation. He who transgresses the doctrine of Christ or of the Gospel, and does not remain in the same, does not have God, that is, he does not enjoy the grace of God or the communion of God, which we have through the Word of the Gospel apprehended by faith. For without faith it is impossible to please God, Heb. XI, 16. Therefore the Vulgate rightly rendered: Everyone who recedes from the doctrine of Christ, and the Syriac: He who passes over and does not remain in the doctrine of Christ. Nor indeed is there any reason why we should explain ἔχειν as knowledge. For in truth he who remains in the doctrine of Christ has both the Father and the Son, he does not merely show that he has them. Nor is having the Father and the Son in this way to show that the will of the Father and the Son is known. St. John is accustomed to use this phrase concerning the communion which we have with the Father and the Son through faith held in the Word. Syriac: He does not have God as a friend. He who has the Father and the Son, consequently has also the Holy Spirit, because these three are one, 1 John V, 7. He is therefore a temple of the Holy Trinity, John XIV, 23; 1 Cor. III, 6; c. VI, 19. That is a tautology, to remain in the doctrine of Christ, or to have the same, and to have knowledge of the will of Christ. Would anyone doubt that the doctrine of Christ exhibits His will? But God was never known to anyone, except through the Son, Matt. 11, 26; John I, 18; and not even to Moses, whom the Son Himself sent and instructed, Exodus III and IV.

Latin:

Vers. 9. Πᾶς ὁ παραβαίνων καὶ μὴ μένων ἐν τῇ διδαχῇ τοῦ Χρι- στοῦ, Θεὸν οὐκ ἔχει.] Παραβαίνειν eximie dicitur, qui legem Dei contemnit, ut diximus Ebr. II, 2. Contemnit autem legem Dei, qui in Evangelio non perstat. Est enim hic μένειν pro διαμένειν. Qui id facit, Deum non habet, id est, non novit, ut Epistola Johannis II, 23. Nam Deus hoc tempore non no- scitur, nisi per Filium, ut olim per Mosen.

Ὁ μένων ἐν τῇ διδαχῇ τοῦ Χριστοῦ.] Permanens dictis & factis.

Οὗτος καὶ τὸν πατέρα, καὶ τὸν υἱὸν ἔχει.] Is ostendit no- tam sibi esse voluntatem & Patris & Filii. Ita sæpe habui- mus nosse pro ostendere nosse, locutione Hebræis admodum familiari. Παραβαίνειν, & μένειν opposita sunt. Amat æ- quipollentibus idem efferre, & tum affirmative, tum negative mentem suam explicare S. Johan- nes. Hic ergo iterum characterem habemus di- ctionis Johanneæ. Ideo non ad transgressionem le- gis demum abeundum, ut denique inferatur non persistentia in Evangelica doctrina, quum συνωνύ- μως κατὰ θέσιν & κατ’ ἄρνησιν idem tradatur. Qui transgreditur doctrinam Christi vel Evangelii, & non permanet in eadem, Deum non habet, id est, Dei gratia non fruitur aut communione Dei, quam per Verbum Evangelii fide apprehensum habemus. Sine fide enim impossibile est Deo placere, Ebr. XI, 16. Ideo recte Vulgatus reddidit: Omnis, qui recedit à doctrina Christi, & Syrus: Qui transit & non permanet in doctrina Christi. Nec vero est, quod ἔχειν de notitia explicemus. Nam revera ha- bet & Patrem & Filium, qui in doctrina Christi manet, non tantum ostendit se habere. Neque ita habere Patrem & Filium est ostendere, notam esse Patris & Filii voluntatem. De communione, quam cum Patre & Filio habemus per fidem Verbo ha- bitam, S. Johannes hac phrasi uti consuevit. Sy- rus: Deum non habet amicum. Qui Patrem & Fi- lium habet, consequenter habet & Spiritum San- ctum, quia hi tres unum sunt, 1. Joh.V, 7. Templum ergo est S. Trinitatis, Joh. XIV, 23. 1. Cor. III, 6. c. VI, 19. Ταυτολογία illa est, manere in doctrina Chri- sti, seu eandem habere, & habere cognitionem volun- tatis Christi. Num doctrinam Christi quis ambige- ret exhibere ejus voluntatem? Deus autem nun- quam & nulli notus fuit, nisi per Filium, Matth. 11, 26. Joh. I, 18. ac ne Mosi quidem, quem Filius ipse misit, & instruxit, Exodi III. & IV.

## 1:10
Vers. 10. If anyone comes to you.) If anyone insinuates himself into your Churches.

And does not bring this doctrine.) And does not bring that doctrine which is in the Gospel. If anyone professes that he abhors the Gospel.

They do not always profess that they abhor the Gospel, who do not bring the Evangelical doctrine. Often they pretend that they bring the same, and profess themselves to be Evangelicals. The devil himself transforms himself into an Angel of light through the Lord, if his ministers transform themselves into ministers of righteousness, 2 Cor. XI, 13, 14, 15. And the discourse is about Doctors and seducers, not about the seduced.

Do not receive him into your house.) This is not said of those who have always been strangers to the Church, as can be seen in 1 Cor. V, 10. But of those who wish to be held as brothers, and overturn the doctrine.

External and political conversation is not prohibited, but ecclesiastical communion, by which one is received either into the house of the Church with danger and scandal, or even into more intimate conversation. For the hearts of the innocent can easily be seduced, Romans XVI, 18, or affected by scandal, when they see such conversation with Pseudo-Prophets, so that they believe it does not matter much between doctrines whose Doctors are so familiar with each other. Those false Doctors Ebion, Cerinthus, or others who insinuated themselves into that Church seem to have given the cause for writing the Epistle. With the danger of perversion of yourself or others excluded, and scandal removed, communication of nature with heretics is not forbidden by divine law, especially if necessity, or piety, or grave utility persuades it, says Tirinus the Jesuit. But Jesuit practice and the Spanish inquisition do not observe that observation at all. But St. John does not only advise this, as it seemed to some, but commands it, and adds a most grave reason for the interdict in v. 11. But why should this be restricted only to those who wish to be held as brothers? Is there not also danger from those who have always been strangers to the Church?

Such as certainly many were in John's age, even from the Cerinthians and Ebionites, with whom St. John did not even want to remain in one bath. And do not say greeting to him.) It signifies that the familiarity of such is to be avoided. And it was the custom for many nations not even to speak to those whom they abhorred. Herodotus, Thalia: He gave no word. And Polymnia: Nor did he converse: John the Disciple of the Lord, when going to the bath in Ephesus, when he had seen Cerinthus inside, leaped out of the bath, not washed, saying that he feared the bath would collapse, since Cerinthus, the enemy of the truth, was inside, so the interpreters of Irenaeus III, 3. The same reports about Ebion, Eusebius l. III, hist. Eccl. c. 25. Theodoret l. II, de haeret. fab. Epiphanius, haer. XXX, mentions that Ebion was, either by a mnemonic error, or also because Ebion was present in the bath together with Cerinthus.

Latin:

Vers. 10. Εἴ τις ἔρχεται πρὸς ὑμᾶς.) Si quis se insinuet in vestras Ecclesias.

Καὶ ταύτην τὴν διδαχὴν ὀ φέρει.) Et non afferat doctrinam illam, quæ est in Evangelio. Si quis profitetur se abhorrere ab Evangelio.

Non semper profitentur abhorrere sese ab Ev- angelio, qui non afferunt doctrinam Evangelicam. Sæpe simulant se afferre eandem, & profitentur se Evangelicos. Transformat se diabolus ipse in An- gelum lucis per Dominum, si ministri ejus in ministros justitiæ se transformant 2. Cor. XI, 13. 14. 15. Et de Doctoribus ac seductoribus sermo est, non de seductis.

Μὴ λαμβάνετε αὐτὸν εἰς οἰκίαν.) Hoc non dicitur de iis, qui alieni semper fuere ab Ecclesia, ut videre est 1. Cor. V, 10. Sed de iis, qui volunt fratres haberi, & doctrinam evertunt.

Non prohibetur conversatio externa & Politi- ca, sed communio Ecclesiastica, qua vel in domum Ecclesiæ cum periculo & scandalo quis recipitur, vel etiam ad intimicrem conversationem. Facile enim seduci corda innocentum possunt, Roman. XVI, 18. aut scandalo affici, ubi talem conversa- tionem cum Pseudo-Prophetis vident, ut credant, non multum interesse inter doctrinas, quarum Doctores adeo inter se familiares sunt. Causam scribendæ Epistolæ videntur dedisse illi falsi Do- ctores Ebion, Cerinthus, aliive, qui se in Eccle- sia illa insinuarunt. Secluso perversionis periculo seu tui, seu aliorum, & semoto scandalo, non vetatur ju- re divino vel communicatio naturæ cum hæreticis, præsertim si vel necessitas, vel pietas, vel gravis utili- tas eam suadeat, inquit Tirinus Jesuita. Sed praxis Jesuitica, & inquisitio Hispanica observationem illam minime observat. Non autem tantum con- sulit hoc S. Johannes, ut quibusdam visum, sed præcipit, ejusque gravissimam rationem addit in- terdicti v. 11. Cur autem id restringendum solum ad eos, qui fratres haberi volunt. Annon etiam pe- riculum ab iis, qui alieni semper fuere ab Ecclesia.

Quales certe multi fuere Johannis ævo, etiam è Cerinthianis & Ebionitis, cum quibus ne quidem in uno balneo manere voluit S. Johannes. Καὶ χάρειν ἀὐτῷ μὴ λέγετε.) Significat talium familiari- tatem devitandam. Et mos erat multis gentibus, ne allo- qui quidem, quos aversarentur. Herodotus Thalia: Λόγον ὐ̓δένα ἐδίδε. Et Polymnia: ὐ̓δὲ διελέγετο: Johannes Domini Discipulus cum in Epheso iens labari, cum vidisset intus Cerin- thum, exsiliit de balneo, non lotus, dicens quod timeat, ne bal- neum concidat, cum intus esset Cerinthus veritatis inimicus, ita Irenæi interpretes III, 3. Refert idem de Ebione Eusebius l. III. hist. Eccl. c. 25. Theodoretus l. II. de hæret. fab. Epiphanius hær. XXX. Ebionem fuisse memorat sive per ἁμάρ- τημα μνημονευτικὸν, sive etiam quod una cum Ce- rintho Ebion balneo interfuerit.

## 1:11
Vers. 11. For he who says to him greeting.) A synecdoche or even a hyperbole. For he wishes to say, he who cultivates friendship with such a one. See what we have said on Matt. XVIII, 17. Saying greeting, bidding him hail. He participates in his evil works.) He comes into a share of the guilt, as an approver. A similar phrase 1 Tim. 5, 22. See Ps. 50, 18.

This is not a hyperbole here, but it is to be understood both of the spiritual salutation, by which the faithful and fellow-members in the Church of Christ salute each other with the holy kiss of peace, which is a symbol of spiritual love rooted in sincere faith and arising from it, Rom. XVI, 16; 1 Cor. XVI, 20; 2 Cor. XIII, 10; 1 Pet. V, 14; and of the honorable address and votive congratulation, which was in use among the Orientals, by which one exhibits honor to the enemies of the truth through simulation or other reason not without scandal, flatters, or applauds them: and of familiar conversation and more prolonged discourse, as the word salutation is sometimes wont to be taken more broadly. See 2 Kings IV, 29; Luke X, 4; Acts XVIII, 22. It is certainly known that it is forbidden for anyone to have a meeting with Doctors who do not bring the doctrine of Christ, which is instituted either by favor of that heterodoxy, or with the danger of our seduction, or with the scandal of one's neighbor, and especially of the weak. Because he who in such a way says AVE to them at all; he communicates in their evil works. These explanations certainly include one another, and therefore they are rightly joined. If it is not permitted to converse familiarly with seducers, much less are they to be held honorably and in esteem, let alone to be applauded, and least of all are they to be embraced with the kiss of holy communion as members of the mystical body. Concerning communication with the evil works of such, Cornelius à Lapide has this: By greeting a heretical teacher, one seems to favor and applaud his dogma and heresy, and to cherish it, and to promote it by one's authority, favor, hospitality, and resources. For just as he who receives into his house a thief practicing the art of stealing is considered to cooperate in his thefts, and therefore is punished according to the laws as a receiver of thieves, because he gives the thief a receptacle and hiding place: And he who lets a house to a harlot so that she may commit harlotry is considered to cooperate in her harlotry, says Navarrus in his Manual, ch. 17, no. 195. If anyone receives into his hospitality a heretic coming into a city so that he may dogmatize in it and spread heresy, he is considered to cooperate in the propagation of his doctrine and heresy. St. John forbids here every conversation, every fellowship, every commerce with heretics, for this is more than an ave. The Apostles and their disciples certainly held such honor that they would not even verbally communicate with any of those who had adulterated the truth. Cf. what is said about these things in the preface to the digression, Vol. I, System. Theol., p. 882, et seqq. Toward the end of this verse, some Latin codices add: Behold, I have foretold you, that you may not be confounded in the day of the Lord. But these are spurious, even if they are admitted by Lyranus himself, Hugo, Dionysius, and Thomas Aquinas.

Latin:

Vers. 11. Ὁ γὰρ λέγων αὐτῷ χαίρειν.) Συνεκδοχὴ vel etiam ὑπερβολή. Vult enim dicere, qui cum tali amicitiam colit. Vide quæ à nobis ad Matth. XVIII, 17. Λέγων χαίρειν jubens salvere. Κοινωνεῖ τοῖς ἔργοις αὐτοῦ τοῖς πονηροῖς.) In partem venit cul- pæ, tanquam approbator. Par locutio 1.Tim. 5, 22. Vid. Pf. 50, 18.

Non est hic ὑπερβολὴ, sed intelligendum id tum de salutatione spirituali, qua sese fideles ac concor- pores in Ecclesia Christi sacro pacis osculo salu- tant, quod symbolum est amoris spiritualis in fide sincera radicati, & ex ea oriundi, Rom. XVI, 16. 1. Cor. XVI, 20. 2. Cor. XIII, 10. 1. Petr. V, 14. tum de honorifica compellatione, ac votiva congratula- tione, quæ in usu fuit apud Orientales, qua hosti- bus veritatis quis honorem per simulationem, aliave ratione non sine scandalo, exhibet, adula- tur, vel applaudit iisdem: tum de familiari conver- satione, ac prolixiori colloquio, prout quandoque largius solet accipi vox salutationis. Vid. 2. Reg. IV, 29. Luc. X, 4. Act. XVIII, 22. Certum omni- no est, cuivis interdictum esse cum Doctoribus, Christi doctrinam non afferentibus, congressui, qui vel favore heterodoxias illius, vel cum peri- culo seductionis nostri, vel cum scandalo proxi- mi, & cumprimis infirmorum instituitur. Quia qui tali ratione ullatenus AVE illis dicit; is commu- nicat operibus ipforum malis. Includunt sane ista explicationes sese mutuò, ideoque recte conjun- guntur. Si non licet familiariter cum seductoribus conversari, multo minus honorifice ac in pretio il- li habendi, nedum applaudendum iisdem, minime omnium osculo sanctæ communionis œu membra corporis mystici complectendi erunt. De com- municatione cum operibus talium malignis Corne- lius à Lapide ita habet: Salutando hæreticum dogma- tisten videtur dogmati & hæresi ejus favere & applau- dere, illudque fovere, & promovere sua autoritate, favore, hospitio, facultatibus. Sicut enim qui furem artem furandi exercentem domo excipit, censetur ejus furtis cooperari, ac proinde juxta leges quasi furum receptator punitur, quia furi dat receptaculum & la- tebras: Et qui meretrici, ut meretricetur, elocat do- mum, censetur cooperari ejus meretricio, ait Navar- rus in Manuali c. 17. num. 195. Si qui hæreticum ve- nientem in urbem, ut in ea dogmatizet, hæresinƀspar- gat, hospitio excipit, censetur ejus doctrinæ & hæresis propagationi cooperari. Vetat hic S. Johannes omne colloquium, omne consortium, omne commercium cum hæreticis, hoc enim plus est, quam ave. Apostoli certe & eorum Discipuli tantum habuerunt hono- rem, ut neque verbotenus communicarent alicui eorum, qui adulteraverant veritatem. Conf. quæ de his in præfat. ad digress. Tom. I. System. Theol. p. 882. seqq. Sub finem hujus versus codices non- nulli Latini addunt: Ecce, prædixi vobis, ut in die Domini non confundamini. Sed ista νόθα sunt, etsi ab ipso Lyrano, Hugone, Dionysio, & Thoma Angli- co admittantur.

## 1:12
V. 12.

Vers. 12. Having many things to write unto you.) Having many things which I could write, not useless to you.

I did not wish by paper and ink.) Namely to write, which is expressed in the following epistle v. 13. Moreover, there is a twofold acceptation of the word to write, proper or improper. For improperly, both he who speaks and he who does good to anyone is said to write upon his heart Prov. III, 3. Jerem. XXXI, 33.

It is not permitted to observe any example of that improper inscription. Those cited passages are irrelevant. For there, to write upon the heart is not to do good to anyone, but to imprint firmly upon one's own mind, Prov. III, 3. But Jerem. XXXI, 33, that phrase is employed concerning the interior information of the mind and the impression of the divine law upon our heart through the illumination of the mind and the conversion of the heart. But why Grotius brought in his proper and improper inscription here, is not clear. Cornelius: I did not wish by paper and ink, not as if I could not write more because of a lack of paper and ink, but because I judge that those things should not be committed to paper and ink, (so the Syriac) that is, they should not be written, but communicated by word of mouth, as follows, either because they are secret, or because letters can perish, or fall into the hands of infidels, who interpret all our things wrongly; or because the living voice is more effective and more pleasing than written ones. The act of the living voice has I know not what latent energy, and it sounds more strongly in the ears of the Disciples when transfused from the mouth of the Author.

But I hope to come unto you.) Into that city where you are. In the Manuscript: For I hope to be with you.

And mouth to mouth to speak.) The former accusative, placed in the Greek manner, for which the Latins would place the ablative. The same locution in Greek, Num. XII, 8. But similar to 1 Cor. XIII, 12. Face to face.

That our joy may be fulfilled.) Fulfilled for full, just as begotten and the like. And this is said comparatively, because there is fuller joy from mutual sight than from the commerce of letters. See Rom. I, 12 and 2 Tim. I, 4, where there is a like locution.

Cornelius gathers from these things that this epistle was written and sent not to Babylon, as Clement of Alexandria says, but to some city of Asia or Greece, near to Ephesus. For from there, he says, St. John, now aged and almost decrepit, could and was accustomed to run out to the neighboring cities of Asia to instruct and confirm them in the faith, but not to Babylon, which is so remote; which things we leave in the middle. In the Greek

Latin:

V. 12.

Vers. 12. Πολλὰ ἔχων ὑμῖν γράφειν.) Multa habens, quæ scribere poteram, vobis non inutilia.

Οὐκ ἐβουλήθην διὰ χάρτου καὶ μέλανος.) Nempe γράψαι, quod exprimitur sequente epistola v. 13. Est autem duplex ac- ceptio vocis γράψαι, propria vel impropria. Improprie enim & qui dicit, & qui bene cuiquam facit, dicitur cordi ejus in- scribere Prov. III, 3. Jerem. XXXI, 33.

De inscriptione ista impropria nullum observare licet exemplum. Loca ista adducta aliena sunt. Non enim ibi inscribere cordi est benefacere cuiquam, sed animo suo firmiter imprimere, Prov. III, 3. Jerem. vero XXXI, 33. de interiori mentis informatione ac legis divinæ impressione in corde nostra per illustra- tionem animi & conversionem cordis phrasis ea adhibetur. Quorsum autem hic propriam & impropriam suam inscriptionem adduxerit Gro- tius, non liquet. Cornelius: Nolui per chartam & atramentum, non quasi ob defectum chartæ & atra- menti plura scribere nequeam, sed quod censeam ea non committenda esse chartæ & atramento, (ita Syrus) hoc est, non esse scribenda, sed oretenus com- municanda, ut sequitur, sive quia secreta sunt, sive quia literæ perire, vel in infidelium, qui perperam omnia nostra interpretantur, manus incidere possunt; sive quia viva vox est efficacior & gratior quam scri- ptæ. Habet nescio latentis energiæ quid vivæ vo- cis actus, & in aures Discipulorum de Autoris ore transfusa fortius sonat.

Ἀλλὰ ἐλπίζω ἐλθεῖν πρὸς ὑμᾶς.) In eam urbem, ubi vos estis. In Manuscripto: Ἐλπίζω γὰρ γίνεσθαι πρὸς ὑμᾶς.

Καὶ στόμα πρὸς στόμα λαλῆσαι.) Accusativus prior, Græco more positus, pro quo Latini ponerent Ablativum. Eadem locutio in Græco, Num. XII, 8. Similis vero 1. Cor. XIII, 12. Πρόσωπον πρὸς πρόσωπον.

Ἵνα ἡ χαρὰ ἡμῶν ᾖ πεπληρωμένη.) Πεπληρωμένη pro πλήρης, quomodo γεγεννημένη & similia. Et dictum hoc comparate, quia plenius gaudium ex conspectu mutuo, quam ex com- mercio literarum. Vid. Rom. I, 12. & 2. Tim. I, 4. ubi par locutio.

Colligit ex hisce Cornelius, hanc epistolam scri- ptam & missam non Babylonem, ut ait Clemens Alexandr. sed ad aliquam Asiæ vel Græciæ urbem, Epheso vicinam. Inde enim, inquit, ad vicinas Asiæ urbes in fide erudiendas & confirmandas excurrere poterat & solebat S. Johannes jam grandævus, & pene decrepitus, non vero in Babylonem adeo remo- tam; Quæ nos in medio relinquimus. In Græco

# 3 John

## 1:1 Introduction
[Abraham Calov, Biblia Novi Testamenti Illustrata (Vol. 2, Part 2). English: machine translation, The Faith Received (Mere Orthodoxy); the original follows each comment.]
ANNOTATIONS ON THE THIRD EPISTLE OF ST. JOHN

Latin:

ANNOT TERTIAM S EPIST

## 1:1 Argument
ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

With a preceding inscription he prays that he may fare well, inasmuch as he has been exhilarated by the report concerning his faith, highly commending his hospitality toward strangers, but complaining about Diotrephes, whence he exhorts him not to imitate him, and praises Demetrius, and gives hope of his own arrival. Finally, with a vow of peace, and a salutation performed in the name of friends, after he has bidden the friends greetings, he concludes the little epistle.

There are three parts: I. The exordium, containing the inscription and the vow with joy, to verse 4. II.

is ἡμῶν [our], not vestrum [your], as the Latin has it. For St. John was as much rejoicing to see, teach, and console his hearers, as they were rejoicing in his appearance, doctrine, and consolation. Compare Rom. 1:12.

Latin:

'ARGUMENTUM ET PAR- TITIO.

Prævia inscriptione precatur, ut feliciter agat, siquidem exhilaratus sit nuncio de fide ipsius, commendans valde hospitali- tatem ejus erga peregrinos, conquerens vero de Diotrephe, unde hortatur, ne eum imitetur, laudatque Demetrium, ac spem facit de adventu suo. Denique pacis voto, & salutatione nomine amico- rum peracto, postquam salvere amicos jus- sit, epistolium concludit.

Partes tres sunt: I. Exordium, inscriptionem & votum cum gaudio continens, ad vers. 4. II.

est ἡμῶν nostrum, non vestrum, ut Latinus habet. Tam enim S. Johannes gaudebat videre, docere & consolari suos auditores, quam illi gaudebant ejus aspectu, doctrina & consolatione. Confer Rom. I, 12.

## 1:1
Verse 1. ὁ Πρεσβύτερος..) See the beginning of the preceding epistle. Γαΐῳ τῷ ἀγαπητῷ.) It is a Roman name. The age hardly allows that this is the same Gaius who is named in Rom. 16:23 and 1 Cor. 1:14, or who is in Acts 19:29 and 20:4. The word was very common, but among those well known and friends, it was sufficient to say the praenomen: Soft ears rejoice in a praenomen, says Horace. Such is that 'O Titus' in Ennius and Cicero. Ἀγαπητὸς is a flattering appellation which Christians used among themselves, as in Rom. 16:5, 8, 9, 12, 1 Cor. 4:17, Eph. 6:21, Col. 1:7, ch. 4:9, 2 Tim. 1:2, Philem. 1:16. This Gaius lived in one of the churches which are mentioned in the Apocalypse.

There is no reason why Gaius, the famous host of St. Paul at Corinth, Rom. XVI, verse 23, should not be present, unless perhaps there is a preconceived opinion about the author of the epistle being not John the Apostle, but some other Presbyter. For so say Bede, Hugo, the Gloss, Lyranus, Dionysius the Carthusian on this passage, Ambrosiaster on Rom. XVI, and many others. Compare 1 Cor. I, 13, 14. Cajetan and Catharinus do indeed doubt it; but no solid reason for doubting appears. Onuphrius in his Chronicle makes him a Roman, Lucius Dexter a Spaniard; both determine that he was the third Bishop of Milan. However, the opinion of the aforementioned interpreters, that he was Paul's host at Corinth, seems preferable. Athanasius in his Synopsis testifies that he was familiar with John. Dorotheus makes that Pauline Gaius the Bishop of Ephesus, Sedulius of Thessalonica; but in a Bishop, hospitality is most highly commended, 1 Tim. III, 2, Tit. I, 8. What Mariana and Serarius relate about the same monarch of Asia does not sufficiently agree with his hospitality, and is destitute of firm authority.

Ὃν ἐγὼ ἀγαπῶ ἐν ἀληθείᾳ.] As in the preceding epistle, verse 1.

Latin:

Vers. 1. ὁ Πρεσβύτερος..) Vide initio epistolæ præcedentis. Γαΐῳ τῷ ἀγαπητῷ.) Est nomen Romanum. Vix fert æ- tas, ut idem sit hic Cajus, qui nominatur Rom. XVI, 23. & 1. Cor. I, 14. aut qui in Actis XIX, 29. & XX, 4. Vocabulum erat valde commune, sed inter bene notos & amicos sufficie- bat prænomen dicere: Gaudent prænomine molles Auriculæ. ait Horatius. Tale illud ô Tite apud Ennium & Cicero- nem. Ἀγαπητὸς blanda appellatio, qua Christiani inter se utebantur, ut Rom. XVI, 5. 8. 9. 12. 1. Cor. IV, 17. Ephes. VI, 21. Coloss. I, 7. c. IV, 9. 2. Tim. I, 2. Philem. I, 16. Vixit hic Cajus in aliqua Ecclesiarum, quarum mentio in Apoca- lypsi.

Causa nulla est, cur Cajus præsens non sit fa- mosus ille hospes S. Pauli Corinthius, Rom. XVI. vers. 23. nisi forte præconcepta opinio de Auto- re epistolæ non Johanne Apostolo, sed alio quo- dam Presbytero. Ita enim Beda, Hugo, Glossa, Lyranus, Dionysius Carthusianus in h. l. Ambrosia- ster ad Rom. XVI. & plerique alii. Conf. 1. Cor. I, 13. 14. Cajetanus & Catharinus dubitant qui- dem; sed non apparet solida dubitandi ratio. Onuphrius in Chron. Romanum facit, Lucius Dexter Hispanum; uterque tertium Mediola- nensem Episcopum fuisse eum statuit. Præferen- da autem videtur Interpretum dictorum senten- tia, quod hospes Pauli Corinthius fuerit. Athanasius in Synopsi eum Johanni fuisse familiarem testatur. Episcopum Cajum illum Paulinum Ephesinum facit Dorotheus, Thessalonicensem Sedulius, in Episcopo autem maxime commendatur hospitalitas, 1. Tim. III, 2. Tit. I, 8. Quæ Mariana, & Serarius de eo- dem Asicæ Monarcho tradunt, non satis conve- niunt ejus hospitalitati, firmaque autoritate de- stituuntur.

Ὃν ἐγὼ ἀγαπῶ ἐν ἀληθείᾳ.] Ut epistola præcedente com- mate 1.

## 1:2
Ἀγαπητὲ.] The epistle begins after the inscription.

Verse 2.

Περὶ πάντων.] As regards all things. Thus Phil. I, 7, chap. II, 19.

Εὔχομαί σε εὐοδοῦσθαι לְהַצְלָחָה.] See Rom. I, 10, 1 Cor. XVI, 2.

Καὶ ὑγιαίνειν.] This is placed as if parenthetically. For it refers back to the word εὐοδοῦσθαι. But because εὐοδοῦσθαι is the greater part of ὑγιαίνειν, therefore after the name of the genus, the most excellent species has been added.

Καθὼς εὐοδοῦταί σου ἡ ψυχὴ.] ψυχὴ is used here for the whole soul, as in Matt. XXII, 37, Mark XII, 30, 33, Luke I, 27, Eph. VI, 6, Col. III, 23. I do not doubt that you are of such a mind as I could wish. I wish the same regarding your body and other matters: It is to be wished that there be a sound mind in a sound body.

Pagninus and the Tigurines understand the words περὶ πάντων as concerning all the faithful, omitting the particle σὲ, which is, however, read in all Greek, Syriac, and Latin codices. The Syrian has explained the sense more correctly: In every matter I pray for you, that you may prosper and be healthy, just as your soul prospers; and Vatablus: Just as you are well in soul, so I desire you to be well in all things. Cornelius also interprets the Vulgate in this way, concerning all things, that is, in all things, yet your soul is yourself: with whom Tirinus has rendered this sense: as if to say, I desire that all things which concern your family, business, income, and work may turn out most happily for you, just as I hear that you are doing very well. Which is also handed down by Bede. This sense does not seem to be rejected: For that περὶ πάντων, which pertains to all matters, embraces more than the health of the body. This is hinted at by the word ὑγιαίνειν, but that εὐοδοῦσθαι περὶ πάντων implies more.

Latin:

Ἀγαπητὲ.] Post inscriptionem incipit epistola.

Vers. 2.

Περὶ πάντων.] Quod attinet ad res omnes. Sic Phil. I, 7. cap. II, 19.

Εὔχομαί σε εὐοδοῦσθαι לְהַצְלָחָה.] Vide Rom. I, 10. 1. Co- rinth. XVI, 2.

Καὶ ὑγιαίνειν.] Hoc velut παρενθετικῶς positum est. Nam redditur ad vocem εὐοδοῦσθαι. Sed quia τὸ εὐοδοῦσθαι maxima pars est τὸ ὑγιαίνειν, ideo post generis nomen addita est species excellentissima.

Καθὼς εὐοδοῦταί σου ἡ ψυχὴ.] ψυχὴ hic pro toto animo po- nitur, ut Matth. XXII, 37. Marc. XII, 30. 33. Luc. I, 27. Ephes. VI, 6. Col. III, 23. Non dubito quin animo sis tali, qualem optare possem. Idem opto de corpore & rebus aliis : Optandum est, ut sit mens sana in corpore sano.

Verba περὶ πάντων de omnibus fidelibus Pa- gninus & Tigurin. intelligunt, omittentes parti- culam σὲ, quæ vero in omnibus Græcis, Syriacis & Latinis Codicibus legitur. Sensum rectius ex- posuit Syrus : In omni re oro ego pro te, ut prospere pergas & sis sanus, sicut prospere agit anima tua; & Vatablus: Sicut animo bene habes, ita opto te per omnia bene habere. Sic etiam interpretatur Cor- nelius Vulgatam de omnibus, id est, in omnibus ani- ma tamen tua ipsi est tu ipse: cum quo Tirinus hunc sensum reddidit: q. d. Opto tibi felicissime ce- dant omnia, quæ familiam tuam, negotia proventus, & opus concernunt, sicut audio te optime habere. Qui etiam à Beda traditus est. Non videtur repro- bandus hic sensus: Nam illud περὶ πάντων, quod attinet ad res omnes, plura complectitur quam sa- nitatem corporis. Hæc voce ὑγιαίνειν innuitur, illa vero εὐοδοῦσθαι περὶ πάντων plura important.

## 1:3
Verse 3.

For I rejoiced greatly.] See above II, 4.

When the brethren came.] When certain Christians came from your parts. This is a present tense for a past.

And of your testifying to the truth.] Who bear witness of your sincerity. Μαρτυρῶ usually governs the dative, Luke IX, 22. Acts XIV, 3. ch. XV, 8. ch. XXII, 5. Rom. X, 2. Gal. IV, 15. Matt. XXIII, 31.

As you walk in truth.] This is an explanation of what preceded. In truth, as if to say, that is, how you order your whole life sincerely, namely, as befits a Christian in deed, not in name. The word σὺ is absent in the manuscript.

Truth in the latter place seems to denote sincerity in faith and charity, but in the former, the truth of the Gospel. For those who receive the truth of the Gospel as is fitting, walk in sincere faith and charity.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

Ἐχάρην γὰρ λίαν.] Vide supra II, 4.

Ἐρχομένων ἀδελφῶν.] Cum Christiani quidam venere ex vestris partibus. Est hic Præsens pro Præterito.

Καὶ μαρτυρούντων σου τῇ ἀληθείᾳ.] Qui testimonium perhi- bent de tua sinceritate. Μαρτυρῶ solet regere Dativum, Luc. IX, 22. Act. XIV, 3. c. XV, 8. c. XXII, 5. Rom. X, 2. Gal. IV, 15. Matth. XXIII, 31.

Καθὼς σὺ ἐν ἀληθείᾳ περιπατεῖς.] Est explicatio ejus quod præcessit. Ἐν ἀληθείᾳ, quasi di- cat, id est, quomodo tu sincere vitam omnem instituas, nempe, ut decet Christianum re, non nomine. Abest σὺ in Manuscripto.

Ἀλήθεια posteriori loco sinceritatem in fide & charitate videtur notare, priori vero veritatem Evangelii. Nam qui veritatem Evangelii, pro- ut par est, suscipiunt, in fide ac charitate sincera ambulant.

## 1:4
I have no greater joy than these.] Other codices have ταύτης. Μειζοτέραν is a comparative made from a comparative to intensify the meaning, just as ἐλαχιστότερος is a comparative from a superlative, Eph. III, 8.

That I may hear my children walking in truth.] In the manuscript it is in the truth, that is, according to the Gospel. Clearly the same construction as John XV, 13, where we said that ἵνα is explanatory of ταύτης which had preceded. My children, that is, those whom I instructed, 1 Tim. I, 2, 18. 2 Tim. I, 2. ch. II, 1. Philem. 10. John indeed, as also Peter, labored especially among the Jews, but when the opportunity was given, they did not omit to instruct the Gentiles also, as Peter did Cornelius.

Here therefore Grotius acknowledges that the Apostle John is the author of the epistle, who labored especially among the Jews with Peter. The Vulgate here is barbaric: I have no greater thanks of these, that is, greater than these. For it is a Grecism, and the codices do not have χάριν, but χαρὰν, that is, joy, if you except a few. Bartholomew of Peter has it thus in this place. The ancient Biblical concordances collected by Hugo of Saint-Cher, Cardinal of the family of Saint Dominic, consistently read, I have no greater joy than these. For this reading is found in those concordances in three places, namely, under the word major, the word habeo, and the word gaudium, and Isidorus Clarius is a witness that he saw ancient Latin codices that had it so. The Complutensian Bible and the Royal Bible derived from it also have it thus. If all these things could have been considered by the Roman correctors, there is little doubt they would have received Cardinal Hugo's reading into the text, as it is sufficiently clear that it is the genuine writing of our interpreter, and it is lucid and clearly conformable to the Greek codex. This diversity arose from the fact that a few less correct Greek codices read χάριν here, which sounds as grace, whereas almost all others have χαρὰν, joy. From this flowed two different interpretations, of which the one that is of the inferior reading occupies most of our codices that are in our hands today. The Syriac rendered it: No joy is greater to me than that I should hear my children walking in the truth. St. Jerome in Chapter V to the Ephesians celebrates a certain axiom of Christ: Never be joyful, except when you have seen your brother in charity.

PART II. The eulogy of Gaius's hospitality.

Latin:

Μειζοτέραν τούτων οὐκ ἔχω χαρὰν.] Alii Codices habent ταύτης. Μειζοτέραν est ad intendendam significationem com- parativus è comparativo factus, quomodo ἐλαχιστότερος comparativus è Superlativo, Eph. III, 8.

Ἵνα ἀκούω τὰ ἐμὰ τέκνα ἐν ἀληθείᾳ περιπατοῦντα.] In Ma- nuscripto ἐν τῇ ἀληθείᾳ, id est, secundum Evangelium. Planè eadem constructio, quæ Joh. XV, 13. ubi diximus ἵνα esse ex- positivum ταύτης quod præcesserat. Ἐμὰ τέκνα, id est, eos, quos ego institui, 1. Tim. I, 2. 18. 2. Tim. I, 2. c. II, 1. Philem. 10. Johannes quidem, ut & Petrus maxime circa Judæos labora- bant, sed occasione data non omittebant instituere & gentes, ut Petrus Cornelium.

Hic ergo agnoscit Grotius, Johannem Aposto- lum Autorem esse epistolæ, qui cum Petro maxime inter Judæos laboravit. Vulgatus hic barbare: Majorem eorum non habeo gratiam, id est, majo- rem his. Est enim Græcismus, neque χάριν habent Codices, sed χαρὰν, id est, gaudium, si paucos ex- cipias. Bartholomæus Petri sic habet h. l. Vete- res Concordantiæ Bibliorum collectæ ab Hugone Ca- rensi Cardinali ex familia sancti Dominici constan- ter legunt, majus his non habeo gaudium. Tribus enim locis hæc lectio in illis Concordantiis reperi- tur, scilicet verbo major, verb. habeo, verb. gau- dium, & Isidorus Clarius testis est sibi visos veteres Latinos codices, qui sic haberent. Habent sic etiam Biblia Complutensia & Regia inde orta. Quæ omnia si considerari potuissent à correctoribus Ro- manis: vix dubium est Cardinalis Hugonis lectio- nem in textum fuisse recepturos, utpote quam satis liqueat esse germanam nostri Interpretis scriptu- ram, eamque dilucidam, & Græco Codici plane conformem. Diversitas hæc inde nata est, quod pauci quidam minus correcti Codices Græci hic le- gunt χάριν, quod sonat gratiam, cum plerique omnes habeant χαρὰν gaudium. Unde fluxerunt duæ diversæ interpretationes, quarum ea, quæ est deterio- ris lectionis plerosque Codices nostros, qui hodie sunt in manibus, occupat. Syrus reddidit: Major illa lætitia mihi nulla est, quam ut audiam filios meos ambulare in veritate. Celebrat S. Hieronymus in Cap. V. ad Eph. axioma quoddam Christi, nunquam læti sitis, nisi cum fratrem videritis in charitate.

PARS II. Elogium hospitalitatis Caji.

## 1:5
Ver. 5.

Ἀγαπητὲ πιστὸν ποιεῖς.] You are doing a good thing. For thus אִישׁ אֱמֶת is translated ἀγαθὸς in Neh. VII, 2. elsewhere δίκαιος.

ὄ ἐὰν ἐργάσῃ εἰς τοὺς ἀδελφοὺς καὶ εἰς τοὺς ξένους.] Read, as in the Manuscript: Ἀδελφοὺς καὶ ταῦτα ξένους, brothers and indeed pilgrims: and thus the Latin reads. ὃ ἐὰν if anything, as in Matt. XII, 36. chap. XIV, 7. chap. XV, 5. chap. XVI, 19. Gal. VI, 7. Eph. VI, 8.

In favor of the Latin, and of one MS., other most agreeing codices are rashly abandoned. And Cornelius himself observes that the καὶ here has the same value as especially. Therefore the matter comes to the same thing. Cf. Mark XVI, 7. tell the disciples and, that is, especially Peter. He also adds Matt. XIII, 14. Bartholomew of Peter: That this, he says, is not in the Greek, and it disturbs the sense somewhat. For the Apostle seems to commemorate two certain things, namely Gaius's beneficence toward the poor Christians of his own city and his own nation, and likewise toward the Christian pilgrims or strangers who were arriving there. Furthermore, others explain πιστὸν more emphatically as a thing worthy of your faith with Vatablus: others as fidelity, as if to say, the fidelity which you vowed to Christ in baptism, concerning keeping his precepts, among which the first is that of charity and beneficence toward one's neighbor, you perform in reality. By strangers, Cornelius understands both the Apostolic men, who by traveling disseminated the Gospel, as Bede wishes, and those who, proscribed by the Gentiles, were wandering as exiles, as Hugo and the Interlinear Gloss wish, and also the faithful traveling for any other title or cause, as Dionysius wishes. For GOD commended the care of these to the faithful by His own example. Deut. X, 18. Tertullian praises hospitality in the primitive Churches, joining the communication of peace, and the appellation of brotherhood, and the token of hospitality, book on prescription, chap. 20, whom St. John so commends in Gaius, that he might the more incite the same man to this virtue. Praised virtue grows, as St. Augustine says, hom. 25, between L. and to praise is the sharpest stimulus for moving.

Latin:

Vers. 5.

Ἀγαπητὲ πιστὸν ποιεῖς.] Rem facis bonam. Nam sic אִישׁ אֱמֶת vertitur ἀγαθὸς Neh. VII, 2. alibi δίκαιος.

ὄ ἐὰν ἐργάσῃ εἰς τοὺς ἀδελφοὺς καὶ εἰς τοὺς ξένους.] Lege, ut in Manuscripto: Ἀδελφοὺς καὶ ταῦτα ξένους, fra- tres & quidem peregrinantes: & sic legit Latinus. ὃ ἐὰν si quid, ut Matth. XII, 36. cap. XIV, 7. cap. XV, 5. cap. XVI, 19. Gal. VI, 7. Eph. VI, 8.

In gratiam Latini, & unius MS. Codices teme- re deseruntur alii plerique consentientes codi- ces. Et observat Cornelius ipse, τὸ καὶ hic idem valere, quod præsertim. Eodem ergo res redit. Conf. Marc. XVI, 7. dicite discipulis &, id est, im- primis Petro. Addit & Matth. XIII, 14. Bar- tholomæus Petri: Illud hoc, inquit, non est in Græco, & nonnihil turbat sensum. Videtur enim Aposto- lus duo quædam commemorare, scilicet Caji benefi- centiam in pauperes Christianos suæ civitatis suæque gentis, item in Christianos peregrinos seu extra- neos, qui illuc adveniebant. Porro alii πιστὸν ma- gis emphatice explicant rem tuæ fide dignam cum Vatablo: alii fidelitatem, q. d. fidelitatem, quam Christo in baptismo vovisti, de servandis ejus præceptis, inter quæ primum est charitatis, & be- neficentiæ erga proximum, reipsa præstas. Per peregrinos Cornelius intelligit tum viros Aposto- licos, qui peregrinando disseminabant Evangelium, uti vult Beda, tum eos, qui à gentilibus proscripti exules peregrinabantur, ut vult Hugo & Glossa in- terlinearis, tum fideles quolibet alio titulo vel causa peregrinantes, ut vult Dionysius. Horum enim curam DEUS suo exemplo fidelibus commendavit. Deuter. X, 18. Laudat Tertullianus in Ecclesiis primitivis hospitalitatem, conjungens communi- cationem pacis, & appellationem fraternitatis & contesserationem hospitalitatis, libr. de præscript. cap. 20. quem ita commendat in Cajo S. Johan- nes, ut eundem magis ad hanc virtutem extimu- let. Laudata virtus crescit, dicente S. Augustino hom. 25. inter L. & laudare est acerrimus stimulus movendi.

## 1:6
Vers. 6.

Who have borne witness to your love.) The construction is as just now in 3. Before the Church.) Before the Ephesian Church. Whom you will do well to send forward.) It seems one should read ἐποίησας, the following words show it. You did well is of one praising, as we said Acts X, 33. 1 Cor. VII, 8. Phil. IV, 14. Jas. II, 8. 19. 2 Pet. I, 19. To send forward here is to dismiss with travel provisions, as Tit. III, 13. Worthily of God.) That is, as we owe to GOD. A similar locution Col. I, 10. and 1 Thess. II, 12. Concerning the matter see Matt. X, 40.

A bold emendation of the sacred text again, without any authority, without any necessity. Although Cornelius cites Hugo, who reads in the Latin, he nevertheless changes nothing in the text, rendering the sense thus: Q. d. To whom if you continue to do good, by receiving them with hospitality, feeding, helping, directing, giving travel provisions, you will lead them worthily of God, q. d. you will cause them to be able to pursue their journey conveniently, and to migrate to another place, whither they are tending, which is a pious work, and worthy of God. The Greek is explained more simply, whom you will benefit by leading them worthily of God. Or as Jerome in chap. I to Titus: Whom you will do best if you send forward worthily of God. Here again the candor of Bartholomäus Petri is to be praised, by which he imitates Estius: Then he adds, says the Apostle speaking of the same strangers, whom you will benefit by leading them worthily of God. Thus it is read in better Latin books conformably to the Greek, and so it is in the text of Lyra and Thomastri. The sense and plain order of the words is this: Whom if you shall have led worthily of God, you will have done a good thing, and worthy of your piety. You will lead, not by accompanying, but by providing travel provisions and other things opportune for the journey, or you will send them forward conveniently, securely, liberally. Conf. Rom. XVI, 2.

Latin:

Vers. 6.

Οἳ ἐμαρτύρησάν σέ τῇ ἀγάπῃ.) Constructio qualis mo- do 3. Ἐνώπιον Ἐκκλησίας.) Coram Ecclesia Ephesina. Οὓς καλῶς ποιήσας προπέμψας.) Legendum videtur ἐποί- ησας, ostendunt id sequentia. Καλῶς ἐποίησας est laudan- tis, ut diximus Actor. X, 33. 1. Cor. VII, 8. Phil. IV, 14. Jac. II, 8. 19. 2. Petr. I, 19. Προπέμπειν hic est cum viatico dimit- tere, ut Tit. III, 13. Ἀξίως τῦ Θεῦ.) Id est, sicut DEO debemus. Similis loquu- tio Col. I, 10. & 1. Thess. II, 12. De re vide Matth. X, 40.

Audax iterum emendatio textus sacri, sine ulla autoritate, sine ulla necessitate. Cornelius etsi Hugonem, in Latino legentem deducis, alleget, in textu tamen nihil mutat, sensum ita reddens: Q. d. Quibus si benefacere pergas, excipiendo illos hospitio, alendo, juvando, dirigendo, dando viati- cum, deduces illos digne Deo, q. d. facies ut commode iter suum prosequi, & alio, quo tendunt, commigrare possint, quod est opus pium, Deoque dignum. Simpli- cius Græca exponuntur, quos beneficio afficies de- ducens digne Deo. Vel ut Hieronymus in cap. I. ad Tit. Quos optime facies, si præmiseris digne Deo. Laudanda hic iterum ingenuitas Bartholomæi Pe- tri, qua Estium imitatur: Tum addit, inquit, Apo- stolus loquens de iisdem peregrinis, quos benefacies de- ducens digne Deo. Ita legitur in Latinis libris melio- ribus conformiter Græcis, & ita est in textu Lyra- ni & Thomastri. Sensus & planus ordo verborum est hic: Quos si digne Deo deduxeris, rem bonam fe- ceris, & tua pietate dignam. Deduces non comi- tando, sed viaticum, & alia ad iter opportuna præ- bendo, vel transmittes commode, secure, liberali- ter. Conf. Rom. XVI, 2.

## 1:7
Vers. 7.

For for the sake of His name they went out.) In the Manuscript: For for the sake of the name they went out: for for the sake of the name, that is, they were cast out from Judea by the unbelieving Jews on account of Christ. For the name by excellence is the name of Christ, Jas. II, 7. See also what we said Acts V, 11. Taking nothing from the Gentiles.) In the Manuscript from the heathens, as Matt. VI, v. 7. chap. XVIII, 17. They could have been helped in that calamity by the mercy of those outside. But they preferred to owe everything to Christians.

Bede understands it not of exile or ejection, but of profession, that they might evangelize the name of God and Christ: others simply, that they undertook this journey for the sake of piety and GOD, whence it is right that they be received worthily of God: the following words seem to hint that the proclamation is being looked to, receiving nothing from the Gentiles, because they preached the Gospel to the Gentiles for free. For this cause, namely, as Bartholomäus Petri has it, lest they should give any offense to the Gospel of Christ. Just as Paul also in Asia and Achaia without support, which would be provided by the converted Gentiles,

preached Christ, because the heathens were not accustomed to support their teachers, and because the Pseudo-Apostles disseminated their doctrines without the burden of those whom they taught. Concerning which matter there is much in the Apostle, 1 Cor. IX, 2. 2 Cor. XI, 7. and following, chap. XII, 13. and following. Which Cornelius a Lapide thinks can be accepted thus, because they were despoiled of their goods by the Gentiles on account of the faith of Christ. But it is one thing to receive nothing from the Gentiles, and another to be despoiled.

Latin:

Vers. 7.

὘πὲρ γὰρ τῦ ὀνόματος αὐτῦ ἐξῆλθον.) In Manuscripto: ὘πὲρ γὰρ τῦ ὀνόματος ἐξῆλθον: ὑπὲρ γὰρ τῦ ὀνόματος, id est, à Judæa ejecti sunt per Judæos incredulos ob Christum. Nomen enim per excellentiam nomen Christi, Jac. II, 7. Vide & quæ diximus Act. V, 11. Μηδὲν λαμβάνοντες ἀπὸ τῶν ἐθνῶν) In Manuscripto ἀπὸ τῶν ἐθνικῶν, quomodo Matth. VI. v. 7. cap. XVIII, 17. Potuerant in ista calamitate adjuvari miseri- cordia τῶν ἔξω. Sed maluerunt omnia Christianis debere.

Beda non de exilio, aut ejectione, sed de profe- stione, ut nomen Dei & Christi evangelizarent, intelligit: alii simpliciter, quod pietatis & DEI causa hoc iter susceperint, unde par sit eos digne Deo suscipi: Præconium respici verba sequen- tia innuere videntur, nihil accipientes à gentibus, quod nempe gratis gentibus prædicarint Evan- gelium. Hac, scilicet, ut Bartholomæus Petri ha- bet, de causa, ne quod offendiculum darent Evan- gelio Christi. Sicut & Paulus in Asia & Achaia sine sustentatione, quæ à gentibus conversis præberetur,

Christum annunciavit, quia Ethnici non assueverant suos magistros alere, & quia Pseudo-Apostoli sine eorum, quos docebant, gravamine suas doctrinas disse- minabant. Qua de re multa sunt apud Apostolum, 1. Cor. IX, 2. 2. Cor. XI, 7. & seqq. cap. XII, 13. & seqq. Quod Cornelius a Lapide ita accipi posse pu- tat, quia a gentibus ob fidem Christi bonis spoliati sunt. Sed aliud est nihil accipere a gentibus spoliari.

## 1:8
Vers. 8.

We etc.) We Christians everywhere. We ought to receive such.) The Manuscript has to receive, that is indeed to help, as in the Greek, Psalm XXX, 1. Suidas explains it as to welcome. That we may become fellow-workers for the truth.) That as much as is in us we may promote the Gospel by contributed help. A similar locution is 2 Cor. I, 24.

The Greek to take hold of is to occupy, so that we do not wait until they themselves come to us, but we anticipate them, invite them into our house, nay, we urge them, as Oecumenius says. Conf. Luke XXIV, v. 29. John XVIII, 12. chap. XIX, 1. Rightly, however, others before Grotius observe that to receive and reception signify every duty, protection, care, help. The Apostle joins himself to others either through the figure of communication of the person of the wealthy faithful, so that he may render them more eager to spend on the poor, who had left everything for the sake of Christ, as Bede has it: But if he is said not to have had his own resources, he could nevertheless help others who were well-off by exhorting, as Lyra advises: he could also help the strangers from public funds collected by the wealthy. Συνεργοι are called here those who administer necessities to those who preach the truth, and to those who sustain tribulations and exiles for the truth of the faith, according to the interpretation of Lyranus. The rich, says Bede, insert themselves into the virtues of the poor, who possess spiritual gifts, while they share their riches with those holy poor. Therefore, in many ways he stimulates Gaius to continue in hospitality: 1. by praising his liberality, 2. by proposing the eulogy which he received before the whole Church, 3. by commending that work as faithful and proper for a Christian, 4. that this work is worthy of GOD, 5. that it is bestowed upon those who preach the name of GOD, or propagate it by their profession, 6. that it is bestowed upon those who have been deserted by the Gentiles, or have received nothing, 7. that we may thus cooperate with the truth and the Gospel, and be rendered συνεργοι of the ministers of the Word. Compare 1 Pet. IV, 9; Heb. XIII, 2.

Latin:

Vers. 8.

Ημεις &c.) Nos Christiani ubique locorum. Οφειλομεν απολαμβανειν τες τοιέτες.) Manuscriptus απολαμβανειν, id vero est opitulari, ut in Græco, Psalm. XXX, 1. Suidas explicat υποδεχεσθαι. Ινα συνεργοι γενωμεθα τη αληθεια.) Ut quantum in nobis est Evangelium promoveamus col- lata ope. Similis loquutio est 2. Cor. I, 24.

Græcum καταλαμβανειν est occupare, ut non ex- pectemus, donec ipsi veniant ad nos, sed eos præ- veniamus, in domum nostram invitemus, imo aga- mus, dicente Oecumenio. Conf. Luc. XXIV. v. 29. Job. XVIII, 12. c. XIX, 1. Recte tamen observant ante Grotium alii suscipere & susceptionem signifi- care omne officium, protectionem, curam, opem. Jungit se Apostolus aliis vel per communicationis figuram personæ fidelium divitum, ut eos alacrio- res reddat ad erogandum pauperibus, qui omnia propter Christum dimiserant, ut Beda habet: Qui vero si dicatur proprias facultates non habuisse, poterat tamen juvare alios, qui pollebant facul- tatibus hortando, ut Lyra monet: poterat & e publicis symbolis a divitibus collatis peregrinis succurrere. Συνεργοι dicuntur hic, qui admini- strant necessaria illis, qui veritatem prædicant, & illis, qui pro veritate fidei tribulationes & exilia sustinent, interprete Lyrano. Divites, inquit Beda, sese virtutibus pauperum, spiritualia dona ha- bentium inserunt, dum iis sanctis pauperibus de suis divitiis impertiuntur. Multis ergo modis sti- mulat Cajum, ut in hospitalitate pergat 1. laudan- do ejus liberalitatem, 2. elogium, quod receperit coram tota Ecclesia proponendo, 3. opus illud ceu fidele & Christiano proprium commendando, 4. quod hoc opus dignum sit DEO, 5. quod in eos conferatur, qui nomen DEI prædicant, aut pro- fessione sua propagant, 6. quod in eos confera- tur, qui a gentibus deserti sunt, aut nihil acceperunt, 7. quod ita cooperemur veritati & Evangelio, ac συν- εργοι reddamur ministrorum Verbi. Confer 1. Petr. IV, 9. Ebr. XIII, 2.

## 1:9
Vers. 9.

Εγραψα τη Εκκλησια.) I wrote to your Church, that I might commend them to you as brothers. In the Manuscript: Εγραψα τι τη Εκκλησια. But the Latin reads εγραψα αν, I would have written, but I did not wish to waste my effort.

The Vulgate incorrectly has 'I would have written,' whereas the original text has 'I wrote,' as Erasmus, Vatablus, Clarius, and Cajetan have rendered it, who, as Cornelius notes, acknowledge that the Vulgate is corrupt here. But that Grotius, preceded by Gagnejus, Sevurius, and Cornelius, pretends that the Interpreter read εγραψα αν, that can be proven by no document. It is nothing new for the Latin Interpreter to have hallucinated. Therefore, not trusting this explanation, Cornelius adds: that he himself understood the αν. But that would also have been from a private interpretation. For nothing should be inferred or added to Scripture. Cornelius urges that it is more congruent, that which the Latin has: I would have written indeed, but I did not write, because that proud Diotrephes does not receive us or our letters; but can he not complain about his letter not being received with the reverence that was fitting, for the sake of which he also promises that he himself will come. Furthermore, the Jesuit urges that there are no letters of St. John written to the Church, and that he would have written them in vain, since he knew they would not be received, nay, that those who had received them would be harassed by Diotrephes, verse 10. But from this passage it is confirmed entirely that the second Johannine epistle was written to that Church in which Gaius was active. However, he is not speaking of his letters in verse 10, but of the brethren, because he cast those who received them out of the Church. And could not letters have reached the Church through Gaius or another, without Diotrephes knowing? Would the work have been lost to the Church just because Diotrephes was so evil? Flacius suspects: that St. John is indicating that he then wrote for the first time to that whole Church about helping those evangelists, so that, having commended them in this way, he gave both public letters to all and private letters to Gaius.

Ἀλλ’ ὁ φιλοπρωτεύων αὐτῶν Διοτρεφής.] Here also a plural is joined to a singular collective, as often. Diotrephes here was one of the Presbyters of that Church in which Gaius was, having been made a Christian from a Gentile, and at that time aspiring to the then-vacant Episcopate. He was, however, of that class of men who did not admit to their assemblies the Jews, even though they professed Christ, if they observed the rites of the law—which Christians in Judea were doing up to these times, as Sulpitius teaches us. Of such a character was he who inserted these things into the Epistle of Ignatius to the Philippians: Εἴτις μετὰ ἰουδαίων ἐπιτελεῖ τὸ πάσχα ἢ τὰ σύμβολα τῆς ἑορτῆς αὐτῶν δέχεται, κοινωνός ἐστι τῶν ἀποκτεινάντων τὸν Κύριον. But the Apostle John was accustomed to grant much to converted Jews, as is apparent from the Jewish observation of the Passover throughout Asia. And John the Presbyter, himself a Jew by birth, imitated him. See Irenaeus to Victor and Eusebius ch. V, 22. 23. 24.

Οὐκ ἐπιδέχεται ἡμᾶς.] It is a metonymy. He does not admit us, that is, our admonitions, our letters of recommendation.

Grotius again brings in another John and his own letters of recommendation, which he has conceived in his mind; for the rest, he acts according to his custom, peddling conjectures. He censures three things especially about Diotrephes: ambition, slander, and inhospitality. Bede notes that he was also a heretic. Similarly Bartholomew of Petra, who says it is credible that he was one of those Jews who were Christians in name only, who thought the faith of Christ should be received in such a way that the ceremonial law of Moses was kept at the same time. For at the beginning of the Christian religion it suffered no greater adversaries in doctrine than these Judaizers, as we can learn from Epiphanius in heresies 28, 29, 30, which are those of the Cerinthians, Nazarenes, and Ebionites. Paul is accustomed to call the teachers of these Judaizers Pseudo-Apostles. Who were certainly most hostile to the true disciples of Christ, who neglected legal matters, and to the true Apostles of Christ, who strenuously preached the cessation, nay, the harm, of the observation of ceremonial law after the Gospel had been published, as is manifest from the Acts of the Apostles and the Pauline epistles. But St. John does not hint at that, for he would undoubtedly have acted more severely against the same man and would have warned Gaius and others to beware of his seduction. Unless perhaps that is to be gathered from what is added about excommunication in verse 10. He notes his pride above all, from which it happened that he dared to oppose John himself and to excommunicate the faithful, whence his name is 'nourished by Jove,' as Vatablus takes that name Diotrephes as an appellative, which others, however, more correctly take as a proper name. L. Dexter has this about him: In Christian circles, Diotrephes hindered guests arriving for the sake of pilgrimage to the Spains. But this evil Bishop was deposed because of his crimes and pride: But that age did not yet know bishops, therefore they could not be cast out.

Latin:

Vers. 9.

Εγραψα τη Εκκλησια.) Scripsi Ecclesiæ vestræ, ut illos vobis commendarem tanquam fratres. In Manuscripto: Εγραψα τι τη Εκκλη- σια. At Latinus legit εγραψα αν, scripsissem, sed nolui ope- ram perdere.

Vulgata male habet scripsissem, quum textus ori- ginalis habeat scripsi, ut reddidere Erasmus, Vata- blus, Clarius, Cajet. qui notante Cornelio agno- scunt, Vulgatam hic esse corruptam. Quod autem Grotius, cui præivit Gagnejus, Sevurius, Cornelius, prætendant Interpretem legisse εγραψα αν, id nullo documento probari potest. Nihil novi est, hallucinatum esse Latinum Interpretem. Ideo non fidens huic explicationi Cornelius addit: ipsum το αν subintellexisse. Sed id etiam ab ιδια επιλυσει fuasset. Non enim inferendum, vel addendum quid Scripturæ.
