Urget Cornelius, congruentius esse illud, quod Latinus habet: Scripsissem utique, sed ideo non scripsi, quia nos nostrasque literas non recipit su- perbus ille Diotrephes; sed annon queri potest de non suscepta ea, qua par erat, reverentia a Diotre- phe epistola sua, cujus gratia etiam seipsum ad- venturum spondet. Urget porro Jesuita, quod nullæ extent S. Johan- nis literæ scriptæ ad Ecclesiam, & frustra eas scripsif- set, cum sciret, eas non recipiendas, imo qui eas re- cepissent, vexandos à Diotrephe, vers. 10. Sed ex hoc loco confirmatur omnino, secundam epistolam Johanneam ad Ecclesiam illam, in qua agebat Cajus, exaratam esse. Non autem de literis suis vers. 10. sed de fratribus agit, quod illos suscipientes de Ec- clesia ejecerint. Et annon ad Ecclesiam per Ca- jum, aut alium literæ pervenire poterant, inscio Diotrephe? Num ideo opera penes Ecclesiam perdita fuiffet, quod Diotrephes tam malus erat? Flacius suspicatur: Id indigitare S. Johannem, se tunc primum ad totam illam Ecclesiam de juvandis illis Evangelistis scripsisse, ut ita illis commendatis tum publicas ad omnes, tum privatas ad Gajum de- derit literas.

Ἀλλ’ ὁ φιλοπρωτεύων αὐτῶν Διοτρεφής.] Hic quoque singulari collectivo subjungitur plurale, ut sæ- pe. Diotrephes hic fuit aliquis ex Presbyteris ejus Ecclesiæ, in qua erat Cajus, ex gentili factus Christianus, & Episcopa- tum tunc vacantem ambiens. Is vero ex illo hominum erat genere, qui Judæos, quanquam Christum professos, si legis ritus observabant, quod in Judæa Christiani faciebant ad hæc usque tempora, ut Sulpitius nos docet, ad suos cœtus non admittebant. Talis ingenii fuit, qui in Epistolam Ignatii ad Philippenses ista infarfit : Εἴτις μετὰ ἰουδαίων ἐπιτελεῖ τὸ πά- σχα ἢ τὰ σύμβολα τῆς ἑορτῆς αὐτῶν δέχεται, κοινωνός ἐστι τῶν ἀποκτεινάντων τὸν Κύριον. Johannes autem Apostolus mul- tum solebat largiri Judæis conversis, ut ex Judaica per Asiam Paschatis observatione apparet. Et hunc imitabatur Johan- nes Presbyter, Judæus & ipse ortu. Vide Irenæum ad Victo- rem & Eusebium c. V, 22. 23. 24.

Οὐκ ἐπιδέχεται ἡμᾶς.] Est Metonymia. Non admittit nos, id est, monita nostra, συστατικὰς nostras.

Iterum alium Johannem suasque systaticas, quas animo præcepit, ingerit Grotius; de cæ- tero facit pro more, conjecturas venditans. Tria autem taxat imprimis de Diotrephe, ambitionem, maledicentiam, & inhospitalitatem. Beda notat etiam hæreticum fuisse. Similiter Bartholomæus Petri, qui, credibile est, inquit, fuisse quempiam ex illis Judæis titulotenus Christianis,qui Christi fidem ita suscipiendam putabant, ut simul servaretur lex ce- remonialis Mosis. Neque enim initio Christianæ reli- gionis ea majores ullos in doctrina adversarios passa est, quam istos Judaizantes, ut ex Epiphanio discere possumus hæresi 28. 29. 30. quæ sunt Cerinthiorum, Nazaræorum, & Ebionitarum. Horum Judaizan- tium magistros solet Paulus appellare Pseudo-Apo- stolos. Qui utique veris Christi discipulis, legalia ne- gligentibus, & veris Christi Apostolis, cessationem imo noxam, ceremonialis post divulgatum Evangelium observationis strenue prædicantibus erant infestissimi, ut ex Actis Apostolorum & epistolis Paulinis manife- stum est. Sed id S. Johannes non innuit, gravius si- ne dubio acturus adversus eundem,& Cajum alios- que de seductione ipsius cavenda moniturus. Nisi forte ex eo id colligendum sit, quod de excommu- nicatione vers. 10. subjicitur. Superbiam imprimis ejus notat, ex qua factum, quod Johanni ipsimet se opponere, atque excommunicare fideles ausus fuerit, unde nomen ejus à Jove nutritus, uti nomen illud Διοτρεφὴς pro Appellativo habet Vatablus, quod tamen alii rectius pro nomine proprio acci- piunt. L. Dexter de ipso ita habet: In Christianis Diotrephes impediebat hospites ad Hispanias pere- grinationis causa devenientes. At hic malus Epi- scopus propter scelera & superbiam depositus est: Sed Episcopos ista ætas nondum norat, dejici ergo non poterant.

## 1:10
Verse 10.

Διὰ τοῦτο ἐὰν ἔλθω.] If my affairs permit, that I may pass over to you.

Ὑπομνήσω ἀυτῦ τὰ ἔργα, ἃ ποιεῖ, λόγοις πονηροῖς φλυαρῶν ἡμᾶς.] I will show him of what a thing he makes himself unworthy, because he slanders me while I am following in the footsteps of the Apostle John. Ὑπομνήσκει is properly to bring to memory, הזכיר. But by a certain transference it is taken for any way of admonishing, Tit. III, 1. 2. Pet. I, 12. Φλυαρεῖν is to chatter, to babble, in the glosses. But neuter verbs are sometimes accustomed to be used transitively. See 1 Tim. V, 13 for who the babblers are.

Καὶ μὴ ἀρκέμενος ἐπὶ τέτοις.] Not considering that enough.

Budaeus, in his Commentaries on the Greek language, translates the word ὑπομνήσω as: I will judge: which is a forensic term. Oecumenius translates it as I will punish. He seems to call Diotrephes' slanders 'chatter' out of contempt. How great a madness it is, says Seneca in epistle XCII, to fear being defamed by the infamous?

He does not admit those coming from Judea, who are devoted to the law, to his communion, contrary to what Paul had commanded in Rom. XIV, where there is προσλαμβάνεσθαι, which is what ἐπιδέχεσθαι is here.

And those who are willing. Namely, to admit them himself, if there are any presbyters or among the common people who are more lenient.

He hinders. Namely, by that authority which he had secured for himself among most people, as the fiercest defender of Christian liberty.

And casts them out of the Church. He brings it about by faction that those more lenient ones, as being more Jews than Christians, are kept from communion. To cast out of the Church is to excommunicate, which the Jews otherwise called making one a synagogue-outcast. See what we have said at Luke VI, 22; John IX, 22; XII, 42; XVI, 2.

Hugo understands this as exclusion from the place and assembly, especially in the agape and the banquet after the Eucharist. Dionysius the Carthusian, however, interprets it as excommunication itself from the assembly of the faithful. Bartholomaeus Petri thinks that ejection was carried out if anyone had received someone who did not confess that the observation of legal ceremonies was even now necessary for salvation.

Latin:

Vers. 10.

Διὰ τοῦτο ἐὰν ἔλθω.] Si res meæ permittent, ad vos ut transcurram.

Ὑπομνήσω ἀυτῦ τὰ ἔργα, ἃ ποιεῖ, λόγοις πονηροῖς φλυαρῶν ἡμᾶς.] Ostendam illi quam rem faciat se indignam, quod mihi obtrectat instanti vestigiis Johannis Apostoli. Ὑπομ- νήσκει propriè est in memoriam reducere הזכיר. Sed per translationem quandam sumitur pro quovis modo monere, Tit. III, 1. 2. Petr. I, 12. Φλυαρεῖν est garrire, blatterare, in glof- sis. Sed verba neutra poni solent interdum transitive. Qui sint φλύαροι vide 1. Tim. V, 13.

Καὶ μὴ ἀρκέμενος ἐπὶ τέτοις.] Id non satis habens.

Verbum ὑπομνήσω Budæus in comment. lingu. Græc. vertit: Judicabo: quod verbum forense sit. Oecumenius puniam. Garritum vocare Diotrephis calumnias per contemptum videtur. Quanta de- mentia est, inquit Seneca epist. XCII. vereri ne infa- meris ab infamibus?

Οὔτε ἀυτὸς ἐπιδέχεται τὲς ἀδελφὲς.] Non admittit illos ex Judæa venientes, legi deditos, ad suam communionem, contra quam Paulus præceperat Rom. XIV. ubi προσλαμβά- νεσθαι est, quod hic ἐπιδέχεσθαι.

Καὶ τὲς βελομένως.] Nempe ἀυτὸς ἐπιδέχεσθαι, si qui Pres- byteri aut in plebe sunt leniores.

Κωλύει.] Nempe ea autoritate, quam apud plerosque sibi paraverat, tanquam Christianæ libertatis acerrimus vindex.

Καὶ τῆς Ἐκκλησίας ἐκβάλλει.] Efficit factione, ut illi leniores, tanquam Judæi magis, quam Christiani, abstineantur à communione. Ἐκ τῆς Ἐκκλη- σίας ἐκβάλλειν est מנדה ἀφορίζειν, quod aliter Judæi dicebant ἀποσυνάγωγον ποιεῖν. Vide quæ diximus ad Luc. VI, 22. Joh. IX, 22. XII, 42. XVI, 2.

Hugo de exclusione à loco & cœtu præsertim in agape, & convivio post Eucharistiam accipit. Dionysius tamen Carthusianus de ipsa excommu- nicatione è cœtu fidelium interpretatur. Ejectio- nem illam factam putat Bartholomæus Petri, si quis recepisset aliquem, qui non fateretur legalium ceremoniarum observationem esse etiam nunc necessa- riam saluti.

## 1:11
Vers. 11.

Beloved, do not imitate the evil, but the good. Do not imitate the harshness of that Diotrephes and those like him, even though you too have been called from the Gentiles. A similar warning is in Isaiah VIII, verse 11.

A warning necessary even among those who are not bad. It is easier, says Jerome in epistle VII, to imitate evils, and you quickly imitate the vices of those whose virtues you cannot attain.

He who does good. He who strives to do well, namely to as many as possible. See Mark 3, v. 4; Luke 6, v. 9, 33, 35. מיטיב.

Is of God. He has a divine nature. A phrase of the Apostle John in his 3rd epistle, 10; 5, 19.

He who does evil has not seen God. Here is the past tense for the present, and 'to see' for 'to know': but to know means to know as one ought, and to show it by deeds. The phrase is taken from 1 John 3, 6.

It is a general axiom, not to be restricted only to beneficence; because doing good must flow from faith. But he who is endowed with faith is of God. Conversely, he who does evil does not know God, that is, does not believe in God, because faith is effective through good works, which sense is supported by a comparison with 1 Epist. ch. III, 6. ch. IV, 7.

Latin:

Vers. 11.

Ἀγαπητὲ, μὴ μίμε τὸ κακὸν, ἀλλὰ τὸ ἀγαθὸν.] Noli illius Diotrephis & similium duritiem imitari, quan- quam & tu ex gentibus vocatus es. Simile monitum Esaiæ VIII. vers. 11.

Monitio etiam apud non malos necessaria. Pro- clivius est, inquit Hieronymus ep. VII. malorum imitatio, & quorum virtutes assequi nequeas, cito imitaris vitia.

Ὁ ἀγαθοποιῶν.) Qui bene facere studet, nempe quamplu- rimis. Vide Marc. 3. v. 4. Luc. 6. v. 9. 33. 35. מיטיב.

Ἐκ τῦ Θεῦ ἐστιν.) Divinam habet indolem. Loquutio Jo- hannis Apostoli in epistola III, 10. V, 19.

Ὁ κακοποιῶν ἑχ ἑώρακε τὸν Θεὸν.) Est hic Præteritum pro Præsenti, & ὁρᾷν pro nosse: nosse vero pro nosse, ut oportet, & id rebus ostendere. Loquutio est sumpta ex 1. Joh. 3, 6.

Generale est axioma, non restringendum tan- tum ad beneficentiam; quia benefacere ex fide fluat oportet. At qui fide præditus est, ex Deo est. Ex adverso qui male facit, non novit Deum, id est, non credit in Deum, quia fides efficax est per bona opera, cui sensui favet collatio cum 1. Epist. c. III, 6. c. IV, 7.

## 1:12
Ver. 12.

Demetrio.) He too was called by the Gentiles, but among the mild ones.

Memartyrētai apo pantōn.) He has testimony from all who know him. See 1 Timothy III, ver. 7. Martyreisthai is used in the same way in Acts VI, ver. 3 and ch. XVI, v. 2. Being good is understood.

Kai hyp' autēs tēs alētheias.) That is, he has testimony also from the things themselves. By comparison, truth is said to be what is less accustomed to deceive, proofs, than the testimonies of men, as the masters of the oratorical art teach.

And we also bear witness.] To him, of course. We also render him testimony of probity and piety. We, that is, I and others who are at Ephesus.

And you know that our testimony is true.] It is worthy of belief, John 5:31, ch. 7:13, 14, ch. 21:24, 1 John 5:6. In the manuscript, οἶδας.

Serarius suspects: that this Demetrius is the one who once, as overseer of the craftsmen of Diana, stirred up a sedition against St. Paul at Ephesus, Acts 19:24, who afterwards, repenting and weighing his sin with fervor, exchanged persecution for the propagation of life. But Cornelius warns that the histories of the ancients reveal nothing of the sort. Ambrosius Catharinus and Alphonsus Salmero think he was a bishop. Lucius Dexter makes him the brother of Gaius. All those things are uncertain. But this is certain, that such bishops as the Papists make were not then in the nature of things. Regarding those words 'and you know that our testimony is true,' Barthol. Petri says: This particle can teach us that the author of this epistle is none other than John the Apostle, who is accustomed to use this expression, as is to be seen in the Gospel ch. 19:35 and ch. 21:24. An assertion of this kind agrees with John, as one of the twelve first Apostles chosen by Christ the Lord. The Apostle adds this testimony of his, as Bede and Lyranus advise, so that he may more effectively move Gaius to the imitation of Demetrius in the constancy of beneficence, ignoring the threats of Diotrephes.

Latin:

Vers. 12.

Δημητρίῳ.) Erat is quoque à gentibus vocatus, sed inter lenes.

Μεμαρτύρηται ἀπὸ πάντων.) Ab omnibus, qui eum norunt, habet testimonium. Vi- de 1. Timoth. III. vers. 7. Μαρτυρεῖσθαι eodem modo su- mitur Actor. VI. vers. 3. & cap. XVI. v. 2. Subintelligitur ὄν- τι ἀγαθός.

Καὶ ὑπ᾽ ἀυτῆς τῆς ἀληθείας.) Id est, testimonium habet etiam à rebus ipsis. Ex comparate dicuntur ἀλήθεια, quod minus solent fallere, τεκμήρια, quam hominum testimonia, ut docent oratoriæ artis magistri.

Καὶ ἡμεῖς δὲ μαρτυρῦμεν.] Αὐτῷ scilicet. Nos quoque pro- bitatis ac pietatis testimonium ei reddimus. Nos, id est, ego & alii, qui Ephesi sumus.

Καὶ οἴδατε ὅτι μαρτυρία ἡμῶν ἀληθής ἐστι.] Est fide di- gna, Joh. 5, 31. cap. 7, 13. 14. cap. 21, 24. 1. Joh. 5, 6. In Ma- nuscripto οἶδας.

Serarius suspicatur: Demetrium hunc esse il- lum, qui olim Praefectus artificum Dianae contra S. Paulum Ephesi seditionem concitavit, Act. XIX. vers. 24. qui postea poenitens peccatum suum fer- vore pensans, persecutionem in propagationem vitae commutavit. Sed Cornelius monet, nil tale pro- dere veterum historias. Ambrosius Catharinus & Alphonsus Salmero putant, Episcopum fuisse. Lu- cius Dexter facit eum Caji fratrem. Incerta illa sunt omnia. Id autem certum, tales Episcopos, quales Papistae faciunt, tum in rerum natura non fuisse. Ad verba illa & nosti quoniam (quod) te- stimonium nostrum verum est, Barthol. Petri: Vel haec, inquit, particula docere nos potest, non alium esse hujus epistolae Autorem, quam Johannem Apo- stolum, qui hoc sermone uti solet, ut est videre Ev- angelii cap. XIX. vers. 35. & cap. XXI, 24. Con- gruit hujusmodi cum autoritate asseveratio Jo- hanni, tanquam uni ex duodecim primis à Christo Domino electis Apostolis. Addit vero hanc suam testificationem Apostolus monente Beda & Lyra- no, ut efficacius permoveat Cajum ad imitationem Demetrii in constantia beneficentiae, neglectis mi- nis Diotrephis.

## 1:13
Verse 13. Ἀσπάζεταί σε τὰ τέκνα τῆς ἀδελφῆς σε τῆς ἐκλεκτῆς.) The children of her sister to whom it is written, who were then at Ephesus on business. See what we have said in the preface to the Pauline Epistle to the Ephesians. For τῆς ἐκλεκτῆς other books have ἔκλεκτῆς without the article, but others have ἔυδεκτῆς, which I think is the true one, so that it may be a proper name, just like Ἐκλεκτή: and the Hebrew name of this woman would have been נלקת.

Again, what audacity the man has, to depart from the received reading at his own pleasure: because he saw clearly that it does not fit for the same name to be believed to have been that of both sisters. But one must remain with the reading which has hitherto been found in the common codices. For he had no codices to name for his own invention of ἔυδεκτῆς. However, it appears sufficiently from this, which Oecumenius and Serarius also urge, that that name is appellative, not proper, and an epithet of some particular Church, as if it were said: Thee, O elect Church of the Corinthians, the children of thy sister greet, e.g., the faithful and elect Church of the Ephesians. Cornelius is inept when he says that it appears more clearly from the Greek that τὸ Electæ refers to tuæ and not to sororis, in this way: The children of τῆς ἀδελφῆς σε τῆς ἐκλεκτῆς greet thee, that is, of thy sister, I say, who art elect, or who, as thou art named, so art thou in reality elect. Whence the Gothic Bible, as Mariana testifies, reads: The children of thy sister Electa greet thee, that is, O Electa, in the vocative case. These are his words, which, however, he himself later saw were forced, acknowledging more plainly that τὸ Electæ refers to the word sister, and he finally slips into the view that this name is appellative, but of a woman. But enough of these things before. Some Greek and Latin codices, as Cornelius also notes, add: Grace be with thee. Amen. And the Syriac: Grace be with you, Amen, which is a greeting both worthy of St. John and frequent in Paul. The little word of confirmation Amen, passed over by Grotius, is read in all Greek codices.

GLORY TO GOD IN THE HIGHEST, AND ON EARTH PEACE, GOOD WILL TOWARD MEN, AMEN.

TATA IN THE WORLD OF ST. JOHN.

A eulogy of hospitality illustrated by the contrary example of Diotrephes, and by the good testimony of Demetrius, at verse 12. III. A conclusion making a hope of arrival with a vow and reciprocal greetings, at verse 13.

Latin:

Vers. 13. Ἀσπάζεταί σε τὰ τέκνα τῆς ἀδελφῆς σε τῆς ἐκλεκτῆς.) Filii sororis ejus ad quam scribitur, qui tum erant Ephesi ob negotia. Vide quæ diximus in anteloquio ad Epistolam Pau- linam ad Ephesios. Pro τῆς ἐκλεκτῆς alii libri habent sine ar- ticulo ἔκλεκτῆς, alii vero ἔυδεκτῆς, quod verum puto, ut sit nomen proprium, sicut Ἐκλεκτή: & Ebræum nomen hujus fœminæ fuerit נלקת.

Rursus, quæ hominis audacia est, pro lubitu à recepta lectione discedit: quia probe vidit non convenire, ut idem nomen credatur fuisse utrius- que sororis. Sed manendum est in lectione, quæ hactenus in Codicibus usitatis inventa est. Nullos enim codices pro sua nuncupatione ἔυδεκτῆς no- minare habuit. Apparet autem hinc satis, quod & Oecumenius ac Serarius urgent, nomen illud Ap- pellativum esse, non proprium, & Epitheton Ec- clesiæ alicujus particularis, ac si dicatur: Te, ô electa Corinthiorum Ecclesia, salutant filii sororis tuæ, v. g. fideles & electæ Ecclesiæ Ephesiorum. Ineptus est Cornelius, dum è Græco clarius id ap- parere ait, τὸ Electæ referri ad tuæ non ad sororis, hoc modo: Salutant te filii τῆς ἀδελφῆς σε τῆς ἐκλεκτῆς, id est, sororis tui,tui inquam,quæ es electa, sive quæ uti nominaris, ita revera es electa. Unde Biblia Gothica, teste Mariana, legunt: Salutant te filii sororis tuæ Electæ, id est, ô Electa, in Vocativo casu. Hæc ille, quæ tamen ipse postmodum vidit contorta esse, agnoscens planius τὸ Electæ referri ad vocem sororis, eoque tandem dilabitur, esse no- men hoc Appellativum, sed fœminæ. Sed de his satis antea. Nonnulli Græci & Latini Codices, no- tante etiam Cornelio, addunt: Gratia tecum Amen. Et Syrus: Gratia vobiscum, Amen, quæ salutatio & S. Johanne digna & Paulo frequens. Vocula certe confirmationis Amen, à Grotio præterita, in omni- bus Codicibus Græcis legitur.

GLORIA IN EXCELSIS DEO, ET IN TER- RA PAX, HOMINIBUS BONA VOLUN- TAS, AMEN.

TATA IN S. JOHANNIS OLAM.

Elogium hospitalitatis contrario Diotrephis exem- plo, & testimonio Demetrii bono illustratum, ad vers. 12. III. Conclusio faciens spem adventus cum voto & salutationibus reciprovis, ad vers. 13.

# Jude

## 1:1 Argument
[Abraham Calov, Biblia Novi Testamenti Illustrata (Vol. 2, Part 2). English: machine translation, The Faith Received (Mere Orthodoxy); the original follows each comment.]
THE EPISTLE OF JUDE. SINGLE CHAPTER. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

With a preliminary inscription and greeting, St. Jude indicates the cause of these letters, namely, an exhortation necessary for the fight for the faith, on account of the impious and heretics who deny our only Lord Jesus Christ: therefore he sets forth the punishment of the unbelieving Israelites and the apostate angels and the fornicating Sodomites, and compares the heretics to them; whose impurity and blasphemy he refutes by the example of Michael the Archangel, denouncing woe upon them, and describing them graphically both by the examples of Cain, Balaam, and Korah, and by similarities to clouds, trees, waves of the sea, and wandering stars; and intimating their punishment in the final judgment as foretold by Enoch. He therefore exhorts the faithful, that, mindful of the Apostolic words concerning the mockers of the last times, they should avoid sectarians, build themselves up in the faith, and praying, persevere in the love of God, awaiting the mercy of Christ unto eternal life; finally, he advises how they ought to conduct themselves toward those who err; and he ends with a doxology.

There are two parts of the Apostolic treatment, of which the first is the inscription, the vow or prayer and the exor-

Latin:

ANNO A EPISTOLA CAPUT UNICUM. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Praevia inscriptione, & salutatione, S. Judas causam harum literarum indicat, necessari- am nempe ad pugnam pro fide, ob impios & haereticos, unum herum nostrum Jesum Chri- stum abnegantes, cohortationem: ideo in- credulorum Israelitarum & Apostatarum Angelorum, & fornicatorum Sodomita- rum poenam sistit, iisque comparat haereti- cos; quorum impuritatem, & blasphemi- am, exemplo Michaelis Archangeli, redar- guit, vae illis denuncians, ac describens eos graphice tum exemplis Cain, Balaami, & Cora, tum similibus à nubibus, arboribus, maris fluctibus, stellis erraticis; poenamq; eorum, in judicio novissimo ab Enocho prae- dicto, intimans. Hortatur itaque fideles, ut memores verborum Apostolicorum, de irrisoribus novissimorum temporum, secta- rios vitent, in fide se mutuo aedificent & orantes perseverent in charitate DEI, ex- spectantes misericordiam Christi ad aeter- nam vitam; denique monet, quomodo se erga errantes exhibere debeant; & δοξο- λογίᾳ finit.

Partes duae sunt tractationis Apostolicae, qua- rum prima inscriptio, votum vel precatio ac exor-

## 1:1
Verse 1.

Jude, a servant of Jesus Christ. He does not add Apostle, which Apostles are accustomed to do in epistles even to private individuals. Furthermore, if this epistle had been held to be Apostolic, it would have been translated into all languages and received by all Churches: which now has been otherwise. Wherefore I am altogether led to believe that this Epistle is of Jude, Bishop of Jerusalem, who was in the times of Hadrian a little before Barchochebas. For to Simeon, whose epistle we believe the one called the second of Peter to be, succeeded Justus, in Hebrew צַדוֹק Σαδωκός, to him Zacchæus, to Zacchæus Tobias, to Tobias Benjamin, to Benjamin John, to John Matthias, to Matthias Philip, that is, פּרָא כי, or פִּי לִבִּי, to Philip Seneca, that is, שָׂנְכָה, to Seneca another Justus, to him Levi, to him Ephres, to Ephres Joseph, he whom I call Jude. This epistle was written especially against the Carpocratians, as was that of Simeon. Wherefore, since it is engaged in the same argument, it is no wonder if he both adapts the same ancient histories and uses words sometimes the same as Simeon, sometimes slightly changed. He writes, however, to the Jews by race, Christians by religion, dispersed everywhere.

And brother of James.

I think this was added by the Scribes, so that Judas might be believed to be an Apostle here, just as we have noted certain additions in that epistle of Simeon. At the threshold of the Epistle, there is both the ὑπογραφὴ or subscription, as they call it, consisting of a mention of the name and office, and a distinguishing periphrasis for identifying the author, verse 1; and the ἐπιγραφὴ or inscription, with a designation of those to whom the epistle was written, and also a εὐχὴ or prayer, verse 2. The author of the Epistle calls himself first by his proper name, Jude, then by his office, a servant of Jesus Christ: by which name St. Peter also styled himself in 2 Ep. I, verse 1, as did St. James in Chapter I, verse 1, and also St. Paul, both with the added epithet of Apostle, Rom. I, verse 2, Tit. I, verse 1, and without the same, or simply in Phil. I, verse 1. Finally, lest any other Jude be imagined, he names himself the brother of James, who is known to have been from the College of the Apostles from a comparison of Matt. X, verse 3, Mark III, verse 18, ch. VI, v. 3, ch. XV, verse 40, John VI, verse 16, Acts I, 13. Although this is not only had from the title, which the Epistle bears as such, Ἰούδα τοῦ Ἀπο- στόλου ἐπιστολὴ καθολικὴ, but also in the text itself as an integral and undoubted part of the Epistle; yet Grotius, such is the man's rashness, preferred to brand the words ἀδελφὸς δὲ Ἰακώβου as spurious, contrary to the faith of all the Codices, rather than subscribe to the truth, so that he might exclude the author from Apostolic dignity. But by what arguments, I ask, will it be shown that the text of this epistle is corrupt, a suspicion which not only the Greek Codices, but also all the versions, which here agree entirely, most strongly exclude. With which also agrees the appellation of Jude in Luke, who likewise calls him Jude, namely the brother of James, ch. VI, verse 16, and Acts I, v. 13.

But the fact that Jude did not add the word Apostle does not make the present epistle more doubtful than that which was inscribed by St. Paul to the Philippians, in which he also called himself only a servant of Jesus Christ, although besides that, that periphrasis 'brother of James' sufficiently teaches that no other Jude is understood than the Apostle. But what he says, that if this Epistle had been considered Apostolic, it would have been turned into all languages, in that we detect no strength of consequence. For since the Greek language was everywhere common in that age, it could be read in the same, as the original. Add that writings of undoubted divinity were not immediately translated into different languages, let alone all, and it may be doubtful whether even to this day they have been converted into all languages? Finally, what is said, that it was not received by all the Churches, that also does not prove that Jude the Apostle is not the author. For some could have doubted it at some time, which happened to other Canonical Scriptures as well, even if they did not have just causes for doubting, such as certainly is not that which Jerome brought forward, from the mind of others, in his catalogue of Illustrious men, namely that the Author takes testimony in it from the book of Enoch, which is Apocryphal. Since Jude did not have the prophecy of Enoch from that Apocryphal book, but from tradition, and especially from divine inspiration. And Jerome adds in the same place concerning this Epistle: 'Nevertheless, it has earned authority through antiquity and use, and is counted among the holy Scriptures'; and in his Epistle to Paulinus he expressly ascribes it to Jude the Apostle. Eusebius also counts it among those which were contradicted by some, which however he says are acknowledged by many, book II of Ecclesiastical History, ch. 23, book VI, ch. 13.

But because of this doubt of some, the Blessed Luther, and the Magdeburg Centuriators, and if any others of our own are found agreeing with them, can be no less excused for having said that this Epistle was not of the same authority in the Church, than Cajetan the Cardinal from among the Papists, who says: 'This Epistle is of less authority than those which are of certain authority.'

But to us it is entirely certain that the author of this Epistle is St. Jude the Apostle, whence we have no doubt at all concerning its Apostolic and divine authority, of which we are made certain both by the internal criteria of the writing, which you might rightly call pearls (as Hilary says of the whole Scripture in sermon VI on Matthew), which within a small bulk includes the sum of many sesterces; and then indeed it is confirmed by the testimonies of the ancients, and the councils. Of the former, Clement of Alexandria, as witnessed by Eusebius in book VI of Ecclesiastical History, chapter 14, in his books of Outlines, instituted a compendious explanation of all the Scriptures of both Testaments, not even omitting those Scriptures which are doubted, I understand the epistle of Jude, etc. Origen in chapter XIII of Matthew says: 'Jude wrote an epistle of few verses indeed, but full of the powerful words of heavenly grace.' Epiphanius on the Gnostic heresy. Wherefore concerning these, he says, (the Gnostics) the Holy Spirit moved in the Apostle Jude says: Whatever things they know naturally as dumb animals, in these they are corrupted, etc. Athanasius in the Synopsis, Gregory Nazianzen in his poems, Oecumenius in this place, Ephrem the Syrian expressly count this Epistle among the Canonical ones, and among the Latins, Cyprian, Tertullian de habit. muliebr. cap. 8, Jerome, Ambrose, Augustine, Rufinus, Philastrius, Cassian, Prosper, Gelasius, Fulgentius, Primasius, Gregory the Great, Bede, Rabanus, Remigius, and others. See Jodocus Coccejus in thes. Cathol. T. I. l. 6. p. 370. From these indeed the Council of Carthage III. num. 47, Laodicea c. 58, the Roman under Damasus, etc.

That which Jude verse 17, which some object, refers to the sayings of the Apostles, that can no more prejudice Apostolic authority than the later Petrine epistle, because Peter likewise referred to the precepts of the Apostles, 2 Ep. III, 2, and to the Epistles of Paul verse 15. We pass over that some think that the Apostle Peter took many things from this Epistle, which he would by no means have done if he had not held it to be Apostolic. Concerning which Tirinus: He wrote, he says, at least before the 31st year from the death of Christ, in which (as Onuphrius relates in his Chronicle) St. Jude with his brother Simon the Canaanite underwent martyrdom in Persia. It was written therefore about six years before the second Epistle of St. Peter, who transcribed very many sentences from the Epistle of Jude almost word for word into his own, which can be seen arranged by parallels in Cornelius à Lapide. Salmero preceded Tirinus regarding this, that Peter took these things from St. Jude, nor does Cornelius deny it, but he is doubtful whether Peter took them from Jude so that he might confirm those sayings, or whether Jude received them from Peter, as Baronius at the year 68, Adam Sasbouth, Hugo, Lorinus, Thomas Anglicus, and Primaticcius maintain here, according to whom it must be determined that Jude did not meet his death in the year of Christ 64, but after St. Peter, and thus after the year 68, since Peter is believed to have written his second epistle shortly before his death, in that year, as the same Cornelius observes. Which opinion is to be preferred. Yet, speaking accurately, neither should be said, whether Peter took his from Jude, or Jude from Peter, since both were θεόπνευστος, or wrote by divine inspiration, whence it is more correctly said that the holy Spirit of GOD inspired the same or almost the same things in both, just as it is established concerning the holy quartet of the Evangelists. Wherefore Hornejus did not accurately enough call the Epistle of Jude a compendium of the latter Epistle of Peter. However, St. Jude seems to have used the same words which St. Peter had used before: in order to designate more expressly those heretics whom St. Peter had predicted would come. For just as St. Peter, 2 Ep. II, 1, says, ἔσονται, ψευδοδιδάσκαλοι, οἵτινες παρεισάξουσιν, THERE SHALL BE false teachers, who SHALL PRIVILY BRING IN heresies of destruction, so St. Jude, verse 4, παρεισέδυσαν γάρ τινες, FOR THERE WERE CERTAIN MEN WHO HAD CREPT IN, &c. The former prophesied of those who were to come, the latter designated those present, whom the former had predicted.

Concerning another Jude, whom Grotius makes the author of the Epistle, perhaps such a thing never entered anyone's mind before him; certainly in all of antiquity no trace of it is found. Nor does the faction of Bar-Cochba, who sold himself as the Messiah, contribute anything to this, whom it is in no way likely that Jude noted. Epiphanius rather observes that the heretics noted by him were the same, namely the Gnostics: Cornelius à Lapide says that the heresies of Simon Magus, the Nicolaitans, and Cerinthus were already born at that time, and that those of the Gnostics, Ebion, Menander, Basilides, Saturninus, Valentinus, Marcion, and the like, would soon be born from them, and are refuted by St. Jude: which we concede regarding the former, but not regarding the latter. For he notes, according to Oecumenius, those who were seducing others at that time. Whom he therefore teaches should be avoided and fled from, graphically depicting their morals, concerning which

Athanasius in the Synopsis: Since certain men had crept in and were teaching that it is ἀδιάφορον, indifferent, to sin, even for those who deny the Lord, he found it necessary to write and render the brethren cautious. And at the beginning, Athanasius continues, he exhorts them to contend and remain in the faith delivered to them. Then he casts off such men as seducers, and denounces that they should have absolutely no communion with them, knowing that it is not enough to have been called, unless they also walk worthily in that calling, for the reason that the Lord also destroyed the former people led out of Egypt when He saw they did not persist in the faith, and did not spare the Angels who did not keep their own order. For this reason one must withdraw from such men. And that Michael the Archangel did not endure the blasphemy of the devil. He teaches, therefore, that the destruction of these men will be like that of the Sodomites. Afterwards, having exhorted them to good morals and prayed for the stability of their faith from the Lord, he closes the Epistle.

Just as these things excellently exhibit the whole argument of the Epistle, so they sufficiently teach how alien the things handed down here are from Bar-Cochba, and that they do not concern Pseudo-Christs or those from the Jews adhering to them, but heretics seducing the faithful in the Christian Church, and are properly directed against present seducers, even if they are to be observed at all times. There is also nothing in it—to add this at least in passing—that Athanasius says these things are opposed to the dogma of Simon, that faith alone suffices for salvation without works, or that it could be reprobated only on that account, because faith, which is alone and without works, by no means either justifies or saves, and not as if works contributed anything to justification or salvation. The heresy of the Carpocratians is long after Jude. For Carpocrates lived at the beginning of the reign of Antoninus Pius, about the year 183 after Christ was born, or certainly, as Theodoret wishes, under his predecessor Hadrian. Nor does the refutation of Jude sufficiently fit the heresy of Carpocrates, since Carpocrates feigned two Gods of a completely different and dissimilar nature and denied the resurrection of the dead: which are by no means noted or refuted here.

But dismissing this Jude, as an alien, and one introduced only by Grotius, some things must still be noted concerning Jude the Apostle, the true author of the Epistle. He was, as we have said, the brother of James the Less, that is, who was surnamed the brother of the Lord, and of Simon, whose mother was Mary, who was also called the mother of James, Mark XV, verse 40. The father was Alphaeus. The mother was later married to Cleophas, and is called the sister of the Blessed Virgin Mary, John XIX, 25. Therefore James is called the brother of the Lord, Galatians I, verse 19, by a Hebrew phrase, that is, a cousin. By which name Jude also comes in the Arabic inscription of the Epistle, for it reads thus: The Catholic Epistle of St. Jude the Brother of the Lord; where, however, the Syriac and the Ethiopian have in its place 'brother of James,' as he is called in verse 1. That those sisters were that Mary and the Blessed Θεοτόκος, not only Eccius, Cardinal Toletus on John p. 214, and Maldonatus on Matthew XII, verse 47, but also Cardinal Hugo of St. Victor and the Glossator on Galatians I, Anselm and Bede on Galatians V, and indeed even Jerome against Helvidius and on Matthew XII, and also Theodoret on Luke VI, have asserted, with James Faber Stapulensis contradicting in vain concerning one Mary out of three, Baronius in the Apparatus chapter IV, Suarez part III, disp. 5, q. 28, art. 1, Cornelius à Lapide in this place. Nor is it necessary that we say that James the brother of the Lord, and his brothers Jude, Simon, and Joses, are so named because they were begotten by Joseph, the spouse of the Blessed Virgin, from a prior marriage, for which opinion Cornelius à Lapide praises many patrons. For thus, he says, Nyssenus thought in oration II on the resurrection, Origen, Theophylactus, and Euthymius on Matthew XIII, Clement of Alexandria here, Epiphanius heresy LI, Chrysostom in his oration on the Annunciation, Hilary canon I on Matthew, Ambrosiaster on Galatians I, Oecumenius, and Cajetan. He also adds the Arabic version, which has 'Jude the son of Joseph the Carpenter'; to which opinion, however, Cornelius does not subscribe, since Joseph was a celibate, and St. Jerome hands this down in tract 23. Nor does the Arabic version in either the London or Leiden edition have such an inscription. Nor do we think they were called brothers of the Lord because Alphaeus, their parent, was a full brother of Joseph, the spouse of Mary, which even if we admit with Hegesippus in Eusebius book III, chapter 11, the reason for the appellation is nevertheless closer, which the Holy Spirit Himself indicates in John XIX, 25, expressly calling Mary their mother the sister of the Blessed Virgin, from which the letter of the Scripture is not to be rashly departed, so that we understand her only as a kinswoman, just as Cornelius wishes, as also Blessed Polycarp and our Lyserus in his Harmony, chapter LXX. In this matter, B. Chemnitius in his Harmony of the Gospels is of the same opinion as us; James, he says, is called the son of Alphaeus, namely of that Alphaeus who was the husband of Mary of Cleophas, the sister of the Lord's mother. Paul in Galatians 1, verse 19, calls him the brother of the Lord, and Josephus also names him so in book 20 of the Antiquities.

The name Judas is derived from praise and confession, which seems to have been taken from the celebrated Patriarch Judah, Genesis 49, verse 8. And since the same name was also given to Judas the betrayer of the Lord, for the sake of distinction, as the blessed Chemnitius holds in the aforementioned place, he was called by the surname Thaddaeus, Mark 3:18; either because this name also implies confession, praise, and thanksgiving by reason of its Hebrew etymology, as the blessed Chemnitius maintains, and the blessed Gerhard in Matthew 10, verse 3; or, as Cornelius prefers, following Angelo Caninio in his Loca Novi Testamenti, book 13, because it is derived from the Syrian תד, meaning breast, as if he were called 'breast-like,' merciful and beneficent. He was also called Lebbaeus from the heart, as if endowed with a heart, or from a lion, on account of his leonine fortitude, or on account of wisdom, which pleases B. Gerhard and Fr. Junius, Matt. X. verse 35. Although indeed Eusebius lib. I. Hist. cap. 13. and Nicephorus lib. II. Hist. cap. 40. place two Thaddeuses along with some others, namely the Apostle and one of the LXX. disciples, which the Greeks also have in the Menologion: yet Jerome in Matt. X., Fulgentius serm. IX., Bede in Acts I., and the Latins in the Martyrology and divine office acknowledge only one, and therefore this Judas must be that Thaddeus of ours, who converted King Abgar of Edessa and the Edessenes to the faith.

To those sanctified in God the Father.] Thus 1 Cor. XII. sanctified in Christ Jesus. For through Christ, extraordinary holiness is given to Christians. In the Manuscript it is: To those beloved in God the Father, as the Latin reads.

And kept in Jesus Christ.] It is a past participle for the present. It signifies that they are kept in Christ, namely so that they may receive a reward from him in his own time. Compare 1 Thess. II, 23. where the same word τηρεῖσθαι is used. Add 1 Cor. XI, 2. Eph. V, 27.

Called.] He shows the source of every good, the calling from mere grace. Thus also 1 Cor. I, 2.

As regards the inscription or the object of those to whom this epistle was written, we admit that the epistle was directed to the Jews converted to the faith of Christ who were dispersed here and there, which most also maintain, and Estius gathers from v. 17: Be mindful of the words which were spoken before by the Apostles, if indeed Peter predicted this in 2 ep. II, who wrote both epistles to the Jews: But this argument does not hold, because Paul also predicted about the mockers of the last times in 1 Thess. IV, even though he wrote to the Gentiles. But Estius rightly observes: That the Greek can be clearly rendered thus: To those who are sanctified in God the Father, and kept in Jesus Christ, called. So that the order is: Namely to the called, who are sanctified in God the Father, and kept in Jesus Christ; understand, he writes this epistle. For called, the Greek κλητοῖς, is a noun, not a participle, as if you were to say, the vocates. Since this was not noticed, someone added the conjunction And, as if it were missing, although it does not explain the sense, but rather obscures it. For the sense is, This epistle is written to the called, that is, to the faithful, who indeed have been sanctified in God the Father, as the Author and principle of all holiness, and in Jesus Christ, who redeemed them, have been guarded and kept by the same God the Father, so that they might not perish by being seduced by deceivers, John VI, 39. cap. XVII. v. 12. For Judas writes these things as to the elect, just as Peter also in his first epistle to the elect strangers, etc. For although among those to whom the Apostles wrote their epistles there were some not elect: yet they wrote primarily for the sake of the Elect. Calvinist Interpreters Fr. Junius, Phil. Pareus, Caspar Sibelius, as also Dan. Heinsius, having changed the Apostolic order, read it thus: Called by God the Father, sanctified and kept in Jesus Christ, but to this end, that they might provide a safeguard for their particular, solely efficacious calling, as can be seen in Caspar Sibelius. We, however, believe that one should persist in the reading approved by many and most ancient Codices. Estius acknowledges that the word ἡγιασμένοις (sanctified) is to be preferred to the other ἠγαπημένοις (beloved), even though Oecumenius read it so, since it is more suited to the purpose, because by the mention of this benefit, sanctification, he immediately recalls and deters them from the impurities of the Simonian school.

Latin:

Vers. 1.

Ἰύδας Χρισῦ Ἰησῦ δῦλος.] Non addit Ἀπόςολος, quod Apostoli facere solent in epistolis etiam ad privatos. Dein- de, si Apostolica fuisset habita hæc epistola, versa fuisset in linguas omnes, & recepta per omnes Ecclesias: quod nunc aliter se habuit. Quare omnino adducor, ut credam hanc Epistolam esse Judæ Episcopi Hierosolymitani, qui fuit Adria- ni temporibus paulo ante Barchochebam. Nam Simeoni, cujus esse credimus epistolam, quæ Petri altera dicitur, succes- sit Justus, Ebraice צַדוֹק Σαδωκός, huic Zacchæus, Zacchæo Tobias, Tobiæ Benjamin, Benjamini Johannes, Johanni Matthias, Matthiæ Philippus, id est, פּרָא כי, vel פִּי לִבִּי, Philippo Seneca, id est, שָׂנְכָה, Senecæ Justus alter, huic Le- vi, ei Ephres, Ephræ Josepheti is, quem dico Judas. Scripta est autem hæc epistola adversus Carpocratianos maxime, ut & illa Simeonis. Quare cum in eodem versetur argumento, non mirum si & easdem historias veteres illi aptat, & verbis modo iisdem quibus Simeon, modo paulum commutatis uti- tur. Scribit autem ad Judæos gente, religione Christianos, ubique dispersos.

Ἀδελφὸς δὲ Ἰακώβυ.]

Hoc additum puto esse a Scribis, ut Judas hic esse Aposto- lus crederetur, quando & in illa Simeonis epistola quædam addita notavimus. In limine Epistolæ tum ὑπογραφὴ subscriptio, quam vocant, mentione nominis & officii, ac περι- φράσει διακριτικῇ ad autorem dignoscendum constans vers. 1. tum ἐπιγραφὴ vel inscriptio, desi- gnatione eorum, ad quos exarata est epistola, tum εὐχὴ vel votum vers. 2. habetur. Autor Epi- stolæ vocat se primum nomine proprio Judam, tum ab officio, Jesu Christi δοῦλον servum : quo nomine sese etiam nuncupavit S. Petrus 2. Ep. I. vers. 1. ut & S. Jacobus Cap. I. vers. 1. necnon S. Paulus & cum addito Apostoli epitheto, Rom. I. vers. 2. Tit. I. vers. 1. & sine eodem, vel simpli- citer Phil. I. vers. 1. Denique ne alius quispiam Judas fingatur, nominat sese fratrem Jacobi, quem ex Apostolorum Collegio fuisse è collatione Matth. X. vers. 3. Marc. III. vers. 18. cap. VI. v. 3. cap. XV. vers. 40. Johann. VI. vers. 16. Actor. I, 13. constat. Quod etsi non tantum è titulo habea- tur, quem talem gerit Epistola, Ἰούδα τοῦ Ἀπο- στόλου ἐπιστολὴ καθολικὴ, sed etiam in ipso textu ceu parte Epistolæ integrali & indubia; Grotius tamen, quæ Viri est temeritas, præter omnium Codicum fidem maluit verba ἀδελφὸς δὲ Ἰακώβου ceu notha traducere, quam veritati subscribere, ut à dignitate Apostolica Autorem excluderet. Sed quibus, obsecro, argumentis docebitur, tex- tum hujus epistolæ corruptum esse, quam suspi- cionem non tantum Græci Codices, sed etiam versiones omnes ex asse hic conspirantes, fortis- sime excludunt. Quibus consonat quoque ap- pellatio Judæ apud Lucam, qui eum itidem Ju- dam, Jacobi scil. fratrem vocat cap. VI. vers. 16. & Actor. I. v. 13.

Quod vero Judas non addiderit vocem Ἀπό- στολος, non magis dubiam reddit præsentem epi- stolam, quam eam, quæ à S. Paulo Philippensibus inscripta est, in qua etiam se tantum nominavit servum Jesu Christi, quanquam præterea illa πε- ρίφρασις frater Jacobi satis doceat, nullum alium Judam, quam Apostolum intelligi. Quod au- tem dicit, si Apostolica fuisset habita hæc Episto- la, versa fuisset in linguas omnes, in eo nullum consequentiæ nervum deprehendimus. Quum enim Græca lingua ubique ævo illo vulgata fue- rit, in eadem, ceu originali legi poterat. Adde, quod Scripturæ indubitato divinæ non statim in diversas linguas nedum omnes translatæ sint, & dubium esse possit, an vel ad hunc diem in lin- guas omnes sint conversæ? Quod denique dici- tur, quod non per omnes Ecclesias recepta fuerit, nec id probat Judam Apostolum autorem non esse. Nam potuere aliqui de eo aliquando du- bitare, quod aliis etiam Canonicis Scripturis con- tigit, etsi justas dubitandi causas non habuerint, qualis certe illa non est, quam adduxit, ex alio- rum mente Hieronymus in catalog. viror. Illustr. quod nempe Autor de libro Henoch, qui Apocry- phus est, in ea affumat testimonium. Siquidem non ex Apocrypho illo libro, sed tum è traditio- ne, tum imprimis ex divina inspiratione vatici- nium Enochi habuerit Judas. Et addit Hierony- mus l. c. de hac Epistola: Autoritatem tamen ve- tustate jam & usu meruit, & inter sanctas Scriptu- ras computatur; Et in Epist. ad Paulin. eandem diserte Judæ Apostolo adscribit. Eusebius etiam illis eandem accenset, quibus à nonnullis contra- dictum, quas tamen à multis agnosci ait libr. II. Hist. Eccl. c. 23. lib. VI. c. 13.

Ob hanc autem nonnullorum dubitationem ex- cusari non minus possunt B. Lutherus, ac Cen- turiatores Magdeburgenses, & si qui alii è no- stris inveniantur ipsis consentientes, quod non ejusdem autoritatis in Ecclesia hanc Epistolam fuisse dixerint, quam è Pontificiis Cajetanus Car- din. qui minoris, inquit, autoritatis est hæc Episto- la iis, quæ sunt certæ autoritatis.

Nobis vero omnino certum est, autorem hu- jus Epistolæ S. Judam esse Apostolum, unde nec de autoritate Apostolica & divina dubium no- bis ullum, de qua tum interna scripti κριτήρια nos certos reddunt, quam margaritas merito (quod de tota Scriptura Hilarius serm. VI. in Matth.) dixeris, quæ sub exigua mole multorum summam includit sestertiorum; tum vero confir- mant veterum testimonia, & concilia. Ex illis Clemens Alexandrinus teste Eusebio lib. VI. Hist. Eccles. cap. 14. in libris ὑποτυπώσεων omnium utriusque Testamenti Scripturarum compendiosam instituit enarrationem, ne illis quidem prætermis- fis Scripturis, de quibus ambigitur, Judæ episto- lam intelligo &c. Origenes in cap. XIII. Matth. Judas, inquit, scripsit epistolam paucorum quidem versuum, at plenam efficacibus verbis gratiæ cæle- stis. Epiphanius hæref. Gnostic. Quare de his, inquit, (Gnosticis) commotus Spiritus Sanctus in Apostolo Juda ait: Quæcunque naturaliter tanquam muta animantia norunt, in his corrumpuntur &c. Athanasius in Synopsi, Gregorius Nazianzenus in carm. Oecumenius in h. l. Ephrem Syrus accen- sent hanc Epistolam diserte Canonicis, & è Latinis, Cyprianus, Tertullianus de habit. muliebr. cap. 8. Hieronymus, Ambrosius, Augustinus, Ruffinus, Phi- lastrius, Cassianus, Prosper, Gelasius, Fulgentius, Primasius, Gregorius Magnus, Beda, Rabanus, Re- migius, aliique. Vid. Jodocus Coccejus in thes. Ca- thol. T. I. l. 6. p. 370. Ex hisce vero Concilium Car- thaginense III. num. 47. Laodicen. c. 58. Romanum sub Damas. &c.

Quod Judas vers. 17. quod nonnulli objici- unt, remittit ad Apostolorum dicta, id non magis Apostolicæ autoritati præjudicare potest, quam epistolæ Petrinæ posteriori, quod Petrus itidem ad Apostolorum præcepta, 2. Ep. III, 2. & ad Pau- li Epistolas vers. 15. remisit. - Tacemus, quod non- nulli sentiant, Petrum Apostolum ex hac Episto- la multa transsumsisse, quod facturus minime fuisset, si pro Apostolica eam non habuisset. Quo de Tirinus: Scripit, inquit, saltem ante an- num 31. à morte Christi, quo (ut Onuphrius in Chron. tradit) S. Judas cum fratre suo Simo- ne Cananæo martyrium in Perside subivit. Scri- pta igitur fuit circiter sexennio ante secundam Epistolam S. Petri, qui plurimas ex Judæ Epi- stola sententias pene verbotenus in suam trans- scripsit, quas per parallela digestas videre est apud Cornelium à Lapide. Tirino quoad hoc, quod Petrus hæc è S. Juda desumpserit, Salmero præivit, nec abnuit Cornelius, sed anceps est, an- ne Petrus ea è Juda sumpserit, ut eos dicta con- firmaret, an vero Judas illa acceperit à Petro, ut volunt Baronius ad ann. 68. Adamus Sasbouth, Hugo, Lorinus, Thomas Anglicus, & Primaticcius hic, juxta quos statuendum, Judam non an. Chri- sti 64. sed post S. Petrum, adeoque post ann. 68. mortem oppetiisse, quum Petrus secundam suam paulo ante mortem, illo anno scripsisse credatur, uti observat idem Cornelius. Quæ sententia præ- ferenda. Neutrum tamen accurate loquendo di- cendum, sive quod Petrus è Juda, sive quod Judas è Petro suam desumserit, quum uterq; θεόπνευστος fuerit, vel divina inspiratione scripserit, unde re- ctius dicitur, eadem vel pene eadem utrique in- spirasse sanctum DEI Spiritum, quemadmodum id de sancta Evangelistarum quadriga constat. Quapropter nec accurate satis Hornejus Judæ epistolam compendium posterioris Petrinæ dixit. Usus autem iisdem verbis videtur S. Judas, qui- bus antea S. Petrus: ut illos hæreticos, quos S. Pe- trus venturos prædixerat, expressius designaret. Nam uti S. Petrus 2. ep. II, 1. ἔσονται, inquit, ψευ- δοδιδάσκαλοι, οἵτινες παρεισάξουσιν, ERUNT falsi Doctores, qui SUBINTRODUCENT hæreses perditionis, ita S. Judas vers. 4. παρεισέδυσαν γάρ τινες INGRESSI erant quidam &c. Ille de futu- ris vaticinatus, hic præsentes, quos ille prædixit, designavit.

De Juda alio, quem Autorem facit epistolæ Grotius, nemini forte ante ipsum tale quid in mentem venit; in universa certe antiquitate nul- lum ejus vestigium habetur. Neque quicquam Barchochebæ, qui se pro Messia venditavit, factio huc facit, quam notasse Judam nullo modo fit verisimile. Epiphanius potius notatos hæreticos ab eodem observat, Gnosticos nempe: Cornelius à Lapide ait, hæreses Simonis Magi, Nicolaitarum, & Cerinthi jam tum natas, ac mox ex iisdem na- scituras Gnosticorum, Ebionis, Menandri, Basilidis, Saturnini, Valentini, Marcionis & similium à S. Juda confutari: quod de prioribus concedimus, non item de posterioribus. Notat enim secun- dum Oecum. eos, qui tum temporis alios seduce- bant. Quos proinde cavendos & fugiendos do- cet, mores eorum graphice depingens, de quo

Athanasius in Synopsi: Cum quidam subingressi docerent, ἀδιάφορον indifferens esse peccatum et- iam eorum, qui Dominum negant, necesse habuit, ut scriberet & cautos redderet fratres. Et initio quidem, pergit Athanasius, hortatur eos, ut certent atque in tradita sibi fide maneant. Deinde abjicit tales tanquam seductores, & denunciat, ne pror- sus ullam cum ipsis communionem haberent, scien- tes, non esse satis, vocatos esse, nisi etiam digne am- bulentur in ista vocatione, eo quod & priorem po- pulum Dominus ex Ægypto eductum, cum in fide videret non persistere, perdiderit, & Angelis ordinem suum non custodientibus, non pepercerit. Hac ratione secedendum esse à talibus. Et Michaë- lem nempe Archangelum non sustinuisse blasphemi- am diaboli. Docet itaque perditionem istorum sicut Sodomitarum futurum. Posthæc adhortatus ad bonos mores & fidei stabilitatem à Domino appreca- tus claudit epistolam.

Quæ uti eximie totum epistolæ argumentum exhibent, ita quam aliena sint, quæ hic tradun- tur à Barchocheba, nec Pseudo-Christos aut iis adhærentes è Judæis, sed hæreticos in Christia- na Ecclesia fideles seducentes concernant, & ad- versus præsentes seductores proprie directa sint, etsi omni tempore observanda, satis docent. Ni- hil etiam de eo, ut obiter saltem id attexam, A- thanasius, quod opposita hæc sint dogmati Simo- nis, quod sola fides sufficiat ad salutem sine operi- bus, quod non nisi ea ratione reprobari potuit, quod fides, quæ sola & sine operibus est, neuti- quam vel justificet vel salvet, non vero quasi ope- ra quicquam ad justificationem vel salutem con- ferant. Carpocratianorum hæresis longe poste- rior est Juda. Carpocrates enim vixit sub ini- tium imperii Antonini Pii circa annum à Christo nato 183. aut certe quod Theodoretius vult, sub ejus antecessore Adriano. Nec satis convenit elenchus Judæ Carpocratis hæresi, siquidem Carpocrates duos Deos diversæ penitus ac dissimi- lis naturæ finxerit ac resurrectionem mortuorum negarit: Quæ hic minime notantur aut convel- luntur.

Sed misso hoc Juda, ceu ἀλλοτρίῳ, nec nisi à Grotio ingesto, de Juda Apostolo vero epistolæ autore adhuc monenda nonnulla. Fuit ille, ut diximus, frater Jacobi minoris scilicet, qui fra- ter Domini cognominatus est, & Simonis, quo- rum mater fuit Maria, quæ & mater Jacobi di- cta, Marc. XV. vers. 40. Pater Alphæus. Mater nupta postea fuit Cleophæ, & Soror B. Mariæ Vir- ginis dicitur, Johan. XIX, 25. Ideo Jacobus frater Domini vocatur Galat. I. vers. 19. phrasi Ebræa, hoc est consobrinus. Quo nomine venit etiam Judas in Arabica inscriptione epistolæ, ita enim habet: Epistola B. Judæ Fratris Domini Catholica; ubi tamen Syrus, & Æthiops ejus loco habent frater Jacobi, ut in vers. 1. vocatur. Fuisse autem sorores Mariam illam, & Beatam Θεοτόκον, non tantum Eccius, Cardinalis Toletus in Joh. p. 214. & Maldonatus in Matth. XII. vers. 47. sed & Cardin. Hugo de S. Victore ac Glossator in Galat. I. Anshelmus & Beda ad Galat. V. imo & Hierony- mus contra Helvid. & in Matth. XII. nec non Theodoretus ad Luc. VI. asseruere, nequicquam contradicente Jacobo Fabro Stapulensi de una Ma- ria ex tribus, Baronio in appar. cap. IV. Suarezio part. III. disp. 5. q. 28. art. 1. Cornelio à Lapide in h. l. Nec vero est, ut fratrem Domini Jaco- bum, & fratres ejus Judam Simonem & Joses di- camus ex eo nuncupatos, quod à Josepho sponso B. Virginis ex priori conjugio procreati sint, cujus sententiæ multos laudat patronos Corne- lius à Lapide. Sic enim, inquit, opinatus est Nysse- nus orat. II. de resurr. Origenes, Theophylactus, & Euthymius in Matth. XIII. Clemens Alexan- drinus hic, Epiphanius hær. LI. Chrysostomus orat. de annunc. Hilarius can. I. in Matth. Am- brosiaster ad Gal. I. Oecumenius & Cajetanus. Ad- dit & Arabicam versionem, quæ habeat, Judas filius Josephi Fabri; cui tamen sententiæ non subscribit Cornelius, siquidem Joseph cælebs fue- rit, idque tradat S. Hieronymus tract. 23. Nec Arabica versio in editione sive Londinensi, sive Leidensi talem inscriptionem habet. Nec fratres Domini dictos censemus ideo, quod Alphæus Pa- rens ipsorum Josephi Mariæ sponsi germanus fue- rit, quod etsi admittamus cum Egesippo apud Eu- sebium l. III. cap. 11. ratio tamen appellationis vi- cinior est, quam ipse Spiritus Sanctus indicat Jo- han. XIX, 25. Mariam matrem ipsorum diserte vo- cans B. Virginis sororem, à qua Scripturæ litera te- mere discedendum non est, ut cognatam tantum intelligamus, quemadmodum vult Cornelius, ut & B. Polycarp. Lyserus noster harm. c. LXX. No- bis hic ὁμόψηφος est B. Chemnitius harm. C. L. Jacobus, inquit, vocatur Alphæi filius, scilicet illius Alphæi, qui fuit maritus Mariæ Cleophæ, sororis matris Domini. Paulus Gal. I. vers. 19. vocat ipsum fratrem Domini, & ita etiam Josephus l. XX. An- tiqu. ipsum nominat.

Judas nomen à laude & confessione habet, quod à celebri Patriarcha Juda accepiffe vide- tur, Gen. XLIX. v. 8. Et quum idem etiam Judæ proditori Domini impositum fuerit, distinctio- nis causa, censente B. Chemnitio l. c. Thaddæi co- gnomento nuncupatus est, Marc. III, 18. sive quod & hoc nomen confessionem, laudationem, & gra- tiarum actionem etymi Ebræi ratione importet, ut B. Chemnitius vult, & B. Gerhardus in Matth. X. vers. 3. sive, quod præfert Cornelius, præeunte Angelo Caninio in loc. Nov. Test. l. XIII. quod à Syro תד mammæ, quasi mammæus, misericors & boneficus dictus sit. Vocatus & Lebbæus à corde, quasi corde præditus, vel leone, ob leoninam fortitudinem, vel ob sapientiam, quod B. Gerhar- do & Fr. Junio placet, Matth. X. vers. 35. Quan- quam vero Eusebius lib. I. Hist. cap. 13. & Nicepho- rus lib. II. Hist. cap. 40. duos cum nonnullis aliis Thaddæos ponant, Apostolum nempe & unum è LXX. discipulis, quod & Græci habent in Meno- logio: Unum tamen tantum agnoscit Hieronymus in Matth. X. Fulgentius serm. IX. Beda in Actor. I. & Latini in Martyrol. & offic. divin. ideoque hunc Judam Thaddæum illum esse oportet no- strum, qui Abgarum Regem Edessæ & Edessenos ad fidem convertit.

Τοῖς ἐν Θεῷ Πατρὶ ἡγιασμένοις.] Sic 1. Cor. XII. ἡγιασμένοις ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ. Per Christum enim data est Christianis sanctitas eximia. In Manuscripto est : Τοῖς ἐν Θεῷ Πατρὶ ἠγαπημένοις, quomodo legit Latinus.

Καὶ Ἰησοῦ Χριστῷ τετηρημένοις.] Est Participium Præteritum pro Præsenti. Significat eos servari in Christo, nempe ut ab eo suo tempore præmium ac- cipiant. Confer 1. Thessal. II, 23. ubi idem verbum τηρεῖσθαι. Adde 1. Cor. XI. 2. Eph. V, 27.

Κλητοῖς.] Ostendit fontem omnis boni, vocationem ex mera gratia. Sic & 1. Cor. I, 2.

Inscriptionem vel objectum eorum, ad quos scripta hæc epistola, quod attinet, ad Judæos ad fidem Christi conversos hinc inde dispersos dire- ctam epistolam admittimus, quod plerique etiam statuunt, & è v. 17. colligit Estius: Memores esto- te verborum, quæ prædicta sunt ab Apostolis, siqui- dem id prædixerit Petrus 2. ep. II. qui ad Judæos utramque epistolam scripserit: Sed hoc argumen- tum non stringit, quia etiam Paulus de illusori- bus novissimorum temporum prædixit 1. Thess. IV. etsi ad gentiles scripserit. Recte autem observat Estius: Græca sic perspicue reddi posse: Iis, qui in Deo Patre sanctificati sunt, & Jesu Christo servati, vocatis. Ut ordo sit: Vocatis nempe iis, qui in Deo Patre sanctificati sunt, & Jesu Christo servati; sub- audi, scribit hanc epistolam. Nam vocatis, Græca κλητοῖς, nomen est, non participium, ac si dicas, vocatitiis. Quod cum non adverteretur, adjecit aliquis copulam Et, tanquam deesset, cum ea sen- sum adeo non explicet, ut magis obscuret. Est enim sensus, Scribi hanc epistolam vocatis, id est, fideli- bus, qui nimirum in Deo Patre, tanquam omnis sanctitatis Autore & principio sanctificati sunt, & in Jesu Christo, qui eos redemit ab eodem Deo Patre custoditi & servati, ne à deceptoribus sedu- cti pereant, Joh. VI, 39. cap. XVII. v. 12. Scribit enim hæc Judas, tanquam electis, quemadmo- dum & Petrus in prima epistola electis advenis &c. Quamvis enim inter eos, quibus scripserunt Apo- stoli suas epistolas, essent quidam non electi: tamen scribebant imprimis propter Electos. Cal viniani Interpretes Fr. Junius, Phil. Pareus, Ca- spar Sibelius, ut & Dan. Heinsius ordine Aposto- lico mutato sic legunt: Vocatis à Deo Patre, san- ctificatis & Jesu Christo servatis, sed eo fine, ut vocationi suæ particulari, solum efficaci, præsidium parent, ut apud Casparem Sibelium videre est. Nos autem persistendum censemus in lectione à pluri- mis & antiquissimis Codicibus probata. Vocem ἡγιασμένοις sanctificatis præferendam esse alteri ἠγαπημένοις, etsi ita legerit Oecumenius, agnoscit Estius, siquidem id magis instituto accommoda- tum sit, quum hujus beneficii, sanctificationis, mentione statim revocet ac deterreat eos ab im- munditiis scholæ Simonianæ.

## 1:2
Verse 2.

Mercy to you and peace, and love be multiplied.] Mercy and peace is also in that which is called the second of John, and often in Paul. That be multiplied is in 1 Pet. I, 2. Love in the greeting of Paul Eph. VI, 23.

The same wish is almost that of St. Peter 2 ep. I, 1. The Vulgate rendered it be fulfilled. But how will the mercy of GOD be fulfilled? Lorinus, with Hugo and Thomas Anglicus, rashly suggests that the mercy of God is begun through the remission of sins; but is fulfilled when grace is superadded, that is, according to their Lexicon, the habit of charity is infused. Certainly, as mercy denotes mercy in God: so in GOD nothing can be added to it. For it is infinite. But that the mercy of GOD is to be multiplied, not in itself, but in relation to us, is to be wished, which happens when the gifts of the same, peace and charity, are multiplied in us, and the full assurance of the grace and mercy of GOD, by which he embraces us in Christ, is increased, so that we may stand and persevere more and more strengthened in that grace of God. Which Judas prays for, because he was about to exhort them to preserve the faith, the fruits of which are peace, and tranquility of conscience, and charity, or love toward God and neighbor. Hornejus wants it to be intended through the multiplication of peace and charity, so that God may hold those whom he has once deemed worthy of his peace and friendship as more friendly and dearer day by day: But that was already included in the multiplication of mercy and divine grace, if it is explained according to Hornejus. It is better, however, to show how the wish fits the treatment: Namely, the multiplication of mercy, when the faith, the preservation of which he intends, is increased: of peace, when it is not disturbed by apostasy or sins that devastate the conscience: of love, when out of love for God, heretics and impure and foul sinners are shunned, and charity is shown toward those who are erring.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

Ἔλεος ὑμῖν καὶ εἰρήνη, καὶ ἀγάπη πληθυνθείη.] Ἔλεος & εἰρήνη est & in ea, quæ secunda Johannis dicitur, & apud Paulum sæpe. Illud πληθυνθείη 1. Petr. I, 2. Ἀγάπη in salu- tatione Pauli Eph. VI, 23.

Idem fere votum est S. Petri 2. epist. I, 1. Vulgatus reddidit adimpleatur. Sed quomodo misericordia DEI adimplebitur? Temere Lorinus cum Hugone, ac Thoma Anglico inchoari misericordiam Dei per remissionem peccatorum; adimpleri vero, quando gratia superadditur, hoc est juxta Lexicon ipsorum, habitus charitatis infunditur. Sane uti ἔλεος misericordiam in Deo notat: Ita in DEO nihil superaddi ei potest. Est enim illa infinita. Multiplicari autem DEI misericordiam non in se, sed ratione nostri optandum, quod sit quum dona ejusdem pax & charitas in nobis multiplicantur, & πληροφορία de DEI gratia & misericordia, qua nos in Christo complectitur, augetur, ut in illa Dei gratia magis magisque roborati stemus, ac perseveremus. Quod precatur Judas, quia hortaturus erat ad fidem conservandam, cujus fructus sunt pax, & tranquillitas conscientiæ, & charitatis, vel dilectio erga Deum & proximum. Hornejus vult id per multiplicationem pacis & charitatis intendi, ut amiciores & chariores indies habeat Deus, quos semel pace atque amicitia sua dignatus est: Sed id jam comprehensum fuit multiplicatione misericordiæ & gratiæ divinæ, si ea juxta Hornejum exponatur. Præstat autem ostendere, quomodo votum tractationi conveniat: Multiplicatio scilicet misericordiæ, cum fides, cujus conservationem intendit, augetur: pacis, cum ea non turbatur per apostasiam aut peccata conscientiam vastantia: dilectionis, cum ex amore Dei fugiuntur hæretici & impuri fœdique peccatores, & charitas erga errantes exhibetur.

## 1:3
Ver. 3.

Ἀγαπητοὶ (Beloved).] Thus 1 Cor. 4:13, ch. 10:14, ch. 15:58, 2 Cor. 12:19, Eph. 5:1, Phil. 2:12, ch. 4:1, 1 Thess. 2:8, Heb. 6:9, Jas. 1:16, 19, ch. 2:5, 1 Pet. 2:11, ch. 4:12, 2 Pet. 3:17, 1 John 3:20, 21, ch. 4:1, 3, 11.

Πᾶσαν σπουδὴν ποιούμενος (Giving all diligence).] A similar phrase in 2 Pet. 1:5.

Γράφειν ὑμῖν περὶ τῆς κοινῆς σωτηρίας (To write to you concerning the common salvation).] Of those things which pertain to the common salvation. Thus κατὰ κοινὴν πίστιν (according to the common faith), Tit. 1:4. In the Manuscript: Κοινῆς ἡμῶν σωτηρίας (our common salvation), for which the Latin reads ὑμῶν (your).

Ἀνάγκην ἔσχον γράψαι ὑμῖν παρακαλῶν (I found it necessary to write to you, exhorting).] That is, εἰς τὸ παρακαλεῖν (to exhort). I had nothing more important to write than to warn you about the present dangers.

This is as it were the exordium of the epistle. But it contains the proposition, while the necessity of writing is explained, on account of a twofold cause concerning the common salvation: both the exhortation to contend for the faith once delivered, v. 3, and the caution concerning the most wicked heretics who had crept in among them, v. 4. These two things the Apostle subsequently executes in the body of the epistle.

Ἐπαγωνίζεσθαι ἅπαξ παραδοθείσῃ τοῖς ἁγίοις πίστει (To contend for the faith once delivered to the saints).] He calls the doctrine itself πίστιν (faith) by metonymy, such as is also in Acts 6:7 and elsewhere. He says it was once delivered to the saints, that is, to those who are now saints, namely by the Apostles, as 1 Cor. 11:2, 23, ch. 15:3, where the same word παραδιδόναι (to deliver) is used. See also 2 Pet. 2:21. And he says once: because nothing is to be changed regarding that doctrine. Ἐπαγωνίζεσθαι τῇ πίστει (to contend for the faith) is to defend it well, not to allow it to be snatched from oneself. For ἐπὶ here stands for 'for'.

By πίστιν (faith) is rightly understood the faith which is believed, or the doctrine of faith. Therefore, some Reformed [theologians] in vain gather from the faith once delivered that the truly faithful cannot fall from faith, following the lead of Calvin on this passage, such as Fr. Junius and Casp. Sibelius. For the very word παραδοθεῖσα (delivered) teaches that the discourse is about the doctrine of faith, which corresponds not so much to the confidence of the heart as to the doctrine of the Gospel, as the learned Dr. Samuel Pomarius rightly [argues] in his Academic lectures on this passage, comparing for that signification of faith Rom. 1:5, Eph. 4:5, 1 Tim. 4:1, ch. 5:19, Gal. 1:23. They also explain it concerning the doctrine of faith in the Reformed school, Beza and Piscator. However, 'once delivered' is understood by some not in terms of quantity, but of quality, so that it is the same as 'certainly, absolutely,' as in Exod. XXXIII, 5, Psalm LXII, 12, Psalm LXXXIX, 38, and below in 5, and that the doctrine of the faith is signified as having been perfectly delivered. Thus Lyranus, Cornelius, and Glassius in Grammat. S. p. 462. 'There is great emphasis,' says Flacius, 'in that description of the true faith or religion, where he says, which was once delivered to the saints.' For he wishes to indicate that it was delivered once, fully and most sufficiently, and that no innovations, or additions of human inventions, or dogmas, or other traditions are to be admitted: just as later Satan overwhelmed the truth with new additions. Lorinus on this passage: 'The faith once delivered,' he says, 'must be preserved as much as possible, that is, in the same way it was first delivered in its purity and integrity; nothing is to be introduced from one's own judgment.' But it is said to be delivered to the saints, that is, according to some, to the Prophets and Apostles, the holy men of GOD, 2 Pet. I, last verse, as B. Gerhard says: 'These saints,' he says, 'are none other than the Prophets and Apostles, who learned the mystery of the faith through immediate divine revelation.' Others supply the preposition, 'which was delivered by the holy Prophets and Apostles,' like the Arabic of Erpenius, 'which they, the pure or holy, delivered to us, or for us.' So also the Carthusian. Others, however, more simply take it in the Dative, 'which was once delivered to the saints, or to the holy Church.' This sense is expressed by the London Arabic edition, translated by B. Johannes Ernestus Gerhardus, 'which was delivered to the saints once.' And Bede: 'praying not to learn another faith than that which was once delivered to you by the Apostles, but to contend for this always even unto death.'

But while the faithful are commanded to contend for the faith, what is more certain than that they ought also to defend the faith against those who attack it, as much as they can? For one must contend with prayer, word, and every effort. And Cornelius himself, although he denies that the simple and unlearned should contend by disputing, had to admit that they ought to contend by constantly asserting and defending the truth and the faith. But how can they assert and defend it against τοὺς ἀντιλέγοντας (those who contradict) unless they assert and defend the doctrine of the faith from the Word of GOD, which cannot be done without disputation, for which the simpler sort do not need artificial Logic, since natural Logic itself, in those endowed with some judgment, dictates consequences in the clear passages of Scripture, by which those who contradict the same may be confounded. He gives here the reason, says Cornelius, for the words 'certain men have crept in,' why it behooves them to contend earnestly for the faith, because, namely, heretics attack it sharply and deceitfully. He also praises the statement of the Pontiff: 'Terrible,' he says, 'is the sentence of Innocent III, dist. 83, c. error: Error, he says, which is not resisted, is approved, and truth, when it is not defended, is oppressed; for to neglect to disturb the perverse when you can is nothing else than to foster them.' He speaks especially to Prelates, but also to others in their order. And the 'super' (earnestly), he says, denotes a huge, sharp, and continuous zeal for contending and resisting the enemies of the faith, and as it were an ἄσπονδον πόλεμον, that is, an irreconcilable war. For 'super' signifies a strenuous and, as it were, superhuman struggle, so that by contending they, as it were, surpass themselves like athletes, who in the arena transcend their own strength and themselves, while the matter concerns the highest thing, namely victory and life. Item: The 'super' denotes another and, as it were, a second struggle, as if to say: 'I first contended with you against idolatry and idolaters; now you contend with me a second time against heresy and heretics,' for this is

— ἐπαγωνίζεσθαι (to contend earnestly). Thus Nazianzen in his oration on the Maccabees says: Προηγωνίζατο πατὴρ, ἐπαγωνιεῖται παῖδες, that is, 'The father contended first, the sons will contend afterwards.' And although we may prefer the explanation of Grotius as simpler; yet these things can be urged against Cornelius himself Κατ' ἄνθρωπον (according to man).

Latin:

Vers. 3.

Ἀγαπητοὶ.] Sic 1. Cor. 4, 13. cap. 10, 14. cap. 15, 58. 2. Cor. 12, 19. Eph. 5, 1. Phil. 2, 12. cap. 4, 1. 1. Thessal. 2, 8. Ebr. 6, 9. Jac. I, 16. 19. c. 2, 5. 1. Petr. 2, 11. c. 4, 12. 2. Petr. 3, 17. 1. Joh. 3, 20. 21. cap. 4, 1. 3. 11.

Πᾶσαν σπουδὴν ποιούμενος.] Par loquutio 2. Petr. I, 5.

Γράφειν ὑμῖν περὶ τῆς κοινῆς σωτηρίας.] De iis, quæ pertinent ad communem salutem. Sic κατὰ κοινὴν πίστιν, Tit. I, 4. In Manuscripto: Κοινῆς ἡμῶν σωτηρίας pro quo Latinus legit ὑμῶν.

Ἀνάγκην ἔσχον γράψαι ὑμῖν παρακαλῶν.] Id est, εἰς τὸ παρακαλεῖν. Nihil potius habui, quod scriberem, quam ut vos monerem de periculis præsentibus.

Est hoc veluti exordium epistolæ. Sed complectens propositionem, dum exponitur scriptionis necessitas, ob geminam causam communem salutem concernentem, tum exhortationem ad agonismum pro fide semel tradita, v. 3. tum cautionem de hæreticis pessimis, qui irrepserant penes ipsos v. 4. Quæ duo deinceps exsequitur Apostolus in corpore epistolæ.

Ἐπαγωνίζεσθαι ἅπαξ παραδοθείσῃ τοῖς ἁγίοις πίστει.] Πίστιν vocat ipsam doctrinam per Metonymiam, qualis est & Actor. VI, 7. & alibi. Eam dicit semel traditam sanctis, id est, iis, qui nunc sancti sunt, nempe per Apostolos, ut 1. Cor. XI, 2. 23. cap. XV, 3. ubi eadem vox παραδιδόναι. Vide & 2. Petr. II, 21. Et dicit semel: quia de ea doctrina nihil immutandum. Ἐπαγωνίζεσθαι τῇ πίστει est eam bene tueri, non sinere sibi eripi. Ἐπὶ enim hic valet pro.

Per πίστιν recte fides quæ creditur, vel doctrina fidei intelligitur. Ideo frustra Reformati nonnulli ex fide semel tradita colligunt, vere fideles excidere fide non posse, præeunte Calvino in h. l. ut pote Fr. Junius & Casp. Sibelius. Nam vel ipsa vox παραδοθεῖσα de fidei doctrina sermonem esse docet, quæ non tam fiducia cordis, quam doctrina Evangelii convenit, ut recte Dn. D. Samuel Pomarius in prælect. Acad. ad h. loc. conferens pro significatione illa fidei Roman. I. vers. 5. Ephes. IV. vers. 5. 1. Tim. IV. v. 1. cap. V, 19. Galat. I, 23. De doctrina fidei explicant etiam in Reformatorum- schola Beza & Piscator. Semel autem tradita à nonnullis intelligitur non ratione quantitatis, sed qualitatis, ut idem sit, quod certo, prorsus, ut Exod. XXXIII, 5. Psalm. LXII, 12. Psalm. XXCIX, 38. & infra 5. & doctrina fidei perfecte tradita innuatur. Ita Lyranus, Cornelius & Glassius in Grammat. S. p. 462. Magna emphasis est, ait Flacius, in illa verae fidei religionisve descriptione, quod inquit, quae semel sanctis tradita est. Vult enim indicare, semel eam plene ac sufficientissime esse traditam, nec admittendas esse ullas novationes, aut addita- menta humanorum inventorum, vel dogmatum, vel traditionum aliarum : Sicut postea satan no- vis additamentis veritatem obruit. Lorinus in h. l. Conservanda, inquit, semel tradita fides, quantum fieri potest, id est, quo primum modo tradita est in sua puritate ac integritate; nihil ex arbitrio suo introducendum. Tradita autem dicitur san- ctis, id est, juxta nonnullos, Prophetis & Apo- stolis sanctis DEI hominibus, 2. Petr. I. vers. ult. quomodo B. Gerhardus: Sancti hi, inquit, non sunt alii, quam Prophetae & Apostoli, qui per im- mediatam revelationem divinam mysterium fidei didicerunt: Alii subaudiunt praepositionem, quae à sanctis Prophetis & Apostolis tradita, ut Arabs Erpenii, quam tradiderunt eam puri, vel sancti nobis, vel ad nos. Sic & Carthusianus. Simplicius tamen alii in Dativo accipiunt, quae sanctis, vel sanctae Ecclesiae semel tradita est. Quem sensum exprimit Arabica Londinensis editio, interprete B, Johanne Ernesto Gerhardo, quae tradita est ad sanctos semel. Et Beda: deprecans non aliam fi- dem discere, quam eam, quae semel tradita est vobis ab Apostolis, sed pro hac certari semper usque ad mortem.

Certare autem pro fide dum jubentur fideles, quid certius est, quam eosdem etiam fidem con- tra eos, qui impugnant, tueri debere, quantum possunt. Certandum enim prece, verbo studioque omni. Et Cornelius ipse quamvis neget, simplices, & rudes disputando certare, fateri necessum ha- buit, certare eosdem debere, veritatem, fidemque constanter asserendo tuendoque. Quomodo vero asserere, ac tueri contra τὺς ἀντιλέγοντας possunt, nisi è Verbo DEI asserant, ac tueantur doctri- nam fidei, quod sine disputatione fieri nequit, ad quam simplicioribus non opus est Logica arti- ficiali, quum ipsa Logica naturalis aliquo judi- cio praeditis in luculentis Scripturae locis conse- quentias dictitet, quibus confundantur eidem contradicentes. Dat hic causam, inquit Corne- lius, ad verba subintroierunt quidam, cur opor- teat eos supercertare pro fide, quia videlicet eam, acriter & dolose impugnant haeretici. Laudat & dictum Pontificis: Terribilis, inquit, est senten- tia Innocentii III. dist. 83. c. error: Error inquit, cui non resistitur, approbatur, & veritas, cum minime defensatur, opprimitur; negligere quippe cum possis deturbare perversos, nihil aliud est, quam fovere: loquitur Praelatis praecipue, sed & ca- teris suo ordine. Et τὸ super, inquit, notat ingens, acre & continuum certandi & resistendi hostibus fidei studium, ac quasi ἄσπονδον πόλεμον, id est, ir- reconciliabile bellum. Tò enim super significat stre- nuum & quasi super vires certamen, ut certando seipsos quasi superent instar athletarum, qui in ago- ne suas vires & seipsos quasi transcendunt, dum de summa rei puta victoria & vita agitur. Item: Tò super notat alterum & quasi secundum certa- men, q. d. Ego vobiscum primo certavi contra idololatriam & idololatras; vos mecum jam secun- do certate contra haeresin & haereticos, hoc enim est

— ἐπαγωνίζεσθαι. Sic Nazianzenus orat. de Macca- bæis ait : Προηγωνίζατο πατὴρ, ἐπαγωνιεῖται παῖ- δες, id est, primo certavit Pater, postea certabunt filii. Etsi autem Grotii explicationem ceu simpliciorem præferamus ; Κατ' ἄνθρωπον tamen hæc contra Cornelium ipsum urgeri possunt.

## 1:4
Ver. 4.

Παρεισέδυσαν γάρ τινες ἄνθρωποι.] They have crept in secretly. Thus παρεισῆλθον (crept in), Gal. II, ver. 4; παρεισάξουσι (will bring in secretly), 2 Pet. II, v. 1. He designates the Carpocratians, as we have said.

Οἱ πάλαι προγεγραμμένοι εἰς τῦτο τὸ κρῖμα.] The translation is taken from the fact that sentences used to be recited from a writing, Ps. 149, v. 4. And κρῖμα (judgment) here is for κατάκριμα (condemnation), for punishment. Thus you have κρῖμα in Matt. 23, v. 14; Mark 12, v. 40; Luke 20, v. 47; Rom. 5, v. 16; chap. 11, v. 33; Gal. 5, v. 10; James 3, v. 1. This punishment God decreed long ago against those who reject the Gospel, so that they bring upon themselves, through evil dogmas and wicked acts, the greatest infamy even among us Christians. See 2 Thess. I, 12, 13; 2 Tim. II, 16; 2 Pet. II, 3. But that passage 2 Pet. II seems to be especially regarded, where these very men are foreshadowed.

Chronology conflicts regarding the Carpocratians, if it is referred to the Apostle Jude, as the epistle must by all means be referred; although it is more likely that the followers of Simon, even if he was already dead, and the Nicolaitans are being looked at. That the passage 2 Pet. II, 2 is being referred to cannot be proven: and therefore it should have been taught that these things look not to divine reprobation, but to Apostolic pre-signification (which explanation is approved by Cornelius à Lapide from Dionysius). Nor were these things written long after Peter, since both St. Peter and St. Jude treat of the same heretics, not indeed as present or just now emerging; but he instructed the faithful against the same as seducers about to enter shortly. Add that St. Peter likewise speaks of the judgment already long ago decreed for them in verse 3, οἷς τὸ κρῖμα ἔκπαλαι ὐκ ἀργεῖ. Therefore, the prior interpretation of Grotius regarding the divine decree, not from an absolute good pleasure, but from the just judgment of GOD made on account of unbelief and impiety, holds itself more correctly. But the gloss of Piscator is impious, that those were destined by the eternal decree of GOD to that impiety, by which they draw upon themselves judgment or eternal damnation. For thus God is rendered the cause of that impiety, and consequently of sin. That impiety certainly did not please Tossanus, who interprets it far more correctly thus: who already long ago, that is, from eternity, were previously written in the book of GOD for that punishment, namely for eternal damnation, which they had merited by their impiety and obstinacy. Cf. B. Franzius, tract. de interpret. Script. Orac. III.
