And that the Jesuits cannot digest such things, even if they are not entirely alien to the Calvinists in the doctrine of predestination, Cornelius is an argument: He says, the impious Beza impiously thinks that they were delivered into a reprobate sense by God, without ordination to demerits. For he says, I say that nothing can be found prior to the decree of GOD in time or order, without GOD being despoiled of his divinity. Is this not a Satanic voice? Which makes a Satan out of God, that is, makes the author of evil and of a reprobate sense out of the Author of good.

Ἀσεβεῖς.] 2 Pet. II, 6. Τὴν τῦ Θεῦ ἡμῶν χάριν μετατιθέντες εἰς ἀσέλγειαν.] Simeon predicts the Ἀσελγείας of those men in ch. II, 2. 18. χάρις τῦ Θεῦ is the Gospel, under whose name they ensnared others, but in reality they transformed the Gospel into a licentious doctrine. Χάρις Θεῦ is called the Gospel by metonymy, as in Heb. XII, 5. and elsewhere.

The first thing which he censures in them is that grace, that is, not the Gospel itself (for that meaning has not yet been proven, nor does that word occur in Heb. XII, verse 5, nor from its proper meaning to Metonymically one must rashly turn aside) but those who transfer what is proposed in the Gospel, and has been done for us in Christ, John 1:17, not only practically, maliciously abusing the same, but dialectically εἰς ἀσέλγειαν into wantonness (the Apostle does not say grace transformed, but μετα[τιθέν]τες transferring, though the matter easily comes to the same thing, namely in reality the Evangelical doctrine transformed into a wanton doctrine) which deed, when they taught, that the lusts do not conflict with the grace proposed in the Gospel; but that they consist well with it; teaching that it is permitted for Christians to freely indulge in concupiscence, gluttony, and lust, as Peter 2. epist. 2, v. 9. promising them liberty, while they themselves are servants of corruption, as Cornelius à Lapide says is noted from Oecumenius regarding the Nicolaitans, Simonians, and Gnostics, who, although they were most impure, pretended that they were teachers of the pure Gospel, and under that pretext led away women burdened with sins, as he says, instituting nocturnal rites, in which they promiscuously perpetrated every obscenity: And he adds: The Gnostics were indeed so obscene that they were called Borborites, that is, filthy, because they traduced even the sacred histories and scriptures themselves by explaining them according to their own lusts, as Epiphanius narrates at length in heresy 26, Irenaeus book 1, chapter 20, and Clement VII in the Stromata. Which the most impudent Jesuit transfers by most atrocious calumny to Blessed Luther, whom almost every page in Luther's writings confounds, and convicts of diabolical accusation. But how Papists, preferring whoredoms to marriage, and adorning sodomy with praises, can be absolved from that crime, that they convert Christianity into Priapism, let the Jesuits themselves consider. Compare here what Blessed Johann Ernst Gerhard has in his epistle of Jude, page 31, concerning Johann de la Casa, not beardless then, as Harding excused, but Archbishop and Apostolic Legate, when he praised sodomy in verse. Concerning Sixtus IV, it is established that for three summer months he gave his household members permission to practice the sodomitical abomination, etc. Concerning Simon, the patriarch of heretics, Blessed Augustine says in On Heresies, chapter 1: He taught, he says, the detestable filthiness of using women indiscriminately. He offered to his disciples a certain harlot, Selene, whom he had made his companion in crimes, and images of both himself and the same harlot to be adored, which he had also established at Rome by public authority as if they were statues of the gods. Tertullian, book on the soul, chapter 34, concerning the same: He redeemed a certain Tyrian Helena from a place of public lust with money, a reward worthy of himself for the Holy Spirit. To which belongs their dogma, that the soul is not polluted by vices, but only the flesh. Whence the Simonians did not condemn the wicked life of their own, just as neither did the Gnostic heretics, as noted by L. Danaeus on the cited book of Augustine. From which impious school proceeded Menander, who embraced the promiscuous intercourse of women, and felt that all mere filthiness, as a fruit of the grace of God toward men, and finally that good and holy morals, which are commanded by the law of God, should be abolished and antiquated through the preaching of the grace of God as now useless and a vain endeavor, and the Saturnians, from a certain Saturninus, who is reported by Augustine to be the witness who confirmed the Simonian filthiness in Syria. Furthermore, the Nicolaitans, by the seducer Nicolaus, who is said to have permitted the free use of his wife to anyone, asserted the indifferent use of women, with the deed of the teacher turned into a most filthy sect, as Augustine has in chapter V, concerning whom Revelation 2:6. And concerning their most filthy obscenities, Tertullian in the book On Prescription. Καὶ τὸν μόνον Θεὸν καὶ Δεσπότην τὸν Κύριον ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦν χριστὸν ἀρνύμενοι) In the Manuscript: Καὶ τὸν μόνον Δεσπότην καὶ Κύριον ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦν χριστὸν ἀρνύμενοι. The name Δεσπότης is given to Christ also in 2 Peter 2:18, where the same men are discussed. They denied Jesus, because they said he was a man born of a man, and many of their own were his equals. Therefore they did not acknowledge him as their redeemer and through that as Master and Lord.

This other impious dogma was, which St. Jude notes here in the heretics of his time, the denial of the Deity of Christ. But they are said not only not to have acknowledged him as their Redeemer, and through that as Master and Lord, because they said he was a man born of a man, and many of their own were his equals: But their heresy consisted in this, that they denied our Lord JESUS Christ to be τὸν μόνον Θεὸν καὶ Δεσπότην, and thus they denied, just as Peter also speaks of the same, τὸν ἀγοράσαντα αὐτὲς Δεσπότην, 2. epist. 2, 1. and that that Master is called κατ' ἐξοχὴν & ἀντονομαστικῶς, namely ὁ μόνος Θεὸς, that one GOD, and that he redeemed them with the price of his blood.

We seek the argument for the Deity of CHRIST from here against the Socinians: He who is that only Master GOD and our Lord, he is that one true GOD. But Christ, as the Apostle testifies, is that only Master GOD and our Lord. Therefore. The major premise shines with its own light, and is conceded by the Socinians themselves, that τὸν μόνον Δεσπότην is no one else than that one true God.

The minor premise is evident from the words themselves, which flow in such a way that it clearly appears that the discourse is about one and the same subject, or that he is the same τὸν μόνον Δεσπότην Θεὸν καὶ Κύριον ἡμῶν, namely JESUS Christ himself, for where the text does not distinguish, it is not for us to distinguish. The article would have been correctly repeated again, if one were that Master God, and another our Lord Jesus Christ, especially since the adversaries confess that the name Κυρίς is used with the article where it is attributed to Christ. Now, since those names are comprehended under one article, and it refers itself to all, is it not sufficiently manifest that they all pertain to describing one and the same subject? Which argument the adversaries cannot refute, since they themselves use the same. Enjedinus in 1 Thess. 3:11, p. 365. This very thing, he says, is confirmed by the fact that a single article is placed before both nouns in Greek, which signifies that both are to be understood as referring to the same person. Furthermore, 2. that those whom St. Jude notes did not deny the supreme God, but denied that Jesus Christ is that one Lord God and our Lord. For they are not read to have entered into the Church of Christ at that time who denied the supreme God, but those who denied that Christ is that one Lord God and our Lord; many false teachers have existed from that age, in whose footsteps the Neo-Photinians and Nestorians now follow: such were the Menandrians, Ebionites, and Cerinthians.

Oecumenius wishes the Nicolaitans and Simonians to be noted here. But they did not deny the supreme Lord, but denied that Christ is God. Concerning which Cornelius à Lapide says: The Nicolaitans, against whom St. Jude writes, denied that Christ is God, for they claimed that God only dwelt in Christ, as Ignatius reports in epistle 9 and Irenaeus in book 3, chapter 11. Concerning Simon and other heretics of his time, St. Ignatius writes thus to the Trallians on page 69: They name Christ, not that they may preach Christ, but that they may spurn Christ,

and they bring forth the law, not that they may establish the law, but that they may announce things contrary to the law, for they alienate Christ from the Father. They reject the law of Christ and his birth from a Virgin, blushing at the cross and denying the passion, and not believing in the resurrection. They profess an unknown God, they think Christ is unbegotten, and they do not confess that the Holy Spirit is. Some of them say that the Son is a mere man, but others say that he himself is the Father, he himself the Son, and he himself the Holy Spirit, and they say that the creature is not the work of God through Christ, but of some other strange power. Beware therefore of such, lest you take snares for your souls. And p. 77. Flee those heresies without God, for they are the invention of the Devil, of the serpent the author of evils, who through the woman seduced Adam, the father of our race. But flee also his evil offspring, I mean Simon the firstborn of his race, and Menander and Basilides, and the whole collection of his malignity, and those worshippers of man the Ebionites, whom the Prophet Jeremiah asserted to be cursed. 3. A parallel passage confirms this opinion, 2 Pet. 2:1, where it likewise treats of those false Teachers who deny τὸν ἀγοράσαντα αὐτὸς Δεσπότην that Master who bought them, who is none other than our God Jesus Christ, whence deservedly Didymus, Oecumenius, Beda, Lyranus, Hugo, and other doctors of the Church have interpreted the present passage concerning Christ, which opinion the Arabic translation also approves, explaining the one Lord as concerning Christ; as also the Syriac: Denying him who is the only Lord our God Jesus Christ, as also the Ethiopic, likewise omitting the copulative particle: And denies that only Lord Jesus Christ. We add 4. that Jesus in the refutation of this heresy subjoined is said to be ὁ κύριος λαὸν ἐκ γῆς Αἰγύπτω σώσας v. 5. concerning which later; and 5. that in the doxological conclusion our Savior is celebrated as the only wise God.

Enjedinus objects in his explanation of the passage, p. 433. 1. that this passage proves nothing solidly because of the ambiguous reading, and that the reading of the old Interpreter is confirmed from five other passages of Scripture, in which Christ is called the one and only Lord, 2 Cor. 8:16. 2. That the copula inserted between God and Lord signifies that two Lords are being treated here. 3. Socinus in Antiw. p. 379. (whom Crellius follows in De Deo & attr. divin. p. 104, Volckelius l. V. de V. R. c. 10. p. 422.) urges that it would be no light inconsistency, nay an absurdity of speech, to call Jesus Christ first the only Master GOD, and afterwards our Lord, as if distinguishing him by a different appellation. Because it is more to be the only Master GOD than our Lord, and all of this is openly contained in that. But to our argument from the unity of the article, Enjedinus, Socinus, and the rest reply that that rule is not perpetual, that one article placed before in Greek implies a single subject.

Response to 1. All the different readings that have been observed serve to confirm our faith. The Complutensian edition certainly, which has τὸν μόνον Θεὸν καὶ δεσπότην τὸν Κύριον Ἰησοῦν Χριστὸν, confirms even better that all these things are said of Christ, as Beza had rightly noted, whom Enjedinus in vain accuses of contradiction, because he previously proved from there that all these things are said of Christ, because one article is placed before all, now on the contrary from the fact that there are several articles, he gathers the same. For the different position of the articles must be attended to. Now since the other article is not placed immediately after the copulative καὶ in this Complutensian edition, but is prefixed to the word κύριος, who not entirely unskilled in Greek letters does not see that it is better confirmed from this that the preceding τὸν μόνον Θεὸν, καὶ δεσπότην are said of that Lord Jesus Christ? Add that the adversaries do not deny that the name δεσπότης in the singular number in the N.T. is proper to the one supreme God, and they wish that to cohere with the word τὸν μόνον Θεὸν; and to express one subject. Now indeed who that δεσπότης is, that edition explicitly explains, while it immediately adds τὸν Κύριον Ἰησοῦν Χριστὸν, where certainly it cannot be denied that JESUS Christ has been called δεσπότην. Besides this reading, the Vulgate Latin exhibits another, omitting the name of GOD, (which Beza found to have been missing in two Greek Codices also) in this manner, and the only Master and our Lord JESUS Christ: from which reading, even if it cannot be proved that Christ is called GOD, it is nevertheless rightly concluded that the same is pointed out as the only Master, because of the arguments adduced: Which name likewise does not befit anyone except the one GOD, who is the only Master and Ruler. Conf. Theol. natur. & revel. p. 511. But the reading of the Greek Codices is altogether to be preferred to the reading of the Latin edition, since the former is found in most all, and those the most approved, Codices.

To 2. Response. No one is ignorant that the argument from the copula is very frivolous, which is very often taken exegetically. And how often is mention made of GOD and the Father in the N.T. But will the adversaries admit that two are being treated, because of the interpolated copula, because it is said Θεὸς καὶ Πατὴρ, GOD and Father.

To 3. Response. There is no incongruity, let alone absurdity of speech, in the first name being used as the sole Ruler God, and then the name our Lord being applied to the same. Certainly no greater than when in the O.T. the same God is called first יהוה, and afterwards אלהים GOD. For the name יהוה is far more august and eminent than the name אלהים and includes it. But what is more frequent than for GOD to be pointed out as our God Jehovah? And what is that absurdity, when first that Master, or that sole Ruler is named, and afterwards our Lord is added, so that we may profess with true faith that He who is the Ruler of all things is also our Lord. We have said more about this in Theol. nat. & rev. p. 514.

To 4. Response. Even if it be admitted that a single article also occurs somewhere only where the discourse is about two different subjects, nevertheless ordinarily a single article implies a single subject. Which Enjedinus himself confessed above. But there is no reason why we should depart from this ordinary usage here. Nay, rather other arguments confirm the same, and teach that all these names comprised under one article are here assigned to CHRIST. Compare, however, with this passage what has been said regarding the parallel in Peter.

Nor indeed is it to be judged here with Piscator, as if the heretics noted by St. Jude only denied JESUS their Master by their base life: just as Oecumenius: In what way, he says, do they not deny Christ, who by an impure and unclean life, as if by a clamorous proclamation, renounce and alienate the Master of all temperance. For concerning Jesus not as Master and Teacher, but as God, as Master, and as Sovereign, having been denied, St. Jude speaks clearly, and indeed as the only God: where Bede rightly says: Whatever person you name in the same holy and undivided Trinity, he is the only God, and when you name the whole Trinity at once, you name the only true God.

Latin:

Verf. 4.

Παρεισέδυσαν γάρ τινες ἄνθρωποι.] Latenter irrepsere. Sic παρεισῆλθον, Gal. II. verf. 4. παρεισάξουσι 2. Petr. II. v. 1. Carpocratianos, ut diximus, designat.

Οἱ πάλαι προγεγραμμένοι εἰς τῦτο τὸ κρῖμα.] Translatio inde sumpta, quod sententiæ ex scripto recitari solebant, Psal. 149. v. 4. Et κρῖμα hic est pro κατάκριμα pro pœna. Sic κρῖμα habes Matth. 23. v. 14. Marci 12. v. 40. Luc. 20. v. 47. Rom. 5. v. 16. cap. 11. v. 33. Galat. 5. v. 10. Jacob. 3. v. 1. Hanc pœnam Deus pridem decrevit in eos, qui Evangelium rejici- unt, ut sibiipsis per mala dogmata & flagitiosos actus sum- mam accersant etiam apud nos Christianos infamiam. Vide 2. Thessal. I, 12. 13. 2. Tim. II, 16. 2. Petr. II, 3. Sed præci- pue respici videtur locus ille 2. Petr. II. ubi hi ipsi homines præsignificantur.

De Carpocratianis repugnat Chronologia, si ad Judam Apostolum referatur, uti referenda omni- no est epistola, Simonis etsi jam mortui sectato- res, & Nicolaitas spectari potius verisimile est. Locum 2. Petr. II, 2. respici, probari non potest: ideoque non ad reprobationem divinam, sed ad præsignificationem Apostolicam, (quæ explica- tio Cornelio à Lapide è Dionysio probatur) hæc spectare docendum erat. Neque longo post Pe- trum tempore hæc scripta esse, quum de iisdem hæreticis, uterque agat & S. Petrus & S. Judas, non quidem ceu præsentibus, vel jamjam emer- gentibus; sed adversus eosdem ceu seductores propediem subingressuros, fideles instruxerit. Adde quod S. Petrus itidem de judicio jam olim iisdem decreto loquatur vers. 3. οἷς τὸ κρῖμα ἔκ- παλαι ὐκ ἀργεῖ. Rectius itaque se habet prior Grotii interpretatio de decreto divino non ex ab- soluto beneplacito, sed justo DEI judicio ob in- credulitatem & impietatem facto. Impia autem est Piscatoris glossa, illos æterno DEI decreto de- stinatos esse ad istam impietatem, qua sibi judici- um seu damnationem æternam attrahunt. Ita enim Deus redditur causa istius impietatis, adeo- que peccati. Non sane placuit illa impietas Tos- sano, qui longe rectius ita interpretatur, qui jam olim, id est, ab æterno sunt prius conscripti in li- bro DEI ad illam pœnam, videlicet ad æternam damnationem, quam impietate & pertinacia sua fuerunt promeriti. Conf. B. Franzius tract. de interpret. Script. Orac. III. Nec concoquere ta- lia posse Jesuitas, etsi in doctrina de prædestina- tione à Calvinianis non omnino alienos, Corne- lius argumento sit: Impie, inquit, impius Beza censet, eos traditos in reprobum sensum à Deo, sine ordinatione ad demerita. Nam DEI decreto, in- quit, nihil vel tempore vel ordine prius inveniri posse, dico, quin DEUS divinitate spolietur. An- non Satanica hæc vox? Quæ ex Deo facit satanam, puta ex Autore boni facit autorem mali & reprobi sensus.

Ἀσεβεῖς.] 2. Petr. II, 6. Τὴν τῦ Θεῦ ἡμῶν χάριν μετατιθέντες εἰς ἀσέλγειαν.] Ἀ- σελγείας illorum hominum prædicit Simeon c. II, 2. 18. χάρις τῦ Θεῦ est Evangelium, sub cujus nomine illi alios inesca- bant, sed revera Evangelium transformabant in doctrinam libidinosam. Χάρις Θεῦ per Metonymiam Evangelium dici- tur, ut Ebr. XII, 5. & alibi.

Primum, quod in ipsis taxat, est, quod gratiam hoc est, non ipsum Evangelium, (illa enim signi- ficatio nondum probata est, nec Ebr. XII. vers. 5. vox illa occurrit, neque à propria significatione ad Metonymicam temere deflectendum est) sed quæ in Evangelio proposita, nobisque in Christo fa- cta est, Joh. I. 17. transferant, non tantum practice, malitiose eadem abutendo, sed dialectice εἰς ἀσέλ- γειαν in libidinem (non dicit Apostolus gratiam transformatam, sed μετα[τιθέν]τες tranferentes, res vero facile eodem redit, nimirum revera Evan- gelicam doctrinam transformatam in doctrinam li- bidinosam) quod factum, quando docuere, gratiæ in Evangelio propositæ non repugnare libidines; sed cum illa probe consistere; docentes Christianis lice- re libere indulgere concupiscentiæ, gulæ, & veneri, uti Petrus 2. epist. 2, v. 9. libertatem illis promit- tentes, quum ipsi sint servi corruptionis, uti Cornelius à Lapide ex Oecumenio notari inquit Nicolaitas, Simonianos, Gnosticos, qui cum es- sent impurissimi, simulabant se puri Evangelii esse Doctores, eoque prætextu mulierculas onu- stas peccatis, ut ait, abducebant, instituen- tes nocturna sacra, in quibus omnem obscœni- tatem promiscue perpetrabant: Additque: Adeo vero obscœni erant Gnostici, ut dicti sint Borbo- ritæ, id est, cœnosi, quia ipsas etiam sacras hi- storias & scripturas ad suas libidines explicando traducebant, uti fuse narrat Epiphanius hær. 26. Irenæus l. 1. c. 20. Clemens VII. Strom. Quæ per atrocissimam calumniam ad B. Lutherum trans- fert impudentissimus Jesuita, quem omnes fere in Lutheri scriptis pagellæ confundunt, & Diaboli- cæ criminationis convincunt. Quomodo au- tem Papistæ scortationes conjugio præferentes, & Sodomiam laudibus ornantes ab isto crimine, quod Christianismum convertant in Priapismum absol- vi possunt, ipsimet Jesuitæ dispiciant. Conf. hic quæ B. Johann. Ernestus Gerhardus in epist. Judæ pag. 31. habet de Johann. de la Casa, non imberbi tum, ut Hardingus excusavit, sed Archi- Episcopo, & Legato Apostolico, cum Sodomiam carmine laudaret. De Sixto IV. constat, quod tribus mensibus æstivis flagitium Sodomiticum ex- ercendi familiaribus suis facultatem dederit &c. De Simone Patriarcha hæreticorum B. Augustinus de hæresib. c. 1. Docebat, inquit, detestandam tur- pitudinem indifferenter utendi fœminis. Miner- vam mero meretricem quandam Selenem, quam sibi sociam scelerum fecerat, imaginesque & suam & ejusdem meretricis discipulis suis præbebat ado- randam, quas & Romæ tanquam simulachra Deorum autoritate publica constituerat. Tertul- lianus l. de anima c. 34. de eodem: Helenam quandam Tyriam de loco libidinis publicæ pecunia redemit dignam sibi mercedem pro Spiritu Sancto. Quo facit dogma eorum, quod anima non pol- luatur vitiis, sed tantum caro. Unde scelera- tam suorum vitam non damnarunt Simoniani, uti nec Gnostici hæretici notante L. Danæo ad l. cit. August. Ex qua impia schola prodiere Menander, qui concubitum mulierum promiscu- um amplexus, omnemque meram turpitudinem tanquam gratiæ DEI erga homines fructum, bonos denique & sanctos mores, qui lege DEI jubentur, per gratiæ DEI prædicationem, ut jam inutiles, & vanum studium tolli & antiquari sensit, & Saturniani, à quodam Saturnino, qui turpitudi- nem Simonianam in Syria confirmasse perhibetur, Augustino teste. Porro Nicolaitæ seductore Ni- colao, qui conjugis suæ liberum usum quibus- libet permisisse fertur, indifferentem usum fœmina- rum asserebant, facto Præceptoris in sectam turpissimam verso, ut habet Augustinus c. V. de quibus Apocal. 2, 6. Et de obscœnitatibus eo- rum turpissimis Tertullianus libr. de Præscri- ption. Καὶ τὸν μόνον Θεὸν καὶ Δεσπότην τὸν Κύριον ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦν χρι- στὸν ἀρνύμενοι) In Manuscripto: Καὶ τὸν μόνον Δεσπότην καὶ Κύριον ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦν χριστὸν ἀρνύμενοι. Datur Christo no- men Δεσπότης etiam 2. Petr. 2, 18. ubi de iisdem homini- bus agitur. Abnegabant Jesum, quia eum dicebant homi- nem natum ex homine, & multos suorum ipsi pares. Non ergo eum pro suo redemptore & per id Hero ac Domino agno- scebant.

Alterum hoc dogma impium erat, quod in hæreticis sui temporis hic notat S. Judas, ab- negatio Deitatis Christi. Non autem tantum non agnovisse dicuntur eum pro suo Redem- ptore, & per id Hero ac Domino, quia di- xerint hominem natum ex homine, & mul- tos suorum ipsi pares: Sed hæresis eorum in eo consistebat, quod negarint Dominum nostrum JESUM Christum esse τὸν μόνον Θεὸν καὶ Δεσπό- την, adeoque inficiati sint, uti & Petrus de iisdem loquitur, τὸν ἀγοράσαντα αὐτὲς Δεσπότην, 2. epistol. 2, 1. & quod Herus ille sit κατ' ἐξοχὴν & ἀντονομαστικῶς dictus, nempe ὁ μόνος Θεὸς, unus ille DEUS, & quod redemerit eos pretio sanguinis sui.

Argumentum hinc petimus Dei- tatis CHRISTI contra Socinianos: Qui est ille solus Herus DEUS & Dominus noster, il- le est unus ille verus DEUS. At Christus te- ste Apostolo est ille solus Herus DEUS & Do- minus noster. Ergo. Major sua luce radiat, & conceditur ab ipsis Socinianis, τὸν μόνον Δεσπότην nullum alium esse, quam unum illum verum Deum.

Minor patet ex ipsis verbis, quæ ita fluunt, ut luculenter appareat, de uno eodemque sub- jecto sermonem esse, vel eundem esse τὸν μό- νον Δεσπότην Θεὸν καὶ Κύριον ἡμῶν, nimirum ipsum JESUM Christum, ubi enim textus non distin- guit, nostrum non est distinguere. Articulus recte repetitus fuisset denuo, si alius foret unus ille Herus Deus, alius Dominus noster Jesus Chri- stus, præsertim cum fateantur adversarii, nomen Κυρίς cum articulo adhiberi, ubi Christo tribui- tur. Nunc cum sub uno articulo comprehen- dantur illa nomina, isque ad omnia sese refe- rat, annon satis manifestum est ea omnia ad unum idemque subjectum describendum pertinere? Quod argumentum reprobare non possunt Ad- versarii, quum ipsimet eodem utantur. Enjedi- nus in 1. Thess. 3, 11. p. 365. Hoc ipsum, inquit, con- firmatur ex eo, quod utrique voci unicus tantum in Græco præpositus est Articulus, quod significat de eodem utramque esse accipiendam. Accedit 2. quod illi, quos notat D. Judas, non negarint Deum summum, sed negarint, Jesum Christum esse unum illum Herum Deum & Dominum nostrum. Non enim leguntur introiisse tum temporis in Eccle- siam Christi, qui negarint summum Deum, sed qui Christum negarint unum illum Herum Deum esse, & Dominum nostrum, plurimi inde ab ista ætate extitere falsi Doctores, quorum jam insistunt ve- stigiis Neo-Photiniani, & Nestoriani: quales fue- re Menandriani, Ebionitæ, Cerinthiani.

Oecumenius vult, Nicolaitas, ac Simonianos hic notari. At illi non negarunt summum Domi- num, sed negarunt, Christum esse Deum. Quo de Cornelius à Lapide: Nicolaitæ, contra quos scri- bit S. Judas, negabant Christum esse Deum, aje- bant enim Deum in Christo tantum habitasse, uti re- fert Ignatius epistola 9. & Irenæus l. 3. c. 11. De Simo- ne aliisque sui temporis hæreticis. S. Ignatius ad Trallian. ita scribit p. 69. Nominant Christum, non ut Christum prædicent, sed ut Christum spernant,

& legem proserunt, non ut legem statuant, sed ut con- traria legi annuncient, Christum enim alienant à Pa- tre. Legem vero Christi & nativitatem ex Virgine abjiciunt, crucem erubescentes & passionem negan- tes, & resurrectioni non credentes. Deum inco- gnitum profitentur, Christum ingenitum putant, & neque quia est Spiritus Sanctus confitentur. Quidam vero eorum Filium hominem purum esse dicunt, alii autem ipsum dicunt esse Patrem, ipsum Filium, ipsumque Spiritum Sanctum, & creaturam non ope- ra Dei esse per Christum dicunt, sed alterius cujus- dam extraneæ virtutis. Cavete ergo à talibus ne su- matis laqueos animabus vestris. Et p. 77. Fugite il- las sine Deo hæreses, Diaboli enim sunt adinventio, serpentis autoris malorum, qui per mulierem sedu- xit Adam, patrem generis nostri. Fugite vero & malas soboles ejus, Simonem dico primogenitum ge- neris ejus, & Menandrum & Basilidem, & totam collectionem malignitatis ipsius, & illos hominis cul- tores Ebionita, quos maledictos esse Ieremias Pro- pheta asseruit. 3. Confirmat hanc sententiam locus parallelus 2. petr. II. 1. ubi itidem de illis falsis Do- ctoribus agitur, qui negant τὸν ἀγοράσαντα αὐτὸς Δεσπότην Herum illum, qui redemit eos, qui nul- lus est alius, quam Deus noster Jesus Christus, unde merito Didymus, Oecumenius, Beda, Lyra- nus, Hugo, aliique Ecclesiæ doctores præsentem locum de Christo interpretati sunt, quam senten- tiam comprobat quoque Arabica translatio, uni- cum Dominum de Christo explicans; nec non Sy- riaca: Eum negans, qui est solus Dominus Deus no- ster Jesus Christus, ut & Æthiopica, particulam co- pulativam itidem omittens: Et negat illum solum Dominum Iesum Christum. Addimus 4. quod Je- sus in confutatione hærefeos istius subjuncta dica- tur ὁ κύριος λαὸν ἐκ γῆς Αἰγύπτω σώσας v. 5. quo de postea; quodq; 5. in conclusione δοξολογικῇ Sal- vator noster celebretur, ut solus sapiens Deus.

Excipit Enjedinus in explic. Loc. p. 433. 1. lo- cum hunc propter ambiguam lectionem nihil solide probare, & veteris Interpretis lectionem confir- mari ex aliis quinque Scripturæ locis, in quibus Christus unus & solus Dominus vocatur 2. Cor. 8, 16. 2. Copulam interjectam inter Deum & Do- minum significare de duobus Dominis hic agi. 3. Socinus in Antiw. p. 379. (quem sequitur Crellius de Deo & attr. divin. pag. 104. Volckelius l. V. de. V. R. c. 10. p. 422.) urget haud levem fore incon- cinnitatem, imo sermonis absurditatem, prius ap- pellare Jesum Christum solum herum DEUM, & postea Domini nostri, tanquam diversa appella- tione eum insignire. Quia plus sit esse solum herum DEUM, quam Dominum nostrum, totumque hoc illo aperte continetur. 4. Ad argumentum vero nostrum ab unitate articuli regerunt Enjedi- nus, Socinus & reliqui, regulam eam non esse per petuam, quod unus articulus præpositus in Græco inferat unicum subjectum.

Respond. ad 1. Omnes quæ observatæ sunt diversæ lectiones, fidei nostræ confirmandæ inserviunt. Complutensis certe editio, quæ ha- bet τὸν μόνον Θεὸν καὶ δεσπότην τὸν Κύριον Ἰησοῦν Χριστὸν, mejius etiam confirmat hæc omnia de Christo dici, ut recte notarat Beza, quem frustra Enjedinus contradictionis postulat, quod ante inde probarit, hæc omnia de Christo dici, quod unus sit omnibus præpositus articulus, nunc contra ex eo, quod plures sunt articuli, idem colligit. Di- versus enim positus articulorum attendendus venit. Jam cum articulus alter non post copu- lativum καὶ immediate ponatur in hac editione Complutensi, sed voci κύριος præfigatur, quis Græcarum literarum non plane imperitus non videt melius hinc confirmari, quod de illo Do- mino Jesu Christo dicantur præcedentia τὸν μό- νον Θεὸν, καὶ δεσπότην? Adde quod non diffitean- tur adversarii, nomen δεσπότης in singulari nume- ro in N. T. uni summo Deo proprium, adhiberi, idque cohærere velint cum voce τὸν μόνον Θεὸν; unumque subjectum exprimere. Jam vero quisnam δεσπότης ille sit, diserte ista editio ex- plicat, dum immediate addit τὸν Κύριον Ἰησοῦν Χριστὸν, ubi certe negari non potest δεσπότην nuncupatum esse JESUM Christum. Præter hanc lectionem aliam exhibet vulgata Latina, omittens nomen DEI, (quod in duobus eti- am Græcis Codd. defuisse comperit Beza) hoc pacto, & solum Dominatorem & Dominum nostrum JESUM Christum: è qua lectione etsi Christum DEUM dictum esse probari nequeat, eundem tamen solum Dominatorem indigitatum esse recte concluditur, ob argu- menta adducta: Quod nomen itidem non con- venit nisi uni DEO, qui est solus herus & Do- minator. Conf. Theol. natur. & revel. pag. 511. Præferenda autem omnino lectio vulgata Græcorum Codd. lectioni Latinæ editionis, quum illa in plerisque omnibus, iisque proba- tissimis Codd. reperiatur.

Ad 2. Resp. Perquam frivolum esse argu- mentum à copula, quam sæpissime ἐξηγητικῶς accipi, nemo nescit. Et quoties DEI & Pa- tris mentio fit in N. T. Num vero de duobus agi admittent adversarii, ob copulam interpo- sitam, quia dicitur Θεὸς καὶ Πατὴρ, DEUS & Pater.

Ad 3. Resp. Nulla est inconcinnitas, ne- dum absurditas sermonis, primum nomen solus Dominator Deus, deinde nomen Dominus no- ster adhiberi de eodem. Non major certe, quam cum in V. T. idem Deus dicitur primum יהוה, ac postmodum אלהים DEUS. Nam & nomen יהוה longè augustius & eminemtius est nomine אלהים idque complectitur. Quid autem fre- quentius, quam DEUM indigitari Deum Iehovam nostrum? Et quænam illa absurditas, cum primum ille Herus, vel Dominator ille uni- cus nominatur, postmodum additur Dominus noster, ut qui rerum omnium Dominator est, eundem etiam Dominum nostrum vera fide pro- siteamur. Plura de eo diximus Theol. nat. & rev. p. 514.

Ad 4. Resp. Etiamsi admittatur, unum arti- culum etiam alicubi tantum occurrere, ubi de duobus diversis subjectis sermo est, ordinarie tamen unicus articulus innuit unicum subje- ctum. Quod ipse Enjedinus fassus est supra. Non est autem cur ab hoc ordinario usu hic re- cedamus. Quin argumenta potius alia confir- mant eundem, docentque omnia hæc nomina sub uno articulo comprehensa CHRISTO hic assignari. Confer autem cum hoc loco, quæ ad parallelum Petrinum dicta.

Nec vero hic cum Piscatore censendum, qua- si hæretici á S. Juda notati tantum vita sua tur- pi abnegarint JESUM Herum suum: quem- admodum Oecumenius: Quo pacto, ait, Chri- stum non negant, qui impura & immunda vita quasi clamoso præconio totius temperantiæ Magi- strum abdicant & alienant. Nam de Jesu non ut- Magistro & Doctore, sed ut Deo, ut Hero, & Dominatore abnegato diferte loquitur S. Judas, & quidem ut solo Deo: ubi recte Beda: Quam- cunque in eadem sancta & indivisa Trinitate per- sonam nomines, solus Deus est, & cum simul to- tam Trinitatem nominas, solum verum Deum no- minas.

## 1:5
Ver. 5. I wish to remind you, though you know this once for all] In the Manuscript: I wish to remind you also, knowing all things once for all. Just as the Latin also reads. When he says all things, he understands all things narrated in the Old Testament. Since those Jews had learned them from their earliest age, they needed only a brief indication to be reminded of them. Thus 2 Pet. 1:12. I will not be negligent to remind you always of these things, though you know them.

That the Lord, having saved the people out of the land of Egypt, afterward destroyed those who did not believe] The Lord here, as in matters of the Old Testament, is YHWH, which the Greeks translate as Lord, because it was read as Adonai. For what is JESUS here in the Latin comes from an abbreviation in Greek books, in which it was written IS for IESUS. Moreover, afterward here has the force of, on the contrary, just as again is taken in Matt. 4:1 and Jas. 5:18. He destroyed them, namely, by serpents, by diseases, by the Angel, by the hands of the Levites. See 1 Cor. 10:6, 8, 9, and 10. Heb. 2:2. He says did not believe instead of were disobedient, because those who do not obey show that they do not believe, or do not believe as they ought. Thus Heb. 4:2, the word is said not to have been mixed with faith in those who heard it.

The treatment follows the proposition, in which he first recalls to the memory of the faithful the example of the Israelites, then of the fallen Angels, and finally of the Sodomites. The Israelites both sinned often, and especially after they were saved out of Egypt, and perished through unbelief, whose example he brings forward in the first place, because he had just noted the heretics for their denial of JESUS Christ as Hero and our GOD, and had judged it necessary that the faithful be warned against their seduction. For the same Lord had saved the Israelites out of Egypt, namely the Son of God, who appeared first to Moses in the burning bush, then to the Israelites in the pillar of cloud and fire at the Red Sea, as is evident from Exod. ch. 3 and ch. 14. That Angel, in whom is the name of the Lord, ch. 23:20, whose voice they were to observe, and in whom they were to place their trust. But they, not believing, brought destruction upon themselves through that unbelief of theirs, as the Apostle teaches in Heb. 4:2. It is clear therefore that Christ is designated here: (1.) Because the name Lord with the article is accustomed to denote Christ in the New Testament, and according to Socinus's rule in Anti-Wujek, p. 368, when it is placed subjectively, it is to be understood of Christ. (2.) The discourse is about that Lord whom the heretics are said to have denied. But that was our Lord JESUS Christ: Which argument is the more compelling because the Apostle intends to exhort them to constancy of faith in the Lord Christ, lest, seduced by heretics, they deny the same and perish with the Israelites through unbelief. For the argument ought to correspond to the proposition. (3.) That Lord is therefore said to have saved the Jewish people out of Egypt, from whom the Jews converted to the Christian faith are warned not to fall away through unbelief. But they are warned not to fall away from JESUS the Lord, lest they perish like the Israelites. Therefore it is not the disobedience of the Israelites that is noted, but their unbelief, just as in Heb. 4, ver. 2, they are said to be excluded from the rest because the word was not mixed with the faith of those who heard it. (4.) We have demonstrated that this Lord led or saved the Israelites out of Egypt from Is. 64, ver. 9, in our Apodixis on the pre-existence of the Son of God, book 1, ch. 13. (5.) Which is likewise evident from Moses, if the passages of Exodus ch. 3, ch. 14, ch. 23, and what we have said regarding them are compared. (6.) He

was their Savior out of Egypt, whom they tempted in the desert. But they are said to have tempted Christ in the desert, 1 Cor. 10:13, concerning which we treated in the aforementioned chapter 7. (7.) He is understood by the Lord the Savior of the people out of Egypt, to whom as Lord the work of salvation belongs. But that belongs to Christ, indeed there is no salvation outside of him, Acts 4:12. Add (8) That some Greek Codices have the word JESUS here, and all Latin Codices read the same consistently. The things that Grotius brings forward concerning the different reading rely on mere conjectures, and I confess I do not understand what the fact that IS was written for IESUS has to do with this. (9.) That the Ancients interpret this passage concerning the Lord JESUS. (10.) That there is one Lord, as in the Old, so in the New Testament, nor does the diversity of times in that part effect anything, Deut. 6:4, Mark 12:29. By these things, therefore, as Estius rightly says, the heresy of the Ebionites and Photinians is destroyed, who deny that Christ existed before Mary: And of the Arians, who took away true Deity from Christ. For that Angel bore the tetragrammaton name of the Lord, Exod. ch. 3, ch. 20, and elsewhere. But how these things can be consistent with the fact that Estius says this Angel bore the person of the Lord, I do not see. For if this Angel only bore the person of the Lord, he certainly was not Jehovah himself. That once for all, about which Heinsius says nothing sound, B. Glassius in his Sacred Grammar, p. 412, explains thus: Although I know that you hold these things as known, yet once more, while I am in this tabernacle, I will remind you of it. Cornelius à Lapide: as if to say, I do not wish to teach you, because you have already learned and know those things, but only to suggest them, and as a monitor to recall them to memory. He says this for the sake of modesty, so that he may not seem to accuse them of ignorance, but rather to praise them for their knowledge. Thus St. John says in his 1st Epistle, chapter 2, verse 21: I have not written to you as to those who are ignorant of the truth, but as to those who know it, as if to say: I am persuaded that you know these things which I write, whence I do not teach them, but refresh and confirm them, so that those things which you have well begun to believe, you may perfect better by persevering. Who, however, for the sake of the Vulgate, also brings forward another interpretation: More congruously, he says, you may refer the word semel by a Hebrew transposition to the word salvans, for it is opposed to the word secundo, which follows, so that the sentence is to be arranged thus: Knowing that JESUS, having once saved the people from the land of Egypt, secondly destroyed those who did not believe, and thus some Greek codices read: for then the sense is plain, connected, and vigorous. The Syriac version follows, which translates: That God according to one time delivered the people from Egypt, and the Arabic: That JESUS in the first turn or firstly delivered his people from Egypt. But because those codices are few, he adds: Thirdly and most plainly, knowing once, that is, altogether and entirely all things, so that it is not necessary for me to teach them again, and for you to hear and learn them again. Thus Cicero in his speech for Dejotarus: When, he says, you are easily entreated, Caesar, you are also accustomed to be entreated once, once, that is, altogether and entirely, so that it is not necessary to entreat you further. Again, once, that is, in sum or in summary, as if to say, knowing once, that is, all things in summary. Thus Quintilian, book 11, chapter 1: And that I may embrace all things once, and book 10, chapter 3: Finally, that I may say once what is most powerful, privacy in dictating is lost, that is, that I may say it in summary. The reason for this phrase is that very word once, which signifies at one time for all, so that afterwards it is not necessary for anything to be added. Finally, once, that is, irrevocably, as if he were saying, knowing all things once, that is, fully, firmly, and irrevocably, so that you cannot forget them. Blessed Gerhard agrees with this latter explanation: Ἅπαξ once is certainly and immutably, you know this, that the Lord, after He had liberated the people from Egypt, nonetheless afterwards destroyed the unbelievers, Num. 14, 29.37. ch. 26, 64. Heb. 3, 17. ch. 4, 2. We prefer, however, the middle interpretation because of the word τὸ δεύτερον.

Latin:

Vers. 5. Ὑπομνῆσαι δὲ ὑμᾶς βύλομαι εἰδότας ὑμᾶς ἅπαξ τῦτο] In Manuscripto: ὑπομνῆσαι καὶ ὑμᾶς βύλομαι εἰδό- τας ἅπαξ πάντα. Quomodo & Latinus legit. Omnia cum dicit intelligit omnia narrata in Vetere Testamento. Ea cum semel illi Judæi gente à prima ætate didicissent, brevi tantum indicio opus habebant, ut eorum reminiscerentur. Sic 2. Petr. 1, 12. Οὐκ ἀμελήσω ἀεὶ ὑμᾶς ὑπομιμνήσκειν περὶ τύτων καίπερ εἰδότας.

Ὅτι ὁ κύριος λαὸν ἐκ γῆς Αἰγύπτω σώσας, τὸ δεύτερον τὸς μὴ πιςεύσαντας ἀπώλεσεν] Ὁ κύριος hic, ut in rebus Veteris Testamenti est יהוה, quod Græci vertunt κύριος, quia legebatur אדוני. Nam quod hic in Latino est JESUS, venit ex Græcorum librorum compendio, in quibus scriptum fuit ῖς pro ἧς. Δεύτερον autem hic valet, ex contrario, quo- modo & πάλιν sumitur Matth. 4, 1. & Jac. 5, 18. Perdidit nempe per serpentes, per morbos, per Angelum, per manus Levitarum. Vide 1. Cor. 10, 6. 8. 9. & 10. Ebr. 2, 2. μὴ πι- ςεύσαντας dicit pro ἀπειθήσαντας, quia qui non obediunt, ostendunt, se non credere, aut non credere ut oportet. Sic Ebr. 4, 2. ὁ λόγος dicitur μὴ συγκεκραμένος τῇ πίσει τοῖς ἀκύ- σασι.

Propositionem excipit tractatio, in qua in me- moriam primum revocat fidelibus exemplum Is- raëlitarum, tum Angelorum lapsorum, denique Sodomitarum. Israëlitz tum sæpe prævaricati sunt, tum imprimis, postquam ex Ægypto sal- vati sunt, & per ἀπισίαν perierunt, quorum exemplum primo loco adducit, quia proxime à JESU Christi Heri & DEI nostri abnegatione hæreticos notarat, & adversus seductionem eo- rundem fideles monendos necessarium esse du- xerat. Israëlitas enim idem Dominus salvarat ex Ægypto, Filius nempe Dei, qui in rubo ar- dente primum Mosi, deinde in columna nubis & ignis ad mare rubrum Israëlitis apparuit, ut è cap. 3. & cap. 14. Exodi constat. Angelus ille, in quo est nomen Domini, cap. 23, 20. cujus vocem ob- servare, & in quem fiduciam collocare debebant. Sed illi μὴ πιςεύσαντες per illam incredulita- tem suam sibi exitium accersivere, ut Aposto- lus docet Ebr. 4, 2. Patet ergo Christum hic designari: (1.) Quia nomen ὁ κύριος cum ar- ticulo Christum solet notare in Novo Testamen- to & juxta Socini regulam in Anti-Wujek. pag. 368. cum subjective ponitur, de Christo intelli- gendum est. (2.) De illo Domino sermo est, quem negasse dicuntur hæretici. At is erat Dominus noster JESUS Christus: Quod ar- gumentum eo magis stringit, quia ad constan- tiam fidei in Dominum Christum hortari instituit Apostolus, ne per hæreticos seducti eundem abnegent, & cum Israëlitis per ἀπισίαν intere- ant. Debet enim argumentum propositioni convenire. (3.) Ille ergo Dominus ex Ægy- pto salvasse populum Judaicum dicitur, a quo Judæi ad fidem Christianam conversi ne defici- ant per incredulitatem monentur. At monen- tur, ne à JESU Domino deficiant, ne pariter ut Israelitæ pereant. Ergo non notatur Israë- litarum inobedientia, sed ἀπισία, uti Ebr. 4, vers. 2. dicuntur exclusi à requie, quia ver- bum non erat mixtum τῇ πίσει fide audientium illud. (4.) Hunc Dominum Israëlitas ex Æ- gypto deduxisse vel salvasse ex Es. 64. vers. 9. Apodoxi de præexist. Filii Dei libr. 1. cap. 13. de- monstravimus. (5.) Quod pariter è Mose constat, si conferantur loca Exodi cap. 3. cap. 14. c. 23. & quæ ad illa diximus. (6.) Is

Salvator ipsorum fuit ex Ægypto, quem illi ten- tarunt in deserto. At Christum in deserto ten- tasse dicuntur, 1. Cor. 10., 13. quo de l. c. cap. 7. actum. (7.) Ille per τὸν κύριον Salvatorem populi ex Ægypto intelligitur, cui ut Domino convenit opus salvationis. At id Christo con- venit, imo extra eum non est salus, Actor. 4, 12. Adde (8) Quod nonnulli Codices Græci hic vocem ὁ ἰησοῦς habeant, omnesque Latini Co- dices eandem constanter legant. Quæ affert. Grotius de diversa lectione, meris conjecturis nituntur, & quid huc facit ῖς pro ῆς scriptum fuisse, fateor me non intelligere. (9.) Quod de Domino JESU Veteres interpretentur hunc locum. (10.) Quod unus sit Dominus, ut in Veteri, ita in Novo Testamento, nec ea in par- te temporum diversitas quicquam efficiat, Deut. 6, 4. Marc. 12, 29. Per hæc ergo, ut recte Estius, destruitur hæresis Ebionitarum & Photinianorum, negantium Christum fuisse ante Mariam: In & Arianorum, qui Christo veram Deitatem ade- merunt. Portabat enim Angelus ille nomen Do- mini tetragrammaton, Exod. c. 3. c. 20. & alibi. Quæ vero quomodo consistere possint cum eo, quod Estius hunc Angelum personam Domini ges- sisse ait, non video. Nam si Angelus hic per- sonam Domini tantum gessit, utique non fuit Jehovah ipse. Illud ἅπαξ, de quo ὀδὲν ὑγιὲς Heinsius, B. Glassius in Gramm. S. p. 412. ita ex- plicat: Etsi scio vos hæc tenere cognita, tamen se- mel adhuc, dum scilicet in tabernaculo hoc sum, vos de eo commonefaciam. Cornelius à Lapide: quasi d. Non volo vos docere, quia jam illa didi- cistis & scitis, sed tantum ea suggerere, & in me- moriam quasi commonitor revocare. Dicit hoc mo- destiæ causa, ne videatur eos inscitiæ arguere, sed potius laudare a scientia. Sic S. Johannes ait epist. 1. cap. 2. vers. 21. Non scripsi vobis quasi igno- rantibus veritatem, sed quasi scientibus eam, quasi d. Persuadeo mihi, vos hæc, quæ scribo, scire, unde ea non doceo, sed refrico & confirmo, ut quæ credere bene cœpistis, melius perseverando perficiatis. Qui tamen in Vulgatæ gratiam etiam aliam affert interpretationem: Magis congrue, inquit, τὸ semel per trajectionem Ebraicam referas ad τὸ salvans, opponitur enim τὸ secundo, quod sequitur, ut sententia ita sit or- dinanda: Scientes quod JESUS semel populum de terra Ægypti salvans, secundo eos, qui non crediderunt, perdidit, & ita legunt nonnulli Co- dices Græci: tunc enim sensus planus est, conne- xus & nervosus. Accedit Syrus, qui vertit: Quod Deus secundum unum tempus populum ex Ægypto liberavit, & Arabicus: Quod JESUS in vice prima vel primo populum suum ex Ægypto libe- ravit. Sed quia pauci illi sunt Codices, addit: Tertio & planissime scientes semel, id est, omni- no & prorsus omnia, ita ut me iterum ea doce- re, & vos iterum ea audire & discere non sit necesse. Sic Cicero pro Dejotario: Cum facile, ait, exorari Cæsar, tum semel exorari soles, semel, id est omnino & prorsus, ut amplius te exora- re non sit necesse. Rursum semel, id est ad sum- mam vel in summa, quasi d. scientes semel, id est summatim omnia. Sic Quintilianus l. 11. cap. 1. Et ut semel ait omnia complectar, & l. 10. c. 3. Denique ut semel quod est potentissimum dicam, secretum in dictando perit, id est, ut in summa dicam. Hujus phrasis ratio est, ipsum illud semel, quod significat una vice pro omnibus, ita ut postea non oporteat quid addi. Denique se- mel, id est irrevocabiliter, quasi dicat, scientes omnia semel, id est, plene firmiter & irrevocabiliter, ut eorum oblivisci non possitis. Cui postremæ explicationi annuit B. Gerhardus: Ἅπαξ semel est certe & immutabiliter hoc scitis, quod Dominus postquam populum ex Ægypto liberasset, nihilo tamen minus postea incredulos perdidit, Num. 14, 29.37. cap. 26, 64. Ebr. 3, 17. cap. 4, 2. Præferimus tamen mediam interpretationem ob vocem τὸ δεύτερον.

## 1:6
Verse 6. Angels who did not keep their own beginning) Their beginning, that is, the state in which they were from the beginning. Metonymy. Minutius: They lost the simplicity of their substance, burdened and immersed in vices. The book on the death of Moses says of the same: Aza and Azael, descending from heaven, corrupted their way. Christ of their Prince: He has not stood in the truth, John 8, 44. Conversely, of the good Angels, Hierocles: Nor if they should ever happen to be, [do they lose] either their own essence or the goodness of the Father.

The other example of the fallen Angels also fits well, because they drew eternal punishment upon themselves through apostasy from their Lord, by which he confirms that Christ is that one Ruler or Master GOD, through whom Paul teaches that the Angels were created, Col. 1, 16. and David Ps. XXXIII. 6. As in the former example the benefit of Redemption and salvation, which Peter had designated in the parallel, is noted, so here the benefit of creation is insinuated, because the Angels defected from GOD the Creator, not keeping their origin or blessedness, in which they were created, or their original and principal condition, but deserting their own οἰκητήριον, that glorious state in which they were established. For they are said not to have kept, in the parallel 2 Pet. 2, 4, ἁμαρτήσαντες, sinning or offending against GOD their creator. Concerning which Estius: They did not keep their origin, that is, they fell away and deprived themselves of the dignity and happiness in which they had been created; they did not retain that gratuitous gift of their first condition. The fables of the book on the death of Moses are unworthy of refutation, especially when we are occupied here with Exegetics. We have, however, spoken of those and similar trifles in System. Theol. Vol. IV, where the sin of the Angels and their state before the fall and their modern state are also treated more fully.

But having left their own dwelling] Having deserted the places of the upper light, they came to the lower regions.

For the judgment of the great day, he has kept them in eternal bonds under darkness] that is, by an inescapable law he wills that they be detained in places removed from the upper light around the earth until the time of judgment. The same sense and similar words in 2 Pet. 2, 4.

Grotius seems to describe the sin of the Angels in such a way that they came to the lower regions, and thus he does not deny the fabulous book on the death of Moses, that descending from heaven they corrupted their way, such inventions about Aza and Azael, the sons of God, that they used the company of Naama, etc., l. c. p. 362, we have refuted; and we showed that these do not refer to the evil Angels, but to the good ones, according to the mind of the Authors. Although we are not unaware that Cardan, Valesius, and Delrio refer these to the evil Angels. Estius has it thus: But they deserted their domicile or habitation, that is, by sinning they deserted their heavenly habitation, as an honorable station in which they had been placed. For raising themselves against GOD through pride, they could preserve neither the honor of their nature nor of their place. The rest of 2 Pet. 2, 4 has already been explained. Blessed Gerhard has it thus in this place. The fall of the Angels is described, (1.) negatively, they did not keep their origin, that is, the honor of their angelic dignity, as Oecumenius explains. There are indeed still among the Angels principalities,

Ephes. 6, v. 12, but infernal, not heavenly. (2.) affirmatively, they left their domicile. The Syriac, their habitation. Having left their own dwelling. They were the armies of GOD Zebaoth, placed in a certain station, but having become deserters, they deserted it. Piscator explains it thus: Rebelling against GOD, they aspired to higher glory and even equality with God, and therefore, because of this crime of high treason, they were forced to leave their heavenly domicile, 2 Pet. 2, 4. The same Blessed Gerhard in disp. Isag. Book on evil Angels ch. 9. §. 5. warns that this sense is also not inconvenient: GOD was their dwelling, so that just as He willed to dwell in them through grace and intimate presence, so also they ought to have dwelt in GOD through obedience, but they deserted this dwelling, having turned from GOD to themselves. Which sense we judge to be preferred. The Arab, according to Cornelius: He cast the Angels, who did not keep their Principality, but deserted their order and office, into extreme darkness, bound in eternal chains, reserving them in them to this great day, the day of judgment.

Furthermore, although they are kept in eternal bonds under darkness, those bonds do not prevent them from being able to wander here and there by divine permission, as is evident even from the history of Job, and they achieve at least this, that they are never free, but as captives bound by chains and deprived of liberty, nor can they expect liberty for eternity, because the bonds are eternal. The bonds, says Cornelius, are spiritual, namely, the divine power holding them, and their obligation and binding by that power to the prison, hell, and eternal punishment. For to this God has so bound and constrained them that they can never and nowhere shake it off or escape it, and therefore they are called eternal, because although demons are permitted to dwell in this air and tempt men until the day of judgment, yet wherever they go, they carry this obligation and binding, and thus their own punishment and fire, around with them like slaves carrying their chain. These things, however, do not sufficiently agree with those which follow later in Cornelius: He reserved, he says St. Peter, to be tormented, see the things said there. St. Jude refers the 'reserved' rather to eternal chains. That is to say: He reserved them for eternal chains, with which on the day of judgment He will bind them and shut them up in prison and eternal fire.

But by the dark place, not the air, which Episcopius also wished (l. 4. Instit. p. 346) and Fuller (l. 3. Miscell. cap. 14), but hell is denoted, we have said regarding the Petrine passage: Concerning which Estius: Some by the name of darkness understand the dark air, into which as into a prison the demons have been cast down, and as it were hidden until that judgment. Thus Clement of Alexandria in a short commentary on this passage, and after him Bede, the Interlinear Gloss, Lyranus, Cajetan, and Adam. But because Blessed Peter calls that place into which they have been thrust Tartarus, which is a name not of the air but of hell: therefore we think it more probable that hell is signified. Although both is true, that they have been cast down into hell, and into this dark air, as into a prison. I would wish one thing still to be observed, that this judgment against the angels is ascribed to the Lord, who saved the people out of Egypt, Jesus, and by this His Deity is established against heretics, who denied the same. Which I see is also noted by Estius. Therefore the sense is, the Lord Jesus, as soon as the deserting angels sinned, cast them down from heaven into a dark place, that is, he thrust them into hell, in which, as if by certain bonds, and those perpetual, he kept those delivered and bound, and keeps and detains them, until they are exhibited to himself for that universal judgment before the whole world, about to receive the sentence of their condemnation.

Latin:

Vers. 6. ᾿Αγγέλυς τὺς μὴ τηρήσαντας τὴν ἑαυτῶν ἀρχὴν) Principium suum, id est, statum in quo à principio fuerunt. Μετωνυμία. Minutius: Simplicitatem substantiæ suæ onusti & immersi vitiis perdiderunt. Liber de morte Mosis ait de iisdem. Aza & Azael cælo descendentes viam suam corruperunt. Christus de eorum Principe: Ἐν τῇ ἀληθείᾳ ὐχ ἑστηκεν Joh. 8, 44. Contra de bonis Angelis Hierocles: Μηδὲ ἂν λάθῃ πότε γιγνόμενοι, μήτε τῆς ἑαυτῶν ὐσίας, μήτε τῆς τῦ πατρὸς ἀγαθότητος.

Alterum exemplum Angelorum lapsorum etiam probe convenit, quia illi per apostasiam à Domino suo pœnam æternam sibi attraxerunt, quo confirmat, Christum esse unum illum Dominatorem seu Herum DEUM, per quem Paulus Angelos creatos esse docet, Col. 1, 16. & David Psal. XXXIII. 6. ut in priori exemplo beneficium Redemptionis & salvationis, quod in parallelo Petrus designarat, notatum, ita hic beneficium creationis insinuatur, quia Angeli à DEO Creatore defecerunt, non servantes suam originem vel beatitudinem, in qua conditi erant, vel originalem & principalem suam conditionem, sed deserentes proprium οἰκητήριον gloriosum illum statum, in quo constituti erant. Nam non servasse dicuntur in parallelo 2. Petr. 2, 4. ἁμαρτήσαντες peccantes vel delinquentes contra DEUM conditorem suum. Quo de Estius: Non servarunt suam originem, id est, exciderunt ac privarunt se dignitate & felicitate, in qua fuerant creati, donum illud gratuitum primæ conditionis non retinuerunt. Fabulæ libri de morte Mosis indignæ sunt refutatione, imprimis ubi hic in Exegeticis occupamur. Diximus tamen de illis & similibus nugis in System. Theol. Tom. IV. ubi etiam de peccato Angelorum, & statu ante lapsum ac moderno fusius actum.

Ἀλλὰ ἀπολιπόντας τὸ ἴδιον οἰκητήριον] Desertis lucis supernæ locis venere ad inferiora.

Εἰς κρίσιν μεγάλης ἡμέρας δεσμοῖς ἀῖδίοις ὑπὸ ζόφον τετήρηκεν] id est lege ineluctabili vult illos in locis à luce superna remotis circa terram detineri ad tempus usque judicii. Idem sensus & verba similia 2. Petr. 2, 4.

Videtur Grotius peccatum Angelorum ita describere, quod ad inferiora venerint, & ita fabuloso libro de morte Mosis haud abnuere, quod descendentes de cælo viam suam corruperint, qualia commenta de Aza & Azaële filiis Dei, quod consuetudine Naamæ usi sint, &c. l. c. p. 362. profligavimus; neque ad Angelos malos, sed ad bonos ea ex mente Autorum spectare ostendimus. Etsi Cardanum, Valesium, & Delrionem ad Angelos malos hæc referre haud ignoramus. Estius ita habet: Sed dereliquerunt suum domicilium sive habitaculum, id est peccando cælestem habitationem, velut stationem honorabilem, in qua collocati fuerant, deseruerunt. Nam erigentes se adversus DEUM per superbiam neque naturæ neque loci primævum honorem conservare potuerunt. Cætera 2. Petr. 2, 4. jam expedita sunt. B. Gerhardus ita habet in h. l. Describitur lapsus Angelorum, (1.) ἀποφατικῶς negative, non servarunt originem, id est Angelicæ dignitatis honorem, ut exponit Oecumenius. Sunt quidem adhuc inter Angelos ἀρχαὶ,

Ephes. 6, v. 12. sed infernales non cælestes. (2.) καταφατικῶς affirmative, reliquerunt domicilium suum. Syrus habitationem. Ἀπολιπόντες τὸ ἴδιον οἰκητήριον. Erant exercitus DEI Zebaoth, collocati in certa statione, sed transfugæ facti il- lam deseruerunt. Piscator sic exponit : DEO rebellantes altiorem gloriam atque adeo æqualita- tem cum Deo affectarunt, & proinde propter hoc crimen læsæ Majestatis domicilium suum cæ- leste coacti sunt relinquere 2. Petr. 2, 4. Idem B. Gerhardus in disp. Isag. L. de Ang. malis c. 9. §. 5. hunc quoque sensum non incommodum esse mo- net, DEUS erat ipsorum οἰκητήριον, ut igitur in illis voluit habitare per gratiam & intimam præ- sentiam: ita quoque debebant ipsi in DEO ha- bitare per obedientiam, sed deseruerunt hoc οἰκητή- ριον à DEO ad seipsos conversi. Quem sensum præferendum censemus. Arabs apud Corneli- um: Projecit Angelos, qui non servaverunt su- um Principatum, sed dereliquerunt suum ordinem & officium, in tenebras extremas, alligatos in vin- culis æternis, reservando in eis ad hunc diem ma- gnum, diem judicii.

Porro quanquam æternis vinculis sub caligine serventur, ea tamen vincula non impediunt, quo minus hinc inde divina permissione vagari pos- sint, ut vel ex historia Jobi constat, idque sal- tim præstant, ut nunquam liberi sint, sed ve- luti captivi vinculis constricti libertate privati, nec in æternum, quia æterna sunt vincula, li- bertatem expectare habeant. Vincula, inquit Cornelius, hæc sunt spiritualia, puta vis divina eos detinens, atque obligatio & alligatio eorum per illam ad carcerem, gehennam & pœnam æ- ternam. Huic enim Deus eos ita alligavit & a- strinxit, ut eam nusquam & nunquam excute- re vel evadere queant, ideoque vocantur æterna, quia licet dæmones usque ad diem judicii permit- tantur in hoc aëre versari & tentare homines, ta- men ipsi quocunque vadant, hanc obligationem & alligationem, adeoque ipsam suam pœnam & incendium, tanquam mancipia catenam suam circumferunt. Hæc vero non satis consonant illis, quæ postea sequuntur apud Cornelium: Re- servavit, cruciandos ait S. Petrus, vide ibi dicta. S. Judas τὸ reservavit potius refert ad vinculis æ- ternis. Q. d. Reservavit eos ad vincula æterna, quibus in die judicii eos vinciet & compinget in carcerem & ignem æternum.

Per locum autem caliginosum non aërem, quod voluit etiam Episcopius l. 4. Instit. pag. 346. & lo- Fullerus l. 3. Miscell. cap. 14, sed infernum deno- tari ad locum Petrinum diximus: Quo de Esti- us: Quidam nomine caliginis aërem caliginosum intelligunt, in quem velut in carcerem dejecti sunt dæmones, & velut reconditi usque ad illud ju- dicium. Ita Clemens Alexandrinus in commen- tariolo hujus loci, & post eum Beda, Glossa in- terlinearis, Lyranus, Cajetanus & Adamus. Sed quia B. Petrus tartarum vocat eum locum, in quem sunt detrusi, quod non aëris sed inferni no- men est: idcirco probabilius arbitramur infernum significari. Quanquam utrumque verum est, & in infernum, & in aërem hunc caliginosum, ut in carcerem dejectos esse. Unum adhuc observa- ri velim, τῷ κυρίῳ, qui salvavit populum ex Ægypto, Jesu adscribi hoc judicium adversus Angelos, eoque stabiliri ejusdem Deitatem ad- versus hæreticos, qui eandem inficiabantur. Quod video etiam ab Estio notatum esse. Ita- que sensus est, Dominus Jesus Angelos desertores, simul atque peccaverunt, è cælo præcipitatos in locum caliginofum, id est, in infernum detrusit, in quo velut quibusdam vinculis, iisque perpetuis tra- ditos & adstrictos servavit, ac servat detinetque, dum sibi ad judicium illud universale exhibeantur coram toto mundo sententiam suae condemnationis accepturi.

## 1:7
Vers. 7. As Sodom and Gomorrah and the cities around them) Adama and Zeboim שדכו Jerem. XLIX, 18. And he said cities for men, as the Greeks also often do: For cities are men, not a wilderness.

Having committed fornication in a manner similar to these and having gone after other flesh) 2. Petr. 2, 10. but especially those who walk after the flesh in the lust of defilement, where we said that by the word flesh, or, as it is here, other flesh בשר זר, is understood not only that which does not agree with the laws of nature, but all that which is not our own, that is, outside of marriage. For those inhabitants of Sodom and the neighboring cities, like the Carpocratians, were abandoned to every kind of Venus. Nor is the word ἐκπορνεύεσθαι less general, in the way the Hebrew זנה is accustomed to be translated. See also what we said about the word πορνείας at Matth. 5, 32.

They are set forth as an example) an example of those who are about to be ungodly, 2. Petr. 2, 6. And well are they set forth, that is, they are placed as if before the eyes. See Hebr. 6, 8. 12, 1. 2.

Suffering the punishment of eternal fire) In the Manuscript ὑπερέχου- σαι, so that the sense may be that they exhibit those burned cities as an instance of the eternal fire which awaits the ungodly.

Interpreters raise a doubt concerning the pronoun τούτοις, because others take it for τούταις, so as to refer to the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah, by an Enallage of gender, as Beza does: Others wish it to look to the Angels, to whom those cities were similar in whoredom, as Ludov. Capell. in Spicil. page 127. Others judge that they are only compared in general with the evil Angels and the Israelites, who fell away through apostasy and infidelity, which is spiritual whoredom: See Glassius Gramm 5. p. 572. and B. Joh. Ernest. Gerh. in h. l. But there is no need for all those, if it be said that the Masculine pronoun looks to the sense, as is accustomed to be done, not the word πόλεις itself: provided that by cities, men in the cities are understood. In the word ἐκπορνεύσασαι there is an emphasis, as if to say, inflamed by whoredom, or poured out into whoredom because of the preposition ἐκ, because they gave themselves to whoredom even to the point of exhaustion, which B. Luther rightly expressed, they have whored themselves out. Furthermore, this example looks to the former character of the heretics, by which they were marked for turpitude. To which, in the Sodomites, the punishment of eternal fire is assigned, not the fire which burned the cities: For that was only an instance of eternal fire, and is extinguished at last, if it be not already extinguished, but the infernal fire, which will torment men, is simply ἄσβεστος, Marc. IX. 48. Whence the Socinians, Episcop. l. III. Inst. page 97, vainly deny the eternity of infernal fire from this passage, because, forsooth, the fire of which St. Jude speaks is also called eternal, even if it is extinguished. For I deny that the discourse here is about such a fire: nor do I admit that both, that which fell from heaven, Gen. XIX, and the infernal one, are designated at the same time. Wherefore there is no need for the Grotius reading, since the received reading of the word ὑπέχουσαι holds itself very well, and is retained even by the Vulgate. The sense therefore is: Those cities, sustaining the punishment described in Genesis, namely of fire and sulfur, are set forth as an example of eternal fire, that is, of the punishment of the ungodly in eternal fire. For the punishment of those cities was so horrible that it was a certain notable figure of Gehenna. Which explanation Estius rightly prefers to the other, that those cities are set forth to sinners as an example in that they sustain the punishment of eternal fire: For how, he says, are those cities set forth as an example to sinners by the fact that they sustain the punishment of eternal fire, when the history of Genesis does not speak of the punishment of eternal fire, and an example must be taken from history? To omit that an example must be taken from a known thing: but it was not known to the sinners against whom the argument is here made that the Sodomites were being tormented by eternal fire. Concerning which punishment of infernal fire, Gregory the Great, XIV. Moral. c. 10. In the very quality of the vengeance, he says, he noted the stain of the crime; for sulfur has a stench, fire has heat; therefore, those who had burned with perverse desires from the stench of the flesh, it was fitting that they should perish at the same time by fire and sulfur. Schlichtingius, although he understands this passage only of that sulfurous fire of Gen. XIX, yet says it is called eternal by reason of the effect, or of eternal subversion by metalepsis.

Latin:

Vers. 7. Ὡς Σόδομα καὶ Γόμοῤῥα καὶ αἱ περὶ αὐτὰς πόλεις) Adama & Zeboim שדכו Jerem. XLIX, 18. Et πόλεις dixit pro hominibus, ut & Graeci saepe: Πόλις γάρ εἰσιν ἄνδρες, οὐκ ἐρημία.

Τὸν ὅμοιον τούτοις τρόπον ἐκπορνεύσασαι καὶ ἀπελθοῦσαι ὀ- πίσω σαρκὸς ἑτέρας) 2. Petr. 2, 10. μάλιστα δὲ τοὺς ὀπίσω σαρ- κὸς ἐν ἐπιθυμίᾳ μιασμοῦ πορευομένους, ubi diximus voce car- nis, sive, ut hic est, carnis alienae בשר זר intelligi non tantum eam, quae naturae legibus non convenit, sed omnem, quae nostra non est, id est, extra matrimonium. Nam & illi Sodomorum vicinarumque urbium habitatores, sicut Carpocratiani, in omnem Venerem erant projecti. Nec minus generale Verbum ἐκπορνεύεσθαι, quomodo verti solet Ebraeum זנה. Vide & quae de voce πορνείας diximus ad Matth. 5, 32.

Πρόκεινται δεῖγμα) ὑπόδειγμα μελλόντων ἀσεβεῖν, 2. Petr. 2, 6. Et bene πρόκεινται, id est, velut ob oculos positae sunt. Vide Ebr. 6, 8. 12, 1. 2.

Πυρὸς αἰωνίε δίκην ὑπέχουσαὶ) In Manuscripto ὑπερέχου- σαι, ut sensus sit, eas urbes incensas instar exhibere ignis ae- terni, qui impios expectat.

De pronomine τούτοις dubium movent Inter- pretes, quod alii pro τούταις, ut ad civitates So- domam & Gomorrham referant, per Enallagen generis cum Beza accipiunt: Alii ad Angelos, qui- bus similes in scortatione fuerint istae civitates, spectare volunt, ut Ludov. Capell. in Spicil. pag. 127. Alii in genere tantum cum Angelis malis & Israelitis conferri censent, qui per apostasiam & infidelitatem defecere, quae spiritualis est scorta- tio: Vid. Glassii Gramm 5. p. 572. & B. Joh. Er- nest. Gerh. in h. l. Sed illis omnibus opus non est, si dicatur, pronomen Masculinum sensum respi- cere, quemadmodum fieri solet, non verbum ipsum πόλεις: siquidem per civitates homines in ci- vitatibus intelligantur. In voce ἐκπορνεύσασαι emphasis est, q. d. scortando effervefactae, seu in scortationem effusae ob praepositionem ἐκ, quod ad defatigationem usq; scortationi operam dederint, quam B. Lutherus recte expressit, sie haben sich ausgehuret. Caeterum hoc exemplum spectat ad priorem haereticorum characterem, quo notati erant à turpitudine. Cui in Sodomitis poena affi- gnatur ignis aeternus, non ignis, qui civitates exus- sit: Ille enim tantum instar erat ignis aeterni, & exstinguitur tandem, si nondum extinctus sit, sed ignis infernalis, qui homines torquebit, ἄσβεστος est simpliciter, Marc. IX. 48. Unde frustra ex hoc loco ignis infernalis aeternitatem negant Sociniani, Episcop. l. III. Inst. pag. 97. quod nempe ignis, de quo S. Judas, etiam aeternus dicatur, etsi extinguatur. Nego enim de tali igne hic sermonem esse: neque admitto utrumque, & illum, qui de coelo delapsus est, Gen. XIX. & infernalem simul designa- ri. Quapropter nec Grotiana opus est lectione, quum recepta vocis ὑπέχουσαι optime sese habeat, à Vulgata etiam retenta. Sensus ergo est: Civitates illae sustinentes poenam in Genesi descriptam scilicet ignis & sulphuris, propositae sunt in exemplum ignis aeterni, id est, punitionis impiorum in igne aeterno. Nam illarum civitatum tam horribilis poena fuit insignis quaedam figura gehennae. Quam explica- tionem merito alteri, quod illae civitates in eo, quod sustineant poenam ignis aeterni propositae sunt peccatoribus in exemplum, praefert Estius: Nam quomodo, inquit, civitates illae per hoc, quod sustinent poenam ignis aeterni sunt peccatoribus in exemplum propositæ: cum de pœna ignis æterni Ge- nesis historia non loquatur, exemplum autem ab historia petatur? Ut omittam, quod exemplum sumi debeat à re nota: notum autem non erat pec- catoribus, adversus quos hic agitur, Sodomitas æterno igne cruciari. De quo ignis infernalis sup- plicio Gregorius M. XIV. Moral. c. 10. In ipsa qualitate ultionis, inquit, notavit maculam cri- minis, sulphur quippe fætorem habet, ignis ardo- rem; qui itaque ad perversa desideria ex carnis fæ- tore arserant, dignum fuit, ut simul igne ac sul- phure perirent. Schlichtingius etsi non nisi de igne illo sulphurco Gen. XIX. locum hunc intelligat; æternum tamen dici ratione effectus ait, aut sub- versionis æternæ per metallipsin.

## 1:8
Vers. 8.

Ὁμοίως μέντοι καὶ ὗτοι) ὅμως μέντοι in the Manuscript, that is, nevertheless, although they have such great examples before them.

Ἐνυπνιαζόμενοι) Isaiah 56 verse 10. הזים is translated ἐνυπνιαζόμενοι. It signifies, however, imagining foolish things, just like those who dream. Moses Maimonides uses that Hebrew word in this way in the preface to the Guide for the Perplexed for the Arabs, among whom הזא stands for the Hebrew הזם, which is to be insane.

Σάρκα μὲν μιαίνεσι) They corrupt males and females. Ἐπιθυμίᾳ μιασμᾶ in the cited passage 2 Peter 2:10.

Κυριότητα δὲ ἀθετᾶσι) Κυριότητος καταφρονῶντας, 2 Peter 2:10, from which we see that ἀθετεῖν here means to despise, as in 1 Thessalonians 4:8. בגר is translated sometimes as ἀθετεῖν and sometimes as καταφρονεῖν.

Δόξας δὲ βλασφημῦσι) The discourse grows. For by δόξας he understands those who are in the highest honors, τὰς ἐξυσίας τὰς ὑπερεχέσας. Thus δόξας & τρέμεσι βλασφημῶντες, 2 Peter 2:10. It is no wonder that the Carpocratians did this, who held all ancestral laws for nothing.

This is rather an application, and indeed to all those things which had preceded in the examples; first, that they corrupt the flesh with wicked lusts by the example of the Sodomites: Second, that they despise the dominion of that one Lord and GOD, the same one Lord and true God; just as Clement of Alexandria and others explain this, denying it by the example of the unbelieving Israelites; who tempted Christ in the desert, soliciting the Divine power of this their Leader: Third, that they blaspheme his glory by the example of the evil angels, who, since they have not at all affected the same glory, do not cease to blaspheme the Divine Majesty and glory of the Lord Jesus. Clement of Alexandria understands the word ἐvυπνιαζόμενοι as those dreaming to themselves by their own imagination lusts and reprobate desires, to which Estius, Gagneius, Vatablus, and Cornelius do not disagree, referring it to nocturnal illusions and pollutions. Epiphanius preceded Grotius, referring these dreams to the fabulous trifles of the Gnostics, so that they are said to be dreaming, that is, delirious, wandering, and saying things which they do not know, as is said later: Whatever they are ignorant of, they blaspheme. Which sense is not to be disapproved. For this pertains not only to the defilement of the flesh, but also to other things which are added. To which the Arab also goes. Those who are dreamers are also likened to them. How often false prophets are called dreamers, because they preached not the oracles of God, but their own dreams and inventions: Which sense Cornelius says fits this passage very well. Compare Deuteronomy 13:3, Jeremiah 22:25, chapter 27:9, 29:18, Zechariah 10:2. Irenaeus, book 1, chapter 20, calls the Gnostics oniropompos, because they sold their own dreams as if they were Divine oracles. Epiphanius, heresy 26. They brought forth, he says, a forged Gospel of the Apostle Philip, and from it mere dreams and ravings to establish their own impure dogmas (such truly monstrous dogmas) they produced, as the catalogues of heretics by Irenaeus, Augustine, and others teach.

Specifically, it is said first of them: σάρκα μὲν μιαί- νουσι σαρκὸς ἐν ἐπιθυμίᾳ μιασμᾶ πορευομένης: Vulgate: Who follow after the flesh, and its carnal appetites, in the concupiscence of uncleanness (in Greek, of contamination and pollution) they walk. Jerome, book 1 against Jovinian: Who follow after the flesh in the desires of pollution. Oecumenius says: He attacks the lusts and filthiness of the heretics of his own age, such as the Simonians, Nicolaitans, and Gnostics. Theodoret, book 1, Heretical Fables: Who, he says, were of the sect of Simon, and boldly gave themselves over to every lust and intemperance. Ephrem, Vol. 1, sermon on those who entice the soul to unchastity, since there is nothing evil in it, cites this epistle. But some interpret δόξας in the plural here, and in Peter, as referring to heavenly mighty works or angels, about whom the heretics had invented many unworthy things to their injury; following the lead of Clement of Alexandria, to whom Estius adds his support, because of what follows concerning Michael not wishing to contend with the Devil, and because of the things that are held in verse 10. Horneius also agrees in this place. But most have explained it concerning the Political Magistrate. It seems, however, that not only because of the word blasphemy, which properly tends toward God, but also because the discourse appears to grow, the Divine Majesty is regarded, which the heretics of that time were blaspheming in many ways: whence also the prophecy of Enoch is brought against the same ones concerning the judgment περὶ πάντων τῶν σκληρῶν, ὧν ἐλάλησαν κατ' ἀυτῶ ἁμαρτωλοὶ ἀσεβεῖς. Thus Bede and Hugo interpret δόξας as the Divine power, wisdom, goodness, and majesty, which were being blasphemed when the mysteries hidden in the scriptures were depraved by the heretics. Cajetan and Arias Montanus interpret it as the truly glorious person of Christ according to both natures, his miracles, heavenly doctrine, resurrection, and ascension, which were δόξαι, 1 Peter 1:11, and were denied by the Simonians and other heretics, who denied that Christ was truly born and suffered. The Syriac rendered it: they are not moved by majesty while they blaspheme. Some understand by δόξας the Apostolic sentences or dogmas. To this opinion is also reduced that Petrine passage: Δόξας ἐ τρέμουσι βλασφημοῦντες, they do not fear to introduce sects, as the Vulgate translates, sub-understanding ἐπάγειν, so that they may obtain their own sects, they blaspheme the sentences of scripture, as it were, according to the interpreter at 2 Peter 2:10. Cornelius à Lapide: how bold and self-pleasing they are is clear from the fact that they dare to introduce new opinions, fashioned from their own brain, against the common doctrine and consensus of the Church and the Fathers, and thus to make sects. But that meaning of sects is unusual: δόξα indeed denotes an opinion, but it never occurs for a sect: nor is it fitting to insert any word into scripture. For whence will that ἐπάγειν be deduced? And that δόξας in Peter denotes glory rather than opinion, let alone a sect, the preceding noun τῆς κυριότη- τος sufficiently teaches; which two are also joined together in St. Jude in this place, where if you interpret δόξας as sects, as the parallelism demands the same sense, who is going to produce the sense, They blaspheme sects? Cornelius saw this well, therefore he says: Δόξας (in Jude) cannot be translated as sects, for heretics do not blaspheme sects, but covet them. But why should the Petrine one not simply be retained? Δόξας ἐ τρέμουσι βλασφη- μοῦντες, They do not fear to blaspheme Majesties, so that the participle is placed for the infinitive verb through a customary Greek idiom: because it is familiar to the Greeks to use participles for Infinitives. Add that the sense is also full in this way, if the participle is retained: They do not fear or do not dread blaspheming Majesties: Which sense the Syriac regarded, and a comparison with the present place of Jude sufficiently teaches that it is implied that they blaspheme Majesties (without any fear, boldly and impudently, as Peter has it).

Which, as we have said, we judge should be referred to the majesty or glory of Christ, rather than to the majesties or earthly ones of Emperors and Kings or the heavenly ones of Angels: 1. because δόξα is never attributed to an Emperor or King in the New Testament; δόξα of Kings or of kingdoms indeed occurs in Matthew 4:8: but it nowhere appears that an Emperor or King is understood by δόξα. On the contrary, however, δόξα is most frequently attributed to Christ, who is called crowned with glory, Heb. 2:8, 9, Lord of glory, 1 Cor. 2:8, James 2:1, of whose glory we are to stand according to Jude v. 24, of whose glory and majesty [it is spoken] everywhere, Matt. 25:30, 31, Mark 10:37, Luke 9:26, ch. 24:26, John 1:14, ch. 2:11, ch. 17:5, 22, 24, 1 Tim. 3:16, Tit. 2:13, 2 Pet. 1:17, Apoc. 5:13, etc., and much glory, Matt. 24:30, Mark 13:26, Luke 21:27, 2. Because St. Peter also said δόξας in the Plural concerning Christ, which the Prophets searched into, τὰς μετὰ ταῦτα δόξας 1 epist. 1:11, which those Pseudo-Prophets blasphemed in return. 3. As blasphemy properly tends toward God: So there is no reason why we should depart from this proper sense. Altensteig proved that in Lexic. Theol. page 102, from Augustine, Thomas, Bonaventure, Hugo, etc. 4. The heretics of that time are not read to have afflicted Magistrates with curses. But they afflicted GOD and Christ with much blasphemy.
