Simon denied that God made the world, and asserted that he himself was Christ, and likewise wanted to be believed to be Jove, as Augustine testifies in ch. 1 of his book on heresies. and he had said (in the same author) that he had given the law of Moses to the Jews in the person of the Father on Mount Sinai, that he had appeared putatively in the person of the Son in the time of Tiberius, and afterwards had come upon the Apostles in the fiery tongues of the Holy Spirit; but that Christ had neither come nor suffered anything from the Jews. Whose disciple Menander, around the year 72, encrusted the same blasphemies in another way: For whatever Simon had said he was, Menander professed himself to be, denying that anyone could have salvation unless he had been baptized in his name, he taught that he was the Savior of the whole world, and furthermore he embraced the promiscuous intercourse of women, as if it were a fruit of the grace of God and mercy toward men. From whose impious school Saturninus and Basilides, distinguished by their monstrous blasphemies against Christ, emerged, so that I shall not now adduce the blasphemies of the Nicolaitans, and of those who emerged from them, according to Epiphanius and Augustine, the Gnostics, Ebionites, and Cerinthians. 5. This interpretation of the blasphemies against Jesus and his δόξας is consistent with the proposition of Jude, since he deemed it necessary to write against those who denied Jesus the Lord and Master, that only God who is our Redeemer and Savior. No mention is made in the proposition concerning the detraction of the Magistrate. 6. St. Jude explains himself, what he understands by blasphemy, v. 10 seq., namely that they blaspheme those things which they do not understand. But these heretics undoubtedly understood the power of the Magistrate, whence these things are more correctly understood concerning the mysteries of the faith concerning the τὰς δόξας glories of Christ. 7. What St. Jude subjoins concerning the judgment of diabolical blasphemy, which not even the Archangel dared to bring, provoking to divine rebuke, when he disputed with Satan about the body of Moses, what else do they argue than that it is a matter not of blasphemy against the magistrate, but against God, and that it is taught to be of such importance that the angels, even though superior in power and strength to the Devil (as St. Peter hints in the parallel passage), and the Archangel Michael himself acknowledged himself unequal to avenging it, and therefore committed its judgment to God alone.

For the gravity of that transgression is exaggerated by this very fact, that those 'daring, self-willed' ones 'blaspheme glories' [Jude 8], fearing nothing, because it is so great that not even the Archangel himself or Angels can judge and avenge it according to its merit, but submit it to the immediate judgment of God. 'He did not dare,' says St. Jude concerning the Archangel Michael, 'to bring a judgment of blasphemy, but said, The Lord rebuke you.' But they do not fear to blaspheme those things which they have not seen, fearing nothing of the divine judgment. 8. There is added the prophecy of Enoch, which is cited, in which not so much the punishments regarding the insults spoken against the Magistrate, as those regarding 'the hard things' which were uttered against the 'Lord,' that Oecumenical Judge, are looked to in express words, v. 15. 9. On the contrary, he commends the believers to that Savior who shall present them 'before his glory' [Jude 24] blameless, that they may see that glory which heretics do not fear to blaspheme, which the Father gave to him, John 17. v. 28, 'with exceeding joy,' as it is held here v. 24. 10. Therefore the holy Apostle attributes 'glory and majesty' in the final doxology to the 'only wise God our Savior,' v. 25, that he may teach that the glory which the heretics do not fear to snatch away from him is to be celebrated in him for all eternity, and may excite the faithful to celebrate the same. Thus the proposition, the treatment, the principal arguments of the same, and the conclusion agree excellently. Finally, this opinion, that the 'glories' of Jesus the Savior are looked to by the Apostle, was not new, but was approved by Bede and other Interpreters named before.

Latin:

Vers. 8.

Ὁμοίως μέντοι καὶ ὗτοι) ὅμως μέντοι in Manuscripto, id est, nihilominus, quamvis tanta exempla habeant an- te se.

Ἐνυπνιαζόμενοι) Esa. 56 vers. 10. הזים vertitur ἐνυ- πνιαζόμενοι. Significat autem stulta imaginantes ita ut ii, qui somniant. Utitur sic illa voce Ebræa Moses Maimoni- des in anteloquio Ducis dubitantium Arabibus, apud quos est הזא pro Ebræo הזם est insanire.

Σάρκα μὲν μιαίνεσι) Corrumpunt mares & fœminas. Ἐ- πιθυμίᾳ μιασμᾶ dicto loco 2. Petr. 2, 10.

Κυριότητα δὲ ἀθετᾶσι) Κυριότητος καταφρονῶντας, 2. Petr. 2, 10. unde videmus, ἀθετεῖν hic esse contemnere, ut 1. Thess. 4. vers. 8. בגר, modo ἀθετεῖν modo καταφρονεῖν vertitur.

Δόξας δὲ βλασφημῦσι) Crescit oratio. Nam δόξας in- telligit eos, qui in summis sunt honoribus, τὰς ἐξυσίας τὰς ὑπερεχέσας. Sic δόξας & τρέμεσι βλασφημῶντες, 2. Pet. 2, 10. Non mirum id fecisse Carpocratianos, qui leges avi- tas omnes pro nihilo ducerent.

Est hic potius applicatio, & quidem ad omnia illa, quæ in exemplis præcesserant; primum quod carnem corrumpant nefandis libidinibus exemplo Sodomorum: Deinde quod dominationem illius unius Heri ac DEI despiciant, eundem unum il- lum Herum, Deumque verum; quemadmodum hoc explicant Clemens Alexandr. aliique negan- tes exemplo Israëlitarum incredulorum; qui Chri- stum in deserto tentarunt, Divinam hujus Ducto- ris sui potentiam solicitantes: Tertio quod gloriam ejus blasphement exemplo Angelorum ma- lorum, qui quum eandem gloriam ne quicquam affectarint, blasphemare non intermittunt Divi- nam Domini Jesu Majestatem, & gloriam. Ver- bum ἐvυπνιαζόμενοι Clemens Alexandr. de somni- antibus sibi imaginatione sua libidines & reprobas cupiditates intelligit, cui non abnuit Estius, Ga- gnejus, Vatablus, & Cornelius ad illusiones & pol- lutiones nocturnas referunt. Grotio vero præivit Epiphanius somnia hæc referens ad fabulosam Gnosticorum nugacitatem, ut somniantes dicantur, id est, delirantes errantes & dicentes, quæ non sciunt, ut postea dicitur: Quæcunque ignorant, blasphemant. Qui sensus non improbandus. Nam pertinet hoc non solum ad carnis commaculatio- nem, sed etiam ad alia, quæ adduntur. Quo etiam abit Arabs. Assimilantur illis etiam hi, qui videntes sunt somnia. Quomodo Pseudoprophe- tæ sæpius vocantur somniantes, eo quod non Dei oracula, sed sua somnia, & commenta prædica- rent: Quem sensum huic loco valde congruere ait Cornelius. Conf. Deut. XIII. 3. Jer. XXII. 25. cap. XXVII. 9. XXIX. 18. Zach. X. 2. Irenæus l. I. c. 20. Gnosticos vocat oniropompos, quod sua so- mnia quasi oracula Divina venditarent. Epiphani- us hær. XXVI. Philippi, inquit, Apostoli confi- ctum Evangelium proferebant, & ex eo mera somnia & deliramenta ad sua impura dogmata stabilienda (qualia dogmata vere portentosa) producebant, ceu catalogi haereticoru Irenai, August. alioru docens.

In specie primo de illis dicitur σάρκα μὲν μιαί- νουσι σαρκὸς ἐν ἐπιθυμίᾳ μιασμᾶ πορευομένης: Vul- gatus: Qui post carnem sequentes carnem, ejusq; ap- petitus carnales) in concupiscentia immunditiae (Grae- ce contaminationis & pollutionis) ambulant. Hie- ronymus l.I. contr. Jovin. Qui post carnem ambulant in desideriis pollutionis. Taxat, inquit Oecumenius, haereticorum sui aevi puta Simonianorum, Nicolaitaru, Gnosticorum libidines & spurcitias. Theodoretes l.I. Haeret. fabul. Qui secta, inquit, Simonis erant, au- dacter se omni libidini & intemperantiae debedant. E- phrem. T. I. serm. de iis, qui animam ad impudicitia pelliciunt, cu nihil mali sit, adducit hanc epistolam. Δόξας vero in plurali hic, & apud Petrum nonnulli de caelestibq virtutibus, vel Angelis interpretantur, de quib9 ad eorum injuriam multa indigna confinxe- rint haeretici; praeeunte Clemente Alexandrino, qui- bus accedit Estius, quod sequatur de Michaele no- lente conciliari Diabolo, & ob ea, quae v.10. habentur. Accedit & Hornejus in h.l. Sed de Magistratu Politi- co exposuere plerique. Videtur tamen non tantum propter vocem blasphemiae, quae proprie in Deum te- dit, sed etiam quia crescere orationem apparet, Ma- jestatem Divinam respici, quam multis modis bla- sphemabant haeretici illius temporis: unde & ad- ducitur adversus eosdem Enochi vaticinium de ju- dicio περὶ πάντων τῶν σκληρῶν, ὧν ἐλάλησαν κατ' ἀυτῶ ἁμαρτωλοὶ ἀσεβεῖς. Ita Beda, & Hugo de po- tentia, sapientia, bonitate & majestate Divina δόξας interpretantur, quae blasphemabantur, cum myste- ria in scripturis latetia depravata sunt ab haereticis. Cajetanus, & Ariasmontanus Christi personam vere gloriosam secundum utramq; naturam, miracula, do- ctrinam caelestem, resurrectionem, ascensionem, quae erant δόξαι, 1. Petr. I. 11. & negabantur à Simonianis, aliisq; haereticis, Christum vere natum & passum inficiantibus. Syrus reddidit, à majestate non mo- ventur, dum blasphemant. Nonnulli per δόξας sen- tentias vel dogmata Apostolica intelligunt. Ad hanc sententiam reducitur etiam Petrinum illud: Δόξας ἐ τρέμουσι βλασφημοῦντες, sectas non metuunt intro- ducere, ut vertit Vulgatus, subintelligens ἐπάγειν, ut sectas suas obtineant, sententias scripturae bla- sphemant, q. d. interprete ad 2. Petr. 2,10. Cornelio à Lapide: quam sint audaces & sibi placentes, liquet ex eo, quod contra communem Ecclesiae Patrumque do- ctrinam & consensum audeant novas opiniones ex suo cerebro confictas inducere, itaq; sectas facere. Sed illa sectarum significatio insolens est: Δόξα opinionem quidem notat, pro secta vero nunquam occurrit: Neque convenit verbum aliquod scripturae inge- rere. Unde enim deducetur illud ἐπάγειν? Et δόξας apud Petrum potius gloriam, quam opinionem, ne- dum sectam notare, praecedens nomen τῆς κυριότη- τος satis docet; quae duo etiam apud S. Iudam h.l. cojunguntur, ubi si δόξας de sectis interpreteris, uti parallelismus eundem sensum postulat, ecquis pro- diturus est sensus, Sectas blasphemant? Vidit id pro- be Cornelius, ideo inquit: Δόξας (apud Iu- dam) verti nequit sectas, nec enim haeretici sectas blasphemant, sed ambiunt. Cur vero non simpli- citer Petrina retinenda? Δόξας ἐ τρέμουσι βλασφη- μοῦντες, Majestates non verentur blasphemare, ut participium ponatur pro verbo infinitivo per usi- tatum Graecismum: quia Graecis familiare est participiis uti pro Infinitivis. Adde quod & ita plenus sit sensus, sit retineatur participium: Ma- jestates non verentur vel non metuunt blaspheman- tes: Quem sensum Syrus respexit, & collatio cum Iudae praesenti loco satis docet, id innui, quod Ma- jestates (sine ullo metu audacter & procaciter, ut Petrus habet) blasphement.

Quæ, ut diximus, ad majestatem, seu gloriam Christi potius referenda censemus, quam ad ma- jestates seu terrenas Imperatorum & Regum seu cæ- lestes Angelorum: 1. quia nunquam δόξα in No- vo Testamento tribuitur Imperatori aut Regi; Regum aut δόξα regnorum quidem Matth. IV. 8. occurrit: sed per δόξαν Imperatorem aut Regem intelligi nu- spiam comparet. Ex adverso vero frequentissime δόξα tribuitur Christo, qui δόξῃ coronatus, Ebr. II. 8. 9. Κύριος τῆς δόξης, 1. Cor. II. 8. Jac. II. 1. di- citur, cujus gloriæ sistendi sumus secundum Judam v. 24. de cujus gloria & majestate passim, Matth. XXV. 30. 31. Marc. X. 37. Luc. IX. 26. cap. XXIV. 26. Joh. I. 14. cap. II. 11. cap. XVII. 5. 22. 24. 1. Tim. III. 16. Tit. II. 13. 2. Petr. I. 17. Apoc. V. 13. &c. & gloria mul- ta, Matth. XXIV. 30. Marc. XIII. 26. Luc. XXI. 27. 2. Quia etiam S. Petrus δόξας in Plurali dixit de Christo, quas scrutati sint Prophetæ τὰς μετὰ ταῦτα δόξας 1. epist. I. 11. quas Pseudo-Prophetæ illi con- tra blasphemarint. 3. Ut blasphemia proprie vergit in Deum: Ita ab hoc proprio sensu cur disceda- mus, causa nulla est. Probavit illud Altensteig. in Lexic. Theol. pag. 102. ex Augustino, Thoma, Bo- naventura, Hugone &c. 4. Non leguntur hæretici istius temporis Magistratus maledictis affecisse. DE- UM autem, & Christum blasphemia multa affece- re. Simon Deum negabat mundum fecisse, seque Christum esse asserebat, itemque Jovem se credi vo- lebat, Augustino teste cap. I. de hæres. ac dixerat (apud eundem) se in monte Sina legem Mosis in Pa- tris persona dedisse Judæis, tempore Tiberii in Filii persona putative apparuisse, postea se in linguis igneis Spiritus Sancti super Apostolos venisse; Christum au- tem nec venisse, nec a Judæis quicquam pertulisse. Cu- jus discipulus Menander circ. ann. 72. easdem bla- sphemias, alia ratione, incrustavit: Quicquid enim se Simon esse dixerat, hac se Menander esse professus est negans, quenquam habere posse salutem nisi in suo nomine baptizatus fuisset, se totius mundi Salvatorem esse docuit, adhæc concubitum mulierum promiscuum amplexus est, tanquam gratia Dei & misericordia erga homines fructum. E cujus schola impia Satur- ninus, & Basilides portentosis in Christum blasphe- miis insignes prodiere, ut Nicolaitarum, & qui ab ipsis prodiere, autore Epiphanio & Augustino, Gno- sticorum, Ebionitarum, ac Cerinthianorum blasphe- mias jam non adducam. 5. Propositioni Judæ con- sentanea est hæc de blasphemiis in Jesum ejusque δόξας interpretatio, quum necessum duxerit ad- versus eos scribere, qui Jesum Dominum & Herum unicum illum Deum abnegarunt, qui Redemptor, & Salvator noster est. De detractione Magistratus nulla in propositione facta est mentio. 6. S. Judas semetipsum explicat, quid intelligat per blasphemi- am, v. 10. sequ. quod nempe ea, quæ non intelligunt, blasphement. Magistratus autem potestatem sine dubio intellexere isti hæretici, unde de mysteriis fidei τὰς δόξας glorias Christi concernentibus hæc rectius intelliguntur. 7. Quæ de judicio blasphemiæ diabolicæ, quod ne quidem Archangelus ausus fue- rit ferre ad divina increpationem provocans, sub- jungit S. Judas, quum ille disceptaret cum Satana de Mosis corpore, quid aliud arguunt, quam quod de blasphemia non contra magistratum, sed contra Deum agatur, eademq; tanti momenti esse docea- tur, ut impares sese Angelos, etsi potentia & forti- tudine Diabolo superiores (ut S. Petrus in loco pa- rallelo innuit) imparem etiam sese ipse Archange- lus Michaël ad eam vendicandam agnoverint, a- deoque uni DEO ejus judicium commiserint.

Exaggeratur enim eo ipso gravitas istius præva- ricationis, quod Τολμηταὶ ἀυθάδεις illi δόξας ἐ τρέ- μυσι βλασφημέντες, nihil scilicet veriti, quod tan- ta ea sit, quam nec ipse Archangelus Angelive ali- judicare ac vindicare pro merito possint, sed judi- cio Dei immediato submittant. Οὐκ ἐτόλμησεν in- quit S. Judas de Archangelo Michaële, κρίσιν ἐπε- νεγκεῖν βλασφημίας, ἀλλ' εἶπεν ἐπιτιμήσαι σοι ὁ Κύριος. Illi vero non verentur ea, quæ non viderunt, blasphemare, nihil metuentes divinum judicium. 8. Accedit prophetia Enochi adducta, in qua non tam pœnæ quoad convitia adversus Magistratum dicta, quam quoad Τὰ σκληρὰ, quæ adversus Κύριον Domi- num, Judicem illum Oecumenicum prolata sunt, verbis expressis respiciuntur, v. 15. 9. Ex adverso credentes commendat illi Servatori, qui eos κατε- νώπιον τῆς δόξης ἀυτῦ coram gloria sua inculpatos si- stet, ut gloriam illam videant, quam heretici bla- sphemare non verentur, quam ipsi Pater dedit, Joh. 17. v. 28. ἐν ἀγαλλιάσει, ut hic habetur v. 24. 10. Ideo δόξαν καὶ μεγαλωσύνην in δοξολογία fina- li tribuit S. Apostolus, ceu μόνῳ σοφῷ Θεῷ Σωτῆρι ἡμῶν, v. 25. ut quam eripere ipsi gloriam hæretici non verentur, in ipso celebratum iri in omnem æ- ternitatem doceat, ac fideles ad eandem celebran- dam excitet. Ita propositio, tractatio, argumenta præcipua ejusdem & conclusio eximie consonant. Denique hæc sententia, δόξας Jesu Servatoris ab Apostolo respici, non nova, sed Bedæ, aliisque an- tea nominatis Interpretibus probata fuit.

## 1:9
Vers. 9.

But Michael the Archangel, when contending he disputed with the Devil about the body of Moses, did not dare to bring a judgment of blasphemy, but said, The Lord rebuke you.) A 'judgment of blasphemy,' 2 Pet. ch. II. v. 11, 'a blasphemous judgment,' is the vengeance which one takes by cursing. Simeon had denied in the epistle that the angels do this when they have to contend with authorities, although impious ones, which we explained there. Jude adds further that the angels do not do this even when they have a struggle with the Devil, who also himself, although impious, received a certain power from GOD over this world, whence he is called 'world-ruler.' Those words 'The Lord rebuke you' do not differ in sense, and almost not at all in sound, from those which are in the Greek of Zech. ch. III. v. 2, 'The Lord rebuke you in you': יגער יהוה בך, which words the great Angel pronounces, who is also called יהוה there, because he acts the part of God against the Devil. We said that he who is called both Angel and יהוה there is Michael, by this argument, that he was at that time as it were the defender of the Jews, Dan. XII. 5, and now under Christ of the Christians, Apoc. XII. 7. To which Hermas III. 8 also looks. But the writer of the book which was called in Hebrew פטירת משה, and in Greek indeed ἀνάληψις Μωσέως, had attributed the same words to Michael contending against the Devil about the body of Moses, which Michael by God's command wished to hide, Deut. XXXIV. 6, but the Devil to bring out into the open, so that the people might be enticed to idolatry (that this was to be feared if that body had appeared, Josephus IV. 8 also testifies); from which Jude took these things, using it as a concession. The Rabbis were accustomed to attribute to both angels and great men those words which they could have plausibly said. Such is that which we shall have concerning Enoch, and that which Heb. XII. 21, Acts VII. 26. You have similar things in the Midrash on Deuteronomy, in Aboth of Rabbi Nathan, and others. Origen calls that book of the 'Assumption' in De Principiis III. 2, and Epiphanius in the Synopsis, nor do I doubt that the narrative which is in Clement, Strom. VI, is taken from the same place. Origen mentions a similar struggle between good and bad angels concerning the salvation and destruction of Abraham in his 35th homily on Luke. In the Hebrew book which is called דברי הימים של משה, certain words of the Devil to Moses before his death are reported, and the ministries which the angels showed to Moses. But the words which are read here do not appear in that book. Whence it is credible that that book of the 'Assumption' has long since perished. Ἀρχάγγελος is שר ראשון Dan. ch. X. 13, where the discourse is about the same Michael. See also 1 Thess. IV. 16.

A 'judgment of blasphemy' is the vengeance of blasphemy from the object, that is, concerning blasphemy, not the vengeance which one takes by cursing or blaspheming. Κρί-

σιν ἐπενεγκεῖν is to bring judgment or vengeance. Not to revile good Angels, what is singular about that? And what would it contribute here, that Angels do not revile? Or, that the word Judas uses, do not blaspheme? Who would presume that Angels, when they must contend with the impious, revile authorities, or afflict them with insults and blasphemies? Furthermore, if malediction is to be understood not as an insult, but as a just judgment, when Angels pray for the rebuke or malediction of the Lord: do they not in that sense revile? Just as Moses, in decreeing and pronouncing a curse upon any transgressor of the law, is rightly said to revile them, by the voice of the law, and δικαϛικῶς judicially, as a ministerial Judge, subordinate to God the principal Judge. That rebuke of the Lord also is not verbal but real, the most grave vengeance of God the just Judge, on account of the blasphemy which Michael prayed against the Devil. Cornelius à Lapide: Note, he says, St. Michael could have restrained the insolence of the Devil by himself and by his own power, because he is more powerful and superior to him, but he preferred out of modesty and reverence to transfer this work and this mighty work to God, whom he prefers as he does in name, so much more he refers to him in heart and work, and to ask from him that he might compress the Devil. You say: it is said that the Archangel disputed with the Devil about the body of Moses, there is no mention of blasphemy. Learn that that dispute was according to common opinion in the cause of idolatry, which the Devil desired to be promoted, contending that the body of Moses should not be buried, or striving to dig it out from the monument in which God himself had buried it, so that it might be raised up for worship. 'I admit that opinion: but we learn from the words of St. Jude that the 'discourse' or disputation of the Devil was joined with blasphemy, just as also that Satanic institution was directed toward blaspheming the name of the Lord on account of the idolatry to be sanctioned among the people of God.

We readily agree that those words ἐπιτιμήσαι σοι Κύριος are the same as the words in Zech. 3:2. But the Angel there who is imprecating Satan is an Angel, not one who bears the person of Jehovah, but Jehovah himself, the Angel of the new covenant, the Son of God, which we demonstrated in the cited passage. As for the comments which Grotius has from the Papists concerning an Angel who was formerly the defender of the Jews and is now the defender of the Christians, Hermas does not deserve to be heard, St. John has nothing, for whom Michael is the one fighting for us, whose ἐξυσία is celebrated there with a loud voice, that is, Christ, Rev. 12:7, 10. Whom we also judge to be understood in Dan. 12:1 by the great Prince Michael. But that Michael the Archangel, whom Jude names here, is different from that great Prince, that the former is from the number of created angels, while the latter is the Lord and Creator of the created angels, the Prince of the host of the Lord, from a comparison with Josh. 5:14. We establish Rev. 12:7, 10, and we taught that the passage in Dan. 10:13 does not hinder us in the explanation of the same: not to mention that Franc. Junius also explains Michael in this passage as the Son of God. Whom Pareus likewise explained as the Son of God, as did also Joh. Cocceius in his Last Words of Moses § 1722.

Furthermore, we are not taught that Michael wished to hide the body of Moses, Deut. 34:6, but that God himself buried the body of Moses: whether that was done by the angelic work of Michael, or indeed immediately by God, is not expressed, and it is not even possible to gather from that whether that dispute was over burying the body of Moses, or indeed over digging it up from the grave? The former of which Cornel. à Lap. asserted, and attributed to Chrysostom, Ambrose, and others; the latter pleased the blessed Joh. Gerhard and his blessed Son, Joh. Ernst Gerhard, who praises the same authors for that opinion. It could therefore be said that, since the Devil contended with the Archangel not without blasphemy against God, with a most grave imprecation, a most severe punishment was denounced against him, and the body of Moses was withdrawn by the LORD. That it had already been buried, the Mosaic passage testifies; but it was not simply withdrawn, but life was restored, and it was indeed withdrawn into heaven, from which Moses appeared on the holy mountain with Elijah, who was likewise taken up into heaven, but without death and burial, and thus alive, Matt. XVII.

Oecumenius indeed maintains that the Devil did not wish to grant this to the Archangel who was about to provide service in burying the body of Moses, but brought an accusation against Moses on account of the killing of the Egyptian, as if Moses were not worthy of that honorable burial, with whom Aretha also agrees; the Jews in Capellus in Spicilegium, p. 128, bring forward another cause of the litigation. B. Gerhard says the cause of the dispute was that the Devil attempted to reveal the body of Moses, which had been buried secretly by the Lord in the valley, to the sons of Israel to provide an occasion for idolatry, to which opinion Thomas Anglicus, Cajetan, Salmero, Titelmann, Arias Montanus, Gagneius, Saa, Fevardentius, Estius, Lancellotus, Lorinus, Cornelius a Lapide, Tirinus in the place cited are brought; Didacus in his Sermon on Moses, Stella on Luke, Cosmas Magalianus in his preface to Joshua, Franz de Mendoza Vol. I on the books of Kings, p. 144, Alphonsus de Mendoza in Theological Controversies, p. 44. Jacobus Bonfrerius in the Pentateuch, p. 1062, Leonh. Marius in the Pentateuch, p. 1066, as well as B. Chemnitius part I of the Loci Theologici, p. 124, B. Walther in his Harmony of the Bible, Hornejus in this place, as also Chrysostom and Ambrose, from which the superstitious and idolatrous cult of relics in the Papacy can be refuted; since God himself, to preclude the occasion of worshipping the relics of Moses, buried Moses, and wished Michael to resist the Devil who was intending the cult. The figment of Serarius, even if it seems probable to Cornelius, namely that the Devil contended that the body of Moses should be brought into the land of promise, and not be buried outside of it in Moab, as a region addicted to him in the cult of idols, so that he might not receive any harm from it, just as he complained he had received from the tomb of St. Babylas in Daphne, as the life of St. Babylas has it, and from it Baronius Vol. IV, is unworthy of being refuted.

But if it is inquired whence St. Jude took these things, there are indeed those who derive them from the Apocryphal book of the Assumption of Moses, Salmero, Cornelius a Lapide, Tirinus, whom some think lost, also Schindler in his Pentaglot Lexicon, p. 1041, to whom Grotius here adds himself: Others, however, wish them to still exist, such as Gilbert Gaulmin, who edited that book in Hebrew, printed at Constantinople and Venice, at Paris with notes and a Latin version: But how will it be proved that that book existed in the time of St. Jude? Who will allow himself to be persuaded that the Apostle, if that had even existed then, would have wished to bring forward anything like history from such a fabulous writing, since by that reasoning the Jews could easily have presumed that that book contained true histories? For although, as Estius objects, the Apostle, endowed with the divine Spirit, could distinguish between the true and false of such a book, it was nevertheless in the interest of the faithful that a book in which false things were contained should not be brought forward and approved: lest those false things in it should also be believed to have been approved. St. Athanasius in his Synopsis certainly rejected this Assumption of Moses in his own time along with another writing akin to this, whose title is the Testament of Moses: Compare Sixtus Senensis, book II of the Bibliotheca, p. 109. Others derive these from the book of Enoch, likewise Apocryphal, with a similar judgment, deserving the same censure; which Cornelius observes regarding Jerome in his epistle to Titus and Origen in book IV of De Principiis. Others say these proceeded from the tradition of the elders; to which, however, if they are admitted, nothing is lost from the perfection of Scripture, nor is anything added to Papistic traditions, because such things do not pertain to articles of faith or the necessary institution of morals. But what need is there to inquire much whence Jude, who was inspired by God, had these things? Since through divine inspiration, or from the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, he had everything that he handed down, just like other men divinely inspired who were writers of the Canonical books.

But St. Jude, indicating that there was a dispute about the body of Moses, speaks of that very body which was buried on Mount Nebo, not of that, as Grotius feigns with Fr. Junius in the Theatrum Biblicum, p. 1982, about which Moses prophesied, and which he prefigured with ceremonies and types, whose antitype was Joshua the Priest, Zech. III. 1, 2, which he says was the body of both Moses and Christ: of Moses indeed insofar as he prophesied about it through oracles, figures, and sacrifices; but of Christ, insofar as in Christ is the completion of the Mosaic prophecies, types, and sacrifices, Col. II. 17. But by that reasoning the body of Christ could also have been called the body of David and other Prophets. Why therefore would the Archangel be said to have disputed specifically about the body of Moses?

Latin:

Vers. 9.

Ὁ δὲ Μιχαὴλ ὁ Ἀρχάγγελος, ὅτε τῷ Διαβόλῳ διακρι- νόμενος διελέγετο περὶ τῶ Μωσέως σώματος, ἐκ ἐτόλμη- σε κρίσιν ἐπενεγκεῖν βλασφημίας, ἀλλ' εἶπεν, ἐπιτιμήσαι σοι Κύριος.) Κρίσις βλασφημίας, 2. Petr. cap. II. vers. 11. κρί- σις βλάσφημος, est ultio, quam quis sumit maledicendo. Negaverat in epistola Simeon, id Angelos facere, ubi cum imperiis, quanquam impiis, certandum habent, quod ibi exposuimus. Addit Judas amplius, ne tum quidem id fa- cere Angelos, ubi cum Diabolo certamen habent, qui & i- pse, quanquam impius, potestatem quandam à DEO in hunc mundum accepit, unde κοσμοκράτωρ dicitur. Illa verba ἐπιτιμήσαι σοι Κύριος. nihil sensu differunt, sono pene nihil ab illis, quæ sunt in Græco Zach. cap. II. v. 2. ἐπιτιμήσαι Κύ- ριος ἐν σοὶ: יגער יהוה בך, quæ verba pronunciat An- gelus magnus, qui & יהוה ibide mvocatur, quod Dei par- tes agat adversus Diabolum. Illum qui ibi & Angelus & יהוה dicitur, esse Michaelem diximus, hoc argumento, quod ille eo tempore quasi defensor esset Judæorum, Dan XII. 5. nunc sub Christo Christianorum, Apoc. XII. 7. Quo spectat & Hermas III. 8. Sed & eadem verba Michaeli con- traDiabolum decertanti de corpore Mosis, quod Michael ex Dei imperio volebat abscondere, Deut. XXXIV. 6. Dia- bolus autem in apertum proferre, ut ad idololatriam popu- lus alliceretur, (quod sc. metuendum fuisse, si id corpus ap- paruisset, testatur & Josephus IV. 8.) tribuerat scriptor li- bri, qui Ebraice dicebatur פטירת משה: Græce vero ἀνάληψις Μωσέως: unde hæc desumpsit Judas, velut con- cesso utens. Solebant Rabbini & Angelis & magnis homi- nibus ea tribuere verba, quæ veresimiliter dicere potuerunt. Tale illud, quod de Enocho habebimus, & illud quod Ebr. XII. 21. Act. VII. 26. Similia habes in Midrasch ad Deute- ronomium, in Aboth Rabbini Mathan & aliis. Librum illum ἀναλήψεως nominant Origenes περὶ ἀρχῶν III. 2. & Epiphanius in Synopsi, nec dubito, quin indidem sit de- sumpta narratio, quæ est apud Clementem Strom. VI. Si- mile certamen inter Angelos bonos & malos de Abrahæ sa- lute & interitu commemorat Origenes homilia in Lucam 35. In libro Ebraico, qui vocatur דברי הימיח של משה referuntur verba quædam Diaboli ad Mosen ante mortem e- rus & ministeria, quæ Angeli Mosi exhibuere. Sed quæ hic leguntur verba, in eo libro non comparent. Unde credibile sit librum illum ἀναλήψεως pridem intercidisse. Ἀρχάγγε- λος est שר ראשון Dan. c. X. 13. ubi de eodem Michaele ser- mo. Vide & 1. Thess. IV. 16.

Κρίσις βλασφημίας ultio est blasphemiæ ab ob- jecto, id est, de blasphemia, non ultio, quam quis sumit maledicendo vel blasphemando. Κρί- a

σιν ἐπενεγκεῖν est judicium vel ultionem ferre. Non maledicere bonos Angelos, quid singu- lare est? Et quid huc faceret, quod Angeli non maledicant? Vel, quod Verbum Judas adhi- bet, non blasphement? Ecquis præsumet An- gelos, cum certandum ipsis cum impiis, impe- riis maledicere, vel convitiis, & blasphemiis ea af- ficere? Porro si maledictio intelligenda non con- vitii, sed justi judicii, quum imprecentur Angeli increpationem, vel maledictionem Domini: an- non ea ratione maledicunt? quemadmodum Mo- ses maledictum decernens & pronuncians quem- vis legis transgressorem maledicere illis recte dici- tur, voce legis, & δικαϛικῶς judicialiter, tanquam Judex ministerialis, Deo Judici principali subor- dinatus. Illa etiam increpatio Domini non verba- lis sed realis est ultio gravissima Dei justi Judicis, ob blasphemiam, quam imprecatus Michaël est Diabolo. Cornelius à Lapide: Nota, inquit, poterat S. Michaël per se suaque vi compescere inso- lentiam Diaboli, quia eo potentior est & superior, sed maluit ex modestia & reverentia hoc opus & hanc virtutem transferre in Deum, quem uti no- mine præfert, ita multo magis corde & opere refert, ab eoque postulare, ut Diabolum comprimeret. Di- cis: disceptasse cum Diabolo Archangelum dici de corpore Mosis, non fieri mentionem blasphemiæ. Disce- ptationem illam fuisse ex communi sententia in cau- sa idololatriæ, quam Diabolus premotam cupie- bat, corpus Mosis, ne sepeliretur, contendens, vel id è monumento, quo Deus ipse id condiderat, eruere satagens, ut ad cultum erigeretur. 'Admitto illam sententiam: sed διάλεξιν vel disputationem Diaboli cum blasphemia conjunctam fuisse, ex verbis S. Judæ discimus, quemadmodum etiam ad nomen Domini blasphemandum propter idolo- latriam in populo Dei sanciendam illud Satanicum institutum directum fuit.

Illa vero verba ἐπιτιμήσαι σοι Κύριος facile ea- dem esse cum verbis Zach. III. 2. annuimus. Sed ibi Angelus imprecans id Satanæ est Angelus, non qui Jehova personam gerat, sed Jehova ipse, Ange- lus fœderis novi, Filius Dei, quod loco laudato de- monstravimus. De Angelo vero defensore quondam Judæorum, eodemque nunc Christia- norum defensore, quæ commenta à Papistis ha- bet Grotius, Hermas non meretur audiri, S. Jo- hannes nihil habet, cui Michaël pro nobis pu- gnans est, cujus ἐξυσία voce magna decantata ibi, hoc est, Christus, Apoc. XII. 7. 10. Quem etiam Dan. XII. 5. per magnum Principem Michaëlem intelligi censemus. Michaëlem vero Archangelum, quam hic Judas nuncupat, ab illo Principe ma- gno diversum, illum è numero creatorurn Ange- lorum, hunc Angelorum creatorurn Dominum & Creatorem esse, Principem exercitus Domini è collatione Job. V. 14. Apoc. XII. 7. 10. statuimus, Nec officere nobis locum Dan. X. 13. in explicatione ejusdem docuimus: ut taceamus, Franc. Junium etiam hoc loco Michaëlem de Filio Dei explicare. Quem pariter de Filio Dei exposuit Pareus, ut & Job. Coccejus in ultimis Mosis §. 1722.

Porro Michaëlem voluisse corpus Mosis abs- condere, Deut. XXXIV. 6. non docemur, sed De- um ipsumet Mosis corpus sepeliisse: Angeline Mi- chaëlis opera id factum, an vero immediate à Deo, no exprimitur, ac ne id quidem inde colligere est, quod διάλεξις illa fuerit super corpore Mosis sepe- liendo, an vero è sepulchro eruendo? Quorum prius Cornel. à Lap. asseruit, & Chrysostomo, Ambrosio, aliisque tribuit; posterius placuit B. Job. Gerhardo, ejusque B. Filio, Joh. Ernesto Gerhardi, eosdem autores pro ea sententia laudanti. Dici itaque possit, quum non absque blasphemia Dei con- tenderet Diabolus cum Archangelo, cum im- precatione gravissima, severissimam vindictam illi denunciatam, & a DOMINO corpus Mo- sis subductum esse. Quod jam sepultum fuisse locus Mosaicus testatur; subductum autem non simpliciter fuit, sed reddita vita, & subductum quidem in cœlum, e quo cum Elia, itidem in cœ- lum, sed citra mortem & sepulturam, adeoque vi- vo transvecto Moses in monte sacro apparuit, Matth. XVII.

Oecumenius quidem statuit, quod Archan- gelo in Mosis corpore sepeliendo ministerium præbituro id concedere noluerit Diabolus, sed accusationem attulerit contra Mosen propter cæ- dem Ægyptii, quasi Moses honorifica ista sepul- tura dignus non esset, cum quo & Arethas fa- cit; aliam causam litigii proferunt Judæi apud Capell. in spici. p. 128. B. Gerhardus causam disce- ptationis dicit, quod Diabolus conatus sit cor- pus Mosis a Domino in valle clam sepultum filiis Israël patefacere ad occasionem præbendam idolatriæ, in quam sententiam adducitur Thomas Anglicus, Cajetanus, Salmero, Titelman- nus, Ariasmontanus, Gagnejus, Saa, Fevardentius, Estius, Lancellotus, Lorinus, Cornelius a Lapide, Tirinus in b. l. Didacus Serm. de Mose, Stella in Lucam, Cosmas Magalianus præfat. in Josuam, Franz. de Mendoza Tom. I. in libb. Reg. p. 144. Alphonsus de Mendoza controv. Theol. pag. 44. Jacobus Bonfrerius in Pentat. p. 1062. Leonh. Ma- rius in Pentat. pag. 1066. necnon B. Chemnitius part. I. LL. p. 124. B. Waltherus in Harm. Bibl. Hornejus in h. l. ut & Chrysostomus & Ambrosius, e qua cultus superstitiosus & idololatricus reli- quiarum in Papatu refelli potest; siquidem Deus ipse, ut occasionem præcluderet reliquias Mosis colendi, Mosen sepeliverit, Michaëlemque Dia- bolo cultum intendenti resistere voluerit. Serarii figmentum, etsi Cornelio probabile videatur, con- tendisse nempe Diabolum, ut corpus Mosis inferretur in terram promissionis, nec extra eam in Moab, utpote regione sibi in idolorum cultu addicta, se- peliretur, ne ab eo aliquod damnum acciperet, uti accepisse se a S. Babyla sepulchro, in Daphne questus est, sicut habet vita S. Babylæ, & ex ea Baronius Tom. IV. indignum est, quod refellatur.

Unde autem hæc desumpserit S. Judas, si disquira- tur, sunt quidem, qui e libro Apocrypho ἀναλή- ψεως Μωϋσέως hæc deducunt, Salmero, Cornelius a Lapide, Tirinus, quem nonnulli deperditum pu- tant, etiam Schindlerus in Lexic. Pentagl. p. 1041. quibus hic accedit Grotius: Alii tamen etiamnum extare volunt, utpote Gilbertus Gaulminus, qui li- brum illum Ebraice Constantinopoli, & Venetiis excusum, Parisiis cum notis ac versione Latina edi- dit: Sed tempore S. Judæ librū illum extitisse, quo- modo probabitur? Ecquis persuaderi sibi patietur, Apostolum ex ejusmodi fabulosa scripta, si maxi- me id tum extitisset, aliquid instar historiæ adduce- re voluisse, quum ea ratione facile Judæi præsume- re potuissent, librum illum veras historias cotine- re? Quamvis enim, quod obvertit Estius, Apostol9 Spiritu divino præditus discernere potuerit inter ejusmodi libri vera & falsa, intererat tamen fide- lium, ne liber, in quo falsa continebantur, adduce- retur, & probaretur: ne & falsa illa in eo probasse crederentur. Reprobavit utique suo jam tempore S. Athanasius in Synopsi hanc Mosis Ascensionem cum alia huic affini fcriptura, cujus titulus est Te- stamentum Mofis : Conf. Sixtus Senensis l. II. Bibl. pag. 109. Alii hæc ex libro Enoch. itidem Apocrypho, parili judicio, deducunt, eandem merentes censu- ram; quod de Hieronymo in epist. ad Tit. & Origine IV. περὶ ἀρχῶν observat Cornelius. Alii ex tradi- tione majorum hæc profecta esse dicunt; quibus tamen, si admittantur, nec Scripturæ perfectioni quicquam decedit, nec Papisticis traditionibus quicquam accedit, quia talia non pertinent ad ar- ticulos fidei aut morum institutionem necessariam. Quid vero opus multum disquirere, unde hæc ha- buerit Judas θεόπνευστος? Quum per θεοπνευσί- αν, vel ex inspiratione Spiritus Sancti omnia habu- erit, quæ tradidit, pariter ut alii viri divinitus in- spirati librorum Canonicorum Scriptores.

De corpore autem Mofis disceptationem fuisse S. Judas indicans loquitur de illo ipso corpore, quod in monte Nebo sepultum est, non de eo, ut cum Fr. Junio fingit Grotius in Theatr. Bibl. pag. 1982. de quo Moses vaticinatus est, & quod præfi- guravit ceremoniis & typis, cujus antitypus fuit Jo- sua Sacerdos, Zach. III. 1. 2. quod & Mosis, & Chri- sti corpus fuisse, ait: Mosis quidem quatenus is de eo prophetavit, oraculis, figuris, sacrificiis; Christi vero, quatenus in Christo est complementum Mosaicorum vaticiniorum, typorum, sacrificiorum, Col. II. 17. Sed ea ratione corpus Christi etiam corpus Davidis & aliorum Prophetarum dici potuisset. Cur ergo peculiariter de corpore Mosis disceptasse dicere- tur Archangelus?

## 1:10
Verse 10.

But these men, whatever things they do not know, they blaspheme] 2 Pet. II. 12, in things which they are ignorant of, blaspheming, where we said that the Carpocratians did not understand how much use laws and governments were to upright men. See also what we said on Rom. XIII.

Others explain these things regarding blasphemy against God and divine matters: Even Cornelius: The Simonians, he says, and the Gnostics blaspheme with intolerable audacity and impudence, and curse those things which they are ignorant of, and which surpass the grasp of them, as being carnal, namely God, and the attributes of God, the mysteries of Christ, and heavenly, sublime, and divine things. Thus Epiphanius, heresy XXVI. The Gnostics, he says, blaspheme not only Abraham, Moses, Elijah, and the whole choir of the Prophets, but also God, who chose them, etc.

Ὄσα δὲ φυσικῶς ὡς τὰ ἄλογα ζῶα ἐπίστανται, ἐν τούτοις φθείρονται] Most living creatures observe the distinctions of the sexes. From them at least those men ought to have learned. But they pervert this very thing both by their actions and by their dogma of ἀδιαφορίας. Compare what we have said on 2 Peter II, verse 16, where there is ἄφωνον, that which is there in the preceding [verses] and in this place ἄλογον: the Latins are accustomed to call them mute animals, for the reason that they lack the use of speech. Φθείρονται ישׁחתו, that is, they corrupt themselves, the passive for a reciprocal verb. Jeremiah [speaks] of such as ובערו, they become brutish, chapter X, v. 8.

Oecumenius explained these things thus: Whatever they know by natural impulse or appetite as irrational, or mute or brute animals, these they pursue while acting senselessly, and [they are] like horses or swine desiring females. Estius: He finds, he says, and explains what he had said before: They indeed defile the flesh. But those things, he says, which they know naturally by the senses alone, as if they were animals lacking reason, such as those things especially which they perceive by taste and touch, in these they are corrupted through gluttony and drunkenness and various lusts, that corruption, namely, by which the dignity of the human condition is disgraced and harmed in the body, which carnal sins are certainly accustomed to do. Naturally is opposed to reason and judgment, which beasts lack, to which therefore men become similar when the brutal motions of the senses lack the bridle of reason or do not restrain or moderate. Epiphanius explains this passage in the heresy of the Gnostics. Similarly, Blessed Gerhard: 'But those things which naturally, etc.' that is, those things which they know like brute animals, namely what manner is to be observed in food, drink, sleep, and the use of Venus, are corrupted in them, namely through harmful abuse.

Latin:

Vers 10.

Οὗτοι δὲ ὅσα μὲν οὐκ οἴδασι, βλασφημῦσι] 2. Petr. II. 12. ἐν οἷς ἀγνοῦσι βλασφημῦντες, ubi diximus Carpocratia- nos non intellexisse, quanto usui viris probis essent leges & imperia. Vide etiam quæ diximus ad Rom. XIII.

De blasphemia in Deum & res divinas alii hæc explicant: Etiam Cornelius: Simoniam, inquit, & Gnostici intoleranda audacia & impudentia blasphe- mant, & maledicunt ea, quæ ignorant, quæq; eorum, utpote carnalium captum superant, scilicet Deum, Deique attributa, mysteria Christi, res cælestes, sub- limes, & divinas. Ita Epiphanius hæres. XXVI. Blasphemant Gnostici, ait, non solum Abraham, Mo- sen, Eliam, & omnem Prophetarum chorum, sed eti- am Deum, qui ipsos elegit, &c.

Ὄσα δὲ φυσικῶς ὡς τὰ ἄλογα ζῶα ἐπίστανται, ἐν τούτοις φθείρονται] Pleraque animantia observant sexuum discri- mina. Ab istis saltem discere debuerant isti. At hoc i- psum illi & actibus suis & ἀδιαφορίας dogmate pervertunt. Confer quæ diximus ad 2. Petr. II. vers. 16. ubi est ἄφωνον, id quod ibi in præcedentibus & hoc loco ἄλογον: muta ani- mantia ea solent dicere Latini, ideo quod sermonis usu care- ant. Φθείρονται ישׁחתו, id est, semel depravant, passivum pro verbo reciproco. Jeremias de talibus ובערו bruse- scunt cap. X. v. 8.

Oecumenius hæc ita exposuit: Quæcunque na- turali impetu vel appetitione tanquam irrationabi- lia, seu muta vel bruta animantia norunt, hæc sectantur infanientes, fæminarumque appetentes e- qui, vel porci. Estius: Reperit, inquit, & expli- cat, quod ante dixerat: Carnem quidem maculant. Quæ vero, inquit, naturaliter solis sensibus, ac si essent animalia rationis expertia cognoscunt, ut ea maxime, quæ gustus tactuque percipiunt, in iis per comessationes & ebrietates, & varias libidi- nes corrumpuntur, ea nimirum corruptione, quæ dignitas humanæ conditionis in corpore debonesta- tur ac læditur, quod utique facere solent peccata carnalia. Naturaliter opponitur rationi & judi- cio, quo bestiæ carent, quibus proinde similes siunt ho- mines, quando brutales sensuum motus fræno rationis non cohibent aut moderantur. Exponit hunc lo- cum Epiphanius in hæresi Gnosticorum. Similiter B. Gerhardus: Quæ vero naturaliter, &c. id est, quæ tanquam bruta animantia norunt, nempe quis modus in cibo, potu, somno & usu veneris observandus, in illis corrumpuntur, videlicet per noxium abusum.

## 1:11
Verse 11.

Woe to them) It is a voice lamenting their condition. It is the same voice as in Matthew 11:21 and often elsewhere, both in the Gospels and in the Apocalypse, as in 1 Corinthians 11:16.

Because they have walked in the way of Cain) Cain took away the fleeting life from his brother: they take away eternal life from their brothers. To walk in the way (הלך בדרך) is to imitate the deeds of someone, 2 Peter chapter 2, verse 16.

And have run greedily in the error of Balaam for reward) That is, they have committed the same error as Balaam, and that for a reward. 'Have run greedily' (ἐξεχύθησαν) means they have erred, they have declined. Just as Psalm 72:2, כאין שפכה אשרי, in Greek 'my steps had well-nigh slipped' (παρ' ὀλίγον ἐξεχύθη τὰ διασήματά με). But 'for reward' (μισθῶ) stands for 'for a reward' (ἀντὶ μισθῶ). Thus the Greeks say: 'I bought it for five drachmae.' Heraclitus: 'It is hard to fight with anger; for it buys what it wants with the soul.' Aeschines: 'The priestess was bought with blood.' Menander concerning the adulterer: 'For it is the price of death.' The sense of this passage is: Just as Balaam was an instigator of lusts for the sake of a reward, so also are they. Compare 2 Peter 2:15 and what is said there.

And perished in the gainsaying of Core) It is an aorist for the future: or for the present, so that we may take 'they perish' for 'they rush into destruction': 'The gainsaying of Core', that is, 'as that of Core'. For that particle is often understood among the Hebrews. Here is that word which in the books of Moses is translated as 'what', which often signifies sedition. That was a sedition against Moses, this against Christ. See what we have said concerning the word 'to be spoken against' (ἀντιλέγεσθαι) in Luke chapter 2, verse 34, Romans chapter 10, verse 21, Hebrews chapter 12, verse 5. All these things denounce to the Carpocratians that destruction into which they fell through Barchochebas, the parts of his sect.

Blessed Gerhard understands this concerning the diverse vices and sins which flourished among the heretics of his time. They follow the example of Cain, who first made a divorce from the Church of God, Genesis 4:5, 'The Burden of the Church', chapter 28. Through Cain the Apostle taxes envy. For Cain killed his brother out of envy. Through Balaam he taxes avarice, who prophesied evilly for a reward. Through Core, who contradicted Moses and stirred up sedition against him, he taxes disobedience. Through clouds he denotes pride. For the proud lift themselves up like clouds, obscuring the true Sun; they are without the water of wisdom, and are carried about by the winds of vanity. Through fruitless trees is understood sloth. For the idle bring forth not good, but indigestible or late fruit. Through the raging waves of the sea he understands the irascible. Through 'spots' (σπιλάδας) in feasts, the gluttonous. He names these three, says Cornelius, above others, because they were three enemies of the faith and holiness of God, and wished to seduce the faithful and destroy the Church, whence they were types and forerunners of Simon, the Gnostics, and the heretics. For Cain killed Abel, the first offspring of the faith and the Church: Balaam wished to destroy the people of the Hebrews, who were worshippers of the true God, and his Church. Core, by coveting the priesthood, rebelled against Moses, and by his schism made the synagogue empty and destroyed it. Concerning the followers of Balaam noted by Saint John, see Apocalypse 2:19. Philastrius in his book on Heresies lists the Balaamites among the heretics. For their heresy was that it is permitted to commit fornication and to eat things sacrificed to idols, which Cornelius observes here. Blessed Gerhard in 2 Peter 2, p. 284, teaches that false teachers follow the way of Balaam: 1. By reason of false doctrine, because as Balaam was disobedient to the mouth of the Lord, and went against His Word to Balak, King of the Moabites: so false teachers desert the way of truth prescribed in the Word of the Lord. 2. By reason of an impious life. Just as Balaam, for his own advantage and to retain royal favor, gave counsel to Balak that the daughters of the people of Moab should entice the Israelites into love for them and at the same time also into idolatry: so false teachers are authors to others for following the license of the flesh and lusts. 3. By reason of avarice, because false teachers, just as Balaam, depart from the straight way of truth for the sake of revenues, prebends, and dignities. What Grotius here mixes in concerning the Carpocratians following Barchochebas, without the authority of any ancient history, neither fits here by reason of time, nor in any way agrees as to the matter itself. For Barchochebas was a Jew; Carpocrates and his followers professed themselves to be Christians. He sold himself as the Messiah, concerning whom Dio writes in 'Hadrian', which Baronius refers to the year of Christ 130, the eleventh of Hadrian: At which time indeed the leader of the Jews was Barchochebas; which name, if one wishes to interpret it, signifies a star (for because it had been written in the oracles: 'A star shall rise out of Jacob'; he proclaimed himself sent by God), a man who, although in the rest of his manner of life he was a bloody and nefarious robber, yet by that very appellation, as if a star fallen from heaven, he falsely feigned that he would bring light and the hope of salvation to those who, as men from the number of slaves, were oppressed by the heavy yoke of servitude and afflicted by miserable hardships. But the Carpocratians by no means accepted Barchochebas as the Messiah: rather, they most impudently affirmed that they themselves and their teacher Carpocrates were better than Christ. For they blasphemed that our Lord Jesus Christ was a mere man, and that he lived a life purer in holiness, not only that he was equal, if he wished to renounce the world more than he did. Barchochebas not only did not admit those who professed themselves to be Christians, but even afflicted them most grievously: Concerning which Justin Martyr to Antoninus Pius: 'In the recent Jewish war, Barchochebas, the leader and prince of the Jewish defection, ordered only the Christians to be dragged to severe punishments unless they denied Christ and cursed him.' And Dio: 'Barchochebas, the leader of the Jewish faction, killed with all manner of tortures those Christians who were unwilling to bear aid to him against the Roman soldiers.' What, therefore, Carpocrates has to do with Barchochebas, or either of them with the present passage, does not appear.

Latin:

Vers. 11.

Οὐαὶ ἀυτοῖς) Est vox conditionem eorum deplorans. Est eadem vox Matth. 11, 21. & alibi sæpe, tum in Evangeliis, tum in Apocalypsi, ut 1. Cor. 11, 16.

Ὅτι τῇ ὁδῷ τῶ Καΐν ἐπορεύθησαν) Cain fratri vitam cadu- cam ademit: illi fratribus adimunt æternam. Πορεύεσθαι ὁ- δῷ הלך בדרך, est facta alicujus imitari, 2. Petr. cap. 2, vers. 16.

Καὶ τῇ πλάνῃ τῶ Βαλαὰμ μισθῶ ἐξεχύθησαν) Id est eun- dem errorem errarunt, quem Balaam, idque pro mercede Ἐξεχύθησαν est errarunt, declinarunt. Sicut Ps. 72, v. 2. כאין שפכה אשרי Græce παρ' ὀλίγον ἐξεχύθη τὰ διασή- ματά με. Μισθῶ vero pro ἀντὶ μισθῶ. Sic dicunt Græci: ὠνησάμην πέντε δραχμῶν. Heraclitus: Χαλεπὸν θυμῷ μά- χεσθαι. ψυχῆς γὰρ ὠνεῖται. Æschines: Αἵματος ἡ ἱερείη ὠνία. Menander de adultero: Θανάτε γάρ ἐσιν ὤνιον Sen- sus hujus loci est: Sicut Balaam mercedis causa incentor fu- it libidinum, sic & illi. Confer 2. Petr. 2, vers. 15. & ibi dicta.

Καὶ τῇ ἀντιλογίᾳ τῶ Κορὲ ἀπώλοντο) Est ἀόριστος pro fu- turo: aut pro præsenti, ut pereunt sumamus pro ruunt in exitium: Ἀντιλογία τῶ Κορὲ, id est, ὡς τῶ Κορὲ. Nam il- la particula sæpe apud Ebræos subintelligitur. hic est ea vox, quæ in libris Mosis transfertur quod sæpe seditionem significat. Illa erat seditio con- tra Mosen, hæc contra Christum. Vide quæ diximus de ver- bo ἀντιλέγεσθαι Luc. cap. 2, v. 34. Rom. cap 10, v. 21. Ebr. cap. 12, vers. 5. Hæc omnia denuntiant Carpocratianis e- xitium illud, in quod per Barchochebam, sectæ rpartes ejus, inciderunt.

De diversis vitiis & peccatis, quæ inter hære- ticos sui temporis viguerint, hæc intelligit B. Gerhardus. Sequuntur exemplum Caini, qui pri- mus ab Ecclesia Dei divortium fecit, Gen. IV. 5. onus Ecclesiæ, cap. XXVIII. Per Cain Aposto- lus taxat invidiam. Cain enim ex invidia occi- dit fratrem. Per Balaam taxat avaritiam, qui male pro mercede divinavit. Per Core, qui con- tradixit Mosi & seditionem contra eum movit, taxat inobedientiam. Per nubes denotat superbiam. Superbi namq; se elevant ut nubes, obscurantes verum Solem, sunt sine aqua sapientiæ, & circumferuntur à ventis vanitatis: Per arbores infructuosas intel- ligitur acedia. Nam otiosi non bonum sed indige- stum vel tardum fructum afferunt. Per fluctus feri maris intelligit iracundos. Per σπιλάδας in epulis gulosos. Nomines hos tres, inquit Cornelius, præ aliis, quia tres fuere Dei fidei & sanctitatis hostes, ac fideles seducere & Ecclesiam perdere voluerunt, un- de fuerunt Simonis, Gnosticorum & hæreticorum typi & prodromi. Cain enim Abelem primam fidei & Ecclesiæ propaginem occidit: Balaam voluit perde- re populum Ebræorum, qui erat veri Dei cultor, ejusque Ecclesia. Core ambiendo sacerdotium rebella- vit Mosi, suoque schismate synagogam fecavit & perdi- dit. De Blaami sectatoribus à S. Johanne notatis, vid. Apoc. II. 19. Philastrius l. de Hær. Balaamitas recenset inter hæreticos. Hæresis enim eorum erat licere fornicari & vesci idolothytis, quod hic ob- servat Cornelius. B. Gerhardus in 2. Petr. II. p. 284. falsos Doctores viam Balaami sequi docet, 1. ra- tione falsæ doctrinæ, quia ut Balaam fuit ori Domini inobediens, & contra ipsius Verbum ad Regem Moa- bitarum Balacum abiit: Sic falsi Doctores viam ve- ritatis in Verbo Domini præscriptam deserunt. 2. Ra- tione impiæ vitæ. Sicut Balaam sui commodi & re- tinendæ gratiæ Regiæ dedit Balaco consilium, ut filiæ populi Moabitici in sui amorem & simul etiam ad idolatolatriam pellicerent Israëlitas : Sic falsi Doctores ad licentiam carnis & libidines sectandas aliis sunt autores. 3. Ratione avaritiæ, quia falsi Doctores æque ac Bileamus ob reditus, præbendas & digni- tates à recta veritatis via decedunt. Quæ de Car- pocratianis sectatis Barchochebam citra ullius hi- storiæ antiquæ autoritate hic Grotius admiscet, ne- que ratione temporis huc faciunt, neque ullate- nus quoad rem ipsam congruunt. Barchochebas e- nim Judæus erat, Carpocrates & sectatores ej9 Chri- stianos se profitebantur. Ille sese venditabat pro Messia, de quo Dio in Hadriano, quæ ad ann. Chri- sti 130. Hadriani undecimum refert Baronius: Quo quidem tempore Judæorum Dux erat Barchochebas; quod nomen si lubet interpretari, astrum significat (nam quod scriptum esset in oraculis : Orietur stella ex Jacob; se divinitus missum pronunciabat) vir quanquam reliqua vitæ ratione cruentus ac nefa- rius prædo, ipsa tamen appellatione tanquam sidus de cælo delapsum, se illis, qui velut homines ex mancipiorum numero gravi servitutis jugo oppressi, atque miseris ærumnosis afflicti affictique erant, lu- cem ac spem salutis allaturum falso commentus est. Carpocratiani autem minime Barchochebam pro Messia suscipiebant: Seipsos autem & Præcepto- rem suum Carpocratem Christo meliores esse im- pudentissime affirmabant. Dominum enim no- strum Jesum Christum purum hominem fuisse, & vitæ sanctitate puriorem vivere, non modo esse parem, si plus quam ille mundo renunciare velit, blasphemabant. Barchochebas eos, qui Chri- stianos se profitebantur, non modo non admit- tebat, sed etiam gravissime affligebat: Quo de Ju- stinus Martyr ad Antonin. Pium: Proximo bello Judaico Barchochebas defectionis Judæorum Dux & Princeps solos Christianos ad gravia supplicia, nisi Christum abnegarent & maledictis incesserent, pro- trahi jussit. Et Dio: Barchochebas Dux factionis Judæorum nolentes sibi Christianos adversus Roma- num militem ferre subsidium, omnimodis cruciati- bus enecat. Quid ergo vel Carpocrates ad Barcho- chebam, vel uterque ad locum præsentem faciat, non apparet.

## 1:12
Verse 12.

Οὗτοί εἰσιν ἐν ταῖς ἀγάπαις ὑμῶν σπιλάδες) They are a disgrace to your Agapae, that is, the feasts which were concluded with the memory of the Lord's death. See 2 Peter 2, verse 13, where some codices, as also some here, have ἐν ταῖς ἀπάταις αὐτῶν by a manifest error. What is σπιλάδες here is σπῖλοι in the epistle of Simeon, מומים, Deut. XXXII, 5.

Συνευωχούμενοι ὑμῖν) And this is taken from that epistle.

Ἀφόβως ἑαυτοὺς ποιμαίνοντες) considering pleasure to be luxury in the daytime, as we have judged should be read in the said epistle. But the words which are here refer to those of Ezekiel XXXIV. 2. 8. 10. הרועים אותם where in the Greek it is ἐβόσκοντο ἑαυτούς. While they fatten themselves, they neglect the flock. Ἀφόβως here is securely, מבטח Prov. 1, 33, by metonymy, because he who has care also fears.

Cornelius observes that feasts were accustomed to be instituted after the celebration of the Holy Supper, but frugal and pious ones, and he renders the sense thus: Now the sense is that which the Syriac gives: These are they who in their delights defile, both the body with gluttony, and the mind with drunkenness, greed, and lust, and the guests with perverse doctrine and heresy, just as with detraction, evil-speaking, and shameless words and looks; for they have eyes full of adultery and unceasing sin, as Saint Peter says in his 2nd epistle, II. 14; see what is said there. The Arabic translates: These are they who provoke guilt upon you, because, namely, they defile you with heresy, gluttony, and lust, and therefore make you guilty and liable to divine wrath and vengeance. In these, therefore, that saying of Tertullian in De Jejun. contra Psychicos, ch. 17, is true: 'Among you, agape boils in the pots, faith grows warm in the kitchens, hope lies in the dishes.' But agape is greater than these, because through it your young men sleep with their sisters; for luxury and lasciviousness are the appendages of gluttony. For the Gnostics, being full, by granting their wives to others, used to say: 'Arise and perform the agape with a brother,' or Epiphanius, heresy 26. Thus also Blessed Gerhard on 2 Peter ch. II, v. 13, p. 252: 'In your public banquets they are spots, that is, like spots, he practices in them shameful things, and things worthy of all reproach, and by this reason they show themselves to be polluted both in mind and body.' In the abstract there is great emphasis, for as we call a notably wicked man a wickedness: so the Apostle calls false teachers, as being notably spotted and defiled, spots and defilements. But especially both Apostles look to this, that they are spots and disgraces to the Church, whose members they wish to be considered, and they associate themselves with its assembly, and meanwhile expose the name of Christians, nay, of Christ himself, to the blasphemy of enemies. Luther in his commentary on this passage: 'They imagine for themselves that they adorn Christianity, just as the sun and moon decorate the sky, that they are most precious treasures, just as gold and gems: But Peter calls them spots and defilements.'

Clouds without water) Thus 'waterless springs,' 2 Peter ch. II, v. 17.

Carried about by winds) There it is 'clouds driven by a storm.' He notes two things in them: that they brought forth no good fruit, and that they were inconstant. See also James 1, v. 6, and what is said there. They are 'a man of wind' in Hosea 9:7.

Others say that heretics are called clouds because of their swelling and pride, because they exalt themselves like clouds, and boast that their doctrine comes from the clouds and heaven. Clouds without water, that is, barren, unfruitful, which seem to promise water for the refreshment of men and the fertility of the earth, but do not provide it. Thus the Gnostics put forward an empty name of knowledge and doctrine, but did not provide it, says Didymus, according to that in Prov. XXV, v. 24: 'Clouds and wind and rain not following, a man who is boastful and does not fulfill his promises.' Bede: 'Just as barren clouds,' he says, 'are carried about by the winds; so heretics are swept away into various errors of vices by the winds, that is, by the breaths and suggestions of demons.' Again, just as a cloud is dispersed and vanishes like smoke by the wind: So also heretics are dissipated and vanish by their own spirit of vanity. Thus St. Athanasius concerning Julian the Apostate, now reigning and beginning to rage against the faithful: 'Let us withdraw,' he says, 'a little, O friends, for it is a little cloud, which quickly passes and vanishes,' as Socrates testifies, book II, ch. 12. Cf. Job VII, 9. Oecumenius: 'Just as a cloud,' he says, 'without water, agitated by winds, does not refresh the places over which it hangs with water, but covers them with darkness and obscures them: So heretics do not irrigate, refresh, and make fruitful souls with saving speech, but darken them with detestable teachings.' John Huss on this passage: 'Clouds agitated by winds excite a storm, and obscure the splendor of the Sun: So heretics disturb the peace of minds, excite seditions, and obscure the Sun of righteousness with the darkness of errors.' John Huss also gives another reason for the comparison with the Interlinear gloss: 'Where there is a fountain without water, there is mud and mire: But in these there is not the water of inundating grace, but the mud of defiling malice.' Nor is it a wonder, because they have forsaken the fountain of living water. They are therefore fountains not inundating, but rather defiling, not calming the heat of pleasure but more truly exciting it, not refreshing but infecting, not sanctifying but polluting.

Autumn trees) If you look at the usage of the word, it means autumn trees. But the etymology of the word is more regarded, so that it says they are like trees whose fruit perishes immediately. Thus willows are 'fruit-destroying' to Homer, which Pliny XVI. 26 translates as 'fruit-destroying.' Those things which these men gather are not going to last long. A similar comparison in Isaiah I, 30.

Without fruit) For no good use: being barren of good works. See Matthew XIII, 22. Mark IV, 19. Eph. V, 11. Titus III, v. 14. 2 Peter I, 18. Add Matthew XXI, 19.

Twice dead) They will perish twice. See Matthew X, 28. Neither will they have a good end here, nor in the other age. A similar passage in Jeremiah LI, 58: 'stripped twice.'

The Vulgate indeed rendered it 'autumnal trees', that is, of the end of autumn. For it is usual, as B. Gerhard notes on 2 Pet. 2, p. 294, for some trees to bloom at the end of autumn contrary to the nature of the season, which farmers judge to be a sign that they will shortly die. Some explain ὧν φθίνει ἡ ὀπώρα in this way, 'whose fruit withers', which indeed bear some fruit, but corrupt and withered, which either because of a lack of sap and nourishment or because of worms eating them, falls off before maturity. Whence the Arab rendered it: 'Trees of corrupt fruits.' Such, says Cornelius, are heretics, who are not only dead, but also deadly, because they not only extirpate their own and others' good works and fruits of piety, but even infect and intoxicate them with the pestiferous poison of heresy: so Beda, Salmero, Catharinus, and others. Some think Φθινόπωρον in B. Gerhard is the same as τὸ μετόπωρον after autumn, that is, the winter season. Plutarch in Sympos. VIII. 'For autumn seems to be like old age to the revolving year.' This explanation can easily be reconciled with the preceding one, for the end of autumn is the beginning of winter. But the discourse rises in the Apostle. First he calls them δένδρα φθινοπωρινὰ, which are next to καρποφόροις or τελεσκαρπῶσι, then ἄκαρπα entirely, thirdly ἀποθανόντα, and finally ἐκριζωθέντα. Epiphanius, as Cornelius notes here in Heresy XXXI, and Irenaeus in book 1, c. 33, compare Gnostics and heretics to fungi, which come forth from trees as if they were their excrement, and arise in a single night, and soon die. For thus heretics have come forth from us, they arise suddenly, and die most quickly, says St. Augustine on Ps. 57.

Ἐκριζωθέντα) And here is an Aorist for the future. They will be uprooted; not even the name of the sect will remain. You have the verb ἐκριζόω in Matt. 13:19, 15:13, Luke 17:6; it corresponds to the Hebrew נתשׁ, Jer. 1:10, and עקר Dan. 7:8, Zeph. c. 2:4. Regarding the thing itself, see Is. 40:24, Prov. 12:3, Is. 50:24, Ez. c. 17:9, Mal. 4:1. They will not be as fortunate as Nebuchadnezzar, whose root was preserved, Dan. 4:12, 20, 23.

They are called Δένδρα ἐκριζωθέντα, according to B. Gerhard, both because they are deprived of all spiritual communion with Christ and his mystical body, and because as certain a destruction threatens them as trees uprooted, and because from them, as from trees torn up by the roots, no fruit can any longer be hoped for. OEcumenius and others cited by Cornelius think this is more than 'twice dead'. For the dead can revive and sprout again if the root remains in healthy soil, but those uprooted have no hope of life. But Cornelius asks, if one explains 'uprooted' as 'twice dead', why would the Apostle use synonyms where every single word has its own weight? OEcumenius says they are uprooted from Paradise, that is, the Lord's Church, and cast out to be gathered for the eternal fire. For what state or root can he have who is cast out by all because of his gluttony for pleasure?

Latin:

Vers. 12.

Οὗτοί εἰσιν ἐν ταῖς ἀγάπαις ὑμῶν σπιλάδες) Dedecori sunt vestris Agapis, id est conviviis, quæ memoria mortis Do- minicæ claudebantur. Vide 2. Petr. 2, vers. 13. ubi quidam Co- dices, ut & hic nonnulli ἐν ταῖς ἀπάταις αὐτῶν errore manife- sto. Quod hic σπιλάδες id in epistola Simeonis σπῖλοι מומים, Deut. XXXII, 5.

Συνευωχούμενοι ὑμῖν) Et hoc de illa epistola transsumptum est.

Ἀφόβως ἑαυτοὺς ποιμαίνοντες) ἡδονὴν ἡγούμενοι τὴν ἐν ἡμέ- ρᾳ τρυφήν, ut in dicta epistola legendum censuimus. Sed verba quæ hic sunt, respiciunt ilia Ezechielis XXXIII. 8. 10. הרועים אותם ubi in Græco ἐβόσκοντο ἑαυτούς. Se dum saginent, gregem negligunt. Ἀφόβως hic est secure מבטח Prov. 1, 33. per Metonymiam, quia qui curam habet, is & metuit.

Cornelius observat convivia post S. Cœnæ ce- lebrationem institui consuevisse, sed frugalia & pia, sensumque ita reddit: Jam sensus est, quem dat Syrus: Isti sunt, qui in deliciis suis commacu- lant, tum corpus crapula, tum mentem ebrietate, gula, libidine, tum convivas prava doctrina & hæresi æque ac detractione, maledicentia atque im- pudicis verbis & aspectibus, habent enim oculos plenos adulterii & incessabilis delicti, ut ait S. Pe- trus 2. epist. II. 14. vide ibi dicta. Arabicus vertit: Isti sunt provocantes super vos reatus, quia scilicet vos hæresi, gula & libidine commaculant, idcoque ira & vindicta divina reos & obnoxios- faciunt. In hisce ergo verum est illud Tertulliani de Jejun. contra Psychicos cap. 17. Apud te A- gape in cacabis fervet, fides in culinis calet, spes in ferculis jacet. Sed major his est agape, quia per hanc adolescentes tui cum sororibus dormiunt, appendices scilicet gulæ luxuria atque lascivia sunt. Gnostici enim saturi, uxores suas aliis concedendo, dicebant: Surge & fac agapen cum fratre, aut Epiphanius hær. 26. Sic etiam B. Gerhardus ad 2. Petr. cap. II. v. 13. pag. 252. In conviviis vestris publicis sunt maculæ, hoc est, instar macularum, exercet in illis turpia, & omni vituperatione di- gna, atque hac ratione sese & animo & corpore pollutos esse ostendunt. In abstracto est magna emphasis, ut enim hominem insigniter sceleratum vocamus scelus: Sic Apostolus falsos Doctores ut- pote insigniter maculatos & inquinatos vocat ma- culas & inquinamenta. Cumprimis vero uterq; Apostolus eo respicit, quod sint maculæ & probra Ecclesiæ, cujus membra haberi volunt, ac cœtui ejus sese associant, atq; interim Christianorum, imo ipsius Christi nomen blasphemiæ hostium exponunt. Lutherus in comment. hujus loci. Imaginantur sibi, quod Christianismum ornent, sicut sol & luna cœlum condecorant, quod sint pretiosissima κειμήλια, sic- ut aurum & gemmæ: Sed Petrus eos vocat macu- las & inquinamenta.

Νεφέλαι ἄνυδροι) Sic πηγὰς ἀνύδρους, 2. Petr. cap. II. vers. 7.

Ὑπὸ ἀνέμων παραφερόμεναι) Ibi est νεφέλαι ὑπὸ λαίλαπος ἐλαυνόμεναι. Duo notat in illis, quod nihil ferrent bonæ frugis, & quod inconstantes essent. Vide & Jac. 1, v. 6. & ibi dicta. Sunt אִישׁ רוּחַ Oseæ 9, 7.

Alii nubes vocari hæreticos ob tumorem, & fastum ajunt, quod instar nubium se extollant, suamque doctrinam è nubibus & cœlo venire ja- ctitent. Nubes sine aqua, id est steriles, infœcun- dæ, quæ videntur aquam ad hominum refrigerium & terræ fœcunditatem promittere, sed eam non præstant. Ita Gnostici nomen inane scientiæ, & doctrinæ præferebant, sed eam non præstabant, ait Didymus, juxta illud Prov. XXV. v. 24. Nubes & ventus & pluviæ non sequentes, vir gloriosus & promissa non complens. Beda: Sicut nubes ste- riles, ait, à ventis circumferuntur; ita hæretici ventis, id est, flatibus & suggestionibus Dæmonum in diversos vitiorum raptantur errores. Rursum sicut nubes à vento instar fumi dispellitur & eva- nescit: Ita & hæretici suo vanitatis Spiritu dissi- pantur & evanescunt. Ita S. Athanasius de Juliano Apostata jam regnante & in fideles grassari inci- piente: Secedamus, ait, paululum, ô amici, est enim nubecula, quæ cito præterit & evanescit, teste Socra- te libr. II. cap. 12. Conf. Job. VII. 9. Oecumenius: Sic- ut nubes, inquit, sine aqua agitata ventis, ea loca, quibus incumbit, non refrigerat aqua, sed caligine obducit, & obfuscat: Ita hæretici animas salutari ser- mone non irrigant, recreant, & fœcundant, sed dete- stabilibus documentis obtenebrant. Joh. Hussus in h. l. Nubes ventis agitatæ tempestatem excitant, & Solis splendorem obfuscat: Sic hæretici mentium quietem turbant, seditiones excitant, tenebris erro- rum Solem justitiæ obfuscat. Reddit & aliam com- parationis rationem Joh. Hussus cum gloss. Inter- lin. Ubi est fons sine aqua, ibi est lutum & limus: Sed in istis non est aqua inundantis gratiæ, sed lutum inquinantis malitiæ. Nec mirum, quia dereliquerunt fontem aquæ vivæ. Sunt ergo fontes non inundan- tes, sed potius inquinantes, non calorem volupta- tis sedantes, sed verius suscitantes, non reficientes, sed inficientes, non sanctificantes, sed pollu- entes.

Δένδρα φθινοπωρινὰ] Si usum vocis respicias, dicit arbo- res autumnales. Sed magis respicitur ἐτυμολογία vocis, ut dicat eos similes esse arboribus, quarum fructus perit illico. Sic salices Homero ὠλεσίκαρποι, quæ Plinius XVI. 26. ver- tit frugiperdas. Ea quæ isti congerunt, non diu sunt dura- tura. Similis comparatio Esaiæ I. 30.

Ἄκαρπα] Nulli bono usui: quippe bonorum operum ste- riles. Vide Matth. XIII. 22. Marc. IV. 19. Eph. V. 11. Tit. III. v. 14. 2. Petr. I. 18. Adde Matth. XXI. 19.

Δὶς ἀποθανόντα] Bis peribunt. Vide Matth. X. 28. Ne- que hic habebunt bonum exitum, neque in seculo altero. Si- mile apud Jer. LI. 58. עַרְעֵר bis nudata.

Vulgata quidem reddidit arbores autumnales, hoc est extremi autumni. Solent enim, ut B. Ger- bardus ad 2. Petr. II. p. 294. nonnullæ arbores ex- tremo autumno præter temporis rationem florere, quod agricolæ judicant esse signum, illas brevi emo- rituras. Quidam sic exponunt ὧν φθίνει ἡ ὀπώρα, quo- rum fructus marcescit, quæ fructum quidem ali- quem ferunt, sed corruptum & marcidum, qui vel succo nutrimentoque deficiente vel vermibus exe- dentibus ante maturitatem decidit. Unde Arabs reddidit: Arbores corruptorum fructuum. Tales, inquit Cornelius, sunt hæretici, qui non tantum sunt mortui, sed & mortiferi, quia non tantum sua, sed & aliorum bona opera & pietatis fructus extirpant, imo pestifero hæresis veneno inficiunt, & intoxicant: ita Beda, Salmero, Catharinus & alii. Quidam Φθινόπωρον apud B. Gerhardum, putant esse idem, quod τὸ μετόπωρον post autumnum, hoc est, tempus brumale. Plutarchus in Sympos. VIII. Ἔοικε γὰρ τῷ ἐν- ιαυτῷ περιϊόντι, οἷον γῆρας εἶναι τὸ φθινόπωρον. Hæc explicatio cum præcedente facile conciliari potest, autumni enim extremitas brumæ est initium. As- surgit autem apud Apostolum oratio. Pri- mo illos vocat δένδρα φθινοπωρινὰ, quæ proxime absunt a καρποφόροις sive τελεσκαρπῶσι, deinde ἄκαρπα prorsus, tertio ἀποθανόντα, postremo ἐκ- ριζωθέντα. Epiphanius, notante hic Cornelio hæ- resi XXXI. & Irenæus libr. 1. c. 33. Gnosticos & hæ- reticos comparant fungis, qui ex arboribus prodeunt quasi eorum excrementa, unaque nocte oriuntur, & mox emoriuntur. Sic enim hæretici ex nobis prodie- runt, repente oriuntur, occiduntque citissime, ait S. Augustinus in Ps. LVII.

Ἐκριζωθέντα) Et hic est Aoristus pro futuro. Radicitus exscindentur; ne nomen quidem Sectæ erit reliquum. Ver- bum ἐκριζόω habes Matth. XIII. 19. XV. 13. Luc. XVII. 6. re- spondet Ebræo נתשׁ, Jerem. I. 10. & עקר Dan. VII. 8. Soph. c. II 4. De re ipsa vide Es. XL. 24. Prov. XII. 3. Es. L. 24. Ez. c XVII. 9. Mal. IV. 1. Non erunt tam felices quam Nabu- chodonosor, cui radix servata est, Dan. IV. 12. 20. 23.

Δένδρα ἐκριζωθέντα vocantur, B. Gerhardo In- terprete, tum quia omni communione spirituali cum Christo & corpore ejus mystico sunt privati, tum quia tam certus ipsis imminet interitus ac ar- boribus radicitus excisis, tum ex illis tanquam ab arboribus radicitus evulsis nullus amplius sperari possit fructus. OEcumenius, aliique apud Corne- lium censent, plus hoc esse, quam τὸ bis mortuæ. Mortuæ enim reviviscere, & repullulare possunt, si radix in terra sana consistat, ac eradicatæ nullam vitæ spem habent. Prætert autem Cornelius, si τὸ eradicatæ quis explicet bis mortuæ, sed cur adhiberet Synonyma Apostolus, ubi singula verba singula pondera? OEcumenius, à Para- diso, id est, Domini Ecclesia eradicantur, & foras projecti ad ignem æternum colliguntur. Qua- lem enim habere statum aut radicem potest, qui ob voluptatis ingluviem ab omnibus projici- tur?

## 1:13
Ver. 13.

I had many things to write, but I do not wish to with ink and pen.] In the manuscript here also is οὐκ ἐβουλήθην instead of οὐ θέλω. Then γράψαι σοι.

But I hope to see you immediately, and we shall speak mouth to mouth.] The sense is the same as in the preceding epistle, verse 12. But here he posits more for certain that he will speak with Gaius.

Peace be to you. In the Hebrew manner שׁלוֹם לָךְ. See 1 Pet. 5:14.

The brethren greet you. Those who are at Ephesus and know you. But in the manuscript, the brethren, that is, all Christians.

Greet the friends by name. That is, greet the friends who are among you, not generally, but individually. See Acts 1:15, Exodus 33:12, Psalm 47:4.

Interpreters here note the courtesy and affability of St. John, who wishes friends to be greeted by name, yet does not name them because they were very many, and lest he offend anyone by passing them over or preferring another. Greet also our friends, he says, that is, according to Osiander's interpretation, just as if I had consigned the names of all to you. For by mutual greetings, which are inserted into letters, fraternal benevolence is fostered and confirmed, whereas otherwise many friendships are dissolved by excessive, long-lasting silence. Let us thus greet the brethren, so that we may pray for good things for them from the heart from God the Father, His only-begotten Son, and the Holy Spirit.

TO WHICH ONE AND TRIUNE GOD BE PRAISE, HONOR, AND GLORY FOR ALL ETERNITY, AMEN.

ANNOTATIONS ON THE EPISTLE OF ST. JUDE.

containing the proposition comprised in the causes of the writing, is placed first; to the other, the celebration of GOD is subjoined: The former is an instruction concerning the fleeing of heretics, exhibiting especially both their guilt and their punishment, up to verse 16. The latter is an exhortation concerning the observing of precautions necessary against apostasy, up to verse 26.

THE FIRST INSTRUCTIVE PART. Concerning the fleeing of heretics.

Latin:

Vers. 13.

Πολλὰ εἶχον γράφειν, ἀλλ᾽ ὀ θέλω διὰ μέλανος καὶ καλάμε.] In Manuscripto est hic quoque ὐκ ἐβυλήθην pro ὀ θέλω. De- inde γράφαι σοι.

Ἐλπίζω δὲ ἐυθέως σε ἰδεῖν, καὶ ςόμα πρὸς ςόμα λαλήσομεν.] Sensus idem, qui in præcedente epistola commate 12. Sed hic magis pro certo ponit, fe cum Cajo collocuturum.

Εἰρήνη σοι.] Ebræo more שׁלוֹם לָךְ. Vide 1. Petr. V, 14.

Ἀσπάζονταί σε οἱ ἀδελφοὶ.] Qui Ephesi sunt & te norunt. At in Manuscripto οἱ ἀδελφοὶ, id est, Christiani omnes.

Ἀσπάζε τὺς φίλως κατ᾽ ὄνομα.] Id est, saluta amicos, qui apud vos sunt, non generatim, sed singulos. Vid. Act. I, 15. Exodi 33, 12. Psalm. 47, 4.

Notant hic Interpretes comitatem & affabilita- tem S. Johannis, qui amicos vult salutari nomina- tim, eos tamen non nominat, quia plurimi erant, & ne quem prætereundo, aut alteri præponendo offendat. Saluta etiam nostros amicos, inquit, id est, interprete Osiandro, perinde, ac si omnium nomina tibi consignassem. Salutationibus enim mutuis, quæ literis inseruntur, benevolentia fraterna fovetur at- que confirmatur, cum alias multæ amicitia nimio diuturno silentio dissolvantur. Ita autem salutemus fratres, ut illis ex animo bona precemur à Deo Patre, Filio ejus unigenito, Spiritu Sancto.

CUI DEO UNI ET TRINO SIT LAUS, HONOR, ET GLORIA IN OMNEM ÆTERNITATEM, AMEN.

OTATA AD AM S. JUDÆ.

dium propositionem in causis scriptionis compre- hensam continens, præmittitur, alteri celebra- tio DEI subjungitur: Prior est informatio de hæ- reticis fugiendis, eorum imprimis exhibens tum culpam, tum pœnam, ad v. 16. Posterior est adhor- tatio de observandis cautelis adversus apostasiam necessariis, ad vers. 26.

PARS PRIOR INFORMA- TORIA. De fugiendis hæreticis.

## 1:13
Vers. 13. Wild waves of the sea] יגרשׂ Is. ch. LVII. 20. Add Eph. IV. 14. Just as savage waves disturb the sea, so do these the whole world. Thus Cicero compares seditious tribunes to winds, and the people to the sea. The word ἀγρία is transferred from wild fruits and living creatures to all harsh things. In the Glossary ἄγριος is savage.

Foaming out their own shames] An excellent expression. For just as waves belch forth filth from the bottom of the sea, so they bring their desires out into the open from their heart. Seneca uses the word despumandi (to foam off) in a similar matter, and Jerome, who often imitates him, does so here regarding the Ocean: The belly, boiling with wine, quickly foams out into lusts. Αἰσχύνας is used figuratively for those things of which they ought deservedly to be ashamed בשר.

Just as he had previously compared heretics to trees: so now to the waves of the sea: designating thus both their inconstancy, because like the sea they are perpetually fluctuating in their dogmas: and their seditious movements, because like the effervescing sea they cannot be at rest: And just as wild waves [shake] a ship; so they, turbulent, seditious, and tumultuous, shake and agitate the Church.

Wandering stars] The Hebrews call those stars who are Teachers, or who take upon themselves the role of Teachers. See what was said at Matt. ch. XXIV. v. 29. Some stars are called ἀπλανεῖς (fixed) by Cicero and 'fixed', others πλανῆται, which are called now wandering, now vagrant, by others erratic. He compares the Carpocratians to these, therefore, because they did not keep themselves in one station, that is, in the doctrine once delivered by the Apostle. See above 3. and 12.
