He notes not only the errors of the heretics, but also the inconstancy and mutability of the errors, as Bede, Oecumenius, and others explain: which is evident from the history of those who came forth from the unhappy school of Simon. Cajetan, however, wishes to indicate not celestial planets, whose motions are constant, but meteors and fiery exhalations, which Aristotle in Meteor. I calls stars running about in the air. Plato in Rep. book II calls merchants πλανήτας ἐπὶ τὰς πόλεις, 'planets of the cities', because they wander through and roam about cities for the sake of merchandise. The Syriac translates 'seductive stars', the Arabic 'dark stars', such as are exhalations which, when ignited, seem to fall from the sky like stars: Likewise 'will-o'-the-wisps', or wandering fires, which lead travelers into pathless places, rivers, or precipices. Very similar are heretics, who wish to be seen as most brilliant stars and great lights of the Church, but they are erratic stars, and who through their doctrine do not illuminate the minds of men, but rather seduce them and lead them away into errors. Compare Isidore of Pelusium, book IV, ep. 58.

To whom the gloom of darkness is reserved forever] An excellent opposition: They wish to be called stars, but perpetual darkness awaits them. Moreover, the words are taken from 2 Pet. ch. II. v. 17, where see what is said.

The punishment is now expressed more clearly. Ζόφος τοῦ σκότους is a Hebrew phrase for 'dark gloom', that is, most dense darkness, which in Matt. VIII. 12, ch. XXII. v. 13, ch. XXV. v. 30 are called 'outer darkness', that is, the outermost, most remote from the region of light. The Vulgate rendered it, 'storm of darkness'. Less appropriately. But Bede is correct when he says, they will be sent into the eternal darkness of torments, who in the Church of God were introducing the darkness of errors under the name of light.

Latin:

Vers. 13. Κύματα ἄγρια θαλάσσης] יגרשׂ Es. c. LVII. 20. Adde Eph. IV. 14. Sicut sævi fluctus mare turbant, ita isti orbem totum. Sic tribunos seditiosos ventis, populum mari comparat Cicero. Vox ἀγρία à feris fructibus & animantibus ad omnia dura transfertur. In Glossario ἄγριος immanis.

Ἐπαφρίζοντα τὰς ἑαυτῶν αἰσχύνας] Egregie dictum. Nam sicut fluctus sordes ex imo maris eructant: ita illi ex corde cupiditates suas in apertum educunt. Despumandi voce in pari re utitur Seneca, & eum sæpe imitans Hieronymus, cujus hoc est ad Oceanum: Venter mero æstuans cito despumat in libidines. Αἰσχύνας figurate dictum pro iis, quorum merito pudere eos deberet בשר.

Uti prius compararat arboribus hæreticos: Ita jam fluctibus maris: designans ita eorum tum inconstantiam, quod instar maris perpetuo in dogmatibus suis fluctuent: tum seditiosos motus, quod instar maris effervescentis quiescere nequeant: Et uti fluctus feri navim; ita ipsi turbulenti, seditiosi & tumultuosi Ecclesiam concutiunt & exagitant.

Ἀστέρες πλανῆται] Stellas vocant Ebræi eos, qui Doctores sunt, aut Doctorum sibi personam sumunt. Vide quæ dicta ad Matth. cap. XXIV. v. 29. Stellarum aliæ dicuntur ἀπλανεῖς inerrantes Ciceroni & infixæ, aliæ πλανῆται, quæ modo errantes, modo vagæ, aliis erraticæ dicuntur. His ergo Carpocratianos comparat, quia se non tenebant in una statione, id est, in doctrina, semel ab Apostolo tradita. Vide supra 3. & 12.

Notat non tantum errores hæreticorum, sed etiam errorum inconstantiam, & mutabilitatem, ut Beda, Oecumenius & alii explicant: 'quod ex eorum, qui è Simonis infelici schola prodiere, historia constat. Cajetanus tamen non planetas cælestes, quorum motus constantes sunt, sed meteora & exhalationes igneas indicari vult, quæ Aristot. I. Meteor. dicuntur stellæ discurrentes in aëre. Plato l. II. de Rep. mercatores vocat πλανήτας ἐπὶ τὰς πόλεις planetas urbium, quia urbes mercium causa pervagantur, & oberrant. Syrus vertit stellæ seductrices, Arabs stellæ caliginosæ, quales sunt exhalationes, quæ accensæ instar stellarum è cœlo cadere videntur: Item ignes fatui, vel errantes, qui viatores in avia, flumina, vel præcipitia deducunt. Simillimi sunt hæretici, qui videri volunt lucidissima sidera, & Ecclesiæ magna lumina, sed sunt stellæ erraticæ, quique per doctrinam suam non illuminant hominum mentes, sed potius eos seducunt, & ad errores abducunt. Conf. Isidorus Pelusiota l. IV. ep. 58.

Οἷς ὁ ζόφος τοῦ σκότους εἰς αἰῶνα τετήρηται] Egregia oppositio: Volunt dici sidera, sed perpetuæ eos tenebræ expectant. Sunt autem verba desumpta ex 2. Petr. c. II. vers. 17. ubi dicta vide.

Pœna jam disertius exprimitur. Ζόφος τοῦ σκότους phrasi Ebrea caligo est tenebricosa, hoc est, tenebræ densissimæ, quæ Matth. VIII, 12. c. XXII. v. 13. cap. XXV. v. 30. vocantur tenebræ exteriores, hoc est, extimæ, à regione lucis remotissimæ. Vulgata reddidit, procella tenebrarum. Minus commode. Recte autem Beda dicente, in tenebras tormentorum mittentur æternas, qui in Ecclesia Dei sub nomine lucis tenebras inducebant errorum.

## 1:14
Vers. 14.

And Enoch, the seventh from Adam, prophesied to these) The Rabbis were accustomed, as I just said, to attribute to both angels and great men those sayings which they could have said. But those words which are cited here, as fitting well for the Carpocratians, were found in a book which was called the Apocalypse of Enoch, which Celsus used, and he produced a fragment from it, which you have in Origen against Celsus, book V. From there Irenaeus also took what he has in IV. 30. Tertullian drew this from there and transferred it into his book on idolatry. Enoch had preceded him, predicting that all elements, all the census of the world, what is contained by heaven, what by sea, what by earth, would turn into idolatry, and that the spirits of the deserting angels would be consecrated as God against the Lord. And concerning the adornment of women, he says that Enoch commanded his son Methuselah to hand down to his descendants the knowledge of those things which he himself had heard by hereditary tradition. Clement of Alexandria in his excerpts cites from the same source: And I came to all the flocks. In the same place, a little later, he says it was handed down by Enoch that the deserting angels were those who were teachers to men of astronomy, divination, and other arts. The Jews attributed faith to that book: for it is cited in the Zohar. George Syncellus possessed a Greek book by that name, from which Joseph Scaliger gave us a sufficiently large part in his most learned notes on Eusebius: In which there are also those things about the arts which men received through the ministry of angels. I believe that in the beginning the book was small, but that with time everyone added to it what he wished, as has often happened in those more abstruse books. He says, however, 'prophesied to these,' because he predicted that which is to happen to them. A similar construction is in Jerem. XXVII. verse 15, and elsewhere. Enoch is called the seventh from Adam, that is, the seventh of men, if Adam is counted as the first.

It is not hinted by Jude that these things were taken from a certain book. He does not say that Enoch wrote these things, but that he prophesied; which Flinsbachius, in his book on the conjectures of the end times, wishes to be understood as a real prophecy, that it was a type of the eternity to be expected after the six millennia of the world, just as bodily death effectively dominated the earlier Fathers of the Church, namely Adam, Seth, Enoch, Kenan, Mahalaleel, and Jared, on account of sin, but could not exercise its force and power upon the seventh, Enoch: so also, through the six thousand years during which this world will stand, it will dominate all men, but in the seventh millennium, which is to be the beginning of eternal and heavenly life, its sting having been lost, it will be utterly abolished. To this, says the blessed Gerhard, Jude seems to look when he says that Enoch, the seventh from Adam, prophesied concerning the final judgment. Which opinion is therefore approved with the blessed D. Harbarto, Disp. Theol. page 986. and the blessed D. Gerhard, commentary on Genesis, page 172. It is more correctly explained as a verbal prophecy, which some think was expressed in writing, though most deny it. Of those, some think that that writing of Enoch has perished, others that it survives. We acknowledge that it survives, because Jude preserved it for us here, not, however, taken from any book or tradition, but received from divine inspiration. That a book of such a kind existed in the time of Jude himself cannot be shown by any solid document, much less that it is the one which some today are peddling. The things which are brought forward concerning the Apocalypse of Enoch do not taste of that age, so that they should be believed to have existed in the time of Jude. As for what Cornelius brings from Tertullian, On the Apparel of Women, chapter 3, that this book was preserved from the flood in the ark, or restored from memory by Noah through the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, how, I ask, will that be proven? Cornelius himself admits that the book of Enoch, which is cited by Tertullian, Irenaeus, and Jerome in his Description of Ecclesiastical Writers on Enoch, by Didymus and Bede in this place, by Athanasius in his Synopsis, and by Clement of Alexandria in book VI of the Stromata, teems with errors, inasmuch as it asserts that the sons of God in Gen. VI were angels, who begat giants from the daughters of men through hot tears flowing from the eyes of the angels, which St. Augustine, City of God 18. 38, deservedly calls a fable. Such is what Tertullian cites from the book of Enoch in his book On the Apparel of Women, c. 10, namely that those angels were condemned who taught women to adorn and paint themselves, to weave golden and silver garments, to dye wool, etc. He also adds to those things what he says in chapter IV on idolatry, that Enoch predicted that demons would convert all elements and everything that is on earth and in the sea into idolatry. Nor are those things which are cited from the same in the Testament of a better sort, as far as authority is concerned. the Twelve Patriarchs. With Origen and Procopius cited, concerning those things which were to happen to them, according to the prophecies of Enoch regarding the sins and punishments of the Hebrews, concerning the Redeemer of the world being killed by the Jews, concerning the slaughter, servitude, and eternal reprobation of the Hebrews. What of the fact that Cornelius, in his work on Ecclesiastical Writers, praises Jerome in [the entry for] Jude, and St. Augustine in the aforementioned place and in Book XV of The City of God, chapter 23, teaches that the things written in the book of Enoch do not have certain faith, for the reason that their excessive antiquity made them suspect, lest they be supposititious or corrupted: (to which he could also have added Origen in the aforementioned place and in Homily 28 on Numbers) and adds that Jude does not cite a book, but a prophecy of Enoch, which could have been vocal and verbal. Drusius, indeed, in [his commentary on] Enoch chapter 22, does not doubt that the book of Enoch still exists today; Bouldoucus also vehemently commends the book of Enoch in [his work] On the Church before Moses, which he thinks was preserved in Noah's ark, Book I, chapter 14, citing in its favor Irenaeus, Justin, Clement of Alexandria, Athenagoras, Tertullian, Methodius, Cyprian, Lactantius, Severus Sulpitius, Proclus, and Psellus. Cedrenus writes of Enoch: 'This man first learns and teaches letters,' to which Zonaras, Andr. Hojus in his sacred and profane history, p. 6, and Ludovicus Ballenster in his onomatographia, page 356, agree, and Jacobus Pamelius in his notes to Tertullian asserts that this antediluvian book [existed] with Tertullian. The alphabets of Enoch were also produced both by Hepburn and by Joh. Augustinus Pantheus in his Voarchadumia (thus he calls the book published in the year 1539), etc. Even Peter Martyr in Genesis complains that the writings of Enoch have perished. To our blessed Gesner, the opinion of those who affirm that there was a use of letters in the time of Enoch, and that the words of Enoch could not have been retained without the aid of letters, also seemed more probable. Blessed Bangius says that it is placed beyond all doubt that some Enochian writing once existed. Yet that opinion, as we have said, rests on no foundation, that Enoch consigned any prophecy to letters; most have wished to deduce it from this passage of Jude, in which, however, nothing is held concerning a writing of Enoch. Nor is the question of whether writing or characters of letters existed before the flood free from controversy, since some maintain that Moses was the very first to carve anything with letters, such as Blessed Quistorpius in this place, as also Blessed Waltherus in his Bibliothecal Workshop, p. 1180. And although Blessed D. Thomas Bangius in The Heaven of the East, which he gave to me, Exercise I on the book of Enoch, refers the origin of letters to Adam, page 9. (whose various forms of the alphabet, produced by Adam, by Theseus Ambrosius, who said that angelic characters were handed down to Adam, and by Jacobus Bonaventura Hepburn in his Golden Rod, and by Laurentius Schrader in his Italian Monuments, he discussed in Exercise II.) Nevertheless, Blessed Gerhard rightly establishes in his Exegesis on Holy Scripture, page 31, that the beginning of the Canonical Scripture was made by the Son of God in the carving of the stone tablets. But as for what Blessed Bangius argues, that if an Enochian writing had not existed, so many Greek as well as Latin Fathers—Origen, Augustine, Tertullian, Jerome, Clement of Alexandria, etc.—would by no means have called it to their aid, that, in our judgment, is not sufficient at all, since others could have been seduced by one, as we have been taught by the example of the tradition of Chiliasm of Papias and his followers: nor is it certain concerning Origen; indeed, the contrary is held in Homily 28 on Numbers, that that book is not held in authority among the Hebrews. And in Book V against Celsus, Origen warned that the authority of the letters of Enoch is not great in the Churches (but it would certainly have been great if any genuine book of Enoch had existed).

Jerome also, on Titus 1, says that the book of Enoch is apocryphal and not received among the scriptures of the Church, even though he asserts that Jude placed a testimony from that apocryphal work, which is likewise clear concerning Augustine from Book XVIII of The City of God, chapter 38. 'What of Enoch,' he says, 'the seventh from Adam? Is it not also proclaimed in the Canonical Epistle of the Apostle Jude that he prophesied?' The excessive antiquity of their (Noah's and Enoch's) writings, because of which they seemed to be held as suspect, lest false things be brought forth for true, caused them not to be in authority among the Jews and among us; but the purity of the canon does not receive them, not because the authority of those men who pleased God is rejected, but because those things are not believed to be their own. Therefore, the matter returns almost entirely to Tertullian alone, in his book On the Apparel of Women, c. 3, whose acumen, however, in the authority of the book of Enoch, Blessed Bangius himself taught was futile, page 18. Who furthermore, on page 23, solidly proved that the writing of Enoch by no means deserves Canonical authority, [and is] worthy not only to be thrust down to the lowest benches of apocryphal books, but also to lie cast on the ground among the refuse of fictitious lies and fables, having brought forward the testimonies of Augustine and Jerome themselves, as well as the authorities of Hier. Zanchius, who denies that any monument of letters was consigned by Enoch in Tom. VIII of his Theological Works, On Holy Scripture, page 353, and Andr. Rivetus in Exercise 49 on Genesis, who is entirely persuaded that this book is supposititious and written by certain Jews, because in the Church of God before the Babylonian captivity no mention is made in any of the books of the Prophets of such a rare treasure, which it is not credible that Moses, if it existed in the nature of things, would have been ignorant of, who would also have mentioned the writings of Enoch if they had existed then; as also Franciscus Junius in Tom. I of his Works, page 1298, Pareus in Genesis, as well as Jos. Scaliger in his notes on Eusebius, p. 245, who judges the book to be clearly fictitious and concocted by the Jews, and cites many things from it, but not without weariness and hatred (who, however, was mistaken in this, that he said the passage in the epistle of Jude was manifestly excerpted from this fragment, which was one of the causes for him to publish it); and from the Papists, Mich. Medina in his work On the Right Faith in God, Book V, 1, p. 220, Joh. Marius Scribonius in Sermon XVII on the epistle of Jude, p. 259, and from our own, Blessed Quistorpius on this passage. He could have added Blessed Waltherus's Bibliothecal Workshop, p. 1180, who proves that no book under the name of Enoch, either Canonical or Acanonical, ever existed, and [discusses] the ancient and modern book (a fragment of which not only Scaliger, but also Athanasius Kircherus, rendered into Latin in his Oedipus Aegyptiacus, Gymn. Hieroglyph. class. II. Gramm. c. 2. §. 4. p. 69. he published) [It is] apocryphal and to be rejected, concocted by converted Jews after the times of the Apostles, taking the occasion from the battle of Michael with the Devil, and the prophecy of Enoch mentioned by Jude. But the blessed Bangius also demonstrates how fabulous the fragment from the book of Enoch concerning the Watchers is, p. 25. and following, and that it is a Jewish offspring wrapped in Platonic swaddling clothes, taken up by the impure hands of Christians, etc. Wherefore, what the blessed Bangius says, that some Enochian writing once existed, is to be understood without doubt concerning a writing sold as Enoch's. For he does not prove that from Augustine, book XV. de C. D. ch. 23. We cannot indeed deny that that Enoch, the seventh from Adam, wrote some divine things, since the Apostle Jude says this in his Canonical Epistle; because Jude does not say that Enoch wrote, but that he prophesied: Nor does he add his vote to Jerome, that the passage of Jude is cited from the work of Enoch, much less to Scaliger, that it is excerpted from a fragment of the Enochian book, p. 244. in the notes to Eusebius, since no trace of the Apostolic passage appears in the remainder of the Enochian booklet, the vanity of which fragment he also convinces from that Testament of the XII Patriarchs cited by Origen and Procopius of Gaza, which Robert Grosseteste, Bishop of Lincoln, in the year 1242, donated to the Athenian truth, having been forged by a certain Rabbi.

But some dispute in vain about it, whether Jude has these things from some writing or from tradition, such as Beza, John Prideaux in his inaugural oration on the Wisdom of the Egyptians, Weller in his Hexapla, Cornelius a Lapide, Jacob Gordon, Tirinus, Menochius, Luc. Osiander, Georg. Rostius in this place; since a third [option] is given, namely that St. Jude had it from divine revelation, and although it is free for a Holy writer to select certain things even from a profane writing which contribute to edification, it is not easily to be conceded that this happens in prophecies. Whence Gregory Primaticcius in his commentary on this place, page 167, rashly contends that these things were taken from the apocryphal Enoch. But William Postell was mistaken when he believed he had found the book of Enoch; Mirandulanus was deceived when he bought it for a large sum of money; of whom Reuchlin reports the latter, and Conrad Gesner the former in his Bibliotheca, under the title Enoch. Nor, however, would that tradition help unwritten Papist traditions, because this tradition is not unwritten, but was related into scripture, if it is to be conceded that it is a tradition.

Προεφήτευσε δὲ καὶ τότοις, says St. Jude; the Vulgate has 'of them' [de iis], as in Heb. 1:7, πρὸς τὲς ἀγγέλες is 'of the angels' [de Angelis], although even without a preposition the sense holds for itself, 'he prophesied to them' [vaticinatus est iis]. For we must believe that things which were previously said or written were also said or written for us, Rom. 15:4. But he is not called the seventh from Adam because he is the seventh man, but the seventh Patriarch, if the beginning of the numbering is made from Adam.

Λέγων ἰδὲ ἦλθε Κύριος) The past tense for the future. Thus Psalm 51:3, יבא אלהינו that is, 'he will execute vengeance,' according to the Chaldean interpreter. For this the Rabbis say שם אתי, the Syrians סק אתי.

Λέγων is DICENS [SAYING]. He says that Enoch did not write these things, but said them, although τὸ λέγειν is also used of scripture, and thus it is indefinite; therefore it cannot be proven from the words of Jude that the prophecy of Enoch was consigned to writing. But Grotius dozed when he said the past tense was used for the future. Ἦλθε denotes not a past time, but an indefinite one, and thus either Present or Past, unless it is drawn to one or the other by the circumstances of the text. Here, however, it is rather the Present, since Jude speaks as if the Lord were already coming, so that we may cherish his advent in our minds at all times. Moreover, from the fact that Christ is called Κύριος absolutely and without the article, the Deity of Christ is confirmed, since Socinians contend that this name without the article designates Jehovah; because in the Greek translation of the Old Testament the name Κύριος without the article, as if it were a proper name, was almost always used to express Jehovah, the proper name of God, as Socinus has it in his response to chapter 17 of Wujeck, p. 141. Concerning which [see] at length in Theol. Natur. & revel. p. 496 seqq. He is designated here by the name Κύριος, whose servant [δῦλον] Jude calls himself, and whom those who deny the only Master God and our Lord [τὸν μόνον Δεσπότην Θεὸν καὶ Κύριον ἡμῶν] he threatens will be judged, v. 2, 14; who saved the people from Egypt, destroyed the unbelievers, and keeps the apostate angels for eternal darkness until the day of eternal judgment, v. 6; whom the Archangel implored, so that he might rebuke the Devil contending about the body of Moses, v. 9.

against whom the ungodly spoke hard words, whom he is said to be coming to convict [ἐξελέγξαι], v. 15; whose Apostles are introduced, v. 17; whose mercy the faithful are commanded to await for eternal life, v. 21; who will present them blameless before his glory at his coming, v. 24, etc. But who is that Lord [κύριος], if not Jesus Christ, of whom Enoch therefore prophesied: ἰδὸ ἦλθε Κύριος, מרן אתא. Which formula of anathema was accepted among the Jews, and used by St. Paul, 1 Cor. 16:22, and seems to have taken its origin from this prophecy, which was not then unknown among the people of God. That was the formula of the extreme anathema, which is called חרם. For besides the Niddui, they had the Cherem, and that both simple, and Maranatha or Samatha, [meaning] the Lord or the Name comes, because τὸ ὄνομα by antonomasia denotes Jehovah the Lord; for he who was separated from the fellowship of the Church by Maranatha in this way was subjected to the extreme judgment of the supreme Lord the Avenger.

In his holy myriads) מרבבת קדש Deut. XXXIII. v. 21. where the LXX have: with myriads of Kadesh: as Aquila has: from myriads of holiness, where Aquila more correctly believes קדש to be an appellative. But the LXX correctly translated מ by σύν. We have noted that angels are called holy at 1 Thess. III. 13, where there is no need to repeat what was said. A similar description of God is in Dan. ch. VII. v. 10.

Latin:

Vers. 14.

Προεφήτευσε δὲ καὶ τούτοις ἕβδομος ἀπὸ Ἀδὰμ Ἐνώχ) Solebant, ut modo dixi, Rabbini & Angelis & viris magnis tribuere ea dicta, quæ dixisse poterant. Ea vero verba, quæ hic citantur, ut Carpocratianis bene convenientia, reperiebantur in libro, qui dicebatur Ἀποκάλυψις Ἐνὼχ, quo usus est Celsus, & particulam ex eo produxit, quam habes apud Origenem contra Celsum libro V. inde etiam sumpsit Irenæus, quod habet IV. 30. Tertullianus inde hausit hoc & in librum de idololatria transtulit. Antecesserat Enoch prædicens omnia elementa, omnem mundi censum, quæ cœlo, quæ mari, quæ terra continen- tur, in idololatriam versuros Dæmonas, & Spiritus desertorum Angelorum, ut pro Deo adversus Dominum consecrarentur. Et de cultu fœminarum l. ait Enochum filio suo Mathu- salæ mandasse, ut notitiam eorum, quæ ipse hæreditaria traditione audierat, posteris suis tradere. Clemens Ale- xandrinus in excerptis indidem citat : Καὶ ἦλθον ἶχε ἶλας πά- σας. Ibidem paulo post ab Enocho ait traditum, Angelos disertores fuisse, qui hominibus Magistri fuerint Astrono- miæ, Divinationis aliarumque artium. Judæi ei libro fi- dem tribuebant: nam citatur in Zohar. Habuit Georgius Syncellus librum Græcum eo nomine, unde nobis partem satis magnam dedit Josephus Scaliger in doctissimis ad Euse- bium notis : In qua & illa sunt de artibus, quas homines Angelorum ministerio acceperint. Credo initio librum fu- isse exiguum, sed cum tempore quemque ea, quæ voluit, ei addidisse, ut in libris illis abstrusioribus factum est sæpe. Dicit autem προεφήτευσε τέτοις, quia prædixit id, quod il- lis est eventurum. Par constructio Jerem. XXVII. vers. 15. & alibi. Dicitur autem Enoch septimus ab Adamo, id est, hominum septimus, si Adam primus numeretur.

E libro quodam hæc desumpta esse non innui- tur à Juda. Non dicit scripsisse hæc Enochum, sed prophetasse; quod Flinsbachius libr. de con- ject. extrem. tempor. intellectum vult de reali prophetia, quod typus fuerit æternitatis post sex mundi millenarios expectandæ, sicuti mors corpo- ralis in priores Patres Ecclesiæ, scilicet in Adam, Seth, Enoch, Kenan, Mahalaleel, & Jared propter peccatum efficaciter dominata est, in septimum vero Enoch suam vim atque potentiam exercere non potuit: ita quoque per sex millia annorum, quibus mundus hic stabit, in omnes homines domi- nabitur, sed in septimo millenario, qui initium æternæ ac cœlestis vitæ futurus est, amisso aculeo suo prorsus abolebitur. Huc videtur, inquit B. Gerhardus, respicere Judas, quando Enochum septimum ab Adamo de extremo judicio vatici- natum dicit. Quæ sententia proinde cum B. D. Harbarto Disp. Theol. pag. 986. & B. D. Gerharde comment. in Gen. pag. 172. probata est. Recti- us explicatur de verbali prophetia, quam scripto expressam nonnulli censent, plerique negant. Ex illis quidam interiisse eam scripturam Eno- chi, alii superesse putant. Superesse agnoscimus, quia Judas eam nobis hic servavit, non tamen è li- bro aliquo vel traditione depromptam, sed ex inspi- ratione divina acceptam. Librum ejusmodi ipsius Judæ tempore extitisse nullo documento solido ostendi potest, nedum eum esse, quem hodie nonnulli venditant. Quæ adducuntur de ἀποκαλύψει Ἐνὼχ, eam ætatem non sapiunt, ut Judæ tempore extitisse credi debeant. Quod Cornelius è Tertulliano de habit. mulier. cap. 3. af- fert, librum hunc à diluvio servatum in arca, aut à Noah afflatu Spiritus Sancti memoriter redin- tegratum, quomodo obsecro probabitur? Fate- tur Cornelius ipse, librum Henoch, qui citatur à Tertulliano, Irenæo & Hieronymo descript. Eccles. in Henoch, Didymo & Beda in h. l. Athanasio in Synopsi, & Clement. Alexandr. l. VI. Strom. erro- ribus scatere, utpote quod asserit, filios Dei Gen. VI. fuisse Angelos, qui ex filiabus hominum per calidas lacrymas ex oculis angelorum profluentes, gigantes genucrint, quam S. August. 18. Civit. 38. merito fa- bulam appellat. Tale est, quod ex libro Henoch citat Tertullianus lib. de cultu fœminar. c. 10. scilicet damnatos esse angelos, qui docuerunt fœminas se or- nare & fucare, aureas & argenteas vestes texere, vellera tingere, &c. Illis accenset etiam, quod cap. IV. de idol. ait Henoch prædixisse, quod Dæ- mones omnia elementa & cuncta, quæ in terra marique sunt, in idololatriam converterent. Nec melioris commatis, quantum ad autoritatem, sunt, quæ citantur ex eodem in testam. XII.Patriarchar. Origeni & Procopio laudato, de his quæ even- tura ipsis erant, secundum vaticinia Enochi de Ebræorum flagitiis & suppliciis, de mundi Redem- ptore à Judæis occidendo, de Ebræorum clade, ser- vitute & reprobatione perenni. Quid? quod Hi- eronymum laudet Cornelius de Script. Eccles. in Juda, & S. Augustinum l. c. & lib. XV. de Civit. Dei cap. 23. docentis, non habere certam fidem, quæ in libro Enoch scribuntur, eo quod nimia an- tiquitas illa suspecta fecerit, ne supposititia vel de- pravata sint: (quibus etiam Origenem l. c. & hom. 28. in Numer. adjungere poterat) addatque, Ju- dam non citare librum, sed prophetiam Henoch, quæ potuerit esse vocalis & verbalis. Drusius qui- dem in Henoch cap. 22. non dubitat librum He- noch adhuc hodie extare, vehementer etiam com- mendat librum Henoch Bouldoucus de Ecclesia ante Mosen, quem in arca Noæ conservatum putat lib. I. cap. 14. adducens pro illo Irenæum, Justinum, Clementem Alex. Athenagoram, Ter- tullianum, Methodium, Cyprianum, Lactantium, Severum Sulpitium, Proclum & Psellum. Cedre- nus de Henocho scribit: Οὗτος πρῶτος γράμ- ματα μανθάνει καὶ διδάσκει, cui annuit Zona- ras, Andr. Hojus in histor. sacr. & prophan. p. 6. Ludovicus Ballenster in onomatograph. pag. 356. librumque hunc antediluvianum cum Tertullia- no adstruit Jacobus Pamelius in notis ad Tertull. Alphabeta etiam Henochi producta sunt tum ab Hepburno, tum à Joh. Augustino Pantheo in Voarchadumia (sic vocat librum Anno 1539. editum) &c. Etiam Petrus Martyr in Gen. que- ritur, scripta Enochi periisse. Nostro quoque B. Gesnero probabilior visa est eorum sententia, qui affirmant, tempore Henochi fuisse literarum usum, neque Henochi verba absque literarum adminiculo retineri potuisse. B. Bangius extra omnem du- bitationis aleam positum dicit extitisse aliquan- do aliquod scriptum Henochium. Nullo tamen, ut diximus, fundamento nititur ea sententia, quod Enoch prophetiam aliquam literis consigna- rit; plerique ex hoc loco Judæ eam deducere voluerunt, in quo vero nihil de Enochi scripto habetur. Neque scripturam aut literarum cha- racteres ante diluvium extitisse controversia va- cat, quum nonnulli Mosen omnium primum ali- quid literis exarasse statuant, utpote B. Quistor- pius in h. l. ut & B. Waltherus in officin Bibl. p. 1180. Et quamvis B. D. Thomas Bangius in Cœ- lo orientis, quod mihi donavit, Exer. I. de li- bro Henochi ad Adamum referat literarum o- riginem pag. 9. (cujus varias alphabeti formas ab Adamo à Theseo Ambrosio, qui Angelicos cha- racteres Adamo traditos dixit, à Jacobo Bonaventu- ra Hepburno in aurea virga, Laurentio Schradero in monument. Ital. productas discussit exercit. II.) Canonicæ tamen Scripturæ initium à Filio Dei in exarandis tabulis lapideis factum recte statuit B. Gerhardus Exeg de Scr. S. pap. 31. Quod vero B. Bangius arguit, nisi extitisset scriptum Henoche- um, neutiquam illud ad partes vocassent tot Pa- tres Græci pariter ac Latini, Origenes, Augusti- nus, Tertullianus, Hieronymus, Clemens Alexandri- nus, &c. id, nostro judicio, minime sufficit, quum ab uno alii seduci potuerint, ut in traditione Chi- liasmi Papiæ exemplo, & Sectatorum ejus edocti sumus: neque de Origene id constat, imo contra- rium hom. 28. in Num. habetur, librum illum apud Ebræos in autoritate non haberi. Et l. V. contr. Cels. monuit Origenes, quod non magna sit literarum E- nochi autoritas in Ecclesiis (magna autem utique fu- isset, si liber Enocheus aliquis genuinus extitisset)

Hieronymus etiam ad Tit. I. Apocryphum nec inter Ecclesiæ scripturas receptum dicit Enochi librum, etsi ex isto Apocrypho Judam testimonium posuisse asserat, quod similiter de Augustino ex l. XIIX. de Civ. Dei cap. 38. liquet. Quid Henoch, inquit, septi- mus ab Adam? Nonne etiam in Canonica Epistola Apostoli Judæ prophetasse prædicatur? Quorum (Noachi & Henochi) scripta, ut apud Judæos & a- pud nos in autoritate non essent, nimia fecit anti- quitas, propter quam videbantur habenda esse suspe- cta, ne proferrentur falsa pro veris; sed ea castitas canonis non recipit, non quod eorum hominum, qui Deo placuerunt, reprobetur autoritas, sed quod ista esse non credantur ipsorum. Ad solum ergo Tertul- lianum sere res redit libr. de habit. mulier. c. 3. cu- jus vero acumen frustraneum inEnochi libri auto- ritate docuit ipse B. Bangius pag. 18. Qui porro p. 23. solide probavit, Henochi scriptum Canonicam auto- ritatem minime mereri, dignum, quod non tantum ad Apocryphorum librorum ima subsellia detrudatur, sed etiam inter commentitiorum mendaciorum & fabularum quisquilias humi abjectum jaceat, ad- ductis ipsius Augustini & Hieronymi testimoniis, necnon autoritatibus Hier. Zanchii, qui ab Enocho aliquod literarum monumentum consignatum ne- gat Tom. VIII. Op. Theol. de S. Script pag. 353. & Andr. Riveti exerc. 49. in Gen. qui librum hunc supposititium esse & à quibusdan Judæis conscriptum sibi omnino persuadet, quod in Ecclesia Dei ante Ba- bylonicam captivitatem in nullis Prophetarum li- bris fiat mentio tam rari thesauri, quem non cre- dibile est, si in rerum natura esset, Mosen latuisse, qui etiam scriptorum Henochi meminisset, si tunc exti- tissent; ut & Francisci Junii Tom. I. Op. pag. 1298. Parei in Genes. necnon Jos. Scaligeri not. in Euseb. p. 245. qui librum plane esse commentitium censet, & à Judæis confictum, multaque ex eodem citat, sed non sine tædio & odio (qui tamen in eo falsus fuit, 'quod locum in epist. Judæ manifeste ex hoc fragmento excerptum dixit, quæ inter alias cau- sa ipsi fuerit illud edendi;) & è Pontificiis Mich. Medinæ de rect. inDeum fide l. v. 1. p.220. Job. Ma- rii Scribonii Serm. XVII. in epist. Jud. p. 259. è no- stris B. Quistorpii ad h. l. Addere potuisset B. Wal- theri officinam Bibl. p. 1180. qui probat nullum li- brum sub nomine Enochi, vel Canonicum, vel Aca- nonicum unquam fuisse, librumque pristinum & modernum, (cujus fragmentum non tantum Sca- liger, sed etiam Athanasius Kircherus Latinitate donatum in Oedipo Ægypt. Gymn. Hieroglyph. class. II. Gramm. c. 2. §. 4. p. 69. edidit) Apocryphum esse & rejectitium, à Judæis conversis post Apostolo- rum tempora, occasione capta ex Michaëlis pugna cum Diabolo, & Henochi prophetia à Juda comme- morata concinnatum. Sed & demonstrat B. Ban- gius, quam fabulosum sit fragmentum ex libro Eno- chi de Egregoris p. 25. & sqq. idq; fætum esse Judai- cum Platonicis fasciis involutum, Christianorum impuris manibus susceptum &c. Quapropter quod B. Bangius extitisse aliquando ait aliquod scriptum Henocheum, intelligendum sine dubio de scripto pro Henocheo venditato. Nam non probat illud Augustini l. XV. de C. D. c. 23. Scripsisse quidem non- nulla divina Enoch illum septimum ab Adam ne- gare non possumus, quum hoc in Epistola Canonica Apostolus Judas dicat; quia non dicit Judas He- nochum scripsisse, sed prophetasse: Nec calculum ad- dit Hieronymo, quod locꝫ Judæ ex opere Henochi cite- tur, nedum Scaligero, quod è fragmento Heno- chiani libri excerptur sit, p. 244. in not. ad Euseb. siquidem Apostolici loci nullum in residuo Heno- chiani libelli fragmento appareat vestigium, cujus fragmenti vanitatem etiam ex illo Testamento XII. Patriarcharum ab Origene, & Procopio Gazao citato, quod a Rabbino quodam confictum Ro- bertus Grossetestus, Linconiensis Episcopus, Anno 1242. veritate Atheniensi donavit, convincit.

Frustra autem de eo disputant nonnulli, an Ju- das ex aliquo scripto, an ex traditione hæc ha- beat, utpote Beza, Joh. Prideax in orat. in- aug. de Sapient. Ægypt. Wellerus in Hexapl. Cor- nelius a Lapide, Jacob. Gordon. Tirinus, Meno- chius, Luc. Osiander, Georg. Rostius in h. l. siqui- dem detur tertium, nimirum e revelatione divina id habuisse S. Judam, & quamvis S. Scriptori libe- rum sit, ex profano etiam scripto quædam selige- re, quæ faciunt ad ædificationem, in prophetiis ta- men id usu venire non facile concedendum. Unde temere Gregor. Primaticcius in comment. in h. l. pag. 167. ex Henochi apocrypho hæc deprompta esse contendit. Falsus vero fuit Guilhelmus Po- stellus, cum credidit, se librum Henochi invenisse; deceptus Mirandulanus, cum grandi pecunia eum emit; quorum hoc Reuchlinus refert, illud Conr. Gesnerus in Bibl. tit. Enoch. Neque tamen illa traditio juvaret quicquam Papisticas traditiones non-scriptas, quia hæc traditio non est non- scripta, sed in scripturam relata, si traditio esse concedatur.

Προεφήτευσε δὲ καὶ τότοις, inquit S. Judas, Vulgata habet de iis, ut Ebr. I. 7. πρὸς τὲς ἀγγέλες est de Angelis, quamvis etiam sine præpositione sensus sibi constet, vaticinatus est iis. Nam quæ antea dicta vel scripta sunt, nobis dicta vel scripta etiam esse credendum, Rom. XV. v. 4. Septimus autem ab Adam non dicitur, quod septimus sit homo, sed septimus Patriarcha, si ab Adamo ini- tium numerationis fiat.

Λέγων ἰδὲ ἦλθε Κύριος) Præteritum pro futuro. Sic Psal. LI. v. 3. יבא אלהינו id est, vindictam faciet, in- terprete Chaldæo. Pro eo Rabbini dicunt שם אתי Syri סק אתי.

Λέγων est DICENS. Non scripsisse, sed di- xisse hæc Enochum ait, quamvis etiam de scri- ptura τὸ λέγειν adhibeatur, adeoque indefinitum sit; proinde ex verbis Judæ probari non potest, quod vaticinium Henochi scriptura consigna- tum fuerit. Dormitavit autem Grotius, cum Præteritum pro futuro adhibitum dixit. Ἦλθε non præteritum tempus, sed indefinitum notat, ad- eoque vel Præsens vel Præteritum, nisi circum- stantiis textus ad alterum pertrahatur. Hic vero potius Præsens est, quum quasi jamjam veniat Dominus, loquatur Judas, ut omni tempore ani- mo adventum ejus foveamus. Ex eo autem quod Christus Κύριος vocatur absolute, & sine articulo, Deitas Christi comprobratur, quum id nomen sine articulo Jehovam designare, Soci- niani contendant; quia in Veteris Testamenti Græca translatione nomen Κύριος sine articulo, tanquam si proprium nomen esset, ad Jehovah proprium Dei nomen exprimendum fere usur- patum, ut habet Socinus resp. ad cap. 17. Wujeck. p. 141. Quo de prolixe in Theol. Natur. & revel. p. 496. seqq. Ille κυρίε nomine hic insignitur, cujus δῦλον se Judas vocat, & quem τὸν μόνον Δε- σπότην Θεὸν καὶ Κύριον ἡμῶν abnegantes judica- turum minatur v. 2. 14. qui populum ex Ægypto salvavit, non-credentes perdidit, angelos aposta- tas caligini æternæ ad diem judicii æterni servat v. 6. quem, ut Diabolum de corpore Mosis con- tendentem increparet, imploravit Archangelus v. 9.

adversus quem dura verba loquuti sunt impii, quos ἐξελέγξαι venturus dicitur, v. 15. cujus Apo- stoli introducuntur, v. 17. cujus misericordiam ad vi- tam æternam exspectare fideles jubentur, v. 21. qui eosdem inculpatos sistet coram gloria sua in adventu suo, v. 24. &c. Quis autem ille κύριος, nisi Jesus Christus, de quo proinde vaticinatus est He- noch: ἰδὸ ἦλθε Κύριος מרן אתא Quæ for- mula anathematis inter Judæos recepta, & a S. Paulo adhibita, 1. Cor. XVI. 22. & ex hac prophe- tia in populo Dei tum non ignota videtur origi- nem cepisse. Fuit ista formula extremi anathe- matis, quod חרם dicitur. Nam præter Mid- dui habebant Cherem, idque tum simplex, tum Maranatha vel Samatha Dominus, vel Nomen ve- nit, quia τὸ ὄνομα κατ' ἀντονομασίαν notat Jeho- vam Dominum, objiciebatur enim per Mara- natha hoc modo a consortio Ecclesiæ separatus, extremo Domini summi Vindicis judicio.

Ἐν ἁγίαις μυριάσιν ἀυτῦ) מרבבת קדש Deut. XXXIII. v. 21. ubi LXX. σὺν μυριάσι Καδής: ut Aquila ἀπὸ μυριά- δων ἁγιασμὲ, ubi Aquila rectius credit קדש esse appella- tivum. At LXX. recte מ verterunt per σύν. Ἁγίυς vocari Angelos notavimus ad 1. Thess. III. 13. ubi quæ dicta, nihil opus repeti. Similis Dei descriptio Dan. cap. VII. v. 10.

## 1:15
Vers. 15.

To execute judgment upon all) What Enoch then either said or could say, with the flood impending, Jude could conveniently refer to that great slaughter which was impending over the contumacious Jews. You have κρίσιν ποιεῖν also in John V. 27. The Hebrews say עשה משפט.

And to convict all the ungodly of them) ἀυτῶν is absent in the manuscript. Ἐλέγξαι יכח is the same as to punish.

concerning all the works of their ungodliness which they have ungodly committed) ἀσεβεῖν רשע this pertains to deeds.

And concerning all the hard things which they have spoken against him) This pertains to words. Σκληρὰ are things hard to hear, John ch. VI. v. 60. Gen. ch. XLII. vers. 7, 30. So also 1 Sam. ch. XX. v. 7. 2 Paral. ch. III. v. 13. Prov. XVIII. 24. עתקים. Such words Lamech had spoken in the time of Enoch.

Ungodly sinners) Injurious to men and to God.

This is a remarkable perversion of an illustrious prophecy, which obtains no other than a single sense concerning the final judgment, which Grotius distorts into a double sense, one of Enoch, another of Jude, and both of them entirely alien: affixing to the former the sense of an impending divine judgment in the universal flood; to the latter, a particular divine judgment against the Jews in the slaughter of Bar Kokhba. Which glosses cannot even stand together, because Jude testifies that Enoch had prophesied to those very people against whom he is acting, teaching that that judgment of the Lord, concerning which he himself prophesied, pertains to those against whom he acts in his epistle. But what indeed is a judgment, which had already passed away so many centuries before in a universal cataclysm, to those who were living in the time of Jude, or were to live thereafter? And if Enoch prophesied concerning the flood, how could Jude the Apostle terrify heretics, or their followers in his own age, with this prophecy? How can the same statement have one sense and then another concerning such diverse divine judgments? Nor indeed does he bring forward the prophecy of Enoch merely by some accommodation, but testifies that it concerns them, just as it does any other men. Moreover, the Holy Spirit fortified this prophecy with a kind of special care, as if foreseeing such a corruption; and that not by one, but by a manifold reason. For he was not content to use the pronoun τέτοις, and to apply the universal judgment to them, but he established that universality so diligently that it could not have been done more diligently, lest, forsooth, the universal judgment, which we expect on the last day, should be converted into some particular judgment.

To execute, he says, judgment upon ALL. Cyprian expressed the sense to Novatian: to execute judgment upon all. Similarly the Arabic, that all flesh may be judged. For we must all be made manifest before the judgment seat of Christ. 2 Cor. 5:10. He adds further καὶ ἐξελέγξαι πάν- τας τοὺς ἀσεβεῖς ἀυτῶν, and to convict ALL their ungodly ones, i.e., of ALL, concerning whom he is about to execute judgment. First, he teaches that all men in general are to be judged, then that all the ungodly in the whole human race are to be convicted and refuted of their impiety: so that he might express the judgment that will be in the future pantocritical day universally, and also specifically, because he was designating the business with the ungodly themselves, the condemnatory judgment of the ungodly, not of some only of a certain time, but of all who have ever lived or are living. He adds, moreover, the universality of evil works, περὶ πάντων τῶν ἔργων τῆς ἀσεβείας ἀυτῶν, concerning ALL their works of impiety, and further, ὧν ἠσέβησαν, WHATEVER they have done impiously. Similarly in general, and universally, he embraces ALL impious words, which will come into judgment, καὶ περὶ πάντων τῶν σκληρῶν, and concerning ALL the hard things WHATEVER they have spoken against him. Furthermore, indefinitely, but in a universal sense, he comprehends all sinners; ἁμαρ- τωλοὶ ἀσεβεῖς, who, namely, have departed in impiety and have not repented. To these are added other arguments from the context. For by that pronoun κατ' ἀυτῦ, St. Jude looks back to κύριον, that Lord, whose coming Enoch had predicted, concerning whom the Apostle had warned that he was denied by the heretics, i.e., Christ, who is about to come visibly with innumerable legions of Angels and Saints, to execute judgment, Matt. 25:31. Furthermore, while he makes mention of τῶν πάντων σκληρῶν, he makes application to those hard things by which they have transgressed against him with their blasphemies, the heretics, v. 8, 10. And lest we doubt that he is still speaking of the same, he subjoins v. 16, Οὗτοί εἰσι γογγυσταὶ, these are murmurers, noting both their hard words, calling them murmurers and complainers, whose mouth speaks proud things against the Lord himself, and their wicked desires, and their impious deeds, so that the application might be clearer, especially that these men admired persons for the sake of gain: which is most clear to be about the heretics of that time. Finally, that it might be clearer than light that the discourse is about the final judgment, he not only alleges predictions made about the same by the Apostles of the Lord concerning the ἐσχάτῳ χρόνῳ, v. 18, but he also instructs the faithful about the preparation for the last judgment, how they ought to conduct themselves, so that they may be able to be presented immaculate, κατ' ἐνώπιον τῆς δόξης ἀυτῦ in the SIGHT of the glory of the Lord himself, which he prays for, namely, of him who is about to come visibly to judgment in his Majesty, Matt. 25:31, which finally are explained in the Vulgate by adding these words: in the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. All of which things will be dragged by nothing but manifest violence to the slaughter of the seditious under the leader Barchocheba, of which there is neither a trace nor a footprint in this whole epistle.

That Jude is not inventing what Enoch could have said in his own time, but that the words of the very prophecy of the Patriarch Enoch are brought forward, is clearly taught by that expression: προεφήτευσε, he prophesied; and λέγων, saying: which, when it occurs in the Scripture of the New Testament, indicates not what a Prophet could have said, but what he did say, and in what words exactly he said it, Matt. ch. 7, v. 7; Luke 1:67.

This Catholic writing is to the Jews converted to the faith of Christ, not to those who were clinging to a Pseudo-Christ. He deals with heretics, not with such seditious persons who are outside the Church. He deals with such a judgment in which an account must be rendered for words, deeds, and wicked desires, which fits neither the judgment of the flood, nor the punishment of the Jewish faction, nor did the Lord come with many thousands to those judgments. We have already proved before that that Lord, whose coming is predicted in this place, is Christ Jesus our Lord, whom, just as myriads of myriads of Angels surround, Apoc. 5:11, so he is about to come with all the Angels, Matt. 25:31. Those most holy companions of the Lord will be present, leading the same in glory, Matt. 25:31; Luke 9:26; 1 Thess. 1:7, about to gather those to be judged, Matt. 25:31. Mark 13:27, about to separate the gathered, Matt. 13:49, about to thrust the damned into hell, Matt. 13:41, about to carry the faithful up into the heavens, 1 Thess. 4:17. But such distorted expositions arise without doubt from the Socinian hypothesis, that the ancients were not certain about the final judgment.

Latin:

Vers. 15.

Ποιῆσαι κρίσιν κατὰ πάντων) Quod tunc Enoch aut dixit aut dicere potuit, imminente diluvio, idem Judas ad in- gentem illam internecionem, quæ Judæis contumacibus imminēbat, referre commode potuit. Κρίσιν ποιεῖν habes & Joh. V. 27. Ebræi dicunt עשה משפט.

Καὶ ἐλέγξαι πάντας τὲς ἀσεβεῖς ἀυτῶν) ἀυτῶν abest in Ma- nuscripto. Ἐλέγξαι יכח idem est castigare.

περὶ πάντων ἔργων ἀσεβείας ἀυτῶν ὧν ἠσέβησαν) ἀσεβεῖν רשע hoc ad facta pertinet.

Καὶ περὶ πάντων τῶν σκληρῶν, ὧν ἐλάλησαν κατ' ἀυτῦ) Hoc ad dicta. Σκληρὰ dura auditu, Joh. cap. VI. v. 60. Gen. cap. XLII. vers. 7. 30. Sic & 1. Sam. cap. XX. v. 7. 2. Paral. c. III. v. 13. Prov. XVIII. 24. עתקים. Talia verba Lamech loquutus erat Enochi tempore.

Ἁμαρτωλοὶ ἀσεβεῖς) In homines Deumque injurii.

Insignis perversio hæc est illustris vaticinii, quod non nisi unicum sensum obtinet de ex- tremo judicio, a Grotio ad duplicem sensum, alium Henochi, alium Judæ, & utrumque pror- sus alienum detorquet: Illi sensum affingens imminentis judicii divini in diluvio universali; huic divini judicii particularis adversus Judæos in clade Barchochebæ. Quæ glossæ neque consiste- re possunt simul, quia Judas Enochum vati- cinatum esse τέτοις illis, contra quos agit, testa- tur, judicium istud Domini, de quo ipse vati- cinatus est, illos attinere docens, contra quos in sua epistola agit. Quid vero ad illos, qui tem- pore Judæ vivebant, aut deinceps victuri erant, judicium, quod ante tot secula jam præterierat in universali cataclysmo? Et si de diluvio vati- cinatus est Henoch, quomodo hoc vaticinio ter- rere potuit hæreticos, eorumve sectatores sua ætate Judas Apostolus? Quomodo alium atque alium sensum de tam diversis judiciis divinis ha- bere potest idem dictum? Nec vero per accom- modationem tantum aliquam prophetiam Heno- chi affert, sed eosdem, uti alios quosvis homi- nes, concernere testatur. Munivit insuper pe- culiari veluti cura hoc vaticinium Spiritus San- ctus, utpote prævidens ejusmodi corruptelam; idque non una, sed multiplici ratione. Non enim contentus pronomen τέτοις adhibere, il- lisque applicare universale judicium, sed uni- versalitatem istam tam diligenter adstruxit, ut non potuerit diligentius, ne scilicet universale judicium, quod in die novissimo exspectamus, in particulare quoddam judicium convertatur.

Ποιῆσαι, inquit, κρίσιν κατὰ πάντων judicium fa- cere contra OMNES. Sensum expressit Cy- prianus ad Novat. facere judicium de omnibus. Similiter Arabs, ut judicetur omnis caro. Omnes enim nos manifestari oportet ante tribunal Chri- sti. 2. Cor. V. 10. Addit porro καὶ ἐξελέγξαι πάν- τας τοὺς ἀσεβεῖς ἀυτῶν, & arguere OMNES im- pios eorum, scil. OMNIUM, de quibus judicium facturus est. Prius in genere omnes homines ju- dicatum iri docet, deinde arguendos & de impie- tate convincendos omnes in toto genere humano im- pios: ut tum universaliter judicium exprimeret in die pantocritico futurum, tum specialiter, quia cum impiis ipsi negotium, judicium condemnato- rium impiorum, non quorundam tantum certi temporis, sed omnium, qui unquam vixere, aut vivunt, designaret. Addit insuper universalita- tem operum improborum, περὶ πάντων τῶν ἔργων τῆς ἀσεβείας ἀυτῶν, de OMNIBUS operibus im- pietatis ipsorum, ac porro, ὧν ἠσέβησαν, QUI- BUSCUNQUE ipsi impie egerunt. Simili- ter in genere, ac universaliter OMNIA impia dicta complectitur, quæ in judicium venient, καὶ περὶ πάντων τῶν σκληρῶν, & de OMNIBUS duris ὧν ἐλάλησαν κατ' ἀυτῦ QUÆCUNQUE loquuti sunt contra ipsum. Præterea indefinite, at sensu uni- versali comprehendit omnes peccatores; ἁμαρ- τωλοὶ ἀσεβεῖς, qui scilicet in ἀσεβείᾳ discessere, nec poenitentiam egerunt. His accedunt & alia e contextu argumenta. Nam pronomine il- lo κατ' ἀυτῦ respicit S. Judas κύριον Dominum il- lum, cujus adventum prædixerat Enochus, de quo abnegato ab Hæreticis monuerat Apostolus, h. e. Christum, qui visibiliter adventurus est, cum innu- meris legionibus Angelorum & Sanctorum, ut ju- dicium faciat, Matth. XXV. 31. Adhæc dum τῶν pántwn sklhroun mentionem facit ad illa sklhpa, quibus kat' autou contra ipsum prævaricati sunt blasphemiis suis hæretici v. 8. 10. applicationem facit. Et ne de iisdem se loqui adhuc ambiga- mus, subjungit v. 16. Οὗτοί εἰσι γογγυσταὶ, hi sunt murmuratores, eorum notat tum verba dura, murmuratores & querulos vocans, quorum os lo- quitur superba contra ipsummet Dominum, tum desideria prava, tum facta impia, ut applicatio sit luculentior, imprimis quod personas mirarentur isti, quæstus causa: Quæ de hæreticis istius tempo- ris agere luculentissimum est. Denique ut luce clarius constaret, de extremo judicio sermonem es- se, non modo prædictiones allegat de eodem ab Apostolis Domini factas de ἐσχάτῳ χρόνῳ, v. 18. sed etiam de præparatione ad novissimum judicium instruit fideles, quales se gerere debeant, ut scilicet immaculati sisti possint, κατ' ἐνώπιον τῆς δόξης ἀυτῦ in CONSPECTU gloriæ ipsius Domini, quod vo- vet, nempe illius, qui visibiliter venturus est, ad ju- dicium in Majestate sua, Matth. XXV. 31. quæ de- nique in Vulgata explicantur additis hisce ver- bis in adventu Domini nostri Jesu Christi. Quæ omnia non nisi manifesta violentia trahentur ad cædem seditiosorum sub Duce Barchocheba, de qua nec vola, nec vestigium in tota hac epi- stola.

Non autem fingere Judam, quæ Enoch suo tempore dicere potuerit, sed afferri verba ipsius- met vaticinii Patriarchæ Henoch, luculenter do- cet illa loquutio: προεφήτευσε vaticinatus est; & λέγων dicens: quæ quando in Scriptura Novi Te- stamenti occurrit, non quid dicere potuerit Pro- pheta, sed quid dixerit, & quibus omnino verbis dixerit, indicant Matth. cap. VII. v. 7. Luc. I. 67.

Scripta hæc Catholica est ad Judæos conversos ad fidem Christi, non ad eos, qui adhærebant Pseu- do-Christo. De hæreticis agit, non de talibus seditiosis, qui sunt extra Ecclesiam. De tali agit judicio, in quo ratio reddenda de dictis, factis, & desideriis pravis, quod nec judicio diluvii, nec supplicio factionis Judaicæ convenit, nec ad illa judicia cum multis millibus venit Dominus. Dominum illum, cujus adventus prædicitur hoc loco, Christum Jesum Dominum nostrum esse, jam antea probavimus, quem uti μυριάδες μυ- ριάδων Angelorum stipant, Apoc. V. v. 11. ita cum omnibus Angelis venturus est, Matth. XXV. v. 31. Aderunt illi sanctissimi comites Domini, eundem glorioso deducentes, Matth. XXV. v. 31. Luc. IX. v. 26. 1. Thess. I. v. 7. judicandos congre- gaturi, Matth. XXV. v. 31. Marc. XIII. v. 27. congregatos separaturi, Matth. XIII. v. 49. da- mnatos ad infernum detrusuri, Matth. XIII. 41. fideles in cælos subvecturi, 1. Thess. IV. v. 17. Oriuntur autem strabæ ejusmodi expositiones sine dubio ex hypothesi Sociniana, quod antiquis non constiterit de judicio extremo.

## 1:16
Verse 16.

Οὗτοί εἰσι γογγυσταὶ) Here again Jude began to speak in his own words. Γογγυσταὶ are those who willingly disparage their superiors, as we said 1 Cor. ch. 10, v. 10, מתאוננים, Num. 11:1.

They do not only come under that name who murmur against the magistrate, but also those who murmur against God, and the discourse is about such in 1 Cor. 10:10, as also in the present place.

Μεμψίμοιροι) Not content with moderate things: not desiring to be within their own fortune, as Propertius speaks. In the Glossary, μεμψίμοιρος is a complainer, μεμψιμοιρία is a secret detractor according to Clement of Alexandria, Paedagogus 1.9. Those men were complaining about the Roman Empire, than which, however, no external rule had been or was to be milder for the Jews.

It is not read that the false prophets complained about the Roman Empire: nor do these things sound of such complaints, but of complaining voices in general, which proceed from a μεμψίμοιρος, incredulous, and impatient mind. B. Geu Hopfner in his practical tract on the Holy Supper explains it as those who are not content with their lot, but complain about their state in which they have been placed by God. Oecumenius and others translate it as censurers, who censure the portion and lot of others, and who strive to find fault with everything and always.

Κατὰ τὰς ἐπιθυμίας αὑτῶν πορευόμενοι) The epistle which is called the second of Peter calls the same men walking in the lust of uncleanness. They followed all kinds of lusts.

These desires are impious cravings against the first and second table: and therefore they extend more broadly than the ἐπιθυμίαι σαρκὸς ἐν ἀσελγείαις, of which St. Peter speaks in 2 Ep. II. 18.

Καὶ τὸ στόμα αὐτῶν λαλεῖ ὑπέρογκα) And this is from the same epistle II. 18. They boasted wonderful things about those powers, which were superior to the creators of the world.

This likewise is more general, which is clear from 2 Pet. II. v. 18. They speak especially proud things, when they exalt themselves against God. Ὑπέρογκα are things swollen beyond measure, as Erasmus rendered it. Bede: They speak grand things, and their whole discourse is pride. Conf. Ps. XII. 5. Concerning Marcus and the Gnostics, Irenaeus: Calling themselves perfect, as if no one could be equaled to the magnitude of their knowledge, not even if you name Paul or Peter, or some other of the Apostles, but that they have known more than all, and have alone drunk in the magnitude of that knowledge which is of ineffable power. And that they are in a height above every power. Wherefore

and to do all things freely, having no fear in anyone.

Showing partiality for the sake of gain) Supply 'they are'. To show partiality to the person of a powerful man הדר פני גדול Levit. ch. XIX. v. 15. is to judge in favor of him who is more powerful. Thus they flattered the rich who were in the Church, by favoring their vices, and that so they might make gain from their largesse. Thus also 2 Pet. II. 14. enticing unstable souls, having a heart trained in covetous practices.

Cornelius a Lapide: They flatter, he says, the powerful and the rich, they praise and extol them wonderfully, pretending that they admire their excellence, talent, wisdom, wealth, virtues. So Oecumenius. Thus Simon flattered Nero, and as if admiring him, won his favor for himself. Thus Marcus the heretic, says Irenaeus in book I, ch. 9, courted purple-clad and very wealthy women, and thus drained their wealth. They hunt for gain, therefore: whence Ignatius, ep. III, calls the heretics of his own age seekers of others' goods, greedy for money, and like whirlpools.

PART II. Exhortation concerning the necessary precautions to be observed against apostasy.

Latin:

Vers. 16.

Οὗτοί εἰσι γογγυσταὶ) Hic iterum Judas incepit suis verbis loqui. Γογγυσταὶ sunt, qui libenter obtrectant su- perioribus, ut diximus 1. Cor. cap. X. v. 10. מתאוננים, Num. XI. 1.

Non tantum eo nomine veniunt, qui adver- sus Magistratum, sed etiam qui adversus Deum murmurant, & de talibus sermo est 1. Cor. X. 10. ut & in præsenti loco.

Μεμψίμοιροι) Non contenti modicis : non cupientes intra fortunam suam esse, ut Propertius loquitur. In Glossario μεμψίμοιρος querulus, μεμψιμοιρία λαθραῖος ψυ- γὸς apud Clementem Alexandrinum Pædagog. I. 9. quere- bantur illi de Imperio Romano, quo tamen nullum exter- num Judæis fuerat, aut futurum erat lenius.

Falsos Prophetas questos esse de Romano Im- perio non legitur : nec de talibus querelis hæc sonant, sed de querulis vocibus in genere, quæ ex μεμψίμοιροι incredulo & impatienti animo proficiscuntur. B. geu Hopfnerus in tract. Pract. de S. Cœna explicat, qui non sunt contenti sua forte, sed queruntur de statu suo, in quo sunt a Deo collocati. Oecu- menius & alii vertunt reprehensores, qui portio- nem & sortem aliorum reprehendunt, quique omnia ac semper student vituperare.

Κατὰ τὰς ἐπιθυμίας αὑτῶν πορευόμενοι) ἐν ἐπιθυμίᾳ μιασμοῦ πορευομένους vocat eosdem homines epistola, quæ secunda Petri dicitur. Omnia illi libidinum genera sectabantur.

Hæc desideria cupiditates impiæ sunt contra primam & secundam tabulam : ideoque latius pa- tent, quam ἐπιθυμίαι σαρκὸς ἐν ἀσελγείαις, de quibus S. Petrus 2. ep. II. 18.

Καὶ τὸ στόμα αὐτῶν λαλεῖ ὑπέρογκα) Et hoc ex eadem epistola II. 18. Mira jactabant de virtutibus illis, qua su- periores essent mundi fabricatoribus.

Hoc itidem generalius est, quod e 2. Petr. II. v. 18. liquet. Superba imprimis loquuntur, quum adversus Deum sese efferunt. Ὑπέρογκα sunt supra modum turgida, ut Erasmus reddidit. Beda : Loquuntur grandia, & totus eorum sermo superbia est. Conf. Ps. XII. 5. De Marco & Gno- sticis Irenæus: Perfectos semetipsos vocantes, quasi nemo possit exæquari magnitudini agnitionis ipso- rum, nec si Paulum aut Petrum dicas, vel alium quendam Apostolorum, sed plus omnibus se cogno- visse, & magnitudinem agnitionis illius, quæ est in- enarrabilis virtutis solos ebibisse. Esse autem se in altitudine super omnem virtutem. Quapropter

& libere omnia agere, nullum in nullo timorem ha- bentes.

Θαυμάζοντες πρόσωπα ὠφελείας χάριν) Supple εἰσι. Θαυ- μάζειν πρόσωπον δυνάστου הדר פני גדול Levit. c. XIX. v. 15. est judicium gratificari ei, qui potentior est, Sic illi divitibus, qui in Ecclesia erant adulabantur, vitiis eorum favendo, idque ut ex eorum largitionibus quæstum facerent. Sic & 2. Petr. II. 14. δελεάζοντες ψυχὰς ἀστηρίκτους, καρδίαν γεγυμνασμένην πλεονεξίαις ἔχοντες.

Cornelius a Lapide : Adulantur inquit, potenti- bus & divitibus, eos mirifice laudant & extollunt, fingentes se admirari eorum excellentiam, ingenium, sapientiam, opes, virtutes. Ita Oecumenius. Sic Simon adulatus Neroni, eumque quasi admirans ejus gratiam sibi conciliavit. Sic Marcus hæreticus, ait Irenæus libro I. cap. 9. purpuratas & ditissimas mu- lieres coluit, itaque eorum opes emunxit. Quæstum ergo aucupantur : unde hæreticos sui ævi Ignatius ep. III. vocat alienorum appetitores, pecuniarum ra- paces, & quasi vortices.

PARS II. Adhortatio de observandis cautelis adversus apostasiam necessariis.

## 1:17
Ver. 17.

But you, beloved) You who ought to be very different from them.

Remember the words which were spoken before) That is, which were said long ago. The same expression in 2 Pet. II. 3. Understand, however, not only those which were committed to writing, but also those which were handed down by word of mouth.

By the Apostles of our Lord Jesus Christ) Especially by Peter, Paul, John. Or from this you may see that this writer was somewhat later than the Apostles.

Latin:

Vers. 17.

Ὑμεῖς δὲ ἀγαπητοὶ) Vos qui multum ab illis distare de- betis.

Μνήσθητε τῶν ῥημάτων τῶν προειρημένων) Id est, quæ pridem dicta sunt. Eadem loquutio 2. Petr. II. 3. Intellige autem non tantum quæ scriptis mandata, sed & quæ voce dicta per manus tradebantur.

Ὑπὸ τῶν Ἀποστόλων τοῦ Κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ) Maximè à Petro, Paulo, Johanne. Vel hinc videas, scriptorem hunc posteriorem aliquanto fuisse Apostolis.

## 1:18
Ver. 18.

That in the last time) That is, finally באחרית הימים, which is accustomed to be translated in the last days, 2 Tim. III. 1. in the last of the times, 1 Pet. I. 20. In the Manuscript here it is in the last of the time.

There will be mockers walking according to their own desires of ungodliness) Taken from 2 Pet. III. 3. that there will come in the last of the days mockers walking according to their own desires. They are called mockers especially because they would mock the resurrection. That 'of ungodliness' is construed with 'the desires', and is in place of an adjective, which are desires of impieties, that is, clearly impious. For 'there will be' the Manuscript has 'there will come'.

Some warnings are general, others are specific. General ones are partly while those things which they had received from other Apostles are called to memory, and he confirms these by their own testimonies, so that they might be made the more certain of their truth: by which method the authority of the other Apostles' letters is simultaneously won; partly while heretics separating themselves from the Church are pointed out as to be avoided. There was no need that he should refer to traditions: for they had the writings of those Apostles, and those Apostolic prophecies exist in the Holy Scriptures, 1 Tim. ch. IV. v. 1, 2 Tim. ch. III. v. 1, 2 Pet. ch. II. v. 3, ch. III. v. 3, which Cornelius himself acknowledges are referred to here, because there the faithful are forewarned to beware of heretics about to be born, and already in part born. Which was also done by St. John, 1 ep. IV. and ep. II. Jas. I. 16. But that is no consequence: St. Jude refers to other Apostles, therefore he himself was not an Apostle. Or even: Therefore he himself is much later than the Apostles. We readily grant, however, that those epistles of other Apostles, to which St. Jude referred, were written earlier. But they had predicted to them that in the last time there would be mockers, walking according to their own desires in impieties, scoffers, who mock all things divine and human. Which Cornelius applies to the Gnostics, who mocked

GOD'S providence and judgment, so that without fear of Him they might freely indulge their lusts, 2 Pet. chap. III. verse 4. But Jude speaks of the last time.

Latin:

Vers. 18.

Ὅτι ἐν ἐσχάτῳ χρόνῳ) Id est tandem באחרית הימים, quod verti solet ἐν ἐσχάταις ἡμέραις, 2. Tim. III. 1. ἐπʼ ἐσχάτων τῶν χρόνων, 1. Petr. I. 20. In Manuscripto est hic ἐπʼ ἐσχάτου τοῦ χρόνου.

Ἔσονται ἐμπαῖκται κατὰ τὰς ἐπιθυμίας ἑαυτῶν πορευόμενοι τῶν ἀσεβειῶν ) Sumptum ex 2. Petr. III. 3. ὅτι ἐλεύσονται ἐπὶ τῶν ἐσχάτων τῶν ἡμερῶν ἐμπαῖκται κατὰ τὰς ἰδίας ἐπιθυμίας αὐτῶν πορευόμενοι. Dicuntur ἐμπαῖκται maximè quod re- surrectionem irriderent. Illud τῶν ἀσεβειῶν construitur cum τὰς ἐπιθυμίας, estque vice ἐπιθέτου, quæ cupiditates sunt im- pietatum, id est plane impiæ. Pro ἔσονται Manuscriptus habet ἐλεύσονται.

Monita alia sunt generalia, alia vero specia- lia. Generalia partim dum in memoriam re- vocantur ea, quæ ab Apostolis aliis acceperant, & confirmat hæc sua ipsorum testimoniis, ut de eorum veritate eo certiores reddantur : Quo pacto simul autoritas conciliata Apostolorum alio- rum literis; partim dum hæretici separantes se ab Ecclesia fugiendi innuntur. Non opus erat, ut ad traditiones remitteretur : Habuere enim istorum Apostolorum scripta, & extant vatici- nia illa Apostolica in S. literis, 1. Tim. c. IV. v. 1. 2. Tim. c. III. v. 1. 2. Petr. c. II. v. 3. cap. III. v. 3. quæ hic respici Cornelius ipse agnoscit, quia ibi præmonentur fideles, ut caveant hæreticos mox nascituros, & ex parte jam natos. Quod etiam a S. Johanne factum, 1. epist. IV. & epist. II. Jac. I. 16. Nulla autem est illa consequentia, S. Judas remit- tit ad alios Apostolos, ergo ipse non fuit Apostolus. Aut etiam : Ergo ipse Apostolis multo posterior est. Id autem facile largimur, prius scriptas es- se illas epistolas aliorum Apostolorum, ad quas S. Judas remisit. Prædixerant autem ipsis, quod in extremo tempore futuri sint illusores, secun- dum desideria sua ambulantes in impietatibus, empæctæ, qui omnia divina & humana irrident. Quod Gnosticis applicat Cornelius, qui illuserint

DEI providentiam & judicium, ut sine ejus metu libere suis indulgerent libidinibus, 2. Petr. cap. III. verf. 4. Sed Judas loquitur de ἐσχάτῳ χρόνῳ.

## 1:19
Verse 19.

These are they who separate themselves) Supply themselves, which it is not necessary to add, since it is accustomed to be understood among the Hebrews as much in the active as in the passive. It is the same as what he will say presently, those who doubt, who separate or distinguish themselves from others, as if they were much wiser and more experienced than others, with great contempt for others, פפרדים.

Sensual) They care for nothing but the things of this life 1 Cor. II. 14. Jas. III. 15. Tertullian, though Montanizing, seized upon this name against those who adhered to the Roman Church.

Not having the Spirit) They boast that they have wonderful inspirations, but they have none.

He now notes the schismatics of his own time, who were segregating themselves from the Church, and consequently also those whom they were seducing. Oecumenius: Who separate, that is, who lead men away and separate them outside the bounds of the Church, outside the faith and the sacred tabernacle of the Church. He notes them as animal not only from the sensitive and vegetative soul: because they do not follow reason, but sense, and live in the lusts of the flesh; but because reason is corrupted, especially in those who are not reborn, by the soul taken universally; since they follow nothing but the leading of their own soul, which is truly corrupted by original sin, not having the Spirit. For they are opposed to each other, the sensual and the spiritual, 1 Cor. II. v. 14. ff.

Latin:

Verf. 19.

Οὗτοί εἰσιν οἱ ἀποδιορίζοντες) Supple ἑαυτοὺς, quod addi nihil necesse est, quum soleat subaudiri apud Ebræos tam in activo, quam in passivo. Idem est quod modo dicet διακρινομένους, qui semet a cæteris separant sive distin- guunt, quasi multo sapientiores ac peritiores essent aliis, cum magno contemptu aliorum פפרדים.

Ψυχικοὶ) Non curant nisi res hujus vitæ 1. Cor. II. 14. Jac. III. 15. Hoc nomen contra eos, qui Ecclesiæ Romanæ ad- hærebant, Tertullianus sed Montanizans arripuit.

Πνεῦμα μὴ ἔχοντες) Jactant se miras habes inspirationes, at nullas habent.

Notat jam schismaticos, sui temporis, qui semet- ipsos segregabant ab Ecclesia, adeoque & illos, quos seducebant. Oecumenius: Qui disterminant, id est, qui extra Ecclesiæ terminos, extra fidem & sacrum Ecclesiæ tabernaculum homines abducunt & separant. Animales notat non tantum ab anima sensitiva & vegetativa: quod non rationem se- quuntur, sed sensum, vivuntque in concupiscentiis carnis; sed quia corrupta est vel maxime ratio pe- nes eos, qui renati non sunt, ab anima universim accepta; siquidem non nisi animæ suæ, quæ vero per peccatum originis corrupta est, ductum se- quuntur, Spiritum non habentes. Nam oppo- nuntur sibi invicem ψυχικοὶ καὶ πνευματικοὶ, 1. Cor. II. v. 14. seqq.

## 1:20
Verse 20.

But you, beloved, building up yourselves on your most holy faith) Those words on your most holy faith are postponed in the Manuscript, and are joined with the following exhortation to prayers, which certainly require faith. Moreover, both to build up and to be built up are accustomed to be used simply for to give progress and to progress, or to rise up, Acts chap. XX. v. 32. Coloss. II. v. 7.

Praying in the Holy Spirit) With the Holy Spirit dictating, Rom. VIII. 26.

Latin:

Verf. 20.

Ὑμεῖς δὲ ἀγαπητοὶ τῇ ἁγιωτάτῃ πίσει ἐποικοδομοῦντες ἑαυ- τοὺς) Illa τῇ ἁγιωτάτῃ πίσει in Manuscripto postponuntur, & conjunguntur cum sequente exhortatione ad preces, quæ certe fidem requirunt. Solet autem & ἐποικοδομεῖν & ἐποικοδομεῖσθαι simpliciter poni pro dare profectum & pro- ficere, sive assurgere, Actor. cap. XX. v. 32. Coloss. II. v. 7.

Ἐν Πνεύματι ἁγίῳ προσευχόμενοι) Dictante Spiritu Sancto, Rom. VIII. 26.

## 1:21
Verse 21.

Keep yourselves in the love of God) The love of God can be and is spoken of sometimes as the way we love God, sometimes as the way God loves us. The former meaning fits this passage better. Devote effort to keep yourselves in love toward God, which is done both through prayers and through pious acts. The expression is not unlike John 17:11.

Praying for the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ unto eternal life) Mercy, חסד, a benefit. Unto eternal life, through which we may attain eternal life. It is indeed promised. But that which is liberally promised retains the name of a benefit from its own source.

There are special admonitions: first, that they should build themselves up in the faith once delivered; next, that they should pray in the Spirit; then, that they should keep themselves in the love of God; and further, that they should constantly and patiently await the hope, the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ. Thus, by the word ἐποικοδομεῖν, the duty of the pious is indicated, who ought not to acquiesce lazily in the measure of faith, but rather should study the Holy Scriptures more and more, and cultivate and strengthen their faith by the study of them, as Junius notes on this passage, B. Glassius, Gramm. S. p. 542. According to Cornelius, St. Jude opposes to that 'building up' which he mentioned in the preceding verse, those who 'separate themselves,' i.e., the Gnostics, who by heresy separate themselves, as from the faith, so from the structure of Christ: 'But you, O believers, constantly insist upon and adhere to the faith already received, and all together build yourselves up.' But because that is not of our own virtue, there is need of prayer, that the grace of God may supply us with strength. The Apostle therefore adds that we should pray in the Spirit: for our prayers also proceed from the Spirit, and must be done in Spirit and truth, John IV. 24. For the Holy Spirit is the Spirit of grace and supplications, Zech. XII. 10. Furthermore, pains must be taken by the reborn, that they may be kept in the love of God, both by the study and scrutiny of the divine Word, and by pious, unwearied prayer: hence the Apostle adds, waiting for the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ unto eternal life. For by meditation on the divine Word we are stirred up, and confirmed in that hope, that we may confidently, patiently, and constantly await that mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ unto eternal life, as being that which he himself acquired for us by his most holy obedience, and by his satisfactory passion and death. By ἀγάπην Θεῦ, therefore, it is better to understand the love of God for us, in which we must take the greatest pains to be preserved, which is bound up with that mercy of Jesus Christ which we await unto eternal life. Of which love the faithful are certain, that they can be separated from it neither by death, nor by life, &c., as being that which is founded in Christ Jesus, Rom. VIII. 38, 39. Those who understand it actively concerning the charity by which we love God, by which we sincerely adhere to God, and in him as the highest good uniquely rest, and passively by which we are loved by God, do not depart from this interpretation, which is to be preserved, lest we fall from it through heresy and blasphemy, but rather that the mercy and love of God may be multiplied in us, v. 2. But since a double sense cannot hold at the same time, it is better that the love of God be explained uniquely in the passive sense, as we have said.

Latin:

Verf. 21.

Ἑαυτοὺς ἐν ἀγάπῃ τοῦ Θεοῦ τηρήσατε) Ἀγάπη τοῦ Θεοῦ & dici potest & dicitur modo qua Deum diligimus, modo qua Deus nos diligit. Huic loco prior significatio melius con- venit. Date operam, ut vosmet conservetis in dilectione erga Deum, quod fit tum per preces tum per actus pios. Locutio non dissimilis Joh. XVII. 11.

Προσευχόμενοι τὸ ἔλεος τοῦ Κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ εἰς ζωὴν αἰώνιον) Ἔλεος חסד beneficium. Εἰς ζωὴν αἰώνιον per quod consequamur vitam æternam. Est quidem ea pro- missa. Sed quod liberaliter promittitur, ex suo fonte nomen beneficii retinet.

Specialia monita sunt, primum ut fide se- mel tradita seipsos ædificent, deinde ut in Spiritu precentur, tum ut seipsos in charitate Dei ser- vent, ac porro ut spem, misericordiam Domini nostri Jesu Christi constanter ac patienter expe- ctent. Ita verbo ἐποικοδομεῖν piorum officium in- nuitur, qui non debent oscitanter acquiescere in demenso fidei, quin magis ac magis studeant sacris literis, & fidem suam studio earum excolant ac statuminent, ut cum Junio in h. l. B. Glassius Gramm. S. pag. 542. Opponit, secundum Cor- nelium, S. Judas τὸ superædificantes illi, quod dixit v. præced. Hi sunt, qui segregant semetipsos q. d. Gnostici per hæresin separant se, uti a fide, ita a fabrica Christi: Vos autem, ô fideles, fidei jam re- ceptæ constanter insistite, inhærete, & omnes simul vos superædificate. Quia vero id virtutis nostræ non est, oratione opus est, ut Dei gratia vires nobis sufficiat. Addit ergo Apostolus, ut in Spiritu oremus: nam & preces nostræ a Spiritu proficiscuntur, & in Spiritu ac veritate fieri de- bent, Joh. IV. 24. Spiritus Sanctus enim est Spiritus gratiæ & precum, Zach. XII. 10. Porro opera dan- dæ renatis, ut in dilectione Dei custodiantur, tum Verbi divini studio & scrutinio, tum oratione pia indefessa: inde addit Apostolus, προσδεχόμενοι τὸ ἔλεος τῦ Κυρίʊ ἡμῶν Ἰησῦ Χρισῦ εἰς ζωὴν αἰώ- νιον. Verbi enim divini meditatione nos exci- tamur, & confirmamur in illa spe, ut confiden- ter, patienter, ac constanter eam misericordiam Domini nostri Jesu Christi ad vitam æternam ex- pectemus, utpote quam ipse acquisivit nobis obedientia sanctissima, & passione ac morte sa- tisfactoria. Per ἀγάπην ergo Θεῦ præstat amo- rem Dei erga nos intelligere, in quo ut conserve- mur opera danda maxime, qui cum illa misericor- dia Jesu Christi, quam ad vitam æternam expecta- mus, devinctus est. De quo amore certi sunt fi- deles, se nec per mortem, nec per vitam, &c. ab illo separari posse, utpote qui in Christo Jesu fun- datus est, Rom. VIII. 38. 39. A qua interpretatione non discedunt, qui & active de charitate, qua Deum diligimus, intelligunt, qua nos Deo sincere adhæremus, & in eo ceu summo bono unice ac- quiescimus, & passive qua diligimur a Deo, quæ conservanda, ne per hæresin & blasphemiam ea excidamus, sed magis magisq; misericordia & dile- ctio Dei in nobis πληθυνθείη, multiplicetur, v. 2. Sed quum geminus sensus simul obtinere ne- queat, præstat unice dilectionem Dei passive, ut diximus, explicari.

## 1:22
Vers. 22.

Καὶ ὓῦς μὲν ἐλεεῖτε διακρινόμενοι) Manuscript: Καὶ ὓῦς μὲν ἐλέγχετε διακρινομένες, and the Latin reads no differently. But the sense here seems to be: Reprove those who prefer themselves to others. For thus is διακρίνειν taken, 1 Cor. ch. IV. 7. Moreover, this is a passive for a reciprocal, after the Hebrew manner, Niphal for Hitpael.

Latin:

Vers. 22.

Καὶ ὓῦς μὲν ἐλεεῖτε διακρινόμενοι) Manuscriptus : Καὶ ὓῦς μὲν ἐλέγχετε διακρινομένες, nec aliter legit Latinus. At sensus hic videtur esse: Reprehendite illos, qui se cæteris præferunt. Ita enim sumitur διακρίνειν, 1. Cor. cap. IV. 7. Est autem hic Passivum pro reciproco more Ebræo Niphal pro Hitpaël.

## 1:23
Vers. 23.

Οὓῦς δὲ ἐν φόβῳ σώζετε) Ἐν for by. Ἐν φόβῳ with terror of divine wrath injected. But that is not in the Manuscript in this place. Moreover, σώζειν is attributed to men in its own way, 1 Cor. VII. v. 16, 1 Tim. IV. 16.

Ἐκ τῦ πυρὸς ἁρπάζοντες) Proverbial. See 1 Cor. III. v. 12, Zech. III. 2, מצל מאש. There follows in the Manuscript: Οὓῦς δὲ ἐλεᾶτε ἐν φόβῳ, that is, have mercy on those who have already fallen, fearing lest something similar happen to you also, Rom. XI. 20.

Μισῦντες καὶ τὸν ἀπὸ τῆς σαρκὸς ἐσπιλωμένον χιτῶνα) And this is proverbial, from Leviticus XIII. 47, 48. Μισεῖν here is metonymically to flee. Just as that which is touched by leprosy or another disease is said to be μιαίνεται, Heb. XII. 15. So also σπιλῦσθαι to be defiled. Thus Servius on the fourth Aeneid speaks of a garment infected by a wound. The sense is: All things through which the evil dogmas or examples of the Carpocratians could creep in must be diligently avoided.

To the admonitions concerning our own preservation and salvation are subjoined admonitions concerning a neighbor, especially one who is erring, of whom the greatest account must be taken, who errs either out of infirmity and is seduced by others, of whom we ought to have mercy, or out of affected ignorance or malice, whom, that we may save him, it is necessary to terrify with the fear of the judgment of the Lord, so that we may snatch him as if from the fire of the impending judgment, 2 Thess. I. 8. The case of the nominative teaches that the word διακρινόμενοι does not look to those of whom we are commanded to have mercy, but rather to those to whom it is commanded. Therefore they are warned that, having made a selection, they should have mercy on such. The Vulgate indeed has it otherwise here: And some indeed argue, being judged: Save others, snatching them from the fire: but on others have mercy in fear. But those things do not agree with the Greek Codices, and Cornelius admits this as regards the third member: But on others have mercy, he says, these are now missing in the Greek, in which consequently the sentence is two-membered, whereas in the Latin it is three-membered. Its sense therefore is, as if to say: Sharply reprove the teachers of heresy themselves, as if judged and condemned by their own judgment as well as that of God and men, so that others may fear: but bring back their disciples to the faith partly by fear, partly by mercy and clemency, according to the character of each.
