Anyone understands that the Greek has it more correctly. Nor do some observe without reason that the word διακρίνεσθαι is not passive, but of active signification in the New Testament, Matt. ch. XXI. v. 21, Mark ch. XI. v. 23, Acts ch. X. v. 20, ch. XI. v. 12, James I. v. 6, ch. II. v. 4, and that διάκρισιν brings in a judgment of discretion between the infirm and the stubborn adults, and those who err as seducers out of ignorance and malice: See Gal. VI. v. 1. 2. Timoth. II. v. 24. as well as Joh. V. 34. 1. Thess. II. 16. 1. Tim. IV. 16. Snatching them from the fire as if from a conflagration, and pulling them out as if by laying a hand upon them ἁρπάζοντες, which is a violent snatching, and a desirable snatching, as Jerome says on Ezech. ch. XVIII. Then indeed the Apostle commands that we hold in hatred the garment spotted by the flesh, that we do not connive at the vices of our neighbor, much less participate in them, but that we pursue them with the utmost hatred and flee from them. Piscator translates: Holding in hatred that garment which is spotted by the flesh. The Apostle, however, seems to refer to the impurities by which he who had touched anything unclean was contaminated, Apoc. III. 4. This, therefore, is what the holy Apostle wants, that they should indeed have pity on those who are erring, even those who are already in the danger of the guilt of their own hellfire, but yet in such a way that they do not connive at their sins, or defile themselves with the same. By the spotted garment some understand hypocrisy, and the appearance of piety with which some clothe themselves, while being inwardly polluted by lust; others understand the flesh, which is as it were the garment of the soul, which the Gnostics called Borborites used to stain with filthy lusts, v. 8; others understand concupiscence, which we are commanded to put off like the old man with his deeds; Cornelius prefers to understand base and carnal morals and affections, which are as it were the garment of the soul, or a base manner of living, soiled by lusts, because sordid works are as it were the sordid garments of the soul: But these last two interpretations can well be joined. Clement of Alexandria: The spotted garment is when the Spirit is polluted by carnal concupiscences: Conf. v. 12. The sense is, says Cornelius, as if to say: see to it, O faithful, that in dealing with the Gnostics you do not contaminate the white garment of innocence, which you received in baptism, with their impurity and lust, but clearly hate and execrate it. See Cant. V. v. 3. This is Beza's explanation: A hyperbole taken from the prohibitions of legal pollutions, as if he were saying: I want you, as far as those wicked men are concerned, to abstain from their company, nay, in a certain way to execrate whatever they have even touched as if it were polluted. Therefore ἀπὸ τῆς σαρκὸς is translated from the contact of the flesh. Which sense Erasmus also brings forward, but prefers the former, having this to say about this whole passage: The sense, otherwise obscure here, is that they should draw some to Christ with gentleness, having regard for the persons, and deter others from sinning by fear, and that they should hate not the men themselves, but the base affections, which he here calls the garment of the flesh spotted. Unless you prefer to interpret it in this sense, holding in hatred not only the base deeds of the flesh themselves, but also the garment contaminated by the flesh, that is, whatever in any way pertains to baseness. The Greek conjunction καὶ supports this interpretation, yet the former squares better with those things which follow immediately: Now to him who is able. Hold vices in hatred, not men, and do not usurp glory for yourselves, but attribute it to God, who is able to render them good from being evil.

Latin:

Vers. 23.

Οὓῦς δὲ ἐν φόβῳ σώζετε) Ἐν pro per. Ἐν φόβῳ terrore injecto iræ divinæ. Sed non est id in Manuscripto hoc loco. Σώζειν autem hominibus tribuitur suo modo, 1. Cor. VII. v. 16. 1. Tim. IV. 16.

Ἐκ τῦ πυρὸς ἁρπάζοντες) Proverbiale. Vide 1. Cor. III. v. 12. Zach. III. 2. מצל מאש. Sequitur in Manuscripto : Οὓῦς δὲ ἐλεᾶτε ἐν φόβῳ, id est, jam lapsorum miseremini, me- tuentes, ne & vobis quid simile eveniat, Rom. XI. 20.

Μισῦντες καὶ τὸν ἀπὸ τῆς σαρκὸς ἐσπιλωμένον χιτῶνα) Et hoc proverbiale est ei Levitici XIII. 47. 48. Μισεῖν hic Me- tωνυμικῶς est fugere. Sicut μιαίνεται dicitur id, quod lepra aut alio morbo contactum est. Ebr. XII. 15. Sic & σπιλῦσθαι sordescere. Sic vestem vulnere infectam dicit Servius ad IV. Æneidos. Sensus est : Cavenda diligenter omnia, per quæ mala dogmata aut exempla Carpocratianorum possent ir- repere.

Monitis nostri conservationem & salutem con- cernentibus monita de proximo, imprimis errante, cujus maxime habenda est ratio, subjunguntur, qui vel ex infirmitate errat, ac seductus ab aliis est, cujus misereri debemus vel ex ignorantia af- fectata aut malitia, quem ut salvemus, metu ju- dicii Domini terrere oportet, ut eum veluti ex igne judicii imminentis eripiamus, 2. Thess. I. 8. Vocem διακρινόμενοι non respicere eos, quo- rum misereri jubemur, sed potius illos, quibus id præcipit, casus nominandi docet. Ideo illi monentur, ut delectu habito talium misereantur. Vulgatus quidem aliter hic habet : Et hos qui- dem arguite judicatos : Illos salvate de igne rapien- tes : aliis autem miseremini in timore. Sed ea non conveniunt Græcis Codicibus, idque quo- ad tertium membrum fatetur Cornelius : Aliis autem miseremini, inquit, hæc jam desunt in Græco, in quo proinde bimembris est sententia, cum in Latino sit trimembris. Sensus ejus ergo est, q. d. Ipsos hæresis Doctores acriter arguite, quasi tam suo, quam Dei & hominum judicio judicatos & condemnatos, ut cæteri timeant : eorum vero discipulos partim timore, partim miseratione & cle- mentia pro cujusque indole ad fidem reducite. Qui- libet intelligit, Græca rectius habere. Nec abs re observant nonnulli, vocem διακρίνεσθαι non passive, sed activæ significationis esse in Novo Testamento, Matth. cap. XXI. vers. 21. Marc. cap. XI. v. 23. Act. cap. X. v. 20. cap. XI. v. 12. Jac. I. v. 6. cap. II. v. 4. & διάκρισιν inferre judicium discretionis inter infirmos, & præfractos adultos, & seductores ex ignorantia & malitia errantes : Vid. Gal. VI. v. 1. 2. Timoth. II. v. 24. necnon Joh. V. 34. 1. Thess. II. 16. 1. Tim. IV. 16. Ἐκ τῦ πυρὸς velut ex incendio rapientes, & quasi injecta manu extrahentes ἁρπάζοντες, quæ rapina est violenta, & rapina optabilis dicente Hieronymo ad Ezech. cap. XVIII. Tum vero jubet Apostolus, ut odio ha- beamus tunicam a carne maculatam, proximi vitiis ne conniveamus, nedum communicemus, sed illa odio summo prosequamur ac fugiamus. Piscator vertit: Odio habentes eam tunicam, quæ sit a carne maculata. Respicere autem videtur Apostolus ad immunditias, quibus contaminabatur, qui ali- quid immundi attigerat, Apoc. III. 4. Hoc ergo est, quod vult S. Apostolus, ut misereantur qui- dem errantium, etiam eorum, qui in periculo culpæ propriæ jam versantur ignis infernalis, sed ita ta- men, ut peccatis eorum non conniveant, aut iisdem semetipsos commaculent. Per tunicam macula- tam hypocrisin nonnulli intelligunt, & speciem pietatis, qua se nonnulli amiciunt, interius libidine polluti, alii carnem, quæ est veluti vestis animæ, quam Gnostici Borboritæ dicti maculabant spurcis libidinibus, v. 8. alii concupiscentiam, quam ut veterem hominem exuere jubemur cum actibus suis, Cornelius mavult turpes & carnales mores, & affectus intelligere, qui sint quasi vestis animæ, vel turpem vivendi modum, sordidatum libidini- bus, quia sordida opera sint quasi sordida indu- menta animæ: Sed probe conjungi possunt hæ postremæ duæ interpretationes. Clemens Ale- xandrinus: Maculata tunica est, cum Spiritus concupiscentiis pollutus est carnalibus : Conf. v. 12. Sensus est, inquit Cornelius, q. d. videte, & fideles, ne agendo cum Gnosticis vestem candidam innocentiæ, quam in baptismo accepistis, eorum im- puritate & libidine contaminetis, sed illam plane odite & execramini. Vid. Cant. V. v. 3. Bezæ hæc est explicatio : Hyperbole ab interdictis pol- lutionum legalium sumpta, ac si diceret : Volo, quod ad illos sceleratos attinet, vos ab illorum con- gressu abstinere, imo quodammodo quicquid illi vel contigerunt, tanquam pollutum execrari. Ideo ἀπὸ τῆς σαρκὸς converti a carnis contactu. Quem sensum quoque affert Erasmus, sed primis præ- fert, de toto hoc loco ita habens : Sensus alioqui subobscurus hic est, ut alios mansuetudine tra- hant ad Christum, habita ratione personarum, alios metu deterreant a peccando, & oderint non ipsos homines, sed turpes affectus, quos hic vestem carnis maculatam vocat. Nisi mavis in hunc interpretari sensum, odio habentes, non solum ipsa turpia facta carnis, verum etiam vestem a carne contaminatam, hoc est, quicquid ullo modo ad tur- pitudinem pertinet. Ad hanc interpretationem facit Græca conjunctio καὶ, tamen prior magis qua- drat cum his, quæ mox sequuntur : Ei vero qui potest. Habete odio vitia non homines, & glo- riam ne vobis usurpetis, sed Deo tribuatis, qui potest illos ex malis reddere bonos.

## 1:24
Ver. 24.

To him who is able to keep (Τῷ δὲ δυναμένῳ φυλάξαι ἀυτὲς ἀπταίςυς) In the Manuscript it is φυλάξαι ἡμᾶς ἀπταίςυς. But the Latin reads ὑμᾶς, not badly, as it is in Rom. XVI. 25. which passage Jude seems to have had before his eyes; there it is σηρίξαι, which is here φυλάξαι ἀπταίςυς, for he who sustains someone, guards him, that he may not fall. Xenophon and Plutarch use the word ἀπταίςυ. In Hebrew לא נפל. Paul joins together στηρίξειν φυλάσσειν ἀπὸ τῶ πονηρᾶ in 2 Thess. III. 3. The following words show that it concerns God. Καὶ ςῆσαι κατενώπιον δ' δόξης ἀυτῦ ἀμώμυς ἐν ἀγαλλιάσει) Thus παραςῆσαι ὑμᾶς ἁγίες καὶ ἀμώμες, Coloss. I. 22. And in the Manuscript, instead of ἀμώμως it is ἀμέμπτες, as in 1 Thess. III. v. 13. Κατενώπιον δ' δόξης ἀυτῦ as if you were to say before his majesty. Thus also δύναμις Θεῦ for God, Luke XXII. 69. Ἐν ἀγαλλιάσει בּשׂשׂון with the highest joy; namely, then when the pious shall enter into the kingdom of God.

Latin:

Vers. 24.

Τῷ δὲ δυναμένῳ φυλάξαι ἀυτὲς ἀπταίςυς) In Manuscripto φυλάξαι ἡμᾶς ἀπταίςυς. At Latinus legit ὑμᾶς, non male, quomodo est Rom. XVI. 25. quem locum ob oculos habuisse videtur Judas, ibi est σηρίξαι, quæ hic φυλάξαι ἀπταίςυς, qui aliquem sustinet, is eum custodit, ne cadat. Voce ἀπταίςυ utuntur Xenophon & Plutarchus. Ebræis לא נפל. Στηρίξειν φυλάσσειν ἀπὸ τῶ πονηρᾶ conjungit Paulus 2. Thess. III. 3. De Deo agi ostendunt sequentia. Καὶ ςῆσαι κατενώπιον δ' δόξης ἀυτῦ ἀμώμυς ἐν ἀγαλλιάσει) Sic παραςῆσαι ὑμᾶς ἁγίες καὶ ἀμώμες, Coloss. I. 22. Et in Manuscripto pro ἀμώμως est ἀμέμπτες, ut 1. Thess. III. v. 13. Κατενώπιον δ' δόξης ἀυτῦ quasi dicas coram majestate ipsius. Sic & δύναμις Θεῦ pro Deo, Luc. XXII. 69. Ἐν ἀγαλλιάσει בּשׂשׂון cum summo gaudio; nempe tunc cum pii intrabunt in regnum Dei.

## 1:25
Ver. 25.

To the only wise God (Μόνῳ σοφῷ Θεῷ) Thus also 1 Tim. I. 17. It is said thus, because he alone has wisdom from himself. To our Savior (Σωτῆρι ἡμῶν) This name is not always given to Christ, but sometimes also to God, as the Principal cause of our salvation, as 1 Tim. II. 3. Tit. I. 2. III. 4. But the Manuscript adds: διὰ Ἰησῦ Χρισῦ Κυρίε, which the Latin also reads. Glory and majesty, power and authority (Δόξα κὴ μεγαλωσύνη κράτος κὴ ἐξεσία) In the Manuscript is read δόξα, μεγαλωσύνη, κράτος κὴ ἐξεσία והודה כבוד ועז. You have glory and power in a similar exclamation in 1 Pet. IV. v. 11. and V. 12. Jude added authority ממשׂל, acknowledging in God not only power, but also the right of commanding, and majesty גדלה which word we have also in Heb. I. 3. VIII. 1. Both now and to all ages (Καὶ νῦν καὶ εἰς πάντας τὲς ἀιῶνας) In the Manuscript is before all time and now, that is, just as it had them before all

Vers. 25.

Μόνῳ σοφῷ Θεῷ) Sic & 1. Tim. I. 17. Sic dicitur, quia solus sapientiam a se habet. Σωτῆρι ἡμῶν) Hoc nomen non semper Christo, sed interdum & Deo datur, tanquam causæ Principi salutis nostræ, ut 1. Tim. II. 3. Tit. I. 2. III. 4. Sed Manuscriptus adjicit: διὰ Ἰησῦ Χρισῦ Κυρίε, quæ & Latinus legit. # Revelation

## 1:1 Introduction
[Abraham Calov, Biblia Novi Testamenti Illustrata (Vol. 2, Part 2). English: machine translation, The Faith Received (Mere Orthodoxy); the original follows each comment.]
I. N ANNOT APOCALY HAN

Latin:

I. N ANNOT APOCALY HAN

## 1:1 Introduction: Grotian Preface
GROTIAN PREFACE.

The reasons why there has been doubt concerning the authority and author of this book, I judge to be that it was long in the hands of few, not added to the Codices given to the public, lest the hatreds of those in power against Christians should be inflamed by those things which are predicted here concerning Rome. Furthermore, because those things which are said here concerning the resurrection, concerning the thousand years, concerning Gog and Magog, they agree in sound with Jewish books, and although here they are taken in a different sense, nevertheless by Cerinthus and Christians Judaizing more than is right, they were snatched into a clearly Jewish sense, as also that concerning Jerusalem having fallen from heaven. But truly those to whom it is deservedly believed, believed this book to be of the Apostle John: Justin against Trypho, Irenaeus IV. 37. 50. V. 30. Tertullian against Marcion IV. and in many other places, with whom agree Clement of Alexandria, Origen, Cyprian, and after them many others. I will add on this matter the passage of Dionysius of Alexandria: I indeed would not dare to reject the book, many brethren holding it in esteem. But taking the opinion concerning it to be greater than my own understanding, I suppose that the interpretation according to each part is something hidden and more wonderful. For even if I do not understand, yet I suspect that some deeper meaning lies in the words, not measuring and judging these by my own reasoning, but giving more to faith, I have thought them to be higher than to be grasped by me. I believe, however, that this book was kept by John the Presbyter, a disciple of the Apostle: hence it happened that it was believed by some through error to be his work. But that in some books it is inscribed John the Theologian, it happened from no other cause than that after Origen, Christians gave to John, with better right, the title which the Platonists give to Orpheus. That this is true appears from Origen himself, Athanasius, Chrysostom, and both Cyrils.

OBSERVATIONS.

The causes why there has been doubt concerning the authority of the Apocalypse are not so much those concerning the concealment of the writing for fear of persecution, and concerning the time, thus it has it now, and will always have it. Thus the Latin also reads: Always honor, and your name, and praises will remain. But why not concerning Christ? whom he had called above the only Master, God, and our Lord v. 4. and who is that God our Savior, and the only wise, wisdom itself hypostatic, Prov. chap. VIII. v. 23. to whose glorious sight the elect are to be presented at the final advent. And Christ is joined in a similar doxology with God the Father, Apoc. V. v. 13. to him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb be blessing and honor, and glory, and power for the ages of ages: because the Son and the Father are one, John chap. X. v. 30. Which magnificent doxology Oecumenius calls that by which St. Jude concludes the epistle: which at the same time contains a silent vow and prayer, that namely God may keep the faithful immaculate, and present them into the sight of his glory, that they may exult before him, and praise him for the ages: Which finally he opposes to the blasphemy of Simon, Ebion, Cerinthus, and others, which derogated from the glory of Christ, Psal. XXXII. 11. Is. XXXV. v. 10. 1 Pet. I. v. 9. He adds the word AMEN, which is both of one wishing and of one confirming. We conclude with the Ethiopian: The epistle of Jude the brother of James is finished, and glory to GOD for the ages of ages; AMEN, and AMEN.

Latin:

PRÆLOQUIUM GROTIANUM.

CUr de hujus libri autoritate & autore addubitatum sit, causas esse arbitror, quod diu in paucorum fuerit manibus, non additus Codicibus in vulgus datis, ne accenderentur imperantium in Christianos odia ex his quæ de Roma hic prædicuntur. Deinde, quod quæ hic dicuntur de resurrectione, de mille annis, de Gogo & Magogo, ea sono congruunt cum Judaicis libris, & quanquam hic sensu politæ alio, attamen a Cerintho & Christianis plus æquo Judaizantibus, in sensum plane Judaicum rapiebantur, ut & illud de Hierosolymis ex cœlo delapsis. At vero Apostoli Johannis esse hunc librum credidere illi quibus merito creditur, Justinus contra Tryphonem, Irenæus IV. 37. 50. V. 30. Tertullianus adversus Marcionem IV. & aliis multis in locis, quibus consentiunt Clemens Alexandrinus, Origenes, Cyprianus, & post eos alii multi. Adjiciam de hac re Dionysii Alexandrini locum : Ἐγὼ δὲ ἀθετῆσαι μὲν ἐκ ἂν τολμήσαιμι τὸ βιβλίον πολλῶν ἀυτὸ διὰ σπυδῆς ἐχόντων ἀδελφῶν. Μείζονα δὲ τ' ἐμαυτῦ φρονήσεως τὴν ὑπόληψιν τὴν περὶ ἀυτῦ λαμβάνων κεκρυμμένην εἶναί τινα καὶ θαυμασιωτέραν τὴν καθ' ἕκαςον ἐκδοχὴν ὑπολαμβάνω. καὶ γὰρ εἰ μὴ συνίημι, ἀλλ' ὑπονοῶ γε νῦν τινα βαθύτερον ἐγκεῖσθαι τοῖς ῥήμασιν, ἐκ ἰδίᾳ ταῦτα μετρῶν καὶ κρίνων λογισμῷ, πίσει δὲ πλέον νέμων ὑψηλότερα ἢ ὑπ' ἐμῦ καταληφθῆναι νενόμικα. Credo autem a Johanne Presbytero Apostoli discipulo custoditum hunc librum: inde factum, ut ejus esse opus a quibusdam per errorem crederetur. Quod autem in quibusdam libris inscribitur Ἰωάννε Θεολόγε non aliunde factum est, quam quod post Origenem Christiani, quem titulum Orpheo dant Platonici, meliori jure dederunt Johanni. Id verum esse apparet ex ipso Origene, Athanasio, Chrysostomo & Cyrillo utroque.

OBSERVATIONES.

CAusæ, cur dubitatum fuerit de autoritate Apocalypseos non tam illæ de scripti ob metum persecutionis occultatione, deque tempus, sic & nunc habet, & habebit semper. Sic legit & Latinus: Semper honos, noménque tuum, laudesque manebunt. Cur vero non de Christo? quem supra τὸν μό- νον Δεσπότην, Θεὸν, καὶ Κύριον ἡμῶν dixerat v. 4. & qui est ille Θεὸς Σωτὴρ ἡμῶν, ac μόνῳ σοφὸς, sapientia ipsa hypostatica, Prov. cap. VIII. v. 23. cujus glorioso conspectui sistendi sunt electi in ad- ventu novissimo. Et conjungitur in simili do- ξολογίᾳ Christus cum Deo Patre, Apoc. V. v. 13. τῷ καθημένῳ ἐκ τῷ θρόνῳ καὶ τῷ ἀρνίῳ ἡ εὐλογία καὶ ἡ τιμὴ, καὶ ἡ δόξα, καὶ τὸ κράτος εἰς τὼς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων : quia Filius & Pater unum sunt, Joh cap. X. v. 30. Quam δοξολογίαν magnificam vo- cat Oecumenius, qua epistolam concludit S. Ju- das : quæ simul tacitum votum, & precationem continet, ut scilicet Deus fideles servet imma- culatos, & in conspectum gloriæ suæ sistat, ut exultent coram illo, eumque laudent in secula : Quam denique opponit Simonis, Ebionis, Ce- rinthi & aliorum blasphemiæ, quæ derogabant Christi gloriæ, Psal. XXXII. 11. Es. XXXV. v. 10. 1. Petr. I. v. 9. Addit vocem AMEN, quæ & optantis, & confirmantis. Concludimus cum Æthiope : Absoluta est epistola Judæ fratris Jaco- bi, & gloria DEO in secula seculorum; AMEN, & AMEN.

## 1:1 Introduction: N. J. Tata on the Inscription of S. John
N. J. TATA ON THE INSCRIPTION OF S. JOHN.

They are reviewed in antiquity for the Cerinthian error, regarding the ἐπιγραφῇ: because John called himself not Apostle, but Theologian, and because of the diversity of style from the Evangelical and Apostolic S. John, and also regarding the subject matter and the sentiments, in which some, like Erasmus, not sufficiently fair to this most divine book, observed at the end of his notes, that they missed Apostolic gravity. To which, however, Beza responded in his annotations and B. Gerhard in his exegesis on Holy Scripture.

John did not take the name of Theologian for himself, but he who made the inscription of the book, by which he wished rather to assert the same for John the Apostle than to abrogate it from him. For John the Apostle alone from that primitive antiquity, when the Apocalypse obtained an ἐπιγραφὴν, bore this name, which was afterwards also given to Gregory Nazianzen on account of his assertion of the eternal Deity of the λόγος of the Son of God. He himself, however, called himself a Servant of Jesus Christ in ch. 1. 1., by which name both Paul and Jude expressed their Apostleship. Athanasius in his Synopsis joined both the name of Evangelist and Theologian. Whether this title was given to John the Apostle before or only after Origen is not clear. B. Gerhard in his exegesis cites Dionysius, who in an epistle written to John while he was in exile on Patmos attributed this name to him. Furthermore, the diversity of style in this book from the remaining Johannine writings is not so great that there do not also appear in this writing indications of Johannine diction. S. John uses the word Λόγος concerning the Son of God in his Gospel ch. 1. 1. 1. 14., in his first epistle ch. 1. 1. The same name occurs concerning Him in Apoc. XIX. 13. Καὶ καλεῖται τὸ ὄνομα ἀυτῶ ὁ λόγος τῷ Θεῷ. To which Paræus also refers in ch. 1. 2. And conformity is observed not only by collation, which Beza from ch. I. 7. and in

He institutes [a comparison] with Gospel ch. XIX. 37, and Flacius ch. I. 2, with Gospel ch. XIX. 35, and 1 John I. 1, but in many other small points. In expressions familiar to John the Apostle if to any other, such as testimony, to testify, to keep the words of God, to guard the Word of God, the faith of Jesus, washing through the blood of Jesus, etc. In the appellation of the Son of God, that he is called the Lamb of God, John I. 29, 36, and Rev. V. 6, 8, 12, 13, ch. VI. 16, ch. VII. 9, 10, 11, 17, etc., where although the word ἀρνίον is used, it was not however unusual for the Evangelist, ch. XXI. 15. In the assertion of the divine nature and the explanation of the benefits of the Son of God, which argument, both because of the heresies of that age and because of saving faith, which looks to that, was most necessary, was not neglected in the Apocalypse, even though it is not didactic but prophetic, and thus also in the scope of John the Apostle, which he prefixed to his writing, John XX. last, and 1. John I. 4. observation, to which the Holy Spirit aimed in this revelation given to St. John, no less than in the rest of his writings which are θεοπνέυστοις [God-breathed]: To which it contributes, that in the Apocalypse that highest head of faith, and the hinge of religion concerning the office of Christ the Savior, is proposed in especially illustrious words just as in the Gospel and the former epistle, as hardly elsewhere. For what is more splendid than that sum of such great doctrine, Jesus Christ loved us, and washed us through his blood, and made us Priests and Kings to our God, ch. I. And that: You are the Lamb slain, and have redeemed us through your blood out of every tribe, and have made us Priests, ch. V. and concerning faith overcoming sin and death ch. II. 10 Be faithful, etc. etc. ch. XII. 11. they overcame through the blood of the Lamb. For the rest, Flacius is correct: The phrase does not much abhor from the style of John, if one considers that visions ought to have been described in one kind of speech, but histories in another, and that John wished rather to record those words which he heard in the vision than to weave them in his own kind of speech, just as other God-breathed writings were not written down by the words of amanuenses, but of the Holy Spirit, by whom they were dictated, who, as it seemed good to him, used now this and now that kind of speech. What? That the blessed Cluverus judges concerning the style p. 4. The style, against which certain fastidious critics feel, is so similar to the remaining writings and phrases of John the Apostle, that nothing could be more similar. For with the prophetic kind of speaking removed, which must necessarily differ from the historical, the formulas of speaking are entirely Johannine.

But I do not see what can be desired in this writing regarding Apostolic gravity: which, as Beza says, is certainly very short, if you remove those things which are copied word for word from the Prophets. Far otherwise Basil, Gregory, Cyril, Epiphanius, Irenaeus, Hippolytus, as Aretas testifies, who not only thought this book (as Dionysius of Alexandria did) to have been written by a holy man, but also openly claimed it for John the Apostle: they would certainly never have done that, if they had noticed no traces of Apostolic gravity.

Some also quibble about the indication of the name made here by John, differently than is observed in the Gospel or Epistles. But did not the Evangelist also build up the certainty of his Gospel from a singular description and commendation of himself ch. XIX. 35, ch. XXI. 24, even if in this place, in the manner of the Prophets, Daniel, and others, he expresses his name, [while] there, as a historiographer, he circumlocutes with a certain periphrasis?

Moreover, in that cause which Grotius brought forward in the first place, something ὕπουλον [insidious] seems to be hidden: Namely, as he contends that the Apocalypse refers to the times of the Apostles by the visions which it exhibits, and exhibits their state: So he also draws the same back to pagan Rome, so that the predictions which occur in it concerning the great Anti-Christ may be obscured, and twisted to any other person whatsoever, I think Barchochebas and the like, so that they do not seem to touch the Roman Anti-Christ: concerning which in the discussion of the annotations.

As for the second cause, the Apocalypse was not only snatched into a Jewish sense by Cerinthus and the Judaizers, but was also ascribed by some (even by Gaius, as Eusebius testifies, b. III, ch. 28) to Cerinthus himself as its author. For Dionysius, Bishop of Alexandria, reporting in his book on the promises, in Eusebius, b. VII, Ecclesiastical History, ch. 25, says that the same man, wishing to prefix a name of great authority to his own inventions to convince others, gave the title of John to his work: Which opinion he himself indeed rejects in the place cited by Grotius, yet he does not vindicate the Apocalypse for John the Apostle, but says that he calls this man John; and I do not deny that the book was written by John: For I confess that it is the work of some holy man and one inspired by the divine Spirit. But that this very person is the Apostle, the son of Zebedee, the brother of James, whose is that Gospel which is inscribed according to John, and the Catholic Epistle, I would not easily concede. Which Dionysius presumed from the genius and form of speaking (of which we have already treated) and from the flow and arrangement of the Apocalypse: also introducing something about another John, surnamed Mark, who is commemorated in Acts XII, to whom, however, he does not assign this book either: Whether this is he, he says, who wrote the revelation, is not clear to me. For he did not come into Asia together with Barnabas and Paul, but returned to Jerusalem. I think, therefore, that it is another, namely one of those who were in Asia. For it is handed down that there were two tombs at Ephesus, each marked with the name of John. It is therefore clearly evident from Dionysius that he himself by no means held John the Evangelist to be the author of the Apocalypse, whose arguments, however, are less solid, nor did they easily cause a scruple for anyone, except for Erasmus, a Pyrrhonian man, and certainly not for the ancient Doctors of the Church, if by chance you except Eusebius, who is wavering here, of whom Beza says: I certainly do not care for Eusebius, in whom all learned men find a lack of judgment in most of his writings. Regarding the twin John of Ephesus, it has already been said enough in the Johannine epistles how uncertain that tradition is. Beza is more inclined toward John surnamed Mark, if the style allowed one to conjecture an author other than John the Evangelist, because the character of the Gospel of Mark and of this book is similar and almost the same, not only in words but also in most formulas of speech. But Flacius rightly says: If faith is to be placed in those Fathers who approached closer to this century, as is certainly most just, such as Justin, Tertullian, Irenaeus, Apollonius, Theophilus of Antioch, Eusebius b. IV, ch. 24, whose testimonies can be referred to in their own place and time, it can be affirmed that it was held in that first century as being by John the Apostle. For why would these men confirm so certainly that it was by John the Apostle, if they had known that doubtful opinions of their predecessors had existed concerning it? Nor does Eusebius himself produce any witness of significant authority from the Doctors of this or the following century who denies that it is by John the Apostle: nor indeed can he cite anyone from the third century after this one except Dionysius of Alexandria. But neither his testimony, nor the reasons which he brings forward, seem to be of such weight as to exclude this Apocalypse of John from the number of the approved books of the New Testament. Which indeed not even Dionysius himself presumed. For he acknowledged that the author was θεόπνευστον (divinely inspired). But Eusebius even expressly ascribed the Apocalypse to John the Apostle, as Flacius likewise observes: Nay, Eusebius himself says in his Chronicle: In the fourteenth year of Domitian, and the ninety-seventh of Christ, while Domitian, the second after Nero, was persecuting the Christians: and under him the Apostle John, having been banished to the island of Patmos, saw the Apocalypse, which Irenaeus interprets.

Nor indeed without reason did the ancients hold the Apostle John to be the author. For they remembered that he produced it around the end of Domitian's reign, at which time John is said to have returned from Patmos, and they had as witnesses the Asian churches to which it is dedicated. For Irenaeus, at the end of his book, corrects that number of the beast written in Greek as χις, by the authority of those who saw John, indicating it to be χξς, that is 666. Flacius also brings forward other internal criteria which refer to John as the author, which may be read there. We have Grotius agreeing with us on this, so that there is no need for more. We do, however, append some testimonies from antiquity concerning the author, the Apostle John, lest any doubt should perhaps linger in anyone from that remark of Dionysius about John the Presbyter being different from the Apostle, or even from Beza's suspicion regarding John Mark.

Among the Latins, Tertullian, in book IV against Marcion, ch. 5, convicts Marcion from the succession of bishops: We have, he says, the churches that are pupils of John. For even if Marcion rejects his Apocalypse, the order of bishops, traced back to its origin, will stand with John as its author. Hilary, in his prologue to the Psalms, on Apoc. V. 4, says that the lament of the author is that of the APOSTLE. Ambrose also acknowledged the Apostle as the author in book V on repentance, ch. 9. How could John say that one should not pray for a sin that is unto death, who wrote in the Apocalypse, it is commanded to the Angel in the Church of Pergamum: Thou hast there them that hold the doctrine of Balaam, and them that hold the doctrine of the Nicolaitans; likewise repent. Philastrius on heresies, ch. LX. After these are the heretics who do not accept the Gospel according to John and his Apocalypse, and since they do not understand the power of the Scripture, nor do they desire to learn, they remain in heresy, wandering about, so that they even dare to say that it belongs to that heretic Cerinthus. Prudentius, in the year 380, in his 6th hymn before the end: The highest Evangelist, most faithful to his Master, sees with remote eyes the things that were hidden and sealed, the Lamb of the Thunderer himself, reddening with slaughter, who alone unseals the book conscious of the future. Jerome in his epistle to Dardanus, Vol. III of his works, p. 68: We (the Latins) receive both (the epistle to the Hebrews and the Apocalypse of St. John), following not the custom of this time, but the authority of the ancient writers. Which are to be understood concerning the Apostle John from the books of Jerome on Illustrious Men. Doctor. It is established: In the fourteenth year, therefore, (he says concerning the Apostle John,) while Domitian was stirring up the second persecution after Nero, he was banished to the island of Patmos and wrote the Apocalypse, which Justin Martyr and Irenaeus interpret. And in book 1 against Jovinian, ch. 14: The Apostle John saw the Apocalypse, containing infinite mysteries of future things, on the island of Patmos, to which he had been banished by the Emperor Domitian. Augustine, tractate XXXVI on John: And in the Prophet Ezekiel, and in the Apocalypse of John himself, whose this Gospel is, a four-footed animal is mentioned, having four faces, namely of a man, a calf, a lion, and an eagle. And on Holy Virginity, ch. 27. Sulpicius Severus (in the year 440), book II of his History. Domitian banished John the Evangelist to the island of Patmos, where he, having had secret mysteries revealed to him, published the book of the Holy Apocalypse (which indeed is rejected by many, either foolishly or impiously). Prosper (in the year 460) on the promises, part 1, ch. 38: This is also indicated by the Apocalypse of St. John, saying: I saw a great multitude, ch. VII. Add part II, ch. 12. Jornandes (in the year 550), book I: Domitian, after he could not extinguish the Apostle and Evangelist John by putting him into boiling oil, banished him to the island of Patmos, where he saw the Apocalypse. Isidore of Seville (in the year 620), book VI of the Etymologies: John wrote the book of the Apocalypse at the time when he is believed to have been banished to the island of Patmos for the preaching of the Gospel. Eligius (in the year 640), homily VIII: And in the Apocalypse, the Apostle John: Who loved us, he says, and washed us from our sins in his blood. Aldhelm (in the year 680) on the praises of virginity, ch. 3: for this reason also I believe, because he is the one who reclined on the Lord's breast and the fourth fountain of paradise, who especially irrigated the seven churches with inexhaustible streams of doctrine, and Rabanus Maurus (in the year 850), book II on the institution of clerics, ch. 54: John the Evangelist wrote the Apocalypse at the same time that he is said to have been banished to the island of Patmos for the preaching of the Gospel. Rudolphus Ardens (in the year 1020) in his sermon on the commemoration of the departed, on the Apocalypse: Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord: This the Apostle and Evangelist John writes, etc. Peter Damian, sermon V on John the Evangelist: Hence it is that Almighty God raised his mind to such a height of purity and mystical revelation, that He showed him not only the state of the present Church, but also revealed what would happen thereafter unto eternity. Hugh of St. Victor (in the year 1130), in his Erudition. Didascalicon, book IV, ch. 5, on the authority of the Old Testament: The Apostle John wrote the Apocalypse while banished to the island of Patmos: See also Richard of St. Victor, preface to the book of the Apocalypse. Nicholas of Lyra, preface to the Apocalypse. Albert the Great, prologue to the Apocalypse (in the year 1240): The whole Church receives this book as that of the Apostle John, and therefore this is to be held as certain. And so much for the Latin Fathers.

From the Greeks, Justin in his dialogue with Trypho asserts that the Apocalypse is by John the Apostle. Whence Eusebius, book IV of Ecclesiastical History, chapter 24, dealing with Justin's Dialogue with Trypho, says he also mentions the revelation of John, which he expressly says was written by the Apostle, σαφῶς τᾶ Ἀποστόλꙋ ἀυτὴν εἶναι λέγων. Irenaeus, book V against heresies: He says, John the disciple of the Lord in the Apocalypse signified even more clearly concerning the end time and those ten kings who are in it, into whom the empire that now reigns will be divided. Origen, homily VII on John: He adds nonetheless that John also sounds the trumpet through his epistles and the Apocalypse. St. Athanasius in the Synopsis on the Apocalypse has it thus: This book is called by this name because John the Evangelist and Theologian himself saw this revelation on the island called Patmos, and afterwards wrote it down. Epiphanius, heresy LVII. Among whom (the Apostles) also St. John imparted through the Gospel and epistles and the Apocalypse from the same gift of the Holy Spirit. St. Cyril of Alexandria, book I of the Thesaurus, chapter 5. And the Gospel: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God; and in the Apocalypse the SAME John: Who is, who was, and who is to come. He affirms that this was also the opinion of the ancients, book VI on worship in Spirit and truth: And that wise John, who wrote the little book of the Apocalypse, which has been approved by the judgment of the FATHERS, affirms that he saw the souls of the saints under the altar of God. The opinion of Gregory of Nazianzus is held from Arethas of Caesarea, who flourished around the year 560, in his commentary on the Apocalypse. whose judgment concerning this book is as follows: Some of the ancients say this book is foreign to the diction and language of the beloved John, referring it to another: But it is not so: Since Gregory the Theologian numbered this among the genuine and legitimate books: As he teaches me (he says, oration 32), the Apocalypse of John. Eusebius himself reports in Book IV of the History, chapters 23 and 25, [mentions] Theophilus, Bishop of the Church of Antioch, who uses the testimonies of this book against the heresy of Hermogenes, and Melito, Bishop of Sardis, who wrote a book on the Apocalypse of John, just as Cyprian also [does] in On the Exhortation to Martyrdom, chapter III and following, and others acknowledge the Apocalypse as they do other Divine scriptures. Similarly, John of Damascus, circa the year 730, in Book IV of the Orthodox Faith, chapter 18, called this the Apocalypse of John the Evangelist and listed it among the Canonical scriptures. Simeon Metaphrastes, in the year 950, in the martyrdom of St. Antipas: Then also the base of the church and the faith and the foundation of Christian truth and the herald of eternal duration, the most excellent Apostle John, was relegated to the island of Patmos: where, while he was confirming the great assembly of Christ's martyrs with those things which he wrote about the seven Churches, he says Antipas, etc. Suidas, in the year 976, in his Lexicon, also held the Apocalypse to be a writing of John the Evangelist; John the Apostle and Evangelist composed it at the age of one hundred. John Chrysostom also admits his three epistles and the Apocalypse. Similarly, Michael Glycas, in the year 1100, part III of his annals: Domitian relegated John, surnamed the Theologian, to the island of Patmos, where he wrote both the Evangelical history and the revelation. B. Hoë has summarized most of the Fathers who attribute the Apocalypse to St. John in this way. Does not, he says, Melito, Bishop of Sardis, does not Theophilus of Antioch and Justin Martyr, who were all almost contemporaries and did not prolong their lives beyond the sixtieth year after the death of John the Evangelist, clearly confess that the Apocalypse was written by John the Apostle and Evangelist on Patmos? The same is asserted without any hesitation by Dionysius the Areopagite, chapter III of the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy. Irenaeus, Tertullian, Hippolytus, Athanasius, Cyprian, Jerome, Augustine, Ambrose, Theophilus, Apollonius, Origen, Primasius, Philastrius, Andreas of Caesarea, Arethas, Marulus, and others. Indeed, Epiphanius defends this opinion so strongly that he does not fear to consider those who maintain the contrary as heretics. And it is to be observed that most of the named Fathers could have the testimony of the Asiatic Churches in their favor, and thus could not rashly pronounce John the Evangelist as the author of the book. Besides these, Coccius cites in his Thesaurus, Book VI, page 736: From the Greeks, Prochorus in the History of John, chapter 47 (Year 120); Clement of Alexandria, Book VI of the Stromata (Year 200); Dionysius of Alexandria against Nepos, in Eusebius, Book VII, chapter 20 (Year 260); Pamphilus the Martyr for Origen (Year 300); Didymus of Alexandria in the Epistle of Jude (Year 360); Ephrem the Syrian on the apparition of the cross (Year 360); Macarius of Egypt (Year 370), homily 30. Nilus (Year 420) on prayer, chapter 69; John Cassian, Conferences 4, chapter 19 (Year 430); Isidore of Pelusium, Book I, epistle 188 (Year 440); Procopius of Gaza on chapter 47 of Isaiah (Year 530); Leontius (Year 600); Maximus on chapter II of the Divine Names of Dionysius the Areopagite (Year 640); John of Damascus, Book IV of the Orthodox Faith, chapter 18 (Year 730); Simeon Metaphrastes in the martyrdom of St. Antipas (Year 950); Suidas in his Lexicon (Year 970); Michael Glycas, part 3 of his Annals (Year 1100); Nicetas Choniates, Book IV, Orthodox Heresy 23 (Year 1200); Nicephorus Callistus, Ecclesiastical History, Book II, chapter 25 (Year 1300); John Cantacuzenus on the Mahometan Sect (Year 1360); Gennadius Scholarius on the fruition of the Saints, folio 7 (Year 1450); Jagazabo, Abbot of Ethiopia, in the Confession of the Ethiopian Faith (Year 1536); From the Latins, the Brothers of Gaul (Year 170); Zeno of Verona, sermon on the sleep of Jacob (Year 260); Victorinus of Pettau, commentary on the Apocalypse (Year 270); Julius Firmicus Maternus on profane religions, chapter 20 (Year 350); Hilary of Poitiers, prologue to the Psalms (Year 350); Victor of Africa

Book III against the Arians (Year 366); Pacianus, epistle 1 against the Novatians (Year 370); Prudentius, hymn 6 (Year 380); Quintus Julius Hilarion, book on the duration of the world (Year 390); Rufinus on the Creed (Year 390); Innocent I, epistle to Exuperius, chapter 7 (Year 406); Idacius against Varimadus (Year 420); Philip the Presbyter, Book II on Job, chapter 19 (Year 430); Maximus of Turin on the solemnity of Pentecost (Year 430); Sixtus III on Chastity (Year 440); Leo the Great, Epistle LIII, chapter 5 (Year 450); Prosper on the promises, part 1, chapter 38 (Year 460); Caesarius of Arles, Homily V on Easter (Year 470); Salvian of Marseille on the providence of God, Book IV (Year 480); Gelasius, Epistle V (Year 490); Fulgentius, Book I to Monimus, chapter 27 (Year 500); Alcimus Avitus on the praise of chastity (Year 500); Junilius Africanus on the parts of divine law (Year 545); Cassiodorus on Psalm 96 (Year 560); Justus of Urgell on the Song of Songs (Year 540); Jordanes, Book I (Year 560); Pelagius II, Epistle 1 to the Synod of Constantinople (Year 579); Gregory the Great, Book I of the Moralia, chapter 4 (Year 630); Isidore of Seville, Book VI of the Etymologies, chapter 2; Eligius, Homily VIII (Year 640); Ildephonsus of Toledo on the Virginity of St. Mary, chapter 10 (Year 660); Aldhelm on the praises of the Virgin, chapter 5 (Year 680); Bede, prologue to the Apocalypse; Pope Zachary, Epistle XI (Year 740); Alcuin on the divine offices, chapter 39 (Year 750); Ambrose Ansbert on the Apocalypse (Year 760); Haymo on the Apocalypse (Year 820); Angelomus, Book III of Kings, chapter 7 (Year 830); Rabanus Maurus on the institution of the Clergy, Book II, chapter 54 (Year 850); Nicholas I, Epistle 8 to the Emperor Michael (Year 860); Smaragdus in the prologue to the Rule of Benedict (Year 970); Byrhtferth of Ramsey on chapter 45 of Bede's On the Reckoning of Time (Year 980); Radulphus Ardens on the commemoration of the dead (Year 1050); Peter Damian, sermon V on the Gospel of John; Anselm on chapter XV of Romans (Year 1080); Hildebert of Le Mans, epistle 36 (Year 1100); Rupert of Deutz on the last chapter of the Apocalypse; Bernard on the Epiphany of the Lord (Year 1130); Hugh Victor of St. Victor, On the Sacraments, book 2, page 16, chapter 1. Richard of St. Victor, Preface to the Apocalypse (Year 1140). Arnold, Abbot, On the Last Seven Words of the Lord (Year 1160). Godfrey of Viterbo, part 13 of the Chronicle (Year 1170). Innocent III, Sermon 1 on a Martyr (Year 1200). Jacques de Vitry on the Nativity of the Lord. Anthony of Padua, Sermon 3 in Lent (Year 1230). Albert the Great, prologue to the Apocalypse (Year 1240). Bonaventure on chapter 4 of Luke (Year 1260). John of San Gimignano in the Summa, book 7, chapter 6 (Year 1310). Nicholas of Lyra, preface to the Apocalypse (Year 1320). Peter Alias, sermon on the Feast of All Saints (Year 1400). Thomas Waldensis, book 2 of the Doctrine of the Faith, article 2 (Year 1410). Lawrence Justinian, on the limits of life, chapter 2 (Year 1438). Thomas à Kempis, book 4 on cloistral discipline, chapter 12 (Year 1430). Bernardino of Siena, Volume 1, Sermon 26 (Year 1430). John Capistran on the authority of the Pope and the Church, folio 28 (Year 1440).

These things, therefore, concerning the Fathers and ancient Doctors who expressly vindicate the Apocalypse for John the Apostle, from whom those do not differ who perhaps do not expressly name the Apostle as the author, yet by assigning divine authority to this Johannine writing, and by citing it as divine scripture, acknowledge that that John was θεόπνευστον [divinely inspired], nay, that he was of the number of the Apostles, and thus by consequence refer this writing to John the Apostle: whom we refrain from enumerating.

And not only individual Doctors, but also entire councils of both the Eastern and Western Church have either expressly ascribed the Apocalypse to John the Apostle, or by including this Johannine writing among the canonical scriptures, have acknowledged by implication that its author was John the Apostle. Such are the Third Council of Carthage in the year 395, chapter 47; the Fourth Council of Toledo in the year 640, chapter 16; the Council of Friuli in the year 800, in the preface. He also appeals to the authority of many other councils, which the Apocalypse of John Evangelists, and among the divine books they determined it should be received. The aforementioned Fourth Council of Toledo; the Second Synod of Nicaea, year 790, Act 1. Blessed be God, he says, who through the holy Apostle (Rev. 1 & 22) I am the A & Ω.

All of which, therefore, not only heretics—Cerdo, who rejected the Apocalypse as if it were false, as Tertullian testifies in De praescriptione c. 51; Marcion, who spurned the same, as the same author testifies in book 4 against Marcion c. 5; the Alogi and Theodotion, who did not admit the Apocalypse of John, as Epiphanius testifies in Haereses 51 and Augustine in De haeresibus c. 39—called into doubt that it was by John the Apostle, which we said was observed long ago in certain Greek texts and done by Dionysius of Alexandria, and by Erasmus of Rotterdam: add also Zwingli, concerning whom Bullinger writes in his commentary on the Apocalypse; or they even derogated from its divine authority: for which reason the Papists are also accustomed to harass B. Luther. But although in the preface of his earlier edition he himself professed that he could in no way perceive that it was composed by the Holy Spirit, in the later preface, however, 'second thoughts are wiser' are read, in which he indeed left it in doubt whether the author is John the Apostle, yet he says he prohibits no one if he wishes to determine that it is his: Nor is that surprising, since Eusebius himself is also somewhere ambiguous with Dionysius of Alexandria as to whether the Apocalypse is by St. John the Apostle, and the Council of Laodicea, as well as Gregory Nazianzen, omitted it in their catalogues of the Holy Scriptures, and Jerome testifies to Dardanus that the Greeks doubt the Apocalypse against the common consensus of the Latins. Into which class some also refer Gaius, who flourished under the Emperor Severus. flourished: concerning whom Eusebius, book 3, c. 28, handed down nothing other than that he wrote that Cerinthus, through certain revelations written by himself as if by a great Apostle, invented these portents as if they had been shown to him by Angels. For the rest, the same Eusebius says of the Apocalypse in book 3, c. 21: 'Even now there is a divided opinion among many, with some approving it, while others reject it': And c. 22: 'Some reject the Apocalypse of John, but others adjudge it to certain and undoubted scriptures.' Junius in his Questions, c. 4, says that the Apocalypse of John is greatly doubted among the Orientals. Let the Papists therefore accuse and refute those men from among the Fathers, if they still wish to write against Luther. But among the fair and learned, he will easily be held excused. Nor is there anyone among our own who does not accept the Apocalypse as a divine writing, so that some might count it among the canonical books of the second order, not because of its authority, but because the author was once doubted, concerning which we have stated our opinion elsewhere.

But lest we seem to rely only on testimonies concerning the author and authority of this book, although they have great weight in this cause and are fortified by reasons, we shall bring forward certain arguments, comprised however in a single syllogism: That John is to be understood here to whom this revelation was made, who 1. at that time, 2. lived on Patmos, 3. presided over the Asian Churches, 4. was absolutely designated by this name, 5. was specifically called the Theologian, 6. whom Christ embraced with singular love above the other Disciples, 7. to whom such an Apocalypse was fitting above others, 8. who was undoubtedly Θεόπνευστος, 9. could worthily seal the Canonical Scripture with his authority, 10. to whom the phrases occurring in the Apocalypse were familiar, 11. who ought to have been most occupied in asserting the eternal Deity of Jesus, 12. and in explaining his benefits, 13. whom the Lord had chosen above all others to describe his discourses, 14. to whom he most entrusted the highest mysteries, 15. whom he had at hand at his transfiguration, so that he might enjoy the heavenly vision and be present at the conversations of the blessed in heaven, 16. who was held worthy by Christ to remain until he himself should come, 17. and to turn out to be the interpreter of the Danielic oracles, 18. who warned about the Anti-Christ, 19. and likewise about the precursors of the Anti-Christs, 20. who finally testified about Christ as an eyewitness of those things of which he testified. But this John is none other than John the Evangelist and Apostle, in whom all those things meet; and therefore no John other than John the Evangelist and Apostle is to be understood here, to whom this revelation was made.

For as to 1. regarding the time, the doctrine of the Nicolaitans and Balaam emerged at the time when this revelation occurred, and the relegation of John into exile happened, to which it is certain that the age of John the Apostle corresponds. Moreover, we do not find another celebrated by the name of John among the illustrious and holy Doctors of the Church at that age. Regarding John the Presbyter, which some point out, it cannot be taught that he is different from John the Apostle: to which point contributes that of Irenaeus, book 5, c. 25: 'If it were necessary to inquire openly at the present time for his (the Anti-Christ's) name, it would certainly have been published by him who also saw the Apocalypse. For it was seen not long ago, but almost in our own generation, towards the end of the reign of Domitian.' And what Origen observes from Rev. 2:14, homily 20 on Numbers: 'Therefore, in the times of John the Apostle, there were some in that Church to which he was writing, teaching the doctrine of Balaam.' But although John Annius, Salmero, and Hentenius wish for the Apocalypse to have been written before the destruction of Jerusalem, yet we must not doubt that it was written long after that, and at least 25 years later, both because the relegation of John to Patmos was done by Domitian, and because mention is made in it of Antipas the martyr, Rev. 2:13, who suffered under the same Emperor, as is held, and because most of the Fathers agree that St. John wrote it in the year of Christ 97, which was the 14th and final year of the reign of Domitian. See Irenaeus at the end, Eusebius in his Chronicle, Jerome, Primasius, Andreas, Aretas, Alcazar, Baronius, Cornelius a Lapide, and almost all of our own.

2. St. John the Apostle confesses that he was in the Spirit on Patmos for the sake of the Word of God and for the testimony of Jesus Christ, Apoc. 1, 9. But ecclesiastical antiquity testifies that this is true of no one other than John the Apostle. Origen around the year of the Lord 230, commentary on Matthew, tract 12, on chapter 20: According to these things, the sons of Zebedee seem both to have drunk the cup and to have been baptized with the baptism. Since Herod indeed killed James the brother of John with the sword: but the Roman Emperor, as tradition teaches, condemned John, who was giving testimony to the Word of God, to the island of Patmos, just as HE HIMSELF teaches concerning his own martyrdom, not saying who condemned him, but where he was condemned. He says, however, in his revelation in this way: John your brother and companion in tribulation. From this it is understood that he saw this revelation while established on the island. See also Eusebius of Caesarea in his Chronicle under the year of the Lord 97, and Athanasius in his Synopsis, and Primasius in his Prologue.

3. That the Apostle John, and no other, presided over the Asian churches is likewise undoubted. For although he was, like the other Apostles, a teacher of the universal Church, yet at that time, when seven letters were to be sent by the command of the Son of God to the seven churches, he took particular care of the churches of Asia, of which Epiphanius testifies that he spent many years in Asia: 21. & Jerome in the prologue to Matthew, that he was requested by the Bishops of Asia to write more deeply concerning the Divinity of the Savior; whom Jerome also says founded and ruled the Churches of all Asia until the time of Trajan. Irenaeus, book 2, chapter 3, says that the Ephesian Church of Trajan. And the fragment of Polycarp, which Feuardentius produces in Irenaeus, book 3, chapter 3, has this to say about him: John, having been established at Ephesus, who, as if they were ignorant of the law as from the Gentiles, took the beginning of the Gospel from the cause of our redemption, etc. Therefore, the first epistle from John also had to be directed to the Ephesian Bishop. However, it is not established that another John than the holy Apostle lived there, or that he particularly cared for the Asian Churches in that age.

(4.) Only the Apostle and Evangelist John was called by this name absolutely. Mark, of whom Acts 15:37 speaks, is never named simply John, but either simply Mark, verse 39, or this surname joined with the appellation of John. (5.) The name Theologian, which occurs in the inscription of the Apocalypse, was proper to St. John the Evangelist in that age. The Complutensian copy has this inscription: The Apocalypse of the holy Apostle and Evangelist John the Theologian. But the Apostle John deserved this name most of all, because he asserted the Deity of Christ before the other Evangelists. For to theologize Christ is to assert that Christ is God, according to Justin, Eusebius, and other Greek Doctors. By which name Ephrem the Syrian also called him in his work on the appearance of the cross at the time of judgment. Theophylact in the preface.

in the Gospel calls him most theological. (6.) Just as to Daniel, the Man of desires (chapter 9:23), God revealed the secrets of the future before other Prophets, even of the newest years and centuries, and specifically concerning the Anti-Christ, both Eastern and Western, as well as the notable circumstances of the times: So to John, the most beloved of the disciples, He deigned to manifest the fates of the Church with the notes of years and times before other Apostles, he who reclined on the bosom of the Lord, whom Anselm in his praises of the virgin called the sacred recumbent of the Lord's breast, and the Greeks called him the one on the breast, of whom Radulphus Ardens speaks at the cited Apocalyptic passage. This writes John the Apostle and Evangelist, who is chosen a virgin by God, and remained a virgin forever, and reclined at the Supper upon the breast of the Lord Jesus, to whose writings faith is to be given all the more, the more deeply he himself received and wrote the heavenly secrets from the very fountain of the Lord's breast than the others. (7.) If there had been more, all famous in that age by the name of John, yet such a notable revelation was owed to this John before others, which Joachim the Abbot prefers to all other prophecies, concerning which Richard of St. Victor writes in the preface to this place. The prophecy of Blessed John, which is contained in this book, which Christ Jesus, the Mediator of God and men, revealed to him for the enlightening of the holy Church, shines forth the more glorious and clear, the more clear and sublime oracles it describes concerning Christ and the Church. For in this it is more excellent than the prophecies, that they denounce the sacraments fulfilled for the most part concerning Christ and the Church: And just as the Gospel excels the observance of the law, so this Prophecy excels the ancient prophecies looking from afar, which has almost as many sacraments as it has words. Compare Peter Damian, sermon V, on John the Evangelist (8.)

: To predict the future or even to reveal hidden things, especially those concealed in the mind of man, belongs to no one except God and men inspired by God, or Angels by divine revelation. Since, therefore, no other John is found to be inspired by God than the Apostle, the Apocalypse must be entirely vindicated for him, so that one must wonder that Dionysius of Alexandria acknowledges the writing to be inspired by God, and yet prefers to ascribe it to someone other than John the Apostle. Certainly John himself testifies concerning the divine inspiration, that he received the apocalypse from Jesus, that he was in the Spirit, that it was divinely revealed to him: whence to the words: I Jesus sent my Angel to testify to you, Rupert of Deutz says, as if it were said: If you seek the authority of this book, I am Jesus, the Author and Giver of this Apocalypse. This Scripture is not from John, it is not from man, for he did not receive it from man nor does he say so, but by my revealing, who am Jesus, and sending through my Angel: so that just as all Scriptures are of divine authority: so also these writings may be testified and recited to you in the Churches and be at the canonical summit.

(9.) Who else at that time could with authority and as was fitting seal the divine Scripture, than John the Apostle, that elder divinely advanced to such an old age for this purpose, that he might put the final hand to the canon, and seal the same with this anathema in chapter 22, 18. For I testify to everyone hearing the words of the prophecy of this book, etc. Whence Rupert of Deutz on the last chapter of the Apocalypse: As he wished the head or beginning, so also the end of this book to be helmeted, in so far as the whole body of those revelations is fortified, lest anyone dare as if it were contemptible to refute, or cast away any of those things which are written in this book.

(10.) Whose phrases, indeed, which are found in this book, were more familiar than those of St. John the Apostle? Concerning which it has already been said before. What Beza warned concerning the style of Mark the Evangelist being most agreeable to this Johannine one will scarcely find belief among others: A comparison certainly with the writings of John the Apostle has persuaded other most learned critics, both ancient and modern, otherwise.

(11.) John, not some elder or one surnamed Mark, but the Evangelist as an eagle flying high, must have been most occupied in asserting the Divinity of Christ, for the sake of which he himself was even asked by the Bishops of Asia, as one in whose time the heresy of Cerinthus and Ebion sprouted forth, denying the eternal Divinity of Jesus. This was done most diligently in this Apocalypse, from which more than fifty proofs of the Deity of Christ can be produced. Dionysius, not indeed the Areopagite, yet an ancient writer of ecclesiastical history, chapter 3, says of the Apocalypse that he [John] expounds that arcane and mystical vision of the beloved disciple, and the divine and most high Theology of the Lord Jesus, and lifts us up and confirms us through sacred and divine mysteries. Origen, book 1, On Principles: But that you may know that there is one and the same omnipotence of the Father and the Son, just as he is one and the same God and Lord with the Father, hear John in the Apocalypse saying in this way: Thus says the Lord God, who is, and who was, and who is to come, the Almighty.

(12.) As in the Gospel and epistles St. John the Apostle was occupied not only in asserting the eternal Deity of Jesus, but also in explaining his highest benefits: So in the Apocalypse the same is observed to be done with the same clarity, gravity, and majesty, which shines forth immediately even from the preliminary vow, and no less from the hymns and doxologies. as also with other most divine visions of our Savior. (13) Just as the Lord had chosen St. John the Apostle before others to describe his sermons, since the other Evangelists expound more on the deeds than the sayings of Christ, but St. John more on the sayings than the deeds: so it was also most fitting for this Evangelist and Apostle to be entrusted with the sermons and prayers of Christ, which he had in the state of glory: not to any other John, but to this faithful and most enlightened amanuensis.

(14) To which John did he reveal the highest mysteries more than to the Apostle, who, before the other Apostles, drew them as if from the very breast of Christ, who alone knows the Father, and to whom he wills to reveal him.

(15) He deigned to take him with himself in the glorification of his body on the holy mountain, Matt. ch. 17, and to employ him in perceiving the conversation with the blessed heavenly beings Moses and Elijah, just as he also wished him to be present at his most grievous agony on the Mount of Olives, and commended his mother, the Blessed Virgin, to him. To whom, therefore, would he rather have handed down this secret ἀποκάλυψιν, whom would he rather have admitted to heavenly visions and the intuition of his glorious majesty, than this disciple of such great dignity and faith? (16) Whom Christ furthermore held in such regard that, when Peter was as it were indignant, or certainly erring through curiosity, because he was following Christ alongside him, he testified concerning him: If I will him to remain until I come, what is that to you? John ch. 21, 22, which indeed he professed concerning none of the other disciples. For by that reasoning, although that was a hypothetical statement, ἐὰν αὐτὸν θέλω μένειν, he judged John worthy to be preserved for the Church until his glorious advent; why should he not have judged him worthy of those glorious apparitions, by which he preluded his final advent and glorious manifestation in the heavens, and by the revelation of the future state of the Church, of which he could be the Rector and supreme Bishop until the end of the world, a judgment which is found nowhere concerning the other Apostles, nor concerning Peter himself.

(17) Daniel predicted that his prophecies, which he had received concerning the Anti-Christ, would one day be expounded more clearly, ch. XII. 9. Through whom, however, would he have expedited this more than through John the Apostle, an ἐγκόλπιον no less beloved to him than Daniel once was, who sought knowledge of future and hidden things from Christ more than the others, Mark ch. 13, v. 3, John ch. 13, v. 23. Whence also the same John was without doubt the one, and no other, who wept for this reason, that no one could open or look into the sealed book, Apoc. V. Through him, therefore, he deigned to expound the oracles of Daniel, of which Irenæus speaks, book 5, chapter 26: John, the disciple of the Lord, signified even more clearly concerning the final time, and concerning those ten Kings in whom the empire that now reigns is divided, expounding in the Apocalypse what the ten horns were which were seen by Daniel, saying that it was told to him thus: the ten horns which you saw, etc. (18.) That the prophecies concerning both Anti-Christs, especially the Western one, were reserved to be explained by John the Apostle is evident both from a collation of the passages of Daniel and from the first Epistle of John, ch. II. 18, 22, ch. IV. 3, 2nd ep. 7. Who, therefore, just as he warned that the same should be fled from, so he also had to describe the same more openly by his marks, so that he might be fled from: which cannot be denied to have been done in the Apocalypse.

(19.) Just as in the previous epistle he predicted not only concerning that great Anti-Christ, but concerning many other

False Prophets, the holy Apostle predicted; and taught that they were to be avoided, as Anti-Christs, and precursors of that great Anti-Christ: so in the Apocalypse the same exhortations are repeated from the epistles to the Asiatic Churches representing the universal Church, and it is to be seen throughout the whole Apocalypse, so that it is not to be doubted in the least that these things proceeded from the same John. (20) No other witness famous by the name of John was an eyewitness of those things which Christ did, than John the Evangelist, nor is that testimony to be attributed to another disciple of Christ, Apoc. 1, 2. And he signified it sending by his Angel to his servant John: Who testified the Word of God and the testimony of Jesus Christ and whatsoever he saw, the comparison teaches with similar attestations, 1 John 1, 1. That which we have seen, which also we have contemplated with our eyes, which we have seen and heard, we announce to you, John 19, 35. he who saw it bore witness; and chap. 21, 24. This is that disciple, who bears witness of these things, and wrote these things and we know that his testimony is true. Not to mention that some consider that by these words Apoc. 1, 2, John indicates the Gospel written by himself. It is certainly true that John designates his Apostolic function by the testimony of the Word of God and the testimony of Jesus Christ, as appears from v. 9 by comparison. Compare also John ch. 15, 27. Acts 1, 8. chap. 10, 39. 41. 42. Since these things are so, who would still doubt that John the Apostle is the author of this writing, and that it is of Apostolic and altogether divine authority? It is very much to be wondered at, says Ansbertus Ambrosius book X. on ch. Apoc. 22, why there is doubt among (some) Orientals concerning this book; and it is by no means thought to be of full authority, especially since John, a faithful writer of the same history, is retained, and the place in which it was seen, by whom, through whom it was sent, by whom and through whom it was revealed, and by whose testimony it was strengthened, is most openly declared. For lest anyone should doubt concerning those things which are narrated in it, he adds further that he bears witness of them, and that he will come quickly, and he predicted the time, and adds an oath of customary confirmation, and says Amen, that is truly or faithfully.

Nor indeed is any of the criteria of divine books lacking in this writing: all things which can be required in a Canonical writing are found in it in abundance. Moreover, the harmony not only with Ezekiel or Daniel, but with the whole Scripture of the Old Testament is very clear. And how through the Apocalypse, the histories, prophecies, predictions, and mysteries of the Old Testament are to be rightly considered and skillfully explained, is shown by the parallelism exhibited synoptically by the blessed Cluverius on page 17, which should be compared here.

But how falsely the Apocalypse was attributed by some to Cerinthus is clear from the very reading of the Apocalypse, inasmuch as by it the impious dogma of Cerinthus concerning Jesus as a mere man (see Tertullian, book on prescription, ch. 48. Epiphanius heresy LI.) is most frequently and most explicitly refuted. Nor are other dogmas of Cerinthus less refuted in the Apocalypse, concerning which Irenaeus book 3, ch. 25, Eusebius book 3, ch. 18, inasmuch as the world was not made by the supreme God, but, he himself being ignorant, by some other separate power: that the Kingdom of Christ would be earthly, etc.

But it is helpful here to add a catalog of Interpreters, who, doubting nothing that the Apocalypse is the work of the author St. John the Apostle, in great number illustrated the same with commentaries. In the second century indeed Papias and Justin Martyr, as also Irenaeus, even though those have perished. In the third century, however, Victorinus of Pettau the Martyr, and Melito Bishop of Sardis, whose commentaries likewise perished, as also Hippolytus and Methodius, as also in the fourth century Gregory to have received very many things. In the fifth century Augustine or rather Tychonius, and Primasius, as also Gennadius. In the sixth century occur Andrew of Caesarea, Aprigius, and Aurelius Cassiodorus, as also Ambrosiaster. In the seventh, Arethas of Caesarea: In the eighth, Albinus and Bede: In the ninth, Haymo, and Strabus, author of the Ordinary Gloss. In the eleventh, Anselm of Canterbury, and Anselm of Laon, author of the interlinear gloss. In the twelfth, Rupert of Deutz, Richard of St. Victor, Joachim the Abbot: Peter Comestor, Geoffrey of Auxerre. In the thirteenth, Nicholas of Lyra, Hugh the Cardinal, author of the concordances, Augustine of Ancona, John Valeis, Albert the Great, Ubertinus of Casale, Matthias of Sweden. In the fourteenth, Peter Aureol, Thomas not Angelic, but English, Henry of Hesse, John Hayton, John Annius, Jordan of Germany, John Purwen, a disciple of Wycliffe. In the fifteenth, Paul of Burgos, Dionysius of Rykel the Carthusian, Ascensius, Augustine of Rome, Bernardino of Siena, Lorenzo Valla. In the sixteenth, MARTIN LUTHER, Erasmus of Rotterdam, Caelius Pannonius, Petrus Galatinus, Conrad Pellican, Heinrich Bullinger, Martin Borrhaus, Rudolph Gualther, François Vatable, Theodore Bibliander, Tacitus, Nicolaus Zeger, Jacob Tralem, Bruno of Siena, Claudius of Montmartre, Federico of Venice, Helias de Anibaldis, Jean Gagne, Eder, Johannes Hentenius, Johannes Tacelphalus, Nicolaus de Alsentia, Vitalis the Cardinal, William Alabaster, Seraphinus of Terno, Lizarazus, Johannes Benedictus, Johannes Funccius, Arias Montanus, Matthias Flacius, Theodore Beza, David Chytraeus, Benedict Aretius, Jacob Brocard, William Fulke, Erasmus Sarcerius, Nicolaus Selneccer, Victorinus Strigel, Alphonsus Conradus, Franciscus Junius, Petrus Artopaeus, John Foxe, Lucas Osiander. In the seventeenth century Blasius Viegas, Benedict Pererius, Franc. Ribera, Capofagius, Forerius, Joseph de la Haye, Juan Mariana, Luis de Alcázar, Cornelius a Lapide, Jacques Tirinus, Menochius, John Price, Zacharias Muthesius, Raphael Eglinus, Thomas Brightman, Conrad Grafer, John Napier, John Piscator, Aretius, Nicolas Collado, David Pareus, William Perkins, Franciscus Lambertus, Georg Nigrinus, Johannes Wolterus, Philipp Nicolai, Johannes Winckelmann, Matthias Hoë, Johannes Drusius, Joseph Mede, Paulus Tossanus, Franciscus Gomarus, Johann Heinrich Alsted, Petrus Crugosius, Ludovicus de Dieu, Daniel Heinsius, Jacobus Laurentius, Julius a Marenholz, Casparus a Melo, Sebastian Mejer, Balthasar Richter, Jeremias Vietor, Anonymous published at Frankfurt in the year 1618. Anonymous Belgian in the year 1622. Johannes Cluverus, Paul Egardus, Patritius, and Joh. Forbes, Johannes Gerhard, the Weimar Paraphrasts, Gottlieb Heiland, Gerhard Grave, Zacharias Engelhard, Zacharias Hogelius, Anonymous of Christianopolis in the year 1653. Elias Praetorius, Jakob Böhme, and other fanatics of the previous and this century, especially the Chiliasts to be reviewed hereafter, Philipp Heinrich Friedlieb, who collected annotations on all the Biblical books, which was also done by Prückner and Raupius, Hieronymus Kromayer, Johann Heinrich a Diest, Johannes Cocceius, Johannes Christophorus Artopaeus, Matthaeus Hofmann, Johannes Schindler, Johann Andreas Lucius, and one than whom hardly any is worse, HUGO GROTIUS. But in such a great number of interpreters, the blessed Luther in the previous century, and the blessed Cluverus in this our century, together with our blessed Gerhard, whom the Weimar Paraphrase has mostly followed, easily deserve the chief praise above all others, nor do we hesitate to add our vote to the judgment of the blessed Cluverus: Indeed, he says on page 27, among all the commentators on the Apocalypse, whether orthodox or heterodox, I have been able to find no one who has aimed so excellently at the mark as that excellent instrument of God, M. Luther, of most blessed memory, the Theologian; to whom, certainly, if there had been enough leisure from the most serious affairs of the Church with which he was overwhelmed, so that he could have elaborated and unfolded more widely the opinion which he proposed in the German preface to this book concerning its true interpretation, I do not think that such a great crowd of bad interpreters would have dared to appear afterwards. The Calvinists praise their Bullinger, they praise Aretius, they praise Colladon, they praise Pareus and others; I indeed will not hesitate to affirm that they owe to Dr. Luther almost everything that is considered most excellent in their commentaries, and that they would have attained many things much more correctly, had they not sometimes departed too far from the path demonstrated by him.

The Synopsis of Athanasius presents the argument of the book quite conveniently, from which it is pleasing to repeat it: This revelation, he says, John the Evangelist and Theologian himself saw on the island called Patmos on the Lord's Day, and being commanded, he wrote it down, so that he might send it to the seven Churches, namely these: Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia, and Laodicea. But the things which he saw in this vision are many and different. Towards the end he also saw the destruction of the Anti-Christ with the Devil. He is commanded, however, first to write to the individual Angels of the aforementioned Churches, according to the actions of each. Therefore he saw many admirable visions, such as seven golden lampstands and in the midst of them one like the Son of man, and he received the interpretation that those lampstands are the seven Churches and that he who was in the midst was the Lord. Then he saw a door opened in heaven, and the Lord sitting on a throne, and twenty-four Elders, sitting upon thrones and worshipping the Lord. He saw also seven seals being opened, and with each one opened a certain vision appeared. He saw likewise seven Angels, having seven trumpets, and with each one of them sounding a sign came to pass, but with the seventh sounding he heard them saying: The kingdom of the world has become the Lord's. And he saw the ark of the Testament in heaven. Then he saw a woman giving birth and a fiery Dragon, who was pursuing her. The woman indeed was saved in the wilderness, but the Dragon was cast into the fire. After these things he saw a beast having ten horns and seven heads, and its diadem was full of blasphemy. But he did not reveal its name, but the number of its name, namely six hundred sixty-six. And he heard virgins singing and following the Lamb. He saw also an Angel flying through the midst of heaven, and after this one another, after the other, a third also, then he saw also a white cloud, and sitting upon it one like the Son of man, having on his head a golden crown and in his hand a sharp sickle. Finally he saw seven Angels having seven last plagues and golden vials full of the wrath of God. After these things he was carried away in the Spirit into the wilderness and saw a woman sitting upon a scarlet beast, having seven heads:

He saw the beast and the Kings of the earth, wishing to make war with him who sat upon the white horse. And the beast was seized, and with it the False Prophet, who is the Anti-Christ, and he saw them cast into the lake of fire. After these things he saw an Angel descending from heaven, and casting Satan with those who had his mark into the abyss, and shutting it over him, so that he might not seduce the nations any more until the thousand years are consumed. Then he saw the martyrs reigning with glory in Christ, and that Satan after a thousand years is to be released and cast into the lake of fire with the Anti-Christ for ever and ever. After these things he saw a new heaven, a new earth, and a new Jerusalem, and a river of living water, and the servants of God contemplating his face and having his name on their foreheads. When John had seen these things, he fell down wishing to worship the Angel who had shown him all these things. But the Angel forbade his attempt, saying: Do not worship me, but God: for I am your fellow servant. But after he saw these things, he heard from our Lord JESUS himself, that he is the existing one, and he himself is the word of God, which in later times was made flesh for our sake: he was made, I say, perfect Man, and was called the Son of man.

The Apostle himself presents the partition in chapter 1, verse 19. Write the things which you have seen, both the things which are, and the things which must happen hereafter. John therefore deals partly with those things which are, or with the present state of the Church, and partly with those things which were to be hereafter, or with the future state of the Church. But because the Holy Spirit wished to commend these to the Churches by way of an Epistle and prefixed a title to the entire writing, the title occurs first, consisting of the inscription of the book in verses 1 and 2 and the commendation of the same in verse 3; then indeed the work itself, in which, according to the epistolary manner, one must observe first the name of the Author, then the names of those Churches to which the Apocalypse is inscribed: Furthermore, a wish or greeting is added, and finally the stirring up of the reader by the commemoration of the glorious coming of Christ. And these are like an Exordium. There follows afterwards a narrative consisting of seven revelations, the first of which is about the present state of the Church, the rest about the future state: The former concerns a particular Church in Asia properly, but the latter the universal Church. Finally, a conclusion is subjoined in chapter 22 from verse 5. For the Apocalyptic narrative extends up to that point.

The first vision is as it were preparatory, insofar as St. John is called and confirmed to this Prophetic office, and this part is common to chapter 1.
