But insofar as those things are proposed in that vision which were to be written down concerning the state of the Church of that time to the seven Churches of Asia, to which the second and third chapters pertain, this vision is separated from the six remaining ones, which come more specially under the name of Prophecy, since that prophecy is said to be such, not because it predicts future things, but because it reveals present, yet hidden, things: Which here concern the state of the Churches, namely the Ephesian, Smyrnean, Pergamene, Thyatirean, chapter 2, as also the Sardian, Philadelphian, and Laodicean, chapter 3. But prophecy is specifically said to be both FIRST and SECOND: Since in chapter 10, last verse, it is indicated to John: You MUST prophesy AGAIN: where he is solemnly invested with the other prophecy.

The second vision is completed in chapters 4, 5, 6, and 7, in which first the preparation occurs in chapter 4, by the representation of the glory of the Most Holy Trinity, and its glorious celebration in heaven: and in chapter 5, by the representation of the sealed book of special providence, or the fates of the Church, as well as of the Lamb slain, worthy to take the book, and for that reason celebrated by the whole choir of the Church in heaven and on earth.

Then the account of the spectacles seen in the opening of the seals, namely the first, from which a white horse came forth; the second, from which a red horse was seen to come forth; the third, from which a black one was seen to come forth: The fourth, from which a pale one: The fifth, upon the opening of which the souls of the slain were seen under the altar provoking Divine vengeance; and the sixth, from which an earthquake, the darkening of the sun, the bloody face of the moon, the falling of the stars, the rolling up of the heaven, and a most grievous commotion of the mountains and islands and inhabitants of the earth were observed, concerning which is chapter 6, under which also the sealing of the elect in dangers is shadowed forth, and their exaltation to heavenly joys: chapter 7.

The third vision is about the seventh seal opened, and the trumpet-bearing Angels, chapters 8 and 9. And indeed in the seventh chapter a preparation was made for opening the seventh seal, for the sake of which the minds of the faithful were first to be comforted on account of the four Angels restraining the damage of the wind, and that was done through the sealing of the servants of the Lord by the seal-bearing Angel, to avert their injury; whence followed the glorification of God and the Lamb, and John's information concerning the assembly of the heavenly Candidates. Yet this chapter 7 is a preparation for the following things in such a way that it also looks back to the preceding things, and exhibits consolation in those calamities which are predicted there, whence it is not undeservedly considered to pertain with them to the second vision as a general one. But in the following chapter 8, it is related how, after the silence of half an hour, seven trumpet-bearing Angels were brought into view, but before the sounding of the trumpets, through another Angel offering the prayers of the saints to God, the saints were confirmed concerning Divine grace in the future calamity, and thus the IV Angels sounded the trumpet: At the first sounding, hail and fire mixed with sulfur, at the second a burning sea, at the third a star falling from heaven caused damages; at the fourth sounding there followed a darkening of the sun, moon, and stars: At whose sounding the cry of an Angel flying through the midst of heaven, announcing woe, woe, woe, was heard. There follows furthermore chapter 9, concerning the first woe of the fifth trumpet, where from the abyss smoke, and out of the smoke destructive and terrible locusts came forth under King Abaddon, as also the sixth trumpet, which pertained to the second woe, and the release of the four Angels at the Euphrates for the killing of a third part of men. And up to this point the first prophecy extends itself, and thus the third vision is to be terminated here.

The fourth follows, pertaining to the seventh trumpet, chapters 10 and 11, in which first in chapter 10, another strong Angel is seen with a book, swearing concerning the end of time, and handing the book to John to be devoured, so that he might prophesy again, which was a preparation for the second prophecy. Afterwards in chapter 11, the third woe is presented in summary under the measuring of the temple, the casting out of the choir, and the trampling of the holy city, as well as the raising up of the two witnesses, whose power, killing, vivification, and glorification is set forth with the loud voice of the heavenly hosts celebrating God, and the sight of the ark of the covenant in heaven.

Furthermore, the fifth vision, comprised in chapters 12, 13, and 14, is partly under the image of the woman fleeing into the desert after childbirth, for whose sake Michael fights against the Dragon, and the woman had to be hidden, the Church and her persecution under the Antichrist is adumbrated in chapter 12; partly the twin beast is brought forth to describe its power and fraudulence in chapter 13, and the Lamb with the confessors on Mount Sion is opposed to the same, but especially with an Angel preaching the eternal Gospel, another intimating the fall of Babylon, as also a third denouncing eternal damnation to the worshippers of the beast, and the Son of man on a cloud and an Angel with a sharp sickle harvesting the vine of the earth in chapter 14.

The sixth vision exhibits the seven last plagues with the judgment upon the great harlot, and the heavenly rejoicing concerning the same, in the five following chapters. The plagues are enumerated in chapters 15 and 16: In the former, the Angels having them are seen with the victors of the beast standing by the sea of glass singing the song of Moses and the Lamb, receiving the golden vials full of divine wrath: In the latter, however, the seven vials are poured out upon the earth. The judgment of the harlot is proposed in chapters 17 and 18. In the former, the Babylonian harlot herself is depicted in vivid colors: In the latter, however, the fall of the same, with the cause of her fall and the mourning of her lovers over her fall, is described. The rejoicing of the heavenly host over the same, as also the dancing on account of the imminent marriage of the Lamb, and furthermore the appearance of the King of Kings, and the victory over the beast and the false Prophet, chapter 19 exhibits.

In the seventh vision, he adumbrates the binding of the Dragon for a thousand years, his release for a short time, and his gathering of Gog and Magog for battle against the camp of the saints, the destruction of him (Gog) by fire from heaven, and his precipitation into the infernal place, in chapter 20, as well as the blessedness of the Elect under the guise of the new Jerusalem and the Bride of the Lamb in chapters 21 and 22 up to verse 5. To which is subjoined the conclusion and the final end in the chapter, up to verse 9. Finally, the Epilogue of the whole book or epistle is subjoined in verse 10 and following, which is sealed with a most grave exhortation and adjuration, as also with a sigh and a final vow.

Let the distribution of the blessed Luther with his succinct explanation be read in his golden preface: Which, explained in a different sense by a few, the blessed Cluverus exhibits thus in his Apocalyptic dawn: That with the introduction and narrative of chapter 1 prefixed, the revelation contains the former part in the PRESENT vision of chapters 2 and 3, and the latter prophecy in the remaining chapters, and this then first in chapters 4 to 8, then second in the following chapters. Moreover, the first and general prophecy is in chapters 4, 5, 6, and 7, and the special one, defined by certain circumstances of times and things, is in chapters 8 and 9. The general one consists of three segments: The first contains the preparation for the whole prophecy in chapters 4 and 5, in the former of which the Lord himself is depicted with his heavenly glory, palace, court, and this whole gracious government; in the latter, however, his inscrutable providence and foreknowledge are figured by the little book of secrets, together with the opening of the same, which can be done and obtained through Christ alone. The second makes the operative part, comprising the very Dramatic figuration of those things which commonly and universally happen in this our pilgrimage, consisting of six seals in chapter 6. The third has an informative and consolatory vision, what the Angels of darkness are plotting, how they are powerfully resisted by God, and in what manner he protects his elect, and finally gathers them into eternal mansions in chapter 7. The special one is completed by six trumpets, of which four minor ones are treated in chapter 8, and two major ones in chapter 9. The last one, however, as the greatest, provides the material for the new Prophecy and extends through eleven chapters.

As regards the second prophecy, the blessed Cluverus made three parts of it: 1. The introduction or preparation through the new investiture of John in chapter 10. 2. The vision itself, comprising the third woe or the sounding of the seventh Angel's trumpet, from chapter 11 up to chapter 22, verse 6. 3. The epilogue in chapter 22, verses 6, 7, 8, 9. He makes a fourfold vision here: 1. The general one, which is the fourth of the Apocalypse itself, and almost the most brilliant of all the visions, depicting the entire period of the third woe in chapters 11, 12, 13, and 14. He proposes a summary of the same in chapter 11; the treatment itself is completed in three parts: then the preparation or prologue from verse 15 to chapter 12, verse 9; then the narrative depicting the beginning, progress, and the very vigor or climax of the third woe in three types, concerning the woman in exile, the Dragon fighting and laying horrible snares, in chapter 12, and concerning the two beasts in chapter 13, of which the former exhibits the Anti-Christian kingdom according to secular power, the latter the Pseudo-Prophetic state of the same: then the antithesis and antidote, partly concerning Christ the King standing on Mount Zion and his choir opposed to the Anti-Christ, partly concerning the heralds of the Gospel opposed to the Pseudo-Prophet, partly concerning the rest of those killed by the beast, partly concerning the judgment of Christ by the sickle immediately reaping the enemies, in chapter 14. II. The special one, commemorating the pouring out of the seven vials in chapters 15, 16, 17, 18, 19 up to verse 11, in which first the preparation is made in chapter 15, then the simple prophecy is had in chapter 16, afterwards a didactic or informative vision is added, concerning the beast carrying the harlot and the whore riding upon it in chapter 17, concerning the Angel denouncing destruction to Babylon in chapter 18, and concerning the heavenly multitude giving thanks to God in chapter 19, and these are referred by the blessed Cluverus to the fifth vision.

III. The destruction of the beast and Gog in chapters 19 and 20. Which is contained in the sixth vision, completed in two parts; the former is the last war of Christ and the Anti-Christ in the remainder of chapter 19: The latter is the final attempt of the devil and its outcome, with a preparatory narrative prefixed concerning the long captivity of the Dragon and the intermediate state of the world, by which he describes the pious and the impious alike, in chapter 20, verse 10. The blessed Cluverus constitutes the seventh vision concerning the end of the world, namely concerning the appearance of Christ the Judge from verse 11 to the end of chapter 20, and concerning the triumphant Church in chapters 21 and 22 up to verse 5. Finally, he assigns the epilogue of the latter prophecy to verses 6, 7, 8. He assigns the epilogue of the whole Apocalypse, as the fourth part of the book, consisting of the words of both Christ and the Apostle, from verse 9 to the end.

Altogether foreign are the interpretations: I. Of those who wish to describe either the general battle of the flesh and the Spirit in man in the Apocalypse, which they attribute to Arias Montanus, or the dissensions between the good and the wicked, and their outcomes, which they attribute to Tyconius, Primasius, Ansbertus, Anselm, Rupert, Haymo, Richard, Hugh, Thomas and Dionysius the Carthusian, as also to Titelmannus, Cornelius and Cluverus, which is refuted without any difficulty by the variety of times and circumstances.

Nor does the interpretation of Aureolus, Lyranus, Antoninus, Ederus, and Lizorazus hold, whom Cornelius à Lapide, along with Alcazar, says extend the first vision of the seven seals to the times of Julian, the second of the seven trumpets to the Emperor Maurice: the third of the Dragon and the double beast to the victories of Charlemagne: the fourth of the vials to the Emperor Henry IV and Hildebrand or Gregory VII: the fifth of the harlot of Babylon and the beast up to the Anti-Christ: the sixth up to the final judgment; which Alcazar rejects as disjointed, and Cornelius as false, inept, and forced, as Cluverus rightly does.

Nor does the opinion of Abbot Ubertinus and Seraphinus deserve approval regarding the seven states of the Church: first, of foundation in the Apostles; second, of persecution under the Gentile Emperors; third, of prosperity under Constantine; fourth, of division under heretics; fifth, of tranquility and growth under Charlemagne; sixth, of the final persecution under the Anti-Christ; seventh, of the final judgment: for besides the fact that it falsely reserves the Anti-Christ for the last place, this explanation, in the judgment of Cornelius himself, is partly forced, partly imported, and entirely fabricated from human ingenuity.

The Jesuits have devised other and more numerous interpretations, in favor of the Pope, so that he might not be recognized as that Anti-Christ predicted by John: But they are diverse and contrary, and mutually destructive. For Ribera and Bellarmine, as also Blasius de Viegas, twist most of the prophecies to the last times and their own three-year Anti-Christ. Which is therefore the fourth explanation. But Ludovicus ab Alcazar (which is the fifth interpretation) refers the same to the first times, and to the war of the Church with the Jewish Synagogue the earlier chapters from c. 4 to 11, but the later ones up to 20 to the war with paganism: Whom Grotius followed in good part, like a hired advocate of the Roman Pontiff. But that could not even prove itself to the Jesuits themselves. Cornelius certainly rejects the same: 1. because it is new, 2. because it is mystical, not literal, 3. because he makes history out of prophecy, 4. because most places of the Apocalypse speak so clearly from the common explanation of the Doctors of the Church about the last times, that they do not seem able to be twisted to the Church of the Jews and the victorious Gentiles. But when it is opposed to Alcazar by Pareus and others, that the former war with the Synagogue had already been fought before the prophecy was revealed, since that had already lain in ashes together with the temple: that the latter war with paganism, even if it were already raging at that time, would further press Christians most gravely, yet that it was predicted by St. John to be far more atrocious with the Anti-Christ, all interpreters, even the Papists themselves, agree unanimously, and that the judgment of the great harlot and the ruin of Babylon are exhibited not as a thanksgiving for conversion, but as a punishment for whoredom, to be inflicted upon the Anti-Christian kingdom and seat in the last times, and thus to interpret it concerning the conversion of Rome and paganism to the faith of CHRIST under Constantine and his successors, which happened soon around the three-hundredth year of Christ, and concerning the erection of the Roman Church and Pontiff to the empire of the city and the world, is to be insane with reason: Grotius interpolated that opinion with a new invention, but one entirely opposed to all antiquity, namely that the Johannine vision was made before the desolation of Jerusalem: he contends that the burning of Babylon by the Ostrogoths and Totila is designated: but what is indicated by the destruction of the beast, he does not find, unless he were to recur to the times which preceded the ruin of the city in a hysteron proteron, and refer the happiness of the new heaven and new earth to the most flourishing state of the Church, which he makes from the times of Constantine up to the times of Justinian, and interpret the glory of Jerusalem described in Chapter 21 concerning the splendor of the Roman Church under Christian Princes. But that hysteron proteron is by no means to be admitted, nor is it the opinion of the ancients and recent interpreters, constant and resting on the evidence of the sacred text clearer than the sun, that St. John in the final chapters deals with the happiness of the Church militant and the greatest persecutions from Constantine to Justinian, which were troubled by much unhappiness from the Arians and Eutychians, to whom Justinian himself is believed to have been addicted, and other heretics, and by the most grave incursions brought by Attila, Genseric, Totila, and similar other scourges of the earth: but rather that he deals with the beatitude of the Church triumphant which will last for all eternity. For the rest, the refutation of the false interpretations of Alcazar, and how the Cadmean brothers Alcazar with Ribera and Blasius de Viegas and Bellarmine [are refuted], can be read in the Dilucidationes of B. Cluverius, page 38 et seqq. We reserve a fuller discussion of those commentaries, and especially of Grotius, for the explanation of the text itself and its vindications.

Furthermore, sixthly, some judge that the Apocalypse does not proceed in a continuous series of periods, but by one representation of the same periods after another, and exhibits the same things in diverse ways, who again depart into divisions of opinion. Most make the vision of the seven seals and seven trumpets, as well as the vision of the woman in labor, the Dragon and both beasts, and finally of the bound, released, and judged Dragon and the new Jerusalem, universal, that is, according to their second, third, fourth, and seventh review, just as they constitute those particular ones concerning the seven vials and the judgment of the harlot and the ruin of Babylon, namely the fifth and sixth, which is the opinion of Pareus and Henricus à Diest, who wove an exegetical analysis of the Apocalypse from the commentaries of Pareus, and others. Who therefore wish the four periods of the Christian Church to be exhibited in those universal visions in four ways: the first of the Church flourishing and agonizing under the Roman tyrants up to the peace of Constantine the Great in the year 315; the second of the Church reigning and luxuriating under Christian Emperors up to the rise of the Anti-Christ under Boniface III in the year of Christ 606; the third of the Church trodden and oppressed by the Anti-Christ, especially the western one, up to the measuring of the temple or the reformation; the fourth of the Church reformed from Popery and the Papacy declined up to the end of the world.

But in truth, it is not to be believed that the periods of the Christian Church had already been exhibited while the seals were not yet opened, and that St. John had received information about the same while the book was still closed. And not a few things are forced in that explanation, when the trumpets are applied as parallels to the seals, and these to the remaining two visions which they call universal; finally, the order of the visions is disturbed, and particular ones are mixed with universal ones.

Still less do the exegesis of those (VII) agree, who compare the vials also to the seals and trumpets, as Nicolaus Colladus wished, because what was prefigured more obscurely by the seals, [was prefigured] more openly by the trumpets, but most openly by the seven seals: how the vision of the seven vials must also be established as universal, which, however, it is clear concern only the last plagues, and cannot be drawn back to the preceding periods and visions except by force, whence Pareus himself refuted this opinion at chapter 16, 2; although there is some similarity of effects in the six trumpets and the six later vials, yet the seven vials do not entirely correspond to the seven seals and seven trumpets. The reason is clearly held from verse 2, as much of this as of the preceding chapter, regarding time, since the vials begin to be poured out upon the branded ones of the beast in chapter 16, 2, long after the rise of the beast, when the same had already begun to be overcome by some in chapter 15, 2; but the birth of the beast pertains finally to the sixth seal and the fifth trumpet.

But they err greatly, VIII. Who also seek the same periods in the seven epistles: Which, however, others distribute and assign differently; Matthaeus Hoffmannus, called Macharopaeus, wishes the first epistle, the first seal, and the first trumpet to concern the same period, so that the first Angel of the Church, namely the Ephesian, represents the primitive Church and that in its entirety for 343 years: and he explains the same years as the first seal, as also the first trumpet. The second Angel of the Smyrnean Church represents the whole Church again for the following 343 years of the Christian era, which he contends likewise regarding the second seal and the second trumpet, and so on for the remaining Angels of the Churches, and seals, and trumpets: Which therefore in summary exhibit seven times 343 years, so that the whole period of the Church of the New

of the Testament be 2400 years or 24 centuries, which may also be represented by the 24 elders. Which opinion the late ὁ Μακαρίτης proposed with such confidence that in this seventeenth century of the Christian era one must seek the Interpreter of the Apocalypse in that Elder who warned John not to weep, Rev. 5:6, and that he himself was this very person, he hinted not obscurely, Ch. 7, p. 112, 113, Ch. 12, p. 215. But intervening death testifies that he was a false prophet, which did not permit him to unseal the seals, nor to progress beyond the fifth seal in his Apocalyptic chronotaxy, which furthermore rests upon extremely slippery principles, for example, that the seven Angels of the Churches of Asia are seven periods of the entire Church of the New Testament, that those seven are also the trumpeting Angels, and thus that those seven Churches correspond with the trumpets regarding the synchronisms, and that each Angelic trumpet contains seven common jubilees, namely 343 years, and so the whole period of the Church of the New Testament consists of two thousand and four hundred years with a unit, and that the twenty-four elders are as many generations or centuries of years; which to have recited is to have refuted.

Again, the Calvinist Bremensians, Ludovicus Crocius, Johannes Crocius, and Balthasar Willius, draw nine other parallel lines and invent other synchronisms regarding the seven epistles, the seven seals, and the seven trumpets, and indeed even regarding the seven vials. The former, in the preface to his Theological syntagma, which he adorned for the condition, as he says, of the Sardian Church in the year 1636, made the first condition of the Christian Church Apostolic, which was signified to the Ephesian Church from Tiberius up to the Emperor Trajan, which he calls golden, and draws to the white horse of the first seal, and to the first trumpet and the first vial, Rev. 2:1, ch. 6:2, ch. 8:7, ch. 16:2. The second, μαρτυρευμένην, approved from Trajan up to Constantine the Great, signified to the Angel of the Smyrnean Church from the year of Christ 85, to which he refers the vision of John on Patmos for ten days, that is, 240 hours or years, up to the year 325, to which period he refers the red horse and the second vial, Rev. 6:4, Ch. 16:3, and names it iron. The third, Polemical or Eristic, signified to the Angel of the Pergamene Church from Constantine the Great up to Charlemagne, of the third seal, the black horse, the third trumpet, the fall of the great star, and the third vial. The fourth, religious and devout, signified to the Thyatirean Angel under the Roman Papacy from the time of Charlemagne up to Charles V, which he refers to the fourth seal, the fourth trumpet, and the fourth vial, but for what reason he does not explain: perhaps because it pleases him so. The fifth, Political, signified to the Sardian Angel from the empire of Charles V, which he compares to the year 1517, and refers to the fifth seal and the fifth trumpet and vial. The sixth, fraternal, signified to the Philadelphian Angel, which he calls silver and refers to the sixth seal and the sixth trumpet and vial. The seventh, lukewarm, signified to the Laodicean Angel, which pertains to the seventh seal, and likewise the seventh trumpet and vial, called by him leaden, during which there will be silence in heaven for half an hour or 30 years, and mere chaff will lie on the threshing floor of the Church. But since the Apocalypse is written partly about those things which are, and partly about those things which are to be after them, and the seven Epistles, according to the traditional opinion of most Interpreters, contain those things which are historically, but the seals, trumpets, and vials those things which are to be prophetically, Crocius contends against this that the seven epistles are not merely historical, but also truly prophetic; assigning to them, as it appears, a double sense, and asserting ten reasons for the Prophetic sense, but of no value, which his fellow in the same faith, Franc. Gomarus, demolished in his digression on the explanation of the epistle to the Galatians, ch. I, Vol. I of his Works, p. 469 ff., rightly calling Crocius's assertion and corruption of the holy scriptures reckless, and indeed nonsense and an insolent and vain paradox, and showing the vanity of the reasons both from the names of the Churches and from the thing itself. The period of the Ephesian Church can certainly be considered golden with far less right from the epistle given to its Angel than that of the Smyrnean and Philadelphian, if we look at the rebuke of the former, but the praises of the latter: and that the candlestick was moved at Ephesus, or that that Church was taken away after John died, which Crocius asserts, is repugnant to history: how reckless finally Crocius was in predicting the FRATERNAL condition of the Church, as if it had already diminished even then, experience, the teacher of fools, has taught. For who is ignorant that the Φιλαδελφίαν was not at all attempted in the Cassel colloquy, and that that ecclesiastical Syncretism with the Reformed was condemned by the unanimous calculation of those professing the Augsburg Confession; and that fraternity and concord with the Papists, whether brought forward by the Roman Catholics in the charitable colloquy of Thorn in the year 1645, or subsequently by the Calixtines in various Irenics, had no success. Nevertheless, Johannes Coccejus followed Crocius, and not only in the Apocalyptic epistles, but also, which you might wonder at, he attempted to show the same periods in the books of the Old Testament, in Isaiah, in Zechariah, even in the Song of Songs, and where not? He hints that these look to all the Prophets, in his preface to the minor Prophets, saying that the Apocalypse, the last of all, points out to us with an outstretched finger what ALL the former had predicted concerning the affairs of the Christian Church. We have noted the man's wonderful commentaries on the Prophets throughout the illustrated Bibles of the Old Testament. Now from the Song of Songs, which he has also dragged here, but equally by the neck, it is helpful to bring forward such things. His thoughts on the Song of Songs in the preface, which presents a synopsis and marrow of the Song, p. 4, stand thus: The state of the Church commemorating the grace of the sweetness of her beloved or preaching the Gospel is conveniently distinguished into seven periods: The first period is of preaching among the Jews and Gentiles before the worsening persecutions and the destroyed temple, Cant. 1, 5. foll. and ch. 2. The second is of the probation and consolation of the Church in the most grave, long-lasting, and various persecutions, until, with the tyrants destroyed by earthly Princes, peace was granted to it, Cant. III, and IV. The third is of the Church pacified from persecutions and safe from the Gentiles, but beginning to struggle with the false Church and with the domination of men, ch. 5. and 6. v. 9. The fourth is of the true Church shining forth and showing itself in the midst of the false Church until the division, from Ch. 6. v. 9. to Ch. 7, 11. The fifth is of the Church, after peace was sought in vain and the conversion of the opposing multitude or reformation was expected, withdrawing from the great city, and in that withdrawal being harassed until its peace, C. 7, 11. 12. 13. and C. 8. v. 1. 2. 3. The sixth is of the Church established in a new distress after the peace which it had obtained from the secession, C. 8. v. 4. 5. But how will that distress have a place in the silver age and the period of the Philadelphian Church? Those innovators will extricate themselves with difficulty. The seventh period for Cocceius is of the Church aspiring after many struggles to the kingdom of Christ, and the preaching of it in the whole world, Cant. 8. from v. 8. and 14. But how is that to be reconciled with the Crocian thoughts concerning the seventh period, lukewarm, saturnalian, and leaden, and of all the most dangerous? Moreover, we shall perhaps compare the thoughts concerning these Cocceian views on the Apocalypse with the Crocian ones more conveniently in the elucidation of our Epistles and Prophecies.

Let us now hear Balthasar Willius. He, in his commentary on Zechariah, ch. 11, p. 484, describes, he says, primarily the history of the new Church in the Apocalypse under the seven Churches, to which as many epistles are inscribed, seven seals, seven trumpets, and seven vials. And from there he judged that the order should be taken (by a wonderful interpretation) by which he attempts to demonstrate that the final prophecy of Zechariah, ch. 12, 13, and 14, describes in ORDER those same seven periods of the new Church of Christ. Nor indeed does Willius merely feign harmony between those things, but he also seeks the same in the old Church by a new paradox: For the old Church also, he says on p. 414, had its Ephesian, Smyrnean, Thyatiren, Pergamene, Sardian, Philadelphian, and Laodicean period, and indeed a more obscure one in the first two thousand years, but a more illustrious one in the two thousand following: The more obscure Ephesian period began in Paradise through the promulgation of the first promise concerning the seed of the woman who would crush the head of the serpent, Gen. 3:15, and lasted until the parricide of Cain, perhaps for thirty or even more years. The Smyrnean period embraces the slaughter of Abel and the first persecution of the pious, Gen. 4:8. The Pergamene period represents the proclamation and sermon concerning the name of the Lord begun under Enoch at his birth, and afterwards continued under the contradictions of the impious, Gen. 4:26. The Thyatiren period will be figured by that suppression of the pious through the profanity of men and the tyranny of the giants, concerning whom Gen. 6:1, 2, 3, 4. The Sardian period has the reformation of Noah and the flood itself, Gen. 6, 7. The Philadelphian period embraces the time after the flood, up to the time of the Babylonian tower, Gen. 11. The Laodicean period, the passive profanity of men up to the calling of Abraham. Afterwards, the first two thousand years being almost finished, the more illustrious Churches began: the Ephesian, which embraces the calling of Abraham, and the repetition of the promise made to him, and his pilgrimage, as also those of Isaac and Jacob: the Smyrnean, which contains the distresses and servitude in Egypt: the Pergamene, which comprehends the pilgrimage in the desert and the introduction into the land of Canaan: the Thyatiren, which is defined by the time of the Judges: the Sardian, which has the most limpid centuries of the Kings and their ending through the Babylonian captivity: the Philadelphian, which extends after the release from captivity to the time of Aristobulus, who first resumed the royal title. The Laodicean, which is continued from that time to the final destruction. These things Willius, deriving his absurdities through the later chapters of Zechariah, but referring the first rudiments of his opinion to Ludovicus Crocius, and repeating the same in his preface so that 'good things may be said twice and thrice,' nay, even attributing them to the prophet Isaiah (in his commentary on Zechariah XIV, p. 514), as if he had begun to describe the Philadelphian Church after the Sardian in ch. 59:20, 21. But for those commentators, I mean Cocceius and Willius, it was easy to fashion anything out of anything, when they induced their minds to demonstrate those periods of theirs in the Old Testament, whether by Moses, especially in his final words, or Solomon, or Isaiah, Zechariah—I wonder why not also Daniel, and David, and Job—as interpreters and commentators of the Johannine Apocalypse, even for the establishing of the Epistles of the Son of God to the Churches of Asia. These authors, therefore, have rendered the Apocalypse—which according to Salmeron, if it is to be explained, is not undeservedly held to be like the squaring of the circle, of which it is usually said that it is knowable but not yet known, and according to others, and especially Socinus, is a work of immense difficulty and altogether incomprehensible without a singular revelation of God—more intricate and perplexed with their glosses. But in place of prolegomena, let these suffice concerning the various interpretations. For it is not worth mentioning the opinions of those who have already long ago attempted to refer the Apocalypse to the histories of the Old Testament, since they have fashioned a historical but enigmatic book out of a prophetic one.

FIRST GENERAL SECTION, AND INTRODUCTION TO THE PROPHECY, AND AS IT WERE HISTORICAL. EMBRACING AT THE SAME TIME THE FIRST VISION.

Latin:

N. J. TATA IN YPSIN S. JO- NNIS.

Cerinthiano errore, in antiquitate, recensentur, quam de ἐπιγραφῇ : quod non Apostolum, sed Theologum se dixerit Johannes, & styli diversita- te, ab Evangelico & Apostolico S. Johannis, necnon de materia, & sententiis, in quibus Apostolicam gra- vitatem nonnulli desiderarunt, ut Erasmus, non sa- tis æquus libro huic divinissimo in calce notarum suarum observavit. Ad quæ vero respondit Beza in annot. & B. Gerhardus in exeg. de Script. S.

Theologi nomen non Johannes sibi sumpsit, sed qui inscri- ptionem libri fecit, quo asserere potius eundem Johanni Apostolo voluit, quam eidem abrogare. Solus enim Johannes Apostolus ex primæva illa antiquitate, cum ἐπιγραφὴν nacta est Apocalypsis, hoc nomen gessit, quod postmodum etiam Grego- rio Nazianzeno datum est ob assertam λόγος Filii Dei æternam Deitatem. Ipse autem Servum Jesu Christi se vocavit c. 1. 1. quo nomine & Paulus & Ju- das Apostolatum suum expresserunt. Utrumque & Evangelistæ & Theologi nomen conjunxit Atha- nasius in Synopsi. An vero ante vel demum post Origenem hic titulus Johanni Apostolo datus sit, non liquet. B. Gerhardus in exeg. adducit Diony- sium, qui in epist. ad Johannem in Pathmo exulan- tem scripta ipsi hoc nomen tribuerit. Porro tanta non est styli in hoc libro a re- liquis Johanneis scriptis diversitas, quin compa- reant etiam in hoc scripto λέξεως Johanneæ in- dicia. Utitur voce Λόγος de Filio Dei S. Johannes in Evangelio c. 1. 1. 1. 14. in epistola priori cap. 1. 1. Idem nomen de eo occurrit Apoc. XIX. 13. Καὶ κα- λεῖται τὸ ὄνομα ἀυτῶ ὁ λόγος τῷ Θεῷ. Quo etiam refert Paræus cap. 1. 2. Et conformitas observatur non collatione tantum, quam Beza e c. I. 7. & in

Evangelio c. XIX. 37. & Flacius c. I. 2. cum Evan- gelii c. XIX. 35. & 1. Joh. I. 1. instituit, sed in plu- sculis aliis. In vocibus Johanni Apostolo si cui- piam alii familiaribus, ut sunt testimonium, testa- ri, sermones Dei servare, custodire Verbum Dei, fides Jesu, ablutio per sanguinem Jesu, &c. In Filii Dei appellatione, quod vocetur Agnus Dei, Job. I. 29. 36. & Apoc. V. 6. 8. 12. 13. c. VI. 16. c. VII. 9. 10. 11. 17. &c. ubi etsi vox ἀρνίον adhibeatur, ea ta- men non inusitata fuit Evangelistæ, c. XXI. 15. In as- sertione divinæ naturæ & explicatione beneficiorum Filii Dei, quod argumentum tum ob hæreses istius ætatis, tum ob fidem salvificam, quæ illa respicit, maxime necessariam, in Apocalypsi non negle- ctum fuit, etsi ea non didactica, sed Prophetica sit, adeoque in scopi etiam Johannis Apostoli, quem scriptioni suæ præfixit, Job. XX. ult. & 1. Job. I. 4. ob- servatione, ad quem collineavit in hac revelatione S. Johanni data Spiritus Sanctus, non minus quam in reliquis scriptis ejusdem θεοπνέυστοις: Quo fa- cit, quod in Apocalypsi summum illud caput fidei, cardoque religionis de officio Christi Servatoris vel imprimis illustribus verbis æque ac in Evangelio, & priori epistola proponatur, ut vix alibi. Quid enim splendidius illa tantæ doctrinæ summa, Je- sus Christus dilexit nos, & abluit nos per sangui- nem suum, & fecit nos Sacerdotes & Reges Deo nostro, cap. I. Et illa: Tu es Agnus mactatus, & redemisti nos per sanguinem tuum ex omni tribu, & fecisti nos Sacerdotes, c. V. & de fide vincente pec- catum & mortem cap. II. 10 Esto fidelis, &c. &c. c. XII. 11. vicerunt per sanguinem Agni. De cætero recte Flacius: Non admodum abhorret phrasis a stylo Johannis, si cogitetur, alio genere sermonis vi- siones, alio vero historias describi oportuisse, & Johannem potius ea verba, quæ in visione audivit, consignare voluisse, quam suo sermonis genere conte- xere, quemadmodum & alia scripta θεόπνευςα non amanuensium, sed Spiritus Sancti, a quo dictata sunt verbis exarata sunt, qui prout ipsi visum fuit, modo hoc modo alio sermonis genere usus est. Quid? quod B. Cluverus de stylo judicet p. 4. Stylus contra quem nasutuli quidam sentiunt, reli- quis Johannis Apostoli scriptis & phrasibus tam si- milis est, nihil ut esse similius possit. Dempto enim Prophetico dicendi genere, quod necesse est ab histo- rico discrepare, formulæ loquendi prorsus Johan- neæ sunt.

Quid vero in hoc scripto ad Apostolicam gra- vitatem desiderari possit non video: qui, ut Beza inquit, sane sit brevissimus, si ea demas, quæ ad ver- bum ex Prophetis sunt exscripta. Longe aliter Ba- silius, Gregorius, Cyrillus, Epiphanius, Irenæus, Hip- polytus, ut Aretas testatur, qui hunc librum non modo (ut Dionysius Alexandrinus) putarunt a san- cto viro scriptum esse, sed aperte etiam Johanni Apostolo vendicarunt: nunquam id certe facturi, si nulla gravitatis Apostolicæ vestigia animadvertissent.

Tricantur etiam nonnulli de indicatione no- minis a Johanne hic facta secus atque observetur in Evangelio vel Epistolis. Sed annon etiam Evangelista certitudinem Evangelii sui a singulari sui ipsius descriptione & commendatione adstru- xit cap. XIX. 35. cap. XXI, 24. etsi hoc in loco, more Prophetarum, Danielis, & aliorum nomen suum exprimat, ibi tanquam historiographus periphrasi quadam circumloquatur?

Cæterum in causa illa, quam primo loco addu- xit Grotius, ὕπουλόν τι occultari videtur: Nimirum ut Apocalypsin ad tempora Apostolorum visionibus, quas exhibet, resficere, eorumque statum exhibere contendit: Ita etiam ad Romam gentilem retrahit eandem, ut prædictiones, quæ de Anti-Christo ma- gno in ea occurrunt, obscurentur, & detorquean- tur ad alium quemcunque, puto Barchochebam & similes, ne Anti-Christum Romanum tangere vi- deantur: quo de in annotationum discussione.

Quod ad alteram causam non a Cerintho & Ju- daizantibus tantum Apocalypsis in sensum Judai- cum abrepta, sed ipsi Cerintho autori adscripta a nonnullis (etiam a Cajo teste Eusebio l. III. c. 28.) fuit. Credere enim, referente Dionysio Ale- xandrino Episcopo in libr. de promission. apud Eusebium l. VII. Hist. Eccles. c. 25. eundem, cum magna autoritatis nomen ad faciendam fidem com- mentis suis vellet præfigere, Johannis titulum operi suo indidisse: Quam sententiam ipse quidem loco a Grotio laudato reprobat, non tamen Apocaly- psin Johanni Apostolo vindicat, sed Johannem, in- quit, hunc vocare; & librum a Johanne scriptum es- se, non inficior: Fateor enim sancti cujusdam & divi- no Spiritu afflati viri id opus esse. Sed hunc ipsum esse Apostolum Zebedæi filium, Jacobi fratrem, cujus est Evangelium illud, quod secundum Johannem inscri- bitur, & Epistola Catholica haud facile concesserim. Quæ ex genio & forma loquendi, (de qua jam actum) & ex Apocalypseos ductu, & dispositione præsumpsit Dionysius: De alio etiam Johanne co- gnomento Marci, qui Act. XII. commemoratur, aliquid injiciens, cui tamen etiam hunc librum haud assignat: An hic sit, inquit, qui revelationem scripsit, mihi non liquet. Neq; enim una cum Barna- ba & Paulo in Asiam venit, sed Hierosolymam re- versus est. Alium igitur esse censeo, unum scilicet eo- rum, qui in Asia versati sunt. Duo enim apud E- phesum sepulchra fuisse traduntur, utrumq; Johan- nis nomine insignitum. Id ergo liquido ex Dio- nysio constat, quod ipse minime Johannem Evan- gelistam pro Autore Apocalypseos habuerit, cu- jus vero argumenta minus solida sunt, nec facile ulli, nisi Erasmo, Viro Pyrrhonico, non certe anti- quis Ecclesiæ Doctoribus scrupulum injecere, si forte Eusebium hic fluctuantem exceperis, de quo Beza: Eusebium sane nihil moror, in quo docti omnes judicium in plerisque scriptis requirunt. De ge- mino etiam Johanne Ephesino jam ad episto- las Johanneas, quam incerta sit illa traditio, satis dictum. In Johannem Marci cognomento vo- catum propensior Beza, si ex stylo liceret alium, quam Johannem Evangelistam Autorem conjice- re, quod non in verbis tantum, sed etiam in for- mulis dicendi plerisque similis ac pene idem sit Evangelii Marci & hujus libri character. Sed recte Flacius: Si iis habeatur fides Patribus, qui propius accesserunt ad hoc seculum, uti certe justissi- mum est, quales sunt Justinus, Tertullianus, Irenæus, Apollonius, Theophilus Antiochenus, Eusebius l. IV. c. 24. quorum testimonia suo loco & tempore refer- ri possunt, affirmari poterit, eam ut Johannis Apo- stoli illo primo seculo esse habitam. Cur enim hi tam certo Johannis Apostoli esse confirmarent, si dubias de ea extitisse sententias suorum antecessorum cogno- vissent. Nec etiam Eusebius ipse quenquam insi- gnis autoritatis testem ex Doctoribus hujus aut se- quentis seculi producit, qui eam Johannis Apostoli esse neget: nec quidem ex tertio ab hoc seculo quenquam alium præter Dionysium Alexandrinum citare pot- est. Sed neque testimonium ejus, neque rationes, quas affert, tanti videntur esse menti, ut ex numero pro- batorum Novi Testamenti librorum, hanc Johannis Apocalypsin excludant. Quod vero nec ipse Dio- nysius præsumpsit. Agnovit enim Autorem es- se θεόπνευστον. Eusebius vero etiam Johanni Apostolo diserte Apocalypsin adscripsit, obser- vante itidem Flacio : Imo ipse Eusebius in Chro- nico inquit : XIV. Anno Domitiani , Christi vero XCVII. dum secundus post Neronem Domitianus Christianos persequitur : & sub eo Apostolus Johan- nes in Pathmum insulam relegatus Apocalypsin vidit, quam Irenæus interpretatur.

Nec vero citra rationem veteres Johannem A- postolum pro Autore habuere. Nam circa finem Domitiani, quo tempore Johannes ex Patmo re- versus dicitur, eam prodidisse meminerunt, & te- stes Ecclesias Asianas, quibus dedicata est, habue- runt. Irenæus enim in fine libri numerum illum bestiæ Græce scriptum χις, corrigit autoritate eo- rum, qui Johannem viderunt, indicans esse χξς hoc est 666. Affert & alia interna κριτήρια Flacius, quæ Johannem Autorem referunt, quæ illic le- gantur. Habemus in eo Grotium consentientem, ut pluribus opus jam non sit. Subjicimus tamen testimonia nonnulla de Autore Johanne Apostolo ex antiquitate, ne cui forte scrupulus ex illo Dio- nysii de Johanne Presbytero ab Apostolo diverso, vel etiam e Bezæ de Joh. Marci suspicione hæreat.

E Latinis Tertullianus l. IV. contr. Marc. c. 5. Marcionem e successione Episcoporum convin- cit : Habemus, inquit, & Johannis alumnas Eccle- sias. Nam etsi Apocalypsin ejus Marcion respuit: ordo tamen Episcoporum ad originem recensus in Jo- hannem stabit autorem. Hilarius proleg. in Psal. de Apoc. V. 4. fletum autoris dicit APOSTOLI esse. Autorem quoque agnovit Apostolum Ambrosius l. V. de pœnit. c. 9. Quomodo Johannes diceret non orandum pro peccato, quod est ad mortem, qui in A- pocalypsi scripsit, mandatum est Angelo in Ecclesia Pergamensi : Habes illic tenentes doctrinam Ba- laam, & tenentes doctrinam Nicolaitarum simili- ter age pœnitentiam. Philastrius de hæresibus c. LX. Post hos sunt hæretici, qui Evangelium se- cundum Johannem & Apocalypsin ipsius non acci- piunt, & cum non intelligunt virtutem Scripturæ, nec desiderant discere, in hæresi permanent percurtes, ut etiam Cerinthi illius hæretici esse audeant dicere. Pru- dentius anno 380. hymno 6. ante fin. Evange- lista summus, fidissimus Magistri, signata quæ latebant, oculis videt remotis, ipsum Tonantis A- gnum de cæde purpurantem, qui conscium futuri li- brum resignat unus. Hieronymus in epist. ad Dar- danum T. III. op. p. 68. Nos (Latini) utramque (epistolam ad Ebræos & Apocalypsin S. Johan- nis) suspicimus, nequaquam hujus temporis con- suetudinem, sed veterum scriptorum autoritatem sequentes. Quæ de Johanne Apostolo intelli- genda esse ex libr. Hieronymi de Illustr. Eccl. Do- ctor. constat: Quarto decimo igitur anno, (inquit de Johanne Apostolo,) secundam post Neronem per- secutionem movante Domitiano, in Pathmum insu- lam relegatus scripsit Apocalypsin, quam interpre- tantur Justinus Martyr, & Irenæus. Et l. 1. advers. Jovin. c. 14. Johannes Apostolus vidit in Patmo in- sula, quo fuerat a Domitiano Principe relegatus, Apocalypsin infinita futurorum mysteria continen- tem. Augustinus tract. XXXVI. in Johan. Et apud Ezechielem Prophetam, & in Apocalypsi ipsius Jo- hannis, cujus est hoc Evangelium, commemoratur animal quadrupes, habens quatuor personas homi- nis videlicet, vituli, leonis & aquilæ. Et de sanct. Virgin. c. 27. Severus Sulpitius (An. 440.) l. II. Hist. Domitianus Johannem Evangelistam in Patmum insulam relegavit, ubi ille arcanis sibi mysteriis reve- latis librum S. Apocalypsis (qui quidem a plerisque aut stulte aut impie non recipitur) conscriptum edi- dit. Prosper (Anno 460.) de promiss. part. 1. c. 38. Hoc etiam Apocal. S. Johannis designat dicens: Vidi turbam magnam c. VII. Adde part. II. c. 12. Jornandes (an. 550.) l. I. Domitian. postquam Johannem Aposto- lum & Evangelistam in ferventi oleo missum non po- tuisset extinguere, in Patmos insulam eum relegavit, ubi Apocalypsin vidit. Isidorus Hispal. (an. 620.) l. VI. Etymol. Apocalypsin librum Johannes scripsit eo tempore, quo ob Evangelii prædicationem in insulam Patmos creditur relegatus. Eligius (an. 640.) ho- mil. VIII. Et in Apocalypsi Johannes Apostolus: Qui dilexit nos, inquit, & lavit nos a peccatis nostris in sanguine suo. Aldhelmus (anno 680.) de laudibus virg. c. 3. ob hoc etiam reor, quod facer Dominici pe- ctoris accubitor & quartus paradisi gurges, qui po- tissimum septenas Ecclesias inexhaustis dogmatum intribus irrigavit, & Rabanus Maurus (an. 850.) l. II. de institutione cleric. c. 54. Apocalypsin Johan- nes Evangelista scripsit eodem tempore, quo ob Evan- gelii prædicationem in insulam Patmos traditur re- legatus. Rudolphus Ardens (an. 1020) in comme- morat. defunct. serm. de Apocal. Beati mortui qui in Domino moriuntur: Hoc scribit Johannes Apostolus & Evangel. &c. Petrus Damianus serm. V. de Johan. Evangel. Hinc est quod mentem ejus omnipotens Deus ad tantum puritatis ac mysticæ re- velationis culmen erexit, ut ei non modo statum præ- sentis Ecclesiæ ostenderet, sed etiam quid deinceps fu- turum esset usque in perpetuum, revelaret. Hugo Vi- ctor. (an. 1130.) erudit. Didasc. l. IV. c. 5. de autor. V. T. Apocalypsin scripsit Johannes Apostolus in Pat- mos insulam relegatus: Vid. & Richard. Victor. præ- fat. in lib. Apocal. Nicol. Lyran. præfat. in Apocal. Albert. M. Prol. in Apoc. (an. 1240.) Tota Ecclesia recipit hunc librum, ut Johannis Apostoli, & ideo hoc tenendum est pro constanti. Atque hæc de Lati- nis Patribus.

E Græcis Justinus in dial. cum Tryph. Johannis Apostoli esse Apocalypsin asserit. Unde Eusebius l. IV. Hist. Eccl. c. 24. de Justini Dial. cum Tryph. agens Johannis quoque revelationem, inquit, com- memorat, quam ab Apostolo conscriptam esse diferte dicit, σαφῶς τᾶ Ἀποστόλꙋ ἀυτὴν εἶναι λέγων. Irenæus l. V. adv. hæres. Manifestius adhuc, inquit, etiam de novissimo tempore & de iis, qui sunt in eo, decem Re- gibus, in quos dividetur, quod nunc regnat imperium, significavit Johannes Domini discipulus in Apocal. Orig. homil. VII. in Johannem: Addit nihilo minus adhuc & Johannes tuba canere per epistolas suas & Apocalypsin. S. Athan. in synops. de Apoc. ita ha- bet: Hoc nomine vocatur hic liber propterea, quod hanc revelationem ipse Johan. Evang. & Theologus in Patmo insula dicta vidit, posteaq́; conscripsit. Epi- phan. hær. LVII. Inter quos (Apostolos) etiam S. Jo- han. per Evangelium ac epistolas & Apocalypsin ex eodem Spiritus Sancti dono impertivit. S. Cyril. Alex. l. I. thesaur. c. 5. Et Evangelium: In princi- pio erat Verbum, & Verbum erat apud Deum; & in Apocalypsi IDEM Johannes: Qui est, qui erat, & qui venturus est. Idem affirmat, vete- rum hanc etiam fuisse sententiam l. VI. de ado- rat. in Spir. & verit: Atque Johannes ille sapiens, qui Apocalypsis libellum conscripsit, qui PA- TRUM judicio comprobatus est, sanctorum ani- mas sub Dei altari se conspexisse affirmat. Gre- gorii Nazianzeni sententia habetur ex Aretha Cæsariensi, qui circa ann. 560. floruit, in Apocal. comment. cujus crisis de hoc libro ita habet: Qui- dam veterum librum hunc alienum dicunt a di- ctione & lingua dilecti Johannis, ipsum ad alium referentes: Sed non est ita: Siquidem Gregorius Theologus hunc inter germanos & legitimos libros connumeravit: Sicut me docet (inquit orat. 32.) Johannis Apocalypsis. Refert ipse Eusebius l. IV. Hist. c. 23. & 25. Theophylum Antiochenæ Ecclesiæ Episcopum, qui contra hæresin Hermoge- nis libri hujus testimoniis utatur, & Melitonem Sardensem Episcopum, qui librum scripserit de Apocalypsi Johannis, quemadmodum & Cyprianus de exhort. Martyr. c. III. & seqq. aliique Apo- calypsin ut alias scripturas Divinas agnoscunt. Si- militer Joh. Damascenus circ. ann. 730. l. IV. orth. fid. c. 18. Johannis Evangelistæ Apocalypsin hanc dixit, eamque inter Canonicas scripturas re- censuit Simeon Metaphrastes Ann. 950. in marty- rio S. Antipæ: Tunc & ecclesiæ fideique basis & Christianæ veritatis fundamentum atque æternæ diuturnitatis præco Johannes Apostolus præstantissi- mus in Pathmum insulam relegatus est : ubi dum magnam Christi martyrum cœtum iis, quæ de septem Ecclesiis scripsit, confirmaret Antipas inquit, &c. Suidas anno 976. in Lexico Apocalypsin etiam pro Johannis Evangelistæ scripto habuit; Johannes Apo- stolus & Evangelista composuit centenarius. Jo- hannes Chrysostomus etiam ejus epistolas tres & Apocalypsin admittit. Similiter Michaël Glycas Anno 1100. part. III. annal. Domitianus Johan- nem Theologum cognomento in Pathmum insulam relegavit, ubi & Evangelicam historiam & reve- lationem conscripsit. B. Hoë summatim plerosque Patres S. Johanni ἀποκάλυψιν adferentes ita com- plexus est. Annon, inquit, Meliton Episcopus Sar- densis, annon Theophilus Antiochenus & Justinus Martyr, qui omnes σύγχρονοι fere fuerunt, & ul- tra annum sexagesimum post Johannis Evangeli- stæ obitum vitam non protraxerunt diferte Apo- calypsin a Johanne Apostolo & Evangelista in Pathmo scriptam fatentur ? Idem absque omni hæsitatione afferunt Dionyf. Areopagita c. III. Eccles. Hierarch. Irenæus, Tertullianus, Hippolytus, Athanasius, Cyprianus, Hieronymus, August. Am- bros. Theophilus, Apollonius, Origenes, Primasius Philastrius, Andreas Cæsariensis, Aretas, Marulus, & alii. Quin & Epiphanius adeo defendit hanc sententiam, ut diversum statuentes pro hæreticis habere non vereatur. Et observandum, quod plerique inter nominatos Patres testimonium Ecclesiarum Asiaticarum pro se habere, adeoque haud temere Evangelistam Johannem pro Au- tore libri pronunciare potuerunt. Præter istos laudat Coccius in Thesaur. l. VI. p. 736. E Græcis Prochorum in Histor. Joh. c. 47. (Ann. 120.) Clementem Alexandrinum l. VI. Stromat. (Ann. 200.) Dionysium Alexand. advers. Hæc ergo de Patribus & antiquis Doctoribus Johan. Apostolo diferte Apocalypsin vindicantibus, a quibus non discrepant, qui Autorem forte ex- presse non nominant Apostolum, autoritatem tamen Divinam huic Johanneo scripto assignando, & ut scripturam Divinam adducendo, Johannem illum θεόπνευστον, imo ex numero Apostolorum fuisse agnoscunt, adeoque per consequentiam hoc scriptum ad Apostolum Johannem referunt: Quos recensere supersedemus.

Neque solum Doctores singuli, sed etiam integra concilia tum orientalis, tum occidentalis Ecclesiæ Apocalypsin Johanni Apostolo aut diferte adscripserunt, aut Johanneum hoc scriptum inter Canonicas scripturas referendo κατὰ διά- νοιαν Autorem ejusdem Johannem Apostolum fuisse agnoverunt. Qualia sunt Concilium Carthaginense tertium Anno 395. cap. 47. Concilium Toletanum Quartum Anno 640. cap. 16. Concilium Forojuliense Anno 800. in præfat. Ad aliorum multorum conciliorum autoritatem etiam provocat, quæ Apocalypsin Johannis Evangelistæ, & inter divinos libros recipien- dam esse constituerint. Prædictum Concilium Toletanum Quartum; Synodus Nicena secunda Ann. 790. Act. 1. Benedictus Deus, inquit, qui per sanctum Apostolum (Apoc. 1. & 22.) ego sum A & Ω.

Quæ proinde omnia non solum hæreticis, Cer- doni Apocalypsin quasi falsam rejicienti, teste Tertulliano de præscript. c. 51. Marcioni spernen- ti eandem, teste eodem l. 4. contr. Marc. c. 5. Alo- gis & Theodotioni Apocalypsin Johannis non ad- mittentibus, teste Epiphanio hær. 51. & Augusti- no de hæref. c. 39. Johannis Apostoli eam esse in dubium vocarunt, quod in Græcis quibusdam olim observatum, & a Dionysio Alex. factum esse dixi- mus, & ab Erasmo Roterodamo: adde & Zwin- glium: de quo Bullinger. in Apoc. vel etiam di- vinam autoritatem eidem derogaverunt: Quo nomine Pontificii B. Lutherum quoque exagitare solent. Sed quanquam in præfatione prioris edi- tionis professus ipse sit, se nullo modo deprehendere posse, quod a Spiritu sancto confecta sit, in posterio- ri tamen præfatione δεύτεραι φροντίδες σοφώτεραι leguntur, in qua in dubio quidem reliquit, anne Autor Johannes Apostolus sit, neminem tamen pro- hibere ait, si ejusdem esse statuere velit: Neque id mirum, quum etiam alicubi Eusebius ipse cum Dionysio Alex. anne Apocalypsis S. Johannis A- postoli sit, ambiguus sit, concilium etiam Laodi- cenum, ut & Gregorius Nazianz. in catalogo S. Scripturarum eandem præterierint, ac Hierony- mus ad Dardanum testetur, Græcos de Apocalypsi contra communem Latinorum consensum dubitare. In quam classem etiam Cajum referunt nonnulli, qui sub Severo Imperat. floruit: de quo Eusebius l. 3. c. 28. nihil aliud tradidit, quam quod scripserit, Cerinthum per revelationes quasdam a se tanquam a magno Apostolo conscriptas, quæ portenta quasi ab Angelis sibi ostensa commentus sit. De cætero idem Eusebius de Apocalypsi inquit l. 3. c. 21. etiamnum apud multos dispar est opinio, probantibus illam aliis, aliis vero reprobantibus: Et c. 22. Apocalypsin Joh. nonnulli reprobant, alii vero certis & indubita- tis scripturis adjudicant. Junius in quæstionibus c. 4. de Johannis Apocalypsi apud Orientales admo- dum dubitatur. Istos ergo e Patribus accusent & redarguant Papistæ, si dicam Luthero scribere ad- huc velint. Apud æquos & eruditos vero facile excusatus habebitur. Nec est inter nostros, qui Apocalypsin pro scripto divino non suscipiat, ut nonnulli Canonicis secundi ordinis eandem ac- censeant, non ob autoritatem, sed quod de autore dubitatum olim fuerit, de quo alias sententiam nostram diximus.

Ne autem solis testimoniis circa libri hujus Au- torem, & autoritatem videamur inniti, quan- quam ea in hac causa & magnum habeant mo- mentum, & rationibus vallata sint, argumen- ta quædam afferemus, unico tamen solum com- prehensa syllogismo: Ille Johannes hic intelli- gendus est, cui hæc revelatio facta, qui 1. isto tempore, 2. in Patmo vixit, 3. Asiaticis Ecclesiis præfuit, 4. absolute hoc nomine designatus, 5. Theologus peculiariter dictus, 6. quem præ cæ- teris Discipulis Christus singulari amore comple- xus est, 7. cui præ cæteris talis Apocalypsis con- veniebat, 8. qui Θεόπνευσ indubie fuit, 9. Scripturam Canonicam autoritate sua digne ob- signare poterat, 10. cui phrases in Apocalypsi occurrentes familiares fuere, 11. qui maxime oc- cupari debuit in asserenda æterna Jesu Deitate, 12. inque explicandis ejus beneficiis, 13. quem ad sermones suos describendos præ omnibus aliis elegerat Dominus, 14. cui mysteria summa ma- xime concredidit, 15. quem in transfiguratione sua præsto habuit, ut cælesti visione frueretur, & interesset beatorum cælitum colloquiis, 16. qui dignus habitus a Christo ut maneret, donec ipse venerit, 17. utque Danieliticorum oraculorum interpres evaderet, 18. qui de Anti-Christo mo- nuit, 19. de Anti-Christis item præcursoribus, 20. qui denique testatus est de Christo ceu te- stis αὐτόπτης eorum, de quibus testatus. At hic Johannes nullus est alius, quam Johannes Evan- gelista & Apostolus, in quem omnia illa con- veniunt; ideoque nullus Johannes alius, quam Johannes Evangelista & Apostolus hic intelligen- dus est, cui hæc facta sit revelatio.

Nam quod ad 1. de tempore, illi tempori quo con- tigit hæc revelatio, Nicolaitarum & Balaam do- ctrina emersit, & relegatio Johannis in exilium accidit, cui congruere ætatem Johannis Apostoli, certum est. Alium autem Johannis nomine cele- bratum in illustribus & sanctis Ecclesiæ Docto- ribus ista ætate non invenimus. De Johanne Presbytero, quod nonnulli monent, doceri non potest, eum diversum esse a Johanne Apostolo: quo facit illud Irenæi l. 5. c. 25. Si oporteret manife- ste præsenti tempore percontari nomen ejus (Anti- Christi) per ipsum utique editum fuisset, qui & Apocalypsin viderat. Neque enim ante multum temporis visum est, sed pene sub nostro Seculo ad fi- nem Domitiani imperii. Et quod Origenes ob- servat ex Apoc. 2, 14. homil. 20. sup. Numer. Ergo temporibus Johannis Apostoli erant quidam in Ecclesia illa, ad quam scribebat, docentes doctri- nam Balaam. Quanquam vero Joh. Annius, Sal- mero, & Hentenius ante excidium Hieros. Apo- calypsin scriptam velint, dubitandum tamen no- bis non est diu, & 25. minimum annis post il- lud conscriptam esse, tum quia relegatio Johan- nis in Pathmum facta est a Domitiano, tum quia mentio in ea fit Antipæ martyris, Apoc. 2, 13. qui sub eodem Imper. passus est, ut habetur, tum quia plerique Patres annuunt sub ann. Christi 97. qui Imperii Domitiani 14. & ultimus fuit, S. Joh. scripsisse. Vid. Iren. sub fin. Euseb. in Chron. Hieron. Primasius, Andreas Aretas, Alcasar, Ba- ronius, Cornel. a L. & nostri plerique omnes.

2. In Patmo fuisse se in Spiritu propter Verbum Dei & propter testimonium Jesu Christi profitetur S. Joh. Apoc. 1, 19. At de nullo alio quam de Joh. Apostolo id testatur antiquitas Ecclesiastica. Ori- genes circa ann. Domini 230. comment. in Matth. tr. 12. in cap. 20. Secundum hæc videntur & cali- cem bibisse, & baptismo baptizati filii Zebedæi. Quoniam Herodes interfecit quidem Jacobum fra- trem Johannis gladio: Imperator autem Romanorum sicut docet traditio, condemnavit Johannem, dan- tem testimonium Verbo Dei, in Insulam Patmum, sic- ut IPSE de suo Martyrio docet, non dicens, quis eum condemnavit, sed ubi fuit condemnatus. Dicit au- tem in revelatione sua hoc modo: Johannes frater vester & socius in tribulatione. Ex hoc intelligitur, quoniam revelationem hanc in Insula constitutus vi- dit. Vid. & Eusebius Cæsar. in Chron. sub an. Dom. 97. & Athanas. in Synopsi & Primas. in Prol.

3. Asiaticis Ecclesiis Apostolum Johannem non alium præfuisse itidem indubium est. Quan- quam enim pariter ut cæteri Apostoli, universa- lis Ecclesiæ Doctor fuerit, isto tamen tempore, quo mittendæ erant jussu Filii Dei septem epi- stolæ ad septem Ecclesias, curam peculiariter egit Ecclesiarum Asiæ, de quo testatur Epiphanius, quod multos annos in Asia transegerit haec : 21. & Hieronymus in prol. Matth. quod ab Asiae Episcopis solicitatus fuerit de Divinitate Sal- vatoris altius scribere ; quem etiam usque ad Trajanum totius Asiae Ecclesias fundasse, ac re- xisse, ait Hieronymus. Irenaeus l. 2. cap. 3. Ecclesiam Ephesinam a Paulo quidem fundatam, sed Johannem ibi permansisse usque ad Trajani tempus ait. Et fragmentum Polycarpi, quod Feuardentius ad Ire- naei l. 3. cap. 3. producit, ita de eo habet: Jo- hannes ad Ephesum constitutus, qui legem tan- quam ex gentibus ignorabant a causa redemptio- nis nostrae Evangelii sumpsit exordium, &c. Ideo etiam ad Ephesinum Episcopum prima dirigen- da fuit a Johanne epistola. Alium autem Jo- hannem quam S. Apostolum ibi egisse, vel A- siaticas Ecclesias peculiariter ista aetate curasse non constat.

(4.) Solus Apostolus & Evangelista Johannes isto nomine absolute nuncupatus fuit. Marcus, de quo Act. 15, 37. nunquam simpliciter Johannes nominatur, sed vel simpliciter Marcus v. 39. vel hoc cognomento cum Johannis appellatione jun- cto. (5.) Theologi nomen, quod in inscriptio- ne Apocalypseos occurrit, proprium ea aetate fuit S. Johanni Evangelistae. Exemplar Complu- tense hanc inscriptionem habet Ἀποκάλυψις τῦ ἁγίε Ἀποστόλε καὶ Εὐαγγελιστ͂ Ἰωάννε τῦ Θεολόγε. Meruit autem hoc nomen Johannes Apostolus maxime, quod Christi Deitatem pro aliis Evangelistis asseruerit. Nam τὸν χριστὸν θεο- λογεῖν est Christum Deum asserere apud Justinum, Eusebium aliosque Graecos Doctores. Quo no- mine etiam ipsum Ephrem Syrus vocavit de ap- parit. cruc. temp. judic. Theophylactus praefat.

in Evang. vocat eum Θεολογικώτατον. (6.) Ut Danieli Viro desideriorum (cap. 9, 23.) Deus prae aliis Prophetis relevavit arcana futura, etiam no- vissimorum annorum & seculorum, & specia- tim de Anti-Christo utroque cum Orientali tum Occidentali, nec non circumstantias temporum insignes : Ita Johanni discipulorum dilectissimo fata Ecclesiae cum notis annorum & temporum prae aliis Apostolis manifestare dignatus est, qui in sinu Domini recubuit, quem Anshelmus de laudib. virginjt. sacrum Dominici pectoris accu- bitorem, Graeci ἐπιστήθιον dixere, de quo allega- to loco Apocalyptico Radulphus Ardens. Hoc scribit Johannes Apostolus & Evangelista, qui vir- go est electus a Deo, & virgo in aeternum perman- sit, & recubuit in Coena super pectus Domini Jesu, cujus scriptis tanto magis fides adhibenda est, quan- to ipse caelestia secreta de ipsius Dominici pectoris fonte caeteris profundius accepit & scripsit. (7.) Si plures fuissent, omnia ista aetate Johannis no- mine celebres, huic tamen Johanni prae aliis tam insignis revelatio debebatur quam Joachimus Ab- bas omnibus aliis prophetiis praefert, de qua Ri- chardus Victorinus praefat. in h. l. Prophetia B. Johannis, quae in hoc libro continetur, quam ei Mediator Dei & hominum homo Christus Jesus ad illuminandam sanctam Ecclesiam revelavit, tanto gloriosior & lucidior enitescit, quanto luci- diora & sublimiora de Christo & Ecclesia oracula describit. In hoc enim est excellentior prophetiis, quod de Christo & Ecclesia magna ex parte sa- cramenta adimpleta denunciant : Et sicut Evan- gelium legis observantiam, sic ista Prophetia excel- lit veteres a longe respicientes prophetias, quae fere tot habet sacramenta, quot verba. Conf. Petrus Damianus serm. V. de Johanne Evangelista (8.)

: Futura prædicere vel etiam occulta imprimis in animo hominis recondita præfentia, non nisi Deo & hominibus θεοπνεύςοις, vel Angelis ex revela- tione divina convenit. Quum ergo alius Johan- nes θεόπνευςος noh reperiatur quam Apostolus, eidem omnino Apocalypsis vindicanda, ut mirari oporteat Dionys. Alexandr. Θεόπνευςον scriptum agnoscere, idque tamen alii quam Johanni Apo- stolo adscribere malle. Testatur certe Johan. ipse de θεοπνευςίᾳ, quod a Jesu acceperit apocalypsin, quod in Spiritu fuerit, quod divinitus revelata sit ipsi: unde ad verba: Ego Jesus misi Angelum meum testificari vobis Rupertus Tuitiensis, ac si dicatur: Si hujus libri autoritatem quæritis, ego sum Jesus Autor & Dator hujus Apocalypsis. Non est Scriptura hæc a Johanne, non est ab homine, neque enim ab ho- mine accepit illam aut dicit, sed me revelante, qui sum Jesus, & mittente per Angelum meum: ut sicut omnes Scripturæ divinæ autoritatis: ita & hæc scri- pta testificentur & recitentur vobis in Ecclesiis atque in Canonico apice sint.

(9.) Ecquis aliis eo tempore poterat cum autoritate ac prout par erat Scripturam divinam obsignare, quam Johannes Apostolus, senior ille huic fini divinitus ad tantum senium provectus, ut canoni ultimam manum imponeret, & hoc anathemate obsigna- ret eundem cap. 22, 8. Obtestor enim omnem au- dientem verba hæc prophetiæ libri hujus, &c. Unde Rupert. Tuit. ad cap. ult. Apoc. Vt caput sive prin- cipium, ita & finem libri hujus voluit esse galea- tum, quatenus munitum sit totum corpus revelatio- num istarum, ne quis audeat quasi contemptibilem refutare, vel abjicere quippiam eorum, quæ in hoc libro scripta sunt.

(10.) Cujus vero familiares magis fuere phra- ses, quæ in hoc libro reperiuntur, quam S. Jo- hanni Apostolo? Quo de antea jam dictum. Quod de Marci Evangelist. stylo maxime huic Jo- hanneo convenienti monuit Beza vix fidem inve- niet apud alios: Collatio certe cum Johannis A- postoli scriptis aliud eruditissimis Criticis antiquis & recentioribus persuasit.

(11.) Johannes non senior aliquis aut cogno- mento Marcus, sed Evangelista ceu aquila alti- volans maxime occupari debuit in asserenda Di- vinitate Christi, cujus gratia etiam ipse ab Asiæ Episcopis rogatus fuit, utpote cujus tempore Cerinthi & Ebionis hæresis propullulavit, æter- nam Jesu Divinitatem abnegans. Hoc in Apo- calypsi hac cumprimis factum sedulo, ex qua ultra quinquaginta Deitatis Christi documenta possunt produci. Dionysius non Areopagita quidem, ve- tustus tamen Scriptor Ecclesiasticæ historiæ cap. 3. de Apoc. Arcanam illam & mysticam visionem di- lecti discipuli, divinamque Domini Jesu & altissimam Theologiam eum exponere ait, nosque per mysteria sacra & divina attollere atque confirmare. Orige- nes l. 1. de Principiis: Ut autem unam & eandem omnipotentiam Patris & Filii esse cognoscas, sicut unus atque idem est cum Patre Deus & Dominus, audi hoc modo Johannem in Apocalypsi dicentem: Hæc dicit Dominus Deus, qui est, & qui erat, & qui venturus est omnipotens.

(12.) Ut in Evangelio & epistolis S. Johannes A- postolus occupatus fuit non tantum in asserenda Jesu æterna Deitate, sed etiam in explicandis summis ejus beneficiis: Ita in Apocalypsi idem fa- ctum observatur eadem perspicuitate, gravitate atque majestate, quod vel ex voto præliminari sta- tim elucescit, nec minus ex hymnis & δοξολογίαις ut & visionibus aliis Salvatoris nostri divinissi- mis. (13) Quemadmodum S. Johannem Apostolum ad describendas conciones suas præ aliis elegerat Dominus, quum cæteri Evangelistæ magis fa- cta quam dicta Christi exponant, S. Johannes vero magis dicta quam facta: ita huic etiam con- veniebat maxime sermones Christi & orationes, quas in statu gloriæ habuit, concredere S. Evan- gelistæ & Apostolo: non alii cuipiam Johanni, sed huic fideli & illuminatissimo amanuensi.

(14) Cuinam Johanni magis summa mysteria pa- tefecit, quam Apostolo, qui præ cæteris Apo- stolis eadem velut e pectore Christi, qui solus Patrem novit, & cui vult ipsum revelare, hausit.

(15) Hunc dignatus est secum assumere in glori- ficatione corporis sui in monte sacro Matth. c. 17. & colloquio cum beatis cœlitibus Mose & Elia percipiendo adhibere, quemadmodum etiam ipsum voluit interesse suo in monte Oli- veti agoni gravissimo, eidemque matrem suam B. Virginem commendavit. Cui ergo potius arcanam hanc ἀποκάλυψιν tradidisset, quem ma- gis ad cœlestes visiones & gloriosæ majestatis suæ intuitum admisisset, quam hunc tantæ digna- tionis & fidei discipulum? (16) Quem præter- ea eo loco habuit Christus, ut, quum Petrus veluti succenseret, aut certe curiositate delin- queret, quod juxta secum Christum sequere- tur, de ipso testatus sit, si eum volo manere, do- nec veniam, quid ad te, Joh. c. 21, 22. quod sane de nullo discipulorum professus est. Nam ea ratione, tametsi hypothetica illa fuerit loquutio, ἐὰν αὐτὸν θέλω μένειν, dignum judicavit Johan- nem, quem conservaret Ecclesiæ, usque ad adventum suum gloriosum; quidni dignum ju- dicasset gloriosis illis apparitionibus, quibus prælusit adventui novissimo & manifestationi gloriosæ in cœlis, ac revelatione status futuri Ecclesiæ, cujus Rector & Episcopus supremus esse poterat usque ad finem mundi, quale ju- dicium nec de aliis Apostolis, nec de Petro ipso uspiam reperitur.

(17) Daniel prædixit va- ticinia sua aliquando luculentius expositum iri, quæ de Anti-Christo acceperat c. XII. 9. Per quem vero potius id expedivisset, quam per Johannem Apostolum ἐγκόλπιον non minus sibi dilectum, quam quondam erat Daniel, quæ de aliis futurorum & occultorum notitiam a Christo petiit, Marc. c. 13. v. 3. Joh. c. 13. v. 23. Unde etiam idem Johannes sine dubio fuit, non alius, qui ideo flevit, quod librum obsigna- tum nemo referare aut inspicere possit Apoc. V. Per hunc itaque exponere dignatus est Danie- lis oracula, quo de Irenæus l. 5. cap. 26. Mani- festius adhuc etiam de novissimo tempore, & de his, quæ sunt in eo decem Regibus, in quos di- videtur, quod nunc regnat imperium, signifi- cavit Johannes Domini discipulus, in Apocaly- psi edifferens, quæ fuerint decem cornua, quæ a Daniele visa sunt, dicens sic dictum sibi esse de- cem cornua quæ vidisti &c. (18.) De Anti-Chri- sto utroque, imprimis de Occidentali vaticinia explicanda reservata Johanni Apostolo fuisse tum e collatione locorum Danielis, tum ex E- pistola Johannea priori cap. II. 18. 22. cap. IV. 3. 2. ep. 7. constat. Qui proinde uti de eodem fu- giendo monuit: ita etiam notis suis eundem apertius, ut fugeretur, describere debuit: Quod in Apocalypsi factum esse negari non potest.

(19.) Quemadmodum in epistola priori non de ma- gno tantum illo Anti-Christo, sed de multis aliis

Pseudo-Prophetis S. Apostolus prædixit; eosque cavendos esse docuit, ceu Anti-Christos, & ma- gni illius Anti-Christi præcursores: ita in Apo- calypsi easdem adhortationes repeti ex epistolis ad Ecclesias Asiaticas universam Ecclesiam re- præsentantes, totaque Apocalypsi passim vide- re est, ut ab eodem Johanne ista profecta esse minime ambigendum sit. (20) Nullus alius Johan- nis nomine clarus testis αὐτόπτης fuit eorum, quæ Christus fecit, quam Evangelista Johannes, ne- que alii Christi discipulo tribuendam esse illam testificationem, Apoc. 1, 2. Et significavit mittens per Angelum suum servo suo Johanni: Qui testi- ficatus est Verbum Dei & testimonium Jesu Christi & quæcunque vidit, collatio docet cum similibus attestationibus, 1. Joh. 1, 1. Quod vidimus, quod & oculis nostris contemplati sumus, quod vidimus & audivimus, annunciamus vobis, Joh. 19, 35. qui vi- dit testimonium ejus perhibuit; & cap. 21, 24. Hic est discipulus ille, qui testimonium perhibet de his, & scripsit hæc & scimus, quia verum est testi- monium ejus. Ne dicam quod nonnulli censeant istis verbis Apoc. 1, 2. Johannem Evangelium a se scriptum indigitare. Id sane certum est, Johannem testificatione Verbi Dei & testimonii Jesu Christi Apostolicam suam functionem de- signare, quemadmodum e v. 9. collatione ap- paret. Conf. & Joh. c. 15, 27. Act. 1, 8. cap. 10, 39. 41. 42. Quæ quum ita se habeant, quis adhuc ambigeret, Johannem Apostolum hujus scripti autorem, illudque Apostolicæ ac prorsus divinæ autoritatis esse? Mirandum valde est, inquit Ansbertus Ambrosius l. X. in c. Apoc. 22. cur apud Orientales (nonnullos) de hoc libro dubite- tur; ac nequaquam plenæ autoritatis putetur, ma- xime cum & fidelis ejusdem historiæ Scriptor Johan- nes retineatur, & locus, in quo visa fuerit, a quo, per quem missa, a quo & per quem revelata, cujusque testimonio sit roborata apertissime declare- tur. Ne enim quisquam de his, quæ in ea nar- rantur, dubitaret, subjicit adhuc idem, quod te- stimonium perhibet eorum, ac cito se venturum, ac tempus prædixit, solitæque confirmationis addit ju- ramentum, & ait Amen, id est vere sive fideliter.

Nec vero ullum e κριτηρίοις librorum divi- norum in hoc scripto desideratur: omnia quæ in scripto Canonico requiri possunt, in ipso affatim in- veniuntur. Harmonia autem non cum Ezeckie- le solum aut Daniele, sed cum tota Scriptura Veteris Testamenti perquam luculenta est. Et quomodo per Apocalypsin, historiæ, prophetiæ, vaticinia, mysteria Veteris Testamenti recte con- sideranda & dextre explicanda, parallelismo sy- noptice exhibito ostensum a B. Cluverio pag. 17. qui hic conferatur.

Quam falso autem a nonnullis Cerintho Apo- calypsis tributa fuerit, ex ipsa Apocalypseos lectio- ne liquet, utpote qua dogma impium Cerinthi de Jesu mero homine (vid. Tertullian. l. de præ- script. cap. 48. Epiphanius hær. LI.) frequentissi- me ac disertissime profligatur. Nec minus etiam refelluntur in Apocalypsi alia Cerinthi dogmata, de quibus Irenæus l. 3. cap. 25. Eusebius l. 3. cap. 18. utpote mundum non a supremo Deo, sed, igno- rante ipso, ab alia quadam separata virtute factum: Regnum Christi terrenum fore, &c.

Addere autem hic juvat Interpretum catalo- gum, qui nihil dubitantes Apocalypsin S. Johannis Apostoli autoris esse, magno numero eandem commentariis illustrarunt. Secundo quidem se- culo Papias & Justinus Martyr, ut & Irenæus, etsi illa interierint. Seculo autem tertio Victo- rinus Pictaviensis Martyr, & Melito Episcopus Sardensis, cujus commentationes pariter inter- cidere, nec non Hippolytus & Methodius, ut & Seculo quarto Gregorius Nazianzenus, a qui- bus se plurima accepisse Andreas & Arethas Cesa- rienses profitentur. Seculo quinto Augustinus vel potius Tychonius, & Primasius nec non Gen- nadius. Seculo sexto occurrit Andreas Cesari- ensis, Aprigius, & Aurelius Cassiodorus, ut & Ambrosiaster. Septimo Arethas Cæsariensis: Octavo Albinus & Beda: Nono Haymo, & Strabus Glossæ ordin. Autor. Undecimo Ans- helmus Cantuariensis, & Anshelmus Laudunen- sis Autor glossæ interlinearis. Duodecimo Ru- pertus Tuitiensis, Richardus de S. Victore, Joachi- mus Abbas: Petrus Comestor, Ganfredus Antissodo- rensis. Decimo tertio Nicolaus de Lyra, Hugo Cardinalis concordantiarum Autor, Augustinus de Ancona, Johannes Valeis, Albertus Magnus, Uber- tinus de Cassalis, Matthias Suecus. Decimo quar- to Petrus Aureolus, Thomas non Angelicus, sed Anglicus, Heinricus Hassius, Johannes Hayton, Jo- hannes Annius, Jordanus Teutonicus, Johannes Purwen, Wiclefi discipulus. Decimo quinto Pau- lus Burgensis, Dionysius a Rykel Carthusianus, A- scensius, Augustinus Romanus, Bernhardinus Se- nensis, Laurentias Valla. Decimo sexto MAR- TINUS LUTHERUS, Erasmus Roterodamus, Cælius Pannonius, Petrus Galatinus, Conradus Pellicanus, Henricus Bullingerus, Martinus Bor- rhaus, Rudolphus Gualtherus, Franciscus Vatablus, Theodorus Bibliander, Tacitus, Nicolaus Zegerus, Jacobus Tralem, Bruno Senensis, Claudius a monte Martyrum, Fridericus Venetus, Helias de Anibaldis, Johannes Gagnejus, Ederus, Johannes Hentenius, Jo- hannes Tacelphalus, Nicolaus de Alsentia, Vitalis Cardinalis, Guilhelmus Alabaster, Seraphinus de Terno, Lizarazus, Johannes Benedictus, Johannes Funccius, Ariasmontanus, Matthias Flacius, Theo- dorus Beza, David Chytreus, Benedictus Aretius, Jacobus Brocardus, Guilhelmus Fulco, Erasmus Sar- cerius, Nicolaus Selneccerus, Victorinus Strigelius, Alphonsus Conradus, Franciscus Junius, Petrus Ar- topæus, Johannes Foxius, Lucas Osiander. Seculo decimo septimo Blasius Viegas, Bened. Pererius, Franc. Ribera, Capofagius, Forerius, Josephus de la Haye, Joh. Mariana, Ludovicus ab Alcafar, Cornelius a Lapide, Jac. Tirinus, Menochius, Joh. Pricæus, Zacharias Muthesius, Raphael E- glinus, Thomas Brigthmannus, Conradus Graferus, Johannes Napeirus, Johannes Piscator, Aretius, Ni- col. Collado, David Pareus, Guilhelmus Perkinfius, Franciscus Lambertus, Georgius Nigrinus, Johan- nes Wolterus, Philippus Nicolai, Joh. Winckelman- nus, Matthias Hoë, Johannes Drusius, Josephus Medus, Paulus Tossanus, Franciscus Gomarus, Joh. Heinricus Alstedius, Petrus Crugosius, Ludovicus de Dieu, Daniel Heinsius, Jacobus Laurentius, Ju- lius a Marenholz, Casparus a Melo, Sebast. Mejer, Balthasar Richter, Jeremias Vietor, Anonymus Francofurt. editus Anno 1618. Anonymus Belga Anno 1622. Johannes Cluverus, Paul. Egardus, Patritius, & Joh. Forbesius, Johannes Gerhardus, Paraphrastæ Vinarienses, Gottlieb Heiland, Ger- hardus Grave, Zacharias Engelhard, Zacha- rias Hogelius, Anonymus Christianopolis Anno 1653. Elias Prætorius, Jacob Böhm, aliique fanatici superioris ac hujus Seculi, Chiliastæ imprimis de- inceps recensendi, Philippus Henricus Friedlieb, qui in omnes libros Biblicos annotat. collegit, quod & a Prücknero, & Raupio factum, Hierony- mus Kromayer, Johannes Heinricus a Diest, Johan. Coccejus, Johannes Christophorus Artopœus, Mat- thæus Hofmannus, Johannes Schindler, Johan. An- dreas Lucius, & quo vix deterior ullus HUGO GROTIUS. Præcipuam autem in tanto Inter- pretum numero laudem præ omnibus aliis facile meretur B. Lutherus superiori, & B. Cluverus hoc nostro seculo cum B. Gerhardo nostro, quem sequuta maxime est Paraphrasis Vinariensis, neque dubitamus B. Cluveri judicio calculum adjicere: Equidem, inquit ille p. 27. inter omnes sane Apo- calypseos commentatores sive orthodoxos sive hetero- doxos neminem invenire potui, qui tam eximie ad scopum collimarit, quam eximium illud Dei organon M. Lutherus beatiss. recordationis Theolog. cui certe si a gravissimis, quibus obrutus fuit, Ecclesiæ negotiis tantum otii suppetiisset, ut quam in præfatione libri hujus Germanica proposuit de vera ejusdem inter- pretatione sententiam, potuisset elaborare & latius diducere, non arbitror postea tantam malorum in- terpretum turbam prodire ausam fuisse. Laudant suum Calviniani Bullingerum, laudant Aretium, laudant, Colladonem, laudant Paræum & alios; E- quidem non dubitabo affirmare, quæ præstantissima habeantur in illorum commentariis, eos fere D. Lu- thero debere, multaque rectius assecuturos fuisse, nisi interdum a via ab ipso demonstrata longius discessissent.

Argumentum libri satis commode exhibet Synopsis Athanasii, e qua id repetere placet: Hanc revelationem, inquit, ipse Johannes Evange- lista & Theologus in Patmo insula dicta Dominico die vidit, jussusque conscripsit, ut ad septem Ecclesias mitteret, videlicet istas, Ephesum, Smyrnam, Perga- mon, Thyatiram, Sardes, Philadelphiam & Lao- diceam. Quæ vero in hac visione vidit, multa sunt atque differentia. Circa finem perditionem etiam An- ti-Christi cum Diabolo vidit. Jubetur autem pri- mum scribere singulis prædictarum Ecclesiarum Angelis, secundum cujusque actiones. Multas itaque admirabiles visiones vidit, utpote septem candelabra aurea & in medio illorum similem Filio hominis, & interpretationem accepit, candelabra illa esse septem Ecclesias & eum, qui in medio erat, esse Dominum. Deinde januam vidit apertam in cælo, & Domi- num in throno sedentem, & viginti quatuor Seniores, sedentes super thronos & adorantes Dominum.
