Ἀπὸ τῶν ὁ ὢν, ὁ ἦν, καὶ ὁ ἐρχόμενος.] Noluit hos articulos & participia declinare, ut eo magis Dei immutabilitatem ostenderet, quomodo Proclus dicit τῷ ἀεὶ ad Timaeum, ut di- ximus ad Marcum 7, 40. quia vero εἰμὶ non habet partici- pium Praeteritum, ideo ad praeteriti significationem coactus fuit uti voce modi Indicativi. Sic & infra cap. 4, 8. c. 11, 17. Ἐρχόμενος autem significat idem quod Latine futurus, ut & infra cap. 4, 9. & Joh. 16, 13. Actor. 18, 21. & alibi. Ebraei sic usurpant הבא. Sic & 1. Thess. 1, 10. ἀπὸ τῆς ὀργῆς ἐρχομέ- νης idem quod ἀπὸ τῆς μελλούσης ὀργῆς, Matth. 3, 7. Luc. 3, 7. vide & Ebr. 10, 37.

Καὶ ἀπὸ τῶν ἑπτὰ Πνευμάτων, ἃ ἐστιν ἐνώπιον τῦ θρόνε αὐτῦ.] In Manuscripto πνευμάτων τῶν ἐνώπιον: Septem Spiritus & hic & infra cap. 5, 6. & cap. 8, 2. esse Angelos multi putarunt, quia receptum est apud Ebraeos, septem esse Angelos maxi- mos, qui Deo adstent, nempe quomodo septem Principes ad- stabant Regi Persarum, quae aula, quia erat magnificentissima, ideo ad ejus formam Dei aulam formant Ebraei. Vide To- biam cap. 12, 15. Matth. 18, 10. & utrobique a nobis dicta. Adde Hermam II, 9. Clementem Strom. VI. Sed recte omnia qui expendet, & conferet locum, qui est infra cap. 5, 6. ubi itidem Spiritus dicuntur oculi DEI, per quos oculos di- ximus in Zacharia cap. 4, 10. significari multiformem DEI providentiam, eo potius feretur, ut hic existimet, denotari septem illa velut membra providentiae Divinae, quae nominan- tur infra cap. 5, 12. & cap. 7, 11. Et sic erit ἓν διὰ δυοῖν. Opta- tur enim pax a DEO & septem Spiritibus, id est, a DEO per septem hos modos operante. Firmat hanc interpretationem quod infra capite 5. distinguuntur Spiritus & Angeli.

Blasius de Viegas in h. l. Pazmann. l. 13. Hodegi c. 4. Cudssemius in desperat.

## 1:5
Vers. 5.

And from Jesus Christ.] Not only from God the Father working through those modes which we have mentioned, but also from Jesus Christ he wishes all prosperous things for the Churches. So also Paul, Romans 1, 7. 1 Cor. 1, 3. and elsewhere.

The faithful witness.] Even here he used the nominatives indeclinably, so that just as he had signified the immutability of GOD, so also he might signify the immutability of Christ in His testimony and kingdom. See Heb. 13, 8. 2 Cor. 1, 10. But Christ is called the faithful witness, because in all things which He has brought to us in the name of God, and of which many things spoken generally by Christ are explained specifically in this book, He is most worthy to be believed. See Isaiah 55, 5. John 3, 11. chapter 8, 38. c. 18, 37. and concerning the word πιστὸς 1 Tim. 1, 15. The same title is attributed to GOD Himself, Ps. 89, 38.

The firstborn from the dead.] That is, who was the first of the dead to be resurrected to immortal life. See 1 Cor. 15, 20. Colossians 1, 18. and what is said there. Resurrection is a certain birth, Matt. 19, 28. Acts 13, 33.

And the ruler of the kings of the earth.] Matt. 28, 18. below chapter 19, 6. He means this: Do not fear the Kings of this world so as to follow less the precepts and example of Christ, for the power of Christ is so great that, where He wills, He is about to destroy them or subject them to Himself. Daniel had given the same title to GOD, chapter 4, 14.

The kings of the earth are understood either mystically, as a little later, or properly concerning earthly Monarch Kings, crowned heads, such as the Apocalypse will relate ten in succession and many more, with whomsoever the Babylonian harlot has committed fornication. Which acceptance is for that reason more approved by us, because here at the beginning St. John teaches that Christ is superior to all of them for the comfort of the faithful, who could easily be terrified by the ten-horned beast, which was to fight with the Lamb, until the King of Kings and Lord of Lords is openly brought into the battle line to overcome them, Apoc. 17 and 19.

To Him who loved us.] A new sense begins and these Datives are connected with that which follows: To Him be the glory. But this title truly befits Christ, as is to be learned in John 13, 34. chapter 15, 9. In the Manuscript τῷ ἀγαπῶντι, so that perpetual love may be indicated.

And to him who freed us from our sins in his blood.] By his own blood, that is, by suffering death, he rendered us certain of the truth of those things which he had taught, which are such that nothing is more suitable for cleansing souls from vices. Compare Isa. 4:4, Eph. 5:26, Rom. 3:25, ch. 5:9, Eph. 1:7, ch. 2:3, Col. 1:14, Heb. 9:14, ch. 10:19, 29. It is the property of a moist nature, under which blood also falls, to wash. This is indeed transferred to the soul through an excellent allegory. Moreover, Christ is said to have washed us with his blood, because he himself both performed all things that were required for that, and it appears that the effect followed in many. In the Manuscript, 'freed us from our sins'. Arethas mentions both readings.

Latin:

Vers. 5.

Καὶ ἀπὸ Ἰησῦ Χριστῦ.] Non a Deo tantum Patre per illos, quos diximus, modos operante, sed & a Jesu Christo optat Ecclesiis prospera omnia. Sic & Paulus Roman. 1, 7. 1. Cor. 1, 3. & alibi.

ὁ μάρτυς ὁ πιστός.] Etiam hic nominativos usurpavit ἀ- κλίτως, ut sicut DEI immutabilitatem significaverat, ita & Christi in testimonio suo & regno immutabilitatem signifi- caret. Vid. Ebr. 13, 8. 2. Cor. 1, 10. Dicitur autem Christus ὁ μάρτυς ὁ πιστός, quia in omnibus, quae Dei nomine ad nos pertulit, & quorum multa a Christo generaliter dicta in hoc libro specialiter explicantur, dignissimus est cui credatur. Vi- de Esaiam 55, 5. Joh. 3, 11. cap. 8, 38. c. 18, 37. & de voce πιστὸς 1. Tim. 1, 15. Idem titulus DEO ipsi tribuitur, Ps. 89, 38.

ὁ πρωτότοκος ἐκ τῶν νεκρῶν.] Id est, qui mortuorum pri- mus ad vitam resuscitatus est immortalem. Vide 1. Cor. 15, 20. Coloss. 1, 18. & ibi dicta. Resurrectio est nativitas quaedam Matth. 19, 28. Act. 13, 33.

Καὶ ὁ ἄρχων τῶν βασιλέων τῆς γῆς.] Matth. 28, 18. infra cap. 19, 6. Hoc vult: Nolite, quo minus Christi praecepta & exemplum sequamini timere mundi hujus Reges, Christi enim tanta est potentia, ut, ubi volet, eos sit destructurus aut sibi subjecturus. Daniel DEO eundem titulum dederat cap. 4, 14.

Reges terrae vel mystice intelliguntur, ut paulo post, vel proprie de Regibus Monarchis terrenis, capitibus coronatis, quales X. deinceps referet Apo- calyps. & longe plures, quibuscunque scortata est meretrix Babylonica. Quae acceptio ideo magis nobis probata, quod hic in principio statim illis o- mnibus Christum superiorem esse in solatium fide- lium doceat S. Johannes, qui facile bestia decacor- ni terreri poterant, pugnatura cum agno, donec in aciem aperte producatur Rex Regum & Dominus Dominantium eosdem superaturus Apoc. 17. & 19.

Τῷ ἀγαπήσαντι ἡμᾶς.] Novus incipit sensus & conne- ctuntur Dativi hi cum eo, quod sequitur: Αὐτῷ ἡ δόξα. Ve- re autem Christo convenit hic titulus, ut discere est Joh. 13, 34. cap. 15, 9. In Manuscripto τῷ ἀγαπῶντι, ut indicetur perpetua dilectio.

Καὶ λύσαντι ἡμᾶς ἀπὸ τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν ἡμῶν ἐν τῷ αἵματι αὑ- τῶ.] Sanguine suo, id est, morte tolerata certos nos reddi- dit veritatis eorum, quæ docuerat, quæ talia sunt, ut nihil sit aptius ad purgandos à vitiis animos. Confer Esa. 4, 4. Eph. 5, 26. Rom. 3, 25. c. 5, 9. Eph. 1, 7. c. 2, 3. Col. 1, 14. Ebr. 9, 14. c. 10, 19. 29. Humidæ naturæ, sub qua est & sanguis, pro- prium est lavare. Id vero per egregiam ἀλληγορίαν ad ani- mum transfertut. Dicitur autem Christus suo sanguine nos lavisse, quia & ipse omnia præstitit, quæ ad id requirebantur, & apparet secutum in plurimis effectum. In Manuscripto λύσαντι ἡμᾶς ἐκ τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν. Meminit utriusque lectionis Arethas.

## 1:6
Ver. 6.

And he made us a kingdom and priests to God and his Father.] Here again is a locution such as that indicated above. For it is a conjunction with a verb in place of a participle. For the correct locution would have been 'having made'. Then 'kingdom' for 'kings', just as 'priesthood' for 'priest', 1 Pet. 2:5, 9. So also below ch. 5:10. The Latin: 'You have made us a kingdom and priests to our God': And that 'and' before 'Father' is explanatory, as 2 Cor. 1:3, ch. 11:30, Eph. 1:2, Col. 1:3, ch. 2:2, ch. 3:17, 1 Thess. 1:3, 2 Thess. 2:16, Jas. 1:37, ch. 3:9. Concerning the thing itself, we have spoken at the cited passage of Peter. Christians are kings because of their victories over the flesh, the world, and the devil: they are priests because they offer to God a pure body, holy prayers, and works of piety and mercy. We shall therefore more correctly use that saying of the Stoics, 'only the wise man is a priest': concerning which he has excellent things, although not pertaining to those approaching perfection. Hierocles on that saying of the golden poem, 'immortally first'. Justin in his dialogue with Trypho: 'Through the name of his Firstborn Son, having stripped off the filthy garments, that is, the sins, and having been inflamed through the word of his calling, we are the true high-priestly race of God, as God himself testifies, saying that in every place among the nations he offers sacrifices to him and brings pure ones.' Marcus Antoninus in book III: 'For such a man, no longer putting off being already among the best, is a certain priest and minister of the gods, etc.' Also the Chaldean Paraphrast calls him a Priest: In the Manuscript here: 'And he made for us a kingdom to God'.

The greeting and the vow, which John wishes for the churches, we have discussed elsewhere: but the Apostle observes the custom of the Apostles: having prayed for grace and peace for them: and he constitutes the Author of grace and peace as 1. God the Father by the words 'who is, who was, and who is to come', his eternal and immutable essence, which eminently embraces all differences of time, which some seek in the tetragrammaton name יהוה, and consider this periphrasis to be used in its place. Cornelius à Lapide considers it a mimesis or imitation of the Hebrew name. Concerning which in Natural and Revealed Theology, and in the Theological System Vol. II. Regarding the construction here, Gomarus holds thus: Erasmus and Gagnejus contend that it is faulty, as if the Greek words 'from him who is' contained a solecism and provided no sense. Others, on the contrary, determine more modestly and skillfully, and that in two ways: For Joachimus Camerarius and others who follow him posit an ellipsis of the word 'being', namely in this way 'from him who is, who is, etc.', that is, from the existing one, who is. Beza, a most famous interpreter, explains it without an ellipsis, so that this description is like the proper name Jehovah, as in Exod. 3, 'I am who I am'. Which, just as it is subtle, so the former is simpler, to which could also be added that the article 'the' is placed for 'that', and the prepositive article is taken for the postpositive, just as the neuter is unusual in good authors of the Greek language, and is found in Scripture.

2. The Holy Spirit, who is understood by the seven Spirits, because the Author of grace and peace cannot be constituted with the Father, designated by that name, other than the Holy Spirit; who is so named metonymically, i.e., not that he himself is manifold, but that his gifts are manifold, which are insinuated by the number seven, and because that is the number of perfection, by which agreement he is celebrated as sevenfold in his office in the ecclesiastical hymn; and because that same Spirit flows into the seven churches, whose mention has been made, granting grace and peace to them, just as also to all other churches. The passage in Apoc. 8:2 concerning the seven Angels is foreign to this, and no less so Apoc. 5:12, ch. 7:12. For we are neither commanded to pray for grace and peace from Angels without idolatry, nor to ask anything from those things which are offered to God in solemn praise to celebrate the Divine name: Those things are offered to God, as if due to him from the Angels and from us, as also to the Lamb slain for us, such as blessing and glory and wisdom (the celebration of divine wisdom) and grace, and honor, and power, and strength (the praise of power and strength) Apoc. 7:12, which things are not invoked by us or the Angels. For who would say that we ought to pray for grace and peace from blessing and thanksgiving? Those things are also attributed to the Lamb, because he is worthy to receive the praise of power and riches (of goodness, I say, or of the riches of grace) and wisdom, and strength, and honor, and glory, and blessing. Who, then, would say that these are invoked by us and by the Angels? And how can those things be called either members of Divine providence, e.g., thanksgiving and blessing, which is done by us, or eyes of God, or the seven Spirits, which are in the sight of the throne of God.

Double is Alcazar's exposition concerning the seven virtues or attributes of Divine providence: wisdom, fortitude, beneficence, justice, patience, threatening, and severity. But to invoke them is foreign to the Scriptures. Akin to the Grotian gloss is the interpretation of Socinus in his epistle, page 483, that the seven Spirits are nothing other than the manifold virtue and power of Christ, with which he has been endowed by God. But Christ is distinguished from the seven Spirits, where indeed Socinus wishes an exposition and a fuller repetition to be held: but since grace and peace are sought equally and distinctly from Jesus Christ, as from the seven Spirits, and as from him who is, who was, and who is to come: and such an ἐξήγησις, that the name of Jesus Christ is an explanation of the name of the seven Spirits, is unusual, and it is little fitting to pray for anything from the multivarious virtue of Christ. To the angels, indeed, the appellation of the seven Spirits would not be incongruous, if it were permitted to pray for grace and peace from them: which the Papists indeed contend—Hugo, Dionysius, Becanus, Vol. V of his Opuscula, book on the invocation of saints, Trithemius in his Dispersed Causes, Calvin, p. 132, Antonius Ferrandus in his Visions, ch. 28, Vasquez, part 1, disp. 180, no. 3, Pererius, Blasius de Viegas, Ribera, Cornelius a Lapide on this passage. But that does not agree with the analogy of faith. Some excellent critic of our School indeed thought so, although he was a stranger to Papal angel-worship, and modestly submitting himself to the judgment of others more skilled in Sacred matters, to such an extent that he would not have them said, nor written, nay, not even thought, if they were judged to be repugnant to the analogy of faith: since they are entirely repugnant to it, they ought to have been expunged by those who published them after the death of the blessed man, even according to the mind and will of the Author, inasmuch as he did not want them written if they were judged as such by those to whom God has granted a deeper knowledge of Divine things. He evidently opined that such is the majesty of the angels that it might be less inconvenient to seek from them peace and grace, albeit of a lower degree than that which is sought from God; whereas, on the contrary, it is certain from the Scriptures that Divine grace and peace are sought by such Apostolic vows, and the Apostle prays for the same grace and peace from the seven Spirits as he does from him who is, who was, and who is to come, nor is anything of another order or degree of grace and peace found in the Scriptures. This had to be noted here, lest anyone either thoughtlessly stumble against the same stone, or smear the stain of heresy upon the blessed Author,

Johannes Alba, a Spanish Carthusian, indeed acknowledged from the Papists themselves in his Century of Animadversions from both Testaments, ch. 99, that this Johannine invocation does not befit the angels, referring it solely to

Christ, so that there is a certain hypallage in this place and there is described 1. the eternity of Christ, 2. majesty and empire 3. mediation, in this way: Grace be to you and peace from him, who is, and who was, and who is to come, that is, from the eternal Son of God, who always is, and who is to come to judgment to judge the living and the dead; AND (exegetically for that is) from the seven Spirits, who are in the sight of his throne, that is, from him, in whose sight of the throne are the seven Spirits, AND, (that is,) from Jesus Christ. But that hypallage is harsher, nor can it be rashly admitted here.

Socinus, in his book of letters, letter III, p. 482, says that it is not certain that those seven Spirits hear our prayers, if indeed they are something different from Christ himself, etc., and from thence it happens that prayer, with respect to Christ, can deservedly be called invocation, but with respect to those seven spirits, not so; but it may only be gathered from thence that those seven Spirits perform something in the grace and peace which is given and to be conferred upon us by God. But since the wish for grace and peace is made for the same reason by the seven Spirits, and by God and by Christ, it ought not to be denied that the invocation of the seven Spirits, or of him who is designated metonymically by the seven Spirits, is taking place. Just as in the preceding words, grace and peace to you from him, who is, etc. and in the following words: And from JESUS Christ he not only expects grace and peace, but with religious devotion of heart he wishes and prays for them from God and Christ; so also in the intermediate words, and from the seven Spirits equally annexed, he not only expects, but with religious supplication of heart he asks for and prays for grace.

And therefore there is no place for the explanation of the Papists, that grace and peace are from GOD effectively and principally, from Christ meritoriously, from the Angels imperatorially and instrumentally: For it is not asked here how gifts proceed from Angels, but whether it is lawful to invoke Angels so that they may bestow spiritual gifts (by whatever reason it may be)? If indeed St. John's wish and prayer is his invocation of him from whom he wishes grace and peace for the Churches: but nowhere in the Scriptures are we commanded to invoke Angels, nor is there any example of that thing: much less are they equally joined with God and Christ, just as here the seven Spirits are equally connected in the wish to him, who is, who was, and who is to come, and to Christ Jesus. Alcazar himself, a Spanish Jesuit, warned in vestig. Apoc. p. 153, that good Theology does not bear that evangelical grace and peace be asked from Angels. Much less, therefore, will it bear that it be asked equally from both Angels and God. Read, if you please, says Antiochus Brondo Sardus, a monk of Cagliari, in Apoc. I, p. 200, all the salutations of the epistles of Paul, etc., and certainly in none of them will you find Angels interposed between God the Father and the Son. Who also warns that in these intermediate words, for the same reason and from the seven Spirits, the discourse must also be (as in the preceding and following) about the true Author of grace, because of that copulative conjunction AND, not about interceding Angels, otherwise the Arch-Prophet would change both the style and the sense of the same in a few words, which cannot be conceded in any way. Whence it is absolutely certain that by the seven Spirits in this place one must necessarily understand the Holy Spirit, who is joined equally with God the Father and Jesus Christ, as in baptism Matt. 28:19, in the testimony 1 John 5:7. So also in the invocation, 2 Cor. 13:13. And he is the Author of evangelical grace and peace equally as the Father and the Son; and he is in the sight of the throne of God the Father, because he is a sharer of the same power and potency, majesty and glory, which is signified by the throne of GOD, just as it is also said concerning the grace and justice and truth of God, Psalm 89: Justice and judgment are the basis of his throne, grace and truth go before thy face: even though the justice, grace, and truth of God do not differ essentially from God, but are contained in the simplicity of the complex of the Divine nature and glory. Therefore, it is not necessarily understood that the seven Spirits, or the Spirit denominated from seven or manifold gifts, are in the sight of the throne, that is, the Majesty and glory of GOD, as regards ministry, since even praise and magnificence themselves are in the sight of God, Psalm 69, verse 6. The Son of God is before the throne of God, Dan. 7:13. Wisdom is with God, Prov. 8:30. But he is said to be in the sight of the throne of God, because he is in the Divine glory, the Spirit, who is from the face of GOD, Isa. 57:16, or by reason of consubstantiality and equality of honor, because he is of the same essence and glory with the Father and the Son, because ἐνώπιον sometimes implies internal communion or conjunction, just as also Psalm 96:5, glory and honor are said to be ἐνώπιον αὐτῶ before God, to be most fitting to God; as also by reason of procession, origin, and derivation from God, because for that reason he is called the river proceeding from the throne of God and CHRIST, Apoc. 22:1, and the Spirit from GOD, τὸ Πνεῦμα τὸ ἐκ τῶ Θεῶ, 1 Cor. 2:12, especially when here respect is had to the effusion of the gifts of the Spirit into the seven Churches and the Holy Spirit is viewed as such; and so also he is described by reason of economy and office: how the Holy Spirit is said to be given and poured out, Acts 5:33, chap. 2:33. Therefore, most interpret the present place concerning the Holy Spirit, the third person of the Divinity: Justin, Victorinus, Primasius, Ambrose, Bede, Haymo, Rupertus, Ansbertus, which opinion Pererius confesses to be almost common, so much so that he himself did not dare to entirely disapprove of it, being approved and handed down by so many and such great men; but Antiochus Brond. l. c. defends it expressly.

3. From Christ Jesus, who is joined to the Father and the Holy Spirit, though in the last place, without prejudice to dignity and order, because, to be sure, more had to be said about him: just as elsewhere order is not always observed, so that the equality of the persons in the Godhead may be the more confirmed. Christ is described by his Prophetic office, that he is ὁ Μάρτυς ὁ πιστὸς, that witness, that faithful one, of whom Isa. 55, 5. Ps. 89, 38. John 5, 37. ch. 17, 17. ch. 18, 37. 1 Tim. 6, 13. who alone is set forth to be heard by all these, and confirmed his own testimony with his own blood: whereas other martyrs sealed with their blood not their own, but Christ's testimony, which they received from Christ and bore witness to concerning Christ; then by his Kingly office, to which two epithets pertain: First, that he is πρωτότοκος τῶν νεκρῶν, the firstborn from the dead, not by reason of order, but of dignity and causality, because he is the cause of our resurrection. B. Glassius explains this name from the blessed Gerhard in Phil. S. Gramm. p. 55. Christ is called πρωτότοκος ἐκ τῶν νεκρῶν, the firstborn from the dead, that is, the most excellent among all who rise from the dead: which explanation is immediately followed by these words: That he himself might be in all things πρωτεύων, holding the primacy and prerogative. Therefore, Christ is the most excellent of those rising again, both essentially by reason of his person, which is God-man, to which excellence no creature can attain, and effectively, because by his merit and power all believers will rise again to eternal life. I will transcribe the words of my venerable teacher D. Gerhard, by which he remarkably illustrates the given explanation, part 3. harm. Evang. cap. 179. p. 1197. He is notably called the firstborn (from the dead), both because he rose again by his own power, and we shall rise again to eternal life by his power and merit, 1 Cor. 15, 14. Heb. 2, 14. Just as the firstborn is called the strength of his Father, Gen. 49, 3. then because to him, having been raised from the dead as our Lord, we are subject, Rom. 14, 10. Just as the firstborn in the O.T. was the prince of his brothers, Gen. 49, 3. 2. Chron. 21, 3. whence it is immediately added in Rev. 1, 5. & Prince of the Kings of the earth: as much because he himself received the nations and the ends of the earth as an inheritance Psalm 2, 8. Heb. 1, 6. just as the firstborn was the heir of his father's goods, from whose hands the rest received a portion of the inheritance: as also because he himself, the first among those resurrected from the dead, did not return to this natural and animal life, but rose again into eternal life, and entered into heavenly glory. Furthermore, that he is the Prince of the Kings of the earth, or of the whole world, King of Kings and Lord of Lords Rev. 17, 14. & ch. 19, 16. then by his Priestly [office], because he loved us, and washed us from our sins with his blood, both by reason of merit and by reason of efficacy: which washing is from sins, which is mere filth, and uncleanness or impurity in the eyes of God; sin is expiated by the blood of Christ, and we are purified from it by his blood, 1 John 1:7. which purification he both acquired for us, by his blood shed for us, and performs in the very act, through that same blood of his applied in the Word and the Sacrament of Baptism for the purification of our sins, Matt. 26, 27. 1 Cor. 6, 11. First his love is commemorated as the fountain of salvation, John 15, 13. 1 John 3, 10. then the washing from sin, done through the blood of Christ, afterwards the acquisition of Royal and Priestly dignity, which likewise was done by his blood and death, and is applied to us when we are regenerated to the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom, 1 Pet. 1, 3. & we are renewed, that we may be a new creature in Christ, and as spiritual Kings we subjugate our enemies, we dominate the world and the Prince of the world, the devil, through faith, nor do we permit sin to have dominion over us, Rom. 6, 14. 1 John 5, 4. therefore he instructs us with both wisdom and strength and power, so that in fighting against such great enemies we may not fail, but stand firm. He renews us, moreover, so that as Priests we may offer spiritual sacrifices to God, accepted in Christ our high Priest, Rev. 8, 4. 1 Pet. 2, 5, 9.

But the Socinian perversion by Grotius of the washing performed by Christ—that is, that by enduring death he rendered us certain of the truth of those things which he had taught, which are such that there is nothing more to cleanse souls from vices—makes Christ a mere Prophet, removes his Priestly office in the expiation of our sins, and constitutes the death of Christ only as a μαρτύριον [testimony], by which the truth of Christ's doctrine is confirmed, and not truly a λύτρον [ransom], by which a solution and satisfaction was provided for our sins: it detracts from the Kingly office of Christ, which he exercises with the scepter of the Word by Divine virtue and efficacy; finally, it makes us ourselves the authors of our own washing from sins, attributing to ourselves the honor proper to Christ; which, as it has been asserted elsewhere against the destructive heresy of the Socinians, may suffice to have indicated here in a few words.

To him be the glory and the power for ever and ever. Amen.] The same words in 1 Pet. 4, 11. But this Amen is both of one affirming and of one approving.

Latin:

Vers. 6.

Καὶ ἐποίησεν ἡμᾶς βασιλειαν καὶ ἱερεῖς τῷ Θεῷ καὶ Πατρὶ αὐτῶ.] Hic iterum locutio, qualis supra ἐσήμανεν. Est enim copula cum verbo loco participii. Recta enim loquutio fue- rat ποιήσαντι. Deinde βασιλείαν pro βασιλεῖς, sicut ἱεράτευ- μα pro ἱερεῦς, 1. Petr. 2, 5. 9. Sic & infra cap. 5, 10. Latinus: Fecisti nos Deo nostro regnum & Sacerdotes: Et illud καὶ ante Πατρὶ est ἐξηγητικὸν, ut 2. Cor. 1, 3. c. 11, 30. Ephes. 1, 2. Coloss. 1, 3. cap. 2, 2. cap. 3, 17. 1. Thessal. 1, 3. 2. Thessal. 2, 16. Jac. 1, 37. cap. 3, 9. De re ipsa diximus ad dictum Petri lo- cum. Reges sunt Christiani ob victorias de carne, mundo, diabolo: Sacerdotes, quia Deo offerunt corpus purum, pre- ces sanctas, opera pietatis & misericordiæ. Rectius igitur usurpabimus nos dictum illud Stoicorum, μόνος ὁ σοφὸς ἱε- ρεύς: de quo habet egregia, quanquam non ad accedentia ad τὸ τέλειον. Hierocles ad illud aurei carminis ἀθανάτως μὲν πρῶτα. Justinus colloquio cum Tryphone: Διὰ τῦ ὀνόματος τῦ Πρωτοτόκε ἀυτῦ Υἱῦ τὰ ῥυπαρὰ ἱμάτια, τετέστι τὰς ἁμαρτίας ἀπαμφιεσμένοι, πυρωθέντες διὰ τῦ λό- γε τῆς κλήσεως αὐτῦ, ἀρχιερατικὸν τὸ ἀληθινὸν γένος ἐσ- μὲν τῦ Θεῦ, ὡς καὶ ἀυτὸς ὁ Θεὸς μαρτυρεῖ, ἐἰπὼν ὅτι ἐν παντὶ τόπῳ ἐν τοῖς ἔθνεσι θυσίας ἐνκρέσεις αυτῷ καὶ καθαρὰς προσφέροντες. Marcus Antoninus libro III. Ὁ γάρ τοι ἀνὴρ ὁ τοιῦτος, ἐκ ἔτι ὑπερτιθέμενος τὸ ὡς ἐν ἀρίστοις ἤδη εἶναι ἱερεύς τις καὶ ὑπεργὸς Θεῶν &c. Etiam Paraphrastes Chaldæ- us Sacerdotem vocat: In Manuscripto hic: Καὶ ἐποίησεν ἡμῖν βασιλείαν τῷ Θεῷ.

Salutationem, & votum, quod ea, quæ Ecclesiis vovet Johannes, alias expendimus: morem autem Apostolorum servat Apostolus: Gratiam & pa- cem ipsis precatus: Autorem vero gratiæ & pacis constituit 1. Deum Patrem vocibus ὁ ὢν, ὁ ἦν καὶ ὁ ἐρχόμενος, æternam & immutabilem ejus essentiam, quæ eminenter omnes temporum differentias complectitur, quas nonnulli in nomine τετρα- γεαμμάτῳ יהוה quærunt, ejusque loco hanc περί- φρασιν adhibitam censent. Cornelius à Lapide mi- mesin seu imitationem nominis Ebræi esse censet. De quo in Theol. Naturali & Revelata, & Systema- te Theologico Tom. II. De constructione hic ita habet Gomarus: Eam vitiosam esse, quasi Græca verba ἀπὸ τῶ ὁ ὢν solœcismum haberent, nullumque sensum præberent, Erasmus & Gagnejus contendunt. Alii contra modestius & peritius statuunt, idque bifa- riam: Nam Joachimus Camerarius & alii, qui eum sequuntur, ellipsin statuunt vocis ὄντος, nempe hac modo ἀπὸ τῶ ὄντος, ὁ ὢν &c. hoc est, ab existente, qui est. Beza clarissimus Interpres sine ellipsi exponit, ut hæc descriptio sit instar nominis proprii Jehovah, ut Exod. 3. sum qui sum. Quod quemadmodum subtile est, ita prius simplicius, cui & illud addi posset, quod articulus τῶ ponatur pro τότε, & ὁ articulus præpo- sitivus pro postpositivo accipiatur, quemadmodum Neutrum bonis linguæ Græcæ autoribus est insolens, & in Scriptura reperitur.

2. Spiritum sanctum, qui per septem Spiritus in- telligitur, quia gratiæ & pacis Autor cum Patre a- lius eo nomine designatus constitui præter Spiri- tum S. non potest; qui Metonymice ita nuncupa- tur, h.e. non quod multiplex ipse sit, sed quod dona ejus multiplicia sint, quæ numero septenario insinu- antur, & quia perfectionis ille numerus est, quo pa- cto septiformis munere in hymno Ecclesiastico ce- lebratur; & quia in septem Ecclesias influit idem il- le Spiritus, quarum mentio facta, gratiam & pacem iis donans, quemadmodum & in cæteras Ecclesias omnes. Locus Apoc. 8, 2. de septem Angelis alienus hic est, nec minus Apoc. 5, 12. C. 7, 12. Nam nec ab Angelis gratiam & pacem precari quisquam ci- tra idololatriam, nec ab illis, quæ Deo deferuntur in solenni εὐλογίᾳ ad celebrandum nomen Di- vinum, petere aliquid jubemur: Deferuntur illa Deo, ceu ipsi ab Angelis & a nobis debita, ut & A- gno pro nobis occiso, utpote benedictio & gloria & sapientia (sapientiæ divinæ celebratio) & gra- tia, & honor, & potentia, & fortitudo (potentiæ & fortitudinis laus) Apoc. 7, 12. quæ vero non invo- cantur a nobis aut Angelis. Ecquis enim diceret nos a benedictione & gratiarum actione gratiam & pacem precari debere? Agno etiam illa tribuuntur, quod dignus sit accipere laudem potentiæ & divitia- rum (bonitatis, inquam, vel gratiæ divitiarum) & sapientiæ, & fortitudinis, & honorem, & gloriam, & benedictionem. Quis a. diceret, hæc invocari a no- bis & ab Angelis? Et quomodo illa vel membra dici possunt Divinæ providentiæ, v. g. gratiarum actio, & benedictio, quæ a nobis fit, vel oculi Dei, vel Spiritus septem, qui sunt in conspectu throni Dei.

Gemina est Alcasaris expositio de septem virtu- tibus sive attributis Divinæ providentiæ, sapientia, fortitudine, beneficentia, justitia, patientia, commina- tione, & severitate. Sed ea invocare alienum est a Scripturis. Affinis est Grotianæ glossæ & Socini in- terpretatio in epist. pag. 483. Septem Spiritus nihil aliud esse, quam multiplicem Christi virtutem ac po- testatem, qua a Deo donatus est. Sed Christus distin- guitur a septem Spiritibus, ubi quidem Socinus vult expositionem & pleniorem repetitionem haberi: Sed quum æque ac distinctim a Jesu Christo, ut a se- ptem Spiritibus, & uti ab eo, qui est, qui erat, & qui venturus est gratia & pax petatur: & ἐξήγησις talis, ut nomen Jesu Christi explicatio sit nominis septem Spirituum, insolens est, parumq; convenit a virtute multivaria Christi aliquid precari. Angelis sane se- ptem Spirituum appellatio non incongrua foret, si gratiam & pacem ab illis precari liceret: quod con- tendunt quidem Pontificii Hugo, Dionysius, Beca- nus T. V. Opusc. l. de invocat. sanct. Trithemius in dispers. caus. Calv. p. 132. Antonius Ferrandus in vi- sion. c. 28. Vasquez p. 1. disp. 180. num. 3. Pererius, Blasius de Viegas, Ribera, Cornelius a Lapide in h. l. Sed id non convenit analogiæ fidei. Putavit quide ita Criticus aliquis eximius nostræ Scholæ, etsi alie- nus ab Angelolatria Papali, ac modeste se submit- tens aliorum peritiorum in Sacris judicio, adeo, ut ea nec dicta, nec scripta, imo nec cogitata velit, si judi- centur analogiæ fidei repugnare: cui quum omnino repugnent, expungi ab illis, qui post obitum τῶ Μα- καρίτη ea divulgarunt, ex Autoris etiam mente ac voluntate debuissent, utpote qui ea scripta noluit, si talia ab iis, quibus penitiorem rerum Divinarum cognitionem Deus largitus est, judicentur. Nimirum opinatus est, eam esse Angelorum Majestatem, ut pa- cem & gratiam inferioris tamen gradus, quam a Deo petatur, ab iis petere minus inconveniens sit; quum contra e Sacris certum sit, gratiam & pacem Divi- nam talibus votis Apostolicis expeti, & eandem gra- tiam & pacem, quam ab eo, qui est, qui erat, & qui venturus est, a septem Spiritibus precetur Apostolus, nec de gratia & pace alius ordinis aut gradus quic- quam in Sacris habeatur. Quod hic monendum erat, ne vel improvide quis in eundem lapidem im- pingat, vel beato Autori hærefeos macula affricet,

Agnovit sane ex ipsis Pontificiis Johannes Al- ba Hispanus Carthusiefis in cent. Animadv. ex u- troque Test. c. 99. Angelis non convenire hanc in- vocationem Johanneam, referens eandem unice ad

Christum, ita ut hypallage quædam hoc loco sit & describatur 1. Christi æternitas, 2. majestas & impe- rium 3. mediatio, hoc modo: Gratia sit vobis & pax ab eo, qui est, & qui erat, & qui venturus est, id est, ab æterno Dei Filio, qui semper est, & qui venturus est ad judicium ad judicandum vivos & mortuos; ET (ἐξηγητικῶς pro id est) à septem Spiritibus, qui sunt in conspectu throni ejus, id est, ab eo, in cujus throni conspectu sunt septem Spiritus, ET, (id est,) à Jesu Christo. Sed hypallage illa durior est, nec temere hic admitti potest.

Socinus libr. epistolar. epist. III. p. 482. ait, non constare septem illos Spiritus preces nostras audire, si modo sint aliquid diversum ab ipso Christo &c. & in- de fieri, ut precatio, Christi respectu invocatio merito dici possit, respectu vero septem illorum spirituum non item; Sed tantummodo liceat inde colligere, septem illos Spiritus in gratia & pace, quæ nobis Divinitus data, conferenda aliquid præstare. Verum quum eadem ratione gratiæ & pacis votum fiat à septem Spiritibus, & à Deo & à Christo, negari non debet invocationem septem Spirituum, vel ejus, qui per septem Spiritus Metonymice designatur, fieri. Sicut in verbis præcedentibus gratia & pax vobis ab eo, qui est &c. & in verbis sequentibus: Et à JESU Christo gratiam & pacem non expectat solum, sed religiosa cordis devotione à Deo & Christo vovet, & precatur; ita & in verbis intermediis, & à septem Spiritibus æqualiter annexis, non expectat solum, sed religiosa cordis supplicatione gratiam postu- lat & precatur.

Ideoque nec Pontificiorum explicationi locus est, gratiam & pacem esse à DEO effective, & princi- paliter, à Christo meritorie, ab Angelis imperatorie & instrumentaliter: Nam non quomodo dona ab Angelis proveniant, sed an Angelos invocare liceat, ut dona spiritualia (quacunq; tandem ratione) lar- giantur, hic quæritur? Siquidem S. Johannis vo- tum & precatio sit ejus invocatio, à quo gratiam & pacem Ecclesiis vovet: nuspiam autem in Sacris jubeamur Angelos invocare, nec ullum ejus rei ex- emplum habeatur: multo minus illi æqualiter con- junguntur cum Deo & Christo, quemadmodum hic septem Spiritus æqualiter in voto connectun- tur ei, qui est, qui erat, & qui venturus est, & Christo Jesu. Bonam Theologiam non ferre, ut gratia & pax Evangelica ab Angelis postuletur, monuit ipse Al- casar, Jesuita Hispanus, vestig. Apoc. p. 153. Multo ergo minus feret, ut æqualiter & ab Angelis & à Deo ea postuletur. Legito, si placet, inquit Antiochus Brondo Sardus, Calaritanus Monachus, in Apoc. I. p. 200. omnes salutationes epistolarum Pauli &c. & certe in nulla earum Angelos interpositos inter Deum Patrem & Filium reperies. Qui etiam monet, in his verbis intermediis in eadem ratione & à septem Spiritibus sermonem etiam esse debere (ut in præ- cedentibus & consequentibus) de vero Autore gra- tiæ, propter conjunctionem illam Copulativam ET non de Intercessoribus Angelis, alioquin paucis verbis & stylum & sensum ejusdem mutaret Archi- Propheta, quod nequeat ullo modo concedi. Unde certum omnino est, per septem Spiritus hoc loco necessario intelligendum esse Spiritum sanctum, qui cum Deo Patre & Jesu Christo ex æquo conjun- gitur, ut in baptismo Matth. 28, 19. in testimonio 1. Johan. 5, 7. Ita & in invocatione, 2. Cor. 13, 13. Et Autor est æque ut Pater, & Filius gratiæ & pa- cis Evangelicæ; ac in conspectu throni Dei Patris est, quia ejusdem potestatis, & potentiæ, Majesta- tis, & gloriæ, quæ per thronum DEI significatur, consors est, quemadmodum etiam de gratia & ju- stitia ac veritate Dei dicitur, Psalm. 89. Justitia & ju- dicium sunt basis throni sui, gratia & veritas ver- santur coram conspectu tuo: etsi justitia, gratia & veritas Dei à Deo essentialiter non differant, sed in simplicitate complexus Divinæ naturæ & glo- riæ contineantur. Non ergo in conspectu throni, hoc est Majestatis & gloriæ DEI septem Spiritus, vel evoluta Metonymia Spiritus à septem vel multi- plicibus donis denominatus, quòad ministerium es- se necessario intelligitur, quum ipsa etiam laus & magnificentia in conspectu Dei sint, Psalm. 69. vers. 6. Filius Dei ante thronum Dei Dan. 7, 13. Sapientia cum Deo sit, Prov. 8, 30. Dicitur autem in con- spectu throni Dei esse, quia in Divina gloria est, Spi- ritus, qui est à facie DEI, Esa. 57, 16. vel ratione ὁμουσίας & ὁμοτιμίας, quod ejusdem sit essentiæ & gloriæ cum Patre & Filio, quia ἐνώπιον quandoque internam communionem aut conjunctionem infert, uti etiam Psal. 96, 5. gloria & decor dicitur ἐνώπιον αὐτῶ coram Deo esse, Deo maxime convenire; ut & ratione ἐκπορεύσεως, originis & processionis à Deo, quia ideo fluvius dicitur procedens à throno Dei & CHRISTI Apoc. 22, 1. & Spiritus ex DEO, τὸ Πνεῦμα τὸ ἐκ τῶ Θεῶ, 1. Corinth. 2, 12. maxime cum hic respectus habeatur ad donorum Spiritus in se- ptem Ecclesias effusionem ac S. S. κατ' ἔξω specte- tur: adeoque etiam ita describitur ratione ὀικονο- μίας & officii: quomodo dari & effundi dicitur Spiritus sanctus, Actor. 5, 33. cap. 2, 33. Proinde de Spiritu sancto tertia persona Divinitatis præsen- tem locum interpretantur plerique Justinus, Victo- rinus, Primasius, Ambrosius, Beda, Haymo, Ruper- tus, Ansbertus, quam sententiam fere communem esse Pererius fatetur, adeo ut ipse eam, à tot & tan- tis viris probatam & traditam non prorsus impro- bare ausus sit; tuetur vero ex professo Antiochus Brond. l. c.

3. A Christo Jesu, qui Patri & Spiritui sancto, sed postremo loco, citra dignitatis, atque ordinis præjudicium jungitur, quia scilicet de eo copiosius dicendum erat: quemadmodum & alias non sem- per ordo observatur, ut eo magis confirmetur personarum in Deitate æqualitas. Describitur autẽ Christus ab officio tum Prophetico, quod sit ὁ Μάρ- τυς ὁ πιστὸς, ille testis, ille fidelis, de quo Esa. 55, 5. Ps. 89, 38. Joh. 5, 37. c. 17, 17. c. 18, 37. 1. Tim. 6, 13. qui solus est istis omnibus audiendus propositus, suumque testimonium sanguine suo confirmavit: alii a. marty- res non suum, sed Christi testimonium obsignarunt sanguine, quod à Christo acceperunt, & de Christo deposuerunt; tum Regio, ad quod duo epitheta per- tinent: Primo quod πρωτότοκος τῶν νεκρῶν primoge- nitus è mortuis sit, non ratione ordinis, sed dignitatis, & causalitatis, quia causa est resuscitationis nostræ. B. Glassius hoc nomen è B. Gerhardo ita explicat in Phil. S. Gramm. p. 55. Christus dicitur πρωτότο- κος ἐκ τῶν νεκρῶν primogenitus ex mortuis, h.e. præ- stantissimus inter omnes, qui resurgunt ex mortuis: quæ explicatio subjicitur statim his verbis: Ut sit ipse in omnibus πρωτεύων, primatum & prærogativam ob- tinens. Præstantissimus igitur resurgentium est Chri- stus tum ὀσιωδῶς ratione personæ, quæ θεάνθρωπος, quam ad ὑπεροχὴν nulla creatura pertingere potest, tum ἐνεργητικῶς, quia merito & virtute ejus omnes credentes, ad vitam æternam resurgent. Adscribam verba Præceptoris venerandi D. Gerhardi, quibus explicationem datam insigniter illustrat part. 3. harm. Evang. cap. 179. p. 1197. Notanter vocatur primogenitus (ex mortuis,) tum quia propria virtu- te resurrexit, & nos ipsius virtute & merito ad vitam æternam resurgemus, 1. Cor. 15, 14. Ebr. 2, 14. Sicut primogenitus dicitur virtus sui Patris, Genes. 49, 3. tum quia ipsi ex mortuis resuscitato ceu Domino no- stro sumus subjecti, Rom. 14, 10. Sicut primogenitus in V. T. erat princeps fratrum suorum, Genes. 49, 3. 2. Paral. 21, 3. unde statim additur Apoc. 1, 5. & Prin- ceps Regum terræ: tam quia ipse in hæreditatem ac- cepit gentes & fines terræ Psalm. II, 8. Ebr. I, 6. sicut primogenitus erat paternorum bonorum hæres, ex cu- jus manibus reliqui partem hæreditatis capiebant:tum quia ipse primus inter resuscitatos ex mortuis non re- diit in hanc naturalem & animalem vitam, sed re- surrexit in æternam vitam, & ingressus est in gloriam cælestem. Deinde quod Princeps sit Regum terræ, vel orbis universi, Rex Regum & Dominus Domi- nantium Apoc. 17, 14. & c. 19, 16. tum Sacerdotali, quod amarit nos, & laverit nos à peccatis nostris san- guine suo cum ratione meriti, tum ratione efficaciæ: quæ lotio est à peccatis, quod mera spurcities est, & immunditia vel impuritas in oculis Dei, reatu, cum sanguine Christi expiatur peccatum, nosque ab eo, sanguine ipsius purificamur, 1. Johan. I. v. 7. quam purificationem & acquisivit nobis, sanguine suo pro nobis profuso, & perficit actu ipso, per eundem sanguinem suum in Verbo & Sacramento Baptismatos, ad purificationem peccatorum nostro- rum, adhibitum, Matth. 26, 27. 1. Cor. 6, 11. Pri- mum dilectio ejus commemoratur ceu fons salutis, Job. 15, 13. 1. Joh. 3, 10. tum lotio à peccato, facta per sanguinem Christi, postea Regalis, & Sacerdotalis dignitatis acquisitio, quæ itidem sanguine, & mor- te ejus facta est, nobisque applicatur, cum regene- ramur ad hæreditatem regni cælestis, 1. Petr. I, 3. & re- novamur, ut simus nova creatura in Christo, & ceu Reges spirituales hostes nostros subjugamus, mun- do, & Principi mundi diabolo dominamur per fi- dem, nec peccato dominium in nos permittimus, Rom. 16, 10. 1. Job, 5, 4. ideo instruit & sapientia, & viribus, ac potentia, ut in pugnando contra tan- tos hostes ne deficiamus, sed consistamus. Reno- vat insuper nos, ut ceu Sacerdotes hostias spirituales Deo offeramus, acceptas in Christo summo nostro Pontifice, Apoc. 8, 4. 1. Petr. 2, 5. 9.

Sociniana autem Grotii perversio ablutionis à Christo factæ, quod scilicet morte tolerata certos nos reddiderit veritatis eorum, quæ docuerat, quæ ta- lia sunt, ut nihil sit amplius ad purgandos à vitiis animos, Christum merum Prophetam facit, officium ejus Sacerdotale in expiatione peccatorum nostro- rum tollit, & Christi mortem μαρτύριον tantum constituit, quo confirmata veritas doctrinæ Christi non vero λύτρον, quo solutio & satisfactio præstita est, pro peccatis nostris: Regio Christi muneri, quod sceptro Verbi Divina virtute, & efficacia ge- rit, derogat; denique nosmetipsos nostræ ablutio- nis à peccatis autores reddit, honorem Christo pro- prium nobis ipsis attribuens; quæ ut alias contra exitiosam Socinianorum hæresin asserta, hic pau- cis tantum indicasse sufficiat.

Αὐτῷ ἡ δόξα καὶ τὸ κράτος εἰς τὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων Ἀμήν.] Eadem verba 1. Petr. 4, 11. Est autem hoc Amen & affirman- tis & approbantis.

## 1:7
Ver. 7.

Behold he comes with the clouds.] He will be present with a great tempest against the unbelieving Jews and Romans. Christ will indeed be present in the clouds in an eminent way and κατὰ κυριολεξίαν [literally] at his last coming: But every other vengeance which God takes upon his enemies is described figuratively in this way, as in Isaiah 19, 1. Ezek. 1, 4. Psalm 104, 3. Dan. 7, 13. Namely, because from clouds come thunders, lightnings, and hail. And those things which are attributed to God in the Old Testament are accustomed to be attributed to Christ in the New, and in prophecies concerning the new, as in Dan. 7, 13. here below 14, 15.

And every eye shall see him.] From Isa. 40, 5. that is, all shall feel his power. The Hebrews express all senses by the name of vision, as in Exod. 20, 18. Jer. 1, 31. and elsewhere.

And those who pierced him.) Who harassed him and his Church in every way. See Acts 9, 5. The words are taken from Zech. 12, 10. See what we said there. Such sayings are used in various ways: because they were either proverbial before the Prophets used them, or they became proverbial from the writings of the Prophets.

And all the tribes of the earth shall wail because of him.] ἐπ' αὐτὸν that is, because of the evils brought upon him and his Church. ἐπὶ for because of. The Hebrews would say עליו. Thus ἐπὶ τί [why] in Aristophanes, all the tribes of the earth, that is, the Jews at home and abroad: Then also the Roman people and the Roman provinces. And this is taken from the same passage of Zechariah, but with the freedom I mentioned. The word φυλαὶ [tribes] is often used for peoples, as in Gen. 28, 14. Psalm 72, 17. where in the Hebrew it is גוים [nations].

Ναὶ, ἀμήν.] John confirms the future judgments of God. The same is ναὶ & ἀμὴν, just as Ἀββᾶ & πατήρ. But it pleased him to use both languages, because these touch both the Jews and the Gentiles. See 2 Cor. 1:20 and below ch. 22:20.

The pronoun in this doxology refers to Christ, inasmuch as it corresponds in case to τῷ ἀγαπήσαντι and τῷ λούσαντι, just as the discourse is continued concerning him. For it follows: Behold he comes with the clouds, which advent is that of Christ the Judge. Since, therefore, he is celebrated, and glory and strength are attributed to him by this Eucharist, who is to come in the clouds, and whom every eye shall see, there is no doubt that this Eucharist and doxology pertain to Christ. Moreover, Grotius indeed acknowledges that Christ is understood when there is talk of the advent in the clouds for the final judgment: but he seems to understand this advent, which is in the present, not as the final advent, but as the advent to take vengeance against the unbelieving Jews and Romans, which, however, he does not define. This is a remarkable στρεβλότης [distortion]! Which perhaps has not come into the mind of any of the interpreters. For first, as often as Christ is said to be about to come in the clouds in the New Testament, his final advent is understood, Matt. 28:30 [sic], ch. 26:64, Mark 13:26, Luke 21:27. Which is also expressed as with the clouds, Mark 14:26, and sitting upon a cloud, Rev. 14:14, 15, 16. Nor is there talk of any other advent in Dan. 7:13. Then, that advent is understood by which Christ will be visibly seen in a cloud: which will not happen except on the final day. But since Grotius understands the force of this argument, he does not wish to accept it as ocular vision. But one must not depart from the letter without a very grave reason. Concerning the advent of the incarnation, the same is read in some way in Isa. 40:5, that indeed all flesh shall see what the mouth of the Lord has spoken; here, however, mention is made not only of seeing, but also of the eyes, the proper organ of vision: whence proper vision is deservedly understood. Thirdly, there is talk of that advent of the Lord in which the eyes of ALL shall behold the Lord in the clouds: of ALL men, I say: because πᾶς ὀφθαλμὸς ὄψεται αὐτόν [every eye shall see him]. But this will not happen except on the day of universal judgment. It is added: Καὶ οἵτινες, and they who pierced him, that is, EVEN they shall see him. He will be seen not only by the faithful and the pious, but also by the impious. Grotius neglects the particle κ [sic], and understands these things restrictively or determinatively, because he wished to favor his own ψευδερμηνείᾳ [false interpretation], as if only those are said to be about to see the Lord who ἐξεκέντησαν [pierced] him. Which he further determines thus: those who vexed him and his Church in every way: whereas, on the contrary, from Zech. 12:11, if the fulfillment of the prophecy described in John 19:37 is compared, we understand that there is talk of the piercing of Christ, and of those who pierced the Lord on the cross. Which Grotius changes into a merely proverbial expression, for no reason at all. See what has been said there against him. Fourthly, it concerns that advent of the Lord in which all the tribes of the earth shall mourn ἐπ' αὐτὸν [because of him], which is not because of the evils brought upon the Lord and his Church; but because of the Lord himself and the eternal punishments imminent from him, or because of him once neglected or despised through unbelief, inasmuch as he willed to be pierced for our salvation. Concerning all the tribes of the earth, therefore, to whom such mourning is proper, or as regards the unbelievers from all the tribes of the earth, these things are to be understood. Grotius again rashly and ἐξ ἰδίας ἐπιλύσεως [from his own interpretation] takes these things concerning the Jews, at home and abroad, and then concerning the Roman people and the Roman provinces. But the Apostle speaks expressly of ALL the tribes not of certain provinces, but of the EARTH, and understands all, by whom Christ will be seen at his coming with horror, grief, and lamentation. Concerning the place of Zechariah and its comparison with this one of ours, we have already spoken regarding Zechariah. Fifthly, that ναὶ & ἀμὴν [yes and amen] is not only of the approval of the future judgments of God, but also of the desire for the Johannine coming of Christ, just as can be seen from the conclusion of the book, where St. John explains his desire in a similar manner in ch. 22, 20. Moreover, Christ promises his coming both to confirm faith concerning his glory and return for judgment, and to offer consolation to the faithful, to strike terror into the infidels, and to compel them to repentance.

Latin:

Vers. 7.

ἰδὺ ἔρχεται μετὰ τῶν νεφελῶν.] Aderit cum magna tem- pestate adversus incredulos Judæos & Romanos. Eximie quidem & κατὰ κυριολεξίαν in ultimo adventu Christus in nubibus aderit: Sed & omnis alia ultio, quam Deus de ini- micis suis sumit, sic figurate describitur, ut Esaæ 19, 1. Ezech. I, 4. Psalm. 104, 3. Dan. 7, 13. Nempe quia ex nubibus sunt tonitrua, fulmina, grandines. Quæ autem Deo tribuuntur in Vetere Testamento, eadem in Novo, & in vaticiniis de no- vo tribui solent Christo, ut Dan. 7, 13. hic infra 14, 15.

Καὶ ὄψεται αὐτὸν πᾶς ὀφθαλμός.] Ex Esa. 40, 5. id est, sen- tient omnes ejus vim. Ebræi omnes sensus visionis nomine exprimunt, ut Exod. 20, 18. Jer. I, 31. & alibi.

Καὶ οἵτινες ἀυτὸν ἐξεκέντησαν.) Qui ipsum & Ecclesiam ejus omnibus modis vexarunt. Vide Act. 9, 5. Desumpta verba ex Zach. 12, 11. Vide, quæ ibi diximus. Talia dicta varie usurpantur: quia aut erant proverbialia, antequam Prophetæ ponerent, aut ex Prophetarum scriptis facta sunt proverbialia.

Καὶ κόψονται ἐπ' αὐτὸν πᾶσαι αἱ φυλαὶ τῆς γῆς.] Ἐπ' αὐτὸν id est, propter mala ipsi & Ecclesiæ ejus illata. Ἐπὶ pro propter. Ebræi dicerent עליו. Sic ἐπὶ τί quamobrem apud Aristophanem, πᾶσαι αἱ φυλαὶ τῆς γῆς, id est Judæi domi ac foris: Deinde etiam populus Romanus & provinciæ Romanæ. Et hoc ex eodem Zachariæ loco sumptum est, sed ea, quam dixi libertate. Vox φυλαὶ sæpe de populis usurpatur, ut Gen. 28, 14. Psalm. 72, 17. ubi in Ebræo גוים.

Ναὶ, ἀμήν.] Approbat Johannes futura Dei judicia. Idem est ναὶ & ἀμὴν, sicut Ἀββᾶ & πατήρ. Sed placuit uti utroque sermone, quia hæc tangunt & Judæos & gentes. Vide 2. Cor. I, 20. & infra c. 22, 20.

Pronomen in hac δοξολογίᾳ refert Christum, utpote quod casu respondet τῷ ἀγαπήσαντι, & τῷ λούσαντι, sicuti & de ipso continuatur oratio. Sequitur enim: Ecce venit cum nubibus, qui adventus est Christi Judicis. Quum ergo is celebretur, eique gloria & robur tribuatur hac Eucharistia, qui in nubibus venturus est, quemque omnis oculus visurus est, dubium nullum est, Christum hanc Eucharistiam & doxologiam attinere. Cæterum agnoscit quidem Grotius Christum intelligi, cum de adventu in nubibus ad novissimum judicium sermo est: Ast videtur hunc adventum, de quo in præsenti, non de novissimo adventu intelligere, sed de adventu ad ultionem sumendam adversus incredulos Judæos & Romanos, quem tamen non definit. Insignis hæc στρεβλότης! Quæ nulli forte Interpretum in mentem venit. Primo enim quoties Christus in nubibus venturus dicitur in N. Test. adventus ejus novissimus intelligitur, Matth. 28, 30. cap. 26, 64. Marc. 13, 26. Luc. 21, 27. Quod etiam effertur cum nubibus, Marc. 14, 26. & super nube sedens, Apocal. 14, 14. 15. 16. Nec de alio adventu Dan. 7, 13. sermo est. Deinde ille adventus intelligitur, quo visibiliter conspicietur Christus in nube: quod non nisi in novissimo die futurum. Quum autem intelligat Grotius vim argumenti hujus visum non vult accipere de oculari visione. Sed à litera discedendum non est citra gravissimam rationem. De adventu etiam incarnationis idem aliqua ratione Esa. 40, 5. legitur, quod nempe omnis caro visura sit, quod os Domini loquutum sit; hic tamen non visus solum mentio fit, sed etiam oculi organi visionis proprii: unde visio propria intelligitur merito. Tertio de eo adventu sermo est, in quo OMNIUM oculi in nubibus Dominum conspecturi sunt: OMNIUM inquam hominum: quia πᾶς ὀφθαλμὸς ὄψεται αὐτόν. At hoc non futurum, nisi in die παντοκριτικῷ. Additur: Καὶ οἵτινες, & qui ipsum pupugerunt, id est, ETIAM illi videbunt eum. Non solum fidelibus & piis, sed etiam impiis conspicietur. Grotius particulam κ negligit, & restrictive vel determinative hæc intelligit, quia suæ ψευδερμηνείᾳ velificari voluit, quasi illi solu dicantur visuri Dominum, qui ipsum ἐξεκέντησαν. Quod porro ita determinat, qui ipsum & Ecclesiam ejus omnibus modis vexarunt: Quum contra è Zach. 12, 11. intelligamus, si conferatur complementum vaticinii Joh. 19, 37. descriptum, de Christi confixione, & iis, qui confixere Dominum in cruce, sermonem esse. Quod ne quicquam in locutionem mere proverbialem commutat Grotius. Vide quæ illic contra ipsum dicta. Quarto de illo adventu Domini agitur, in quo lugebunt omnes tribus terræ ἐπ' αὐτὸν, quod non est, propter mala Domino & Ecclesiæ ipsius illata; sed propter ipsum Dominum & ab ipso imminentia æterna supplicia, vel propter ipsum quondam neglectum, vel contemptum per incredulitatem, utpote qui configi voluit propter nostram salutem. De- omnibus ergo tribubus terræ, quibus talis luctus proprius est, vel quoad infideles ex omnibus terræ tribubus hæc intelligenda. Grotius iterum temere & ἐξ ἰδίας ἐπιλύσεως de Judæis, domi ac foris, ac de- inde de populo Romano & provinciis Romanis ea ac- cipit. At Apostolus diferte loquitur de OMNIBUS tribubus non certarum provinciarum, sed TER- RÆ, omnesque intelligit, à quibus cum horrore, dolore ac planctu videbitur in adventu suo Chri- stus. De loco Zachariæ ejusque cum hoc nostro comparatione ad Zachariam jam diximus. Quinto illud ναὶ & ἀμὴν non est approbationis tantum judi- ciorum Dei futurorum, sed desiderii etiam adven- tus Christi Johannei, quemadmodum ex conclu- sione libri, ubi desiderium suum simili ratione ex- plicat S. Johannes c. 22, 20. videre est. Adventum autem suum promittit Christus tum ut fidem de gloria, & reditu ad judicium confirmet, tum ut fi- delibus consolationem præbeat, infidelibus terro- rem incutiat, eosque ad pœnitentiam compellat.

## 1:8
Ver. 8.

Ἐγώ εἰμι τὸ Α καὶ τὸ Ω, λέγει ὁ Κύριος ὁ Θεός.) [I am the A and the Ω, says the Lord God.)] In the Manuscript: Ἄλφα καὶ τὸ Ω, not badly. For Ἄλφα was accustomed to be pronounced entirely in that sense. Thus the Alpha of the penultimates in Martial. But Ω was pronounced no otherwise than it was. Ausonius: And the last is ascribed with Argolic marks Ω. For neither was μέγα accustomed to be added, just as neither was μικρὸν to ο, nor ψιλὸν to ε or υ. Moreover, it is a locution taken from the Rabbis, who say מאלף ועד תיו [from aleph to tav], from the beginning to the end, as Jalkuth on 2 Sam., Isaac Benarima on Lev. 26, and contractedly את [et] the beginning and the end in the book Zohar, in the gate of light, in the gates of justice, Bahir, and others. John adapted that locution to the Greek Alphabet, because he himself was writing in Greek. But what he means by this locution will be easily understood from the following: namely, that God is the same and has always been, and therefore his promises are certain: which was formerly signified by יהוה [YHWH] and אשר יהיה [he who will be]. See what was said on Exodus ch. 2, 15 and ch. 6, 5. & add Isa. 41, 4. ch. 44, 6. ch. 48, 12. Plato: God, just as the ancient word says, holding the beginning and the end and the middle of all things that are. ὁ ὢν καὶ ὁ ἧν καὶ ὁ ἐρχόμενος.) [he who is and who was and who is coming.)] above ch. 1, 4. ὁ παντοκράτωρ.) [the Almighty.)] Not without cause is this also added. For it happens to men that they do not fulfill promises either through inconstancy or through impotence: Wherefore both were to be removed from God. Moreover, the Hebrew אלהי צבאות [God of hosts] is accustomed to be translated by παντοκράτωρ.

Nothing solid can be had concerning the origin of the phrase from Rabbinism, since it is not yet established that those writings were prior to the books of the New Testament, and it could have been derived from the received custom of speaking, to which the Holy Spirit accommodated himself. Concerning the names יהוה [YHWH] and אהיה אשר אהיה [I am who I am], it has been spoken expressly in Theol. Natural. & Revelata. Moreover, it should have been added that, for the sake of explanation, it is read thus in most Codices, even if the Latin Vulgate and Montanus do not have the addition in the text, ἀρχὴ ὴ τέλος [the beginning and the end], which implies eternity lacking beginning and end, just as afterwards are joined τὸ Α κὲ τὸ Ω, ὁ πρῶτος κὲ ὁ ἔχατος [the first and the last], by which locution God has been accustomed to describe his eternity, see Isa. 41, 4. ch. 44, 6. ch. 48, 12. which is further designated also by that periphrasis, embracing all circumstances of times, ὁ ὢν, κὲ ὁ ἦν κὲ ὁ ἐρχόμενος [he who is, and who was, and who is coming]. In the word ὁ ἐρχόμενος [he who is coming], that is, ὁ ἐλευσόμενος [he who will come], there is a Hebraism; thus ימים הבאים [the coming days] are the future, and the coming age, i.e., the future in immortal life עולם הבא [the world to come], Glassius Gramm. S. p. 397. Moreover, by so many words the eternal Deity of the Son of God is asserted on account of the heresy of Ebion and Cerinthus, which was taking it away from him with sacrilegious art. At the end also is added the attribute of omnipotence, ὁ παντοκράτωρ [the Almighty]. Grotius thinks that by that word the Lord Zebaoth is expressed, and thus the true God by nature, whose proper appellation that is, is designated: By which, however, at the same time the certainty of those things which are said is established, which the Lord is able to perform by his omnipotence and his infinite virtue; even if they might perhaps seem impossible in our eyes, Zachar. 8, 6. Moreover, that the Son of God himself is speaking these things, a comparison with v. 11. & 17, where he uses the same speech, ἐγώ εἰμι τὸ Α κι τὸ Ω, ὁ πρῶτος κι ὁ ἔσχατος [I am the A and the Ω, the first and the last], clearly teaches: To which may be added, besides the συνέχειαν [continuity] of the text and the name ὁ κύριος [the Lord], designating Christ, the most clear explanation in ch. 22, 13. Concerning which places for demonstrating the eternal Deity of the Son we have treated expressly, having overthrown the contrary exceptions of the Socinians in Apodixi præexsistent l. 2. c. 26, having adduced the consensus of the Ancients: Nazianzen orat. XXXV, Athanasius tract. in Matth. XI, 27, Ambrose book II de fid. c. 3, Rufinus in exposit. symbol., Idacius Clarus l. 3. c. Varim., Phæbadius l. III contr. orthod. Thus, with Pareus saying, whom he had just said would come with the clouds, he now presents him as if ἀπὸ μηχανῆς [from the machine] present for the consolation of the pious and the terror of enemies, as if crying out from heaven: Do you doubt? Behold I am here: I am α & ω the beginning and the end, the almighty &c. Who will intercept or make doubtful my return, who my judgment? Not otherwise than in the Gospel, with the Jews clamoring, he exclaims: I am the light of the world, &c. Furthermore (which is to be noted for the sake of Calvin), presence is not taken away when the coming is promised, because a visible coming is promised: But the presence, by which he is never not present to his own, A & Ω, the Lord Almighty, is invisible, whose ἐπιφάνεια [manifestation] will then take place, when he will show himself in the clouds.

PART III. OF CHAPTER I. Preparation for the visions of John, and the apparition of the Son of man in the first vision.

Latin:

Vers. 8.

Ἐγώ εἰμι τὸ Α καὶ τὸ Ω, λέγει ὁ Κύριος ὁ Θεός.) In Manu- scripto: Ἄλφα καὶ τὸ Ω non male. Nam Ἄλφα eo sensu to- tum pronuntiari solebat. Sic Alpha penulatorum apud Mar- tialem. Ω autem non aliter quam pronuntiabatur. Ausonius: Et suprema notis ascribitur Argolicis Ω. Neque enim addi solebat μέγα, ut nec μικρὸν ad ο, nec ψιλὸν ad ε vel υ. Est autem loquutio à Rabbinis desumpta, qui di- cunt מאלף ועד תיו ab initio ad finem, ut Jalkuth ad 2. Sam. Isaac Benarima ad Lev. 26. & contracte את princi- pium & finis in libro Zohar, in porta lucis, in portis justitiæ, Bahir & alii. Johannes eam locutionem aptavit ad Alphabe- tum Græcum, quia ipse Græce scribebat. Quid autem hac locutione velit, ex sequentibus facile intelligetur: nempe Deum eundem & esse semper & fuisse, ac proinde certa ejus promissa: quod olim significatum per יהוה & אשר יהיה. Vide quæ dicta ad Exodum c. 2, 15. & c. 6, 5. & adde Esa. 41, 4. c. 44, 6. c. 48, 12. Plato: ὁ μὲν δὴ Θεὸς, ὥσπερ καὶ ὁ παλαιὸς λόγος ἀρχήν τε καὶ τελευτὴν, καὶ μέσα τῶν ὄντων ἁπάντων ἔχων. ὁ ὢν καὶ ὁ ἧν καὶ ὁ ἐρχόμενος.) supra c. 1, 4. ὁ παντοκράτωρ.) Non sine causa & hoc additum. Nam hominibus evenit, ut promissa non impleant aut per incon- stantiarn, aut per impotentiam: Quare utrumque à Deo re- movendum fuit. Solet autem per παντοκράτωρ verti Ebræ- um אלהי צבאות.

De origine phraseos è Rabbinismo nihil solidi ha- beri potest, quum illa scripta libris Novi Testa- menti priora fuisse nondum constet, & e loquendi recepta consuetudine derivari potuerit, cui se at- temperavit Spiritus sanctus. De nominibus יהוה & אהיה אשר אהיה ex professo dictum in Theol. Natural. & Revelata. Addi autem debebat, quod ex- plicationis causa, in plerisque Codicibus ita legatur, etsi Vulgata Latina, & Montanus non habeant ad- ditum in textu, ἀρχὴ ὴ τέλος, quod æternitatem principio & fine carentem infert, quemadmodum postea junguntur τὸ Α κὲ τὸ Ω, ὁ πρῶτος κὲ ὁ ἔχα- τος primus & novissimus, qua loquutione æternita- tem suam Deus describere consuevit, vid. Es. 41, 4. c. 44, 6. c. 48, 12. quæ ulterius etiam designata illa periphrasi, omnes temporum circumstantias com- plectente, ὁ ὢν, κὲ ὁ ἦν κὲ ὁ ἐρχόμενος. In voce ὁ ἐρ- χόμενος, id est, ὁ ἐλευσόμενος, Ebraismus est; ita ימים הבאים dies venientes sunt futuri, & sæculum veniens, h.e. futurum in immortali vita עולם הבא Glassius Gramm. S. p. 397. Tot autem verbis Filii Dei æterna Deitas adseritur propter hæresin Ebio- nis & Cerinthi, quæ illam ipsi sacrilega arte detra- hebat. In fine etiam adjungitur omnipotentiæ attri- butum ὁ παντοκράτωρ. Exprimi voce ista Domi- num Zebaoth, adeoque verum natura Deum, cujus illa appellatio propria est, designari existimat Gro- tius: Qua tamen simul eorum, quæ dicuntur certi- tudo stabilitur, quod præstare eavaleat omnipoten- tiæ ti & infinita sua virtute Dominus; etiamsi impossi- bilia videantur forte in oculis nostris, Zachar. 8, 6. Loqui autem hæc ipsummet Filium Dei, collatio cum v. 11. & 17. ubi eadem oratione utitur, ἐγώ εἰμι τὸ Α κι τὸ Ω, ὁ πρῶτος κι ὁ ἔσχατος, luculenter do- cet: Quibus addatur, præter συνέχειαν textus & nomen ὁ κύριος, Christum designans, explicatio luculentissima c. 22, 13. De quibus locis pro demon- stranda æterna Deitate Filii egimus ex professo So- cinianorum profligatis exceptionibus contrariis in Apodixi præexsistent l. 2. c. 26. adducto consensu Veterum Nazianzeni orat. XXXV. Athanasii tract. in Matth. XI, 27. Ambrosii libr. II. de fid. c. 3. Ruf- fini in exposit. symbol. Idacii Clari l. 3. c. Varim. Phæbad. l. III. contr. orthod. Ita, Pareo dicente, quem modo dixerat venturum cum nubibus, jam qua- si ἀπὸ μηχανῆς præsentem sistit in consolationem pio- rum & hostium terrorem, quasi cælitus clamantem: Dubitatis: En adsum: Ego α & ω principium & finis, omnipotens &c. Quis reditum, quis judicium meum intercipiet vel dubium faciet? Non secus atque in Ev- angelio obstrepentibus Judæis exclamat: Ego lux mundi, &c. Cæterum (quod in Calvin. gratiam notandum) præsentia non tollitur, cum adventus promittitur, quia promittitur adventus visibilis: Præsentia autem, qua suis nunquam non adest, Α & Ω, Dominus Omnipotens, est invisibilis, cujus ἐπιφάνεια manifestatio tum fiet, cum in nubibus sese demonstrabit.

PARS III. CAPITIS I. Παρασκευὴ ad visiones Johannis, & apparitio Filii hominis in visione prima.

## 1:9
Ver. 9. Ἐγὼ Ἰωάννης ὁ ἀδελφὸς ὑμῶν.) [I John your brother.)] Of the same faith. I John, namely, that one already designated.

And a companion in the tribulation and kingdom and patience in Christ Jesus.) The Greeks do not seem to have read καὶ ὑπομονῇ. It can, however, be borne, if you interpret βασιλείαν as the right to the kingdom: namely, that John calls himself a participant in adversities, but with the certain hope of a future kingdom, which is the reason why those adversities are endured with a great spirit. Κοινωνὸς is חָבֵר. Ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ is through Christ, Christ giving it.

The account of John describes the person seeing, designates the occasion and place, v. 9, and expresses the manner of the vision, that it was ἐν Πνεύματι, and the day, v. 10, ἐν τῇ κυριακῇ ἡμέρᾳ. Whether this is a preparation for all the visions, or only for the first, is not so clear, nor perhaps does it matter much whether this or that is assumed. John describes himself, however, by regeneration and faith, because he is a brother not by blood but by faith, and by a triple communion with the saints: first in affliction, since he himself was an exile in Patmos; then in the spiritual kingdom, of which Rom. 14, 17, as also in its own time in the heavenly one, Apoc. 22, 5, just as he had said that Christ made us Kings; thirdly in patience, because neither can spiritual Kings be without patience, nor aspire to the heavenly kingdom, 2 Tim. II, 12. Rom. IIX, 16. The determination, ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ, can conveniently be referred to all three, because the affliction of Christians is an affliction in Christ Jesus, which happens and is undertaken for the sake of his name, nor is any other kingdom understood except in Christ Jesus, nor any other tolerance than that which is from the Author himself, and which is sustained for his sake. Some, however, interpret it as the expectation from 2 Thess. III, v. 5, Tit. II, 13. Furthermore, he prefaces very well concerning the fellowship of affliction, patience, and the kingdom, being about to set forth such mysteries in the following prophecy, from which it may be perceived that the universal Church is to be exercised by various afflictions and miseries, which, however, it ought to bravely undergo and overcome by the expectation of the future kingdom, as here the blessed Cluverus.

'I was in the island which is called Patmos for the word of God' &c.] In the manuscript, 'ἐγὼ' is repeated here before 'ἐγενόμην'. Dorotheus, Bishop of Tyre, reports that the Apocalypse was written in Patmos; Eusebius, that it was written in Ephesus. Both are true for distinct parts. The former were seen and written down in Patmos, the latter in Ephesus, as we shall say below. That John was in Patmos by the order of Claudius, and was enlightened there by visions, is reported by Epiphanius in the 'Alogi', without doubt following the ancients. And I think that is true. For others also gather from not-bad arguments that this book began to be written before Jerusalem was destroyed. When the Proconsul of Asia understood that a new sect of Jews had arisen in Ephesus, whose leader was John, and that disturbances were arising from there, such as those which are described in Acts XIX, he wrote about him, as is credible, to Claudius, who was hostile to foreign religions: by whose order John, as if a seditious person, was deported to an island, which was a frequent punishment at that time. L. rei capitalis §. Constat L. Relegati D. de pœnis, especially in the case of sedition L. Capitalium §. solent quidem. D. tit. de pœnis: Paulus, Sententiarum V. tit. XXII. §. 1. Among the seditious, however, were also considered those who stirred up the minds of men with a new superstition L. Si quis aliquid tit. de Pœnis. Islands for this purpose were usually small and nearly deserted, such as Seriphus and Gyaros in Juvenal and Tacitus, Amargus, Cercina, Pandateria. Such also is Patmos in the Aegean. In Tacitus, book XV of the Annals, you have: 'To Cluvidienus Quietus, Julius Agrippa, Blotius Catulinus, Petronius Priscus, Julius Altinus, as if into a file and number, the islands of the Aegean Sea are permitted.' This opinion regarding the deportation of John carried out by Claudius is strengthened by the fact that John begins to count the Roman Emperors from Claudius, just as Ezekiel counts the times from the deportation. What has been handed down by others, that the exile of Patmos was imposed upon John by Domitian, does not stand against these things which we have said. For Vespasian abolished the old edicts against the Christians, as we learn from Tertullian, but Domitian restored them. Therefore, those who had returned home from exile in the time of Vespasian were sent again into the same exile by Domitian. That part of the visions, however, which befell John in the city of Ephesus, pertains to the times of Vespasian, as will also be clear below. John says, however, that he was in Patmos, 'for the word of God and for the testimony of Jesus,' in which parts he had also described the Gospel above, 2. For the Gospel has its precepts with promises: it also has a history of events, which builds authority for the precepts. This doctrine, however, being new, and appearing no less to Pagans than to Jews as a crime of sedition, as we have already said, and as appears in Acts XVII. 6, XXI. 38. But the great consolation of the Christians was in this, that while John was excluded from the lands, heaven was open to him.

The things which Grotius confidently affirms, as is his custom, concerning the different place of writing, are destitute of suitable testimonies. He names Eusebius regarding the Apocalypse written in Ephesus, but he brings forward no passage of his, nor does he teach from where he even has it that the latter parts were written in Ephesus. Nor does it appear from the Apocalypse itself. Epiphanius indeed, in 'Haer. Alog.' LI, almost at the end, says that John prophesied in the times of Claudius Caesar, when he was on the island of Patmos. But more faith should be placed here in Irenaeus, who was not much later than Saint John. He, however, clearly refers the Apocalypse to the times of Domitian. 'His name,' he says, 'would have been published by him who had also seen the Apocalypse, for it was not seen A LONG TIME AGO, but almost in our own age AT THE END OF DOMITIAN'S REIGN.' Which is also confirmed from the Apocalypse itself. For in chapter II, mention is made of Antipas: 'In those days Antipas my faithful witness was killed among you, where Satan's seat is.' Antipas, however, was killed in the time of Domitian, concerning which see Baronius at the year of Christ 39. Jerome certainly assigns the 14th year of Domitian to the writing of the Apocalypse in his book 'De scriptoribus Ecclesiasticis'. Therefore, in the fourteenth year, with Domitian stirring up the second persecution after Nero, he was relegated to the island of Patmos and wrote the Apocalypse. To the times of this Emperor, Eusebius also refers that exile of John in Patmos, in which he saw the Apocalypse, in book III of 'Ecclesiastical History', chapter 33; for he says that John returned from the exile which he had endured on the island after the death of Domitian: which he confirms from Clement of Alexandria in the same place: 'When after the death of the Tyrant John had returned from the island of Patmos to Ephesus, he went also to the neighboring provinces, having been relegated.' Eusebius reports this even more clearly in the same book, chapter 18. In this (Domitian's) persecution, John the Apostle and also Evangelist, who even then survived among the living, is reported to have been relegated to the island of Patmos for the testimony which he bore to the divine Word. Where he appeals to the previously praised testimony of Irenaeus, concerning the Apocalypse seen at the end of the reign of Domitian. Victorinus of Pettau, and also Primasius in his Commentaries on the Apocalypse, report that John was then relegated by Domitian to dig metals. Sulpitius Severus, book II of 'History': 'Domitian, the son of Vespasian, persecuted the Christians, at which time he relegated John the Apostle and Evangelist to the island of Patmos, where he, with secret mysteries revealed to him, wrote and published the book of the holy Apocalypse (which indeed is not received by many, either foolishly or impiously).' Whence Baronius at the year of Christ 92, number 4. He notes the error of Epiphanius, because he refers the exile of John to the time of Claudius, when both Latin and Greek ecclesiastical writers affirm that it happened under Domitian: as does Arethas of Caesarea, who said that the exile of John happened under the reign of Nero, deceived, as he thinks, by the fact that Tertullian in his book 'De praescriptione', chapter 36, recounts the martyrdom of Peter, Paul, and John all together. To say nothing of the fact that Domitian was also called Nero. Therefore, the things which Grotius reports here about this book having begun to be written before Jerusalem was destroyed, and about the Proconsul of Asia who procured this exile under Claudius, are mere inventions. Which he himself devised for the sake of his own very vain gloss concerning the destruction predicted by John. He says that others gather from not-bad arguments that this book of the Apocalypse began to be written before the destruction, but he could neither name them, nor did he produce those not-bad arguments. The argument that the Roman Emperors are to be counted from Claudius, as John begins to count, just as Ezekiel counts times from his deportation, is very slippery and must be considered nothing but bad. For where does John even obscurely hint that his deportation happened under Claudius? Where does he connect the Claudian years with the time of his deportation, so that these can be compared with Ezekiel's computation? Similar is the Grotian fable about a certain part of the visions which occurred to John in the city of Ephesus, not to mention other Grotian inventions occurring here.

St. John says he was on Patmos διὰ τὸν λόγον τῦ Θεῦ, διὰ τὴν μαρτυρίαν Ἰησῦ χρισῦ, which by no means stand as opposites, as if by λόγον τῦ Θεῦ one understands precepts, and by μαρτυρίαν Ἰησῦ promises. For this distribution reeks of Socinian and Arminian vanity: just as the hypothesis that the Evangelical history is added for the sake of reconciling authority to the precept, either solely or chiefly, which most of all exhibits the fulfillment and more abundant declaration or illustration of the divine promises in the Old Testament, and, properly speaking, constitutes their foundation. Therefore, the cause of undergoing exile was the preaching of the divine Word in general. For neither the Jews, addicted to their traditions, nor the pagans, wrapped in gentilism, could endure the sincere proclamation of the Word, much less a public testimony about Christ. But here it is properly a matter of the persecution of the gentiles, which flourished under Domitian, a second Nero (Tertullian calls him in Apolog. cap. 5. a portion of Nero in cruelty)

Latin:

Vers. 9. Ἐγὼ Ἰωάννης ὁ ἀδελφὸς ὑμῶν.) Ejusdem fidei. Ego Johannes nempe ille jam designatus.

Καὶ κοινωνὸς ἐν τῇ θλίψει καὶ βασιλείᾳ καὶ ὑπομονῇ ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ.) Græci non videntur legisse καὶ ὑπομονῇ. Potest tamen id ferri, si βασιλείαν interpreteris jus ad regnum: nempe ut participem se dicat Johannes adversorum, sed cum certa spe regni futuri, quæ causa sit cur illa adversa magno animo perferantur. Κοινωνὸς est חָבֵר. Ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ est per Chri- stum, dante Christo.

Relatio Johannis personam videntem describit, occasionem, & locum designat, v. 9. modumq́; visionis, quod fuerit ἐν Πνεύματι, ac diem exprimit v. 10. ἐν τῇ κυριακῇ ἡμέρᾳ. An vero hæc parasceve sit ad omnes visiones, num ad primam solum, non adeo patet, nec multum fortassis refert, sive hoc, sive il- lud assumatur. Se autem describit Johannes à rege- neratione, ac fide, quod frater non sanguine, sed fide sit, & à communione triplici cum sanctis, primo in afflictione, siquidem ipse in Pathmo exulabat:Dein- de in regno spirituali, de quo Rom. 14, 17. ut & suo tempore in cælesti Apoc. 22, 5. quemadmodum di- xerat Christum nos Reges fecisse: Tertio in pa- tientia, quia nec Reges spirituales sine patentia esse possunt, nec ad regnum cœleste adspirare, 2. Tim. II, 12. Rom. IIX, 16. determinatio, ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ, ad omnia tria commode referri potest, quia affli- ctio Christianorum est afflictio in Christo Jesu, quæ ejus nominis causa contingit, ac suscipitut, nec aliud regnum, nisi in Christo Jesu, nec alia tole- rantia intelligitur, quam quæ ab ipso Autore est, & quæ ipsius causa sustinetur. Nonnulli tamen interpretantur expectationem è 2. Thessal. III. v. 5. Tit. II, 13. Cæterum optime de afflictionis, patientiæ, regnique societate præfatur, sequenti prophetia ta- lia maxime prolaturus mysteria, unde universam Ecclesiam variis afflictionibus & ærumnis exercendam esse perspiciatur, quas tamen futuri regni expecta- tione fortiter subire ac superare debeat, ut hic B. Cluverus.

'Eγενόμην ἐν τῇ νήσῳ τῇ καλευμένῃ Πάτμῳ διὰ τὸν λόγον τῦ Θεῦ &c.] In Manuscripto ἐγὼ hic repetitur ante ἐγενόμην. In Patmo scriptam Apocalypsin tradit Dorotheus Tyri Episcopus: Ephesi scriptam Eusebius. Utrumque verum est distinctis partibus. Priora in Patmo visa & perscripta, posteriora Ephesi, ut infra dicemus.
