Fuisse autem Johannem in Patmo Claudii jussu, & ibi visis illustratum tradidit Epiphanius in Alogis, non dubium quin veteres secutus. Et id verum puto. Nam & alii ante excisa Hierosolyma scribi hunc librum cœpisse argumentis non malis colligunt. Proconsul Asiæ cum intelligeret Ephesi novam exsitere sectam Judæorum, cujus Princeps esset Johannes atque inde turbas oriri, quales illæ, quæ describuntur Act. XIX. scripsit de eo, ut credibile est, ad Claudium peregrinis religionibus inimicum: cujus jussu Johannes, quasi sedifiosus, deportatus est in insulam, quæ frequens pœna eo tempore L. rei capitalis §. Constat L. Relegati D. de pœnis, maxime in causa seditionis L. Capitalium §. solent quidem. D. tit. de pœnis: Paulus sententiarum V. tit. XXII. §. 1. Inter seditionsos autem habiti & illi, qui superstitione nova hominum animos commoverent L. Si quis aliquid tit. de Pœnis. Esetæ autem ad hoc plerumque insulæ exiguæ & prope desertæ, qualis Seriphus & Gyaros apud Juvenalem & Tacitum, Amargus, Cercina, Pandateria. Talis & Patmos in Ægeo. Apud Tacitum XV. annalium habes: Cluvidieno Quieto, Juliæ Agrippæ, Blotio Catulino Petronio Prisco, Julio Altino, velut in agmen & numerum, Ægei maris insulæ permittuntur. Firmat hanc de deportatione Johannis per Claudium facta sententiam, quod Johannes infra Imperatores Romanos à Claudio numerare incipit, sicut tempora Ezechiel à deportatione numerat. Non obstat his quæ diximus id quod ab aliis traditum est à Domitiano Johanni irrogatum Patmi exsilium. Nam vetera contraChristianos edicta sustulit Vespasianus, ut ex Tertulliano discimus, restituit autem Domitianus. Quare qui Vespasiani tempore domum ab exilio redierant, ii iterum in idem exilium missi sunt à Domitiano. Ea autem visorum pars, quæ Johanni in urbe Ephesi obtigit, pertinet ad Vespasiani tempora, ut & infra patescet. Dicit autem Johannes se in Patmo fuisse, διὰ τὸν λόγον τῦ Θεῦ κὰι διὰ μαρτυρίαν Χρισῦ, quibus partibus etiam supra Evangelium descripserat 2. Habet enim Evangelium sua præcepta cum promissis: habet & historiam rerum, quæ præceptis autoritatem adstruit. Hæc autem doctrina, utpote nova, nec Paganis minus quam Judæis in visa in seditionis crimen rapiebatur, ut jam diximus, & apparet Actor. XVII. 6. XXI 38. Magna autem Christianorum consolatio in hoc erat, quod Johanni terris excluso cœlum patuit.

Quæ de diverso scriptionis loco confidenter, ut solet, Grotius affirmat, idoneis destituuntur testimoniis. Eusebium de Apocalypsi Ephesi scripta nominat, sed locum ejus nullum adducit, unde etiam habeat posteriora Ephesi scripta esse non docet. Nec ex Apocalypsi id constat. Epiphanius quidem hær. Alog. LI. sub finem fere, Johannem vaticinatum dicit in temporibus Claudii Cæsaris, quando in Patmo insula erat. Sed magis hic fides habenda Irenæo, qui non multum posterior Sancto Johanne fuit. Hic autem diferte refert Apocalypsin ad Domitiani tempora. Nomen ejus, inquit, per ipsum utique editum fuisset, qui & Apocalypsin viderat, neque enim ANTE MULTUM TEMPORIS visum est, sed pene sub nostro sœculo AD FINEM DOMITIANI IMPERII. Quod etiam confirmatur ex ipsa Apocalypsi. Nam cap. II. Antipas mentio fit: In diebus illis Antipas testis meus fidelis occisus est apud vos, ubi sedes est Satanæ. Antipas autem occisus est Domitiani tempore, quo de videatur Baronius ad ann. Christ. 39. Hieronymus certe annum 14. Domitiani assignat scriptioni Apocalypseos libr. de scriptor. Ecclesiast. Quarto igitur decimo anno secundam post Neronem persecutionem movente Domitiano in Patmos insulam relegatus scripsit Apocalypsin. Ad cujus Imperatoris tempora etiam exilium illud Johannis in Patmo, in quo Apocalypsin vidit, refert Eusebius libr. III. Histor. Eccles. cap. 33. dicit enim Johannem post Domitiani mortem reversum ab exilio, quod in insula pertulerat: Quod ex Clemente Alexandrino ibidem confirmat: Cum post obitum Tyranni ex insula Patmo Ephesum rediisset Johannes ad finitimas quoque provincias relegatus se contulit. Luculentius adhuc id tradit Eusebius libr. eod. cap. 18. In hac (Domitiani) persecutione Johannes Apostolus idem & Evangelista, qui etiam tum in vivis superavit, ob testimonium, quod divino Verbo perhibebat, in insulam Patmum traditur esse relegatus. Ubi provocat ad Irenæi testimonium antea laudatuin, de Apocalypsi sub exitum imperii Domitiani visa. Victorinus etiam Pictaviensis, nec non Primasius in Commentariis in Apocalypsin tradunt, à Domitiano Johannem tum relegatum fuisse ad effodienda metalla. Sulpitius Severus lib. II. Hist. Domitianus Vespasiani filius persequutus est Christianos, quo tempore Johannem Apostolum atque Evangelistam in Patmum insulam relegavit, ubi ille arcanis sibi mysteriis revelatis librum sacræ Apocalypsis (qui quidem à plerisque aut stulte aut impie non recipitur) conscripsit edidit. Unde Baronius ad ann. Christi 92. num. 4. Epiphanii errorem notat, quod ad Claudii tempus exilium Johannis referat, quum sub Domitiano id contigisse tam Latini quam Græci Ecclesiastici scriptores affirment: ut & Aretæ Cæsariensis, qui Johannis exilium sub Neronis imperio accidisse dixit, ex eo, ut putat, deceptus, quod una simul Tertullianus martyrium Petri, Pauli atque Johannis l. de præscript. cap. 36. recenseat. Ut taceam, quod & Domitianus Nero vocatus sit. Mera ergo commenta sunt, quæ hic refert Grotius de libro hoc scribi cœpto ante excisa Hierosolyma, & de Pro-Consule Asiæ, qui exilium hoc penes Claudium procurarsit. Quæ excogitavit ipse in gratiam glossæ suæ vanissimæ de prædicto à Johanne excidio. Dicit alios argumentis non malis id de libro Apocalypseos ante excidium scribi cœpto colligere, sed nec nominare illos potuit, nec argumenta illa non mala produxit. Argumentum de Imperatoribus Romanis à Claudio numerari à Johanne cœptis, sicut Ezechiel à sua deportatione tempora numerat, valde lubricum, nec nisi malum habendum. Ubi enim suam deportationem sub Claudio factam Johannes vel obscure saltim innuit? ubi annos Claudianos cum suæ deportationis tempore connectit, ut cum Ezechielis computo hæc comparari possint. Similis est fabula Grotiana de parte quadam visorum, quæ Johanni in urbe Ephesi obtigerit, ne alia hic occurrentia Grotiana commenta jam attingam.

In Patmo se fuisse dicit S. Johannes διὰ τὸν λόγον τῦ Θεῦ, διὰ τὴν μαρτυρίαν Ἰησῦ χρισῦ, quæ se minime habent ut opposita, quasi per λόγον τῦ Θεῦ præcepta, per μαρτυρίαν Ἰησῦ promissa intelligantur. Hæc enim distributio Socinianam & Arminianam matæologiam redolet: quemadmodum & hypothesis, quod historia Evangelica, autoritatis præcepto conciliandæ gratia sive unice, sive præcipue addatur, quæ maxime promissorum divinorum in Veteri Testamento complementum, & uberiorem declarationem vel illustrationem exhibet, eorumque fundamentum proprie loquendo sistit. Exilii ergo subeundi causa fuit prædicatio Verbi divini in genere. Nam nec sincerum Verbi præconium Judæi traditionibus suis dediti, nec pagani gentilismo involuti ferebant, nedum testimonium publicum de Christo. Sed hic de persecutione gentilium proprie agitur, quæ sub Domitiano, altero Nerone (Tertullianus vocat eum in Apolog. cap. 5. portionem Neronis de crudelitate) viguit.

## 1:10
v. 10. I was in the Spirit] that is, with the Spirit of GOD. Thus also those who are possessed by demons are said to be in an unclean spirit, Mark 1:23, v. 2. He says the same thing that Ezekiel says in other words, the hand of the LORD was upon me. Therefore, what he is about to narrate, he did not see with the senses of the body, but within his mind, as Peter did in Acts 10:10.

The sense is far different when prophets are said to be in the Spirit than when it is said of those possessed that they are in a spirit. For there, it is not an obsession by a good spirit, but rather an ecstasy or an elevation to some vision brought about by the Holy Spirit that is implied. Which the phrase of Ezekiel also suggests. Gomarus observes that 'in the Spirit' is said either of the infinite Spirit of God, so that it is the same as being seized by the Holy Spirit—which pleases Camerarius and Beza—or of a finite spirit, that is, the soul of man, or to signify the sacred meditation of John and the exercise of the soul in prayers and meditation on the word; or to denote the immediate subject of the received Apocalypse, namely the Spirit and the mind, to show that this revelation was not external to the bodily senses, but internal, and an object of the soul, as also happened to the prophets of the Old Testament. For B. Glassius, 'in the Spirit' here is 'seized by the Spirit,' 2 Cor. 12:2. It denotes, he says, that holy enthusiasm by which the holy men of GOD, being seized, were carried out of this world in soul to the blessed sight of the Most Holy Trinity. Nor are there wanting those who think that the words 'in the Spirit' are opposed to that which is 'in the body,' not that those seeing in the Spirit lay aside the body, but that he was as it were caught up out of the body into the third heaven, and they refer that kind among the extraordinary charisms of the New Testament: which explanation is approved by Rupert, the Blessed Cluver, and others. Cf. Apoc. 4:12. Cocceius, however, takes it from the Spirit of God, and does not deny certain visions to the bodily senses: 'To be in the Spirit,' he says, 'signifies to receive in the mind the addresses and visions of the Holy Spirit and meanwhile to have the senses idle: unless we say that voices and forms were also conveyed to his eyes and ears by the Spirit.' Aretas calls it divine possession.

On the Lord's day] Thus Christians called that day which is called by the Jews the first of the sabbaths, because of the resurrection of the Lord, which had happened on that day. On which day the epistles of Paul also teach us that Christian assemblies were accustomed to be held, as Justin does in his second Apology, where, in the manner of the Greeks, he calls it the day of the Sun. You have the name of the Lord's day in the epistle of Ignatius to the Trallians and to the Magnesians, and in the Constitutions of Clement several times, likewise in the passage of Irenaeus which the writer of the responses to the orthodox has preserved for us. Tertullian on the soul speaks of the solemnities of the Lord's day. Thus of old were the feast days, days to the LORD.

From which appellation of the Lord's day it is not obscurely evident that the day of the Lord's resurrection, which we call the day of the Sun, was sanctified in the time of the Apostles, and indeed by the Apostles themselves, for divine worship in place of the Sabbath. Which, as Christ the Sun of righteousness did by his exit from the sepulcher and rising as it were on the earthly horizon, and by his appearance in the midst of the Apostles, when he himself preached with them and committed the sacred ministry a second time, Luke 24, John 20, so it was consecrated by the Apostolic Church for the preaching of the Gospel and other pious uses, 1 Cor. 16:2, Acts 20:7.

FIRST VISION, Concerning the present state of the Churches in Asia. I. DESCRIPTION OF THE APPEARANCE OF THE SON OF MAN.

And I heard a voice behind me as of a trumpet] That 'behind' looks to the passage in Isaiah 30:21. Things that happen from behind are more unexpected. But that 'as of a trumpet' looks to Psalm 47:5 and Zechariah 9:14. He understands a very sonorous voice. For whatever is sonorous is compared to a trumpet, Isaiah 58:1.

In this appearance, 1. a great voice was heard, by which he was warned to turn himself to behold the vision, and it was signified that the mind ought to be bent toward the contemplation of things that would be in the future many centuries later, which no one could foresee from the front. Ambrose, Thomas Anglicus, and Ribera say that John heard the voice from behind here because he was about to hear things that were unknown to the Church. For what is behind us, because it cannot be seen, is considered unknown. The Gloss and Albert think that by this voice from behind it is signified symbolically that these mysteries, which are revealed to John here, are contained in the Law and the Prophets as if in type and figure. Cornelius says this voice was heard from behind so that it might be signified 1. that this revelation is of the Holy Spirit, because the Holy Spirit is not seen by men, and therefore while he shows himself to them as a teacher and monitor, he seems to cause the ears to hear the words of one warning from behind, as Isaiah says chapter 30, verse 21. 2. that God speaking here to John cannot be clearly seen face to face in this life: whence he said to Moses in Exodus 33, 'You shall see my back parts, but my face you shall not be able to see.' 3. that the persecutions heard and prophesied here by John were about to follow Saint John immediately under Trajan, Hadrian, Antoninus, etc. Cocceius seeks another meaning: 'And he heard a word behind.' Perhaps that signifies that Christ is present with his disciples not only as a Leader, but also as a Teacher, nay as a Father; who follows the boy and observes all his footsteps, Isaiah 30:21. And your ears shall hear a word behind you saying: This is the way, walk in it. As he follows John, so Christ follows the Church, so he follows individual believers, like a shepherd his sheep, and shows them the way, and especially calls them back to himself when they do not know where and by what way they are going. Which we leave in the middle. But Cornelius a Lapide rightly rejects the opinion of Alcazar, that the voice was presented to John from behind so that he might understand that he was being called to consider a war that had already passed, because the Apocalypse is a prophecy of future things, not a history of past things. A great voice is said to have been heard like a trumpet, because John is stirred by the trumpet-blast of the divine voice, just as the Israelites were of old to be stirred and called together, Numbers 10:2, 8, to see, hear, indicate, and trumpet through the churches great things.

Latin:

v. 10. Ἐγενόμην ἐν Πνεύματι] id est cum DEI Spiritu. Sic & qui à Dæmonibus possidentur, dicuntur esse ἐν πνεύματι ἀ- καθάρτῳ Marci I. 23, V. 2. Idem dicit quod Ezechiel verbis aliis תהי עלין יד־יהוה. Non ergo quæ jam narrabit, vidit corporis sensibus, sed intra animum, ut Petrus Act. X. 10.

Longe alius sensus est, cum Prophetæ ἐν Πνεύ- ματι esse dicuntur, quam cum de ἐνεργυμένοις di- citur, quod ἐν Πνεύματι sint. Ibi enim non obsessio à spiritu bono, sed vel ecstasis vel evectio ad aliquã visionem à Spiritu Sancto facta innuitur. Quam etiam phrasis Ezechielis infert. Gomarus obser- vat, in Spiritu dici vel de Spiritu infinito Dei, ut idem sit, quod à Spiritu Sancto correptum esse; quod Camerario & Bezæ placet, vel de Spiritu finito, seu anima hominis, aut ut significet sacram Johan- nis meditationem & exercitium animæ in preci- bus & meditatione verbi; aut ut denotet proximum Apocalypseos receptæ subjectum, nempe Spiritum ac mentem, ut ostendat revelationem hanc non fuisse externam corporeis sensibus, sed internam, atque animæ objectum, ut Prophetis etiam Veteris Testamenti accidit. B. Glassio in Spiritu hic est Spiritu correptus, 2. Cor. XII. vers. 2. Denota- tur, inquit, Sanctus ille ἐνθυσιασμὸς, quo sancti DEI homines correpti extra mundum hunc animâ evehebantur ad beatum Sacrosanctæ Trinitatis adspectum. Neque desunt, qui verba in Spiritu opponi ei quod est esse in cor- pore censeant, non quod in Spiritu videntes deponant corpus; sed quod quasi extra corpus fuerit raptus in tertium cœlum, illudque genus inter charismata Novi Testamenti extraordinaria referant: Quæ explicatio Ruperto, Beat. Clu- vero, aliisque probata. Conf. Apoc. IV. vers. 12. De Spiritu tamen Dei accipit Coccejus, nec ab- nuit visa quædam corporeis sensibus: Esse in Spi- ritu, inquiens, significat animo accipere Spiritus Sancti alloquia & ὀπτασίας atque interim sensus otiosos habere: nisi dicamus etiam oculis & auri- bus ejus voces atque formas a Spiritu fuisse ingestas. Θείαν κατοχὴν nominat Aretas.

Ἐν τῇ Κυριακῇ ἡμέρᾳ] Ita Christiani vocarunt eam diem, quæ Judæis dicitur μία σαββάτων ob resurrectionem Domini, quæ ea die contigerat. Qua die conventus Christianos so- litos fieri & Pauli epistolæ nos docent, ut Justinus Apologe- tico secundo, ubi Græcorum more diem eum Solis nominat. Nomẽ Κυριακῆς ἡμέρας habes in Ignatii epistola ad Trallianos & ad Magnetios, & in Constitutionibus Clementis aliquo- ties, item in Irenæi loco, quem servavit nobis Scriptor re- sponsionum ad orthodoxos. Inter Dominicæ solemnia Ter- tullianus de anima. Sic olim festi dies יומי ליהוה.

Ex qua appellatione diei Dominicæ haud ob- scure patet, diem resurrectionis Dominicæ, quam nos Solis vocamus diem, tempore Apostolorum, adeoque ab ipsismet Apostolis cultui divino in lo- cum sabbati sanctificatum fuisse. Quem ut Chri- stus Sol justitiæ, suo egressu ex sepulchro & ortu veluti in horizonte terreno fecit, suaque appari- tione in medio Apostolorum, cum iis prædicavi ipse, & sacrum ministerium commisit iterata vice honoravit, Luc. XXIV. Joh. XX. ita consecratu præconio Evangelii aliisque piis usibus fuit ab Ecclesia Apostolica, 1. Cor. XVI, 2. Act. XX, 7.

VISIO PRIMA, De præsente Ecclesiarum in Asia statu. I. APPARITIONIS FILII HOMINI DESCRIPTIO.

Καὶ ἤκουσα φωνὴν ὀπίσω με ὡς σάλπιγγος] Illud ὀπίσω respicit locum Es. XXX. 21. Magis improvisa sunt, quæ tergo obveniunt. Illud autem ὡς σάλπιγγος respicit Pf. mum XLVII. 5. & Zach. IX. 14. Intelligit autem voc valde sonoram. Nam quicquid sonorum est, tubæ compara- tur, Es. 58, 1.

In hac apparitione 1. vox magna audita, qua monitus est, ut se verteret ad visionem perspi- ciendam, & significatum, mentem flecti debe- re ad rerum multis retro seculis futurarum con- templationem, quas nemo a fronte prospicere potuerit. Ambrosius, Thomas Anglicus & Ribera Johannem hic a tergo audivisse vocem ajunt, quia auditurus erat ea, quæ ignota erant Ecclesiæ. Quod enim post nos est, quia videri nequit, ignotum censetur. Glossa & Albertus putant, hac voce a tergo significari symbolice, quod hæc mysteria, quæ Johanni hic revelantur, in lege & Prophetis conti- neantur quasi in typo & figura. Cornelius vocem hanc a tergo auditam dicit, ut significaretur 1. re- velationem hanc esse Spiritus Sancti, quia Spiritus Sanctus non videtur ab hominibus, ideoque dum se iis doctorem & monitorem exhibet, videtur fa- cere, ut aures audiant verba post tergum monen- tis, ut ait Esaias cap. XXX. vers. 21. 2. quod Deus hic loquens Johanni clare per faciem in hac vita videri nequit: unde Mosi dixit Exod. XXXIII. Posteriora mea videbis, faciem autem meam videre non poteris. 3. quod persecutiones hic a Johanne auditæ & prophetatæ proxime Sanct. Jo- hannem secuturæ erant sub Trajano, Adriano, Antonino, &c. Aliam significationem Coccejus quærit: Pone autem audivit sermonem. Forta id significat, Christum suis discipulis adesse non tantum ut Ducem, sed etiam ut Pædagogum, i- mo ut Patrem; qui sequitur puerum, & ipsius vestigia omnia observat, Es. XXX. vers. 21. Et audient aures tuæ sermonem pone te dicendo: Hæc est via, ambulate in ea. Ut Johannem, ita Ec- clesiam, ita singulos fideles sequitur Christus, vel- ut pastor oves, & viam illis commonstrat, atque imprimis revocat ad se, quando nesciunt, quo & qua vadant. Quæ in medio relinquimus. Al- casaris autem opinionem, a tergo vocem exhi- bitam esse Johanni, ut intelligeret, se vocari ad bellum, quod jam præterierat considerandum, merito rejicit Cornelius a Lapide, quod Apoca- lypsis prophetia sit futurorum, non historia præ- teritorum. Magna autem dicitur audita vox in- star tubæ, quod Johannes divina vocis tubicinio, ut olim excitandi & convocandi fuere Israëli- tæ, Num. X. vers. 2. 8. excitetur ad res magnas videndas, audiendas, indicandas, & per Ecclesi- as ebuccinandas.

## 1:11
Vers. 11.

Saying, I am the A and the Ω, the first and the last. That the Son of God is designated here is clearer than light: For he is called the same later in verse 13, like unto the Son of man, and having professed of himself again in verse 17, I am the first and the last, he added, and the living one and I became dead, and behold I am living. Most interpreters, except the Socinians, acknowledge that eternity is denoted by this periphrasis. Coccejus, however, loves to be singular: I am A & Ω, that is, the highest and the lowest. I am that one who is indeed a stone of stumbling and rejected by men, but chosen and precious with God, 1 Pet. II. v. 4. the head indeed of the Church, but whose full glory is hidden with God, and who am set for a sign which is spoken against, Luke II. 34. First and last. By my right I am the head, because I am the first: Thus the Baptist, John I. 15. He who comes after me, has preceded me, because he was long before me: Him, who was in the beginning, John I. verse 1. who was before all things, and for whom all things are, Col. I. verse 16. who is not changed, who lives forever,

and is the same as the last, and is conquered by no one, Is. XLI. 4. XLIV. 6. XLVIII. 12. He is worthy of that honor, that he should be the Alpha and the highest. For by that word 'last' are signified these things, as also this, that after that King there is no other King, after that Priest no other Priest, after that Doctor no other Doctor, after Christ himself no other Christ. See also Ps. CX. 4. Thou art a Priest forever. But no one can extract these things from that expression, inasmuch as the Son has it in common with the Father.

What you see, write in a book] That is, what you are now about to see and hear. For it is the present for the near future. And 'to see' stands for any sense.

And send to the seven Churches] Namely, a description of this vision. For this does not pertain to the rest of this book. Different visions occurred to John at different times, as also to other Prophets. The Apocalypse makes much use of the number seven: because to the Hebrews it denotes the sum of things.

Furthermore, the writing of those things which he is about to see was entrusted to Saint John, to be consecrated for the use of the Church. Therefore, the recording of the sacred scriptures did not arise from occasion as the Papists wish, but was undertaken by divine command; which was given here to John with a sonorous voice, while others were incited to write by an internal impulse. Nor indeed should the mandate be restricted to this first apparition, but to the whole revelation. He had to record it in a book, not on some separate scrap of paper: concerning which book in chapter XX. 18, Saint John adjures the reader not to dare to add or take away anything, implying that it must be referred to the perpetual and invariable Canon of Scripture, which according to Varinus is one that admits no addition or subtraction, which was to be sealed by this adjuration. That these visions occurred at different times is asserted rashly. Why should they not all have happened on that Lord's Day? Pareus indeed says it is not likely that all were seen on the same Lord's Day: yet he admits that everything hangs together by one thread, and finally thinks that these things can be left in the middle without prejudice to the faith. But why should we not persist in that designation of a single Lord's Day? The traces of a new ecstasy which he seeks in chapter IV. 2 and XVII. 5, even if they are admitted, do not demonstrate that the ecstasies happened on different days, since they could have occurred on one day. And however much some things are said to have been seen in Patmos, some in heaven, some on the seashore, some in the desert, it must not necessarily be established that these partial places were so far apart that the revelation could not have been completed on the same day. And it is evident from the Gospel history how the Devil was in different and most widely separated places during the temptation of Christ. Why could the Holy Spirit not have placed John in those different places in the twinkling of an eye? Nor was such a leading about in the Spirit, or even a repeated ecstasy and accumulated revelation, a weariness to Saint John in one day, as Pareus affirms, but the highest recreation, after he was raised up by Christ, when he was cast down to the ground terrified by His glory, chapter I. 17. Concerning the septenary number, in which the Holy Spirit was delighted in this writing especially, one will be able to read copiously in the blessed Stephanus Clotzius, and those whom he himself alleges in his treatise on Angelolatry, disp. X. p. XVI. th. XVI.

To Ephesus, and to Smyrna, and to Pergamum, and to Thyatira, and to Sardis, and to Philadelphia, and to Laodicea) The Prophets are accustomed to allude to the names of cities, as Micah I. 14, 15. All these names beautifully remind Christians of their duty. Ephesus warns that they ought to be kindled with a desire for eternal things. For 'Ephesis' is desire. Smyrna, that they should be incorrupt, such as is myrrh, concerning which matter we spoke at Matthew II. verse 11. Pergamum, that they should think of sublime things. For Hesychius and Suidas, and Servius on the second book of the Aeneid, note that all sublime things are called 'Pergama' by the Asiatics. Thyatira, 'thysin ateirea', that is, to kill untamed affections in honor of God.

well impressed upon the mind, to hold the precepts of Christ, just as the Sarda gem best impresses signs among all gems. Philadelphia excites to brotherly love, Laodicea to demonstrating justice toward all peoples. These are, moreover, the most noble cities of Ionia, Lydia, Aeolis, and Caria, as appears from Stephanus, Pliny, and Ptolemy.

We do not disapprove of the allusions of names, whether those which Grotius brings forward, or others that could be devised, provided they are not sold as being of undoubted divine intention. Grotius had said before that all other Churches are comprehended under the names of these cities. Others say that the things inculcated upon them pertain to all, at least by accommodation, with Bede; others finally wish the state of all Churches to be designated according to distinct periods of the New Testament, and judge that to be consistent with the opinion of Bede. Indeed, they even seek similar periods of time in the antediluvian world and the state of the Old Church from Abraham onwards; such are the games that the Bremen Syncretists play, so that they may persuade themselves and others that a brotherhood between the Lutherans and the Reformed was predicted by the Holy Spirit under the Philadelphian period, either already imminent or current. But Gomarus warned in his works, p. 472, that what is brought forward from Bede, besides the fact that he is a more recent author and detracts from his own credibility with many inept interpretations of names, is not so much his intention—that these epistles denote the seven parts of the universal Church through mystical prophecy, and that the things written to them historically signify their diverse conditions, and through them, by mystical prophecy, seven distinct conditions of the universal Church in order, as this unusual opinion posits; but that Bede only indicates a secondary use of these epistles, that although the seven Epistles were written only to the Churches of Asia: yet by reason of the communication and utility to be perceived from their examples and warnings, they were written for all. Just as also Paul's epistles to the Romans, Ephesians, Timothy, and Titus, by reason of the mission, pertained to them alone: But by reason of communication and utility they were common to all, according to the nature of the whole of Holy Scripture, Rom. 15, 3 and 2 Tim. 3, 16, 17. To which also pertains that passage of Tertullian against Marcion, book V, chapter 7: 'But we hold that that epistle to the Ephesians was sent to the churches in truth, but Marcion desired to interpolate a title into it at some time, as if he were a most diligent explorer in that matter too. But it makes no difference about the title, since he wrote to all the Apostles, while writing to some.' Which words Bede, imitating, referred these seven epistles to the communication and utility of all, and not to a mystical meaning concerning the conditions of the universal Church, as the exposition of those epistles in Bede demonstrates. Thus Gomarus. In which sense also must be taken what Cocceius brings forward from Aretas concerning Primasius, page 9, in this place. Aretas: By the seven churches and the hebdomadal number, he signified the multitude of churches everywhere, corresponding to the present life, etc. Primasius, that is, all churches are sevenfold. Concerning the elegant allusion of names, also approved by Willius, it pleases me to submit the judgment of Gomarus again: 'It is inept,' he says, 'and unworthy of a learned and pious man, the allusion of words (as if they contained a mystical prophecy), such as Sardis to the Hebrew שרים, Princes, as if the condition of the Church under Princes were signified.' To which is afterwards added, 'To this present state of the Church, the name Sardis sweetly alludes, according to the Venusian poet in his epistles: What the elegant Samos, what the royal Sardis of Croesus.' But I say, what could have been imagined more inept and inelegant? It is of the same flour, then, when it is said the condition of the sixth Christian Church will be FRATERNAL, which is signified to the Angel of the Church of Philadelphia, as if that mystery were signified by the name of the city of Philadelphia. Such also is the fiction derived from the name Laodicea and distorted from Bede of this kind: This last period of the New Testament embraces the final judgment by the very name τὴν λαῶ δίκην.

The arguments among the Bremensians, interpolated by Crocius, are trivial. I. Who can say whether such things as these epistles signify occurred in those seven particular Asian churches? Indeed, who would dare to deny this, unless he wishes to deny the literal and historical sense and leave only that mystical and prophetic one in those epistles, which is to oppose Christ, who says that these things concern ἃ εἶσι. However, the Crocian inference is inconsequent: Why, if it can only be said rashly that the epistles speak of the affairs of those seven churches, can it only be denied stubbornly that by their names the church of the world in distinct times is understood, so that the difference of places enigmatically signifies the difference of times: since it is open that what the Spirit says in the epistles could most aptly have been said of those things which have been done in the Christian Church until now? Resp. The consequence from possibility to actuality is not valid. And how aptly that can be said, the fabricated, sometimes twisted, and very poorly applied explanation teaches. Why also those mere precarious enigmas should be drawn to the differences of times, which the Bremensians invent for themselves at will, rather than to the differences of places in the same age, does not appear. In sum, all things are merely arbitrary.

II. Does Christ only walk among the seven churches? But if Christ is present in all churches, why will the seven churches not be the churches of the whole time of the New Testament? Again, no consequence. Christ is present not only among seven, but in all churches; therefore, what is said about the seven churches must be explained about the churches of the whole New Testament. Only this follows: Therefore Christ beholds, observes, and directs all things that are done in all churches at all times, which are proven here to be observed, and which are disapproved, he wishes to be amended, if things twin to these are found. Of prophets, periods, and events of future things, no shadow or any trace appears here. Nor have we not inculcated again and again that both a historical and a mystical sense underlie the same words, or that a double literal sense is intended by the Holy Spirit in the Holy Scriptures. Crocius had brought forward this argument thus: Because Christ, appearing among the seven lampstands in Apoc. I. 12, 13, does not look only to the seven churches of Asia, but universally to all, as in the last vision of Daniel ch. VII. 13 and X. 5, 6. But, I say, the interpretation of Christ appearing in v. 20 refutes this: The mystery, he says, of the seven stars which you saw in my right hand, and the seven λυχνίας golden lampstands: The seven stars are the angels of the seven churches, and the seven lampstands which you saw are the seven churches: From which it appears that the seven particular churches of Asia are understood; because he expressed these in the preceding v. 11, and explained them most clearly immediately after, when he described both those angels and the churches in the same order, and dictated the epistles to be written to them. For thus first in chapter II. 1, he says: Write to the angel of the Ephesian church: These things says he who holds the seven stars in his right hand, who walks among the seven lampstands: I know your works, etc., by which he describes his accurate knowledge and provident care of both those pastors and the seven churches: so that he both knows and observes their works. But there exists no indication in this place that this is affirmed of the universal church. Nor are the conditions and seven periods of one universal church (which they allege) certain, nor can the seven churches be called such by any use of Holy Scripture. Finally, the seven churches of which

Christ makes mention are seven angels: that which is ascribed by Christ to the seven churches of Asia in the epistles to them. But the seven conditions of one universal church do not have only seven angels or pastors, but a great abundance; indeed, individual periods have abounded with more. Therefore, these are rashly accommodated to the universal church. But as for the testimony cited from Daniel, that proves nothing at all. For in ch. X. 5, 6, not the same, but a certain similar vision of the person of Christ is described: but there is no mention of stars and lampstands, and in ch. VII. 14, the dominion of Christ over all peoples is indicated, but neither pertains to the matter. For if Christ is the Lord and inspector of all peoples: therefore also of the seven churches of Asia: and therefore nothing prevents that which is common to all churches from being accommodated in this place of the Apocalypse to the seven churches alone. Just as Christ, by his ascension, promised that he would prepare a place in heaven (which is common to all the faithful) expressly to the Apostles alone in John XIV. 1, 3, saying: I go to prepare a place for you: where the word you denotes the Apostles alone, even if the thing itself promised does not befit them alone, and in Luke X. 20 he says to the Apostles alone: Your names are written in heaven: which is nevertheless common to all true faithful. So also, although Christ is in the midst of all the churches of the whole world as Lord: that could nevertheless be signified by this vision concerning the seven churches alone.

Of the same moment is that which is brought forward in III: Does Christ only hold seven stars in his hand, the bishops of the seven churches? And did he wish to rule at one church from the fact that he holds seven stars in his hand, and does he not rather wish to be known everywhere, as he who has the messengers of all churches in his hand, and has distinguished all messengers into seven orders? We concede all these things, except the last. For there is not even a jot or tittle in the Scriptures about the angels of all the churches of all times being distinguished into seven orders.

Let the same be the IV. judgment concerning the fourth reason: Is the Spirit thus only the Spirit of the seven particular Churches in Asia, and did He wish to be named by them to us? But in chapter V. 6. these seven Spirits are said to be sent into the whole earth. We grant these things to the ταῖς ἀμφαῖς, but what is this πρὸς ἔπος? The Holy Spirit works in all Churches at all times: Therefore are the certain periods of the ages of the New Testament Church defined here? Did He not also act in the Church of the Old Testament? Are the periods of that also defined here? Not even the Bremensians would say that, even if they maintain that these also can be referred to them, and twist them to that end.

As to what the V. asks: Since Christ says to John, immediately before the dictation of these epistles, that He would dictate to him also the things which must happen after that: by what argument shall we maintain that no future things are contained in the three chapters? Εὐδιάλυτον: Because the things which must happen after that pertain to the other section of the book, not to the first, which concerns in these seven Churches ἅ εἰσι which are.

As to what the VI. urges: How will an opportunity not be given to Jews or scoffers to reject this Prophetic Scripture, if we say that the matters of the seven epistles are included in the Churches of the seven places, when those things which happened to those Churches do not appear written in these epistles: but those things which did not happen do not seem to be written? To the Thyatiran Church the Morning Star is promised. What Morning Star has risen for the Asiatic Churches? Or was the domination of the Saracens and Turks their morning star? Who are those in Sardis who walked with Christ clothed in white? What is the notable conversation of the Philadelphians from the temptation of the whole inhabited world? These things savor of nothing but a private interpretation, and will vanish through the explanation of those places. Those things which Crocius omitted, perhaps because he held them to be less solid, are nevertheless specious, nay, they could be considered more solid; as for instance how the whole seventh book is said to be significativus, and to signify, ἃ δεῖ γενέσθαι, Apoc. I. 1. to which, however, Gomarus has already replied: The word σημαίνειν to signify has a very wide range, and extends generally to any signs, whether they be spoken, or done, or written, whether it be mere history or prophecy: or whether both are present interchangeably and in order. Nay, of this special signification (as if σημαίνειν were to prophesy mystically through the history of some thing) no example is brought forward, neither from the New Testament, nor from the Greek translation of the Old Testament, nor from the ancient usage of the Greeks, as is apparent. Gomarus adds: That it is false that the whole Apocalypse signifies future things: For this is neither said in chapter I, verse 1, where the statement is indefinite: nor could it even be truly said: because it contains not only the prophecy of future things, but also the history of past and present things, as is distinctly handed down in chapter I, verse 9. Nor is it unusual for mere history to be inserted at times in a Prophetic book, just as such is described in Isaiah concerning Sennacherib in chapters XXXVI and XXXVII, and concerning Hezekiah in chapters XXXVIII and XXXIX: and the same is evident from many examples in Jeremiah. Finally, even if (which we have shown to be false) the whole book were significant, and dealt only with future things, it would indeed be a prophecy, but not for that reason mystical (which is what is disputed here), because not a few clear divine prophecies are proposed in both testaments without a hidden mystery: nor is every mystical prophecy described through the history of other things (as was to be proved here), but more often through mere allegory.

As to the eighth argument, which is of this kind: because Laodicea was overturned by an earthquake in the time of Nero before the writing of these epistles: Gomarus replies likewise: Can it be correctly concluded from that: Therefore these seven epistles to the seven Churches of Asia are not merely historical, but mystical by reason of being prophetic: For this is the scope toward which both this and the remaining arguments aim and are directed, but they do not reach it at all. For who is ignorant that under Tiberius, Ephesus, along with eleven other illustrious cities of Asia, collapsed in a horrendous earthquake before the writing of the epistle to the Ephesians, and yet from that no one (unless he is astray) could conclude that that epistle comprises not only history, but also mystical prophecy. Then, since at the same time that Laodicea and Hierapolis collapsed by an earthquake under Nero, the same thing (witness Eusebius in his Chronicles to the year of Christ 66) also happened to the city of Colossae, and indeed before the epistle to the Colossians was written: yet no one has concluded from that that it should be understood not only historically but also mystically, unless ineptly and falsely. Nor can it be retorted that the case of Ephesus and Laodicea is far different. For Ephesus indeed collapsed, but was repaired a little later: but Laodicea, when these epistles were written, had not yet been restored from its ruin, and therefore the epistle sent to the Laodicean Church contains a mystical prophecy; that, I say, cannot rightly be retorted: because that antecedent is openly refuted by the annals of Tacitus. For as he relates in book II of those Ephesus and eleven other cities collapsed and were restored by the remedy of the Emperor's munificence: So also he says of Laodicea being restored in book 14: In the same year, Laodicea, one of the illustrious cities of Asia, collapsed from an earthquake, and recovered by its own resources, without any remedy from us. And Christ shows the same, when he specifically commanded the Laodicean epistle to be written and sent in chapter I, 11, and dictates it in chapter III, 14. For if Laodicea, when this epistle was written, had not existed, the history of the things which are contained in the epistle sent to it would be removed, and the epistle would be (which God forbid) empty and foolish. Wherefore, so that the vanity of the consequence of this eighth argument may be seen, there is no need for any new breath of the Prophetic Spirit, but only for attention.

IX. And Crocius urges this, and Willius repeats it with the others: That the Jews would have been to be converted under the Philadelphian condition, which was not done in that time, Apoc. III. 9. Rom. XI. 25. 26. But this argument is the most vain by far (I use the response of Gomarus, so that I may oppose a companion of the faith), because it contradicts both the express words of Christ and the opinion of the Author, for the proving of which it is brought forward. For the words of Christ concerning the conversion of the Jews are these: Behold δίδωμι I give from the synagogue of Satan of those who say they are Jews, and are not, but lie: Behold I will make them come and worship before thy feet, and know that I have loved thee: By which words not a universal, but a particular conversion of certain Jews is expressly promised by Christ, as that partition demonstrates: I give from the synagogue of those who say they are Jews. Then the explanation related to them, to be called from the Synagogue, when it is said, I will make them (αὐτὺς) come. Finally, because this civil reverence of adoration, to be performed by those Jews, before the feet of the Angel of the Philadelphian Church, because it is said, before thy feet, by which he addresses the Angel to whom he writes, and affirms that it will happen in his time. But this cannot happen when the people of the Jews will be converted, and all Israel will be saved toward the end of the world: because the Philadelphian Angel has already ceased to exist with his Church for many centuries. And therefore this argument, taken from Apoc. III, verse 19, expressly denies what Christ affirms in the same place will happen to the Angel of the Church, to have happened in his time. And what is said about particular Jews being converted, it affirms against the words of Christ, concerning the universal conversion of the Jewish people from the epistle to the Romans XI, verse 26. The patron of this reasoning and paradox contradicts not only the words of Christ, but also opposes his own opinion, which he set out to defend, and while he strives to build it up, he destroys it from the foundations: for if the conversion of the Jews, which is treated here, has not taken place in the time of this Angel, but is only to be in the penultimate condition of the universal Church (as is shown): Therefore the history of this epistle is removed, and a false prophecy remains: against which the opinion concerning history and through it the connection of mystical prophecy in these seven epistles is set forth and to be proved.

X. In place of an argument, Crocius used the fact that not even the whole of these letters can be praised for the bare letter, which might cast a doubt into the minds of sensible people. Gomarus replied: But, I say, to dissolve the falsity of this reasoning (to omit what we have said before), this single demonstration will abundantly suffice for sensible and attentive people. Whatever contains history without any controversy, whose mystical prophecy cannot be proved by any necessary argument, that has mere history. But these seven epistles without any controversy (even by the admission of the author of the objected reasoning) contain history, whose mystical prophecy cannot be proved by any necessary argument, as the examination of the ten reasons, none of which is probable, let alone necessary, proves. Therefore these seven epistles contain mere history. In which response we easily acquiesce: in which manner that whole fabrication of the Bremensians collapses entirely, so that henceforth there is no need to labor over the application, inasmuch as it rests upon no foundation (for that has been destroyed). For it can be various according to the conjectures of the human mind; but if it lacks a foundation, it is always vain.

Latin:

Vers. 11.

Λεγούσης, ἐγώ εἰμι τὸ Α καὶ τὸ Ω, ὁ πρῶτος καὶ ὁ ἔσχατος. Hic esse designatum Filium Dei luce clarius est: Nam vocatur idem postea vers. 13. ὅμοιος υἱῷ ἀνθρώπου, & de se iterum professus vers. 17. ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ πρῶτος καὶ ὁ ἔσχατος adjecit, καὶ ὁ ζῶν καὶ ἐγενόμην νεκρὸς, καὶ ἰδοὺ ζῶν εἰμι. Æternitatem denotari hac periphrasi plerique Interpretes præ- ter Socinianos agnoscunt. Coccejus tamen singu- laris esse amat: Ego sum A & Ω, id est summus & infimus. Ego ille sum hominibus quidem lapis of- fendiculi & reprobatus, sed apud Deum electus & pretiosus, 1. Petr. II. v. 4. caput quidem Ecclesiæ, sed cujus gloria plena apud Deum occultatur, & qui positus sum in signum cui contradicitur, Luc. II. 34. Primus & ultimus. Jure meo caput sum, quia primus sum: Ita Baptista Joh. I. 15. Qui post me venit, me prævenit, quia longe ante me fuit: Eum, qui in initio fuit, Joh. I. vers. 1. qui fuit ante omnia, & propter quem omnia sunt Col. I. vers. 16. qui non mutatur, qui vivit in perpetuum,

& cum ultimis idem est, & à nemine vincitur, Es. XLI. 4. XLIV. 6. XLVIII. 12. Is eo honore dignus est, ut sit ὸ Alpha & summus. Nam illa per ὸ ulti- mus significantur, ut & hoc, quod post ipsum Regem non est alius Rex, post illum Sacerdotem nullus alius Sacerdos, post illum Doctorem nullus alius Doctor, post ipsum Christum nullus alius Christus. Vide & Psal. CX. 4. Tu es Sacerdos in seculum. Sed hæc, ex illa locutione, utpote quam cum Patre com- munem habet Filius, nemo exsculpet.

ὃ βλέπεις γράψον εἰς βιβλίον] Id est quod jam videbis & audies. Est enim præsens pro futuro proximo. Et videre pro quovis sensu.

Καὶ πέμψον ταῖς ἑπτὰ Ἐκκλησίαις] Nempe hujus visi de- scriptionem. Neque enim ad cætera hujus libri hoc perti- net. Diversa visa diversis temporibus Johanni obtigere, ut & Prophetis aliis. Septenario numero multum utitur Apo- calypsis: quia Ebræis rerum summum denotat.

Porro demandata est Sancto Johanni scriptio eorum, quæ visurus est, in librum usui Ecclesiæ consecrandum. Non ergo ex occasione nata est sacrarum literarum consignatio ut Papistæ volunt, sed jussu divino suscepta; qui hic Johanni voce sonora datus, aliis impulsu interno ad scriben- dum instigatis. Neque vero restringendum man- datum ad primam hanc apparitionem, sed ad totam ἀποκάλυψιν. In librum consignare debuit, non in chartulam aliquam separatam: De quo libro cap. XX. 18. obtestatur S. Johannes le- ctorem, ne aliquid addere sive demere ausit, in- nuens eundem ad Canonem Scripturæ perpetu- um & invariabilem, qui juxta Varinum, est μη- δεμίαν πρόθεσιν ἢ ἀφαίρεσιν ἐκδεχόμενον, refe- rendum esse, qui hac obtestatione erat obsignan- dus. Diversis autem temporibus visa hæc conti- gisse, temere asseritur. Quidni illa die Dominica obtigerint omnia? Pareo quidem non est verisimile, eadem Dominica omnia visa: Fa- tetur tamen omnia uno filo cohærere, censet de- nique, hæ posse in medio relinqui salva fide. Sed cur non in illa unius diei Dominicæ de- signatione persistamus? Quæ cap. IV. 2. & XVII. 5. quærit novæ ἐκσάσεως vestigia, etsi admittan- tur, alia atque alia die ἐκσάσεις factas esse, non demonstrant, quum una die contingere potue- rint. Et utut quædam in Patmo, quædam in cœlo, quædam in littore maris, quædam in de- serto visa dicantur, non tamen hæc partialia loca ita dissita fuisse statuendum necessario est, quin eadem die absolvi ἀποκάλυψις potuerit. Et quam diversis maximeque dissitis in locis in tentatione Christi Diabolus fuerit eodem die, ex historia Evangelica constat. Quidni Spiritus Sanctus Jo- hannem ἐν ῥοπῇ ὄμματος in diversis illis locis siste- re potuerit? Nec talis in Spiritu circumductio vel etiam iterata ἔκσασις & cumulata in uno die revelatio S. Johanni fatigatio fuit, uti affirmat Pareus, sed summa recreatio, postquam à Chri- sto erectus fuit, cum gloria ejus territus in ter- ram prosterneretur, cap. I. 17. De numero se- ptenario, quo delectatus in hoc imprimis scri- pto fuit Spiritus Sanctus, copiose legi poterit B. Stephanus Clotzius, & quos allegat ipse in tract. de Angelolatr. disp. X. p. XVI. th. XVI.

Εἰς Ἔφεσον, καὶ εἰς Σμύρναν, καὶ εἰς Πέργαμον, καὶ εἰς θυά- τειρα, κὴ εἰς Σάρδεις, κὴ εἰς Φιλαδέλφειαν, κὴ εἰς Λαοδίκειαν) So- lent Prophetæ alludere ad urbium nomina, ut Michæas I. 14. 15. Hæc nomina omnia Christianos sui officii pulchre admo- nent. Ἔφεσις monet accendi eos debere desiderio rerum æternarum. Ἔφεσις enim est desiderium. Σμύρνα ut sint in- corrupti, qualis est myrrha, qua de re diximus ad Matth. II. vers. 11. Pergamum, ut sublimia cogirent. Sublimia enim omnia dicta Asiaticis Πέργαμα notat Hesychius, & Suidas, & Servius ad secundum Æneidos. Thyatira θύσιν ἀτειρέα, id est, in honorem Dei interficere indomitos affectus.

bene impressa animo, tenere Christi præcepta, sicut inter gemmas omnes signa optime imprimit Sarda. Φιλαδέλφεια ad amorem fraternum, Λαοδίκεια ad justitiam erga populos omnes demonstrandam excitat. Sunt autem hæ urbes no- bilissimæ Ioniæ, Lydiæ, Æolidos, Cariæ, ut ex Stephano, Pli- nio, Ptolomæo apparet.

Nominum allusiones sive quas Grotius affert, sive quæ aliæ excogitari possent, non improba- mus, modo non venditentur illæ ceu indubiæ intentionis divinæ. Sub urbium harum nomi- nibus alias Ecclesias omnes comprehendi, Grotius antea dixerat. Alii quæ illis inculcantur, ad o- mnes pertinere, saltim per accommodationem cum Beda ajunt; alii denique Ecclesiarum omnium sta- tum secundum distinctas Novi Testamenti periodos designari volunt, idque Beda sententiæ consenta- neum judicant. Imō similes etiam periodos temporum in mundo antediluviano & statu Eccle- siæ Veteris inde ab Abrahamo quærunt; quales lu- sus facere Bremenses Syncretistas, ut sub Phila- delphensi periodo seu imminente jam, seu currente inter Lutheranos & Reformatos fraternitatem à Spiritu S. prædictam esse, sibi aliisque persuade- ant. Sed monuit Gomarus oper. p. 472. quod ex Beda adducitur, præterquam quod recentior sit Au- tor, & multis nominum interpretationibus ineptis fidem sibi deroget, ejus non tam esse mentem, hasce epistolas per mysticam prophetiam septem universa- lis Ecclesiæ partes notare, & quæ ad illas scribuntur historice, earum conditiones diversas, & per eas, mystica prophetia, septem Ecclesiæ universalis distin- ctas conditiones ordine significare, quemadmodum insolens hæc opinio statuit; Sed Bedam usum dun- taxat harum epistolarum secundarium indicare, quod licet septem Epistola ad solas Asiæ Ecclesias sint scriptæ: Communicationis tamen & utilitatis ex ea- rum exemplis ac monitis percipiendæ ratione ad o- mnes scripta sunt. Quemadmodum & Pauli episto- læ ad Romanos, Ephesios, Timotheum, Titum rati- one missionis ad eos solos pertinebant: Sed commu- nicationis & utilitatis ratione omnibus fuerunt com- munes pro totius sacræ scripturæ natura, Rom. 15, 3. & 2. Tim. 3, 16. 17. Quo etiam spectat illud Tertul- liani adversus Marcionem libr. V. cap. 7. Ecclesiæ autem veritate epistolam illam ad Ephesios habemus missam, sed Marcion ei titulum aliquando interpola- re gestiit, quasi & in isto diligentissimus explorator. Nihil autem de titulo interest, cum ad omnes Apo- stolos scripserit, dum ad quosdam. Quæ verba imitatus Beda ad communicationem & utilitatem omnium has epistolas septem, non vero ad mysticam de septem universalis Ecclesiæ conditionibus retulit, ut epistolarum illarum apud Bedam expositio demon- strat. Hæc Gomarus. Quo sensu etiam accipienda, quæ ex Areta de Primasio affert Coccejus pag. 9. in h. l. Aretas: Διὰ τῶν ἑπτὰ Ἐκκλησιῶν κὲ τῶ̃ ἑβδομα- δικῶ̃ ἀριθμῷ τὸ τῶν ἁπανταχῆ ἐκκλησιῶν ἐσήμανε πλῆθος τῶν τῷ παρέντι βίῳ συσοίχων, &c. Prima- sius, id est, omnes Ecclesiæ septiformes. De allusione nominum concinna, etiam probata Willio, iterum Gomari judicium subjicere placet: Inepta, inquit, est, & Viro docto, ac pio indigna vocum (quasi pro- phetiam mysticam continerent) allusio, ut Sardium ad Ebræum שרים Principes, quasi Ecclesia sub Prin- cipibus conditio significaretur. Quibus postea additur, ad hunc præsentem Eccl. siæ statum nomen Sardium suaviter alludit, juxta Venusinum Poetam in epistolis: Quid concinna Samos, quid Crasi Regia Sardis. At inquam quid ineptus atque inconcinnius fingi potuit? Ejusdem deinde farinæ est, cum dicitur sextæ Eccle- siæ Christianæ conditio erit FRATERNA, quæ signi- ficatur Angelo Ecclesiæ Philadelphensis, quasi myste- rium illud urbis Philadelphensis nomine significaretur. Quale etiam commentum est è nomine Λαοδίκεια pe- titum & ex Beda detortum hujusmodi: Hæc ultima novi Testamenti periodus ipso nomine τὴν λαῶ δίκην judicium ultimum complectitur.

Minutulæ sunt rationes apud Coccejum è Cro- cio interpolatæ I. An in septem illis particularibus Ecclesiis Asiaticis talia contigerint, qualia hæ epi- stolæ significant, quis potest dicere? Imo quis ausit hoc negare, nisi qui sensum literalem & histori- cum inficiari, solumque mysticum illum & Pro- pheticum in epistolis illis relinquere velit, quod est Christo repugnare, qui ait concernere hæc ἃ εἶσι. Illatio autem Crociana inconsequens est: Quare si non nisi temere dici potest, epistolas loqui de rebus septem illarum Ecclesiarum, non nisi præ- fracte negari potest, per earum nomina intelligi Ec- clesiam orbis in distinctis temporibus, ut locorum differentia ænigmatice temporum differentiam sig- nificet: quum apertum sit de iis, quæ in Ecclesia Chri- stiana hucusque facta sunt, quæ Spiritus in epistolis dicit, aptissime potuisse dici? Resp. A posse ad esse non valet consequentia. Et quam apte id dici pos- sit, conficta, quandoque contorta, pessimeque applicata explicatio docet. Cur etiam ænigmata illa mere precaria potius ad temporum differentias, quas sibi pro arbitrio fingunt Bremenses, quam ad differentias locorum in eadem ætate trahenda sint, non apparet. Summa, omnia sunt mere arbitraria.

II. Christus an tantum ambulat inter septem Eccle- sias? Quod si Christus in omnibus Ecclesiis adest, quare non septem Ecclesiæ erunt Ecclesiæ totius tem- poris Novi Testamenti? Iterum nulla consequentia. Christus adest non inter septem tantum, sed in omnibus Ecclesiis; Ergo quæ de septem Ecclefi- is dicuntur, explicanda de Ecclesiis totius Novi Testamenti. Id tantum sequitur: Ergo Christus omnia, quæ in omnibus Ecclesiis omni tempore geruntur, intuetur, observat, dirigit, quæ hic pro- bantur, observari, quæ improbantur, emendari vult, si gemina his reperiantur. De prophetis, pe- riodis ac eventib9 futurorum hic nulla umbra, vel vestigium ullum apparet. Neque sensum & hi- storicum & mysticum iisdem verbis subesse, vel geminum sensum literalem â Spiritu Sancto in- tendi in Sacris literis sæpe sæpius inculcavimus. Crocius hanc rationem ita protulerat: Quia Chri- stus inter septem candelabra apparens Apoc. I. 12. 13. non ad solas septem Asiæ Ecclesias, sed universaliter ad omnes spectat, ut in ultima visione Danielis cap. VII. 13. & X. 5. 6. At, inquam, Christi apparentis interpretatio v. 20. hoc refellit: Mysterium, inquit, septem stellarum, quas vidisti in dextra mea, & septem λυχνίας candelabra aurea: Septem stellæ An- geli sunt septem Ecclesiarum, & candelabra septem quæ vidisti, sunt Ecclesiæ septem: Ex quibus appa- ret septem particulares Asiæ Ecclesias intelligi; quia hasce in antecedentibus v. 11. expressit, & pro- xime non obscure de iisdem explicavit, cum & Angelos illos & Ecclesias eodem ordine descripsit, iisque scribendas epistolas dictavit. Sic enim pri- mum cap. II. 1. ait: Angelo Ecclesiæ Ephesinæ scribe: Hæc dicit, qui tenet septem stellas in dextra sua, qui ambulat inter septem candelabra: Novi opera tua &c. quibus & pastorum illorum & septem Ecclesia- rum accuratam cognitionem suam & providen- tem curam describit: ut eorum opera & norit & observet. De universali vero Ecclesia illud affir- mari hoc loco nullum extat indicium. Neque et- iam unius universalis Ecclesiæ conditiones ac pe- riodi septem (quas obtendunt) sunt certæ, neque septem Ecclesiæ ullo S. Scripturæ usu appellari possunt. Denique septem Ecclesiarum, quarum

Christus meminit, sunt septem Angeli: id quod septem Asiæ Ecclesiis à Christo in epistolis ad eas adscribitur. Unius vero universalis Ecclesiæ conditiones septem non tantum septem habent Angelos sive Pastores, sed maxima copia, imo singulæ periodi pluribus abundarunt. Quare te- mere hæc ad Ecclesiam universalem accommo- dantur. Quod vero ex Daniele testimonium ci- tatur, illud nihil omnino probat. Nam cap. X. 5.6. non eadem, sed similis quædam personæ Christi visio describitur: Stellarum vero & candelabro- rum nulla mentio, & cap. VII. 14. dominium Christi in omnes populos indicatur, sed neutrum ad rem facit. Nam si omnium populorum Chri- stus est Dominus atque inspector: Ergo & septem Ecclesiarum Asiæ: ideoque nihil obstat, quo mi- nus id, quod omnibus Ecclesiis commune, hoc loco Apocalypseos solis septem Ecclesiis accom- modetur. Quemadmodum Christus se ascensio- ne sua locum in cœlis paraturum (quod fidelibus omnibus commune) solis Apostolis expresse Joh. XIV. 1. 3. promisit dicens: Proficiscor para- turus vobis locum: ubi vox vobis solos Apostolos notat, etsi res ipsa promissa iis solis non conveni- at, & Luc. X. 20. solis Apostolis ait: Nomina vestra scripta sunt in cœlis: quod tamen omnibus vere fidelibus commune. Sic etiam licet Christus sit in medio omnium totius orbis Ecclesiarum tan- quam Dominus: illud tamen hac visione de solis septem Ecclesiis potuit significari.

Ejusdem momenti est, quod III. affertur: An Christus tantum septem stellas tenet manu, Episco- pos Ecclesiarum septem? Et apud unam Ecclesiam voluit dominari inde, quod teneat septem stellas manu sua, & non potius ubique vult innotescere, ut is, qui omnium Ecclesiarum nuntios in manu habet, & omnes nuntios in septem ordines distinxit? Hæc omnia concedimus, postremo excepto. Nam de omnibus omnium Ecclesiarum omnium tempo- rum Angelis in septem ordines distinctis ne gry vel my quidem in Scripturis.

Idem esto IV. judicium de quarta ratione: Ita Spiritus numquid est Spiritus tantum septem Ecclesiarum in Asia particularium, & ab iis deno- minari nobis voluit? Sed cap. V. 6. dicuntur septem hi Spiritus missi in totam terram. Hæc ταῖς ἀμφαῖς largimur, sed quid hæc πρὸς ἔπος? Spiritus San- ctus operatur in omnibus Ecclesiis omni tem- pore: Ergo periodi certæ ætatum Ecclesiæ novi Testamenti hic definitæ sunt? Annon egit etiam in Ecclesia Veteris Testamenti? Etiamne illius periodi hic definitæ? Id ne Bremenses quidem dixerint, etiamsi ad eas etiam hæ deferri posse statuant, eoque detorqueant.

Quod V. quærit: Quum Christus dicat, Jo- hanni statim ante dictationem harum epistolarum se ei dictaturum etiam quæ post deinde debeant fieri: quo argumento adstruemus, in tribus capitibus nul- la futura contineri? Εὐδιάλυτον: Quia quæ deinde debeant fieri, ad alteram sectionem libri per- tinent, non ad primam, quæ concernit in his se- ptem Ecclesiis ἅ εἰσι quæ sunt.

Quæ VI. urgentur: Quomodo non dabitur an- sa Judæis aut contemptoribus hoc Propheticum Scri- ptum abjicendi, si dicamus epistolarum septem res includi, septem locorum Ecclesiis, quum ea, quæ iis Ecclesiis evenerunt, non appareant in his epistolis scripta: at ea, quæ non evenerunt, non videantur scripta? Thyatirensi Ecclesiæ promittitur Phospho- rus. Quis Phosphorus Asiaticis Ecclesiis ortus est? An Saracenorum & Turcarum dominatio earum phosphorus est? Qui Sardibus cum Christo ambula- runt amicti albis? Philadelphensium quæ notabilis conversatio est ex tentatione totius habitabilis? Ea nonnisi ἰδίαν ἐπίλυσιν sapiunt, & per locorum isto- rum explicationem evanescent. Illa quæ è Cro- cianis prætermisit forte quia minus solida habuit, speciosa tamen sunt, imo solida magis censeri queant; utpote quomodo VII. totus liber σημαν- tikὸς significativus dicatur, & significare, ἃ δεῖ γε- νέσθαι, Apoc. I. 1. ad quod tamen jam Gomarus re- spondit: Verbum σημαίνειν significare latissime pa- tet, & ad quævis signa sive sint dicta, sive sint facta, aut scripta se extendit generatim, sive mera sit histo- ria aut prophetia: sive ὑπαλλήλως & ordinatim utrumque insit. Imo specialis hujus significationis (quasi σημαίνειν esset per alicujus rei historiam mysti- ce prophetare) neque ex Novo Testamento, neque ex Græca Veteris Testamenti translatione, neque ex an- tiquo Græcorum usu ullum exemplum adducitur, ut apparet. Addit Gomarus: Falsum esse, totam Apocalypsin futura significare: Hoc enim neque cap. I. v. 1. dicitur, ubi indefinita oratio: neque etiam vere dici potuit: quia non solum futurorum prophetiam continet, sed etiam & præteritorum & præsentium historiam, ut cap. I. v. 9. distincte tra- ditur. Neque insolens est, in libro Prophetico me- ram historiam interdum insertam, quemadmodum talis in Esaia de Zancheribo cap. XXXVI. & XXXVII. deque Ezechia cap. XXXVIII. XXXIX. describitur: idemque multis Jeremiæ exemplis per- spicuum. Denique etsi (quod falsum esse ostendi- mus) totus liber esset significativus, & de rebus fu- turis tantum ageret, prophetia quidem esset, sed non idcirco mystica, (quod hic controvertitur) quia prophetiæ non paucæ divinæ perspicuæ sine latente mysterio in utroque testamento proponuntur: nec omnis etiam mystica prophetia per historiam aliarum rerum (ut hic probandum erat) sed sæpius per me- ram allegoriam describitur.

Quod ad VIII. rationem, quæ hujusmodi est: quia Laodicea tempore Neronis eversa fuit terræ motu ante harum epistolarum scriptionem: Re- spondit itidem Gomarus: An inde recte concludi potest: Ergo septem hæ epistolæ ad septem Asiæ Ec- clesias non sunt mere historicæ, sed mysticæ ratione propheticæ: Hic enim est scopus, ad quem & hæc & reliquæ rationes collimant ac diriguntur, sed eum ne- quaquam attingunt. Quis enim ignorat sub Tibe- rio Ephesum cum aliis undecim illustribus Asiæ urbibus horrendo terræ motu collapsam ante epistolæ ad Ephesios scriptionem, & tamen ex eo nemo (nisi devius) colligere poterit, eam epistolam non solum hi- storiam, sed etiam mysticam prophetiam complecti. Deinde cum eodem tempore, quo sub Nerone Lao- dicea & Hierapolis terræ motu corruerunt, idem (teste Eusebio in Chronicis ad annum Christi 66.) etiam urbi Colossensi acciderit, & quidem ante scri- ptam ad Colossenses epistolam: nemo tamen inde non solum historice sed etiam mystice intelligendum, nisi inepte ac falso concluserit. Neque etiam regeri po- test, Ephesi & Laodiceæ rationem esse longe diver- sam. Ephesum enim collapsam quidem, sed paulo post reparatam: Laodiceam vero cum hæ epistolæ scriberentur, nondum à ruina restauratam, ideoque epistolam ad Laodicenam Ecclesiam missam contine- re mysticam prophetiam, id inquam regeri jure non potest: quia antecedens illud Taciti annalibus aperte refutatur. Nam ut eorum libr. II. Ephe- sum aliasq; undecim urbes collapsas munificentia Im- peratoris remedio restitutas tradit: Sic quoque de La- odicea restaurata l. 14. ait: Eodem anno ex illustri- bus Asiæ urbibus Laodicea tremore terræ collapsa, nullo à nobis remedio, propriis opibus revaluit. I- demque Christus commonstrat, cum nominatim epi- stolam Laodiceam scribi ac mitti præcepit cap. I. 11. e- amque dictat cap. III. 14. Si enim Laodicea, cum hæc epistola scriberetur, non extitisset, tolleretur hi- storia rerum, quæ in epistola ad eam missa continen- tur, & inanis stultaque (quod absit) esset epistola. Quamobrem ut consequentia hujus octavæ rationis vanitas conspiciatur, nullo Spiritus Prophetici novo afflatu, sed sola attentione opus est.

IX. Et hoc urget Crocius, repetitque cum cæte- ris Willius: Judæi sub Philadelphensi conditione fu- issent convertendi, id quod in illo tempore haud fa- ctum, Apoc. III. 9. Rom. XI. 25. 26. Verum hæc ra- tio longe vanissima, (utor responsione Gomari, ut socium fidei opponam) quia & disertis Christi verbis, & sententiæ Autoris, cui probandæ affertur, contradicit. Verba enim Christi de Judæorum con- versione hæc sunt: Ecce δίδωμι do ex synagoga Sa- tanæ eorum, qui se dicunt Judæos esse, nec sunt & mentiuntur: Ecce faciam, ut ipsi veniant & ado- rent ante pedes tuos, & sciant, quod ego dilexi te: Quibus verbis diserte non universalis, sed particu- laris Judæorum quorundam conversio à Christo pro- mittitur, ut partitio illa demonstrat: Do ex syna- goga eorum, qui se dicunt Judæos esse. Deinde ex- plicatio ad illos relata, ex Synagoga vocandos, cum dicitur, faciam ut ipsi (αὐτὺς) veniant. Denique quia hæc reverentia civilis adorationis, à Judæis il- lis præstanda, ante pedes Angeli Philadelphensis Ecclesiæ, quia dicitur, ante pedes tuos, quibus An- gelum, ad quem scribit, compellat, ejusque tempo- re id futurum affirmat. Hoc autem fieri non poterit, cum populus Judæorum convertetur, & totus Israel salvus fiet sub mundi finem: quia Angelus Phila- delphensis jam multis seculis cum sua Ecclesia esse desiit. Ac propterea hæc ratio ex Apoc. III. vers. 19. petita diserte id, quod ibidem Christus Angelo Ec- clesiæ eventurum affirmat, factum ejus tempore negat. Quodque de particularibus ex Judæis convertendis dicitur, illud de universali populi Judaici ex epi- stola ad Rom. XI. vers. 26. conversione, contraque Christi dicta affirmat. Nec Christi solum verbis rationis hujus & paradoxi Patronus contradicit, sed suæ etiam, quam tuendam præfixit, sententiæ adversatur, eamque, cum adstruere studet, fundi- tus diruit: nam si conversio Judæorum, de qua hic agitur, facta non sit hujus Angeli tempore: sed tantum sub Ecclesiæ universalis conditione penulti- ma (ut ostenditur) futura: Ergo tollitur hujus e- pistolæ historia, ac falsa superest prophetia: con- tra quam sententia de historia & per eam mysticæ prophetiæ, in hisce septem epistolis connexione præfi- xa ac probanda statuit.

X. Argumenti loco adhibuit Crocius, quod ne tota quidem pro nuda litera ex hisce literis, quod cordatis scrupulum injiciat, laudari possit. Re- spondit Gomarus: At, inquam, ad hujus ratio- nis falsitatem diluendam (ut ante à nobis dicta omit- tamus) vel unica hæc demonstratio apud cordatos & attentos abunde suffecerit. Quicquid citra ullam controversiam historiam continet, cujus mystica prophetia nullo necessario argumento probari po- test, illud meram habet historiam. Atqui hæ se- ptem epistolæ citra ullam controversiam (fatente etiam objectæ rationis Autore) historiam continent, cujus mystica prophetia nullo argumento necessario probari potest, ut examen rationum decem, qua- rum nulla probabilis, nedum necessaria evincit. Ergo hæ septem epistolæ meram historiam continent. Qua responsione facile acquiescimus: Quo- pacto totum istud commentum Bremensium corruit penitus, ut deinceps de applicatione, utpote quae nullo fundamento (id enim destru- ctum est) nititur, laborandum non sit. Ea enim pro ingenii humani ςοχασμοῖς varia esse potest; sed si fundamento careat, semper vana est.

## 1:12
Ver. 12.

And there) that is, then, an adverb of place for an adverb of time: But this ἐκεῖ is absent in many books. I turned to see the voice that was speaking with me) In the Manuscript λαλεῖ as if in the present tense. There is also a Metonymy here: For he names the voice, when he wished the one who was speaking to be understood. A similar locution in Matt. III. ver. 3. He rightly says, however, that he turned back, because the voice was sounding from behind, as we have already heard.

Some explain 'voice' literally, but 'to see' by Hebrew Catachresis or Synecdoche as 'to perceive' and 'to receive what is heard,' such as Aretas and Haymo, with Cornelius not dissenting; but he had already sufficiently perceived the great voice like a trumpet, yet he desired to know the one speaking. It is better, therefore, to understand by 'voice' the one uttering the voice, as in Job I. 13.

And having turned I saw seven golden lampstands) מנורות זהב. Just as in the temple there was one lampstand with seven lamps, Num. VIII. ver. 2. Zech. IV. ver. 2. So now, as a sign of multiplied grace, seven lampstands having seven lamps each. By these are signified first the seven Asian Churches, then through them also others similar to them, made for the purpose of shining before the world. See Phil. I. ver. 15. John V. ver. 35. Matt. V. ver. 16. The septenary number, as Philo explains in his book on the Heir of Divine Things, dealing with the lampstand of the temple, signifies purity, but gold signifies immunity from all rust: to which also refers that which is below in XXI. ver. 18. 21. The Churches are described here, such as they ought to be.

Latin:

Vers. 12.

Καὶ ἐκεῖ) id est tum, adverbium loci pro adverbio tempo- ris : Sed hoc ἐκεῖ abest in libris multis. Ἐπέστρεψα βλέπειν τὴν φωνὴν, ἥτις ἐλάλει μετ' ἐμῦ) In Manuscripto λαλεῖ quasi in re praesenti. Est & hic Μετωνυ- μία: Nam vocem nominat, cum ipsum qui loquebatur in- telligi vellet. Similis locutio Matth. III. vers. 3. Recte au- tem respexisse se dicit, quia à tergo vox sonabat, ut jam audivimus.

Nonnulli vocem proprie, videre autem per Catachresin Ebraeam sive Synecdochen sentire, & audita excipere exponunt, utpote Aretas & Haymo, non abnuente Cornelio; sed vocem magnam tubae instar jam satis perceperat, lo- quentem autem nosse desiderabat. Praestat er- go per vocem intelligere vocem proferentem, ut Job. I. 13.

Καὶ ἐπιστρέψας εἶδον ἑπτὰ λυχνίας χρυσᾶς) מנורות זהב. Sicut in templo unum erat candelabrum cum septem lucer- nis, Num. VIII. vers. 2. Zach. IV. vers. 2. Ita nunc in si- gnum multiplicatae gratiae septem candelabra septenas habe- tia lucernas. Per has significantur primo septem Ecclesiae Asiaticae, deinde per eas etiam aliae eis similes, in id factae, ut mundo praeluceant. Vide Phil. I. vers. 15. Joh. V. vers. 35. Matth. V. vers. 16. Septenarius numerus, ut Philo ex- plicat libro de haerede rerum divinarum, de candelabro tem- pli agens, puritatem significat, aurum vero immunitatem ab omni rubigine : quo spectat & quod infra est XXI. vers. 18. 21. Describuntur hic Ecclesiae, quales esse de- bent.

## 1:13
Ver. 13.

And in the midst of the seven lampstands one like the Son of man) An angel in the figure of Christ, which Christ is described by such a mark mystically in Daniel 7, ver. 13. 10, ver. 5. See the remarks there, and also at Matt. 8, ver. 20. A similar locution below, ver. 14. In the Manuscript it is read: And in the midst of the lampstands a likeness of the Son of man. Christ is said, however, to be moving in the midst of the lampstands, because He is present with the Churches, just as Moses uses ἐμπεριπατεῖν concerning God, Lev. 26, 11. and Paul 2 Cor. 6, v. 6. and Isaiah chap. 11, ver. 6, uses 'to be in the midst.' You have the thing itself in Matt. 18, v. 20. and 28, v. 20.

The revelation made at the beginning comprises things seen and heard. The things seen are the objects and the person, namely the lampstands and the one like the Son of man: Of the former, both the material is indicated, that they were golden, and the number, that they were seven, by which mystery the seven Churches are noted here, and not indeed all the Churches throughout the whole world, although it is a number of perfection, nor should it be doubted that the Son of man is likewise present in the midst of other Churches, Matt. XVIII. ver. 20. and chap. XXVIII. ver. 20. Because this vision is explained specifically concerning the seven Churches of Asia, ver. 20. No one would say that purity is designated by that number, which is denoted rather by gold, because the Churches, as far as the faithful are concerned, shine and are precious in the purity of doctrine and life, purified by the precious blood of the Son of God, Heb. IX. ver. 25. just as gold shines and is held in value. Nor is the Church called golden only because of charity, but also because, as Cornelius says, it is as if gold is tested, extended, and formed by the fire and hammers of persecutions. The Church is therefore like a lampstand, says Pererius, luminous through the doctrine of the Scriptures, splendid through the brightness of virtues, weighty through the gravity of morals, ductile through obedience, sonorous through preaching, extended through perseverance, upright through hope, founded in God through faith, bound to God through charity. Lampstands, however, strike the eyes before the one who lights them. We see the Churches more easily than Christ, the head, foundation, and Pastor of the Churches, as here B. Cluverus.

The person seen is not some Angel, but Christ Himself: For to Him alone, not to an Angel, does that speech belong: I am the A and the Ω. Likewise: I was dead, and now I live. Through 'man' in the words 'like the son of man,' many of the ancients and moderns definitely understand Christ, which is to be explained thus, not that Christ Himself was not seen, but only 'like Christ': But that the person seen appeared like Christ, as far as the vision is concerned, because He appeared with such magnificence that, although He was in reality Christ Himself, He nevertheless seemed like the son of man, or definitely like Christ, not indefinitely like a man. B. Cluverus explains it thus: He says John [saw one] like the Son of man, because according to the truth of the flesh He appeared as the Son of man; but according to His divine Majesty He surpassed the form of man by much. Gomarus, however, with others prefers to interpret it as some man indefinitely, so as to remove the presence of Christ on earth: For as he says, the human figure accompanied by two Angels revealed itself outwardly to Abraham before He was born, Gen. XVIII. ver. 2. 17. So after He ascended into heaven, not in His own proper body (which will remain in heaven until the day of judgment, Acts III. v. 21.) but under a human appearance, He revealed Himself to the spirit of John, presented inwardly, and in this place is described with the addition of clothing and the external appearance of the body. But that comparison is null. For the Son of God, without flesh, could by a temporary dispensation assume a body of human figure, but in the flesh, to assume another human body above His own flesh, which He never lays aside, does not befit sound Theology. Nor was he seen by John only in an external appearance, but in the very human nature in which he had undergone death, he testified: I was dead, and behold I live, which some phantom could not say. Nor does the whole apparition and the speech which he had to St. John testify that Christ was playing a drama here, but that he presented himself to John conspicuous in divine glory. Coccejus does not deny it: Perhaps, he says, this name is used here, as is customary in the Gospel, to denote Jesus Christ, who is called the Son of man, Psalm VIII, verses 5, 6. It agrees with what is in John V, verse 27, he gave him power also to execute judgment, because he is the Son of man. Pareus more confidently: All things teach that Christ is described by this form, both because he commands John to write the Apocalypse in verse 19, and reveals the following visions to him, chapter IV, verse 1. But the Revealer of the Apocalypse was Christ, both because in verse 18 he says that he lives, but had been dead, and is alive for evermore, and has the keys of hell and of death, which belongs neither to man or human nature, nor to an Angel, but solely to Christ. The description is in large part taken from Dan. VII, verse 10. That he stands in the midst of the candlesticks signifies that Christ is not far away, but is present in the midst of the Church, so that by his Word and Spirit he may rule, direct, defend, and preserve it by his grace, according to the promises, Matt. XVIII, verse 20, chapter XXVIII, verse 20. This is Pareus: Who nevertheless, against the Ubiquitarians, whom he thus accuses, maintains that the human nature of Christ is only in heaven, not on earth, until he returns from there for judgment. But if the Son of man walks in the midst of the Churches, since without his human nature the Son of God neither is, nor is present anywhere after the incarnation, nor can he be called the Son of man, it is necessary, not only in the heavens, but also on earth in the midst of his Churches, that there be present a human nature no less than a divine nature, both of which pertain to the integrity of the person of Christ, and neither of which can exist without the other while maintaining the personal union. The absurdity that Pareus introduces: Christ’s humanity seven Churches in its hand, and that a sword would proceed from his mouth—arises from a confusion of the figure and the thing figured. For what is understood literally in a figure, once the figure is unfolded, is to be explained not literally, but according to the mystery that was shadowed forth; otherwise, one would attribute to Christ seven eyes, seven horns, and feet like burnished bronze. But the nature of the person himself who is figured is one thing, and the nature of these figures is another. The person is said to have been like the Son of man, and, according to Pareus’s interpretation, Christ himself, the Son of man: and it implies that Christ is not far away, but is present in the midst of the Church, not indeed as only half a Christ, but as a whole one, for whose integrity the human nature is absolutely required. Therefore, the Parean objection about Christ having seven Angels and Churches in a corporeal hand (which, in truth, is inserted into the scripture regarding the Churches, but is not found in the scripture) and about a corporeal sword is inept: such things are seen entirely as the letter has them: But that representation did not shadow forth that Christ truly had the Angels in his corporeal hand, but in his power: nor that a corporeal sword went out of his mouth, but the sword of the Word.

Pareus calls us more inept, we who, under the pretext of this vision, defend the image of Christ in temples, contrary to the express word of God. The Carlstadian reformers will never teach that this is repugnant to the express Word of God. But if it is permitted for our eyes to present the image seen here by St. John, which is absolutely necessary for those who conceive this vision in their own minds, why would it not be permitted to exhibit the same painting to the eyes of the body, whether in temples or outside them?
