Those holy ones carry such images on gold and silver coins, but they do not carry them painted or cast in temples; perhaps one should doubt whether they would even refuse golden statues cast or formed in that likeness, if they were gifted them? If such things are forbidden by God, why did Moses cause them to be made in the tabernacle, and Solomon in the temple? How did God command that they be made in the tabernacle, and subsequently also in the temple, by a prescribed likeness or idea?

Ἐνδεδυμένον ποδήρη] Just as the Angels are also described, Ezek. 9, verse 2. Dan. 10, verse 5. In both places in the Hebrew it is בדים, which in Ezekiel the Seventy translate as ποδήρη (long robe), but in Daniel, Theodotion retained the Hebrew word: other interpreters put ἐξαίρετα (excellent things), others βύσσινα (linen things). It is that priestly garment, Exod. 28, verse 38. Levit. 6, verse 10. 16, verse 4. 23. 32. It is given, however, to Angels as likewise to Ministers of God, such as priests are: just as, conversely, the name of Angel is given to a priest in Malachi. But here the poderes (long robe) is given to Christ as High Priest, which title is attributed to him with the best right often in the epistle to the Hebrews. Concerning the poderes, see Josephus and Jerome in the booklet on priestly garments. The same name is also found in Apuleius. What is here ποδήρης is below λίνον λαμπρὸν (bright linen) 15, 6. Byssus is a most splendid kind of linen, about which Pliny 19, verse 1 can be seen.

That Angel in Ezek. IX. verse 2. and Dan. X. 3. is not a created Angel, but the Son of God. As the Weimar Bible, Döling, others of our side, Pareus, etc., rightly [hold]. For that is the priestly habit. But the priesthood does not belong to Angels but only to men, Heb. V. verse 1. The name מַלְאָךְ is given to a priest, which is common, denoting a messenger, Mal. II. verse 8. but are priests therefore to be called angelic spirits, or to be clothed in priestly habit? Angels are indeed seen in linen garments, Apoc. XV. verse 6. but not clothed in the poderes, which is a priestly habit, and since Christ appears clothed in it, Grotius himself acknowledges that his Priesthood is indicated. He presents himself as a Priest in the midst of the Church, because he does not lay aside that office for eternity, and performs it for the Church, Ps. CX. verse 4. both by the intercession of the virtue of his sacrifice, and by our blessing. That others make that garment an indication of gravity and wisdom, that its use was that of Senators, Scribes, and Doctors of the law, Mark XII. 38, and others understand it at the same time as the justice with which we must be clothed, does not fit so well: because the office proper to Christ was to be exhibited, and his adornment, not ours, which we have from him, is presented; therefore Interpreters commonly judge that the priesthood of Christ is noted. Irenaeus, book IV, chapter 32, refers this to priestly dignity. Cornelius a Lapide [says] the poderes is the hyacinthine tunic proper to the Pontiff, from chapter Exod. XXVIII. verse 31, he says, and that by it the Pontificate of Christ is signified, therefore he rejects the opinions of others, nor does he admit the opinion of his Alcazar, as if this prologue of the Apocalypse were represented by the first person and the sum of the whole spectacle (or of the Apocalypse) as genuine, but he wishes these things to look properly at the seven lampstands: Christ here assumes that appearance by which he represents to us his Pontifical office concerning these Churches, and any others, which he corrects, teaches, warns, and perfects, as will be clear in chapters II. and III. For all these things up to chapter IV. pertain to the first part of the Apocalypse, which is about the correction and instruction of the seven Churches and Bishops of Asia. Whence chapter V., where the other, namely the Prophetic part of the Apocalypse begins, another vision and another appearance of Christ, namely as the Lamb slain, is proposed. Secondarily, however, these things also pertain to the fifth chapter and the whole Apocalypse. For Christ here bears that appearance by which he represents his care, protection, and glorification of the faithful: but toward the impious, especially toward the Anti-Christ and his followers, terror and vengeance, which is the argument and scope of the whole Apocalypse. Pareus and Coccejus, asserting that royal majesty is designated by the long robe, hardly find what they might understand by the golden girdle.

From these things, however, it appears that it is unjust and truly sacrilegious that the Roman Pontiff should advertise himself as Vicar throughout the universal Church. For the duties of the absent are accustomed to be supplied, not those of the present, who by the very act are performing that office in the same place and time, the duty of which the vicar arrogates to himself.

Καὶ περιεζωσμένον πρὸς τοῖς μαστοῖς ζώνην χρυσῆν] It was the custom of Kings to wear golden belts, Job 12, verse 18, to which Isaiah 11, verse 5, and Psalm 18, verses 33, 40, allude. The same is attributed to Michael and the Prince of the Angels in Dan. 10, 5, where Theodotion (καὶ ἡ ὀσφὺς ἀυτῶ περιεζωσμένη ἐν χρυσίῳ ὠφάζ). However, just as a linen garment is attributed to Angels below in verse 6, so too is a golden belt. But it is deservedly attributed to Christ, as reigning over the Angels themselves, Eph. 1. 20.

We have already said, and in its proper place demonstrated, that it is not a created Angel Michael, but the Son of God who is understood in Daniel: which passage is parallel to ours: and therefore the same form is seen in both places, so that we may understand the same person of the Son of God to have been seen in both, there before the ἐνσάρκωσιν in an assumed human appearance, here after the ἐνσάρκωσιν in his own body, but conspicuous in singular Majesty, and so that we may not doubt that Daniel and the Johannine Apocalypse explain each other. That the kingly office of Christ is designated is beyond doubt. He made us both Kings and Priests, therefore he himself, as King, or Prince of Kings, as he is called in v. 4, and supreme Pontiff appears. But that a girdle is seen around his breasts contrary to custom, his charity toward the Church is noted. For between the breasts is the heart, the seat of love.

Latin:

Vers. 13.

Καὶ ἐν μέσῳ τῶν ἑπτὰ λυχνιῶν ὅμοιον ὑῷ ἀνθρώπε] Ange- lum in Christi figura, qui Christus tali nota describitur μυ- σικῶς apud Danielem 7, vers. 13. 10, vers. 5. Vide tum ibi, tum ad Matth. 8, vers. 20. dicta. Par loquutio infra 14. vers. In Manuscripto legitur: Καὶ ἐν μέσῳ τῶν λυχνιῶν ὁμοίωμα ὑᾶ ἀνθρώπε. Dicitur autem Christus versari in medio cande- labrorum, quia adest Ecclesiis, sicut & de Deo ἐμπεριπα- τεῖν usurpat Moses, Levit. 26, 11. & Paulus 2. Cor. 6, v. 6. & esse in medio Esaias cap. 11, vers. 6. Rem ipsam habes Matth. 18, v. 20. & 28, v. 20.

Revelatio à fronte facta complectitur visa, & audita. Visa, sunt res & persona, nempe cande- labra, & similis Filio hominis : Illorum indicatur & materia, quod aurea fuerint, & numerus, quod septem, quo mysterio septem Ecclesiae, non ve- ro universae Ecclesiae per totum orbem hic no- tantur, etsi perfectionis numerus sit, neque dubi- tari debeat pariter in medio aliarum Ecclesia- rum praesto esse Filium hominis, Matth. XVIII. vers. 20. & cap. XXVIII. vers. 20. Quia specifi- ce de septem Asiae Ecclesiis haec visio explica- tur, vers. 20. Numero illo puritatem designari nemo dixerit, quae per aurum potius denotatur, quod Ecclesiae doctrina & vitae puritate, quod ad fideles, fulgeant ac pretiosae sint, pretioso sanguine Filii Dei purificatae, Ebr. IX. vers. 25. quemadmodum aurum fulget & in pretio ha- betur. Nec aurea tantum dicitur Ecclesia pro- pter charitatem, sed etiam, quia, Cornelio dicen- te, quasi aurum igne & malleis persecutionum pro- batur, extenditur, formatur. Est ergo Ecclesia quasi candelabrum, inquit Pererius, per doctri- nam scripturarum lucida, per fulgorem virtutum splendida, per gravitatem morum ponderosa, per obedientiam ductilis, per praedicationem sonora, per perseverantiam extensa, per spem erecta, per fidem in Deo fundata, per charitatem Deo ad- stricta. Candelabra autem prius in oculos in- currunt, quam qui accendit ea. Facilius Ec- clesias quam Christum Ecclesiarum caput, funda- mentum ac Pastorem conspicimus, ut hic B. Cluverus.

Persona visa non Angelus aliquis est, sed Chri- stus ipse: Huic enim soli, non Angelo compe- tit illa oratio: Ego sum A & Ω. Item: Ego e- ram mortuus, & jam vivo. Per hominem in verbis similis hominis filio, multi veterum & recentiorum definite Christum intelligunt, quod ita explican- dum, non quod Christus ipse haud visus sit, sed tantum similis Christo: Sed quod persona visa Christo similis apparuerit, quantum ad ὀπτασίαν, quia magnificentia tanta apparuerit, ut quamvis revera Christus ipse fuerit, videretur tamen simi- lis filio hominis, vel Christo definite, non inde- finite homini. B. Cluverus ita explicat: Similem inquit Filio hominis Johannes, quia juxta carnis veritatem ut Filius hominis apparebat; at secun- dum divinam Majestatem hominis formam plu- rimam superabat. Gomarus tamen cum aliis mavult indefinite hominem aliquem interpreta- ri, ut præsentiam Christi in terris tollat: Ut enim inquit, humana figura duobus Angelis stipatus Abrahamo, antequam natus esset, exterius sese patefecit, Gen. XVIII. vers. 2. 17. Ita postquam in cælos ascendit, non suo corpore proprio, (quod in cælis ad diem judicii permanebit Act. III. v. 21.) sed sub specie humana, spiritui Johannis interius objecta sese revelavit, & hoc loco describitur ad- juncto vestitu & corporis externa specie. Sed colla- tio illa nulla est. Filius enim Dei ἄσαρκος po- tuit οἰκονομίᾳ προσκαίρῳ corpus humanæ figuræ assumere, sed ἔνσαρκος supra carnem suam, quam nunquam deponit, aliud humanum corpus assu- mere, sanæ Theologiæ non convenit. Neque externa tantum specie visus est Johanni, sed in ipsa natura humana, in qua mortem subierat, te- status: Ego eram mortuus, & ecce vivo, quod spectrum aliquod dicere non poterat. Neque dramate hic ludere, sed semetipsum Johanni sistere Christum gloria divina conspicuum, uni- versa apparitio & oratio, quam ad S. Johannem habuit, testatur. Non abnuit Coccejus: Fortasse, inquit, hoc nomen hic usurpatur, ut in Evangelio solet, ad notandum Jesum Christum, qui Filius hominis dicitur Psal. VIII. vers. 5. 6. Convenit, quod est Joh. V. vers. 27. potestatem ipsi dedit & judicium faciendi, quia Filius hominis est. Con- fidentius Pareus: Christum describi hac forma omnia docent, tum quod jubet Johannem scribere Apocalypsin vers. 19. & visiones sequentes ei reve- lat, cap. IV. vers. 1. Revelator vero Apocalypseos erat Christus, tum quod vers. 18. dicit, se vivere, sed fuisse mortuum, & esse vivum in secula secu- lorum, & habere claves inferorum & mortis, quod nec homini vel specici humanæ, nec Angelo, sed Christo unice convenit. Descriptio ex Dan. VII. vers. 10. magna parte desumpta est. Quod me- dius stat inter candelabra, significat, Christum non procul abesse, sed præsentem adesse in medio Eccle- siæ, ut Verbo & Spiritu gratia sua eam regat, di- rigat, defendat, servet, juxta promissiones, Matth. XVIII. vers. 20. cap. XXVIII. vers. 20. Hæc Pa- reus: Qui tamen contra Ubiquitarios, quos ita criminatur, pertendit, Humanam Christi natu- ram tantum in cælo, non in terra esse, donec inde ad judicium redeat. Sed si in medio Ecclesiarum ambulat Filius hominis, quum sine humana natura Filius Dei neque sit, neque uspiam præsto sit post incarnationem, neque dici possit Filius hominis, oportet, non in cœlis tantum, sed etiam in terris in medio Ecclesiarum suarum præ- sto esse humanam non minus, quam divinam na- turam, quorum utraque ad integritatem personæ Christi pertineat, neutra sine altera esse possit salva unione personali. Absurdum, quod infert Pareus: Christi Humanitatem habituram in manu sua septem Angelos & septem Ecclesias, rhomphæamq; prodituram ex ore ejus, procedit è confusione fi- guræ & rei figuratæ. Nam quod in figura litera- liter intelligitur, evolutione figuræ facta non li- teraliter, sed secundum μυστήριον, quod adum- bratum, explicandum; alias affingerentur Chri- sto septem oculi, septem cornua, pedes similes au- richalco. Sed alia est ratio personæ ipsius figura- tæ, alia figurarum istarum. Persona dicitur si- milis fuisse Filio hominis, &, interprete Pareo, Christus ipse, hominis Filius: innuitque Christum non procul abesse, sed præsentem adesse in medio Ecclesiæ, non utique dimidium tantum Christum, sed integrum, ad cujus integritatem omnino re- quiritur humana natura. Inepta ergo est obje- ctio Pareana de Christo in manu corporea haben- te septem Angelos & Ecclesias: (quod vero de Ecclesiis inseruit scripturæ, non invenitur in scri- ptura) de rhomphæa corporea: visa omnino talia sunt, uti litera habet: Sed ea repræsentatio non adumbrabat Christum revera in manu sua corpo- rea habere Angelos, sed in potestate sua: non exire corpoream rhomphæam ex ore ejus, sed rhomphæam Verbi.

Ineptiores nos dicit Pareus, qui prætextu visio- nis hujus imaginem Christi in templis tueamur, con- tra expressum Dei verbum. Verbo Dei expref- so id repugnare nunquam docebunt Carlstadiani deformatores. Si autem licet nostris oculis ima- ginem hic S. Johanni visam sistere, quod omni- no necessum est illis, qui concipiunt, mente sua, hanc ὀπτασίαν, cur non oculis corporis picturam eandem exhibere sive in templis, sive extra ea li- ceret? In nummis aureis, & argenteis ferunt ejus- modi imagines sanctuli illi, sed in templis neque pictas, neque fusas ferunt; num etiam aureas sta- tuas ad eam similitudinem fusas aut efformatas haud laturi, si donarentur, forte ambigendum? Si talia à Deo interdicta, qui Moses in taberna- culo, & Salomon in templo fieri fecit? quî Deus ut fierent in tabernaculo, & deinceps etiam in templo, similitudine, vel idea præ- scripta jussit?

Ἐνδεδυμένον ποδήρη] Sicut & Angeli describuntur, Ezech. 9, vers. 2. Dan. 10, vers. 5. Utrobique in Ebræo est בדים, quod in Ezechiele 70. transferunt ποδήρη, in Daniele vero Theodotion retinuit vocem Ebræam: alii interpretes ponunt ἐξαίρετα, alii βύσσινα. Est ea vestis Sacerdotalis, Exod. 28, vers. 38. Levit. 6, vers. 10. 16, vers. 4. 23. 32. Datur au- tem Angelis ut itidem Dei Ministris, quales sunt Sacerdotes: Sicut vicissim Sacerdoti datur Angeli nomen apud Malachi- am. Christo autem hic datur poderes ut Summo Sacerdoti, qui ei titulus optimo jure tribuitur sæpe in epistola ad Ebræ- os. De podere vide Josephum & Hieronymum libello de ve- stibus Sacerdotalibus. Est idem nomen & apud Apulejum. Quod hic ποδήρης infra λίνον λαμπρὸν 15, 6. Byssus li- ni splendidissimum genus, de quo videri potest Plinius 19, vers. 1.

Angelus ille Ezech. IX. vers. 2. & Dan. X. 3. non creatus est Angelus, sed Filius Dei. Ut re- cte Vinariens. Biblia, Döling. alii è nostris, Pareus, &c. Est enim ille habitus Sacerdotalis. Non au- tem Angelis sed hominibus solum sacerdotium convenit, Ebr. V. vers. 1. Datur Sacerdoti no- men, מַלְאָךְ, quod commune est, Legatum no- tans, Mal. II. vers. 8. sed num ideo Sacerdotes vo- candi Spiritus angelici, aut habitu sacerdotali ve- stendi? Linea veste quidem conspecti Angeli, Apoc. XV. vers. 6. non autem podere, qui habi- tus sacerdotalis est, vestiti, quo quum vestitus compareat Christus, Sacerdotium ejus indicari, agnoscit ipse Grotius. Sistit se ceu Sacerdotem in medio Ecclesiae, quod illud officium in aeternum non deponat, & eodem pro Ecclesia fungatur, Psal. CX. vers. 4. tum intercessione virtute sacri- ficii sui, tum benedictione nostri. Quod alii ve- stitum illum gravitatis & sapientiae indicium faciat, quod ejus usus Senatorum, Scribarum & legis Docto- rum fuerit, Marc. XII. 38. alii simul intelligant justitiam nobis induendam, non adeo convenit: quia munus Christo proprium erat exhibendum, ejusque ornatus, non noster, quem ab ipso ha- bemus, sistitur; ideo communiter sacerdotium Christi notari censent Interpretes Irenaeus l. IV. cap. 32. refert hoc ad Sacerdotalem dignitatem. Cornelius a Lapide poderem esse tunicam hyacin- thinam propriam Pontifici, e cap. Exod. XXVIII. vers. 31. ait, propriumque significari eo Christi Pontificatum, ideo alias aliorum opiniones re- probat, nec Alcafaris sui, quasi hic prologus A- pocalypseos prima persona & summa totius spe- ctaculi (vel Apocalypseos) repraesentetur, sen- tentiam ceu genuinam admittit, sed proprie vult haec spectare septem candelabra: Christus hic eam speciem assumit, qua repraesentet nobis officium ejus Pontificale circa hasce Ecclesias, & alias quas- vis, quas corripit, docet, monet, perficit, ut pate- bit cap. II. & III. Haec enim omnia usque ad cap. IV. pertinent ad primam Apocalypseos partem, quae est de correptione & instructione septem Ecclesiarum & Episcoporum Asiae. Unde cap. V. ubi incipit al- tera scilicet Prophetica Apocalypseos pars, alia visio & alia species Christi scilicet quasi Agni occisi pro- ponitur. Secundario tamen haec quoque ad caput quintum, totamque Apocalypsin pertinent. Chri- stus enim hic eam speciem gerit, qua repraesentat suam in fideles curam, protectionem & glorificatio- nem: In impios vero praesertim in Anti-Christum ejusque asseclas terrorem & vindictam, quod est argumentum & scopus totius Apocalypseos. Pa- reus & Coccejus talari veste Regiam Majestatem designari asserentes vix inveniunt, quid per Zo- nam auream intelligant.

Ex his vero apparet, iniquum esse vereque sa- crilegum, quod Romanus Pontifex Vicarium sese per universam Ecclesiam venditet. Absentium enim vices suppleri solent, non praesentium actu ipso, eodem loco & tempore illo mune- re fungentium, cujus vicem sibi arrogat vica- rius.

Καὶ περιεζωσμένον πρὸς τοῖς μαστοῖς ζώνην χρυσῆν] Erat hoc Regum balteos gestare aureos, Job. 12, vers. 18. quo alludit Esaias 11, vers. 5. & Psal. 18, vers. 33. 40. Idem tribuitur Mi- chaëli & Angelorum Principi Dan. 10, 5. ubi Theodotio (καὶ ἡ ὀσφὺς ἀυτῶ περιεζωσμένη ἐν χρυσίῳ ὠφάζ) Tribuitur au- tem ut linea vestis ita & aureus balteus etiam Angelis infra 15. v. 6. Christo autem merito idem tribuitur, ut regnanti su- per Angelos ipsos, Eph. I. 20.

Jam diximus, suoque loco demonstravimus, non Michaëlem Angelum creatum, sed Filium Dei apud Danielem intelligi: Qui locus nostro pa- rallelus est: atque ideo eadem forma utrobique conspicitur, ut eandem personam Filii Dei utro- bique visam esse, ibi ante ἐνσάρκωσιν in assum- pta specie humana, hic post ἐνσάρκωσιν in proprio suo corpore, sed Majestate singulari conspicuo, in- telligamus, utque Danielem & Apocalypsin Jo- hanneam mutuo sese explicare, ne dubitemus. Regale munus Christi designari, extra dubium est. Fecit nos & Reges & Sacerdotes, ideo ipse, ut Rex, vel Princeps Regum, ut v. 4. vocatur, & supre- mus Pontifex apparet. Quod autem præter mo- rem circa mamillas zona videtur, charitas ejus er- ga Ecclesiam notatur. Inter mamillas enim sedes amoris cor est.

## 1:14
Ver. 14.

And his head and his hairs were white, like white wool, as snow] What is attributed to GOD in Daniel VII. ver. 9 is here attributed to Christ. But, as we said regarding Daniel, pure judgments free from turbulent affections are signified. See also Matthew 28. ver. 3. Isaiah ch. I. 18 has a comparison of wool and snow at the same time. That hoary prudence is shadowed forth, which also seemed so to Pareus, we do not much oppose. That also seems more convenient than that the eternity of Christ is seen to be designated by others. Cornelius à Lapide thinks that eternity is described first, and consequently omniscience, omniprudence, and omniprovidence: Cocceius and Blasius de Vigeas were pleased with purity and holiness: which Aretas also asserts is figured. For that in Dan. VII. ver. 9 hoary hairs designate something different from eternity is clear from the fact that the latter is expressed by the name Ancient of Days: but knowledge and providence are hinted at by eyes flaming like fire. The likeness as white wool like snow is accustomed to be applied to purity, Ps. LI, Is. I. Pareus joins them: by the snowy color purity is noted. Therefore John saw Christ venerable in hoariness, to be respected for prudence, innocent in purity, and eternal in age.

And his eyes as a flame of fire] This is attributed to GOD in Ezekiel I. ver. 27, to Michael in Daniel X. ver. 6, and to Christ again below in XIX. ver. 2. Fire penetrates all things. Thus Christ sees through all things, even the most intimate, Heb. IV. ver. 13. Therefore he does not overlook any of the vices of the churches.

Gagneius wishes the omniscient mind of Christ, shining upon the just and burning the reprobate, to be noted; however, it pleases Ribera, Cornelius à Lapide, Alcazar, and Cocceius more that wrath and vengeance against the persecutors of Christians are designated. But wrath and vengeance are signified rather by the following emblem. Yet that eyes seeing through all things are also hinted at for the sake of vengeance can be gathered from Jer. XXXII. 19. His eyes are open, that he may render to the sons of men according to the fruit of their devices. Thus in ch. II. 18, 23, we see fiery eyes applied to divine perspicacity into the hidden and secret recesses of hearts: Cf. Ps. XXXIV. 17, Prov. V. 21, Job XXXIV. 21.

Latin:

Vers. 14.

Ἡ δὲ κεφαλὴ αὐτῶ κέ τρίχες λευκαὶ, ὡσεὶ ἔριον λευκὸν ὡς χιών] Quod DEO apud Danielem VII. vers. 9. idem hic tribuitur Christo. Significantur autem, ut ad Danielem dixi- mus, judicia pura à turbidis affectibus. Vide & Matth. 28. vers. 3. Lanæ simul & nivis comparationem habet Esaias cap. I. 18. Prudentiam canam, quod etiam Pareo visum, adumbrari, non multum repugnamus. Conve- nientius id etiam videtur, quam quod aliis æterni- tas Christi designari videtur. Cornelius à Lapide censet æternitatem primum, consequenter omni- scientiam, omniprudentiam, omniprovidentiam describi: Coccejo & Blasio de Vigeas, puritas & san- ctitas placuit: quam figuratam Aretas etiam asse- ruit. Nam Dan. VII. vers. 9. canos diversi quid ab æternitate designare, ex eo liquet, quod illa sit expressa per nomen Antiqui dierum: Scientia vero & providentia per oculos instar ignis flam- mantes innuitur. Similitudo ut lana alba tan- quam nix puritati adhiberi solet Psal. LI. Es. I. Conjungit illa Pareus: Niveo colore puritas no- tatur. Christum igitur Johannes vidit canitie venerandum, prudentia suspiciendum, puritate in- nocuum, ætate æternum.

Καὶ οἱ ὀφθαλμοὶ αὐτῶ ὡς φλὸξ πυρὸς] Hoc DEO tribui- tur apud Ezechielem I. vers. 27. Michaëli apud Danielem X. vers. 6. Christo iterum infra XIX. vers. 2. Ignis omnia penetrat. Sic Christus omnia etiam intima pervidēt, Ebr. IV. vers. 13. Ideo nulla Ecclesiarum vitia dissli- mulat.

Omnisciam mentem Christi justis lucentem, re- probos incendentem, notari Gagnejus vult, Ribe- ra tamen, Cornelio à Lapide, Alcasari & Coccejo magis placet iram & vindictam in persecutores Christianorum designari. Sed ira & vindicta po- tius sequenti emblemate significatur. Oculos ta- men omnia pervidentes etiam vindictæ causa in- nui, è Jerem. XXXII. 19. colligere est. Oculi ejus aperti sunt, ut reddat filiis hominum secundum fru- ctum adinventionum eorum. Sic cap. II. 18. 23. oculos igneos ad divinam perspicaciam in abdita at- que secreta cordium penetralia applicari vide- mus: Conf. Psal. XXXIV. 17. Proverb. V. 21. Job. XXXIV. 21.

## 1:15
Ver. 15.

And his feet like unto chalcolibanus] And this is attributed to Michael in Dan. X. v. 6, where in the Greek: His legs as the appearance of shining brass, and to the Cherubim in Ezek. I. ver. 17, where the LXX say: as flashing brass. We said that the probity of actions is signified by these. For by feet actions are signified, as we said on John XIII. ver. 10. But there are many of the same things in the vision of Daniel and in this vision of John: because just as there the adversities and prosperities of the Jewish people are predicted: so here those of the Christian people. Suidas says that chalcolibanus is made from glass and stone. But the Latin here translates it as aurichalcum, which Pliny teaches is a most excellent kind of copper, as do the Scholiast on the shield of Hesiod, and Servius. The common people called it aurichalcum because of its shine similar to gold, as is in Festus. Chalcolibanus seems to be a hybrid word from the Greek chalkos and the Syriac laban, which is to shine or to flash. For a similar reason, below, feet like fiery columns are given to the Angel. As if burned in a furnace] Thus Prov. X. ver. 21, kesef nivchar is translated as silver refined. Also tzaraph is translated as to be refined in many places and is said of silver in Ps. LXVI. ver. 9, Zech. XIII. ver. 9. But kaminos here is that which elsewhere is a crucible. Therefore, brass is signified that is both excellent by its own nature and, furthermore, purified by fire.

Some understand the Apostles here because of their fiery zeal and splendor due to their doctrine and life, Is. LII. ver. 7, Rom. X. ver. 15. Aretas, Flacius, Szegedinus, Winckelmannus, Gerhardus, Hogelius, Pererius, Alcazar: the Church to be tested by the fire of the cross, Augustine, Anselm, Haymo; the flesh of Christ flashing with communicated divine majesty, Gregory, Nazianzen, Rupertus, Ribera; most refer it to strength in preserving the Church, Thomas Anglicus, Junius, Hoë, Cluverus, the Vinarienses, which opinion can be properly joined with the preceding.

Not so much the probity of actions as the certainty of delivering the faithful and punishing enemies is hinted at, because the feet are prepared and inflamed for that by the zeal of love and wrath, which Cocceius acknowledges in part, even though he said that wrath inexorable against adversaries is already signified by the eyes seen like a flame of fire. It signifies, he says on this verse, that which is in Is. XXVII. ver. 4. If anyone sets me as a brier and thorn in battle, I will invade it, I will burn it together. Christ by his presence consumes all that is carnal, and burns up all thorns. To Pareus, however, it seems that singular strength and firmness and constancy are signified because of divine power. The blessed Cluverus agrees: The sense of the mystery here is: that Christ stands strongly and inexpugnably, with his feet fixed in his territory as if they were brazen columns: Meanwhile, his heel, bruised by the serpent, is scorched by the fire of tribulation, which, however, he overcomes with invincible solidity, nay, even as if with his own inflamed brass he forces it to a most present and far more terrible destruction. Indeed, just as the flaming eyes of Christ strike terror into enemies, whom he consumes like wax by the power and brightness of his wisdom, and drags out those desiring to hide in darkness, illuminating on the contrary whosoever detests the gloom: So his brazen feet, similarly ignited, testify that he is constant and immovable in protecting the ways of the pious, and, burning with the very heat which they snatched from the furnace of tribulation, they inflict so much the greater horror and ruin upon those subjected to them: These are the words of the blessed Cluverus. Which can be joined with the former. More alien is the opinion of certain ancients concerning the proving of the Church of the last time by vehement pressures, such as the interpretation of Augustine, Primasius, Anselm, Haymo, and also others concerning the Humanity of Christ, which, having been proved in the burning furnace of passions, was at length raised to shining glory. To these, however, Cornelius has been added. The feet of Christ were like unto fine brass in a burning furnace (in the Greek it is burning), that is, says Cornelius, the feet of Christ were most splendid, to wit, the humanity of Christ (which is signified by the feet, as the Deity by the head) was made by the furnace of passion and the cross most splendid and most strong for trampling upon Domitian and his enemies, and for burning him up. Thus Nazianzen in Andrew, and Damascene in Ribera, Rupert, Pannonius, and others, who all understand by the feet the Human nature in Christ. But Cornelius will scarcely obtain this gloss from all those cited. And it is inappropriate for the Deity to be denoted by the head and the Humanity by the feet; since the whole vision properly concerns the Son of man himself, whose members are thus distinctly represented for the sake of symbolic signification, the nature of the Son of man being preserved. For those divine attributes perfect, they do not destroy the human nature; they extol, they do not take away the same, the former of which is asserted against the Nestorians, the latter against the Eutychians and others. Cornelius is therefore inept when he concludes from this signification of the feet of Christ that John did not see a true man, but an image and specter of a man. For from the oἰκονομία of the apparition to the taking away of the truth τῆς ὀσίας or of the Human nature, the inference does not hold. Even though the external figure presented to the mind of St. John was most diverse, just as we see God himself represented by various figures: yet the Person of Christ is present, and thus also his human nature, according to which he is the Son of man, which is represented in this Apocalyptic book now in one habit, now in another, in different images, yet it is always present itself in its substantial form, even if exhibited in the vision in a differently varied habit, by which the same is figured according to other and yet other attributes, without prejudice to the truth of his nature.

And his voice as the voice of waters] Thus concerning the Cherubim, Ez. 1:24 and 43:2. See also below 19:6 and Is. 17:12, Jer. 50:42. As the sound of trumpets, so is the huge sound of the roaring sea. Thus the Gospel is heard far and wide.

Concerning this, Cornelius: This voice, says St. Gregory, Ticonius, Haymo, Seraphinus, and Pererius, is the preaching of the Gospel, so sonorous and powerful that its sound has gone out into all the earth. What roaring of the sea dashed against rocks, what confluences of the most rapid rivers, what cataracts of the Nile have resounded so far? This voice was therefore as of many waters; first because it quenched the thirst for temporal things like water, and cooled the heat of concupiscence: Second because it washed away the stains of sins: Third because it made fruitful the earth of human hearts, so that they might bring forth the fruits of virtues. Fourth because it converted many, nay all nations to Christ, and caused that everyone should invoke and praise God with their own voice. For this is a Music not of eight but of a hundred thousand voices, in the ears of God as sonorous as it is most acceptable. Hence chapter 17:15 it is said: The waters are many peoples, and nations, and tongues. Thus Primasius, Ambrose, Bede, Anselm, Richard, Rupert, Dionysius, and Pannonius. We judge, however, that the latter similarity is most signified, because that voice is to be diffused far and wide, and is to be very sonorous throughout the world. Primasius: In the voice, he says, he shows the Church preaching, to whom it is said, cry out, do not cease (Is. 58). But many waters are many peoples, by whose tongues Christ sounds. Berengandus: By the voice of many waters, the multitude of nations, which runs to the faith of Christ, is signified. And Bede: The voice of confession, of preaching, and of praise resounds not only in Judea, but among diverse peoples. That such a voice becomes Christ is evident through that of Ezekiel: I heard the sound of wings, as the sound of many waters, as the sound of the sublime God, Ez. 1:24.

Latin:

Vers. 15.

Καὶ οἱ πόδες αὐτῶ ὅμοιοι χαλκολιβάνῳ] Et hoc Michaëli tribuitur Dan. X. v. 6. ubi in Græco: Τὰ σκέλη ὡς ὅρασις χαλ- κῶ στίλβοντος, & Cherubinis Ezech. I. vers. 17. ubi LXX. ὡς ἀσράπτων χαλκός. Significari diximus per hæc actionum probitatem. Nam per pedes significantur actiones, ut di- ximus ad Joh. XIII. vers. 10. Sunt autem multa eadem in viso Danielis & in hoc viso Johannis: quia sicut ibi prædi- cantur adversa & prospera populi Judaici: Ita hic populi Christiani. Χαλκολίβανος ex vitro & lapide fieri ait Suidas. At Latinus hic vertit aurichalcum, quod æris genus esse præ- stantissimum Plinius docet, & Scholiastes ad clypeum He- siodi, & Servius. Vulgus ob similem auro fulgorem auri- chalcum dixit, ut apud Festum est. Videtur χαλκολίβανος vox esse hybrida ex Græco χαλκὸς & Syriaco לבן quod est στίλβειν vel ἐξαστράπτειν. Pari de causa infra Angelo dantur pedes quasi columnæ igneæ. Ὠς ἐν καμίνῳ πεπυρωμένοι] Sic Prov. X. vers. 21. כסף נבחר vertitur ἄργυρος πεπυρωμένος. Etiam צרף verti- tur πυρῦσθαι multis in locis & de argento dicitur Psal LXVI. vers. 9. Zach. XIII. vers. 9. Καμίνος autem hic id quod ali- bi χωνευτήριον. Significatur ergo æs & sua natura præstans, & præterea igne purgatum.

Apostolos hic nonnulli intelligunt ignei zeli, & splendoris ob doctrinam & vitam Es. LII. vers. 7. Rom. X. vers. 15. Aretas, Flacius, Szege- dinus, Winckelmannus, Gerhardus, Hogelius, Pererius, Alcafar: Ecclesiam igne crucis pro- bandam Augustinus, Anshelmus, Haymo; car- nem Christi communicata majestate divina co- ruscantem Gregorius, Nazianzenus, Rupertus, Ribera; plerique ad robur in conservanda in Ec- clesia referunt, Thomas Anglicus, Junius, Hoë, Cluverus, Vinarienses, quæ sententia cum præce- dente conjungi probe potest.

Non tam actionum probitas, quam liberandi fideles & puniendi hostes certitudo innuitur, quod pedes parati & inflammati sint ad id Zelo amoris & iræ, quod ex parte agnoscit Coccejus, etsi per oculos instar flammæ ignis visos iram ἀπαραίτητον in adversarios jam significari dixerit. Significa- tur, inquit ad hunc versum, quod est Es. XXVII. vers. 4. Si quis me, ut sentis & spina, posuerit in bello, invadam eam, incendam pariter. Christus sua præsentia concremat omne id, quod carnale est, omnesque spinas exurit. Pareo ramen videtur si- gnificari robur singulare ac firmitas & constan- tia propter divinam potentiam. Concimnius B. Cluverus: Mysterii sensus hic est: Christum fortiter & inexpugnabiliter stare, pedibus tan- quam æreis columnis territorio suo infixis: In- terim contritum à serpente calcaneum ejus igne tribulationis ustulari, quem tamen invicta solidi- tate superet, imo tanquam ære suo inflammato ad præsentissimam longeque terribiliorem per- niciem cogat. Nimirum sicut oculi flammantes Christi terrorem incutiunt hostibus, quos sa- pientiæ suæ vi & fulgore tanquam ceram consu- mit, protrahitque in tenebris delitescere cu- pientes, illuminans contra, quicunque detestan- tur caliginem: Sic pedes ejus ærei similiter igniti constantem eum & immobilem in tuendis piorum viis testantur, ipsoque quem è camino tribulationis corripuerunt æstu flagrantes, tanto majorem subjectis horrorem clademq; inferunt: Hæc B. Cluverus. Quæ cum prioribus conjungi possunt. Alienior est veterum quorundam de Ecclesiæ novissimi temporis vehementis pressurarum probanda sententia, utpote Augustini, Primasii, Anshelmi, Haymonis, necnon aliorum de Hu- manitate Christi interpretatio, quæ in ardenti pas- sionum camino probata tandem ad gloriam fulgen- tem evecta est. Quibus tamen accessit Cornelius. Pedes Christi similes erant aurichalco in camino ar- denti (in Græco est ardentes) hoc est, inquit Cor- nelius, pedes Christi erant splendidissimi, puta hu- manitas Christi, (quæ per pedes significatur, uti Deitas per caput) per caminum passionis & crucis fa- cta est splendidissima & fortissima ad conculcandum Domitianum, suosq; hostes, & ad eum comburendum. Ita Nazianzenus apud Andream, & Damascenus apud Riberam, Rupertus, Pannonius aliiq́, qui omnes per pedes intelligunt Humanam naturam in Christo. Sed hanc glossam vix ab omnibus illis adductis im- petrabit Cornelius. Et inconveniens est per ca- put Deitatem, per pedes Humanitatem notari; quum tota visio proprie ipsummet Filium hominis concernat, cujus membra ita distincte symbolicæ significationis causa salva Filii hominis natura, re- præsentata. Nam attributa illa divina perficiunt, non interficiunt humanam naturam, extollunt non tollunt eandem, quorum illud contra Nestoria- nos, hoc contra Eutychianos alias adstruitur. In- eptus ergo est Cornelius, cum ex hac pedum Chri- sti significatione concludit, Johannem non vidisse verum hominem, sed hominis imaginem & spectrum. Nam ab oἰκονομίᾳ apparitionis ad tollendam veri- tatem τῆς ὀσίας vel naturæ Humanæ non valet con- sequentia. Etsiamsi figura externa menti S. Johan- nis exhibita maxime diversa fuerit, quemadmo- dum variis figuris Deum ipsum repræsentari vide- mus: Persona tamen Christi præsto adest, adeoque natura etiam humana, secundum quam est Filius hominis, quæ modo hoc, modo alio habitu, in diversis imaginibus repræsentatur in hoc Apoca- lyptico libro, semper tamen adest ipsa in sua sub- stantiali forma, etsi habitu diversimodo in visione exhibita, quo eadem secundum alia, atque alia attributa figuratur, salva naturæ veritate.

Καὶ ἡ φωνὴ ἀυτῦ ὡς φωνὴ ὑδάτων] Sic de Cherubinis Ez. I. 24. & XLIII. 2. Vide & infra XIX. 6. & Es. XVII. v. 12. Jerem. L. 42. Sicut tubæ, ita maris clangentis ingens est sonus. Sic Evangelium longe lateque auditur.

De hoc Cornelius : Hæc vox ait S. Gregorius, Ticonius, Haymo, Seraphinus, & Pererius est præ- dicatio Evangelii, ita sonora & potens, ut sonus ejus exiverit in omnem terram. Quis maris fremitus cautibus illisi, quæ fluminum rapidissimorum con- fluges, quæ Nili catadupa tam longe personarunt? Fuit ergo hæc vox quasi aquarum multarum; primo quia aquæ instar restinxit sitim rerum temporalium, & refrigeravit æstum concupiscentiæ: Secundo quia abluit maculas peccatorum: Tertio quia fœcundavit terram cordium humanorum, ut fructus virtutum proferant. Quarto quia multos imo omnes gentes ad Christum convertit, fecitque, ut quique sua voce in- vocent & laudent Deum. Hæc enim est Musica non octo sed centum millium vocum, in auribus Dei uti sonora, ita gratissima. Hinc cap. XVII. 17. dici- tur: Aquæ multi populi sunt, & gentes & linguæ. Ita Primasius, Ambrosius, Beda, Anshelmus, Richar- dus, Rupertus, Dionysius & Pannonius. Postre- mam tamen similitudinem maxime significari cen- semus, quod vox ea se longe lateque diffusura, & valde sonora per orbem futura sit. Primasius: In voce, inquit, Ecclesiam ostendit prædicantem, cui dicitur, clama, ne cesses (Es. LVIII.) Aqua autem multæ populi multi sunt, quorum linguis sonat Chri- stus. Berengandus: Per vocem aquarum multa- rum multitudo gentium, quæ ad fidem Christi con- currit, signatur. Et Beda: Vox confessionis, præ- dicationis & laudis non in Judæa tantum, sed in di- versis populis resonat. Quod autem hujusmodi vox deceat Christum, patet per illud Ezechielis: Au- diebam sonum alarum, quasi sonum aquarum mul- tarum, quasi sonum sublimis Dei Ezech. I. 62.

## 1:16
Verse 16.

And having] Supply 'was'. But in the Manuscript 'having' is missing.

In his right hand seven stars] The stars are Doctors, as we said at Matt. 24:29. To teach in the Christian Church, however, belongs especially to Bishops, whom we shall learn are figured here below in verse 20. Thus also the Apostles are figured by stars below 12:1. Stars are not unlike gems: whence also to poets those things which are gemmed are called starred, as is in Ovid, Metam. 8.

-- Let gems be turned into shining fires. That is, into stars. But gems were accustomed to be worn on the right hand, Jer. 22:24, Hag. 2:24, Sir. 43:13. By that it is signified that good Bishops are of great value to Christ, and are solicitously guarded by him.

That Doctors are understood by stars, there is no need to seek elsewhere. For the explanation of this mystery has been added in verse 20. But seven are counted, not because he does not have all Doctors in his hand, but because Christ was seen here for the sake of the seven Bishops of Asia. The interpretations of the seven stars, as well as of the seven candlesticks and seven Churches, of Victorinus, Tyconius, Ambrose, Bede, Haymo, are alien, because he walked among the candlesticks, but held the stars in his hand: we have from verse 20 that the candlesticks denote the Churches, but the stars the Bishops of the Churches, as well as those concerning the seven Angelic celestial Spirits, as some ancients accepted, Origen in

Num. 21. Hilary on Ps. 124. Nazianzen, oration 32. Jerome on Matt. 18. Maldonatus on Matt. 18. because it is evident from verse 20 and from the epistles themselves that the Bishops of the Churches of Asia are understood by the Angels: as well as those concerning the seven gifts of the Spirit, which is the explanation of Victorinus, Seraphinus, and Montanus, as well as those concerning the seven degrees of things in universality, as Andreas explained in this place. Concerning other expositions, especially that of Alcazar, let his associate Cornelius be seen, who himself calls those inventions, and denies that they are solid and genuine, since he transforms the stars into gems, nay into rings, of which there is no mention here. But he is said to carry them in his right hand, that is, to protect, to observe, to move powerfully for his good pleasure, and to show them as the excellent ornament of his own virtue, indeed through whom he also confounds the force and height of adversaries: Cf. Is. 49:16, John 10:28, 2 Cor. 2:14, Ps. 84:7, as B. Cluverus rightly.

And out of his mouth a sharp two-edged sword proceeding] Again supply 'was'. The Evangelical word proceeding from the mouth of Christ penetrates the innermost parts: and it discerns not only actions, but also good and evil thoughts. See what was said at Heb. 4:12, Eph. 6:17, and below 2:12, 16. Elsewhere a sword signifies vengeance: but what I have said is more convenient to those things which will follow, pertaining to the Churches. Tertullian translates 'a two-edged sword' as 'a sword twice sharpened' in 'Against the Jews', and a third time in 'Against Marcion'. See also below 19:15.

The cited passages sufficiently show that the Word of God is being designated. Its power, however, is to be referred not only to the penetration of the inmost parts of the hearts, but also to their conversion as well as their condemnation. Hearts are said to be rent in salutary contrition, Joel II, to which also the spiritual circumcision of the heart contributes, Deut. XXX. 6, Jerem. IV. 4. By this sword also the διχοτομία of the impious is made, concerning which Luke XII. 48, cf. Apoc. XIX. 15. Tyconius, Primasius, Arethas, Haymo, Anselm, Richard, Victorinus, and Alcasar explain the sword as the Word of God, as Cornelius admits, who, however, rashly abandons that opinion and understands the sword as the sentence of condemnation and the condemnation itself, in which opinion he also cites Andrew, Arethas, Rupert, Bede, Lyra, Seraphinus, and Ribera: But those things pertain to the power and effect of the mystical sword, that is, the divine word, but they are not the sword itself. B. Cluverus more correctly: Christ fights with his mouth, not with horses or chariots, Zech. IV. 6 and ch. IX. 10. Yet not with a mouth that is unarmed, naked, or ineffective, but armed, and indeed with a two-edged sword. For is it not a stupendous power to produce a two-edged sword from the mouth, which penetrates bones and marrow, Heb. IV. 12? The same Lord Messiah agrees, crying out in the Prophet Isa. XLIX. 2: He has made my mouth like a sharp sword; in the shadow of his hand he hid me, and made me a polished arrow; in his quiver he hid me. Rightly, therefore, Victorinus, Augustine (book XX of the City of God, ch. 21), Andrew, Primasius, Anselm, and other Doctors gather from Eph. VI. 17 that this sword is the Word of God, since it proceeds from the mouth, Isa. XI. 4, 2 Tim. II. 8. The Word of Christ is therefore a rhomphaea, by which he crushes and cuts whatever is in the way, by which he amputates the luxury of the flesh, kills the old Adam, drives men to obey his kingdom, strikes down those who stubbornly resist to their destruction, nay, by whose strict and finally irrevocable sentence he consigns the impious to eternal torments of body and soul, Deut. XXXII. verse 41, Isa. LXVI. 16, Matt. XXV. Rupert: This sword of judgment, sharp on both sides, will then go forth from his mouth, and will effectively discern and judge both sides, namely the right and the left, according to their merits.

And his countenance shines as the sun in his strength] His whole face was shining just as the Sun, when it shines most brightly. That is a sign of Majesty, as in Matt. 17, v. 2. Add Hab. 3, 4. The same is attributed to the Angel below .XI. Great, however, is the consolation of the pious, because they themselves, though in their own degree, will be such, Matt. 13, 43.

His Majesty is thus expressed in Dan. X. 6: his face is like the appearance of lightning. Lightning is not easily looked upon with unharmed eyes; so the radiance of the Sun in its meridian strength dazzles and injures the eyes of those who look at it. Pareus himself acknowledges that the divine Majesty and supreme glory, by which the Humanity of Christ shines at the right hand of God in the heavens, is noted. Although Primasius and Tyconius do not incorrectly compare Christ to the Sun, because he was born and suffered and rose again, just as the Sun rises, sets, and emerges again, and Andreas Aretas and Lyranus, because he is the Sun or spiritual light of the world; yet Christ is not called the Sun here, but the appearance of his face is compared to the Sun, not for the splendor of this ἀποκαλύψεως, as Seraphinus, or of the Gospel, as Antoninus, or of the Church in the sixth age, as Joachim Abbas, or of the faithful, as Anselm and Thomas Anglicus, or even of the Roman Church, as Alcafar, whom Cornelius himself rejects here, wished, but to designate Christ himself: Whom Pareus indeed and others explain by the splendor of his glorious body, to which opinion the transfiguration of Christ in Matt. XVII. 2 seems to favor, for in that too his face shone like the Sun, which Ribera and Cornelius adduce. But because the splendor of the glorious body is proper and native to Christ in glory, but here it seems to be understood as symbolic and σημαντικὸς, when his face shone like light and the Sun, his face seems to be designated as gracious toward his own, whom he illuminates with the splendor of his grace, 2 Cor. IV. 6, and whom he will gloriously illuminate in the other life with the light and splendor of his face, Apoc. XXI. 23, c. XXII. v. 5. Which future grace he shows to the faithful by this symbolic apparition; for which sense Cornelius praises Tyconius, Ambrose, Haymo, Rupert, and Pererius. Although we are to be σύμμορφοι to the body of his glory, Phil. 3, 21, and to shine like the Sun, Matt. XIII. 13, yet it is not our glory, but Christ's, with which he will crown us, that is exhibited. I repeat again, says the blessed Cluverus here, that Christ appears here such as the fates of the Church, which will be commemorated hereafter, require. For in order that it may be established that the face of Christ, even if it is as it were obscured by heresies and the shedding of the blood of the pious, and its radiance is intercepted from the inhabitants of the world, nevertheless remains most bright and most shining like the meridian Sun, dazzling the sight of all eyes, so that it can provide most sufficient light to the pious, but blind and stupefy the dim-sighted, such a refulgence of countenance is altogether fitting for him, and therefore below in chapter X. 1, the Angel, opposed to the beast and its dark kingdom, radiates with a similar brightness. Then, just as the Sun illuminates all things, communicates light to the moon, the stars, and the whole orb of the earth, whose face, however, no one can look upon with a direct gaze of the eyes: so the universal Church and its Doctors, whom the Lord sustains with his own hand, borrow light from him, Is. LX. 1 sqq., John I. 9, c. VIII. 12, IX. 5, XII. 35, 46. Thirdly, as the vital radiance of the Sun recreates, vegetates, and gladdens the whole world with its creatures; so the grace shining forth from Christ's countenance is friendly, salutary, and vivifying to all who are made truly partakers of it. Wherefore this comparison of the Savior with the Sun is most pleasant, used also by David in Ps. 19 and 84, and by the holy prophet Malachi in c. IV. Nay, the Lord himself, dwelling among us, when he revealed the glory and power of his kingdom to the Disciples on the mount, imparted the brightness of the Sun to his face, Matt. 17, 2. For which reason the saints desire his face to shine upon them (Ps. 4, 6, and 31, 17, and 67, 2, and 80, 4, 8, 20), and the Priest is commanded to pray for his propitious light for the people, Num. VI. For truly happy and blessed is he upon whose soul the most pleasant voice of that countenance radiates; sad, on the contrary, and placed in the shadow of death, is he to whom this face is hidden, or looked upon as indignantly turned away. Thus, therefore, he shows what he will show himself to be in these things which are revealed in the present ἀποκαλύψει, and he teaches symbolically what the προσκείμενα and ἀξιώματα of his presence and assistance are, when, for instance, our Priest and King walks in the midst of the golden lampstands: 1. Regarding the holiness and divine purity of his judgments through his snow-white hair. 2. Regarding divine omniscience and providence through his eyes of fire. 3. Regarding divine zeal for vindicating the Church through his feet as if burning from a furnace. 4. Regarding the propagation of divine doctrine through his voice sounding like many waters. 5. Regarding the divine direction and conservation of the Doctors of the Word through the stars carried in his hand. 6. Regarding the divine efficacy of the Word through the two-edged sword. 7. Regarding divine grace through the face of splendor, shining upon us like the Sun, signified: In which way the comparison with the Sun also applies here: that just as the Sun illuminates the moon and other stars: so Christ illuminates with his light both the Doctors, as stars, and those who are in a lower place, as the moon, the Auditors: And what other comparisons of this kind are sought from the splendor of the Sun.

Latin:

Vers 16.

Καὶ ἔχων] Supple ἦν. At in Manuscripto deest ἔχων.

Ἐν τῇ δεξιᾷ ἀυτῦ χειρὶ ἀςέρας ἑπτὰ] Stellæ sunt Docto- res, ut diximus ad Matth. XXIV. 29. Docere autem in Ec- clesia Christiana præcipue est Episcoporum, quos hic figu- rari discemus infra 20. Sic & Apostoli per stellas figu- rantur infra XII. 1. Stellæ non dissimiles gemmis: unde & Poëtis quæ gemmata sunt, stellata dicuntur, ut apud O- vidium est Metam. VIII.

-- Gemmæ nitidos vertantur in ignes. Id est in stel- las. Gemmæ autem in manu dextra ferri solebant, Jerem. XXII. 24. Agg. II. 24. Sir. XLIII. 13. Per id significatur, bo- nos Episcopos in magno apud Christum esse pretio, & ab eo solicite custodiri.

Doctores per stellas intelligi, non aliunde opus est petamus. Addita enim est v. 20. mysterii hu- jus explicatio. Septem autem numerantur, non quod non omnes Doctores in manu sua habeat, sed quia conspiciebatur hic Christus septem Epi- scoporum Asiæ gratia. Alienæ sunt interpretatio- nes septem stellarum, tum de septem candelabris, & septem Ecclesiis, Victorini, Tyconii, Ambrosii, Bedæ, Haymonis, quia inter candelabra ambulabat, stellas vero in manu habebat: Candelabra Ecclesias notare, stellas vero Episcopos Ecclesiarum, e v. 20. habemus, tum de septem Angelis Spiritibus cœ- lestibus, ut accepere veteres nonnulli, Origenes in

Num. XXI. Hilarius in Psal. CXXIV. Nazianzenus orat. XXXII. Hieronymus in Matth. XVIII. Maldonatus in Matth. XVIII. quia per Angelos Episcopos Ecclesiarum Asiae intelligi e v. 20. & ex ipsis epistolis evidens est : tum de septem donis Spiritus, quae Victorini, Seraphini, & Montani explicatio est, tum de septem rerum in universalitate gradibus, ut Andreas in h. l. exposuit. De aliis expositionibus, imprimis Alcasaris videatur socius ejus Cornelius, qui ipse ea commenta vocat, ac solida & genuina esse negat, quum transformet stellas in gemmas, imo in annulos, quorum hic nulla est mentio. In manu autem dextra gestare dicitur, id est tueri, observare, potenter movere pro beneplacito, & tanquam eximium virtutis suae decorem ostentare, quippe per quos etiam adversariorum vim & altitudinem confundat : Conf. Es. XLIX. 16. Job. X. 28. 2. Cor. II. 14. Psal. LXXXIV. 7. ut recte B. Cluverus.

Καὶ ἐκ τοῦ στόματος αὐτοῦ ῥομφαία δίστομος ὀξεῖα ἐκπορευομένη] Rursus subaudi ἦν. Sermo Evangelicus ex Christi ore proficiscens intima penetrat : neque actiones tantum, sed & cogitata bona malaque discernit. Vide quae dicta ad Ebr. IV. 12. Eph. VI. 17. & infra II. 12. 16. Alibi gladius ultionem significat : sed quod dixi convenientius est iis, quae sequentur, ad Ecclesias pertinentia. Μάχαιραν δίστομον ensem bis acutum vertit Tertullianus adversus Judaeos, & tertio adversus Marcionem. Vide & infra XIX. 15.

Verbum Dei designari loca adducta satis docent. Ejus autem vis non tantum ad penetrationem intimorum cordium, sed etiam eorundem tum conversionem tum condemnationem referenda. Scindi corda dicuntur in contritione salutari, Joël. II. ad quam etiam facit spiritualis cordis circumcisio, Deut. XXX. 6. Jerem. IV. 4. Hoc etiam gladio διχοτομία impiorum fit, de qua Luc. XII. 48. conf. Apoc. XIX. 15. Gladium de Verbo Dei explicant Tyconius, Primasius, Arethas, Haymo, Anshelmus, Richardus, Victorinus & Alcasar fatente Cornelio, qui vero temere illam sententiam relinquit, & de sententia condemnationis ipsaque condemnatione gladium intelligit, in quam sententiam allegat etiam Andream, Aretam, Rupertum, Bedam, Lyranum, Seraphinum & Riberam : Sed ista ad gladii mystici, hoc est, verbi divini vim & effectum pertinent, non vero gladius ipse sunt. Rectius B. Cluverus : Pugnat ore Christus non equis aut curribus, Zach. IV. 6. & cap. IX. 10. Ore tamen non inermi, nudo, aut inefficaci sed armato, & quidem ense bis acuto. Nonne enim vis stupenda est oris gladium producere ancipitem, qui penetret ossa & medullas Ebr. IV. 12. Consentit idem Dominus Messias clamans apud Prophetam Es. XLIX. 2. Posuit os meum sicut gladium acutum, in umbra manus suae abscondit me, & posuit me in tersam sagittam, in pharetra sua abscondit me. Recte igitur Victorinus, Augustinus, (libr. XX. de civ. Dei cap. 21.) Andreas, Primasius, Anshelmus & caeteri Dd. ex Eph. VI. 17. colligunt, gladium hunc esse Verbum Dei cum ore procedat Es. XI. 4. 2. Tim. II. 8. Est igitur Verbum Christi rhomphaea, qua comminuit inciditque quidvis obvium, qua luxuriam carnis amputat, veterem Adamum occidit, homines ad obediendum regno suo adigit, pertinacius resistentes ad internecionem caedit, imo cujus stricta tandem & irrevocabili sententia impios aeternis corporum animarumque cruciatibus nuncupat, Deut. XXXII. vers. 41. Es. LXVI. 16. Matth. XXV. Rupertus : Iste judicii gladius utraque parte acutus tunc de ore ejus exibit, & utramque partem, dexteram scilicet & sinistram pro meritis efficaciter discernet atque dijudicabit.

Καὶ ἡ ὄψις αὐτοῦ ὡς ὁ ἥλιος φαίνει ἐν τῇ δυνάμει αὐτοῦ] Tota fasies ejus ita splendebat, sicut Sol, cum- splendet maxime. Id signum Majestatis, ut Matth. 17, v. 2. Adde Abac. 3,4. Angelo idem tribuitur infra .XI Magna au- tem piorum consolatio, quod & ipsi,suo tamen gradu tales e- runt, Matth 13, 43.

Majestas ejus ita exprimitur Dan. X. 6. facies ejus sicut aspectus fulguris. Fulgur illæsis oculis non facile aspicitur, ita Solis jubar in vigore me- ridiano perstringit læditq; intuentium oculos. Di- vinam Majestatem gloriamque summam, qua Chri- sti Humanitas ad dextram Dei in cælis refulget, no- tari, Pareus ipse agnoscit. Quanquam vero non inrecte Christum Soli conferant Primasius & Ty- conius, quia natus est & passus & resurrexit, sicut Sol oritur, occidit & rursus emergit, & Andreas Aretas ac Lyranus, quia Sol est seu spiritualis lux mundi; non tamen hic Christus Sol dicitur, sed faciei ejus aspectus Soli comparatur ad splendo- rem non ἀποκαλύψεως hujus, ut Seraphinus, aut Evangelii, ut Antoninus, aut Ecclesiæ in sexta ætate, ut Joachimus Abbas, vel fidelium, ut Ans- helmus & Thomas Anglicus, vel etiam Ecclesiæ Ro- manæ, ut Alcafar, quem ipse Cornelius hic reji- cit, voluere, sed ipsiusmet Christi designandum: Quem de gloriosi corporis splendore Pareus qui- dem & alii explicant, cui sententiæ favere vide- tur transfiguratio Christi Matth. XVII. 2. nam & in illa facies ejus lucebat instar Solis, quo Ribera, Cornelius adducit. Sed quia splendor corporis gloriosi Christo in gloria proprius & nativus est, hic autem symbolicus σημαντικὸς intelligendꝫ pro- prie videtur, cum luxit facies ejus instar lumi- nis & Solis, facies ejus gratiosa erga suos designa- ri videtur, quos splendore gratiæ suæ illuminat, 2. Cor. IV. 6. gloriose in altera vita faciei suæ lu- mine & splendore collustraturus Apoc. XXI. 23. c. XXII. v. 5. Quam gratiam futuram fidelibus hac symbolica apparitione ostentat; pro quo sensu Tyconium, Ambrosium, Haymonem, Rupertum & Pererium laudat Cornelius. Quamvis vero σύμ- μορφοι futuri simus τῷ σώματι τῆς δόξης αὐτ῵, Phil. 3, 21. & fulsuri ut Sol Matth. XIII. 13. Non nostra tamen sed Christi gloria, qua nos coronabit, ex- hibetur. Iterum repeto, inquit hic B. Cluverus, talem hic apparere Christum, qualem Ecclesia fata, quæ deinceps commemorabuntur, requirant. Ut e- nim constet, Christi faciem, etiamsi hæresibus & sanguinis piorum effusionibus quasi obscuretur, & fulgor ejus mundi habitatoribus intercipiatur, ni- hilominus lucidissimam fulgentissimamque manere ad instar Solis meridiani omnium aciem oculorum præstringentis, ut piis lumen sufficientissimum præ- bere, luscisiosis autem excæcare & obstupefacere possit, omnino convenit ipsi hujusmodi vultus efful- guratio, ideoque infra cap. X. 1. Angelus bestia re- gnoque ejus tenebroso oppositus simili fulgore radiat. Deinde sicut Sol illustrat omnia, luna, stellis toti- que adeo terrarum orbi lumen communicat, cujus ta- men faciem directa oculorum acie nemo potest intue- ri: Sic Ecclesia universa ejusque Doctores, quos sua manu sustentat Dominus, ab ipso lumen mutuan- tur, Es.LX. 1. sqq. Joh. I. 9. c. VIII. 12. IX. 5. XII. 35. 46. Tertio ut Solis vitale jubar universum cum crea- turis orbem recreat, vegetat & lætificat; Sic gratia ex Christi vultu exsplendescens, amica, salutaris & vi- vifica omnibus est, qui ejus redduntur vere participes, Quamobrem jucundissima est hæc Salvatoris cum Sole collatio Davidi quoque Psal. 19. & 84. & Sanct. Malachia vati usurpata c. IV. Quin & ipse Domi- nus habitans inter nos, cum gloriam vimque regni sui Discipulis in monte patefaceret, Solis claritatem faciei suæ indidit, Matth. 17, 2. Quam sibi faciem idcirco lucere optant sancti, (Psal. 4, 6. & 31, 17. & 67, 2. & 80, 4. 8. 20.) ejusque lucem precari pro- pitiam jubetur Sacerdos populo Num. VI. Vere enim latus beatusque est, cujus animo amœnissima istius vultus vox irradiat, tristis contra, ac in umbra mor- tis positus, cui tecta hac facies, indignanter aversa prospicitur. Sic ergo qualem sese exhibiturus sit in his, quæ in præsenti ἀποκαλύψει revelantur, ostendit, & præsentiæ, & assistentiæ suæ προσκεί- μενα & ἀξιώματα, qualis illa sit, cum ambulat sci- licet Sacerdos & Rex noster in medio candelabrorum aureorum symbolice docet: 1. Quoad judiciorum sanctitatem & puritatem divinam per capillos ni- veos. 2. Quoad divinam omniscientiam & provi- dentiam per oculos igneos. 3. Quoad divinum ze- lum pro vindicanda Ecclesia per pedes ceu è camino ardentes. 4. Quoad doctrinæ divinæ propagationem per vocem sonoram instar aquarum. 5. Quoad di- vinam directionem & conservationem Doctorum Verbi per stellas in manu gestatas. 6. Quoad divi- nam Verbi efficaciam per gladium ancipitem. 7. Quo- ad divinam gratiam per faciem splendoris, Solis in- star nobis affulgentem, significatam: Quo pacto e- tiam huc facit comparatio cum Sole: quod sicut Sol lunam & stellas alias illuminat: Ita Christus cum Doctores per stellas, tum qui inferiori loco sunt instar lunæ Auditores luce sua illuminet: Et quæ hujusmodi aliæ a splendore Solis petuntur compa- rationes.

## 1:17
Vers. 17.

And when I saw him, I fell at his feet as dead) For fear, as in Joshua V, v. 15, and Dan. VIII. 8, and X. 8, 9, where see Jacchiades. The same happened to the Apostles, Matt. XVII. 6.

And he laid his right hand upon me saying to me Fear) He raised me up with a gesture and voice at the same time, as the Angel did to Daniel in chapter VIII. 18, X. 10, 11. In the Manuscript: He laid his right hand upon me.

Latin:

Vers. 17.

Καὶ ὅτε εἶδον ἀυτὸν, ἔπεσον πρὸς τὲς πόδας ἀυτῶ ὡς νεκρὸς) Præ metu ut Josuæ V, v. 15. & Dan. VIII. 8. & X. 8. 9. ubi Jac- chiadem vide. Idem Apostolis evenit, Matth. XVII. 6.

Καὶ ἐπέθηκε τὴν δεξιὰν ἀυτῶ χεῖρα ἐπ᾽ ἐμὲ λέγων μοὶ Φοβῶ) Gestu simul & voce me erexit, ut Danielem Angelus cap. VIII. 18. X. 10. 11. in Manuscripto: Ἔθηκε τὴν δεξιὰν ἀυτῶ ἐπ᾽ ἐμέ.

## 1:17
Ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ πρῶτος καὶ ὁ ἔσχατος) First, that is, highest in dignity with power much greater than anyone before. Concerning this meaning of the word πρῶτος, see what has been said at John 1:15. Last, that is, the most despised of men, Isaiah 53:3, namely captured, mocked, beaten, scourged, condemned to punishment, and indeed a servile one.

In that sense, without doubt, he professes concerning himself: Ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ πρῶτος καὶ ὁ ἔσχατος, in which he previously testified with a sonorous voice in verse 11, Ἐγώ εἰμι τὸ Α καὶ τὸ Ω, ὁ πρῶτος καὶ ὁ ἔσχατος, and will testify in Revelation 22:13: Ἐγώ εἰμι τὸ Α καὶ τὸ Ω, ἀρχὴ καὶ τέλος, ὁ πρῶτος καὶ ἔσχατος. These things, however, do not treat of the highest in dignity in exaltation and the lowest in the state of humiliation, but rather of the eternal Deity of Christ, whence Athanasius and other ancients prove the eternity and Deity from this title of Christ.

Καὶ ὁ ζῶν] that is, life-giving: in which sense it is also placed in John 6:51 and Acts 7:38. Christ, while acting on earth, had brought life to the dead, and health (which itself is also called life by the Hebrews) to the sick.

Latin:

Ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ πρῶτος καὶ ὁ ἔσχατος) πρῶτος, id est, sum- mus dignitate cum potestate multo majore quam ante quis- quam. De hoc significatu vocis πρῶτος vide quæ dicta ad Joh. I. 15. Ἔσχατος id est, contemptissimus hominum, Es. LIII. 3. nimirum captus, irrisus, verberatus, flagris cæsus, addictus supplicio, & quidem servili.

Eo, sine dubio, sensu de sese profitetur: Ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ πρῶτος καὶ ὁ ἔσχατος, quo antea v. 11. sonora voce testatus est, ἐγώ εἰμι τὸ Α καὶ τὸ Ω, ὁ πρῶτος καὶ ὁ ἔσχατος, & Apoc. XXII. 13. testabitur: Ἐγώ εἰμι τὸ Α καὶ τὸ Ω, ἀρχὴ καὶ τέλος, ὁ πρῶτος καὶ ἔσχα- τος. Hæc autem non de summo dignitate in ex- altatione, & novissimo in exanitionis statu, sed potius de æterna Christi Deitate agunt, unde Atha- nasius & alii veteres æternitatem & Deitatem ex hac appellatione Christi probant.

Καὶ ὁ ζῶν] id est ζωοποιῶν: quo sensu ponitur & Joh. VI. v. 51. & Act. 7, 35. Christus in terris agens vitam attulerat mor- tuis, valetudinem (quæ & ipsa Ebræis vita dicitur) ægrotis.

## 1:18
Verse 18.

Latin:

Vers. 18.

## 1:18
Καὶ ἐγενόμην νεκρὸς) And yet he himself truly underwent death. This is said for this reason, so that it may be known that he is the one who could have compassion on others, Hebrews 4:15. That indeed pertained especially to removing from John that fear taken up from the Majesty of Christ.

Καὶ ἰδὲ ζῶν εἰμι εἰς τὲς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων] I live in such a way that I can provide both temporary and eternal life to you and to others, John 10:28.

The word ζῶν is properly living, 1. by which that life-giving differs, nor is it accepted otherwise in John 6:51 and Acts 7:38: where life is attributed to Christ and to the law received from Moses, and there follows the explanation handed down here by Christ, that indeed he truly had died, but now lives forever. It is not a matter of the state of Christ on earth, but of the state of the same in heaven, that, even though he underwent death, he is now established in a glorious life: by which very thing he effectively raises up John, because, just as he had been handed over to an infamous death on account of sins our [righteousness]: Thus he may have been raised to glorious and eternal life for the sake of our righteousness, by whose majesty one ought therefore not to be terrified and cast down, but cheered and quickened; especially because he obtained the key of death and hell for our sake. He hints at the same time by that reason at the liberation of his Church, as if to say: Just as I have gloriously risen from death, so will I cause that the Church may rise gloriously and triumph from the tribulations by which it seems to be overwhelmed and buried.

Amen] seems to be an interjection by John: and after it the discourse of Christ is continued. The speaking persons are sometimes left unmentioned. See around the end of this book.

This particle of affirmation is more correctly attributed to Christ: because his discourse, which it is not likely that St. John interrupted, is continued without interruption.

And I have the keys of death and of hell] What is said of God, he quickeneth and killeth, he bringeth down to the underworld and bringeth back, 1 Sam. 2:6, and to God belong the issues of death, Ps. 68:20, this Christ also rightfully claims for himself. He can both shut and open the bars of death. A key signifies authority and power, as below 3:2, 20:1. In the Orphic hymns you have: 'Whoever hold the keys of the nether vaults.' In the same hymns and elsewhere keys are often used for power. Thanatos is death: Hades is the state after death. See Matt. 16:10, 1 Cor. 15:55, below 6:8, 20:13-14. This is what Christ means: You shall not die, except where I shall have willed: And I will liberate my Church, where I shall have willed. And the titles and ornaments of Christ will soon be brought back to the memory of the Churches, according to the merit of each.

Cornelius reports various opinions concerning the power of the keys of death and hell, but which are subordinate, if death is taken in a fuller signification: and hell, regarding the state after death, likewise embraces any state whatsoever; because in this way they could easily be held as subordinate: 1. The power of forgiving sins and liberating from death and hell, according to Tyconius, Primasius, Bede, and Rupert. 2. Of punishing enemies with death and Gehenna, according to Andrew and Richard of St. Victor. 3. Of raising the faithful from death and liberating them from hell, according to Lyra and Ribera. 4. Of the power of life and death, of quickening and killing, according to Arethas and Pererius. 5. Of the power of condemning even the Devil himself, the author and president of death and hell, according to Primasius. 6. Of the power of liberating from the death of grace and glory, or of depriving of and granting spiritual and eternal life, according to Viegas. But the one which he brings forward from Alcufar, as if to say: I can loosen or tighten the reins for death, that is, for the demon, to tempt men: I can restrain him and his ministers, so that the temptation may not be greater than what the faithful can endure: nay, I can cause, and in fact will cause, that your very temptation and tribulation may be a means to the greater glory and sublimity of the Church and of each individual, [that] is forced: not only because he understands the Demon and his ministers by death, which suggests the direction of temptations to the greater glory of the Church, which is not found in the text; Nor even the Cornelian [interpretation]: That he opposes this to the Jews and Gentiles threatening death and hell unless they renounced the faith, that he can not only scatter those things and liberate from them, but that he is the Master and Lord of both. For we are taught in Matt. 10:28 that persecutors have no power to send into hell, even though they can kill the body. Nor are these less opposed to the temptation of heretics than of tyrants, from whose seduction and persecution Christ liberates us. Keys in common phraseology imply the power of opening and shutting. Cf. Apoc. 3:7, ch. 9:1-2, ch. 20:1-3, 21. But hell [signifies] the second death, as it is called,

Apoc. 2:11, ch. 20:6, ch. 21:8, or the prison of everlasting damnation. Death properly signifies bodily destruction, according to the mind of the Caesarean, Rupert, B. Cluver, and others. Gomarus notes that by this periphrasis Christ describes both his divine nature, when he calls himself the first and the last, and his human nature, from life restored through resurrection and death endured for us, and that such a species is similarly explained, that he was both Priest and victim, and died for us, John 10:16-17, and having been received into the heavenly sanctuary now lives forever. And that the Royal office is declared by the power (which he metaphorically calls keys) of the underworld and of death, because he overcame death and hell, 1 Cor. 15:54, Heb. 2:14-15, and has the right to liberate and save his own from them, and conversely to destroy his enemies: and therefore he is not a minister of the keys, like others, but truly the Lord.

Latin:

Καὶ ἐγενόμην νεκρὸς) Et ipse tamen mortem revera subiit. Hoc ideo dicitur, ut sciatut is esse qui misereri aliorum posset, Ebr. 4, 15. Id vero maxime pertinebat ad demendum Johan- ni metum illum ex Christi Majestate susceptum.

Καὶ ἰδὲ ζῶν εἰμι εἰς τὲς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων] Ita vivo, ut ti- bi & aliis vitam & temporariam & æternam præstare possim, Joh. X. 28.

Verbum ζῶν proprie est vivus, 1. quo differt illud ζωοποιῶν, neque aliter Joh. VI. 51. Act. VII. 38. accipitur: ubi vita Christo & legi à Mose ac- ceptæ tribuitur, & sequitur ἐξήγησις à Christo hic tradita, quod nempe vere quidem mortuus fuerit, jam autem vivat in æternum. Non agitur de statu Christi in terris, sed de statu ejusdem in cælis, quod, etsi mortem subeirit, jam in vita gloriosa constitutus sit: quo tamen ipso Johan- nem efficaciter erigit, quod, quemadmodum in mortem infamem traditus fuerat propter peccata nostra : Ita ad vitam gloriosam & æternam re- suscitatus sit propter justitiam nostram, cujus ma- jestate proinde non terreri & prosterni, sed ex- hilarari & vivificari debeat; imprimis quia mor- tis & inferni clavem ita nostri causa obtinuerit. Innuit autem simul ea ratione Ecclesiæ suæ libe- rationem , q. d. Sicut ego ex morte gloriosè sur- rexi: ita faciam, ut Ecclesia ex tribulationibus, quibus videtur obrui & sepeliri, gloriosa resurgat ac triumphet.

Ἀμὴν ] videtur esse interlocutio Johannis: & post eam continuari sermo Christi. Personæ loquentes interdum sub- ticentur. Vide circa finem hujus libri.

Rectius hæc asseverandi particula Christo tribuitur: quia oratio ejus, quam interpellasse S. Johannem verisimile non est, sine interruptio- ne continuatur.

Καὶ ἔχω κλεῖς τῦ θανάτε καὶ τῦ ἅδε] Quod de Deo di- citur, vivificat & mortificat, deducit ad inferos & reducit 1. Sam. II. vers. 6. & Dei sunt exitus mortis, Psal. 68. vers. 21. id Christus sibi quoque jure vindicat. Potest claustra mortis & claudere & aperire. Clavis imperium potestatem- que significat, ut infra 3, vers. 2. XX. vers. 1. In Orphicis habes: Ὅσσοι νερθερίων βερίθρων κληῖδας ἔχυσιν. In iisdem hymnis & alibi claves sæpe pro potestate. Θάνα- τος est mors: ᾴδης status post mortem. Vide Matth. 16, 10. 1.Cor. 15, 55. infra 6, 8. 20, 13.14. Hoc vult Christus: Non morieris, nisi ubi ego voluero: Et Ecclesiam meam libera- bo, ubi voluero. Et tituli autem & ornamenta Christi mox in memoriam reducentur Ecclesiis, pro cujusque me- rito.

Varias refert Cornelius de potestate clavium mortis & inferni sententias, sed quæ subordina- tæ sunt, si mors in pleniori significatione suma- tur: & infernus de statu post mortem pariter quemcumque statum complectatur; quia ita fa- cile ὑπάλληλα haberi poterant, 1. Potestas dimit- tendi peccata & liberandi à morte & inferno, juxta Tyconium, Primasium, Bedam & Ruper- tum. 2. Hostes morte & gehenna puniendi, jux- ta Andream & Richardum Victorem. 3. Fideles à morte excitandi & ex inferno liberandi juxta Lyranum & Riberam. 4. De potestate vitæ & mor- tis, vivificandi & occidendi juxta Aretam & Pereri- um. 5. De potestate ipsum etiam Diabolum autorem & Præsidem mortis & inferni condemnan- di juxta Primasium. 6. De potestate à morte gratiæ & gloriæ liberandi, vel spirituali & æterna vita pri- vandi, & donandi juxta Viegam. Quam vero ex Alcufare affert, q.d. Possum morti, id est, dæmoni ad tentandum homines laxare habenas vel contra- here: Possum cohibere eum, ejusque Ministros, ut tentatio non sit major, quam ut fideles possint susti- nere: imo possum facere, & reipsa faciam, ut ipsa vestra tentatio & tribulatio sit medium ad majo- rem Ecclesiæ & cujusque gloriam & sublimitatem, ea coacta est: non modo quod per mortem Dæ- monem intelligat & ministros ejus fideles, quod directionem tentationum ad majorem Ecclesiæ gloriam ingerat, quæ in textu non invenitur; Neque etiam Corneliana: Quod Judæis & genti- libus minantibus mortem & infernum, nisi fidem abnegarent, hoc opponat, quod non tantum illa disjicere possit, indeque liberare, sed utriusque Herus sit, & Dominus. Nam in infernum mit- tendi persecutores nullam habere potestatem Matth. X. 28. docemur, etsi occidere corpus pos- sint. Nec minus hæc opposita sunt tentationi hæ- reticorum, quam tyrannorum, à quorum & sedu- ctione & persecutione nos Christus liberat. Claves usitata phrasi potestatem aperiendi & claudendi inferunt. Conf. Apoc. III. 7. c. IX. 1. 2. c. XX. 1. 2. 3. 21. Infernus vero mortem secundam, ut vocatur,

Apoc. II. 11. c. XX. 6. c. XXI. 8. vel damnationis sem- piternæ carcerem. Mors corporalem interitum proprie significat, ex mente Cæsariensis, Ruperti, B. Cluveri & aliorum. Hac periphrasi Christum tum divinam naturam, cum se primum & ultimum vocat, tum humanam describere à vita per resur- rectionem restituta, & morte pro nobis exantlata, notat Gomarus, eaque similiter exponi talemem speciem, quod Sacerdos atque victima fuerit, ac mortuus pro nobis, Joh. X. 16. 17. & in cæleste sa- crarium receptus jam vivat in æternum. Officium autem Regium declarari à potestate, (quam Me- taphorice claves vocat) inferorum & mortis, quoa mortem & infernum superarit, 1. Cor. XV. 54. Ebr. II. 14. 15. ac jus habeat suos ab iis liberandis ac ser- vandi, & contra hostes perdendi: ideoque clavium non minister, ut alii, sed vere Dominus.

## 1:19
v. 19. Write therefore what you have seen) First write this very vision, intending then to write other things as well. Therefore, that is, because you see me so powerful.

And what they are] The present state of the Churches throughout Asia, under which others are also understood. This will be written in the second and third chapters.

And what is about to happen] Which are future things and will be written in chapter 4 and following.

Latin:

v. 19. Γράψον οὖν ἃ εἶδες) Primum hoc ipsum visum scri- be, scripturus deinde & alia. Οὖν id est, quia me tam po- tentem vides.

Καὶ ἃ εἶσι] Statum præsentem Ecclesiarum per Asiam, sub quibus intelliguntur & aliæ. Hoc scribetur capite secundo & tertio.

Καὶ ἃ μέλλει γενέσθαι] Quæ futura sunt & scribentur capi- te IV. ac deinceps.

## 1:20
Verse 20.

The mystery of the seven stars which you saw on the right hand, and the seven golden lampstands] Supply, write this also. And he calls it a mystery metonymically, that which is signified through mystical figures, as Dan. II. verse 27. Eph. V. 32. So also below XVII. verse 7. The seven lampstands briefly for the mystery of the seven lampstands. In the Manuscript it is read: Which you saw on my right hand.

The seven stars are the Angels of the seven churches] I said at Malach. II. 7, following David Kimchi, that the high priests were called Angels by the Hebrews, because they would carry both the commands of God to the people, and the prayers of the people to God, like unto Angels. We also showed that this kind of speaking came from the Hebrews to the Egyptians, who themselves also called the high priest an Angel. To the high priests of the temple correspond in the Christian Church the Chief Presbyters, the presiding ones among Justin, who by excellence are called Bishops. In like manner to the Priests and Levites correspond Presbyters and Deacons, as can be understood from the prophecy of Isaiah LXVI. verse 21. Not all functions are indeed the same; but it is enough that there is an analogy on account of which a communication of names may be made. These angels of those churches were appointed by John himself, and other bishops succeeded them in their order one after another, as Tertullian teaches us concerning the prescriptions of heretics, and against Marcion IV. and before him Irenaeus III. 3. Here again the seven stars is put for the mystery of the seven stars. A similar locution Gen. XLI. 26. Ezech. V. 1. Dan. IV. verse 19. VII. 17. 23. VIII. 20. 21. Luc. VIII. 12. The reason why stars signify bishops we said above at 16.

Teachers are compared to Angels for various reasons, as for instance both on account of their mission, because they are legates of GOD and Angels, and Teachers of the Church, so that they may propose the will of God, Ps. CIV. 20, 2 Cor. V. 20, and on account of knowledge, by which both shine, 2 Sam. XIV. 20, Eph. III. 9, and on account of truth, because they do not expound their own mind but God's, 2 Cor. XI. v. 11, Gal. I. 8, c. II. 4, 1 Thess. II. 13, and on account of holiness, Matt. XXV. 31, 1 Tim. IV. 12, and on account of vigilant care, Dan. IV. 10, Ez. III. 17, Heb. XIII. 7, Ps. XCI. 11, and on account of the ardor of charity, Luc. XV. 10, 1 Cor. IX. 19, sqq. But that they are to be compared to Angels in that they carry prayers to God, we are nowhere taught, nor is that office attributed to Angels. The things which are said concerning the analogy of the high priest in the Old Testament and the Chief Presbyters, and likewise of the Presbyters and Deacons with the Priests and Levites, are likewise destitute of the authority of Scripture: And if Grotius wished to patronize the Papists in these matters, just as this zeal of his shines forth everywhere, why has he forgotten the supreme Roman Pontiff? If John appointed the bishops of Asia, how are those parts claimed for the Roman Pontiff, whom it is confessed that Saint John certainly was not.

Moreover, the comparison of Doctors with stars is usually instituted partly by reason of the origin of the light from the Sun, which Doctors receive from Christ, the Sun of righteousness; partly by reason of the light, because they glitter like the stars in doctrine and life, and scatter a clear splendor from themselves, and illuminate others, 2 Cor. IV, verse 4; partly by reason of sublimity, because they are placed on high by the sublimity of their office, and, in the manner of stars looking down upon the lands from on high, they are not mixed with earthly things; partly by reason of diversity, because as star differs from star in brightness, so also a difference is given to Doctors regarding gifts, 1 Cor. XV, verse 41, chap. XII, verse 8, seqq. The blessed Glassius fully and elegantly develops this comparison in Rhetor. S., page 226. He shows that it pertains to the ministry, whose face is proposed in the same place, chap. I, v. 16, as the Sun shining in its brightness. As the Sun communicates its light to the stars in heaven: so Christ, the Sun of righteousness, Mal. IV, verse 2, imparts the light of saving knowledge to his faithful servants, 2 Cor. IV, verse 6. The Lord brings out the host of stars in number and calls them all by name, Is. XL, verse 26. He likewise brings out his ministers in the Church as a sacred army against Satan and the world, and calls them by name, Ps. LXVIII, verse 12, as well as their office. God placed stars in the firmament to illuminate the earth, Gen. I, verse 17.
