Let the light of doctrine, which the Ministers of the Church bring, be brought from heaven and derived solely from the heavenly Word, 2 Pet. I, verses 16, 19, which is sweeter than honey to θεοδιδάκτοις (God-taught) souls, Ps. XIX, v. 13, Ps. CXIX, verse 103. If it be done otherwise, let it be the star called wormwood, Apoc. VIII, verse 11, on account of its extreme bitterness and the destruction of the soul. The star led the Magi solely to Christ, Matt. II, v. 9. Let Ministers also look only to Him in teaching, 1 Cor. II, verse 2. Of the stars it is said in Sir. XLIII, verse 11, that they hold their order according to the Word of Jehovah, and do not fail in their watches. Of the ministers of the Word, Heb. XIII, verse 17, that they watch for the souls of men: therefore they ought not to fail in their watches on account of the ingratitude of the world, but by the example of both doctrine and life, they should constantly keep the same order; thus they will be far removed from those wandering stars, for whom the blackness of darkness is reserved forever, Jude, verse 13. Let them also take care that all things are done decently and according to order in the Church, 1 Cor. XIV, verse 40. Of the stars it is said in Jud. V, verse 20, that they fought from heaven against the enemies of the people of God. A most serious battle against devils is proposed to the Ministers of the Word, Eph. VI, v. 12. Let them see to it, therefore, that they fight rightly, 2. Cor. X, verses 2, 4, 5, so that they may be able to glory in the Lord about obtaining the heavenly prize, 2 Tim. IV, verses 7, 8. Of the stars it is said in Gen. I, 14, that together with the Sun and Moon they divide between the day and the night, and are for signs and seasons and days and years. It is the duty of the Ministers of the Word to divide between day and night, light and darkness, that is, to diligently show and inculcate the distinction between good and evil, piety and impiety, Is. V, verse 20, Jer. XV, v. 19, Rom. XIII, verses 12, 13, 2 Cor. VI, v. 14, sqq.; likewise to give signs and seasons, that is, to provide that those things which pertain to the public worship of God are performed rightly and εὐκαίρως (opportune) in the individual parts of the year, lest any ἀταξία (disorder) and confusion occur; likewise to indicate days and years, that is, to preach the acceptable year of the Lord, Is. LXI, v. 2, and to diligently inculcate the final pantocritical day, Acts XVII, verse 31. Of the stars it is said in 1 Cor. XV, v. 41, that they differ from one another in glory. Thus there is a wonderful diversity of the gifts of the Holy Spirit in the Ministers of the Word, 1 Cor. XII, v. 4, seqq. But all luminous stars are commanded to praise the Lord, Ps. CXLVIII, v. 3. Cf. Job XXXVIII, v. 7. Thus let all heralds of the divine Word, however much they may be endowed with χαρίσμασιν (gifts) by the Holy Spirit, and whatever office they may hold in the Church, ardently praise the Lord, and serve Him in the ἁπλότητι (simplicity) of their heart, and cultivate mutual peace and concord among themselves without αὐθαδείᾳ (arrogance) and envy. Then the reward, if they show themselves faithful. And that not only in this life: Christ carries the stars seen by John in His right hand, Apoc. I, 20; let the faithful ὑπηρέται (servants) themselves be certain of the most merciful protection of the hand of the omnipotent Christ, Is. LI, v. 16, but also in the future, Dan. XII, v. 3. But Hoffmann wrongly said that those seven angels were trumpeters, chap. VII. For here the Doctors of the Churches of Asia are noted: But there, heavenly angels were seen. It can neither be, nor ought it to be, that one writes to heavenly angels.

And the seven lampstands, which you saw, are the seven Churches) See above 13. In the Manuscript, 'which you saw' is missing, as it is also in the Latin.

Churches are compared to lampstands by an allusion made to the golden lampstands in the tabernacle, Exod. 25, v. 37, ch. 37, 22; then because the Church does not hide in the dark, but makes itself manifest by its marks, the preaching of the Word and the dispensation of the sacraments, Matt. V, 14, 15, Is. 40, 9; then because it holds forth light and a torch to the world living in darkness, Ps. L, 2, Is. LX, 2, 8. Hoffmann, as well as the Bremensians, understand the universal Church by the seven churches, and wish the same seven ages or periods to be designated, and he indeed thinks that the seven angels are noted here as trumpeters, and transforms them into the Church of the New Testament, consisting of seven angelic jubilees. But that stars and lampstands, angels and churches, whose angels are the Doctors, who are those angels, are confused with the churches, that the universal churches throughout the world are built up from seven determined and, as to the counted number, defined throughout Asia, and that periods or ages are made from the assemblies or their leaders, everyone sees.

THE LATTER SPECIAL AND PROPHETIC SECTION.

PART I. CONCERNING THE REVELATION OF PRESENT THINGS DELIVERED IN THE ASIAN CHURCHES BY THE FIRST VISION.

Latin:

Vers. 20.

Τὸ μυστήριον τῶν ἑπτὰ ἀσέρων ὧν εἶδες ἐπὶ τῆς δεξιᾶς, καὶ τὰς ἑπτὰ λυχνίας τὰς χρυσᾶς] Supple, etiam hoc scribe. Et μυσήριον vocat μετωνυμικῶς, id quod per mysticas figuras significatur, ut Dan. II. vers. 27. Eph. V. 32. Sic & infræ XVII. vers. 7. Τὰς ἑπτὰ λυχνίας breviter pro τὸ μυσήριον τῶν ἑπτὰ λυχνιῶν. In Manuscripto legitur : Οὓς εἶδες ἐν τῇ δεξιᾷ με.

Οἱ ἑπτὰ ἀσέρες Ἄγγελοι τῶν ἑπτὰ ἐκκλησιῶν εἰσι] dixi- mus ad Malach. II. 7. post Davidem Kimchium summos Sa- cerdotes dictos Angelos Ebræis, quia & Dei mandata ad po- pulum, & preces populi ad Deum deferrent Angelorum in- star. Ostendimus etiam hoc loquendi genus ab Ebræis ve- nisse ad Ægyptios, qui & ipsi τὸν ἀρχιερέα dixere Ἄγγελον. Summis Sacerdotibus templi respondent in Ecclesia Christia- na Principes Presbyteri, οἱ προεστῶτες apud Justinum, qui per excellentiam dicti Episcopi. Pari modo Sacerdotibus & Levitis respondent Presbyteri & Diaconi, ut intelligi potest ex vaticinio Esaiæ LXVI. vers. 21. Non sunt quidem omnes functiones eædem; Sed satis est τῶ ἀναλόγῳ propter quod nominum fiat communicatio. Hi ἄγγελοι istarum Ecclesi- arum ab ipso Johanne erant constituti, & illis alii deinceps Episcopi suo ordine successerunt, ut Tertullianus nos docet de præscriptionibus hæreticorum, & adversus Marcionem IV. & ante eum Irenæus III. 3. Hic iterum οἱ ἑπτὰ ἀσέρες positum pro τὸ μυσήριον τῶν ἑπτὰ ἀσέρων. Similis locutio Gen. XLI. 26. Ezech. V. 1. Dan. IV. vers. 19. VII. 17. 23. VIII. 20. 21. Luc. VIII. 12. Causam cur stellæ Episcopos significant supra 16. diximus.

Comparantur Angelis Doctores ob varias cau- sas, utpote tum ob missionem, quod legati DEI sint & Angeli, & Doctores Ecclesiæ, ut volunta- tem Dei proponant, Ps. CIV. 20 2. Cor. V. 20. tum ob scientiam, qua utrique fulgent, 2. Sam. XIV. 20. Eph. III. 9. tum ob veritatem, quia non suam sed Dei mentem exponunt, 2. Cor. XI. v. 11. Gal. I. 8. c. II. 4. 1. Thess. II. 13. tum ob sanctitatem Matth. XXV. 31. 1. Tim. IV. 12. tum ob curam vigilem, Dan. IV. 10. Ez. III. 17. Ebr. XIII. 7. Ps. XCI. 11. tum ob charitatis ardorem, Luc. XV. 10. 1. Cor. IX. 19. sqq. Quod vero Angelis in eo conferendi sint, quod preces ad Deum deferant, nuspiam docemur, neque id officium Angelis tribuitur. Quæ de analogia summi Sacerdotis in Veteri Testamento & Prin- cipum Presbyterorum, itemque Presbyterorum & Diaconorum cum Sacerdotibus & Levitis dicun- tur, Scripturæ autoritate itidem destituuntur : Et si illis patrocinari Pontificiis voluit Grotius, quem- admodum ubique hoc ejus studium effulget, cur summi Pontificis Romani oblitus est? Si Johan- nes Asiæ Episcopos constituit, quomodo illæ partes Romano Pontifici, qualem utique Sanct. Jo- hannem non fuisse in confesso est, vendicantur.

Cæterum comparatio Doctorum cum stellis insti- tui solet partim ratione originis luminis à Sole quod Doctores à Sole justitiæ Christo accipiunt partim ratione lucis, quod coruscent siderum instar doctrina, & vita, ac clarum splendorem de se spargant, aliosque illuminent, 2. Cor. IV. vers. 4. partim ratione sublimitatis, quod in alto positi sint officii sublimitate, & more stellarum terras ex alto aspicientium non misceantur terre- nis: partim ratione diversitatis, quia ut stella à stella claritate differt, ita & Doctorum quantum ad do- na differentia datur, 1. Cor. XV. vers. 41. cap. XII. vers. 8. seqq. Plene & eleganter hanc comparatio- nem evolvit Beat. Glassius Rhetor. S. pag. 226. Ostendit ea ministerii tum dominium, cujus facies instar Solis in fulgore suo lucentis ibidem cap. I. v. 16. proponitur. Ut Sol lucem suam communicat stellis in cœlo: Sic Christus Sol justitiæ Mal. IV. vers. 2. cognitionis salutaris lucem impertit fidelibus suis servis, 2. Cor. IV. vers. 6. Stellarum exercitum edu- cit Dominus in numero & nomine omnes vocat, Es. XL. vers. 26. Idem ministros suos in Ecclesia tanquam exercitum sacrum adversus Satanam & mundum educit, eosque vocat nomine, Psal. LXVIII. vers. 12. tum officium. Stellas posuit Deus in firmamento ad illuminandum terram Genes. I. vers. 17. Lux doctrinæ, quam afferunt Ecclesiæ Ministri sit cœlitus allata & ex solo cœlesti Verbo deducta, 2. Petr. I. vers. 16. 19. quod præ melle a- nimabus θεοδιδάκτοις dulce est, Psal. XIX. v. 13. Psal. CXIX. vers. 103. Secus si fiat, sit stella, absin- thium dicta, Apoc. VIII. vers. 11. ob summam a- maritudinem, animæque perniciem. Stella de- duxit Magos unice ad Christum, Matth. II. v. 9. Hunc solum etiam respiciant docendo Ministri, 1. Cor. II. vers. 2. De stellis dicitur Syr. XLIII. vers. 11. quod secundum Verbum Jehove ordinem suum teneant, nec deficiant in vigiliis suis. De Ministris verbi Ebr. XIII. vers. 17. quod vigi- lent pro animabus hominum: Non igitur in vi- giliis suis deficere debent ob mundi ingratitudinem, sed & doctrina & vitæ exemplo, ordinem eundem constanter servent; ita procul aberunt à stellis illis erraticis, quibus caligo tenebrarum in æternum servata est, Jud. vers. 13. Curent etiam, ut o- mnia decenter, & secundum ordinem in Ecclesia fi- ant, 1. Corinth. XIV. vers. 40. De stellis dicitur Jud. V. vers. 20. quod de cœlis pugnaverint contra hostes populi Dei. Gravissima pugna adversus di- abolos Verbi Ministris proposita est Eph. VI. v. 12. Videant igitur, ut rite depugnent, 2. Cor. X. vers. 2. 4. 5. ut de consequendo præmio cœlesti gloriari in Domino possint, 2. Tim. IV. vers. 7. 8. de stellis di- citur Gen. I. 14. quod una cum Sole & Luna divi- dant inter diem & inter noctem, & sint in signa & tempora & dies & annos. Ministrorum Verbi est di- videre inter diem & noctem, lucem & tenebras, hoc est discrimen boni, & mali, pietatis & impietatis diligenter ostendere & inculcare, Es. V. vers. 20. Jer. XV. v. 19. Rom. XIII. v. 12. 13. 2. Cor. VI. v. 14. sqq. signa item & tempora dare, hoc est, providere, ut quæ ad cultum Dei publicum pertinent, rite & εὐ- καίρως singulis anni partibus peragantur, ne quæ fiat ἀταξία & confusio: dies item & annos indicare, hoc est prædicare annum beneplaciti Domini, Es. LXI. v. 2. & diem ultimam pantocriticam sedulo inculcare, Actor. XVII. v. 31. De stellis dicitur 1. Cor. XV. v. 41. quod gloria inter se differant. Sic donorum Spi- ritus Sancti in Verbi Ministris mira est diversitas, 1. Cor. XII. v. 4. seqq. Omnes vero stellæ luminosæ Dominum laudare jubentur, Psal. CXLVIII. v. 3. Conf. Job. XXXVIII. v. 7. Sic omnes Verbi divini praecones, quantiscunque sint praediti a Spiritu San- cto χαρίσμασιν, & qualecunque in Ecclesia gerant munus, Dominum ardenter laudent, & in cordis ἁπλότητι ipsi serviant, mutuamque inter se absqs αὐθαδείᾳ & invidia colant pacem ac concordiam. Tum praemium, si fideles se exhibeant. Idque non in hac vita solum: Stellas à Johanne visas in dextera sua gerit Christus Apoc. I. 20. de clemen- tissima protectione manus Christi omnipotentis sint certi fideles ipsi ὑπηρέται Es. LI. v. 16. sed & in futu- ra Dan. XII. v. 3. Perperam autem Hoffmannus septem illos Angelos tubicinatores esse dixit cap. VII. Hic enim notantur Doctores Ecclesiarum Asiae: Illic vero Angeli coelestes conspecti sunt. Ad Angelos coelestes scribi neque potest, neque debet.

Καὶ αἱ ἑπτὰ λυχνίαι, ἃς εἶδες, ἑπτὰ Ἐκκλησίαι εἰσὶ) Vide supra 13. In Manuscripto deest ἃς εἶδες, ut & in Latino.

Candelabris conferuntur Ecclesiae allusione fa- cta ad candelabra aurea in tabernaculo, Exod. 25, v. 37. c. 37, 22. tum quia non in obscuro delitescit Ecclesia, sed notis suis verbi praedicatione & sacra- mentorum dispensatione dispalescit, Matt. V, 14.15. Es. 40, 9. tum quia lumen facemque praefert mun- do in tenebris versanti, Psal. L. 2. Es. LX. 2.8. Hoff- mannus ut & Bremenses per septem Ecclesias uni- versam Ecclesiam intelligunt, ejusdemque septem aetates seu periodos designari volunt, & ille qui- dem septem Angelos tubicinatores hic notatos censet, eosque in Ecclesiam Novi Testamenti septem jubilaeis Angelicis constantem transformat. Ita vero astra & candelabra, Angelos & Ecclesias, quarum sunt Angeli, Doctores, qui sunt Angeli illi cum Ec- clesiis confundi, è septem determinatis & quoad numerum numeratum per Asiam definitis univer- sas per orbem Ecclesias extrui, & ex coetibus vel eorum praesidibus periodos vel aetates confici ne- mo non videt.

SECTIO POSTERIOR SPECIALIS ET PROPHETICA.

PARS I. QUA REVELATIONEM PRAESEN- TIUM IN ECCLESIIS ASIATICIS VISIONE PRIMA TRADITAM.

## 2:1 Argument
CHAPTER II.

ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

The command to write given to the Angel of the Ephesian Church, and the epistle dictated to John, in which, after the title of Christ is set forth, he is praised for his labors, and for his vigilance in testing false Apostles, and for his tolerance and patience with evil men: but he is rebuked for having abandoned his first love, and is warned to perform penance, lest the lampstand be moved from its place: finally, he is confirmed in his hatred of the works of the Nicolaitans, and a promise of the fruits of the tree of life is made to those who conquer; to the Bishop of Smyrna, however, testimony is borne by letter of his endured calamity and slander from the synagogue of Satan, and he is encouraged against persecutions by the crown of life, with immunity from the second death promised to those who conquer. The faith of the Bishop of Pergamum is commended, in which he persisted, even though Antipas was killed for the same: but he is reproved for having tolerated the followers of Balaam and the Nicolaitans, with an added admonition to penance, lest by the two-edged sword of the Lord

may come, and by the promise of the hidden Manna, and of a good testimony. Finally, the Bishop of Thyatira is commended by letter for his works, ministry, faith, and patience: Yet the toleration of the impenitent Jezebel is disapproved, with a threat against her and those committing adultery with her. To the others not doing so with her, impunity is promised, and to the victors power over the nations, to rule them with an iron scepter, as also the gift of the morning star.

There are IV parts. The first presents the letter to the Ephesian Bishop to v. 7. The second to the Smyrnean to v. 11. The third to the Pergamene v. 17. The fourth to the Thyatiran to v. 29.

PART I.

FIRST LETTER TO THE EPHESIAN BISHOP.

Vers. 1.

Τῷ Ἀγγέλῳ τῆς Ἐκκλησίας ἐν Ἐφέσῳ γράψον ) Some think this was Timothy. I, some other person of Jewish origin. See Acts XVIII. 25.

Τάδε λέγει ὁ κρατῶν τὲς ἑπτὰ ἀσέρας ἐν τῇ δεξιᾷ αὐτῦ ) Words from chap. I will often be repeated in the following, because in it there is a certain introduction to all that follows. And individual things are adapted to their own places. What Christ says in this place is this: Bishops are precious to me and diligently guarded like gems in a hand. Therefore they ought to attend diligently to themselves, so that they may preserve their purity. For a corrupted gem is easily cast away: which likeness is adapted to Jeconiah Jer. XXII. 24.

Ὁ περιπατῶν ἐν μέσῳ τῶν ἑπτὰ λυχνιῶν χρυσῶν ) The lampstands are the Churches, I walk among them, namely to see if they shine well, if they do not shine enough, that they may be snuffed. If they do not shine even then, that they may be removed from their place as useless. This sense is indicated to us below 5.

In the book of Acts, Apollos is mentioned, but it is not taught that he was the same Bishop of Ephesus. The common opinion, however, is that that Bishop is Timothy, as Lyranus admits, which Aureolus, Viegas, Alcazar, Magalianus in his proem to the epistle to Timothy, Baronius, Cornelius a Lapide, and most of our own, as well as the Reformed, defend, and Cornelius thinks it can be sufficiently inferred from chronology: Since at this time there was no other Bishop at Ephesus than Timothy. For St. Paul, he says, wrote the epistle to Timothy, as to the Bishop of Ephesus, in A.D. 57; but John wrote these things in the year of Christ 97. Timothy, however, died as Bishop of Ephesus in the year 109, which was the tenth of Trajan. For then Onesimus succeeded him in the Ephesian Episcopate, whom St. Paul commends when writing to Philemon. Whence, writing to the Ephesians in the same year of Christ 109, St. Ignatius mentions Onesimus after Timothy, as their already recent Bishop. Simon Episcopius in his lecture on chapters II and III of the Apocalypse thinks that either the head of the Pastors and Ephesian Bishops can be understood, or the college and assembly of them by collection, because there were several Bishops there, Acts XX, 18, 28, and that the letter was not properly destined for them, but delivered to the Church entrusted to their care and inspection, because it is written to them as Angels. But why should we make a plural out of a singular name, and attribute to many persons or to the whole presbytery attributes concerning one individual, or ascribe them to the entire Church, whether in this or in the remaining epistles? Anyone sees that a certain Doctor is partly praised in some things, and partly reproved for some things. But those things which are said generally pertain not only to that particular epistle, but in general to anyone in the universal Church, e.g., that epiphonema: He who has ears to hear, let him hear: He who overcomes, I will give him to eat from the tree of life, etc. Which conclusions of the epistles are truly universal. Nor indeed is it to be gathered from the fact that Christ addresses one Bishop that in that age Bishops were superior to Presbyters, but at most one may presume from that, that some one person was held to be first in age and order; which is not against us.

The author of the Epistle, Christ, does not describe himself by the estimation and care of gems, of which there is no trace here, but by the carrying and use of stars, that is, of Bishops in his hand, because he surely wishes to employ mystical stars, so that by the brightness of both life and doctrine they may shine for others in the worldly darkness: and also by his walking in the midst of the lampstands, not a bodily and local one, which was seen by John in the Spirit, but a mystical and spiritual one, which is signified by that: because just as a Priest in the tabernacle and temple took care of the lampstand, so that the lights in it might burn and shine, and not be extinguished: So may Christ mystically perform this in the Church: And therefore he observed this Bishop, how he conducted himself in the Ephesian Church, in which he was constituted Bishop by the Holy Spirit, Acts XX. 18. However, lampstands are not to be confused with lights: not the former, but the latter shine: and the former cannot be snuffed, but the latter must be snuffed. The lampstands are the mystical Church, but the lights are the Teachers of the Church.

Latin:

CAPUT II.

ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Mandatum scribendi ad Ephesinae Ecclesiae An- gelum datum, & epistola dictata Johanni, in qua praemisso Christi titulo, laudatur ille à la- boribus, & in probandis falsis Apostolis vi- gilantia, ac malorum tolerantia & patien- tia: Reprehenditur vero ob charitatem pri- mam relictam, ac monetur de agenda poeni- tentia, ne candelabrum loco moveatur: deni- que confirmatur in operum Nicolaitarum o- dio, & vincentibus promissio fit fructuum li- gni vitae, Episcopo vero Smyrnensi testimoni- um literis perhibetur toleratae calamitatis, & calumniae à schola Satanae, & erigitur adver- sus persecutiones corona vitae, promissa vin- centibus immunitate à morte secunda. Epi- scopi Pergamensis fides commendatur, in qua perstitit, etsi Antipas ob eandem occisus sit: Redarguitur vero ob toleratos sectatores Ba- laami, & Nicolaitas, addita commonefactio- ne ad poenitentiam, ne gladio ancipiti Domino-

adveniat, & promissione absconditi Manna, & boni testimonii. Denique per epistolam commendatur Episcopus Thyatirensis ab ope- ribus, ministerio, fide & patientia: Improba- tur tamen toleratio Iesabelis impœnitentis, cum comminatione adversus ipsam & scor- tantes cum eadem. Cæteris cum illa non fa- cientibus promittitur impunitas, & victo- ribus potestas super gentes, regendi eas fer- reo sceptro, ut & donum phosphori.

Partes sunt IV. Prima epistolam ad Episcopum Ephesinum exhibet ad v. 7. Secunda ad Smyrnen- sem ad v. 11. Tertia ad Pergamensem v. 17. Quar- ta ad Thyatirensem ad v. 29.

PARS I.

EPISTOLA PRIMA AD EPISCOPUM EPHESINUM.

Vers. 1.

Τῷ Ἀγγέλῳ τῆς Ἐκκλησίας ἐν Ἐφέσῳ γράψον ) Hunc quidam putant fuisse Timotheum. Ego alium aliquem gente Judæum. Vide Act. XVIII. 25.

Τάδε λέγει ὁ κρατῶν τὲς ἑπτὰ ἀσέρας ἐν τῇ δεξιᾷ αὐτῦ ) Sæ- pe repetentur in sequentibus verba ex cap. I. quia in eo est quædam εἰσαγωγὴ ad omnia sequentia. Et singula aptan- tur suis locis. Quod Christus hoc loco dicit, hoc est: Sunt apud me Episcopi pretiosi & diligenter custoditi ut gemmæ in manu. Ideo diligenter attendere sibi debent, ut puri- tatem suam servent. Nam gemma corrupta facile abjici- tur: quæ similitudo aptatur Jechoniæ Jer. XXII. 24.

Ὁ περιπατῶν ἐν μέσῳ τῶν ἑπτὰ λυχνιῶν χρυσῶν ) Candela- bra sunt Ecclesiæ, inter eas ambulo, nempe ut videam, an bene luceant, si non satis lucent, ut emungantur. Si ne sic quidem lucent, ut velut inutiles a loco suo amoveantur. Hic sensus nobis indicatur infra 5.

In libro Actorum Apollo commemoratur, sed eundem Ephesi Episcopum fuisse non docetur. Communis vero sententia est Episcopum illum esse Timotheum, fatente Lyrano, quam tuentur Aureo- lus, Viegas, Alcazar, Magalianus proœm. in epist. ad Timoth. Baronius, Cornelius a Lapide, & pleri- que nostri, ut & Reformati, eamque satis e chrono- logia referri posse putat Cornelius: Siquidem hoc tempore non alius fuerit Episcopus Ephesi quam Timotheus. Nam S. Paulus, inquit, scripsit episto- lam ad Timotheum, quasi ad Episcopum Ephesi, A.C. 57. hæc autem scripsit Johannes anno Christi 97. Ti- motheus vero obiit Ephesi Episcopus anno 109. qui fuit decimus Trajani. Tunc enim successit ei in Epi- scopatu Ephesino Onesimus, quem Philemoni scri- bens commendat S. Paulus. Unde eodem anno Christi 109. scribens ad Ephesios S. Ignatius post Ti- motheum meminit Onesimi, tanquam jam recentis eorum Episcopi. Simon Episcopius in lect. ad cap. II. & III. Apoc. putat vel Antistitem Pastorum & Epi- scoporum Ephesinorum intelligi posse, vel collegium & cœtus eorum collectione, quia plures ibi fuere Episcopi, Act. XX, 18. 28. nec ipsis proprie destina- tam epistolam, sed Ecclesiæ ipsorum curæ & inspe- ctioni traditæ, quia ipsis tanquam Angelis scribitur. Sed cur ex nomine singulari plurale faciendum, & attributa unum individuum concernentia pluri- bus personis vel toti presbyterio tribuamus, aut in- tegræ Ecclesiæ adscribamus, sive in hac sive in reli- quis epistolis? Videt quilibet certum Doctorem partim laudari in quibusdam, partim ob nonnulla reprehendi. Quæ vero generaliter dicta, non ad epistolam tantum illam particularem, sed in genere ad quosvis in universa Ecclesia pertinere, v. g. epi- phonema illud: Qui habet aures ad audiendum, audiat: Qui vicerit, dabo illi edere de arbore vi- ta &c. Quæ epistolarum conclusiones vere uni- versales sunt. Nec vero ex eo, quod unum com- pellat Episcopum Christus colligendum, illa ætate Episcopos superiores fuisse Presbyteris, sed ad sum- mum id præsumere inde licet, unum quempiam ætate, & ordine primum fuisse habitum; quod no- bis adversum non est.

Autor Epistolæ Christus non sese describit a gemmarum, quarum hic nullum vestigium, æsti- mio & cura, sed a stellarum, hoc est, Episcoporum in manu sua gestatione & usu, quod nempe velit ad- hibere mysticas stellas, ut fulgore cum vitæ tum doctrinæ aliis in caligine mundana luceant: nec- non ab ambulatione in medio candelabrorum non corporali & locali, quæ a Johanne visa est, in Spiri- tu, sed mystica & spirituali, quæ per illam significa- ta: quod nempe ut Sacerdos candelabri in taberna- culo, & templo curam gerebat, ut in ea luminaria arderent, ac lucerent, non extinguerentur: Ita my- stice hoc præstet Christus in Ecclesia: Ideoque ob- servavit hunc Episcopum, qualem se gesserit in Ec- clesia Ephesina, in quam a Spiritu Sancto constitu- tus fuit Episcopus Act. XX. 18. Candelabra autem non confundenda cum luminaribus: non illa, sed hæc lucent: nec illa emungi possunt, sed hæc emun- gantur, oportet. Candelabra Ecclesiæ sunt mysticæ, luminaria vero Doctores Ecclesiæ.

## 2:2
Vers. 2.

Οἶδα τὰ ἔργα σε) There are some good men, some good enough, as Cicero distinguishes these in his letters. This Bishop was of the latter kind, as the following indicates. His works are praised here, that is, most things κατὰ τὴν ἐπικράτειαν: Just as God observes both the good and the bad, Prov. XV. 3. and is תֹּכֵן רוּחוֹת Prov. XVI. 2. so also is Christ.

Καὶ τὸν κόπον καὶ τὴν ὑπομονήν σε) one through two for τὴν ἐν τῷ κόπῳ ὑπομονήν, the endurance of labors, and indeed heavy ones, such as are accustomed to weigh upon Bishops. It is a great thing to bear such a burden.

Καὶ ὅτι ὀ δύνη βαστάσαι τες κακές) Used in a diminutive sense. For this is praiseworthy: See Plutarch περὶ ἀοργησίας. In the Manuscript, the καὶ is missing, so that that ὅτι is an explanation of constancy. A person is said to be unable to do something because it is abhorrent to his nature, Matth. XIII. 34. Joh. VIII. 43. XII. 35.

Καὶ ἐπείρασας τὲς λέγοντας ἑαυτὲς Ἀποστόλες εἶναι καὶ ἐκ εἰσίν) Again here the καὶ is in the Hebrew manner in place of a relative: You may also translate it thus: Who say they are Apostles, when they are not. In the Manuscript, εἶναι is missing. They said they were made Apostles through the revelation of Christ, which Paul truly said of himself, but they falsely. To test this was not for just anyone. The best method of discerning them was this, if they secretly sought after money, which they claimed to despise, and overlooked the sins of the rich. Such are those who are described in 2 Cor. XI. 13. and following.

Καὶ εὗρες αὐτὲς ψευδεῖς) You have detected their fallacies.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

Οἶδα τὰ ἔργα σε) Sunt quidam viri boni, quidam satis boni, ut ista distinguit Cicero in epistolis. Episcopus iste ex posteriori erat genere, ut sequentia indicant. Laudan- tur hic opera ejus, id est, pleraque κατὰ τὴν ἐπικράτειαν: Quomodo Deus speculatur & bonos & malos, Prov. XV. 3. & est תֹּכֵן רוּחוֹת Prov. XVI. 2. ita & Christus.

Καὶ τὸν κόπον καὶ τὴν ὑπομονήν σε) ἓν διὰ δυοῖν pro τὴν ἐν τῷ κόπῳ ὑπομονήν, laborum & quidem gravium, quales Episcopis incumbere solent, patientiam. Multum est tale onus perferre.

Καὶ ὅτι ὀ δύνη βαστάσαι τες κακές) Ἐς μειωτικῶς. Lau- dabile enim hoc: Vide Plutarchum περὶ ἀοργησίας. In Manuscripto deest καὶ, ita ut illud ὅτι sit explicatio con- stantiæ. Non posse quis dicitur, quod ab ingenio ejus abhorret, Matth. XIII. 34. Joh. VIII. 43. XII. 35.

Καὶ ἐπείρασας τὲς λέγοντας ἑαυτὲς Ἀποστόλες εἶναι καὶ ἐκ εἰσίν) Iterum hic καὶ more Ebræo est vice relativi: Potes & sic vertere: Qui dicunt, se Apostolos esse, cum non sint. In Manuscripto deest εἶναι. Dicebant se per Christi revelationem factos Apostolos, quod vere de se dicebat Paulus, illi falso. Hoc explorare non erat cujusvis. Opti- ma eos dignoscendi ratio hæc erat, si pecunias, quas con- temnere se dicebant clam appeterent, & divitum peccata dissimularent. Tales sunt, qui describuntur 2. Cor. XI. 13. & sequentibus.

Καὶ εὗρες αὐτὲς ψευδεῖς) Deprehendisti eorum falla- cias.

## 2:3
Vers. 3.

Καὶ ἐβάστασας καὶ ὑπομονὴν ἔχεις διὰ τὸ ὄνομά με) that is, bearing for my name's sake you have endurance. In the Manuscript there is a different order of words, which the Latin codex follows: Καὶ ὑπομονὴν ἔχεις καὶ ἐβάστασας. There is endurance in labors, and there is also in adversities, of which this treats: διὰ τὸ ὄνομά με for my sake, just as Matth. X. 22. διὰ τὸ ὄνομά με is the same as ἕνεκεν ἐμῦ, Matth. V. 11. Βασάζειν נָשָׂא 2. Reg. XVIII. 14. It is said of every thing that is heavy for us, such as are calamities.

In general, he first attributes to himself the knowledge of all things which the Ephesian Angel had done in the administration of his office, especially the Pastoral one, because as Arch-Bishop he performs the inspection of all Bishops and Pastors, and nothing escapes him: which knowledge is not conjectural, but certain and infallible, not of some works only, but indefinitely and universally of all, not as regards the external surface only, but as regards the internal condition, not in effect only, but in heart and affection, with what mind all things are done, whether it redounds from faith and charity, or not? since he himself searches the hearts and reins, Apoc. II. 23. Rightly Episcopius:

By works are understood in this place: 1. All actions, as well immanent as transient, whether internal or external, consistent with the divine will, and as such, that is, actions and the qualities of actions, principles, causes, ends, modes, circumstances, and whatever is knowable in them, so that they may be fully known. 2. Passions also, insofar as they are voluntary and freely undertaken, or endured: for very often both are accustomed to be understood by works in the scriptures. For even if a passion is not an action, because nevertheless the will to suffer is present, by which it happens that we are willing to suffer with an even mind, this action of the will deserves to be called an action: for the will can just as much will to receive according to the will of God and to bear, as to act or produce something of itself. However, the discourse here is not about the works of the Church, which Episcopius wishes, but of the Bishop. Nor indeed is a bare and simple knowledge understood, but a special science, which is called approval, concerning which Ps. 1:6, 2 Tim. 2:19, which befits Christ, inasmuch as He, as Priest and King, not only knows the works of those whom He has set over the Church, but also approves those which are to be approved.

Then specifically patience in labors: that he has sustained and endured the same with ὑπομονῇ, not only regarding the difficulty of the labors, which requires patience, but also regarding zeal, as far as the wickedness of men, which makes the Ecclesiastical office difficult, when we do not connive with them, but resist. That the labor is not of just anyone in the Church, but of the Episcopal office, is acknowledged even by those who say the epistle pertains to the Church, because indeed he understands not just any labor, but that which is in speech and doctrine, 1 Tim. 5:17, 1 Thess. 5:12, cf. 1 Tim. 4:13 seqq., where repentance is to be expected by Teachers and provoked by serious exhortation, and infirmity is to be tolerated: this is the ὑπομονὴ of labors, concerning which Paul had reminded Timothy, 2 Tim. 2:24, cf. Ezek. 34:4, 1 Thess. 5:14. But which patience must be tempered with zeal, lest it degenerate into the laxity of sluggish indulgence and remission. Therefore, it also contributed to the praise of the Bishop, τὴν ἐν τῷ κόπῳ ὑπομονὴν, which is particularly commended: And because you cannot bear the evil, namely, without correcting or expelling them from the Church, as Anselm explains: For thus had Timothy been instructed long ago by St. Paul, 2 Tim. 2:24, cf. Ps. 99:13, Isa. 68:1, Jer. 15:19, Ezek. 3:18, ch. 33:7 seqq., Tit. 1:12. Furthermore, he also commends vigilance against Pseudo-Apostles, which he demonstrated by observing and testing them, which is to be understood concerning the trial by reason of doctrine and the proof of the same from the word of God: because when they persuaded themselves and others that they were Apostles, by his own judgment, they are not, and that that Ephesian Bishop found those false ones: who are Apostles neither by calling nor by doctrine, although they carried both before them: Cf. 2 Cor. 11:13. St. Paul had predicted the danger from such to the Ephesians, Acts 20:29, and that they had arisen and been found there when Timothy was presiding over them, is evident from 1 Tim. 1:3, 2 Tim. 2:17, where the Apostle noted Hymenaeus and Philetus, who were perverting the faith of some; such as perhaps Phygellus and Hermogenes 2 Tim. 1:15. But among them they especially reckon Cerinthus, concerning whom Eusebius, Hist. Eccl. book 3, ch. 28, has this from Gaius: But also Cerinthus, through certain revelations written by him as if by some great Apostle, introduced to us certain prodigies shown to him as if by Angels, affirming that after the resurrection the kingdom of Christ would be on earth, and again that men living in Jerusalem would be subject to the desires and pleasures of the body: And that enemy of the divine scriptures adds that the space of a thousand years would be spent in nuptial feasts, so that he might more easily deceive unskilled men. Which is also confirmed from Dionysius of Alexandria, book 2, on promises, and from Irenaeus, book 1, against heresies, mentioning certain more secret fabrications of the same.

Καὶ ἐκ ἐκοπίασας) לֹא יָגַעְתָּי: See Isa. 16:2, 47:15. That Manuscript also has it thus, not as other books: Κεκοπίακας καὶ ὠ̓ κέκμηκας.

On the contrary, Petrus Faber, Agonist. book 2, ch. 8, suspects, and that probably by the judgment of Cornelius, that there is an error here in the Greek Codices, and that for ἐκοπίασας one should read κέκμηκα: Since it does not seem to him that the Apostle takes κόπον differently in this verse than in the preceding verse. But the Aldine Codex of the New Testament published at Venice in the year 1518, and that of Robert Stephanus published at Paris in the year 1546, and the Basilian in the year 1565, and the Lugdunum in the year 1571, read both, in this way: Καὶ διὰ τὸ ὄνομά με κεκοπίακας καὶ ὀ̓ κέκμηκας: Which is altogether the more approved reading: And thus the Vulgate reads: And you have sustained for my name, and have not failed. Thus also Beza rendered: And for my name you have labored, and have not grown weary. Erasmus Schmidius: Οὐ κέκμηκας you have not grown weary, you have not suffered because of the duration τῷ κόπῳ, you have not turned aside from the straight path. Κάμνω I labor with weariness, or αὐσπαθῶς, as Gregory says of Euclid, κάμνων ἐν ἀποδείξεσιν, assiduously occupied with demonstrations, or ἀλλοπαθῶς to labor studiously. Odyss. ο. ἔνθ᾽ ἔσαν οἱ πέπλοι παμ- πόικιλοι, ὓς κάμεν αὐτὴ, which she herself had labored. Likewise, I am tired, I am weary. Those who read ἐκεκοπία- κας will not be able to sustain the sense of the Vulgate, unless with Cornelius they understand τὸ κοπιᾷν not as simply to labor, but to labor in a perfect act in such a way that in the labor you fail and succumb.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

Καὶ ἐβάστασας καὶ ὑπομονὴν ἔχεις διὰ τὸ ὄνομά με) id est, βαστάζων διὰ τὸ ὄνομά με ὑπομονὴν ἔχεις. In Manuscripto est alius ordo verborum, quem sequitur codex Latinus: Καὶ ὑπομονὴν ἔχεις καὶ ἐβάστασας. Est ὑπομονὴ in laboribus, est & in adversis, de quo hic agitur: διὰ τὸ ὄνομά με mea de causa, sicut Matth. X. 22. διὰ τὸ ὄνομά με idem est, quod ἕνεκεν ἐμῦ, Matth. V. 11. Βασάζειν נָשָׂא 2. Reg. XVIII. 14. De omni re dicitur, quæ nobis gravis est, quales sunt calamitates.

In genere primum notitiam omnium, quæ in ad- ministratione muneris imprimis Pastoralis gesse- rat Angelus Ephesinus, sibi tribuit, quod ceu Ar- chi-Episcopus inspectione omnium Episcoporum & Pastorum fungatur, nec quicquam ipsum fugiat: quæ notitia non est conjecturalis, sed certa & in- fallibilis, non quorundam tantum operum, sed in- definite & universaliter omnium, non quoad ex- ternam tantum superficiem, sed quoad internam conditionem, non in effectu tantum, sed in corde & affectu, quo animo omnia agantur, an ex fide, & charitate redundet, necne? siquidem corda & renes ipse scrutetur, Apoc. II. 23. Recte Episcopius:

Per opera intelliguntur hoc loco 1. actiones omnes, tam immanentes, quam transeuntes, sive internæ & externæ, voluntati divinæ convenientes, & qua ta- les, id est, actiones & actionum qualitates, principia, causæ, fines, modi, circumstantiæ, & quicquid in iis cognoscibile est, ut plene cognoscantur. 2. Passio- nes etiam, quatenus illæ voluntariæ & liberè susce- ptæ sunt, sive latæ: sæpenumero enim utrumque per opera in scripturis solet intelligi. Etiamsi enim passio actio non sit, quia tamen voluntas patiendi adest, qua fit, ut æquo animo velimus pati, hæc actio voluntatis merito dicenda est: voluntas enim tam potest velle recipere juxta voluntatem Dei & ferre, quam agere aut producere aliquid de se. Non tamen hîc de operibus Ecclesiæ, quod vult Episco- pius, sed Episcopi sermo est. Neque vero nuda tantum & simplex notitia intelligitur, sed specialis scientia, quæ approbationis dicitur, de qua Psal. I. 6. 2. Tim. II. 19. quæ Christo convenit, utpote qui tan- quam Sacerdos, & Rex non tantum norit eorum, quos præfecit Ecclesiæ, opera, sed ea etiam probet, quæ probanda sunt.

Deinde in specie patientiam in laboribus: quod sustinuerit & exantlarit eosdem cum ὑπομονῇ non solum quoad difficultatem laborum, quæ patien- tiam requirit, sed etiam quoad zelum, quantum ad improbitatem hominum, quæ difficile reddit munus Ecclesiasticum, cum iis non connivemus, sed resistimus. Laborem non quorumvis in Eccle- sia, sed officii Episcopalis intelligi agnoscunt etiam, qui epistolam ad Ecclesiam spectare ajunt, quod nempe non quemvis laborem, sed eum, qui est in sermone & doctrina, intelligat, 1. Timoth. V. 17. 1. Thess. V. 12. conf. 1. Timoth. IV. 13. seqq. ubi expe- ctanda Doctoribus, & seria exhortatione provo- canda pœnitentia ac infirmitas toleranda: hæc est laborum ὑπομονὴ, de qua Timotheum commone- fecerat Paulus, 2. Tim. II. 24. conf. Ezech. XXXIV. 4. 1. Thess. V. 14. Quæ vero patientia cum zelo tem- peranda, ne in segnis indulgentiæ & remissionis la- xitatem degeneret. Ideo ad laudem Episcopi etiam τὴν ἐν τῷ κόπῳ ὑπομονὴν faciebat, quod peculia- riter commendatur: Et quia non potes sustinere ma- los, scilicet, quin corrigas vel expellas ab Ecclesia, ut exponit Anselmus: Ita enim à S. Paulo infor- matus erat pridem Timotheus, 2. Tim. II. 24. conf. Psal. XCIX. 13. Esa. LXVIII. 1. Jerem. XV. 19. Ezech. III. 18. cap. XXXIII. 7. seqq. Tit. I. 12. Adhæc com- mendat etiam vigilantiam adversus Pseudo-Apo- stolos, quam illos observando & tentando, quod de tentamine ratione doctrinæ, ejusdemque ex verbo Dei probatione intelligendum, demonstravit: quia cum persuaderent sibi aliisque, se esse Aposto- los, ipsomet decernente, non sunt, quodque Epi- scopus ille Ephesinus falsos illos invenerit: qui nec vocatione, nec doctrina Apostoli sint, licet utrum- que præ se ferrent: Conf. 2. Cor. XI. 13. Prædixerat Ephesinis a talibus S. Paulus periculum, Actor. XX. 29. & exortos eos, ac repertos ibi fuisse, cum Timo- theus illis præesset, e 1. Tim. I. 3. 2. Tim. II. 17. con- stat, ubi Hymenæum & Philetum, quorundam fidem pervertentes, notavit Apostolus; quales forte Phy- gellus ac Hermogenes 2. Timoth. I. 15. Illis autem im- primis accensent Cerinthum, de quo Eusebius l. III. Hist. Eccl. cap. 28. ita habet ex Cajo: Sed & Cerin- thus per revelationes quasdam a se tanquam a ma- gno quodam Apostolo conscriptas portenta quædam quasi ab Angelis sibi ostensa commentus nobis intro- duxit, affirmans post resurrectionem regnum Christi in terris futurum, ac rursus homines Hierosolymis degentes cupiditatibus & voluptati corporis obno- xios fore: Additque hostis ille divinarum scriptura- rum, mille annorum spatium in nuptialibus festis transactum iri, quo facilius imperitos homines deci- piat. Quæ etiam ex Dionysio Alexandrini l. II. de promission. confirmat, & ex Irenæi l. I. advers. hæ- ret. secretiora quædam ejusdem figmenta comme- morante.

Καὶ ἐκ ἐκοπίασας) לֹא יָגַעְתָּי: Vide Esaæ XVI. 2. XLVII. 15. Habet sic & Manuscriptus ille, non ut alii libri: Κεκοπίακας καὶ ὠ̓ κέκμηκας.

Ex adverso Petrus Faber l. II. Agonist. c. 8. suspi- catur, idque judicio Cornelii probabiliter, mendum hic esse in Græcis Codicibus, & pro ἐκοπίασας legen- dum κέκμηκα: Quin non videtur ipsi Apostolum aliter κόπον hoc versu, aliter versu præcedente acci- pere. Aldinus vero Codex Novi Testamenti Ve- netiis Anno 1518. editus, & Roberti Stephani editus Parisiis Anno 1546. & Basiliensis Anno 1565. & Lugdunensis Anno 1571. utrumque legunt, hoc mo- do : Καὶ διὰ τὸ ὄνομά με κεκοπίακας καὶ ὀ̓ κέκμηκας: Quæ omnino probatior lectio est: Atque ita legit Vulgata: Et sustinuisti propter nomen meum, & non defecisti. Sic etiam Beza reddidit : Et propter nomen meum laborasti, & non es defatigatus. Erasmus Schmidius: Οὐ κέκμηκας non defatigatus es, non pas- sus es ob diuturnitatem τῷ κόπῳ, te a recta via defle- στι. Κάμνω laboro cum defatigatione, sive αὐσπαθῶς, ut Gregorius de Euclide, κάμνων ἐν ἀποδείξεσιν, assi- due occupatus demonstrationibus, sive ἀλλοπαθῶς studiosè elaborare. Odyss. ο. ἔνθ᾽ ἔσαν οἱ πέπλοι παμ- πόικιλοι, ὓς κάμεν αὐτὴ, quos elaboraverat ipsa. Item fessus sum, defatigatus sum. Qui legunt ἐκεκοπία- κας, senium Vulgatæ sustinere non poterunt, nisi cum Cornelio τὸ κοπιᾷν non simpliciter laborare, sed in actu perfecto ita laborare, ut in labore de- ficias & succumbas, intelligant.

## 2:4
Vers. 4.

Ἀλλ᾽ ἔχω κατά σου) I have, however, something to complain about you. Concerning this locution see Matt. 5:2, 3.

Ὄτι τὴν ἀγάπην σε τὴν πρώτην ἀφῆκας) You have remitted much of that first care for the poor. That care indeed always pertained to Bishops, but it burdened them most in new Churches, where there were not yet Deacons. That ἀφῆκας here does not signify ἀγάπην in every way, but τὴν πρώτην, that is, that which was so fervent. A certain weariness is also accustomed to creep upon sharp minds with time. Wherefore they are to be warned both by others of themselves, and by themselves through prayers and attentive thoughts, as if to be awakened from sleep. Πρώτην, that is, πρωτέραν, as John 1:15, where see the things said.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

Ἀλλ᾽ ἔχω κατά σου) Habeo tamen aliquid, quod de te que- rar. De hac loquutione vide Matth. V. 2, 3.

Ὄτι τὴν ἀγάπην σε τὴν πρώτην ἀφῆκας) Multum remisisti de prima illa cura circa pauperes. Ea cura semper quidem E- piscopos spectavit, sed maxime eos onerabat in novis Eccle- siis, ubi nondum erant Diaconi. Illud ἀφῆκας hic non omni- modam ἀγάπην significat, sed τὴν πρώτην, id est, illam adeo ferventem. Solet etiam acribus animis cum tempore lassi- tudo quædam obrepere. Quare & ab aliis per se monita, & a semetipsis per preces & attentas cogitationes velut e somno excitandi sunt. Πρώτην, id est, πρωτέραν, ut Joh. I. 15. ubi dicta vide.

## 2:5
Verse 5.

Μνημόνευε ὖν πόθεν ἐκπέπτωκας) Consider from what degree of honor you have fallen. Thus we have μνημονεύων in 2 Tim. II. 8. And for the Hebrews זָכַר, זְכֹר is taken in this way. In the Manuscript πόθεν πέπτωκας נָפַלְתָּ.

Καὶ μετανόησον καὶ τὰ πρῶτα ἔργα ποίησον) that is, repent to do the first works.

It is not a matter here of remission in the care of the poor: for there is nothing in the text that points to that: But just as previously the diligent care and vigilance of this Bishop was celebrated with fervor and zeal for the purity of the divine word against the Pseudo-Apostles without any remission or deficiency, so he seems to have become more remiss, having left that first fervor of charity toward God and the divine word: For he is commanded, having done penance, to do the former works: But what are those former works, if not those which the Son of God had previously commended, that he could not tolerate the wicked, that he tested the Pseudo-Apostles, that he labored for the name of the Lord, and was not wearied. It is of such a defect that it is treated here, on account of which the Son of God threatens the removal of the lampstand, which does not seem to be said of some more remiss care of the poor. There follows a correction, which the Son of God adds, namely that he still employs zeal against the works of the Nicolaitans, from which it may be gathered that it was previously a matter of lukewarmness in the refutation. Where also Cornelius a Lapide goes with Pererius, Ribera, Alcafar, and others, although they understand Timothy through this Angel of Ephesus. It seems, therefore, that Timothy, who for 40 years had already been Bishop of Ephesus (for he was Bishop in the year of Christ 57, and the year of Christ 97 was already underway, as I said in verse 1. Therefore, 40 years had already elapsed since the beginning of his episcopate), had grown somewhat lukewarm in preaching the word of God and in the labor of converting the Ephesians, because he saw that the Jews and Gentiles, worshippers of the Ephesian Diana, were persistently resisting him; whence, partly from pusillanimity and lukewarmness, and partly from human prudence suggesting that for the sake of peace it was necessary to act more remissly, lest by excessive zeal he should disturb the Christian cause more and stir up the infidels against himself and his own (as he remembered had happened to St. Paul once at Ephesus, when the crowd shouted against him: Great is Diana of the Ephesians, Acts 19:34), he relaxed somewhat from his former ardor for evangelizing.

As for what Cornelius thinks, that this sin was venial, not mortal, in that he is entirely mistaken. For not only does every sin by its own nature deserve death, but he is also pronounced cursed by the divine voice who does the work of the Lord negligently, Jerem. XLVIII. 10. He adds from Alcafar: For often Prelates sin more through remissness, which creeps in under the guise of prudence, than through imprudence, which [creeps in] under the guise of zeal. Both, however, are a vice, and both are here reproved by Christ: the former in the Ephesian Bishop, the latter in the Thyatirean. But in the epistle to the Thyatirean Bishop nothing of the sort occurs, from which it might be permitted to gather a correction against imprudence committed under the guise of zeal. Rather, remissness is reproved in him in tolerating Jezebel, chap. II. 20; it is not found that her zeal is overly reproved. For the rest, they are rightly observed by Chrysostom homil. 1 on Lazarus, the reasons why a Bishop ought not to grow lukewarm in preaching, even if few or none are converted: First, by the example of fountains, which always gush forth, even if no one draws from them. Second, by the example of Jeremiah, ch. 20:7, who, though mocked by the Jews, is nevertheless commanded by God to preach to them. Third, by the example of Christ, who admonished Judas, even though he was obstinate. Fourth, because those who are good at least become better, and those who are not yet converted may perhaps be converted later. Whence St. Paul commands the same Timothy in 2 Epist. ch. 4, saying: Preach the word, be instant in season, out of season, reprove, entreat in all patience. It is not, however, a wonder that Timothy himself, although previously quite stout-hearted and burning with zeal for the divine word, became more remiss in his old age, since experience not rarely demonstrates that other Bishops, who initially proved themselves full of most ardent zeal, have become more lukewarm in their latest age; and the Angels of the Church of Pergamum, as well as of Thyatira, are both commended for their zeal by the Son of God, and at the same time rebuked because they show themselves too remiss against certain people. Pareus and Sibelius, asserting the inamissibility of faith, and others of the Calvinists, as well as Pererius, Ribera, Alcafar, and Cornel. a Lap. from the Papists, understand this remission in the degrees of love, not the loss of charity itself.

If not, I will come to you quickly, and will move your lampstand out of its place, unless you repent) I will cause your people to flee elsewhere, namely to those places where greater care is taken of the poor. I will come quickly and will move is nothing else than I will quickly move. Thus, having come, offer, Matt. 5:24. Having come, I will heal, Matt. 8:7. Thus, having gone, do, Luke 10:37. Having gone, learn, Matt. 9:13.

That gloss is merely arbitrary. He does not threaten that the people will flee elsewhere, but that the lampstand will be removed, or from his care, as Rupert, Hugo, Richard, Victorinus, Cornelius a Lapide, and others say, some of whom posit a hypallage: I will move your lampstand from its place, that is, I will move you from the place of your lampstand, or from that place, which the words imply more. But why does the Son of God threaten punishment to the Church because of the Bishop's negligence or lukewarmness? That happens, partly because the people or the communion are accustomed to imitate the Bishop: partly because, when heretics are not refuted, they easily fill the Church with their heterodox opinions: hence, therefore, with Pseudo-Apostles or heretics occupying the place, the lampstand of the divine word no longer holds in that seat, in which, namely, the light of the word shines. Therefore, some posit a Metonymy, so that the lampstand is taken for the lamp which is placed on the lampstand. If, however, with Victorinus the Martyr, the people are understood by the lampstand, I will move the lampstand, that is, I will scatter your people, the cause of it is not the neglected care of the poor, but a just rebuke omitted. Because God, by a just judgment, scatters ecclesiastical assemblies on account of heresies tolerated in the Church. For that toleration of heresies arises from contempt of heavenly truth.

Latin:

Vers. 5.

Μνημόνευε ὖν πόθεν ἐκπέπτωκας) Cogita equanto hono- ris gradu decideris. Sic μνημονεύων habemus 2. Tim. II. 8. Et Ebræis זָכַר ita sumitur זְכֹר. In Manuscripto πόθεν πέπτωκας נָפַלְתָּ.

Καὶ μετανόησον καὶ τὰ πρῶτα ἔργα ποίησον) id est, μετανόη- σον πρὸς τὸ ποιῆσαι τὰ ἔργα τὰ πρῶτα.

De remissione in cura pauperum hic non agi- tur: nihil enim in textu est, quod eo respiciat: Sed uti antea celebrata fuit Episcopi hujus sedula cura & vigilantia cum fervore ac zelo pro verbi divini puritate adversus Pseudo-Apostolos fine ulla re- missione vel deficientia, ita videtur remissior ille factus primum illum fervorem charitatis erga Deum & verbum divinum reliquisse: Nam jubetur acta pœnitentia priora opera facere: Quænam vero illa priora sunt opera, nisi quæ prius commendarat Fi- lius Dei, quod malos tolerare non potuerit, quod Pseudo-Apostolos tentarit, quod propter nomen Do- mini laborarit, nec defatigatus sit. De tali hic agi- tur defectu, ob quem minatur Filius Dei dimotio- nem candelabri, quod non videtur de remissiori ali- qua pauperum cura dicendum. Accedit correctio, quam addit Filius Dei, quod nempe zelum adhuc adhibeat adversus opera Nicolaitarum, unde colli- gere licet, prius de tepiditate in elencho actum fuisse. Quo etiam abit Cornelius a Lapide cum Pererio, Ribera, Alcafare, & aliis, etsi Timotheum per Angelum hunc Ephesinum intelligant. Videtur ergo Timotheus, qui per 40. annos jam fuerat Epi- scopus Ephesi (fuit enim Episcopus anno Christi 57. & jam agebatur annus Christi 97. ut dixi vers. 1. Ergo jam ab Episcopatus exordio effluxerant anni 40.) nonnihil intepuisse in prædicando verbo Dei, in labore convertendi Ephesios, eo quod videret Ju- dæos & gentiles Dianæ Ephesiæ cultores sibi perti- naciter obsistere, unde partim ex pusillanimitate & tepore, partim ex prudentia humana suggerente, quod pacis causa oporteret remissius agere, ne ni- mio zelo magis rem Christianam turbaret, & infi- deles contra se suosque suscitaret (ut Ephesi olim S. Paulo contigisse, turba contra eum conclamante: Magna Diana Ephesiorum Actor. XIX. v. 34. me- minerat) de pristino Evangelizandi ardore nonnihil remisit.

Quod vero Cornelius putat, peccatum hoc fuisse veniale, non mortale, in eo omnino errat. Nam non modo peccatum omne natura sua mortem meretur, sed maledictus etiam voce divina pro- nunciatur, qui opus Domini facit negligenter, Jerem. XLVIII. 10. Addit ex Alcafare: Sæpe enim Prælati magis peccant per remissionem, quæ specie prudentiæ\obrepit, quam per imprudentiam, quæ sub specie ze- li. Utrumque tamen vitium est, utrumque hic re- prehenditur a Christo: Prius in Episcopo Ephesino, posterius in Thyatirensi. Sed in epistola ad Thya- tirensem Episcopum nihil tale occurrit, ex qua epanorthosin adversus imprudentiam sub specie zeli commissam colligere liceat. Remissio potius in ipso reprehenditur in toleranda Jesabele cap. II. 20. nimium ejus zelum reprehendi non invenitur. De cætero recte observantur a Chrysostomo homil. I. de Lazaro, causæ, cur Episcopus non debeat te- pescere in concionando, etiamsi pauci aut nulli convertantur: Primo exemplo fontium, qui semper scaturiunt, licet nemo inde hauriat. Secundo ex- emplo Jeremiæ cap. XX. 7. qui irrisus a Judæis, jube- tur tamen a Deo iis concionari. Tertio exemplo Christi, qui Judam, licet obstinatum, admonuit. Quarto quia qui boni sunt saltem fiunt meliores, & qui jam non convertuntur, postea forte converten- tur. Unde eidem Timotheo S. Paulus epist. II. c. IV. præcipit dicens: Prædica verbum, insta opportune, importune, argue, obsecra in omni patientia. Non autem mirum, Timotheum ipsum, etsi antea satis cordatum, & zelo verbi divini flagrantem in sene- ctute remissiorem factum, quum alios etiam Epi- scopos, qui se initio zelo ardentissimo plenos pro- barunt, novissima ætate tepidiores factos experi- entia non raro demonstrarit; atque Angeli Eccle- siæ Pergamensis, necnon Thyatirensis & a zelo com- mendentur a Filio Dei, & simul reprehendantur, quod remissiores se contra quosdam exhibeant. Remissionem in gradibus amoris, non amissionem ipsius charitatis intelligunt Pareus, Sibelius fidem inamissibilem adserentes, alique Calvin. nec non e Pontificiis Pererius, Ribera, Alcafar, Cornel. a Lap.

Εἰ δὲ μὴ, ἔρχομαί σοι ταχὺ, καὶ κινήσω τὴν λυχνίαν σου ἐκ τοῦ τόπου αὐτῆς, ἐὰν μὴ μετανοήσῃς) Efficiam ut plebs tua alio diffugiat, nempe ad ea loca, ubi major habetur cura paupe- rum. Ἔρχομαι ταχὺ καὶ κινήσω nihil aliud est quam ταχὺ κινήσω. Sic ἐλθὼν πρόσφερε, Matth. V. 24. Ἐλθὼν θερα- πεύσω, Matth. VIII. 7. Sic πορευθεὶς καὶ ποίει, Luc. X. 37. πορευθέντες μάθετε, Matth. IX. 13.

Glossa ista mere arbitraria est. Non plebem alio diffugituram minatur, sed candelabrum re- motum iri, sive a cura ipsius, ut Rupertus, Hugo, Richardus, Victorinus, Cornelius a Lapide, alii, e- quibus nonnulli hypallagen statuunt, movebo can- delabrum tuum de loco suo, hoc est, movebo te de loco candelabri tui, seu ab isto loco, quod magis verba inferunt. Qui vero ob Episcopi negligen- tiam, aut tepiditatem pœnam minatur Ecclesiæ Fi- lius Dei? Fit illud, tum quia Episcopum imitari solet populus vel communio: tum quia non re- probatis hæreticis, illi heterodoxis suis opinioni- bus facile replent Ecclesiam: Inde ergo locum oc- cupantibus Pseudo-Apostolis vel hæreticis non amplius candelabrum verbi divini in ea sede obti- net, in quo scilicet lux verbi lucet. Ideo nonnulli Metonymiam statuunt, ut candelabrum accipia- tur pro lucerna, quæ in candelabro ponitur. Si ta- men cum Victorino Martyre populus intelligatur per candelabrum, movebo candelabrum, id est, dispergam plebem tuam, causa ejus non est negle- cta pauperum cura, sed justa ἔλεγξις intermissa. Quia ob toleratas in Ecclesia hæreses Deus justo judicio dispergit cœtus Ecclesiasticos: . Illa enim tolerantia hæresium ex contemptu veritatis cœle- stis oritur.

## 2:6
Verse 6.

But this you have, that you hate the works of the Nicolaitans) With wonderful art he mitigated the rebuke, both with preceding and following praises. Paul uses the same artifice in 1 Cor. 1 and 11. It is sufficiently agreed among the ancients that the Nicolaitans had their name from Nicolaus, one of the first Deacons. But whether those evil dogmas flowed from him, or were falsely sold under his name, is not so. To me, comparing the testimonies of the ancients, the middle opinion pleases: which is this, that Nicolaus, being accused of jealousy, because having a beautiful wife he did not sufficiently bear those kisses of peace customary among Christians of both sexes, ran to the contrary, and by the example of the Laconians and Cato permitted the use of his wife to others, just as if there were no sin in that which was done with the husband and wife willing. But this window having been opened once against Evangelical chastity, afterwards, as evils are wont not to stand where they begin, all lusts were admitted. But those who had despised discipline to that extent, it is no wonder that they permitted themselves soft flesh without any discrimination.

Augustine in his letter to Quodvultdeus, chapter 5, handed down the same things about Nicolaus, observing that that deed of Nicolaus was turned into a most shameful sect, in which the indiscriminate use of women is pleasing. Nor, therefore, is that foulness to be attributed only to the followers of Nicolaus, as some do: Nicolaus himself is held guilty of the same by Augustine, Philastrius, Epiphanius, as also by Tertullian in De praescriptione haereticorum, chapter 46, whence the name of that heresiarch stuck to his followers: after whose example they are rightly called Zwinglians and Calvinists by Zwingli and Calvin, the authors of heresy, Arminians by Arminius, and Socinians by Socinus. But Cocceius is very rash when he judges it clearly rash to say: 'At that time a certain Nicolaus existed, the author of a sect,' and he pretends that it is a mere enigma in the vision, and wishes a Nicolaitan to be a sect-making [person], and to usurp the name of a man besides the name of Christ. But we reject this, not undeservedly, as the enigmas of his own mind. Gomarus disputes on both sides concerning the sect of the Nicolaitans, originating from Nicolaus, finally acceding to the negative: yet the affirmative is proven by Episcopius. The opinion of Hoffmann, that by Nicolaitans are understood Romans or Gentiles, then portending famine to the whole world, does not deserve a refutation. But Saint Augustine does not report only this one error of the Nicolaitans in the aforementioned place: nor even only that other one concerning foods not necessarily separated from those which had been sacrificed to idols, but also concerning other rites of Gentile superstitions admitted: and also certain fabulous notions about the world, with which they mixed the barbarous names of Princes into their disputations, and attributed creation not to God, but to certain powers, which they either fashioned with wonderful vanity or believed in. Epiphanius hints that that heresy gave origin to the Gnostics; Eusebius (Book IV, ch. 29) makes it contemporary with the Cerinthian, while Tertullian, Epiphanius, and Augustine make it earlier. L. Danæus, in his commentary on the aforementioned passage of Augustine, reports from the testimony of a certain Bohemian that some remnants of this sect still existed in Bohemia. It certainly was useful to the Mahometans for proving polygamy, which someone recently did not fear to defend in a very scandalous writing among Christians, worthy of being publicly burned and exterminated. Here, works are dogmas; which are the works proper to heretics: and fruits, by which they are to be distinguished, Matt. VII. 16. just as faith is the work of God, John VI. & v. 5. above called the first works: thus heresy is the work of the Devil, John VIII. 41. 44. the work of the flesh, Gal. V. 20.

which I also hate) Namely, as contrary to the Gospel. In the Manuscript, the 'ἃ' is absent, with the sense remaining intact.

Latin:

Vers. 6.

Ἀλλὰ τοῦτο ἔχεις, ὅτι μισεῖς τὰ ἔργα τῶν Νικολαϊτῶν) Mira arte reprehensionem mitigavit, & antepositis & subjun- ctis laudationibus. Eodem artificio Paulus utitur 1. Cor. I. & XI. Nicolaitas nomen habuisse ab uno primorum Diaconorum Nicolao satis inter veteres constat. Sed an mala illa dogmata ab ipso fluxerint, an vero falso sub ejus nomine fuerint venditata, non item. Mihi veterum testi- monia conferenti media placet sententia: quæ hæc est, Nicolaum accusatum ζηλοτυπίας, quod uxorem pulchram habens usirata illa inter Christianos utriusque sexus pacis oscula non satis ferret, in contrarium cucurrisse, & exemplo Laconum ac Catonis uxoris suæ usuram permisisse aliis, plane quasi in eo, quod marito & uxore volentibus fieret, non peccaretur. Sed hac aperta semel contra Evangelicam castitatem fenestra, postea, ut solent non stare ubi incipiunt mala, tota fore admissas libidines. Qui vero eousque disci- plinam contempserant, eos non mirum est, in molatitias carnes sibi permisisse sine ullo discrimine.

Eadem de Nicolao tradidit Augustin. ad Quod vult Deum c. V. observans factum illud Nicolai in turpisssimam sectam versum esse, in qua placet usus indifferens fœminarum. Nec ergo tantum Ni- colai sectatoribus fœditas illa tribuenda cum qui- busdam: Nicolaus ipse ejusdem reus ab Augu- stino, Philastrio, Epiphanio, ut & Tertulliano de præscript. hær. c. 46. peragitur, unde & sequacibus nomen hæresiarchæ istius hæsit: ad quorum ex- emplum recte a Zwinglio & Calvino, hæreseos Autoribus, Zwingliani & Calviniani, ab Armi- nio Arminiani, a Socino Sociniani nuncupantur. Temerarius autem valde est Coccejus, dum plane temerarium censet dicere: Eo tempore extitisse Ni- colaum quendam, Autorem sectæ, fingitque me- rum ænigma id esse in visione, ac Nicolaitam vult esse sectam facere, & nomen hominis usurpare præ- ter nomen Christi. Sed rejicimus hoc non immeri- to ad ænigmata propriæ mentis. De secta Nicolai- tarum, a Nicolao oriunda in utramque partem disputat Gomarus, negativæ tandem accedens: Episcopio tamen affirmativa probatur. Hoff- manni sententia per Nicolaitas intelligi Romanos sive Ethnicos, tum famem universo mundo omi- nantes, refutationem non meretur. Non autem unum istum errorem tantum Nicolaitarum re- fert l. c. S. Augustinus: nec etiam saltim alterum istum de cibis ab iis, quæ idolis immolata erant, non separatis necessario, sed etiam de aliis ritibus gentilium superstitionum admissis: nec non fabu- losa quædam de mundo, quibus barbara Princi- pum nomina disputationibus suis miscuerint, ac creationem tribuerint non Deo, sed quibusdam potestatibus, quas mirabili vel finxerint vanitate, vel crediderint. Hæresin illam Gnosticis origi- nem dedisse Epiphanius innuit; quam σύγχρονον Cerinthianæ facit Eusebius l. IV. c. 29. priorem ea Tertullianus, Epiphanius & Augustinus. Reli- quias adhuc aliquas sectæ istius in Bohemia fuisse refert ex Bohemi cujusdam testimonio L. Da- næus ad locum dictum Augustini. Mahometa- nis certe ad polygamiam probandam profuit, quam non veritus est nuper nonnemo scripto per- quam scandaloso inter Christianos tueri, digno quod publice comburatur & exterminetur. Ἔργα hic sunt dogmata; quæ ἔργα propria hæreticorum: & fructus, e quibus dignoscendi, Matth. VII. 16. ut fides ἔργον τῦ Θεῦ Joh. VI. & v. 5. supra τὰ πρῶ- τα ἔργα dicta: ita hæresis ἔργον Diaboli, Joh. VIII. 41. 44. ἔργον τῆς σαρκὸς, Gal. V. 20.

ἃ κἀγὼ μισῶ) Nempe ut Evangelio contraria. In Ma- nuscripto abest ἃ sensu salvo.

## 2:7
Verse 7.

he who has ears, let him hear) A formula of one exciting attention, Matt. XI. 5. XIII. 9. 43. Mark IV. 9. 23. VIII. 16. Luke VIII. 8. XIV. 35. below II. 17. 29. XII. 9. This is, as it were, כּלֹא in the Psalms.

What the Spirit says to the Churches) the spirit, that is, this divine vision: concerning this acceptance of this word, see 1 Cor. XII. 3. 10. 1 John IV. 1. 2. 3. Thus in Hermas: That Spirit is the Son of God, that is, that vision. Says, that is, commands to be said to the Churches, namely the Ephesian and others, which were under the care of the Ephesian Bishop.

The spirit nowhere in the sacred scriptures denotes a divine vision; 1 Cor. XII. 3. signifies the Holy Spirit, the third hypostasis of the Holy Trinity, as is clear from the whole context, the author of knowledge, confidence, and the profession of faith in Christ, and not indeed a divine vision. Nor does it occur in v. 10, or even 1 John IV. 1. 2. 3. concerning a divine vision, but concerning men boasting of the Spirit, whom it is permitted to judge by the sacred Scripture. Hermas does not deserve to be heard here among sacred things. Those works of saying, speaking, testifying, announcing, and the like, are personal acts, and designate the hypostasis of the Holy Spirit.

To him who overcomes) To him who suffers himself to be led away from Christianity neither by hunger nor by other inconveniences.

I will give to eat from the tree of life, which is in the midst of the paradise of my God) There is an opposition similar to that in Matt. V. 6. Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied. The LXX put wood for the tree עֵץ. By the fruit of the tree of life, the Holy Spirit is to be understood here, who makes us certain of life, and indeed immortal life. The Law is to the Hebrews the food of the soul, the tree of life, Prov. II. 19. because it gives a happy life on earth. But much more justly Christ, the Author of eternal life, the bread of life, John VI. 35. 41. 48. 50. 51. 58. The tree of life is explained by Philo in 'On the Creation of the World' as piety, in his allegories as the character of perfect virtue. Some of the ancients do not wrongly refer this passage to the Eucharist, because through it, when taken as it ought to be, the Holy Spirit is introduced and increased. In the Manuscript it is in the Paradise. You have that 'of my God' also below III. 12. So also John XX. 17.

The victors are the Elect in the triumphant Church, Ribera, Cornel. a Lap., not so Bellarmine, 'On the Beatitude of the Saints', ch. 18. It does not appear that hunger is being specifically referred to; although it follows concerning the eating of the tree of life: because victory is obtained rather against the seductions of the Nicolaitans, and thus of any heresies whatsoever, which is obtained through faith, as well as against any scandals of vices: therefore, if these things refer to eating, because a magnificent promise of eating from the tree of life is joined, the prohibition of eating things sacrificed to idols is referred to, as that which the Nicolaitans admitted, and consequently the use and enjoyment of all those things which are forbidden by God. For to those who abstain according to the divine prescription, the enjoyment of the fruit of the tree of life is promised by grace, which is Christ, Apocal. XXII. 2. whose fruit, and indeed leaves, are for the healing of the nations. Moreover, the Holy Spirit may indeed be reckoned among the fruits of the tree of life, because Christ both merited for us and provides the same, and the communication of his gifts, from whose fullness we all receive grace for grace, John 1:16. That enjoyment, however, entirely comprises the righteousness of Christ, and his obedience, both active and passive: for that tree of life, that green wood, bore these fruits in his life, passion, and death, Luke 23:31, John 11:24, 1 Corinthians 1:30; we enjoy these through faith in this life. For here we eat of the tree of life and its fruits, and we perceive its sweetness, 1 Peter 2:3. Nor are regeneration, justification, adoption, sanctification, renewal, glorification, and eternal salvation excluded from the fruits of the tree of life, all of which must be attributed to the tree of life, just as the tree of life in the earthly Paradise could have served our first parents with its fruits for the perpetuity of life: so this tree of spiritual life, Christ, serves us with his fruits for a life of grace and glory, spiritual and heavenly, not only temporary, but also eternal. It is not a matter here properly of the certification of life, which is done through the Spirit, but of the communication of life, which is done through the power and efficacy of Christ, to whom Rupert, Anastasius, and Paschasius specifically apply it; who is our life, John 1:2, chapter 14:6, 1 John 1:1, and in the Eucharist he also grants us the vigor of life, communicating himself and his life-giving flesh to us, provided that we enjoy the same through faith. It is the Spirit of God who promises these things, 'I will give to eat of the tree of life': but he himself is not properly the tree of life. For τὸ πνεῦμα λέγων ταῖς Ἐκκλησίαις is introduced in verse 7. And these words are τοῦ Πνεύματος. Christ, that hypostatic wisdom, also comes to Solomon under the name of the tree of life. Compare Proverbs 3:18, chapter 8:22, 23, Luke 11:48. This tree of life is also said to be in the midst of the Paradise of God, both as it refers to the spiritual Paradise, the Church, in whose midst it is situated, because it wishes to communicate itself equally to all; and as it refers to the heavenly one, because all the elect enjoy the same: just as in Revelation 22:2 the tree of life was seen in the middle of the street of the heavenly Jerusalem. However, it appears that this especially regards the enjoyment of heavenly goods in the other life, from the promises of the remaining epistles and the designation of the subject, which is ὁ νικῶν, THE CONQUEROR. For we only truly conquer, so as to enjoy this promise, when we are faithful to the end of life, bringing back the crown of life, verse 10, chapter 7:9. To which some, including the blessed Cluverus, refer the fact that in chapter 22:2 the leaves of the tree of life are said to serve already for the healing of the nations: but the fruits here are not yet perceived, but are to be perceived in the other life, in the heavenly paradise: the promise of which was made to the converted thief, Luke 23:43, into which Paul was also caught up, 2 Corinthians 12:4.

PART II. OF CHAPTER II.

THE SECOND EPISTLE OF THE SON OF GOD TO THE BISHOP OF THE CHURCH OF SMYRNA.

Latin:

Vers. 7.

ὁ ἔχων ὖς, ἀκουσάτω) Formula attentionem excitantis, Matth. XI. 5. XIII. 9. 43. Marc. IV. 9. 23. VIII. 16. Luc. VIII. 8. XIV. 35. infra II. 17. 29. XII. 9. Hoc est, velut כּלֹא in Psalmis.

Τί τὸ Πνεῦμα λέγει ταῖς Ἐκκλησίαις) τὸ πνεῦμα, id est, hoc divinum visum: de qua vocis hujus acceptione vide 1. Cor. XII. 3. 10. 1. Joh. IV. 1. 2. 3. Sic apud Hermam: Ille Spiritus Fi- lius Dei est, id est, visum illud. Λέγει, id est, jubet dici Eccle- siis, nempe Ephesinæ & aliis, quæ sub Ephesini Episcopi cura erant.

Τὸ πνεῦμα nuspiam in sacris literis divinum vi- sum notat, 1. Corinth. XII. 3. Spiritum Sanctum ter- tiam S. Triadis hypostasin, ut e toto contextu li- quet, autorem cognitionis, fiduciæ, & professionis fidei Christi, non vero divinum visum significat. Neque v. 10. aut etiam 1. Johan. IV. 1. 2. 3. de divino visu, sed de hominibus Spiritum jactantibus oc- currit, quos dijudicare per Scripturam sacram li- cet. Hermas hic in sacris audiri non meretur. Ope- ra illa dicere, loqui, testificari, annunciare, & simi- lia, actus sunt personales, ac hypostasin Spiritus Sancti designant.

Τῷ νικῶντι) Ei qui neque inedia neque incommodis aliis patitur se à Christianismo abduci.

ἔώσω φαγεῖν ἐκ τῦ ξύλε ζωῆς, ὅ ἐστιν ἐν μέσῳ τῦ παραδείσε τῦ Θεῦ με) Est oppositio similis isti Matth. V. 6. Μακάριοι οἱ πεινῶντες καὶ διψῶντες τὴν δικαιοσύνην, ὅτι αὐτοὶ χορτασθή- σονται. Ξύλον LXX. ponunt pro arbore עֵץ. Per fructum arboris vitæ intelligendus hic Spiritus Sanctus, qui vitæ & quidem immortalis nos certos facit. Lex Hebræis cibus animæ, arbor vitæ, Prov. II. 19. quia vitam dat felicem in terris. At multo justius Christus, vitæ æternæ Autor ἄρτὸ τῆς ζωῆς Joh. VI. 35. 41. 48. 50. 51. 58. Τὸ δένδρον τῆς ζωῆς Philoni de opificio mundi explicatur ἡ θεοσέβεια, in alle- goriis ὁ τῆς τελείας ἀρετῆς χαρακτήρ. Hunc locum non male ad Eucharistiam referunt veterum quidam, quia per eam, ut oportet sumptam, Spiritus Sanctus introducitur & augetur. In Manuscripto est ἐν τῷ Παραδείσῳ. Illud Θεῦ με habes & infra III. 12. Sic & Joh. XX. 17.

Victores Electi sunt in Ecclesia triumphante, Ribera, Cornel. a Lap. non item Bellarm. de Beat. Sanct. c. 18. Inediam respici peculiariter non ap- paret; Etsi sequatur de esu arboris vitæ: quia vi- ctoria potius adversus Nicolaitarum seductiones, adeoque quarumvis hæresium, quæ per fidem ob- tinetur, necnon adversus scandala quævis vitio- rum: ideo siad esum hæc respiciant, quod pro- missio magnifica de comestione ex arbore vitæ jungatur, prohibitio esus τῶν εἰδωλοθύτων respici- tur, utpote quem admittebant Nicolaitæ, ac conse- quenter usus & fruitio omnium eorum, quæ a Deo prohibita sunt. Abstinentibus enim secun- dum præscriptum divinum promittitur ex gratia fruitio de fructu ligni vitæ, quod Christus est, Apocal. XXII. 2. cujus fructus, imo & folia εἰς θεραπείαν τῶν ἐθνῶν. Fructibus autem arboris vitæ Spiritus sanctus quidem accenseri potest, quod eundem, & donorum ipsius communica- tionem & meruerit nobis Christus, & submini- stret, de cujus plenitudine accipimus omnes gratiam pro gratia, Johan. I. 16. Fruitio autem illa com- prehendit omnino Christi justitiam, & obedien- tiam tum activam tum passivam: hos enim fru- ctus arbor illa vitæ, lignum illud viride tulit in vita, passione ac morte sua, Luc. XXIII. 31. Johan. XI. 24. 1. Corinth. I. 30. hisce fruimur per fidem in hac vita. Hic enim comedimus de arbore vitæ ejusque fru- ctibus, ejusque percipimus svavitatem, 1. Petr. II. 3. Neque excluduntur a fructibus arboris vitæ rege- neratio, justificatio, adoptio, sanctificatio, renova- tio, glorificatio, & salus æterna, quæ omnia arbori vitæ accepta ferre oportet, ut arbor vitæ in Para- diso terrestri primis parentibus fructibus suis ad vitæ perpetuitatem inservire potuisset: Ita hæc spiritualis vitæ arbor Christus suis fructibus no- bis inservit ad vitam gratiæ & gloriæ, spiritualem & cœlestem, non temporariam tantum, sed etiam æternam. Non de certificatione vitæ, quæ per Spiritum fiat, sed de vitæ communicatione pro- prie hic agitur, quæ fiat per vim & efficaciam Christi, ad quem specialiter applicant Rupertus, Anastasius, Paschasius; qui est vita nostra, Johan. I. 2. cap. XIV. 6. 1. Johan. I. 1. & in Eucharistia etiam nobis vitæ vigorem tribuit, semetipsum & carnem suam vivificam nobis communicans, dummodo eadem per fidem fruamur. Spiritus Dei est, qui hæc promittit, dabo ego comedere de arbore vi- tæ: non autem ipse proprie est arbor vitæ. Nam τὸ πνεῦμα λέγων ταῖς Ἐκκλησίαις introducitur v. 7. Et hæc verba sunt τοῦ Πνεύματος. Christus sapien- tia illa hypostatica arboris vitæ nomine etiam Sa- lomoni venit. Conf. Prov. III. 18. cap. VIII. 22. 23. Luc. XI. 48. Dicitur quoque hæc arbor vitæ in medio Paradisi Dei esse, tum qua Paradisum spiri- tualem Ecclesiam, in cujus medio sita est, quod se ex æquo omnibus communicare velit: tum qua cœlestem, quia electi omnes eadem fruantur: quemadmodum Apocal. XXII. 2. in medio plateæ cœlestis Hierosolymæ arbor vitæ visa est. Ma- xime tamen respicere hæc fruitionem bonorum cœlestium in altera vita ex promissis reliquarum epistolarum, & subjecti designatione, quod est ὁ νικῶν, VINCENS, apparet. Nam tum vinci- mus demum, ut hac promissione fruamur, cum ad finem vitæ fideles sumus, coronam vitæ reportan- tes, vers. 10. cap. VII. 9. Quo referunt nonnulli, etiam B. Cluverus, quod c. XXII. 2. folia arboris vitæ dicantur inservire jam sanationi gentium: fructus vero hic nondum percipiantur, sed perci- piendi sint in altera vita, in cœlesti paradiso: Cujus promissio facta est latroni converso, Luc. XXIII. 43. in quem abreptus etiam fuit Paulus 2. Corinth. XII. 4.

PARS II. CAPITIS II.

EPISTOLA SECUNDA FILII DEI AD EPISCOPUM ECCLESIÆ SMYR- NENSIS.

## 2:8
Verse 8.

And to the Angel of the Church in Smyrna write) And here I think not Polycarp is designated, but someone earlier than him. In the Manuscript τῷ ἐν Σμύρνῃ Ἐκκλησίας.

Grotius did not have to designate who was prior to Polycarp in the Smyrnean Church. Nor does the time fit for an earlier one. And the works which are proclaimed here v. 9, and the sufferings against which he is comforted v. 10, suit him very well. Gomarus agrees with most others: Some, he says p. 758 of his works, think Polycarp the Martyr, a disciple of the Apostle John, was the one, which correctly fits the circumstances of time and persecution, and is more probable than that which some v. 1 explain the Angel of the Ephesian Church as Timothy. For although he was placed at Ephesus by Paul, that he might deter from heterodoxy, 1 Tim. 1:3, concerning which it was treated v. 2, yet the rebuke v. 4 does not fit the holiness of Timothy. Nor does Episcopius differ. But Cocceius is too singular, that the Angel of the Church of one town is not addressed, but the Angel of the Church suffering in every place; because the name has an allusion to σμύρναν, which is myrrh, and Cant. 3:6 the Church is called perfumed with myrrh. Although indeed Polycarp underwent martyrdom only under Lucius Verus after about 65 years: it is certain, however, that he was very long-lived, and presided over the office for eighty-six years, as Eusebius testifies, book IV of Church History, chapter 15. Most of our people understand it of Polycarp, and among the Papists, Aureolus, Ribera, Pererius, etc.

These things says the first and the last) He who, although he was of the highest dignity, endured the highest ignominy: Above 1:8. This pertains to this, that the Bishop of Smyrna might not flee from ignominy. In the Manuscript: Ὁ πρωτότοκος καὶ ὁ ἔσχατος.

Who became dead and lived) This pertains to this, that the same Bishop might not be led away from his office by the fear of death, but might be certain that, just as Christ revived, so he too would revive. See the place already indicated above 1:8.

The first and the last are not names of status, as if both the highest dignity and the highest ignominy were noted, but of eternity, so that he might think of saving himself for eternal blessedness from him who is the first and the last.

Latin:

Vers. 8.

Καὶ τῷ Ἀγγέλῳ τῆς Σμύρνῃ Ἐκκλησίας γράψον) Et hic puto non Polycarpum designari, sed aliquem eo priorem. In Manuscripto τῷ ἐν Σμύρνῃ Ἐκκλησίας.

Polycarpo quis prior fuerit in Smyrnensi Eccle- sia non designare habuit Grotius. Neque tempus congruit in priorem. Et opera, quæ hic prædican- tur v. 9. & passiones, adversus quas confortatur v. 10. optime illi conveniunt. Annuit Gomarus cum aliis plerisque: Nonnulli, inquit p. 758. oper. Po- lycarpum Martyrem, discipulum Johannis Apo- stoli fuisse arbitrantur, quod circumstantiis temporis & persecutionis recte convenit, ac probabilius, quam quod nonnulli v. 1. Angelum Ephesinæ Ecclesiæ Ti- motheum exponunt. Quamvis enim Ephesi colloca- tus fuerit a Paulo, ut deterreret ab heterodidascalia, 1. Timoth. I. 3. de qua actum v. 2. tamen reprehensio v. 4. sanctitati Timothei non congruit. Neque in di- versum abit Episcopius. Singularis autem nimium est Coccejus, non compellari Angelum Ecclesiæ unius oppidi, sed Angelum Ecclesiæ patientis in omni loco; quia nomen habet allusionem ad σμύρναν, quod est myrrha, & Cant. III. 6. Ecclesia dicitur perfumigata myrrha. Quanquam vero sub Lucio Vero demum martyrium subierit Polycar- pus post 65. annos circiter: constat tamen, eum μακρόβιον valde fuisse, ac per octoginta & sex an- nos officio præfuisse, teste Eusebio, l. IV. hist. Ec- cles. cap. 15. De Polycarpo intelligunt plerique nostrates, & e Pontificiis Aureolus, Ribera, Pere- rius &c.
