Hæretici mera profunda mysteria venditabant; sed Filius Dei vocat ea profunditates Satanæ. Quo facit illud Irenæi l. III. c. 15. Suasorius & verisimilis est exquirens fucos error, sine fuco autem est veritas. Conf. Rom. XVI. 18. 2. Cor. XI. 13. 1. Tim. VI. 20. Recte habet Andreas παρὰ ψυχὰς, postquam adeo malis & sagacibus impostoribus per simplicitatem morum obsistere haud potestis, utpote profunditates Satanæ non edocti, sicut dicitis, non postulo a vobis verborum cum iis certamen, sed custodiam doctrinæ, quam accepistis, donec hinc vos assumsero.

Οὐ βαλῶ ἐφ’ ὑμᾶς ἄλλο βάρος) Jactant illi se rerum mul- tarum cognitione, eam a vobis non exigo. Βάλλειν βάρος ἐπί τινας, idem quod ἐπιτίθεσθαι βάρος, exigere aliquid, ut ad salutem necessarium, Act. XV. 28.

Rectius alii etiam B. Gerhardus : Non immit- tam vobis tales tribulationes, quales Nicolaitis sum comminatus: Si tantum observaveritis, quæ præcipio. Vel ut B. Cluverus habet: Sufficit vobis militia illa contrà Jezabelem & profunditates ejus Satanicas, quam hactenus fortiter sustinuistis, nec idolis, illecebris, aut viribus ejus supposuistis collum, prælato molli meo jugo, Matth. XI. 29. Non ergo vo- bis aliud quippiam tribulationis, tentationis aut mandati gravioris imponam. Magnum enim onus est, cum scandalis & hæresibus conflictari. De pla- gis tamen & pœnis Jezabalis explicant Osiander, B. Winckelmannus, B. Gerhardus, B. Gravius, de jugo legis, sed minus commode Thomas Szeged. Piscat. Napeirus, Pareus, Sibelius, Ribera, Cornel. a Lap. alii, etiam e nostris B. Chytreus, &c.

## 2:25
Verse 25. Πλὴν) only. Thus πλὴν is taken in Luke 11:41, 12:31, Acts 20:23. It corresponds to the Hebrew אך.

Ὅ ἔχετε) The Evangelical dogma, which you have well perceived.

Κρατήσατε) Retain without any change.

Ἄχρις ἷ ἂν ἥξω) Until I come) Unto the judgment, which, because it is promised for an uncertain day, ought always to be expected by Christians. In the manuscript ἕως ἷ, as in Matt. 2:13 and often elsewhere.

Others prefer to take it concerning the coming to our assumption through death, so that we may retain until the end of life the faith delivered to us, the heavenly deposit, 1 Tim. 1:14, which is called until the end in the following verse.

Latin:

Vers. 25. Πλὴν) tantum. Sic πλὴν sumitur Luc. XI. 41. XII.31. Act.XX.23. Respondet Ebræo אך.

Ὅ ἔχετε) Dogma Evangelicum, quod bene percepistis.

Κρατήσατε) Retinete sine ulla mutatione.

Ἄχρις ἷ ἂν ἥξω) Ad judicium, quod quia incerta die pro- missum est, semper a Christianis expectari debet. In Manu- scripto ἕως ἷ, quomodo Matth.II.13. & alibi sæpe.

Alii malunt accipere de adventu ad nostri per mortem assumptionem, ut ad finem usque vitæ reti- neamus fidem nobis traditam, cœleste depositum, 1. Tim. I.14. quod dicitur ἄχρι τέλες vers. seq.

## 2:26
Verse 26. And he who overcomes) Because he will spurn those evil dogmas. That 'he who overcomes' is always repeated, but it must be understood according to each subject matter.

And he who keeps until the end my works) It is a metonymy. For works are called the precepts concerning works. This very thing is called keeping the commandments below in 12:17, 14:12. To keep the word or the words 3:8, 10, 22:7, 9. There is also a Hebraism here. For the Greek construction would have been 'to him who overcomes and keeps,' with the omission of that 'him' which follows. Until the end, until the end of life. Until death above 10.

Works do not only comprise the precepts concerning works according to the prescription of the tables of the law regarding the love of God and neighbor; but also concerning faith, which is truly a Divine work, John 6:59, Phil. 1:29, 1 John 2:23. The works of Christ are faith, love, peace, kindness, etc., Phil. 2:30, Gal. 5:22, 23, Eph. 5:9. But the works of the devil are unbelief, hatred, anger, pride, 2 Cor. 4:4, Eph. 4:26, James 3:14, 15, 1 John 2:16, 1 John 3:12.

I will give him authority over the nations) I will raise him to the rank of Presbyter, so that he may judge those who live not in a Christian manner, but in an ethnic (heathen) manner. See Matt. XVIII. 17.

Latin:

Vers. 26. Καὶ ὁ νικῶν) Quia ista mala dogmata spernet. Repetitur semper illud ὁ νικῶν, sed intelligendum pro re quaque subjecta.

Καὶ ὁ τηρῶν ἄχρι τέλες τὰ ἔργα με) Est Metonymia. Nam ἔργα dicuntur præcepta de operibus. Hoc ipsum dicitur τηρεῖν τὰς ἐντολάς infra XII.17. XIV.12. Τηρεῖν τὸν λόγον vel τὺς λόγες III.8.10. XXII.7.9. Est & hic Ebraïsmus. Nam Græca constructio fuerat τῷ νικῶντι καὶ τηρῦντι, omisso illo αὐτῷ, quod sequitur. ἄχρι τέλες עד קץ ad finem vitæ. Ἄχρι θανάτε supra 10.

Ἔργα non tantum præcepta de operibus secun- dum præscriptum tabularum legis de dilectione Dei & proximi; sed etiam de fide, quæ vere Divi- num opus est, Joh.VI.59. Phil. I.29. complectuntur 1. Joh. II, 23. Christi opera sunt fides, dilectio, pax, benignitas, &c. Phil. II. 30. Gal.V. 22.23. Eph.V.9. Diaboli vero opera incredulitas, odium,ira,super- bia. 2. Cor.IV. 4. Eph.IV. 26. Jac. III.14.15. 1. Joh. II.16. 1. Joh.III.12.

Δώσω αὐτῷ ἐξουσίαν ἐπὶ τῶν ἐθνῶν) Eveham illum in gra- dum Presbyteri, ut judicet de iis, qui non Christiane, sed ἐθνικῶς vivunt. Vide Matth. XVIII. 17.

## 2:27
V. 27. And he will shepherd them with an iron rod) This is from the elders of the LXX, Ps. 11. 9, where they did not read, as the Masoretes, תרועם, but תרעם from רעה, not from רוע, with the sense remaining the same. For because shepherds rule the flock, therefore rule of any kind is expressed by metonymy through the word for shepherding, even if it tends toward the harm of those who are ruled. This appears in Mic. V. 5. An iron rod is nothing other than a sword, as we said at the second Psalm according to David Kimchi. Figuratively, however, by the sword here is understood the Word of God, of which excommunication is a part. So also below, ch. XII. ver. 5, and XIX. 15.

We do not here deny [this] to Grotius, along with Lyra, Dionysius, Ribera, Corn. a Lapide, Hoen, and B. Gerhard, T. VIII. L.C. on death §. 359.

As the potter's vessels they shall be broken) It is the future for any time, in the Hebrew manner. He will treat them in the way that earthen vessels are accustomed to be broken without hope of restoration, Jer. XIX. 10, 11. Clay, while it is in the hand of the potter, is molded and remolded easily, Jer. XVIII. It is not the same with a broken piece of pottery. The words are from Ps. 11. 9, where in the Greek, 'as a potter's vessel you will break them,' the thing itself alludes to that which was predicted to Jehu, 2 Kings IX. 6. Moreover, it signifies perpetual exclusion from communion, which was the punishment that followed idolaters and adulterers in the first times.

Latin:

V.27.Καὶ ποιμανεῖ αὐτὺς ἐν ῥάβδῳ σιδηρᾷ) Est ex senibus LXX. Psal. 11. 9. ubi non legerunt, ut Masoretz, תרועם, sed תרעם a רעה non a רוע sensu eodem recidente. Nam quia pastores regunt pecus; ideo regimen qualecunque per μετάληψιν exprimitur pascendi vocabulo, etiamfi in malum tendat eorum, qui reguntur. Apparet id Mich. V. 5. Virga ferrea non aliud est, quam gladius, ut ad Psalmum secundum ex Davide Kimchi diximus. Figurate autem per gladium hic intelligitur Verbum Dei, cujus pars est & excommuni- catio. Sic & infra XII. vers. 5. & XIX. 15.

Non abnuimus hic Grotio cum Lyra, Dionysio, Ribera, Corn. a Lapide, Hoen, B. Gerhardo T. VIII. L.C. de morte §. 359.

Ὡς τὰ σκεύη τὰ κεραμικὰ συντριβήσεται) Est futurum pro quovis tempore, more Ebræo. Ita eos tractabit, quomodo vafa fictilia frangi solent sine spe restitutionis Jerem. XIX. 10. 11. Argilla dum in manu est figuli, fingitur & refingitur facile, Jerem.XVIII. Non idem in fictili fracto. Verba sunt e Psal. 11.9.ubi in Græco ὡς σκεῦος κεραμέως συντρίψεις αὐτός, res ipsa alludit ad id, quod prædictum Jehu 2 Reg.IX.6. Si- gnificatur autem exclusio perpetua a communione, quæ pœna idololatras & adulteros primis temporibus seque- batur.

## 2:28
Vers. 28. As I also have received from my Father) They will receive the power of judging from me, just as I received it from the Father. That 'as' signifies some similarity, not parity, as 'just as' in Luke XXII. 29.

There is no need for us to assume that the LXX interpreters read otherwise. For they rendered the sense; they did not express it word for word: nor is it a matter of elevation to the rank of presbyter or the power of excommunication, but of heavenly glory and judgment over the impious, to which the faithful are raised, being about to judge the world and the angels themselves, 1 Cor. VI. 2, 3. By the iron rod, however, not only the efficacy of the Word is designated, but also the gravity of the future judgment, because the iron rod is said to be applied for this reason, that they are to be crushed by it as if they were earthen vessels, about to perish in eternal death. An iron rod, that is, with inflexible justice and immutable sentence. This is also confirmed by the comparison with the judgment given to Christ, John V. 22. Compare with this passage ch. XII. 5, ch. XIX. 15. Dionysius the Carthusian on this passage. He will rule them with an iron rod, that is, in the rigor of justice or with a sentence of condemnation he will send, or direct them to the end owed to them, namely, to the punishments of hell. For they will judge together with Christ, and will approve his sentence. They will be broken, not by ceasing to exist, but by losing all well-being. Alcafar is inept in suggesting that evangelical perfection, as they call it, is shadowed forth under the appearance of an iron rod: or even that the subjection of the nations is promised to Prelates; the words 'until the end' show that it concerns the axiom in eternal life. Cornelius acknowledges this: St. John speaks here of the day of judgment, in which the holy victors and those keeping God's commandments until the end of life will be created by God as Judges of the world, and with Christ will condemn the impious nations, so that they may be broken, that is, irreparably cast down into eternal death and hell. Compare Matt. XIX. 28, Luke XXII. 30, Mal. IV. 3, Wisd. III. 8. Furthermore, Reihing in his Manual. Cath. p. 502, and Tirinus on this passage, rashly conclude the invocation of saints from this place, along with Bellarmine. For Lyranus explains that the perfect are to judge with Christ, and so does Alcafar, for which exposition Tirinus himself cites Victorinus, Arethas, Lyranus, Ribera, and Corn. a Lapide. They also praise the explanation of those who interpret it concerning the power which Christ received from the Father, Ps. II. 9, and which he gave to the preachers of the word, as his ministers, who convert the nations and subjugate the infidels as if on account of the concupiscence of the flesh, and bring them into the obedience of CHRIST by words and examples. Bellarmine himself, on Pastoral Life, Haymo, and Blasius de Viegas interpret it concerning the Church, along with Bede, Primasius, Ansbert, and others. Blasius de Viegas brings forward a twofold sense: the one literal, concerning the universal Church conquering the nations and subjecting them to itself; the other concerning those who opposed themselves to Jezebel, to be established as prelates in the Church: Richard, Anselm, and Thomas Aquinas [interpret it] concerning those who have resisted enemies with an unconquered spirit, to be set over others in the government of the Church.

And I will give him the morning star) It is a metonymy. For he wishes to say, I will give also the brightness, not of just any star, but of Lucifer, who greatly surpasses the other stars. Homer: 'As a star goes among the stars in the dead of night, Hesperus, which stands as the most beautiful star in heaven.' Virgil: 'As when Jupiter, bathed in the waters of the Ocean, whom Venus loves before other fires of the stars, has lifted his sacred face in the sky and dispels the darkness.' 'The morning star' is a locution of the Rabbis. For they say כוכב הבוקר.

He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the Churches) namely, to Thyatira and its neighbors.

Although it may be explained metonymically without absurdity as referring to the glorious brightness, but of the other life, with which the teachers are to shine like the stars, Dan. 12, 3, it does not appear, however, why the proper sense should not be retained. But does not Christ, who is the Morning Star by proper interpretation, Apoc. XXII. 16, most fully communicate Himself to the elect? The Son of God therefore wishes to make His faithful ones participants not only of His glory in judicial power, but also to give Himself wholly with the fullness of the Divinity to them, as if for their own, so that they may be filled with all Divine fullness: which, since it is said in a certain way concerning gracious indwelling in Eph. III, how much more is it to be hoped for in the glorious communion which is expected in the heavens. The glosses of the Carthusian concerning the Angelic society, of the Caesarean concerning the contrition of Lucifer, that is, the Devil; likewise concerning Lucifer, John, and Elijah; and of Lyranus concerning glorification are inconvenient. Rupertus paraphrases thus: After the labor, in which he labors in the present life as if in the night, released and vigilant in the custody of the souls committed to him, I will manifest myself to him, who am the bright and morning star. Beda: Christ, he says, is the morning star, because when the night of the age has passed, He promises and reveals the light of life to the saints, and eternal life. Cocceius clearly perverts this epistle: To whom the woman Jezebel partly signifies the false Prophet, of whom is chap. XIII, that is, the system of false Prophets, and partly the head of all those, the Anti-Christ. And here is seen in summary the confusion of the faithful with those worshipping the beast, the sitting of the Anti-Christ in the temple of God, the introduction of the Church within the gates of hell. And when the Anti-Christ is revealed, then Jezebel is said to have been cast into a bed. The giving of the morning star, however, with Cocceius as author, ought to be understood concerning the beginnings of liberation through the leading out of the Church from Babylon, and its illustration through the Word of truth and the refutation of falsehood, and various charisms in many, and finally its defense against the furies of the world. Who would not laugh, or rather grieve, at such interpretations?

Latin:

Vers. 28. Ὡς κᾀγὼ εἴληφα παρὰ τῆ͂ Πατρός με) Illi a me judicandi potestatem accipient, sicut ego a Patre accepi. Il- lud ὡς aliquam similitudinem non paritatem significat, ut καθὼς Lucæ XXII. 29.

Non opus est, statuamus, aliter legisse LXX. In- terpretes. Reddidere enim sensum; non vero ver- bum verbo expresserunt: neque de evectione in gradum presbyterii aut potestate excommunica- tionis agitur, sed de gloria cœlesti & judicio super impios, ad quod evehuntur fideles, mundum ipsosque Angelos judicaturi, 1. Cor. VI. 2. 3. Per virgam autem ferream non tantum efficacitas Ver- bi, sed etiam gravitas futuri judicii designatur, quia ideo virga ferrea adhiberi dicitur, quod conteren- di eadem sint veluti vasa testacea, æterna morte pe- rituri. Ferrea virga, id est, inflexibili justitia, & im- mutabili sententia. Quod confirmat etiam com- paratio cum judicio, Christo dato, Joh. V. 22. Conf. cum hoc loco cap. XII. 5. cap. XIX. 15. Dionysius Carthusian. in h. l. Reget eos in virga ferrea, hoc est, in rigore justitiæ vel cum damnationis sententia mit- tet, seu diriget eos ad finem eis debitum, puta ad pœ- nas inferni. Nam simul cum Christo judicabunt, & ejus sententiam approbabunt. Confragentur non esse, sed omne bene esse perdendo. Ineptus est Alcafar, Evangelicam perfectionem, quam vo- cant, adumbrari sub specie virgæ ferreæ: vel etiam Prælatis subjectionem gentium promitti, de axio- mate in vita æterna agi verba ἄχρι τέλες docent. Agnoscit id Cornelius: Loquitur hic S. Johannes de die judicii, in quo sancti victores & Dei mandata cu- stodientes usq́; in finem vitæ creabuntur a Deo Judi- ces orbis, & cum Christo gentes impias condemna- bunt, ut confringantur, id est, irreparabiliter in æter- nam mortem & gehennam præcipitentur. Conf. Matth. XIX. 28. Luc. XXII. 30. Mal. IV. 3. Sap. III. 8. Cæterum ex hoc loco invocationem san- ctorum temere concludit cum Bellarmino Reihin- gius in Manual. Cath. p. 502. & Tirinus in h. l. Nam Lyranus explicat, quod perfecti judicaturi sint cum Christo, sic & Alcafar, pro qua ἐκθέσει adfert Tirinus ipse Victorin. Aretam, Lyran.Riber.Cornel. a Lap. laudant etiam eorum explicationem, qui de potestate exponunt, quam accepit a Patre Chri- stus Ps. II. 9. quamq; dedit concionatoribus verbi, tanquam suis ministris, qui convertunt gentes & subjugant infideles quasi propter carnis concupi- scentiam, inque obsequium CHRISTI verbis & exemplis redigunt. Bellarminus ipse de vita Pa- storal. Haymo & Blasius de Viegas de Ecclesia interpretantur cum Beda, Primafio, Ansberto, & aliis. Blasius de Viegas geminum adfert sensum, li- teralem alterum de universa Ecclesia vincente gentes multas sibi subjiciat; alterum de illis, qui se- se Jezabeli opposuerunt prælatis in Ecclesia consti- tuendis: Richardus, Anshelmus, Thomas de Aqui- no de illis, qui animo invicto hostibus restiterint, aliis in Ecclesiæ gubernatione præficiendis.

Καὶ δώσω ἀυτῷ τὸν ἀσέρα τὸν πρωϊνὸν) Est Metonymia. Vult enim dicere, dabo & fulgorem, non qualiscunque stel- læ, sed Luciferi, qui cæteras stellas multum vincit. Homerus: Οἷος δ᾽ ἀςὴρ εἶσι μετ᾽ ἀςράσι νυκτὸς ἀμολγῷ Εσπερος, ὃς κάλλιςος ἐν ἐρανῷ ἵςαται ἀςήρ. Virgilius: Qualis ubi Oceani perfusus Jupiter unda, Quem Venus ante alios astrorum diligit ignes, Extulit os sacrum cælo, tenebrasque resolvit. Αςέρα τὸν πρωϊνὸν locutio Rabbinorum. Dicunt enim כוכב הבוקר.

Ὁ ἔχων ὖς ἀκςσάτω, ὅ τὸ πνεῦμα λέγει ταῖς Ἐκκλησίαις) nempe Thyatiræ & vicinis ejus.

Quanquam explicari Metonymice citra absurdi- tate possit de fulgore glorioso, sed alteriꝫ vitæ, quis fulsuri sunt Doctores instar stellarum Dan. 12, 1. non apparet tamen, cur non retinendus sit sensus pro- prius. Annon vero Christus, qui est Phosphorus ex propria interpretatione, Apoc. XXII. 16. plenis- sime sese communicat electis? Participes ergo red- dere vult Filius Dei fideles suos non tantum gloriae suae in judiciaria potestate, sed etiam sese totum cum plenitudine Divinitatis illis dare, quasi ad pro- prium, ut repleantur omni Divina plenitudine: quod quum de gratiosa inhabitatione certo modo dicatur Eph. III. quanto magis sperandum in glo- riosa communione, quae in coelis expectatur. Incom- modae sunt glossae Carthusiani de Angelica societa- te, Cæsariensis de Luciferi, id est, Diaboli contritio- ne; item de Lucifero Johanne, & Elia; Lyrani de glorificatione. Rupertus ita παραφράζει: Post labo- rem, quo in praesenti vita quasi in nocte laborat, solu- tus ac pervigil in animarum sibi commissarum custo- dia manifestabo ei meipsum, qui stella sum splendida & matutina. Beda: Christus, inquit, est stella matuti- na, quia transacta nocte seculi lumen vitae sanctis pro- mittit, & pandit æterna. Pervertit plane hanc epi- stolam Coccejus: Cui mulier Jezabel partim signi- ficat falsum Prophetam, de quo est cap. XIII. hoc est, systema falsorum Prophetarum, partim illorum omnium caput Anti-Christum. Cerniturque hic ἐν συνόψει confusio fidelium cum adorantibus besti- am, sessio Anti-Christi in templo Dei, Ecclesiae intro- ductio intra portas inferni. Et quando revelatus est Anti-Christus, tunc dicitur Jezabel in lectum con- jecta. Datio autem sideris matutini, Coccejo au- tore debet intelligi de initiis liberationis per edu- ctionem Ecclesiæ e Babylone, ejusque illustrationem per Verbum veritatis & redargutionem falsitatis, variaque in multis charismata, denique ejus defen- sionem contra furores mundi. Quis non rideat vel doleat potius ob tales interpretationes?

## 3:1 Argument
CHAPTER III. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

He is commanded to write to the Angel of Sardis, that although he is said to live, he is dead, and therefore ought to awaken and strengthen others; otherwise he is to be visited by an unexpected judgment; but to those few who have not defiled themselves, white garments are promised, not to be blotted out from the book of life, and to be honored by confession before the Father. To the Philadelphian, who has an open school and had retained the Word of Christ, is promised the subjection of the Pseudo-Jews, and preservation from the hour of universal temptation: and he is warned to retain what he has, with the notable promise that He wishes to make the one who overcomes a pillar in the temple; and to inscribe upon him the name of God and of the new Jerusalem, and His own new name. He reproves the Laodicean for lukewarmness with the threat of being spewed out, crushing his boasting, and suggests counsel on how he might be enriched, clothed, and obtain sight, exhorting to repentance, and inviting him by knocking and the promise of the communion of the supper, and promising his throne to the victor.

There are three parts of the chapter: The first exhibits the fifth epistle to the Bishop of Sardis to v. 7. The second the sixth, to the Philadelphian to verse 13. The third the seventh to the Laodicean to v. 22.

PART I. THE FIFTH EPISTLE TO THE BISHOP OF SARDIS.

Vers. 1. And to the Angel of the Church in Sardis write.) Sardis, the royal city of Croesus according to Horace, was once a most opulent city.

These things says He who has the seven spirits of God) He who has in His power those seven modes of Divine providence, of which above I. 4. and below V. 6. and through them procures the salvation of men.

And the seven stars) He who holds the bishops who perform their duty most dear, and cares for them more than others, and can cast away those who do not perform their duty.

Sardis, a great city of Lydia on the side of Mount Tmolus. Aureolus and Antiochus Brondus make S. Melito its bishop. But he did not yet flourish in the time of S. John. Who he was, is not clear. The description by the seven Spirits refers to the gifts of the Spirit, with which Christ was not endowed by measure according to His Human Nature, John III. 34, and which, κατὰ τὸ μέτρον τῆς δωρεᾶς τοῦ Χριστοῦ, as He Himself wishes to communicate, are distributed to Teachers, Eph. IV. 7. In His hand also are the Bishops, because He has them under His own power.

I know thy works) You do certain things that are fair.

That thou hast a name, that thou livest) Those who do not know your inner self consider you a good Christian. To live here is to live according to Christ.

Καὶ νεκρὸς εἶ) You are wallowing in a hidden sin, and such a one as excludes you from my favor and eternal life. Such are called dead, Eph. II. 1. 1. Tim. V. 6. See what is said at Matth. VIII. 22.

Latin:

CAPUT III. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Jubetur scribere Angelo Sardensi, quod etsi vi- vere dicatur, mortuus sit, adeoque evigila- re, aliosque confortare debeat; caeteroquin inexpectato judicio visitandus; paucis au- tem illis, qui se non commacularunt, pro- mittuntur albae vestes, non expungendis e li- bro vitæ, & confessione coram Patre hono- randis. Philadelphensi, qui apertam scho- lam habeat, & Verbum Christi retinuerat, promittitur subjectio Pseudo-Judæorum, & praeservatio ab hora tentationis universalis: monetque, ut retineat, quod habet, cum pro- missione insigni, quod vincentem velit fa- cere columnam in templo; nomenque Dei & novæ Hierosolymæ, ac novum suum no- men eidem inscribere. Laodicenum ob te- piditatem reprehendit cum comminatione exspuitionis, gloriationem ejus contundens, & consilium, quomodo ditari, amiciri, & visum consequi possit, suggerit, ad pœniten- tiam hortans, & pulsatione ac communionis cœnæ pollicitatione invitans, victori que thronum suum promittens.

Partes capitis tres sunt: Prima epistolam quintam ad Episcopum Sardensem ad v. 7. Altera sextam, ad Philadelphiensem ad vers. 13. Tertia Septimam ad Laodicenum ad v. 22. exhibet.

PARS I. EPISTOLA QVINTA AD EPISCO- PUM SARDENSEM.

Vers. 1. Καὶ τῷ Ἀγγέλῳ τῆς ἐν Σάρδεσιν Ἐκκλησίας γράψον.) Sardes Crœsi Regia Horatio, opulentissima olim urbs.

Τάδε λέγει ὁ ἔχων τὰ ἑπτὰ πνεύματα τοῦ Θεοῦ) Qui in po- testate sua habet septem illos Divinæ providentiæ modos, de quibus supra I. 4. & infrá V. 6. & per eos hominum salu- tem procurat.

Καὶ τοὺς ἑπτὰ ἀστέρας) Qui Episcopos omnes officium facientes charissimos habet, ac plus quam alios curat, & officium non facientes abjicere potest.

Sardis urbs Lydiæ magna ad latus Tmoli mon- tis. Episcopum ejus Aureolus & Antiochus Bron- dus S. Melitonem faciunt. Sed ille S. Johannis tempore nondum viguit. Quis fuerit, non liquet. Descriptio a septem Spiritibus respicit dona Spiri- tus, quibus Christus non ad mensuram instructus est secundum Humanam Naturam, Joh. III. 34. quæque κατὰ τὸ μέτρον τῆς δωρεᾶς τοῦ Χριστοῦ, prout ipse communicare vult, distribuuntur Doctori- bus, Eph. IV. 7. In manu ejus etiàm sunt Episco- pi, quia sub potestate sua eosdem habet.

Οἶδά σου τὰ ἔργα) Quædam facis speciosa.

Ὅτι ὄνομα ἔχεις, ὅτι ζῇς) Qui intima tua non norunt, te pro bene Christiano habent. Vivere hic est secundum Chri- stum vivere.

Καὶ νεκρὸς εἶ) Volutaris in peccato homines latente, ac tali, quod te a meo favore & vita æterna excludat. Tales mortui dicuntur, Eph. II. 1. 1. Tim. V. 6. Vide quæ dicta ad Matth. VIII. 22.

## 3:2
Vers. 2. Be watchful) Pay attention to yourself. Beware of all crimes. For it is not enough to be immune from some. See Matt. XXIV. 42.

And strengthen the things which remain, which were ready to die) In the Manuscript: strengthen the things which remain; which were ready to die, as the Latin reads. Virtues enjoy mutual company. But if one is missing, the others easily perish, God hardening men and delivering them into base desires.

Every vice has stood on the precipice. This, therefore, is what it means: See that by neglecting one crime you do not become altogether wicked, and thereby repentance is rendered more difficult for you. No differently than one who with difficulty forces a boat against the river with oars, if he happens to relax his arms, the current sweeps him headlong down the river. Keep the remnants of a good mind by expelling the poison which is accustomed to kill them little by little.

The life of the body, says Isidore, book I of the Summa Bonorum, from Augustine, is the soul, but the life of the soul is God: And just as the body is dead without the soul, so the soul is dead without God. Concerning spiritual life, Eph. IV. 18; concerning death, Luke IX. 60, 1 Tim. V. 6, James II. 17. Although Rupert makes the sin of this Bishop a carnal one of hidden lust, Primasius and Beda more conveniently argue the negligence of the Bishop in his office, because he is commanded to watch and to strengthen those who were near to spiritual death. Yet that negligence could have arisen from a propensity toward those sins, and delight in them: against which he had already burned with righteous zeal in others, being solicitous neither for his own salvation nor for that of those committed to him, as was proper. See Ez. III. 18, Jerem. XLVIII. 11, Acts XX. 28. However, the other Codices are not to be corrected according to the Manuscript of Grotius and the Vulgate, but vice versa, and those ready to die are rightly understood as Christians who are like dying sheep, Ezech. XXXIV. 16, in whom faith and charity are almost extinguished. For Scripture is accustomed to designate the universality of both persons and things with the neuter gender.

For I have not found thy works perfect before my God) You are inconsistent. You do some things well: others badly: but God does not love His own to be half-hearted. Matt. VI. 24. Understand works here as the sum of those works which are required in the Gospel. A Christian in his warfare, just as Caesar in his armed one, ought to think nothing done, while anything remains to be done. See James 2:10 and the statements there. Christ also called the Father His God above in 2:7, and will say so below in verse 11. Before God, that is, with God as witness and judge.

No works of ours are found full and perfect in the eyes of God because of the sin that clings to us, which in us wars against the law of our mind, Rom. 7:13. Wherefore they are called not fulfilled, either because they are hypocritical, not sincere, or, which I would prefer, because it concerns a Bishop who had not been sufficiently vigilant, nor had he cared for the sheep according to the tenor of the Episcopal office, so that they were found dying, because the discourse is about works of duty that are deficient: just as, if the letters are correct, the Man of God may be complete, equipped for every good work, 2 Tim. 3:17, and it is inculcated to Timothy, ch. 4:5, fulfill your ministry, and it must be said to Archippus, that he fulfill the ministry which he had received in the Lord, that you may fulfill the ministry, Col. 4:7. Compare Acts 14:26.

Latin:

Vers. 2. Γίνου γρηγορῶν) Attende tibi. Cave ab omnibus criminibus. Non enim sufficit, ab aliquibus esse immunem. Vide Matth. XXIV. 42.

Καὶ στήριξον τὰ λοιπὰ, ἃ ἔμελλες ἀπολαβεῖν) In Manuscripto: στήρισον τὰ λοιπὰ; ἃ ἔμελλον ἀποθανεῖν, quomodo legit La- tinus. Virtutes mutuo gaudent comitatu. Quod si una desit, facile pereunt cæteræ, Deo homines obdurante & tra- dente in malos sensus.

Omne in præcipiti vitium stetit. Hoc ergo vult: Vide ne unum crimen negligendo plane fias flagitiosus, atque eo difficilior tibi reddatur pœnitentia. Non aliter quam qui adverso vix flumine lembum Remigiis subigit, si brachia forte remisit, Atque illum in præceps prono rapit alveus amne. Reliquias bonæ mentis serva, expellendo venenum, quod eas paulatim solet interficere.

Vita corporis, inquit Isidorus l. I. de Summ. Bon. ex Augustino, anima, animæ vero Deus: Et sicut corpus mortuum est sine anima, ita anima mortua est sine Deo. De vita spirituali Eph. IV. 18. de morte Luc. IX. 60. 1. Tim. V. 6. Jac. II. 17. Quanquam vero peccatum hujus Episcopi Rupertus faciat carnale occultæ libidinis, convenientius tamen Pri- masius, & Beda negligentiam Episcopi in officio ar- guunt, quia jubetur γρηγορεῖν & στηρίζειν eos, qui morti spirituali vicini erant. Potuit tamen illa ne- gligentia oriri ex propensione in ea peccata, & ob- lectationem in illis: adversus quæ in aliis jam justo zelo exarsit, neque de sua neque de sibi commisso- rum salute, prout par erat, solicitus. Vide Ez. III. 18. Jerem. XLVIII. 11. Act. XX. 28. Non sunt au- tem Codices cæteri ad Manuscriptum Grotii & Vulgatum emendandi, sed vice versa, & recte mo- ribunda intelliguntur de Christianis, qui ovibus moribundis similes sunt, Ezech. XXXIV. 16. in qui- bus fides & charitas pene extincta est. Solet enim Scriptura genere neutro designare universitatem tam personarum, quam rerum.

Οὐ γὰρ εὗρόν σου τὰ ἔργα πεπληρωμένα ἐνώπιον τοῦ Θεοῦ μου) Varius es. Quædam bene agis: alia male: Deus autem non amat niti in solidum suos. Matth. VI. 24. Opera hic intellige τὸν ὁμάδα eorum operum, quæ in Evangelio exi- guntur. Christianus in sua militia, ita ut in armata Cæsar, nil debet actum putare, dum quid agendum superest. Vi- de Jacob. II. 10. & ibi dicta. Christus Patrem etiam su- pra Deum suum dixit II. 7. & dicet infra 11. Coram Deo, id est, Deo teste ac judice.

Plena & perfecta nulla inveniuntur in oculis Dei opera nostra ob adhærens peccatum, quod in no- bis repugnat legi mentis nostræ, Rom. VII. 13. Qua- propter μὴ πεπληρωμένα dicuntur, vel quod hy- pocritica, non sincera, vel, quod malim, quia de E- piscopo agitur, qui non satis vigilans fuerat, nec oves juxta tenorem Episcopalis muneris curarat, ut moribundæ invenirentur, quod de operibus of- ficii deficientibus sermo sit: quemadmodum, si li- teræ præstant, Vir Dei ἄρτιος sit πρὸς πᾶν ἔργον ἀγαθὸν ἐξηρτισμένον 2. Timoth. III. 17. & Timotheo inculcatur cap. IV. 5. Ministerium tuum πληροφό- ρησον, & Archippo dicendum, ut ministerium quod acceperat in Domino, impleat, ἵνα τὴν διακονίαν πληροῖς Col. IV. 7. Conf. Act. XIV. 26.

## 3:3
Verse 3.

Remember therefore how you have received and heard) That is, you have received by hearing. Think again and again what kind of doctrine you have received from the Apostles. In a similar sense we had remember also above 2:5. To take or to receive is accustomed to be said of doctrine, 2 John v. 4, 1 Cor. 11:22, 15:1, 2, Gal. 1:9, Phil. 4:9, Col. 2:6, 1 Thess. 2:13, 4:1, 2 Thess. 3:6.

And keep) Observe these things, not some, but all. Thus we have to keep in John 14:15, 21, 23, 24, ch. 15:10, 20, 1 Tim. 6:14, 1 John 2:3, 4, 5, 3:22, 24, 5:2, 3.

And repent) Do penance for those things of which you are conscious to yourself.

The latter is rather explanatory of the former, what you have received, that is, heard, namely what kind of person you ought to conduct yourself as in your office. How the ministry with the precious deposit of doctrine has been commended to you, namely that you may faithfully guard it and propagate it to others. Keep, persevere in it; as the blessed Gerhard rightly says. Crocius refers this prediction and commination to our times from the beginning of Charles V: Hoffmann also wishes it to look to our times, estimating the danger intimated to the sleepy Sardians by the following commination from the reformation of Bohemia, Carinthia, Austria, and Moravia. But on what foundations? None. Such signs certainly do not agree in any way with the epistles concerning the state of the Johannine time.

If therefore you will not watch, I will come upon you as a thief, and you will not know at what hour I will come upon you) Christ is said to come both when He will come to the universal judgment, and then when He takes each one from this life. See John 21:22. But just as the comparison of the thief is adapted to the last judgment, Matt. 24:43, 1 Thess. 5:2, so also to sudden death, as here, and to other sudden judgments, as below 16:15. But this is said aptly to the matter, because sinners for the most part flatter themselves with this, that they think there will be enough time for them for repentance. Upon you is missing here in the Manuscript. At what hour instead of at what hour. Otherwise it would be said at what hour, as in Matt. 24:42. The guards in the temple also watched at night.

Concerning the particular judgment, because the commination is made to the Sardian Bishop, these things must be accepted, not concerning the universal. Compare Luke 12:39. But because, he says, everyone ought to fear also concerning the last day of this life of his (for in whatever state his last day finds each one, in that the last day of the world will overtake him, since, as each one dies in that day, so he will be judged in that day) hence the last day of each one's life is designated by the same symbol of the thief. Therefore St. Hilary warns in Canon 25 on Matthew. It is fitting that we be prepared, because the ignorance of the day excites the intent solicitude of suspenseful expectation. And St. Augustine in tract 33 on John. The Lord is gentle, the Lord is long-suffering, the Lord is merciful: But the Lord is also just, and the Lord is truthful, He grants you a space for correction, but you love delay more than amendment. You were evil yesterday, be good today. And you have spent the present day in malice, or you always expect to change tomorrow, and you promise yourself much from the mercy of God; as if He, who promised you indulgence through patience, had also promised a longer life. Compare Prov. 27:1, James 4:13, Sir. 18:26, Ps. 95:7, Heb. 3:7, ch. 4:7.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

Μνημόνευε ὖν πῶς εἴληφας καὶ ἤκουσας) Id est, ἀκούων εἴλη- φας. Etiam atque etiam cogita, qualem doctrinam ab Apostolis acceperis. Pari sensu μνημόνευε habuimus & su- pra II. 5. Λαμβάνειν aut παραλαμβάνειν לקח aut קבל de doctrina dici solet. 2. Joh. v. 4. 1. Cor. XI. 22. XV. 1. 2. Gal. I. 9. Phil. IV. 9. Coloss. II. 6. 1. Thess. II. 13. IV. 1. 2. Thess. III. 6.

Καὶ τήρει) Observa ista, non quædam, sed omnia. Sic τηρεῖν habemus Joh. XIV. 15. 21. 23 24. c. XV. 10. 20. 1. Tim. VI. 14. 1. Joh. II. 3. 4. 5. III. 22. 24. V. 2. 3.

Καὶ μετανόησον) Pœnitentiam age de illis, quorum tibi es conscius.

Posterius potius ἐξηγητικὸν est prioris, quod ac- ceperis, id est, audieris, qualem scilicet te in officio tuo gerere debeas. Qualiter ministerium cum chato doctrinæ deposito tibi commendatum sit, vide- licet ut fideliter illud custodias & ad alios propages. Τήρει persevera in eo; ut recte B. Gerhardus. Prædi- ctionem & comminationem hanc ad nostra tem- pora inde ab initio Caroli V. refert Crocius: No- stra etiam tempora respicere vult Hoffmannus pe- riculum somniculosis Sardenfibus comminatione subsequenti intimatum e Bohemiæ, Carinthiæ, Au- striæ, Moraviæ reformatione æstimans. Sed quibus fundamentis? Nullis. Talia ἐνσήματα certe epi- stolis statum temporis Johannei concernentibus nulla ratione congruunt.

Ἐὰν ὖν μὴ γρηγορήσῃς, ἥξω ἐπί σε, ὡς κλέπτης, καὶ ὐ μὴ γνῷς, ποίαν ὥραν ἥξω ἐπί σε) Venire Christus dicitur & quum ad judicium universale veniet, & tunc cum quemque ex hac vita abducit. Vide Joh. XXI. 22. At sicut furis comparatio ultimo judicio aptatur, Matth. XXIV. 43. 1. Thess. V. 2. ita & morti improvisæ, ut hic & aliis judiciis improvisis, ut infra XVI. 15. Apposite au- tem ad rem hoc dicitur, quia peccatores plerumque eo fi- bi blandiantur, quod putant satis sibi temporis fore ad pœnitentiam. Ἐπί σε hic deest in Manuscripto. Ποίαν ὥραν pro κατὰ ποίαν ὥραν. Alioqui diceretur ποίᾳ ὥρᾳ, ut Matth. XXIV. 42. Custodes in templo etiam nocte vi- gilabant.

De particulari judicio, quia comminatio fit Episcopo Sardenfi, hæc accipienda, non de univer- sali. Conf. Luc. XII. 39. August. epist. LXXX. Quia autem, inquit, unusquisque debet etiam de die hujus vitæ suæ novissimo formidare (in quo enim quemque invenerit suus novissimus dies, in hoc eum comprehendet mundi novissimus dies, quoniam, qua- lis in isto die quisque moritur, talis in die illo judica- bitur) hinc ultimus vitæ cujusque dies eodem furis symbolo designatur. Ideo monet S. Hilarius Can. XXV. in Matth. Paratos nos esse convenit, quia diei ignoratio intentam solicitudinem suspensæ expecta- tionis excitat. Et S. Augustinus tr. XXXIII. in Joh. Mansuetus Dominus, longanimis Dominus, mise- ricors Dominus: Sed & justus Dominus, & ve- rax Dominus, largitur tibi spatium correctionis, sea & tu plus amas dilationem, quam emendationem. Malus fuisti heri, hodie bonus esto. Et hodiernum diem in malitia peregisti, vel cras mutare semper ex- pectas, & de misericordia Dei tibi plurimum pollice- ris; quasi ille, qui tibi per patientiam promisit indul- gentiam, promiserit etiam prolixiorem vitam. Conf. Prov. XXVII. 1. Jac. IV. 13. Sir. XVIII. 26. Psal. XCV. 7. 7. Ebr. III. 7. cap. IV. 7.

## 3:4
Vers. 4. But you have a few names in Sardis, which have not defiled their garments) He rouses the Bishop by examples proposed from the common people. Ὀνόματα are persons, as Acts 1:15 & below 11:13. The garment of the soul is the conscience. It is defiled by crimes: It is kept pure through innocence & holiness. Μολυσμὸς is whatever is repugnant to holiness 2 Cor. 7:1, μιάσματα 2 Pet. 2:20, σπῖλοι Jas. 1:27.

The chastisement is tempered by commendation, because he watched against the fornication & idolatry & other wickednesses of the Nicolaitans, and preserved some of them from those stains, 2 Pet. 2:20, Jude v. 25, to whom a notable promise is made: so that the Bishop may be roused to greater vigilance, and others in his Church to holiness. The naming of names for persons seems to look to the enrollment of names in the register of Bishops, which is gathered from the epistle of Ignatius to Heron. But the allegory of garments is used on account of that clothing of the faithful, of which Gal. 3:27. For that is unworthily defiled by sins, as the filth of a soul purified by faith, Acts 15:9, 2 Pet. 2:20. But it is less correctly understood here that the garment is the conscience, which is as it were the garment of the soul, to be whitened first of all by the blood of Christ, Rev. 7:14, Eph. 5:25, Tit. 1:7, & to be adorned with the garment of his righteousness Isa. 61:10. And not to be defiled by the filth of the world: Whence we are commanded to purify ourselves from all filthiness of the flesh and spirit, perfecting holiness in the fear of God 2 Cor. 7:1. Cornelius a Lapide wishes the garment to be called purity & innocence, which they received in baptism along with the white garment and preserved, or at least repaired after it was defiled by sin through repentance. But the chief garment which is put on in Baptism is Christ, and his innocence & righteousness: For as many of you as have been baptized, have put on Christ, Gal. 3:27. Nor is our innocence able to cover the nakedness of the soul, but that garment which Christ offers to us, Rev. 3:18. The Jesuit Alcazar preferred to take the garment as the conscience, for this is cleansed and defiled. To bear a stained garment, says B. Cluverus, and a cauterized conscience I hold as synonyms, 1 Tim. 4:2. Not to have defiled the garments, is not to have defiled the conscience, to have it cleansed by faith in Christ, and to retain the soul addicted to him, Heb. 9:14, or not to have permitted sin to reign in its mortal body, Rom. 6:12. No less because a few names of such a kind were found there. For the Lydians, because it was observed of the same, and the chief inhabitants of Sardis, which was the metropolis, were so infamous among the ancients for lusts, effeminacy, luxury, thefts, and a degenerate life, that they gave place to proverbs, whence, 'A Lydian at noon,' concerning one untimely and intemperately lustful. 'A Lydian plays the tavern-keeper,' was said of an effeminate and degenerate person. For Cyrus, having overcome the Lydians in war, had forbidden them weapons, and commanded them to engage in tavern-keeping and base trades. The same 'Lydian knaves' concerning luxuries, 'The Lydian shuts the door' concerning thieves and those given to filth. See Erasmus, Chiliad 2, Century 6, near the end. Athenaeus, Deipnosophistae, book 12. But it is a great praise of the few, as Primasius says, to remain among the evil and defiled with immaculate garments through the constant brightness of virtues, to which state God calls them. The few holy ones certainly knew that they were in the midst of a multitude of defiled ones, yet remaining themselves immaculate, they groaned according to Ezekiel, and mourned for the iniquity which was done in the midst of them. And they shall walk with me in white.] Pure clothing and white are not the same, for white garments in this place and below III, 18. IV, 4. are shining garments, as we learn in Matt. XVII, 2. and Luke IX, 29. and John XX, 12. And thus take white robes below VI, 11. VII, 9. 13. Those whom the King holds in the greatest honor, he also wishes to be his companions, and to be magnificently clothed. Such were those to him, Christ, in this very life.

White or bright garments correspond to garments not defiled; because those whose consciences have been purified by the blood of Christ, Heb. IX. v. 14. and are not polluted by the filth of the world, are to be adorned with white and splendid garments in the other life; white on account of all-manner of purity and innocence, Luke XXIII, 11. on account of the brightness of glory, on account of the honor of Royal and Priestly dignity, on account of the beauty of triumphs, and the unblemished light and serenity of heavenly happiness, Eccl. IX, 8. See Ap. IV, 4. C. VI, 11. chap. VII, 9. chap. XIX, 4. Among the Romans, candidates or those conspicuous in a white garment were seekers of honors, Kings, triumphers, and those celebrating solemn feasts. But that these things do not sound of the clothing of this life is confirmed both by the comparison with the final promises in the other epistles of the Son of God, and by what is subjoined concerning the book of life. And in the other life we shall properly walk with Christ: For we shall always be with him, 1 Thess. IV, 17. and we shall shine with the brightness of innocence and glory promised here, Matt. XIII, 43. being about to be like the angels, Luke XX, 36. who shone in white garments in their appearances, Acts I, 10. and participants of the glory of Christ, Phil. III, 21. Compare Mark X, 3.

Because they are worthy.] That word worthy signifies a certain congruence between acts and the honor rendered to acts, even if the honor exceeds the acts, as Luke VII, 4.

Dignity is not from our purity: for this is very imperfect, Is. LXIV, 6. Prov. XX, 9. Phil. III, 8. but it arises and is estimated from the innocence and holiness of Christ communicated to us, and the purification made through his blood. For there is no proportion between our inherent holiness and the glory of eternal life, no congruence of dignity: no merit is to be feigned here, whether of congruity or of condignity. One dignity is of testimony, another of merit. A good conscience, the light of works, and afflictions endured for Christ testify that those in whom they excel are worthy of the kingdom of God, Phil. I, 27. 2 Thess. I, 5. But Christ alone makes them worthy through faith. And we walk clothed in white not on account of ourselves, but on account of the honorable garment and covering of Christ apprehended by faith.

Latin:

Vers. 4. Ἀλλ’ ὀλίγα ἔχεις ὀνόματα ἐν Σάρδεσιν, ἃ οὐκ ἐμό- λυναν τὰ ἱμάτια αὑτῶν) Excitat Episcopum exemplis de ple- be propositis. Ὀνόματα sunt personæ, ut Act. I. 15. & infra XI. 13. Vestis animi est conscientia. Ea polluitur crimini- bus: Pura servatur per innocentiam & sanctitatem. Μο- λυσμὸς est quicquid sanctitati repugnat 2. Cor. VII. 1. μιά- σματα 2. Petr. II. 20. σπῖλοι Jac. I. 27.

Temperatur castigatio commendatione, quod adversus scortationem & idololatriam & alia flagi- tia Nicolaitarum vigilaverit, ac illorum nonnullos ab istis maculis præservarit, 2. Petr. II. 20. Jud. v. 25. quibus insignis sit promissio: ut ad majorem vigilantiam Episcopus, sanctimoniam alii in ejus Ecclesia excitentur. Nominum appellatio proper sonis respicere videtur nominum conscriptionem in matriculam Episcoporum, quæ ex Ignatii ad He- ronem epistola colligitur. Vestium autem allego- ria adhibita ob indumentum illud fidelium, de quo Gal. III. 27. Id enim indigne commaculatur per peccata, ceu sordes animæ fide purificatæ, Act. XV. 9. 2. Petr. II. 20. Minus recte autem vestimen- tum hic intelligitur de conscientia, quæ est quasive- stis animæ, dealbanda imprimis sanguine Christi, Apoc. VII. 14. Eph. V. 25. Tit. I. 7. & exornanda vesti- mento justitiæ ejus Es. LXI. 10. Nec coinquinandæ sordibus mundi: Unde purificare nos ipsos jube- mur ἀπὸ παντὸς μολυσμοῦ σαρκὸς καὶ πνεύματος ἐπιτελῶντες ἁγιωσύνην ἐν φόβῳ Θεῦ 2. Cor. VII. 1. Cornelius a Lapide vestem dici vult puritatem & in- nocentiam, quam cum veste candida in baptismo acceperunt & conservarunt, vel certe peccato in- quinatam per pœnitentiam repararunt. Sed quæ in Baptismo induitur vestis præcipua Christus est, ejusque innocentia & justitia: Quotquot enim ba- ptizati estis, Christum induistis, Gal. III. 27. Neque nostra innocentia nuditatem animæ tegere valet, sed vestis illa, quam Christus nobis offert, Apoc. III. 18. Alcazar Jesuita per vestimentum maluit accipere conscientiam, hæc enim mundatur & in- quinatur, Maculatam vestem, inquit B. Cluverus, & cauteriatam conscientiam gerere pro Synony- mis habeo, 1. Timoth. IV. 2. Non polluisse vestes, non polluisse conscientiam est, Christi fide mundatam ba- bere, & retinere animam illi addictam, Ebr. IX. 14. seu concupiscentiis in mortali suo corpore regnum non permisisse, Rom. VI. 12. Non minus quod pau- ca ibi nomina ejusmodi reperta sint. Lydi enim, quod eidem observatum, eorumque præcipui Sardi- um, quæ metropolis erat, incolæ ob libidines, molliti- em, luxum, furta, vitamque degenerem adeo samo- si fuere apud veteres, ut proverbiis locum dederint, unde, Lydus in meridie, de intempestive ac intempe- ranter libidinoso. Lydus cauponatur, in effœmi- natum & denegerem dicebatur. Cyrus enim, supe- ratis bello Lydis, arma interdixerat, cauponarias & viles eis negotiationes præceperat. Idem Λύδων κά- πηκας de lautitiis, λυδὸς τὴν θύραν ἔκλεισι de furaci- bus ac spurcitiæ deditis. Vide Erasmum Chiliad. 2. Centur. 6. sub finem. Athenæum Dipnosophist. li- bro 12. Magna autem laus paucorum, dicente Pri- masio, inter malos inquinatos jugi virtutum nitore immaculatis vestibus permanere, ad quem habi- tum Deus provocat. Sciebant utique pauci san- cti esse in medio sui inquinatorum multitudinem, ipsi tamen immaculati permanentes, ingemisce- bant juxta Ezechiel, & mœrebant ab iniquitate, quæ fiebat in medio eorum. Καὶ περιπατήσουσι μετ' ἐμὲ ἐν λευκοῖς.] Non idem est vestis pura & λευκὴ, nam λευκὰ ἱμάτια hoc loco & infra III, 18. IV, 4. sunt vestes coruscantes, ut discimus Matth. XVII, 2. & Luc. IX, 29. & Joh. XX, 12. Et sic sume στολὰς λευκὰς infra VI, 11. VII, 9. 13. Quos Rex maximo in honore habet, eos & sibi co- mites vult esse, & magnifice vestiri. Tales illi erant Christo in hac ipsa vita.

Vestibus non commaculatis respondent vestes albæ vel candidæ; quia quorum conscientiæ per sanguinem Christi purificatæ sunt, Ebr. IX. v. 14. nec coinquinantur sordibus mundi, vestibus or- nandi sunt albis & splendidis in altera vita; candidis ob omnimodam puritatem & innocentiam, Luc. XXIII, 11. ob gloriæ nitorem, ob dignitatis Regiæ & Sacerdotalis honorem, ob triumphorum decorem, & felicitatis ac gaudii cœlestis intemeratam lucem & serenitatem Eccl. IX, 8. Vid. Ap. IV, 4. C. VI, 11. cap. VII, 9. cap. XIX, 4. Penes Romanos candi- dati vel candida veste conspicui erant honorum pe- titores, Reges, triumphatores, & solaria festa cele- brantes. Non autem de vestitu hujus vitæ hæc so- nare tum collatio cum finalibus promissionibus in cæteris Filii Dei epistolis, tum quæ subjunguntur de libro vitæ, confirmant. Et in altera vita proprie cum Christo ambulaturi sumus: Semper enim cum ipso erimus 1. Thess. IV, 17. & claritate innocentiæ ac gloriæ hic promissa rutilabimus Matth. XIII, 43. ἰσάγγελοι futuri, similes Angelis, Luc. XX, 36. qui niveis vestibus fulserunt in apparitionibus, Act. I, 10. & gloriæ Christi participes, Phil. III, 21. Conf. Marc. X, 3.

Ὅτι ἄξιοί εἰσι.] Vox illa digni congruentiam quandam si- gnificat inter actus & honorem actibus redditum, etiamsi ho- nor superet actus, ut Luc. VII, 4.

Dignitas non è nostra puritate: Hæc enim valde imperfecta est, Es. LXIV, 6. Prov. XX, 9. Phil. III, 8. sed ab innocentia & sanctitate Christi nobis com- municata, & purificatione per sanguinem ejus fa- cta oritur & æstimatur. Nulla enim inter nostram inhærentem sanctimoniam & vitæ æternæ gloriam proportio, nulla dignitatis congruentia: nullum hic meritum fingendum f. de congruo, s. de condi- gno. Dignitas alia est testimonii, alia meriti. Bona conscientia, lux operum, afflictiones propter Chri- stum exantlatæ testantur dignos esse regno Dei il- los, in quibus eminent, Phil. I, 27. 2. Thessal. I, 5. Christus autem solus per fidem dignos facit. Nec propter nos ipsos, sed propter vestem ac tegumen- tum honorabile Christi fide apprehensum albati incedimus.

## 3:5
Verse 5. He who overcomes.] That is, not only those Sardians, but also as many as have overcome the temptations of pleasure and terror in a like manner.

This one shall be clothed in white garments.] He shall be in honor with me, such as Joseph was with Pharaoh, Gen. XLI, 22. 42.

And I will not blot out his name from the book of life.] That is, he shall have a right to eternal life, and he himself shall feel that within himself. The similitude is taken from the custom of cities, among which citizens were inscribed in the White [register], and were erased from it if they had become dishonored. See Luke 10, 20. below 13, 8. chap. 17, 8. chap. 20, 12. 15. chap. 21, 17. But there is a litotes here. For I will not blot out is said for I will diligently preserve. To blot out is to wipe away. See Acts 3, 19. Col. 2, 14. and Exod. 32, 31. 32. with the added place of Luke 9, 26. chap. 12, 8. 9.

He had made mention of the praised names, which, inscribed in the register of Bishops, were approved by Christ himself: now he testifies that their names are inscribed in the book of life, and are not to be expunged from it: which is the register of heaven. We admit a meiosis. Not to be deleted is to be written with the just. Just as in Psalm LXIX, 29. opposites are spoken of synonymously, delete them from the book of the living, that they may not be written with the just. Compare Exod. XXXII, 32. This promise is to be understood not only of the right to eternal life, as being made to him who finally overcomes through faith, but of the actual concession of eternal life. Concerning which book see below Chapter XIII, 8.

For this book does not commemorate God, lest he be deceived by forgetfulness; but it signifies the predestination of those to whom eternal life will be given. For God is not ignorant of them, and reads in this book so that he may know: But rather his very foreknowledge concerning them, which cannot be deceived, is the book of life, in which they are written, that is, foreknown. Anselm: The names, he says, of those are written in the book of life, that is, they are held assigned to life in the memory of Divine predestination. For who is the book of life, if not the memory of God, in which are those who live forever: Conf. Dan. XII, 2. Luc. X, 20. Phil. IV, 3. Ebr. XII, 23.

And I will confess his name before my Father, and before his Angels.)

His name will be read as if from the book of life, in which it is inscribed, which will happen on the last day, when the books will be opened, and among these also the book of life, Apoc. XX, 12. Which profession of the names of those who fearlessly profess the name of Christ, he himself promised, Matth. X, 32.

Latin:

Vers. 5. Ὁ νικῶν.] Id est non illi tantum Sardiani, sed & quotquot pari modo voluptatis ac terroris tentamenta supe- raverint.

Οὗτος περιβαλεῖται ἱματίοις λευκοῖς.] Erit apud me in ho- nore, quali Josephus apud Pharaonem, Gen. XLI, 22. 42.

Καὶ ὐ μὴ ἐξαλείψω τὸ ὄνομα αὐτῦ ἐκ τῆς βίβλυ τῆς ζωῆς.] Id est, jus habebit ad vitam æternam, & ipse id intra se sentiet. Similitudo sumpta à more civitatum, apud quas cives inscri- bebantur Albo, & ex eo eradebantur, si facti essent ἄτιμοι. Vi- de Luc. 10, 20. infra 13, 8. c. 17, 8. c. 20, 12. 15. c. 21, 17. Est autem hic λιτότης. Nam ἐ μὴ ἐξαλείψω dicitur pro diligenter asser- vabo. Ἐξαλείφειν est מחה. Vid. Act. 3, 19. Col. 2, 14. & Exod. 32, 31. 32. addito loco Luc. 9, 26. c. 12, 8. 9.

Nominum laudatorum fecerat mentionem, quæ in matricula Episcoporum inscripta Christo ipsi probabantur: jam illorum nomina inscripta in li- bro vitæ, nec ex eo expungenda esse testatur: quæ est cœli matricula. Μείωσιν admittimus. Non dele- ri est scribi cum justis. Quemadmodum Psal. LXIX, 29. Συνωνύμως dicuntur opposita, dele illos è libro viventium, ne cum justis scribantur. Conf. Exod. XXXII, 32. Non de jure ad vitam æternam tantum hæc promissio, utpote facta illi, qui τελικῶς vincit per fidem, sed de actuali vitæ æternæ concessione intelligenda. De quo libro vide infra Cap. XIII, 8.

Non enim Deum liber iste commemorat, ne obli- vione fallatur; sed praedestinationem significat eo- rum, quibus aeterna dabitur vita. Neq; enim nescit eos Deus, & in hoc libro legit, ut sciat: Sed potius ipsa ejus praescientia de illis, quae falli non potest, li- ber est vitae, in quo sunt scripti, id est, praecogniti. Anshelmus: Nomina, inquit, eorum scripta sunt in libro vitae, id est, assignata tenentur ad vitam in memoria Divinae praedestinationis. Quis est enim liber vitae, nisi memoria Dei, in qua sunt illi, qui vivunt in aeternum: Conf. Dan. XII, 2. Luc. X, 20. Phil. IV, 3. Ebr. XII, 23.

Καὶ ἐξομολογήσομαι τὸ ὄνομα αὐτῶ ἐνώπιον τῶ Πατρός με, καὶ ἐνώπιον τῶν Ἀγγέλων αὐτῶ.)

Legetur quasi è libro vitae nomen ejusdem, in quem inscriptum est, quod fiet in die novissimo, ubi libri pandentur, & inter hos etiam liber vitae, Apoc. XX, 12. Quam professionem nominum Eo- rum, qui Christi nomen intrepide profitentur, ipse promisit, Matth. X, 32.

## 3:6
Vers. 6. He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the Churches.] Namely to the Sardian and to others in Lydia. What I say to the Bishop, I say also to the hearers.

PART II. SIXTH EPISTLE TO THE BISHOP OF PHILADELPHIA.

Latin:

Vers. 6. ὁ ἔχων τὸ ὗς ἀκουσάτω, τί τὸ πνεῦμα λέγει ταῖς Ἐκ- κλησίαις.] Nempe Sardianae & in Lydia aliis. Quae dico Epi- scopo, dico & auditoribus.

PARS II. EPISTOLA SEXTA AD EPISCOPUM PHI- LADELPHENSEM.

## 3:7
Vers. 7. And to the Angel of the Church in Philadelphia write.] It is a city of Mysia, founded by Attalus, whose surname was Philadelphus.

This Bishop of Philadelphia, which is a Decapolis in Asia Minor according to Pliny b. V. c. 48. and Strabo XVI. By Aureolus and Lyranus, who calls this a common opinion, it is believed to be St. Quadratus: concerning whom let Eusebius be read b. III. c. 34. Nicephorus b. I. hist. Eccl. cap. 21. But he flourished around the year of Christ 125, and thus after the Apocalypse was written, and, by the authority of Jerome, he was an Athenian, not a Philadelphian Bishop. It is better therefore to suspend judgment as to who he might have been. He is certainly praised remarkably, and there is promised to him the grace and efficacy of preaching, even for convincing the adversaries themselves, as well as the protection of Christ in the hour of temptation, with an added exhortation that he should guard the purity of the Word and the truth of the faith, with a magnificent promise that he is to be made a pillar in the temple of God, to be adorned with a new name, not another. The present epistle Ludov. Crocius wishes to refer to the fraternal condition of the Christian Church, which he thought had already diminished at that time, i.e., in the year 1635, which, having been delivered from the time of temptation about to come upon the whole world, is about to return as closely as possible to the first love lost under the Apostolic condition, and is about to receive the Jews who are to be converted according to the promise. But 40 years have already flowed by, and there has not yet arisen from the present dawn of that silver period, nor does any hope of it shine forth: Never was there greater discord, less brotherly love in the Church than in these years: with the Reformed themselves torn into parties through the contentions of the hypotheticals with the absolutists, if I may so call them, and between those and these among themselves, which Crocius himself experienced, as well as the various sects, especially those arisen in England, which disturbed the whole kingdom, and gave cause for the King's slaughter; not to mention anything of the sharper contentions against the associates of the Augsburg confession and of these mutually among themselves; through all of which it is so far from the case that brotherly love can be expected, that there rather looms the fulfillment of the prophecy of Christ concerning the Son of man about to come and scarcely finding faith in the world, Luc. XIIX, 18. But what is charity without faith? What? concerning charity in the hearts of men about to expire, Matt. 24:12. about to predominate through impiety and implacability, 2 Tim. 3:1 ff. But concerning the numerous conversion of the Jews in these most recent times, there exists neither any promise, nor conjecture, much less does any hope appear. Cocceius certainly did not dare to rise up thus against his senior colleague: even though he still had his dreams about political peace in the year 1665; which, however, the outcome proves to be too false, especially in these massive upheavals of the Christian world: Who would doubt, he says, regarding those words: Behold, I give some from the Synagogue of Satan to those who say they are Jews, and are not, but lie: Behold, I will make them come and worship before your feet, and know that I have loved you, if anyone sees a people attacked by a long-lasting war on the occasion of the Evangelical doctrine proceeding so far against the hope of the whole world, that the most powerful Monarchs, who say they are Jews, that is, the true people of God, who had been the afflicted of the Lord, are forced to make peace with them, having renounced all right, and indeed even to profess in words that their God has helped them, that that people can usurp these words about themselves, provided that the word of the patience of Christ is retained in that people. Namely, the Son of God, according to this Dreamer, predicted in this letter to the Philadelphian Church, that is, to the Reformed in Belgium, that glory, that from the Synagogue of Satan those who say they are Jews, and are not, the King of the Spains with his own is to come and worship before the seats of the Belgian estates, and is to know that Christ has loved them. Yet he did not foresee, nor could he extract from this letter, that after the Most Catholic King, the Most Christian King was to undertake [war] with the very Defender of the Reformed faith, the King of Great Britain, against the Batavians, the allies of the same faith: nor did he have anything to say about the temptation about to come upon the whole earth: which he here rashly fears is still predicted: Whoever, he says, will diligently search out other prophecies, and the remaining parts of the Apocalypse, corresponding to this period, so that those things which are of the sixth seal, and are said in the seventh trumpet, and chap. 20:11, and which are at the end of chap. 7, he perhaps will understand more about this temptation. Let us therefore leave that investigation to others who are twins in these matters. David Pareus, of primary name among the Reformed, could see no vision here concerning the most recent times, but understood the letter properly as concerning the Philadelphians, to whom also the letter of Ignatius is circulated as having been written. And he explains these things likewise concerning the Jews said to be according to the flesh, and their conversion, but that it was to be a little after those times, while he to whom this letter was given, the Bishop, was still living: he also does not refer the hour of temptation to the final times; but to that late persecution which was then encroaching from Trajan or another tyrant.

Thus says the holy one, the true one.] Christ is called holy also in Acts 3:14. Here, however, is added ὁ ἀληθινός, that is, preeminently holy. For 'true' is often said of that which excels in any given kind. Jer. 2:21, John 1:9, ch. 4:23, ch. 6:32, ch. 15:1, 1 Tim. 6:19, 1 Pet. 5:12, 1 John 4:12. He says this so that the bishops might imitate his holiness as much as possible. In the Manuscript, the order is changed: ὁ ἀληθινός, ὁ ἅγιος.

He who has the key of David.] That is, he who has not only the right of death and hell, as above 1:18, but the most complete authority in the house of God, just as Eliakim had in the house of Hezekiah, who was of the descendants of David. That Eliakim was, as the Constantinopolitans used to speak, the curopalates of Hezekiah, the badge of whose office was the figure of a key woven into the shoulder-piece. See Isaiah 22:22.

he who opens and no one will shut.] Αὐτὴν is not in the Manuscript. It is, however, a purely Hebrew idiom, for which the Greeks would say: Οὗ ἀνοίγοντος οὐδεὶς κλείσει. No one in the palace dares to contradict him, or to act against his commands. In Isaiah 22:22, to which this passage refers, it is read: And he shall open, and there shall be no one shutting, and he shall shut, and there shall be no one opening.

Except he who opens, and no one will shut it.] Better in the Manuscript: Shutting and no one opens, as in Isaiah, that is, he who shuts and no one opens. All things are open to him. The Latin reads these and the preceding words as they are in the Manuscript.

The epithets of Christ are not to be diminished with Alcazar and Grotius, so that one may emerge from two. For it pleased the Son of God to use different ones in the inscription, which are accommodated to the subject matter of the letter. He is therefore called ὁ ἅγιος, that holy one, by which name an excellence is already expressed; because he himself is the Holy of Holies, Dan. 9:24. Cf. 1 John 2:20, because he wants all the bishops subject to him, and indeed all the faithful, to imitate the holiness of the supreme Bishop, 1 John 3:1, 7. But he is called ὁ ἀληθινός, because he wants them to guard the Word of truth, which they have received from him who is Truth itself, John 14:6, Apoc. 3:8, and he promises and distributes distinguished rewards to those struggling for truth and holiness. He is said to have the key of David, because by his power he had given an open door to the Bishop, and was about to give it further for the entry of the Jews, and the communion of the spiritual kingdom of David, Luke 1:32, 33. But that key, as it is wrongly confused by Ansbert with Christ the key-bearer; when he makes Christ the key: so neither can this be understood as the key of the knowledge of Scripture, as Rupert, Anselm, Lyra, Pannonius, and Viegas wish; nor can it be taken as the cross of Christ with Hugo and Albert; even though the opening is made by the merit of the passion and death of Christ: much less of the key by which Christ opened the limbo of the Fathers, as it is imagined by the Papists, in which opinion Cornelius cited Thomas 3rd part, q. 17, art. 1, ad 2: but it is power and faculty for the opening of the house of David, namely of the kingdom or the Church: The key of David, that is, the key of the house of David, or of the Church: because the Church is the spiritual kingdom of David, who is named, because the throne of David was given to Christ, Luke 1:32. He has full power in the government of the Church of opening heaven and receiving into the Church not only the militant, but also the triumphant. To what do the keys of the kingdom of heaven pertain, Matt. XVI, 19. of loosing and binding, Matt. XVIII, 18. John XX, 23. But that which is said, he himself opens, and no one shuts, he shuts, and no one opens, by this is expressed the absolute power of admitting into the house of the Lord, that is, the Church, 1 Tim. III, 15. Heb. III, 6. and of excluding from the same. It is hinted, however, by this title, that the key-bearer here has uniquely unlocked the door of the Church to the Philadelphian Angel, and will continue to unlock it, which no one of the thrones, no one of the angels of Satan can shut. There is, however, a great difference between Christ in the power of the key of David, and Peter, in the power granted to him by Christ, when the keys of the kingdom of heaven were given to him, and, in his person, to the other Apostles. For the power of the former is absolute, supreme, independent, αὐτοκρατορική; the power of the latter is restricted, subordinate, dependent, διακονική. The former is infallible; the latter can fail. Sometimes, as Origen says, he who is sent outside is inside, and he who is outside is seen to be retained inside. Nor does Aegidius Romanus deny this difference: God, he says, by Himself dismisses guilt by cleansing the soul from the stain of guilt, and by releasing the debt of eternal punishment: but Priests dismiss and release by manifesting and showing the remission made or not made. Furthermore, this is the work of one GOD, that our hearts are opened Acts XVI, 14. that they are inclined, 2 Kings XIX, 14. that they are changed, Job XII, verse 24. that they are softened, 2 Chron. XXXIV, 27. that they are broken, 1 Sam. X, 26. that they are converted Luke I, 17. that stony hearts are taken away, and hearts of flesh are put in, Ezek. XXXVI, 26. that new hearts are created, Ps. LI. that our souls are healed Ps. 103:3. that we are made alive dead in sins, Eph. 2:5. that we are raised from the dead. Eph. 5. Who could doubt that all these are Divine effects? for which there is need of Divine power: which in Christ is proper to him by reason of his Divine nature in itself, but communicated to his human nature through the personal union natures: Because in the actions of his office each nature does what is its own, with the communication of the other. But to the teachers of the Word other things are ascribed, not indeed merely in title, or for the sake of honoring the ministry, as the Calvinist Tropists pervert; but properly and truly, yet only ministerially and in the manner of a deacon, and indeed on account of the power of the Word, which they dispense. Rom. 1:16. Heb. 4:12. Finally, note here again the rashness of Grotius in correcting the remaining codices, even though they are most approved and highly consistent, from a manuscript and a Latin codex.

Latin:

Vers. 7. Καὶ τῷ Ἀγγέλῳ τῆς ἐν Φιλαδελφείᾳ Ἐκκλησίας γρά- ψον.] Urbs est Mysiae, condita ab Attalo, cui cognomen erat Philadelpho.

Episcopus hic Philadelphia, quae Decapolis est in minori Asia juxta Plinium l. V. c. 48. & Strabon. XVI. Aureolo & Lyrano, qui communem dicit hanc sententiam, creditur S. Quadratus: de quo legatur Eusebius l. III. c. 34. Nicephorus l. I. hist. Eccl. cap. 21. Sed is floruit circa annum Christi 125. adeoque post scriptam Apocalypsin, &, autore Hieronymo, Atheniensis fuit, non Philadelphensis Episcopus. Praestat ergo ἐπέχειν, quisnam ille fuerit. Lauda- tur certe insigniter, ac promittitur ei praedicationis gratia & efficacia, ad ipsos etiam adversarios con- vincendos, necnon praesidium Christi in hora ten- tationis, addita cohortatione, ut puritatem Verbi & veritatem fidei custodiat, cum pollicitatione magnifica, quod efficiendus sit columna in templo Dei, novo nomine non alio exornanda. Episto- lam praesentem Ludov. Crocius referre vult Ecclesiae Christianae conditionem fraternam, quae jam tum imminuerit, quum ea somniavit, h. e. an. 1635. quae liberata ex tempore tentationis in universum or- bem venturo, ad primam charitatem sub conditio- ne Apostolica amissam, quam proxime reditura sit, Judaeosque secundum promissionem converten- dos exceptura. Sed fluxerunt jam XL. anni, & nondum surrexit è praesenti aurora istius argenteae periodi, nec ulla ejus affulget spes: Nunquam ma- jor discordia, minor Φιλαδελφία fuit in Ecclesia, quam istis annis: in partem discerptis ipsis Refor- matis per contentiones hypotheticorum cum ab- solutistis, ut ita vocitem, & cum illorum tum isto- rum inter sese, quas expertus ipse Crocius est, nec- non sectas multivarias, in Anglia imprimis exortas, quae regnum totum turbarunt, Regisque caedi cau- sam dederunt; ne de acrioribus contentionibus ad- versus socios Augustanae confessionis & horum inter sese mutuo quicquam dicam; per quae omnia tantum abest, ut Φιλαδελφία expectari possit, ut immineat potius vaticinii Christi de Filio hominis venturo fidem vix inventuro in mundo comple- mentum Luc. XIIX, 18. quae autem sine fide est cha- ritas? Quid? de charitate in cordibus hominum expiratura Matth. XXIV, 12. impietate & implaca- bilitate prædominatura, 2. Tim. III, 1. feqq. De Ju- dæorum vero numerosa conversione in hisce no- vissimis temporibus nec promissio ulla extat, nec conjectura, nedum spes aliqua apparet. Coccejus certe sic non ausus fuit assurgere seniori suo colle- gæ: etsi etiam de politica pace somnia sua adhuc anno 1665. habuerit; quæ vero eventus nimis falsa comprobat, in his imprimis decumanis orbis Chri- stiani motibus: Quis dubitet, inquit, ad verba illa: Ecce, do quosdam ex Synagoga Satanæ iis, qui di- cunt, se esse Judæos, & non sunt, sed mentiuntur: Ecce, faciam eos, ut veniant, & adorent coram pe- dibus tuis, & cognoscant, quod ego dilexerim te, si quis videat populum oppugnatum bello diuturno occasione Evangelicæ doctrinæ contra totius mundi spem eo usque procedere, ut potentissimi Monarchæ, qui se dicunt esse Judæos, hoc est verum populum Dei, qui afflictorum Domini extiterant, cogantur pacem cum illis facere, abdicato omni jure, imo verbis etiam profiteri, quod Deus ipsorum ipsos juverit, illum po- pulum posse hæc verba de se usurpare, dummodo in illo populo sermo patientiæ Christi retineatur. Scil. Filius Dei juxta hunc Somniatorem prædixit hac epistola Ecclesiæ Philadelphiensi, hoc est, Reforma- tis in Belgio eam gloriam, quod ex Synagoga Sa- tanæ illi, qui dicunt se Judæos, & non sunt, Rex Hi- spaniarum cum suis venturus sit & adoraturus co- ram sedibus ordinum Belgicorum, & cogniturus, quod Christus ipsos dilexerit. Non prævidit tamen ille, nec eruere potuit ex hac epistola, quod post Regem Catholicissimum Rex Christianissimus su- scepturus sit cum ipso Defensore fidei Reformatæ Magnæ Britanniæ Rege, adversus Socios ejusdem fidei Batavos: nec dicere habuit quicquam de ten- tatione ventura in totam terram: quam hic prædi- ctam temere adhuc metuit: Qui diligenter, inquit, alias rimabitur prophetias, & reliquas Apocalypsis partes, huic periodo respondentes, ut ea, quæ sunt si- gilli sexti, & dicuntur in tuba septima, & cap. XX, 11. & quæ sunt in fine cap. VII. is fortasse amplius de hac tentatione intelliget. Eam ergo indagationem aliis ipsi geminis in commissis relinquamus. Da- vid Pareus, præcipui nominis inter Reformatos, nullam hic videre potuit de novissimis temporib9 visionem, sed de Philadelphenis proprie intellexit epistolam, ad quos etiam Ignatii epistola exarata circumfertur. Et de Judæis pariter secundum car- nem dictis hæc explicat, eorumque conversione, sed paulo post ista tempora futura, vivente adhuc illo, ad quem epistola hæc data est, Episcopo: ho- ram etiam tentationis non ad extrema refert tem- pora; sed ad seram illam persecutionem, quæ à Trajano vel alio tyranno tunc ingruebat.

Τάδε λέγει ὁ ἅγιος, ὁ ἀληθινὸς.] Sanctus Christus dici- tur etiam Act. III. vers. 14. Hic autem additur ὁ ἀληθινός, id est, eximie sanctus. Verum enim sæpe dicitur, id, quod in unoquoque genere eminet. Jerem. II, 21. Joh. I, 9. c. IV, 23. c. VI, 32. c. XV, 1. 1. Tim. VI, 19. 1. Petr. V, 12. 1. Joh. IV, 12. Hoc ideo dicit, ut Episcopi ipsius sanctitatem, quan- tum fieri potest, imitentur. In Manuscripto mutato ordine ὁ ἀληθινὸς, ὁ ἅγιος.

Ὁ ἔχων τὴν κλεῖν τῦ Δαβὶδ.] Id est, qui non tantum mortis & inferni jus habet, ut supra I, 18. sed plenissimum imperium in domo Dei, quemadmodum Eliacimus in domo Ezechiæ, qui erat ex Davidis posteris. Is Eliacimus fuit, ut Constantinopolitani loquebantur, κυροπαλάτης Ezechiæ, cu- jus functionis insigne erat clavis figura intexta epomidi. Vi- de Esaiam XXII, 22.

ὁ ἀνοίγων καὶ ὀδὲις κλείσει αὐτήν.] Αὐτὴν non est in Manu- scripto. Est autem loquutio plane Ebræa, pro qua Græci di- cerent: Οὗ ἀνοίγοντος οὐδεὶς κλείσει. Nemo in palatio ei audet contradicere, aut contra ejus jussa facere. In Esaia XXII, 22. quo hic locus respicit, legitur: Καὶ ἀνοίξει, καὶ ὐκ ἔσαι ὁ ἀπο- κλείων, καὶ κλείσει, καὶ ὐκ ἔσαι ὁ ἀνοίγων.

Ei mh̀ o̔ a̓noígwn, kaì ou̓deìs kleísei au̓th́n.] Melius in Manu- scripto: Kleíwn kaì ou̓deìs a̓noígei, ut in Esaia, id est, kleíont©· u̓deìs a̓noígei. Omnia ei patent. Latinus haec & praecedentia legit ita, ut sunt in Manuscripto.

Epitheta Christi non sunt imminuenda cum Al- cazaro & Grotio, ut ex duobus unum evadat. Pla- cuit enim Filio Dei diversa in inscriptione adhibe- re, quae epistolae materiae accommodata sint. Dici- tur ergo o̔ ạ́gios, sanctus ille, quo nomine jam e̓xo- ch̀ est expressa; quod ipse Sanctus sanctorum sit, Dan. IX, 24. Conf. 1. Joh. II, 20. quia vult, ut supre- mi Episcopi sanctitatem imitentur omnes ipsi sub- jecti Episcopi, imo fideles universi, 1. Joh. III. c. 1, 7. O̔ a̓lhqinòs vero dicitur, quia vult, ut veritatis Verbum custodiant, quod ab eo, qui Veritas ipsa est, acceperunt, Joh. XIV, 6. Apocal. III, 8. & cer- tantibus pro veritate & sanctitate insignia praemia promittit ac distribuit, Habere clavem David di- citur, quia dederat ejus virtute Episcopo ostium apertum, daturusque porro erat ad ingressum Ju- daerum, & communionem regni spiritualis David, Luc. I, 32. 33. Clavis autem illa, uti perperam ab Ans- berto cum clavigero Christo confunditur; cum Christum clavem facit: ita neque de clave intelli- gentiae Scripturae hic sermo, ut Rupertus, Anshel- mus, Lyranus, Pannonius, Viegas volunt; neque de cruce Christi accipi potest cum Hugone & Alber- to; etsi merito passionis & mortis Christi fiat aper- tio: nedum de clave, qua Christus limbum Patrum, qualis a Papistis fingitur, aperuit, quemadmodum in ea sententia Thomam 3. part. q. 17. art. 1. ad 2. ad- duxit Cornelius: sed est potestas & facultas in aper- tionem domus Davidis, regni scilicet vel Ecclesiae: Clavis David, id est, clavis domus David, vel Eccle- siae:quia Ecclesia est regnum spirituale Davidis, qui nominatur, quia Christo datus thronus Davidis, Luc. I, 32. Plenam habet potestatem in Ecclesiae regimine coelum aperiendi & recipiendi in Eccle- siam non militantem solum, sed & triumphantem. Quo pertinent claves regni coelorum, Matth. XVI, 9. solvendi & ligandi, Matth. XIIX, 18. Joh. XX, 23. Quod autem dicitur, aperti ipse, & nemo clau- dit, claudit, & nemo aperit, eo exprimitur absoluta potestas intromittendi in domum Domini, hoc est, Ecclesiam, 1. Tim. III, 15. Ebr. III, 6. & excludendi ab eadem. Innuitur autem hoc titulo, quod cla- viger hic unice Philadelpheno Angelo ostium Ec- clesiae reserarit, & porro reseraturus sit, quam nul- lus thronorũ, nullus Angelorum satanae occludere possit. Magna autem est differentia inter Christum in potestate clavis David, & Petrum, in potestate à Christo illi concessa, cum ipsi, &, in persona ejus, caeteris Apostolis datae sunt claves regni coelorum. Illius enim potestas est absoluta, summa, indepen‐ dens, au̓toxratorikh̀; horum potestas est restricta, subordinata, dependens, diakonikh̀. Illa est infal- libilis; haec fallere potest. Interdum, dicente Ori- gene, qui foris mittitur, intus est, & qui foris est, intus videtur retineri. Nec hanc differentiam diffitetur Aegidius Romanus: Deus, inquit, per se dimittit culpam mundando animam a macula culpa, & sol- vendo debitum poenae aeterna: Sacerdotes vero dimit- tunt & solvunt remissionem factam vel non factam manifestando & ostendendo. Porro unius DEI hoc est, quod corda nostra aperiuntur Act. XVI, 14. quod inclinantur, 2. Reg. XIX, 14. quod immutan- tur, Job. XII, vers. 24. quod emolliuntur, 2. Paral. XXXIV, 27. quod franguntur, 1. Reg. X, 26. quod convertuntur Luc. I, 17. quod corda saxea eximun- tur, & carnea induntur, Ezech. XXXVI, 16. quod corda nova creantur, Psal. VI. quod animae nostrae sanantur Pfal. CIII, 3. quod vivificamur mortui in peccatis, Eph. II, 5. quod resuscitamur à mortuis. Eph. V. Quæ omnia Divina esse ἀποτελέσματα ec- quis ambigat? ad quæ Divina virtute opus est: quæ Christo ratione Divinæ propria est per se, humanæ vero ejus naturæ communicata per unionis perso- nalis gratiam, unde ad ea concurrit secundum u- tramque naturam : Quia in actionibus officii agit utraque natura quod suum est, cum communicatione alterius. Verbi autem Doctoribus alia adscribun- tur, non quidem titulotenus tantum, vel cohone- standi ministerii gratia, ut Calviniani Tropistæ per- vertunt; sed proprie & vere, ast διακονικῶς tantum & ministerialiter, & quidem ob virtutem Verbi, quod dispensant. Rom. I, 16. Ebr. IV, 12. Denique notanda hic iterum temeritas Grotii corrigentis è Manuscripto & Latino Codices reliquos, etsi pro- batissimos, atque apprime consentientes.

## 3:8
Verse 8. I know your works.] Your labor in propagating the Gospel. Behold I have given before you an open door.] Before you instead of to you, as also above 2:14. Understand by the door the opportunity of freely announcing the Gospel, as 1 Cor. 16:9, 2 Cor. 2:12, Col. 4:3, where see the things said. And this agrees well with the things said above: I have opened, and who shall shut? which no one is able to shut it.] Again a Hebraism. The sense: No one will be able to hinder that liberty of preaching.
