By the opening of the door, not only the opportunity of preaching the Gospel is insinuated; but also the removal of impediments and the granting of the faculty for admitting, so that they may be gathered to the Church, and admission may not be prohibited, John 10:3. And Paul preaches that a great door was opened to him at Ephesus, 1 Cor. 16:9, and at Troas 2. Cor. 2:12, and he prays that the Colossians may pray for him, that God may open to him a door of the Word, ch. 4:3, by which he may be able to enter to them through the Word, convert them to the faith, and gather them to the communion of the Church. But that is not done immediately, but through the medium of the Word and its efficacy. It is said, however, in the past tense I have given, even though it is finally to happen, and that on account of the certainty of the thing, in the manner of Scripture. Therefore in the following verse 9 the present is used I give, because it is already imminent. That you have little power.] I have done this because now you have a small Church, which is here called power, that is, an army, צבא, as Matt. 24:30, after the example of Daniel, with whom the Jewish people is called the host of heaven, 8:10. And you have kept my word.] That is, yet you have persisted in observing my precepts. See above 3. And you have not denied my name.] You have not dissembled that you were a Christian לא כפרת.

Others understand it concerning little power: I have not given you many talents of eloquence and other gifts, to which Victorinus of Pettau, Ambrose, Lyra, Dionysius, B. Cluverus, and Gerhard accede, although the latter also joins a small amount of power, by a comparison made to the small number of persecutors, so that they may be resisted: he also joins Grotius's explanation concerning the little flock entrusted to the Church. The former can be joined, the latter not so. For it is a disparate sense. Bede and Haymo with Primasius explain little as humble and modest, because it acknowledges that it can do little, and has small strength. But here the judgment of one's own sense is not expressed, but the judgment of the Son of God himself, by whose testimony the power of the Bishop was very small for accomplishing great things. And who is sufficient for these things, exclaims the Doctor of the Gentiles himself and the leader of the Apostles, 2 Cor. 2:16. Cf. 1 Cor. 1:26, 27, 28. There certainly would not have been lacking to the Bishop the quickness of natural judgment, nor the power of interpretation, nor skill in Scripture; he would also have had senses exercised to discern both good and evil, Heb. 5:14. Who, no matter how instructed with gifts, would not acknowledge that there is little power for those Divine effects of converting those who have been taught in the synagogue of Satan, and whose minds the god of this world has blinded, so that they might not see the light of the Gospel, 2 Cor. 4:4. Therefore, little power is said both by reason of other teachers who are instructed with greater gifts, and by reason of the duties and works to be performed, little, when it is estimated from itself: which, however, is not little when it is estimated from the outpouring of Divine grace: because we carry a heavenly treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellence of the power may be of God and not from us, 2 Cor. 4:7. How the supreme Apostle was among the Corinthians in weakness, in fear, and in trembling, and did not exert himself in the proclamation of human wisdom's persuasive words, but in the demonstration of the Spirit and of power, he himself teaches 1 Cor. 2:3, 4. Not to us, O Lord, not to us, but to your name be glory, Ps. 115. But let no one easily despise anyone on account of small gifts, because God chose the weak things in the world, that he might put to shame those that are strong, 1 Cor. 1:27; let no one also despair on account of his own little power: If the foot should say, I am not the hand, I am not of the body, is it therefore not of the body? And if the ear should say, I am not the eye, I am not of the body, is it therefore not of the body, 1 Cor. 12:14 ff. For God perfects strength for himself not rarely even through the mouth of infants and nursing children, that he may destroy the enemy, Ps. 8:3, and experience often teaches that those who have lesser gifts accomplish more than those who are instructed with more excellent gifts, because the power of the Lord is perfected in infirmity, 2 Cor. 12:9. Cf. Ex. 4:11, Matt. 25:14 ff. See, if you please, a clear example in Rufinus, book 1, ch. 3, of the conversion of a philosopher by a certain simple confessor, whom great bishops could not convert. But although he has little power and small strength to resist; yet the power of the Lord was so perfected in his infirmity, that the grace of the same preserved and defended the Word of the Lord, the deposit of heavenly truth; and he did not deny the name of the Lord, to whatever temptations he was exposed, but constantly professed it. For it is a μείωσις, as in John 1:20 it is said of the Proto-Baptist: And he confessed, and did not deny; for that becomes true confessors, and all Bishops. On the contrary, he is a betrayer of the truth who either does not freely proclaim, or does not freely defend the same, as Chrysostom says in the imperfect work, homily 25. Conf. 1 Peter 3:14, 15. Victorinus in this place: The humble in the world and the rustic in the Scriptures hold the faith immovably.

Latin:

Vers. 8. Οἶδά σου τὰ ἔργα.] Laborem tuum in propagando Evangelio. Ἰδὺ δέδωκα ἐνώπιόν σου θύραν ἀνεῳγμένην.] Ἐνώπιόν σου pro σοι, ut & supra II, 14. Januam intellige occasionem libere annuntiandi Evangelii, ut 1.Cor. XVI, 9. 2.Cor. II, 12. Coloff. IV, 3. ubi dicta vide. Et bene hoc convenit cum dictis supra: Ego aperui, & quis claudet? ἢν ὐδεὶς δύναται κλεῖσαι αὐτόν.] Rursum Hebraismus. Sen- sus: Nemo illam libertatem prædicandi impedire poterit. Per ostii apertionem non tantum occasio prædi- candi Evangelii; sed & impedimentorum remotio & facultatis ad intromittendum concessio infinua- tur, ut colligantur ad Ecclesiam, nec prohibeatur admissio, Joh. X, 3. Et Paulus prædicat, quod sibi magnum ostium Ephesi apertum sit, 1. Cor. XVI, 9. & Troade 2. Cor. II, 12. oratque, ut pro se precentur Colossenses, ut Deus sibi aperiat ostium Verbi, cap. IV, 3. quo per Verbum ingredi ad ipsos, con- vertere ad fidem, & colligere eos ad communio- nem Ecclesiæ queat. Non autem ἀμέσως id fit, sed mediante Verbo, ejusque efficacia. Dicitur au- tem in Præterito δέδωκα, etsi demum id futurum sit, idque ob certitudinem rei, more Scripturæ. Ideo sequenti vers. 9. præsens adhibetur δίδωμι, quod id jamjam immineat. Ὅτι μικρὰν ἔχεις δύναμιν.] Hoc ideo feci, quia nunc modi- cam habes Ecclesiam, quæ hic vocatur δύναμις, id est, exerci- tus, צבא, ut Matth. XXIV, 30. ad exemplum Danielis, apud quem populus Judaicus vocatur צבא השמים δύναμις τῶ ὐρανῶ, VIII, 10. Καὶ ἐτήρησάς με τὸν λόγον.] Id est, tamen perstitisti in ob- servandis præceptis meis. Vide supra 3. Καὶ ὐκ ἠρνήσω τὸ ὄνομά με.] Non dissimulasti te esse Chri- stianum לא כפרת.

Alii de modica virtute intelligunt: Non dedi tibi multa talenta eloquentiæ & aliorum donorum, quibus accedit Victorinus Pictaviensis, Ambrosius, Lyranus, Dionysius, B. Cluverus, Gerhardus, etsi hic conjungat etiam modicum potestatis, comparatio- ne facta ad modicum persecutorum, ut illis resista- tur: conjungit etiam Grotii explicationem de gre- ge pusillo Ecclesiæ concredito. Illa conjungi pot- est, hæc non item. Est enim disparatus sensus. Be- da, & Haymo cum Primafio modicam explicant humilem & modestam, quod agnoscat se parum posse, parvas habere vires. Verum hic non judici- um sensus proprii exprimitur, sed judicium ipsius Filii Dei, cujus testimonio potestas Episcopi valde exigua fuit ad res magnas gerendas. Et quis est ad hæc idoneus, exclamat ipse gentium Doctor & Apostolorum Antesignanus, 2. Cor. II, 16. Conf. 1. Cor. I, 26. 27. 28. Non defuerit sane Episcopo ἀγχίνοια naturalis judicii, non δύναμις ἑρμηνευτικὴ, non peritia Scripturæ; habuerit etiam sensus exer- citatos πρὸς διάκρισιν καλῶ τε καὶ κακῶ, Ebr. V, 14. Quis quantiscunque etiam donis instructus non agnoscat modicam esse virtutem ad Divinos istos effectus convertendi eos, qui in Synagoga satanæ edocti sunt, & quibus Deus hujus mundi mentes excæcavit, ne videant lucem Evangelii, 2. Cor. IV, 4. Exigua itaque virtus dicitur tum ratione aliorum Doctorum, qui majoribus donis instructi sunt, tum ratione munerum & operum perficiendorum, exi- gua, quum ex se æstimatur: quæ vero non exigua, quum æstimatur ex Divinæ gratiæ ἀποῥῥοίᾳ: quia thesaurum cœlestem gerimus ἐν ὀστρακίνοις σκεύε- σιν, ἵνα ἡ ὑπερβολὴ τῆς δυνάμεως ἦ τῦ θεῦ κὰὶ μὴ ἐξ ἡμῶν, 2. Cor. IV, 7. Quomodo ἐν ἀσθενείᾳ ἐν φόβῳ κὰὶ τρόμῳ Apostolus summus inter Corinthios fue- rit, neque præconium ejus ἐν πειθοῖς ἀνθρωπίνης σοφίας λόγοις, ἀλλ’ ἐν ἀποδείξει πνεύματος κὰὶ δυνάμεως sese exeruerit, ipse edocet 1. Cor. II, 3. 4. Non nobis, Domine, non nobis, sed nomini tuo sit glo- ria, Psal. CXV. Nemo autem quenquam facile ob dona modica despiciat, quia τὰ ἀσθενῆ imbecil- lia in mundo elegit Deus, ut pudefaceret ea, quæ sunt robusta, 1. Cor. I, 27. nemo etiam ob modicam suam virtutem desperet: Si dicat pes, non sum ma- nus, non sum de corpore, num idcirco non est de corpore: Et si dicat auris, non sum oculus, non sum de corpore, num idcirco non est de corpore, 1. Cor. XII, 14. seqq. Nam perficit Deus etiam per os infantium & lactentium sibi non raro robur, ut destruat inimicum, Psal. VIII, 3. docetque experi- entia sæpe, illos, qui minora habent dona, plus præ- stare, quam qui donis præstantioribus sunt instru- cti, quia virtus Domini ἐν ἀσθενείᾳ τελειῦται in in- firmitate perficitur, 2. Cor. XII, 9. Conf. Ex. IV, 11. Matth. XXV, 14. seqq. Exemplum luculentum vide sis apud Ruffin. l. 1. c. 3. conversionis Philosophi à quodam simplici confessore, quem magni Episco- pi convertere non potuere. Etsi autem modicam virtutem & potestatem exiguam habeat resistendi; sic tamen virtus Domini perficiebatur in ejus infir- mitate, ut gratia ejusdem conservarit ac defende- rit Verbum Domini, cœlestis veritatis depositum; neque nomen Domini, quibuscunque etiam ten- tationibus expositus, abnegarit, sed constanter professus sit. Est enim μείωσις, ut Joh. I, 20. de Proto-Baptista dicitur: Et confessus est, & non ne- gavit; id enim decet veros confessores, omnesque Episcopos. Contra proditor is veritatis est, qui aut non libere pronuntiat, aut non libere defendit eandem, dicente Chrysostomo in opere imperfect. hom. XXV. Conf. 1. Petr. III, 14. 15. Victorinus in h. l. Humiles in seculo & rustici in Scripturis fidem immobiliter tenent.

## 3:9
Verse 9. Behold I give of the synagogue of Satan of those who say themselves to be Jews, and are not, but lie.] Interpret as above 2:9, and here also supply 'some'.

[Behold I will make them.] After many words are interposed, it is customary for either the word that preceded, or another similar one, to be repeated. Thus here 'behold I will make' is the same as 'behold I give'. For the Hebrews use נתן in this way for שום or שית. See Gen. 3:12, compared with 1:17; Ezek. 34:26, compared with Psalm 21:7.

[That they may come.] A pleonasm, about which we spoke above 2:5, 18. Then 'I will make that they may come' means 'I will make them come'. Thus Luke 5:34, 'to make to fast', in the Syriac, 'to make that they may fast'.

By a notable promise of success in his office, he comforts the Bishop, because he is going to convert even the worst Jews from the very synagogue of Satan, who boast that they are Jews, that is, confessors, and are not, by the ministry and power of the Word, with Divine grace granting, nay, working. Behold I give: and further: Behold I will make them. For it is the work of Divine and infinite power to illuminate and convert the hearts of men, even if the Son of God uses the work and ministry of the Doctors of the Word, Psalm 68:19; Eph. 4:11, 12, 13; Jer. 30:18. Furthermore, that title which the Son of God He attributes to the Jews, who above others wished to be believed to be confessors, that not only are they not confessors, and falsely lie that they are such; but that they are of the synagogue of Satan, he reminds us that the Doctors of the Word can receive the adversaries of the truth with sharper words without abuse, and call a spade a spade without a circuit of words by the example of Christ: who publicly proclaimed the Pharisees, hypocrites who shut the kingdom of heaven to others and exclude themselves from it, children of hell, fools, blind, blind guides, whitewashed sepulchres, full of iniquity, serpents and offspring of vipers in one and the same sermon, Matt. 23. The magnanimous theologian, the blessed Hoë, collected other epithets of heresies in this place, which are worthy to be read here too: That heretics, he says p. 389. They are called the synagogue of Satan, from which we learn that it is not required that we treat Pseudo-Doctors with soft words: Christ led the way with serious zeal, the Prophets led the way, the Apostles led the way, the Church Fathers and most illustrious Doctors led the way, and they repeatedly called heretics seducers, liars, deceitful men, men of blood, destroyers of the foundation, mockers, offspring of vipers, serpents, dogs, robbers, thieves. Although, therefore, we do not approve of a mere and excessive itching for abuse against the enemies of the truth: yet we do not allow ourselves to be constrained as if by shackles, nor our throats to be entirely closed and our tongues restrained by bolts: because sometimes we are urged and compelled to seek hard wedges for a hard knot: we are compelled to render double to heretics, and to mix for them in turn in the cup which they have mixed, Rev. 18:6. Therefore heresy, from which heretics have obtained their name, stands described quite harshly among the Fathers under the comparison and likeness of various animals: Sometimes it is compared to a PARTRIDGE, because it broods over the eggs of others, that is, the Church: sometimes to an APE, because it imitates the gestures and prayers of the Church as much as it can: sometimes to a FOX, because it is crafty: sometimes to a CATERPILLAR, because although it is thin in appearance, yet it is most harmful: sometimes to a SCALY DRAGON, because it does not believe easily: sometimes to an ENTANGLED SERPENT, because it has various contradictions in itself, and can hardly be detected: sometimes it is compared to a BURROWING MOUSE, because it lies hidden and does harm by digging tunnels: to a FLYING BEETLE, because it is easily scattered: to a VIPER, because it kills its mother the Church: to a CUTTLEFISH, because it throws ink, which completely infects and disturbs: heresy is also compared to tares, since it kills the good seed; CHAFF, because it often lies hidden in the Church with the good grain: DEADLY GRASS, because it is not easily distinguished: a MOUNTAIN, because it is proud: a TORRENT, because it adds open force to a lie when it can. It is also called by its effect a LETTER, because it infects and stains the whole man: POISON, because it brings death to souls: SHIPWRECK, because it is the loss of salvation: a TEMPEST, because it disturbs the Church. What wonder, then, if we derive similar epithets from the class of conjugates from heresy to the heretics themselves? Especially since the Son of God also compared seducers not only to Balaam and Jezebel: but also called them liars and indeed the SYNAGOGUE OF SATAN several times. Let those delicate and tender ones go now, who want the enemies of the truth to be treated with a soft arm and not even an austere countenance.

And they shall worship before thy feet.] That is, let them become Christians, and then show honor to thee, as a Bishop, established in lower places. See Acts 22:3. To worship properly means to kiss the hands, but by catachresis to show any sign of honor whatsoever. But to be prostrated at the feet is the greatest submission, 1 Sam. 25:24. Luke 4:7. with the addition of Matt. 4:9. below 15:9.

Not only is the gathering to the Church of the Christians and the assembly of the Bishop of Philadelphia promised, but also the humiliation of the Jews, who like Satan had opposed him until now: by which they will submit themselves, and will suppliantly seek forgiveness for what they have committed against him. With face lowered to the ground they will worship thee, and will lick the dust of thy feet, it is also said of Kings and Queens in Is. 49:12. Add also Is. 45:10. ch. 62:4. Cf. Acts 16:29. ch. 21:20. The Jews were the fiercest enemies of the kingdom of Christ, Acts 7. ch. 13. 14. 17. 18. 22. 28. 1 Thess. 2. etc. and yet the Jews are said here to be converted, so that they humble themselves before the Angel of Philadelphia, and fall at his feet, and indeed even those who were of the synagogue of Satan itself, the brothers of Judas the traitor, Ps. 109:7. Finally, those also who boasted that they were true Jews not according to the flesh, but in the Spirit, and who, adhering to Christ from the opposite side, held those who were deserters of the true faith and execrated them: when in reality they themselves were not confessors and praisers of the true God; but blasphemers, deniers, and did not emulate the faith of the Patriarch Judah, but the infidelity of Canaan and the wickedness of Sodom, Is. 1:10. ch. 57:3. Ezek. 16:45. Regarding adoration, Gomarus has these things against the Papists: When it is preached here that it will come to pass that they will worship from the synagogue of Satan before the feet of the Bishop of Philadelphia: the Papists err, who from similar Prophetic promises, made to the Church, ascribe that to the Roman Bishop alone, and by a completely perverse opinion conclude the tyrannical and idolatrous adoration of the feet of the Pope. Such promises are Isaiah 49:23. Kings shall be thy nursing fathers and their Queens thy nursing mothers, they shall worship thee with face prone to the ground, and shall lick the dust of thy feet, etc. 60:14. The humble children of those who afflicted thee shall come to thee and shall worship the footsteps of thy feet, who disparaged thee, and shall call thee the city of the Lord, Zion of the Holy One of Israel. For nothing else is denoted than (by a likeness taken from civil adoration) spiritual subjection, by which they will reverently bow and submit their hearts concerning the Church and the Word of Christ, proposed through its ministry. For as the eastern peoples abounded in ceremonies: so they not only worshipped Kings, as David 1 Sam. 25:23. and 2 Sam. 9:6. and ch. 14:5. and ch. 24:20. and Solomon 1 Kings 1:53. or Leaders, as Joab 2 Sam. 8:21. but also parents and elders, as Moses his father-in-law Jethro, Exod. 18:7. Solomon his mother, 1 Kings 2:19. and those who were in the place of parents, as the prophet Elisha, 2. 2 Kings 4:37. And the younger brothers, the firstborn, Gen. 27:29 and 49:8. Indeed, even for the sake of honor and to show gratitude, they were prompt to perform duties, both to those who had done them a favor, as Gen. 23:7, and to honorable guests, as Gen. 18:2 and ch. 19:1 (for although they were angels, they were nevertheless thought to be men, Heb. 13:2). And although King Nebuchadnezzar prostrated himself and adored Daniel, it is nevertheless not approved: because that was done out of impulse and pagan superstition, not by right reason: since he held Daniel as a semi-god: just as he also commanded sacrifices to be offered to him, as the following verses argue. Much less does it help that Saul, thinking the specter was the prophet Samuel, adored it, 1 Sam. 28:14, because it was entirely superstition, such as that of those who adore the beast, Rev. 14:9; therefore also the angels, Rev. 19:10 and 22:9, rejected adoration, and Peter, Acts 10:25. But as for the kissing of feet, with the exception of some impious tyrants, no one admitted it: which the Pope arrogates to himself. Indeed, what no tyrant is ever read to have dared, he offers his foot to be kissed by Kings and supreme Emperors who greet him.

Καὶ γνῶσιν, ὅτι ἠγάπησά σε.] Then they will acknowledge how much I have valued you, who have wished to use you, as a chosen instrument, for their conversion.

Latin:

Vers. 9. ἰδὺ δίδωμι ἐκ τῆς συναγωγῆς τῦ Σατανᾶ τῶν λεγό- μενων ἑαυτὺς Ἰυδαίυς εἶναι, κὰὶ ἐκ εἰσιν, ἀλλὰ ψεύδονται.] Inter- pretare ut supra II, 9. & hic quoque subaudi τινὰς.

[ἰδὺ ποιήσω αὐτὺς.] Post multa verba interposita solet re- peti aut vox, quæ præcessit, aut alia similis. Ita hic ἰδὺ ποιήσω idem est, quod ἰδὺ δίδωμι. Nam Ebræi נתן sic usurpant pro שום vel שית. Vide Gen. III, 12. collato I, 17. Ezech. XXXIV, 26. collato Psalm. XXI, 7.

[ἵνα ἥξωσι.] Πλεονασμὸς de quo diximus supra II, 5.18. De- inde ποιήσω ἵνα ἥξωσι faciam venire. Sic Luc. V, 34. ποιῆσαι νησεύειν, in Syriaco, facere, ut jejunent.

Promissione insigni successus in officio confortat Episcopum, quod pessimos etiam Judæos ex ipsa satanæ synagoga, qui se gloriantur Judæos, id est, confessores esse, & non sunt, ministerio & virtute Verbi conversurus sit, concedente imo operante Divina gratia. ἰδὺ δίδωμι Ecce do: & porro: ἰδὺ ποιήσω αὐτὺς. Id enim est opus Divinæ & infinitæ virtutis hominum corda illuminare ac convertere, etsi utatur Filius Dei opera & ministerio Docto- rum Verbi, Psal. LXVIII, 19. Eph. IV, 11. 12. 13. Jer. XXX, 18. Cæterum titulus ille, quem Filius Dei Judæis tribuit, qui præ cæteris confessores credi volebant, quod non modo non sint confessores, & falso sese tales mentiantur; sed quod è Synagoga satanæ sint, commonefacit nos, Doctores Verbi posse adversarios veritatis citra convitium acrio- ribus verbis excipere, ac scapham scapham sine circuitu verborum exemplo Christi dicere: qui Pharisæos hypocritas occludentes aliis regnum cœlorum, & ab eodem seipsos excludentes, filios gehennæ, stultos, cæcos, Ductores cæcos, sepulcra dealbata, plenos iniquitate, serpentes & genimina viperarum una eademque concione publice pro- clamavit, Matth. XXIII. Collegit alia hoc loco hæ- reseon epitheta B. Hoë, Theologus magnanimus, quæ digna sunt, ut hic quoque legantur: Quod hæ- retici, inquit p. 389. Synagoga dicuntur satanæ, inde discimus, non requiri, ut mollibus Pseudo-Doctores verbis tractemus: præivit zelo serio Christus, præivere Prophetæ, præivere Apostoli, præivere Ecclesiæ Patres atque Doctores clarissimi, hæreticosque subinde sedu- ctores, mendaces, viros dolosos, viros sanguinum, fun- damenti eversores, empæctas, genimina viperarum, ser- pentes, canes, latrones, fures nominarunt. Etsi igitur non probamus meram & nimiam convitiorum in ho- stes veritatis pruriginem: tamen nec compedibus qua- si nos constringi, nec fauces prorsus præcludi, & lin- guas repagulis cohiberi patimur: quia interdum ur- gemur & cogimur duro nodo duros quærere cuneos: cogimur reddere hæreticis duplicia, & in poculo, quo miscuerunt, miscere ipsis vicissim, Apoc. XIIX, 6. Pro- pterea hæresis, à qua hæretici nomen suum sortiti, sub comparatione & similitudine variorum animalium satis duriter apud Patres descripta extat: Nonnun- quam comparatur PERDICI, quia alienis ovis, hoc est, Ecclesiæ incubat: nonnunquam SIMIÆ, quia Ecclesiæ gestus & orationes, quantum potest, imita- tur: nonnunquam VULPI, quia subdola est: in- terdum ERUCÆ, quia licet specie tenuis sit, tamen est nocentissima: interdum DRACONI SQUA- MOSO, quia non facile credit: interdum SER- PENTI IMPLICATO, quia varias in se con- tradictiones habet, & vix deprehendi potest: inter- dum confertur MURI ARANEO, quia clam latet, & nocet cuniculis actis: CANTHARO VO- LITANTI, quia facile spargitur: VIPERÆ, quia matrem Ecclesiam occidit: SEPIÆ, quia jacit atra- mentum, quod omnino inficit & turbat: comparatur etiam hæresis zizaniis, quoniam bonum semen ene- cat; PALEÆ, quia sæpe in Ecclesia cum bono gra- no latet: GRAMINI LETHALI, quia non facile dignoscitur: MONTI, quia superbit: TORRENTI, quia mendacio apertam vim cum potest, addit. Dici- tur etiam ab effectu LITERA, quia totum hominem inficit & maculat: VENENUM, quia mortem animis affert: NAUFRAGIUM, quia est amis- sio salutis: TEMPESTAS, quia turbat Ecclesiam. Quid ergo mirum, si ex conjugatorum classe similia epitheta ab hæresi ad ipsos hæreticos derivemus? Præ- sertim cum Filius Dei quoque seductores non tantum Balaamo & Jesabeli comparaverit: sed & menda- ces imo SYNAGOGAM SATANÆ illos aliquoties vocaverit. Eant nunc delicatuli illi, & tenelluli, qui molli brachio & ne austero quidem vultu hostes veri- tatis tractari volunt.

Καὶ προσκυνήσωσιν ἐνώπιον τῶν ποδῶν σε.] Id est, Chri- stiani fiant, & tum tibi, ut Episcopo, honorem exhibeant, constituti in locis inferioribus. Vide Actor. XXII, 3. Προσκυ- νεῖν proprie quidem manus osculari, sed per κατάχρησιν qua- lecunque honoris signum exhibere. Ad pedes autem proster- ni maxima submissio, 1. Sam. XXV, 24. Luc. IV, 7. addito Matth. IV, 9. infra XV, 9.

Non solum aggregatio ad Ecclesiam Christia- norum & cœtum Episcopi Philadelphiensis, sed etiam humiliatio Judæorum, qui instar satanæ ad- versati hactenus eidem erant, promittitur: qua se submittent, & condonationem, quæ adversus ipsum commiserunt, supplices expetent. Vultu in terram demisso adorabunt te, & pulverem pedum tuorum lingent, dicitur etiam de Regibus & Reginis Es. 49, 12. Adde & Es. 45, 10. cap. 62, 4. Conf. Actor. 16, 29. cap. 21, 20. Judæi fuere acerrimi regni Christi hostes, Act. 7. cap. 13. 14. 17. 18. 22. 28. 1. Thess. 2. &c. & con- vertendi tamen hic Judæi dicuntur, ut humilient se coram Angelo Philadelphiensi, & ad pedes ejus devolvantur, & quidem illi etiam, qui ex ipsa syn- agoga satanæ erant, Judæ proditoris fratres, Psal. 109, 7. Denique illi quoque, qui se gloriabantur veros Judæos esse non secundum carnem, sed in Spiritu, & ex adverso Christo adhærentes pro de- sertoribus veræ fidei habebant & execrabantur: quum revera non confessores ipsi ac laudatores ve- ri Dei essent; sed blasphemi, abnegatores, nec Judæ Patriarchæ fidem, sed Canaanis infidelitatem ac So- domorum nequitiam æmularentur, Es. 1, 10. c. 57, 3. Ezech. 16, 45. De adoratione Gomarus hæc ha- bet adversus Pontificios: Cum hic prædicatur fore, ut è satanæ Synagoga adorent ante Episcopi Philadel- phiensis pedes: errant Pontificii, qui ex similibus Pro- pheticis promissionibus, Ecclesiæ factis, illud soli Ro- mano Episcopo adscribunt, & perversa omnino sen- tentia tyrannicam & idololatricam pedum Pontificis adorationem concludunt. Quales promissiones sunt Esaiæ 49, 23. Reges erunt nutritii tui & Reginæ eorum nutrices tuæ, prono in terram vultu adorabunt te, & pulverem pedum tuorum lingent, & c. LX, 14. Ve- nient ad te humiles filii eorum, qui humiliaverunt te & adorabunt vestigia pedum tuorum, qui detrahebant tibi, & vocabunt te civitatem Domini, Zion sancti Israël. Nec enim aliud denotatur, quam (simili- tudine à civili adoratione desumpta) subjectio spi- ritualis, qua reverenter de Ecclesia & Christi Verbo, per illius ministerium proposito, corda sua incurva- bunt ac submittent. Nam ut orientales populi cere- moniis abundarunt: ita non solum Reges adorarunt, ut Davidem 1. Sam. 25, 23. & 2. Sam. 9, 6. & c. 14, 5. & c. 24, 20. & Salomonem 1. Reg 1, 53. aut Duces, ut Joabum 2. Sam, 8, 21. sed etiam parentes & majores, ut Moses Socerum suum Jethronem, Exod. 18, 7. Sa- lomon matrem, 1. Reg. 2, 19. & qui parentum quasi lo- co, ut Prophetam Elisæum, 2. Reg. 4, 37. & fratres mi- nores natu, primogenitum, Gen. 27, 29. & 49, 8. Imo etiam honoris causa & testandi animi, ad officia præ- standa prompti, tum iis, qui benefecerunt, ut Gen. 23, 7. tum hospitibus honestis, ut Gen. 18, 2. & c. 19, 1. (licet enim Angeli essent, homines tamen putabantur Ebr. 13, 2.) Ac quamvis Danielem Rex Nebucadne- zar pronus adorarit, tamen non probatur: quia il- lud ex impetu ac superstitione gentili, non recta ratio- ne factum: quoniam Danielem quasi Semi-Deum habuit: sicut etiam præcepit ei sacrificia offerri, ut se- quentia arguunt. Multo minus juvat, quod Saul spe- ctrum Samuelis Prophetam ratus adorarit 1. Sam. 28, 14. quia omnino superstitio fuit, qualis eorum, qui bestiam adorant, Apoc. 14, 9. ideo & Angeli Apoc. 19, 10. & 22, 9. adorationem respuerunt, & Petrus Act. 10, 25. Pedum vero oscula, exceptis tyrannis non- nullis impiis, nemo admisit: Quod Pontifex sibi arro- gat. Imo, quod nullus unquam tyrannus ausus fuisse legitur, Regibus & Imperatoribus summis pedem osculandum præbet salutantibus.

Καὶ γνῶσιν, ὅτι ἠγάπησά σε.] Tunc agnoscent, quanti te fecerim, qui te, tanquam instrumento electo, uti voluerim ad eorum conversionem.

## 3:10
Vers. 10. Ὅτι ἐτήρησας τὸν λόγον τῆς ὑπομονῆς με.] Because in many adversities you have observed my precept of patience, that is, concerning patience. A double genitive, the other of the cause Of the efficient cause, the other of the matter. This precept is Luke XXI, 19. and elsewhere. In the manuscript it is: Καὶ ἐτήρησας: and thus the Latin reads. Τηρεῖν λόγον, to observe a precept, is a frequent expression in the Gospel of John. The patience of Christ is called that which Christ commanded, also 2 Thess. III, 5.

Λόγος denotes the Word, not a precept or law, which is called νόμος. But the word τῆς ὑπομονῆς μου, says the Son of God, which can be understood of the patience of Christ, and the sufferings patiently endured for us, of the Word of the cross of Christ, as the Gospel is described, 1 Cor. I, 5: Or also of the Word of Christ's constancy in faith, if it introduces the notion of an efficient cause; because perseverance in faith is not only commanded by Christ, but also has Him as its Author, inasmuch as He is the author and finisher of faith, Heb. XII, 2. because ὑπομονὴ everywhere denotes constancy and perseverance in faith, Heb. X, 36. Luke VIII, 15. and thus it can also be understood, Luke XXI, 19. The word of Christ to keep is used not so much of the law as of the Gospel, for which faith and perseverance in faith are necessary. The following words deal with temptations and how we may patiently sustain them; that is included in the promise: Namely, because he has constantly kept the Word of Christ, and has persevered in the faith, therefore the Son of God receives that He will in turn keep him in the hour of temptation, so that he may be able to patiently sustain and overcome the same.

Κἀγώ σε τηρήσω ἐκ τῆς ὥρας τοῦ πειρασμοῦ, τῆς μελλούσης ἔρχεσθαι ἐπὶ τῆς οἰκουμένης ὅλης, πειράσαι τοὺς κατοικοῦντας ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς.] Πειράσαι for εἰς τὸ πειράσαι. Then οἰκουμένη and γῆ here signify the lands of the Roman Empire, as Luke II, 1. The temptation, which is treated here, is the persecution under Nero, of which also below XII. I will keep you untouched from that cruelty, so that you may long be of use to me, since I have found you suitable. Ὥρα is any time, even a sufficiently long one, John V, 15. and 1 John II, 18. And there is a metonymy in the word πειρασμοῦ, because every severe persecution brings temptation. A similar expression is to be rescued from temptation, 2 Pet. II, 9. which is explained there by the example of Lot.

These things cannot be referred to the time of Nero. For John was relegated to Patmos under Domitian, in which he had his visions: But these things were written after he had them, how therefore can the temptation, which is predicted here as future, be referred to the times of Nero? Others explain it concerning the time and persecution of Trajan, which was strong and universal, and flared up like fire, but soon ceased, and passed away like a whirlwind. Concerning which Eusebius l. III. Hist. Eccl. c. 32. Add also Jerome's letter to Trajan. Thus, with Ribera and Alcazar, Cornelius à Lapide, and most of the more learned interpreters, B. Cluverus notes that these things are to be understood of the same persecution: who nevertheless afterwards says: The most certain sense, he says, is that, since the Angel and the Philadelphian Church held an unshaken faith in the recent persecution of Domitian, and did not yield to the stubbornness of the Jews, it will happen henceforth that, having been well tested, they will not be so tempted in the future, nor will it be granted to Satan, when he is soon to ask again to sift and disturb the world for himself, to inflict any harm on the Philadelphians, whether through the Jews rioting under Hadrian, and shaking almost the whole world, or through the Gentiles. B. Gerhard understood it generally concerning the imminent universal persecutions under the Gentile Emperors. More alien is the interpretation concerning the persecution of the Antichrist to come at the end of the world, which was that of Primasius, Caesariensis, and Lyranus: To which, however, Erasmus seemed to accede. Schmidius: If at this time, he says, in the year 1636 and 1637, especially this πειρασμὸς is not in force, I do not know what could be more in force. Thomas Anglicus explained that temptation from the hour of temptation: I will keep you, not so that you are not tempted, but so that you are not overcome by temptation. That does not please Cornelius: For he thinks it should have been said thus, I will keep you in the hour, but not I will keep you from the hour. But Grotius rightly compares the passage

2 Pet. II, 9. Therefore B. Gerhard: I will guard you, so that in the imminent universal persecutions you do not suffer harm to your soul, but that they may turn out for your good. B. Cluverus, although he more approves of preservation from the hour of temptation, nevertheless does not reject the sense concerning rescue out of temptation. Simon Episcopius considers the act of liberation in three ways: 1. As prohibitive of the evil itself, so that it does not invade the Church, or reach it. 2. As an impediment to the evil already invading and pressing on all sides, regarding its highest and extreme force and efficacy, that is, so that it does not harm the saints, but that the pious and faithful may emerge from it unharmed, and be rescued as if from a certain fire. 3. As destructive of the evil itself regarding its force and efficacy in the pious, that is, by which it comes about that they are not struck down by the evil itself, and cast down from the station of their mind, but emerge as victors, and in the very evils, and therefore in death, rejoice and glory. Let the sweet name of calamities and persecutions be noted here, that they are only πειρασμὸς, or temptation, in which the pious can exult, 1 Pet. I, 6. 7. Jas. I, 12. Wis. III, 5. 6. 7. Tob. XII, 13. in which God, who sends it, has promised moreover preservation and liberation, Ps. LXVIII, 20. Ps. XCI, 15. Isa. XLIII, 2. 1 Cor. X, 13. 2 Pet. II, 9. Ps. 34, 5. seqq.

Latin:

Vers. 10. Ὅτι ἐτήρησας τὸν λόγον τῆς ὑπομονῆς με.] Quia in multis adversis observasti præceptum meum patien- tiæ, id est, de patientia. Duplex Genitivus, alter causæ Efficientis, alter materiæ Præceptum hoc est Luc. XXI, 19. & alibi. In Manuscripto est: Καὶ ἐτήρησας: & sic legit Lati- nus. Τηρεῖν λόγον, præceptum observare, loquutio frequens in Evangelio Johannis. Patientia Christi dicitur ea, quam Christus præcepit, etiam 2. Thess. III, 5.

Λόγος Verbum notat, non præceptum vel legem, quæ νόμος dicitur. Verbum autem τῆς ὑπομονῆς μου, inquit Filius Dei, quod de patientia Christi, & passionibus pro nobis patienter exantlatis, de Ver- bo crucis Christi, ut Evangelium describitur, 1. Cor. I, 5. accipi potest: Vel etiam de Verbo constantiæ Christi in fide, si causæ Efficientis notionem infe- rat; quod à Christo non præcepta modo sit perse- verantia in fide; sed etiam eundem Autorem ha- beat, utpote, qui est ἀρχηγὸς καὶ τελειωτὴς τῆς πί- στεως, Ebr. XII, 2. quia ὑπομονὴ passim notat con- stantiarn & perseverantiam in fide, Ebr. X, 36. Luc. IIX, 15. atque ita etiam accipi potest, Luc. XXI. 19. Verbum Christi servare non tam de lege quam Ev- angelio adhibetur, ad quod fide ac fidei perseve- rantia opus est. De tentationibus & ut patienter eas sustineamus, verba sequentia agunt; ea pro- missioni inclusa est: Nimirum quia Verbum Chri- sti constanter servavit, & perseveravit in fide, ideo recipit Filius Dei sese vicissim ipsum servaturum in hora tentationis, ut patienter sustinere ac supe- rare eandem possit.

Κἀγώ σε τηρήσω ἐκ τῆς ὥρας τοῦ πειρασμοῦ, τῆς μελλούσης ἔρ- χεσθαι ἐπὶ τῆς οἰκουμένης ὅλης, πειράσαι τοὺς κατοικοῦντας ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς.] Πειράσαι pro εἰς τὸ πειράσαι. Deinde οἰκουμένη & γῆ hic significant terras Romani Imperii, ut Luc. II, 1. Tentatio, de qua hic agitur, est persecutio sub Nerone, de qua & infra XII. Servabo te ab illa sævitia intactum, ut mihi diu sis usui, quandoquidem idoneum te reperi. Ὥρα est quodvis tempus, etiam satis longum, Joh. V, 15. & 1. Joh. II, 18. Et Μετωνυμία est in voce πειρασμοῦ, quia omnis gravis persecutio affert ten- tationem. Par locutio ἐκ πειρασμοῦ ῥύεσθαι, 2. Petr. II, 9. quod ibi explicatur Lothi exemplo.

Ad Neronis tempus referri hæc nequeunt. In Pathmum enim relegatus fuit Johannes sub Domi- tiano, in qua visiones suas habuit: Scripta autem hæc sunt, postquam eas habuit, quomodo ergo tentatio, quæ hic futura prædicitur, ad tempora Neronis referri potest? De tempore & persecutio- ne Trajani explicant alii, quæ valida fuit & univer- salis, atque instar ignis exarsit, sed mox desiit, & velut turbo transiit. De qua Eusebius l. III. Hist. Eccl. c. 32. Adde & Hieron. ad Trajan. epistolam. Ita cum Ribera & Alcasare Cornelius à Lapide, ac eruditiores plerosque Interpretes de eadem perse- cutione hæc accipere notat B. Cluverus: qui ta- men postea: Sensus certissimus est, inquit, cum Ange- lus & Ecclesia Philadelphena in nupera Domitiani persecutione fidem inconcussam tenuerint, nec Judæo- rum pervicaciæ cesserint, futurum deinceps, ut bene probati imposterum non ita tententur, nec indul- geatur Satanæ, ut quum mox denuo mundum sibi cribrandum ac perturbandum postulaturus sit, Phi- ladelphenis damni quicquam inferat, sive per Judæ- os sub Adriano tumultuantes, totumque pene orbem concutientes, sive per Ethnicos. In genere de im- minentibus universalibus persecutionibus sub Ethnicis Imperatoribus B. Gerhardus accepit. Alie- nior est interpretatio de persecutione Antichristi in fine mundi futura, quæ Primasii, Cæsariensis & Lyrani fuit: Ad quam tamen accedere est visus Er. Schmidius: Si hoc tempore, inquiens, Anno 1636. & 1637. cumprimis hic πειρασμὸς non est in vigore, nescio, quid magis vigere possit. Illam tentationem ἐκ τῆς ὥρας τοῦ πειρασμοῦ Thomas Anglicus expo- suit: Servabo te, non, ut non tenteris, sed ut tentatione non vincaris. Non placet id Cornelio: Putat enim sic dici debuisse, servabo te in hora, non autem ser- vabo te ab hora. Sed recte confert Grotius locum

2. Petr. II, 9. Ideo B. Gerhardus: Custodiam te, ne in imminentibus universalibus persecutionibus damnum animae patiaris, sed ut in bonum tibi cedant. B. Cluverus etsi magis probet praeservationem ab hora tentationis: non reprobat tamen sensum de ereptione ex tentatione. Simon Episcopius actum liberationis tripliciter considerat 1. ut prohibitivum mali ipsius, quo minus invadat Ecclesiam, aut ad eam pertingat. 2. Ut mali jam undique sit malum invadentis & prementis quoad vim & efficaciam summam & extremam impeditivum, id est, ut ne sanctis noceat, sed ut ex illo incolumes evadant pii & fideles, & veluti ex incendio quodam eripiantur. 3. Ut mali ipsius quoad vim & efficaciam ejus in piis destructivum, id est, quo ipso sit, ut malo ipso non percellantur, & de statione mentis dejiciantur, sed victores evadant, & in ipsis malis adeoq; morte gaudeant & glorientur. Notetur hic dulce nomen calamitatum & persecutionum, quod πειρασμὸς tantum sint, vel tentatio, in qua pii exultare possunt, 1. Petr. I, 6. 7. Jac. I, 12. Sap. III, 5. 6. 7. Tob. XII, 13. in qua promisit insuper Deus, qui immittit, conservationem & liberationem, Psal. LXVIII, 20. Ps. XCI, 15. Es. XLIII, 2. 1. Cor. X, 13. 2. Petr. II, 9. Pf. 34, 5. seqq.

## 3:11
Vers. 11. Ἔρχομαι ταχύ.] Shortly I will send that persecution into the churches.

Others interpret it not as the coming to the πειρασμὸν [temptation] of the Church, but as the coming to the τήρησιν [keeping]: Behold, I come quickly to help and crown you. Rupert, Richard, and B. Gerhard [interpret it] as the coming πρὸς κρίσιν [to judgment], so that he may be delivered through death. Gomarus also [interprets it] as the coming to judgment, but a penal one, or to punish the sources; which pleases me because of the comparison with C. II, 5. 16. C. III, 3.

Κράτει ὃ ἔχεις.] Retain then the faith and the profession. I will preserve you in life. See to it that you do not fail through fear. No one has progressed so far that he ought not to be on his guard. 1 Cor. IX, 27.

Similarly Gomarus: Hold what you have, that is, my Gospel delivered to you, keep it with true and constant obedience of faith, charity, and endurance. What did he have? Faith and a good conscience, thus Paul explains it in 1 Tim. I, 18, says Pareus. B. Gerhard: Hold the purity of the Word and the truth of the faith, Apoc. II, 25. Hold, that is, continue to hold, retain constantly. It signifies an act not begun, but continued. The word κρατει indicates that zeal and strength are needed here, because there are many things that could shake these gifts from the faithful, unless they strive to hold them by all means. Therefore, he exhorts to perseverance in the integrity begun, as Pareus does here.

Ἵνα μηδεὶς λάβῃ τὸν σέφανόν σου.) Lest you lose the honor of perseverance, with others receiving it. The loss of dignity burns more vehemently if we not only fall from it ourselves, but also see another possess it, Job 34, 24. Matt. 25, 28.

Lest you lose the crown of glory and life, which is given only to those who persevere to the end; and which is promised to the constant confessors of the Word, Apoc. II, 10. Your crown, that is, the one destined for you. We do not bring in those things which others heap up concerning triumphal, civic, military, naval, etc., crowns. The metaphor is obvious, taken from contests, and used elsewhere by the Holy Spirit, 1 Cor. 9, 25. 2 Tim. 4, 7. 8. 1 Pet. 4, 5, about which we have already treated elsewhere. But whether that custom of the athletes is precisely being referred to, who would snatch with their hands a crown hung from some higher place in a race run as quickly as possible—which Cornelius à Lapide, from Peter Faber's book II, ch. 27 on the Agonistics, wishes to claim—seems to be defined rashly: nor is its attainment to be attributed to our running, but to the Divine grace strengthening us in the faith, by which we as if with a hand apprehend the crown proposed in the Word, Rom. 9, 16. Ne quis auferat coronam tuam [Lest anyone take your crown] is simply: lest the crown be taken from you: therefore one must not scrupulously inquire whether a crown proposed or promised to one, or which he has and possesses through faith, which is taken away from the same on account of deliberate sins and unbelief, and therefore impenitence; if indeed the justified can fall away both totally and finally from Divine grace and eternal salvation, it may be granted to another as if succeeding into his place. Interpreters Cornelius à Lapide and others wish this to be signified in this place, that God is accustomed, when one falls, to substitute another in his place and reward: not that it is to be established at least formally before foreknowledge that the number of the elect is certain, e.g., that so many crowns precisely are decreed, so that if one is taken from one, that one is given to another: which opinion of Alcazar this Cornelius refutes. And Episcopius conveniently warns on p. 576: It is not necessary to labor much concerning the receiving person. For the manner of speaking used in the Scriptures prevails, so that sometimes some action or passion is attributed to persons, even if no account is taken of a person, but the sense is understood impersonally: so that in this place by this phrase: Let no one take your crown, nothing else is indicated than that your crown may not be taken from you. The reason is manifest, because no one obtains the crown of another: and because the punishment or evil, which Christ threatens in this place, is not the transfer of the crown to another, but the snatching away or removal of the crown. For it is not the transfer that properly torments, but the removal. Therefore, the removal itself is chiefly intended, which, because it is accustomed to be done by someone or received from one snatching it away, hence it is that a person is also attributed, by a phrase, as we have said, that is used: just as it is in Luke 6:38. Give and it shall be given to you: a good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and running over they will give into your bosom: that is, they will give, whoever will give, or rather it shall be given to you, and you will receive. Which explanation Episcopius wishes to be noted; so that it may be understood once for all, even if sometimes certain words are subjoined to a verb which is immediately attributed to some person, they cannot yet immediately be attributed in the same way to that person: as in this place and others. Thus 2 Samuel 24, when it is said: And the anger of the Lord added to be angry against Israel, and he incited David against them, etc., it is not to be explained that the anger of the Lord incited, but that he who incited, incited him, impersonally as we have said elsewhere. For every phrase, and the force and efficacy of the phrase, must always be estimated from the principal scope of the place itself, or from the nature of the thing itself, by which it is attributed to someone, whether it can belong, or whether it ought to be attributed to him to whom it seems to be attributed. To which Tirinus does not dissent: See that you retain it, nor let it be snatched from you by another, e.g., by tyrants, by seducers, by demons, etc. For to receive here designates nothing other than to take away, to remove, to carry off: (in the way that the wicked receive, that is, take away from the pious their crown, when they tear them away from piety.) Nor does it necessarily connote transferring to one's own head from another's head: which can be ascribed only to the pious, to whom it does not seem to be alluded here. Whence, although it happens very often that when one falls another is substituted in his place, e.g., men for angels, Gentiles for Jews, David for Saul, Matthias for Judas, Cyprian for Tertullian, Cyril for Origen, Jerome for Rufinus, Augustine for Pelagius, etc., daily experience teaches that this is not perpetual, nor can it be solidly gathered from this verse. But rightly from these words: Hold what you have, that no one may take your crown, Vasquez (part 1, q. 23, disp. 89, c. 10) and Cornelius à Lapide with him gather that God does not absolutely elect anyone to heavenly glory. For if election to glory had been made absolutely, it would be said in vain: Hold what you have, that another may not take your crown: Whence they further conclude: That one absolutely elected is necessarily saved by the efficacious decree of God, and that it is impossible for him to be damned, whatever he may do. To which Tirinus adds his calculation: Much less can it be gathered from this, which Primasius, Bede, Ansbertus and

certain others wish, that the number of those to be saved is certain and predefined before the foreseen final perseverance of individuals, so that neither more are to be saved, nor fewer, nor others than those who are of the said number. But rather with Vasquez, Gregory of Valencia, Lessius, Cornelius à Lapide, and others, I gather the plain opposite from this, namely that God has not absolutely elected us to heavenly glory. Which are to be opposed not only to the Calvinists, but also to the Scotists and Dominicans. See Vol. II, System. Theol., c. X, Q. VI, p. 526. It is not, however, to be inferred from this that God elects to heavenly glory only after foreseen merits, but that He elects after foreseen final faith in the merits of Christ: because eternal life is a gift of God, a free gift in Christ Jesus, Romans 6, last. Although we also agree with Cornelius in this, that it is evident from this that the just can fall away from the grace of God: concerning which Episcopius: Where there is no danger, or harm, nor can there be, and it is known and understood for certain that there is not, and cannot be, there the affection of fear or dread cannot be moved, taken from the persuasion of a harmful event. And Tirinus gathering that any just person, even the most holy, can fall away from holiness and grace. For why else would He warn: hold what you have? Why would He inculcate the danger of losing the crown? Why in all these epistles would He promise the crown to none but the one who overcomes? Why would He threaten so many threats? by so many warnings, by so many rewards he might stir up: Where Pareus is to no purpose, regarding what you have concerning that which is held κατὰ δόξαν, or what seems to be held; because he explains the express letter and the open praise of the Bishop of Philadelphia: as if they are hinted to be deprived of the crown at last, who are commonly held to be faithful, because they do not hold what they had, that is, what they seemed to have, Luke 8:18. It is one thing to have, another to seem to have. And did the Bishop not truly have what he was commanded to hold? Yet it must not be conceded to Cornelius that no one can be certain of his own perseverance and salvation, except as to absolute certainty: for hypothetical certainty is entirely given; if, that is, we do not neglect the means of salvation; nor voluntarily cast away the grace of God through deliberate sins. For the gifts and the calling of God are ἀμεταμέλητα, Rom. 11:29. And God is faithful, by whom we were called into the communion of Jesus Christ, his Son, our Lord, 1. Cor. 1:9. Pareus also refutes some among the Reformed who deny degrees of glory: When he says: Your crown, he hints not obscurely that for each individual his own crown is set forth in heaven. Whence it seems to be able to be gathered that, just as there will be degrees of punishments in hell, so there will be differences of rewards in heaven. My crown is one thing, yours another. The crown of faithful Teachers, who have instructed many unto righteousness, will undoubtedly be more noble: For they shall shine like the stars of the firmament. Jovinian, against whom Jerome disputed, seems to have maintained that the same glory is set forth for all, which some among the orthodox also hold today, from that saying of Christ: Then the righteous shall shine like the sun. But there is nothing more illustrious in created things than the brightness of the sun. Indeed, nothing prevents granting different degrees of brightness, since even now the brightness of the sun is accustomed to be sometimes greater and sometimes lesser.

Latin:

Vers. 11. Ἔρχομαι ταχύ.] Brevi immittam in Ecclesias illam persecutionem.

Non de adventu ad πειρασμὸν Ecclesiae; sed de adventu ad τήρησιν alii interpretantur: Ecce, venio cito te adjuturus & coronaturus. Rupertus, Richardus, & B. Gerhardus de adventu πρὸς κρίσιν, ut per mortem liberetur. Gomarus etiam de adventu ad judicium, sed poenale, vel ad puniendos fontes; quod ob collationem C. II, 5. 16. C. III, 3. placet.

Κράτει ὃ ἔχεις.] Retine tunc fidem & professionem. Servabo te in vita. Tu vide, ne metu deficias. Nemo eo usque profecit, ut non cavere sibi debeat. 1. Cor. IX, 27.

Similiter Gomarus: Tene, quod habes, hoc est Evangelium meum tibi traditum, serva vera ac constanti fidei, charitatis, & tolerantiae obedientia. Quid habebat? fidem & bonam conscientiam, sic exponit Paulus 1. Tim. I, 18. inquit Pareus. B. Gerhardus: Tene puritatem Verbi & veritatem fidei, Apoc. II, 25. Tene, id est, perge tenere, retine constanter. Significat actum non inchoatum, sed continuatum. Verbum κρατει studio & robore hic opus esse indicat, quia plurima sunt, quae fidelibus haec dona excutere possint, nisi tenere omnibus modis contendant. Ad perseverantiam ergo in coepta integritate hortatur, ut hic Pareus.

Ἵνα μηδεὶς λάβῃ τὸν σέφανόν σου.) Ne tu honorem perseverantiae amittas, aliis eum accipientibus. Vehementius urit jactura dignitatis, si non tantum nos ea excidamus, sed & alterum videamus ea potiri, Job. 34, 24. Matth. 25, 28.

Ne amittas coronam gloriae & vitae, quae solis ad finem usque perseverantibus datur; quaeque constantibus Verbi confessoribus promissa est, Apoc. II, 10. Coronam tuam, hoc est, tibi destinatam. Non adducimus ea, quae de coronis triumphalibus, civicis, castrensibus, navalibus, &c. alii congerunt. Metaphora in aprico est, à certaminibus petita, alibique à Spiritu sancto adhibita, 1. Cor. 9, 25. 2. Tim. 4, 7. 8. 1. Petr. 4. 5. de qua alias jam actum. Num autem praecise mos ille Agonistarum respiciatur, qui ex aliquo eminentiore loco appensam coronã incitato quam ocyffime cursu manibus corripiebant, quod ex Petri Fabri l. II. c. 27. Agonistici Cornelius à Lapide vult, temere definiri videtur: neq; nostro cursui, sed Divinae gratiae nos in fide, qua veluti manu apprehendimus coronam in Verbo propositam, confortanti tribuenda ejus consecutio Rom. 9, 16. Ne quis auferat coronam tuam simpliciter est, ne auferatur tibi corona: non ergo scrupulose inqui- rendum; an corona uni proposita aut promissa, vel quam habet ac possidet per fidem, quae eidem pro- pter peccata proaeretica & ἀπιστίαν, adeoq; impoe- nitentiam aufertur; siquidem justificati & ὁλικῶς & τελικῶς excidere possint gratia Divina & salute aeterna, concedatur alteri velut in locum ejusdem succedenti. Interpp. Cornelius à Lapide aliique id significari hoc loco volunt, Deum solere uno ca- dente alium ejus loco & praemio substituere: ne- dum id statuendum saltim formaliter ante praesci- entiam certum esse numerum electorum, v. g. tot praecise coronas esse decretas, ita si una ab uno au- feratur, illa detur alteri: quam Alcazaris sententiam refellit hic Cornelius. Et commode monet Epi- scopius p. 576. Non est necesse admodum laborare de persona accipiente. Ratio enim loquendi in Scri- pturis usitata obtinet, ut personis aliquando actio ali- qua aut passio tribuatur, etiamsi nulla persona ratio habeatur, sed impersonaliter sensus intelligatur: ita ut hoc loco phrasihac: Nullus accipiat coronam tu- am, aliud nihil indicetur, quam ut tibi corona tua non adimatur. Ratio est manifesta, quia nemo al- terius coronam consequitur: & quia poena aut ma- lum, quod hoc loco comminatur Christus, non est translatio coronae ad alium, sed ereptio vel ademptio coronae. Non enim cruciat translatio proprie, sed ab- latio. Itaque precipue intenditur ipsa ablatio, qua quia ab aliquo fieri aut accipi ab eripiente solet, hinc est, quod persona etiam tribuatur, phrasi, ut diximus, usitata: prout est Luc. VI, 38. Date & dabitur vo- bis: mensuram bonam, pressam, agitatam & super- fluentem dabunt in sinum vestrum: id est, dabunt, quicunque dabunt, vel potius dabitur vobis, & vos accipietis. Quam explicationem notari vult Episco- pius; Ut semel intelligatur, etiamsi aliquando verba quaedam subjungantur verbo, quod immediate per- sonae alicui tributum est, ea tamen non statim similiter personae illi tribui posse: ut hoc loco & aliis. Sic 2. Sam. XXIV. cum dicitur: Et addidit irasci furor Domini contra Israëlem, & concitavit Davidem in eos, &c. non explicandum est, furorem Domini concitasse, sed concitasse eum, qui concitavit, impersonaliter ut ali- bi diximus. Semper enim ex scopo principali loci ipsius, aut ex natura rei ipsius, qua alicui tribuitur, an possit competere, an debeat tribui illi cui tribui videtur, aestimanda omnis phrasis est, & phraseos vis & efficacia. Quibus non abnuit Tirinus: Fac reti- neas, nec tibi ab alio eripi sinas, v. g. à tyrannis, à se- ductoribus, à Daemonibus, &c. Accipere enim hic non aliud designat, quam adimere, tollere, auferre: (quomodo improbi accipiunt, id est, adimunt piis co- ronam suam, quando illos à pietate divellunt.) Neq; necessario connotat, transferre in proprium caput ex alieno capite: quod solis piis adscribi potest, ad quos hic non videtur alludi. Unde licet saepissime acci- dat, ut uno cadente alius ejus loco substituatur, v. g. homines Angelis, gentiles Judaeis, David Sauli, Mat- thias Judae, Cyprianus Tertulliano, Cyrillus Origeni, Hieronymus Ruffino, Augustinus Pelagio, &c. id ta- men perpetuum non esse docet quotidiana experientia, neque potest ex hoc versu solide colligi. Recte au- tem ex hisce verbis: Tene, quod habes, ne quis aufe- rat coronam tuam, colligit Vasquez part. 1. q. 23. disp. 89. c. 10. & Cornelius à Lapide cum eo Deum nemi- nem absolute eligere ad gloriam coelestem. Nam si absolute electio ad gloriam facta esset, frustra ele- ctio diceretur: Tene, quod habes, ne alius accipiat coronam tuam: Unde porro concludunt: Absolu- te electum necessario ex efficaci Dei decreto salva- ri, ac impossibile esse eum damnari, quicquid agat Quibus calculum addit Tirinus: Multo minus ex eo colligi potest, quod Primasius, Beda, Ansbertus &

quidam alii volunt, certum ac prædefinitum esse nu- merum salvandorum ante prævisam singulorum fi- nalem perseverantiam, adeo, ut nec plures salvandi sint, nec pauciores, nec alii, quam qui de dicto numero sunt. Quin potius cum Vasquez, Gregorio à Valentia, Lessio, Cornelio à Lapide, & aliis plane contrarium hinc colligo, nempe Deum non absolute nos elegisse ad gloriam cælestem. Quæ opponenda sunt non Cal- vinianis tantum, sed & Scotistis & Dominicanis. Vid. T. II. System. Theol. c. X. Q. VI. p. 526. Non autem ideo inferendum, Deum non nisi post prævisa me- rita ad cælestem gloriam eligere, sed eligere post prævisam fidem in Christi merita finalem: quia vita æterna χάρισμα donum Dei gratuitum est in Chri- sto Jesu, Rom. VI. ult. Quanquam etiam in eo an- nuamus Cornelio, hinc patere, justos posse à gratia Dei excidere: quo de Episcopius: Ubi nullum est periculum, aut damnum, nec potest esse, & nec esse, nec esse posse certo scitur & intelligitur, ibi non potest moveri affectus metus aut timoris persuasione à damnoso eventu sumptam. Et Tirinus colligens, posse etiam quemcunque justum, etsi sanctissimum, à sanctitate & gratia excidere. Cur enim alioqui mo- neret: tene, quod habes? Cur periculum inculcaret amittendæ coronæ? Cur omnibus his epistolis nulli ni- si vincenti promitteret coronam? Cur tot minas in- tentaret? tot monitis, tot præmiis excitaret: Ubi ne- quicquam Pareus, quod habes de eo, quod habetur κατὰ δόξαν, vel quod videtur haberi; quia expressam literam, & Episcopi Philadelphiensis laudationem apertam explicat: quasi corona tandem privari in- nuantur, qui vulgo fideles habentur, quia non te- nent, quod habebant, hoc est, quod videbantur ha- bere, Luc. IIX, 18. Aliud est habere, aliud videri habere. Et annon revera habebat Episcopus, quod tenere jubebatur? Non tamen id concedendum Cornelio, quod nemo certus esse possit de sua per- severantia & salute, nisi quod ad certitudinem ab- soluta: Hypothetica enim certitudo omnino da- tur; si scilicet media salutis non negligamus; nec voluntarie per peccata proæretica gratiam DEI excutiamus. Dona enim & vocatio Dei sunt ἀμε- ταμέλητα, Rom. XI, 29. Et fidelis est Deus, per quem vocati sumus in communionem Jesu Christi, Filii ejus, Domini nostri, 1. Cor. I, 9. Refellit etiam quos- dam ex hoc loco Pareus inter Reformatos, gradus gloriæ negantes: Cum dicit: Coronam tuam, non ob- scure innuit, singulis suam coronam in cælis esse pro- positam. Unde colligi posse videtur, sicut erunt pæ- narum gradus in inferno: sic fore præmiorum diffe- rentias in cælo. Alia corona mea, alia tua. Nobilior haud dubie erit corona Doctorum fidelium, qui mul- tos ad justitiam erudierunt: Fulgebunt enim instar stellarum firmamenti. Jovinianus, adversus quem Hieronymus disputavit, videtur statuisse, omnibus eandem gloriam propositam, quod nonnulli ex ortho- doxis etiam hodie tenent, ex illo Christi: Tunc justi fulgebunt sicut sol. Solis autem fulgore nullus est in rebus creatis illustrior. Nihil vero impedit, diversos fulgoris gradus concedere, cum & nunc solis fulgor quandoque major & minor esse soleat.

## 3:12
Verse 12. Ὁ νικῶν ποιήσω αὐτὸν στύλον ἐν τῷ ναῷ τοῦ Θεοῦ μου.) What he had said to the Bishop he extends also to others, as also above always. And it is a Hebraism: Ὁ νικῶν ποιήσω αὐτὸν, for which the Greeks would say: Τὸν νικῶντα ποιήσω. When he speaks of a pillar, he refers to those two columns which were in the front of Solomon's temple, and because of their firmness were called Jachin and Boaz, 1 Kings 7:15 and 2 Chronicles 3:15, 16, 17. But why he uses this similitude, he will now explain.

Καὶ ἔξω ὐ μὴ ἐξέλθῃ ἔτι.) That is, he will not be forced to flee again, as under Nero: He will remain perpetually in the Sardian Church, just as those columns remained in the temple.

The exhortation to constancy in the faith is followed by a promise, which is commonly for all who conquer through faith, so that it is established that that warning pertains to all as well, not to the Bishop alone. However, remaining in the Philadelphian Church is not promised (Grotius said Sardian by a slip of memory) so that he is not forced to flee again, as under Nero, in which Grotian memory was not faithful again. For he had noted at v. 10 that the Neronian persecution had not passed, but was imminent, and would finally be: nor is this promise to be understood concerning the kingdom of grace, which most others wish, and among the Reformed Joh. Cocceius, Pareus, etc., but concerning the kingdom of glory, and among the Papists Blasius de Viegas, and Jac. Tirinus, with which interpretation standing, Bellarmine's argument for the invocation of Saints collapses: because it is made to those who conquer τελικῶς through faith, and hold what they have until the very end of life, and it is connected with the promise of the crown, which we finally attain in the other life. Simon Episcopius: In that opinion, he says, they seem to be, that they think it should be referred to the state of this present life: therefore, by the temple of GOD, the Church of Jesus Christ militant on earth for God: but to be made a pillar in it is nothing else than to persevere firm and constant, and to support, corroborate, and confirm others by word and example. For pillars are firm by themselves, and then by their own strength support the whole mass of the building: Whence also some wish that perseverance and constancy in the faith once received is promised. But they do not seem to me to speak conveniently: For it cannot be understood what that victory is which is required beforehand and underlies the promise. Then: because the good which is promised is more excellent than to be referred to the spans of this life, and especially those times of persecutions and afflictions. Thirdly: because no such promise is read to have been made, indeed history and experience can abundantly testify that the contrary has sometimes happened. Therefore we think this promise should be extended and referred to the spans of the future life. Gomarus agrees, departing here from other Reformed: That some, he says, accommodate this place to the present life, which is subject to change, having the primary signification of this word, so that it is a promise of perseverance, they hallucinate not a little: because this promise of primary glory belongs only to the victor, that is, to one constant unto death, and is attributed to him. But the sense is not badly expressed by Episcopius: It can be taken, he says, in two ways, either as if there is a defect or ἔλλειψις of a note of similitude among the Hebrews, and it can be read, I will make him as it were a pillar in the temple of my GOD, that is, in the temple of Solomon: or that it be taken simply: I will make him a pillar in the temple of my GOD, that is, heaven. If in the first way, an allusion can be made to those two most famous pillars of Solomon's temple, which, as one may read in 1 Kings 7:21, were tall and most beautiful, adorned with most elaborate architraves and capitals, so that they brought much dignity and decorum to the temple, and stood out among those things which were seen in it for beauty and elegance: so that the sense will be: That those who have conquered are to be crowned with glory and honor before others, and will appear extraordinary, and will be as it were some ornaments among the rest of the inhabitants of heaven, illustrious and excellent. If in the second way: then it must be considered that a pillar is understood not of necessity for supporting, but of ornament for illustrating: or which is a sign of decorum and glory and indeed solid, firm, and stable. But he says that that pillar is not to be erected for the victor, but the victor himself will be a pillar, that is, perpetually and solidly glorious: so that thus the divinity of the promise may be understood. For because men cannot perpetually preserve, and always affect the deserving with glory and honor, hence it is that they erect signs for the dead, through which they as it were continue and preserve the illustrious fame of the dead. But truly Christ will not erect signs for the victors, but will make the victors themselves pillars, that is, he will make them live with glory and eternal honor, or to speak briefly, immortal. Thus also Gomarus: In the temple of God, that is, in the Church triumphant in heaven, so that he may stand out like a pillar, not one that supports the rest (as is said in Gal. 2:9 concerning the primary Apostles, for in heaven this is not required) but only is for an ornament: such as the pillars, as it were typical, are described in the vestibule of Solomon's temple, 1 Kings 7:5, 21. Which glory of the benefit is amplified by perpetual continuation, and he will not go out anymore, that is, from that time. For 'no more', as usually with the future excluded, includes the past time: Thus sometimes it is only referred to the future, as Jer. 22:11. Thus says the Lord to Shallum the son of Josiah, who went out from that place, he will not return here anymore, but in the place to which I have transferred him, there he will die, that is, he will not return at all from that time: for Shallum had never before gone out as a captive outside Judea. Therefore Pareus's excellent place concerning the perseverance of the faithful in the militant Church collapses, as if it were said that those whom Christ once made pillars in his temple, he will never cast out, nor suffer to go out or be moved from the degree of constancy. We do not deny, however, that Richard of St. Victor, Lymnus, and Alcafar accept these concerning the kingdom of grace; just as John and James were called pillars of Christ, i.e., as Lyra has it, I will make him a pillar, i.e. strong and powerful, in faith not only for himself, but also for comforting and confirming others.

Καὶ γράψω ἐπ᾿ ἀυτὸ τὸ ὄνομά τῶ Θεῦ με.] He pursues the translation. For inscriptions were made on pillars, such as those which are called מכתם in the Psalms, for so the Greeks read Psalm 16 and elsewhere, where now the Hebrew books have מכתם. The Greeks translate it στηλογραφία. The name of God, which he says will be written on the pillar, is the name יהוה, which signifies that God will fulfill his promises, as can be understood from Exod. 6:3 and those things which were said here above I, 4 and 8. The sense is that those who were constant in the Neronian persecution will see by the Prophetic Spirit how GOD, according to his promises, will triumph over the Jews and Romans, which is the principal argument of the Apocalypse.

Setting aside those things which do not belong to this place, but pertain to Psalm 16 and Exodus 6, the sense of this remarkable promise is greatly perverted. The names of conquerors were indeed accustomed to be inscribed on columns: the names of the Kings and Princes themselves who erected them were also accustomed to be inscribed on columns: The latter they apply thus: I will inscribe the name of God, so that, namely, they may be named the sons of God. The former thus: That Christ will confess before the Father and the Angels that those victors are the sons of God. It is more fittingly said that the similitude is drawn from an ancient civil custom, in which owners inscribed their own names on their goods, so that they might distinguish them from others' and in that way protect them from injury: just as also statues, which were consecrated to the gods of the nations, bore their inscribed names, and monuments of honor erected by ambitious men, as Absalom's 2 Sam. 18:18, as here Gomarus. What does the vision of the Prophetic Spirit have to do with the name of God or the inscription of the name of God, how God is about to triumph over the Jews and Romans? Are those who are pillars in the Church of God, bearing the inscribed name of God, therefore instructed by the Prophetic Spirit? And what does the triumph over the Jews and Roman gentiles have to do with the Apocalypse? To our explanation and that of Gomarus is added

Episcopius: The name of God shall be written on the conqueror, because he is always to be God's, and is to be possessed entirely by Him, and in him God will glory particularly as in a servant and a brave soldier, whom He will always want to be acknowledged and called His own, and will so clearly separate him from the rest, that when God is about to demand an account and institute a review, then He will acknowledge him as His own and as a disciple of His Christ, and will hold him as His son, that is, an heir of immortal and eternal life according to His promise made through Christ everywhere: John I, 12; 2 Tim. II; Matt. XXV; Rom. II; 2 Thess. I. Moreover, Christ calls God his God, the Father, not because He Himself is not God, but because by reason of His human nature He acknowledges the Father as His God: although the name 'my God' can also be understood as the name of the Most Holy Trinity or the Triune God, whom Christ professes as His God, as man.

And the name of the city of my God, the new Jerusalem, which comes down out of heaven from my God.] This name is the catholic church, namely, free and flourishing under Christian Emperors. It descends from heaven, that is, it has been procured by the admirable benefit of God. See John VI, 33, 37, 41, 42, 50, 51, 58, and the things said there, compare them with those which we shall have below in XXI. The word 'descending' signifies that which is described here as being on earth. In the Manuscript it is ἡ καταβαίνουσα, which sufficiently smacks of the locution of John, who is accustomed to use direct cases for oblique ones.

The name of the city of God, the new Jerusalem, is not to be understood of the city of God in these lands, or of the earthly Jerusalem, but of the city of God in the heavens: because the pillars are heavenly. Which is that glorious city of God exhibited to John in Apoc. XXI. And although it is said to descend (καταβαίνειν), yet nothing else is hinted at than its origin from the heavens, Matt. XXI, 25, nor is it to be concluded from that that it descends into the lands and is on the lands, just as St. John is not said to have seen it descending (καταβαίνουσαν ἐκ τῦ ἐϱανῦ ἀπὸ τῦ Θεῦ) in Apoc. 21, 10, as if he had seen it descending into the lands. For it is and remains the glorious seat of the Elect in the heavens. And St. John saw it when the first heaven and the first earth had already passed away, and the sea no longer existed, Apoc. XXI, 1. How then could he have seen it descending from heaven to earth? Furthermore, while it is called 'new,' the abolition, or annihilation, or destruction of the old seems to be hinted at, Heb. VIII, v. last. It is called Jerusalem because it was the metropolis of the holy land, and the seat of divine rest, and the sanctuary which prefigured heaven: and in it He manifested His glory, if indeed it is manifested most fully in heaven, and God is there, where the tabernacle of God is with men, Apoc. XXI, 3. Episcopius also notes that that phrase, 'descends from the heavens,' indicates the heavenly fatherland, the knowledge and awareness of which cannot be had except through free and gracious heavenly revelation, by which it can be comprehended neither by sense nor by mind, but can only be believed as revealed from heaven, and by which it is now revealed and known by us. The Church, he says, does not properly descend from heaven to earth, but ascends from earth to heaven through faith and hope, even if faith and all gracious gifts are also said to descend from heaven. Whatever in the Holy Scriptures exceeds human powers, and has God as its Author, is said to be from heaven, and to descend from heaven, Luke XX, 4; James III, 15. Concerning which city, having foundations, whose architect and builder is God, Heb. XI, 10, and which remains eternally, Heb. XIII, 14, the conquerors are made more certain through faith; that they are to be its citizens, or if the name of the city of God signifies that glory and Majesty which is to be in that city, which Episcopius prefers, the glory of the same promised to them is to be understood. The former, however, is simpler. For it bears the name of the city inscribed, because it pertains to that city.

And my new name.] This new name of Christ is King of Kings and Lord of Lords, as can be seen below in XIX, 16. See also above II, 17.

We admit that new name, as one which He obtained after the passion, all power having been given to Him in heaven and on earth, Matt. XXVIII, 19. For under Christ the King of Kings we shall be kings ruling before God, and having under our feet the impious and Demons, the world and the Prince of the world, Apoc. III, 21; c. I, 6; c. V, 10; c. XXII, 5. Others understand the new name figuratively, so that it denotes glory, as Gomarus observes from the epistle Phil. II, 9, that is, he will reign with me. Others, on the contrary, take it properly, and indeed more conveniently to the preceding signification of the name: and some [take it as] Son of God: others the name of Christ; some the name of Jesus; but what if it is rather understood as King of Kings, Lord of Lords? Such a name is established as inscribed on the glorious Christ, Apoc. XIX, 16. But these are not opposites. For when the name of King of Kings is inscribed, [it means] that we shall be heavenly kings through Him and under Him, and thus twins to Christ Jesus, and promoted to that dignity by His merit. Therefore Blessed Gerhard: The new name of Christ shall be written on him, that is, it shall be manifest that those pillars were erected in heaven by Christ through the passion and death, by which He obtained that new name, as a monument in His victory, and that the glory of all the saints is to be attributed to Him. One must be careful, however, not to say with Episcopius that Christ obtained the name of Son of God more excellently when He was raised from the dead. Which opinion has been refuted among the Socinians. Paul teaches that Christ was declared or manifested to be the Son of God through the resurrection from the dead, Rom. I, 4. He does not say that He was made the Son of God through the same. Nor does the name of Son of God, which belongs to Christ, admit of degrees or of 'more and less'. Finally, what Episcopius observes, that the dominion of Christ will cease after this life, does not agree with that name of Christ, King of Kings. For of his kingdom there shall be no end, Luke 1:33. Although, therefore, the kingdom of grace is to cease, the kingdom of glory will nevertheless endure forever, nor will it have any end. For he will never cease to sit at the right hand of God and on the throne of God the Father: just as the Elect also will sit on the throne of Christ forever, and are to receive an eternal kingdom. From which most illustrious διηγήσει (exposition) of the promise it is clear that the Jesuits, Cornelius à Lapide along with Alcazar, whom they cite from this, have not attained its meaning, as if to say: I will make this man such a solid and illustrious pillar in virtue, that he may be for an honor and glory to God, and to the Church, and to the great Christ, so that he himself may be as it were a trophy erected by Christ for the honor of God the victor and the Church. For as many as shall behold him and his manners, so holy, will say that he is a pillar of God, of the Church, and of Christ, so that he may seem to bear written on his forehead: This is a pillar, nay rather a trophy of God, of Christ, and of the Church, because in him shines forth, and is proposed to be read by all, the greatness of the grace and virtue of God. It is a Catachresis, for it is said to be written, because it is so conspicuous and illustrious, as if it were written on the forehead. It is clear that our blessed Cluverius expressed the meaning of the divine promise far more correctly and harmoniously, when he presented this inscription thus: To JEHOVAH the Best and Greatest GOD and his Father, this ORNAMENT AND FIRMAMENT, eternal and immovable, of the new city founded by Him with omnipotent and glorious power, JESUS CHRIST THE TRIUMPHER, AUTHOR of eternal peace, life, and joy, with Satan trampled underfoot, and death abolished, and all evils entirely blotted out, gratefully and most joyfully has placed.

Latin:

Vers. 12. Ὁ νικῶν ποιήσω αὐτὸν στύλον ἐν τῷ ναῷ τοῦ Θεοῦ μου.) Quæ ad Episcopum dixerat ad alios quoque extendit, ut & supra semper. Et est Ebraismus: Ὁ νικῶν ποιήσω αὐτὸν, pro quo Græci dicerent: Τὸν νικῶντα ποιήσω. Cum columnam dicit, respicit duas illas columnas, quæ erant in fronte templi Salomonis, & ob firmitatem vocabantur Jakin & Booz, 1. Reg. VII, 15. & 2. Paral. III, 15. 16. 17. Cur autem hac similitudine utatur, jam explicabit.

Καὶ ἔξω ὐ μὴ ἐξέλθῃ ἔτι.) Id est, non iterum cogetur effu- gere, ut sub Nerone: Perpetuo manebit in Ecclesia Sardiana, sicut columnæ illæ manebant in templo.

Adhortationem ad constantiam in fide sequitur promissio, quæ communiter omnibus per fidem vincentibus sit, ut monitum illud ad omnes etiam pertinere, non ad solum Episcopum constet. Non autem promittitur permansio in Philadelphensi Ecclesia (Sardianam per memoriæ lapsum dixit Grotius) ne iterum cogatur effugere, ut sub Nero- ne, in quo iterum fida non fuit Grotiana memoria. Nam persecutionem Neronianam non præteriisse, sed imminere, ac futuram demum esse ad v. 10. an- notarat: neque promissio hæc de regno gratiæ in- telligenda, quod alii pleriq; volunt, & è Reforma- tis Joh. Cocceus, Pareus &c. sed de regno gloriæ, & è Pontificiis Blasius de Viegas, & Jac. Tirinus, qua in- terpretatione stante corruit Bellarmini argumen- tum pro invocatione Sanctorum: quia facta est illis, qui per fidem τελικῶς vincunt, & ad finem usque vitæ tenent, quod habent, & connexa est cum pro- missione coronæ, quam demum in altera vita con- sequimur. Simon Episcopius: In ea quidem, inquit, sententia esse videntur, ut ad vitæ hujus præsentis sta- tum referend.um putent: proinde per templum DEI Ecclesiam Jesu Christi in terris Deo militantem: Co- lumnam autem fieri in ea aliud nihil esse, quam fir- mum & constantem perseverare, aliosque verbo & exemplo fulcire, corroborare & confirmare. Colu- mnæ enim per se firmæ sunt, & robore deinde suo to- tam ædificii molem sustinent: Unde etiam quidam perseverantiam & constantiam in fide semel accepta perpetuam promitti volunt. Sed non videntur illi mihi convenienter loqui: Nec enim intelligi potest, quænam illa sit victoria, quæ prærequiritur & sub- sternitur promissioni. Deinde: quia excellentius est bonum, quod promittitur, quam ut ad spatia vitæ hujus referatur, & imprimis illa persecutionum & afflictionum tempora. Tertio: quia nulla talis pro- missio facta legitur, imo contrarium aliquando eve- nisse historia & experientia abunde testari possunt. Itaque ad spatia vitæ futuræ extendendam & refe- rendam existimamus hanc promissionem.
