Annuit Gomarus, ab aliis Reformatis hic discedens: Quod quidam hunc locum, inquit, ad præsentem vitam, quæ mutationi est obnoxia, accommodant, habita hujus vocis significatione prima, ut sit promissio per- severantiæ, non parum hallucinantur: quia victori, hoc est, ad mortem constanti hæc primæ gloriæ pro- missio competit tantum, ac tribuitur. Sensus autem non male exprimitur ab Episcopio: Dupliciter, in- quit, accipi potest promissio vel ut sit defectus sive ἔλλειψις notæ similitudinis apud Hebræos, & legi pos- sit, faciam eum veluti columnam esse in templo DEI mei, id est, in templo Salomonis: vel ut simpliciter accipiatur: faciam eum columnam in templo DEI mei, id est, cælo. Si primo modo allusio fieri potest ad duas illas celeberrimas templi Salomonis columnas, quæ uti legere est 1. Reg. VII, 21. proceræ & pulcherri- mæ erant, epistyliis atque capitellis operosissimis orna- tæ, ita ut multum templo afferrent dignitatis & de- coris, & inter illa quæ in illo videbantur pulchritu- dine atque elegantia eminerent: ita, ut sensus sit fu- turus: Illos, qui vicerint, gloria & honore præ aliis coronandos, & egregios apparituros, velutique orna- menta aliqua inter reliquos cæli incolas futuros illu- stres atque eximios. Si secundo modo: tum consi- derandum est, columnam intelligi non necessitatis ad fulciendum, sed ornatus ad illustrandum: sive quæ signum est decoris & gloriæ & quidem solidum, fir- mum & stabile. Illam autem columnam non eri- gendam esse victori dicit, sed ipsum victorem colu- mnam futurum, id est, perpetuo & solide gloriosum: ut ita divinitas promissionis intelligatur. Quia enim homines perpetuo conservare nequeunt, & gloria honoreque semper afficere benemeritos, hinc est, quod mortuis signa erigant, per quæ gloriam eorum quasi continuent & conservent illustrem fa- mam mortuorum. At vero Christus non eriget signa victoribus, sed victores ipsos faciet columnas, id est, vivere eos cum gloria & æterno honore fa- ciet, sive ut breviter dicam, immortales. Ita & Gomarus: In templo Dei, hoc est, in Ecclesia tri- umphante in cælis, ut emineat instar columnæ, non quæ suffulciat reliquos, (ut Gal. II, 9. de primariis Apostolis dicitur, nam in cælo hoc non requiritur) sed tantum ornamento sit: quales columnæ quasi typicæ in vestibulo templi Salomonis, 1.Reg.VII, 5, 21. describuntur. Quæ gloriæ beneficii perpetua conti- nuatione amplificatur, nec foras egredietur am- plius, hoc est, ab eo tempore. Nam non amplius, ut plerumque excluso futuro, includit tempus præte- ritum: Sic interdum tantum ad futurum refer- tur, ut Jerem. XXII, 11. Hæc dicit Dominus ad Sellum filium Josiæ, qui egressus est de loco illo, non revertetur huc amplius, sed in loco, ad quem transtu- li eum, ibi morietur, hoc est, omnino ab eo tempore non revertetur: nunquam enim prius Sellum capti- vus extra Judæam exiverat. Corruit ergo locus Parei egregius de perseverantia fidelium in mili- tante Ecclesia, quasi dicatur, quos Christus semel fecit columnas in templo suo, eos nunquam ejiciet foras, neque exire vel dimoveri de gradu constan- tiæ patietur. Non diffitemur tamen Richardum de S. Victore, Lymnum & Alcafarem hæc de regno gratiæ accipere; sicut Johannes & Jacobus colu- mnæ dicti sunt Christi, q. d. ut Lyr. habet, faciam illum columnam, h. e. fortem & potentem, in fide non solum per se, sed & pro aliis confortandis & confirmandis.

Καὶ γράψω ἐπ᾿ ἀυτὸ τὸ ὄνομά τῶ Θεῦ με.] Persequi- tur translationem. Nam in columnis fiebant inscriptio- nes, quales sunt, quæ in Psalmis dicuntur מכתם ita enim legere Græci Psalm. XVI. & alibi, ubi nunc libri He- braici habent מכתם. Vertunt Græci στηλογραφία. Nomen Dei, quod ait scriptum iri in columna, est nomen יהוה, quod significat Deum impleturum promissa, ut in- telligi potest Exod. VI, 3. & iis, quæ dicta hic supra I, 4. & 8. Sensus est, eos, qui in persecutione Neroniana constantes fuerint, visuros Spiritu Prophetico, quomodo DEUS secundum sua promissa triumphaturus sit de Judæis & Romanis, quod præcipuum est Apocalypseos argumen- tum.

Missis illis, quæ hujus loci non sunt, sed ad Psal. XVI. & Exod. VI. pertinent, sensus valde perver- titur insignis hujus promissionis, Solebant utique triumphatorum nomina inscribi columnis: Sole- bant & Regum ac Principum eorum nomina inscri- bi columnis, qui easdem erexerunt: Hoc posterius sic applicant: Inscribam nomen Dei, ut sc. nominen- tur filii Dei. Prius ita: Quod Christus coram Patre & Angelis confessurus sit victores illos esse filios Dei. Convenientius dicitur similitudinem dedu- ctam esse ab usu civili antiquo, in quo possessores suis bonis sua inscribebant nomina, ut ea ab alienis distinguerent, & eo modo ab injuria tutarentur: quemadmodu etiam statuis, quæ consecratæ erant gentium Diis, eorum nomina inscripta præfere- bant, ac monumenta honoris ab ambitiosis homi- nibus erecta, ut Absolomi 2 Sam. XXVIII, 18. ut hic Gomarus. Quid ad nomen Dei vel inscriptio- nem nominis Dei facit visio Spiritus Prophetici, quomodo Deus de Judæis & Romanis trium- phaturus sit? Num illi, qui columnæ in Ecclesia Dei sunt, inscriptum Dei nomen gerentes Spiritu Prophetico ideo instructi sunt? Et quid ad Apoca- lypsin triumphi de Judæis & Romanis gentili- bus? Nostræ & Gomari explicationi accedit

Episcopius: Nomen Dei scribetur in Vincente, quia semper Dei futurus est, & ab eo totus possidendus est, & in eo Deus tanquam in servo ac milite forti pecu- liariter gloriabitur, quem semper suum agnosci & dici volet, & ita clare a reliquis separabit, ut quan- do Deus rationem postulaturus est, & recensionem in- stituturus, tum eum ut suum & Christi sui discipulum agniturus sit, & pro filio suo, id est, hærede vitæ im- mortalis & æternæ habiturus juxta promissionem suam per Christum factam passim Joh. I, 12. 2. Tim. II, Matth. XXV, Rom. II. 2. Thess. I. Cæterum Deum suum vocat Christus Deum Patrem, non quod ipse Deus non sit, sed quod ratione Humanæ na- turæ Patrem Deum suum agnoscat : quanquam etiam nomen Dei mei intelligi possit nomen SS. Trinitatis vel triunius DEI, quem Deum suum Christus profitetur, ut homo.

Καὶ τὸ ὄνομα τῆς πόλεως τῦ Θεῦ μᾶ, τῆς καινῆς Ἰεϱυ- σαλὴμ, ἡ καταβαίνει ἐκ τῦ ἐϱανῦ ἀπὸ τῦ Θεῦ μᾶ.] Hoc nomen est ἐκκλησία καθολικὴ nempe libera & florens sub Imperatoribus Christianis. Ea ex cœlo descendit, id est, Dei beneficio admirabili procurata est. Vide Joh. VI, 33. 37. 41. 42. 50. 51. 58. & ibi dicta, confer cum eis, quæ habe- bimus infra XXI. Verbum descendendi significat id, quod hic describitur in terris fore. In Manuscripto est ἡ καταβαί- νουσα, quod satis redolet locutionem Johannis, qui rectis uti solet pro obliquis.

Nomen civitatis Dei novæ Hierosolymæ non de civitate Dei in his terris, vel Hierosolyma terre- stri, sed de civitate Dei in cœlis accipiendum : quia columnæ sunt cœlestes. Quæ est gloriosa illa DEI civitas Johanni exhibita Apoc. XXI. Etsi autem di- catur καταβαίνειν, non tamen aliud, quam origo de cælis innuitur, Matth. XXI, 25. nec quod in terras descendat, & in terris sit inde concludendum, quemadmodam nec Apoc. 21, 10. καταβαίνουσαν ἐκ τῦ ἐϱανῦ ἀπὸ τῦ Θεῦ vidisse S. Johannes dicitur, quasi in terras viderit descendentem. Est enim & manet sedes gloriosa Electorum in cœlis. Et vidit S. Johannes illam, quando jam primum cœlum & prima terra abierat, & mare non amplius extabat, Apoc. XXI, 1. Quomodo ergo de cœlo in terram descendentem vidisset? Porro dum nova dicitur, defitio, sive annihilatio seu destructio veteris innui videtur, Ebr. IIX. v. ult. Hierusalem dicitur, quia ea metropolis terræ sanctæ erat, & sedes requietis divinæ, & sacrarium, quod cœlum præfigurabat: & in ea gloriam suam manifestabat, siquidem plenis- sime in cœlo manifestatur, ibique Deus, ubi taber- naculum Dei est cum hominibus, Apoc. XXI, 3. Phrasin etiam illam, descendit è cœlis, Episcopius notat, indicare patriam cælestem, cujus cognitio & notitia haberi non potest, nisi per liberam & gratio- sam cælestem revelationem, qua nec sensu nec mente comprehendi, sed cælitus revelata credi tantum potest, & qua jam revelatur & cognoscitur à nobis. Ecclesia non proprie, inquit, descendit ex cælo in terram, sed è terra in cælum ascendit per fidem & spem, etsi fides etiam & dona omnia gratiosa cælitus descendere di- cantur. Quicquid in S.literis humanas vires exce- dit, & Deum habet Autorem, è cœlo esse, & de- scendere è cœlo dicitur, Luc. XX, 4. Jac. III, 15. De qua civitate, fundamenta habente, cujus τεχνίτης & δημιεργὸς est Deus, Ebr. XI, 10. quæque æternum permanet, Ebr. XIII, 14. certiores redduntur vin- centes per fidem; quod ejusdem futuri sint cives, vel si civitatis Dei nomen significet gloriam illam & Majestatem, quæ in civitate illa futura est, quod mavult Episcopius, gloria ejusdem ipsis promissa intelligenda. Prius tamen simplicius est. Nomen enim civitatis inscriptum gerit, quod ad civitatem illam pertineat.

Καὶ τὸ ὄνομά με τὸ καινὸν.] Hoc novum nomen Christi est βασιλεὺς βασιλέων καὶ Κύριος Κυρίων, ut videre est infra XIX, 16. Vide & supra II, 17.

Admittimus illud novum nomen, utpote quod consequutus est post passionem, data ei omni po- testate in cœlo & in terra, Matth. XXIX, 19. Sub Christo enim Rege Regum nos Reges erimus co- ram Deo imperantes, & sub pedibus habentes im- pios & Dæmones, mundum & Principem mundi, Apoc. III, 21. c. I, 6. c. V, 10. c. XXII, 5. Alii novum nomen figurate intelligunt, ut gloriam notet, ob- servante Gomaro ex epist. Phil. II, 9. id est, mecum regnabit. Alii contra proprie, & quidem convenien- tius antecedenti nominis significationi accipiunt : ac quidam Filii Dei : alii Christi nomen ; nonnulli no- men Jesu; sed quid si potius Rex Regum, Dominus Dominorum intelligatur ? Quale nomen Christo glorioso inscriptum statuitur, Apoc. XIX, 16. Sed hæc opposita non sunt. Nam cum inscribitur nomen Regis Regum, nos fore per illum & sub illo Reges cœlestes, adeoque Christo Jesu geminos, ejusque merito ad illam dignitatem provectos. Ideo B. Gerhardus : Nomen Christi novum in eo scribetur, id est, manifestum erit, columnas illas in cælo à Christo per passionem & mortem, qua nomen illud novum consecutus est, tanquam in victoria sua monumen- tum erectas fuisse, illique omnium sanctorum glo- riam acceptam esse ferendam. Cavendum tamen, ne cum Episcopio dicatur nomen Filii Dei Chri- stum excellentius consequutum esse, quando ex mortuis resuscitatus est. Quæ sententia in Soci- nianis profligata est. Christum per resurrectio- nem ex mortuis Filium Dei declaratum esse vel manifestatum, Paulus docet Rom. I, 4. Filium DEI per eandem factum esse non dicit. Neque nomen Filii Dei, quod Christo competit, admittit gradus vel magis & minus. Denique quod Episcopius ob- servat, dominium Christi cessaturum esse post hanc vitam, non congruit cum illo nomine Christi Regis Regum. Nam regni ejus non erit finis, Luc. I, 34. Etsi ergo regnum gratiæ cessaturum est, re- gnum tamen gloriæ in æternum durabit, nec fi- nem ullum habiturum est. Nunquam enim desinet sedere ad dextram Dei & in throno Dei Patris: quemadmodum & Electi sedebunt in throno Christi in æternum, ac regnum accepturi sunt æter- num. Ex qua διηγήσει promissionis illustrissima patet, sensum ejus non assecutos Jesuitas, Corne- lium à Lapide cum Alcafare, quem hinc depro- munt, q. d. Ego hunc virum tam solidum & illu- strem in virtute columnam efficiam, ut & Deo, & Ecclesiæ, & Christo magno sit honori & gloriæ, ut ipse sit quasi trophaum in Dei victoris & Ecclesiæ decus à Christo erectum. Quotquot enim ipsum ipsiusque mores tam sanctos intuebuntur, dicent, illum esse co- lumnam Dei, Ecclesiæ & Christi, ita, ut videatur in fronte scriptum gerere : Hic est columna, imo tro- phæum Dei Christi & Ecclesiæ, quia in ipso resplendet, omnibusque legenda proponitur magnitudo gratiæ & virtutis Dei. Est Catachresis, scribi enim dici- tur, quod tam conspicuum sit & illustre, ac si in fronte scriptum esset. Patet longe rectius & concinnius promissionis divinæ sensum expressisse B. Cluve- rum nostrum, quum hanc inscriptionem ita exhi- buit : JEHOVÆ OPT. M. DEO & Patri suo, hoc novæ civitatis ab eo omnipotenti & gloriosa vir- tute conditæ DECUS ET FIRMAMENTUM sempiternum immobile, JESUS CHRISTUS TRI- UMPHATOR, æterna pacis, vitæ ac lætitiæ AU- TOR, pessundato satana, abolitaque morte, dele- tis in universum malis omnibus gratulabundus lætis- simus posuit.

## 3:13
Verse 13.

He that hath an ear, let him hear what the Spirit saith unto the churches.] To the church of Philadelphia, and to others in that part of Mysia.

Indeed, not only to them, but to all the churches are these things written. Therefore, it is said indefinitely to the churches, both in this and in the other epistles of the Son of God. And these things concerning the epistle written by the command of the Son of God to the Philadelphian Angel or Bishop: which I selected many years ago, so that when the Son of God—ah! come, Lord Jesus, come to the blessed departure, come!—has called me away from the church militant, it may be declared in place of a funeral oration at the obsequies; not that I acknowledge myself equal to him, or worthy of such great eulogies and rewards, I who weigh and deplore my unworthiness daily; but because I humbly and with true confidence of heart worship God the Father of all grace in the name of Jesus, that He may render me worthy in Christ Jesus, and may cause, by the power of His Spirit, that I may firmly and constantly hold what I have, and through faith may overcome, and may implore my Lord Jesus, who is my only confidence and my hope, with most ardent sighs, that on account of His most holy obedience even unto death, and indeed the death of the cross, He may establish me as an immovable pillar here in the temple of my God, in the spiritual, and one day in the heavenly Jerusalem, which shall go out no more, that He may write upon me the name of my God, and the name of the city of my God, the new Jerusalem, which descendeth out of heaven from my GOD, and His own new name. Amen, my Jesus, Amen!

PART III. THE SEVENTH EPISTLE TO THE ANGEL OF LAODICEA.

Latin:

Vers. 13.

Ὁ ἔχων ὖς ἀκκσάτω, τί τὸ Πνεῦμα λέγει ταῖς Ἐκκλησίαις.] Ecclesiæ Philadelphenæ, & aliis in illa parte Mysiæ.

Imo non illis tantum, sed omnibus Ecclesiis hæc scripta sunt. Ideo indefinite ταῖς Ἐκκλησίαις di- citur cum in hac, tum in cæteris Filii Dei epistolis. Atque hæc de epistola jussu Filii Dei ad Philadel- phensem Angelum vel Episcopum perscripta: quam ante complures annos selegi, ut quando Fi- lius Dei, ah! veni, Domine Jesu, veni ad beatam ἀ- νάλυσιν, veni! me ex Ecclesia militante evocavit, concionis funebris loco in exequiis declaretur; non quod parem illi, tantisque elogiis ac præmiis dignum memet agnoscam, qui meam indignita- tem quotidie expendo, & deploro; sed quod hu- militer & vera cordis fiducia Deum Patrem omnis gratiæ in nomine Jesu venerer, ut dignum me in Christo Jesu præstet, faciatque Spiritus sui virtu- te, ut firmiter, & constanter teneam, quod habeo, ac per fidem vincam, & Dominum Jesum meum, qui unica fiducia mea, & spes mea, ardentissimis su- spiriis implorem, ut propter sanctissimam obe- dientiam suam usque ad mortem, & quidem mor- tem crucis me columnam immotam hic in templo Dei mei, in spirituali, & olim in cœlesti Hicrosolyma constituat, quæ foras non egrediatur amplius, ut scribat super me nomen Dei mei, & nomen civi- tatis Dei mei, novæ Hierusalem, quæ descendit de cœlo à DEO meo, & nomen suum novum. Amen, mi Jesu, Amen!

PARS III. EPISTOLA SEPTIMA AD ANGELUM LAODICENSEM.

## 3:14
Verse 14.

And unto the angel of the church in Laodicea write.] It is a city of Lydia on the river Lycus, where, before the arrival of Paul there, some church existed from the dispersed Jews.

It is near to Colossae, first called Diospolis, then Rhome, and finally restored by Antiochus the son of Stratonice, and called Laodicea in honor of his wife Laodice, as Pliny testifies, book V, ch. 49. Col. IV, 16. Aureolus, in the year of Christ 172, calls that bishop Sagaris, with Eusebius, book IV, ch. 24, stating that he was crowned with martyrdom. The epistle consists of a most grave rebuke of his lukewarmness and pride in spiritual poverty, v. 15, 16; then a most sweet provision of wholesome counsel and an invitation to repentance, v. 18; then a most splendid promise made to those who overcome through faith, v. 21, with the customary clause for giving audience to the Spirit.

Thus saith the Amen.] He made a noun from an adverb, just as the Latins say, a clear morning, that tomorrow, yesterday's tomorrow. Isa. LXV, 16. God is called the God of Amen. Moreover, Christ signifies that He is the one through whom all promises are fulfilled, which Paul said in 2 Cor. I, 20: All the promises in Christ are Amen.

The faithful and true witness.] Above I, 5. He repeats this here so that the certainty of the promises concerning eternal life may rouse the languid.

The beginning of the creation of God.] Of the new creation, which is treated in 2 Cor. V, 17; Gal. VI, 15. See also Col. I, 15 and Jas. I, 18. He says this so that the Laodicean Bishop may take an example for himself from Christ, who truly is the beginning of the ways of God.

The Son of God assumes to himself those names which are most accommodated to the argument of the epistle. Ὁ ἀμηνὰ with an undoubted and infallible truth concerning those things of which he argues with the Bishop, and which he threatens to him: as well as those which he suggests and promises to him: Which name is proper to God himself, Isa. LXV, 16. It confirms that Christ is true God, who is also truth itself, John XIV, 5, and in whom all promises are ναὶ & ἀμὴν, 2 Cor. I, 20. And because he has testified of these things on earth in the days of his flesh, and makes us, as witnesses in heaven of one essence with the Father and the Holy Spirit, certain of them, 1 John V, 7. He is called Ὁ μάρτυς ὁ πι- στὸς κἠ ἀληθινὸς by a most eminent reason, as in Apoc. I, 5, as θεάνθρωπος God and Man, the author or principle of every creature, who has all things in his hand: as one who by infinite power created all things, to whose communion he has been admitted even according to his Human nature, sitting on the very throne of God the Father. Conf. Heb. I, 2, 3. We do not see why we should accept κτίσιν as a new creature with the Socinianizing Grotius, since there is no necessity to depart from the proper signification; especially because the creation of all things is everywhere attributed to him, Ps. XXXIII, 6, Prov. IIX, 30, John I, 2, Col. I, 16, Heb. I, 2. The Laodicean could not take an example from Christ regarding a new creation; because Christ had no need of a new creation, regeneration, or renovation: but we are a new creature in Christ, 1 Cor. V, 17. But it is an effective principle, not a material one of creation: because through him all things were created, πάντα γὰρ τὰ αἴτια ἀρχαὶ, according to the Philosopher, book IV, Metaph. ch. 1. Therefore the Arians impiously proved from this that Christ was the first and a mere creature. Add that ἀρχὴ can also be explained as Prince, just as Christ is called ὁ ἄρχων, the Prince of the Kings of the earth, Apoc. I, 5.

Latin:

Vers. 14.

Καὶ τῷ Ἀγγέλῳ τῆς ἐν Λαοδικείᾳ Ἐκκλησίας γράψον.] Urbs est Lydiæ ad Lycum amnem, ubi ante Pauli eo adventum Ec- clesia aliqua erat ex Judæis dispersis.

Vicina est Colossis primum Diospolis, deinde Rhome nuncupata, denique ab Antiocho filio Stra- tonices instaurata, & in gratiam uxoris Laodiceæ Laodicea vocata, teste Plinio l. V. c. 49. Col. IV, 16. Episcopum illum Sagarem dicit Aureolus an. Chri- sti 172. Eusebio l. IV. c. 24. perhibente martyrio co- ronatum. Epistola constat tum gravissima χλιαρό- τητος ipsius & superbiæ in spirituali egestate repre- hensione v. 15. 16. tum suavissima consilii salutaris subministratione & ad pœnitentiam invitatione, v. 18. tum splendidissima vincentium per fidem fa- cta pollicitatione, v. 21. cum consueta clausula ad audientiam Spiritui præstandam.

Τάδε λέγει ὁ Ἀμήν.] Ex adverbio fecit nomen, sicut Lati- ni dicunt, clarum mane, cras illud, cras hesternum. Esa.LXV, 16. Deus vocatur אלהי אמן. Signficat autem Christus se eum esse, per quem omnia promissa implentur, quod Paulus dixit 2.Cor.I, 20. Omnia promissa in Christo esse Amen.

Ὁ μάρτυς ὁ πιςὸς καὶ ἀληθινὸς.] Supra I, 5. Id ideo hic re- petit, ut promissorum de vita æterna certitudo languidos excitet.

Ἡ ἀρχὴ τῆς κτίσεως τῦ Θεῦ.] Novæ creationis de qua agi- tur 2.Cor. V, 17. Gal.VI, 15. Vide & Col. I, 15. & Jac. I, 18. Hoc ideo dicit, ut Laodicenus Episcopus à Christo sibi exemplum sumat, qui vere est ראש דרכי אל.

Nomina Filius Dei ea sibi assumit, quæ cum ma- xime argumento epistolæ accommodata sunt. Ὁ ἀμηνὰ veritate indubitata atque infallibili cum eo- rum de quibus arguit Episcopum, quæque ei mina- tur: tum eorum, quæ ipsi suggerit & pollicetur: Quod nomen ipsi Deo proprium, Esa. LXV, 16. Christum verum Deum esse confirmat, qui etiam ipsa veritas est Joh. XIV, 5. & in quo omnes promif- siones ναὶ & ἀμὴν sunt, 2. Cor. I, 20. Et quia testatus est de hisce in terris in diebus carnis, nosq; ceu te- stes in cœlis unius cum Patre & Spiritu sancto essen- tiæ certos reddit de illis, 1. Joh. V, 7. Ὁ μάρτυς ὁ πι- στὸς κἠ ἀληθινὸς vocatur eminentissima ratione, ut Apoc. I, 5. ceu θεάνθρωπος Deus & Homo, autor vel principium omnis creaturæ, qui in manu sua habet omnia: utpote qui virtute infinita creavit omnia, ad cujus communionem admissus est etiam secundum Humanam naturam considens in ipso Dei Patris throno. Conf. Ebr. I, 2. 3. Cur κτίσιν de creatura nova cum Grotio Socinianizante accipia- mus, quum nulla necessitas sit discedendi a propria significatione, non videmus; imprimis quia creatio omnium rerum ipsi passim tributa est, Ps. XXXIII, 6. Prov. IIX, 30. Joh. I, 2. Col. I, 16. Ebr. I, 2. Exem- plum a Christo quoad novam creationem sumere sibi non potuit Laodicenus; quia Christus nova creatione, regeneratione aut renovatione opus non habuit: nos autem nova creatura sumus in Christo, 1. Cor. V, 17. Principium autem effectivum est, non materiale creationis: quia per ipsum creata sunt omnia, πάντα γὰρ τὰ αἴτια ἀρχαὶ, secundum Philosophum l. IV. Metaph. c. 1. Ideo impie Aria- ni hinc probabant Christum primam esse ac me- ram creaturam. Adde, quod ἀρχὴ etiam de Prin- cipe explicari possit, uti ὁ ἄρχων Princeps Regum terræ Christus dicitur. Apoc. I, 5.

## 3:15
Vers. 15.

Οἶδά σε τὰ ἔργα.] He describes that kind of men who approach the assemblies of Christians and aggregate themselves to them, but do not institute their life according to the norm of the Gospel, such as Paul also describes in 2 Tim. III, 5, 7. See also Matt. VII, 22, and Heb. X, 29. He to whom Epictetus refers in Arrian IV, 7, was not far from this: ἐπεπώπηκας ἤδη τῶν τῇ ῥίζῃ κάτω, τὰ δ᾽ ἄνω μακροὶ ἔτι ἀνθεῖ.

Ὅτι ὔτε ψυχρὸς εἶ, ὔτε ζεστός.] They are cold who have no knowledge of the Gospel, and therefore no Christian motions. They are fervent who are endowed with Christian love, which is compared to fire, as is all love. In the Glossary, ζεσὸς is fervent, boiling. See Cant. IIX, 7.

The Son of God appeals to his omniscience, in whose light he sees and penetrates all things, even the innermost and hidden recesses of the heart, Apoc. III, 23. Heat and cold are understood in a more significant degree, as Andreas Caesariensis, from the interpretation of Gregory Nazianzen, renders what? ἀκριβῶς ζεῖν, ἢ ἀκριβῶς ἀποψύχεθαι, to be significantly fervent or significantly cold. The Grotian interpretation is not unlike the interpretation of Riccardus, Ambrose in sermon IV on Ps. CXIIX, Bede, and Arethas, who by the cold understand the infidel, who has some excuse for his sins because of the ignorance in which he lives: By the lukewarm, a Christian, who is considered worse than the cold, because he sins more gravely in the same kind of sin than the infidel, on account of the knowledge of the truth and the more ample benefits received from God, Luke XII, 17, 2 Pet. II, 21. Blessed Gerhard also favors this sense, and it is analogous to the exposition of Victorinus: That the cold are heretics, the hot are Catholics, the lukewarm are politicians (or Syncretists) who, for their own advantages, pretend to be now heretics, now Catholics, or favor both, wish to reconcile both, and desire both to be admitted into mystical communion. To Gregory the Great, book XXXIV, moral. ch. 2, the hot is he who has charity; the cold is he who exists in mortal sin but acknowledges his fault; the lukewarm is he who is in sin but does not acknowledge it, and through hypocrisy pretends to be good. To Haymo, Anselm, Lyranus, and Cassian, collat. IV, ch. 12 and 19, the lukewarm is he who fluctuates between virtues and vices, and who would indeed like to live from virtue and avoid sins, but shuns the struggle with vices and the labor of virtue.

Latin:

Vers. 15.

Οἶδά σε τὰ ἔργα.] Describit id hominum genus, qui cœ- tus Christianorum adeunt, & eis se aggregant, sed vitam non instituunt ad normam Evangelii, quales & Paulus describit 2. Tim. III, 5. 7. Vide & Matth. VII, 22. & Ebr. X, 29. Non longe hinc abibat ille, ad quem Epictetus apud Arianum IV, 7. ἐπεπώπηκας ἤδη τῶν τῇ ῥίζῃ κάτω, τὰ δ᾽ ἄνω μακροὶ ἔτι ἀνθεῖ.

Ὅτι ὔτε ψυχρὸς εἶ, ὔτε ζεστός.] Frigidi sunt, qui nullam ha- bent Evangelii notitiam, ac proinde nec ullos motus Christia- nos. Fervidi, qui præditi sunt Christiana dilectione, quæ igni comparatur, ut amor omnis. In Glossario ζεσὸς fervidus, fer- fens. Vide Cant. IIX, 7.

Ad omniscientiam suam provocat Filius Dei, in cujus luce videt ac penetrat omnia, etiam intimos & abditos cordis recessus, Apoc. III, 23. Calor & fri- gus intelliguntur in gradu insigniori, ut Andr. Cæ- sar. ex interpretatione Gregor. Nazianz. reddit quid? ἀκριβῶς ζεῖν, ἢ ἀκριβῶς ἀποψύχεθαι insigniter fer- vere vel insigniter frigere. Grotiana interpretatio non absimilis est interpretationi, Riccardi, Ambrosii serm. IV. in Psal. CXIIX. Bedæ & Aretæ, qui per fri- gidum intelligunt infidelem, qui aliquam habet propter ignorantiam, in qua versatur, peccatorum suorum excusationem: Per tepidum Christianum, qui deterior frigido existimatur, quia eodem pec- cati genere gravius peccat, quam infidelis propter notitiam veritatis, & ampliora a Deo accepta bene- ficia, Luc. XII, 17. 2. Petr. II, 21. Cui sensui favet etiam B. Gerhardus estque analogus expositioni Victori- ni: Frigidos esse hæreticos, calidos Catholicos, tepidos politicos (vel Syncretistas) qui pro suis commodis jam hæreticos jam Catholicos se simulant, aut utrisꝙ fa- vent, utrosque conciliare volunt, utrosque in com- munionem mysticam admissos cupiunt. Gregorio M. l. XXXIV. moral. c. 2. calidus est, qui charitatem habet; frigidus, qui in peccato mortali existit, sed culpam suam agnoscit; tepidus est, qui est in pec- cato, sed illud non agnoscit, & per hypocrisin pro- bum se simulat. Haymoni, Anshelmo, Lyrano & Cas- siano collat. IV. c. 12. & 19. tepidus est, qui inter vir- tutes & vitia fluctuat, quique ex virtute quidem vivere & peccata vitare vellet, sed certamen cum vitiis & virtutis laborem refugit.

## 3:16
Vers. 16.

Ὄφελον ψυχρὸς εἴης, ἢ ζεσός.] This is because it is a lighter matter to be ignorant of the truth than, having known it, not to use it. Luke II, 48. 2 Peter II, 21, where see the remarks. Add that there is greater hope of health in the intemperate (ἐν ἀκολάστῳ) than in the incontinent (ἐν ἀκρατεῖ), as Aristotle shows. ὄφελον, לוֹ, אחלי are used by Dioscorides, Galen,

Others explain it thus: I wish you were either hot, fervently pious, or cold, sensibly wicked, for then you would either be kindled by heat to progress bravely, or be stimulated by cold to repent quickly from a shameful, dangerous, and damnable state. Gloss: He does not wish, he says, for him to be cold simply, but such a one of whom there might be greater hope. The discourse, says Thomas Anglicus, is about the cold, not regarding coldness and guilt, but regarding the greater ease of disposition. For the lukewarm is more dangerous than the cold, both because of greater forgetfulness and sloth, from which he does not notice his danger; but secure in it, he rests and sleeps, and because of the danger of abandonment by God: especially because lukewarmness is joined to and usually arises from great self-importance, pride, presumption, and contempt of God and divine things. For the lukewarm persuade themselves that they are good, and they live securely, as if needing nothing, fearing nothing, just as is added here: You say that I am rich, and need nothing. Coldness, says Gregory the Great, Part III, Pastoral Rule, admonition 35, is before lukewarmness under hope; but lukewarmness after coldness is in despair, that is, he who is still in sins does not lose the confidence of conversion, but he who has become lukewarm after conversion has at the same time withdrawn the hope that existed for the sinner. Acedia, says Climacus in the chapter on acedia, is a relaxation of the soul, and a dissolution of the mind, a faint-heartedness in exercise, a hatred of one's profession, a beatifier of worldly things, a detractor of God as if He were unfeeling and existing without kindness, astonished in the singing of Psalms, weakening in prayer, iron-like in ministry, lazy in the work of hands, disobedient in obedience. Whence Cassian. in the same place, observing, we have often seen those who are cold and carnal, that is, secular and pagan, arrive at spiritual fervor; those who are lukewarm and animal we have not seen at all. Chrysostom, book on the fall. The root, he says, of despair is sloth, and not only the root, but it is its nurse and mother. For just as a garment generates and nourishes a moth: so sloth not only generates despair from itself, but feeds and fosters it. However, that 'I wish you were cold rather than lukewarm' is to be taken not absolutely, but with the exception of repentance, i.e., unless you repent, because the conscience of duty renders the neglect of it and the punishment more severe, Luke 12:44, 45. The cold are also better for this reason, that they bring forth the mind of their own soul, and do not show one thing in words while hiding another in their breast: and because they often sin out of ignorance, thinking they are offering true worship to God, 1 Tim. 1:13. John 16:2, therefore, having been taught better things, they bear excellent fruits of amendment, or, conscious of more serious crimes, they gain profit more quickly, Matt. 21:31, 32. Whereas, on the contrary, the lukewarm admit contrary things at the same time, and deem that they can serve Jehovah and Baal equally, Christ and Belial equally, God and the belly or Mammon equally, 2 Kings 17, Matt. 6:24, 2 Cor. 6:15, Rom. 16:18, Phil. 3:19. They are like amphibious animals, and as Victorinus speaks, they are all things to all men. ψυχροὶ, the cold, says B. Glassius, Rhet. Sacr. p. 265, in that respect of the lukewarm, are praiseworthy in that they openly profess what kind they are, and do not hide one thing in words and another in their breast: since they labor with the blindness of nature, if they are taught about better things, they are often laudably amended: which can hardly be hoped for in the lukewarm, who have the appearance of piety but deny its power. The sense therefore is: You ought to have been placed in extreme degrees, so that you might be judged. Therefore, the lukewarm in this place is not one who relaxes somewhat from charity, for who could not easily be rendered ambiguous in that way, whether he is sufficiently fervent? Nor does Andr. Caesar warn without reason: in works indeed, that which keeps the middle is not to be rejected: but in the end, the middle or lukewarm is disapproved by all.

Οὕτως ὅτι χλιαρὸς εἶ.] Οὕτως here is worth 'therefore'. In the glossary, χλιαρὸν is lukewarm. Aristotle, Galen, and others use it. χλιαρὸς is סכך. Hermas calls these 'doubtful' in III, 8. Καὶ ὔ ζεσὸς, ὔτε ψυχρὸς.] He explains more clearly what χλιαρὸς is. Μέλλω σε ἐμέσαι ἐκ τῦ ςόματός μ8.] He continues the comparison. Lukewarm things are ἐμετικὰ, Celsus I, 2. He who is accustomed to vomit after food, if he does it easily, ought to take water as if it were lukewarm beforehand. But Christ signifies that such men are troublesome to Him, just like those things which cause nausea. Christ vomits out those whom He ceases to admonish. It is equal in translation to when someone is said to be unable to digest something.

Regarding the word μέλλω, for which the word 'I will begin' is held in the Vulgate, B. Hoë observes that God does not immediately pour out the full cataracts of His wrath upon us, but proceeds gradually in sending punishments, just as is evident from the example of Pharaoh: B. Cluverus presses the Greek word. Not precisely, he says, have I vomited or will I vomit, but hesitatingly, as it were, μέλλω σε ἐμέσαι, that is, I am in the state of vomiting, unless, of course, you have done penance, which He commands in verse 19, and urges and demands with the most serious reasons, Ps. 103:8.

Latin:

Vers. 16.

Ὄφελον ψυχρὸς εἴης, ἢ ζεσός.] Hoc ideo, quia levius est verum ignorare, quam cognito non uti. Luc. II, 48. 2. Petr. II, 21. ubi dicta vide. Adde, quod sanitatis major spes ἐν ἀκολά- σῳ quam ἐν ἀκρατεῖ, ut ostendit Aristoteles. ὄφελον, לוֹ, אחלי Utuntur Dioscorides, Galenus,

Alii sic explicant: Utinam vel calidus, ferventer pius, vel frigidus, sensibiliter malus esses, tunc enim vel calore accendereris ad fortiter progredien- dum, vel frigore exstimulareris ad celeriter resipi- endum à probroso, periculoso & damnabili statu. Glossa: Non optat, ait, eum frigidum simpliciter, sed talem, de quo major spes habeatur. Sermo est, inquit Thomas Anglicus de frigido, non quantum ad frigidi- tatem & culpam, sed quantum ad dispositionis majo- rem facilitatem. Tepidus enim periculosior est frigo- re tum ob majorem oblivionem & socordiam, ex qua non advertit suum periculum; sed securus in eo quie- scit & dormit, tum ob periculum derelictionis à Deo: imprimis quia tepor conjunctus est & oriri solet ex magna præsidentia, superbia, præsumptio- ne & contemptu Dei & rerum divinarum. Persua- dent enim tepidi sibi, se bonos esse, ac secure vi- vunt, quasi nullius egentes, nihil timentes, quem- admodum hic additur: Dicis, quod dives sum, & nullius egeo. Frigus, inquit Gregorius M. III. part. pastor. admonit. 35. ante teporem sub spe est; tepor autem post frigus in desperatione, id est, qui adhuc in peccatis est, conversionis fiduciam non amittit, qui vero post conversionem tepuit, simul spem, quæ erat de peccatore, subtraxit. Acedia, inquit Climacus cap. de acedia, est remissio animæ, & resolutio men- tis, pusillanimitas exercitationis, odium professionis, mundanorum beatificatrix, detractrix Dei quasi in- viscerosi, & existentis sine benignitate, attonita in Psalmodia, infirmans in oratione, in ministerio fer- rea, in opere manuum pigra, in obedientia improba. Unde Cassian. l. c. observante, sæpe vidimus de frigi- dis atque carnalibus, id est, de secularibus ac paga- nis ad spiritualem pervenire fervorem, de tepidis at- que animalibus omnino non vidimus. Chrysostomus libr. de lapsu. Radix, ait, desperationis est ignavia, & non solum radix, sed est nutrix ejus & mater. Nam sicut vestimentum & tineam generat & nutrit: Ita ignavia non solum gignit ex se desperationem, sed alit & fovet. Accipienda autem illa, utinam frigi- dus esses potius quam tepidus, non absolute, sed cum exceptione resipiscentiæ, h. e. nisi resipiscas, quo- niam officii conscientia neglectum illius & pœnam graviorem reddit, Luc. XII, 44. 45. Frigidi etiam ideo meliores sunt, quod animi sui mentem profe- rant, nec aliud verbis ostentent, aliud in pectore occultent: & quia sæpe ignorantia peccant, putan- tes se cultum verum præstare Deo, 1. Tim. I, 13. Joh. XVI, 2. ideo meliora edocti præclaros emendatio- nis fructus ferunt, aut graviorum sibi criminum conscii citius lucrisiunt, Matth. XXI, 31. 32. Quum ex adverso tepidi contraria simul admittant, ac pa- riter Jehovæ & Baali, pariter Christo & Belial, pa- riter Deo & ventri vel Mammonæ servire posse au- tument, 2. Reg. XVII. Matth. VI, 24. 2. Cor. VI, 15. Rom. XVI, 18. Phil. III, 19. Sunt quasi animalia am- phibia, & ut Victorinus loquitur, ad omnes omnia sunt. ψυχροὶ frigidi, inquit B. Glassius Rhet. Sacr. p. 265. in eo respectu tepidorum, laudabiles sunt, quod palam profitentur, quales sint, neque aliud verbis, aliud pectore claudunt: cum cæcitate naturæ laborent, si de melioribus edoceantur, sæpe laudabiliter emen- dantur: quod in tepidis, pietatis speciem habentibus, & vim ejus abnegantibus, vix sperari potest. Sensus igitur est: In extremis gradibus oportebat te esse posi- tum, ut dijudicari possis. Non ergo tepidus hoc lo- co est, qui de charitate nonnihil remittit, ecquis enim ita non possit facile ambiguus reddi, numne satis fervidus sit? nec abs re monet Andr. Cæsar. in operibus sane, quod medium servat, non est re- spuendum: in fine autem medium seu tepidum ab omnibus improbatur.

Οὕτως ὅτι χλιαρὸς εἶ.] Οὕτως hic valet אל־כן igitur. In glossario χλιαρὸν tepidum. Utuntur Aristoteles, Galenus & alii. χλιαρὸς סכך. Hos dubios vocat Hermas III, 8. Καὶ ὐ ζεσὸς, ὔτε ψυχρὸς.] Clarius explicat,quid sit χλιαρὸς. Μέλλω σε ἐμέσαι ἐκ τῦ ςόματός μ8.] Prosequitur compara- tionem. Tepida sunt ἐμετικὰ, Celsus I, 2. Qui vomere post cibum solet, si ex facili facit, aquam tanquam tepidam ante debet assumere. Significat autem Christus tales homines sibi esse molestos, sicut illæ, quæ nauseam movent. Evomit Chri- stus, quos admonere desinit. Par translatione cum quis dici- tur rem aliquam concoquere non posse.

Vocem μέλλω, pro qua in Vulgata habetur vox incipiam, B. Hoë observat, Deum non plenas iræ suæ cataractas super nos protinus effundere, sed gradatim in immittendis pœnis procedere, quem- admodum exemplo Pharaonis constat: B. Cluve- rus Græcam vocem premit. Non præcise, ait, evomui aut evomam,sed cunctabundus quasi μέλ- λω σε ἐμέσαι, hoc est, in eo sum, ut evomam, nisi scilicet pœnitentiam egeris, quam vers. 19. impe- rat, & gravissimis rationibus urget & flagitat, Ps. CIII, 8.

## 3:17
Vers. 17. Ὅτι λέγεις πλύσιός εἰμι καὶ πεπλύτηκα, καὶ ὐδενὸς χρείαν ἔχω.] It is a gradation. It is much to be rich: but more, when he is rich, to be further enriched: but the greatest is to be in need of absolutely nothing. Such do they seem to themselves, who feel some kind of faith in themselves, and profess Christianity: and when they have these, they think nothing is lacking to them for salvation. See James 2:25. A figure of such are the Israelites of the ten tribes, who also said they were rich, Zech. 12:8. Καὶ ἐκ οἶδας, ὅτι σὺ εἶ ὁ ταλαίπωρος καὶ ὁ ἐλεεινὸς.] He shows that he who thought himself happy is so unhappy that he ought to move the mercy of all: and that in the highest degree, which the added article indicates. Ταλαίπωρος is שרוד, Judg. 5:27. Καὶ πλωχὸς.] Needy of things necessary for salvation. Καὶ τυφλός.] Not seeing how miserable you are. He said τυφλὸν by way of increase for one who is blear-eyed, as will appear below. Καὶ γυμνὸς.] Lacking justice, which is the clothing of Christians. Below 19:8.

He explains what he had said, because you are lukewarm, that is, partly bad, partly good, bad secretly, good apparently: hence you stroke yourself, please yourself, are proud, presume, as if all things were going well with you in every respect. For you say the opposite by grace of faith and virtues: and I am in need of nothing to obtain perseverance and salvation: whereas if you were cold, you would already feel by the very biting cold that you are naked, deprived of the garment of righteousness, blind, lacking spiritual intelligence, not acknowledging your poverty, not hungering or thirsting for righteousness, Matt. V, 6. poor, destitute of faith and charity, and truly miserable, pitiable on account of the guilt of sin and the most present destruction of damnation. You do not know what, with your heart explored and weighed according to the standard of the divine word, you ought most of all to know, 1 Cor. 11, 28. 1 Cor. 13, 5. Gal. 6, 4. Gregor. lib. 34. Moral. c. 2. He asserts that he is rich, who is exalted through arrogance, but he is proven poor, blind, naked: Poor, because he does not have the riches of virtues; blind, because he does not see the poverty which he suffers; naked, because he has lost the first robe: But it is worse, because he does not even acknowledge that he has lost it. He calls him first miserable in soul and body ταλαίπωρον Rom. VIII, 24. into which misery sin precipitates us: then ἐλεεινὸν, pitiable, on account of the death and condemnation which sin brings: whose misery is known more to others than to the miserable man himself. Rom. 6. last. Deut. 27, 26. Gal. 3, 10. Furthermore πτωχὸν on account of spiritual poverty, because he is destitute of all virtues Luke 21, 21. Ps. 14, 3. c. 53, 4. Rom. 3, 20. 21. Eph. 4, 18. 19. τυφλὸν without increase, utterly blind, Job 9, 40. Matt. 15, 14. Whose thoughts the god of this world has blinded, 2 Cor. 4, 4. Eph. 4, 18. c. 5, 14. 2 Pet. 1, 9. and γυμνὸν naked, lacking the garment of righteousness. Conf. Luke XVI, 15. c. XIX, 5. Prov. XXXI, 2.

Latin:

Vers. 17. Ὅτι λέγεις πλύσιός εἰμι καὶ πεπλύτηκα, καὶ ὐδενὸς χρείαν ἔχω.] Est gradatio. Multum est, divitem esse: plus vero, cum dives sit, adhuc locupletari: maximum vero nul- lius plane rei indigere. Tales sibi videntur,qui fidem qualem- cunque in se sentiunt, & Christianismum profitentur: & hæc cum habeant, putant sibi nihil deesse ad salutem. Vide Jac. II, 25. Talium figura Israelitæ decem tribuum, qui & ipsi se divites dicebant, Zach. XII, 8. Καὶ ἐκ οἶδας, ὅτι σὺ εἶ ὁ ταλαίπωρος καὶ ὁ ἐλεεινὸς. ] Eum, qui felicem se putabat, ostendit ita esse infelicem, ut omni- um misericordiam commovere debeat: idque in summo gra- du, quod indicat appositus articulus. Ταλαίπωρος שרוד, Judic. V, 27. Καὶ πλωχὸς.] Egens rerum ad salutem necessariarum. Καὶ τυφλός.] Non videns, quam sis miser. Τυφλὸν dixit κατ' αὔξησιν pro lippiente, ut infra apparebit. Καὶ γυμνὸς.] Carens justitia, quæ vestitus est Christiano- rum. Infra XIX, 8.

Explicat, quod dixerat, quia tepidus es, id est, partim malus, partim bonus, malus occulte, bonus apparenter:hinc teipsum palpas,tibi places,super- bis,præsumis,quasi bene omni ex parte tecum age- retur. Dicis enim diversum gratia fide & virtuti- bus: & nullius egeo ad perseverantiam & salutem consequendam: quod si frigidus esses, jam ipso fri- gore pungente sentires, quod sis nudus, privatus veste justitiæ, cæcus, intelligentia spirituali carens, non agnoscens tuam egestatem, non esuriens aut sitiens justitiam, Matth. V, 6. pauper, fide ac chari- tate destitutus, & vere miser, miserabilis ob peccati culpam & præsentissimum damnationis exitium. Non nosti, quod explorato corde tuo, & ad nor- mam verbi divini expenso maxime scire debebas, 1. Cor. 11, 28. 1. Cor. 13, 5. Galat. 6, 4. Gregor. lib. 34. Moral. c. 2. Divitem se esse asserit, qui per arrogan- tiam extollitur, sed pauper, cæcus, nudus arguitur: Pauper,quia virtutum divitias non habet; cæcus,quia nec paupertatem, quam patitur, videt; nudus, quia primam stolam amisit: Sed pejus est, quia nec se perdidisse agnoscit. Miserum primum dicit anima & corpore ταλαίπωρον Rom. IIX, 24. in quam mi- seriam nos peccatum præcipitat: deinde ἐλεεινὸν, miserabilem, ob mortem & condemnationem, quam peccatum affert:cujus miseria magis est aliis, quam ipsi misero cognita. Rom. 6. ult. Deut. 27, 26. Gal. 3, 10. Adhæc πλωχὸν ob paupertatem spiri- tualem,quod omnibus virtutibus destituatur Luc. 21, 21. Psal.14, 3. c.53,4. Rom.3, 20. 21. Eph. 4, 18. 19. τυφλὸν sine ἀυξήσει prorsus cæcum, Job. 9, 40. Matth.15, 14. Cui excæcavit Deus hujus mundi τὰ νοήματα, 2.Cor. 4, 4. Eph. 4, 18. c. 5, 14. 2. Petr.I,9. & γυμνὸν nudum justitiæ veste carentem. Conf. Luc. XVI, 15. c. XIX, 5. Prov. XXXI, 2.

## 3:18
Ver. 18. I counsel thee.) He could have commanded. But he prefers to assume the role of one advising, because that which he is about to say is most useful to this Bishop and those like him. Buy gold of me.) To buy is to acquire with some labor, as Prov. 3:14, 23:23. Gold here is a permanent affection, through which God and neighbor are loved. It is acquired by the taming of the flesh and assiduous prayers. See Matt. 13:45. Tried in the fire.) Proved by fire. For ἐκ as the Hebrew מן is often a mark of the instrument. Πυρῶν is to prove, to refine. The best gold is that which has been thoroughly purified by fire. See above 1:15. That thou mayest be rich.) That you may receive greater gifts daily, not in opinion, but in reality, 1 Tim. 6:17, Tit. 3:6, 1 Cor. 4:8, 2 Cor. 8:9. And white raiment that thou mayest be clothed.) That you may also acquire for yourself splendid garments with which to be clothed, that is, works proceeding from love. Lest the shame of thy nakedness appear.) ערוה which is translated now as shame, now as nakedness. This saying is therefore like earth of clay, twice the same. But shameful parts through figurative speech signify sins. These in a man who has been amended no longer appear. God does not remember them. And anoint thine eyes with eyesalve, that thou mayest see.) Anatolius also writes collyrium. Others wish it to be written κολύριον from the fact that it checks the flow, because it stops a flux: others collyrium, because it is made in the form of a certain bread. You have some descriptions of eyesalves against diseases of the eye in the sixth book of Celsus, where he also says to anoint, which is here ἐγχρίειν. This manuscript has ἐγχρίσαι thine eyes, that is, obtain from God a clear view of the mysteries of God and of future things.

To buy here is not to acquire with any labor; but freely, and without money, as Is. 55:1, 2. God himself explains: You who have no silver, make haste, buy, come, buy without silver and any exchange. Why do you weigh out silver not for bread and your labor not for satiety. Buy, he says, without silver. For he did not seek a price from us, who paid the price of his own blood for us, says Ambrose, book on Joseph, ch. VII. What can a miserable and wretched man, what can a poor and naked man contribute of his own? what price to bring? and how shall a blind man work, that he may receive sight? The gloss of Grotius savors of Pelagianism and Popery. To Thomas Anglicus, buying is a disposition of free will: Dionysius the Carthusian. Buy, he says, with a price, not condign, but congruous; for acts of faith, hope, repentance, and others are prices, that is, dispositions, by which this grace is bought with great labor, that is, acquired, as here Cornelius, who nevertheless does not hesitate here to praise the theologian's opinion: Nazianzen, he says, in his oration on Holy Baptism, answers: That God, because of his immense goodness, by which he desires our salvation, esteems our desire for grace and salvation as a price. O wonderful speed of beneficence, exclaims Nazianzen! O easy method of contracting! This good is proposed to you to be bought with the sole price of the will; God esteems the appetite itself in place of a great price: he thirsts to be thirsted for, he offers drink to those desiring to drink; when a benefit is sought from God, he thinks himself to be benefited: he is a prompt, munificent, and prolix nature, he gives more pleasantly than others receive. Moreover, the Apostle testifies that God also works that willing, Phil. 2:13. It is God who works in you both to will and to perform. He prescribes, therefore, a counsel and a remedy, but one which he himself has in his own hand, and wishes to impart liberally, he requires only our receiving; that what he offers freely, and can alone confer, may be received by the hand of faith. Against troubles, misery, and poverty, the most purified gold of unfeigned faith, by which he may become rich in faith, and be rich in the Lord, 1 Pet. 1:7, 1 Tim. 1:5, 2 Tim. 1:5, Jas. 2:5, Luke 12:21, Jer. 9:23, 24, 1 Cor. 1:29, 30, 31. For faith is the gift and work of the Lord, John 6:29, Phil. 1:29. And it arises from the word of God, which is purer and more precious than all gold, and through it is given to us, Rom. 10:17, Ps. 19:11, Ps. 119:7, Prov. 30:5, 1 Cor. 1:5, Col. 2:2. I counsel thee, that thou mayest acquire from me for thyself the true knowledge of God and faith through true repentance, diligent meditation on the word, and devout prayer, that thou mayest become rich in all knowledge and doctrine, 1 Cor. 1:5, rich in faith Jas. 2:5. Against nakedness, the white garments of the most perfect righteousness of Christ, whom we put on through faith Gal. 3:27, Rev. 19:8, which alone can cover the shame of our nakedness Gen. 3:7, 21, Is. 64:16, which Christ alone provides for us. From me, he says, acquire for thyself those garments: by whose blood the stoles of the saints are made white, Rev. 7:14, and who clothes us with the garments of salvation, and surrounds us with the robe of righteousness, as a bridegroom adorned, Is. 61:10, that we may shine with the righteousness of the Bridegroom himself, Ps. 45:8, ff. Cf. Luke 15:22. Against blindness he provides the remedy of the eyesalve of the Holy Spirit, which is conferred by oil, Ps. 45:8, by which, through the medium of the word, the eyes of our mind are anointed and illuminated, that we may see, Eph. 1:18, 1 John 2:7. By the author B. Gerhard it is most simply explained thus: Groan to God, that he may give you through the word and the Holy Spirit illuminated eyes of the intellect, Eph. 1:18, that, liberated from spiritual blindness, you may salutarily acknowledge me as Savior and the mediator of your soul.

Latin:

Vers. 18. Συμβουλεύω σοι.) Poterat imperare. Sed mavult suadentis personam sumere, quia id, quod dicturus est, isti E- piscopo & ejus similibus est utilissimum. Ἀγοράσαι χρυσίον παρ' ἐμὲ.) Emere est comparare cum ali- quo labore, ut Proverb. III, 14. XXIII, 23. Aurum hic est af- fectus permanens, per quem diligitur Deus & proximus. Is comparatur edomatione carnis & precibus assiduis. Vide Matth. XIII, 45. Πεπυρωμένον ἐκ πυρὸς.) Probatum igne. Nam ἐκ ut מן Ebræum sæpe nota est instrumenti. Πυρῶν est probare, exco- quere. Aurum optimum est, quod igne perpurgatum est. Vi- de supra I, 15. Ἵνα πλουτήσῃς.) Ut majora indies dona accipias, non in opinione, sed in re, 1. Tim. VI, 17. Tit. III, 6. 1. Cor. IV, 8. 2. Cor. IIX, 9. Καὶ ἱμάτια λευκὰ ἵνα περιβάλῃ.) Compares tibi etiam splen- didas vestes, quibus amiciaris, id est, opera ex dilectione pro- cedentia. Μὴ φανερωθῇ ἡ αἰσχύνη τῆς γυμνότητός σου.) ערוה quod modo αἰσχύνη, modo γύμνωσις vertitur. Est ergo hoc dictum, sicut terra luti bis idem. Pudenda autem per figuratam locu- tionem significant peccata. Ea in homine emendato non amplius apparent. Non meminit eorum Deus. Καὶ κολλύριον ἔγχρισον ἐπὶ τοὺς ὀφθαλμούς σου, ἵνα βλέπῃς.) Κολλύριον scribit & Anatolius. Alii volunt κολύριον scribi πα- ρὰ τὸ κολλύειν τὸ ῥεῦν, quod fluxum sistat: alii κολλύριον, quod fiat ad formam panis cujusdam. Collyriorum adversus oculi morbos descriptiones habes aliquas libro sexto Celsi, ubi & inungere dicit, quod hic ἐγχρίειν. Manuscriptus hic ἐγχρίσαι τοὺς ὀφθαλμούς, id est, impetra a Deo clarum conspectum my- steriorum Dei & rerum futurarum.

Emere hic non est cum labore aliquo compara- re; sed gratis, & sine pecunia, ut Es. 55, 1.2. Deus ipse explicat: Qui non habetis argentum, properate, emi- te, venite, emite absq; argento & ulla commutatione. Quare appenditis argentum non in panibus & labo- rem vestrum non in saturitate. Emite, inquit, sine ar- gento. Neque enim pretium quæsivit à nobis, qui pro nobis pretium sanguinis sui solvit, ait Ambrof. lib. de Joseph. c. VII. Quid miser & miserabilis, quid pau- per & nudus de suo conferre possit? quod afferre pretium? & quomodo cæcus operabitur, ut visum recipiat? Sapit glossa Grotii Pelagianismum & Pa- pismum. Thomæ Anglico emptio est dispositio liberi arbitrii: Dionysius Carthusian. Eme, inquit, pretio, non condigno, sed congruo; actus enim fidei, spei, pœ- nitentiæ, aliique sunt pretia, id est, dispositiones, qui- bus magno labore emitur, id est, comparatur hæc gra- tia, ut hic Cornelius, qui tamen hic laudare non du- bitat Theologi sententiam: Nazianzenus, inquit, orat. in S. Baptisma respondet: Deum ob ingentem suam bonitatem, qua nostram salutem optat, nostrum desiderium gratiæ & salutis æstimare pro pretio. O miram, exclamat Nazianzenus, beneficentia cele- ritatem! O facilem contrahendi rationem! Hoc bonum solo voluntatis pretio emendum tibi pro- ponitur; appetitionem ipsam Deus ingentis pretii loco æstimat: sitit sitiri, bibere cupientibus potum præbet; cum à Deo beneficium petitur, beneficio se affici putat: prompta, munifica ac prolixa natura est, jucundius dat, quam alii accipiunt. Illud autem velle etiam Deum operari testatur Apostolus Phil. II, 13. Deus est, qui operatur in vobis & velle & per- ficere. Consilium itaq; & remedium præscribit, sed quod ipse in manu sua habet, & liberaliter imperti- re vult, requirit tantum nostram λῆψιν; ut manu fi- dei accipiatur, quod gratis offert, ac solus conferre potest. Adversus ærumnas, miseriam, & egestatem aurum fidei infucatæ purgatissimum, quo in fide ditescat, & in Domino divers sit, 1. Pet. I, 7. 1. Tim. I, 5. 2. Tim. I, 5. Jac. II, 5. Luc. XII, 21. Jer. IX, 23. 24. 1. Cor. I, 29. 30. 31. Donum enim & opus Domini est fides, Joh. VI, 29. Phil. I, 29. Et è verbo Dei, quod omni auro mundius & pretiosius oritur, ac per illud no- bis donatur, Rom. X, 17. Psal. XIX, 11. Pf. CXIX, 7. Prov. XXX, 5. 1. Cor. I, 5. Col. II, 2. Suadeo tibi, ut ve- ram Dei cognitionem & fidem per veram pœni- tentiam, sedulam verbi meditationem, ac devotam orationem a me mihi compares, ut dives fias in omni cognitione & doctrina, 1. Cor. I, 5. dives fide Jac. II, 5. Contra nuditatem vestimenta alba justi- tiæ Christi perfectissimæ, quem induimus per fidem Gal. III, 27. Apoc. XIX, 8. quæ sola nuditatis nostræ turpitudinem tegere potest Gen. III, 7. 21. Es. LXIV, 16. quæ solus Christus nobis præbet. Παρ᾽ ἐμοῦ in- quit, a me tibi compara illa vestimenta: cujus san- guine dealbantur stolæ sanctorum, Apoc. VII, 14. quique induit vestimentis salutis, & circumdat nos indumento justitiæ, quasi sponsum decoratum, Es. 61, 10. ut justitia ipsius Sponsi nostri coruscemus, Pfal. 45, 8. feqq. Conf. Luc. 15, 22. Contra cæcita- tem remedium præbet collyrium Spiritus sancti, qui oleo confertur, Pf. 45, 8. quo, mediante verbo, inunguntur & illuminantur oculi mentis nostræ, ut videamus, Eph. I, 18. 1. Joh. II, 27. B. Gerharde Autore simplicissime sic exponitur: Ingemisce ad De- um, ut det tibi per verbum & Spiritum sanctum illu- minatos oculos intellectus, Eph. I, 18. ut a spirituali cæcitate liberatus me Salvatorem & animæ tuæ me- dium salutariter agnoscas.

## 3:19
Ver. 19. As many as I love.) That is, those whom I have not decided to cast off and harden entirely because of long-standing sins. For here φιλῶ is said not absolutely, but comparatively, as elsewhere μισεῖν. See 2 Cor. 2:24, Gal. 6:11.

Ελέγχω καὶ παιδεύω.) I rebuke with words, I chastise with blows. Thus you have the word ἐλέγχω in John 8:46, 1 Tim. 5:20; but παιδεύειν in 1 Cor. 11:32, 1 Tim. 1:20, Heb. 12:7. The words are taken from Prov. 3:12.

Ζήλωσον ὖν.) Grow warm, you who are lukewarm: for ardent love is called ζῆλος, קִנְאָה, Num. 11:29, Psalm 69:10, and elsewhere. In the manuscript: Ζήλευε ὖν.

He gives the reason why he rebuked the Bishop so severely, because it was done out of affection and fatherly love. Cf. Ps. 28:33, Job 5:17, 1 Cor. 10:13. It is better to be corrected by God on account of sins than to be pampered and fattened for punishment, Prov. 27:16, Job 21:7, 17, Ps. 73:3, 18, Jer. 12:1 ff., Mal. 3:15. Concerning zeal and the fervor of piety, see John 2:17, 1 Cor. 11:31, 2 Cor. 7:11, ch. 11:2, Gal. 4:14, Tit. 2:14.

Καὶ μετανοήσον.) Out of love for me, correct your life. You see here the alternating actions of Christ and men regarding conversion.

Μετανοεῖν brings about a transformation of the mind for the better, Rom. 12:2, which, just as it does not exist without the sorrow of preceding sin, so it is also inseparably joined with faith effective through charity; indeed, it intimately embraces the same. Which, therefore, is not our work or of our own powers, but of divine grace, Jer. 31:18, Ezek. 36:26, Ps. 51:12.

Latin:

Verf. 19. Ἐγὼ ὅσους ἐὰν φιλῶ.) Id est, quos non plane ob diuturna peccata abjicere & obdurare constitui. Dicitur enim hic φιλῶ non absolute, sed comparate, ut alibi μισεῖν. Vide 2. Cor. 2, 24. Gal. 6, 11.

Ελέγχω καὶ παιδεύω.) Reprehendo verbis, castigo verbe- ribus. Sic verbum ἐλέγχειν habes Joh. 8, 46. 1. Tim. 5, 20. παι- δεύειν vero 1. Cor. 11, 32. 1. Tim. I, 20. Ebr. 12, 7. Sumpta verba ex Proverb. 3, 12.

Ζήλωσον ὖν.) Incalesce tu tepide: Nam ardens amor ζῆλος dicitur קִנְאָה Num. 11, 29. Psalm. 69, 10. & alibi. In Manu- scripto: Ζήλευε ὖν.

Causam reddit, cur Episcopum tam severe ob- jurgarit, quod id factum ex affectu & amore pater- no. Conf. Pf. XXVIII, 33. Job. V, 17. 1. Cor. X, 13. Præ- stat a Deo corripi propter peccata, quam foveri & ad pœnam saginari Prov. XXVII, 16. Job. XXI, 7. 17. Pf. LXXIII, 3. 18. Jer. XII, 1. feqq. Mal. III, 15. De ze- lo deque fervore pietatis vid. Joh. II, 17. 1. Cor. XI, 31. 2. Cor. VII, 11. c. XI, 2. Gal. IV, 14. Tit. II, 14.

Καὶ μετανοήσον.) Ex amore in me vitam corrige. Vides hic alternas circa conversionem actiones Christi & hominum.

Μετανοεῖν infert animi in melius transmutatio- nem, Rom. XII, 2. quæ sicut absque dolore antece- dentis peccati non est: sic etiam cum fide per cha- ritatem efficaci inseparabiliter conjuncta est, imo eandem intime complectitur. Quæ proinde non nostrum opus aut virium nostrarum, sed gratiæ di- vinæ est, Jer. 31, 18. Ezech. 36, 26. Psal. 51, 12.

## 3:20
Verf. 20. ἰδού ἕστηκα ἐπὶ τὴν θύραν κὶ κρούω.) He returns to the door but in a different sense, just as the shepherd simile is used in various ways in John 10. But someone might say, why does he who has the key knock? I will say, because a bolt was fastened to the door, which had to be removed. That bolt is the habit of sinning.

Ἐάν τις ἀκούσῃ τῆς φωνῆς με.) For those who knock are accustomed to call out at the same time, 'Open,' as in comedies. And this calling and knocking signify thoughts injected by God to warn the sinner's conscience. God does this for some time, not always. For he hardens many who are stubborn.

Καὶ ἀνοίξῃ τὴν θύραν.) If he admits the salutary warnings.

Καὶ εἰσελεύσομαι πρὸς ἀυτόν.) And here is redundant in the Hebrew manner. And it is absent in certain codices. Nor does the Latin read it. Christ enters where he gives his Spirit.

Ecce, sto ad ostium cordis, Cant. 5:5 ff., with my Spirit, so that it may be opened by his grace, Acts 16:16, and I knock, so that I may awaken the dormant and dead soul. Christ knocks, however, as blessed Gerhard teaches, 1. by the hammer of the law. 2. By the hammer of the cross. 3. By the hammer of death, to which add the knocking of miracles and prodigious operation, by which he is also accustomed to awaken the sleeping world, Luke 23:47, 54. He knocks 1. by external calling. 2. By internal impulse and address. It is signified, however, that he awaits the conversion of men, and offers them his grace and heavenly benefits, through the preaching of the word Is. LXV, 2. Nor does he only knock with the hammer of the law, Jer. XXIII, 29, but primarily also with the scepter and power of the Gospel, Ps. XLV, 7; CX, 2; for he uses both staves, both the sad or bitter and the pleasant, Zech. 11, 7, because by knocking he grants the power of opening, which efficacy is proper to the word of the Gospel, Rom. 1, 16. And therefore when his voice or the word of grace, Eph. I, 14, which is Spirit and life, John VI, 63, is joined with the efficacious knocking; by which it is brought about that the door is opened, through which also the Lord enters to us, that he may dwell in us through faith, John 14, 23; Eph. III, 17; Prov. I, 30; ch. IX, 1, seqq. It is evident, however, from this that God is not anticipated by the free will of man, but anticipates us through exciting grace, John VI, 44, and that man can fail to respond to God who excites and calls out, can stop up his ears and heart, and keep the door of his soul closed, Prov. I, 24; Ps. 95, 8; Is. 65, 2; Acts 7, 51; Matt. 23, 37. To Bellarmine, book I, ch. 11, on grace and free will, who urges this passage: if they do not have the sufficient aid of opening, why, I ask, does the Lord knock? Is he therefore ignorant that they cannot open? Gomarus answers: It does not follow: man ought to open to Christ who knocks: therefore he can by the powers of free will; since in this way the duty of man is denoted, to which he is bound, but not the natural faculty of performing it. For what Bellarmine objects, that this is repugnant to the knowledge and wisdom of God: that he would knock at a door where there is no one inside who can open; that is deservedly denied: since the knocking pertains to convincing the proud deafness and contumacy of the reprobate, Is. VI, 10, and Job XII, 20. and it is an instrument of the conversion of the elect: which God, as he teaches and demands outwardly by the word, so he effects inwardly by his Spirit, by regenerating the blind mind and the hardened will, and by endowing them with new qualities, as the sole cause by reason of the habit, and as the principal cause by reason of the operation: for by reason of the habit man is a mere subject, not a cause: but by reason of the operation he is a co-cause, cooperating with God, and therefore it is rightly attributed to God as the first and principal efficient cause, and also as the helper: but to man as a cause not coordinated with the powers of supernatural regeneration, who is endowed with spiritual life, whence he produces the actions of life; nor is he only acted upon by the Spirit, but he also acts under the Spirit and with the Spirit. Add the explanation of Ludovicus de Ponte on the parallel passage Cant. V, 2, book VIII, in Cant. Exhort. 8. which is as follows: That voice 'open' is to be taken by way of an efficacious command, in the manner in which Christ the Lord said to the deaf and dumb man 'Ephphatha', which is 'be opened', and immediately his ears were opened, Mark VII, 34. But since the Lord was accustomed to heal the whole man outwardly and inwardly through his miracles, the efficacy of that voice toward the body indicated the efficacy of the internal voice toward the soul, to which he also said 'be opened' to hear and speak what I command you, by the power of which (note) the soul immediately, although freely, obeyed the voice of the Lord and decided to fulfill the commands. The efficacy of this voice is shown when Christ the Lord raised three dead persons with a single voice, saying: 'Maiden, or young man, arise', etc. Matthew was dead when he said to him: 'Follow me', and with this single voice he granted him life, because he soon gave his consent rejoicing. For he had scarcely said to Saul: 'I am Jesus of Nazareth, whom you persecute', when he opened the door of his heart, saying, 'Lord, what do you want me to do?' Thus, therefore, when God says efficaciously to the breast: 'Open to me', he soon opens the door of the heart. For the voice so sounds in his heart that he wishes to open without delay. Whence man opens the door in such a way that God himself is also said to open, because man does not open except through the aid of grace coming from God, as St. Luke insinuated, speaking of the woman named Lydia, Acts XVI, 14. Whose heart, he says, the Lord opened to attend to those things which were said by Paul.

Whence the blessed Gerhard concludes, book II, Conf. Cathol. part 3, art. 22, ch. IV, p. 578: Therefore man opens the door of his heart not by the natural powers of free will, but by new powers given through preventing and exciting grace, just as those raised from natural death rise again not by their own powers, but by new powers given in the resurrection.

And I will sup with him, and he with me.] It is a great honor to have a King as a guest. But by the banquet is understood joy, both of Christ for the converted sinner, and of the converted sinner for Christ dwelling in him. For great joys are accustomed to be expressed by the similitude of banquets. Luke XII, 37; XV, 23.

Not only joy and gladness, but mutual communion, which is the cause of joy, is primarily designated. For he sups with us, and we with him, when he offers us spiritual food, the Manna of his word, and his flesh, himself, as that bread of life which came down from heaven: both in the word of the Gospel and in the sacrament of the Eucharist, John VI; 1 Cor. X, 16; and we enjoy his most sweet communion, which is a certain foretaste of the eternal banquet and of the marriage which he has prepared for his bride, Is. XXV, 65; Matt. VIII, 11; Rev. XIX, 7. Furthermore, Christ the bridegroom is affected in turn by the breasts of the bride, that is, by love, by ointments, that is, by spiritual gifts, by lips, that is, by prayers, confessions, and praises, Cant. IV, 10; ch. V, 1.

Latin:

Verf. 20. ἰδού ἕστηκα ἐπὶ τὴν θύραν κὶ κρούω.) Redit ad ostium sed alio sensu, sicut pastoris similitudo varie usurpatur Joh. X. At dicat aliquis, cur pulsat qui clavem habet? Dicam, quia pessulus erat obditus ostio, qui amoveri debebat. Is pessulus est peccandi consuetudo.

Ἐάν τις ἀκούσῃ τῆς φωνῆς με.) Nam solent qui pulsant simul clamare, aperi, ut in Comœdiis. Et clamor hic & pulsatio si- gnificant cogitata a Deo injecta ad monendam peccatoris conscientiam. Id Deus aliquandiu facit non semper. Multos enim sui contumaces obdurat.

Καὶ ἀνοίξῃ τὴν θύραν.) Si salutaria monita admittat.

Καὶ εἰσελεύσομαι πρὸς ἀυτόν.) Καὶ hic παρέλκει more E- bræo. Et abest in codicibus quibusdam. Neque legit Latinus. Intrat Christus, ubi Spiritum suum reddit.

Ecce, sto ad ostium cordis, Cant. V, 5. fqq. cum Spi- ritu meo, ut id aperiatur ejus virtute, Act. XVI, 16. & pulso, ut sopitam & mortuam animam excitem. Pulsat autem Christus, B. Gerhardo docente, 1. per malleum legis. 2. Per malleum crucis. 3. Per malleum mortis, quibus adde pulsum miraculorum, & prodi- giosæ operationis, quo etiam stertente mundū exci- tare solet, Luc. 23, 47. 54. Pulsat 1. per vocationem ex- teriore. 2. Per impulsum & affatū interiorem. Signifi- catur autem, quod expectet hominum conversionem, & offerat illis suam gratiam & beneficia cælestia, per verbi prædicationem Ef.LXV,2. Nec tantum pul- sat legis malleo, Jer. XXIII, 29. sed imprimis etiam sceptro, & virtute Evangelii, Psal. XLV, 7. CX, 2. utroque enim baculo utitur & tristi, vel acerbo & amæno, Zach.11,7. quia pulsando vim largitur ape- riendi, quæ efficacia verbo Evangelii propria est, Rom. 1,16. Ideoque cum pulsu efficaci vox ejus vel verbum gratiæ, Eph.I, 14. quod Spiritus est & vita, Joh.VI,63. conjunctum est; quo præstatur,ut janua aperiatur,per quod etiam ingreditur Dominus ad nos,ut per fidem habitet in nobis, Joh. 14, 23. Eph. III, 17. Prov. I, 30. c. IX, 1. seqq. Patet autem hinc, Deum non præveniri à libero hominis arbitrio,sed prævenire nos per excitantem gratiam, Joh.VI,44. ac posse hominem Deo excitanti & acclamanti non respondere, aures & cor obturare, & ostium animæ occlusum tenere, Prov. I, 24. Ps.95,8. Esa.65, 2. Act.7, 51. Matth. 23, 37. Bellarmino l. I. c. 11. de grat. & libero arbitr. hunc locum urgenti, si non habent sufficiens auxilium aperiendi, cur obsecro Dominus pulsat? an igitur ignorat,eos aperire non posse? Respondet Gomarus : Non sequitur : Christo pulsanti homo aperire debet : Ergo viribus liberi ar- bitrii potest ; siquidem denotatur hoc modo officium hominis, ad quod tenetur, non autem naturalis effici- endi facultas. Nam quod Bellarminus objicit, hoc re- pugnare Dei scientiæ & sapientiæ: quod pulsaret ostium, ubi nemo intus sit, qui aperire possit ; illud me- rito negatur : quoniam pulsatio pertinet ad reprobo- rum superbam surditatem & contumaciam convin- cendam, Es. VI, 10. & Job. XII, 20. & instrumentum est conversionis electorum: quam Deus, ut verbo do- cet atque exigit foris, sic suo Spiritu intus, mentem ca- cam & voluntatem obduratam regenerando, novisque qualitatibus donando efficit, ut causa sola ratione ha- bitus, & ut causa principalis ratione operationis: nam habitus ratione homo merum est subjectum, non cau- sa: operationis vero συναίτιον,cooperans Deo,ideoque recte Deo tribuitur, ut causæ primæ ac principali Effi- cienti, atque etiam adjuvanti: homini vero ut causæ non coordinatæ viribus regenerationis supernatura- lis, quæ vita spirituali donatur, unde actiones vitæ producit ; neque solum à Spiritu agitur, sed etiam sub Spiritu ac cum Spiritu agit.Addenda explicatio Lu- dovici de Ponte in locum Parallelum Cant. V, 2. libr. IIX. in Cant. Exhort.8. quæ ita habet: Vox illa ape- ri accipienda est per modum imperii efficacis, ad mo- dum, quo Christus Dominus homini surdo & muto dixit Ephatah, quod est adaperire, & statim aperta sunt aures ejus, Marc. VII.34. Cum autem Dominus per miracula sua totum hominem foris & intus sana- re consueverit, efficacitas illius vocis erga corpus indi- cabat efficacitatem vocis internæ erga animam, cui etiam dixit adaperire ad audiendum & loquen- dum, quæ tibi jubeo, virtute cujus (nota) statim ani- ma, etsi libere voci Domini obedivit, & implere jussa decrevit. Efficacia autem hujus vocis ostenditur, cum Christus Dominus tres mortuos unica voce suscitavit, dicens : Puella,vel adolescens, surge &c. Mortuus erat Matthæus, cum ei dixit: Sequere me, & hac unica voce largitus est ei vitam, quia mox gaudens consen- sum præstitit. Vix enim Saulo dixit: Ego sum Jesus Nazarenus, quem tu persequeris, cum aperuit ostium cordis, dicens, Domine, quid vis me facere ? Sic igitur cum Deus efficaciter pectori dicit: Aperi mihi, mox aperit ostium cordis. Ita enim vox sonat in corde ipsius, ut sine mora velit aperire. Unde ita homo aperit ja- nuam, quod ipse Deus etiam dicatur aperire, quo- niam homo non nisi per auxilium gratiæ à Deo pro- veniens aperit, sicut D. Lucas insinuavit, loquens de muliere Lydia nomine, Act. XVI, 14. Cujus Deus, in- quit,aperuit cor intendere iis, quæ dicebantur à Paulo.

Unde concludit B. Gerhardus l. II. Conf. Cathol. part. 3. art. 22. c. IV. p. 578. Ergo homo cordis ostium aperit non naturalibus liberi arbitrii viribus, sed novis per gratiam prævenientem & excitantem donatis viri- bus, sicut resuscitati ex morte naturali non suis, sed novis in resuscitatione datis viribus resurgunt.

Καὶ δειπνήσω μετ’ ἀυτῦ, καὶ ἀυτὸς μετ’ ἐμῦ.] Magnus ho- nos Regem habere convivam. Per convivium autem intelli- gitur gaudium, tum Christi ob conversum peccatorem, tum peccatoris conversi ob Christum in se habitantem. Solent enim magnæ lætitiæ exprimi conviviorum similitudine. Luc. XII, 37. XV, 23.

Non gaudium tantum & lætitia, sed mutua com- munio, quæ gaudii causa, imprimis designatur. Nã cœnat nobiscum, & nos cum ipso, cum præbet no- bis cibum spiritualem, Manna verbi sui, & carnem suam, seipsum, ceu panem illum vitæ, qui de cœlo venit: tum in verbo Evangelii, tum in sacramento Eucharistiæ Joh. VI. 1. Cor. X, 16. nosque ipso frui- mur suavissima ejus comunione, quæ πρόγευσμα quoddam convivii sempiterni & nuptiarum, quas sponsæ suæ præparavit, Es. XXV, 65. Matth. IIX, 11. Apoc. XIX, 7. Porro afficitur Christus sponsus vi- cissim uberibus sponsæ, hoc est, amore, unguentis, hoc est, donis spiritualibus, labiis, hoc est, precibus, confessionibus, laudibus, Cant. IV, 10. c. V, 1.

## 3:21
Vers. 21.

To him that overcometh I will give.) The same expression as above 12. He who shall have overcome, namely, the habit of sin.

To sit with me in my throne.) That is, on the throne which I will give to him. See above III, 21, and what was said there, and John XVII, 24.

As I also overcame.) All temptations. Concerning this victory, a mystical prediction in Isaiah 63.

And I sat down with my Father in his throne.) That is, in that throne which the Father gave to me. Psalm CX. Dan. VII, 9. 14. Matth. XXII, 44. below XXII, 1.

Rightly the throne of Christ, which he himself gives to the faithful, making them Kings before God, Apoc. I, 5. c. V, 10. from the throne of God the Father, in which Christ sat down, exalted to the right hand of God the Father, to the right hand of the Majesty on high, Psal. CX, 1. Heb. I, 3. For that is a great glory, but finite; this, however, is a glory truly immense and infinite, the glory of God the Father himself, to whose communion Christ has been raised according to his human nature, is signified. Hence the same throne is of God and the Lamb, Apoc. XXII, 1. and the same glory is offered to GOD and the Lamb, Apoc. V, 13. c. VII, 10. Which difference Pareus himself acknowledges: He says, I will not grant him to sit on the throne of the Father, which is the right hand of the Father, to sit at which is a dignity befitting only Christ the head, but on my throne. Conf. Heb. I, 13. The particle therefore ὡς denotes not parity, but some likeness, as often elsewhere Matth. V, 48. 1. Petr. III, 3. To sit with Christ on his throne is to be a participant in his kingdom and power over enemies, which is infinite to him and according to all fullness, οὐκ ἐκ μέτρου, not by measure, but to us it belongs κατὰ τὸ μέτρον τῆς δωρεᾶς according to the measure of his gift, John III, 34. Eph. IV, 7. The throne of God is unique, it is eternal and uncreated: the thrones of the blessed are many, and prepared by God, Matth. XXV, 31. 34. cap. XIX, 28. XX, 23. Luke XXII, 30. To sit on a throne, says Haymo, is to be a participant in the judicial power of Christ. The sense therefore is, I will grant that after victory he may reign with me in heaven 2. Tim. II, 12. Ap. II, 26. c. XXI, 5. Just as I conquered through passion, death, and resurrection, and sat down with the Father on his throne, Eph. I, 20. c. IV, 10. Alcafaris's gloss: To the throne of Christ perfect men are exalted, not in the future, but in this life, while they are placed in the seat of the highest peace, and as they sit and enjoy that peace, God subjects to them the motions of temptations, just as God subjects enemies to Christ sitting and reigning. For nothing more apt could be promised to one shaking off lukewarmness, that spiritual peace, which they who resolve to serve Him perfectly partake of from Christ, and that throne which they enjoy, and the mastery of their own affections: this cannot be approved even by His associate, Cornelius a Lapide. For he denies that this sense is literal and genuine. He wishes the prize of the heavenly kingdom to be promised. Finally, Gregory rightly advises in Homily XXXVII on the Gospel: Let the magnitude of the rewards delight the mind; but let not the struggle of labors deter it. For no one will be crowned unless he has struggled lawfully.

Latin:

Vers. 21.

Ὁ νικῶν δώσω ἀυτῷ.) Eadem loquutio, quæ supra 12. Qui vicerit, nempe peccati consuetudinem.

Καθίσαι μετ’ ἐμῦ ἐν τῷ θρόνῳ μ8.) Id est, in solio, quod ego ipsi dabo. Vide supra II, 26. & ibi dicta, & Joh. XVII, 24.

Ὡς κἀγὼ ἐνίκησα.) Tentationes omnes. De hac victoria mystica prædictio Esa. 63.

Καὶ ἐκάθισα μετὰ τῦ Πατρός με ἐν τῷ θρόνῳ ἀυτῦ.) Id est in eo solio, quod Pater mihi dedit. Psalm. CX. Dan. VII, 9. 14. Matth. XXII, 44. infra XXII, 1.

Recte thronus Christi, quem ipse dat fidelibus, faciens eos Reges coram Deo, Apoc. I, 5. c. V, 10. à throno Dei Patris, in quo consedit Christus, exal- tatus ad dextram Dei Patris, ad dextram Majestatis in excelsis Psal. CX, 1. Ebr. I, 3. Nam illo gloria ma- gna sed finita; hoc autem gloria vere immensa & infinita, ipsiusmet Dei Patris gloria, ad cujus com- munionem evectus est Christus secundum Huma- nam naturam innuitur. Hinc idem thronus est Dei & agni, Apoc. XXII, 1. eademque gloria DEO & Agno defertur, Apoc. V, 13. c. VII, 10. Quam diffe- rentiam agnoscit Pareus ipse: Non inquit dabo ei sedere in throno Patris, qui est dextra Patris, ad quam sedere dignitas est, soli Christo capiti conve- niens, sed in throno meo. Conf. Ebr. I, 13. Par- ticula ergo ὡς non paritatem, sed similitudinem ali- quam notat, ut sæpe alias Matth. V, 48. 1. Petr. III, 3. Sedere cum Christo in throno ejus, est esse parti- cipem regni & potestatis ejus super hostes, quæ ipsi infinita & secundum omnem plenitudinem, ἐκ ἐκ μέτρ8, non ad mensuram, nobis autem κατὰ τὸ μέ- τρον τῆς δωρεᾶς secundum mensuram doni ejusdem competit, Joh. III, 34. Eph. IV, 7. Thronus Dei uni- cus est, æternus est & increatus: throni beatorum plures sunt, & parati à Deo, Matth. XXV, 31. 34. cap. XIX, 28. XX, 23. Luc. XXII, 30. Sedere in thro- no, inquit Haymo, est participem esse judiciariæ potestatis Christi. Sensus itaque est, dabo, ut post victoriam mecum regnet in cœlo 2. Tim. II, 12. Ap. II, 26. c. XXI, 5. Sicut ego vici per passionem, mor- tem & resurrectionem, & consedi cum Patre in throno ejus, Eph. I, 20. c. IV, 10. Alcafaris glossa: Ad thronum Christi viri perfecti exaltantur, non in fu- tura, sed in hac vita, dum in altissimæ pacis sede collocantur, ac ipsis sedentibus & ea pace fruenti- bus Deus illis tentationum motus subjicit, sicut Chri- sto sedenti atque regnanti Deus subjicit inimicos. Ni- hil enim aptius promitti potuit teporem excutienti, quam pax illa spiritualis, quam a Christo partici- pant, qui ei perfecte servire decernunt, ac thronus ille quo fruuntur, & affectuum propriorum domi- natio: nec ipsi ejus socio, Cornelio a Lapide, pro- bari potest. Negat enim hunc sensum esse litera- lem & genuinum. Vult promitti brabeum regni cœlestis. Postremo recte monet Gregorius hom. XXXVII. in Evangel. Delectet mentem magnitu- do præmiorum; sed non deterreat certamen labo- rum. Nam non coronabitur, nisi qui legitime cer- taverit.

## 3:22
v. 22. He that hath an ear, let him hear what the Spirit saith unto the churches) Namely, to the Laodicean, and to others near to it.

Why should we understand as definite, and restrict to those churches, what is said indefinitely, with Christ not restricting it: For those things were said to the churches, so that all who have ears ought to hear. And therefore, even if they were said primarily to those churches; they nevertheless pertain to all, Rom. XVI. 4.

Latin:

v. 22. Ὁ ἔχων ὖς, ἀκουσάτω, τὶ τὸ Πνεῦμα λέγει ταῖς Ἐκκλη- σίαις) Nempe Laodicenæ, & aliis ei proximis.

Cur quod indefinite dicitur, non restringente Christo, nos definite intelligamus, & ad illas Ec- clesias restringamus: Illa enim dicta sunt Eccle- siis, ut audire debeant omnes, qui aures habent. Ideoque etsi πρώτως illis Ecclesiis sint dicta; ad omnes tamen pertinent, Rom. XVI. 4.

## 4:1 Argument
PART II. THE PROPHETIC APOCALYPSE, IN WHICH THE REVELATION OF FUTURE THINGS IN ALL THE CHURCHES IS COMPLETED IN SIX VISIONS. SECOND VISION, AND ITS I. PREPARATION. I. THE REVEALER OF FUTURE THINGS, THE TRIUNE GOD, GLORIOUSLY SEEN. CHAPTER IV. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

With the door of heaven opened, John is commanded to ascend and see, and he sees a throne, and One sitting upon it with great majesty, and twenty-four Elders as assessors on as many thrones with golden crowns, and the things which proceeded from that throne; also a sea of glass before the throne and four living creatures around the same, to whom, as they sing the trisagion and glorify God, the twenty-four Elders fall down before Him who sits on the throne, and, having cast down their crowns, celebrate Him as the Creator of all.

There are two parts: I. Things seen concerning the representation of Him who sits on the throne, to v. 8. II. Things heard concerning the celebration of the same in heaven, to v. 11.

PART I. Things seen concerning the representation of Him who sits on the throne.

Grotian Continuation.
