After the completed vision containing salutary warnings to the seven Bishops and Churches, under whose example other Bishops and Churches are also understood, there follow other visions which occurred to the Apostle at different times, and were afterwards reduced into one volume: which also happens in other prophecies, often even without the distinction of time being noted, but given to be understood from those things which are contained in each place. Now these visions pertain to the affairs of the Jews, up to the end of the twentieth chapter: then to the most flourishing state of the Christian Church up to the end. But just as the ancient Prophets do not touch upon Assyrian, Babylonian, or Egyptian affairs, except insofar as they are connected with Jewish affairs, that is, for predicting the evils which the Jews were to suffer from them, and in turn the punishments which God was about to exact from those nations, so that the pious might be forewarned against the foreseen evils, and in the evils themselves might receive comfort from the foreseen vengeance; so also here the Apostle predicts first the injuries of the Jews and Romans against the Christians, then the severe judgments of God against the Jews, and further against the idolatrous Romans, so that the Christians might understand that evils do not happen to them except by the singular disposition of God, nor are they neglected by God in the evils themselves, who has both predetermined certain times for those evils, and is about to exact most bitter punishments to avenge the blood of the martyrs. But just as Isaiah chapter VI. and Ezekiel chapter VIII., about to prefigure the judgments of God, see the divine Majesty and angelic service appearing in the Jerusalem temple; so also John in Patmos sees in an ecstasy the Majesty of God and Christ and the angelic service shining forth in heaven itself, and the leaders of the Jerusalem Church being assumed into it, so that they might contemplate future things with Him, and know that they are not only highly cared for by God, but also that they make one family with the angels of God and Christ: and that they are citizens of the heavenly fatherland by hope and by right, Phil. III. 20. Eph. II. 6. Heb. XII. 12.

Grotius errs heaven-wide in the economy of the visions; whatever may be the case regarding the time of the visions, about which we have warned somewhat in the Prolegomena. For that the visions pertain to the affairs of the Jews up to the end of chapter XI, then to the affairs of the Romans up to the end of chapter XX, then to the most flourishing state of the Christian Church up to the end, is an unheard-of distortion of the whole prophecy: and a commentary clearly arbitrary, of which not even an obscure trace is detected in the text; or has been able to be detected by any Interpreter thus far. And how would God have predicted here the fates of the Jews, whose temple and Republic had already been destroyed 25 years before? How can the affairs of the pagan Romans be considered to be exhibited up to the 20th chapter, when neither the visions, nor the times, for example those 1260 angelic days, that is, as many years, in any way fit? Furthermore, that the blessedness not of the militant, but of the triumphant Church is described in the last two chapters is as clear as when it is cloudless at midday. What, finally, do the leaders of the Jerusalem Church have to do with this? That they existed when this vision occurred will never be taught.

Another vision is indeed designated thus: After these things or after that vision of the Son of man described in chap. I., and the letters dictated by his command to the seven Angels by the Son of God himself, I saw, and behold, a door opened in heaven. The prior vision took place on earth, where he saw the Son of man walking in the midst of the seven golden candlesticks, that is, the Churches: The latter in the heavens, with the door of heaven opened to John. In the former he heard a person appearing with Majesty: in the other he did not hear God seen on a majestic throne. Furthermore, it is not clear that this vision happened at another time. Most Interpreters think that all those visions happened on the same Lord's day: nor does it seem necessary to some that a new ecstasy occurred here, not a continuation of the former, but only a higher illumination, which we leave to its own place. But unless those visions follow one another in order, nothing certain will easily be had from this revelation, which was truly made to that end, that in order, those things which are to follow in the Church, may be designated, therefore the numbers determining the times have also been expressed. But that such an ascension is commanded here, as was that of the Angels on Jacob's ladder, Gen. XXVIII, whence will it be proved? He could ascend to a certain point, but he did not ascend into heaven itself. For heaven can be opened everywhere, the Majesty of God can be displayed everywhere, as to Moses on the mountain, Exod. XXIV. 16, to Ezekiel beside the river Chebar, chap. I. 3, to Stephen on earth, Acts VII. 55. It is evident, however, from the summary compilation of those things which were to be shown, that not past or present things, but those which were then to be future, had been shown to John. Against which Cocceius brings forward in vain the instance concerning the book to be opened by the Lamb, chap. V, and concerning the Son born to the woman and caught up to the throne of God, chap. XII. For this latter was then still entirely among the things that are to be: but the former, with respect to St. John, to whom the vision was made, was likewise to be future: for when the book was first shown to him sealed, it was still to be unsealed for him at last, even though to Christ the Lamb of God and to God all things are naked and open, and have no need of unsealing, ἃ δεῖ γενέσθαι, which it BEHOOVES to happen, which is not an absolute necessity, but a hypothetical one on account of the divine decree. 1 Cor. XI. 9. Luke XVII. 1.

Latin:

PARS II. APOCALYPSEOS PROPHETICA, QUA REVELATIONEM FUTURORUM IN ECCLESIIS UNIVERSIS, SEX VISIONIBUS ABSOLUTA. VISIO SECUNDA, EJUSQUE I. PA- RASCEVE. I. REVELATOR FUTURORUM TRIUNUS DEUS GLORIOSE VISUS. CAPUT IV. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Aperto cæli ostio ascendere & videre jubetur Jo- hannes, videtque thronum, & in eo seden- tem cum magna majestate, ac assessores XXIV. Seniores in totidem thronis cum co- ronis aureis, & quæ e throno illo prodiere; necnon mare crystallinum coram throno & IV. animantia circa eundem, quibus trisa- gion concinentibus, & Deum glorificantibus concidunt XXIV. Seniores coram Sedente in throno, cumque, abjectis coronis, ceu Crea- torem omnium celebrant.

Partes duæ sunt I. Visa circa repræsentationem Sedentis in throno, ad v. 8. II. Audita quoad cele- brationem ejusdem in cælo, ad v. 11.

PARS I. Visa circa repræsentationem Sedentis in throno.

Συνέχεια Grotiana. Post absolutum visum monita salutaria continens ad se- ptem Episcopos & Ecclesias, sub quorum exemplo alii quoque Episcopi atque Ecclesiæ intelliguntur, sequuntur visa alia, quæ diversis temporibus Apostolo obtigere, & postea in unum volumen redacta sunt: quod & in prophe- tiis aliis evenit, sæpe etiam non annotato temporis discri- mine, sed dato intelligi ex iis, quæ loco quoque continen- tur. Pertinent autem hæc visa ad res Judæorum, usque ad finem capitis vicesimi: deinde ad statum florentissimum Ecclesiæ Christianæ ad finem usque. Sicut autem Prophetæ veteres non tangunt res Assyrias, Babylonicas, Ægyptias, nisi quatenus connexæ sunt cum rebus Judaicis, id est, ad prædicenda mala, quæ Judæi ab illis erant perpessuri, & rur- sum pœnas, quas ab illis gentibus sumpturus erat Deus, ut & præmunirentur pii adversus mala prævisa, & in ipsis ma- lis solatium acciperent ex prævisa ultione; ita & hic Apo- stolus prædicit primum injurias Judæorum & Romanorum in Christianos, deinde severa Dei judicia adversus Judæos, & porro adversus Romanos idololatras, ut intelligerent Christiani, neque sibi mala evenire, nisi singulari Dei dispo- situ, neque in ipsis malis se a Deo negligi, qui & certa tempora illis malis præfinierit, & acerbissima supplicia sumpturus sit ad vindicandum martyrum sanguinem. Sic- ut autem & Esaias cap. VI. & Ezechiel cap. VIII. præsigni- ficaturi Dei judicia, divinam Majestatem & Angelicum fa- mulatum vident in templo Hierosolymitano apparentem; ita & Johannes in Patmo videt ἐν ἐκςάσει Dei & Christi Ma- jestatem & Angelicum famulatum relucentem in ipso cœ- lo, & eo assumi præsides Ecclesiæ Hierosolymitanæ, ut cum ipso futura contemplentur, norintque, non tantum a Deo se summe curari, verum & unam se facere cum An- gelis Dei ac Christi familiam: & cives cœlestis patriæ se esse spe ac jure, Phil. III. 20. Eph. II. 6. Ebr. XII. 12.

Toto cœlo errat Grotius in οἰκονομίᾳ visorum; quicquid sit de visionum tempore, quo de nonni- hil in Prolegomenis monuimus. Nam ad res Judæo- rum visa usque ad finem cap. XI. pertinere, inde ad res Romanorum usque ad finem cap. XX. deinde ad statum florentissimum Ecclesiæ Christianæ ad finem usque, inaudita ςρεβλότης est totius prophe- tiæ: & commentarius plane arbitrarius, cujus ne obscuriusculum quidem vestigium in textu de- prehenditur; aut deprehendi hactenus ab ullo In- terprete potuit. Et quomodo prædixisset hic Deus fata Judæorum, quorum templum & Resp. jam ante 25. annos destructa erant? Quomodo res Romanorum gentilium usque ad XX. caput exhi- beri censeri potest, quum nec visiones, nec tem- pora v. g. illi 1260. dies Angelici, hoc est, totidem anni ullatenus quadrent? Porro non Ecclesiæ mi- litantis; sed triumphantis beatitudinem postre- mis duobus capitibus describi tam clarum est, quam cum sudum est in meridie. Quid denique Præsides Ecclesiæ Hierosolymitanæ huc faciunt? quos tum fuisse, cum hæc visio obtigit, nunquam docebitur.

Alia visio ita quidem designatur: Post hæc vel post visionem illam Filii hominis cap. I. descri- ptam, & expeditas jussu ejus literas, ad septem Angelos ab ipso Filio Dei dictatas, εἶδον vidi, καὶ ἰδὲ & ecce, ostium apertum in cœlo. Prior visio in terris facta, ubi vidit Filium hominis in medio septem candelabrorum aureorum, hoc est, Ec- clesiarum ambulantem: Posterior in cœlis, aper- to Johanni cœli ostio. In priori audivit personam cum Majestate apparentem: in altera Deum in throno Majestatico conspectum non audivit. Cæ- terum alio tempore hanc visionem accidisse non liquet. Plerique Interpretes omnes illas visiones eadem die Dominica contigisse censent: neque id necessum videtur quibusdam novam hic ecsta- sin, non prioris continuationem, sed altiorem solum illuminationem factam, quod nos suo lo- co relinquimus. Nisi autem ordine sese visa illa excipiant, nihil facile certi ex hac revelatione habebitur, quæ vero ea fini facta, ut ordine, quæ sequutura sint in Ecclesia, designentur, ideo nu- meri etiam tempora determinantes expressi sunt. Quod vero ascensio talis hic jubeatur, qualis An- gelorum fuit in scala Jacobæa Genes. XXVIII. un- de probabitur? Ascendere potuit aliquousque, sed in cœlum ipsum non ascendit. Ubique enim cœlum aperiri potest, ubique Majestas Dei exhi- beri, ut Mosi in monte Exod. XXIV. 16. Ezechie- li secus flumen Chobar cap. I. 3. Stephano in terra, Actor. VII. 55. Patet autem e summaria complexio- ne eorum, quæ ostendenda erant, non præterita, vel præsentia, sed quæ tum futura erant, Johanni exhibita fuisse. Ad quæ nequicquam instantiam Coccejus dat de libro ab Agno aperiendo, cap. V. de Filio mulieri nato, & ad thronum Dei rapto. cap. XII. Nam hoc posterius tum omnino adhuc erat inter τὰ μέλλοντα: Prius autem illud respe- ctu S. Johannis, cui visio facta, futurum itidem erat: nam quum primum liber ipsi obsignatus ex- hiberetur, adhuc ille demum ipsi resignandus erat, etsi Christo Agno Dei & Deo omnia sint nu- da & aperta, neque resignatione opus habeant, ἃ δεῖ γενέσθαι, quæ OPORTET fieri, quæ neces- sitas non est absoluta, sed hypothetica ob decre- tum divinum. 1. Cor. XI. 9. Luc. XVII. 1.

## 4:2
Ver. 2.

And immediately I was in the spirit) He did not ascend into heaven in body, but in an ecstasy, which is called Spirit also above I. 10.

Whether he ascended in body, or in mind alone, is not defined. St. John says only that he was caught up in the Spirit. Which is also certain concerning the rapture of Paul, who indeed does not know whether he was caught up in the body or indeed out of the body, 2 Cor. XII. 2, 3. Gomarus says that that ἐν πνεύματι, in the Spirit, is explained probably in two ways: either so that the Holy Spirit is understood as the author of the translation into heaven, as Paul says 2 Cor. XII. 4, I was caught up into Paradise: or so that it denotes the spirit or mind of John, that he was there by a vision of the mind, namely where he was called, that is, in heaven.

And behold a throne was set in heaven) Of God the Father as appears below 5. V. 7. So also Isaiah VI. 1 sees God on a throne, namely prepared for exercising judgments. Add Daniel VII. 9, where ἐτίθεσαν, which is ἔκειτο here. For κεῖσθαι is accustomed to mean the same as to be placed, as 1 Tim. I. 9, 1 Thess. III. 3. All these things allude to the old tabernacle. This throne corresponds to the sanctuary.

Even if it can be admitted that there is an allusion to the old tabernacle, yet the state of the New Testament is not exhibited by this; but as it was a figure of heavenly things there, the glorious state of the Elect in heaven is shadowed forth. But we are nowhere taught that the throne of divine Majesty corresponds to the sanctuary. For the sanctuary shadowed forth heaven, as the Apostle testifies, Heb. IX. 25. Grotius invents these things, so that he may teach that the state of the primitive Jerusalem Church is figured in this place. But this is a mere ἰδία ἐπίλυσις, hitherto unheard of in the Church, and in no way agreeing with the text, in which it is too clear that the divine Majesty in the heavens is represented to John as visible to the Elect, so that, namely, the author of the glorious revelation may be exhibited, and the authority and majesty of the revelation made to John may be shown.

And upon the throne one sitting) God the Father in the likeness of a King. Therefore that throne is called by the Hebrews כסא כובד, θρόνος δόξης, a Royal throne. In the Manuscript more briefly, and he who sits. Nor does the Latin say otherwise.

Interpreters vary in this place. Some, like Grotius here, wish God the Father, the first person of the most holy Trinity, to be presented; to whom also our blessed Cluverus accedes, because the Son, the Lamb, appears standing in the midst of the throne, and the seven lamps, illuminating all things before the throne, designate the Holy Spirit. Blessed Gerhard, with Blessed D. Hoë and others, judge that Christ is exhibited in this vision in his glory. But it is better in our judgment to say that here the Triune God, or the most holy Trinity, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, sitting on the throne, is figured: 1. because heavenly things, and things stored up in the divine secrets, in the counsel of the most holy Trinity, were to be manifested, which equally concern all three persons of the Divinity. 2. The Revealer of the ἀποκάλυψις seemed to be presented as the Triune God, just as afterwards Christ is exhibited as the biune resigner of the Apocalyptic book, chap. V. 3. The Trisagion is acclaimed by the four living creatures to the three persons of the most holy and undivided Trinity, not to one only. 4. Which the Seraphic Trisagion and the vision described in Is. VI more confirm, by which Catholic Doctors commonly acknowledge the most holy Trinity to have been exhibited and celebrated. 5. Glory, justice, grace, holiness, omnipotence, and whatever other divine attributes are exhibited here, are common to the most holy Trinity. 6. The work of creation, which is celebrated here, is likewise an undivided work ad extra. 7. The Doxology, which is performed in the heavens, equally pertains to all persons of the most holy Trinity. 8. Nor indeed is it therefore that Christ, because he is afterwards represented as the Lamb of God in c. VII, is himself torn into different persons, but just as elsewhere in the Scriptures the Triune God and the biune Christ are exhibited without multiplication or duplication of person: so it is by no means inconvenient for the same to be done here in the visions. For theology is distinct from the economy. The Son of God, when he is viewed in the simple complex of the divinity as of one essence with the Father and the Holy Spirit, then in the economy as the Word made Flesh, the Son of God became the Son of man, and God was manifested in the flesh, which is proper to him alone, and not common with the Father and the Holy Spirit. 9. Here he whose voice was heard, Christ the God-man, is distinguished from him who is seen sitting on the throne. 10. As to Moses, Exod. XXIV, the glory not of the Father alone, or of the Son alone, but of the most holy Trinity was exhibited on the mountain: so it is consistent that the same is also exhibited here. Cornelius agrees against Alcazar: Furthermore, Alcazar thinks that here, as in Is. VI, the sitter was God the Father only. But others think far better that it was God absolutely, as he is common to the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. For it alludes to the throne in Is. VI. 1, where the sitter was the Triune and One God, or the holy Trinity, as I showed in that place. Whence also here, just as there, the holy animals continually acclaim to Him the trisagion, namely Holy, Holy, Holy, as if they were saying Holy Father, Holy Son, Holy Spirit: for these three are most holy, and are the very primeval uncreated, essential, and immense holiness.

In the divine theonography, both He who sits upon the throne, those who sit around the throne, those which proceed from the throne, those which are seen in the sight of the throne, and those which are seen in the midst of the throne, have been described by St. John. He who sits on the throne is not in the reality of the thing, but ἐν ὁράσει (in vision) is like a Jasper and Sardius stone, with a rainbow surrounding the throne similar in ὁράσει (vision) to an Emerald. No earthly thing, no created or finite thing can shadow forth the very truth of the Majesty sitting on the throne. Therefore, it is only presented in the vision according to some likeness or other, just as not even other heavenly things can be presented; much less that immense and infinite Majesty of God. We judge that the divine glory is shadowed forth by the Jasper stone, because that gem is by far the most splendid: nor does the blessed D. Hoë differ, l. II. Comment. pag. 71. The Jasper is a mirror of the highest perfection in God. For just as the Jasper is held to be the most noble gem and, because of its perfection, the most precious and indeed the primary one, to which nothing can be compared: So God is one and alone the most perfect, subsists in Himself, has all things, and needs nothing of anyone, 2 Maccab. XIV. v. 35. The Jasper is the most precious gem among all. The Jasper shines the most: So also the divinity holds the first place in heaven and on earth, and has an incomprehensible splendor. Thus far the blessed Hoë. By the Sardius is signified divine justice: because it is fiery, and God is a consuming fire regarding His immense justice, Deut. IV. Heb. XII. By the rainbow and the Emerald color of the same, which is especially pleasing in a rainbow, divine grace is shadowed forth, of which the rainbow, the gracious covenant of God, ought to be some monument, recalling to our memory, just as by the session on the throne the majestic and omnipresent rule of God is denoted. Thus the interpretations of others can be reconciled in some way, even if they are either not adequate or not so convenient. Haymo, Albertus, the Gloss, Ansbertus, and others understand by the Jasper the divinity of Christ, which is common to Him with the Father and the Holy Spirit; even if they refer the Sardius to the Humanity, not with us to the Deity, reddened with the blood of love. But this was not yet the place for representing the Humanity of Christ or the τῆ οἰκονομίᾳ (economy). For concerning the Lamb, who redeemed us with His blood, a peculiar vision had to be presented, ch. V, as the one by whose merit the resignation of the book was acquired. But the explanation of Victorinus, Augustine, Bede, Primasius, and Rupert is clearly alien, who understand two judgments in the two stones, in the Jasper that which was done by water, in the Sardius that which will be in the future at the consummation of the age by fire. That the Sardius, which is of a red color and fiery, signifies vengeance against enemies and a red color, and the justice of God because of its heat, has been observed by others also. Furthermore, it is handed down concerning the Sardius that because of its fiery color it is terrifying and formidable to wild beasts: So although God is more lovable to the pious through the Jasper: Yet He is also a just and most sharp avenger of impiety, having eyes that are flaming and as if reddening from anger: which consideration of color squares especially well with the declaration of divine providence, as the blessed D. Hoë also has here. Andreas of Caesarea: The Sardius, he says, is compared to God because of terror. For the Sardius has the appearance of fire. Since God cannot be endured if He were to use the rigid judgment of justice: the Sardius deservedly offers an argument of a clement and good God: for since it is a stone that is both terrifying and, as they say, bears the appearance of fire, which they report is not only a cause of fear to beasts and monsters; but also has the power of curing pains and ailments which arise in our body. For the great Epiphanius says that it, if applied, heals tumors and wounds inflicted by iron. Justice therefore tempered by mercy, such as the divine is, is best designated in this way. Divine justice both bestows rewards on the pious and punishments on the impious; and it is estimated either according to rigor or κατ' ἐπιείκειαν (according to equity): Gomarus praises the opinion of those who think that by the Jasper (whose species is more frequently green) the eternal life of God is noted, which flourishes and as it were greens and gives life: but by the Sardius the justice and judgment which He exercises, as He is a consuming fire, Heb. XII. 19. and from whose sight, sitting on the throne, fire flashed, Dan. VII. 9. 10. The Emerald of a green color, which is also most beautiful in a rainbow and most pleasing to the sight, most rightly denotes, in the judgment of others also, divine grace that is always green. By the rainbow, says Ambrose, which was given to Noah as a sign of reconciliation and the pacification of God with men, the clemency and mercy of God is fittingly signified, which surrounds the seat of God, that is, the Church, i.e., protects and governs it on all sides, and defends it from visible and invisible enemies. But concerning the Emerald, Franc. Rueus, book II. de gemm. ch. 4. p. 210. The most pleasant of green gems and held as the first. For no color has equally pleased the eyes; because the sight of these is most soothed by the greenness. And afterwards: Therefore the most select Emerald is that which, being most green, most lucid, and most pure, constantly fills or satisfies the eyes with its own greenness, so infecting the neighboring air that it yields neither to the sun, nor to shadows, nor to lamps: but rather it always irradiates with a perpetual and stubborn green brightness, always offering the sight of itself with a persistent and most hard substance. But nothing is so green to our hearts, nothing so refreshes the eyes of the mind, as divine mercy. Furthermore, they ascribe most excellent powers to the Emerald, as the same Rueus observes, against all poisons, so that from this it has long since been tested that it is able to save the poisoned from death when devoured in powder at the weight of eight grains of barley. What is more useful against the poison of the Devil and death itself than divine clemency? But His grace and mercy surround the seat of God, just as here the rainbow with an Emerald aspect surrounded the divine throne. Conf. Exod. XXXIV. 6. 7. Ps. XXV. 10. Ps. XCIX. 15. Ps. CIII. 4. Sir. II. 23. chap. XVIII. 4. Blessed Hoëus supports us here again, whose comparison of divine mercy with the emerald it pleases me to subjoin; Just as therefore, he says on page 74, the emerald holds the palm among all green gems, and most greatly refreshes and sharpens the sight: So also by divine mercy we are most greatly vigorous, we flourish, we bloom, and our eyes are most greatly refreshed by it: not the splendor of gold, not the fervor of honors brings such delights to the eyes as the grace and clemency of God: By this goodness Jacob was recreated, just as he himself confesses: I have seen the Lord face to face, and my soul has been saved. Then just as the emerald frees from the most dangerous diseases: So divine mercy provides the most immediate health of body and soul. For by this alone Hezekiah obtained the prolongation of his life, and the healing of the epidemic abscess: this mercy the Canaanite woman implored, saying: Lord, son of David, have mercy on me. Just as the emerald drives away poisons: So mercy drives away the toxin of sin. Ps. CIII. v. 12. Fourthly, just as the eyes of a serpent are said to melt away from the sight of an emerald: So the mercy of God wards off the blows of the infernal serpent from the faithful, and most powerfully dispels them, puts demons to flight, binds that dragon and roaring lion, so that it can in no way harm or injure the pious. Fifthly, the emerald is said to restrain storms: What restrains the fury, what restrains the storm of divine wrath and punishment more strongly than the very mercy of God, which He does unto thousands who love Him,

I do not see the opinion of Andreas and Aretas as foreign to this interpretation of ours of the three gems, to which Cornelius a Lapide assents: He says, Andreas, Aretas, and Ribera are excellent: The Jasper, they say, because it is the firmest gem, green and often translucent, as Pliny testifies in book 37. 8., signifies the splendor and beauty of the divinity that is always green and flourishing. The Sardius, because it is of a blood-red and fiery color, and as Aretas says, strikes terror into wild beasts, signifies first the fiery, that is, the most sublime and most efficacious nature of God. Second, his justice, terror, and vengeance against the impious precursors or followers of the Anti-Christ: for by this it is pre-signified and predicted in the Apocalypse: whence GOD most excellently displays his appearance here, and assumes the habit of an avenger. For he is accustomed to assume an appearance and habit similar to the matter and thing about which the action is concerned. Third, Abulensis. and others assert that joy is kindled by the Sardius: therefore the Sardius aptly signifies that immense glory and happiness of God, from which his immense pleasure and joy flows. To this point is what Alcazar page 979, letter C, hands down, that the Sardius is a part and origin of the Amethyst, and that this is manifest from the fact that in some gems which are found, the Sardius is discerned in one part, the Amethyst in the other. The Amethyst, however, which has the color of wine, is a symbol of heavenly delights and of the divine Nectar, which gladdens the heart far more than Falernian wines, and inebriates it with joy, according to that of the Psalmist: They shall be inebriated with the abundance of thy house, and thou shalt make them drink of the torrent of thy pleasure. The Sardius therefore signifies the same. And afterwards: More generally and genuinely Ribera, Viegas, Pererius and others here and there: The rainbow, they say, is the mercy of God, which surrounds the throne of God on all sides. Item: The Emerald, which wonderfully refreshes the eyes with its greenness, and so, as Solinus testifies in chapter 17, surpasses herbs and grasses in greenness, nay, infects and colors those nearest to it with its greenness, nor does it change it in shadow, by lamps, or in the Sun, signifies the mercy of God that never grows old, but is always green, wonderfully consoling us as if it were new and fresh. The Emerald, says Pliny in book 37, chapter 5, fills the eyes with its greenness and beauty, never satiates, and therefore serves the purpose of a most beautiful mirror. Whence Nero watched the battles of the gladiators through an Emerald. Joachim Abbas should be heard: in the Jasper the person of the Father is expressed, which is the principle of all life: In the Sardius, which reflects a blood-red color, the Son is indicated; by the Emerald, which excels in greenness, the Holy Spirit is signified, who excites hearts to the hope of glory through the gifts of his thanks. The rainbow, however, is said to be seen κυκλόθεν τοῦ θρόνου, which is not to be taken precisely regarding a circular form, since a cycle is said ἐν πλάτῃ, even if it had only the form of that, or it is to be held as ἐξαιρέτῳ and singular, just as Blessed Luther also observes here that he saw the rainbow circularly round or closed on all sides.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

Καὶ εὐθέως ἐγενόμην ἐν πνεύματι) Non corpore in cœlum ascendit, sed ἐκτασίᾳ, quæ Spiritus dicitur etiam supra I. 10.

Num corpore ascenderit, an animo solum, non definitur. Solum Spiritu correptum se fuisse ait S. Johannes. Quod etiam de Pauli raptu con- stat, qui vero non novit, num raptus erat in cor- pore an vero extra corpus 2. Corinth. XII. 2. 3. Gomarus illud ἐν πνεύματι in Spiritu bifariam, inquit, exponitur probabiliter: vel ut Spiritus San- ctus intelligatur translationis in cœlum autor, ut Paulus ait 2. Corinth. XII. 4. Raptus sum in Para- disum: Vel ut spiritum seu mentem Johannis notet, quod fuerit mentis visione ibi, nimirum quo voca- batur, hoc est in cœlo.

Καὶ ἰδὲ θρόνος ἔκειτο ἐν τῷ ὐρανῷ) Dei Patris ut appa- ret infra 5. V. 7. Sic & Esaias VI. 1. Deum in solio videt, nempe paratum ad judicia exercenda. Adde Danielem VII. 9. ubi ἐτίθεσαν quod hic ἔκειτο. Solet enim κεῖσθαι idem valere quod poni ut 1. Tim. I. 9. 1. Thessal. III. 3. Allu- dunt omnia ad vetus tabernaculum. Solium hoc respondet adyto.

Ad vetus tabernaculum alludi etiamsi admit- ti possit, non tamen hoc Novi Testamenti status exhibetur; sed ut ibi figura erat cœlestium, adum- bratur status gloriosus Electorum in cœlis. So- lium vero Majestatis divinæ respondere adyto nu- spiam docemur. Adytum enim adumbravit cœ- lum, teste Apostolo Ebr. IX. 25. Fingit ista Gro- tius, ut statum primitivæ Ecclesiæ Hierosolymi- tanæ hoc loco figurari doceat. Sed hæc mere ἰδία ἐπίλυσις est, hactenus in Ecclesia inaudita, neque ullo pacto textui conveniens, in quo Ma- jestatem divinam in cœlis Electis conspicuam Jo- hanni quadantenus repræsentari nimis luculen- tum est, ut nempe autor revelationis gloriosæ exhibeatur, & autoritas ac majestas revelationis Johanni factæ ostendatur.

Καὶ ἐπὶ τῶ θρόνε καθήμενος) Deus Pater Regis specie. Ideo solium illud vocatur Ebræis כסא כובד θρόνος δό- ξης, solium Regale. In Manuscripto brevius καὶ ὁ καθήμε- νος. Nec aliter Latinus.

Variant hoc loco Interpretes. Nonnulli ut hic Grotius Deum Patrem, primam sacrosanctæ Trinitatis personam sisti volunt; quibus etiam accedit B. Cluverus noster, quod Filius Agnus in medio throno consistens appareat, Spiritum Sanctum septem lampades, omnia coram thro- no illuminantes, designent. B. Gerhardus cum B. D. Hoë & alii Christum hac visione in gloria sua exhiberi censent. Sed præstat nostro judicio dicere, hic Deum Triunum, vel sacrosanctam Trinitatem, Patrem, Filium, & Spiritum S. in throno sedentem figurari: 1. quia cœlestia, & in arcanis divinis, in consilio SS. Trinitatis repo- sita manifestanda erant, quæ ex æquo ad omnes tres Divinitatis personas spectant. 2. Revelator ἀ- ποκαλύψεως Triunus Deus sistendus videbatur, quemadmodum postea resignator libri Apocaly- ptici Christus biunus exhibetur cap. V. 3. Trisa- gion quatuor animantium acclamatur tribus SS. & individuæ Trinitatis personis, non uni tantum. 4. Quod magis confirmat trisagion Seraphicum & visio Es. VI. descripta, qua SS. Trinitatem ex- hibitam & celebratam esse communiter Dd. Ca- tholici agnoscunt. 5. Gloria, justitia, gratia, sanctitas, omnipotentia, & quæ alia attributa di- vina hic exhibentur, communia sunt SS. Trinita- ti. 6. Opus creationis, quod hic celebratur, iti- dem ceu opus ad extra indivisum est. 7. Δοξολο- γία, quæ in cœlis peragitur, ex æquo pertinet ad omnes SS. Trinitatis personas. 8. Nec vero ideo, quod Christus ceu Agnus Dei postea repræsente- tur c. VII. in diversas ipse personas discerpitur, sed quemadmodum alias in Scripturis Deus Triunus & Christus biunus sine multiplicatione vel duplicita- te personæ exhibetur: Ita idem hic in visionibus fieri minime inconveniens. Nam & θεολογία di- stincta est ab οἰκονομίᾳ. Filius Dei cum in simplici complexu divinitatis ut unius cum Patre & Sp. S. essentiæ spectatur, tum in οἰκονομίᾳ ut Verbum Ca- ro factum, Filius Dei factus est Filius hominis, & Deus manifestatus est in carne, quod ipsi uni pro- prium, non cum Patre ac Spiritu Sancto commu- ne est. 9. Distinguitur hic ille, cujus vox est audita, Christus θεάνθρωπος, ab eo, qui in throno se- dens conspicitur. 10. ut Mosi Exod. XXIV. gloria non Patris solius, aut solius Filii, sed SS. Trinitatis exhibita est in monte: ita eandem etiam hic exhi- beri vero est consentaneum. Annuit contra Alca- sarem Cornelius: Porro Alcazar censet tam hic, quam Es. VI. sessorem fuisse Deum Patrem tantum. Verum longe melius alii censent, fuisse Deum absolu- te, prout communis est Patri, Filio & Spiritui S. Al- ludit enim ad thronum Es. VI. 1. ubi sessor fuit Deus trinus & unus, sive sancta Trinitas, ut ibidem ostendi. Unde & hic æque ac ibi sancta animalia ju- giter acclamant ei trisagion, scilicet Sanctus, San- ctus, Sanctus, quasi dicant Sanctus Pater, Sanctus Filius, Sanctus Spiritus Sanctus: Hi enim tres san- ctissimi sunt, ipsaque primæva increata, essentialis & immensa sanctitas.

In θεονογραφίᾳ divina tum qui in throno sedet, tum qui circa thronum assident, tum quæ de thro- no procedunt, tum quæ in conspectu throni, tum quæ in medio throno conspiciuntur, a S. Johanne descripta sunt. Sedens in throno non in rei veri- tate, sed ἐν ὁράσει similis est lapidi Jaspidi & Sardio, cum iride thronum circumfundente simili ὁράσει visione Smaragdino. Veritatem ipsam Majestatis sedentis in throno nulla res terrena, nulla res crea- ta aut finita adumbrare potest. Exhibetur ergo tantum illa in visione secundum qualemcunque similitudinem, quemadmodum ne alia quidem cœlestia exhiberi possunt; nedum immensa illa atque infinita Dei Majestas. Per lapidem Jaspi- dem adumbrari censemus divinam gloriam, quia gemma illa longe splendidissima est: neque discre- pat B. D. Hoë l. II. Comment. pag. 71. Jaspis specu- lum est summæ perfectionis in Deo. Sicut enim Ja- spis pro gemma nobilissima & ob perfectionem suam pretiosissima quin & primaria habetur, cui nulla æquiparari potest: Ita Deus unus & solus est per- fectissimus, in se subsistit, habet omnia, nec indiget ullius, 2. Maccab. XIV. v. 35. Jaspis pretiosissima gemma inter omnes est. Jaspis maxime fulget: Ita & divinitas primas tenet in cœlo & in terra, & splendorem habet incomprehensibilem. Hacte- nus B. Hoë. Per Sardium significatur divina justi- tia: quia ignea illa est, & Deus est ignis consu- mens quoad immensam justitiam, Deut. IV. Ebr. XII. Per iridem & colorem ejusdem Smaragdi- num, qui præcipue gratus in iride est, adumbrata est divina gratia, cujus monumentum aliquod esse debuit Iris fœdus Dei gratiosum, nobis in memo- riam revocans, quemadmodum per sessionem in throno regimen Dei Majestaticum & omnipræ- sens denotatur. Ita conciliari aliqua ratione alio- rum interpretationes possunt, etsi vel non adæ- quatæ, vel non tam commodæ. Haymo, Albertus, Glossa, Ansbertus, & alii per Jaspidem divinitatem Christi intelligunt, quæ ipsi cum Patre & Spiritu S. communis est; etsi Sardium ad Humanitatem, non nobiscum ad Deitatem referant, sanguine amoris rubentem. Sed hic nondum locus erat re- præsentandæ Christi Humanitatis vel τῆ οἰκονο- μία. De Agno enim, qui nos sanguine suo rede- mit, peculiaris visio exhibenda erat, c. V. utpote cujus merito resignatio libri acquisita est. Victori- ni vero, Augustini, Bedæ, Primafii & Ruperti ex- plicatio plane aliena est, qui in lapidibus duobus judicia duo intelligunt, in Jaspide illud, quod per aquam factum, in Sardio illud, quod per ignem in consummatione seculi futurum. Sardium, qui ru- bei coloris & igneus est, vindictam adversus ho- stes & colorem rubeum, & justitiam Dei propter ardorem significare, aliis etiam observatum. Por- ro de Sardio traditur, quod propter igneum colo- rem feris sit terrificus & formidabilis: Ita licet Deus Jaspide amabilior sit erga pios: Attamen ju- stus quoque & acerrimus impietatis vindex est, o- culos flammeos & præ ira quasi rubentes habens: quæ coloris consideratio apprime ad divinæ pro- videntiæ declarationem quadrat, ut hic itidem B. D. Hoë habet. Andreas Cæsariensis: Sardius, in- quit, ob terrorem confertur Deo. Habet enim Sar- dius ignis speciem. Quandoquidem ferri non po- test Deus, si rigido uti vellet justitiæ judicio: me- rito clementis & boni argumentum præbet Sar- dius: quippe cum & terrens & ignis speciem præ se ferens, ut ajunt, lapis sit, quem non solum ti- mori esse ferunt beluis atque monstris; sed etiam vim habere curandi dolores & molestias, quæ no- stro corpori innascuntur. Ait enim Magnus Epi- phanius, ipsum, si applicetur, mederi tumoribus, ferroque illatis vulneribus. Justitia itaque miseri- cordia temperata, qualis divina est, optime ita designata. Justitia divina & piis præmia tribuit, & impiis supplicia; & æstimatur vel secundum rigo- rem, vel κατ' ἐπιείκειαν: Gomarus laudat illorum sententiam, qui per Jaspidem (cujus species frequen- tior viret) Dei vitam æternam, quæ viget ac quasi viret & vivificat: per Sardium vero justitiam & judicium, quod exercet, notari putant, ut ignis con- sumens est Ebr. XII. 19. & a cujus in solio sedentis conspectu ignis emicuit, Dan. VII. 9. 10. Smarag- dus viridis coloris, qui etiam in iride pulcherri- mus, & visui gratissimus est, gratiam divinam sem- per virentem rectissime, aliorum etiam judicio, denotat. Per Iridem, inquit Ambrosius, quæ in si- gnum reconciliationis & pacificationis Dei cum hominibus data est Noe, congrue clementia & misericordia Dei significatur, quæ sedem Dei, id est, Ecclesiam circumdat, h. e. undique protegit & gubernat, & a visibilibus atque invisibilibus ho- stibus defendit. De Smaragdo vero Franc. Rueus libr. II. de gemm. c. 4. p. 210. Viridium gemmarum jucundissima primaque habita. Nullus namq́, color oculis æque placuit; quod horum acies virore maxime demulceatur. Et postea: Selectissima itaq́, Smarag- dus ea est, quæ viridissima, lucidissima ac purissima existens suo quidem virore oculos constanter explet satiatve, ita vicinum aërem inficiens, ut neq́, soli, neq́, umbris seu lucernis cedat: quin potius perpetuo con- tumaciq́, virenti fulgore semper irradiat, sui semper præbet conspectum substantia pertinaci ac durissima. Nihil autem ita cordibus nostris viret, nihil ocu- los mentis ita reficit, quam divina misericordia. Porro vires adscribunt Smaragdo præstantissimas, observante eodem Rueo, adversus venena omnia, ut & hinc octo granorum hordei pondere in pol- line devorata venenatos a morte vindicare potens jam pridem explorata sit. Quid magis contra ve- nenum Diaboli mortemque ipsam prodest, quam divina clementia? Cingit autem sedem Dei ejus gratia & misericordia, ut hic iris Smaragdino aspe- ctu thronum divinum ambiebat. Conf. Exod. XXXIV. 6. 7. Psal. XXV. 10. Psal. XCIX. 15. Ps. CIII. 4. Sir. II. 23. cap. XVIII. 4. Suffragatur hic iterum nobis B. Hoëus, cujus comparationem misericor- diæ divinæ cum Smaragdo subjicere placet; Sicut ergo, inquit pag. 74. Smaragdus inter omnes virides gemmas palmam obtinet, & visum maxime reficit & acuit: Ita & misericordia divina summopere vigemus, viremus, floremus, & oculi nostri pluri- mum ea reficiuntur: non auri splendor, non hono- rum fervor tantas oculis affert delicias, quantas gra- tia & clementia Dei: Hac bonitate recreabatur Ja- cob, quemadmodum ipse fatetur: Vidi Dominum de facie ad faciem, & salva facta est anima mea. Deinde sicut Smaragdus a morbis liberat periculo- sissimis: Ita misericordia divina sanitatem corporis ac animæ præsentissimam præstat. Hac enim sola vi- tæ prorogationem Ezechias, & apostematis epide- mialis sanationem impetravit: hanc mulier Cana- næa misericordiam imploravit, inquiens: Domine fili David, miserere mei. Sicut Smaragdus venena pellit: Ita misericordia pellit toxicum peccati. Psal. CIII. v. 12. Quarto sicut ab aspectu Smaragdi serpen- tis diffluere oculi perhibentur: Ita misericordia Dei ictus infernalis serpentis a fidelibus arcet, ac vali- dissime dispellit, dæmones fugat, draconem illum & leonem rugientem ligat, ne quicquam piis obesse & nocere possit. Quinto Smaragdus tempestates cohibe- re dicitur: Quid furorem certius, quid tempesta- tem iræ ac pœnæ divinæ fortius cohibet ipsa Dei mi- sericordia, quam facit in millia diligentibus ipsum,

Nec aliena video ab hac no- stra trium gemmarum interpretatione Andreae & Aretae sententiam, cui adstipulatur Cornelius a Lapide : Optime, inquit, Andreas, Aretas, & Ribera: Jaspis, inquiunt, quia firmissima est gem- ma, viridis & saepe pellucens, teste Plinio libr. 37. 8. significat splendorem & pulchritudinem divinitatis semper virentis ac florentis. Sardius quia sangui- nei & ignei coloris est, & ut ait Aretas, feris ter- rorem incutit, significat primo igneam, id est, sub- limissimam & efficacissimam Dei naturam. Secun- do ejusdem justitiam, terrorem & vindictam in impios Anti-Christi praecursores vel asseclas: hac enim in Apocalypsi praesignatur & predicitur: unde optime ejus speciem hic ostentat DEUS, ac vin- dicis habitum assumit. Solet enim assumere speciem & habitum similem materiae & rei, de qua agitur. Tertio Abulens. & alii asserunt, Sardio gaudium accendi: apte ergo Sardius significat immensam il- lam Dei gloriam & felicitatem, ex qua manat im- mensa ejus voluptas & laetitia. Huc facit quod Al- cazar pag. 979. litera C. tradit, Sardium partem esse & originem Amethysti, idque ex eo manife- stum esse, quod in nonnullis gemmis, quae inveniun- tur, una parte Sardius, altera Amethystus cerna- tur. Amethystus autem, qui colorem habet vini, sym- bolum est deliciarum caelestium, & Nectaris di- vini, quod longe magis quam vina Falerna laetifi- cat cor, illudque gaudio inebriat, juxta illud Psal- tis: Inebriabuntur ab ubertate domus tuae, & tor- rente voluptatis tuae potabis eos. Idem ergo signifi- cat Sardius. Et postmodum: Magis generatim & genuine Ribera, Viegas, Pererius & alii passim: Iris, inquiunt, est Dei misericordia, quae undique thronum Dei circumdat. Item: Smaragdus, qui sua viriditate oculos mire recreat, adeoque teste Solino cap. 17. virore superat herbas & gramina, imo sibi proxima virore suo inficit & colorat, nec eum in umbra, lucernis, aut Sole immutat, significat Dei misericordiam nunquam senescentem, sed semper virentem, quasi novam & recentem mire nos con- solari. Smaragdus ait Plinius libr. 37. cap. 5. suovi- rore & pulchritudine oculos implet, nunquam sa- tiat, & proinde pulcherrimi speculi vicem obit. Un- de Nero gladiatorum pugnas per Smaragdum spe- ctabat. Joachimus Abbas sit audiendus, in Jaspi- de persona Patris exprimitur, quae vitae omnis principium est: In Sardio, qui colorem refert san- guineum, Filius indicatur, per Smaragdum, qui viriditate praecellit, Spiritus Sanctus significatur, qui per gratiarum suarum dona corda ad spem gloriae excitat. Iris autem visa dicitur κυκλόθεν τοῦ θρόνου, quod non praecise de forma circulari acci- piendum, quum cyclus ἐν πλάτῃ dicatur, utut il- lius tantum formam habuerit, vel pro ἐξαιρέτῳ & singulari habendum, quemadmodum & B. Luthe- rus hic iridem circulariter rotundam seu undique clausam se vidisse observat.

## 4:4
Vers. 4.

And round about the throne were four and twenty thrones, and upon the thrones I saw the four and twenty elders sitting) The article shows that certain Presbyters are understood, namely of the Jerusalem Church, who were then XXIV, after the likeness of as many principal Priests who had been in the temple at the time of Solomon 1 Paral. XXIV. 17. Josephus VII. 11. Mention is made of these Presbyters, without the number being expressed, in Acts XV. 2. 4. 6. 23. XVI. 4. But the Presbyters sit around the throne of God, because they judge in the Church in the place of God. Thus Clement of Alexandria understood it in Strom. VI. And note that in the Old Testament the Angels stand by the throne: in the new the Presbyters sit. In the Manuscript it is only: I saw elders sitting. clothed in white garments) With the highest dignity. See above I. 13. III. 4. 18. That ἦν is absent in the Manuscript, not badly.

The article is too meager an indication of certain Presbyters, which it is very well known is most frequently used among the Greeks without any designation of a certain thing: whence it is called most trivial by Scaliger. But it is not likely that there were XXIV Presbyters of the Jerusalem Church before the Jerusalem desolation. But much less is that to be asserted about the time following the desolation, or the time of the Johannine vision. But in truth, Grotius, as he is very bold in his commentaries, not only places XXIV Presbyters there at the time of this vision; but also treats them with the highest dignity, and adorns them with Royal insignia. He is not consistent with himself, however, when he observes that the Hebrews also give crowns to the just in the other world. For he himself wishes that not the state of the other world be regarded here, but the form of the Jerusalem Church; which, why it should be exhibited to John in heaven as something abstruse or to be in the future, when Grotius seems to establish that the state of that time, present and most well-known to John, is being set forth. Therefore, other interpreters more rightly decide that the state of the Church triumphant in heaven is adumbrated. There is no doubt that those XXIV principal Priests, when they were in the temple at the time of Solomon, 1 Par. XXIV. 7, nay and XXIV Prefects of the Singers c. XXV, were a figure then of the whole Israelite Church or of the entire people, who were gathered in that Church, to whose communion also belonged all the faithful throughout the world in the time of the O.T., as well as the Christian Church in the N.T., and as to the spiritual sacrifices, which were to be offered by all, and as to the Music and Psalmody pleasing to God, and the praises to be sung in the Church, and that they had led the whole assembly and represented it: Just as in a council of Presbyters the Church is said to be held representatively: then also of the Church of the Elect in heaven, which presents the sacrifices of prayers and Eucharistic sacrifices with Music and heavenly doxology to God. But here is properly exhibited the heavenly assembly of the blessed, which that eating with the holy Angels, and the common chorus of heavenly Singers consisting of the Spirits of the just made perfect and of any blessed ones and the holy Angels, sufficiently teaches. Although some interpret these things concerning the twenty-four Presbyters as twenty-four persons, such as Rupertus, who understands the first twelve as the Judges who were before the seat of David after Joshua, from Othniel down to Samuel, and the latter twelve as the Apostles temporally succeeding Christ, the son of David; and Andreas, Caesar, Aretas, and Hier. Prad. as the twelve Patriarchs, sons of Jacob, and the twelve Apostles of the New Testament; and Ambrose as the twenty-four Fathers of the Old Testament, whose seats were the twenty-four books of the Old Testament: yet neither can any mortal define which individuals sat upon the heavenly thrones, nor do those definitions square in any way. For St. John, to whom this vision was exhibited and who was still living among mortals, certainly belonged to the number of the twelve Apostles: therefore he was not sitting with the other Apostles on the heavenly thrones. And why were these in the Old Testament selected above others? Were all those Judges, or even all the sons of Jacob, raised to heavenly thrones, some of whom certainly received little praise from the Holy Spirit? And why should they be preferred to the most holy Kings of the Jewish people, who were highly extolled by the Holy Spirit? But perhaps it matters little to know which of the heavenly beings were seen sitting on the thrones: it is more useful to investigate who are designated by these twenty-four heavenly beings. But how piously, how wisely the divine throne is made a figure of the apostate Roman see, and the twenty-four heavenly Presbyters a figure of twenty-four mitred Bishops, the Pope's slaves, men often unlearned and impious, or whether the former are said to represent the latter, let the judgment rest with the prudent.

Those approach closer to the truth who, with Gregory (Book IV, in Reg. ch. IX, 24), make the elders holy preachers, mature in senses and grave in morals, who surround the throne of God because they love the Creator above others; and therefore, through the highest contemplation and conversation, they rest more closely to Him. Or those who say that all the saints of the Old and New Testament are represented here. But we cannot add our vote to either opinion, because other Elect are distinguished from the twenty-four elders, and the four living creatures. Wherefore it seems most simple that by the twenty-four elders seen sitting here, the whole assembly of the Ministers of the Word is represented, just as by the four living creatures, the Doctors who inform the universal Church, raised into celestial glory, are noted, to whom a greater degree of glory falls. For although the promise of sitting on the throne of Christ is made to all saints (Rev. 3:21), it is nevertheless promised in a peculiar way and thus in a more eminent degree to the Apostles and their successors in the preaching of the Word (Matt. 19:28, Luke 22:30), the fulfillment of which promise is here exhibited to be looked upon by the very eyes. They are indeed exhibited here in golden vials, full of the prayers of the saints, and in the harps of the saints' music (ch. 5:8). But indefinitely. And although the new song, which is sung by them (ch. 5:9), is common to all the Elect, nothing prevents it from being attributed peculiarly to the Ministers of the Word, who lead the whole assembly with both the sacrifices of prayers and sacred songs: nor are they undeservedly called redeemed from all tribes and languages and peoples and nations; since the universality of the Ecclesiastical order is represented to be seen in these twenty-four elders. To which opinion it furthermore seems to favor that in Rev. 8:11, the twenty-four elders, established with the four living creatures in the circuit of the throne, are distinguished from that great multitude of the Elect without number seen from every nation and tribe and all peoples and languages (v. 9). For it is perhaps difficult to see them distinctly as the representative celestial Church—if one may call it so—exhibited in the four living creatures and the twenty-four elders; and then the universal collective Church; but not to be separated from one another, nor is it convenient to say that the assembly is exhibited distinctly both collectively according to individuals, and representatively according to certain heads, and that in one and the same vision. Whence it is better to separate the other individuals seen in the promiscuous assembly from the twenty-four elders and the four living creatures exhibited gradually, and to attribute to these, as heads, some excellence or preeminence of degrees of glory over them. Blessed Luther understands all ministers of the Word, but celebrating the Lamb of God on this earth with the harp of the Word, and singing; Clement of Alexandria (Book VI, Stromata), Lyra, Mede, and Döling understand the ministers of the New Testament; Blessed Cluver understands the presbyters, even the laity. Our interpretation is favored by what Blessed Hoëus observes (p. 24) concerning the number twelve, that it is no less a number of full and consummated virtue than the number seven and one thousand, as witnessed by Jerome (Book XVI, commentary on Ezekiel), Augustine (Book XX, De Civitate Dei, ch. 5, and in the enarrations on Psalm 86), and Gregory the Great (Book X, Moralia, ch. 29), so that in this way, by the former twelve, all the sacred heralds of the Old Testament are understood, and by the latter, all of the New Testament. Ticonius, Bede, Primasius, and Arias Montanus (on Zech. 4:19) think the twenty-four elders signify the universal Church, which is crowned by God, and renders its crowns to God as received from Him.

Furthermore, Grotius's invention is analogous to Alcazar's interpretation, that the twenty-four elders are the Chief Priests, and that the discourse is not about the throne of God, which He has in the heavens, but about the new throne of the kingdom of heaven, which Christ and the Apostles preached; that is, about the throne which the Church has. But Cornelius a Lapide refutes this in the same society: It is a question here of the throne of God, he says, which He has in heaven, and not in the Church, as is evident from the following, where he teaches that in the circuit of this throne were celestial Spirits and the blessed, clothed in white, and crowned with golden crowns, crying Holy, Holy, Holy, etc. Again, from the fact that he says in verse 5 that lightnings, voices, and thunders proceeded from the throne; for these proceed from heaven, not from the earth. Finally, Alcazar says that the Apocalypse is like a revolving stage, in which, by certain machines, the frame being suddenly turned, another scene is shown, so that a forest, for example, may seem to be suddenly converted into a palace: for thus this celestial throne is changed as if into a terrestrial one: which little accords with divine gravity and Majesty.

Therefore, as for the white garments, not so much the Priesthood, as Alcazar wishes, but the charity and glory of the blessedness of the twenty-four elders is indicated, as Cornelius likewise acknowledges; just as the golden crowns on their heads denote their victory, triumph, and kingdom.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

Καὶ κυκλόθεν τοῦ θρόνου θρόνοι εἴκοσι τέσσαρες, καὶ ἐπὶ τοὺς θρό- νους εἶδον τοὺς εἴκοσι τέσσαρας πρεσβυτέρους καθημένους) Arti- culus ostendit certos Presbyteros intelligi, nempe Eccle- siae Hierosolymitanae, qui tum erant XXIV. adinstar toti- dem praecipuorum Sacerdotum, qui in templo fuerant tem- pore Salomonis 1. Paral. XXIV. 17. Josephus VII. 11. Horum Presbyterorum, numero non expresso, mentio fit Act. XV. 2. 4. 6. 23. XVI. 4. Sedent autem Presbyteri circa Dei so- lium, quia Dei vice in Ecclesia judicant. Sic Clemens Alexan- drinus accepit Strom. VI. Et nota in Veteri Testamento apud solium stare Angelos: in novo sedere Presbyteros. In Manuscripto tantum est: Εἶδον πρεσβυτέρους καθημένους. περιβεβλημένους ἐν ἱματίοις λευκοῖς) Cum summa dignita- te. Vide supra I. 13. III. 4. 18. Illud ἦν abest in Manuscripto, non male.

Nimis exile indicium certorum Presbytero- rum est articulus, quem apud Græcos frequentissi- me adhiberi sine ulla rei certæ designatione notis- simum est: unde nugacissimus Scaligero dictus est. Ecclesiæ autem Hierosolymitanæ XXIV. Presby- teros ante Hierosolymitanam desolationem fuisse non est verisimile. Sed multo minus id de tempore desolationem sequuto, aut tempore visionis Jo- hanneæ asserendum. Verum enim vero Grotius ut in commentis suis valde audaculus non solum vi- sionis hujus tempore XXIV. Presbyteros eo locat; sed etiam summa dignitate illos mactat, ac Regiis insignibus exornat. Non constans tamen in eo si- bimetipsi, cum observat etiam Ebræos justis dare coronas in altero seculo. Vult enim ipse respici hic non statum alterius seculi, sed formam Ecclesiæ Hierosolymitanæ; Quæ cur Johanni in cœlis tan- quam aliquid abstrusi vel deinceps futuri exhibe- retur, quum statum illius temporis præsentem Jo- hanniq; notissimum sisti Grotius statuere videa- tur. Rectius itaq; Interpretes alii adumbrari statum Ecclesiæ triumphantis in cœlis decernunt. Dubium nullum est XXIV. illos præcipuos Sacerdotes, quū tempore Salomonis in templo erant, 1. Par. XXIV. 7. imo & XXIV. Cantorum Præfectos c. XXV. fi- guram fuisse tum totius Ecclesiæ Israëliticæ vel universi populi,qui colligebatur in illa Ecclesia,ad cujus etiam communionem pertinebant omnes per orbem fideles tempore V. T. necnon Ecclesiæ Christianæ in N. T. & qua sacrificia spiritualia, quæ ab omnibus offerenda, & qua Musicam & Psalmodiam Deo gratam,laudesque inEcclesia de- cantandas, & cœtui toti præivisse, eundemque re- præsentasse: Sicut in concilio Presbyterorum Ec- clesia repræsentativa haberi dicitur: tum etiam Ec- clesiæ Electorum in cœlis, quæ sacrificia precum & Eucharistica cum Musica & δοξολογίᾳ cœlesti Deo sistit. Sed hic proprie exhibetur panegyris beatorum cœlestis, quod illa comestio cum sanctis Angelis, & communis chorus cœlestium Canto- rum ex Spiritibus justorum perfectorum ac beato- rum quorumvis & sanctis Angelis constans satis docet. Quanquam autem hæc nonnulli de Presby- teris numero XXIV. de totidem personis accipi- ant, utpote Rupertus per priores XII. Judices, qui ante sedem David fuere post Josuam ab Ottho- niele usq; ad Samuelem, per posteriores XII.Apo- stolos Christo Davidis filio temporaliter succe- dentes, & Andreas Cæsar. Aretas & Hier. Prad. duodecim Patriarchas, filios Jacobi, & XII. Apo- stolos N. T. Ambrosius XXIV. Patres Vet. Test. quorum sedilia fuerint XXIV. libri V. T. intelli- gens: non tamen vel mortalium quisquam definire poterit, quænam individua in thronis cœlestibus consederint, vel illæ definitiones ullatenus qua- drant. Nam ad Apostolorum duodenarium nu- merum pertinebat utiq; S. Johannes, cui visio ista exhibita est, quiq; adhuc inter mortales agebat: non ergo cum cæteris Apostolis in thronis cœle- stibus considebat: Et cur isti in V. T. præ cæteris selecti? An omnes illi Judices, aut etiam omnes fi- lii Jacobi ad thronos cœlestes evecti, quorum cer- te nonnulli a Spiritu S. laudem exiguam reporta- runt? Et cur illi præferrentur Regibus Judaici po- puli sanctissimis,maximopere a Spiritu S. deprædi- catis?Sed parum fortassis refert scire,quinam e cœ- litibus in thronis sedere visi sint:id magis ex usu est indagare, quinam per hos XXIV. cœlites sint de- signati. Sed quam pie, quam sapienter thronus di- vinus figura sedis Romanæ apostaticæ, XXIV. Presbyteri cœlestes XXIV. mitratorum Episco- porum Papæ mancipiorum, hominum sæpe indo- ctorum atque impiorum figura constituantur, aut illi hos repræsentare dicantur, penes cordatos esto judicium.

Propius accedunt ad veritatem, qui cum Gre- gorio l. IV. in Reg. c. IX. 24. Seniores faciunt sanctos predicatores, maturos sensibus & moribus graves, qui thronum Dei ambiunt, quia præ cæteris condito- rem diligunt; ideoq; per altissimam contemplationem & conversationem ei vicinius requiescunt. Vel qui omnes sanctos Vet. & N. T. hic repræsentari ajunt. Sed neutri sententiæ calculum adjicere possumus, quod & Electi alii a Senioribus XXIV. distinguan- tur, & IV. animalia. Quapropter simplicissimum videtur per XXIV. Presbyteros hic considere visos repræsentari totum cœtum Ministrorum Verbi, ut per IV. animalia Doctores, qui Ecclesiam uni- versam informant, in cœlestem gloriam evecti no- tentur, quibus major gradus gloriæ obtingit. Nam etsi omnibus sanctis confessus in throno Christi promittatur, Apoc. III. 21. peculiariter tamen atque ita eminentiori quodam gradu Apostolis eorumq; in Verbi præconio successoribus promissus est, Matth. XIX. 28. Luc. XXII. 30. cujus promissionis complementum hic oculis ipsis spectandum exhi- betur. Exhibentur quidem hic in phialis aureis, plenis thymiamafi sanctorum προσευχαὶ, & in Citharis sanctorum Musica c. V. 8. Sed indefi- nite. Et quamvis commune est omnibus Electis canticum novum, quod ab illis decantatur, c. V. 9. Nihil tamen vetat peculiariter id tribui Ver- bi Ministris, qui præeunt cum precum sacrificiis, tum canticis sacris toti cœtui: nec immerito re- dempti illi dicuntur ex omnibus tribubus & lin- guis & populis & gentibus; quum universitas ordinis Ecclesiastici repræsentetur in hisce XXIV. Senioribus conspicienda. Cui sententiæ id præ- terea videtur favere, quod Ap. VIII. Seniores XXIV. v. 11. cum IV. animantibus in circuitu thro- ni constituti a populo illo multo Electorum sine numero ex omni gente ac tribu omnibus populis & linguis v. 9. conspecto distinguuntur. Durum enim forte est distincte quidem illis videri cum Ec- clesiam cœlestem repræsentativam, quam ita vo- care liceat in IV. animantibus & XXIV. Senioribus exhibitam; tum Ecclesiam universam collecti- vam; sed non sequestrari ab invicem, nec conve- niens dicere, distincte cœtum exhiberi tum colle- ctive secundum individua, tum repræsentative ju- xta quædam capita, idque in una eademq; visione. Unde præstat cætera individua in cœtu promiscuo visa separare a XXIV. Senioribus & IV. animalibus sensim exhibitis, & his ceu capitibus aliquam gra- duum gloriæ ἐξοχὴν vel præeminentiam præ illis attribuere. Omnes ministros Verbi B. Luther. sed his in terris Agnum DEI cythara verbi celebran- tes, & canentes intelligit; Ministros N. T. Clemens Alex. VI. Strom. Lyra, Medus, Döling. Presby- teros, etiam Laicos B. Cluver. Pro qua interpre- tatione nostra favet, quod observat B. Hoëus, p. 24. de numero duodenario, quod ille non minus quam numerus septenarius & millenarius plenæ consummatæq; virtutis numerus sit, teste Hierony- mol. XVI. comment. in Ezech. & Augustino l. XX. de Civ. Dei c. 5. & in enarrat. Psal. XXCVI. Gre- gor. M. l. X. Moral. c. 29. ut hoc pacto per priorem duodenarium omnes sacri præcones V. T. & per posteriorem omnes N. T. intelligantur. Ticonius, Beda, Primasius & Ariasmontanus in Zach. IV. 19. censent XXIV. Seniores significare universam Ec- clesiam, quæ a Deo coronata est, & coronas suas Deo acceptas refert.

Porro analogum est Grotii commentum Alca- zaris interpretamento, quod XXIV. Seniores sint Principes Sacerdotum, nec de throno Dei, quem habet in cœlis, sed de throno novo regni cœlorum, quod prædicavit Christus & Apostoli, sermo sit; id est, de throno, quem habet Ecclesia. Quod vero refellit in eadem societate Cornelius a Lapide: A- gi hic de throno Dei, inquit, quem habet in cœlo, non autem in Ecclesia, patet ex sequentibus, ubi docet, in circuitu throni hujus fuisse cælestes Spiritus ac beatos vestitos albis, & coronatos coronis aureis, clamantes Sanctus, Sanctus, Sanctus &c. Rursum ex eo, quod ait v. 5. de throno processisse fulgura, voces & toni- trua, hæc enim e cælo prodeunt, non e terra. Denique Alcazar ait, Apocalypsin esse quasi scenam versati- lem, in qua subito machinis quibusdam converso pe- gmate, alia species ostenditur, ut sylva, verbi gratia, in palatium subito converti videatur: Sic enim thro- num hunc cælestem quasi in terrestrem mutari: quod parum congruit divinæ gravitati & Majestati.

Quod ergo ad vestimenta alba non tam Sacer- dotium, ut vult Alcazar, quam charitas & gloria beatitudinis XXIV. Seniorum, agnoscente itidem Cornelio, indicatur; quemadmodum coronæ au- reæ in capitibus eorum victoriam, triumphum, & regnum eorum denotant.

## 4:5
Verse 5.

And out of the throne proceeded lightnings and voices and thunders) In many Manuscripts the order is this, and thunders and voices. Lightnings and thunders signify the threats of God against the impious. See below 8:5, 10:4, 5, 11:19, 14:2, 15:1, 16:18, 19:6. Voices are in the thunders themselves below 10:3, that is, He does not only threaten generally, but also predicts special punishments.

And seven lamps of fire burning) An allusion to the candelabrum of the temple, having seven lamps. By the candelabrum, however, the Jerusalem Church is signified, as other Churches above 1:20.

which are the seven spirits of God) The seven lamps on the lampstand signify the many modes of divine providence, through which the Jerusalem Church is governed, just as the world is governed by the seven planets. They are, indeed, in the mystery. In the Manuscript: ἁ ἐσι τὰ ἑπτὰ, not a bad construction.

We send a commentary on the Jerusalem Church; what was the point of it being represented and shown to St. John in heaven? The seven Spirits are not seven modes of divine providence through which the Church is governed, just as modern astronomers will not admit that the world is governed by seven planets, inasmuch as they have observed and count more planets. But they are the manifold gracious effects of the Holy Spirit in the Church; which proceed from the divine throne into the faithful no less than lightnings, voices, and thunders into the unfaithful: so that the administration of the one sitting on the throne may be shadowed forth as no less gracious than just and severe, such as He will show Himself to be in those things which are now to be foretold to the Church. For thus God is accustomed to exhibit His Majesty, justice, and wrath in visions through lightnings and thunders, as was done on Mount Sinai in the promulgation of the law, Exod. XIX. 16. Alcazar's interpretation, that the thrones of God are all the faithful, and from them proceed voices, that is, pious discourses joined with lightnings and thunders, because they have a joined heavenly power signified in the thunder, and the illustration of a pious life and holy example noted by the lightning, can neither in any way be held as mystical with Cornelius, nor in any way be admitted as consistent. The same, almost like Grotius, understands by these seven lamps the seven gifts and virtues of divine providence. Cornelius a Lapide [understands] the seven primary Angels; but without foundation, nay, against the analogy of the vow in Apoc. I. 4. Blessed Hoë does not dissent from our interpretation, that by the lightnings and thunders are understood the severe judgments of God, as in Psalm XVIII. v. 8.

Ps. 97:3-4. Through the seven Spirits of God, the seven or manifold gifts of the Holy Spirit. Paul, and others, and B. Gerhard, as to the thunders and lightnings: It is most simply referred to the penetrating power of the Gospel, Matt. 24:27, the thunder and strong voice of the heavenly Word, Ps. 68:3, Mark 3:17, which has sounded throughout the whole world by the command of Christ, through which He gathered to Himself a Church from all kingdoms and peoples, and prostrated all human or worldly wisdom and power, 2 Cor. 10:5, through the seven Spirits: The Holy Spirit, he says, with seven, that is, manifold gifts, power, and operation, inasmuch as He converts men through the Word of the Gospel, kindles the fire of faith and divine love in hearts, leads them to the kingdom of Christ, saves, etc. With this exposition agrees what some establish, that those fiery lamps are a symbol of the illumination of minds for the right recognition of God, and of the inflammation of hearts for the loving of God and neighbor. Cf. Acts 2:3, fiery tongues; Matt. 3:11, He will baptize with fire. If anyone should wish to refer the Word of the Law to the thunders and the Word of the Gospel to the seven lamps at the same time, he will not contradict our interpretation; since the Law refers to the justice and wrath of God, but the Gospel and the ministry of the Spirit, which is of reconciliation, to grace, 2 Cor. 3. Gomarus observes this sense: Some think it is typically noted that the Law of God is signified by terrible signs, because it was delivered on Mount Sinai in that manner; and its office is to terrify sinners: on the contrary, however, the Gospel is shadowed forth by the pleasant signs of the lamps, because the Holy Spirit illuminates, cherishes, and comforts us: concerning which two things 2 Cor. 3 is discussed. and Heb. 12:18 is discussed: But others think otherwise. But it seems most probable that by the lightning, voices, and thunders, as in the promulgation of the Law, Exod. 19, it is designated that God is the most powerful and just Author of the punishments to be sent into the world, as is evident from a comparison of Rev. 8:5, ch. 10:3-4, ch. 16:18. Then, that He is the preserver of the Church by His Spirit, who recreates, illuminates, and directs the faithful with His perfect gifts: and therefore it is depicted by lamps, and indeed seven in number, as has been declared in Rev. 1:4. And that seems to be shadowed forth by the seven lamps of the lampstand of the tabernacle, Exod. 37:23 and Zech. 4:2. For as the tabernacle was illuminated by them: so the universal Church, shadowed forth by the tabernacle (just as the temple of the Lord is also called by Paul), is illuminated by the Holy Spirit with manifold light. Both of which pertain to the consolation of the faithful: the former indeed so that faith concerning the justice of God against the impious enemies of the Church may be established: the latter, however, so that confidence concerning the care and mercy of God toward the Church against temptations may be established. v. 5. I explained the seven burning lamps in Theol. natur. & Revel. Anti-Crellio p. 1539. Thus also B. Danhauerus in Anti-Christo-Soph. p. 299. which went out from the throne: he explains that they were burning before the throne with B. Luther, Erasm. Schmiedius, but these are not opposites. For they are kindled by heavenly fire from the throne, and by the grace of Him who sits on the throne. Crugotius understands the angels inconveniently. Anselm, Thomas, and Szegedin interpret the voice of thunder thus, that St. John perceived some intelligible voice with the thunder. Jerome, with us, judges that the judgments of God are signified, on Dan. 7:9-10.

Latin:

Vers. 5.

Καὶ ἐκ τῦ θρόνυ ἐκπορεύοντο ἀσραπαὶ καὶ φωναὶ καὶ βρόνται) In plurimis Manuscriptis ordo hic est, καὶ βρόνται καὶ φωναὶ Fulgura & tonitrua fignificant minas Dei contra impios. Vide infra VIII. 5. X. 4. 5. XI. 19. XIV. 2. XV. 1. XVI. 18. XIX. 6. Voces sunt in ipsis tonitribus infra X. 3. id est, non genera- liter tantum minatur, sed & speciales pœnas prædicit.

Καὶ ἑπτὰ λαμπάδες πυρὸς καιόμεναι) Allusio ad candela- brum templi, septem habens lucernas. Per candelabrum autem significatur Ecclesia Hierosolymitana, ut aliæ Eccle- siæ supra I. 20.

ἁί εἰσιν ἑπτὰ πνεύματα τῦ Θεῦ) Septem lucernæ in cande- labro significant multos modos divinæ providentiæ, per quos Ecclesia Hierosolymitana gubernatur, sicut mundus gubernatur per septem Planetas. Εἶσι nempe in mysterio. In Manuscripto: ἁ ἐσι τὰ ἑπτὰ, non mala constructione.

Mittimus commentum de Ecclesia Hierosolymita- na, quam in cælis repræsentari & ostendi S. Johanni quid attinebat? Septem Spiritus non sunt septem modi divinæ providentiæ, per quos gubernata Ec- clesia, sicuti mundum per septem planetas guber- nari hodierni Astronomi non admittent; utpote qui plures observarunt & numerant planetas. Sed effecta gratiosa Spiritus S. multiplicia in Ecclesia; quæ non minus procedunt a throno divino in fi- deles, quam fulgura, voces ac tronitrua in infide- les: ut ita adumbretur administratio sedentis in throno non minus gratiosa, quam justa & severa, qualem sese exhibitura sit in his, quæ Ecclesiæ jam prædicenda sunt. Sic enim Deus exhibere solet in visionibus suam Majestatem, justitiam atq; iram per fulgura & tonitrua, ut in monte Sinai factum in promulgatione legis, Exod. XIX. 16. Alcazaris in- terpretatio, quod throni Dei sint fideles omnes, & ab his procedant voces, id est, sermones pii con- juncti fulguribus & tonitruis, quia conjunctam ha- bent virtutem cœlestem in tonitru significatam, & piæ vitæ ac sancti exempli illustrationem fulgure notatam, neq; ut ullo modo mystica cum Cornelio haberi, neque ut ullo modo consentanea admitti potest. Idem fere, ut Grotius, per septem hasce lampades septem divinæ providentiæ dotes & vir- tutes intelligit. Cornelius a Lapide septem prima- rios Angelos; sed citra fundamentum, imo contra analogiam voti Apoc. I. 4. Nostræ interpretatio- ni non abnuit B. Hoë, quod per fulgura & tonitrua Dei severa judicia intelligantur, ut Psal. XVIII. v. 8.

Psal. XCVII. 3. 4. Per septem Spiritus Dei don septem vel multiplicia SpiritusSancti. Paulo alite B. Gerhardus, qua tonitrua & fulgura: Simplicis- sime refertur penetrans virtus Evangelii Matth XXIV. 27. tonitru & fortis vox Verbi cœlestis, Psal LXVIII. 3. Marc. III. 17. quæ in toto orbe ex mandat Christi sonuit, per quam ex omnibus regnis & popu- lis Ecclesiam sibi collegit, & omnem sapientiam ac po- tentiam humanam sive mundanam prostravit, 2. Co- rinth. X. 5. qua septem Spiritus: Spiritus S. inquit, cum septem hoc est multiplicibus donis, virtute & ope- ratione, utpote qui per Verbum Evangelii homines convertit, ignem fidei & amoris divini in cordibus accendit, ad regnum Christi deducit, salvat &c. Cum hac expositione congruit, quod quidam statuunt, lam- pades illas igneas esse symbolum illuminationis men- tium ad Deum recte agnoscendum, & inflammatio- nis cordium ad diligendum Deum & proximum. Conf. Act. II. 3. linguæ igneæ Matth. III. 11. Baptiza- bit igne. Si ad tonitrua Verbum legis, ad septem lam- pades Verbum Evangelii quis simul referre velit, haud contradicet nostræ interpretationi; quum justitiam & iram Dei referat lex, gratiam vero Ev- angelium & ministerium Spiritus, quod est recon- ciliationis, 2. Cor. III. Hunc sensum observat Go- marus: Nonnulli typice notari putant, signis quidem terribilibus legem Dei, quod ea ratione in monte Si- nai esset tradita; ejusq́; officium sit terrere peccatores: contra vero signis jucundis lampadum Evangelium adumbrari, quod Spir. S. nos illuminet, foveat ac con- soletur: de quibus duobus 2. Cor. III. & Ebr. XII. 18. differitur: Alii vero aliter. Sed maxime probabile vi- detur, fulgure, vocibus, ac tonitruis, ut in legis pro- mulgatione, Exod. XIX. designari, Deum pœnarum in orbem immittendarum esse Autorem præpotentem ac justum, ut ex collatione Apoc. VIII. 5. c. X. 3. 4. cap. XVI. 18. patet. Deinde Ecclesiæ conservatorem esse suo Spiritu, qui donis perfectis suis recreat, illuminat ac dirigit fideles: ideoq́; lampadibus, & quidem numero septem depingitur, ut Apoc. I. 4. declaratum est. Id- que videtur lucernis septem lampadis tabernaculi Exod. XXXVII. 23. & Zach. IV. 2. adumbratum. Nam ut iis tabernaculum illustrabatur: Sic Spiritus S. luce multiplici universa Ecclesia per tabernacu- lum adumbrata (sicut etiam templum Domini a Paulo appellatur) illustratur. Quorum utrumq́; ad fidelium consolationem pertinet: illud quidem ut fi- des de Dei justitia adversus impios Ecclesiæ hostes: hoc vero ut fiducia de Dei cura & misericordia erga Ecclesiam adversus tentationes stabiliatur. v. 5. Se- ptem lampades ardentes exposui in Theol natur. & Revel. Anti-Crellio p. 1539. Sic & B. Danhaue- rus Anti-Christo-Soph. p. 299. quæ exiere a thro- no: ardentes eas fuisse coram throno explicat cum B. Luthero, Erasm. Schmiedius, sed hæc opposita non sunt. Igne enim cœlesti accenduntur a throno, ejusque gratia qui sedet in throno. Incommode Angelos intelligit Crugotius. Vocem tonitrui sic interpretantur Anshelmus, Thomas, Szegcdinus, quod cum tonitru vocem aliquam intelligibilem perceperit S. Johannes. DEI judicia significari Hieronym. nobiscum censet ad Dan. VII. 9. 10.

## 4:6
v. 6. And before the throne as a sea of glass, like unto crystal) In the tabernacle and temple there had been the Sea, that is, the huge laver, Exod. 30:18, 1 Kings 7:23, 2 Chron. 4:2. But by this sea, that is, the laver full of water, the Jerusalem populace is signified. For waters are peoples, below 17:15. Sea, a multitude, Hab. 2:15. But it is called a glassy sea, that is, the waters which were in the laver. As the glassy pontus in Horace: because God perceives both the actions and the thoughts of the people, in which sense we have the glassy sea also below 15:2. But this sea was so glassy that it resembled crystal, on account of the supreme purity of that Jerusalem populace which had given its name to Christ; which purity is described in Acts 2 and 4. The proper brightness of crystal. Ezek. 1:22, כעין הקרח is translated as the appearance of crystal.

That the Jerusalem populace is represented by the glassy sea is as unheard of hitherto as it is utterly absurd. And what analogy is there here that the Presbyters of Jerusalem are those sitting on the thrones, but the sea is the faithful populace? The impious are compared to the sea, Is. 58. And many peoples are many waters, Rev. 17. But nowhere are the faithful compared to the sea, or come under the name of a glassy sea: And some explain it concerning the world, because it is called a sea on account of the multitude of men, and this sea is pellucid to God, because all words and deeds are pellucid in the eyes of God, Ps. 139:11-12, Heb. 4:13, and because the fortune of the world is truly glassy and fragile, see Büllinger, Piscator, Napeirus, Pareus, Ribera, and of our own, B. Chytraeus, D. Winckelm., D. Hoë. No one is found who explains it of the populace of the faithful; Crugotius understands it of the Elect of the O.T.; Hofmannus of the visible Church; Cotterius of the life of the faithful. The elect are indeed admitted to the enjoyment of the crystalline sea, which proceeds from the throne of God and the Lamb: But by what reason the name of crystalline sea fits them, does not appear. Pererius and Cornelius a Lapide think that the seat of the Elect is signified not on earth and in the heavens: his own empyrean heaven, which is called a sea on account of its amplitude, because it is most vast: glassy on account of its subtlety and tranquility. Andreas Caesar. and Aretas understand the angels and the blessed themselves by the glassy sea: although for Aretas it is also those waters which are above the firmament of heaven, or the crystalline heaven itself, which Andreas Caesar chooses, just as the empyrean heaven pleased Pererius and a Lapide, and for Tirinus the palace of God is called a sea on account of its amplitude, and glassy and crystalline on account of its subtlety, tranquility, splendor, and solidity. But it is a matter of religious scruple for us to ascribe a local palace to God as if He were a worldly monarch. For Ribera, the glassy sea is the present age, through which, as if through a sea, we pass to the gate of blessedness. But everyone sees how unsuitable those expositions are. Joachim of Fiore comes closer to the truth, that the glassy sea is Holy Scripture, because it is transparent and like a mirror: And Ambrose, for whom the bronze sea in Solomon's temple is the O.T., the glassy sea is the N.T. And Dionysius the Carthusian and Alcasar, for whom the glassy sea is penance: because penance is a sea on account of its bitterness and abundance of tears, similar to crystal on account of the firmness of the resolve to avoid sins henceforth and to enter upon a new life. But the most ancient interpretation, approved by most of the Fathers and other interpreters, is most fitting, that Baptism is signified by the glassy sea: 1. Because Baptism has the vastness of the sea, the transparency of glass, and the firmness and solidity of crystal. 2. Just as glass is permeable to the rays of the Sun: so the baptized soul is illuminated by the rays of grace from God, as Hugh says. The faithful who are baptized, as Rupert says, which Cornelius cites here, are in this life glassy, i.e., lucid, but fragile, weak, mortal; but after the resurrection they will be like crystal, that is, solid, robust, and immortal. 3.
