Baptism is deservedly called a sea; because it is not only an open fountain for the house of Jacob, Zech. 13:1, but it is open to all peoples and nations, as the common laver of regeneration for all, Tit. 3:5. And a crystalline sea on account of the illumination which occurs in Baptism: so that the sea signifies the vastness, but the crystal the power and efficacy of baptism. This sea is in the sight of the throne: because Baptism is at the threshold of the Church and is the approach to the throne and kingdom of God, John 3:5. 4. We admit that there is a reference to the analogy of the bronze sea made by Solomon. Therefore, just as the priests washed themselves in it before they were admitted to the sanctuary, 1 Kings 7:23, so there is need of the washing of baptism and the sacrament of initiation, that we may be admitted into the Church, and for entrance into the kingdom of heaven, as many of us as wish to be priests before God, Rev. 1:5. Everyone who desires to approach the throne of God must pass through the sea of Baptism. 5. Thus from the throne of God proceeds the Word of the Law and the Gospel, and before the throne is the Sacrament of Baptism, because God sitting on the throne gathers to Himself a Church through the Word and Sacraments. Before the throne of God, says the blessed Cluverus, are the gifts of the divine Spirit and life with the sea: by the former it is fitting that all who approach Him be enlightened, by the latter, purified. 6. Baptism is prefigured by the Red Sea, in which the army of Pharaoh was suffocated, Exod. XIV. v. 27. which reasoning the blessed Gerhardus uses here. 7. Victorinus, and Tyconius, Primasius, Anselmus, Rupertus, Beda, Haymo, Richardus, Lyranus, and the Gloss. ordinar. approve this interpretation with their suffrage. Strabus, Thomas, most of our countrymen, Osiander, the blessed Hoë, the blessed Gerhardus, the blessed Cluverus, the blessed Clotzius in his disputation on the Sacrament of Baptism, who in §. 25 brings forward this reasoning: Just as in the Apocalypse the state of the Church of the New Testament, which it either had in his time or was to have thereafter until the consummation of the age, is delineated for John from chapter IV to XX: So in this chapter IV and V, by a general vision and one as it were preparatory to the following prophecy, the state of the Church of the New Testament, which it was to maintain from the beginning to the end, is exhibited by those types and colors which are then repeated sporadically throughout the whole Apocalypse in chapters XI, XIV, XV, XIX. That sea, therefore, is understood here which pertains to the state of the Church militant in this age, and represents it, the type of which is exhibited here to John. See also the blessed Quistorp the Elder. Frobenius explains it concerning the word of God, Thomas, Cluverus, Grave, and Dürfeld concerning Baptism and the Word.

And in the midst of the throne, and round about the throne) that is, of the four living creatures one was on the steps that were before the throne. See 1 Kings X. v. 19. Two on the sides: one behind, and thus they were closer to the throne than the Elders. The steps are taken as a part of the throne.

Four living creatures) In the tabernacle, in the temple of Solomon, and in the vision of Ezekiel there are two equal figures, composed of the forms of four living creatures. Here, however, as the following things teach us, there are four distinct forms of living creatures. Why so? Because all things in the New Testament are known more distinctly than in the Old. The four living creatures in this place are the four Apostles, or Apostolic men who were then at Jerusalem as the standard-bearers of the camps of Christ.

Full of eyes before and behind) From Ezekiel, where by the word עינים, that is, eye, we said that colors are signified. Those colors, however, signify here the multiform gifts of God, through which the Apostles knew both present and future things, Matt. XIII. 52.

Latin:

v. 6. Καὶ ἐνώπιον τῦ θρόνε ὡς θάλασσα ὑαλίνη, ὁμοία κρυ- ςάλῳ) In tabernaculo & templo fuerat. Mare, id est, la- brum ingens, Exod. XXX. 18. 1. Reg. VII. 23. 2. Paral. IV. 2. Significatur autem per hoc mare, id est labrum aqua ple- num, plebs Hierosolymitana. Aquæ enim sunt populi infra XVII. 15. Mare, multitudo Ab. II. 15. Dicitur autem mare vi- treum, id est, aquæ, quæ erant in labro. Sicut pontus vitreus Horatio: quia Deus & actiones & cogitata populi perspicit, quo sensu mare vitreum habemus & infra XV. 2. Sed hoc mare ita vitreum, ut crystallum referret, propter summam puritatem plebis Hierosolymitanæ ejus, quæ Christo no- men dederat; quæ puritas describitur Act. II. & IV. Crystalli proprius candor. Ezech. V. 22. כעין הקרח vertitur ὡς ὅρα- σις κρυστάλλυ.

Plebelem Hierosolymitanam per mare vitreum ex- hiberi, uti inauditum hactenus, ita prorsus abso- num est. Et quæ hic analogia sedentes in thronis esse Presbyteros Hierosolymitanos, mare vero esse plebem fidelem? Impii mari comparantur, Es. LVIII. Et populi multi aquæ multæ, Ap. XVII. Nu- spiam autem fideles mari conferuntur, aut maris vitrei nomine veniunt: Et explicant nonnulli de mundo, quod propter hominum multitudinem mare dicatur, & pellucidum hoc mare sit Deo, quod omnia dicta & facta in oculis Dei pellucida Psal. CXXXIX. 11. 12. Ebr. IV. 13. quodque mundi fortuna vere vitrea & fragilis sit, vid. Büllinger, Piscator, Na- peirus, Pareus, Ribera, & e nostris B. Chytraus, D. Winckelm. D. Hoë. De plebe fidelium nemo inveni- tur, qui explicet; de Electis V. T. intelligit Crugo- tius; de Ecclesia visibili Hofmannus; de vita fidelium Cotterius. Electi sane ad maris crystallini, quod a throno Dei & Agni procedit, fruitionem admittun- tur: Sed qua ratione ipsis maris crystallini nomen conveniat, non apparet. Pererius & Cornelius a La- pide Electorum potius sedem non in terris & in cœlis significari censent: cœlum suum empyræum, quod mare dicatur ob amplitudinem, quia vastissi- mum est: vitreum ob subtilitatem & tranquillita- tem. Andreas Cæsar. & Aretas ipsosmet Angelos & beatos per mare vitreum intelligunt: quanquam A- retæ etiam illud aqua sint super firmamentum cæli, vel cælum ipsum crystallinum, quod Andreas Cæsar. eligit, uti Pererio, & a Lapide cœlum empyræum placuit, Tirino palatium Dei mare dictum ob am- plitudinem, vitreum & crystallinum, ob subtilita- tem, tranquillitatem, splendorem, soliditatem. Sed Deo ceu Monarchæ terreneo palatium locale ad- scribere nobis religio est. Riberæ mare vitreum est præsens seculum, per quod quasi per mare transi- mus ad portam beatitudinis. Sed quam inconve- nientes illæ expositiones sint, nemo non videt. Magis accedit ad veritatem Joach. Abbas, mare vi- treum esse Scripturam Sacram, quia hæc pellucida est, & quasi speculum: Et Ambrosius cui mare æneum in templo Salomonis est V. T. mare vitreum est N. T. Et Dionysius Carthuf. atque Alcasar, quibus mare vitreum est pœnitentia: quia pœnitentia est mare ob amaritudinem & copiam lacrymarum, simile crystallo ob firmitatem propositi de peccatis dein- ceps cavendis & vita nova ineunda. Sed maxime convenit antiquissima Interpretatio, Patribus ple- risq; & aliis Interpp. probata, Baptismum per mare vitreum figurari: 1. Quod Baptismus habeat maris amplitudinem, vitri perspicuitatem, & crystalli firmi- tatem ac soliditatem. 2. Sicut vitrum Solis radiis est pervium: ita anima baptizata radiis gratiæ a Deo illustratur, dicente Hugone. Fideles baptizati, Ruperto dicente, quod hic affert Cornelius, in hac vita sunt vitrei, i. e. lucidi, sed fragiles, infirmi, mortales; at post resurrectionem erunt similes crystallo, id est, solidi, robusti, & immortales. 3. Me- rito mare vocatur Baptismus; quia non tantum apertus fons est domui Jacob Zach. XIII, 1. Sed omnibus populis & gentibus patet, ceu commune omnium lavacrum regenerationis, Tit. III. 5. Et mare crystallinum ob illuminationem, quæ fit in Baptismo: ita ut mare amplitudinem, crystallus autem virtutem ac efficaciam baptismi significet. Mare hoc in conspectu throni est: quia Baptismus in limine Ecclesiæ & aditus ad thronum & regnum Dei, Joh. III. 5. 4. Admittimus respici ad analo- giam maris ænei a Salomone facti. Ut ergo in illo sese lavabant Sacerdotes, antequam ad sanctua- rium admitterentur, 1. Reg. VII. 23. Ita baptisma- tis lavacro & sacramento initiationis opus est, ut in Ecclesiam admittamus, & ad ingressum re- gni cœlorum, quotquot Sacerdotes esse volumus coram Deo, Apoc. I. v. 5. Omnis qui ad thronum Dei cupit accedere, debet per Baptismi mare transire. 5. Sic a throno Dei procedit Verbum Legis & Evangelii, & coram throno est Sacra- mentum Baptismi, quia Deus in throno sedens per Verbum & Sacramenta sibi Ecclesiam colli- git. Ante thronum Dei, ait B. Cluverus, sunt do- na divini Spiritus & vitæ cum mari : illis illustra- ri, hoc purgari oportet omnes ad illum accedentes. 6. Baptismus præfiguratus est per mare rubrum, in quo exercitus Pharaonis suffocatus est Exod. XIV. v. 27. qua ratione hic utitur B. Gerhardus. 7. Approbant suffragio suo hanc interpretationem Victorini, & Tyconii, Primasius, Anshelmus, Ru- pertus, Beda, Haymon, Richardus, Lyranus, Gloss. ordinar. Strabus, Thomas, plerique nostrates, O- siander, B. Hoë, B. Gerhardus, B. Cluverus, B. Clo- tzius disput. de Baptism. Sacram. qui §. 25. hanc rationem affert: Sicut Johanni in Apocalypsi status Ecclesiæ, Novi Testamenti, quem suo tempore vel habuit vel post habitura erat usque ad consumma- tionem seculi a cap. IV. ad XX. delineatur: Ita hoc cap. IV. & V. visione generali & ad prophetiam se- quentem quasi præparatoria status Ecclesiæ Novi Te- stamenti, quam ab initio ad finem usque obtinere debebat, exhibetur iis typis & coloribus, qui dein per totam Apocalypsin sparsim repetuntur cap. XI. XIV. XV. XIX. Illud ergo mare hic intelligitur, quod pertinet ad statum Ecclesiæ militantis in hoc seculo, eumq́; repræsentat, cujus typus hic Johanni exhibe- tur. Vid. & B. Quistorp. Senior. De verbo Dei ex- plicat Frobenius, de Baptismo & Verbo Thomas, Cluverus, Grave, Dürfeld.

Καὶ ἐν μέσῳ τῦ θρόνε, καὶ κύκλῳ τῦ θρόνε) id est, de qua- tuor animalibus unum erat in gradibus qui ante folium. Vi- de 1. Reg. X. v. 19. Duo a lateribus: unum retro, ac sic propiores erant solio, quam Presbyteri. Gradus sumuntur ut pars solii.

Τέσσαρα ζῶα) In tabernaculo, in templo Salomonis & in viso Ezechielis duæ sunt figuræ pares, compositæ ex qua- ternorum animantium formis. Hic vero, ut sequentia nos docent, quatuor formæ animantium distinctæ. Quare id? quia omnia in Novo Testamento distinctius quam in vetere noscuntur. Quatuor animalia hoc loco sunt quatuor Apo- stoli, aut Apostolici viri qui tunc erant Hierosolymis velut vexilliferi castrorum Christi.

Γέμοντα ὀφθαλμῶν ἔμπροσθεν καὶ ὄπισθεν) Ex Ezechiele, ubi per vocem עינים, id est, ὀφθαλμὸς, diximus significa- ri colores. Illi autem colores hic significant multiformia Dei dona, per quæ Apostoli norant & præsentia & futura, Matth. XIII. 52.

## 4:7
Verse 7. And the first living creature like a lion) I do not doubt that this is Peter, placed at the front of the throne because of his primacy, fervent in spirit, and in this similar to a lion.

And the second living creature like a calf) שור which signifies an ox, the Greek Interpreters translate as calf in very many places. The ox signifies patience: by which I think James the brother of the Lord is designated.

And the third living creature having the face as a man) In goodness man surpasses the other living creatures. I think, however, that Matthew is designated, who is said to have remained for a long time in Judea. In the Manuscript it is as a man, just as the Latin also has it. Face as פנים in Ezekiel is everything that falls into sight, not the face alone.

And the fourth living creature like a flying eagle) It signifies the speed of the ministry: which is certainly proper to Paul, who was frequently at Jerusalem, Acts IX. v. 7, Gal. I. v. 18, ch. II. v. 1, Acts XV. v. 2, ch. XXI. v. 17. And well as flying, because he was always in a course.

Latin:

Vers. 7. Καὶ τὸ ζῶον τὸ πρῶτον ὅμοιον λέοντι) Non dubito quin hic sit Petrus ob principatum collocatus in fronte solii, fervens animo, & in hoc leoni similis.

Καὶ τὸ δεύτερον ζῶον ὅμοιον μόσχῳ) שור quod bovem si- gnificat, μόσχον vertunt Græci Interpretes plurimis in locis. Bos patientiam significat : per quam designari puto Jaco- bum fratrem Domini.

Καὶ τὸ τρίτον ζῶον ἔχον τὸ πρόσωπον ὡς ἄνθρωπος) Boni- tate homo antecedit animantia cætera. Puto autem desi- gnari Matthæum, qui diu dicitur mansisse in Judæa. In Ma- nuscripto ὡς ἀνθρώπυ, quomodo & Latinus. Πρόσωπον ut פנים apud Ezechielem est omne id quod in conspectum ca- dit, non facies sola.

Καὶ τὸ τέταρτον ζῶον ὅμοιον ἀετῷ πετωμένῳ) Celeritatem ministerii significat : quod certe Paulo proprium, qui sæ- pius Hierosolymis fuit Act. IX. v. 7. Gal. I. v. 18. cap. II. v. 1. Act. XV. v. 2. c. XXI. v. 17. Et bene πετωμένῳ, quia semper erat in cursu.

## 4:8
Verse 8.

And the four living creatures, each one of them having six wings) Bishops are equated to Angels. Apostles, however, to the Seraphim, the highest of the Angels. For this is taken from Isa. VI. v. 2. The Apostles cover their face before God through humility in the mind, and through the discipline of the body, in which are fasts. Their feet, that is, those things of which one ought to be ashamed, namely sins, they cover through a contrite heart and an amended life. They fly, however, through faith and love: Behold six wings, truly excellent. By these oars one goes to the throne of God. Round about and within they are full of eyes) that round about pertains entirely to this, not to the preceding. For the six wings which cover the face, and the shameful parts, and with which one flies, cannot be round about. But round about and within means, outside and inside. Those multiform gifts given to the Apostles were both in the mind and appeared outwardly. Thus 1 Kings VII. 36, within, round about, that is, within and round about or outside. These are vain inventions about the four Apostles who were then at Jerusalem as the standard-bearers of the camps of Christ, Peter, James the brother of the Lord, Matthew, and Paul. What history, whether Biblical or Ecclesiastical, hands down such a thing? That colors are signified by eyes has, so far as I know, come into no one's mind: just as it is very inconsistent that the multiform gifts of God be noted by colors, through which the Apostles knew both present and future things: which, even if it be true in part concerning the Apostles, Matt. XIII. 52, it is not handed down.

If it be asked what is truly to be understood by the four living creatures, we answer that it is certain to us, 1. that the four primary angels are not meant, as Cornelius a Lapide wishes, along with Pererius and Hieronymus Prado, and also Franciscus Gomarus: because those living creatures sing together with the twenty-four elders concerning the redemption made for them by the blood of the Lamb, Apoc. V. v. 9. But were the angels redeemed by Christ? 2. Much less the four cardinal virtues, as Aretas reported from certain others: for here subjects are denoted. Neither a song, nor redemption, nor other things assigned here are appropriate to virtues. 3. For the same reasons, the opinion of Origen in homily I on Ezekiel and of Nazianzen, cited by Sixtus Senensis, is to be rejected, that by these four living creatures are signified the four faculties and powers of the human soul, because indeed certain persons and personal actions are designated here. 4. Nor does it in any way agree with the interpretation of Ansbert, Jerome, Abulensis, and others, that Christ is understood, who in his incarnation was man, in his passion a calf, in his resurrection a lion, in his ascension an eagle. For the subjects were distinct. And Christ is exhibited by the Lamb in the midst of the throne distinctly from those four living creatures: Or 5. Lyranus's interpretation concerning the four patriarchal churches. 6. Similarly, the explanation of others is very foreign, concerning the four attributes of divine providence, which is strong, as a lion; swift and penetrating, as an eagle; sweet and lovable, as a man; long-suffering and patient, as an ox. For these pertain to the one sitting on the throne, not to the four living creatures around the throne. 7. Indeed, the exposition in Aretas is discordant, that by this fourfold form the world, both great and small, is designated, consisting of the four elements; as if the lion signifies fire, the ox earth, the man air, the eagle water: To have recited these is to have refuted them. Nor does the interpretation of Pareus concerning all the saints of the New Testament triumphing in heaven deserve approval; or 9. that of Brightman concerning all the ministers and doctors of the divine Word. For the four living creatures are distinguished from the elders. Those who say that the four evangelists are meant approach closer 10. to the truth; yet in such a way that perhaps St. Paul occupied the place of the fourth, since John was a spectator, not an assessor. Which explanation is almost accepted regarding Ezekiel I: most making Mark the lion, whose beginning in the Gospel starts from the cry and roar of St. John like a lion in the desert: they say the calf is St. Luke, whose beginning starts from the old priesthood of Zacharias. They say St. Matthew is figured in the man, whose beginning is the human genealogy of Christ.

The eagle [represents] St. Paul, who penetrated as far as the third heaven. If John himself is said to be represented, Ribera observes that these animals were represented not as they were then, but as they were to be thereafter and at that time about which he prophesies. But let it be that those four were seen here: Mark, Luke, Matthew, and Paul: but who are signified by them? For there is no doubt that others are signified by the four animals: As in the whole Apocalypse, that which is seen is one thing, and that which is signified by that vision is another. Pererius and Viegas think that all the Prelates of the Church are represented in these four animals, and Gvaltherus explains this in Sixtus Senensis, how we have here a type of a good Prelate, namely that he ought to be strong as a lion, laborious as an ox, clement and compassionate as a man, contemplative as an eagle. But you would seek such things in Papal Prelates in vain. Others designate the four Doctors of the Church, namely St. Gregory as the easy man, St. Ambrose as the strong lion, St. Jerome as the laborious and solid ox, St. Augustine as the sublime eagle. But that meaning is too narrow. Alcafar wishes not only the four Evangelists to be understood, but the Apostles and Apostolic men, who are Cherubim in knowledge and wisdom, and Seraphim in ardor and zeal. But neither is that meaning adequate: Therefore, just as all Ministers of the Word who preside over certain and defined Churches are signified by the twenty-four Elders, so all Doctors who serve the universal Church with public writings, and are not restricted to informing only a certain Church, are signified by the four mystical animals; even if they happen to be in charge of one or another diocese and province. Such as were not only the Apostles and Evangelists, but such as are today Doctors in the Church, who inform the universal Church chiefly by their writings, just as that was done by the Fathers, as we call them. Which opinion is proved first because those who are represented by the four animals say that they were redeemed from every tribe, tongue, and people; which cannot be said of the four Evangelists or particular Doctors, but is rightly said of various Catholic Doctors of all times throughout the world: then because they are distinguished from the twenty-four Elders, whom there is no doubt designate Ministers of the Word; just as they are distinguished from that innumerable multitude of the Elect triumphing in heaven: whence it is gathered that they signify neither any promiscuous elect, nor any Ministers of the Word: then because the animals, as being more distinguished, precede the Elders who follow in singing divine praises. Although therefore the Elders sit on thrones, the animals are nevertheless ἐν μέσῳ τοῦ θρόνου κὴ κύκλῳ τοῦ θρόνου: Although those shine with white garments and golden crowns; the animals are nevertheless full of eyes on all sides, which signifies that they are watchful, and have other eyes on the way, and make things accessible to themselves, and work on all sides with the greatest alacrity, wisdom, and perspicacity: those have a certain seat as it were, these fly perpetually, and keep watch for the whole Church: then because that tradition of Irenaeus concerning the four Evangelists seems to have flowed from the very school of St. John, although a little changed, as is accustomed to happen; since the Evangelists are indeed signified, but not they alone. Anshelmus favors our opinion: The Evangelists and other holy preachers are called animals, who, being gentle and well-spirited, animate others, who do not speak according to persons, but according to the office of fourfold preaching. Albertus: By the four animals all Preachers and especially the four Evangelists are signified. They are called 4 animals, because their preaching is taken from the four Gospels; and the Evangelists themselves sustain, guard, and defend the Church of Christ even to the present by these doctrines or Evangelical books. Dionysius: The four animals in this book do not always designate the four Evangelists, but also all the Doctors of the Church who follow their doctrine. Blessed Cluverus, who wishes to be signified by the Elders both those teaching by the word and those holily ruling and governing the Church, such as Princes also are, the guardians of both tables and of Evangelical doctrine, 1 Tim. V. v. 17. But he explains the four animals on p. 185. As I understand the Evangelists by the animals in the most common exposition of the Church, so I judge that one must by no means stop at those four alone, but that the mystery must be extended to the rest also, who either taught by living voice by traveling through diverse regions, or even when those ministries ceased, performed the same by true and salutary writings. But I do not wonder that the name has stuck to those four, I mean Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John, since they delivered the complete and infallible norm of the Gospel not to one city or people alone, but to many, nay, to all tribes and tongues, and are thus Evangelists by a double right, inasmuch as they both propagated the Gospel to and fro by living voice while traveling through various regions of the world, and commended the same to all nations by a perennial and never-dying Scripture. For these Evangelists were chosen from every tribe and people and tongue: Those four Evangelists were of one people only. Therefore after them other Evangelists are commemorated, Eph. IV. v. 11, such as Chrysostom reports Priscilla and Aquila to be there, and such as Philip was, Acts XXI. v. 8, not bound to one city or nation only; but preaching here and there in Samaria, Gaza, Azotus, Caesarea, and other places, Acts VIII. v. 5, 26, 40. Timothy 2 Tim. IV. v. 5, who was called from the Ephesian Church to Paul, so that he might be sent to other nations, and Titus, after he had informed the Cretans, was sent away into Dalmatia, 2 Tim. IV. Which Evangelists Paul in 1 Cor. XII. v. 28, 29, has embraced under the general title of Doctors. Since, therefore, to act as an Evangelist is to announce the eternal Gospel of Christ not to one people only, but to various or all nations and languages, certainly under the reign of the beast, that is, the Roman Pontiff, such Evangelists or Evangelizing Angels, chap. XIV. v. 6. are predicted to arise; as the blessed Cluverus rightly concludes: who therefore establishes two kinds of Evangelists. Others, he says, are those who, traveling the lands themselves with a living voice, announce the Gospel, such as those whom Eusebius describes in book III of Church History, chap. 31, and whoever are or have been like them. I add, especially the Apostles, the teachers of the whole world. Others are those who, absent in body, accomplish the same thing by the Spirit and by writings. Such were, after the Apostles, Ignatius, Clement, Quadratus, Justin, Irenaeus, Dionysius, Jerome, Augustine, and many others in every century. In more recent memory, Luther, Chemnitius, Brentius, Melanchthon, and others, especially the theologians of this and the previous age, the Academics. For they are the ones who both instruct the diverse nations flowing to them and send teachers to them, and with accurately elaborated writings hold a torch before the churches. This is what he says, referring to the oration of the blessed Chemnitius on the origin of Academies, delivered in the introduction of the University of Julia. In this, however, we differ from the blessed Cluverus, in that he wishes the present state of the Church and the teachers in it to be prefigured, whereas we, even if we admit that the kind of people they were in the Church militant is shadowed forth, yet here their heavenly glory is described, in that they incessantly thunder forth their δοξολογία [doxology] and, clothed in white garments and crowned with golden crowns, they triumph, we do not doubt.

Moreover, they are full of eyes before and behind, not only because of understanding, but also because they attend to the whole Church, Acts 20:28, 1 Peter 5:2, and are vigilant on every side. They are compared to a lion, because they are of undaunted spirit in adversity; to a calf, because they are laborious and industrious, 1 Timothy 5:18; to a man, because they ought to be humane, 2 Timothy 2:24, especially toward the infirm, Romans 14:1; to an eagle, because they preach not human dreams, but heavenly doctrine, primarily Christ, 1 Corinthians 2:2, who is true God and man, designated by the eagle and the man, as this blessed Gerhard [says], and the lion is of the tribe of Judah, Revelation 5:2, and has prostrated all enemies, and offered himself to God as a sweet-smelling savor, Ephesians 5:2, just as in the Old Testament calves were offered to God. But this implies how varied the gifts of God are: in one, leonine magnanimity excels, Isaiah 31:4, Amos 3:4, Proverbs 28:1. In another, bovine endurance of labors, Deuteronomy 33:17, Proverbs 14:4; in a third, human moderation and prudence, Daniel 4:15, chapter 7:4, Hosea 11:4; in a fourth, aquiline perspicacity and swiftness, Job 9:26, Isaiah 40:31, Jeremiah 4:13, chapter 48:10.

They are seen having six wings, like the Seraphim, Isaiah 6:3, because of equal zeal and diligence in executing the parts of their office; then also because of reverence, because they fear the divine majesty: therefore they cover both their face and their feet with their wings, concerning which Andreas of Caesarea [says]: The animals, as it seemed to the great Dionysius, covered their faces with two wings for this reason, their feet with two, and flew with the two in the middle, from which it is evident that their fear concerning sublime things and things deeper than their comprehension, and the reverence through which they are lifted by their middle wings to the divine rays as if by heavenly balances. Compare Exodus 33:22, Ezekiel 19:3. But through ταπεινοφροσύνην [humility] in the mind, and through the δαλαγωγίαν [discipline] of the body, in which there are fasts, as also through contrition of heart and amendment of life through faith and love, as if by six excellent wings, one goes to the throne of God; nor is this implied in this place, where the discourse is not about the manner of arriving at the throne of God, but about those who move around the throne: nor is there a description of the Elect and Ministers of the Word, much less are the causes of salvation defined, nor is it consistent with the analogy of faith: because no one comes to the Father except through me, says Christ, namely apprehended by faith, John 14:6, and in this one name is the salvation of all, Acts 4:12.

PART II. DIVINE ΔΟΞΟΛΟΓΙΑ [DOXOLOGY]. Verse 8 of the same.

And they have no rest day and night) This Paul explains in Acts 20:31. As much as nature allowed, they suffered no time to be free from labors for the praise of God. Taken from Isaiah 62:6.

This is to be understood simply and absolutely, not restrictedly, 'as much as nature allowed.' For just as the eyes were carried around on every side without rest, so also there was no rest from the celebration of God. Just as the Angels always sing their τρισάγιον [trisagion] without intermission or weariness, so also the Elect in heaven, being ἰσάγγελοι [equal to the angels]. They have rest from all labor and trouble, Revelation 14:3. But from crying out and psalmody they have no rest, because this brings true rest and supreme pleasure in the Lord, but not trouble or weariness.

Saying holy, holy, holy, holy, holy, holy, holy, holy, holy) In very many manuscripts it is read only three times, as in Isaiah. And it is the custom of the Hebrews to repeat a word three times in matters which they wish to be vehemently inculcated, Jeremiah 22:29, Ezekiel 21:27.

God the Almighty) יהוה צבאות [LORD of Hosts]. See above I. 8. He who was, and who is, and who is to come) who promises, and performs what is promised, and will perform, see above I. 4.

As divine glory, divine justice, and divine grace were depicted by notable gems: so in this doxology of the four animals, divine holiness and omnipotence and eternity are celebrated. But the threefold repetition is held, not because divine holiness is vehemently inculcated; but because of the mystery of the most holy Trinity, because the Father is holy, the Son is holy, the Holy Spirit is holy, which the ancients taught with great consensus, and it is evident from the collation of the Isaianic passage, and those things which are said there. Nor is God the Almighty the same as יהוה צבאות, because by the former the omnipotence of God is expressed, by the latter His αὐτουσία [self-existence] and power over all things. Finally, by those words 'He who was, and who is, and who is to come,' not the execution of promises, but the interminable and immutable eternity of the Triune God is designated, which is expressed in this way for our comprehension according to the differences of all times. just as it is also designated shortly after by the words τῷ ζῶντι εἰς τὼς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. Some refer the first part, 'who was', to the Father and creation; 'who is', to the Son and redemption; and 'who is to come', to the Holy Spirit and beatification. For God does not live only in Himself, as life itself, eternal and uncreated; but He is the cause of the life of all, whether natural, or supernatural through grace, or heavenly through the glory of beatitude, Psal. XXXVI. 5. Joh. I. 5. c. XIV. 6.

Latin:

Vers. 8.

Καὶ τέσσερα ζῶα ἓν καθ᾽ἓν αὐτῶν ἔχων ἀνὰ πτέρυγας ἓξ) Episcopi Angelis æquantur. Apostoli autem Seraphinis Angelorum summis. Nam desumptum hoc ex Esa. VI. v. 2. Faciem coram Deo tegunt Apostoli per ταπεινοφροσύνην in animo, & per corporis δυλαγωγίαν, in qua sunt jejunia. Pedes, id est, ea quorum pudere debet, peccata scilicet, te- gunt per cor contritum, & vitam emendatam. Volant autem per fidem & dilectionem : Ecce alas sex, sane egregias. His remigiis ad solium Dei itur. Κυκλόθεν καὶ ἔσωθεν γέμουσιν ὀφθαλμῶν) κυκλόθεν istud omnino huc pertinet, non ad præcedentia. Alæ enim sex quæ tegunt faciem, & pudenda, & quibus volatur, non possunt esse in circuitu. Sed κυκλόθεν καὶ ἔσωθεν valet, extra & intus. Dona illa multiformia Apostolis data, & in ani- mo erant, & foris apparebant. Sic 1. Reg. VII. 36. ἔσωθεν, κυκλόθεν, id est, ἔσωθεν καὶ κυκλόθεν sive ἔξωθεν. Vana hæc sunt commenta de quatuor Aposto- lis, qui tum Hierosolymis velut vexilliferi castro- rum Christi fuerint, Petro, Jacobo fratre Domi- ni, Matthæo & Paulo. Quænam historia sive Bi- blica, sive Ecclesiastica tale quid tradit. Per ocu- los etiam colores significari hactenus, quod sciam, nemini in mentem venit: quemadmodum in- concinnum valde, per colores multiformia Dei dona notari, per quæ Apostoli norant & præsen- tia & futura: Quod etsi ex parte de Apostolis ve- rum sit, Matth. XII. v. 52. traditum non est.

Quid vero per quatuor animalia intelligendum sit, si quæratur, respondemus, certum id nobis esse, 1. non intelligi Angelos quatuor primarios, ut cum Pererio & Hieronymo Prado, Cornelius a Lapide vult, nec non Franciscus Gomarus: quia concinunt illa animalia cum viginti quatuor Se- nioribus de redemptione sibi per sanguinem A- gni facta, Apoc. V. v. 9. Num vero Angeli a Chri- sto redempti sunt? 2. Nedum quatuor virtutes cardinales, ut Aretas e quibusdam retulit: Hic enim supposita denotantur. Virtutibus nec can- ticum, nec redemptio, nec alia hic assignata con- veniunt. 3. Iisdem rationibus reprobanda O- rigenis homil. I. in Ezech. & Nazianz. apud Six- tum Senensem sententia, per hæc quatuor anima- lia significari quatuor facultates & vires animæ humanæ, quod nempe hic designatæ sint certæ personæ & actiones personales. 4. Neque ulla- tenus congruit Ansberti, Hieronymi, Abulens. aliorumque interpretatio, Christum intelligi, qui in incarnatione fuit homo, in passione vitulus, in resurrectione leo, in ascensione aliqua. Distin- cta enim fuerunt supposita. Et Christus per A- gnum in medio throni ab illis quatuor animalibus distinctim exhibitus est: Aut 5. Lyrani de qua- tuor Patriarchalibus Ecclesiis. 6. Similiter per- quam aliena est explicatio aliorum de quatuor at- tributis providentiæ divinæ, quæ fortis, ut leo; ve- lox & penetrans sit, ut aquila; svavis & amabilis, ut homo; longanimis & patiens, ut bos. Hæc enim pertinent ad sedentem in throno, non ad quatuor animalia circa thronum. 7. Absona vero apud Aretam est ἔκθεσις per hoc quadriforme mundum tam magnum, quam parvum designari ex quatuor elementis consistentem; quasi leo significet ignem, bos terram, homo aërem, aquila aquam: Quæ recitasse est refutasse. Neque 8. calculum meretur Parei de omnibus Novi Testamenti san- ctis in cælo triumphantibus interpretamentum; aut 9. Brightmanni de omnibus Verbi divini Mi- nistris & Doctoribus. Distinguuntur enim a Presbyteris quatuor animalia. Propius 10. ad veritatem accedunt, qui quatuor Evangelistas consedisse dicuntur; ita tamen ut quarti locum occuparit forte S. Paulus, quum Johannes spe- ctator fuerit, non adsessor. Quæ explicatio circa Ezech. I. fere recepta est: plerisque leonem Mar- cum facientibus, cujus principium in Evangelio incipit a clamore & rugitu S. Johannis velut leo- nis in deserto: vitulum esse dicunt S. Lucam, cujus principium incipit a sacerdotio veteri Za- chariæ. S. Matthæum in homine figuratum ajunt, cujus principium est humana genealogia Christi.

Aquilam S. Paulum, qui in cœlum tertium usque penetravit. Si Johannes ipse repræsentatus dica- tur, observat Ribera, hæc animalia repræsentata fuisse non qualia tum erant, sed prout futura de- inceps & eo tempore erant, de quo vaticinatur. Sed esto quod hic visi sint quatuor illi, Marcus, Lucas, Matthæus & Paulus: quinam vero per illos significati? Nam per quatuor animalia alios significari dubium nullum est: Ut in tota Apoca- lypsi aliud est, quod videtur, aliud quod viso illo significatur. Pererius ac Viegas existimant, in qua- tuor hisce animalibus omnes Ecclesiæ Prælatos repræsentari, idque explicat Gvaltherus apud Sixtum Senensem, quomodo boni Prælati typum hic habeamus, quod nempe debeat esse fortis ut leo, laboriosus ut bos, clemens & compatiens ut homo, contemplativus ut aquila. At talia temere in Prælatis Papalibus quæsiveris. Doctores qua- tuor Ecclesiæ alii denominant, hominem nempe facilem esse S. Gregorium, leonem fortem S. Am- brosium, bovem laboriosum & solidum S. Hiero- nymum, aquilam sublimem S. Augustinum. Sed significatio illa nimis angusta est. Alcafar non tantum quatuor Evangelistas, sed Apostolos, vi- rosque Apostolicos, qui Cherubim scientia & sa- pientia, Seraphim ardore ac zelo sunt, intelligi vult. Sed nec ea significatio adæquata est: Ideoq; ut per viginti quatuor Presbyteros omnes Mini- stri Verbi, qui certis & definitis præsunt Ecclesiis: ita per quatuor animalia mystica omnes Docto- res, qui universali Ecclesiæ scriptis publicis in- serviunt, nec ad certam solum Ecclesiam infor- mandam adstricti sunt; etiamsi forte uni aut alteri diœcesi ac provinciæ sint præfecti. Quales erant non tantum Apostoli & Evangelistæ, sed hodie- que Doctores sunt in Ecclesia, qui scriptis præci- pue universam Ecclesiam informant, quemad- modum id a Patribus, quos vocamus, factum est. Quæ sententia probatur primo quia redemptos illi se dicunt, qui per quatuor animalia repræsen- tati ex omni tribu, lingua & populo; quod de qua- tuor Evangelistis aut peculiaribus Doctoribus dici non potest, recte autem de variis per orbem omnium temporum Doctoribus Catholicis dici- tur: tum quia a viginti quatuor Senioribus distin- guuntur, quos Verbi Ministros designare dubium non est; æque ut & ab innumerabili illa multitu- dine Electorum in cælis triumphantium discer- nuntur: unde nec quosvis promiscue electos, nec quosvis Verbi Ministros significare colligi- tur: tum quia animalia ceu insigniora præcedunt, quæ sequuntur Presbyteri in concinendis laudi- bus divinis. Etsi ergo Seniores in thronis sedeant, animalia tamen ἐν μέσῳ τοῦ θρόνου κὴ κύκλῳ τοῦ θρόνου sint: Etsi illi albis vestibus & aureis coronis ful- geant; animalia tamen plena undiquaque oculis sunt, quod præstat, aliisque oculatis in via, quæque sibi pervia faciunt, & summa alacritate, sapientia & perspicacia sua undique operantur: illi certam veluti sedem habent, hæc perpetuo volant, pro- que universa Ecclesia excubant: tum quod tra- ditio ista Irenæi de quatuor Evangelistis ex ipsa S. Johannis schola videatur profluxisse, etsi pau- lulum, ut fieri consuevit, immutata; quum Ev- angelistæ quidem signati sint, non autem soli. Nostræ sententiæ favet Anshelmus: Animalia di- cuntur Evangelistæ & cæteri sancti prædicatores, qui mansueti & bene animati cæteros animant, qui non dicunt secundum personas, sed secundum offi- cium quadrifariæ prædictionis. Albertus: Per qua- tuor animalia omnes Prædicatores & præcipue qua- tuor Evangelistæ signati sunt. Dicuntur autem præ- ser- dicatores 4. animalia, quia de quatuor Evange- liis prædicatio eorum sumitur; ipsiq́; Evangelistæ his doctrinis seu Evangelicis libris usq́; in præsens Ec- clesiam Christi sustentant, custodiunt ac defendunt. Dionysius: Quatuor animalia in hoc libro non semper quatuor Evangelistas, sed & omnes Do- ctores Ecclesiæ, qui eorum doctrinam sequuntur, designant. B. Cluverus, qui per Presbyteros signifi- cari vult tum docentes verbo, tum sancte regentes & gubernantes Ecclesiam, quales etiam Princi- pes sunt custodes tabulæ utriusque & doctrinæ Evangelicæ, 1. Tim. V. v. 17. Animalia vero qua- tuor ita explicat p. 185. Ut per animalia Evangeli- stas tritissima Ecclesiæ expositione intelligo, sic in so- lis quatuor illis nequaquam subsistendum, sed my- sterium ad reliquos etiam dilatandum censeo, qui vel viva voce regiones diversas perambulando do- cuerunt, vel etiam cessantibus illis ministeriis id- ipsum veris ac salutaribus scriptis præstiterunt. Nomen autem in istis quatuor, Matthæo, inquam, Marco, Luca & Johanne hæsisse nihil miror, quan- doquidem bi integram & infallibilem Evangelii normam non uni duntaxat civitati aut populo, sed multis, imo omnibus tribubus & linguis tradide- runt, duplicíq́; adeo jure Evangelistæ sunt, quippe qui & varias orbis regiones peragrantes ultro citroq́; Evangelium viva voce propagarint, & Scriptura perenni ac nunquam intermoritura idem cunctis gentibus commendarint. Hi enim Evangelistæ ex omni tribu & populo & lingua electi fuerunt: Illi quatuor Evangelistæ unius tantum populi erant. Ideo post illos alii commemorantur Evangelistæ, Eph. IV. v. 11. quales ibi Priscillam & Aquilam re- fert Chrysostomus, & qualis Philippus fuit, Actor. XXI. v. 8. non uni tantum civitati aut genti obstri- ctus; sed passim Samariæ, Gazæ, Azoto, Cæsareæ & aliis locis prædicans, Actor. VIII. v. 5. 26. 40. Timotheus 2. Tim. IV. v. 5. qui ab Ephesina Ec- clesia ad Paulum vocatus, ut ad alias gentes mitte- retur, & Titus, postquam Cretenses informarar, in Dalmatiam ablegatus, 2. Tim. IV. Quos Evan- gelistas Paulus 1. Cor. XII. v. 28. 29. generali Do- ctorum titulo complexus est. Quum ergo Evan- gelistam agere sit æternum Christi Evangelium non uni tantum populo, sed aut variis aut omni- bus gentibus & linguis annunciare, certe sub re- gno bestiæ, id est, Romani Pontificis, tales Evan- gelistæ vel Evangelizantes Angeli, cap. XIV. v. 6. exorituri prædicuntur; ut recte B. Cluverus col- ligit: qui proinde duo genera Evangelistarum con- stituit. Alii sunt, inquit, qui viva voce ipsimet ter- ras obeuntes Evangelium annunciant, quales fue- runt illi, quos Eusebius describit lib. III. Histor. Ec- cles. cap. 31. & quicunq́; illis sunt aut fuerunt simi- les. Addo ego, imprimis vero Apostoli, universi orbis Doctores. Alii qui corpore absentes idipsum Spiritu & scriptis efficiunt. Quales fuerunt post Apostolos Ignatius, Clemens, Quadratus, Justinus, Irenæus, Dionysius, Hieronymus, Augustinus & multi alii quovis seculo. Recentiori memoria Lu- therus, Chemnitius, Brentius, Melanchthon & alii, præsertim Theologi hujus & superioris ætatis Aca- demici. Illi enim sunt, qui & diversas nationes ad se confluentes erudiunt, iisq́; Doctores mittunt, & scri- ptis accurate elaboratis Ecclesiis facem præferunt. Hæc ille, remittens ad orationem B. Chemnitii de Academiarum origine in introductione Universita- tis Juliæ habitam. In eo tamen a B. Cluvero disce- dimns, quod ipse statum Ecclesiæ præsentem & Doctores in eadem figurari velit, nos autem, etsi quales illi fuerint in Ecclesia militante adumbrari, admittamus: hic tamen gloriam eorum cœlestem describi, qua indefinenter suam δοξολογίαν into- nant & vestimentis albis vestiti, coronisque aureis redimiti triumphant, nulli ambigimus.

Pleni autem oculis sunt ante & retro, non tan- tum ob intelligentiam, sed etiam, quia attendunt toti Ecclesiæ, Act. XX. 28. 1. Petr. V. 2. & undiqua- que vigilant. Conferuntur leoni, quod in adversis animo sint imperterrito; vitulo, quod laboriosi sint & industrii, 1. Tim. V. 18. homini, quia humani esse debent, 2. Tim. II. 24. præsertim erga infirmos, Rom. XIV. 1. aquilæ, quia non humana somnia, sed doctrinam cœlestem prædicant, imprimis Chri- stum, 1. Cor. II. 2. qui est verus Deus & homo, per aquilam & hominem designatus, ut hic B. Gerhar- dus, & leo est de tribu Juda, Apoc. V. 2. & omnes hostes prostravit, seque Deo in odorem suavitatis obtulit, Ephes. V. v. 2. ut Veteri Testamento vituli Deo oblati sunt. Id autem innuitur, quam dona Dei varia sint, in uno præcellere magnanimita- tem leoninam, Esa. XXXI. v. 4. Amos III. v. 4. Prov. XXVIII. v. 1. in altero bovinam laborum to- lerantiam, Deut. XXXIII. v. 17. Prov. XIV. v. 4. in tertio humanam moderationem & prudentiam, Dan. IV. v. 15. cap. VII. v. 4. Ose. XI. v. 4. in quarto aquilinam perspicaciam & celeritatem, Job. IX. 26. Esa. XL. 31. Jer. IV. 13. c. XLVIII. 10.

Conspiciuntur habentes sex alas, ut Seraphim Esa. VI. v. 3. ob parilem zelum & diligentiam in exequendis partibus officii; tum etiam ob reve- rentiam, quod metuant majestatem divinam: ideo & faciem & pedes alis suis obtegant, de quo An- dreas Cæsariensis : Animalia, ut Magno Dionysio visum est, duabus alis ob id facies suas tegebant, duabus pedes, duabus mediis volabant, quo hinc constet ipsorum circa sublimia & captu suo profun- diora metus, & reverentia per quam alis mediis ad divinos radios tanquam cælestibus libramentis alle- ventur. Conf. Exod. XXXIII, v. 22. Ezech. XIX. 3. Per ταπεινοφροσύνην autem in animo, & per cor- poris δαλαγωγίαν, in qua jejunia sunt, ut & per cordis contritionem & vitæ emendationem per fidem & dilectionem ceu egregias sex alas ad so- lium Dei iri neque hoc loco innuitur, ubi non de modo perveniendi ad solium Dei, sed de iis, quæ circa thronum versantur, sermo est: neque Ele- ctorum & Ministrorum Verbi descriptio habe- tur, nedum causæ salutis definiuntur, nec analo- giæ fidei consentaneum est: quia nemo venit ad Pa- trem, nisi per me, inquit Christus, scilicet fide ap- prehensum, Joh. XIV. v. 6. & in hoc uno nomine salus est omnium, Actor. IV. v. 12.

PARS II. ΔΟΞΟΛΟΓΙΑ DIVINA. Vers. eodem 8.

Καὶ ἀνάπαυσιν ἐκ ἔχωσιν ἡμέρας καὶ νυκτὸς) Hoc Paulus explicat Act. XX. v. 31. Quantum natura sinebat, nullum tempus vacare patiebantur a laboribus pro Dei laude. Sum- ptum ex Esa. LXII. 6.

Simpliciter hoc, & absolute intelligendum, non restricte, quantum natura sinebat. Ut enim oculi undiquaque circumferebantur sine requie: ita etiam nulla requies erat a celebratione Dei. Quemadmodum Angeli semper suum τρισάγιον concinunt sine intermissione aut defatigatione; sic etiam Electi in cælis, utpote ἰσάγγελοι. Re- quiem habent ab omni labore ac molestia, Apoc. XIV. v. 3. Sed a clamore & psalmodia requiem non habent, quia hæc veram in Domino quietem & summam voluptatem affert, non autem mole- stiam vel defatigationem.

Λέγοντα ἅγιος, ἅγιος, ἅγιος, ἅγιος, ἅγιος, ἅγιος, ἅγιος, ἅγιος, ἅγιος) In plurimis Manuscriptis ter tantum legitur ἅγιος, ut apud Esaiam. Et Ebræorum mos est ter vocem repetere in rebus quas vehementer inculcatas volunt, Jer. XXII. 29. Ezech. XXI. 27.

Ὁ Θεὸς ὁ παντοκράτωρ) יהוה צבאות. Vide supra I. 8. Ὁ ἦν, καὶ ὁ ὤν, καὶ ὁ ἐρχόμενος) qui promittit, ac promissa præstat, & præstabit, vide supra I. 4.

Ut depicta erat divina gloria, divina justitia, divina gratia per insignes gemmas: Ita in hac qua- tuor animalium δοξολογία celebratur divina san- ctitas & omnipotentia & æternitas. Repetitio autem trina habetur, non quod vehementer in- culcetur divina sanctitas; sed ob mysterium sacro- sanctæ Trinitatis, quia sanctus Pater, sanctus Fi- lius, sanctus Spiritus Sanctus, quod magno con- sensu veteres docuere, & e collatione loci Esaiani, atque eorum, quæ ibi dicta sunt, luculentum est. Neq; ὁ Θεὸς ὁ Παντοκράτωρ, idem est quod יהוה צבאות quia illo Dei omnipotentia, hoc αὐτου- σία & potestas super omnia exprimitur. Deniq; illis ὁ ἦν, καὶ ὁ ὢν, καὶ ὁ ἐρχόμενος non promissorum exe- cutio, sed interminabilis & immutabilis Dei triunius æternitas designatur, quæ nostro captu secundum omnium temporum differentias ita exprimitur; quemadmodum ea etiam vocibus τῷ ζῶντι εἰς τὼς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων paulo post designata est. Non- nulli prius illud, qui erat, ad Patrem & creatio- nem, qui est, ad Filium & redemptionem, & qui venturus est, ad Spiritum S. & beatificationem re- ferunt. Nec enim Deus in se tantum vivit, ut ipsa vita æterna & increata; sed causa est vitæ omnium tum naturalis tum supernaturalis per gratiam, tum cœlestis per beatitudinis gloriam, Psal. XXXVI. 5. Joh. I. 5. c. XIV. 6.

## 4:9
Vers. 9.

And when the living creatures give glory and honor and thanksgiving to Him who sits on the throne, who lives forever and ever) A magnificent description of God. Thus also below V. v. 14. Glory is given to God for His power, honor for His attributes, thanks for His benefits. Εὐχαριστία is תודה, for which the Latin interpreter here placed 'benedictionem' [blessing]; concerning this permutation of words, see what we said at Matth. XXVI. v. 24. Δώσῃ and shortly after πεσοῦνται are futures for any time, in the Hebrew manner.

By δόξαν we admit that the glory of God is given for His power, by τιμὴν indeed honor for His majesty, immutability, and divine holiness, and finally by εὐχαριστίαν for His grace and divine justice. Thus God is celebrated by the four living creatures for His divine properties and attributes, which is especially fitting for that most arduous matter. Glory is rendered to Jehovah as the eternal, omnipotent, and wise maker of all things, honor as to the only Holy One and the one who sanctifies all things, and thanksgiving as to the perennial and inexhaustible source of all goods. He Himself is known and proclaimed as life, and the eternal fountain of all life and joy. He is ὁ ὢν, in whom are all things, and from whom are all things, and through whom are all things. To Him alone be all honor forever.

Latin:

Vers. 9.

Καὶ ὅταν δώσῃ τὰ ζῶα δόξαν καὶ τιμὴν, καὶ εὐχαριστίαν τῷ καθημένῳ ἐπὶ τῷ θρόνῳ τῷ ζῶντι εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων) Magnifica Dei descriptio. Sic & infra V. v. 14. Gloria Deo datur ob potentiam, honos ob proprietates, gratiæ ob be- nefacta. Εὐχαριστία est תודה, pro quo benedictionem hic posuit Latinus Interpres, de qua vocum permutatione vide quæ diximus ad Matth. XXVI. v. 24. Δώσῃ & mox πεσοῦνται sunt futura pro quovis tempore, more Ebræo.

Per δόξαν gloriam Dei ob potentiam dari ad- mittimus, per τιμὴν vero honorem ob majesta- tem, immutabilitatem & sanctitatem divinam, per εὐχαριστίαν denique ob gratiam & justitiam divi- nam. Ita celebratur Deus a quatuor animalibus ob proprietates & attributa divina, quæ materia maxime ardua illa imprimis decet. Gloria Jehove tanquam æterno, omnipotenti & sapienti omnium factori, honor tanquam soli Sancto, & omnia san- ctificanti, gratiarum actio tanquam perenni & in- exhausto omnium bonorum fonti redditur. Ipse tan- quam vita, omnisq; vitæ & gaudii sempiterna sca- turigo cognoscitur & prædicatur. Ipse est ὁ ὢν, in quo omnia, & a quo omnia, & per quem omnia. Ipsi soli omnis honor in secula.

## 4:10
Vers. 10.

The twenty-four elders will fall before Him who sits on the throne, and will worship Him who lives forever and ever) The Jerusalem elders faithfully follow the Apostles. To fall to the ground, and προσκυνεῖν, which in this place is to kiss the feet, are the highest signs of honor. See Isaiah XLIX.

And they will cast their crowns before the throne) Namely, thus testifying that they received whatever right they have to the kingdom from God. Thus Tiridates, in Tacitus, Annal. XV, places the royal insignia before the effigy of Caesar.

Latin:

Vers. 10.

Πεσοῦνται οἱ δεκατέσσαρες πρεσβύτεροι ἐνώπιον τοῦ καθημένου ἐπὶ τοῦ θρόνου, καὶ προσκυνήσουσι τῷ ζῶντι εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων) Apostolos Presbyteri Hierosolymitani fideliter subsequuntur. Procidere in terram, & προσκυνεῖν quod hoc loco est pedes osculari, summa sunt honoris signa. Vide Esaiam XLIX.

Καὶ βάλουσι τοὺς στεφάνους αὑτῶν ἐνώπιον τοῦ θρόνου) Nimi- rum sic testantes se quicquid habent juris ad regnum a Deo accepisse. Sic Tiridates apud effigiem Cæsaris ponit insigne Regium apud Tacitum Annal. XV.

## 4:11
Vers. 11.

Saying, You are worthy, O Lord and our God, the Holy One, to receive glory and honor and power) Ὁ ἅγιος is absent in the Manuscript, as it is also in the Latin. By δύναμιν here is understood metonymically a confession of power: just as the Hebrews also use עז. Compare what is below in XI. 17.

For You created all things, and because of Your will they are and were created) It is the same as what the Jerusalem Church says, with the Apostles leading, in Acts IV. v. 24 and Nehem. IX. v. 6. In vain do the Jews hate us, since we worship no other God than the maker of the world and its parts, whom also The Jews call Him their God. In the manuscript it is: διὰ θέλημα τίσυ by the error of one letter for διὰ θέλημα τὸ σῦ. They were already men, because you had willed it, and they were created, that is, created again through Christ. See above chapter III. 14. Our writers are also accustomed, when they speak of names, to use the neuter gender. See Eph. I. v. 10. John XI. v. 32. as it is in the Latin, and in certain Greek copies. Here is fulfilled what Isaiah XXIV. v. 23 had predicted, that God would be glorified in Jerusalem in the sight of His servants.

It is not the Jerusalem Presbyters who follow the Apostles and Evangelists and chief Doctors, but all the Ministers of the Word throughout the world and the ages. Τὸ προσκυνεῖν according to the usage of Scripture in general is to worship, not to kiss feet. The casting down of crowns testifies to humility and the acknowledgment of unworthiness, because they wear crowns by no merit of their own. More correctly, therefore, Cornelius a Lapide: Note here a triple gesture of reverence, which denotes the wonderful humility and veneration of the Elders. For first they fall down and cast their faces to the ground as if to kiss the soil; second, they worship; third, they cast their crowns before God. The first signifies eager haste and profound reverence; the second, the just worship of latria owed to God; the third, the entire truth, sincerity, and gratitude of the soul, while they strip off their crowns and all their dignity, and as it were abdicate them from themselves, and resign and return them to God, as if to the true Lord of them. Furthermore: A crown is first a symbol of perfection and completion: but God alone is most perfect, and the true crown and completion of all things; second, of victory and triumph; third, of happiness; fourth, of empire and kingdom; fifth, of majesty and glory, which originally and fully belong to God alone, and are derived from Him through streams and communicated to creatures, especially the saints. Cf. Ps. CIV. v. 1. 1 Chron. XXIX. v. 11. Isa. XXVI. v. 12. Jas. I. v. 17.

The Δοξολογία according to the more approved codices is as follows: Ἄξιός εἶ, Κύριε, λαβεῖν &c. The other names therefore are redundant. They celebrate glory likewise, as the four living creatures, and honor and divine power with thanksgiving, as they confess and proclaim that which has shown itself in gracious preservation and protection. The reason is added from the creation of all things, and their preservation according to His gracious will. There is no reason why we should take the last word in a different sense regarding the new creation. For it can be understood in the proper sense: Because you created all things, and by your will they are, exist, and are sustained: which pertain primarily to divine omnipotence and goodness. Power, as Cocceius rightly says, is demonstrated in two ways: 1. because all things that are, are the work of God; 2. because they are on account of the will of God, that is, they were brought into being by the mere moment of His will, and as it were by His calling. Otherwise Gomarus: God is the efficient cause of the world, not only creating, but also the end, Rom. XI. v. 36.

II. THE UNSEALER OF THE BOOK, CHRIST THE GOD-MAN.

Latin:

Vers. 11.

Λέγοντες, ἄξιος εἶ ὁ Κύριος καὶ ὁ Θεὸς ἡμῶν, ὁ ἅγιος λα- βεῖν τὴν δόξαν, καὶ τὴν τιμὴν, καὶ τὴν δύναμιν) Ὁ ἅγιος abest in Manuscripto, ut & in Latino. Per δύναμιν hic intelligi- tur μετωνυμικῶς potentiæ confessio: quomodo & Ebræi עז usurpant. Confer quod infra XI. 17.

Ὅτι σὺ ἔκτισας τὰ πάντα καὶ διὰ τὸ θέλημά σου εἰσὶ καὶ ἐ- κτίσθησαν) Idem est quod Ecclesiæ Hierosolymitanæ præ- euntibus Apostolis dicit Actor. IV. v. 24. & Nehem. IX. v. 6. Frustra Judæi nos odio habent, cum non alium Deum co- lamus, quam mundi partiumque ejus opificem, quem & suum Deum dicunt Judæi. In Manuscripto est: διὰ θέλη- μα τίσυ errore unius literæ pro διὰ θέλημα τὸ σῦ. Erant jam homines, quia tu volueras, & conditi sunt, id est, iterum conditi per Christum. Vide supra cap. III. 14. Solent nostri Scriptores etiam cum de nominibus loquuntur, neu- tro genere uti. Vide Ephes. I. v. 10. Joh. XI. v. 32. ut est in Latino, & in Græcis exemplaribus quibusdam. Impletur hic quod prædixerat Esaias XXIV. v. 23. fore ut Deus glori- ficaretur in Jerusalem in conspectu servorum suorum.

Apostolos ac Evangelistas & Doctores præcipuos sequuntur non Hierosolymitani Presbyteri, sed omnes per orbem & secula quavis Verbi Ministri. Τὸ προσκυνεῖν ex usu Scripturæ in genere est ado- rare, non pedes osculari. Coronarum abjectio hu- militatem & indignitatis agnitionem testatur, quod nullo suo merito coronas gestent. Rectius ergo Cornelius a Lapide: Nota hic triplicem re- verentiæ gestum, qui miram Seniorum humilitatem & venerationem denotat. Nam primo procidunt & projiciunt faciem suam in terram quasi humum osculaturi; secundo adorant; tertio mittunt coronas ante Deum. Primum significat alacrem festinatio- nem & profundam reverentiam; secundum justum & Deo debitum latriæ cultum; tertium integram animi veritatem, sinceritatem & gratitudinem, dum suas coronas omnemq; dignitatem exuunt, & quasi a se abdicant, atque Deo, quasi vero earum Domino, resignant & reddunt. Porro: Corona pri- mo symbolum est perfectionis & complementi: Deus autem solus est perfectissimus, verumq; omnium co- ronis & complementum; secundo victoriæ & trium- phi; tertio felicitatis; quarto imperii & regni; quin- to majestatis & gloriæ, quæ originaliter & plene soli Deo competunt, & ab eo per rivulos derivantur & communicantur creaturis, præsertim sanctis. Conf. Psal. CIV. v. 1. 1. Par. XXIX. v. 11. Esa. XXVI. v. 12. Jac. I. v. 17.

Δοξολογία secundum probatiores codices ita habet: Ἄξιός εἶ, Κύριε, λαβεῖν &c. Cætera ergo nomina abundant. Gloriam pariter, ut quatuor animalia, & honorem celebrant & potentiam divinam cum gratiarum actione, utpote quæ sefe in conservatione ac tuitione gratiosa exhi- buit, confitentur ac deprædicant. Ratio additur a creatione omnium, eorumque secundum gra- tiosam voluntatem conservatione. Verbum po- stremum non est, cur alio sensu accipiamus de creatione nova. Nam intelligi potest sensu proprio: Quia tu creasti omnia, & per volunta- tem tuam sunt, existunt, & sustentantur omnia: Quæ ad divinam omnipotentiam & bonitatem im- primis faciunt. Potentia, ut recte Coccejus, de- monstratur duobus modis, 1. quia omnia, quæ sunt, Dei opus sunt, 2. quia propter voluntatem Dei sunt, hoc est, solo momento voluntatis, & quasi vocatione, adducta sunt. Aliter Gomarus: Deus causa mundi est efficiens non solum procreans, sed etiam finis, Rom. XI. v. 36.

II. RESIGNATOR LIBRI CHRISTUS ΘΕΑΝΘΡΩΠΟΣ.

## 5:1 Argument
CHAPTER V. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

He sees a book in the right hand of Him who sits on the throne, sealed with seven seals, and when an Angel asks who is worthy to open the book, and none is found who could do it, he weeps bitterly, but one of the Elders raises him up through the victory of the lion of the tribe of Judah, the root of David, and behold he saw in the midst of the throne a Lamb slain, having seven horns and seven eyes, receiving the book, and heard Him proclaimed by the four living creatures and the twenty-four Elders as worthy to open it, with innumerable Angels and every creature acclaiming.

There are two parts: I. The description of the Unsealer of the sealed book, to v. 7. II. The celestial harmonic music in praise of the Unsealer, to v. 14.

PART I. The description of the Unsealer of the sealed book.

Ver. 1. And I saw upon the right hand of Him who sits upon the throne a book)

For it is the custom to carry with us the books which we magnify; and to place them at the right hand is to wish to execute them.

Thus, here occurs 1. the vision of the book. 2. The question of the angels concerning the unsealing. 3. John's weeping over the unsealer. 4. The information of the Elder, comforting John, concerning the Unsealer. By the former members, by way of negation (κατ᾽ ἄρσιν), every mere creature in heaven and on earth is excluded from this office. By the latter member, however, that one is defined who is able and willing to unseal the book. That Elder describes his suppositum, which consists of human and divine nature, calling him the Lion of the tribe of Judah by reason of origin, as regards his human nature, and the root of David, as regards his divine nature, according to which David was begotten and sustained by him, not otherwise than as a tree sprouts from a root and is preserved by its vigor: then his office, both Royal, according to which he comes under the name of the Lion, King of all living creatures: and Prophetic, according to which the opening of the book is appropriated to him; and Priestly, to which pertains his slaughter as the Lamb immolated for us on the altar of the cross: then his state, both of exaltation, that he was in the midst of the throne, that he is worthy to receive the book and to open it, and of previous emptying, by which he was humbled even unto death: then the cause and principle of the power of unsealing the book, which arises from the eminence and glory of this person, because that Lamb has seven horns, which imply his infinite power, and seven eyes, which imply his immense knowledge, communicated to him according to his human nature: then the victory, which he obtained through passion and death, conquering the infernal lion: since through this victory he obtained for us that we might be made participants of the divine mysteries contained in the sealed book. Therefore, as to the first point, the vision of the book, the mystical book was shown to St. John not by custom or for the estimation of the book, but for a peculiar signification and for the representation of the things described in the book; it is held in the right hand for the sake of a good omen, for the faithful, who are one day to be placed at the right hand, and not for the sake of signifying execution, concerning which the truth of the divine book does not permit one to doubt.

Γεγραμμένον ἔσω, καὶ ἔξωθεν κατασφραγισμένον σφραγίσιν ἑπτὰ) It must be distinguished thus, as we have written: For it does not say the book was written inside and outside: but written inside: sealed outside. But that he says the book was sealed with seven seals is a πρόληψις (anticipation). For he saw the book with one seal, but with that opened, he learned there were six sealed parts. For there were seven volumes, each sealed, so that the second was wrapped in the first (for the Hebrew pages were volumes, מגלוח), the third in the second, and so on in succession.

These Grotius-like interpretations do not displease: Although many others [interpret] the book as written inside and outside, whence those who refer it to the book of Scripture, Origen homily XVI on Exodus, Ambrose, Eusebius, Augustine, Jerome, Bede, Hugo, Primasius, Ansbertus, [interpret] it as written on the outside by reason of the literal sense, and on the inside by reason of the spiritual; on the outside in respect of external preaching, on the inside in respect of saving power. But this book only reveals future things, therefore it is not the whole of Scripture. Others, with Hilary in his preface to the Psalms, understand by the book Christ during his passion: on the inside regarding the torments of his soul, on the outside regarding the scourges and wounds, as Bernard has it in his first sermon on the feast of Easter. But it is Christ who opens the book, not the book itself. More conveniently, Andreas of Caesarea and Arethas understand the decree and memory of God, in which all men are described, or the inscrutable abyss of the works and judgments of God. Oecumenius, Lyranus, and Aureolus think this book is the divine predestination, which is closed to us unless it is revealed from the right hand of God, or the book of life, in which the names of the elect are written. But those things might perhaps be referred to a part of this mystical book, since mention is made of the book of life in the same place; here, however, something more is designated, not indeed, as Lyranus—whom Maldonatus supports in the notes brought forward by Cornelius—wishes, the divine omniscience itself, but something which God predicts by the power of his omniscience concerning the fates of the Church and of his elect, as well as of their enemies. But the opinions of Ambrose, that this book is the chronology of the world and the seven seals are the seven ages of the world, and of others, that this book is the handwriting of Adam's sin, that is, the obligation and guilt of sin, are entirely foreign. For what do these have to do with prophecy? Alcafar understands by the book the seals themselves and their mysteries, and thinks that the salvation of believing Jews and the damnation of unbelievers is contained therein, but it is evident that the book is distinguished from its seals; and those things concerning the Jews had already been accomplished and were public to the whole world. Hieronymus Pradus on Ezekiel 2:10 refers the seven seals to the greatest calamities of the Church, but too generally, as Cornelius a Lapide admits. The book must therefore be understood as the divine providence concerning the fates of the Church, and those things still future, not only in this, but also in the future age, not only regarding the Church in itself, but also regarding the enemies of the Church. The sum is that the book itself is a prophecy which was now to be revealed through its resignation, and so it is like a sealed book before it is resigned. Others say this book is written inside and out because they were accustomed to write on both sides of the parchment, interior and exterior, and this is because whatever happens in time, God has foreseen from eternity, and what was hidden in God from eternity is made manifest in the execution of the divine decrees. Which Pineda, book V, on the things of Solomon, ch. 30, says the book is sealed because it is written in secret signs and characters, as was the custom among the Egyptians and Chinese, does not fit, because the seals were real, which were to be resigned. Therefore the book is sealed with seven seals because the judgments of God are hidden until they are manifested, either by revelation or by fulfillment. If Cornelius a Lapide is to be heard, the whole Apocalypse is occupied in the description of this book and its seven seals, so that it has two parts: in the former, namely from this chapter up to the 11th, the seals are referred to and explained; in the latter, from chapter 11 to the end, those things which were written in the book itself are referred to and read. But more correctly, the opening of the seven seals ends with the silence made in heaven for half an hour, Apoc. 8:1. And therefore, with all seven seals now opened, those things which were written in the opened book will be read and related; with this opinion standing, which he brings from Ribera, namely that the seals of the book are not to be understood as if, upon their being loosened, that which John narrates he saw upon the loosening of each one was read in the book, just as upon the loosening of the first seal he narrates that he saw a white horse, upon the loosening of the second a red one, upon the loosening of the third a black one, upon the loosening of the fourth a pale one, etc. For he does not read these in the book, but saw that with each seal opened, the individual things lying hidden under them were revealed and shown to him. For nothing could be read in the book except after the resignation of all seven seals: for only when all were referred to could the book be opened and read, not before. For the book was rolled up, and thus sealed on the outside with seven seals: Therefore that which John saw upon the unsealing of each seal, he saw not in the book, as being still closed by the other seals, but as if hidden under the seal itself, and made manifest upon its being opened.

Latin:

CAPUT V. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Videt librum in dextra sedentis in throno obsi- gnatum septem sigillis, & quærente Angelo, quis dignus sit aperire librum, nullog; reper- to, qui id posset, plorat amare, sed unus e Senioribus erigit eum per victoriam leonis de tribu Juda, radicis David, & ecce vidit in medio throni Agnum occisum, septem cor- nua & septem oculos habentem, accipere li- brum, & a quatuor animalibus & viginti quatuor Senioribus ceu dignum aperire de- prædicari audivit, acclamantibus Angelis innumeris & creatura universa.

Partes duæ sunt: I. Προσπογραφία Resignatoris libri obsignati, ad v. 7. II. Musica cælestis harmo- nica in laudem Resignatoris, ad v. 14.

PARS I. Προσπογραφία Resignatoris libri obsignatio.

Vers. 1. Καὶ εἶδον ἐπὶ τὴν δεξιὰν τῶ καθημένο ἐπὶ τῶ θρόνο βιβλίον)

Mos enim est libros quos magnificamus, nobiscum ferre; Et ad dextram ponere, est velle exequi.

Occurrit itaque hic 1. libri visio. 2. Angeli de resignstione quæstio. 3. Johannis ob resignatorem illacrimatio. 4. Senioris, consolantis Johannem, deResignatore informatio. Prioribus membris κατ᾽ ἄρσιν excluditur quævis creatura mera in cœlo & in terra ab hoc munere. Posteriori autem mem- bro definitur unicus ille, qui resignare librum va- leat ac velit. Describit autem Senior ille ejus tum suppositum, quod humana constet ac divina natu- ra, Leonem dicens de tribu Juda ratione originis, quoad humanam naturam, & radicem Davidis, quoad divinam naturam, secundum quam David ab ipso procreatus ac sustentatus est, non secus at- que arbor e radice propullulat, & conservatur ejusdem vigore: tum officium & Regium, secun- dum quod Leonis Regis omnium animantium no- mine venit: & Propheticum, juxta quod referatio libri eidem appropriatur; & Sacerdotale, ad quod pertinet occisio ejus tanquam Agni pro nobis im- molati in ara crucis: tum statum, & exaltationis, quod fuerit in medio throni, quod dignus sit acci- pere librum, & aperire, & præviæ exinanitionis, qua humiliatus est usque ad mortem: tum potesta- tis resignandi librum causam, & principium, quæ e personæ istius cum eminentia & gloria oritur, quia Agnus ilie septem habet capita, quæ infini- tam ejus potentiam, & septem oculos, qui immen- sam ejus scientiam, secundum humanam naturam ipsi communicatam inferunt: tum victoriam, quam per passionem, & mortem obtinuit, vincens leo- nem infernalem: Siquidem per hanc victoriam id nobis obtinuerit, ut participes reddi possimus di- vinorum mysteriorum, libro obsignato compre- hensorum. Quod ergo primum ad libri visionem, non ex more, vel æstimio libri, sed ex peculiari si- gnificatione, & ob rerum in libro descriptarum re- præsentationem S. Johanni exhibendam visus est liber mysticus, qui in dextra habetur boni ominis causa, pro fidelibus, olim etiam ad dextram sta- tuendis, non vero significandæ executionis causa, de qua dubitare non permittit libri divini veritas.

Γεγραμμένον ἔσω, καὶ ἔξωθεν κατασφραγισμένον σφραγίσιν ἑπτὰ) Ita hoc distinguendum, ut scripsimus: Non enim di- cit librum intus & extra scriptum: sed intus scriptum: extra signatum. Quod autem dicit, septem signis librum fuisse signatum, est πρόληψις. Vidit enim librum cum uno sigillo, sed eo aperto didicit sex esse partes fignatas. Erant enim septem volumina, singula signata, ita ut primo effet in- volutum secundum, (nam paginæ Ebrææ erant volumina, מגלוח( secundo tertium, atque ita deinceps.

Non displicent hæc Grotiana: Etsi plerique alii librum intus, & extus scriptum, unde qui ad librum Scripturæ referunt, Origenes homil. XVI. in Exod. Ambrosius, Eusebius, Augustinus, Hie- ronymus, Beda, Hugo, Primasius, Ansbertus, eum nonnulli foris scriptum dicunt ratione sensus li- teralis, intus ratione spiritualis; foris respectu ex- ternæ prædicationis, intus respectu salvificæ vir- tutis. Sed hic liber tantum revelat futura, non ergo est universa Scriptura. Alii cum Hilario præfat. in Psalm. Christum per librum intelligunt in passione intus & foris scriptum, intus quoad animæ tormenta, exterius quoad flagella, & vulne- ra, ut habet Bernhardus serm. I. in fest. Pasch. Sed Christus est, qui aperit librum, non vero liber ipse. Paulo convenientius Andreas Cæsariensis, & Aretas intelligunt decretum, & memoriam Dei, in qua omnes homines descripti sunt, sive operum & judiciorum Dei inscrutabilem abyssum. OEcumenius, Lyranus, & Aureolus librum hunc esse prædestinationis divinæ, quæ nobis clausa est, nisi a dextra Dei reveletur, vel librum vitæ, in quo sunt Electorum nomina scripta. Sed ea ad partem libri hujus mystici forte referri queant, quum in eodem libri vitæ mentio fiat; hic autem aliquid amplius designatur, non quidem, ut Ly- ranus, cui Maldonatus suffragatur in notis a Cor- nelio adductis, vult, ipsa omniscentia divina, sed quoddam, quod vi omniscientiæ suæ prædicit Deus de fatis Ecclesiæ, ac Electorum suorum, ut & hostium ipsorum. Alienæ autem prorsus sunt sen- tentiæ, Ambrosii, hunc librum esse chronologiam mundi, & septem sigilla esse septem mundi ætates, & aliorum, hunc librum esse chirographum peccati Adæ, puta obligationem, & reatum peccati. Quid enim hæc ad prophetiam? Alcafar per li- brum intelligit ipsa sigilla, eorumque mysteria, censetque eo contineri salutem Judæorum creden- tium & damnationem incredulorum, sed apertum est, librum a suis sigillis distingui; & illa de Judæis jam peracta erant, & publica toti mundo. Hie- ronymus Pradus ad Ezech. II. v. 10. septem sigilla ad maximas Ecclesiæ calamitates refert, sed nimis generaliter, fatente Cornelio a Lapide. Intelligen- dus ergo liber providentiæ divinæ de fatis Eccle- siæ, iisque adhuc demum futuris, nec in hoc tan- tum, sed etiam in futuro seculo, non tantum quo- ad Ecclesiam per se, sed etiam quoad hostes Ecclesiæ. Summa est liber ipse prophetia, quæ jam revelanda erat per ejusdem resignationem, itaque obsignati libri instar est, antequam resignetur. Alii scri- ptum dicunt hunc librum intus & foris, quia scri- bere solebant ab utraq; parte membranæ interio- ri & exteriori, idque ideo, quia quicquid fit in tempore, Deus prævidit ab æterno, & quod ab æterno in Deo fuit absconditum, id in decreto- rum divinorum exequutione in tempore sit mani- festum. Quod Pineda lib. V. de reb. Salom. c. 30. librum signatum dicit, quia scriptus arcanis notis, & characteribus, ut Ægyptiis & Sinensibus rece- ptum, non congruit, quia vera fuere sigilla, quæ resignanda erant. Septem itaque sigillis liber ob- signatus, quia judicia Dei occulta sunt, donec ma- nifestentur, vel per revelationem vel per comple- mentum. Cornelius a Lapide si audiendus, tota apocalypsis occupatur in descriptione hujus libri, & septem sigillorum ejus, ut duæ ejus sint partes: priore, hoc scilicet capite usque ad XI. referantur & explicantur sigilla; altera a cap. XI. usque ad fi- nem referantur & leguntur ea, quæ scripta erant in ipso libro. Sed rectius apertio septem sigillo- rum finitur cum silentio in cælo facto per semiho- rium, Apoc. VIII. v. 1. Ideoque apertis jam omnibus septem sigillis legentur & referentur, quæ in libro aperto scripta erant; hac stante sententia, quam ex Ribera affert, nimirum signacula libri non ita intelligenda esse, quasi illis solutis legeretur in li- bro id, quod quolibet soluto vidisse se narrat Jo- hannes, uti soluto primo sigillo narrat se vidisse equum album, soluto secundo rufum, soluto ter- tio nigrum, soluto quarto pallidum, &c. Hæc enim non legit in libro, sed singulis sigillis apertis, singula sub iis latentia, & clausa referari, sibique ostendi vidit. Nihil enim in libro legi poterat, nisi post resignationem omnium septem sigillorum: omnibus enim referatis demum aperiri potuit, & legi liber, non ante. Erat quippe liber convolu- tus, itaque forinsecus septem sigillis obsignatus: Ergo id quod sub cujusque sigilli reserationem vidit Johannes, non in libro, utpote adhuc aliis sigillis clauso, sed sub ipso sigillo quasi abscondi- tum, eoque aperto patefactum vidit.

## 5:2
Vers. 2.

And I saw a strong Angel) In the Old Testament, God executes all things through Angels: in the new, the greatest things through Christ, the lesser through Angels. But the greater the matter being transacted, the greater the Angel who ministers. ἰσχυρὸς is אל, which title is given to great Angels. See below ch. 10:1, ch. 18:21. Those were great Angels, but there are certain things reserved for Christ.

Proclaiming with a loud voice) ἐβόα ἐν ἰσχύϊ, Dan. 3:4, קרא בחיל. In the Manuscript ἐν φωνῇ μεγάλῃ, a Hebrew idiom.

Who is worthy to open the book, and to loosen its seals) that is, to open by loosening, for the book, or parts of the book, could not be opened unless the seal were also loosened. You have similar things in compound expressions elsewhere, as Col. 2:5, compared with the passage Acts 11:23.

The name אל is nowhere given to great Angels; but it is proper to the one God, which we have shown by induction in our Divine Onomatology in our Natural and Revealed Theology. Nor indeed is the reason for the Greek word ἰσχυρὸς the same, which is also attributed to a created Angel: although in Apoc. 10:1, by 'strong Angel' no other than the uncreated Angel, the Son of God, is understood. Some understand Gabriel here, because this name signifies the strength of God. He cries out like a herald with a loud voice, so that he may be heard throughout the whole heaven, and indeed on earth, because no one was found, either in heaven or on earth, who was able to open the book. Ἄξιός is worthy, by some here it is explained as suitable. Neither could anyone be found worthy to open the book hidden in the secrets of God, nor suitable. If he had been worthy, there could not have been doubt about his ability. Let us therefore retain the proper meaning of the word. However, to open is not to fulfill those things which had been predicted in the book through the redemption of the human race, predicted in the Old Testament, as Ambrose wishes, for here it is a question of the manifestation of future things: That redemption had already been accomplished then, and to open the seals is to be understood as it sounds, just as the sealing of the book by seven seals is likewise properly understood. Whence the gloss of Cornelius Alcafaris is deservedly disapproved, that to open the book and to loosen the seals is nothing other than for Christ to make an abundance of His Spirit available to men, so that they might be able to recognize the mysteries.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

Καὶ εἶδον Ἄγγελον ἰσχυρὸν) In V. Test. Deus omnia per Angelos exequitur: in novo per Christum maxima, minora per Angelos. Quo autem major res agitur, eo major Ange- lus ministrat. ἰσχυρὸς אל quod cognomen magnis Ange- lis datur. Vide infra cap. X. v. 1. cap. XVIII. v. 21. Magni illi erant Angeli, sed sunt quædam Christo reservata.

Κηρύσσοντα φωνῇ μεγάλῃ) ἐβόα ἐν ἰσχύϊ, Dan. III. vers. 4. קרא בחיל. In Manuscripto ἐν φωνῇ μεγάλῃ locu- tione Ebræa.

Τίς ἄξιός ἀνοῖξαι τὸ βιβλίον, καὶ λῦσαι τὰς σφραγῖδας αὐτοῦ) id est, ἀνοῖξαι λυσάμενος, non poterat enim aperiri liber, aut libri partes, nisi sigillo quoque referato. Similia in συνδέτοις habes alibi, ut Col. II. 5. collato loco Act. XI. 23.

Nomen אל nuspiam magnis Angelis datur; sed uni Deo proprium est, quod per inductionem, in Onomatologia divina in de Theologia naturali & revelata ostendimus. Nec vero eadem ratio vocis Græcæ ἰσχυρὸς, quæ etiam creato Angelo tribui- tur: quamvis Apoc. X. v. 1. per Ἄγγελον ἰσχυρὸν nul- lus alius quam increatus Angelus Dei Filius intelli- gatur. Nonnulli Gabrielem hic intelligunt, quia hoc nomen significat fortitudinem Dei. Clamat autem Præconis instar voce magna, ut per totum cœlum exaudiatur, imo & in terra, quia nemo sive in cœlo, sive in terra inventus est, qui librum ape- rire valuerit. Ἄξιός est dignus, a quibusdam hic exponitur idoneus. Neque dignus quisquam inve- niri potuit ad aperiendum librum in arcanis Dei reconditum, neque idoneus. Si dignus fuisset, de ἱκανότητι dubitari non potuisset. Retineamus ergo propriam vocis significationem. Aperire autem non est implere ea, quæ in libro prædicta erant, per generis humani redemptionem, in Vest. Test. prædictam, ut Ambrosius vult, hic enim de futuro- rum manifestatione agitur: Redemptio illa jam tum facta erat, & aperire signacula intelligendum, prout sonat, quemadmodum obsignatio libri per septem sigilla proprie itidem intelligitur. Unde merito improbatur a Cornelio Alcafaris glossa, aperire librum & solvere signacula non esse aliud, quam Christum sui Spiritus copiam hominibus facere, ut mysteria possint agnoscere.

## 5:3
Vers. 3.

Καὶ οὐδεὶς ἐδύνατο ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ, οὐδ᾽ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς, οὐδὲ ὑποκάτω τῆς γῆς ἀνοῖξαι τὸ βιβλίον, οὐδὲ βλέπειν αὐτὸ) No living thing. Ὑποκάτω τῆς γῆς, that is, in the sea, as also below in 13. And so in Exodus chapter XX, after במימ is added מתחת לארץ. See what we have said from the opinion of the Hebrews in Psalm XLIV, v. 2. Again ἀνοῖξαι τὸ βιβλίον, οὐδὲ βλέπειν, for ἀνοίξαμενοι βλέπειν.
