For sealed pages cannot be looked into unless the seals are broken, Isaiah XXIX. 11.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

Καὶ οὐδεὶς ἐδύνατο ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ, οὐδ᾽ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς, οὐδὲ ὑποκάτω τῆς γῆς ἀνοῖξαι τὸ βιβλίον, οὐδὲ βλέπειν αὐτὸ) Nulla res vivens. Ὑποκάτω τῆς γῆς, id est, in mari, ut & infra 13. Itaque Exod. cap. XX. post במימ additur מתחת לארץ. Vide quæ ex Ebræorum sententia diximus Psal. XLIV. v. 2. Rur- sus ἀνοῖξαι τὸ βιβλίον, οὐδὲ βλέπειν, pro ἀνοίξαμενοι βλέπειν. Non possunt enim introspici paginæ obsignatæ, nisi ruptis sigillis, Esa. XXIX. 11.

## 5:4
Vers. 4.

Καὶ ἐγὼ ἔκλαιον πολὺ, ὅτι οὐδεὶς ἄξιός εὑρέθη ἀνοῖξαι κῂ ἀνα- γνῶναι τὸ βιβλίον, ὔτε βλέπειν αὐτὸ) There is a gradation: no one could open, nor read, nay, not even look into it at all. John had learned among the Hebrews that the decrees of God were called sealed, which were certainly going to be, if not in individual men, certainly in classes of men. Moreover, the decrees of God pertaining to the Jews are signified here, which Christ predicted in summary, Matthew XXIV, Luke XXI, but here much more explicitly.

Alcazar therefore falsely thinks that these mysteries were known to the XXIV Elders and the IV living creatures, and that John only desires that the book be opened, not for himself and his own, but for others, both faithful and infidels. Since no one was found who could open the book, and not even look upon it, much less read it and understand it, which Cornelius rightly opposes to his associate.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

Καὶ ἐγὼ ἔκλαιον πολὺ, ὅτι οὐδεὶς ἄξιός εὑρέθη ἀνοῖξαι κῂ ἀνα- γνῶναι τὸ βιβλίον, ὔτε βλέπειν αὐτὸ) Est gradatio: nec ape- rire quis poterat, nec legere, imo nec introspicere saltem. Didicerat Johannes apud Ebræos decreta Dei obsignata dici, quæ certo erant futura, si non in singulis hominibus, certe in generibus hominum. Significantur autem hic de- creta Dei pertinentia ad Judæos, quæ Christus summatim prædixit, Matth. XXIV. Luc. XXI. hic vero multo expli- catius.

Falso itaque censet Alcazar XXIV. Senioribus & IV. animalibus haec mysteria cognita fuisse, Jo- hannem autem id tantum optare, non ut sibi suis- que, sed ut aliis tum fidelibus, tum infidelibus li- ber aperiatur. Quum nullus inventus sit, qui li- brum aperire, ac ne quidem respicere illum, ne- dum eum legere, ac intelligere, quod recte socio opponit Cornelius.

## 5:5
Vers. 5.

And one of the elders) See how great is the honor of the Elders. An Angel teaches Daniel, who desires to know future things: a Presbyter teaches John. The sense is: That it would be revealed by God to one of the Jerusalem Presbyters, so that Christ, through John, might make known to the Jerusalem Church all things that pertained to it.

Do not weep) Do not grieve so. You shall have what you desire.

The sense of Grotius is clearly irrational and alien. For who will admit that by the heavenly Elder, whether he was a Prophet or some other more honorable citizen of heaven, a Jerusalem Presbyter was signified? And what do those deeds of the Church made known through John have to do with the Jerusalem Church? These are Grotian dreams, which did not even come into anyone's mind before him, not even in a fever. Those who make that Elder either St. Peter with Lyranus, or St. Matthew with Dionysius, or St. Luke with Alcazar, or with others the holy Patriarch Jacob, feel this way more by guessing than by reasoning. The latter, however, is approved by the blessed Gerhard, because the name of Lion is attributed to Christ from the prophecy of Jacob.

Behold, the lion has conquered, he from the tribe of Judah) Has conquered means he has obtained that which you thought was desperate. That 'the lion from the tribe of Judah' shows in a more sublime sense in Christ, who was from the tribe of Judah, as the Genealogies teach, and the writer to the Hebrews ch. VII. v. 13, 14, that the prophecy of Jacob in Gen. XLIX. v. 9 was fulfilled, to which can be added that of Num. XXIV. v. 17. And because of those words of Jacob, the Lion was always on the standard of Judah. There is, however, an emphasis here: He who appears as a lamb, is in reality a lion.

The root of David) A metonymy. For he wishes to say a shoot from the root of David, which was said of Hezekiah in Isa. XI. v. 1. There is the same metonymy in Hosea XIV. v. 6, and in the said chapter of Isaiah, verse 10, which passage Paul adapts to Christ in Romans XV. v. 12. Add Isa. LIII. v. 2, 1 Macc. I. v. 11. This title applies especially to Christ, in whom all the old prophecies of the saints are fulfilled in a much more excellent sense. Formerly temporal things were announced, eternal things lay hidden. Thus also below ch. XXII. v. 16.

The victory of Christ, although it extends to the power of unsealing the book, is not, however, completed by that alone. The lion of the tribe of Judah conquered the infernal lion, when he wished to devour the whole human race: nor did he only redeem us from his jaws, Col. I. 14, ch. III. v. 15, but he also acquired for us the grace of the Holy Spirit, so that God might deign to open heavenly mysteries to us through his Spirit, and teach us about them, we who are natural, not understanding the things which are of the Spirit of God, 1 Cor. II. v. 14. But as Christ is said to be from the tribe of Judah by reason of his temporal birth and human nature, so there is no need for us to refer the other name to the same, and explain it metonymically, since a proper meaning has a place, that he is the root of David, which produced David himself; therefore the root and the offspring of David are distinguished, Rev. XXII. v. 16. I am the root and the offspring of David: root as to his divine nature, offspring and shoot as to his human nature. Root, that is, the foundation, source, and author of the life of David, from whom he himself drew sap and fatness also, Rom. XI. 17. David does not call him his root, says St. Bernard in sermon 1 on Easter, but he himself is the root of David, because he carries, and is not carried. Rightly, David, you holily call your Son your Lord, because you do not carry the root, but the root carries you. He is called a Lion, however, both because of the excellence of his strength, Prov. XXX. v. 4, and because of his heroic act, and because of his royal dignity. Christ, as Augustine says in sermon XLVI on various topics, ch. 2, because of fortitude; the Devil, because of ferocity; the former is a lion for conquering, the latter a lion for harming. As a Lamb in his passion, so a Lion in his resurrection, because through it he demonstrated his strength by overcoming death and crushing the head of the infernal serpent, Gen. III. 15, Hos. XIII. 14, Rom. I. v. 4. A Lion in the calling of the Gentiles, because a lion strikes terror into living creatures with his voice, so that they fail as if stunned and struck by force, as Ambrose says in book VI of the Hexaemeron, ch. 3. What Drusius has in book 10 of his Praeterita, p. 410, seems to favor Grotius: A lion from the tribe of Judah, for he was from the tribe of Judah, whose emblem was a lion, which was also carved on the standard of that tribe out of linen of three colors. These words were inscribed: Arise, O Lord, and let your haters be scattered, and let your enemies flee from you. One should see Jonathan on Num. II. v. 3, Abraham the son of David the Levite in his historical cabala, fol. 28, c. 3, and Moses on Gen. XLIX. 9, a lion's whelp of Judah.

To open the book and the seven seals thereof) There is a syllepsis here. For 'to open' is properly said of pages, but 'to loose' is used for seals, as above. The sense is 'to open the book by loosing the seals.' Daniel, a figure of Christ, reads what others were not able to read, Dan. V. 8 and following.

Latin:

Vers. 5.

Καὶ εἷς τῶν πρεσβυτέρων) Vide quantus honor Presby- terorum. Danielem desiderantem res futuras cognoscere, docet Angelus: Johannem Presbyter. Sensus est: Alicui ex Presbyteris Hierosolymitanis a Deo patefactum fore, ut Christus per Johannem Ecclesiae Hierosolymitanae cogni- ta faceret omnia, quae ad ipsam pertinerent.

Μὴ κλαῖε) Noli ita dolere. Habebis quod optas.

Sensus Grotii plane ἄλογος est καὶ ἀλλότριος. Ecquis enim per Seniorem coelestem, seu Prophe- ta fuerit, ceu alius quispiam honoratior coeli civis, Presbyterum Hierosolymitanum significatum ad- mittet? Et quid facta illa Ecclesiae per Johannem patefacta ad Ecclesiam Hierosolymitanam? So- mnia haec Grotiana sunt, quae ne per febrim qui- dem ulli in mentem ante ipsum venerunt. Qui Seniorem illum vel S. Petrum cum Lyrano, vel S. Matthaeum cum Dionysio, vel S. Lucam cum Al- cazare, vel cum aliis S. Patriarcham Jacobum fa- ciunt, magis divinando quam ratiocinando ita sentiunt. Postremum tamen probatur B. Gerhar- do, quia a vaticinio Jacobi Christo nomen Leonis tribuitur.

Ἰδοὺ ἐνίκησεν ὁ λέων, ὁ ἐκ τ̃ φυλῆς Ἰούδα) Ἐνίκησεν est ob- tinuit id, quod tu desperatum putabas. Illud ὁ λέων ἐκ τ̃ φυλῆς Ἰούδα, ostendit sensu sublimiore in Christo, qui ex tri- bu erat Judae, ut Genealogiae docent, & scriptor ad He- braeos c. VII. v. 13. 14. impletum vaticinium Jacobi Gen. XLIX. v. 9. cui addi potest & illud Num. XXIV. v. 17. Et propter illa verba Jacobi Leo fuit semper in vexillo Judae. Est autem hic ἔμφασις: Qui ut agnus apparet, revera est leo.

Ἡ ῥίζα Δαβίδ) Μετωνυμία. Vult enim dicere surculum ex radice Davidis, quod de Ezechia dictum Esa. XI. v. 1. Est autem eadem metonymia Oseae XIV. v. 6. & in dicto capite Esaiae commate 10. quem locum Christo aptat Paulus Ro- man. XV. v. 12. Adde Esa. LIII. v. 2. 1. Macc. I. v. 11. Eximie autem hic titulus in Christum competit, in quo omnia re- sum bonarum vaticinia vetera in sensu multo excellentiore implentur. Olim enuntiabantur temporalia, latebant aeter- na. Sic & infra c. XXII. v. 16.

Victoria Christi etsi ad reserandi librum pote- statem sese extendat, non tamen ea sola absolvi- tur. Vicit leo de tribu Juda leonem infernalem, cum totum genus humanum devoratum vellet: nec redemit nos tantum ex faucibus ejusdem, Col. I. 14. cap. III. v. 15. sed acquisivit nobis etiam gra- tiam Spiritus S. ut Deus per Spiritum suum nobis mysteria coelestia aperire dignaretur, nosque de iisdem edoceret, qui ψυχικοὶ sumus, non intelli- gentes ea, quae sunt Spiritus Dei, 1. Cor. II. v. 14. Ut vero ex tribu Judae Christus dicitur ratione na- tivitatis temporalis, & naturae humanae, ita non opus est, ut ad eandem etiam referamus alterum nomen, idque metonymice explicemus, quum propria significatio locum habeat, quod radix David sit, quae Davidem ipsum produxit; ideo di- stinguitur radix, & genus David, Apoc. XXII. v. 16. Ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ ῥίζα καὶ τὸ γένος τοῦ Δαβίδ: ego sum radix, & genus David: radix quoad divinam, genus & propago quoad humanam naturam. Radix, id est, firmamentum, fons, & autor vitae Davidis, ex quo ipse succum & pinguedinem quoque hausit, Rom. XI. 17. Non dicit David radix ejus, inquit S. Bern- bardus serm. 1. in Pasch. sed ipse radix David, quia portat, & non portatur. Merito David sancte Fi- lium tuum vocas Dominum tuum, quia tu non ra- dicem portas, sed radix te. Leo autem dicitur tum propter roboris excellentiam, Prov. XXX. v. 4. tum propter actum heroicum, tum propter axiama Re- gium. Christus, dicente Augustino serm. XLVI. de diversis cap. 2. propter fortitudinem, Diabolus, propter feritatem, ille leo ad vincendum, iste leo ad nocendum. Ut Agnus in passione, ita Leo in resur- rectione, quia per eam suam fortitudinem demon- stravit mortem superando, & serpentis infernalis caput conterendo, Gen. III. 15. Hos. XIII. 14. Rom. I. v. 4. Leo in gentium vocatione, quia leo voce sua terrorem animantibus incutit, ut quasi vi atto- nita atque icta deficiant, dicente Ambrosio lib. VI. Hexaëm. cap. 3. Grotio favere videntur, quæ ha- bet Drusius lib. 10. præter. p. 410. Leo ex tribu Ju- da, nam erat ex tribu Juda, quorum insigne leo, qui etiam in vexillo tribus illius sculptus erat ex lino trium colorum. Adscripta erant hæc verba : Surge Domine & dissipentur osores tui, & fugiant ini- mici tui a te. Videndi sunt Jonathan Num. II. v. 3. Abraham Davidis filius Levita in cabala historica fol. 28. c. 3. & Moses Gen. XLIX. 9. catulus Leonis Juda.

Ἀνοῖξαι τὸ βιβλίον καὶ τὰς ἑπτὰ σφραγῖδας αὐτῦ) Est hic σύλληψις. Nam ἀνοῖξαι proprie de paginis dicitur, de sigillis λύσαι ut supra. Sensus est ἀνοῖξαι τὸ βιβλίον λύσας τὰς σφραγῖδας. Daniel, Christi figura, legit, quod alii legere non valebant, Dan. V. 8. & seqq.

## 5:6
Verse 6.

And behold, and in the midst of the throne, and of the four living creatures, and in the midst of the elders) That 'and' after 'behold' here is redundant in the Hebrew manner. Christ, however, appears here in the form of a Lamb in the middle place between the Apostles and the Elders, clearly so that He may be an example to both the one and the other.

A Lamb standing) living. This pertains to the resurrection.

As though it had been slain) as one who had been slaughtered: that is, dripping with blood and showing wounds. σφάττειν and σφαγίζειν are words proper to victims, Gen. 35:10, Exod. 12:6, ch. 29:11, 16, 20, and elsewhere often below in ch. 13:8.

He is seen as a Lamb, by which the merit of the passion is designated, by which illumination and revelation were procured for us; for the Lamb was slain, as Bernard says, but the Lion conquered. He is indeed compared elsewhere to a Lamb because of meekness and patience, Isa. 53:6, as also because of innocence, 1 Pet. 1:18, and likewise beneficence, because we are clothed with the fleece of Christ. But here the Paschal and sacrificial Lambs of the Old Testament are regarded, because the Lamb slain for us is introduced as prefigured by them, and therefore His immolation on the altar of the cross is designated, by which, as that Lamb of God bearing the sins of the world, He was made a propitiation for us, nay, not for our sins only, but for the sins of the whole world, John 1:29, 1 John 2:2. Therefore He is seen in the midst of the throne, both on account of the communion of the glory of the seat and of majestic rule, and on account of mediation between God and men. For He is seen in the midst of the throne and of the four living creatures, and in the midst of the four Elders. St. John was wonderfully delighted by the word 'Lamb,' so much so that in the Apocalypse he has called Christ by this name twenty-seven times. For with Paul he knows nothing except Jesus, and Him crucified, 1 Cor. 2:2. In the words 'as though it had been slain,' the particle 'as' is explained by others as the Caph of truth, John 1:14; others, with Andrew of Caesarea, say that He was seen as a slain Lamb, because Christ, rising again, still preserved the scars of His wounds.

Having seven horns) Great powers for subduing enemies, Ps. 75:6, 11, Ps. 72:22, and elsewhere. Thus below, the Kings who sustained the Roman Empire are called the horns of the Roman Empire. A wonderful thing, a horned lamb, and indeed seven-horned. After the highest patience, the highest powers.

And seven eyes) I would think that here also, by 'eyes,' in the Hebrew manner, colors are understood, as above in ch. 4:8.

Which are) namely in mystery, as above in ch. 4:5. In the Manuscript 'which are' (οἵ εἰσιν). Either construction is good.

'Seven spirits of God sent into all the earth') in as many ways as God has always used in governing the universe, in just as many ways does Christ use in governing, protecting, and defending the Church.

Latin:

Vers. 6.

Καὶ ἰδὺ, καὶ ἐν μέσῳ τῦ θρόνυ, καὶ τῶν τεσσάρων ζώων, καὶ ἐν μέσῳ τῶ πρεσβυτέρων) Illud καὶ post ἰδὺ hic παρέλκει more Ebræo. Christus autem Agni specie apparet hic medio loco inter Apostolos & Presbyteros, nimirum ut his & illis sit exemplo.

Ἀρνίον ἑστηκὸς) vivens. Hoc ad resurrectionem pertinet.

Ὡς ἐσφαγμένον) ut qui mactatus fuerat: id est, cruore manans & vulnera ostentans. σφάττειν & σφαγίζειν verba propria victimis Gen. XXXV. v. 10. Exod. XII. v. 6. c. XXIX. v. 11. 16. 20, & alibi sæpe infra c. XIII. v. 8.

Agnus videtur, quo meritum passionis desi- gnatur, quo nobis illuminatio & revelatio parta est; occisus enim est Agnus, dicente Bernhardo, sed Leo vicit. Confertur quidem alias Agno pro- pter mansuetudinem & patientiam, Esa. LIII. v. 6. ut & propter innocentiam, 1. Pet. I. v. 18. nec non beneficentiam, quia vellere Christi induimur. Sed hic respiciuntur Agni Paschales, & sacrificiales Ve- teris Testamenti, quia Agnus pro nobis mactatus introducitur illis figuratus, ideoq; immolatio ejus in ara crucis designatur, qua ceu Agnus ille Dei portans peccata mundi pro nobis factus est pro- pitiatio, imo non pro nostris tantum, sed pro to- tius mundi peccatis, Joh. I. v. 29. 1. Johan. II. v. 2. Ideo in medio throni conspicitur tum ob gloriæ solii & regiminis Majestatici communionem; tum ob mediationem inter Deum & homines. Nam in medio throni & quatuor animalium, & in medio quatuor Seniorum conspicitur. Voce Agni mire delectatus est S. Johannes, adeo ut in Apo- calypsi vigesies septies Christum hoc nomine nun- cuparit. Nihil enim cum Paulo novit, nisi Jesum, cumq; crucifixum, 1. Cor. II. 3. In verbis ὡς ἑσφα- γμένον ab aliis particula ὡς explicatur, ut Caph ve- ritatis, Johan. I. v. 14. alii cum Andrea Cæsar. tan- quam occisum Agnum illum visum dicunt, quod Christus resurgens servarit adhuc vulnerum ci- catrices.

Ἔχον κέρατα ἑπτὰ) Ingentes vires ad domandos hostes, Psal. LXXV. v. 6. 11. Psal. LXXII. v. 22. & alibi. Sic infra Reges, qui imperium Romanum sustentabant, vocantur Imperii Romani cornua. Res mira, agnus cornutus, & qui- dem septicornis. Post summam patientiam, summæ vires.

Καὶ ὀφθαλμὺς ἑπτὰ) Putem & hic per ὀφθαλμὺς more Ebræo intelligi colores, ut supra c. IV. v. 8.

Ἅ εἰσι) nempe in mysterio, ut supra c. IV. v. 5. In Manu- scripto οἵ εἰσιν. Utravis constructio bona est.

'Eπτὰ πνεύματα τõ Θεõ ἀπεσταλμένα εἰς πα̃σαν τὴν γη̃ν) quot modis Deus semper usus est in gubernando universo, totidem modis Christus utitur in gubernanda, tuenda, vindi- canda Ecclesia.

## 5:7
Verse 7.

And he came, and has taken] a pleonasm, concerning which see above VI. v. 5. and elsewhere. Εἴληφεν in the Manuscript, because a vowel follows. From the right hand of him sitting upon the throne the book) For all the counsels of God are open to him: And he has the right of revealing them to whom he wishes.

By seven horns supreme, nay divine, power is understood, because seven is the number of perfection; by seven eyes, immense knowledge or omniscience: which are the infinite gifts of the Holy Spirit, with which Christ is anointed not by measure, John III. verse 34. Horns signify kingdoms and Royal power, 1 Sam. XI. v. 10. Ps. XCII. v. 11. Ps. CXXXII. v. 7. Ps. LXXXIX. verse 25. Dan. VIII. v. 20, 21. Jer. XLVIII. v. 25. Zech. I. v. 13. Rev. XVII. v. 12. sometimes it denotes strength and excellence simply, Deut. XXXIII. v. 17. Ps. XVIII. v. 3. Ps. XXII. v. 22. Ps. LXV. v. 11. Ps. LXXXIX. v. 18. Lam. II. v. 3, 17. By horns, says Primasius, power is understood, by seven, universality. And the diversity of words produces one understanding. For by horns are signified the most excellent gifts of the Holy Spirit, with which Christ reigns throughout the world in his Church. But by seven eyes the Spirit of knowledge, wisdom, science, understanding, prudence, discernment, and counsel is designated, because with these eyes Christ looks upon all things hidden in God, permeates all lands, sees and knows all things, perceives the hearts of all, Isa. XI. v. 2, 3. Zech. IV. v. 10. Wis. I. v. 2. ch. VII. v. 23. Eph. I. v. 7. Through his Spirit the Lamb observes all, illuminates all, comforts all, in whom divine knowledge is inseparably joined with immense power. Therefore they are called the seven Spirits sent into all the earth metonymically, that is, the infinite gifts of the Spirit, by which the Lamb that was slain, now the unconquered Lion, exerts himself throughout all the earth, both by his omnipotence and his omniscience, especially in the government of the Church. Therefore he is said to have taken the book from the right hand of him sitting on the throne, because he received that power of taking and opening that book, which is a truly immense power. For it is implied that he is admitted to the communion of divine power, which is designated by the right hand of God, and of omniscience and providence, which the book expresses. Wherefore he is also celebrated after this for his divine power and wisdom. According to his human nature, says Blessed Gerhard, he received infinite power and wisdom from the Father. He has seven horns, therefore he is strong in power to strike down the enemies of the Church: He has seven eyes, therefore he watches in care for the Church. Even if the Son of man, through the union of divinity with flesh, was Lord and God even in the womb of his mother, Luke I. v. 43, II. v. 11, yet nothing prevents him from being said to have received it afterwards, namely from him from whom all things are always received. For our King and head Jesus Christ so possesses all things delivered to him, that he nevertheless always receives the same from the Father, and imparts them to his body, which is the Church. Thus, ascending to the heavens long ago, he received gifts for us, the remission of sins, righteousness, the Spirit, Ps. LXVIII. v. 19. But nevertheless, perpetually sitting at the right hand of God, he intercedes for us, Heb. VII. v. 25, Rom. VIII. v. 34, obtaining and bringing to the Father all things, whatsoever he bestows upon us, so that in all things God may be glorified. Similarly, he now receives this Apocalypse, of which, however, he had been aware even before through the union of his divinity and the presence of the Spirit. But so that he may communicate it to his whole Church further through the Angel ministering it to John, and through his hand, as Blessed Cluverus rightly says here. On the words he has taken, etc., Blessed Gerhard: There is denoted 1. the mystery of the personal union, 1. Tim. III. verse 16. 2. the communication of idioms resulting from it, which befell Christ according to his human nature, namely that Christ, God and man, after his exaltation in the unity of his person, sits and reigns on the throne of majesty and glory; yet so that according to his divine nature he had from eternity in his right hand the book of divine decrees, mysteries, and judgments, sealed; but according to his human nature he received in time the divine virtue of opening the book, and full dominion through the union and exaltation of his human nature. Alien are the interpretations of Alcazar concerning the seven endowments of divine providence, almost twin to those of Grotius, concerning the seven Angels of the Churches of Asia, of Joachim, concerning the seven primary Angels, of Pererius, Ribera, Cornelius, concerning the seven ages of the world from Adam until the end of the world, of Ambrose, concerning all the empires of the Kingdom of Dionysius.

Latin:

Vers. 7.

Καὶ ἦλθε, καὶ εἴληφε ] πλεονασμός, de quo supra VI. v. 5. & alibi. Εἴληφεν in Manuscripto, quia vocalis sequitur. 'Εκ τη̃ς δεξια̃ς τõ καθημένο ἐπὶ τõ θρόνυ βιβλίον) Ipsi e- nim omnia Dei consilia patent: Et jus habet ea patefaciendi quibus vult.

Per cornua septem potentia summa, imo divi- na, quia septenarius est perfectionis numerus, in- telligitur; per septem oculos immensa scientia vel omniscentia: quæ sunt infinita Spiritus Sancti do- na, quibus unctus est Christus οὐκ ἐκ μέτρου Iob. III. vers. 34. Cornua regnúm & Regalem pote- statem significant, 1. Sam. XI. v. 10. Psal. XCII. v. 11. Psal. CXXXII. v. 7. Psal. LXXXIX. vers. 25. Dan. VIII. v. 20. 21. Jer. XLVIII. v. 25. Zach. I. v. 13. Apoc. XVII. v. 12. quandoque robur & excel- lentiam simpliciter denotat, Deut. XXXIII. v. 17. Psal. XVIII. v. 3. Psal. XXII. v. 22. Psal. LXV. v. 11. Psal. LXXXIX. v. 18 Thren. II. v. 3. 17. Per cor- nua, inquit Primasius, potestas intelligitur, per se- ptem universitas. Et diversitas vocabulorum unum profert intellectum. Cornibus enim significan- tur excellentissima Spiritus Sancti munera, quibus per orbem in sua Christus regnat Ecclesia. Per septem autem oculos Spiritus cognitionis, sapien- tiæ, scientiæ, intelligentiæ, prudentiæ, discretio- nis & consilii designatur, quia his oculis intuetur Christus omnia abdita in Deo, omnes permeat terras, videt & cognoscit omnia, omnium corda perspicit, Esa. XI. v. 2. 3. Zach. IV. v. 10. Sap. I. v. 2. cap. VII. v. 23. Eph. I. v. 7. Per Spiritum suum A- gnus observat omnes, illuminat omnes. confortat omnes, in quo scientia divina cum potentia im- mensa inseparabiliter conjuncta est. Ideo dicun- tur septem Spiritus missi in omnem terram metonymice, id est, dona infinita Spiritus, quibus per omnem terram sese exerit Agnus occisus, jam Leo invictus, tum omnipotentia tum omniscien- tia sua vere divina, in regimine imprimis Ecclesiæ. Ideo dicitur accepisse è dextra sedentis in throno librum, quia accepit potestatem illam librum il- lum accipiendi & referandi, quæ vere immensa est potestas. Nam admitti ita innuitur ad commu- nionem divinæ potentiæ, quæ dextra Dei designa- tur, & omniscientiæ ac providentiæ, quam liber exprimit. Quapropter celebratur etiam post ob divinam potentiam & sapientiam. Secundum hu- manam naturam, inquit B. Gerhardus, infinitam potentiam & sapientiam a Patre accepit. Habet cor- nua septem, ergo pollet robore ad hostes Ecclesiæ pro- sternendos: Habet oculos septem, ergo vigilat in cura pro Ecclesia. Etiamsi Filius hominis per unionem di- vinitatis cum carne Dominus fuerit & Deus in utero etiam matris suæ, Luc. I. v. 43. II. v. 11. nihil tamen impedıt, quo minus postea etiam accepisse dicatur, ab eo videlicet, à quo semper accipiuntur omnia. Nam omnia sibi tradita sic habet Rex & caput no- strum Jesus Christus, ut eadem nihilominus semper à Patre accipiat, & corpori suo, quod est Ecclesia, im- pertiat. Sic pridem cælos conscendens accepit pro nobis dona, remissionem peccatorum, justitiam, Spi- ritum, Psal. LXVIII. v. 19. At nihilominus perpe- tuo sedens ad dextram Dei intercedit pro nobis, Ebr. VII. v. 25. Rom. VIII. v. 34. impetrans & accepta fe- rens Patri omnia, quæcunq́; nobis tribuit, ut in omni- bus Deus glorificetur. Similiter nunc accipit Apo- calypsin istam, cujus tamen & antea per unionem divinitatis, & præsentiam Spiritus fuerat conscius. Sed ut eam ministrante Angelo Johanni, persǫ; ejus manum toti porro Ecclesiæ suæ communicet, ut hic recte B. Cluverus. Ad verba ἔληφεν, &c. B. Ger- hardus: Denotatur 1. mysterium personalis unionis, 1. Tim. III. vers. 16. 2. inde resultantis communica- tionis idiomatum, quæ Christo secundum humanam naturam obtigit, quod videlicet Christus Deus & homo post suam exaltationem in personæ unitate sedet & regnat in throno majestatis & gloriæ; ita tamen ut secundum divinam naturam una cum Patre & Spiritu Sancto librum divinorum decre- torum, mysteriorum, & judiciorum ab æterno in manu dextra sua habuerit signatum; sed juxta hu- manam naturam in tempore acceperit divinam virtutem aperiendi librum, ac plenum dominium per unionem ac exaltationem humanæ naturæ. A- lienæ sunt interpretationes de septem dotibus di- vinæ providentiæ Alcazaris, fere gemina Grotia- næ, de septem Angelis Ecclesiarum Asiæ, Joachi- mi, de septem Angelis primariis, Pererii, Riberæ, Cornelii, de septem mundi ætatibus ab Adamo us- que ad finem mundi, Ambrosii, de omnibus Re- gni imperiis Dionysii.

## 5:8
Verse 8.

Καὶ ὅτε ἔλαβε τὸ βιβλίον ] Namely, that he might relate what follows in ch. VI. v. 1.

Τὰ τέσσαρα ζῶα ] Other apostles, who burned with no less desire than John to know what was about to happen to the Jews.

Καὶ εἰκοσιτέσσαρες πρεσβύτεροι] Imitators of the Apostles, as above ch. IV. 10. 11.

Ἔπεσον ἐνώπιον τῶ ἀρνίυ ] They showed to Christ the same honor that they had shown to God, ch. IV. 10.

The Vulgate has: Et cum aperuisset [And when he had opened]: from whose error Bede seeks a mystery in it, how the book is said to be opened first, when the seals were only opened afterwards; others invent a prolepsis; Alcazar often says this book was opened and then closed again. Cornelius a Lapide thinks it should be explained as, when he had opened, that is, when he had begun to open. But all those things are wiped away, for in the Greek codices it is written, when he was opening the book, and Cornelius acknowledges that Primasius, Arias, and others read it that way too. The heavenly psalms clearly teach that not an honor next to God, but the same honor as God, was shown to Christ.

Ἔχοντες ἕκαστος κιθάρας ] Instruments of praise, Ps. 32, v. 2. 43, v. 4. 57, v. 9. 71, v. 22. 92, v. 21. 98, v. 5. 108, v. 2. 147, v. 7. 150, v. 7. Sirach 39, v. 20. The preaching of the Word is understood. In the Manuscript: Ἕκαστος κιθάραν.

Καὶ φιάλας χρυσᾶς γεμούσας θυμιαμάτων ] And this is taken from the temple. There were many kinds of vials there, for libations, for blood, for wine, concerning which we have said some things at Zech. IX. 15. ch. XIV. 20. But here are understood bowls, in which there was incense and other perfumes: which Cornutus thinks are called acerræ among the Latins. See what was said at 1 Chron. IV. v. 22.

Αἵ εἰσιν αἱ προσευχαὶ τῶν ἁγίων ) An excellent comparison and taken from Ps. 141, v. 2. Just as the perfumes of the temple ascended toward heaven and smelled sweet (see Exod. 30, v. 34), so the prayers of the pious go to God, Acts 10, v. 4, 31. Sir. 35, v. 20. And they are pleasing to Him; see below ch. 8, v. 3, 4. ch. 18, v. 13. Philo, concerning those sacrificing, says that by incense is signified the purest rational spirit of the one sacrificing. Clement, Strom. VI: They call the just soul the truly holy altar, and holy prayer the incense from it. Origen against Celsus VIII: The ruling faculty of each of the just is an altar for us, from which truly and intellectually sweet-smelling incense is sent up, prayers from a pure conscience.

Not the preaching of the Word, but the harmonious celebration and proclamation of God is signified, which is performed in heaven with the libations of prayers: for there is perpetual music there, perpetual sacrifices of prayers: the former for benefits received, the latter for the same to be continued eternally. For although the blessed cannot fall from glory, yet they perpetually [pray] for the continuation of the same offer incense, and because they persevere continually in prayer, they are also preserved and remain perpetually in glory. Which explanation, as it flows from the letter, is to be embraced as the simplest of all. (Whether it follows from this that the Saints in heaven pray for us.) For nothing of the sort is said here. We shall speak of the passage Apoc. VIII. v. 3. in its own place. Concerning heavenly pleasure, the hearing of those to whom the harmonies of the heavens and the concert of the Angels, the sweet-sounding organs of all the saints, sound incessantly.

Vials are pious and chaste thoughts, from which incense exhales here. To Rupert, Bede, Richard, Hugo, and Viega, vials are hearts dilated by charity. (Harp.) The harp is a musical instrument which, stretched with ten strings, was accustomed to be struck with a plectrum, according to Josephus, lib. VII. antiq. cap. 12., which occurs in 1 Sam. X. v. 5., 1 Paralip. XVII. v. 28., cap. XXV. v. 3, 6., Job XXX. v. 31., Ps. XXXIII. verf. 2., XLIII. verf. 4., LVII. v. 9., LXXI. v. 21., LXXXVIII. verf. 5., CVIII. v. 2., CXLVII. v. 7., CL. v. 3. In the beginning, as Isidore testifies in lib. II. Orig. cap. 21., it was similar to the human chest, because just as the voice is produced from the chest; thus the song was produced from it, which in the Doric tongue is called kithara.

Concerning the vials, which were vessels with a wide mouth, sacred in Exod. XXVII. v. 3., Num. VII. v. 13., such as were golden in the temple, 1 Reg. VII. 50., as also for symposia, Amos VI. v. 6., destined, cf. Exod. XXX. verf. 7., Ps. CXLI. v. 2. But Cornelius is inept, and indeed very childishly so, while he gathers that organs, harps, lyres, (Ap. XIX. v. 2. are material harps in heaven?) and flutes will have a place in heaven from this passage and c. XIV. v. 2., because the melody of instruments is greater and sweeter than that of voices. How much more harmoniously do Andreas and Aretas say that by harps is denoted τὸ εὐαγγέλιον καὶ εὐχὴν τῆς εἰς θεὸν δοξολογίας, that is, the consonant sweetness of divine celebration: because just as the harp is an instrument of joy: so the Spirit himself celebrates rejoicing in God, Eph. V. verf. 18, 19. Pannonius, by harps, understands the spiritual harmony resulting from the consonance of various virtues, through which the saints always praise God. And Guilhelmus Parisiensis, lib. 21. de universo part. 2. fol. 166., the mouth of every glorified person will be like a harp of innumerable strings and innumerable pipes, and there will be a sonority from the mouth of each one, a concert of voices or of innumerable sounds and of a sweetness inconceivable to us here, consonant with one another and audible to the ears of that perfection at once. St. Augustine passed over this in lib. XXII. de Civ. Dei cap. 30. He also admonishes with a holy song, where I read or hear: Blessed are they who dwell in thy house, O Lord, for ever and ever they will praise thee, all the members and viscera of thy incorruptible body, which we now see distributed through various uses of necessity and motions, since then there will not be necessity itself, but full, certain, secure, everlasting happiness, they will progress in the praises of God. For all those of whom I have now spoken, who now lie hidden in the number of bodily harmony, will not lie hidden, disposed inwardly and outwardly through all parts of the body, and with other things, which will seem great and wonderful there, they will inflame rational minds to the praise of such an Artificer with the delights of rational beauty.

All of which Alcuin made his own in lib. III. de atern. beat. sanct. c. 22., cf. Ps. CXXVI. 1, 5., Isa. XXVI. 29., c. XXV. 10., c. LI. 11., cap. LXV. 14., Apoc. 11. 8, 9., c. VII. 9, 10., c. XI. 16, 17., c. XII. 6., 6. XIV. 2., c. XV. 2., c. XIX. 1, 3. seqq.

PART II. Psalmody sung in praise of the Resigner of the book. Verf. 9. Καὶ ᾄδουσιν ᾠδὴν καινὴν Pindar says that new songs are more approved.

See Psalm 33. 3., 40. 4., 96. 1., 149. 1., Isa. 41. 10. That of the same Pindar: ψυχῇ δ' ἐνεσθῶσιν ὡραίοις πάσαις μολπαῖς μάκαροι μέγα ᾄδουσιν ἐν ὕμνοις.

It is called new, because the singers are new, (Why is a new song, new matter concerning Christ's incarnation, passion, redemption, which alone is new, called a song?) that which is new upon the earth, Jerem. XXXI. 22., and concerns our innovation.

S. Bernhard in Cant. Truly, he says, new, whose matter knows no antiquity, whose grace knows no weariness, which is always fresh with love, more recent in use. For it is truly new, which renews the souls of men to eternal blessedness.

Finally, it is read, do not remember the former things, and do not consider the ancient things: for behold I do new things; rightly new things which are by no means concluded by the laws of the nature running from antiquity.

Cf. Ps. XXXIII. v. 3., Ps. XL. 1., Ps. XCVI. 1., Ps. XCVIII. 1. Λέγοντες Ἄξιος εἶ λαβεῖν τὸ βιβλίον, καὶ ἀνοῖξαι τὰς σφραγῖδας αὐτοῦ Worthy art thou to know and reveal the mysteries of God, thou who hast suffered so much, done so much for the honor of God. Ὅτι ἐσφάγης More is understood than is said.

For from the fact that he is said to have been slain, it is to be understood that he offered himself to death, that he might serve God and benefit men. Καὶ ἠγόρασας τῷ θεῷ ἡμᾶς that is, εἰς τὸ λατρεύειν θεῷ.

Luc. 2. verf. 74. When he says us, he understands Christians, of all places and times, whom Christ freed from sins, at a great cost, namely of his own life, Rom. 3. v. 24., 1 Cor. 1. v. 30., 6. 20., 7. 27., 1 Petr. 1. 18., 2 Petr. 2. 11., Gal. 4., and elsewhere. So also below 14. 4. Ἐν τῷ αἵματί σου in the Manuscript: ἐν τῷ αἵματι, in the manner of διάματι. 1 Ioh. 5. 6. Ἐκ πάσης φυλῆς, καὶ γλώσσης, καὶ λαοῦ, καὶ ἔθνους From all the tribes of Israel, and from men of so many languages, whether they be the more lingering ones, who are wont to be called λαοὶ, as Greeks and Italians, or Barbarians, to whom the name ἰδῶν is especially appropriate. λαοὶ φυλῇ, γλώσσῃ is in Daniel 3. 3. Verf. 10. Καὶ ἐποίησας αὐτοὺς the discourse passes from the first plural to the third: not badly: because they speak both of themselves and of others. Βασιλεῖς καὶ ἱερεῖς Even in this life in some sense, above c. 1. 6. In the Manuscripts βασιλεία: abstract for concrete, in the Hebrew manner, as ἱεράτευμα, 1 Petr. 2. v. 5, 9. And so the Latin reads here. Καὶ βασιλεύσουσιν ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς that is, ὧν βασιλεύσουσιν ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς. Other Manuscripts have, as the Latin also reads, καὶ βασιλεύσομεν ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς, for ἵνα βασιλεύσωμεν, so that the discourse is properly about the Apostles and Presbyters, to whom it is given to rule the Church. See above 2. 27. and 4. 4. And this kingdom on earth is heavenly: for what he binds on earth, is bound in heaven, Matth. 18. 18.

These things are not to be understood concerning the dignity of merit regarding Christ himself, as if he had merited for himself any grace by his active and passive obedience: but by reason of us, because he receives the book to be opened for us, spent for our sake, for nothing of those things written in it was hidden from him, since in him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, Col. II. v. 3., and he himself knows all things, Job XXI. v. 17., just as he redeemed us with his blood, and made us Kings and Priests.

Whence the paraphrase of B. Gerhard rightly has: Because thou hast redeemed us with thy own blood, therefore it is just that we should also say that the divine power of governing thy Church according to human nature, as well as the knowledge of the future state of the Church, was given to thee to manifest to others. But the discourse is not about our Regal and Priestly dignity in this life, much less about the rule of Churches, proper to Presbyters and Apostles; because these are common to the Elect from every tribe and language and people and nation: but the Apostles were from one people only: but about our dignity in another life. That we shall reign on earth is to be understood concerning the new earth, in which righteousness dwells, 2 Pet. 3:13, Rev. 21:1.

Vers. 8.

Καὶ ὅτε ἔλαβε τὸ βιβλίον ] Nempe ut referraet, quod sequitur c. VI. v. 1.

Τὰ τέσσαρα ζῶα ] Apostoli alii, qui non minore quam Johannes desiderio flagrabant noscendi quæ Judæis erant e- ventura.

Καὶ εἰκοσιτέσσαρες πρεσβύτεροι] Imitatores Apostolorum, ut supra c. IV. 10. 11.

Ἔπεσον ἐνώπιον τῶ ἀρνίυ ] Proximum honorem ei honori, quem Deo exhibuerant, c. IV. 10. Christo exhibuere.

Vulgata habet: Et cum aperuisset: ex cujus errore Beda mysterium in eo quærit, quomodo prius dicatur apertus liber, cum postea demum aperta sint sigilla; alii prolepsin fingunt, Alcazar sæpius librum hunc apertum & deinde iterum clausum dicit. Cornelius a Lapide explicandum censet, cum aperuisset, id est, aperire cœpisset. Sed ea omnia in spongiam incumbunt, in Græcis e- nim codicibus habetur, cum aperiret librum, at- que ita etiam legisse Primasium, Ariam, & alios, agnoscit Cornelius. Christo non proximum Deo sed eundem cum Deo honorem exhibitum esse Psalmodiæ cœlestes luculenter edocent.

Ἔχοντες ἕκαστος κιθάρας ] Instrumenta laudis Psal. 32, vers. 2. 43, vers. 4. 57, vers. 9. 71, vers. 22. 92, vers. 21. 98, vers. 5. 108, vers. 2. 147, vers. 7. 150, vers. 7. Sirach. 39, vers. 20. Intelligitur Verbi prædicatio. In Manuscripto: Ἕκαστος κιθάραν.

Καὶ φιάλας χρυσᾶς γεμούσας θυμιαμάτων ] Et hoc de templo sumptum. Multa ibi erant phialarum genera, ad liba, ad sanguinem, ad vinum, de quibus quædam dixi- mus ad Zachar. IX. 15. c. XIV. 20. Hic autem intelligun- tur pateræ, in quibus erat thus & suffimenta alia: quas apud Latinos acerras dici putat Cornutus. Vide quæ dicta 1. Pa- ralip. IV. v. 22.

Αἵ εἰσιν αἱ προσευχαὶ τῶν ἁγίων ) Egregia comparatio & desumpta ex Psal. 141, vers. 2. Sicut suffimenta templi ad- cendebant cœlum versus, & bene olebant (vid. Exod. 30, vers. 34.) Ita preces piorum ad Deum eunt, Actor. 10, vers. 4 .31. Sir. 35, vers. 20. Eique gratæ sunt, vide infra c. 8, vers. 3. 4. cap. 18, vers. 13. Philo de sacrificantibus, per suffitum ait significari τὸ καθαρώτατον τῦ θύοντος πνεῦμα λογικόν. Clemens Strom. VI. βωμὸν δὲ ἀληθῶς ἅγιον τὴν δικαίαν ψυχὴν, καὶ τὸ ἀπ' αὐτῆς θυμίαμα τὴν ὁσίαν εὐχὴν λέ- γυσιν. Origenes contra Celsum VIII. βωμὸς μὲν εἰσιν ἡμῖν τὸ ἑκάστυ τῶν δικαίων ἡγεμονικὸν, ἀφ' ὗ ἀναπέμπεται ἀληθῶς, καὶ νοητῶς εὐώδη θυμιάματα, προσευχαὶ ἀπὸ συνειδήσεως κα- θαρᾶς.

Non Verbi prædicatio, sed harmonica Dei cele- bratio, & deprædicatio fignatur, quæ cum liba- mentis precum in cœlis peragitur: Ibi enim perpe- tua Musica, perpetua precum sacrificia: illa ob beneficia accepta, hæc ob eadem æternum conti- nuanda. Etsi enim beati excidere gloria non pos- sint, perpetuo tamen pro ejusdem continuatione suffimenta offerunt, & ideo quia in precatione continuo perfeuerant, in gloria etiam perpetuo conferuantur & permanent. Quae explicatio, ut ex litera fluit; ita ceu omnium simplicissima amplectenda. (An ex b.l. conflet, Sanctos in caelis pro nobis orare.) Nihil enim tale hic dicitur. De loco Apoc. VIII. v. 3. suo loco dicturi fumus. De coelesti voluptate, auditus illorum, quibus incessanter fonant harmonie caelorum, & concentus Angelorum dulcisona organa omnium sanctorum. Porro citharae fecundum Andream fignificant concinnam, fuauemque Dei laudem, thymiamata fignificant sacrificium, quod fideles per sanctimoniam Deo offerunt.

Phiale sunt piae castaeque cogitationes, ex quibus hic thymiamata exhalat. Ruperto, Beda, Richardo, Hugoni, Viega phialae sunt corda charitate dilatata. (Cithara.) Cithara est instrumentum fuit musicum, quod decem chordis intensum plectro feriri confueuit apud Iosephum lib. VII. antiq. cap. 12. quod occurrit 1. Sam. X. v. 5. 1. Paralip. XVII. v. 28. cap. XXV. v. 3. 6. Iob. XXX. v. 31. Pfal. XXXIII. verf. 2. XLIII. verf. 4. LVII. v. 9. LXXI. v. 21. LXXXVIII. verf. 5. CVIII. v. 2. CXLVII. v. 7. CL. v. 3. Initio teste Isidoro lib. II. Orig. cap. 21. pectori humano fimilis fuit, quod veluti vox de pectore; ita ex ipsa cantus ederetur, quod Dorica lingua κιθάρα vocatur.

De phialis, quae vafa erant ore patulo, sacris Exod. XXVII. v. 3. Num. VII. v. 13. quales in templo erant aureae, 1. Reg. VII. 50. ut & symposiis, Amos VI. v. 6. destinatae, conf. Exod. XXX. verf. 7. Pfal. CXLI. v. 2. ineptit vero Cornelius, & quidem valde pueriliter, dum organa, citharas, chelydes, (Ap. XIX. v. 2. an cithara materiales in caelo?) tibias in calo locum habituras ex h. l. & c. XIV. v. 2. colligit, quia maior & suauior fit melodia instrumentorum quam vocum. Quanto concinnius Andreas & Aretas per citharas notari ajunt τὸ εὐαγγέλιον καὶ εὐχὴν τῆς εἰς θεὸν δοξολογίας, hoc est, consonantem suauitatem celebrationis diuinae: quia sicut cithara laetitiae instrumentum est: Ita laetari in Deo Spiritus ipse celebrat, Ephef. V. verf. 18. 19. Pannonius, per citharas intelligit spiritualem harmoniam ex variarum virtutum consonantia resultantem, per quam sancti Deum semper laudant. Et Guilhelmus Parifienfis lib. 21. de vniuerfo part. 2. fol. 166. os cujuscunque glorificati erit sicut cithara chordarum innumerabilium & innumerabilium fistularum, & erit sonoritas ex ore uniuscujusque, glorificati hominis concentus vocum five sonorum innumerabilium & incogitabili nobis hic fuauitate sibi inuicem consonantium, & auribus perfectionis illius simul audibilium. Praeterat S. Augustinus lib. XXII. de Civ. Dei cap. 30. Admonet etiam sancto cantico, ubi lego vel audio: Beati qui habitant in domo tua, Domine, in fecula feculorum laudabunt te, omnia membra & viscera incorruptibilis corporis tui, quae nunc videmus per usus necessitatis varios & motus distributa, quoniam tunc non erit ipsa necessitas, sed plena, certa, fecura, fempiterna felicitas, proficient in laudibus Dei. Omnes quippe illi, de quibus jam fum loquutus, qui nunc latent harmonie corporalis numeri, non latebunt intrinfecus & extrinfecus per corporis cuncta dispositi, & cum ceteris rebus, quae ibi magna & mirabiles videbuntur rationales mentes in tanti Artificis laudem rationabilibus pulchritudinis delectatione succendent.

Quae omnia sua fecit Alcuinus lib. III. de atern. beat. sanct. c. 22. conf. Pfal. CXXVI. 1. 5. Efa. XXVI. 29. c. XXV. 10. c. LI. 11. cap. LXV. 14. Apoc. 11. 8. 9. c. VII. 9. 10. c. XI. 16. 17. c. XII. 6. 6. XIV. 2. c. XV. 2. c. XIX. 1. 3. feqq.

PARS II. Psalmodia in laudem Refignatoris libri decantata. Verf. 9. Καὶ ᾄδουσιν ᾠδὴν καινὴν Ait Pindarus cantionum nouas magis probari.

Vide Pfalm. 33. 3. 40. 4. 96. 1. 149. 1. Ef. 41. 10. Ejusdem Pindari illud: ψυχῇ δ' ἐνεσθῶσιν ὡραίοις πάσαις μολπαῖς μάκαροι μέγα ᾄδουσιν ἐν ὕμνοις.

Novum dicitur, quia cantores sunt novi, reno- (Cur novum canticum, materia nova de Christi incarnatione, paffione, redemptione, quae sola est novum dicatur?) illud fuper terram, Ierem. XXXI. 22. & innovationem nostram concernit.

S. Bernhard. in Cant. Vere, inquit, novum, cujus nescit antiquitatem materia, fastidium gratia, quae semper est amore recens, usu recentior. Vere enim novum, quod animos hominum ad aeternam innovat beatitudinem.

Denique legitur, ne memineritis priorum, & antiqua ne intuemini: nova quippe ego facio; jure novas quae ab antiquo currentis natura nequaquam conclufa sunt legibus.

Conf. Pfal. XXXIII. v. 3. Pfal. XL. 1. Pfal. XCVI. 1. Pfal. XCVIII. 1. Λέγοντες Ἄξιος εἶ λαβεῖν τὸ βιβλίον, καὶ ἀνοῖξαι τὰς σφραγῖδας αὐτοῦ Dignus qui noris & patefacias Dei arcana, qui ad Dei honorem tanta passus es, tanta fecisti. Ὅτι ἐσφάγης Plus intelligitur quam dicitur.

Nam ex eo quod interfectus dicitur, intelligendum est quod femet morti obtulit, ut Deo ferviret, & hominibus prodeffet. Καὶ ἠγόρασας τῷ θεῷ ἡμᾶς id est, εἰς τὸ λατρεύειν θεῷ.

Luc. 2. verf. 74. Nos cum dicit, Christianos intelligit, omnium locorum & temporum, quos Christus à peccatis liberavit, magno impendio, vitae scilicet suae, Rom. 3. v. 24. 1. Cor. 1. v. 30. 6. 20. 7. 27. 1. Petr. 1. 18. 2. Petr. 2. 11. Gal. 4. & alibi. Sic & infra 14. 4. Ἐν τῷ αἵματί σου in Manuscripto: ἐν τῷ αἵματι, quomodo διάματι. 1. Ioh. 5. 6. Ἐκ πάσης φυλῆς, καὶ γλώσσης, καὶ λαοῦ, καὶ ἔθνους Ex omnibus tribubus Ifraelis, & ex tot linguarum hominibus, five illi moratiores sint, qui λαοὶ dici folent, ut Graeci & Itali, five Barbari, quibus eximie competit ἰδῶν nomen. λαοὶ φυλῇ, γλώσσῃ est apud Danielem 3. 3. Verf. 10. Καὶ ἐποίησας αὐτοὺς tranfit fermo à prima plurali ad tertiam: non male: quia & de fe loquuntur, & de aliis. Βασιλεῖς καὶ ἱερεῖς Etiam in hac vita sensu aliquo, supra c. 1. 6. Manuscriptis βασιλεία: abstractum pro concreto, more Ebraeo, quomodo ἱεράτευμα, 1. Petr. 2. v. 5. 9. Et ita hic legit Latinus. Καὶ βασιλεύσουσιν ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς id est, ὧν βασιλεύσουσιν ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς. Alii Manuscripti habent, ut & Latinus legit, καὶ βασιλεύσομεν ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς, pro ἵνα βασιλεύσωμεν, ut proprie de Apostolis & Presbyteris fermo fit, quibus datum est regere Ecclesiam. Vide supra 2. 27. & 4. 4. Et hoc regnum in terris coeleste est: nam quod ligat in terris, ligatum est in coelo, Matth. 18. 18.

Non hac intelligenda de dignitate meriti quoad ipsum Christum, quasi meruerit sibi obedientia sua activa & passiva aliquam gratiam: sed ratione nostri, quod merite, nostri gratia impenso, librum nobis aperiendum accipiat, ipsi enim nihil eorum absconditum erat, quae in eo scripta, quum in ipso absconditi sint omnes thefauri scientiae & cognitionis, Col. II. v. 3. & ipse norit omnia, Iob. XXI. v. 17. quemadmodum nos redemiffi fanguine suo, Regesque ac Sacerdotes fecit.

Unde recte habet paraphrasis B. Gerhardi: Quia proprio tuo fanguine nos redemisti, idco aequum est, ut etiam fecundum humanam naturam divinam virtutem Ecclesiam tuam gubernandi, ut & cognitionem futuri Ecclesiae status ad manifestandum aliis tibi datam esse dicamus. Non autem de Regali ac Sacerdotali nostra dignitate fermo est in hac vita, nedum de regimine Ecclesiarum, Presbyteris, & Apostolis proprio; quia communia Electorum haec sunt ex omni tribu & lingua & populo & gente: Apostoli autem ex uno tantum populo erant: sed de dignitate nostra in altera vita. Illud regnabimus in terra intelligen- dum de terra nova, in qua habitat justitia, 2. Petr. III. v. 13. Apoc. XXI. v. 1.

## 5:11
Verse 11.

And I heard as it were the voice of many angels round about the throne and the living creatures and the elders) The agreement between the angels and the Church is noted: and the angels are placed in the outermost circle, as those who serve not only God, but also the Church, Heb. 1:14. So also below ch. 7, v. 11. And the number of them was myriads of myriads and thousands of thousands) In Daniel 7:10, 'And thousands of thousands ministered unto him, and ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him.' And this reading of ours is in Arethas. Compare Deut. 33:2, Ps. 68:8, Heb. 12:22.

Latin:

Vers. 11.

Καὶ ἤκουσα ὡς φωνὴν Ἀγγέλων πολλῶν κύκλῳ τοῦ θρόνου καὶ τῶν ζώων καὶ τῶν πρεσβυτέρων) Notatur consensio inter An- gelos & Ecclesiam : & Angeli ponuntur in extimo ambitu, ut qui non Deo tantum, sed & Ecclesiae inserviant, Ebr. 1, 14. Sic & infra c. 7, v. 11. Καὶ ἦν ὁ ἀριθμὸς αὐτῶν μυριάδες μυριάδων καὶ χιλιάδες χιλι- άδων) In Daniele 7, 10. ורבן רבן קדמוהי יקומון אלף אלפים ישמשוניה : χιλιὰς χιλιάδος ἐλητούρ- γει αὐτῷ καὶ μυρίας μυριάδες παρειστήκασιν αὐτῷ. Et nostra haec lectio est apud Aretham. Conf. Deut. 33, v. 2. Psal. 68, 8. Ebr. 12, 22.

## 5:12
Verse 12.

Saying with a loud voice) They approve of those things which the Apostles and Elders preach. 'Saying' is rightly referred to 'myriads,' namely according to the meaning.

The discourse is not about the militant Church, but the triumphant, which Cornelius a Lapide acknowledges against his Alcazar, who foolishly gathers from this the sacrifice of the Mass; namely, that all these things were seen in heaven, not on earth, and denote the glory of heavenly things, not earthly. That number of angels is truly innumerable, because myriads of myriads are spoken of indefinitely.

Worthy is the Lamb that was slain to receive power, and riches, and wisdom, and strength, and honor, and glory, and blessing] Seven names of praise corresponding to the seven Spirits. In the Latin it is read 'divinity,' where it was written by the interpreter 'riches,' πλοῦτον. But the confession of Christ's liberality is signified. An equal number is below 7:12, where for 'riches' we have 'thanksgiving.' Power (gebura), strength (koach), dominion (oz).

Through those seven divine attributes and immense praises, the following are claimed for Christ: 1. Power, which is authority, Matt. 28:18, Mark 5:20, Luke 4:36, ch. 5:17, ch. 6:19, ch. 8:46, ch. 9:1, ch. 21:27. 2. Riches, divine all-sufficiency, the inexhaustible fullness of the riches of grace, Ps. 36:10, John 1:17, Acts 11:33, Eph. 2:4, Gen. 17:1. That the Vulgate version is faulty here, when it rendered it 'divinity,' the notable agreement of the Greek and other codices shows. 3. Wisdom, immense wisdom, just as in him are said to be hidden all the treasures of wisdom, Col. 2:3, and he himself is full of wisdom, Luke 2:40, and according to his divine nature he is the very hypostatic wisdom of God, Prov. 8:23, Luke 11:47. 4. Strength, he brings in fortitude, might, and infinite power, Isa. 63:3, Phil. 3:21. 5. Honor is attributed to him on account of the dignity of adoration, whence God is called Elohim from adorability, Phil. 2:5. 6. Glory on account of divine majesty, Col. 2:9, which is the glory of Jehovah, whence he is called the Lord of glory, 1 Cor. 2:8. 7. Blessing on account of the grace and all-embracing benediction which we have from Christ and in Christ, Eph. 1:3, John 1:14, Gen. 12:3, Gal. 3:16. They profess this concerning the Lamb slain, and thus concerning Christ according to his human nature, which was made a partaker of divine glory through hypostatic communication and exaltation to the right hand of God, Col. 2:9, Phil. 2:9-10. God does not give his glory to another, Isa. 42:8. But the Lamb is of one essence with God, John 10:30. Nor would the glory of the Father be given to him, unless he were one with the Father: and although he differs according to his human nature, this nevertheless does not subsist as its own, but in the very hypostasis of the Word, and constitutes one subsistent being with him. Therefore, glory is not given to another by transfer, but is conferred upon the flesh, united to the Word consubstantial with the Father, subsisting in the Word himself through hypostatic communion. He acknowledges this with Arethas: That the Lamb has received

the book is to be understood according to the human nature, St. Anselm: the man who was made received from the right hand of the one sitting, that is, from the Word united to himself. And: Blessing and honor to him who sits on the throne, to God the Father and the Lamb, according to the flesh: As also Albert: Worthy, he says, to receive, so that humanity may possess all things: likewise Dionysius the Carthusian, who confirms this from Damascene, that to the humanity of Christ, by reason of its hypostatic union with the Word, the fullness of grace and wisdom was given and belongs. I add also Cornelius Jansen in Concord. Evangel. ch. 136. The human nature received that brightness which the divine nature had from eternity, when the human nature was endowed with immortality, and raised into heaven, and through the conjunction of itself with the divine nature into the unity of the same person, it was then made a sharer of glory. Cardinal Cajetan in Sent. decima, quest. 4, on John 17:3. The Lord asks, he says, that this be carried out, namely, that his eternal glory be derived into himself according to his human nature: What? that Maldonatus observes regarding that passage, that all interpreters understand it concerning the clarification of his humanity, not his Deity. Regarding the name above every name, Phil. 2, v. 9. that all the Fathers prove from the Scriptures that omnipotence is understood, Vasquez teaches in book II de adorat. disput. VIII. cap. 10. that Christ obtained this name by grace, in so far as he was made man; although he had it from eternity, in so far as he is God, Lombard acknowledges in book III. sent. dist. 18. lit. C.

Vers. 12.

Λέγοντες φωνῇ μεγάλῃ) Approbant ea quae Apostoli & Presbyteri praedicant. Λέγοντες recte referetur ad μυριάδες, nempe κατὰ τὸ σημαινόμενον.

De Ecclesia sermo est non militante, sed trium- phante, quod agnoscit Cornelius a Lapide contra Alcasarem suum, inepte hinc sacrificium Missae colligentem; haec scilicet omnia visa esse in coelo, non in terra, & denotare gloriam coelestium non terrestrium. Numerus ille Angelorum vere in- numerus, quia myriades myriadum indefinite di- cuntur.

Ἄξιόν ἐστι τὸ ἀρνίον τὸ ἐσφαγισμένον λαβεῖν τὴν δύναμιν, καὶ πλοῦτον, καὶ σοφίαν, καὶ ἰσχὺν, καὶ τιμὴν, καὶ δόξαν, καὶ εὐλογίαν] Septem laudum nomina respondentia septem Spi- ritibus. In Latino legitur divinitatem, ubi ab interprete scriptum fuit divitias, πλοῦτον. Significatur autem confessio liberalitatis Christi. Par numerus infra 7, 12. ubi pro πλοῦ- τος habemus εὐχαριστίαν. VIII. v. 46. cap. IX. v. 1. cap. XXI. v. 27. 2. πλοῦτος divitiae, omnisufficientia divina, plenitudo divitia- rum gratiae inexhausta, Psal. XXXVI. v. 10. Joh. I. v. 17. Actor. XI. v. 33. Ephes. II. v. 4. Gen. XVII. v. 1. Vitiosam autem hic esse Vulgatam versionem, cum divinitatem reddidit, consensus insignis Grae- corum & aliorum codicum docet. 3. Σοφία im- mensa sapientia, sicut in ipso absconditi dicuntur omnes thesauri sapientiae, Col. II. v. 3. & ipse plenus est sapientia, Luc. II, v. 40. estque secundum di- vinam naturam ipsa sapientia Dei hypostatica, Prov. VIII. v. 23. Luc. XI. v. 47. 4. ἰσχὺς fortitu- dinem, robur, & potentiam infinitam infert Esa. LXIII. v. 3. Phil. III. v. 21. 5. Τιμὴ tribuitur ei ob ἀξίωμα adorationis, unde אלהים dicitur Deus ab adorabilitate, Phil. II. v. 5. 6. δόξα ob ma- jestatem divinam, Coloss. II. v. 9. quae est יהוה τοῦ, unde Dominus gloriae vocatur, 1. Corinth. II. v. 8. 7. Εὐλογία ob gratiam & benedictionem omnige- nam, quam a Christo, & in Christo habemus, Eph. I. v. 3. Joh. I. v. 14. Genes. XII. v. 3. Galat. III. v. 16. Profitentur hoc de Agno occiso, adeoque de Chri- sto secundum humanam naturam, quae particeps facta est divinae gloriae per communicationem hy- postaticam & exaltationem ad dextram Dei, Col. II. 9. Phil. II. v. 9. 10. Gloriam suam Deus alteri non dat, Esa. XLII. v. 8. Sed Agnus est unius cum Deo essentiae, Joh. X, v. 30. Nec ipsi daretur glo- ria Patris, nisi unum esset cum Patre: ac licet se- cundum humanam naturam differat, haec tamen non propria, sed ipsa τοῦ λόγου hypostasi subsistit, & cum ipso unum constituit ὑφισάμενον. Non ergo datur gloria alteri per μετάβασιν, sed confer- tur carni, τῷ λόγῳ Patri ὁμοουσίῳ, unitae per κοινω- νίαν ὑποστατικὴν subsistenti ἐν αὐτῷ τῷ λόγῳ. A- gnoscit id cum Aretha: Τὸ εἰληφέναι τὸ ἀρνίον τὸ

βιβλίον κατὰ τὸ ἀνθρώπινον νοητέον, S. Anshelmus : accepit homo factus de dextra sedentis, id est, à Ver- bo sibi unito. Et: Benedictio, & honor sedneti in thro- no Deo Patri & Agno, secundum carnem : Ut & Albertus : Dignus est, inquiens, accipere, ut hu- manitas scilicet omnia possideat: necnon Dionysius Carthusianus, qui id è Damasceno confirmat, quod humanitati Christi ratione suæ hypostaticæ unionis tum Verbo data est, & competit plenitudo gratiæ & sapientiæ. Addo & Cornelium Jansen. in Concord. Evangel. cap. 136. Humana natura ac- cepit illam claritatem, quam divina natura ha- buit ab æterno, quando humana natura immorta- litæ donata est, & in cælum sublata, & per con- junctionem sui cum divina natura in unitatem personæ ejusdem, tum illa gloriæ consors effecta. Cardinal. Cajetanus in Sent. decim. quæst. 4. de Johan. XVII. v. 3. Petit Dominus, inquit, ut exe- quutioni mandetur hoc, scilicet, quod gloria sua æterna derivetur in seipsum secundum humanam naturam: Quid? quod ad illum locum observet Maldonatus, omnes Interpretes eum accipere de clarificatione humanitatis, non Deitatis. Per no- men supra omne nomen, Philipp. II. v. 9. Patres omnes ex Scripturis probare, intelligi omnipoten- tiam, docet Vasquez lib. II. de adorat. disput. VIII. cap. 10. quod nomen Christum per gratiam ob- tinuisse, in quantum factum est homo; etsi id ha- buerit ab æterno, in quantum Deus est, Lombar- dus agnoscit lib. III. sent. dist. 18. lit. C.

## 5:13
Vers. 13.

Καὶ πᾶν κτίσμα, ὅ ἐστι ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ] in the heaven, namely, the lowest, middle, and highest, as the Hebrews distinguish. Καὶ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς, καὶ ὑποκάτω τῆς γῆς, καὶ ἐπὶ τῆς θαλάσσης ἅ ἐστι, καὶ τὰ ἐν αὐτοῖς, πάλας ἤκουσα λέγοντας) It is a prosopopoeia, by which speech is attributed to inanimate or mute things, so that they may be shown to obey not only God, but also to serve Christ and his glory, Phil. 2. v. 9. 10. Heb. 1, v. 6. See similar things in Deut. 32, v. 1. Isa. 1. v. 2. Hab. III. v. 10. Psalm 19, v. 1. and elsewhere. In the Manuscript it is πάντα ἤκουσα λέγοντα. I take that καί before the words ἐπὶ τῆς θαλάσσης exegetically, namely, so that the preceding Hebrew locution may be explained by the more familiar Greek, just as Ἀββᾶ is explained by πατήρ. See what is above in chapter 5, v. 3. But I take that τὰ ἐν αὐτοῖς in such a way that those things are signified which are intimate within living beings and things, and escape the eyes of men; by the argument of the passage in Psalm 103, verse 1, where in the Greek it is πάντα τὰ ἐντός μου. The opening of the seals shows that there are no creatures that do not serve Christ.

He joins into one choir of those glorifying, with those who are in heaven, all who are on earth, who rest under the earth in their monuments, and who are in the sea with all things that are in them, as in Psalm 147, verse 1, seq. Isa. LX. verse 5. 9. so that there is no need to transfer these to irrational and inanimate creatures, as was done by Andreas of Caesarea, Rupert, and others. If by under the earth demons are understood; their confession is indeed forced, yet due, as is bowing or adoration, Phil. II. 10. There is no need, therefore, for a prosopopoeia, nor that we extend these to souls in purgatory. For what is said in Psalm 6, verse 6: Shall thanks be given to you in hell? is to be understood κατά τι, in that reason and manner by which we living ones praise God, namely, with a common and public voice before the living. Such a distribution of creatures was held also in v. 3 of this our chapter, where certainly by τὰς ὑποκάτω τῆς γῆς neither inanimate things nor demons are understood, whom it was not necessary to mention as not being admitted to that dignity. For they are eternally excluded from the blessed vision of God. However, this passage does nothing for purgatory, both because, according to Bellarmine in book II de Purg. c. 6. and Maldonatus in Tom. II. disp. de Sacram. p. 171, Jesuits of great name as witnesses, it is not yet certain to the Papists whether purgatory is below or above the earth, both because, as Bellarmine admits, inanimate creatures under the earth can be understood, as Lyranus also explained, and because Gregory the Great and Rupert say demons and the damned, Ambrose and Theodoret say the dead; Bellarmine says he probably understands the Fathers who were in limbo. Τῷ καθημένῳ ἐπὶ τῷ θρόνου καὶ τῷ ἀρνίῳ] Thus also below 7, 10. c. 14, 4. 22, 3. Ἡ εὐλογία, καὶ ἡ τιμὴ, καὶ ἡ δόξα, καὶ τὸ κράτος εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων, ἀμήν] See a similar doxology above I. 6. 1. Tim. 6, 16. 1. Petr. 4, 11. Jude 25. Rom. 11, 36. 16, 27. Gal. 1, 5. Eph. 3, 21. Phil. 4, 20. 2. Tim. 4, 18. Heb. 13, 21. 2. Petr. 3, verse 18.

Latin:

Vers. 13.

Καὶ πᾶν κτίσμα, ὅ ἐστι ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ] in cælo nempe infi- mo, medio & summo, ut distinguunt Ebræi. Καὶ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς, καὶ ὑποκάτω τῆς γῆς, καὶ ἐπὶ τῆς θαλάσ- σης ἅ ἐστι, καὶ τὰ ἐν αὐτοῖς, πάλας ἤκουσα λέγοντας) Est προ- σωποποιΐα, qua sermo tribuitur inanimis aut mutis rebus, ut ostendantur illa omnia parere, non Deo tantum, sed & Chri- sto & ejus gloriæ inservire, Phil. 2. v. 9. 10. Ebr. 1, v. 6. Simi- lia vide Deutet. 32, v. 1. Esa. 1. v. 2. Abac. III. v. 10. Psalm. 19, v. 1. & alibi. In Manuscripto est πάντα ἤκουσα λέγοντα. Illud κὴ ante verba ἐπὶ τῆς θαλάσσης sumo ἐξηγητικῶς, nempe ut præcedens locutio Ebræa per Græcam notiorem explice- tur, sicut Ἀββᾶ explicatur per πατήρ. Vide quæ supra cap. 5, v. 3. Illud autem τὰ ἐν αὐτοῖς ita sumo ut significen- tur ea quæ in animantibus rebusque sunt intima, & oculos hominum effugiunt; argumento loci Psalm. 103, vers. 1. u- bi in Græco πάντα τὰ ἐντός μου. Ostendit sigillo- rum apertio nullas esse creaturas quæ Christo non ser- viant.

Conjungit in unum glorificantium chorum, cum iis, qui in cælo sunt omnes, qui in terra sunt, qui sub terra in monumentis suis quiescunt, & qui in mari cum omnibus, quæ in ipsis, uti Psal. 147, vers. 1. seq. Esa. LX. vers. 5. 9. ut non o- pus sit ad creaturas irrationales & inanimes hæc transferre, quemadmodum ab Andrea Cæsariensi, Ruperto, & aliis factum. Si sub terra intelligan- tur Dæmones; confessio ipsorum coacta quidem est, debita tamẽ, uti incurvatio vel adoratio, Phil. II. 10. Non opus ergo prosopopœia, nec ut ad animas in purgatorio hæc extendamus. Quod enim Psal. 6, vers. 6. dicitur: Num in inferno tibi gratiæ agentur? intelligendum κατά τι, ea ratione & modo, quo nos viventes Deum laudamus, nimi- rum voce communi & publica coram viventibus. Talis creaturam distributio habebatur & v. 3. hujus capitis nostri, ubi certe per τὰς ὑποκάτω τῆς γῆς non res inanimatæ, neq; Dæmones intelligun- tur, quos ad eam dignationem non admitti, nihil opus erat commemorari. Sunt enim à beata Dei visione æternum exclusi. Nihil autem facit hic lo- cus pro purgatorio, tum quia Bellarmino lib. II. de Purg. c. 6. & Maldonato Tom. II. disp. de Sacram. p. 171. Jesùitis magni nominis testibus, nondum constat Pontificiis an purgaorium sit subtus vel su- per terram, tum quia fatente Bellarmino per crea- turas sub terra inanimes intelligi possunt, uti etiam Lyranus exposuit, tum quia Gregorius M. & Ru- pertus Dæmones & damnatos, Ambrosius & Theo- doretus mortuos; Bellarminus Patres, qui in limbo erant, probabiliter intelligere, ait. Τῷ καθημένῳ ἐπὶ τῦ θρόνου καὶ τῷ ἀρνίῳ] Sic & infra 7, 10. c. 14, 4. 22, 3. Ἡ εὐλογία, καὶ ἡ τιμὴ, καὶ ἡ δόξα, καὶ τὸ κράτος εἰς τὲς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων, ἀμὴν] Similem δοξολογίαν vide supra I. 6. 1. Tim. 6, 16. 1. Petr. 4, 11. Judæ 25. Rom. 11, 36. 16, 27. Gal. 1, 5. Eph. 3, 21. Phil. 4, 20. 2. Tim. 4, 18. Ebr. 13, 21. 2. Petr. 3, vers. 18.

## 5:14
Verse 14.

Καὶ τὰ τέσσαρα ζῶα λέγοντα τὸ Ἀμήν] Approving that which the Angels indeed confessed in words, but the whole world in reality. And he said τὸ Ἀμήν because it was a received expression in the Church. Καὶ οἱ πρεσβύτεροι ἔπεσον καὶ προσεκύνησαν] They showed honor, not to God only, as above 4, 10, but also to Christ. But as for what is added here in some codices, ζῶντι εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων, it is missing in the Manuscript. Therefore, the same glory, the same honor, the confession of the same divine power is shown to the Triune God sitting on the throne, and to the Lamb Christ, who according to his human nature has been raised to the same throne of divine majesty and made συνθρόνῳ. These things clearly refute the Calvinist impiety, which refuses to attribute divine glory to Christ according to his human nature, which even the Elect themselves, and all creatures, attribute in heaven, on earth, under the earth, in the sea, with all the holy Angels singing in harmony, according to that Psalm XCVII. 8. Heb. I. 6. All the Angels shall worship him.

Latin:

Vers. 14.

Καὶ τὰ τέσσαρα ζῶα λέγοντα τὸ Ἀμήν] Approbantes id, quod Angeli quidem verbis, mundus autem totus reipsa fate- batur. Et dixit τὸ Ἀμὴν quia vox erat recepta in Ecclesia. Καὶ οἱ πρεσβύτεροι ἔπεσον καὶ προσεκύνησαν] Honorem ex- hibuere, non Deo tantum, ut supra 4, 10. sed & Christo. Quod vero hic in nonnullis codicibus additur, ζῶντι εἰς τὲς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων, deest in Manuscripto. Eadem ergo gloria, idem honor, ejusdem vir- tutis divinæ confessio exhibetur Deo Triuni in throno sedenti, & Agno Christo secundum humanam naturam in eundem majestatis divinæ thronum evecto & συνθρόνῳ facto. Quæ luculenter refel- lunt Calvinianam impietatem, Christo secun- dum humanam naturam divinam gloriam tribu- ere renuentem, quam ipsi etiam Electi, & o- mnes creaturæ tribuunt in cælis, in terra, sub ter- ra, in mari, concinentibus omnibus sanctis Ange- lis, juxta illud Psal. XCVII. 8. Ebr. I. 6. Adorabunt eum omnes Angeli.

## 6:1 Argument
III. THE UNSEALING OF THE SIX SEALS. CHAPTER VI. ARGUMENT, AND PARTITION. Upon the first seal being unsealed, a white horse comes forth, with a crowned rider: The second, a red one, with a rider girded with a sword: The third, a black one, with a rider equipped with a balance, measuring out the grain: The fourth, a pale one, with a rider named Death: In the fifth, when opened, the souls of those slain for the word of God are seen, seeking vengeance, and being given white robes, they are ordered to rest for a while: Upon the sixth being opened, an earthquake occurs, the Sun is darkened, the Moon becomes bloody, the stars fall, the heaven flees, the mountains and islands are moved from their places, and the Kings on earth wish to fall upon the mountains and rocks, and to be hidden from the wrath of him who sits on the throne and of the Lamb. There are two parts: The former contains the unsealing of the first four seals, with the exhortation of the four living creatures to look upon those things which come forth, up to verse 8. The latter exhibits the unsealing of the fifth and sixth seals, and the things seen and heard concerning them, up to verse 17. PART I. THE UNSEALING OF THE FOUR FIRST SEALS. I. THE UNSEALING OF THE FIRST SEAL. Verse 1.

Καὶ εἶδον ὅτι ἤνοιξε τὸ ἀρνίον μίαν ἐκ τῶν ἑπτὰ σφραγίδων] The song now being finished. Μίαν, that is, the first, as appears from what follows. Thus μία σαββάτων, the first between two Sabbaths. Καὶ ἤκουσα ἑνὸς ἐκ τῶν τέσσαρα ζώων λέγοντος, ὡς φωνὴ βροντῆς, ἔρχου] It seems that the leader of the Apostolic band, Peter, who had also been the first in the preaching of the Gospel, of which there will be talk here, is addressing John here. Ἑνὸς, that is, πρώτου, because δευτέρου, τρίτου, τετάρτου follows: just as we have already had μίαν. A voice like thunder is a great and resonant voice, whence both John and his brother are called sons of thunder, Mark III. v. 17. Come, namely so that you may hear the singular circumstances of those things which Christ had predicted to us in general, Matthew 24, so that through you all may the more recognize the admirable providence of God concerning Jewish affairs.

Latin:

III. SEX SIGILLORUM RESERATIO. CAPUT VI. ARGUMENTUM, ET PARTITIO. Referato primo sigillo prodit albus equus, cum equite coronato: Secundo rufus, cum equite gladio cincto: Tertio niger, cum equite trati- na instructo, annonam demetiente: Quarto pallidus, cum equite Morte: Quinto aperto conspiciuntur animæ occisorum propter ver- bum Dei, vindictam expetentes, datis albis stolis adhuc quiescere jubentes: Sexto aperto fit terræ motus, obtenebratur Sol, Luna fit san- guinea, stellæ decidunt, cælum fugit, montes & insulæ sedibus suis dimoventur, Regesque in terris montibq & petris corrui, atq; ab ira sedentis in throno & agni, occultari optant. Partes sunt duæ: Prior quatuor priorum sigillo- rum resignationem, cum quatuor animalium hor- tatu, ad ea spectanda, quæ prodeunt, continet, us- que ad v. 8. Posterior quinti & sexti sigilli resignati- onem, & circa ea visa & audita exhibet usq; ad v. 17. PARS I. QUATUOR PRIORUM SIGILLORUM RESIGNATIO. I. RESIGNATIO PRIMI SIGILLI. Vers. 1.

Καὶ εἶδον ὅτι ἤνοιξε τὸ ἀρνίον μίαν ἐκ τῶν ἑπτὰ σφραγίδων] Absoluto jam cantu. Μίαν, id est, primam, ut ex sequentib. apparet. Sic μία σαββάτων, prima inter duo Sabbata. Καὶ ἤκουσα ἑνὸς ἐκ τῶν τέσσαρα ζώων λέγοντος, ὡς φωνὴ βροντῆς, ἔρχου] Videtur Johannem hic alloqui princeps Apo- stolici cœtus, Petrus, qui & in prædicatione Evangelii, de qua hic agetur, primus fuerat. Ἑνὸς, id est, πρώτου, quia sequitur δευτέρου, τρίτου, τετάρτου: quomodo jam & μίαν habuimus. Vox tanquam tonitru, est vox magna & fono- ra, unde & Johannes & frater ejus dicti υἱοὶ βροντῆς, Marc. III. v. 17. Veni, nempe ut audias circumstantias singulares eorum, quæ generatim Christus nobis prædixerat, Matth. 24. ut eo magis per te omnes agnoscant admirabilem Dei circa res Judaicas providentiam.

## 6:2
Verse 2. Καὶ εἶδον καὶ ἰδὺ ἵππος λευκὸς] There are red, black, white, and varied horses in Zechariah, c. VI, which signify, as we have said, the Chaldeans, Persians, Alexander, and the Kings of both Syria and Egypt from Seleucus and Lagus. But there the horses are joined in four-horse chariots in the manner of war, here they are κέλητες or single horses to signify a swift journey with power. Therefore Psalm XIV. v. 5, where in the Hebrew there is רכב, that is, ride, the Greeks put βασίλευε. And in Ecclesiastes X. 7. and Zach. 3, a horse is put as a sign of power. ἵππος ὃς ὕψος, καὶ ἀξίωμα ὑγιὲς, Achmeti 233. Instead of the varied horses in this prophecy, a pale horse will come. This rider, the leader of the army, is Christ himself, who is seen now not as a lamb, but as a King. That is manifest below XIX. v. 11. 12. 13, whence it follows that the white horse, upon which he sits, is his Gospel because of its purity. See above I. 14. The rest of the riders who follow are Angels, the administrators of divine providence.

Καὶ ὁ καθήμενος ἐπ᾽ αὐτὸν ἔχων τόξον] The bow threatens before it strikes: Thus also Christ. See Psalm VII. 13. XI. 2. LX. v. 4. in the Greek: where by the bow Basil understands threats. All things that harm are called weapons metaphorically. Thus in Homer: τίσειαν Δαναοὶ ἐμὰ δάκρυα σοῖσι βέλεσσι, that is, by plague. See Deut. XXXII. 23. Hab. III. 8. Hosea I. 5. Ps. XVIII. 15. XXVIII. 2. LXIV. 3. LXXVII. 18. CXX. 4. CXXVII. 5. CXLIV. 6. In the Manuscript also it is ἐπ᾿ αὐτὸν, not ἐπ᾿ αὐτῷ.

Καὶ ἐδόθη αὐτῷ στέφανος] He is crowned as a victor.

Καὶ ἐξῆλθε νικῶν καὶ ἵνα νικήσῃ] Here the first καὶ is causal. He is crowned for this reason, because he had both conquered and will conquer. He had conquered many Jews by the power of his word, Acts 2 and thereafter, and he will conquer the stubborn with his many and varied weapons. The weapons of God are primarily three: war, famine, and pestilence, Lev. XXVI. 17. and following, Deut. 28, verse 52. and following, 1 Sam. 24, verse 13. 2 Chron. 20, 9. Jer. 14, 12, 15, 2. 21, 7. 24, 10. 27, 8. 32, 36. 34, 17. 38, 2. 42, 17. 44, 13. Ezek. 5, 12. 17. 6, 11. 12. 7, 15. 12, 16. 14, 21. Christ imitates the providence of God. These are the beginnings of sorrows in the words of Christ, Matthew 24, 8. War is accustomed to precede: from war, devastation is born, and from that, evils either double or triple coincide at the same time.

The first and sixth seal bring auspicious and happy things in the spiritual advent of grace, and the last [brings] the bodily glory of Christ to the kingdom, which he gathers in these lands, and to the glorious kingdom to be granted to the elect in the final judgment, until which time the souls of the martyrs are commanded to rest. Included in the intermediate four seals were the bodily evils impending over the Church and the world, as in the seventh seal the spiritual evils to be inflicted upon the same by the heresies and Anti-Christian idolomania, which are revealed by the opening of the seals performed by the Lamb. Where the interpretation reported by Andreas does not deserve refutation, of those who explained the opening of the seven seals as concerning the birth, baptism, miracles, accusation, crucifixion, burial, and descent into hell of Christ; or as it seemed to Rupert, concerning the birth, cross, resurrection, ascension of Christ, the mission of the Holy Spirit, the calling of the Gentiles, and the universal judgment; since those things do not correspond, and John is not dealing here with past events, but with future ones, and is expounding a prophecy delivered to him; or the opinion of Ambrose, that by the seven seals are signified those things which have happened and will happen to the seven holy ages of the world. Moreover, four living creatures are employed to show the four horses, conformably to the individual visions, which Grotius rashly defines by the denomination of the Apostles, not defined in the ἀποκαλύψει. Peter, although first among the Apostles in order, is not prince in dignity. For they were this, as Cyprian says, and the Canon Law approves in C. loquitur, Caus. 24. q. 1., the other Apostles were equal, as was Peter, endowed with an equal partnership of both honor and power: Why it is conferred upon the first animal, namely the lion, does not appear. For he was not of such leonine fortitude that he was not terrified more than others, both in the passion of Christ denying his Lord, and in his conversation with the Jews Judaizing for the favor of the Pseudo-Apostles, Gal. II. Whoever, however, he may have been who is signified by the first animal, the leonine virtue of the Evangelizers contributes greatly to the primordial propagation of the Gospel, which from

With the victorious rider on the first white horse in first arms, and from there it is promoted by the Johannine vision. However, it is not by the horse, but by the rider that Christ the King is designated, who sits upon the teachers of the Word, inasmuch as they are understood more correctly by horses than the Gospel itself, and they serve Christ by the course of the Gospel for the purpose of propagating it swiftly. There is one white horse, but in that one is designated the universality of all, who ought to be white and bright with the brightness and light of a purer doctrine, and then also of a holier life, and to carry none but Christ through the world, 1 Cor. 2:2. Moreover, the course of this rider is not defined, except that it is said that he has both conquered thus far, and will conquer hereafter, and therefore deservedly wears a crown. Not therefore only as King, who is introduced earlier seen as a Lamb, but also as victor, always august. Who had conquered as a lion both in the resurrection and in the calling of the Gentiles through the Apostles, and in the destruction of the enemies, the Jews, and of the Republic and the temple and their worship, and also in the conversion of some to the Gospel. Cf. Zech. 9:10, ch. 10:3 ff., ch. 13:8, 9, ch. 14:8 ff. Who furthermore was to conquer always until the consummation of the age, not only in the violent persecution of the Gentile tyrants, but also in the fraudulent persecution of the heretics, the Arians, and others, as also in the fraudulently violent and violently fraudulent persecution of the Antichrist of both kinds, Eastern and Western. Such a victor, although he is hinted at here as showing himself in a peculiar and illustrious manner to the previous centuries, amidst the very most atrocious persecutions of his own; yet this is not to be understood exclusively, but is to be extended entirely to the other fates of the Church until the consummation of the age and the consummated victory of his own, shown in ch. 7; just as the evils, both bodily and spiritual, comprised under the seven seals, although they are to follow one another in a certain order by reason, yet they will extend themselves until the end of the world, and the final punishment of the enemies of the Church, and indeed the consummated reward of the faithful. Nor indeed can we agree either with those who, with Petrus Aureolus and Viega, understand by the one sitting on the white horse Gaius Caligula, who in no matter harassed the Church, or with those who, with Luther, Osiander, Hoë, and Danhaw. Anti-Christ. p. 308, as also Döling. Dürfeld, understand those who are carried by the white horse, because they persecute the pious in the peace of the Republic, but conquer by the judgment of the world: or with D. Gravius, who understands the Roman Empire or the Gentile Emperors themselves, who attacked and conquered the Christians for over 300 years. For although the Christians spiritually conquered the persecutors through the blood of the Lamb and the Word of their testimony, Apoc. 12:11, yet the Roman persecutors obtained an external, bodily, and before the world plausible victory, until Constantine the Great. Whiteness, he says, of this horse indicates the supreme Majesty of the Emperors, which had its beginning in C. Julius Caesar and was derived to all his other successors, so that they used white horses and triumphal garments in their triumphs and inaugurations. The whiteness of horses and garments was also a sign of justice. For the Roman Emperors, under the pretext of justice, wanted to eradicate the Christian religion as a plague of the Empire, judging Christians as evildoers, unworthy even of enjoying the usury of life. By the bow of this rider is denoted the speed of the persecutions undertaken against the Christians through all the provinces of the empire. By the crown granted to this rider, both the Royal authority and the triumphs which the persecutors arrogated to themselves over the Christians are understood. Diocletian and Maximian proceeded to such impiety that they erected triumphal statues to themselves for Christ conquered and eradicated, because his sect had been pernicious to the Roman Empire. And this John expresses when he adds in v. 2: And a crown was given to him, and he went out conquering and to conquer. This is the Blessed Doctor Gravius. John Fox understands by these four horses the four Monarchies, Irenaeus book IV, ch. 38.
