Ticonius, Primasius, Beda, Glossa, Albertus M., Haymo, Thomas, Flacius, Chytraeus, Cramerus, Vinariens., Hoffmannus, and from the Reformed Bullinger, Aretius, Piscator, Szegedin, Napeir, Pareus, Forbesius, as also Riccardus, Joseph Mede, Diestius the epitomizer of Pareus, Colladon, Coccejus, Crugotius, and from the Papists Ribera, Cornelius à Lapide, and finally Cotterius, judge that Christ is signified by the first horse, propagating the Gospel through the world by the ministry of the Apostles: Nor does our Hugo disagree. Nor is there any doubt that all things more correctly fit Christ, who is carried through the world by the Evangelists of peace as if on a white horse, Isa. 52:2, which was done especially in the time of the Apostles, and shortly after, as long as the Church remained a virgin, and he triumphs as victor, just as the Roman victors entered on a white horse. By the bow the efficacy of the Word is designated, Ps. 45:6, Heb. 4:12. The crown is a sign of dominion and victory. He went out, as one who had already conquered, and was to conquer hereafter, as a strong one powerfully prostrating all the wisdom and power of the world, and of its Prince, Satan, and crushing him under the feet of the faithful, Rom. 16:20, conquering especially the idolatry of the Gentiles, so that peoples and Kings might fall down before him, Ps. 45:6, inasmuch as they are converted to him, Ps. 22:28, 29, 30, Ps. 72:10, 11, Isa. 49:23, ch. 60:1 ff. That those are called horses mystically who attack something with valid impetus and a high spirit, and hasten to accomplish it, is evident from the example of Elijah and Elisha, who are called the horsemen of Israel, 2 Kings 2:12, ch. 13:14, for which reason that name is also attributed to Angels, Zech. 1:8, 2 Kings 2:11, ch. 6:17. And for the sake of consolation, a joyful image is set forth beforehand, and the trumpets of the three heresies, and the seductions of Antichrist, and the threefold Woe, a more joyful vision is intimated, preceding the Son of God, interceding for the Church with a golden censer. Add that in this manner Christ showed Himself again most recently, Apoc. XIX. v. 11. Behold a white horse, and he that sat upon him was called faithful and true, and in justice he judgeth and fighteth. Whence Primasius rightly says: This horse, he says, can be understood in the Apostles and preachers of the truth of the Church, whitened by grace beyond custom, whose rider is Christ. For which reason he is also said to hold an arrow, which is most aptly compared to the preaching of the Word of God; which, having pierced the interiors of men, can bring forth the fruit of faith. Tertullian has similar things in his book against the Jews, chapter IX. Victorinus, Ticonius, Augustine, Andreas, Arethas in part, Anselm, likewise Haymo, Lyra, B. Gerhard, B. Cluver, B. Winckelmann; It is proposed, he says, the victory of Christ in the diffusion of the Gospel through the whole world until the end of the world, although the Devil and all powerful tyrants resist. For Christ, through the ministry of the Apostles and Apostolic men, who are designated by the horse, propagates His Gospel, and therefore as a rider bends and directs his horse at his nod, and indeed sometimes even pricks it with spurs, that is, permits them to be afflicted, and yet by His power breaks through. He had a bow. Thus the Messiah is introduced in Isaiah XLIX, saying: The Lord hath made my mouth like a sharp sword; in the shadow of his hand he hath hid me, and hath made me a polished arrow. And indeed aptly preaching, when the Lord adds strength, is compared to an arrow flying most swiftly, because in a short time it filled the world, just as it is said in Isaiah 11: The earth is filled with the knowledge of Jehovah (a crown was given to him). This adorns the victory of Christ. And indeed, just as a horse moves now here, now there, at the guidance and nod of its rider; so also the Apostles and Apostolic men, having followed the direction of the Holy Spirit, have entered now this, now that region. Just as a horse stimulated by spurs proceeds more strongly: so also the Apostles and Apostolic men, although they were forced to suffer many things for the name of Christ; nevertheless, they proceeded strenuously in performing their duty. Andreas of Caesarea attributes the crown and the bow to the Apostles and preachers, but the rest to Christ. But the horse is a participant in the glory of its rider, whom it carries, and Christ fights, conquers, is crowned, and triumphs through his horses, 2 Corinthians 2:14. Romans 15:17-18. Revelation 12:11, chapter 14:14. Albert the Great: Christ, he says, presiding over the Church, wields the armor of sacred doctrine against the impious. The white horse is the company of the first preachers, who are called a horse on account of their fortitude, boldness, and the neighing of their preaching; likewise on account of the speed of running and patience. White on account of the baptismal grace by which they were washed, and the greater clarity of knowledge. But he went out from the narrowness of Judea, conquering by converting a few of the Jews to the faith, so that he might conquer more of the Gentiles. Similarly, Blessed Cluverus applies these things particularly to the earlier times, since up to Constantine the Great, for a space of almost 250 years, the conflict of this rider with his enemies and his victory were very illustrious, when he not only promoted his empire far and wide, but also compelled the Roman Emperor himself to worship his fasces and to swear by his scepter and crown; and the effects of the first seal shone forth sufficiently splendidly at the end of the reign of Domitian, by which he lifted the persecution commanded against the Churches with contrary edicts, and also while Nerva was reigning; concerning which Tertullian in his Apologeticus: Domitian also once attempted something similar, a portion of Nero in cruelty; but as a man he quickly desisted, so that he even recalled those whom he had sent into exile. Which is also established concerning his successor Nerva, as he was one who ordered all exiles to be recalled by a decree of the Senate and to receive back their property. Whence also St. John returned to Ephesus from Patmos, and traveling through the neighboring provinces, he planted Churches, or watered and propagated those already planted; as can be read in Irenaeus, Clement of Alexandria, and Eusebius. Concerning whom Dio says of Nerva: He absolved those who had been accused of impiety, and restored the exiles. He also permitted no one to be accused of impiety or of Jewish ritual. Tertullian, who flourished in those times, is a clear witness to the fulfillment of this vision of the seal, in his book Against the Jews, chapter 7, number 96. Thus he says: The Lord God says to my Lord Christ, whose right hand I have held, that the nations may hear him: I will break the strengths of Kings, I will open doors before him, and cities will not be closed to him: Which we see fulfilled. For to whom does God the Father hold the right hand, if not to Christ, his Son? Whom all nations have heard, that is, in whom all nations have believed, whose preachers the Apostles are also shown to be in the Psalms of David: Their sound, he says, has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world. For in whom else have all nations believed, if not in Christ, who has already come? For to whom have other nations also believed, the Parthians, Medes, Elamites, and those who inhabit Mesopotamia, Armenia, Phrygia, Cappadocia, and the inhabitants of Pontus, and Asia and Pamphylia, those dwelling in Egypt and the region of Africa which is beyond Cyrene, the Romans and inhabitants, then also in Jerusalem and the rest of the nations, as now the varieties of the Gaetulians, and the many borders of the Moors, all the ends of the Spains, and the diverse nations of the Gauls, and the places of the Britons inaccessible to the Romans. But subject to Christ are also the Sarmatians and Dacians and Germans and Scythians and many hidden nations and provinces and many islands unknown to us, and which we are less able to enumerate? In all of which places the name of Christ, who has already come, reigns, as the gates of all cities are opened before him, and to whom none are closed, before whom iron bars have been crushed, and bronze valves have been opened; although these things are also to be understood spiritually, by which the hearts of individuals besieged in various ways by the Devil have been unlocked by the faith of Christ, yet they have been clearly fulfilled, as in all these places the people of the name of Christ dwell. For who could have reigned over all, if not Christ the Son of God?

Grotius boasts much indeed about the victory of many Jews after the times of John or from this vision, but he brings forward no documents or testimonies of antiquity, from which he might have more easily proven the contrary. And that those things which Christ predicted in Matthew 24 concerning Judea and the destruction of Jerusalem are explained here is a precarious hypothesis of Grotius, which chronology openly contradicts. For these visions happened long after that destruction: Why then would the Holy Spirit prophesy about things already long since accomplished? Those trifles are more vain than fig-leaf nonsense: such as Cornelius has already defeated in his Alcazar, who opposes to him and others that this vision embraces only what is to come in the Church. Nor can we say without cause concerning the Grotian exposition what Cornelius says of his own gloss on chapter 5, verse 1, page 105. This whole exposition seems an ingenious accommodation rather than a genuine explanation, just as Proba Falconia accommodated and adapted Virgil's Aeneid to Christ and the deeds of Christ: and Eudocia, wife of the Emperor Theodosius the Younger, composed her Homeric centos from the same out of Homer. But Cornelius joins our opinion: I say, he says, that by this symbol of the white horse and the rider is signified the most warlike and most victorious state of the primitive Church. For the horse is first a symbol of war. Second, it is a symbol of empire. Third, it is a symbol of victory. I say therefore, first, the white horse are the Apostles and other heralds of the Gospel, such as St. Ignatius, Polycarp, Dionysius, etc. through whom Christ conquered the world and subjected it to Himself: Thus Aretas, Andreas, Haymo, Tyconius, Ribera, Pererius, and others everywhere, who followed St. Irenaeus, the first and ancient author of this explanation, all agree and conspire in this with one voice. Secondly, the rider of this horse is Christ. Thirdly, the bow is the Holy Scripture, or the Word of God, from which proceed as many arrows as there are words and sentences. Fourthly, this horse is white, so that it may signify that this battle will be joyful and festive, inasmuch as it will have a certain victory as its end. Whence also Christ is distinguished by a crown, because He is King and victor, a victor, I say, not like a leader of camps among men, who kills the enemy while he subdues him, but who, while subduing him, makes a friend out of an enemy, a pious man out of an impious one, nay, makes him His own soldier, whom He uses as a kind of new arrow to strike and subdue others. For Christ, from the enemies prostrated and struck by Him, forges for Himself new arrows, with which He may pierce others with love of Him. For this is what this arrow does, namely the charity and love of Christ, so that those struck by it are not content with their own salvation alone, but thirst for the salvation of all others, and ardently procure it. Wherefore they shoot and strike others with the same arrow of theirs with which they themselves have been pierced. Hence this arrow is called by Isaiah an elect arrow. And the Psalmist: The arrows, he says, of the mighty are sharp, Psal. CXIX. where S. Augustine: The arrows, he says, of the mighty are sharp are the words of God. Behold, they are cast and they pierce hearts, so that love may be excited, not destruction brought about. It shoots the heart of the lover, so that it may help the lover, it shoots so that it may make a lover. And, thy arrows are sharp (hence the peoples shall fall under thee) in the hearts of the King's enemies, Psal. XLIX. vers. 6. The symbol of this victory is a white horse. Coccejus also agrees, except that he wishes the rider to signify doctors and rulers: The victory achieved, he says, signifies the confirmation of the Gospel among the Jews as if converted, or as convicted. The victory to be achieved signifies the end of the Gospel sent to the nations, so that the whole world may be subjected to Christ. Conf. 2. Corinth. X. v. 4. 5. 2. Tim. IV. v. 7. Pomponius Laetus has these things concerning the triumph of Diocletian and Maximian: After the chariots of the triumphers made of gold and precious stones, which four horses vying with snow in whiteness were drawing. But that Cornelius à Lapide says the custom of Roman prelates, that the new Pope is to receive possession of the Pontificate at the Lateran, is taken from this vision of ours, while they are accustomed to ride to him on white horses, because the Pope is the vicar and successor of Christ, is exceedingly vain and futile. For it is not that the prelates are thus ridden, but that the prelates might be hinted to be the horses of Christ, if they were true leaders, of whom Heb. XIII. v. 17. but because they know well that they do not carry Christ, they do not wish to be his horses, and they themselves prefer to be riders, namely, not of the teachers of the Word as if they were mystical horses, but of their own asses, their brethren in ignorance, not of the Word of God, but of human traditions: nor does Christ need a successor, because he perseveres in his most holy office without a successor, Heb. VII. vers. 23. 24. or a vicar, because being everywhere present he performs his office, not absent, as earthly Kings might need vicars, because they cannot be present everywhere themselves.

II. THE OPENING OF THE SECOND SEAL.

Latin:

Vers. 2. Καὶ εἶδον καὶ ἰδὺ ἵππος λευκὸς] Sunt apud Zachariam equi rufi, nigri, albi, varii, c. VI. qui signifi- cant, ut diximus, Chaldæos, Persas, Alexandrum & Re- ges tum Syriæ, tum Ægypti ex Seleuco & Lago. Sed ibi equi juncti per quadrigas bellico more, hic κέλητες sive sin- gulares ad significandum iter properum cum potentia. Ita- que Psalm. XIV. v. 5. ubi in Hebræo est רכב, id est, equita, Græci ponunt βασίλευε. Et Ecclesiastæ X. 7. & Zach. 3. e- quus ponitur pro potentiæ signo. ἵππος ὃς ὕψος, καὶ ἀξίω- μα ὑγιὲς, Achmeti 233. Pro equis variis in hac prophetia veniet equus pallidus. Eques hic agminis ductor, Christus ipse est, qui jam non ut agnus, sed ut Rex conspicitur. Ma- nifestum id infra XIX. v. 11. 12. 13. unde sequitur, equum can- didum, cui insidet, esse Evangelium ipsius ob puritatem. Vi- de supra I. 14. Cæteri qui sequuntur equites Angeli sunt di- vinæ providentiæ administri.

Καὶ ὁ καθήμενος ἐπ᾽ αὐτὸν ἔχων τόξον] Arcus minatur, an- tequam feriat: Sic & Christus. Vide Psalm. VII. 13. XI. 2. LX. v. 4. in Græco: ubi per arcum minas intelligit Basilius. Omnia quæ nocent μεταφορικῶς vocantur tela. Sic apud Homerum: τίσειαν Δαναοὶ ἐμὰ δάκρυα σοῖσι βέλεσσι, id est, peste. Vide Deut. XXXII. 23. Abac. III. 8. Oseæ I. 5. Ps. XVIII. 15. XXVIII. 2. LXIV. 3. LXXVII. 18. CXX. 4. CXXVII. 5. CXLIV. 6. In Manuscripto quoque est ἐπ᾿ αὐτὸν, non ἐπ᾿ αὐτῷ.

Καὶ ἐδόθη αὐτῷ στέφανος] Coronatus est tanquam victor.

Καὶ ἐξῆλθε νικῶν καὶ ἵνα νικήσῃ] Hic prius καὶ est αἰτιολογι- κὸν. Ideo coronatus est, quia & vicerat, & vincer. Vice- rat multos Judæos vi verbi sui, Act 2. & deinceps, & vincet contumaces multis & variis telis suis. Tela Dei potissimum tria sunt, bellum, fames & pestilentia, Lev. XXVI. 17. & seqq. Deut. 28, vers. 52. & seqq. 1. Sam. 24, vers. 13. 2. Paral. 20, 9. Jer. 14, 12, 15, 2. 21, 7. 24, 10. 27, 8. 32, 36. 34, 17. 38, 2. 42, 17. 44, 13. Ezech. 5, 12. 17. 6, 11. 12. 7, 15. 12, 16. 14, 21. Dei providentiam Christus imitatur. Hæ sunt ἀρχαὶ ὠδίνων in Christi verbis Matth. 24, 8. Solet præcedere bellum: ex bello vastitas nasci & inde mala aut bina, aut terna in idem tempus congruunt.

Primum & sextum sigillum Ecclesiæ auspicata & felicia afferunt in spirituali adventu gratiæ, & novissimo corporali gloriæ Christi ad regnum, quod in his terris colligit, & ad gloriosum regnum con- cedendum electis in judicio novissimo, quousque animæ martyrum quiescere jubentur. Intermediis quatuor sigillis inclusa erant mala corporalia Ec- clesiæ & orbi imminentia, ut septimo sigillo mala spiritualia ab hæresibus & idolomania Anti-Christia- næ eidem inferenda, quæ patefiunt reseratione si- gillorum ab Agno facta. Ubi refutationem non meretur ab Andrea relata eorum interpretatio, qui septem sigillorum apertionem de Christi nati- vitate, baptismo, miraculis, accusatione, crucifixio- ne, sepultura, & descensu ad inferos; vel ut Ruperto visum, de nativitate, cruce, resurrectione, ascensio- ne Christi, missione Spiritus S. gentium vocatione & judicio universali exposuere; quum nec congruant illa, nec Johannes de præteritis, sed de futuris hic agat, ac prophetiam exponat sibi traditam; aut Am- brosii sententia, per septem sigilla significari ea, quæ septem mundi ætatibus sanctis contigerunt & contin- gent. Adhibentur autem ad ostendendos quatuor equos quatuor animalia, visis singulis conformi- ter, quæ temere Apostolorum denominatione defi- nit Grotius, non definita in ἀποκαλύψει. Petrus, etsi primus inter Apostolos ordine, non princeps dignitate. Hoc enim erant, dicente Cypriano, & ap- probante jure Canonico C. loquitur, Caus. 24. q. 1. æque & cæteri Apostoli, quod fuit & Petrus, pari con- fortio præditi & honoris & potestatis: Cur primo ani- mali, leoni nempe, conferatur, non apparet. Non enim adeo leoninæ fuit fortitudinis, quin præ aliis terreretur, & in passione Christi Dominum suum abnegans, & in conversatione cum Judæis in gra- tiam Pseudo Apostolorum Judaizans, Gal. II. Quis- quis autem fuerit, qui primo animali significatus est, leonina Evangelizantium virtus aporime facit ad primordialem Evangelii propagationem, quæ ab

Equite victore in equo primo candido primis ar- mis, & inde à visione Johannea promota est. Non autem per equum, sed per equitem Rex designatur Christus, qui insidet Verbi Doctoribus, utpote qui rectius per equos intelliguntur, quam Evange- lium ipsum, & ad velociter propagandumper cursum Evangelii Christo inserviunt. Unus est equus al- bus, sed in uno illo universitas omnium designata, qui albi & candidi esse debent candore & lucetum doctrinæ purioris, tum vitæ etiam sanctioris, nec nisi Christum portare per orbem, 1. Cor. II. 2. Hujus autem equitis cursus non definitur, nisi quod dica- tur, eundem & vicisse hactenus, & deinceps victu- rum, adeoq; merito coronam gerere. Non ergo tan- tum ut Rex, qui prius ut Agnus visus introducitur, sed etiam ut victor, semper augustus. Qui vicerat ut leo & in resurrectione & in gentium per Apostolos vo- catione, hostiumque Judæorum & Reip. ac templi, cultusque eorum deletione, quorundam etiam ad Evangelium conversione. Conf. Zach. IX. 10. c. X. 3. seqq. c. XIII. 8. 9. c. XIV. 8. seqq. Qui porro victu- rus erat semper usque ad consummationem seculi non in persecutione tantum violenta, tyrannorum gentilium, sed & fraudulenta hæreticorum, Aria- norum, & aliorum, ut & fraudulenter violenta & violenter fraudulenta Anti-Christi utriusque, Orien- talis, & Occidentalis. Qualem victorem cum arcu suo etsi peculiariter, & illustri ratione se se priorib. seculis inter ipsas atrocissimas suorum persecutio- nes exhibiturum hic innuatur; id tamen non ex- clusive intelligendum, sed ad cætera Ecclesiæ fata usque ad consummationem seculi, & victoriam suorum consummatam cap. VII. exhibitam omni- no est extendendum; quemadmodum & mala tum corporalia tum spiritualia sub septem sigillis comprehensa, etsi certæ ratione suo se consecutura sint ordine, se tamen porrigent usque ad mundi finem, hostiumque Ecclesiæ finale supplicium, fi- delium vero consummatum præmium. Neq; vero astipulari possumus vel illis, qui cum Petro Aureolo & Viega per insidentem equo albo Cajum Cali- gulam, qui nulla in re Ecclesiam divexarit, vel Magistratus coronâ suâ ad opprimendos confessores abutentes cum Luthero, Osiandro, Hoë & Danhaw. Anti-Christ. pag. 308. ut & Döling. Dürfeld, intelli- gunt, qui equo albo vehantur, quia in pace Reip. persequuntur pios, vincunt autem mundi judicio: vel cum D. Gravio, Romanum imperium seu ipsos Imperatores Ethnicos intelligente, qui Christianos ultra 300. annos oppugnarunt & vicerunt. Quam- vis enim Christiani spiritualiter persecutores vice- runt per sanguinem Agni & Verbum testimonii, A- poc. XII. v. 11. tamen externam, corporalem & coram mundo plausibilem victoriam persecutores Romani obtinuerunt, usque ad Constantinum M. Albedo, inquit, hujus equi summam Imperatorum Majesta- tem indigitat, quæ in C. Julio Cæsare initium ha- buit & ad reliquos omnes ejus successores est deri- vata, ita ut in suis triumphis & inaugurationibus candidis usi sint equis & vestimentis triumphalibus. Fuit quoque albedo equorum & vestium signum justi- tiæ. Imperatores enim Romani sub prætextu justi- tiæ Christianam religionem, tanquam pestem Im- perii eradicare voluerunt, Christianos tanquam ma- leficos, indignos esse, quin vitæ usurâ fruerentur, ju- dicantes. Per arcum hujus equitis summa persecu- tionum per omnes provincias imperii contra Christi- anos susceptarum celeritas denotatur. Per coro- nam equiti huic concessam tum Regia autoritas, tum triumphi, quos sibi persecutores de Christianis ar- rogarunt, intelliguntur. Diocletianus & Maximi- nianus ad tantam processerunt impietatem, ut sta- tuas sibi de Christo victo & eradicato triumphales erexerint, eo quod secta illius pernitiosa Imperio Ro- mano fuerit. Et hoc exprimit Johannes, quando v. 2. addit: Et data est ei corona, & exivit vin- cens & ut vinceret. Hæc B. Doct. Gravius. Jo- bannes Foxus per hos quatuor equos quatuor Monarchias, Irenæus libr. IV. cap. 38. Ticonius, Primasius, Beda, Glossa, Albertus M. Haymo, Tho- mas, Flacius, Chytræus, Cramerus, Vinariens. Hoff- mannus, & è Reformatis Bullinger, Aretius, Pi- scator, Szegedin, Napeir, Pareus, Forbesius, ut & Riccardus, Joseph Medus, Diestius Parei Epito- mater, Colladon, Coccejus, Crugotius, è Pontificiis Ribera, Cornelius à Lapide, denique Cotterius, Christum per equum primum Evangeli- um per orbem ministerio Apostolorum adhi- bito propagantem significari censent: Nec ab- nuit Hugo noster. Neque dubium est, quin omnia rectius Christo conveniant, qui per Evangelistas pacis velut candido equo vehitur per orbem, Esa. LII. v. 2. quod imprimis factum tempore Aposto- lorum, & paulo post, quoadusque Ecclesia virgo mansit, & victor triumphat, ut victores Romani equo albo ingrediebantur. Per arcum efficacia Verbi designatur, Psal. XLV. v. 6. Ebr. IV. v. 12. Corona signum dominii est & victoriæ. Exiit, ut qui jam vicerat, ac porro victurus erat, ceu for- tis omnem sapientiam ac potentiam mundi, ac Principis ejusdem, Satanæ potenter prosternens, eumque sub pedes fidelium conterens, Roman. XVI. v. 20. idololatriam maxime gentilium vin- cens, ut populi & Reges coram ipso procidant, Psal. XLV. v. 6. utpote ad ipsum conversi Psalm. XXII. v. 28. 29. 30. Psalm. LXXII. vers. 10. 11. Esa. XLIX. 23. cap. LX. v. 1. & seqq. Equos mystice dici, qui cum valido impetu excelsoque animo a- liquid aggrediuntur, & perficere properant, Eliæ & Elisæi exemplo constat, qui equites Israëli dicti, 2. Reg. II. v. 12. cap. XIII. v. 14. qua de causa etiam Angelis id nomen tributum, Zach. I. v. 8. 2. Reg. II. v. 11. cap. VI. v. 17. Et solatii causa præmittitur læta imago, ac tubicinia trium hæresium, & Anti- christi seductiones, ac Væ triplex intimatura visio lætior antecedit Filii Dei, cum thuribulo aureo pro Ecclesia intercedentis. Adde quod ea ratio- ne sese exhibuit iterum novissime Christus, Apoc. XIX. v. 11. Ecce equus albus, & qui sedebat super eum, vocabatur fidelis, & verax, & in justitia judi- cat & pugnat. Unde recte Primasius: Iste equus, inquit, potest in Apostolis & prædicatoribus verita- tis Ecclesiæ intelligi super morem gratia dealbatæ, cujus sessor est Christus. Propter quod & sagittam tenere dicitur, quæ prædicationi Verbi Dei aptissime comparatur; quæ hominum interiora transfixa possint fidei fructum afferre. Paria habet Tertullia- nus lib. advers. Jud. cap. IX. Victorinus, Ticonius, Augustinus, Andreas, Arethas ex parte, Anshel- mus, item Haymo, Lyra, B. Gerhardus, B. Clu- verus, B. Winckelmannus; Proponitur, inquit, vi- ctoria Christi in diffusione Evangelii per universum mundum usque ad finem mundi, licet resistant Dia- boli & omnes potentes tyranni. Nam Christus per ministerium Apostolorum & Apostolicorum viro- rum, qui per equum designantur, propagat Evan- gelium suum, ac proinde tanquam sessor equum su- um ad nutum inflectit, & dirigit quin & pungit non- nunquam calcaribus, id est, affligi illos permittit, & tamen virtute sua perrumpit. Habebat arcum. Ita Messias Esa. XLIX introducitur, dicens: Po- suit Dominus os meum, tanquam gladium in um- bra manus suæ abscondit me, & posuit me in sagit- tam tensam. Et sane apposite prædicatio, cum Do- minus addit robur, cum sagitta concitatissime vo- lante confertur, quia brevi tempore mundum re- plevit, quemadmodum Esa. XI. dicitur. Terra re- pleta est cognitione Jehove (data est ei corona.) Hec victoriam Christi condecorat. Et sane quem- admodum equus ad ductum & nutum sessoris sui jam hac, jam illac incedit; ita etiam Apostoli & Apostolici viri directionem Spiritus Sancti se- quuti, jam hanc jam illam regionem ingressi sunt. Quemadmodum equus calcaribus stimulatus for- tius progreditur: Ita & Apostoli virique Aposto- lici, licet ob Christi nomen multa perpeti coacti fuerint; nihilominus tamen strenue in peragendo officio perrexerunt. Andreas Cæsariens. Aposto- lis & prædicatoribus coronam, & arcum tribuit, cæreri Christo. Sed particeps est equus gloriæ equitis sui, quem portat, & Christus per equos suos pugnat, vincit, coronatur, triumphat, 2. Co- rinth. II. v. 14. Rom. XV. v. 17. 18. Apoc. XII. v. 11. cap. XIV. v. 14. Albertus M. Christus, inquit, Ec- clesiæ præsidens contra impios gerit sacræ doctrinæ armaturam. Equus albus est prædicatorum pri- morum cœtus, qui dicuntur equus propter for- titudinem, audaciam, & hinnitum prædicationis; item propter currendi velocitatem & patientiam. Albus propter gratiam baptismalem, qua sunt ab- luti, & majorem claritatem cognitionis. Exivit autem de angustia Judæa vincens paucos de Judæ- is convertendo ad fidem, ut vinceret plures de gentibus. Similiter applicat hæc B. Cluverus pecu- liariter ad priora tempora, siquidem usque ad Con- stantinum M. toto ferme 250. annorum spatio perillustris fuerit equitis hujus cum hostibus con- flictus, & victoria, quum non tantum longe, la- teque imperium suum promovit, sed ipsum etiam Imperatorem Romanum suos adorare fasces suo- que jurare sceptro & coronæ compulerit; & effe- ctus primi sigilli extremo Domitiani principatu, quo demandatam adversus Ecclesias persecutio- nem contrariis edictis sustulit, nec non imperan- te Nerva initia jam emicuerint satis splendida; de quo Tertullianus in Apologet: Tentavit ali- quando & Domitianus simile aliquid, portio Nero- nis in crudelitate; sed quasi homo cito destitit, ita ut etiam eos, quos in exilium miserat, revocaret. Quod etiam de Nerva successore constat, utpote qui exules omnes Senatusconsulto revocari, & facultates recipere jussit. Unde etiam S. Johan- nes rediit in Ephesum è Patmo, & vicinas pera- grans provincias, Ecclesias plantavit, aut plantatas irrigavit & propagavit; ut apud Irenæum, Clemen- tem Alexandrin. & Eusebium legere est. De quo Dio in Nerva: Eos, inquit, qui rei facti erant im- pietatis, absolvit, exulesque restituit. Neminem quoque impietatis aut ritus Judaici accusari per- misit. De complemento etiam visionis hujus si- gilli Tertullianis testis est luculentus, qui istis temporibus floruit, lib. advers. Judæos, cap. VII. n. 96. Sic dicit Dominus Deus Christo meo Domi- no, cujus tenui dextram, ut exaudiant illum gentes: fortitudines Regum disrumpam, aperiam ante il- lum portas, & civitates non claudentur illi: Quod ipsum adimpletum videmus. Cui enim dextram tenet Pater Deus, nisi Christo, Filio suo? Quem exaudierunt omnes gentes, id est, cui crediderunt omnes gentes, cujus & prædicatores Apostoli in Psal- mis David ostenduntur: In universa, inquit, terra exivit sonus illorum, & usque ad terminos terræ verba eorum. In quem enim alium universæ gentes crediderunt, nisi in Christum, qui jam venit? Cui enim & aliæ gentes crediderunt, Parthi, Medi, Elamitæ, & qui inhabitant Mesopotamiam, Ar- meniam, Phrygiam, Cappadociam & incolentes Pontum, & Asiam & Pamphyliam, immorantes Ægyptum & regionem Africæ, quæ est trans Cyre- nem, inhabitantes, Romani & incolæ, tunc & in Hierusalem & cæteræ gentes, ut jam Getulorum va- rietates, & Maurorum multi fines, Hispaniarum omnes termini, & Galliarum diversæ nationes, & Britannorum inaccessa Romanis loca. Christo ve- ro subdita & Sarmatarum & Dacorum & Germa- norum & Scytharum & abditarum multarum gen- tium & provinciarum & insularum multarum nobis ignotarum, & quæ enumerare minus possu- mus? In quibus omnibus locis Christi nomen, qui jam venit, regnat, utpote ante quem omnium civi- tatum portæ sunt apertæ, & cui nullæ sunt clausæ, ante quem seræ ferreæ sunt comminutæ, & valvæ æreæ sunt apertæ; quanquam & ista spiritualiter sint intelligenda, quo præcordia singulorum variis mo- dis à Diabolo obsessa fide Christi sint reserata, atta- men perspicue sunt adimpleta, utpote in quibus omnibus locis populus nominis Christi inhabitet. Quis enim omnibus regnare potuisset, nisi Christus Dei Filius?

De victoria multorum Judæorum post tempo- ra Johannea vel inde ab hac visione multa qui- dem jactitat Grotius, sed nulla affert documen- ta vel antiquitatis testimonia, è qua contrarium facilius probaverit. Et explicari hic ea, quæ Matth. XXIV. de Judæa & excidio Hierosoly- mitano prædixit Christus, precaria est Grotii hypothesis, cui chronologia aperte refragatur. Nam visa hæc longe contigere post excidium illud: Qui ergo de rebus jam pridem peractis vaticinaretur Spiritus Sanctus? Nugæ illæ sunt gerris ficulis vaniores: quales in suo Alcazare jam profligavit Cornelius, qui ei aliisque oppo- nit, quod hæc visio tantum futura in Ecclesia complectatur. Nec immerito de Grotiana ex- positione dicere possumus, quod Cornelius de socienni sua glossa ad cap. V. 1. pag. 105. Tota hæc expositio videtur potius ingeniosa accommoda- tio, quam genuina explicatio, quomodo Proba Fal- conia Æneidem Virgilii accommodavit & adapta- vit Christo, Christique gestis: atque de eisdem ex Homero suos Homerocentones composuit Eudocia, uxor Theodosii junioris Imperatoris. Accedit au- tem nostræ sententiæ Cornelius: Dico, inquit, hoc sinibolo albi equi & equitis significari bellico- sissimum & victoriosissimum primitivæ Ecclesiæ sta- tum. Nam equus primo symbolum est belli. Se- cundo symbolum est imperii. Tertio symbolum est victoriæ. Dico ergo primo equus albus sunt Apo- stoli, aliique præcones Evangelii, ut S. Ignatius, Poly- carpus, Dionysius, &c. per quos Christus orbem de- bellavit, sibique subjecit: Ita Aretas, Andreas, Hay- mo, Tyconius, Ribera, Pererius & alii passim, qui secuti S. Irenæum primum & priscum hujus ex- plicationis Autorem, in eo uno ore consentiunt & conspirant omnes. Secundo Sessor hujus equi est Christus. Tertio arcus est sacra Scriptura, vel Verbum Dei, de qua tot procedunt sagittæ, quot verba & sententiæ. Quarto equus hic est albus, ut significet lætum, & festivum fore hoc prælium, utpote finem habiturum certam victoriam. Unde & Christus corona insignitur, quia Rex est & vi- ctor, victor inquam non ut Dux castrorum apud homines, qui hostem dum subigit, occidit, sed qui cum subigendo ex hoste faciat amicum, ex impio pium, imo faciat eum militem suum, quo quasi nova sagitta utatur ad alios feriendos & subigen- dos. Christus enim ex hostibus à se prostratis & percussis conflat sibi novas sagittas, quibus- alios sui amore transfigat. Hoc enim facit hæc sa- gitta, puta charitas & amor Christi, ut ea per- cussi non sua solius salute sint contenti, sed omnium aliorum salutem sitiant, eamque ardenter procu- rent. Quocirca alios eadem sua sagitta, qua ipsi confixi sunt, sagittant & feriunt. Hinc ab Esaia vocatur hæc sagitta electa. Et Psaltes: Sagittæ, ait, potentis acutæ, Psal. CXIX. ubi S. Augustinus: Sagittæ, ait, potentis acutæ verba Dei sunt. Ecce jaciuntur & transfigunt corda, ut amor excitetur, non interitus comparetur. Sa- gittat cor amantis, ut adjuvet amantem, sagittat ut faciat amantem. Et, sagittæ tuæ acutæ (hinc populi sub te cadent) in corda inimicorum Regis, Psal. XLIX. vers. 6. Hujus victoriæ symbolum est equus albus. Consonat & Coccejus, nisi quod Sessorem significare Doctores & rectores velit: Victoria parta, inquit, significat Evangelii βεβαίωσιν, confirmationem inter Judæos velut conversos, vel ut convictos. Victoria paranda significat finem missi Evangelii ad gentes, ut totus mundus Christo sub- jiciatur. Conf. 2. Corinth. X. v. 4. 5. 2. Tim. IV. v. 7. Pomponius Lætus de triumpho Diocletiani & Maximiani hæc habet: Post triumphantium currus ex auro & lapillis pretiosis, quem trahe- bant quatuor equi candore certantes cum nive. Quod vero Cornelius à Lapide morem præsulum Romanensium Novum Pontificem ad Latera- num Pontificatus possessionem accepturum ex hac visione nostra desumptum ait, dum equis al- bis ei adequitare solent, quia Pontifex vicarius & successor est Christi, perquam vanum est & futi- le. Non enim præsulum ita equitatus, sed præ- sules equos Christi esse innueretur, si veri essent ἡγέμενοι, de quibus Ebr. XIII. v. 17. sed quia pro- be norunt, se non gestare Christum, ejus equi esse nolunt, & equites ipsi malunt esse insidentes scil. non Verbi Doctoribus ceu equis mysticis, sed asinis suis ignorantiæ fratribus, non Verbo Dei, sed traditionibus humanis: neque Christus vel successore indiget, quia perseverat in suo san- ctissimo munere sine successore, Ebr. VII. vers. 23. 24. vel vicario, quia ubique præsens suo fun- gitur officio, non absens, uti Reges terreni vica- riis indigeat, quod ubique ipsi præsto esse ne- queant.

II. RESERATIO SECUNDI SIGILLI.

## 6:3
Vers. 3.

And when he had opened the second seal, I heard the second living creature saying, come] That second animal is, if I am not mistaken, Matthew, whose words are XXIV. vers. 7. For nation shall rise, and kingdom against kingdom, where we said that by kingdom a province is understood, and we showed it from Isaiah, who calls the Nomes of Egypt thus XIX. 2.

Too rashly is Matthew defined here again, nor is the 24th chapter of Matthew compared without begging the question, which deals partly with the destruction of Jerusalem, partly with the consummation of the age. Neither fits the present prophecy. For that had already been accomplished; this can only be referred to the sixth seal. The Caesarean [Eusebius] thinks that by this second animal, the calf, the sacrifices of the martyrs are figured, who offered themselves for the truth of religion, with whom agree Aretas, Anselm, the Ordinary Gloss, Thomas, Richard, Napier, Pareus, Crugotius, Diestius: Add also Ribera, and Cornelius à Lapide. Concerning wars and mutual slaughters [are] Ticonius, Bullinger, Aretius, Piscator, Junius, Forbes, Mede, B. Luther, Flacius, Chytræus, Winckelmann, Danhauer, Cluver, Gravi, Dëling, Dürfeld. Concerning the persecutions of Christians in particular, and also more generally concerning any wars whatsoever [are] B. Hoë, B. Gerhard, Vinariens. concerning wars stirred up by barbarians Hoffmann, concerning the last war of the Romans against the Jews Coccejus.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

Καὶ ὅτε ἤνοιξε τὴν δευτέραν σφραγῖδα ἤκουσα τοῦ δευτέρου ζώου λέγοντος, ἔρχου] Secundum istud animal est, nisi fallor, Matthæus, cujus sunt verba XXIV. vers. 7. Ἐγερθήσεται γὰρ ἔθνος, καὶ βασιλεία ἐπὶ βασιλείαν, ubi per βασιλείαν pro- vinciam intelligi diximus, & ostendimus ex Esaia, qui No- mos Ægypti sic vocat XIX. 2.

Nimis temere hic iterum definitur Matthæus, nec sine petitione principii Matth. XXIV. cap. confertur, quod de excidio Hierosolymæ partim, partim de consummatione seculi agit. Neutrum convenit præsenti vaticinio. Nam illud jam peractum erat; hoc non nisi ad sextum sigillum referri potest. Cæsariensis hoc secundo anima- li vitulo censet martyrum sacrificia, qui pro veritate religionis seipsos obtulerunt, figura- ri, quocum faciunt Aretas, Anshelmus, Glos- sa ordin. Thomas, Riccardus, Naperius, Paræus, Crugotius, Diestius: Adde & Riberam, & Cor- nelium à Lapide. De bellis & mutuis cædibus Ticonius, Bullinger, Aretius, Piscator, Ju- nius, Forbesius, Medus, B. Lutherus, Flacius, Chytræus, Winckelmannus, Danhauer, Cluver. Gravi, Dëling, Dürfeld. De persecutionibus Christianorum in specie, necnon generalius de quibusvis bellis B. Hoë, B. Gerhardus, Vi- nariens. de bellis à barbaris excitatis Hoffmannus, de ultimo Romanorum bello contra Judæos Coccejus.

## 6:4
Vers. 4.

And there went out another horse red] The red horse signifies not obscurely the shedding of blood. That appears in 1. Kings III. 22. where in the Greek there is red waters, that is, bloody waters.

And to him that sat upon it) To the Angel. In the Manuscript it is in him that sat, by him.

Ἐδόθη αὐτῷ] Here αὐτῷ is redundant in the Hebrew manner. But in the manuscript, αὐτῷ is missing.

Λαβεῖν τὴν εἰρήνην ἐκ τῆς γῆς] He takes peace from the land of Judea, and the places in which the Jews were. In the manuscript, ἐκ is absent, without prejudice to the sense. He speaks here, however, of the wars of the Jews with their neighbors or those inhabiting the same towns, such as that of the Jews living in Beroea against the Philadelphians; concerning which Josephus [writes in] XX. 1, which preceded the famine of which we shall treat shortly.

Ἴνα ἀλλήλυς σφάξωσι] The neighbors [slaughter] the Jews, the Jews the neighbors, and indeed even Jews [slaughter] Jews.

Καὶ ἐδόθη αὐτῷ μάχαιρα μεγάλη] חרב, which the Greeks translate sometimes as μάχαιραν, sometimes as ῥομφαίαν, signifies in the Prophets warlike slaughter, as in Jerem. XVI. 4, Ez. XIV. 21, and in many other places.

That the discourse is about wars is beyond doubt. But to take peace from the earth is general, not specifically concerning the land of Judea, to which it is rashly restricted. Nor is peace said to be taken away only from the Jews, or the places in which the Jews were, who, as far as converts or Christians are concerned, were dispersed throughout the world. Few things will be brought forward, at any rate, concerning wars brought upon converted Jews, and indeed after the destruction of the city. Such things are therefore invented without cause. Although indeed Ambrose, Aretas, Montanus, Pareus, and others make not only this, but also the following two horsemen [represent] Christ; yet others—Ticonius, Primasius, Beda, Haymo, Lyranus, Thomas, Joachimus, Aureolus, Pannonius, Ribera, Viega, Pererius—more correctly [make them represent] the Devil, who is a murderer from the beginning, John ch. VIII, verse 44. Cornelius here refutes his Alcazar, who makes the rider of the red horse the boldness of the first Christians in proclaiming their faith, who took worldly peace from the earth and substituted the true peace of God (such as the Evangelical is), Matth. X, verse 34. He himself, however, chooses the opinion that the red horse signifies the Gentiles, with whom Christ is to fight, so that the state of the martyrs succeeding the Apostolic [age] is here hinted at, and the ten bloody persecutions of the Christians are signified, which were from Nero up to Constantine the Great for 250 years; and thus the rider is Trajan, Antoninus, Severus, Decius, Valerianus, Aurelianus, Julianus, Maximinus, Diocletianus, and Maximinianus, Roman Emperors. Nor do those disagree who, with Haymo, understand it of the angels who stirred up wars in the world on account of the contempt of the Gospel, or of the body of the Devil, that is, the multitude of the reprobate, whose rider is the Devil. Thus also Augustine explains the red horse as the wicked people, and its rider as the Devil. Primasius: Just as he promises joy concerning the good for the victory of the Church, so he foretells caution concerning the evil from the foreknowledge of future things. For this red horse, as if bloody with the blood of others, not his own, is predicted to fight against the victorious Church, when it is implied that he takes peace from the earth, which is also taught by the bow and by the sword. Which (the sword of the Roman Empire) Fromondus understands; others more correctly interpret it as the sword of the bloody persecution of the Christians. For Diocletianus triumphed over the Goths, Bastarnae, Carpi, Sarmatians, Quadi, Egyptians, and Persians; Maximinianus, however, over the Franks, Alemanni, Britons, and Mauritanians. But since those two Caesars were victorious in all wars, they thought that happiness on account of the persecution of the Christians was being repaid to them by the gods; whence they raged more cruelly day by day; and from this it happened that Diocletian in the East and Maximian in the West slaughtered an innumerable multitude of Christians with various tortures, and determined to extinguish Christianity in the whole world. Which happened quite otherwise. For just as GOD in the first state of the Church wished faith to grow by the sowing of the Word; so in the second He wished it to be irrigated by the blood of the martyrs and to germinate more abundantly. For by the example of such great fortitude, and the light of miracles, which shone everywhere in the martyrdoms and the martyrs, countless numbers were converted to the faith. The blessed Gravius also understands the slaughters and shedding of blood, but he places the completion of that matter in the year 180, from the persecutors of the Church themselves and their mutual conflicts with one another, from which time the Emperors and provincial governors and military leaders harassed themselves so greatly with mutual wars and seditions for the sake of imperial dignity that the strength of the empire was weakened, and by the incursion of barbarian nations the peoples and provinces, and among them the Christians too, were miserably afflicted, and the golden peace clearly vanished. But the blessed Cluverus wishes to be taught by these things: 1. that it does not happen in the world without the foreknowledge and permission of GOD that, while Christ is intent on propagating His kingdom everywhere through His satellites, Satan perpetually opposes Himself and stirs up wars and dissensions everywhere in the world. Indeed, sometimes he destroys no small number of mortals with mutual slaughters and rages with a great sword against the inhabitants of the earth. 2. The first operation of this horseman showed itself quite quickly and maturely under the empire of Ulpius Trajan, who succeeded Nerva in the Principate. See Pliny, book X, ep. 97; Freculphus, Vol. II, Chron. book 2, chap. 10. 3. Just as the victory of Christ among the nations shone more evidently up to Constantine: so after his death we perceive that hatreds, dissensions, distractions, seditions, and wars flourished as much as possible in the human race up to the times of Charlemagne. For after Satan felt himself cast down and driven from the dignity and his divine eminence, which he had most unjustly possessed until the age of Constantine, he conceived powerful angers against the inhabitants of the earth and sea, and did not cease to wear them down with continuous fights and calamities among themselves, until, with the imperial diadem transferred to Charles, a certain greater serenity of peace and rest from barbarian incursions seemed to shine forth: with another kingdom meanwhile established, I mean the Pontifical, by whose fraudulence the same Dragon could subsequently impose upon the human race and foist various superstitions and deceptions upon the nations in place of the true worship of Christ. Others explain the persecutions of the Christians as those instituted by the pagan Emperors, and that most conveniently. The blessed Hoeus says that under Trajan the red horse raged incredibly against the Christians and the principal lights of the Church, both through Asia and Africa and through all of Europe, for fourteen years; see Cent. III, Magdeb. c. 2, book 12, seqq. Under Severus so much blood was shed that it flowed into the rivers: which, however, perhaps does not apply here. For this was not done on account of the profession of the name of Christ. You would more correctly refer here to the fact that under Aelius Hadrian, Alexander, Bishop of Rome, was burned in a burning furnace with 1250 others, and that ten thousand Christians are read in Henry of Erfurt to have been crucified on Mount Ararat for the sake of the faith of Christ, and that under Decius peace was so taken away that, as Nicephorus testifies in book V, chap. 29, it is not as easy to recount all the men who were killed in that persecution as it is to count the sand of the sea.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

Καὶ ἐξῆλθεν ἄλλος ἵππος πυῥῥὸς] Equus is rufus אדורב non obscure sanguinis effusionem significat. Apparet id 1. Reg. III. 22. ubi in Græco est ὕδατα πυῥῥὰ, id est, cruentæ aquæ.

Καὶ τῷ καθημένῳ ἐπ’ αὐτὸν) Angelo. In Manuscripto est ἐν τῷ καθημένῳ, per eum.

Ἐδόθη αὐτῷ] Hic αὐτῷ abundat more Ebræo. Sed in Manuscripto deest αὐτῷ.

Λαβεῖν τὴν εἰρήνην ἐκ τῆς γῆς] Aufert pacem è terra Judæa, & locis, in quibus erant Judæi. In Manuscripto abest ἐκ salvo sensu. Loquitur autem hic de bellis Judæorum cum vicinis aut eadem oppida habitantibus, quale fuit Judæo- rum in Berœa habitantium contra Philadelphenos; de quo Josephus XX. 1. quod antecessit annonæ caritatem, de qua mox agetur.

Ἴνα ἀλλήλυς σφάξωσι] Judæos vicini, vicinos Judæi, imo & Judæi Judæos.

Καὶ ἐδόθη αὐτῷ μάχαιρα μεγάλη] חרב quod modo μά- χαιραν, modo ῥομφαίαν vertunt Græci, apud Prophetas si- gnificat occidionem bellicam, ut Jerem. XVI. 4. Ez. XIV. 21. & multis aliis locis.

De bellis sermonem esse dubio vacat. Sed au- ferre pacem è terra generale est, non speciatim terram Judæam concernens, ad quam temere id restringitur. Neq; tantum à Judæis pax auferenda dicitur, aut locis, in quibus Judæi erant, qui quod ad conversos, vel Christianos attinet, passim per orbem dispersi erant. Pauca afferentur utiq; de bellis Judæis conversis illatis, & quidem post exci- dium urbis. Gratis itaque talia finguntur. Quan- quam vero Ambrosius, Aretas, Montanus, Pareus, alii non solum hunc, sed etiam sequentes duos equites Christum faciant; rectius tamen alii, Ti- conius, Primasius, Beda, Haymo, Lyranus, Thomas, Joachimus, Aureolus, Pannonius, Ribera, Vie- ga, Pererius Diabolum, qui homicida est ab ini- tio Johan. cap. VIII. vers. 44. Cornelius refellit hic Alcazarem suum, sessorem equi rufi facien- tem audaciam primorum Christianorum in sua fi- de promulganda, qui pacem mundanam de ter- ra sustulerunt, & veram Dei pacem (qualis est Evangelica) substituerunt, Matth. X. vers. 34. Ipse vero eam eligit sententiam, quod equus ru- fus significet gentiles, cum quibus pugnaturus sit Christus, ut hic Martyrum status Apostolico succedens innuatur, ac decem persecutiones cru- entæ Christianorum significentur, quæ à Nerone usque ad Constantinum M. per 250. annos fuere; adeoque fessor sit Trajanus, Antoninus Severus, Decius, Valerianus, Aurelianus, Julianus, Ma- ximinus, Diocletianus & Maximinianus Rom. Imperatores. Nec disconveniunt, qui de An- gelis, qui in mundo excitarunt bella propter Ev- angelii contemptum, vel de corpore Diaboli seu multitudine reproborum, quorum fessor est Dia- bolus, cum Haymone intelligunt. Sic & Augu- stinus equum rufum exponit malum populum, & sessorem ejus Diabolum. Primasius: Sicut de bono lætitiam pro Ecclesiæ victoria pollicetur: Sic de malo cautelam prænuntiat ex præscientia futu- rorum. Nam iste equus rufus velut cruentus san- guine alieno non suo, contrarius victrici Eccle- siæ prædicitur repugnare, quando pacem de terra insinuatur auferre, quod & arcu docetur, & gladio. Quem (gladium de imperio Romano) Fromon- dus intelligit, rectius alii de gladio truculentæ Christianorum persequutionis interpretantur. Nam Diocletianus de Gothis, Bastarnis, Carpis, Sarmatis, Quadis, Ægyptiis, Persis; Maximinianus vero de Francis, Alemannis, Britannis & Mauri- tanis triumphavit. Cum vero duo isti Cæsares omni- bus bellis victores essent; felicitatem istam propter persecutionem Christianorum à Diis sibi rependi existimabant; unde crudelius indies sæviebant; & hinc factum est, ut Diocletianus in Oriente, Maxi- mianus in Occidente innumerabilem Christiano- rum multitudinem variis suppliciis trucidarint, statuerintque Christianismum toto orbe extinguere. Quod secus omnino accidit. Nam sicut DEUS in primo Ecclesiæ statu, seminatione Verbi fidem vo- luit crescere; Ita in secundo Martyrum sanguine vo- luit irrigari & uberius germinare. Nam exem- plo tantæ fortitudinis, & luce miraculorum, quæ undique in martyriis & martyribus coruscabant, innumeri ad fidem convertebantur. Cædes & sanguinis profusiones intelligit quoque B. Gra- vius, sed è persecutorum ipsorummet Ecclesiæ mutuis inter se digladiationibus, collocans ejus rei complementum in annum 180. a quo Impera- tores & provinciarum præsides, bellique duces ob dignitatem Imperatoriam sese mutuis bellis & se- ditionibus tantopere divexarunt, ut imperii vires lalefactarentur, & irruptione barbararum genti- um populi ac provinciæ & in his Christiani quo- que misere affligerentur, & aurea pax plane eva- nesceret. Sed B. Cluverus his doceri vult, 1. non sine præscientia & permissione DEI evenire in mundo, quod, dum Christus regno suo passim per satellites suos propagando incumbit, perpetuo sese opponit Satanas, bellaque & dissidia ubivis ter- rarum excitat. Imo nonnunquam non ingentem mortalium numerum mutuis lanienis perdit, gladio- que magno grassatur in terræ incolas. 2. Primam hujus equitis operationem sat cito matureque se ex- eruisse sub imperio Ulpii Trajani, qui Nervæ suc- cessit in Principatu. Vid. Plin. lib. X. ep. 97. Frecul- phus Tom. II. Chron. l. 2. cap. 10. 3. Sicut victoria Christi inter gentes usque ad Constantinum eviden- tius enituit: Sic post ejus decessum odia, dissensio- nes, distractiones, seditiones, bellaque in genere humano quam maxime viguisse usque ad Caroli Magni tempora deprehendimus. Postquam enim dejectum se exturbatumque dignitate & divina sua eminentia sensit Satanas, quam ad Constantini usque ætatem possederat injustissime, validas con- cepit iras adversus terræ marisque habitatores, eosque continuis inter se pugnis & calamitatibus atterere non destitit, donec translato in Carolum diademate imperiali paulatim pacis quædam major serenitas atque à barbaricis incursionibus quies e- micare visa est: Constituto interim alio regno, Pontificio inquam, cujus fraudulentia deinceps i- dem Draco humano generi imponere, ac gentibus pro vero Christi cultu varias obtrudere superstitio- nes ac deceptiones posset. De persequutionibus Christianorum alii explicant ab Imperatoribus paganis institutis, idque commodissime. B. Höëus sub Trajano, inquit, equus rufus incredibiliter in Christianos & præcipua Ecclesiæ lumina tum per Asiam, & Africam, tum per universam Eu- ropam per annos quatuordecim sæviit; vid. Cent. III. Magdeb. c. 2. l. 12. seqq. sub Severo tantum san- guinis fusum est, ut in fluvios flueret: quod ta- men forte huc non facit. Non enim ob nominis Christi professionem hoc factum. Rectius huc referas, quod sub Ælio Hadriano Alex. Rom. Episcopus cum aliis 1250. in furno ardenti crema- tus, quodque decem millia Christianorum in mon- te Ararat, propter Christi fidem apud Henricum Erfordensem crucifixa leguntur, & quod sub De- cio pax ita sublata, ut Nicephoro lib. V. cap. 29. teste, tam non sit facile, omnes homines recense- re, qui in persecutione ista interfecti sunt, quam arenam maris numerare.

## 6:5
Verse 5.

Kaì ὅτε ἤνοιξε τὴν σφραγῖδα τὴν τρίτην, ἤκυσα τῦ τρίτυ ζώε λέγοντος, ἔρχυ] I think this is Paul, to whom Agabus predicted this scarcity of grain, Acts 11, verse 28. There were many evils of that kind. Ἔσονται λιμοὶ, Matthew 24, verse 7; Luke 21, verse 11; but most notable is that predicted by Agabus, where οἰκυμένη is Judea. That scarcity fell in the Principate of Claudius, as both the passage in Acts indicates and Josephus in Antiquities 20.2, where we read: Πολλῶν ὑπ’ ἐνδείας ἀναλωμάτων φθειρόμενον, and in the same book, chapter III, where he calls it μέγαν λιμὸν κατὰ τὴν Ἰυδαίαν. Καὶ ὁ καθήμενος ἐπ’ αὐτόν] The angel who had received that prefecture from Christ. ἔχων ζυγὸν ἐν τῇ χειρὶ αὑτῦ] For it is customary in a severe grain shortage for portions of bread to be weighed out to individuals either by magistrates or by heads of families.

It is again rashly defined that Paul was the third living creature: nor are these things less precariously restricted to Judea, which were spoken generally. Aureolus indeed refers it to the empire under Titus, who had surrounded and stormed Jerusalem: But those things had already preceded. Nor does the interpretation of those who understand heretics by the black horse, who holds a deceitful balance in his hand, fit: which is that of Augustine, Primasius, Andreas, Bede, Anselm, Strabus, Albert, Thomas the Englishman, Joachim, and Gagneius, and especially concerns the Arians, who wonderfully devastated the Church for three hundred and more years soon from the time of Constantine. Which opinion the blessed Cluverus defends especially speciously, refuting the proper sense concerning the scarcity of grain and bodily famine with these reasons: 1. because it cannot be explained what that preservation of wine and oil means. 2. That great angel, to whom it is said, do not harm, cannot be indicated. 3. In the following seal mention of famine is made. 4. The concern of all four living creatures should concern not so much a shortage of food as the mystical famine of the Word of God. 5. Among the general evils by which the world is pressed, some place must also be given to deceptions and heresies. To which, therefore, Hoffmann from our side is added. Thus also they explain concerning the spiritual famine, which is in Amos 8, on account of the corruptions of heretics, with Primasius and the Gloss. Ordin., Anselm and Thomas, as well as Pererius, Ribera, Cornelius à Lapide, as also Riccardus, Pareus, Crugotius, Diestius. But the arguments of the blessed Cluverus seem to us by no means sufficiently pregnant for us to abandon the literal sense and recur to allegory. For why could not 1. a famine be sent, and a lack of necessary food, while oil and wine, which serve more for luxuries, are left safe? 2. That that horseman is the Devil, to whom it is commanded, μὴ ἀδικήσῃς, there is no doubt. For from him all evils have arisen, the evil of fault, and, which that draws after it, the evil of punishment, to which famine pertains, Deut. chap. XXVIII. For false teachers are not understood with sufficient convenience by the horsemen who ride upon the black horse, and who is that black horse? Do they themselves hold a balance in their hand, that they might measure out wheat and barley, when they would prefer to measure not with a balance, but with a full granary? 3. In the following seal mention is also made of a sword. Must the sword in the second seal therefore be taken improperly? 4. The concern of the four living creatures is not detected here regarding the mystical famine of the Word of God, but regarding war, regarding famine, and regarding death with subsequent damnation. 5. Not only general evils are recounted here, but special ones, namely of war, of famine, and of death, which is predicted to the impious in place of punishment, to the fourth part of the earth, and that remaining part holds in its embrace, namely war and famine as also the beasts of the earth. Wherefore, since we do not see sufficiently effective reasons not to depart from the literal sense, we judge that one must adhere to the same and we understand Antoninus, Maximinus, Decius, and others, in the year of Christ 160, 235, 250, with B. Luther, Flacius, Osiander, Chytraeus, Winckelmann, Walther, Cramer, Gerhard, Danhauer, Döling, Dürfeld, Kromayer, Bullinger, likewise Aretius, Czegedin, Calladon, Brightman, Piscator, Junius, Napier, Forbes, as also Cotterius. By the black horse, says B. Gravius, is denoted famine and the scarcity of provisions, for the black color suits the famished, as is explained in Lam. IV. 7, 8. To the rider is attributed a balance, a fitting instrument for famine, especially when provisions are not so much measured as weighed, the scarcity of which, as regards wheat and barley, is specifically expressed as the material of necessary bread for food, verse 6, while oil and wine, which serve more for luxuries, are ordered to remain safe. The ancients called a choenix the daily food of a servant, that is, as much as was given to a servant for food in the space of one day, and it was sold for one denarius, that is, 4 asses, which price was considered too high among the ancients. The fulfillment of this punishment partly falls into the times of the Emperor Maximinus, under whom for some years there were no harvests, partly into the reign of M. Antoninus, partly into that of Decius, Euseb. bk. IX. ch. 8, where Eusebius reports that in the times of Maximinus there was such a scarcity of provisions that one measure of wheat was sold for two thousand and five hundred Attic drachmae. Add also the famine in the time of Gallienus. For although famine does not so much affect the Church specifically as it is a public calamity; which is also to be understood concerning wars and other evils designated here; yet they are figurative public evils, both because the Church and the faithful were also to be involved in them and therefore to be informed about them, and because the Gentiles transferred the blame for them onto the Christians, and from that arose more serious persecutions against them. And therefore, soon after those calamities, the voices of the martyrs are heard, countless numbers of whom had been dragged to punishments because of these public calamities. B. Gerhard: It is prefigured, he says, the scarcity of provisions and famine, because famine renders the faces of men lurid and black, Lam. IV. verse 8. He who sits on this horse has a ζυγὸν, a balance, in his hand, because in famine provisions are not sold by the bushel, but by the balance, as spices are wont to be sold, Levit. XXVI. verse 26, Ezech. IV. verse 10. And this opinion seems to be preferred before others. For first, the prophecy here is still concerned with bodily evils and afflictions. 2. The rest that follow do not concern spiritual things but bodily ones, slaughter and killing and famine, death or pestilence, the cruelty of the beasts of the earth, the martyrdoms of the saints, and the final judgment. 3. Spiritual afflictions of heresies follow under the seventh seal and the Angelic trumpets. 4. A recapitulation or rather a collection of all the plagues, which occurred under the IV. seal, commands us to understand the preceding things according to the letter, to which it adds the cruelty of wild beasts. 5. Christ on the white horse helps us here against those bodily evils, as one who has conquered the Devil with all his power. Therefore he is seen like a triumphant King. He also protects us against heresies, or evil Angels and Doctors, as that Angel of the covenant, and he procures efficacy for our prayers by his Priestly intercession, ch. VIII. 6. Thus everything flows more correctly and in the right order, nor does the συνέχεια suffer violence. For both those bodily evils last until the consummation of the age, and until then heresies with the Anti-Christ will last, both being cast into the abyss: furthermore, both follow one another according to the succession and series of times, as indicated by the opened seals and the sounding trumpets, as history testifies, and the fulfillment, the best interpreter of any prophecies. That famine brought forward by Grotius from Acts XI. 28 under Claudius had already passed, and therefore could not be predicted here. Joseph Mede understands the severe administration of justice through the Roman Empire, under Septimius and Alexander, from which they obtained their name. There remains the gloss of Alcazar, but it is again sufficiently inept, who makes the rider of this horse poverty through personification, and that voluntary, to which Cornelius says: These, he says, are mystical, not literal, and they suppose this horse just as the first to be Christ's, the contrary of which I have taught above from the common opinion of Interpreters.
