Vers. 5.

Kaì ὅτε ἤνοιξε τὴν σφραγῖδα τὴν τρίτην, ἤκυσα τῦ τρίτυ ζώε λέγοντος, ἔρχυ] Hunc puto esse Paulum, cui hanc anno- næ caritatem prædixit Agabus, Actor. XI. vers. 28. Fue- runt multa mala ejus generis. Ἔσονται λιμοὶ, Matth. 24, vers. 7. Luc. XXI. vers. 11. sed maxime insigne illud ab A- gabo prædictum, ubi οἰκυμένη est Judæa. Ea caritas inci- dit in Principatum Claudii, ut & locus Actorum indicat, & Josephus antiquæ historiæ XX. 2. ubi legimus: Πολλῶν ὑπ’ ἐνδείας ἀναλωμάτων φθειρόμενον, & eodem libro cap. III. ubi μέγαν λιμὸν κατὰ τὴν Ἰυδαίαν vocat. Καὶ ὁ καθήμενος ἐπ’ αὐτόν] Angelus, qui à Christo eam præfecturam acceperat. ἔχων ζυγὸν ἐν τῇ χειρὶ αὑτῦ] Solent enim in gravi annona partes panum singulis appendi aut à magistratibus, aut à pa- tribus familias.

Temere iterum definitur, Paulum fuisse ter- tium animal: nec minus precario hæc restringun- tur ad Judæam, quæ generaliter dicta sunt. Re- fert quidem Aureolus ad imperium sub Tito, qui Hierosolymam obsidione cinxerat & expu- gnarat: Sed ista jam præcesserant. Neque eo- rum convenit interpretatio, qui per equum ni- grum hæreticos intelligunt, qui stateram dolo- sam in manu sua habet: Quæ Augustini, Pri- masii, Andreæ, Bedæ, Anshelmi, Strabi, Al- berti, Thomæ Anglici, Joachimi, & Gagneji, est, & præcipue Arianos respicit, qui mire Ec- clesiam vastarunt per trecentos & amplius an- nos mox à Constantini tempore. Quam sen- tentiam imprimis speciose propugnat B. Clu- verus, hisce rationibus proprium sensum de annonæ caritate ac fame corporali refellens, 1. quia explicari non possit, quid sibi velit illa vini & olei præservatio. 2. Angelus ille ma- gnus, cui dicitur, ne læseris, indicari nequeat. 3. In sequenti sigillo famis mentio fiat. 4. O- mnium quatuor animalium solicitudo non tam eduliorum penuriam, quam mysticam Verbi Dei famem concernat. 5. Inter generalia quibus pre- mitur mundus mala, omnino etiam aliquis de- ceptionibus, & hæresibus locus dandus sit. Quibus proinde accedit è nostris Hoffmannus. Sic etiam de fame spirituali, qua de Am. VIII. ob corruptelas hæreticorum, explicant cum Primasio, & Gloss. Ordin. Anshelmus & Tho- mas, necnon Pererius, Ribera, Cornelius à Lapide, ut & Riccardus, Pareus, Crugotius, Diestius. Verum argumenta B. Cluveri nobis minime satis prægnantia videntur, ut literam de- seramus, & ad allegoriam recurramus. Nam quidni 1. fames immitti possit, & defectus ali- menti necessarii, oleo & vino, quæ delitiis ma- gis inserviunt, salvis relictis? 2. Eques ille quia Diabolus sit, cui præcipitur, μὴ ἀδικήσῃς, du- bium nullum est. Ab eo enim omnia mala or- ta sunt, malum culpæ, &, quod illud post se trahit, malum pœnæ, ad quod fames pertinet, Deuter. cap. XXVIII. Nam falsi Doctores per e- quites non satis commode intelliguntur, qui su- per equo nigro equitant, & quisnam ille niger equus est? Num ipsi stateram in manu habent, ut triticum atque hordeum admetiantur, quum non statera, sed pleno horreo admetiri mallent. 3. In sequenti sigillo etiam gladii mentio facta. Num ergo gladius in secundo sigillo ideo impro- prie accipiendus? 4. Animalium quatuor solicitu- do hic non deprehenditur circa mysticam Verbi Dei famem, sed circa bellum circa famem, & circa mortem cum subsequa damnatione. 5. Non gene- ralia hic tantum mala recensentur, sed specialia, nimirum belli, famis, & mortis, quæ pœnæ loco impiis prædicitur, ad quartam partem terræ, & illa reliqua in complexu suo habet, nempe bel- lum, & famem ut & bestias terræ. Quapropter quum non videamus sat efficaces rationes, ne à proprietate literæ discedamus, eidem inhæren- dum censemus & intelligimus famem corpora- lem sub Aurelio Antonino, Maximino, Decio, aliis, anno Christi 160. 235. 250. cum B. Luthe- ro, Flacio, Osiandro, Chytreo, Winckelmanno, Walthero, Cramero, Gerhardo, Danhauero, Dölingio, Dürfeld, Kromayero, Bullingero item, Aretiō, Czegedino, Calladon, Brigthmanno, pi- scatore, Junio, Napeiro, Forbesio, ut & Cotte- rio. Per equum nigrum, inquit B. Gravius, denotatur fames & annonæ caritas, niger enim co- lor famelicis congruit, ut exponitur Thren. IV. 7. 8. Sessori tribuitur statera aptum instrumentum fami, præsertim quando non tam mensuratur quam appenditur annona, cujus caritas quantum ad triticum & hordeum alimenti necessarii panis ma- teriam speciatim exprimitur, vers. 6. oleo & vi- no, quæ deliciis magis inserviunt, salvis manere jussis. Chœnicem vocabant veteres diurnum ci- bum servilem, hoc est, quantum servo unius diei spatio in cibum dabatur, & vendebatur denario uno, hoc est, IV. assibus, quod pretium apud ve- teres nimis magnum æstimabatur. Complementum hujus pœnæ partim incidit in tempora Maximini Imp. sub quo aliquot annis nullæ messes fuerunt, partim in M. Antonini, partim in Decii impe- rium, Euseb. l. IX. cap. 8. ubi refert Eusebius, quod Maximini tempora tanta fuerit annonæ caritas, ut una tritici mensura bis mille, & quingentis At- ticis venderetur. Adde & famem tempore Gal- lieni. Quamvis enim fames non tam Ecclesiam peculiariter afficiat, quam publica sit calamitas; quod & de bellis, aliisque malis hîc designatis intelligendum; figurata tamen sunt mala publi- ca, cum quod Ecclesia & fideles iisdem etiam in- volvendi ac proinde de illis informandi fuerant, tum quod gentiles culpam eorum in Christianos transtulerint, atque inde ortæ sint persecutiones graviores adversus eosdem. Ideoque mox post ca- lamitates illas audiuntur voces martyrum, quo- rum innumeri ob calamitates istas publicas ad supplicia abrepta fuerant. B. Gerhardus: Præfigu- ratur, inquit, caritas annonæ & fames, quia fa- mes reddit hominum facies luridas, atras, Thren. IV. vers. 8. Insidens huic equo habet ζυγὸν libram in manu, quia in fame annona non modiis vendi- tur, sed statera, quæ vendi solent aromata, Le- vit. XXVI. vers. 26. Ezech. IV. vers. 10. Atque hæc sententia præ aliis probanda videtur. Nam primo versatur hîc prophetia adhuc in malis & affli- ctionibus corporalibus. 2. Cætera quæ sequun- tur, non spiritualia concernunt sed corporalia, in- terfectionem & cædem & famem, mortem vel pestem, bestiarum terræ crudelitatem, martyria sanctorum, & judicium novissimum. 3. Spiri- tuales hæresium afflictiones sequuntur sub sigillo septimo & tubis Angelicis. 4. Recapitulatio vel potius collectio omnium plagarum, quæ sub IV. sigillo facta, jubet antecedentia secundum lite- ram intelligere, quibus illa addit ferarum sæviti- am. 5. Christus in equo albo nobis succurrit hîc adversus mala illa corporalia, utpote qui devicit Diabolum cum omni potestate. Ideo instar Re- gis triumphantis conspicitur. Idem adversus hæ- reses nos tuetur, vel Angelos & Doctores malos, ceu Angelus ille fœderis, & orationibus nostris Sacerdotali sua intercessione efficaciam conciliat cap. VIII. 6. Sic omnia rectius & justo ordine flu- unt, nec vim patitur συνέχεια. Nam & mala illa corporalia durant usque ad seculi consummatio- nem, & eo usque hæreses cum Anti-Christo tum conjiciendo in barathrum durabunt : adhæc u- traque juxta successum & seriem temporum, quemadmodum sigillis referatis & tubis clangen- tibus indicata sunt, sese excipiunt, teste histo- ria, & complemento, optimo interprete quo- rumvis vaticiniorum. Fames illa Grotio adducta ex Actor. XI. 28. sub Claudio jam transierat, ideo- que hic prædici non potuit. Joseph. Medus intel- ligit justitiæ per Imperium Romanum severam ad- ministrationem, sub Septimio & Alexandro, in- de nomen adeptis. Restat Alcasaris glossa, sed satis iterum inepta, qui sessorem hujus equi per Prosopopœiam paupertatem facit, eamque vo- luntariam, ad quæ Cornelius: Hæc, inquit, my- stica sunt, non literalia, atque supponunt hunc e- quum æque ac primum esse Christi, cujus contra- rium superius ex communi Interpretum sententia docui.

## 6:6
And I heard a voice in the midst of the four living creatures) Of Agabus to Paul.

That these things concerning the prediction of Agabus are irrelevant here, we have already warned from the Chronology. That Paul is one of those four living creatures, and indeed the third in order, is assumed precariously.

Saying, a choenix of wheat for a denarius, and three choenixes of barley for a denarius] This so singular circumstance signifies great providence. For not only is the scarcity of provisions, which is also famine to Cicero, indicated, but also what the price will be, both for wheat, which is σῖτος by excellence, and for barley. The eating of barley is less good. Therefore it was wont to be given to soldiers as a punishment, as we learn from Livy and Vegetius. The eating of wheat is most suitable for man. Now a choenix of wheat is as much as a healthy man needs for a day, as the learned have observed from the third and seventh books of Herodotus, others also from Hippocrates, Diogenes Laërtius, and Athenaeus. But a denarius is as much as a man working strenuously could earn in a day, as can be seen in Matt. ch. XX. v. 2. Now indeed, if a poor man who earned a denarius a day had a wife and children, he certainly could not feed them from the choenix. Indeed, even a bachelor was forced to live, or to eat less than nature required, or to lack a roof, clothes, and furniture, all of which had to be bought from that daily wage. Barley was cheaper, but less pleasing. Josephus, Jewish War V. 27, translates choenix as two sextarii. So also the Glossary. Another Glossary translates it as a semodius.

And do not harm the oil and the wine) It was said to the Angel, do not diminish anything either from the vintage or from the olive harvest. Let these retain their custom. Ἀδικεῖν by βλάπτειν is to harm, to diminish, as above II. 11. Injuries of the sky are accustomed to harm all crops. But then, with Christ dispensing, crops necessary for life were cut off, those not necessary were abundant. The use of oil for delights: instead of wine, water could be drunk.

Pliny set the price of fine flour in an average market at 40 asses for a modius of flour, that is, four denarii, Book XVIII of Natural History, chapter 4. Therefore, a choenix of flour, which is the eighth part of a modius, and the daily food of slaves, is to be set at five asses, or half a denarius. Whence it is clear that a price twice as high is indicated here than there was in an average market; and therefore that a famine is entirely signified, with individual choenices of wheat selling for individual denarii.

THE UNSEALING OF THE FOURTH SEAL.

Latin:

Καὶ ἤκουσα φωνὴν ἐν μέσῳ τῶν τεσσάρων ζώων) Agabi ad Paulum.

Hæc de Agabi prædictione hic ἀλλότρια esse, jam è Chronologia monuimus. Paulum unum es- se ex istis quatuor animalibus, & quidem tertium in ordine precario assumitur.

Λέγουσαν, χοῖνιξ σίτου δηναρίου, καὶ τρεῖς χοίνικες κριθῆς δη- ναρίου] Hæc tam singularis circumstantia magnam providen- tiam significat. Neque enim caritas tantum annonæ, quæ fames etiam Ciceroni, indicatur, sed & quod futurum sit pretium, tum tritico, qui σῖτος per excellentiam, tum hordeo. Hordei pastus minus bonus. Ideo militibus in pœ- nam dari solebat, ut ex Livio & Vegetio discimus. Tri- tici pastus maxime homini convenit. Est autem χοῖνιξ tri- tici tantum, quanto homo sanus in diem indiget, ut ex He- rodoti libro tertio & septimo observarunt eruditi, alii etiam ex Hippocrate, Diogene Laërtio, & Athenæo. Denari- us vero tantum, quantum quoque die mereri poterat homo, strenue laborans, ut videre est Matth. cap. XX. v. 2. Jam vero si homo pauper qui denarium merebat in diem, habe- ret uxorem & liberos, certe eos ἐκ τοῦ χοίνικος alere non poterat. Imo & cælebs vivere cogebatur, aut minus, quam natura exigebat, edere, aut carere tecto, vestibus, & su- pellectile, quæ omnia ex diurna illa mercede comparar de- bebant. Hordeum erat vilius, sed minus placebat. Jose- phus belli Judaici V. 27. χοίνικα bisilbre vertit Latinus. Sic & Glossarium. Aliud Glossarium vertit semodium.

Καὶ τὸ ἔλαιον, καὶ τὸν οἶνον μὴ ἀδικήσῃς) Dicebatur An- gelo, noli quicquam imminuere aut de vindemia, aut de olivitate. Retineant ista suum morem. Ἀδικεῖν per βλά- πτειν est lædere, imminuere, ut supra II. 11. Cœli injuriæ solent omnes fruges lædere. Tunc autem, Christo dispen- sante, intercidebant fruges ad vitam necessariæ, non ne- cessariæ affluebant. Olei usus ad delitias: pro vino aqua bibi potuit.

Plinius pretium similaginis annona media sta- tuit in modios farinæ asses 40. hoc est, quatuor denarios, libr.XVIII. histor. Natur. cap. 4. Chœ- nici ergo farinæ, quæ octava pars modii est, ac diurnus servorum cibus, quinque constituendi asses, aut semidenarius Unde patet duplo hic majus pretium indici, quam mediocri annona fuerit; ideoque omnino caritatem significari, singulis chœnicibus tritici singulis denariis vene- untibus.

SIGILLI QUARTI RESIGNATIO.

## 6:7
Vers. 7. And when he opened the fourth seal, I heard the voice of the fourth living creature, saying, come) I think this is James, called the brother of the Lord, who predicts diseases, James I. verses 20, 21, and indeed to the rich, to whom the scarcity of grain does less harm.

A truly excellent reason why James is to be understood, because he warned here about the sick, how they ought to conduct themselves. Others say that the eagle, seeking the heights most swiftly and remarkable for the sharpness of its sight, is introduced because there is the greatest need for these virtues against such a great heap of evils pressing in at once, 1 Cor. 7:29 ff., Rom. 8:18.

Latin:

Vers. 7. Καὶ ὅτε ἤνοιξε τὴν τετάρτην σφραγῖδα, ἤκουσα φωνὴν τοῦ τετάρτου ζώου, λέγοντος, ἔρχου) Hunc puto esse Jacobum fratrem dictum Domini, qui morbos prædicit, Jac. I. vers. 20. 21. & quidem divitibus, quibus caritas annonæ minus nocet.

Egregia vero ratio cur Jacobus intelligendus, quia hic de aegrotis, quales se gerere debeant, monuit. Alii aquilam excelsa celerrime petentem & perspicacia visus insignem introduci ajunt, quod his virtutibus adversus tantam malorum pariter ingruentium congeriem maxime opus sit, 1. Cor. VII. 29. seqq. Rom. VIII. 18.

## 6:8
And I saw and behold a pale horse] Thus the poets speak of pale death.

And he who sat upon it, his name is Death] This is first a Hebraizing expression, 'he who sat his name' for 'the name of him who sat'. Next, it is to be noted that by the name of death is signified metonymically pestilence and lethal diseases; which we showed at Matt. 24:7. Pestilence is accustomed to follow famine, 'after famine, pestilence' is a Greek proverb. Thus also in Matthew and Luke they are named after famines, pestilences. Here, however, the Angel is given a name from the thing which he was administering.

And Hades follows with him] Those diseases drag [people] into the sepulcher. Death and Hades are accustomed to be joined, 1 Cor. 15:55, below 20:13, 14.

That horse seems to signify that malignant impulse by which someone threatens death to another by whatever means. The rider, however, is the Devil himself, a murderer from the beginning, John 8:44. Regarding hell, the word Hades is explained by B. Gerhard, L. C. de Morte § 173; by Lyra, Thomas, Ribera, Cluver, Ravanell; as the sepulcher by Alcafar, Piscator, Hoë; as both by B. Winckelmann. The first interpretation is approved by us, because by that word ordinarily, if not perpetually, hell and the state of the damned is denoted. See Matt. 11:23, ch. 16:18, Luke 16:23, Acts 2:27, 31, 1 Cor. 15:53, Apoc. 1:12. Compare Ps. 18:5, 6, 49:15, 55:16, 116:3, Prov. 5:5, 7:27, 9:18, Is. 28:15. Therefore the punishments of the impious are noted.

v. 8. And authority was given to him over the fourth part of the earth) It is to be understood here, to him and the two previous Angels. For now the effects of three Angels are drawn together into one. 'Over the fourth part of the earth' not everywhere, but in the fourth part of Judea. Thus Christ will move the terror closer and closer by certain degrees, tempering severity with great patience.

To kill with the sword] This is of the first Angel.

And with famine] This of the second. Josephus also narrates in Antiquities XX. 8 that certain priests perished by famine.

And with death] With pestilential diseases. This of the third. The Vulgate perverts it, rendering, 'power was given to him over four parts of the earth.' Thus no one would be excepted. Death is taken for pestilence also in Exod. 5:3, 9:3, 16, 2 Sam. 24:13, 14, 1 Kings 8:37, Num. 14:12, 1 Chron. 21:12, 14, 2 Chron. 20:8, Jer. 24:10, ch. 44:13, Ezek. 5:11, 17, ch. 6:11. By the pronoun 'to them' the previous riders on the red and black horse are included. Therefore the Vulgate rendered it wrongly in the singular.

And by the beasts of the earth] It is accustomed to follow the devastation of fields and the deaths of men, so that with no one resisting, the number of wild beasts increases, with great destruction to travelers, Deut. 32:29, Lev. 26:22, Ezek. 5:17, 14:15, 21. In the Manuscript [it is] 'and the fourth part of the beasts of the earth,' as if it were a matter of the death also of beasts, not of death by beasts.

Compare 2 Sam. 24, verse 13, Jer. 21, verses 7, 9, ch. 15, verses 2, 3, ch. 34, verse 17, ch. 44, verse 13, Ezek. 6, verses 11, 12, ch. 8, verses 5, 16, ch. 33, verse 27, Am. 4:5 ff. These refer, however, partly to the reign of Trajan, concerning which Aurelius Victor [writes] in the Epitome on Trajan: 'At that time, much more destructively than under Nerva, the Tiber flooded with great ruin of buildings: And a severe earthquake occurred through many provinces, and a cruel pestilence, and famine and fires.' Compare Eusebius, book IV, ch. 1 and 2. And that Trajan on one day sometimes brought forth ten thousand beasts for the spectacles, and as many gladiators, Dio is witness: partly to the reign of Antoninus Verus, under whom there was such a plague that villas, fields, and towns everywhere were deserted without a cultivator and fell into ruins and forests, and to the rule of Commodus and Gallus Valerianus, under whom a huge number of men were consumed by plague, and also to the reign of Diocletian, under whom plague and the scarcity of grain lasted for an entire decade. See Euseb. l. VII. c. 12. l. VIII c. 15. l. IX. c. 8. partly in the times of Decius, and partly in the times of Gallus, under whom the plague raged for a full 15 years, Euseb. l. VII. cap. 22. l. IX. cap. 8. Lyranus and Aureolus understand by the pale horse the persecution of Domitian, Andreas of Caesarea that of Diocletian, Ribera that of Trajan, which, by the testimony of Eusebius, was most bitter. But all those have already been designated under the second seal and the red horse. Alcafar wishes to signify by this death the death of martyrs as well as of other believers, for instance, Jews converted to Christ; but hell, or condemnation, follows this death in the present. Cornelius also rightly warns that this horse is not a friend, but an enemy; and that it does not have Christ as its rider, but the Devil, and that Alcafar's explanation is too narrow, because this seal, as well as the preceding ones, restricts itself to the Jews, which was also done by Grotius. Yet it is not precisely a fourth part of men that is understood, but with a finite number put for an infinite one, a great multitude of men of that time and those places in which those punishments were raging. But the gloss of Thomas Anglicus, Dionysius, Gagney, Richard, Viega, and others, understanding by the pale horse hypocrites who oppose the Gospel by their evil life and crimes: so that these three horses signify three enemies of the white horse, that is, of the Church and of Christ; namely, that the red signifies the world, the black the Demon, the pale the flesh, has no place: which sense Cornelius admits is more moral than literal: preferring to all others the explanation of Joachim, Seraphinus, Firmanus, Pannoniensis, and Pererius, who understand by this pale horse the sect of Mahomet. But that belongs to the heresies and the seventh seal and the angelic trumpets. Hoffmann, led by his own clearly arbitrary interpretation, fixes here the fourth period of the Church from the year of Christ 1062 to the year 1404, because by the sword, indeed, bodily wars between Emperors, Kings, and Pontiffs, which especially the Anti-Caesars and Anti-Popes stirred up, are to be understood; but famine, death, or plague and wild beasts are to be explained spiritually, and by famine the ignorance of the truth, by plague its malicious opposition; but by wild beasts those beasts are to be designated of which mention is made in Apoc. VIII. But if one of these plagues, war, is to be understood according to the letter as a bodily war, why should we take the others spiritually, when they, as often as they are joined in Scripture, always occur in the same and indeed literal sense. And who will suffer these to be dragged to the third century and beyond: when there still remain seven trumpets under the seventh seal, and seven vials are yet to be poured out in succession? John. Coccejus wishes to refer by the sword and the taking away of peace from the earth to Gessius Florus, the procurator of Caesar Nero, the first incendiary of the Jewish war. But he refers the famine to the Doctrine of Balaam, and mercenary bishops, and those eagerly affecting worldly power, under whom, however, Christians are to be multiplied, signified by the grain and the must. But by death he understands Jezebel, by hell the adulterers of Jezebel, that is, Kings and Princes, handing over their power to the harlot to hold the peoples in error, as if in a second death. But just as the earth is rashly restricted to Judea, and the war is ineptly referred to preceding times, so everyone sees how merely arbitrary the rest of these comments are.

PART VI. CHAPTER VI. EXHIBITING THE UNSEALING OF THE FIFTH AND SIXTH SEAL

UNSEALING OF THE V. SEAL.

Ezech. 5, 17. 14, 15. 21. In Manuscripto καὶ τὸ τέταρτον τῶν ϑηρίων τῆς γῆς, quasi agatur de morte e- tiam bestiarum, non de morte per bestias.

Conf. 2. Sam. 24, vers. 13. Jerem. 21, vers. 7. 9. cap. 15, vers. 2. 3. cap. 34, vers. 17. cap. 44, vers. 13. Ezech. 6, vers. 11. 12. cap. 8, vers. 5. 16. cap. 33, vers. 27. Am. 4, 5. seqq. Referunt autem haec partim ad Trajani imperium, quo de Aurelius Victor in Epit. de Trajano: Eo tempore multo perniciosius quam sub Nerva Tiberis inundavit magna clade aedium: Et terrae motus gravis per provincias multas, atroxque pestilentia, famesque & incendia facta sunt. Conf. Euseb. l. IV. cap. 1. & 2. Et Trajanum uno die in- terdum decem bestiarum millia ad spectacula pro- duxisse, totidemque gladiatorum, testis est Dio: partim ad imperium Antonini Veri, sub quo tan- ta lues fuit, ut passim villae, agri, atque oppida sine cultore deserta in ruinas, sylvasque conces- serint, & ad Commodi, ac Galli Valeriani re- gimen, sub quo ingens hominum numerus peste absumtus, nec non ad Diocletiani imperium, sub quo pestis & annonæ caritas per integrum decen- nium duravit. Vid. Euseb. l. VII. c. 12. l. VIII c. 15. l. IX. c. 8. partim in Decii, partim in Galli tempo- ra, sub quo lues totos XV. annos sæviit, Euseb. l. VII. cap. 22. l. IX. cap. 8. Lyranus & Aureolus per equum pallidum persequutionem Domitiani, An- dreas Cæsariensis Diocletiani, Ribera Trajani, quæ, Eusebio teste, acerrima fuit, intelligunt. Sed illæ omnes jam sub sigillo secundo, & equo rufo designatæ sunt. Alcafar per mortem hanc si- gnificari vult mortem tam martyrum, quam alio- rum fidelium, puta Judæorum ad Christum con- versorum; verum mortem hanc in præsenti se- quitur infernus, seu condemnatio. Recte etiam monet Cornelius, equum hunc non esse amicum, sed inimicum; nec sessorem habere Christum, sed Diabolum, & explicationem Alcafaris arctio- rem esse, quod sigillum hoc, uti & præcedentia Judæos restringat, quod & à Grotio factum. Non tamen præcise quarta hominum pars, sed nu- mero finito pro infinito posito, magna multitu- do hominum istius temporis & istorum locorum, in quibus illæ pœnæ grassabantur, intelligitur. Non autem Thomæ Anglici, Dionysii, Gagnei, Ri- chardi, Viegæ & aliorum glossa, per equum palli- dum hypocritas intelligens, qui sua mala vita & sceleribus Evangelio adversantur: ut hi tres equi significent tres hostes equi albi, id est, Ecclesiæ & Christi; scil. rufus significet mundum, niger Dæ- monem, pallidus carnem, locum habet: quem sensum magis moralem esse quam literalem, fate- tur Cornelius: præferens omnibus aliis Joachi- mi, Seraphini, Firmani, Pannonii, & Pererii ex- plicationem, qui per hunc equum pallidum in- telligunt sectam Mahometis. Sed illa ad hæreses & septimum sigillum, tubasque Angelicas pertinet. Hoffmannus sua ductus plane arbitraria ἐπιλύσει hic figit quartam Ecclesiæ periodum ab anno Chri- sti 1062. ad annum 1404. quod per gladium qui- dem bella corporalia inter Imperatores, Reges, Pontifices, quæ imprimis Anti-Cæsares & Anti- Papæ moverunt, intelligenda sint; fames autem mors, vel pestis & feræ spiritualiter explicandæ sint, & per famem ignorantia veri, per pestem malitiosa ejus oppugnatio; per feras autem be- stiæ illæ, quarum Apoc. VIII. mentio fit, designen- tur. Sed si una istarum plagarum bellum secundum literam de corporali intelligenda bello, cur reli- quas spiritualiter accipiamus, quum illæ, quo- ties in Scriptura conjunguntur, semper eodem & quidem literali sensu occurrant. Et quis patie- tur hæc abripi ad seculum tertium, & ultra: quum adhuc sub sigillo septimo septem tubæ restent, ac septem phialæ deinceps effundendæ adhuc sint? Johan. Coccejus per gladium & ablationem pacis à terra respici vult Gessium Florum, procuratorem Cæsaris Neronis, primum belli Judaici incendia- rium. Famem autem refert ad Doctrinam Bala- am, & Episcopos mercenarios, & mundanam potestatem certatim affectantes, sub quibus ta- men multiplicandi Christiani, per frumentum & mustum significati. Per mortem autem intelligit Jesabelem, per infernum adulteros Jesabelis, hoc est, Reges & Principes, tradentes meretrici po- testatem suam ad populos in errore, tanquam morte secunda continendum. Sed ut terra temere restringitur ad Judæam, & bellum inepte refertur ad tempora antegressa, ita quam mere arbitraria in his commentis reliqua sint, nemo non videt.

PARS VI. CAPITIS VI. EXHIBENS QUINTI ET SEXTI SIGILLI RESERATIONEM

SIGILLI V. RESIGNATIO.

## 6:9
Ver. 9.

And when he opened the fifth seal, I saw under the altar the souls of the men who had been slain for the word of God, and for the testimony of the Lamb, which they had] What things are in heaven; they are accustomed to be explained among the Jews by the figure of sensible things, in the temple as we have already seen several times. Thus the Martyrs correspond to the victims, Phil. 2, ver. 17. 2 Tim. 4, ver. 6. In the temple was the altar of victims. At the foot of that altar the blood of the victims was poured out, Levit. 1, ver. 5. chap. 3, ver. 7. chap. 7, ver. 1. chap. 8, ver. 15, 18. chap. 9, v. 18. Is. 29, ver. 2. That blood placed in the sight of the sanctuary reminded GOD, as it were, of the sacrifice performed for Him. Much more do the souls do this, that is, the Spirits of the Martyrs placed in the sight of Christ, under the covenant of God 2 Macc. chap. 7, ver. 36. The blood of Abel Gen. chap. 4, ver. 10. demands vengeance. So too the souls of the martyrs. For it is of natural equity.

Blasius de Viegas notes that Bernard, in sermon 4 on the feast of All Saints, takes this altar to be the humanity of Christ, and teaches that the souls of the Martyrs are for now under the altar, because they only see the humanity of Christ, but after the day of judgment they are to be placed above the altar, that is, they will enjoy the beatific vision when they receive their bodies: He himself, however, understands the places where the bodies of the martyrs lie buried. Jacob Tirinus, having followed Gregory the Great, book II of the Morals, ch. 6, as it appears, explains it concerning the desire of the souls of the martyrs for both the resurrection and the judgment: And for Tirinus, under the altar is in heaven, that is, from the secret heavenly inner chamber, suppose from the place of happiness and glory, or from the choir destined for the Martyrs in heaven. And the Papists assert that souls are tormented in purgatorial fire, which differs from the infernal only in duration, whereas Bellarmine denies it. that Martyrs come into purgatory, l. II. de Purgat. c. 1. and he confesses that the Roman Church has not yet defined where Purgatory is, l. II. de Purgat, c. 6.

If he should suffer what he did, justice would be straight. I interpret souls here as spirits, in the way that word is taken in Matthew chap. X. ver. 28. So also below 20, ver. 4. Those souls, released from the body, testify much more than blood to the death endured. Christ remembers that death and avenges it through His own steps, but, as we have said, tempering the severity with wonderful patience, and He gives time to curable dispositions, so that the punishment may pertain to the few, if that can be done, and the example to the many. These things are comprehended in those seven Spirits mentioned before. By the word of God the Gospel of Acts 4, ver. 31. chap. 6, ver. 7. chap. 8, ver. 14. Then in the Manuscript and other books it is only, for the testimony which they had, just as the Latin also reads, so that God is to be understood from the preceding. Which they had, that is, the testimony which they retained to the very end. So also below 12, ver. 17. Of those having the testimony of Jesus. The testimony is the same as that which is rendered both to God and to Christ: to God as the Author, to Christ as the truthful messenger.

Verf. 9.

Καὶ ὅτε ἤνοιξε τὴν πέμπτην σφραγῖδα, εἶδον ὑποκάτω τοῦ θυσιαστηρίου τὰς ψυχὰς τῶν ἀνθρώπων τῶν ἐσφαγμένων διὰ τὸν λόγον τοῦ Θεοῦ, καὶ διὰ τὴν μαρτυρίαν τοῦ ἀρνίου, ἣν εἶχον] Quæ in cœlo sunt; solent inter Judæos explicari per figu- ram τῶν αἰσθητῶν, in templo ut jam aliquoties vidimus. II. de Purgat. c. 1. fateturque Ecclesiam Romanam nondum definivisse, ubi sit Purgatorium l. II. de Purgat, c. 6.

Εἴκε πάθοι τά κ᾿ ἔρεξε, δίκη κ᾿ ἰθεῖα γένοιτο. Ψυχὰς hic interpretor πνεύματα, quomodo ea vox sumitur Matth. cap. X. vers. 28. Sic & infra 20. vers. 4. Ejus mortis Christus meminit & ulciscitur eam per gradus suos, sed severitatem, ut diximus, mira pati- entia temperans, & tempus dat ingeniis sanabilibus, ut pœna ad paucos, si fieri id possit, exemplum ad multos per- tineat. Hæc comprehenduntur in septem illis ante memo- ratis Spiritibus. Λόγῳ Θεοῦ Evangelium Actorum 4, vers. 31. cap. 6, vers. 7. cap. 8, vers. 14. ## 6:10
And they cried with a loud voice] That cry heard shows what the matter itself seems to demand.

Saying how long, O Master, the holy and true] It appears from the above 3, ver. 7, 14 that these things are to be referred to Christ. Christ is called Master also in 2 Pet. 2, ver. 11. For all this dispensation of patience and severity concerning the Jews has been handed over to Christ. Matt. 21, ver. 44. 22, ver. 7. Luke 19, ver. 12, 14, 27.

Do you not judge and avenge our blood] That is, by judging you avenge, our blood, suppose that of Stephen, of James the son of Zebedee, who was the brother of this John, and of others whose names are hidden from us. Optatus of Milevis: Even if a martyr, yet not yet avenged.

From those dwelling upon the earth] In Judæa which was called the land and the inhabited world by way of excellence.

Thus far concerning the opening of the four seals, the four living creatures in their holy office, in rousing and admonishing St. John to attention,

(the other seals had no need of such admonition; because the very voice of those crying under the altar, and that horrible transformation of nature perceived at the opening of the sixth seal were enough to rouse St. John) The living creatures watch generally in the militant Church, but now those things are represented which happen in heaven. In the Grotian explanation of the fifth seal opened, it is most to be desired that he restricts the souls of the slain to the converted Jews, whereas the vision sounds generally concerning the souls of the martyrs, and that he refers it to the times preceding the destruction of the temple, whereas on the contrary the vision itself was later than the destruction, and John was relegated to Patmos only under Domitian, but the temple was destroyed only under Vespasian. Alcafar restricts that voice to Christians slain by Jews, but it is deservedly rejected by Cornelius, and why should only Jewish martyrs or Christians slain by Jews be understood? Cornelius understands the martyrs to be all those slain in persecutions up to the Anti-Christ, whom he imagines will come only at the end of the world, perhaps with Christ or the Messiah of the Jews. But it was not yet time to prophesy here concerning the Anti-Christ, much less concerning the extreme times of the world. For the great Anti-Christ will follow only when the seventh seal is opened, and indeed when the sixth Angel sounds, Apoc. IX. 13. seqq. and thereafter. Although therefore the cry of the martyrs may perhaps last until then; and consequently, as new spirits of the just and perfect slain for the name of Christ are added, it might seem to grow heavier, (which, however, I would not affirm, since they are commanded to rest: although this also is certain, that by that command it is only indicated that the time for universal divine vengeance is not yet, and that therefore it is to be awaited.) Here, however, the series is not to be rashly neglected, and the souls of those who, whether in warlike persecutions or in public calamities arising therefrom, remained constant in the profession of the name of Christ, and especially of those who poured out their blood for the Word of the Gospel, are to be understood, whose condition, however, in this imploration of vengeance is equal to that of others slain in subsequent persecution, and their cry is the same. St. John saw God sitting on the throne just as he saw the myriads of Angels in the Spirit. But the manner of the vision is ineffable to us: he saw the souls of the slain, not of those whose death hell follows, but who poured out their blood on account of the Word of God. He saw for their comfort their glorious state under the altar, and the adornment of white robes, so that they might not allow themselves to be deterred from the profession of the name of Christ by persecutions and cruel torments, Matth. X. 28. Rom. VIII. 18.

Some apply these in general indeed to all times of the Church, but specifically to the martyrs slain under Trajan, which was done by the blessed Cluverus. Most others, with Petrus Aureolus, understand them as those slain during the time of the ten persecutions up to Constantine the Great, to which the blessed D. Gerhard and the blessed D. Gravius accede. Alcafar understands the souls of the slain before the devastation of the City: namely, that they are seeking vengeance from the Jews and the persecutors of Christians, and that in this life, namely that God should cut them off through Titus, Hadrian, etc. Whom Grotius followed with nothing but blind impulse. For this destruction had already happened. But by the souls under the altar, Lorinus on 2 Pet. III. 8, with Baronius T. I. annal. Ann. LV. 1. XV., understands the bones of the martyrs hidden under the altars. Cornelius à Lapide assigns a double altar, as for instance that of burnt offerings, on which victims were sacrificed, and beneath which he says the bodies of the martyrs were buried which formerly from the sanction of Felix I were accustomed to be buried under the altar, as attested by Augustine, sermon XI on the saints, Anselm, and Richard: But in this way the soul will be placed for the body: which synecdoche of a part for a part is unheard of: then of the incense, to which the souls, having been translated after death, as it were rest, exhaling a perpetual incense of praise to God. Although indeed in the vision the true altar of incense may have been exhibited; yet as nothing is commemorated here concerning the altar of burnt offerings: So neither is the altar of incense introduced otherwise than for the sake of mystical signification; not as if the souls cling to a place of happiness and glory proper to the martyrs under some heavenly altar, which Cornelius wishes; but through that altar Christ was signified, Heb. XIII. 10. Ἔχομεν θυσιαστήριον, whence Richard with Ambrose and Haymo understand Christ in this place, under whose protection the souls of the departed live, and enjoy his joyful and glorious vision. Albert: Under the protection and fellowship of Christ, who is called the altar, made from the earth in the virgin. Cf. Apoc. VII. 19. That the souls of the martyrs are seen beneath the altar, by this it is signified that the souls of the piously departed, especially of the martyrs, are in the hand of Christ, under the protection and shadow of Christ until the day of judgment, immune from all dangers and adversities, Wis. III. 1. Acts VII. 59. 1 Pet. IV. 19, says Blessed Gerhard. For one must not believe with the Greeks and Vigilantius that souls sleep after death, which does not agree with their crying out. Whence Jerome, against Vigilantius, deservedly called him the Sleeper, and added: You, while awake, sleep, and while sleeping, write.

They are said to be slain because of the word of God and (exegetically, that is) because of the testimony of the Lamb: because in the Word of God there is especially the testimony concerning the Lamb slain for our sins, and concerning death, and the Devil triumphing through the resurrection; inasmuch as he conquered as the Lion of the tribe of Judah. That great cry, however, is not directed so much to vengeance as, as Chrysostom has in Psalm IX, to confounding the strength of the adversaries by God, so that they may acknowledge the power and divinity of Christ; and also to declaring the desire for the final judgment and the final liberation of the Church. Concerning which Cornelius à Lapide does not speak badly: I say these souls primarily do not so much ask for the punishment and condemnation of those who injure and persecute, as for the liberation of the innocent, that is, of themselves and their own, who are afflicted by injury. For this is what the Hebrew word נקם signifies, that is, to vindicate, when it is constructed with the preposition מן, that is, from, out of, away from. And the Greek ἐκδικέω, when it is constructed with the preposition ἐκ, as is done here: For they desire to be vindicated from those who dwell upon the earth, that is, from the inhabitants on the earth. Thus 1 Kings XXIV. 14, David says to Saul: May the Lord judge between me and you, and may the Lord vindicate me from you, but let not my hand be upon you. Vindicate, that is, deliver me from your so sharp persecution, for he does not imprecate the death and vengeance of God upon Saul to his face: For he says: Let not my hand be upon you: As if he were to say: Far be it that I should kill you, even if I had you in my hand: for I do not wish for your death, but for my own liberation and safety from you, and I seek it. Luke adds in XVIII. 3, and the appeal to the judges and vindicators of Israel, Gideon, Samson, etc., who delivered Israel from the rod of the Philistines and other nations, and asserted them into liberty; even if they often did that with the slaughter of the enemies. Secondarily, however, and consequently (so Cornelius continues) they also desire vengeance properly so called out of a zeal for justice, as if they were saying: How long, just Lord, do you not execute justice, so that you may deliver us and the innocent Church, but punish the persecutors, so that all may praise and celebrate your justice toward both? For the blood of the martyrs demands this. For it is the same thing to say that the souls seek vengeance as to say that their blood demands it. Therefore the souls do not cry out from impatience or a desire for vengeance, but from an intimate desire both for the final and plenary liberation of the Church, and for union with their resurrected bodies. Gregory the Great, book II, Morals, ch. 6: Their great cry is a great desire both for the resurrection and for judgment. Indeed, each person cries out the less, the less he desires, and expresses a greater voice, the more fully he pours himself into the desire for the thing. It is not to be believed in a carnal sense that they are inflamed with a desire for vengeance, since we know that even enemies are loved by them, placed here through the abundance of charity. But it is manifest that they prayed against the kingdom of sin, and asked for such things out of a desire for that kingdom of which we say: Thy kingdom come. And we understand this to have been revealed to them by the foreknowledge of divine wisdom, that the impious are also inevitably to be punished with eternal punishment and that, until the end of the age, with the fountain of heavenly grace flowing, many are still to be joined to the fellowship of the holy martyrs. Having received this answer, they are filled with ineffable joy, which we rightly believe to be figured by the white robes, as Cluverus has on page 249. By those dwelling on the earth, not the worshippers of the beast, as Cocceius wishes, not the inhabitants of Judea, which Grotius has not yet taught to be called the inhabited world, but generally those who persecute Christians on earth are understood: against whom God exercises the judgments of his justice both in this age and in the future, both of which are comprehended here. He hints, says Blessed Gravius, at the same time, that corporal punishment is also to be inflicted upon tyrants, as much private in their tragic end, as public by Constantine the Great, but finally that eternal punishment is to follow in the abyss of hell. Regarding the argument of the Papists for the intercession of the blessed, Blessed Hülsemann replied in his Manual on page 925: The consequence deduced from the example of the martyrs in the Apocalypse seeking the vindication of their blood, what, I ask, does it do for the intercession of the blessed for any others whatsoever, living in any place and time? But does it follow that he who prays for himself also sees a camp-follower in a Cistercian monastery suffering from toothache? What madness is this? Then indeed Ribera, Viegas, and Cornelius deny that the souls cried out properly; but they understand by the souls of the departed the bodies, which are said to have cried out to heaven, just as the blood of Abel is said hyperbolically to cry out to heaven: What has this to do with the intercession of the Saints in heaven, properly so called? Others, like the commentator of Ambrose, Ansbertus, Haymo here, and Bernard, explain it not as a zeal for vindictive justice, as Saa and others do here, but as a zeal for glory, so that the Martyrs indicate their desire, how they wish that their bodies be delivered from corruption and joined to their souls, which is to happen only on the last day. What, likewise, does this help the prayers of the Blessed for any others whatsoever?

Latin:

Καὶ ἔκραξαν φωνῇ μεγάλῃ] Clamor iste auditus ostendit quid res ipsa exigere videatur.

Λέγοντες ἕως πότε ὁ Δεσπότης ὁ ἅγιος καὶ ἀληθινὸς] Hæc ad Christum referenda apparet ex superioribus 3, vers. 7. 14. Christus Δεσπότης dicitur & 2. Petr. 2, vers. 11. Nam omnis hæc dispensatio patientiæ & severitatis circa Judæos Christo est tradita. Matth. 21, vers. 44. 22, vers. 7. Luc. 19, vers. 12. 14. 27.

Οὐ κρίνεις καὶ ἐκδικεῖς τὸ αἷμα ἡμῶν] Id est, κρίνων ἐκδικεῖς, nostrum sanguinem, puta Stephani, Jacobi Zebedæidæ, qui hujus Johannis frater, & aliorum. quorum nomina nos la- tent. Opratus Milevitanus: Etsi martyris, at nondum vin- dicati.

Ἐκ τῶν κατοικούντων ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς] In Judæa quæ γῆ & οἰκου- mένη per excellentiam dicebatur.

Hactenus circa quatuor sigillorum apertio- nem IV. animalia suo fancto officio, in excitan- do & commonendo ad attentionem S. Johanne,

(cætera figilla tali commonitione opus non ha- bebant; quia vox ipsa clamantium sub altari, & horribilis illa naturæ μεταμόρφωσις ad sexti sigil- li apertionem percepta satis excitare S. Johannem poterant) Animalia in Ecclesia militante gene- ratim vigilant, nunc autem repræsentantur, quæ in cœlo fiunt. In Grotiana vero sigilli quinti re- ferati explicatione id maxime desiderandum, quod animas occisorum restringat ad Judæos con- versos, quum generaliter de martyrum animabus sonet visio, quodque ad tempora antegressa exci- dium templi referat, quum ex adverso visio ipsa posterior fuerit excidio, & in Patmum relegatus Johannes demum sub Domitiano sit, templum vero sub Vespasiano demum destructum fuerit. Alcafar restringit vocem istam ad Christianos à Judæis occisos, sed merito rejicitur'à Cornelio, & cur intelligendi solum vel Judaici martyres vel oc- cisi à Judæis Christiani? Cornelius Martyres o- mnes in persecutionibus usque ad Anti-Chri- stum, quem sub finem mundi demum, forte cum Christo vel Messia Judæorum, venturum com- miniscitur, occisos intelligis. Sed nondum hic de Anti-Christo, nedum de extremis mundi tem- poribus vaticinari tempus erat. Sequetur enim Anti-Christus Magnus uterque demum septimo aperto sigillo, & quidem clangente sexto Angelo, Apoc. IX. 13. seqq. & deinceps. Etsi ergo marty- rum clamor eo usque forte duret; & proinde no- vis occisorum pro nomine Christi justorum per- fectorum Spiritibus accedentibus ingravescere videri possit, (quod tamen non affirmarim, quum quiescere jubeantur: quamvis & hoc certum sit, mandato isto solum innui, nondum tempus esse u- niversalis vindictæ divinæ, adeoque id expectan- dum esse.) Hic tamen series non temere negli- genda, & animæ eorum, qui sive bellicis perse- cutionibus, sive inde oriundis calamitatibus pu- blicis constantes permansere in nominis Christi professione, & maxime illorum, qui pro Verbo Evangelii sanguinem suum profudere, intelligen- dæ videntur, quarum tamen in hac vindictæ im- ploratione cum aliis subsequentibus persecutio- nis mactatis par est ratio, idemque clamor. Vi- dit S. Johannes Deum in throno sedentem pro- ut Angelorum myriadas vidit in Spiritu. Modus autem visionis nobis ἀνεκδιήγητος est: vidit ani- mas occisorum, non eorum, quorum mortem in- fernus sequitur, sed qui propter Verbum Dei sanguinem fuderunt. Vidit in solatium eorum sta- tum gloriosum sub altari, & stolarum albarum or- natum, ut ne persecutionibus & tormentis crude- libus à professione nominis Christi sese absterreri patiantur, Matth. X. 28. Rom. VIII. 18.

Applicant hæc nonnulli in genere quidem ad o- mnia Ecclesiæ tempora, speciatim vero ad marty- res sub Trajano occisos, quod à B. Cluvero fa- ctum. Alii plerique cum Petro Aureolo ad occisos tempore decem persecutionum usque ad Constanti- num M. quibus B. D. Gerhardus & B. D. Gravius accedunt. Alcafar animas occisorum ante vasta- tionem Urbis intelligit: Petere nempe eos vindi- ctam de Judæis Christianis & Christianorum per- secutoribus, eamque in hac vita, scilicet ut Deus eos exscindat per Titum, Adrianum &c. Quem non nisi cæco impetu sequutus est Grotius. Hoc enim excidium jam factum erat. Per animas au- tem sub altari Lorinus in 2. Petr. III. 8. cum Baro- nio T. I. annal. Ann. LV. 1. XV. ossa martyrum sub altaribus recondita intelligit. Cornelius à Lapide duplex assignat altare, ut puta tum holocaustorum, in quo victimæ immolabantur, & sub eo sepulta dicit corpora martyrum, quæ olim è fanctione Fe- licis I. confueverint fub altari fepeliri, tefte Au- gust. ferm. XI. de sanct. Anshelmo, Richardo: Sed ita anima ponetur pro corpore: quæ Synecdoche partis pro parte inaudita est: tum thymiamatis, ad quod post mortem animæ translatæ, quasi re- quiescunt, juge thymia ma laudis Deo exhalan- tes. Quanquam vero in visione altare thymia ma- tis verum exhibitum sit; tamen uti de altari holo- caustorum hic nihil commemoratur: Ita nec alta- re thymiamatis aliter introducitur, quam mysticæ significationis causa; non quasi sub altari quodam cœlesti, quod Cornelius vult, animæ hæreant in loco felicitatis & gloriæ martyrum proprio; sed per altare illud significatus fuit Christus Ebr. XIII. 10. Ἔχομεν θυσιαστήριον, unde Riccardus cum Ambrofio, & Haymone hoc loco Christum intelli- gunt, sub cujus protectione animæ defunctorum vivunt, & visione ejus læta & gloriosa fruuntur. Albertus: Sub protectione & consortio Christi, qui dicitur altare, factum de terra in virgine. Conf. Apoc. VII. 19. Quod animæ martyrum subtus al- tare videntur, eo fignificatur, quod animæ pie defun- ctorum præsertim martyrum sint in manu Christi, sub præsidio & umbra Christi usque ad diem judicii ab omnibus periculis & adversis immunes, Sap. III. 1. Actor. VII. 59. 1. Petr. IV. 19. inquit B. Ger- hardus. Neque enim cum Græcis, & Vigilantio cre- dendum, animas post mortem q. dormire, quod cum clamore ipsarum non convenit. Unde Hie- ron. c. Vigil. merito eum Dormitantium dixit, ad- diditque: Tu vigilans dormis, & dormiens scribis.

Occifi dicuntur διὰ τὸν λόγον τῦ θεῦ καὶ (exe- getice, id est) διὰ τὴν μαρτυρίαν τῦ ἀρνίε: quia in Verbo Dei præcipue est testimonium de Agno ma- ctato propter peccata nostra, & super morte, at- que Diabolo triumphante per resurrectionem; utpote qui vicit ceu Leo de tribu Juda. Clamor au- tem ille magnus non tam ad vindictam directus est, quam, ut Chrysostomus in Psal. IX. habet, ad confundendam à Deo adversariorum fortitudinem, ut agnoscant Christi potentiam & divinitatem; necnon ad declarandum defiderium judicii novis- simi & finalis Ecclesiæ liberationis. Quo de non male Cornelius à Lapide: Dico hasce animas pri- mario non tam poscere injuriantium & persecuto- rum punitionem & condemnationem, quam inno- centium puta sui suorumque afflictarum ab injuria liberationem. Hanc enim significat Ebr. נקם id est, vindicare, quando construitur cum Præpo- sitione מן id est, à, ex, de. Et Græcum ἐκδικέω, quando construitur cum Præpositione ἐκ, uti hic fit: Optant enim vindicari ἐκ τῶν κατοικόντων ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς, id est, ex habitantibus in terra. Sic 1. Reg. XXIV. 14. ait David ad Saul. Judicet Dominus in- ter me & te, & ulciscatur me Dominus ex te, non autem sit manus mea in te. Ulciscatur, id est, li- beret me ex tua tam acri persecutione, non e- nim in os imprecatur Sauli necem, & ultionem Dei: Ait enim: Manus mea non sit in te: Quasi dicat: Absit, ut te occidam, esto, habuerim te in manu mea: non enim tibi mortem, sed mihi à te liberationem & salutem opto, & quæro. Ad- dit Luc. XVIII. 3. & appellationem judicum & vindicum Israëlis Gideonis, Simsonis, &c. qui Israëlem à virga Philistinorum aliarumque gen- tium exemerunt, & in libertatem asseruerunt; esto id fecerint sæpe cum hostium strage. Se- cundario tamen, & consequenter (ita pergit Corne- lius) optant quoque vindictam proprie dictam ex zelo justitiæ, quasi dicant: Usquequo, Domi- ne juste, non facis justitiam, ut nos & Ecclesiam insontem liberes, persecutores vero punias, ut o- mnes laudent & celebrent tuam in utrosque justi- tiam? Hanc enim postulat martyrum sanguis. Idem enim est dicere, animas petere vindictam, quod dicere sanguinem earum illam deposcere. Non ergo clamant animæ ex impatientia, vel cu- piditate vindictæ, sed ex intimo desiderio tum fi- nalis & plenariæ liberationis Ecclesiæ, tum unio- nis cum corporibus resuscitatis. Gregor. M. l. II. Moral. c. 6. Magnus earum clamor, magnum est de- siderium tum resurrectionis tum judicii. Tanto vero quisque minus clamat, quanto minus desiderat, & tanto majorem vocem exprimit, quanto se in rei desi- derium plenius effundit. Non carnali sensu creden- dum est, cupiditate eos ultionis accendi, cum ab eis hic positis per affluentiam charitatis, inimicos quoque diligi noverimus. Sed eos manifestum est contra pec- cati regnum orasse, & talia illius regni desiderio po- stulasse, de quo dicimus: Adveniat regnum tuum. Et hoc iis divina sapientiæ præscientia intelligimus revelatum, quod & impii æterna sint inevitabiliter pœna plectendi & usque ad finem seculi fonte cælestis gratiæ profluente multi sint adhuc sanctorum mar- tyrum consortio sociandi. Quo illi accepto respon- so inenarrabili lætitia cumulantur, quam stolis a'- bis recte credimus figuratam, ut habet Cluverus pag. 249. Per habitantes in terra non bestiæ adora- tores, ut Coccejus vult, non Judææ inhabitatores, quam οἰκουμένην dici nondum docuit Grotius, sed generatim illi, qui in terra persequuntur Christia- nos, intelliguntur: adversus quos Deus vi suæ ju- stitiæ judicia tum in hoc seculo tum in futuro ex- ercet, quæ utraque hic comprehenduntur. Innuit, inquit B. Gravius, simul, pœnam etiam corpora- lem tyrannis infligendam esse, tam privatam in tragico eorum exitu, quam publicam à Constanti- no M. tandem vero secuturam esse æternam in inferni barathro. Quod ad Pontificiorum argu- mentum pro intercessione beatorum B. Hülsem. in Man. respondit pag. 925. Consequentia deducta ab exemplo Martyrum vindicationem sanguinis sui in Apocalypsi petentium, quid obsecro facit pro intercessione Beatorum pro aliis quibuscunque, quocunque loco & tempore viventibus? Anne vero sequitur, qui orat pro seipso, is quoque videt calo- nem in Cisterciensi monasterio dentibus laborare, quæ hæc insania? Tum vero Ribera, Viegas, Corne- lius negant, animas proprie clamasse; sed per animas defunctorum corpora intelligunt, quæ dicantur cla- masse in cælum, quomodo sanguis Abel dicitur hy- perbolice clamare in cælum: Quid hoc ad interces- sionem Sanctorum in cælis, proprie sic dictam? Alii ut commentator Ambrosii, Ansbertus, Haymo hic, & Bernhardus exponunt non de zelo justitiæ vin- dicativæ, ut Saa, & alii hic, sed de zelo gloriæ, ut indicent Martyres desiderium suum, quam optent, ut corpora ipsorum à putredine vindicentur, & a- nimab9 conjungantur, quod in novissima demum die futurum est. Quid itidem hoc juvat Beatorum pro quibuscunque aliis preces?

## 6:11
Vers. 11.

Καὶ ἐδόθησαν ἑκάστοις στολαὶ λευκαὶ) In the Manuscript: Καὶ ἐδόθη αὐτοῖς ἑκάστῳ στολὴ λευκή. First, the name of a person is given to the souls, by synecdoche, of which we spoke at Luke 16:2. It would have been a long time to put off the martyrs until the time of the universal resurrection. They were worthy of some prerogative, as the ancients say. While comforts are given to other souls, honor is given to them, which is indicated by the shining robes, as we see above III. 4.5.18. IV 4. But Christ was also going to give them a kingdom in his own time, which time is called the first resurrection below XX. 24. Grotius does not sufficiently explain what he understands by the white robes, nor what kind of kingdom he thinks is to be given to them. He says it is at least an honor and a prerogative. But he does not teach what that honor is, or what that prerogative is. Hoffmann says that the outcry of the souls is the state of the militant Church of today, accusing the Papacy, rashly and relying on inept subtleties; he says the answer given from heaven is a modern revelation of future things (but what is that? perhaps such as that of the new Prophets, or one he fashioned for himself?), and he says the white robes represent a declaration of innocence, because whiteness is a symbol of innocence and holiness. But what comfort could the souls of the slain receive from this here? Did they ever doubt either their own innocence or its divinely promised manifestation, Ps. 37:6? Cocceius's interpretation on p. 75 is not unlike this. White robes were given to them for a time, i.e., their cause was justified in the world through the repression of the persecutors, so that they were compelled to give glory to GOD, Chap. 11:13, and to grant peace to the Church. Cf. Chap. 3:4. For the fifth epistle written to the Angel of Sardis promises that it will come to pass that some, who had not defiled their garments, shall walk with Christ in white. Wherefore, if the first pacification of religion after the war waged by Charles V in Germany is understood here, the order of the history of the prophecy, both of the epistles and of the seals, will fit properly. How alien these things are in this place, we leave to others to judge. For Andreas Caesar and Bernard, the white robes are full purity, rest, and the certain hope of blessedness. The white robe is more correctly explained by others as the glory and blessedness of the soul, the vision, and the enjoyment of God: which is white not so much because it is a symbol of the purity and innocence of the martyrs, as because it is bright and splendid, Rev. 3:5, Chap. 7:13, 14. Thus Augustine, Sermon 11 on the Saints. Gregory in Psalm 4 of the Penitential Psalms, verse 10. Bede, Anselm, Richard, Haymo, and others. Compare concerning the fine linen robe, Gen. 41:42, 1 Chron. 15:27, Esth. 6:11, Sir. 6:30, 32, ch. 50:11.

Ἵνα ἀναπαύσωνται εἰς χρόνον.] Let them rest, that is, let them await vengeance. Χρόνον, that is, not much time, about thirty years.

Ἕως ὗ πληρωθῶσι καὶ οἱ σύνδουλοι αὐτῶν καὶ οἱ ἀδελφοὶ αὐ- τῶν, οἱ μέλλοντες ἀποκτένεσθαι ὡς καὶ αὐτοὶ.] Fellow servants, like James the brother of the Lord: brothers, like other Christians from the common people slaughtered by the Jews in many places. There is also a metonymy here: until they are completed, that is, until their number is completed. The more who are avenged, the more will also perish. Thus judges are often accustomed to reserve a great crowd of guilty persons for one time of punishment, as the Jews were for the time before Passover.

Grotius drew these things from the Jesuit Alcafare, who says that it signifies that vengeance is to be deferred until the number of martyrs to be killed by the Jews is completed, upon the completion of which he would punish them and cut them off through Titus and the Romans. But another Jesuit, Cornelius à Lapide, had already refuted him, teaching that these things are to be referred to all martyrs and to the end of the world. St. Gregory, lib. 2, Moral. cap. 4: To answer the souls is to show that they ought to await the gathering of their brothers, to instill into their minds the willingness to await the delays, so that when they desire the resurrection of the flesh, they may also rejoice in the increase of the brothers to be gathered.

VI. THE OPENING OF THE SEAL.

Latin:

Vers. 11.

Καὶ ἐδόθησαν ἑκάστοις στολαὶ λευκαὶ) In Manuscripto: Καὶ ἐδόθη αὐτοῖς ἑκάστῳ στολὴ λευκή. Primum animabus datur personæ nomen, κατὰ συνεκδοχὴν de qua diximus ad Luc. 16, 2. Longum fuerat martyres rejicere ad tempus resurre- ctionis universalis. Digni erant aliqua prærogativa, ut ve- teres loquuntur. Cum aliis animabus dentur solatia, illis datur honos, qui per stolas fulgentes indicatur, ut videmus supra III. 4.5.18. IV 4. Sed & regnum illis daturus erat Chri- stus suo tempore, quod tempus dicitur resurrectio prior in- fra XX. 24. Non explicat satis Grotius, quid per stolas al- bas intelligat, nec quale regnum ipsis dandum pu- tet. Honorem saltim & prærogativam dicit. Sed quis honor ille, quæ prærogativa sit, non docet. Hoffmannus ut vociferationem animarum statum Ecclesiæ militantis hodiernum, Papatum accusan- tis, temere, & ineptis innixus argutiis dicit; sic responsum cœlitus datum modernam futurorum revelationem (quænam vero illa? talis forte, qua- lis novellorum Prophetarum, aut quam sibimet- ipsi finxit?) stolas vero albas declarationem inno- centiæ figurare ait, quia candor innocentiæ & san- ctitatis symbolum est. Sed quid inde hic solatii accipere poterant animæ occisorum? Anne du- bitarunt illæ unquam, vel de innocentia sua, vel de ejusdem in lucem productione divinitus pro- missa, Psal. XXXVII, 6. Non absimile est Cocceji interpretamentum p. 75. Datæ sunt ipsis pro tem- pore stolæ albæ, h. e. justificata est ipsorum causa in mundo per repressionem persecutorum, ut cogerentur DEO gloriam dare Cap. XI, 13. & Ecclesiæ pacem concedere. Conf. Cap. III, 4. Nam epistola quinta ad Sardensem Angelum scripta promittit, futu- rum, ut quidam, qui suas vestes non maculave- rant, ambulent cum Christo in albis. Quare si hic intelligatur pacificatio religionis prima post bellum à Carolo V. in Germania gestum, ordo hi- storiæ prophetiæ tum epistolarum tum sigillo- rum probe conveniet. Quæ quam ἀλλότρια sint hoc loco, aliis judicare relinquimus. Andreas Cæsar. & Bernhardus stolæ albæ sunt plena puritas, quies, & spes certa beatitudinis. Rectius stola alba ab aliis explicatur de gloria, & beatitudine animæ, visione, ac fruitione Dei: Quæ alba non tam quod symbolum puritatis & innocentiæ martyrum sit, quam quia lucida est, & splendida, Apoc. III. v. 5. Cap. VII, 13. 14. Ita Augustinus serm. XI. de Sanctis. Gregor. in Psalm. IV. Pœnit. vers. 10. Beda, Anshel- mus, Richardus, Haymo, alii. Confer de stola bys- sina, Gen. XLI. vers. 42. 1. Par. XV, 27. Esth. VI, 11. Sir. VI, 30. 32. c. L, 11.

Ἵνα ἀναπαύσωνται εἰς χρόνον.] Requiescant, id est, expectent vindictam. Χρόνον, id est, temporis non multum, annos ad- modum triginta.

Ἕως ὗ πληρωθῶσι καὶ οἱ σύνδουλοι αὐτῶν καὶ οἱ ἀδελφοὶ αὐ- τῶν, οἱ μέλλοντες ἀποκτένεσθαι ὡς καὶ αὐτοὶ.] Conservi ut Jacobus frater Domini: fratres, ut alii de plebe Christiani multis in locis ab Judæis trucidati. Est autem & hic με- τωνυμία donec compleantur, id est, donec compleatur eo- rum numerus. Quo plures vindicabuntur, eo & plures peribunt. Sic sæpe solent Judices magnam nocentium tur- bam in unum supplicii tempus reservare, ut Judæi in tempus ante Pascha.

Hausit hæc Grotius è Jesuita Alcafare, qui, significat, inquit, differendam esse vindictam, donec numerus martyrum à Judæis occidendorum com- pleatur, quo completo se eos puniturum, & excisu- rum per Titum & Romanos. Sed illum jam pro- fligarat alius Jesuita Cornelius à Lapide, docens, hæc ad omnes martyres & ad finem mundi refe- renda esse. S. Gregorius lib. II. Moral. cap. 4. Respondere animabus est, ut collectionem fratrum expectare debeant, eorum mentibus libenter expectan- di moras infundere, ut cum carnis resurrectionem appetunt, etiam ex colligendorum fratrum augmento gratulentur.

VI. SIGILLI RESIGNATIO.

## 6:12
Verse 12.

Καὶ εἶδον κᾀμότε ἤνοιξε τὴν σφραγῖδα τὴν ἕκτην, καὶ σει- σμὸς μέγας ἐγένετο.] The sixth seal comprises the omens that preceded the war between the Jews and the Romans. Among these are earthquakes in various places, Matt. 24:7, Luke 21:10, concerning which matter we have spoken at those places. Just as the judgment

of GOD upon the Jews was an image and a pledge of the universal judgment: so almost equal prodigies precede it.

Καὶ ὁ ἥλιος μέλας ἐγένετο ὡς σάκκος τριχίνος.) The sun failed by a fourth part of its diameter in the fifth year of Claudius. Dion 60. Σάκκοι τριχινοι or δέῤῥαι τριχιναὶ, Exod. 26:7, Zech. 13:14, are haircloths made from the hair of goats, and the Latin translator understood it no differently here.

And the moon became as blood.) A huge eclipse of the moon, in the seventh year of Claudius. Understand blood as dark, as also in Joel II, 31. Poets compare such eclipses to rust. In the Manuscript ἡ σελήνη ὅλη &c.

Latin:

Vers. 12.

Καὶ εἶδον κᾀμότε ἤνοιξε τὴν σφραγῖδα τὴν ἕκτην, καὶ σει- σμὸς μέγας ἐγένετο.] Sextum sigillum complectitur præ- sagia, quæ bellum inter Judæos & Romanos præcessere. In his sunt σεισμοὶ κατὰ τόπες, Matth. XXIV. v. 7. Luc. XXI. vers. 10. qua de re ad ea loca diximus. Sicut judicium

DEI in Judæos imago fuit & arrhabo judicii universalis: ita paria ferme ante se habent prodigia.

Καὶ ὁ ἥλιος μέλας ἐγένετο ὡς σάκκος τριχίνος.) Sol quarta parte diametri defecit, quinto anno Claudii. Dion LX. Σάκκοι τριχινοι sive δέῤῥαι τριχιναὶ, Exod. XXVI, 7. Zach. XIII, 14. sunt cilicia ex hircorum pilis, nec aliter hic accepit Latinus.

Καὶ ἡ σελήνη ἐγένετο ὡς αἷμα.) Ingens lunæ defectio, anno Claudii septimo. Sanguinem intellige atrum, ut & Joel II, 31. Poëtæ tales defectus ferrugini comparant. In Manuscripto ἡ σελήνη ὅλη &c.

## 6:13
Vers. 13.

And the stars of heaven fell to the earth. And if this is frequent, it is considered among prodigies. Lucan among the omens of civil war: - - - And flying torches through the void of heaven.

As a fig tree casts its unripe figs when shaken by a great wind.) A comparison taken from Isa. XXXIV. v. 4. ὄλυνθοι are grossi, as in the Glossary, פגים Cant. II, 13. Now grossi are unripe figs: Tertullian against Hermogenes called them bitter; for σειομένη, in the Manuscript it is σελευομένη.

Latin:

Vers. 13.

Καὶ οἱ ἀστέρες τoυ̃ οὐρανoυ̃ ἔπεσον εἰς τὴν γη̃ν. Et hoc si frequens sit, inter prodigia habetur. Lucanus inter præsagia belli civilis: - - - Cœloque volantes Obliquas per inane faces.

Ὡς συκη̃ βάλλει τoὺς ὀλύνθους αὐτη̃ς ὑπὸ μεγάλε ἀνέμε σειομένη.) Comparatio desumpta ex Esa. XXXIV. v. 4. ὄλυνθοι grossi, ut in Glossario, פגים Cant. II, 13. Sunt autem grossi ficus immaturæ: acerba dixit Tertullianus contra Hermogenem pro σειομένη, in Manuscripto est σελευομένη.

## 6:14
Vers. 14.

And the heaven was parted as a scroll when it is rolled up.) Isa. XXXIV. vers. 4. The heaven shall be rolled up as a scroll. A rolled-up book cannot be read. Thus he says it will be in heaven, so that nothing can be seen. Therefore understand ἀπεχωρίσθη as from sight, namely by dense clouds, taking away the view. Seneca about such a time: But a heavy and black vapor broods over the lands, it has covered the citadels of the gods and the highest houses with an infernal appearance.

And every mountain and island were moved out of their places.) It is a hyperbole. For he wishes to say that some mountains and islands were cast from their place, namely by that earthquake of which he had spoken. See Jerem. IV, 24. Pliny II, 80, about an earthquake: Maritime places are shaken most of all, nor are mountainous ones free from such an evil. The same brings examples of moved mountains, II, 73, and Tacitus records in Annals II that mountains sat down in Asia for that reason. Seneca about an earthquake c. 4, deserts mountains, and c. 26. Every shore of the sea is subject to movement, which he shows by examples. The Hebrews call all maritime places islands, indeed even those adjacent to all. In the Manuscript for ἐκινήθησαν it is ἀπεκίνησαν, the active for the passive: just as we say: the earth moves, the year turns.

And the kings of the earth.) The sons and daughters of Agrippa, who are called kings in this way, just as the daughters of kings are called queens in Tragedies because of the dignity of their birth. But it is also the custom of the Hebrews to call all governors kings. See what is in Acts IV, 16.

And the great men.) אדירים Jerem. XIV, 7. Dan. III. v. 25. Nahum. II, 5. Zach. XI, 2. Suetonius uses the word Megistanes, Caligula, and Tacitus in Annals XV, where he speaks of the Armenians, and Seneca, and our Mark VI, 21.

And the captains of thousands.) שרי אלפים. Exodus XVIII. v. 21. and elsewhere.

And the rich men.) who are strong in wealth.

And the mighty men.) Soldiers, Judg. V, 22. Jerem. XLIX. v. 21. Lam. I, 16.

Every slave and every freeman.) All kinds of men, the highest, the middle, the lowest, without any distinction, will be terrified by such great portents.

They hid themselves in the caves and in the rocks of the mountains.) because they are thought to be the safest in an earthquake. Seneca: What hiding-place do we foresee, what help, if the world itself causes ruins: if this which protects and sustains us, upon which cities are situated, which some have called the foundation of the world, splits and totters? See Isa. II, 18.

And they say to the mountains and to the rocks, fall on us, and hide us.) Personification taken from Hosea X. v. 8. See Luke XXIII, 30. And fall on us, is nothing else here than overshadow us: just as, shadows fall, Virgil said.

From the face of him who sits on the throne and of the Lamb.) Here too John mixes his own words with the words of the Jews, as above c. II, 24. For they wanted to be covered against the evils signified by so many portents. But John shows that those evils come from the wrath of God & Christ.

Latin:

Vers. 14.

Καὶ ὁ οὐρανὸς ἀπεχωρίσθη ὡς βιβλίον ἑλισσόμενον.) Esa. XXXIV. vers. 4. Ἑλιγήσεται ὁ οὐρανὸς ὡς βιβλίον. Liber convolutus legi non potest. Ita in cœlo ait fore, ut nihil possit conspici. Itaque ἀπεχωρίσθη intellige ἀπ' ὄψεως, densis nimirum nebulis, conspectum adimentibus. Seneca de tali tempore: Sed gravis & ater incubat terris vapor, Obtexit arces cœlitum & summas domos Inferna facies.

Καὶ πα̃ν ὄρος καὶ νη̃σος ἐκ τω̃ν τόπων αὐτω̃ν ἐκινήθησαν.) Est ὑπερβολὴ. Vult enim dicere aliquos montes & insulas loco suo dejectas, nempe illo, de quo dixerat, terræ motu. Vide Jerem. IV, 24. Plinius II, 80. de terræ motu: Maritima autem maxime quatiuntur, nec montosa tali malo carent. Idem exempla affert emotorum montium, II, 73. & sedisse in Asia montes ea de causa Tacitus memorat Annalium II. Seneca de terræ motu c. 4. desert montes, & c. 26. Omnis ora maris obnoxia est motui, quod exemplis ostendit. Omnia maritima Ebræi insulas vocant, imo & omnibus adsita. In Manuscripto pro ἐκινήθησαν est ἀπεκίνησαν, activum pro passivo: sicut dicimus: terra movet, vertit annus.

Καὶ οἱ βασιλει̃ς τη̃ς γη̃ς.) Agrippæ filii & filiæ, qui sic βασιλει̃ς dicuntur, sicut Regum filiæ ἄνασσαι in Tragœdiis ob ortus dignitatem. Sed & præsides omnes vocare מלכים βασιλέας mos Ebræis. Vide, quæ Act. IV, 16.

Καὶ οἱ μεγιστα̃νες.) אדירים Jerem. XIV, 7. Dan. III. v. 25. Nahum. II, 5. Zach. XI, 2. Utitur Megistanum voce Suetonius, Caligula, & Tacitus Annalium XV. ubi de Armeniis & Seneca, & Marcus noster VI, 21.

Καὶ οἱ χιλιάρχοι.) שרי אלפים. Exodi XVIII. v. 21. & alibi.

Καὶ οἱ πλούσιοι.) qui opibus valent.

Καὶ οἱ ἰσχυροὶ.) Milites, Judic. V, 22. Jerem. XLIX. v. 21. Lam. I, 16.

Πα̃ς δoυ̃λος καὶ πα̃ς ἐλεύθερος.) Omnia hominum genera, summi, medii, infimi, nullo discrimine, tantis portentis perterrebuntur.

Ἔκρυψαν ἑαυτοὺς εἰς τὰ σπήλαια καὶ εἰς τὰς πέτρας τω̃ν ὀρω̃ν.) quia ea in terræ motu tutissima putantur. Seneca: Quam latebram prospicimus, quod auxilium, si orbis ipse ruinas agitat: si hoc quod nos tuetur ac sustinet, supra quod urbes sitæ sunt, quod fundamentum quidam orbis esse dixerunt, discedit ac titubat? Vide Esa. II, 18.

Καὶ λέγουσι τοι̃ς ὄρεσι καὶ ται̃ς πέτραις, πέσετε ἐφ' ἡμα̃ς, καὶ κρύψατε ἡμα̃ς.) Προσωποποιία desumpta ex Oseæ X. v. 8. Vide Luc. XXIII, 30. Et cadite super nos, nihil hic aliud est, quam obumbrate nos: sicut, cadunt umbræ dixit Virgilius.

Ἀπὸ προσώπου τoυ̃ καθημένου ἐπὶ τoυ̃ θρόνου καὶ τoυ̃ ἀρνίου.) Hic quoque Judæorum verbis sua verba permiscet Johannes, ut supra c. II, 24. Nam illi voluerunt tegi adversus mala tot prodigiis significata. At Johannes ostendit, illa mala venire ex ira Dei & Christi.

## 6:17
Vers. 17.

For the great day of his wrath has come.) They said the great day of his wrath, that is, most mournful times, Lam. I, 12. Rom. IX, 22. c. XIII, 4. 1. Thess. I, 10.

And who is able to stand?) That is, to survive so many and such great evils? For that is what it is to stand, Ezra IX, 15. Luke XXI, 36. See also the Latin version, Ps. 13:39, 36:13. Again he derived these from his Alcazar: except that he explained the signs of the destruction of the city a little differently: the earthquake as the great disturbance of things which happened at Jerusalem when they stirred up sedition and war against the Romans: the blood of the moon as the punishment for the blood of Christ shed: the fall of the stars as the slaughter of James, Stephen, etc.: the folding up of the heaven as the departure of the Christians from the city: the migration and secession of mountains and islands as the removal of all difficulties for invading and occupying the city: the fear of those saying to the mountains: Fall upon us as the immense fear of the Jews on account of the imminent severe vengeance. But because all those things were already past, and it is not history that is held here, but prophecy about future things, it is manifest that those things are foreign. Nor were there Kings at Jerusalem, of whom verse 15 speaks, whence Grotius here had need of a new commentary about the sons of Agrippa. And how could the Jerusalemites say: Hide us from the face of the Lamb, who did not acknowledge Christ as the Lamb of God, nor ever feared his face? Although indeed Ambrose and Rupert refer these also to the reprobation and destruction of the Jews, just as they wish those things which are held in the following chapter to pertain to the calling of the Gentiles; yet neither the chronology, nor the letter of the text, nor the mystical application agrees, as it carries with it coercion. Blessed Gerhard refers it to the times of the Anti-Christ. But it is necessary to depart from the letter in such a way, for which there is no necessity, even if Victorinus, Ticonius, Primasius, Cæsariensis, Anselm, and others of the Ancients have led the way; and Blessed D. Hoë, Pareus, and others have embraced the same opinion. Lord D. Gravius likewise accepts the allegorical interpretation, but applies it to other times after Constantine the Great up to the tyranny of the Saracens. Thus nothing certain can be had when one departs from the letter of the text. Which is especially to be seen also in Cocceius and others. Meanwhile, Blessed Gerhard himself acknowledges in LL. CC. de Consumm. Sec. §. 9. p. m. 339, that most of the ancients accommodate these things to the very destruction of the world to be in the last day, since in Isaiah XXXIV, verse 4, the destruction of the world seems to be described in almost the same words. Compare Jerome and Cyril of Alexandria in the commentary on Isaiah Chapter 34. Eusebius, book 11 of the preparation of the Gospel, the chapter on the renewal of the world. Chrysostom in the homily to the Neophytes. Augustine in Psalm 103. Bede and Primasius in the commentary on this place. The Prophetic text parallel to ours, Isaiah XXXIV, verse 4 seqq., confirms this sense, where in that third verse the vengeance of the Lord to be exercised against the Anti-Christian army is described, and it is hinted that the consummation of the world is joined with the same or will immediately follow it, verse 4, namely that every army (of the stars) of heaven is to be folded up like a scroll, and every army withers, just as the leaf of the vine withers, and the dry leaf of the fig tree: i.e., that slaughter of the entire Anti-Christian army will be as certain as the folding up of the entire army of the stars of heaven will be at some time, at the end of the age, as certain as the destruction of all the creatures of the earth, because all living things except man will then perish no less than the leaves of the vine, and the fig tree, and all vegetables, and all creatures.

But the exposition of Aureolus and Lyranus is violent, who refer these to the persecution of Diocletian, as if it were said to the blessed in heaven: Fall upon us, that is, protect us. But if we adhere to the letter of the text, from which one must not depart without the greatest necessity, especially in such hidden things, there is no doubt that the discourse is about the signs that will immediately precede the last judgment. Let us collect the arguments. First, it fits aptly with the cry of the souls of the slain provoking the judgment of GOD, that it is about the last judgment, as if a real response were rendered to the souls. Then, the propriety of the words can be best retained, because all those seven members [fit], if we understand these things about the signs of the last judgment and the judgment itself. Which is manifest from the analogy and collation of other places of Scripture dealing with the signs of the last day: For it is gathered not obscurely that notable earthquakes will precede the day of total destruction, 2. Petr. III, 10. 12. Apoc. XXI, 1. What is held in Matthew XXIV, 7 about the earthquake is called the beginnings of future sorrows. The obscuration of the Sun and Moon is indicated in Matthew XXIV, 29, Luke XXI, verse 25. Only here is the blood-red form of the moon added. The fall of the stars from heaven is likewise established from Matthew XXIV, 29. The folding up of heaven from Ps. CII, 27, Is. XXXIV, v. 4, and those things which are said about the commotion of the powers of heaven in Matthew XXIV, 29, Luke XXI, 26. The migration of mountains and islands from their places from the immense commotion of the sea in Luke XXI, 25, the flight of the sea, Apoc. XXI, 1, and by collation of the time of the flood sent in, Matthew XXIV, 37, there is no reason for us to speak about the complaints of the infidels concerning the last judgment. Cf. Ap. I, 7. Thirdly, therefore, those things which are said in verse 15 about the Kings of the earth and the Princes and the rich, and the strong, and all slaves and free men, hiding themselves in tombs, and in the rocks of the mountains, and those things which are said about the great day of the wrath of him who sits on the throne, and of the Lamb, v. 16, 17, can be applied to no other time more correctly than to the day of universal judgment, which no one of the impious will be able to escape or endure. Cf. Wisdom V. Fourthly, those things which follow about the elect being marked, and being led from the waves of persecutions to the harbor of eternal blessedness, and also being fed and refreshed by the Lamb, cohere best: since the condemnation of the impious and the salvation of the faithful pertain equally to the extreme judgment. Fifthly, the parallel place Luke XXIII, 30 is like a clear commentary, which without doubt is to be understood about the last day, not only of the Jewish polity, but also of the whole universe. For as regards the impious, their last day coheres with the last day of the world. The overthrow of the city is certainly a notable type of the destruction of the world, by the confession of all Interpreters. Cf. Is. II, 19, Hos. X, 8. Concerning the dread of the infidels on that great day, Gregory the Great, book 17 of the Morals, chapter 21. Who could endure his wrath, whose very gentleness could not be endured.

Latin:

Vers. 17.

Ὅτι ἦλθεν ἡ ἡμέρα ἡ μεγάλη τη̃ς ὀργη̃ς αὐτoυ̃.) Illi dixere ἡ ἡμέρα ἡ μεγάλη τη̃ς ὀργη̃ς, id est, tempora luctuosissima, Lam. I, 12. Rom. IX, 22. c. XIII, 4. 1. Thess. I, 10.

Καὶ τίς δύναται στη̃ναι;) Id est, superesse tot & tantis malis? Id enim est stare Esdr. IX, 15. Luc. XXI, 36. Vide & Latinam versionem, Psal. XIII, 39. c. XXXVI, 13. Iterum hæc ex Alcazare suo derivavit: nisi quod ille paulo aliter signa excidii urbis expo- fuerit: Terræ motum de magna rerum perturba- tione, quæ Hierosolymis accidit, cum seditionem & bellum contra Romanos concitarunt: Lunæ sanguinem de supplicio pro fuso sanguine Christi, stellarum casum de nece Jacobi, Stephani &c. com- plicationem cæli de discessione Christianorum ex urbe, migrationem ac secessioneın montium & in- sularum de difficultatum omnium amotione ad in- vadendam & occupandam urbem: metum dicen- tium ad montes: Cadite super nos de ingenti ti- more Judæorum ob imminentem vindictam seve- ram. Sed quia illa omnia jam præterita erant, & non historia hic, sed prophetia de futuris ha- betur, aliena illa esse in propatulo est. Nec Re- ges fuere Hierosolymæ, de quibus vers. 15. unde commento novo hic opus habuit Grotius de A- grippa filiis. Et quomodo dicerent Hierosolymi- tani: Abscondite nos à facie Agni, qui Christum Dei Agnum non agnoverunt, nec ejus faciem unquam timuerunt? Quanquam vero hæc etiam Ambro- sius, & Rupertus ad Judæorum reprobationem, & excidium referant, uti quæ Cap. seq. habentur, ad vocationem gentium pertinere volunt; non con- venit tamen vel chronologia, vel textus litera, vel applicatio mystica, utpote coactionem secum in- ferens. B. Gerhardus ad tempora Anti-Christire- fert. Sed ita discedere oportet à literà, cujus rei nulla necessitas est, etsi Victorinus, Ticonius, Pri- masius, Cæsariensis, Anshelmus, aliique Veterum præiverint; B. D. Hoë etiam Pareus, & alii ean- dem amplexi sint sententiam. Dn. D.
