Gravius allegoricam interpretationem pariter acceptat, sed ad alia tempora post Constantinum M. usque ad tyrannidem Saracenorum applicat. Ita nihil certi haberi potest, cum à litera textus discedi- tur. Quod imprimis etiam in Coccejo, & aliis vi- dere est. Interim agnoscit ipse B. Gerhardus in LL. CC. de Consumm. Sec. §. 9. p. m. 339. ple- rosque ex veteribus ad ipsam mundi destructio- nem in novissima die futuram isthæc accommo- dare, quum Esa. XXXIV. vers. 4. iisdem fere ver- bis mundi interitus describi videatur. Confer Hie- ronymum & Cyrillum Alexandrinum in comm. su- per Esaiam Cap. 34. Euseb. lib. 11. de præparat. Ev angel. Cap. de mundi innovat. Chrysostom. in hom. ad Neoph. Augustin. in Psalm. CIII. Bedam & Pri masium in comm. h. l. Confirmat hunc sensum textus Propheticus huic nostro parallelus Esa. XXXIV. vers. 4. seqq. ubi versu illo tertio, vindi- cta Domini adversus exercitum Anti-Christia- num exercenda describitur, & cum eadem con- juncta vel eandem statim sequutura innuitur con- summatio mundi Vers. 4. quod nempe omnis exer- citus (stellarum) cæli convolvendus sit instar Epi- stolæ, & omnis exercitus tabescit, uti folium vitis tabescit, & folium siccum ficus: q. d. tam certa erit illa strages Anti-Christiani exercitus universi, quam certa erit aliquando, in fine seculi, exercitus stellarum cæli omnium convolutio, quam certus creaturarum terræ omnium interitus, quia animan- tia omnia præter hominem, non minus tum interitura sunt quam folia vitis, & ficus omniumque vegetabi- lium, & creaturæ universæ.

Violenta vero est Aureoli, & Lyrani expositio, qui referunt hæc ad persecutionem Diocletiani, quasi beatis in cælo diceretur: Cadite super nos, id est, protegite nos. Literæ autem textus, à quo citra maximam necessitatem, præsertim in tam abditis discedendum non est, si inhæreamus, de signis proxime antegressuris novissimum judici- um sermonem esse, dubium nullum est. Colli- gamus argumenta. Primum apte congruit ad cla- morem animarum occisorum DEI judicium pro- vocantium, quod de judicio novissimo agatur, quasi realis responsio animabus reddatur. Dein- de proprietas verborum optime retineri potest, quod omnia illa septem membra, si hæc de ju- dicii novissimi signis, & ipso judicio, intelliga- mus. Quod ex analogia & collatione aliorum locorum Scripturæ de signis extremæ diei agen- tium manifestum est: Nam terræ motus insignes ante diem πανωλεθριαν præcessuros haud obscure colligitur 2. Petr. III, 10. 12. Apoc. XXI, 1. Quæ Matth. XXIV, 7. de terræ motu habentur, initia futurorum dolorum dicuntur. Solis & Lunæ ob- scuratio indicata est Matth. XXIV, 29. Luc. XXI. vers. 25. Solum hic addita lunæ sanguinea forma. Stellarum de cælo casus constat itidem è Matth. XXIV, 29. Cæli convolutio è Ps. CII, 27. Es.XXXIV. v. 4. & iis, quæ de virium cæli commotione dicun- tur Matth. XXIV, 29. Luc. XXI, 26. Montium & insularum de locis suis migratio ex ingenti maris commotione Luc. XXI, 25. maris fuga, Apoc. XXI, 1. & collatione temporis immissi diluvii, Matth. XXIV, 37. de querelis infidelium circa novissimum judicium non est, quod dicamus. Conf. Ap. I, 7. Tertio itaque nulli alii tempori rectius applicari possunt, quæ vers. 15. de Regibus terræ & Principi- bus & divitibus, & fortibus, & servis omnibus & liberis, sese abscondentibus in sepulchris, & in petris montium, & quæ de magno iræ die sedentis in thro- no, & Agni v. 16. 17. dicuntur, quam diei panto- critico, quem nec effugere impiorum quisquam poterit, nec sustinere. Conf. Sap. V. Quarto quæ sequuntur de electis præsignandis, & è persecutio- num fluctibus ad portum æternæ beatitudinis per- ducendis, necnon pascendis, & reficiendis ab Agno, cohærent optime: quum ad judicium ex- tremum æque pertineat impiorum condemnatio, & fidelium salvatio. Quinto luculenti commentarii instar est locus parallelus Luc. XXIII, 30. Qui sine dubio de die novissimo intelligendus est, non so- lum politiæ Judaicæ, sed etiam totius universitatis. Quoad impios enim cohæret ultimus ipsorum; & ultimus mundi dies. Typus certe insignis est eversio urbis excidii orbis, omnium Interpretum confessio- ne. Conf. Es. II, 19. Ose. X, 8. De pavore infidelium in magno illo die Gregor. M. l. XVII. moral. cap. 21. Quis ejus iram toleret, cujus & ipsa non potuit man- suetudo tolerari.

## 7:1 Argument
EXHORTATION OF THE FAITHFUL ON ACCOUNT OF THE OPENING OF THE SEVENTH SEAL. CHAPTER VII.

ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

St. John sees angels throughout the whole world attempting to restrain the blasts of saving doctrine: but another angel, prescribing a limit to them, and sealing the 144,000 of the elect from the tribes of Israel. He also sees an innumerable multitude in heaven rejoicing with the angels before God and the Lamb, and is informed by one of the Elders concerning them, whence they came, who they are, and what blessedness they now enjoy.

There are two parts: The former is that which is carried out on earth concerning the blasts of the winds and the sealed foreheads of the faithful, up to verse 8. The latter represents the state of the blessed in heaven, as many as have washed their robes in the blood of the Lamb in these lands, up to verse 10.

PART I. CONCERNING THE ANGELS RESTRAINING THE BLASTS OF THE WINDS, AND THEIR COERCION.

Ver. 1. And after these things I saw four angels upon the four corners of the earth.] Namely, of Judea. It is customary for the whole world, just as for its parts, to be distributed into four portions. See Matt. XXIV, 31. The manuscript has μετὰ τῦτο, that is, immediately after that which was narrated last. Γωνίαι מִגּוֹת: thus the outermost parts of anything are called by the Hebrews. These angels had received power, though a limited one, both to restrain calamities and to send them in, as appears below in verse 2.

Holding the four winds of the earth.] Winds signify any kind of calamity, such as slaughter, diseases, poverty. See Achmet. Jerem. 18, 17. ch. 49, 36. ch. 51, 1. Dan. 7, 2. where see the remarks.

That the wind should not blow upon the earth.] That is, that devastation might not be brought upon the fields. But ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς is not in the manuscript.

Most make this chapter the second part of the sixth seal, which we admit thus far, because these things still pertain to the opening of the sixth seal. Meanwhile, it is not incorrectly established here as a preparation for the seventh seal. For just as the houses of the Hebrews were to be marked before the angel striking Egypt passed through, Exod. XII, 7, and before the wicked Jews were struck, the holy ones were to be marked with a peculiar sign, Ez. IX, 4; so before heresies occupied and infected the world, the tribes of Israel according to the Spirit were to be preserved and sealed, lest the malignant angels should harm the assembly of the elect.

However, the name of the earth is not to be restricted to Judea, just as those tribes were not contained within the same boundaries of the Jewish land, but were scattered everywhere, even the Israelites themselves, 1 Pet. I, 1; Jas. I, 1, not to mention the Gentiles. From this sealing, however, and the cause of it, it is clear that the sealed ones did not dwell in the heavens, but on the earth. For there, no sealing is needed, especially so that no harm may be brought upon anyone. For there is no death there, no pain, Ap. XXI, v. 4. The victorious crowd, indeed, clothed in white robes and carrying palms in their hands, celebrates a triumph in the heavens, which consisted of all peoples, equally from the Jews and the Gentiles. But the tribes of Israel according to the Spirit were still to be sealed by the angel ascending from the rising of the sun while in the militant Church.

That μετὰ ταῦτα, however, sufficiently indicates the order, and thus teaches that these things are less correctly referred by Primasius, Haymo, and Ansbert to the time before Christ, and by Alcazar and Grotius to the time before the destruction of the city. For those things were past; how, therefore, could a prophecy be made concerning them? Nor can the calling of the Gentiles be conveniently understood by them, as Ambrose does, which had likewise preceded in an illustrious manner through the sending of the Apostles into the world. And the discourse is made concerning all the tribes of the Israel of God. Andreas, Beda, Ribera, and Pererius refer them to the happiness of the Church that will follow soon after the Anti-Christ; when countless numbers from the Gentiles and Jews are to be chosen for grace and glory; which opinion Cornelius à Lapide corrects in such a way that he understands the sealed ones to be the faithful converted from the Jews to Christ, partly before the Anti-Christ, and partly, and for the greater part, after the Anti-Christ. To which explanation we cannot add our vote, both because he understands the Israelites according to the flesh, by which method none from the Gentiles would have been sealed and chosen; and because of that fiction concerning the greater part of the Jews to be converted after the Anti-Christ, which arises from a hypothesis that is clearly precarious, or rather false, that upon the Anti-Christ being slain, all Israel is to be converted to Christ: and because it is easily convicted of falsehood: since after the Anti-Christ nothing will remain to be expected further, much less a notable conversion of the Jews. For Christ will destroy him by His glorious coming, 2 Thess. II, 8; Ap. XX, 10.

Wherefore we accede to the opinion of those who understand the efforts of Satan not only under the reign of the Anti-Christ, as Pareus and others wish, along with most of the Ancients, nor only under the four Caesars who were to persecute the Church after Diocletian and Maximian—Severus, Maximinus, Licinius, and Maxentius—as Lyranus and Aureolus have interpreted: but during all that time which was to follow until the consummation of the age, and especially under both Anti-Christs, striving everywhere throughout the world to hinder the blasts of the saving doctrine. Those four angels, therefore, are not called the four Emperors of Lyranus, nor the Roman Empire, ruling over the four winds, that is, the quarters of the world, as Primasius, Ansbert, Anselm, and Beda explain, nor properly false teachers, as it seemed to some: but true angels, and those not good, as Toffanus wishes, who, although they are sometimes employed for punishments, Gen. XIX, 2. Kings XIX, yet they cannot be called ἀδικῆσαι, which is had in verse 2: nor do they intend the corruption of the whole earth, or oppose the blasts that bring salvation; but they are evil, which it is not new to call angels absolutely, Rom. VIII, 38; 1 Cor. VI, 3; ch. IV, 9; 2 Pet. II, 11; Apoc. IX, 14, and they have their own princes, Dan. X, v. 13, 20, so that the primary angels under the empire of Satan are hinted to be pressing upon the four corners, or quarters, of the earth; since throughout the whole world, or all parts of the earth, they strive to hinder the fruit of the Gospel, Luke VIII. The four winds, however, are not natural, as Cornelius wishes, although Satan can also delay and disturb those, Ephes. II, 2; Job I, 19, but mystical, because the things which happen concerning the winds in nature are common to the good and the evil. Nor can Satan delay all the winds throughout the world, nor is he persuaded that he can. And therefore by winds St. Anselm best understands preachers: because (these are his words:) as the wind, shaking the clouds, irrigates the earth, and makes it bear fruit, and gladdens the face of the earth: So preaching irrigates, gladdens, and renders minds fruitful to God. The winds of the earth, says Dionysius, are called preachers, who cool the hearts of the hearers, infuse the breath of spiritual life, and bring the cloud of overshadowing grace. To these agree Strabus, Rupertus, Lyra, Albertus, and very many others. Compare also the four chariots, and John III, 8, the operation of the Holy Spirit compared to wind in the reborn, and the coming of the Holy Spirit with the blowing of a wind, Acts II, the communication with the breathing, John XX, 22, the spirit of life in the wheels, Ez. I, 20, 21, the calling of the South wind, that it may blow through the garden of the Church, Cant. IV, 16. Blessed Claverus, with these comparisons added: Just as by winds all things are animated and vegetated and refreshed, which otherwise would rot: So God, by sending forth His Spirit through the preaching of the heavenly Word, renews the face of the earth, Psalm CIV, 31, Rom. I, 16, Psalm XIX, 9, Psalm CXIX, 92. Just as winds enter the earth by hidden passages, vegetate, and make it fruitful: So the Evangelical breathing of the Holy Spirit penetrates earthly hearts, and excites divine motions, Heb. IV, verse 12, Luke XXIV, 32. And just as trees are defended by the breathings of the winds from the injury of worms and caterpillars: So those who excel others in virtue are, by the breath of the sacred inspiration, defended from sloth, sluggishness, and the rot of pride, 2 Tim. I, 6, Heb. III, 13, Acts XIII, 43. Likewise just as winds [propel] ships on the sea: So these mystical breaths promote the Churches, so that, progressing through the waves of this worldly sea, they may reach the harbor of eternal happiness, Acts 9, 31. & ch. 17. 11.

Blessed Gerhardus agrees, except that, departing from the letter, he understands by Angels false Doctors, of whom he says: They hinder sincere Doctors in their ministry, which is the ministry of the Spirit, Genesis.

VI, 3. Ez. I, 20. Joh. III, 8. Actor. II, 2. 2. Cor. III, 6. He manifested Himself in the Spirit or wind; so that the word of the Gospel may be preached purely and incorruptly throughout the whole world, according to God's command, and that men may feel from it life-giving consolation and the recreation of their souls; and that they may not fail on account of the heat of divine wrath and the sorrows of the soul, Isa. LVII, 16. The blessed Grave agrees entirely: By these four Angels are understood malignant Spirits, who have attempted with all their might to infest the Church, flourishing in all parts of the world, through heretics. Among these heretics, the chief were those who, relying on political power, were able to impede the course of the Gospel, namely Arius, Macedonius, Photinus, Donatus, Eunomius, Nestorius, Eutyches, Mahomet, the Roman Pope, etc. The scope of these was to prohibit the wind by frauds and arms, that is, the saving power and operation of the Holy Spirit through the Ministry of the Word and Sacraments. For the Spirit blows where it wishes, Joh. 3, 8. Act. 2, 2. But just as, when natural winds cease, putrefaction is introduced, with manifest ruin to trees and fruits: So also, when the spiritual wind ceases, that is, the gracious operation of the Holy Spirit through the Word and Sacraments, its saving fruit is impeded with manifest corruption of faith and morals among Christians. This was acknowledged in his time under the middle Papacy in the year 1395, in a commentary by the blessed Luther published here in 1528 with a preface, and applied to the studies of the Roman Antichrist by Johannes Purvey, a disciple of Wycliffe, whom Mornay teaches to be the author in Mysterium Iniquitatis, p. 1108. They are sent, he says, by God for the testing of the good and the deception of the evil (1 Kings XXII, 21. 2 Chron. XVIII, 20.) and by their Prince the devil, as much as they can for the subversion of all. And they stand, that is, they are prepared to harm the Church, upon the four corners of the earth, i.e. upon every region of the world, the east, the west, the north, and the south. Holding the four winds, that is, all the true preachers and Doctors of the four Evangelists: because the devil knows well that in the time of the persecution of the Antichrist nothing would be more necessary than the preaching of the Gospel: And therefore he strives to have it detained in every place as much as he can. Which no one can now doubt has been fulfilled, while by the effort of the Prelates of the Church all preachers of the Gospel are prohibited. For let someone preach to our Prelates and Pseudo-Prophets the perfection which they profess, the Apostolic one, then they will cry out that he is a heretic and a Lollard worthy to be burned. Grotius does not explain whether good or evil Angels are noted: Only those holding the wind are holding back the calamity. But what is that, that the wind should not blow upon the earth? Perhaps also that the calamity should not be sent, which the Grotian explanation of the wind as calamity seemed to demand? But Grotius does not mean that; but on the contrary, he explains it in such a way that devastation is brought upon the fields, unless the particle of negation is to be believed to have been omitted, or that 'if' has been placed in its stead, since he refers these things to a time of deep peace.

Μήτε ἐπὶ τῆς θαλάσσης.] The sea in this book signifies a great people, such as the Jerusalemite people was in particular. See above IV, 6. Achmes interprets it as a kingdom.

Μήτε ἐπὶ πᾶν δένδρον.] Manuscript: Μήτε ἐπὶ δένδρα. By the name of trees are signified those things which are made from trees, such as cities, but especially the temple, which is also called Lebanon among the Prophets, for the reason that it consisted of the trees of Lebanon. See what we have said at Jerem. XXI, 14. XXII, 7. 23. XLVI, 23. Zach. XI, 5. These things pertain to the time of King Agrippa, under whom there was deep peace in Judea, Josephus II, 17.

What does the Jerusalemite people have to do with this, and what were the Angels doing around it, prohibiting the wind from blowing? What does the temple have to do with this? Was it so that the calamity (for this is what was noted by the wind

by Grotius's authority) should not blow upon the Jerusalemite people, and the four Angels held back the calamity from the temple? What, finally, do the past times of King Agrippa have to do with this, where the prophecy is about future things? By the earth and sea, others understand men living on the earth, in the sea or in islands; by the tree, they understand the Christian, compared to a fruit-bearing tree, Psalm I, 3. XCII, 13. Jerem. 17, 8. The blessed Cluverus thinks that by the earth are meant men given to earthly things, in the sea those fluctuating in various ways, and by the tree, he who has received the faith and is now prepared to bear fruit, is shadowed forth with Anselm, and he observes that Strabo, Rupert, Lyranus, and Albert subscribe to that interpretation. But just as those Angels attempt to hold and impede the saving blasts of the spiritual winds: So they are prepared to inflict harm in an iniquitous manner upon the inhabitants of the earth, the sea, and any tree, which the subsequent account of verses 2 and 3 teaches. For it is said that it was given to them ἀδικῆσαι τὴν γῆν καὶ τὴν θάλασσαν, which is to inflict injury or harm, which, although it is alien to God to inflict injury, he can nevertheless permit the same by a just judgment, John 8, 3. It is said to those Angels, μὴ ἀδικήσατε τὴν γῆν. For although God as a just Judge can permit this against those who adhere to the earth, or are given to earthly things, Coloss. 3, v. 1, and who fluctuate in various ways with vices, like the sea, Is. 57, v. last, as also to test every tree or the faithful one who is prepared to bear fruit; he does not, however, even will that, because of his long-suffering and immense mercy, Exod. 34, v. 6, by which he rather invites them to repentance through the heralds of the Word and the ministry of his Spirit, Rom. 2, 4, or because of his fatherly love, so that the pious may not be tempted beyond their strength, 1 Cor. 10, 13. But how demons delay the operation of the Holy Spirit, the Holy Scripture teaches throughout, and experience, as much by the obsession and blinding of ears and minds, Luke 8, 11. 2 Cor. 4, 4, as by the heretical depravation of the Word, Rom. 16, v. 17. Ephes. 4, 14. 2 Pet. 2, 17. chap. 3, 16. Jude v. 12, as by the promulgation of interdicts against purer doctrine, such as were issued under pagan tyrants, and are still issued by the Anti-Christ, by which a check is put upon saving doctrine, and the South wind is said to blow through the garden of the Church, so that its spices may flow, Cant. IV, 16.

Latin:

PARACLESIS FIDELIUM OB SIGILLI SE- PTIMI RESIGNATIONEM. CAPUT VII.

ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Videt S. Johannes Angelos per totum orbem ventorum salutaris doctrinæ flatus inhibere conantes: sed Angelum alium, iisdem ter- minum præscribentem, & electorum 144000. ex tribubus Israël signantem. Vi- det & turbam innumeram in cælis cum Angelis Deo, & Agno congratulantem, & de illa à Seniore aliquo informatur, unde venerint, quinam sint, & qua beatitudine jam fruantur.

Partes duæ sunt: Prior ea, quæ in terris geruntur de flatibus ventorum, obsignatisque frontibus fi- delium ad v. 8. Posterior repræsentat statum beato- rum in cælis, quotquot in sanguine Agni stolas suas dealbarunt in his terris, ad v. 10.

PARS I. DE ANGELIS VENTORUM FLATUM IN- HIBENTIBUS, ET EORUM COERCI- TIONE.

Vers. 1. Καὶ μετὰ ταῦτα εἶδον τέσσαρας ἀγγέλες ἐπὶ τὰς τέσσαρας γωνίας τῆς γῆς.] Nempe Judææ. Solent ut totus terrarum orbis, ita ejus partes in quatuor portiones distribui. Vide Matth. XXIV, 31. Manuscriptus habet μετὰ τῦτο, id est, statim post id, quod ultimo narratum est. Γωνίαι מִגּוֹת: ita Hæbræis dicuntur extima quæque. Hi Angeli potestatem sed limitatam acceperant, & retinendi clamitates & immittendi, ut apparet infra 2.

Κρατῶντας τὲς τέσσαρας ἀνέμους τῆς γῆς.] Venti significant qualemcunque calamitatem, ut occidio- nem, morbos, pauperiem. Vide Achmetem. Jerem. 18, 17. c. 49, 36. c. 51, 1. Dan. 7, 2. ubi dicta vide.

Ἵνα μὴ πνέῃ ἄνεμος• ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς.] Id est, ut vastitas agris in- ferretur. Sed ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς non est in Manuscripto.

Plerique hoc caput faciunt alteram sigilli sex- ti partem, quod hactenus admittimus, quod hæc ad apertionem sexti sigilli adhuc faciant. Interim non inrecte hic constituitur præparatio ad sigillum septimum. Ut enim signandæ, antequam Ange- lus percutiens Ægyptum transiret, erant domus Ebræorum Exod. XII, 7. & antequam Judæi scele- rati percuterentur, sancti peculiari signo notan- di erant, Ez. IX, 4. Ita priusquam hæreses orbem occuparent, atque inficerent, præservandæ erant tribus Israëlisfecundum Spiritum, ac obsignandæ, ne Angeli maligni electorum cœtui obessent.

Non autem terræ nomen ad Judæam restringon- dum, quemadmodum nec illæ tribus ex iisdem intra terræ Judaicæ terminos continebantur, sed passim, ipsi etiam Israëlitæ dispersi erant, 1. Petr. I, 1. Jac. I, 1. nedum gentiles. Ex hac vero signa- tura, & causa ejusdem luculentum est, signatos non in cælis egisse, sed in terra. Nam illic nulla signa- tura opus est, imprimis ne damnum alicui infe- ratur. Nulla enim ibi mors, nullus dolor, Ap. XXI, v. 4. Turba quidem victrix stolis albis amicta, & palmas in manibus gerens triumphum agit in cælis, quæ ex omnibus populis, è Judæis pariter, & gen- tibus constabat. Sed tribus Israël secundum Spiri- tum ab Angelo ab ortu Solis ascendente signandæ adhuc in militante agebant Ecclesia.

Illud autem μετὰ ταῦτα indicat satis ordinem, adeoque docet, hæc minus recte à Primasio, Hay- mone, & Ansberto ad tempus ante Christum, ab Al- casare & Grotio ad tempus ante excidium urbis referri. Nam ista præterita erant, quî ergo de il- lis prophetia fieri poterat? nec per illa cum Am- brosio commode intelligi gentium vocationem, quæ pariter illustri modo præcesserat per Apostolorum in orbem emissionem. Et de tribubus Israelis Dei universis sermo fit. Andreas, Beda, Ribera & Pe- rerius referunt ea ad Ecclesiæ felicitatem mox post Anti-Christum sequuturam; quum innumeri ex gentibus, & Judæis eligendi sint ad gratiam & gloriam; quam sententiam ita corrigit Cornelius à Lapide, ut signatos fideles è Judæis conversos ad Christum partim ante Anti-Christum, partim & potiori parte post Anti-Christum intelligat. Cui explicationi calculum adjicere non possumus, tum quod Israëlitas secundum carnem intelligat, quo pacto nulli è gentibus fuissent signati & ele- cti; tum ob illud de potiori Judæorum parte post Anti-Christum convertenda commentum, quod ex hypothesi plane precaria imo falsa, quod An- ti-Christo cæso omnis Israël ad Christum con- vertendus sit, oritur: tum quod facile id falsitatis convincatur: Siquidem post Anti-Christum nihil restabit amplius expectandum, nedum insignis conversio Judæorum. Hunc enim adventu suo glo- rioso delebit Christus, 2. Thess. II, 8. Ap. XX, 10.

Quapropter illorum accedimus sententiæ, qui satanæ conatus non tantum sub regno Anti-Chri- sti, ut Pareus vult, & alii, cum Veteribus plerisque, nec solum sub quatuor Cæsaribus post Diocletia- num & Maximinum, Ecclesiam insectaturis, Se- vero, Maximino, Licinio & Maxentio, ut Lyra- nus & Aureolus interpretati sunt: Sed omni illo tempore, quod sequuturum erat usque ad con- summationem seculi, & imprimis sub Anti-Chri- sto utroque, præpedire salvificæ doctrinæ flatus pas- sim per orbem satagente, intelligunt. Quatuor ergo illi Angeli non sunt dicti quatuor Imperato- res Lyrani, nec Romanum Imperium, quatuor ven- tis, id est, mundi plagis imperans, ut explicant Pri- masius, Ansbertus, Anshelmus, Beda, nec proprie falsi Doctores, ut quibusdam visum: Sed veri An- geli, iique non boni, ut vult Toffanus, qui quan- doque quidem suppliciis adhibiti, Genes. XIX. 2. Reg. XIX. non tamen dici possunt ἀδικῆσαι, quod v. 2. habetur: neque intendunt universæ terræ cor- ruptionem, aut flatibus saluti feris obsistunt; sed mali, quos absolute Angelos vocari non novum Rom. VIII, 38. 1. Cor. VI, 3. cap. IV, 9. 2. Petr. II, 11. Apoc. IX, 14. habentque suos Principes, Dan. X. v. 13. 20. ut adeo primarii Angeli sub satanæ im- perio quatuor angulis, vel plagis terræ incumbe- re innuantur; siquidem per totum orbem, seu omnes terræ partes, præpedire Evangelii fructum conentur, Luc. VIII. Quatuor autem venti non sunt naturales, prout Cornelius vult, etsi & illos re- morari, & turbare possit satanas, Ephes. II, 2. Job. I, 19. sed mystici, quia quæ circa ventos in natura fiunt, communia sunt bonis, & malis. Nec omnes per orbem ventos remorari potest, vel se posse persuasus est satanas. Ideoque per ventos prædi- catores optime intelligit S. Anshelmus: quia (quæ verba ejus sunt:) sicut ventus, excutiens nubes, irrigat terram, & facit fructificare, & faciem ter- ræ exhilarat: Sic prædicatio irrigat, lætificat, fœ- cundasque Deo reddit mentes. Venti terræ, inquit Dionysius, dicuntur prædicatores, qui audientium corda refrigerant, spiritualis vitæ flatum infundunt, nubem obumbrantis gratiæ afferunt. Quibus an- nuunt Strabus, Rupertus, Lyra, Albertus, & pleri- que alii. Conf. & quatuor currus, & Joh. III, 8. ope- rationem Spiritus S. vento comparatam in rena- tis, & adventum Spiritus S. cum flatu venti, Act. II. communicationem cum afflatu, Joh. XX, 22. Spi- ritum vitæ in rotis, Ez. I, 20. 21. vocationem Au- stri, ut perflot hortum Ecclesiæ, Cant. IV, 16. B. Cla- verum, cum additis hisce comparationibus: Sic- uti ventis animantur & vegetantur & reficiuntur omnia, quæ alioqui putrescerent: Sic Deus emitten- do Spiritum suum per Verbi cælestis prædicationem faciem terræ renovat, Psalm. CIV, 31. Rom. I, 16. Psalm. XIX, 9. Psal. CXIX, 92. Sicut venti occultis terram meatibus subintrant, vegetant, fœcundant- que: Sic sancti Spiritus Evangelica spiratio terrena corda penetrat, motusque divinos excitat, Ebr. IV. vers. 12. Luc. XXIV, 32. Et sicut arbores ventorum spiraculis à vermium bruchorumque injuria defen- duntur: Sic qui alios virtute antecellunt, spiratio- nis sacræ afflatu ab ignavia, focordia, fastusque pu- tredine, 2. Tim. I, 6. Ebr. III, 13. Actor. XIII, 43. Item sicut venti naves in mari: Sic mystici hi flatus Ecclesias promovent, ut in mundani hujus pelagi an- dis progredientes æternæ felicitatis portum teneant, Act. 9, 31. & c. 17. 11.

Consonat B. Gerhardus, nisi quod à litera dis- cedens per Angelos intelligat falsos Doctores, de quibus inquit: Illi impediunt sinceros Doctores in suo ministerio, quod est ministerium Spiritus, Genes.

VI, 3. Ez. I, 20. Joh. III, 8. Actor. II, 2. 2. Cor. III, 6. In Spiritu seu vento sese manifestavit; ut verbum Evangelii in toto terrarum orbe, juxta Dei man- datum pure & incorrupte prædicetur, ac homi- nes ex eo vivificam consolationem & animarum recreationem sentiant; nec ob æstum iræ divinæ & animæ dolores deficiant, Esa. LVII, 16. Annuit ex asse B. Grave: Per quatuor hosce Angelos intel- liguntur maligni Spiritus, qui per hæreticos Eccle- siam in omnibus orbis terrarum partibus florentem infestare omnibus viribus conati sunt. Ex his hæ- reticis præcipui fuerunt illi, qui potentia politica freti, cursum Evangelii impedire potuerunt, videl. Arius, Macedonius, Photinus, Donatus, Eunomius, Nestorius, Eutyches, Mahometes, Papa Roma- nus &c. Horum scopus fuit, fraudibus & armis prohibere ventum, hoc est, vim & operationem Spiritus sancti salutiferam per Ministerium Verbi & Sacramentorum. Spiritus enim, ubicunque vult, spirat, Joh. 3, 8. Act. 2, 2. Quemadmodum autem cessantibus ventis naturalibus putredo introdu- citur, cum manifesta arborum, & fructuum per- nicię: Ita quoque cessante vento spirituali, gra- tiosa sc. Sp. S. per Verbum, & Sacramenta opera- tione, salutaris ejus fructus impeditur cum mani- festa fidei & morum apud Christianos corruptio- ne. Quod agnovit suo tempore sub medio Papatu An. 1395. in comment. à B. Luthero An. 1528. hic cum præfatione edito, & ad Antichristi Romani studia applicavit Johannes Purvejus, discipulus Wic- lefi, quem Autorem esse docet Mornæus in myster. iniquit p. 1108. Mittuntur, inquit, à Deo ad proba- tionem bonorum & deceptionem malorum (1. Reg. XXII, 21. 2. Par. XIIX, 20.) & à Principe suo dia- bolo, quantum possunt ad subversionem cunctorum. Et stant, id est, parati sunt ad nocendum Ecclesiæ, su- per quatuor angulos terræ, i.e. super omnem plagam mundi, orientem, occidentem, boream & austrum. Tenentes quatuor ventos, id est, omnes Veros præ- dicatores & Doctores quatuor Evangelistarum: quia diabolus bene novit, quod tempore persecutionis Anti- Christi nihil magis esset necessarium, quam prædica- tio Evangelii: Et ideo nititur eam detineri in omni loco quantum potest. Quod nemo jam ambigere po- test impletum, dum pro nisu Prælatorum Ecclesiæ pro- hibentur omnes Prædicatores Evangelii. Prædicet namque aliquis Prælatis nostris & Pseudo-Prophetis perfectionem, quam profitentur, Apostolicam, tunc hæreticum clamabunt, & Lolardum merito combu- rendum. Grotius non explicat, bonine, an mali An- geli notentur: Solum tenentes ventum sunt tenen- tes calamitatem. Quid autem est illud, ne flet ven- tus super terram? Forte & ne immittatur calami- tas, quod videbatur postulare Grotiana explica- tio venti pro calamitate? Id vero non vult Gro- tius; sed contra ita explicat, ut vastitas agris infera- tur, nisi omissa credenda particula negandine, vel ut ejus loco positum sit siquidem, quum hæc ad tempus altæ pacis referat.

Μήτε ἐπὶ τῆς θαλάσσης.] Mare in hoc libro magnum po- pulum significat, qualis imprimis erat Hierosolymitanus. Vi- de supra IV, 6. Regnum interpretatur Achmes.

Μήτε ἐπὶ πᾶν δένδρον.] Manuscriptus: Μήτε ἐπὶ δένδρα. Arborum nomine significantur, quæ ex arboribus fiunt, ut ur- bes, sed maxime templum, quod & Libanus dicitur apud Pro- phetas, ideo, quod ex Libani arboribus constaret. Vide quæ diximus ad Jerem. XXI, 14. XXII, 7.23. XLVI, 23. Zach. XI, 5. Pertinent hæc ad tempus Regis Agrippæ, sub quo alta Judææ pax fuit Josephus II, 17.

Quid huc facit populus Hierosolymitanus, & quid agebant Angeli circa illum, prohibentes, ne flaret ventus? Quid templum huc facit? Num ne flaret calamitas (hæc enim per ventum notata

Grotio Autore) super populum Hierosolymita- num, & templum quatuor Angeli calamitatem tenuere? Quid denique huc tempora Regis Agrip- pæ præterita, ubi Prophetia habetur de futuris? Per terram, mare, alii homines in terra, in mari seu insulis habitantes, per arborem Christianum, arbori frugiferæ comparatum, Psal. I, 3. XCII, 13. Jerem. 17, 8. intelligunt. B. Cluverus per ter- ram habitantes homines terrenis deditos, in mari varie fluctuantes, per arborem eum, qui fidem re- cepit, jamque paratus est fructum facere, adum- brari cum Anshelmo autumat, illique interpre- tationi subscribere Strab. Rupert. Lyran. & Al- bert. observat. Ut autem Angeli isti tenere, ac præpedire ventorum spiritualium salutiferos fla- tus conantur: Ita damnum iniqua ratione habi- tatoribus terræ, maris, & arbori cuivis inferre parati sunt, quod subsequens relatio v. 2. 3. do- cet. Nam datum illis dicitur ἀδικῆσαι τὴν γῆν καὶ τὴν θάλασσαν, quod est, injuriam vel damnum in- ferre, quod etsi à Deo alienum injuriam nempe immittere, Johan. 8, 3. permittere tamen ean- dem justo judicio potest. Dicitur illis Angelis, μὴ ἀδικήσατε τὴν γῆν. Nam quamvis Deus ceu justus Judex hoc permittere possit adversus illos, qui terræ adhærent, vel terrenis dediti sunt, Coloss. 3. v. 1. & qui vitiis varie fluctuant, maris instar, Es. 57. v. ult. ut & ad probandum arborem quam- que seu fidelem, qui fructum ferre paratus est; non tamen vel illud vult ob longanimitatem & misericordiam suam immensam, Exod. 34. v. 6. qua potius eos ad pœnitentiam invitat per Ver- bi præcones & Spiritus sui ministerio, Rom. 2, 4. vel hoc ob paternam dilectionem, ne pii supra vires tententur, 1. Cor. 10, 13. Quomodo autem remorentur dæmones operationem Spiritus san- cti, Scriptura sacra passim docet, & experientia, ut- pote tum per aurium mentiumque obsessionem & excæcationem, Luc. 8, 11. 2. Cor. 4, 4. tum per hæreticam Verbi depravationem, Rom. 16. v. 17. Ephes. 4, 14. 2. Petr. 2, 17. cap. 3, 16. Jud. v. 12. tum per interdictorum purioris doctrinæ promulga- tionem, qualia sub tyrannis paganis edita fuere, atque eduntur adhuc ab Anti-Christo, quibus do- ctrinæ salutari sufflamen injicitur, & Auster per- hibetur hortum Ecclesiæ perflare, ut fluant aro- mata ejus, Cant. IV, 16.

## 7:2
Vers. 2. And I saw another angel ascending from the rising of the sun.] From Christ, who is called ἀνατολὴ, Luke I, 78. Therefore Christians used to pray toward the east. This was a greater Angel. In the Manuscript ἀπὸ ἀνατολῶν, as in Matthew II, 2.

Having the seal of the living God.] Bringing commands from the King, as the highest Ministers of Kings are accustomed to do. Σφραγὶς by synecdoche denotes a Royal constitution, because such constitutions are accustomed to be sealed.

And he cried with a loud voice to the four angels.] To the same four who were indicated before.

To whom it was given.] Again a Hebraism אשׁר להם. To harm the earth and the sea.] To harm the earth and the peoples. Concerning this improper meaning of the word ἀδικεῖν see above II, 11. VI, 6. God is also accustomed to use the works of angels to punish the impious, Gen. 19, 21. 2 Sam. 24, 16. 2 Kings 19, 35.

By the present Angel one is not to understand the Holy Spirit with Cocceius and Alcazar. Grotius understands it as an Angel Minister, which Piscator, Pererius, Bellarmine, Ribera, Estius, Cornelius à Lapide, and Dürfeld also seem to hint at regarding the meaning. Other Papists, whom Grotius willingly gratifies in the matter of the Anti-Christ, understand Elijah, who, with Gagneius as author, will oppose the raging Anti-Christ, and will convert many to Christ, and will mark them with the cross of Christ.

But having dismissed their trifles with the Ancients Ambrose, Ansbert, Primasius, Bede, Haymo, Anselm, as also Richard, the ordinary and interlinear gloss, Thomas, Bullinger, Aretius, Crugotius, Forbesius, Cotterius, Pareus, B. Gerhardus, B. Cluverus, Flacius, Winckelmannus, and not a few others of our own, we judge that Christ is this Angel, who is excellently called an Angel because of his most eminent mission, another Angel, by the otherness of his nature, ascending from the rising, because he is the ἀνατολὴ ἐξ ὕψες, Luke 1:65. And he has the sign of the living GOD, or rather the seal, because he is not only the character τῆς ὑποστάσεως τῦ Θεῦ, Heb. 1:2, and the Father has sealed him, but the Elect are sealed in him and through him, to whom the seal of the Holy Spirit is given, by which the Elect are sealed in their heart, 2 Cor. 1:29. For the Holy Spirit is the Spirit of the Son, Gal. 4:6, because he proceeds from him from eternity, and is given in time, and is imprinted upon the elect as a seal, Acts 2:33, 2 Tim. 2:19. What more? That he alone knows who are to be sealed, Rev. 2:23. and he is also introduced under this office, Ezek. 9:3. Nor does that conjunction suit another, until we seal, σφραγίσωμεν, I with the Father, let us seal, I say, with the seal of the Holy Spirit, the servants of the Triune GOD, as the Weimar Paraphrasts have it with B. Gerhardus (others do not so conveniently join the ministering Angels), to whom also that great cry with the efficacy of commanding the evil Angels by his own authority belongs, as well as the definition of the terms and the manner of the injury, not to mention that he is the same Angel who is in Rev. 10:3, who is likewise the Son of God. The explanation of Aureolus and Lyranus is incongruous, by which they understand Constantine the Great through the other Angel, for nowhere are Emperors called Angels; the comment of Bonaventure in the prolegomena to the life of St. Francis, that this Angel is St. Francis and his Franciscan followers, is inept, and to have recited it is to have refuted it. Furthermore, the propriety of the word indicates that σφραγῖδα ought not to be taken for a constitution, but for a seal, from which one must not depart, and the very mention of the forehead, on which they were to be sealed, to which indeed what a constitution would do does not appear. Add that Grotius himself in verse 3 explains the signature from a comparison of the passage in Ezek. 9.

Latin:

Vers. 2. Καὶ εἶδον ἄλλον ἄγγελον ἀναβαίνοντα ἀπὸ ἀνατολῆς ἡλίου.] A Christo, qui vocatur ἀνατολὴ, Luc. I, 78. Ideo Chri- stiani ad orientem orabant. Hic erat major Angelus. In Ma- nuscripto ἀπὸ ἀνατολῶν, quomodo Matth. II, 2.

Ἔχοντα σφραγῖδα Θεῦ ζῶντος.] Mandata à Rege afferentem, ut solent summi Regum Ministri. Σφραγὶς per συνεκδο- χὴν constitutionem Regiam notat, quia tales constitutiones obsignari solent.

Καὶ ἔκραξε φωνῇ μεγάλῃ τοῖς τέσσαρσιν ἀγγέλοις.] Iisdem quatuor, qui ante indicati.

Οἷς ἐδόθη αὐτοῖς.] Rursum Ebraismus אשׁר להם. Ἀδικῆσαι τὴν γῆν καὶ θάλασσαν.] Nocere terræ & populis. De hac impropria significatione vocis ἀδικεῖν vide supra II, 11. VI, 6. Solet etiam Deus ad puniendos impios Angelorum opera uti, Gen. 19, 21. 2. Sam. 24, 16. 2. Reg. 19, 35.

Per Angelum præsentem non intelligendus Spiritus Sanctus cum Coccejo, & Alcafare. Gro- tius de Angelo Ministro intelligit, quod etiam quantum ad significationem innuere videntur Pi- scator, Pererius, Bellarminus, Ribera, Estius, Cor- nelius à Lapide, Dürfeld. Alii Papistæ, quibus Grotius in materia de Anti-Christo lubenter grati- ficatur, intelligunt Eliam, qui sævienti Anti-Chri- sto, Gagnejo autore, se opponet, multosque con- vertet ad Christum, ac cruce Christi signabit.

Sed missis illorum nugis cum Veteribus Am- brosio, Ansberto, Primasio, Beda, Haymone, Anshel- mo, ut & Ricchardo, glossa ordin. & interlin. Thoma, Bullingero, Aretio, Crugotio, Forbesio, Cotterio, Pa- reo, B. Gerhardo, B. Cluvero, Flacio, Winckel- manno, aliisque è nostratibus non paucis Christum hunc Angelum esse censemus, qui Angelus excel- lenter dicitur ob missionem eminentissimam, An- gelus alius, alietate naturæ, ascendens ab ortu, quia ἀνατολὴ ἐξ ὕψες, Luc. I, 65. & signum habet DEI vivi, vel sigillum potius, quia non tantum chara- cter est τῆς ὑποστάσεως τῦ Θεῦ, Ebr. I, 2. ipsumque signavit Pater, sed in ipso & per ipsum signati Electi, cui sigillum Spiritus S. datum, quo Electi obsignantur in corde, 2. Cor. I, 29. Spiritus San- ctus enim est Filii Spiritus, Gal. IV, 6. quia ab ipso procedit ab æterno, & donatur in tempore, ac electis ceu sigillum imprimitur, Act, II, 33. 2. Tim. II, 19. Quid? quod ipse solus norit qui signandi sint, Apocal. II, 23. & sub hoc officio introductus quoque sit, Ezech. IX, 3. nec alii convenit illa con- junctio, donec σφραγίσωμεν signemus, ego cum Patre, signemus, inquam, sigillo Spiritus S. servos DEI Triunius, ut cum B. Gerhardo Paraphrastæ Vinarienses habent (non ita commode alii jun- gunt Angelos Ministros) cui etiam clamor ille magnus cum efficacia Angelis malis ἀυτεξυσίως imperandi convenit, ac terminorum, & modi læ- sionis definitio, ut taceam, quod idem Angelus sit, qui Ap. X, 3. qui pariter est Filius Dei. Incon- grua est Aureoli & Lyrani explicatio, qua per Angelum alium Constantinum M. intelligunt, nu- spiam enim Imperatores Angeli vocantur; in- eptum Bonaventuræ commentum in proleg. vit. S. Francisci, hunc Angelum esse S. Franciscum, ejusque asseclas Franciscanos, quod recitasse est refutasse. Cæterum σφραγῖδα non pro constitu- tione, sed pro signaculo accipi debere, vocis pro- prietas indicat, à qua recedendum non est, & ipsa mentio frontis, in qua signandi erant, ad quam vero quid constitutio faciat, non apparet. Adde quod Grotius ipse vers. 3. de signatura è collatione loci Ezech. IX. explicet.

## 7:3
Verse 3. Saying, do not harm the earth or the sea or the trees.] Do not bring devastation upon the lands, nor slaughter upon the peoples, nor fire upon the cities or the temple.

But how does the event correspond to this interdict, if it is especially posited that the destruction of the city preceded it? Was there not devastation brought upon the lands, slaughter upon the peoples, and fire upon the cities and the temple? But how could these things be brought about against the will of GOD?

Until we seal the servants of our GOD on their foreheads.] In Ezekiel 9, the Angel is commanded to seal with a ת, which signifies the law, those who had kept the law, and this so that they might be safe at the time when the Chaldeans were about to break into Jerusalem. Thus here, the Christians who were in Jerusalem and in all Judea are commanded to be sealed with the cross, the mark of Christians, so that they might be exempted from the common evils of the Jews. And this is what Eusebius says in History 3.5. Moreover, the people of the church in Jerusalem, according to a certain oracle given by revelation to those approved there before the war, were commanded to depart from the city and to inhabit a certain city of Perea, which they call Pella, in which those who had believed in Christ had migrated from Jerusalem, as if the holy men had completely failed, and the divine justice was then pursuing them, as well as the royal metropolis of the Jews and the whole Jewish land, for having committed such outrages against Christ and his Apostles, utterly destroying that very generation of the impious from among men. We seal those things which we wish to be guarded. But on the forehead, because it was the custom in the East to write the names of masters on the foreheads of slaves, which appears not only from that passage of Ezekiel, but also from Aristophanes, who introduced Babylonian slaves onto the stage with their foreheads inscribed, as we have said from Hesychius under the words Σαμίων, δῆμος and Ἱσρίανα. And it is the custom for Christians to mark their forehead with the sign of the cross. Tertullian mentions this in De Corona: Julianus in Cyril book VI, and others. See also below 9:4. But this enigmatic sealing on the forehead clearly corresponds to that time when Eusebius says the Christians left Jerusalem, namely not only before the siege, but also before the war of the Jews against the Romans.

Latin:

Vers. 3. Λέγων, μὴ ἀδικήσατε τὴν γῆν μήτε τὴν θάλασσαν, μήτε τὰ δένδρα.] Neque vastitatem terris, neque occidionem populis, neque urbibus aut templo incendium inferte.

Quomodo vero huic interdicto respondit eventus, si maxime ponatur id præcessisse exi- tium urbis? Annon vastitas terris, occidio popu- lis, incendium urbibus & templo illatum? Quæ vero quomodo inferri poterant contra volunta- tem DEI?

Ἄχρις ᾗ σφραγίσωμεν τὺς δύλυς τῦ Θεῦ ἡμῶν ἐπὶ τῶν με- τώπων ἀυτῶν.] In Ezechiele IX. jubetur Angelus signare per ת, quod legem significat, eos, qui legem servaverant, idque ut salvi essent eo tempore, quo Chaldæi Hierosolyma erant irrupturi. Ita hic Christiani, qui Hierosolymis & in omni Judæa erant, jubentur signari cruce, nota Christianorum, ut communibus Judæorum malis eximerentur. Et hoc est, quod dicit Eusebius Historiæ III, 5. Οὐ μὴν ἀλλὰ καὶ τῦ λαῦ τῆς ἐν Ἱε- ροσολύμοις ἐκκλησίας, κατά τινα χρησμὸν τοῖς αὐτόθι δοκίμοις δι ἀποκαλύψεως ἐκδοθέντα, πρὸ τῦ πολέμυ μεταστῆναι τῆς πό- λεως, καί τινα τῆς Περαίας πόλιν οἰκεῖν κεκελευσμένης, Πέλλαν αὐτὴν ὀνομάζυσιν, ἐν ᾗ τῶν εἰς χριστὸν πεπισευκότων ἀπὸ τῆς Ἱε- ροσολύμων μετῳκισμένων, ὡς ἀν παντελῶς ἐπιλελοιπότων ἁγίων ἀνδρῶν, αὐτήν τε τὴν Ἰυδαίων βασιλικὴν μητρόπολιν, καὶ σύμπα- σαν τὴν Ἰυδαίαν γῆν, ἡ ἐκ Θεῦ δίκη λοιπὸν αὐτὺς, ὥστε τοσαῦτα εἶς τε τὸν χρισὸν, καὶ τὺς Ἀποσόλυς αὐτῦ παρηνομηκότας μετήῃει, τῶν ἀσεβῶν ἄρδην τὴν γενεὰν αὐτὴν ἐκείνην ἐξ ἀνθρώπων ἀφανί- ζυσα. Signamus ea, quæ custodiri volumus. In fronte au- tem, quia is mos erat in Oriente, Dominorum nomina servis in fronte scribere, quod non ex illo tantum Ezechielis loco apparet, sed & ex Aristophane, qui Babylonios servos cum fronte inscripta introduxit in scenam, ut diximus ex Hesy- chio vocibus Σαμίων, δῆμος & Ἱσρίανα. Et Christianis mos frontem crucis signaculo terere. Meminit Tertullianus de corona: Julianus apud Cyrillum lib. VI. & alii. Vide & in- se- fra IX, 4. Plane autem congruit hæc ænigmatica signatio in fronte, in illud tempus, quo Eusebius ex Hierosolymis exiis- se dicit Christianos, nempe non ante obsidionem tantum, sed & ante bellum Judæorum in Romanos.

## 7:4
Verse 4. And I heard the number of those who were sealed, one hundred and forty-four thousand sealed from every tribe of the sons of Israel.] They make this sum twelve thousand twelve times, which our writer then divides into twelve tribes: not that this was precisely the number of all, or equal in each tribe: but that by such a number, as by μυρίας in Greek, a very huge multitude is expressed. Thus concerning the same Jews believing in Christ, how many myriads are there? Acts 21:50. In the Manuscript, those words are missing, and I heard the number of those who were sealed.

There is no word here about the signature of the cross; nor is it to be referred only to the Jews who were converted, but to all the faithful persevering in the faith; because those who are not sealed do not belong to the assembly of the Elect: nor was the sealing done here so that they might be exempted from the common evils of the Jews, as that they might be confirmed in the grace of God, 2 Tim. 2:19. Therefore, the interpretation from Eusebius about those who were saved in Pella is vain in this place. How would this sealing fit into a time not only before the siege, but also before the war of the Jews against the Romans, when the same thing is finally commanded here long after those times? Not to mention that there was by no means such a great number of those converted from the Israelites to Christ who moved from Jerusalem to Pella. Furthermore, it is not to be thought that a literal sealing is noted, which was never done to anyone on the forehead; but by this symbol was signified the exemption of the sealed from injury, as certainly some sign, whatever it may have been, was given to those Angels, so that they would not harm those who were marked with the same.

Latin:

Vers. 4. Καὶ ἤκουσα τὸν ἀριθμὸν τῶν ἐσφραγισμένων ἑκατὸν κὶ τεσσαράκοντα τέσσαρες χιλιάδες ἐσφραγισμένοι ἐκ πάσης φυ- λῆς ὑιῶν Ἰσραήλ.] Hanc summam faciunt duodena millia duo- decies, quam deinde scriptor noster in duodecim tribus par- titur : uon quod aut præcise is fuerit numerus omnium, aut in singulis tribubus æqualis: sed quod per talem numerum, ut Græce per μυρίας ingens admodum multitudo exprimatur. Sic de iisdem Judæis in Christum credentibus, πόσαι μυριάδες εἰσὶ; Act. XXI, 50. In Manuscripto desunt illa, καὶ ἤκουσα τὸν ἀριθμὸν τῶν ἐσφραγισμένων.

De signatura crucis nullum hic habetur ver- bum; nec ad Judæos tantum conversos, sed ad omnes fideles in fide perseverantes, ea referenda; quia qui non obsignati sunt, illi non pertineant ad cœtum Electorum: nec tam obsignatio hic facta, ut communibus Judæorum malis eximeren- tur, quam ut confirmarentur de gratia Dei, 2. Tim. II, 19. Vanum ergo hoc loco est interpretamen- tum ex Eusebio de illis, qui sospitati sunt in Pella. Quomodo conveniret hæc obsignatio in tempus non ante obsidionem tantum, sed & ante bellum Judæorum in Romanos, quum longe post illa tempora eadem demum hic præcipiatur? Ut ta- ceam, quod tantus illorum numerus ex Israelitis ad Christum conversis minime fuerit, qui Hiero- solymis Pellam concesserunt. Cæterum non pu- tandum, propriam signationem notari, quæ ne- mini unquam in fronte facta; sed symbolo hoc significata fuit exemptio signatorum à læsione, ut certe Angelis illis aliquod signum, quodcunq; illud fuerit, datum, ne illis, qui eodem notati sunt, nocerent.

## 7:5
Vers. 5. Of the tribe of Judah twelve thousand sealed.] The number twelve always pleased the Jews much on account of the offspring of Jacob. Hence twelve springs in Elim, Exod. XV, 27. Twelve pillars around the altar of Moses, Exod. XXIV, 4. Twelve loaves of the presence, Levit. XXIV, 5. Twelve gems in the breastplate of the High Priest, Exod. XXIV, 4. As many stones in the Jordan, Jos. IV, 2. Victims often in the same number, Num. VII, 3. 87. XXIX, 17. Ezra VIII, 34. and many instruments of the temple, Num. I, 3. 84. 85. 86. Twelve prefects under Solomon, 1 Kings IV, 7. Under the bronze sea twelve oxen, 1 Kings X, 20. Twelve cubits of the altar in length, as many in breadth according to Ezek. XLIII, 17. Jacob had had twelve sons: But when it is a matter of successions, the Levites are omitted and from Joseph two stocks are made, Ephraim and Manasseh, according to the testament of Jacob, which is observed here also. But Levi is numbered here, because in Christ that tribe had a right to a share with the others: but Dan is omitted, because that tribe had long since dwindled to one family, the Hushim, as the Hebrews say, which family itself seems to have perished in wars before the times of Ezra. For in Chronicles, where the posterity of the Patriarchs is recorded, Dan is omitted. And perhaps that is predicted in Amos VIII, verse 14. John of Antioch narrates that few survived from the tribe of Dan, and that they fled into Phoenicia.

Others add this reason for the omitted Danite tribe, that it had long since turned itself away from the worship of the true Israel of GOD through detestable idolatry, and therefore that name had been deservedly omitted, Jud. XVIII, 30. Grotius, the advocate of the Roman curia, seems to have been ashamed of the reason which the Papists are accustomed to assert, namely that that tribe was omitted because the Antichrist is to arise from it. For it does not have any appearance of probability.

Of the tribe of Gad twelve thousand.) No order is preserved, because all are equal in Christ.

Add that it ought to be clear from this that the Israelites according to the flesh are not being regarded here, but the Israel of God, Galat. VI, 16. For Scripture is accustomed to designate things of the New Testament with the names of the Old Testament. And just as the Israelites hoping in the Messiah were the truly faithful people of God, so Christians, named from that promised Messiah Christ, constitute the people of GOD in the New Testament, as many of them as place their trust in Christ, Rom. X, 9. There are also those who seek some rationale of order in the spiritual signification of the names, because in the first place Judah is placed as the acknowledger and confessor of God, Rom. X, 9. 10. Secondly, Reuben, the son who is looked upon, because we cannot be preserved from the harm of demons without the gracious look of God, Psalm XCI, 13. nor does the Lord look upon anyone unless he truly acknowledges and celebrates God, Psalm CIII, 3. 4. Rom. IX, 15. 16. Heb. XI, 6. Thirdly, Gad, from bagad comes a troop, and happily, ἐν τύχῃ as the LXX have it, Gen. XXX, 11. because the faithful fight in troops and happily against spiritual enemies, Apoc. XII, 7. 11. Fourthly, Asher, from the blessedness which is the consequence of that battle and victory, Apoc. XII, 10. Fifthly, Naphtali, from the wrestlings with God, which must be undertaken by the faithful Israelites after the example of Israel, Gen. XXXII, 28. Sixthly, Manasseh, because on account of divine delights they ought to forget the house of their Father, Psalm XLV, 11. & of all his labors, Gen. XLI, 51. Seventh שמעון, because they are certainly heard by God, Ps. XCI, 15. Eighth לוי, from our holier union with God our husband, Is. LIV, 5. Ninth יששכר from reward, which is God himself, Gen. XV, 1. Heb. XI, 6. Tenth זבלון from the dwelling of God in us. For the more we are united to God, and receive his rewards, the more closely we experience him dwelling with us, Jas. IV, 8. Eleventh יוסף because God will at length take away all reproach from his own, Is. XXV, 8. Twelfth בן ימין son of the right hand, because on the last day the faithful shall be set at the right hand of the Lord, Matt. XXV, v. 33. The ancients do not reject this mystical reasoning, to whom Viegas is also added, of whom Cornelius says: Ambrose, Primasius, Rupert, Bede, and Viegas give a mystical cause for this order: Because, they say, in the conversion of man and the spiritual life, the first is Judah, that is, the confession of true faith and of one's own sins. The second is Reuben, that is, son of vision. The sons of vision are the works of the mighty works, which faith itself prescribes. The third is Gad, that is, girded for overcoming temptations. For as the Wise Man says: Son, when you come to the service of God, prepare your soul for temptation. The fourth is Asher, that is, blessed. For blessed is the man, says St. James, who endures temptation: for when he has been proved, he shall receive the crown of life. The fifth is Naphtali, that is, breadth; because he who has overcome the temptations of the heart acquires great breadth and confidence in God. The sixth is Manasseh, that is, forgetfulness, because he who is a victor over temptation experiences divine consolation, and forgets all earthly things. The seventh is Simeon, that is, hearing; because he who forgets earthly things is capable of hearing and perceiving divine things. The eighth is Levi, that is, borrowed; because he who aspires wholly to God considers himself a stranger in the world, and as it were borrowed. The ninth is Issachar, that is, reward, which is amply owed to such a stranger. The tenth is Zebulun, that is, habitation: because God dwells in such a one. The eleventh is Joseph, that is, addition or increase: because such a one increases daily in grace and mighty works. The twelfth is Benjamin, that is, son of the right hand; because such a one is raised to the right hand of God in heaven.

Latin:

Vers. 5. Ἐκ φυλῆς Ἰούδα δώδεκα χιλιάδες ἐσφραγισμένοι.] Numerus duodenarius multum semper placuit Judæis ob Ja- cobi sobolem. Ideo duodecim fontes in Elim, Exod. XV, 27. Duodecim columnæ circa altare Mosis Exod. XXIV, 4. Duo- decim panes προθέσεως, Levit. XXIV, 5. Duodecim gemmæ in pectorali Pontificis, Exod. XXIV, 4. totidem in Jordane lapides, Jos. IV, 2. victimæ sæpe numero eodem, Num. VII, 3. 87. XXIX, 17. Esdræ VIII, 34. & multa templi instrumenta, Num. I, 3. 84. 85. 86. præfecti à Salomone duodecim, 1. Reg. IV, 7. sub mari æneo boves duodecim, 1.Reg. X, 20. Duode- cim cubiti altaris in longum, totidem in latum apud Ezech. XLIII, 17. Filii Jacobo fuerant duodecim: Sed ubi de succes- sionibus agitur, omittuntur Levitæ & de Josepho duæ fiunt stirpes Ephraimi & Manassis ex Jacobi testamento, quod & hic observatur. Sed annumeratur hic Levi, quia in Christo ea tribus pars jus habebat cum cæteris: omittitur vero Dan, quia jam olim ea tribus ad unam familiam Hussim reciderat, ut ajunt Ebræi, quæ ipsa familia bellis interiisse videtur ante Esdræ tempora. Nam in Paralipomenis, ubi posteritas Pa- triarcharum memoratur, Dan omittitur. Et forte id prædi- citur apud Amosum VIII. vers. 14. Ex Danis tribu paucos superfuisse, eosque in Phœnicem profugisse narrat Johannes Antiochenus.

Addunt alii hanc causam omissæ tribus Dani- ticæ, quod illa jam olim sese à veri Israëlis DEI cultu per idololatriam detestandam averterit, idæoque nomen illud omissum merito fuerit, Jud. XIIX, 30. Rationis, quam Pontificii asserre solent, quod nempe ideo omissa sit illa tribus, quod ex eadem Anti-Christus oriturus sit, videtur puduisse Advocatum Romanæ curiæ Grotium. Nec enim ullam illa verisimilitudinis speciem habet.

Ἐκ φυλῆς Γὰδ δώδεκα χιλιάδες.) Nullus servatus ordo, quia omnes in Christo pares.

Adde, quod ita constare debuerit, non respici hic Israelitas secundum carnem, sed Israëlem Dei, Galat. VI, 16. Solet enim Scriptura nominibus Ve- teris Testam. designare res Novi Test. Et uti Israë- litæ in Messiam sperantes populus Dei vere fide- lis erant, sic Christiani à Christo Messia illo pro- misso denominati populum DEI constituunt in N. Testamento, quotquot eorum in Christum fiduciam collocant, Rom. X, 9. Sunt & qui ordi- nis aliquam rationem in fignificatione nominum fpirituali quærunt, quod primo loco יהודה Dei agnitor & confessor pofitus sit, Rom. X, 9. 10. Se- cundo ראובן filius adspectus, quod fine gratiofo DEI afpectu præfervari à damno Dæmonum non possimus, Pfalm. XCI, 13. nec refpiciat quen- quam Dominus, nisi Deum vere agnofcat & ce- lebret, Pfal. CIII, 3. 4. Rom. IX, 15. 16. Ebr. XI, 6. Tertio Gad à בגד venit turma, & feliciter, ἐν τύ- χῃ ut LXX. habent, Gen. XXX, 11. quod fideles turmatim, ac feliciter contra hoftes fpirituales prælientur, Apoc. XII, 7. 11. Quarto אשר à beati- tudine, quæ confequens eft illius prælii, & victo- riæ, Apoc. XII, 10. Quinto נפתלי à luctationibus cum DEO, quæ fidelibus Ifraëlitis obeundæ ad exemplum Ifraëlis, Gen. XXXII, 28. Sexto מנשה quod ob divinas delectationes oblivifci debeant domus Patris sui, Pfalm. XLV, 11. & omnium labo- rum fuorum, Gen. XLI, 55. Septimo שמעון, quod certo à Deo exaudiantur, Pfal. XCI, 15. Octavo לוי, à copulatione noftra cum Deo marito noftro fanctiori, Ef. LII, 5. Nono יששכר à mercede, quæ eft ipfe Deus, Gen. XV, 1. Ebr. XI, 6. Decimo זבלון ab habitatione Dei in nobis. Quanto magis enim Deo copulamur, ejusque præmia percipi- mus: eo propius eum nos cohabitantem experi- mur, Jac. IV, 8. Undecimo יוסף quia auferet Deus tandem omne opprobrium à fuis, Ef. XXV, 8. Duo- decimo בן ימין filius dextræ, quia in noviffimo die fideles ad dextram Domini fiftentur, Matth. XXV. v. 33. Non abnuunt huic rationi myfticæ veteres, quibus accedit etiam Viegas, de quo Cornelius: Myfticam caufam hujus ordinis dat Ambrofius, Primafius, Rupertus, Beda & Viegas: Quia in- quiunt in converfione hominis & vita fpirituali primus eft Judas, id eft, confeffio veræ fidei & pec- catorum fuorum. Secundus eft Ruben, id eft, filius vifionis. Filii vifionis funt opera virtutum, quæ præfcribit ipfa fides. Tertius eft Gad, id est, accin- ctus ad tentationes fuperandas. Nam ut ait Sapi- ens: Fili accedens ad fervitutem Dei, præpara ani- mam tuam ad tentationem. Quartus eft Afer, id eft, beatus. Beatus enim eft vir, ait S. Jacobus, qui fuffert tentationem: quoniam cum probatus fuerit, accipiet coronam vitæ. Quintus eft Nepthali, id eft, latitudo; quia qui vicit tentationes cordis, ma- gnam latitudinem & fiduciam in Deo acquirit. Sextus eft Manaffe, id eft, oblivio, quia qui ten- tationis victor divinam experitur confolationem, terrenorum omnium oblivifcitur. Septimus est Si- meon, id eft, auditio; quia qui terrena oblivifcitur, capax eft, ut audiat & percipiat divina. Octavus eft Levi, id eft, mutuatus; quia qui totus ad Deum adfpirat, peregrinum fe in mundo, & quafi mutua- tum arbitratur. Nonus est Iffafchar, id est, mer- ces, quæ tali peregrino ampla debetur. Decimus est Zabulon, id est, habitatio: quia in tali inhabitat Deus. Undecimus eft Jofeph, id eft, additio vel incrementum: quia talis quotidie gratia & virtute accrefcit. Duo- decimus eft Benjamin, id eft, filius dextræ; quia talis ad dextram Dei evehitur in cælo.

## 7:8
Ver. 8.

Ἐκ φυλῆς Ἰωσὴφ δώδεκα χιλιάδες.] That is, from the tribe of Ephraim: for Manasseh, who himself is also named above from Joseph. Therefore the right of having the name of the firstborn of the father is given, as Amos V, 6. Psalm LXXVIII, 68. Ezek. XXXVII, 16.

Since this enumeration is to be taken generally, and it is signified indefinitely that the number of Israelites, that is, of those who are truly faithful in Christ and conquering through Christ, whom the Lord will preserve for himself from the power of Satan, so that no harm may be brought upon them, will be great: it is manifest that these things are wrongly snatched away to the numerous conversion of the Jews toward the end of the world, about which there is deep silence in the Scriptures. For if this were only about the Jews to be converted to Christ, it would have to be said that the Gentiles are excluded from the number of those sealed with the seal of God, and thus from the Elect of the Lord, 2 Tim. II, 19. How false that is, the following vision of the innumerable crowd seen in heaven from various peoples teaches. Let the Jew Apella believe that at the end of the world 12,000 will be converted to Christ from each of the tribes of the Jews, but that no one from the tribe of Dan will be, as Ribera trifles in this place. Cornelius does not believe that, because it is not likely that from every tribe at the end of the world there will be born and to be saved precisely the same number, so that not even one more is born and saved from Judah than from Reuben or another tribe. It also does not seem worthy of the majesty of the Apocalypse to descend to these minutiae, even if they were true. Secondly, it is not likely that no one from the tribe of Dan is to be saved. For the Danites, when they see the Antichrist killed and themselves deluded by him, will curse him and look to their own salvation. The latter is to oppose trifles with trifles. Furthermore, it would have sufficed, as Cornelius warns, to say: From each of the twelve tribes twelve thousand were sealed, but he repeats this number for each tribe, saying: From the tribe of Judah twelve thousand sealed, from the tribe of Joseph twelve thousand sealed, etc. both because this is the custom of the Hebrews, as I showed Num. VII, 18, and because God, just as much as John, delights in this iteration of the lot of each one so happy and blessed, and as it were takes pleasure with the sealed ones themselves, so that he may signify how much he values them, and at the same time honors and decorates those very ones by addressing and designating them one by one, and indicates that they are most acceptable to him. These things he [says] from Alcazar.

PART II. CONCERNING THE GREAT CROWD IN HEAVEN AND ITS BLESSEDNESS.

Latin:

Verf. 8.

Ἐκ φυλῆς Ἰωσὴφ δώδεκα χιλιάδες.] Id est, ex tribu Ephrai- mi: nam Manaffes, qui & ipfe ex Jofepho fupra nominatus eft. Datur ergo jus habendi πρωτοτόκων patris nomen, ut Amos V, 6. Pfalm. LXXVIII, 68. Ezech. XXXVII, 16.

Quum hæc ἐξαρίθμησις generaliter accipienda fit, & indefinite fignificetur, magnum fore nume- rum Ifraëlitarum, id est, vere fidelium in Chrifto & per Chriftum vincentium, quos à poteftate satanæ sibi præservabit Dominus, ne monumen- tum illis inferatur: manifestum est perperam hæc ad Judæorum numerosam sub finem mundi con- versionem, de qua altum est in Scripturis silen- tium, abripi. Nam si de Judæis hic solum agere- tur ad Christum convertendis, dicendum fuerit, gentes à numero signatorum sigillo DEI, adeoque ab Electis Domini excludi, 2. Tim. II, 19. Quod quam falsum sit, sequens visio de innumera turba è variis populis in cœlo visa edocet. In fine mun- di ex singulis Judæorum tribubus 12. millia ad Christum conversum iri, neminem autem ex tri- bu Dan, ut hoc loco Ribera nugatur, credat Ju- dæus Apella. Non credit id Cornelius, quia non est verisimile, ex qualibet tribu in fine mundi na- scituros æque ac salvandos fore præcise eodem nu- mero, ut ne unus quidem amplius è Juda quam ex Ruben aliave tribu nascatur & salvetur. Non et- iam dignam videtur Apocalypseos Majestate, ad hasce minutias descendere, etiamsi veræ essent. Se- cundo non est verisimile, nullum ex tribu Dan sal- vandum esse. Danitæ enim cum videbunt Anti- Christum occisum, seque ab eo delusos, eum exe- crabuntur & saluti suæ consulent. Quod poste- rius est nugas nugis opponere. Porro suffecisset, monente Cornelio, dicere: Ex singulis duodecim tribubus signati sunt duodecim millia, sed iterat hunc numerum, per singulas tribus, dicendo: Ex tribu Juda duodecim millia signati, ex tribu Jo- seph duodecim millia signati &c. tum quia hic mos est Ebræorum, ut ostendi Num. VII, 18. tum quia Deus æque ac Johannes hac iteratione sortis cujusque tam felicis & beatæ delectatur, & quasi cum ipsis signatis dissuaviatur, ut significet, quanti eos faciat, simulque illos ipsos sigillatim compellando & designando honoret & decoret, sibique acceptissi- mos esse indicet. Hæc ille ex Alcafare.

PARS II. DE TURBA MAGNA IN COELIS EJUS- QUE BEATITUDINE.

## 7:9
Ver. 9.

Μετὰ ταῦτα εἶδον, καὶ ἰδὲ ὄχλος πολὺς, ὃν ἀριθμῆσαι οὐδεὶς ἐδύνατο ἐκ παντὸς ἔθνους καὶ φυλῆς, καὶ γλωσσῶν.] See above V, 9. However, the promise of God made to Abraham is looked back upon. This is referred incidentally to Jewish matters, so that it may be understood how much comfort those exiles from Judea who were Christians had when they saw innumerable companions of their faith from the Gentiles. For Syria was full of Christians. In the Manuscript, in a more Hebraic phrasing: Μετὰ ταῦτα εἶδον ὄχλον πολὺν, καὶ ἀριθμῆσαι οὐδεὶς ἐδύνατο.

How God knows and defends his own in the dangers of this life; whom he not only marks himself, but also seals in his hand, so that he may never forget them, Is. XLIX, 16. the heavenly vision has already taught: It follows therefore how he eternally refreshes those snatched from every affliction after this life, shadowed forth by a new vision. Which, as they altogether cohere in the case of the sealed, defense in this life, and glorification in the other life: So Grotius most absurdly says that this vision is only incidentally joined to the former, and perversely declares it to be about some consolation to be perceived by the Jewish Christians who were exiles from the accession of the nations to the faith of Christ. For the text, clearer than the sun, teaches that the joy not of those still acting on earth, but of those triumphing in heaven, is shadowed forth here. And the difference of both groups is in the open. For that group of the militant Church is contained by a certain number, so that it may be established that God has them in a numbered state, 2. Tim. II. verse 19. although the faithful cannot be numbered in the human manner on earth; yet they do not equal the number of the elect in heaven, who are therefore called innumerable here. The former group is distinguished into certain tribes, because the Churches on earth are separated by their own places and boundaries; but the group of the elect in heaven enjoys the same heaven, the same blessedness in heaven, without any difference of tribes. On earth, a marking is necessary because of the admixture of hypocrites, which has no place in heaven: where the wheat is now separated from the tares, and only the elect have been gathered into the bundle of the living, Matt. XIII, 40. 1 Sam. XXV, v. 29. On earth, the marked are not beyond danger and afflictions: but those who are seen with white robes and palms, no heat burns them any longer, no tears are wrung out.

Standing before the throne and before the Lamb.] That is, having their mind not depressed to the earth, but raised to heavenly things. See above IV, 4. In the Manuscript: Standing upon the throne and before the Lamb. Ἐπὶ with the Genitive often signifies near.

Latin:

Vers. 9.

Μετὰ ταῦτα εἶδον, καὶ ἰδὲ ὄχλος πολὺς, ὃν ἀριθμῆσαι οὐδεὶς ἐδύνατο ἐκ παντὸς ἔθνους καὶ φυλῆς, καὶ γλωσσῶν.] Vide supra V, 9. Respicitur autem promissio Dei, facta Abra- hamo. Hoc obiter ad res Judaicas refertur, ut intelliga- tur, quantum solatium extorres isti ex Judæa Christiani habuerint, cum innumeros viderent ex gentibus suæ fidei consortes. Nam Syria plena erat Christianorum. In Ma- nuscripto locutione magis Ebraica: Μετὰ ταῦτα εἶδον ὄχλον πολὺν, καὶ ἀριθμῆσαι οὐδεὶς ἐδύνατο.

Quomodo Deus suos in hujus vitæ periculis norit, ac defendat; quos non signat tantum ipse, sed etiam in manu sua consignat, ne eorum un- quam obliviscatur, Es. XLIX, 16. jam docuit visio cœlestis: Sequitur itaque quomodo ereptos ex omni afflictione post hanc vitam æternum refi- ciat, nova adumbratum visione. Quæ uti omni- no penes signatos cohærent, defensio in hac vi- ta, & glorificatio in altera vita: Sic perabsurde obiter tantum Grotius hanc visionem priori con- jungi ait, ac perverse declarat illam de solatio aliquo ex accessione gentium ad fidem Christi à Judæis Christianis extorribus percipiendo. Non enim in terra adhuc agentium, sed in cœlo tri- umphantium gaudium hic adumbrari, textus Sole clarior docet. Et differentia utriusque cœtus in aprico est. Ille enim militantis Ecclesiæ cœtus numero certo continetur, ut constet Deum eos in numerato habere, 2. Tim. II. vers. 19. quam- vis humano more numerari nequeant fideles in terris; non tamen exæquare eos numerum electo- rum in cælis, qui proinde innumerabiles hic di- cuntur. Prior cœtus in certas tribus est distinctus, quia separatæ sunt locis & terminis suis Ecclesiæ in terris; at electorum cœtus in cælis sine ulla tribuum differentia eodem gaudet cælo, eadem in cælis beatitudine. In terra signatura opus est ob admixtionem hypocritarum, quæ in cælo nullum locum habet: ubi jam triticum à zizaniis separatum, solique electi in fasciculum viventi- um collecti sunt, Matth. XIII, 40. 1. Sam. XXV. v. 29. In terra signati non sunt extra periculum & afflictiones: at qui cum albis vestibus & palmis visuntur, illos æstus nullus urit amplius, nullæ ex- primuntur lacrymæ.

Ἑστῶτες ἐνώπιον τοῦ θρόνου καὶ ἐνώπιον τοῦ ἀρνίου.] Id est, mentem habentes, non ad terras depressam, sed ad cœlestia erectam. Vide supra IV, 4. In Manuscripto: Ἑστῶ- τα ἐπὶ τοῦ θρόνου καὶ ἐνώπιον τοῦ ἀρνίου. Ἐπὶ cum Genitivo sæpe significat juxta.

## 7:9
And palms in their hands.] The palm is a sign of victory. Gellius III, 6. But just as their own honor was given to the martyrs; so now to the confessors, that is, those who, to bear witness to Christ, had not indeed conquered death, but had conquered either torments, or prison, or poverty, or exiles, reproaches, and other evils of that kind. Here again, as several times above, ἦσαν is understood.

The words as they sound do not concern those who lift up their hearts on high, Col. III, 1, and have their citizenship in heaven, Phil. III, 20, yet still walk by faith, not yet by sight, 2 Cor. V, 7. But they treat of those who already stand before the throne of God in heaven, as is most clear from a comparison of Apoc. IV, 10, c. V, 6. 7, c. XXI, 3. 4, c. XXII, 1, and also from the clothing of the triumphant, Apoc. 3, 5, Cap. 19, 14, and the palm, the sign of victory, which is not perfect except by death, the last enemy, 1 Cor. XV, 26, being overcome, and the epinikion, which is proper not to those militant on earth, but to those triumphant in heaven, who here constitute, as it were, one symphonic choir with the Angels, v. 9. Grotius could have been taught here about the white robes by the Jesuit Cornelius, a friend and supporter of the Jesuits: The white robe, as I said c. VI, 11, was a garment of honor, glory, and triumph. Hence it was a Priestly garment, namely the linen tunic. And this is alluded to here; for he says v. 14, They have washed their robes, etc., therefore they are before the throne of God, and serve him day and night in his temple. For the Saints in heaven will be Kings and Priests of God, as he said c. V, 10. Therefore this robe of the Saints signifies first the purity, chastity, and whiteness of conscience: Secondly, the serenity, cheerfulness, and joy resulting therefrom: Thirdly, happiness and glory: Fourthly, hymns, thanksgivings, and doxologies, which as Priests they will continually sing to God, who gave them victory, triumph, and eternal glory. And we have not yet said anything about the explanation of the heavenly Elder, who those are who are seen here, which is so arranged that it uniquely fits the blessed in heaven, both as to the term from which, whence they came, namely from afflictions, whereas on the contrary travelers here dwell in dangers and calamities, and as to the splendid clothing, that they have made their robes white, not are still making them, by the sprinkling and cleansing of the blood of Christ, 1 John I, 7, Heb. IX, 14, c. X, 22, and as to the term to which, that they are before the throne of God, and in the temple of God, Apoc. XXI, 22, and as to the continuous act, that they serve God nights and days, which does not befit the present life of man, but the other, where there is no weariness day or night, Apoc. IV, 8, and as to the state of blessedness, as far as the Lord is concerned, under whom they dwell most happily. Conf. Ap. 21, 3. 7. & as far as the heap of goods is concerned, with which they abound most abundantly, which are described partly negatively, that neither hunger nor thirst afflicts them, that is, by meiosis, that they will be filled with the satiety of all goods that the faithful can hunger and thirst for, John IV, 14, cap. VI, 13, Matt. V, 6, and that they will be affected by neither the heat of the Sun nor any heat of temptations; but on the contrary the Sun of righteousness will pour upon them light, salvation, and life and joy, Mal. IV, 2, Isa. LX, 19, Ap. XXI, 23, c. XXII, 5, and finally that there will be no cause for tears for them, but tears are to be wiped away, to be changed into laughter, jubilation, and joy, John XVI, 22, Isa. LXV, 13, Luke VI, 21, partly positively, that they are to be fed most sumptuously by the Lamb, who is in the midst of the throne, and refreshed most sweetly by living waters, Apoc. XXI, 4, Ps. XXXVI, 9. John X, 11, of which delights, although the elect perceive a certain foretaste here; yet they will not perceive that fullness, which is expressed here in many and most emphatic words, except in heaven. How jejunely all these things are received by Grotius is placed in the sun's disk. The ancients explain with us concerning the Elect in heaven or the martyrs killed in any century, such as Joachim, or those killed under Diocletian, which pleased Lyranus, or concerning the Gentiles converted to Christ in the time of Constantine the Great, which is the opinion of Aureolus. But Ambrose, Ticonius, and Bede interpret most correctly concerning all the blessed who enjoy the vision of God, whose state and happiness is shadowed here, so that the faithful may not allow themselves to be deterred from the profession of the name of Christ by calamities and afflictions.

Latin:

Καὶ φοίνικες ἐν ταῖς χερσὶν αὐτῶν.] Palma signum victoriæ. Gellius III, 6. Sicut autem martyribus suus datus est ho- nor; ita nunc confessoribus, id est, qui ad testimonium Christo reddendum non quidem mortem vicissent, sed aut tormenta, aut carcerem, aut paupertatem, aut exilia, oppro- bria, & alia id genus mala. Hic rursum, ut supra aliquoties ἦσαν subintelligitur.

Verba prout sonant, non de iis, qui sursum cor- da attollunt, Col. III, 1. & πολίτευμα in cælis ha- bent Phil. III, 20. adhuc tamen per fidem ambu- lant, nondum per speciem, 2. Cor. V, 7. Sed de iis agunt, qui jam coram throno Dei consistunt in cælis, ut luculentissimum est è collatione Apoc. IV, 10. c. V, 6. 7. c. XXI, 3. 4. c. XXII, 1. nec non è vestitu triumphantium, Apoc. 3, 5. Cap. 19, 14. & palma, victoriæ signo, quæ non est perfecta, nisi morte, hoste novissimo, 1. Cor. XV, 26. superata & ἐπινικείῳ, quod non militantium in terris, sed triumphantium in cælis proprium est, qui cum Angelis unum quasi chorum symphoniacum hic constituunt, v. 9. De stolis albis edoceri hic pote- rat Grotius à Jesuita Cornelio, amicus & fautor Jesuitarum: Stola alba, ut dixi c. VI, 11. erat vestis honoris, gloriæ & triumphi. Hinc erat vestis Sacer- dotalis, puta poderis byssina. Et ad hanc hic alludi- tur; ait enim v. 14. Laverunt stolas suas, &c. ideo sunt ante thronum Dei, & serviunt ei die ac nocte in templo ejus. Erunt enim Sancti in cælo Reges & Sacerdotes Dei, ut dixit c. V, 10. Stola ergo hæc San- ctorum significat primo conscientiæ puritatem, casti- tatem, & candorem: Secundo inde consequentem serenitatem, hilaritatem & lætitiam: Tertio feli- citatem & gloriam: Quarto hymnos, gratiarum actiones, & doxologias, quas quasi Sacerdotes jugiter canent Deo, qui eis dedit victoriam, triumphum & gloriam æternam. Nec adhuc quicquam diximus de Senioris cœlestis explicatione, quinam illi sint, qui hic conspecti, quæ sic comparata est, ut unice beatis in cælo conveniat, tum qua termi- num à quo, unde venerint illi, nimirum ex af- flictionibus, quum ex adverso hic viatores in pe- riculis & calamitatibus versentur, tum qua splen- didum vestitum, quod candidas fecerint non ad- huc faciant vestes Agni aspersione ac mundatio- ne sanguinis Christi, 1. Joh. I, 7. Ebr. IX, 14. c. X, 22. tum quoad terminum ad quem, quod coram thro- no Dei sint, & in templo Dei, Apoc. XXI, 22. tum quoad actum continuum, quod noctes atque dies serviant Deo, quod non convenit præsenti homi- nis vitæ, sed alteri, ubi nulla est defatigatio die ac nocte, Apoc. IV, 8. tum quoad beatitudinis sta- tum, quantum ad Dominum, sub quo habitant felicissime. Conf. Ap. 21, 3. 7. & quantum ad bono- rum cumulum, quibus affluunt abundantissime, quæ describuntur partim ἀρνητικῶς, quod nec fa- mes, nec sitis eos anget, id est, per μείωσιν, quod re- plebuntur satietate omnium, quæ esurire & sitire possunt fideles, bonorum, Joh. IV, 14. cap. VI, 13. Matth. V, 6. quodque nec Solis ardore, nec ullo æsta tentationum afficientur; sed ex adverso Sol justitiæ ipsis lucem, salutem & vitam ac lætitiam affusurus sit, Mal. IV, 2. Esa. LX, 19. Ap. XXI, 23. c. XXII, 5. nec denique ulla lacrymarum causa illis futura, sed lacrymæ abstergendæ, in risum, jubilum, & gaudi- um commutandæ sint, Joh. XVI, 22. Es. LXV, 13. Luc. VI, 21. partim θετικῶς, quod ab Agno, qui in medio throni est, & pascendi sint lautissime, & aquis viventibus reficiendi suavissime, Ap. XXI, 4. Ps. XXXVI, 9. Joh. X, 11. quarum delitiarum etsi προποτισμὸν quendam electi hic percipiant; ea ta- men plenitudine, quæ multis maximeque empha- ticis verbis hic exprimitur, non nisi in cœlis per- cepturi sunt. Quæ omnia quam jejune à Gro- tio accipiantur, in Solis disco positum est. Veteres nobiscum de Electis in cœlo vel martyribus quo- libet seculo occisis, utpote Joachimus, vel de oc- cisis sub Diocletiano, quod placuit Lyrano, vel de gentilibus ad Christum tempore Constantini M. conversis, quæ est Aureoli sententia, explicant. Rectissime autem Ambrosius, Ticonius, & Beda de beatis omnibus, qui visione Dei fruuntur, in- terpretantur, quorum status & felicitas hic ad- umbratur, ne calamitatibus & afflictionibus fide- les à professione nominis Christi absterrefi se pa- tiantur.

## 7:10
Vers. 10.

And they cry with a loud voice.] Namely those confessors from the Jews, and those who were gathered from the Gentiles. Salvation to our God who sits upon the throne.] It is a Metonymy. For he calls salvation thanks for the salvation received: Just as power above I, 6, cap. V, 17, is the acknowledgment of power. And to the Lamb.] As above V, 13.

Latin:

Vers. 10.
