Καὶ κράζουσι φωνῇ μεγάλῃ.] Nempe confessores illi ex Judæis, & qui ex gentibus erant aggregati. Ἡ σωτηρία τῷ Θεῷ ἡμῶν τῷ καθημένῳ ἐπὶ τοῦ θρόνου.] Est Metonymia. Nam salutem vocat gratiam ob acceptam salutem: Sicut κράτος supra I, 6. cap. V, 17. est potentiæ agnitio. Καὶ τῷ ἀρνίῳ.] Ut supra V, 13.

## 7:11
Vers. 11.

And all the angels stood round about the throne and the elders and the four living creatures. For the Apostles also, who were at Jerusalem, and the Elders had gone out together. See the same words concerning the Angels above V, 11. And they fell before the throne on their faces, and worshipped God, saying, Amen. Just as the Apostles and Elders approve the song of the Angels in V, 11, 12, 13, 14, so here the Angels sing in response to the confessors, as fellow-citizens of one kingdom.

That cry of a loud voice concerning salvation sounds not in hope, but in reality, not begun, but consummated. For salvation is spoken of by antonomasia, and is to be understood in the most excellent sense: not concerning the preservation of temporal life. Eusebius, who described these things in Book III of Church History, ch. V, does not say that the Apostles and Elders, together with other believers, went out from Jerusalem and entered Pella by divine oracle for the sake of preserving their lives; nay, he testifies in the same place that the destruction of the city was a divine vengeance for the crimes committed both against Christ and against his Apostles, inasmuch as they had taken them from life, just as had been predicted to the Apostles by Christ, John XV, verse 20, Chapter XVI, v. 1, 2.

Latin:

Vers. 11.

Καὶ πάντες οἱ Ἄγγελοι εἱστήκεισαν κύκλῳ τοῦ θρόνου καὶ τῶν πρεσβυτέρων καὶ τῶν τεσσάρων ζώων.] Nam & Apostoli, qui Hierosolymis fuerunt & Presbyteri una erant egressi. Vide eadem verba de Angelis supra V, 11. Καὶ ἔπεσον ἐνώπιον τοῦ θρόνου ἐπὶ τὸ πρόσωπον αὐτῶν, καὶ προσ- εκύνησαν τῷ Θεῷ, λέγοντες, Ἀμήν.] Sicut Angelorum cantum approbant Apostoli & Presbyteri V, 11. 12. 13. 14. sic confesso- ribus accinunt hic Angeli, ut populares unius regni.

Clamor ille vocis magnæ de σωτηρίᾳ non in spe, sed in re, non inchoata, sed consummata sonat. Sa- lus enim κατ᾽ ἀντονομασίαν dicitur, & excellentis- sima ratione exaudienda est: non de temporalis vitæ conservatione. Apostolos & Presbyteros simul cum aliis fidelibus Hierosolymis egressos Pel- lam ex divino oraculo vitæ conservandæ ergo in- gressos esse, non ait Eusebius, qui hæc descripsit lib. III. Hist. Eccl. c. V. imo testatur ibidem excidium urbis ultionem fuisse divinam, ob admissa tum in Christum, tum in ejus Apostolos scelera, utpote quos è vita sustulerant, quemadmodum Aposto- lis à Christo prædictum fuerat, Joh. XV. vers. 20. Cap. XVI. v. 1. 2.

## 7:12
Vers. 12.

Blessing, and glory, and wisdom, and thanksgiving, and honor, and power, and might be unto our God for ever and ever, amen. These are also the words of the Angels explaining that which preceded, Amen. The same words as above V, 12, except that here is thanksgiving, for which there is riches in the same sense there. For thanksgiving is the acknowledgment of liberality, which is called riches by us. That thanksgiving (εὐχαρισία) of words and wealth (πλοῦτος), or the proclamation of the riches of God, confirms what we said above, that the riches of divine grace are being designated. For to this is properly owed thanksgiving (εὐχαρισία), or the act of giving thanks. Regarding the passage, Bernard says in Sermon XIII on the Song of Songs: whence the rivers of thanksgiving go forth, they return, so that they may flow again: In the same way the Apostle says: Giving thanks in all things. Whatever wisdom, whatever virtue you trust you possess, attribute it to the virtue of God, to the wisdom of God, to Christ. Regarding the word Amen, Cornelius says not inappropriately from Alcafar: This repetition of Amen signifies a vehement assertion, arising from a greater penetration and a greater admiration of the divine goodness, which raised miserable men, lost by sin, through the blood and death of Christ to such great salvation and glory.

Latin:

Vers. 12.

Ἡ εὐλογία, καὶ ἡ δόξα καὶ ἡ σοφία, καὶ ἡ εὐχαριστία, καὶ ἡ τιμὴ, καὶ ἡ δύναμις, καὶ ἡ ἰσχὺς τῷ Θεῷ ἡμῶν εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων, ἀμήν.] Sunt hæc quoque verba Angelorum illud, quod ante- cessit, Amen explicantium. Voces eædem, quæ supra V, 12. nisi quod hic εὐχαρισία, pro quo ibi πλοῦτος sensu eodem. Nam εὐχαρισία est agnitio liberalitatis, quæ πλοῦτος nostris dicitur. Illa vocum εὐχαρισία gratiarum actio & πλοῦτος divitiæ, seu divitiarum Dei deprædicatio confir- mat, quod supra diximus, divitias gratiæ divinæ de- signari. Huic enim proprie debetur εὐχαρισία, vel gratiarum actio. Ad locum, ait Bernh. Serm. XIII. in Cant. unde exeunt, revertuntur gratiarum flumi- na, ut iterum fluant: Qualiter dicit Apostolus: In omnibus gratias agentes. Quicquid sapientiæ, quic- quid te virtutis habere, confidis Dei virtuti, Dei sapi- entiæ, deputa Christo. De voce Amen non incom- mode ex Alcafare Cornelius: Hanc Amen iteratio- nem significare vehementer asseverationem, ortam ex majori penetratione, majorique admiratione divinæ bonitatis, quæ homines miseros & peccato perditos per Christi sanguinem & mortem ad tantam salutem & gloriam evexit.

## 7:13
Clothed in white robes.] Illustrious in deeds. See above III, 4. 5. 18. c. IV, 4. c. VI, 11.

Latin:

Περιβεβλημένοι στολὰς λευκὰς.] Illustres factis. Vide supra III, 4. 5. 18. c. IV, 4. c. VI, 11.

## 7:13
Verse 13. And one of the elders answered.] Answered (ἀπεκρίθη) here is simply said, as in Matthew 11:25 and elsewhere, following the example of the Hebrew ענה.

Saying to me, who are these who are clothed in white robes and whence have they come?] That Elder was someone famous for the prophetic gift, by whom even the Apostle is not afraid to be taught, just as Paul was by Agabus. See above 5:5.

Latin:

Vers. 13. Καὶ ἀπεκρίθη εἷς ἐκ τῶν πρεσβυτέρων.] Ἀπεκρίθη hic est simpliciter dixit, ut Matth. XI, 25. & alibi ad Exemplum scilicet Ebræi ענה.

Λέγων μοι, ὗτοι οἱ περιβεβλημένοι τὰς στολὰς λευκὰς τίνες εἰσὶ καὶ πόθεν ἦλθον;] Is Presbyter fuit aliquis Prophetico dono clarus, à quo etiam Apostolus doceri non veretur, ut ab Aga- bo Paulus. Vide supra V, 5.

## 7:14
Verse 14. And I said to him, My Lord, you know.] My Lord, a gentle form of address, as in John 20:15. Thus the Hebrews also say אדני to one unknown.

And he said to me, these are they who come out of the great tribulation.] From those places where Stephen, where James the son of Zebedee were killed; where they themselves lived in the greatest dangers, vexed in every way. See 1 Thessalonians 2:14, Hebrews 10:32, 33.

But whence come those determinations about the places of the dangers of Stephen and James, and why are they referred only to these dangers, and not to the killing, or why are they restricted only to the martyrs; if indeed the entire crowd of the Elect seems to be exhibited here. For they are said to have whitened their robes not in their own blood, but in the blood of the Lamb, and it had already been treated in chapter 6:9 ff. concerning the souls of the martyrs. Not only martyrs, but all the pious come out of afflictions, Acts 14:21, 2 Timothy 3:12, Job 16:20, 21, Romans 8:29, Colossians 1:24, Hebrews 12:2. Grotius therefore assumes those things gratuitously, and without scripture (ἄτερ γραφῆς), and therefore they are rejected with the same ease with which they are asserted.

And they washed their robes, and made them white in the blood of the Lamb.] They washed and made white (ἔπλυναν καὶ ἐλεύκαναν) for having washed they made white (πλύναντες ἐλεύκαναν). And to whiten (λευκαίνειν) here is not to bleach, but to render more adorned. Just as wool becomes more beautiful by the blood of purple, so their garments become more beautiful by the blood of Christ. Moreover, their garments are said to be, that is, their consciences dyed with the blood of Christ, not because they bore death, but because they were near to death, and thus imitated Christ.

Latin:

Vers. 14. Καὶ εἶπον αὐτῷ, Κύριέ με, σὺ οἶδας.] Mi Domine, blanda compellatio, ut Joh. XX, 15. Sic Ebræi etiam ignoto dicunt אדני.

Καὶ εἶπέ μοι, ὗτοί εἰσιν οἱ ἐρχόμενοι ἐκ τῆς θλίψεως τῆς με- γάλης.] Ex illis locis, ubi Stephanus, ubi Jacobus Zebedaides occisi; ubi ipsi vixere in summis periculis, vexati omnibus modis. Vide 1. Thess. II, 14. Ebr. X, 32. 33.

Unde vero illæ determinationes de locis peri- culorum Stephani, & Jacobi, & cur ad pericula tantum hæc, non ad occisionem referuntur, aut cur restringuntur solum ad Martyres; siquidem universa turba Electorum hic exhiberi videatur. Stolas enim non suo, sed Agni sanguine dealbasse dicuntur, actumque jam erat c. VI, 9. seqq. de mar- tyrum animabus. Ex afflictionibus non martyres solum, sed omnes pii veniunt, Act. 14, 21. 2. Tim. 3, 12. Job. 16, 20. 21. Rom. 8, 29. Coloss. 1, 24. Ebr. 12, 2. Gratis ergo assumit illa Grotius, & ἄτερ γραφῆς, ideoq; ea facilitate illa rejiciuntur, qua asseruntur.

Καὶ ἔπλυναν τὰς στολὰς αὐτῶν, καὶ ἐλεύκαναν αὐτὰς ἐν τῷ αἵμα- τι τῦ ἀρνίυ.] Ἔπλυναν καὶ ἐλεύκαναν pro πλύναντες ἐλεύκαναν. Et λευκαίνειν hic non est albare, sed ornatiores reddere. Sicut purpuræ sanguine pulchrior fit lana, ita ipsorum vestes Christi sanguine. Dicuntur autem vestes illorum, id est, conscientiæ tinctæ Christi sanguine, non quod mortem tulerint, sed quod morti proxima, & Christum sic sint imitati.

## 7:15
Verse 15. Therefore they are before the throne of God.] That is, in the sight of God. They are of the highest concern to Him.

This is a remarkable phrase of distortion: to be dyed with the blood of Christ is to be near to death by shedding blood after the example of Christ. Who will bear this depravity? The blood is said to be of the Lamb, who was sacrificed for us: by it, consciences are said to be cleansed from dead works or sins, Hebrews 9:14, because the blood of Christ cleanses us from all sin, 1 John 1:7, because we have been expiated by the blood of the same: for He Himself was made a propitiation for us, 1 John 2:2. Which the Levitical purifications long ago prefigured, whence the Lamb is said to be slain from the foundation of the world, Revelation 13:8, Psalm 51:19, Hebrews 9:14. Concerning which Ambrose says: Because the souls of the elect, which before were wrapped in the blackness of sins, took on the whiteness of purity through the redemption of the blood of Christ: And Haymo: As if it were said: they belong to the number of the Elect for this reason, that they are seen to have been washed in the blood of the Lamb. Therefore, it is not by the imitation of the example of Christ, through which no one arrives at the throne of God, just as no one can imitate His holiness or His patience, or drink the cup of His passion which He Himself drank, even though we ought to drink the one which He offers to us, Matthew 20:22. For that one was so horrible that He Himself tearfully prayed against it three times, Matthew 26:39 ff. But by the application of the merit of Christ we aspire to stand before the throne of GOD, for eternal life in Christ Jesus is a gift (χάρισμα) of God, Romans 6, last verse. But that light interpretation, that to be before the throne of God and the Lamb brings about nothing else than to be in the sight of God and of the highest concern to Him, which finds no parallel passage in Scripture, nor exhausts the emphasis of the words, nor in any way suffices for similar passages, inasmuch as by them the enjoyment of the glorious and most blessed vision of God is accustomed to be designated, which is also expressed by sitting on the throne of Christ. Compare Revelation 4:10, chapter 5:8, 11, chapter 3:21.

And they serve him day and night in his temple.] The same sense as above, ch. 4, 8. And it is a similitude taken from the Levites, of whom some were always keeping watch in the temple, Ps. 136, 1. And it is a silent consolation. The Jewish temple indeed, which is nothing else but wood, δένδρα, will perish, but there will be another temple consisting of pious minds and pure bodies.

All these things correspond to Rev. 4, 8. But there the discourse was concerning the λατρεία in heaven. The saints are indeed called temples of GOD both as to body and as to soul, 1 Cor. 6, 15, 20; ch. 3, 16. But here those victors are said to be in the temple of God, and to serve God in the same, nights and days, which does not befit the state of this life; for night is ordained for rest, day for labor, and it is said of the elect in Rev. 21, 22 that the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are their temple.

And he that sitteth on the throne shall dwell among them.] Σκηνώσει here is, he shall be to them in the place of a tabernacle, he shall protect them against heat and injuries. In this sense שכן is said of the cloud, Num. 9, 18, 22, and is translated σκιάζειν, and Ps. 5, 13 in the Greek is κατασκηνώσεις. In the Latin, which Jerome expressed according to the Hebrew, you shall protect: where in the Hebrew is תסך from סכך which elsewhere is wont to be translated by σκιάζειν, ἐπισκιάζειν, συσκιάζειν, likewise by σκεπᾶν and ἐπισκεπᾶν. The sense is: Here God will keep them safe at Pella from all those evils which await the contumacious Jews in the greatest degree.

That explanation of Grotius concerning security at Pella is too cold, which does not correspond to those magnificent words about him who sits on the throne, who will be in the place of a tabernacle to the elect. Which are explained far more eminently by the heavenly voice, Rev. 21, 3: Behold the tabernacle of God is with men, and he will dwell with them, and they shall be his people, and God himself shall be with them, their God. Therefore, by that σκήνωσις is designated not only divine protection against any adversities whatsoever, but also the illumination of heavenly grace, and the familiar conversation of GOD with the elect, as with members of his household. Compare Isa. 4, 5, 6.

Latin:

Vers. 15. Διὰ τῦτό εἰσιν ἐνώπιον τῦ θρόνε τῦ Θεῦ.] Id est, in conspectu Dei. Summæ illi curæ sunt.

Insignis hæc est phrasis στρεβλότης: sanguine Christi tingi esse ad exemplum Christi sanguinem fundendo morti proximum esse. Quis hanc de- pravationem feret? Sanguis dicitur Agni, qui pro nobis mactatus est: eo tinctæ conscientiæ mun- dari dicuntur ab operibus mortuis seu peccatis, Ebr. IX, 14. quia sanguis Christi emundat nos ab omni peccato, 1. Joh. I, 7. quia expiati sumus per sangui- nem ejusdem: factus enim ipse nobis est propitiatio, 1. Joh. 2, 2. Quod jam olim Leviticæ purificationes præfigurarunt, unde Agnus dicitur occisus ab ori- gine mundi Apoc. 17, 13. Psal. 51, 19. Ebr. 9, 14. Quo de Ambrosius: Quia animæ electorum, quæ antea erant nigredine peccatorum involutæ, per redemptionem san- guinis Christi candorem munditiei affumpserunt: Et Haymo: Ac si diceretur: propterea pertinent ad nu- merum Electorum, quod in sanguine Agni videntur abluti. Non ergo imitatione exempli Christi, per quam nemo ad thronum Dei pervenit, uti nec quisquam vel sanctitatem, vel patientiam ejus imi- tari, vel calicem passionis ejus bibere potest, quem ipse bibit, etsi eum bibere debeamus, quem ipse nobis propinat, Matth. 20, 12. Ille enim tam hor- ribilis fuit, ut ipse eum tribus vicibus flebiliter de- precatus sit, Matth. 26, 39. sqq. Sed applicatione me- riti Christi eo adspiramus, ut coram throno DEI consistamus, χάρισμα enim τῶ Θεῶ est vita æterna in Christo Jesu, Rom. 6. v. ult. Levis autem illa interpretatio, coram throno Dei & Agni esse, nihil aliud infert, quam in conspectu Dei & summæ illi curæ esse, quæ nec in Scriptura ullum parallelum lo- cum reperit, nec emphasin verborum exhaurit, nec similibus locis ullatenus sufficit, utpote quibus fruitio visionis gloriosæ & beatissimæ Dei designari consuevit, quæ etiam per τὸ sedere in throno Chri- sti exprimitur. Conf. Ap. 4, 10. c. 5, 8. 11. c. 3, 21.

Καὶ λατρέυυσιν αὐτῷ ἡμέρας καὶ νυκτὸς ἐν τῷ ναῷ αὐτῶ.] Idem sensus, qui supra cap. 4, 8. Et est similitudo sumpta à Levi- tis, quorum semper aliqui in templo pervigilabant, Pf. 136, 1. Et est tacita consolatio. Templum quidem Judaicum, quod nihil aliud est nisi ligna, δένδρα, peribit, sed erit aliud tem- plum constans ex piis mentibus, purisque corporibus.

Hæc omnia respondent Ap. 4, 8. Ibi autem de λατρείᾳ in cœlis sermo erat. Templa quidem DEI dicuntur Sancti & quoad corpus & quoad animam, 1. Cor. 6,15. 20. c. 3, 16. Sed hic dicuntur victores illi, in templo Dei esse, Deoque in eodem servire, noctes atque dies, quod hujus vitæ statui non congruit; nox enim ordinata est quieti, dies labori, & de ele- ctis dicitur Ap. 21, 12. quod Dominus omnipotens Deus, & Agnus ipsorum templum sit.

Καὶ ὁ καθήμενος ἐπὶ τῶ θρόνω σκηνώσει ἐπ’ αὐτύς.] Σκηνώσει hic est, erit ipsis vice tabernaculi, proteget eos contra æstum & injurias. Hoc sensu שכן dicitur de nube, Num. 9, 18. 22. & vertitur σκιάζειν, & Pf. 5, 13. in Græco est κατασκηνώσεις. In Latino, quod ad Ebræum expressit Hieronym. proteges : ubi in Ebræo תסך à סכך quod alibi verti solet per σκιάζειν, ἐ- πισκιάζειν, συσκιάζειν, item per σκεπᾶν & ἐπισκεπᾶν. Sensus est : Hic Pellæ eos Deus tutos præstabit ab omnibus illis ma- lis, quæ Judæos contumaces manent maxima.

Nimis frigida est illa Grotii de securitate in Pel- læ explicatio, quæ non respondet magnificis istis verbis de sedente in throno, qui tabernaculi vice ele- ctis erit. Quæ longe eminentius exponuntur à voce cœlesti, Ap. 21, 3. ἰδὺ ἡ σκηνὴ τῶ Θεῶ μετὰ τῶν ἀν- θρώπων, ἰ̓ σκηνώσει μετ’ αὐτῶν, ἰ̓ αὐτοὶ λαοὶ αὐτῶ ἔσονται, ἰ̓ αὐτὸς ὁ Θεὸς ἔσται μετ’ αὐτῶν, Θεὸς αὐτῶν. Designatur itaque per illam σκήνωσιν non tantum protectio divina contra quasvis adversitates, sed & cœlestis gratiæ illuminatio, & familiaris DEI cum Electis, ceu domesticis, conversatio. Conf. Efa. 4, 56

## 7:16
Ver. 16. They shall hunger no more, neither thirst any more.) They shall have wherewith to live, who before were often in the greatest penury, see 1 Cor. 4, 11; 2 Cor. 11, 27; Phil. 4, 12.

Neither shall the sun light on them, nor any heat.) They shall lack inconveniences. For the Hebrews are wont to express all inconveniences by heat, whether from the sun or from a burning wind, which the Greek interpreters call καύσωνα, these words and the preceding being taken from Isa. 49, 10, where in the Greek: Neither shall the heat nor the sun smite them: where κάυσων is put for שרב, but elsewhere the same word explains the Hebrew קדים, that is, the East wind, as Job 27, 21; Jer. 18, 17; Ez. 17, 10; ch. 19, 12; Hos. 12, 1; ch. 13, 16. You have a description of both heat, from the sun and from the wind, in Jonah 4, 8.

Latin:

Vers. 16. Οὐ πεινάσωσιν ἔτι, ὐδὲ διψήσωσιν ἔτι.) Habebunt unde vivant, qui antea in summa sæpe fuerunt penuria, vide 1. Cor. 4, 11. 2. Cor. 11, 27. Phil. 4, 12.

Οὐδὲ ἐμὴ πίσῃ ἐπ’ αὐτὺς ἥλιος, ὐδὲ πᾶν καῦμα.) Carebunt incommodis. Nam Ebræi incommoda omnia solent exprime- re per æstum, sive à Sole, sive ab urente vento, quem Græci In- terpretes καύσωνα vocant, desumpta verba hæc & præcedentia ex Esa. 49, 10. ubi in Græco: Οὐδὲ πατάξει αὐτὺς ὁ κάυσων ὐδὲ ὁ ἥλιος: ubi κάυσων ponitur pro שרב, alibi vero eadem vox explicat Ebræam קדים, id est, Eurum, ut Job. 27, 21. Jer. 18, 17. Ez. 17, 10. c. 19, 12. Os. 12, 1. c. 13, 16. Descriptionem utrius- que æstus tum à Sole, tum à vento habes Jon. 4, 9.

## 7:17
Ver. 17. For the Lamb which is in the midst of the throne.) Above ch. 5, 6. He shall feed them, and shall lead them unto living fountains of waters.) So the Latin reads, not as other codices have, living fountains. There will therefore be a transposition for fountains of waters of life, waters of life in the Hebrew manner are living waters, perennial waters, a living stream, as Virgil also speaks. But because it is very sweet to quench thirst with a flowing stream, therefore every consolation and everything that refreshes us is expressed by that image. See Ps. 23, 1; Ps. 36, 9; and 42, 1. And Christ alludes to this in John 4, 10, 11, 14; ch. 7, 38. In Isa. 49, 10, for these words you have: כי מרחמם ינהגם ועל מבועי מים ינהלם. In Greek: He that has mercy on them shall comfort them, and by the fountains of waters shall lead them. In Latin: For he that has mercy on them shall rule them, and shall lead them to the fountains of waters.

And God shall wipe away every tear from their eyes.) From Isa. 25, 8, where in the Greek: The Lord God has taken away every tear from every face. To wipe away sickness, mourning, grief, by a figure drawn from tears, Cicero also said. And there is somewhat more in the word of wiping away, which we have here, than in that of taking away, which Isaiah has. The Apocalypse uses the same expression again below in 21, 4. That remarkable promise is wonderfully emptied: the discourse is about the satiety of heavenly goods for the heavenly Elder; because the question had been instituted concerning the state of those who, having been freed from all afflictions, were established before the throne of God in the heavens. They will not have a desire for earthly things; because in GOD they will have the complement of all goods. Every heat of the Sun is removed, every καῦμα, whether from a burning wind, or from wherever. The καῦμα of the sun is noted in Matt. XIII, 6, and πύρωσις, 1 Pet. I, v. 12. But who in this life is clearly free from every inconvenience? Here the burden and heat of the day must be borne, Matthew XX, 12; there, however, is rest from all labor and troubles, Ap. 14, 13; ch. 21, 4. To which also the latter refers, Isa. 49, 10. Conf. Acts 3, 20, 21. There is no heat there of a restless conscience, of divine wrath, or of the fire of Gehenna, Apoc. XXI, 5. The Lamb is said to be about to shepherd them, who is in the midst of the throne, and to lead them to the fountains of living water. Therefore they are present with the Lamb. Whom, therefore, the Elect are said to follow, Apocal. 14, 3. That fountain of living water is crystalline, proceeding from the throne of God and the Lamb, Apoc. XXII, 1, of the fullest delights and pleasures, with which the elect are to be refreshed, who have come out of the waters of tribulations, to be exhilarated abundantly and forever by the waters of the streams of glorious grace and gracious glory of the Holy Spirit. The wiping away of all tears brings about the exclusion of every kind of sorrow and sadness, or the removal of the cause of all weeping, which happens nowhere in these lands, certainly it does not happen to the faithful saved in Pella, but is to be expected only in the heavens, Isa. LXV, 13; Ap. XXI, 4. Cardinal Vitalis in his moral mirror teaches the beauty of the word of the Holy Scriptures: that spiritual delights are denoted by drink rather than food, for seven reasons and analogies: The first is that drink delights the sight as much by its clarity as by its color. The second, that by its subtlety it changes the taste. The third, that by its limpidity it carries nourishment to individual members and unites it to them inseparably. The fourth, that by its power it restores what was lost. The fifth, that by its subtlety it penetrates the whole body: whence the famished and failing immediately resume vigor and strength upon drinking wine. The sixth, that by its satiety it quenches thirst, and yet provokes an appetite for eating. The seventh, that by its ease and sweetness it easily enters the innermost parts of the belly. He adds to these seven gifts of drink that seven rewards or gifts of the reward of the Blessed are denoted: namely, first, contemplation without discontinuation; second, fruition without interruption; third, love without separation; fourth, power without corruption; fifth, wisdom without concealment; sixth, purification without rebellion; seventh, concord without discretion.

THIRD VISION. THE OPENING OF THE SEVENTH SEAL, AND THE BLAST OF THE SIX TRUMPETER ANGELS.

Latin:

Vers. 17. Ὄτι τὸ ἀρνίον τὸ ἀναμέσον τῶ θρόνυ.) supra c. 5, 6. Ποιμανεῖ αὐτὺς, κὴ ὁδηγήσει αὐτὺς ἐπὶ ζωῆς πηγὰς ὑδάτων.) Sic legit & Latinus, non ut alii Codices habent, ζώσας πηγάς. Erit ergo trajectio pro πηγὰς ὑδάτων ζωῆς, ὕδατα ζωῆς Ebræo more sunt ὕδατα ζῶντα, aquæ perennes, flumen vivum, ut & Virgilius loquitur. Quia vero valde est Dulce, sitim salientis aquæ restinguere rivo, ideo omne solatium & omne id, quod nos recreat, ea imagine exprimitur. Vide Pf. 23, 1. Pf. 32, 9. & 42, 1. Et huc alludit Chri- stus Joh. 4, 10. 11. 14. c. 7, 38. In Esa. 49, 10. pro his verbis habes: כי מרחמם ינהגם ועל מבועי מים ינהלם. Græce : ὁ ἐλεῶν αὐτὺς παρακαλέσει καὶ διὰ πηγῶν ὑδάτων ἄξει αὐτούς. Latine : Quia miserator eorum reget eos, & ad fontes aqua- rum portabit eos.

Καὶ ἐξαλείψει ὁ Θεὸς πᾶν δάκρυον ἐκ τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν αὐτῶν.) Ex Esa. XXV, 8. ubi in Græco: Ἀφεῖλε Κύριος ὁ Θεὸς πᾶν δά- κρυον ἀπὸ παντὸς προσώπε. Abstergere ægritudinem, luctum, dolorem, ducta à lacrymis figura, dixit etiam Cicero. Et est aliquanto plus in verbo abstergendi, quod hic habemus, quam in illo auferendi, quod habet Esaias. Utitur Apocalypsis ea- dem locutione rursus infra XXI, 4. Insignis illa promissio mirum quantum evacua- tur: De satietate bonorum coelestium sermo est Se- niori cœlesti; quia quæstio instituta erat de illorum statu, qui ex afflictionibus omnibus liberati coram throno Dei in cœlis constituti erant. Non habe- bunt rerum terrenarum desiderium; quia in DEO habebunt omnium bonorum complementum. Removetur omnis æstus Solis, omne καῦμα, sive ab urente vento, seu undecunque. Solis καῦμα notatur Matth. XIII, 6. & πύρωσις, 1. Petr. I. v. 12. Quis vero in hac vita ab omni incommodo plane liber est? Hic pondus & æstus diei portandus, Mat- thæi XX, 12. ibi autem requies est ab omni labore & molestiis, Ap. 14, 13. cap. 21, 4. Quo etiam ultima- to respicitur Esa. 49, 10. Conf. Act. 3, 20. 21. Nul- lus ibi æstus inquietæ conscientiæ, iræ divinæ, aut ignis gehennæ, Apoc. XXI, 5. Agnus dicitur il- los pasturus, qui in medio throni est, & ducturus ad fontes aquæ vivæ. Agno ergo adsunt. Quem pro- inde sequi dicuntur Electi, Apocal. 14, 3. Fons ille aquæ vivæ crystallinus est, procedens de throno Dei & Agni, Apoc. XXII, 1. plenissimarum delitiarum & voluptatum, quibus electi reficiendi sunt, qui ex aquis tribulationum venerunt, aquis fluentorum gratiæ gloriosæ & gloriæ gratiosæ Spiritus S. affa- tim, & in æternum exhilarandi. Abstersio omnium lacrymarum, omnimodam mœroris & tristitiæ ex- clusionem, vel causæ omnis lacrymandi remotio- nem infert, quæ nullibi locorum in his terris con- tingit, fidelibus certe in Pella servatis non contin- git, sed in cœlis demum expectanda, Esa. LXV, 13. Ap. XXI, 4. Cardinalis Vitalis in speculo morali S. Scriptorum verbo pulchritudo docet: Delitias spirituales potius denotari per potum, quam cibum, ob septem causas & analogias: Prima est, quod potus tam claritate quam colore delectet aspectum. Secun- da, quod sua subtilitate immutet gustum. Tertia, quod sua limpiditate ad membra singula deportet, cis- que inseparabiliter uniat nutrimentum. Quarta, quod sua potestate restauret deperditum. Quinta, quod sua subtilitate corpus penetret totum: unde famelici & deficientes hausto vino statim resumunt vigorem & vi- res. Sexta, quod sua satietate sedet sitim, & tamen edendi provocet appetitum. Septima, quod sua facili- tate & suavitate facile subeat intima ventris. Addit hisce septem dotibus potus denotari septem præmia vel dotes præmii Beatorum: scil. primo contemplationem sine discontinuatione; secundo fruitionem sine inter- ruptione; tertio dilectionem sine separatione; quar- to potentiam sine corruptione; quinto sapientiam sine occultatione; sexto mundationem sine rebellione; septimo concordiam sine discretione.

VISIO TERTIA. SEPTIMI SIGILLI APERTIO, ET SEX AN- GELORUM TUBICINUM CLANGOR.

## 8:1 Argument
CHAPTER VIII.

ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

After the seventh seal is opened, and the silence of half an hour, seven Angels with trumpets are seen, whose blast, however, is anticipated by another Angel, with a golden censer, and fire poured out onto the earth: but at the first blast, hail and fire with blood consume a third part of the trees, with all the grass: at the second, a mountain burning with fire falls into the sea, and destroys a third part of the creatures in it: at the third blast, a great star falls from heaven, like a torch, infecting a third part of the rivers and fountains with the bitterness of wormwood: At the fourth, a third part of the Sun, Moon, and Stars is darkened, and soon an Angel is seen flying through the heaven, and denouncing a triple Woe to the lands, on account of the three following trumpets. There are two parts: The first is preparatory and historical, concerning the silence of half an hour, and the Angel with the golden censer, to v. 5. The other is Prophetic, concerning the trumpeting of the four Angels with the lesser trumpets, to v. 13.

PART I. PREPARATORY TO THE ANGELIC TRUMPETS.

Vers. 1. And when he opened the seventh seal.] The final decree containing seven parts concerning the clauses of the siege, and the siege of the city of Jerusalem.

There was silence in heaven for about half an hour.] That is, those winds, of which we treated above VII, 1, did not rest for long; Menander also used ἡμιώριον for a minimal time, as Pollux testifies. See Tob. 11, 14. Below, μία ὥρα for a short time, v. 12, ch. 18, 10, 17, 19. The heaven is also said to be silent among the Latins when the winds cease.

Latin:

CAPUT IIX.

ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Post apertum septimum sigillum, & semihorii silentium septem Angeli cum tubis viden- tur, quorum tamen clangorem antevertit alius Angelus, cum aureo thuribulo, & igne in terram effuso: primo autem clangente grando & ignis cum sanguine tertiam par- tem arborum, cum gramine omni consu- mit: secundo mons igne ardens in mare ca- dit, tertiamque partem creaturarum in il- lo perdit: ad tertii clangorem stella magna de cælo decidit, instar facis, tertiam flumi- num & fontium partem amaritudine ab- sinthii inficiens: Ad quarti obtenebratur tertia pars Solis, Lunæ & Stellarum, mox- que conspicitur Angelus per cælum volans, & triplex Væ, ob tres tubas sequentes, ter- ris denuncians. Partes duæ sunt: Prima parascevastica & historica est, de semihorii silentio, & Angelo, cum aureo thu- ribulo, ad v. 5. Altera Prophetica de quatuor Ange- lorum cum tubis minoribus tubicinio, ad v. 13.

PARS I. PRÆPARATORIA AD TUBICINIA ANGELICA.

Vers. 1. Καὶ ὅτε ἤνοιξε τὴν σφραγῖδα τὴν ἑβδόμην.] Ultimum decretum septem partes continens de clausulis obsidii, & ob- sidio urbis Hierosolymorum.

Ἐγένετο σίγη ἐν τῷ ὀρανῷ ὡς ἡμιώριον.] Id est, non diu venti illi, de quibus actum supra VII, 1. quievere, ἡμιώριον pro mini- mo tempore usurpavit & Menander, teste Polluce. Vide Tob. 11, 14. Infra μία ὥρα pro tempore exiguo 17. v. 12. c. 18, 10. 17. 19. Silere cœlum etiam Latinis dicitur, cum cessant venti.

## 8:2
Vers. 2. And I saw the seven angels who stand before God.] Those of the inner admission, of whom we spoke at Matt. 18, 10. God does not use these except for extraordinary matters.

And seven trumpets were given to them.] Trumpets indicate future battles, Jer. 42, 14; Hos. 3, 6; ch. 5, 8, and elsewhere. The hebdomad, as in other things; so where there is mention of plagues, it signifies that nothing is missing. And so those threats of God against the descendants of Jacob are fulfilled here, Levit. 26, 28.

The half-hour interval teaches that a new vision is deservedly begun here. Since, therefore, the seventh seal has now been opened and the whole book fully unsealed, visions concerning the future and the state of the Church, both militant and triumphant, are revealed: just as in the first vision the state of the present Church and in the second the general events of the world, or political evils, were exhibited, or rather bodily calamities and persecutions; which are now followed by ecclesiastical evils and spiritual calamities imminent from heresies. B. Cluverus says that, having premised what pertained to knowing the general face of the world's government, the Holy Spirit now proceeds to the special symbols of the greatest mutations of the world; and that this order can be clearly gathered, among other things, from the fact that upon the opening of the seventh seal the whole book of the judgments of GOD is laid open to the Lamb, and thus provides a distinct reading of the decrees written therein. While it is still closed, the contents cannot but present themselves to the eyes in a somewhat more obscure and confused manner. Grotius repeats his old song about the siege of Jerusalem and pretends that its causes and description are exhibited. For neither trace nor vestige of this is found in the text, nor does it harmonize with either chronology or ecclesiastical history. Nor indeed is a rest from the winds indicated. For those winds were not harmful, but salutary; which therefore the evil Angels were trying to restrain; but they were coerced by the Son of God, the Angel of the covenant of grace. Holy Scripture knows nothing of a septenary of the more intimate admission of Angels: outside of which, in such matters as are of mere revelation, to be wise is to be foolish. Meanwhile, the place and their office indicate that not evil ones, even if they were heralds of evils, much less heretics themselves, were designated by these Angels, but that they were seen to be good Angels, whose office it was to denounce evils, so that they might be the more rightly guarded against and endured. For weapons foreseen do less harm. Trumpets were given to them; just as their use was in declaring wars and dangers, Ezek. 33:3, Amos 3:6, Zeph. 1:15, as also in the excitation of spirits for battles, Job 39:24, Jer. 51:27, 1 Cor. 14:8. But it is rashly asserted that the threats denounced by the trumpet-blasts concern the descendants of Jacob. Why would there be a special account here of those who had already been rejected by the just judgment of God? For by the sound of the trumpets are they warned, and are those informed, whom it also concerns? Why should such intercessory prayers be made, and with an Angel intervening for those hardened, and utterly and almost universally desperate ones, against whom God, as Grotius admits, was no longer willing to restrain His wrath? For prayers ought to be made not against, but according to the divine will. Which could not but be known to the Angel Mediator. For that Angel is μεγάλης βυλῆς, of the great counsel, Is. IX, 6. according to the LXX. Interpreters, the very hypostatic wisdom of GOD, Proverbs VIII, 24. Concerning the silence in heaven for half an hour, we leave aside the futile commentaries of Brightman regarding the three-year tranquility of the Church under Constantine and Licinius, of Lyranus regarding the secret persecution of Julian the Apostate, of Bede and Anselm regarding the rest after the killing of the Anti-Christ, of Rupert regarding the quiet after the day of judgment, and we judge most simply that attention is being excited, or that a tranquility from heresies is designated for a brief interval of time, before those things indicated by the Angelic trumpets break out into violence and disturb the peace of the Church. For if some mystery is to be sought here as well, even though the heresy of the Ebionites had already begun to creep in at that time; yet that which is predicted about the third part of the trees being consumed was still finally to come. If a day is counted for a year, Apoc. XII, 6, a watch, or a fourth part of a day, is to be understood: If the space of two weeks or half a month, half an hour will be a single week. Whence it is evident that whether half an hour is taken in the common sense or the mystical, a very small interval is designated. Concerning the tranquility of the Church, however, Fromondus also explained it with Richard, and judged it to be of only 45 days, namely after the death of the Anti-Christ. But Jerome teaches in the latter chapters that all plagues will follow this quiet. Haymo and Bernard, following Gregory the Great, interpret this silence mystically as the quiet of contemplation, when the soul, by repressing the tumult of thoughts, enters into the secret of internal quiet, as if into a certain silence. More fully: it is a silence 1. Of attention, such as that in Acts XV, 12, ch. XXI, 40. 2. Of admiration, as in Zech. II, 13, Luke II, 19, 47. 3. Of celebration, as in Psalm LXII, 2.

Latin:

Vers. 2. Καὶ εἶδον τὲς ἑπτὰ ἀγγέλες οἳ ἐνώπιον τῶ Θεῶ ἑστήκα- σι.] Illos interioris admissionis, de quibus diximus ad Matth. 18, 10. His Deus non utitur nisi ad res eximias.

Καὶ ἐδόθησαν ἀυτοῖς ἑπτὰ σάλπιγγες.] Tubæ indicant pu- gnas futuras Jer. 42, 14. Ose. 3, 6. c. 5, 8. & alibi. Hebdomas, sicut in rebus aliis; ita ubi plagarum est mentio, significat ni- hil deesse. Itaque implentur hic illæ Dei adversus Jacobi po- steros minæ, Levit. 26, 28.

Novam hic merito inchoari visionem inter- stitium semihorarium docet. Quum ergo jam se- ptimum sigillum apertum, & totus liber plene re- seratus sit; visiones de futuris, & statu Ecclesiæ cum militantis tum triumphantis revelantur: quemad- modum prima visione status Ecclesiæ præsentis, & secunda generalia orbis facta, vel mala Politica exhibita sunt, aut potius calamitates ac persecutio- nes corporales; quas nunc excipiunt mala Ecclesia- stica, & calamitates spirituales ab hæresibus immi- nentes. B. Cluverus præmissis, quæ ad generalem re- giminis mundi faciem cognoscendam spectabant, nunc ad specialia maximarum mundi mutationum symbola Spiritum S. progredi ait; eumque ordinem inter alia luculenter ex eo colligi posse, quod ad septimi sigilli solutionem totus judiciorum DEI liber Agno traditus patescat, adeoque distinctam decretorum ibi- dem scriptorum lectionem suppeditet. Quo adhuc clauso contenta non possunt non obscurius quodam- modo & confusius sese oculis ingerere. Grotius anti- quam suam cantilenam de obsidione Hierosolymorum repetit, ejusque causas & descriptionem exhiberi fingit. Hujus enim in textu nec vola nec vestigium reperitur, neque consonat vel chronologia, vel hi- storia Ecclesiastica. Nec vero quies à ventis indi- catur. Illi enim venti non fuere noxii, sed saluti- feri; quos proinde cohibere mali Angeli conaban- tur; sed coërciti illi à Filio Dei, Angelo fœderis gratiæ. De Angelorum intimioris admissionis septenario Scriptura S. nihil novit: Extra quam in talibus, quæ meræ revelationis sunt, sapere est desipere. Interim non malos, etsi malorum præ- nuncios, nedum hæreticos ipsos designari per hos Angelos, sed visos esse Angelos bonos, locus & offi- cium eorum indicat, quod erat mala denunciare, ut caveri ac sustineri eo rectius possint. Tela enim prævisa minus nocent. Datæ illis tubæ; quemad- modum earum usus erat in bellis & periculis indi- cendis, Ezech. 33, 3. Amos 3, 6. Soph. I, 15. ut & in animorum ad prælia excitatione, Job. 39, 34. Jerem. 51, 27. 1. Cor. 14, 28. Minas autem per tubicinia de- nunciatas Jacobi posteros concernere temere asseri- tur. Cur illorum peculiaris hic haberetur ratio, qui justo Dei judicio jam reprobati erant. Nam clan- gore tubarum monentur, & informantur illi, quos etiam concernit? Cur tales preces intercessoriæ fierent & Angelo interveniente pro istis obduratis, & prorfus ac universaliter fere desperatis, adversus quos Deus, fatente Grotio, non ultra voluit iram suam cohibere? Preces enim fieri debent non contra, sed juxta divinam voluntatem. Quæ Angelo Mediatori non poterat non esse cognita. Est enim Angelus ille μεγάλης βυλῆς, magni consilii, Es. IX, 6. juxta LXX. Interpp. ipsa sapientia DEI hypostatica, Proverb. VIII, 24. De silentio in cœlo semihorario relinquimus commenta futilia Brightmanni de triennali Ecclesiæ sub Constantino & Licinio tranquillitate, Lyrani de clancularia Juliani Apostatæ persecutione, Bedæ & Anshelmi de requie post interfectum Anti-Christum, Ruperti de quiete post diem judicii, & simplicissime censemus attentio- nem excitari, vel ad breve temporis intervallum tranquillitatem ab hæresibus designari, antequam Angelicis tubis indicatæ in nervum erumpant, & quietem Ecclesiæ turbent. Nam si aliquod etiam hic mysterium quærendum, etsi illo tempore jam Ebionitarum hæresis serpere cœperit; id tamen quod de tertia parte arborum consumenda prædicitur, adhuc demum futurum erat. Si dies pro anno numeratur Apoc. XII, 6. vigilia, vel quarta pars diei intelligenda: Si spatium duarum hebdomadum vel dimidii mensis, semihora erit unica hebdomas. Unde constat sive sensu vulgari sumatur semihora, sive mystico, perexiguum intervallum designari. De tranquillitate tamen Ecclesiæ etiam cum Richardo Fromondus exposuit, eamque tantum 45. dierum futurarum censuit, post necem scilicet Anti-Christi. Sed hanc quietem sequuturam omnes plagas Hieronymus circa posteriora capp. docet. Haymo & Bernhardus post Gregorium M. mystice de quiete contemplationis hoc silentium interpretantur, quando anima cogitationum tumultus reprimendo in internæ quietis secretum, quasi in quoddam silentium ingreditur. Plenius: est silentium 1. Attentionis, quale illud Act. XV, 12. cap. XXI, 40. 2. Admirationis, ut Zach. II, 13. Luc. II, 19. 47. 3. Celebrationis, ut Pfalm. LXII, 2.

## 8:3
Ver. 3.

Καὶ ἄλλος Ἄγγελος ἦλθε.] The Angel of the prayers of the Church, as is understood from what follows. The Hebrew book Chasidin and Tertullian on Prayer mention such an Angel.

Καὶ ἐσάθη ἐπὶ τὸ θυσιαστηρίυ.] At the golden altar, on which incense was offered. By that altar, Clement in Strom. VII and Origen understand pious souls: ἐπὶ here is again 'at' or 'by', as we said above VII, 9.

What kind of Angel that is, must be said from nowhere else than the Scriptures: which know no other who, by a diversity of nature, performs the priesthood, and carries out the incense or golden altar and intercession, and makes the pleasing odor ascend to the altar of God, τὴν ὀσμὴν τῆς ἐυωδίας, and carries the prayers of the Saints to God, and makes them pleasing and ratified, than the Angel of the face of the Lord, the Angel Redeemer, the Angel Mediator, the Angel Intercessor, the Angel of the covenant of grace, the bread-basket of divine grace, Christ Jesus, Isa. LXIV, 6, Gen. XLVIII, v. 16, Job XXXIII, 23, Ezek. XXIII, 20, Mal. III, v. 1, John I, 14, 17. Therefore He is said to offer ταῖς προσευχαῖς by the ellipsis of the preposition σὺν, with the prayers. Conf. Lev. XXVI, 24, Deut. XXXII, 43. But by the altar, pious souls are nowhere understood in sacred writings: It is the seat on which sacrifices were offered, θυσιαστήριον, on which incense was offered. Therefore, since spiritual sacrifices are offered in Christ and upon Christ, Christ is compared to the altar, Heb. XIII, 10. Here Christ is said to have approached the altar, by which it is hinted that He wished to perform the parts of a Priest. Something of this kind is read nowhere of any created Angel. He stands at the altar of the divine good pleasure, once promised, now performed, always proposing to the Father ineffably how He, by His decree, suffered and sacrificed for His sheep, fulfilled the will of God, and by sustaining the punishment due to sins, removed all the power of Satan, Psalm CX, 4, Heb. VII, 25, Ch. IX, 24, as here B. Cluverus. Which I approve more than what Andreas has in this place: This altar is Christ, in whom the holy and liturgical virtue of the odor consists, and the martyric offerings are presented. B. Gerhard, p. 58, also teaches that Christ is understood by the Angel, from Blasius de Viegas, p. 340. Most interpreters confess that this Angel is Christ the Lord. Nor can they aptly accommodate to another what is placed in this place. For whose else is it to offer the incense of the universal Church, that is, prayers, in a golden censer under the appearance of such Majesty? Whose is it, except Christ's, to have sent part of the fire, with which the golden censer was filled, onto the earth, and to have inflamed them with the fire of divine love and the ignited gifts of the Holy Spirit. Which Fromondus wrongly and ἄτερ γραφῆς (without Scripture) understands of one from the order of Seraphim, some of Michael, others of Gabriel. For Angels are nowhere said to offer sacrifices, or to procure for them the odor of a good fragrance. The Gloss and Thomas understand the holy Apostles by θυσιαστήριον, Coccejus & Cramer understand the faith of the Saints, Cotterius the death of Christ, Danhawerus and Coccejus the merit of Christ, Doling the necessity of the Saints: But we hinted above that either Christ or His humanity is noted, which pleased most, Primasius, Augustine in Sermon XCVIII de temp., Bullinger, Cornelius à Lapide, etc.

Ἔχων λιβανωτὸν χρυσοῦν.] I think it should be read λιβανωτὸν so that χρυσοῦν is said in the Attic manner. Thus also below in 3, I think it should be read τὴν λιβανωτόν. For in the Glossary, λιβανωτὶς is a censer, a thurible. But λιβανωτὸς is frankincense itself, 1 Paral. IX, 29, in Herodotus, Theophrastus, Galen. The Scholiast on the Clouds of Aristophanes: 'It is one thing to be libanos and another to be libanotos. For libanos is the tree itself, but libanotos is the fruit of the libanos.' Naturally, the more accurate ones distinguished thus. Otherwise, it is certain that libanos is also used for the aromatic. Therefore Ammonius: 'Libanos and libanotos differ. For libanos is commonly both the tree and that which is burned: but libanotos is only that which is burned.' We said above that it is solemn for the Jews to express the things of heaven by the words of the temple, 1 Kings VII, 50, המחתות זהב, in Greek θυίσκαι χρυσαῖ, in Latin censers of purest gold.

Even if elsewhere the word λιβανωτὸς is not used except for the fruit of τοῦ λιβάνου, should the reading, approved by all manuscripts, be corrected for that reason? Should not a metonymy of the container for the thing contained rather be admitted, lest Scripture be altered? Does the Holy Spirit not use the word differently than profane writers? The censer, according to B. Cluver, is the body of Christ, and his heart is truly golden, that is, pure, precious, and incorrupt, which, full of the love of God and of us, offered most effective fragrances or prayers for us, Eph. 5:2.

Καὶ ἐδόθη αὐτῷ θυμιάματα πολλὰ, ἵνα δώσῃ ταῖς προσευχαῖς τῶν ἁγίων πάντων ἐπὶ τὸ θυσιαστήριον τὸ χρυσοῦν τὸ ἐνώπιον τοῦ θρόνου.] The Latin reads τὰς προσευχὰς when it translates concerning prayers. And rightly so. For it is a locution in which the signifier and the signified are intermingled, as if he were saying: He received many incenses, so that he might cast those incenses, which are the prayers of all the saints, upon that altar which is before the throne. Thus above in 5:8, incenses are said to be prayers. Concerning such a mixing of members of the comparison we have spoken at Matt. XXIII, 25. and Heb. IX, 15. 'To give' upon the altar is a term proper to sacred rites. Just as the altar of incense was near to the inner sanctuary, so here it is shown to be near to the throne of God, which corresponds to the inner sanctuary. And it is called the altar of incense, θυσιαστήριον, because not only victims, but whatever is offered to GOD, is called θυσία. In Hebrew also מזבח קטרת.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

Καὶ ἄλλος Ἄγγελος ἦλθε.] Angelus precum Ecclesiæ, ut ex sequentibus intelligitur. Talis Angeli meminit Ebræus liber Chasidin & Tertullianus de Oratione.

Καὶ ἐσάθη ἐπὶ τὸ θυσιαστηρίυ.] Ad altare aureum, in quo suffitus fiebant. Per id altare pios animos intelligunt Clemens Strom. VII. & Origenes: ἐπὶ hic rursus est juxta, ut supra diximus VII, 9.

Qualis Angelus ille sit, non aliunde, quam è Scripturis dicendum est: quæ alium natura diversitate, qui sacerdotio fungatur, thymiamavel altare aureum & intercessionis peragat, gratumque odorem ad altare Dei ascendere faciat τὴν ὀσμὴν τῆς ἐυωδίας, ac preces Sanctorum ad Deum deferat, gratas ac ratas efficiat, nullum alium norunt, quam Angelum faciei Domini, Angelum Redemptorem, Angelum Mediatorem, Angelum Intercessorem, Angelum fœderis gratiæ, divinæ gratiæ panarium Christum Jesum, Esa. LXIV, 6. Gen. XLIIX, v. 16. Job. XXXIII, 23. Ezech. XXIII, 20. Mal. III. v. 1. Joh. I, 14. 17. Ideo dicitur offerre ταῖς προσευχαῖς per ellipsin Præpositionis σὺν cum precibus. Conf. Lev. XXVI, 24. Deut. XXXII, 43. Per altare autem nuspiam pii animi in sacris intelliguntur: Sedes est, in qua offerebantur sacrificia, θυσιαστήριον, in quo suffitus fiebant. Ideo cum in Christum & super Christum sacrificia spiritualia offerantur, altari confertur Christus, Ebr. XIII, 10. Hic ad altare Christus dicitur accessisse, quo in- nuitur, quod voluerit Sacerdotis partes exsequi. Quale quid de nullo creato Angelo uspiam legi- tur. Stat ad altare beneplaciti divini, olim pro- missi, nunc præstiti, proponens semper Patri inenar- rabiliter, quomodo ipsius decreto passus litaverit pro ovibus suis, Dei voluntatem impleverit pœnamque pec- catis debitam sustinendo omnem satanæ potestatem sustulerit, Psalm. CX, 4. Ebr. VII, 25. Cap. IX, 24. ut hic B. Cluverus. Quod magis probo, quam quod hoc loco habet Andreas: Altare hoc Chri- stus est, in quo sancta & liturgica virtus odoris constat, & martyrica hostiæ offeruntur. Christum per Angelum intelligi etiam è Blasio de Viegas p. 340. docet B. Gerhardus p. 58. Hunc Angelum esse Christum Dominum plerique Interpretes confi- tentur. Neque enim alteri apte accommodare pos- sunt, quæ hoc loco ponuntur. Cujus enim alterius est universæ Ecclesiæ incensa, hoc est, orationes in aureo thuribulo tantæ Majestatis specie offerre? Cu- jus est, præterquam Christi, de igne, quo thuribulum aureum erat impletum, partem in terras misisse, eas- que divini amoris igne & ignitis Spiritus S. donis in- flammasse. Quod perperam & ἄτερ γραφῆς de ali- quo ex ordine Seraphinorum Fromondus, de Mi- chaele nonnulli, alii de Gabriele intelligunt. Nu- spiam enim Sacrificia offerre, vel iis odorem bo- næ fragrantiæ conciliare dicuntur Angeli. Glossa & Thomas per θυσιαστήριον S. Apostolos, Coccej. & Cramer. fidem Sanctorum, Cotterius Christi mortem, Danhawerus & Coccejus Christi meritum, Doling. necessitatem Sanctorum intelligunt: Verum notari vel Christum, vel ejus humanitatem supra innui- mus, quod plerisque placuit Primasio, Augustino Serm. XCIIX. de temp. Bullingero, Cornelio à La- pide, &c.

Ἔχων λιβανωτὸν χρυσοῦν.] Puto legendum λιβανωτὸν ita ut χρυσοῦν sit Attice dictum. Sic & infra 3. legendum puto τὴν λιβανωτόν. Nam λιβανο- τὶς acerra, thuribulum in Glossario. At λιβανωτὸς thus ipsum, 1. Paral. IX, 29. Herodoto, Theophrasto, Galeno. Scholiastes ad nebulas Aristophanis: Ἄλλο λίβανος καὶ ἄλλο λιβανωτός. λίβανος μὲν γὰρ αὐτὸ τὸ δένδρον, λιβανωτὸς δὲ ὁ καρπὸς τοῦ λιβάνου. Nimirum sic distingwebant accuratiores. Alioqui certum est etiam pro aromate dici λίβανον. Itaque Ammonius: Λίβανος καὶ λιβανωτὸς διαφέρει. Λίβανος μὲν γὰρ κοινῶς καὶ τὸ δένδρον καὶ τὸ θυμιώμενον: λιβανωτὸς δὲ μόνον τὸ θυμιώμενον. Diximus supra solemne Judæis res cœli per verba templi exprimere, 1. Reg. VII, 50. המחתות זהב, Græce θυίσκαι χρυσαῖ, Latine thuribula de auro pu- risima.

Esto alias non usurpetur vox λιβανωτὸς nisi de fructu τοῦ λιβάνου, num ideo lectio, omnibus codi- cibus probata, corrigenda? Annon metonymia contenti pro continente potius admittenda, ne Scri- ptura immutetur? Annon aliter vocem accipere Spiritus Sanctus, quam prophani Scriptores? Thuribulum B. Cluvero est Christi corpus, & cor ejus est vere aureum, id est, purum, pretiosum & in- corruptum, quod amore Dei & nostri plenum odo- ramenta seu preces efficacissimas pro nobis obtulit, Ephes. V, 2.

Καὶ ἐδόθη αὐτῷ θυμιάματα πολλὰ, ἵνα δώσῃ ταῖς προσευχαῖς τῶν ἁγίων πάντων ἐπὶ τὸ θυσιαστήριον τὸ χρυσοῦν τὸ ἐνώπιον τοῦ θρόνου.] Latinus legit τὰς προσευχὰς cum vertit de orationibus. Et recte. Est enim loquutio, in qua permiscetur significans & significatum, quasi dicat: Accepit multos suffitus, ut eos suffitus, qui sunt omnium Sanctorum preces, injiceret in altare illud, quod est apud solium. Sic supra V, 8. suffitus dicuntur esse preces. De tali permixtione membrorum comparationis diximus ad Matth. XXIII, 25. & Ebr. IX, 15. Dare in aram vox propria sacris. Sicut ara suffituum pro- pinqua erat adyto, ita hic ostenditur propinqua Dei solio, quod adyto respondet. Et dicitur ara suffituum, θυσιαστήριον quia non victimæ tantum, sed quicquid DEO offertur, dici- tur θυσία. Ebraice quoque מזבח קטרט.

## 8:4
Ver. 4.

And the smoke of the incense went up with the prayers of the saints before God.

GOD, delighted by the assiduous piety of the Christians, did not wish to restrain any longer His wrath against the Jews, whose cruelty toward the Christians had been so great. I think the Latin [translator] here read τῆς προσευχῆς τῶν ἁγίων, and rightly so. For in such cases the singular and plural numbers are used interchangeably. And 'that is' or 'that' τῆς προσευχῆς is understood. For it is explained toward what that vision tended.

There is no need for a different reading, which should not have been invented, but asserted by the authority of the codices; whatever the Latin [translator] saw, whose oversights are too frequent, the reading of the authentic text should not be tampered with for his sake, especially because he did not always render word for word. 'Much incense' is said to be given to the Angel, because to him is granted the power of all aromatics to be offered: there was given to him the fullness of grace and εὐωδίας, and the ineffable groanings of the Spirit Himself interceding for us, Rom. VIII, 26, so that he might give to the prayers of the saints the same, that is, so that he might render them prayers of good odor on the altar before the throne, by which they might ascend to God, and God might smell the odor of their sweetness, Gen. VIII, 20. He himself has the most precious aromatics of his own oblation, Eph. V, 2, which he adds to the prayers of the saints, so that they may be effective. For they do not have efficacy, except from the passion and merit of Christ, John XVI, 23. Coloss. III, 17. Heb. XI, 6. The saints, says Albert the Great, commit their prayers to Christ, that He may offer them to the Father. He himself renders them accepted. For Christ, with Primasius as author, stands over the Church, having a golden censer, that is, an immaculate body, conceived by the Holy Spirit coming upon it: which He offered for redeeming the whole world as an oblation and sacrifice to God for an odor of sweetness. But the same is said to have received of the prayers of the Saints, and to have offered them, because through Him the prayers of all can sweetly reach God, Heb. XIII, 15. 1 John II, 2. Conf. Lev. XVI, 13. Therefore, by incense we judge that the burning of incense and the prayers of the faithful are designated together, Apocal. V, 8. Psalm CXLI, 2. Cant. III, 6. Conf. Num. XVI, 46. Forbes distinguishes the odors from the prayers, unlike in Chapter V, and that only to show how and through whom it happens that the prayers of the Saints are odors, that is, pleasing to GOD. To Cotterius it seems an unworthy thing for an Angel to offer prayers, and therefore Christ, he says, breathes a fragrance, with which He imbues and aids the prayers of the Saints approaching the Father in His name.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

Καὶ ἀνέβη ὁ καπνὸς τῶν θυμιαμάτων ταῖς προσευχαῖς τῶν ἁγίων ἐνώπιον τοῦ Θεοῦ.]

DEUS delectatus assidua Christianorum pietate non ultra cohibere voluit iram suam adversus Judæos, quotum tanta in Christianos crudelitas fuerat. Puto Latinum hic legisse τῆς προσευχῆς τῶν ἁγίων, & recte. Nam in talibus numerus singularis & pluralis usurpantur promiscue. Et subauditur τοῦτ' ἔστι, aut illud τῆς προσευχῆς. Explicatur enim quo visum illud tetenderit.

Non opus est diversa lectione, quæ non fin- genda erat, sed codicum autoritate asserenda; quicquid viderit Latinus, cujus παροράματα ni- mis frequentia sunt, in ejus gratiam non solici- tanda lectio textus authentici, imprimis quia non semper verbum verbo reddidit. Data dicuntur Angelo θυμιάματα πολλὰ, quia ipsi potestas omnium aromatum offerendorum concessa est: Data ipsi gratiæ & εὐωδίας plenitudo, ipsiusque Spiritus pro nobis intercedentis gemitus inenarrabi- les, Rom. IIX, 26. ut daret ταῖς προσευχαῖς oratio- nibus sanctorum eadem, id est, ut redderet eas boni odoris preces in altari coram throno, quo ascen- derent ad Deum, & odoraretur Deus odorem sua- vitatis earum, Gen. IIX, 20. Ipse habet aromata pretiosissima suæ oblationis, Eph. V, 2. quæ addit precationibus sanctorum, ut efficaces sint. Nam non habent illæ efficaciam, nisi à Christi passione ac merito, Joh. XVI, 23. Coloss. III, 17. Ebr. XI, 6. Sancti, inquit, Albertus M. orationes suas commit- tunt Christo, ut eas Patri offerat. Ipse eas reddit ac- ceptas. Christus enim Primasio autore, stat super Ecclesiam, habens aureum thuribulum, id est, corpus immaculatum, Spiritu sancto superveniente conce- ptum: Quod pro mundo universo redimendo obtu- lit oblationem & hostiam Deo in odorem suavitatis. Accepisse autem de orationibus Sanctorum idem dicitur, & obtulisse, quia per ipsum omnium pre- ces ad Deum possunt suaviter pervenire, Ebr. XIII, 15. 1. Joh. II, 2. Conf. Lev. XVI, 13. Per thymia- mata itaque suffitus, & preces fidelium cum plerisque designari censemus, Apocal. V, 8. Psalm. CXLI, 2. Cant. III, 6. Conf. Num. XVI, 46. Forbesius odo- res à precibus distinguit secus ac Cap. V. idque tan- tum ad ostendendum, quomodo & per quem eve- niat, ut Sanctorum preces sint odores, id est, DEO gratæ. Cotterio res indigna Angelo altaris videtur offerre preces, ideoque Christus, inquit, spirat ni- dorem, quo preces Sanctorum in nomine ipsius Patrem adeuntium imbuat & juvet.

## 8:5
Ver. 5.

And the Angel took the censer.] The censer, as we have already said.

And he filled it with the fire of the altar.] Read 'it' [feminine], of the sacrificial altar, of course, which is called [the altar] of burnt offerings because of its most important part. The fire, which is on that altar, signifies the wrath of God. See what we have said at Mark IX, 46. And throughout the Prophets fire is the wrath of GOD.

And he cast it into the earth.] Namely that fire or coals, he poured out the wrath of God into Judea. For thus 'earth' is taken in this part of the Apocalypse. Thus fire is poured into Jerusalem, Ezek. X, 2.

And there were voices and thunders.] That is, voices of thunders, as we said above IV, 5, for the same 'voice of thunder' VI, 1.

Καὶ ἀστραπαὶ καὶ σεισμός.] All these things signify that new threats have come from God, namely through many portents, which Josephus records, and Eusebius in his Chronicle, and partly also Tacitus. Thus we have also had lightning and thunder in the sense of threats above at IV, 5. To ἀστραπὰς you may rightly refer the battle lines and gleaming arms seen clashing in the sky, as Tacitus speaks, the fiery sword, as Josephus, and the fact that the temple shone with sudden fire. To βροντὰς & φωνὰς the voice heard in the temple,

μεταβαίνωμεν ἐντεῦθεν, to the earthquake, because the bronze gate opened of its own accord. See Josephus VI, 31. and Tacitus, Histories V.

Why should we introduce another altar here, and not retain the one that was commemorated before? For the Angel Mediator does not pour out the fire of wrath, but of divine love, which he had reconciled with his incense, the effects of which on the earth—not only Judea, but the whole world, because the sound pertains to the whole world—followed, salutary, not destructive. For Φωναὶ βροντῶν are also voices that befit the sons of thunder, that is, the Apostles, as James and John were called by Christ himself, Bnehargem Mark III, 17. as also lightnings, by which they shine on earth with the splendor of virtues, as Gregory Nazianzen says of Basil the Great: His sermon was thunder, and his life was lightning. The Word of the Gospel is also compared to lightning, Matt. XXIV, 27.

But earthquakes are the mystical commotions of the souls of men who have hitherto clung to earthly things, but are converted to God, by which hearts of stone are removed, and hearts of flesh are put in, Ezek. XXXVI, 26. so that they do not seek the things that are on earth, but those that are above in heaven, Coloss. III, 2. That fire is the Spirit of grace and of supplications, Zech. XII, v. 10. which was given in the form of fire, Acts II, 2. it kindles our prayers, Mark IX, 49. John IV, 24. and sent down from heaven it remains with us always in the temple of our heart, just as the sacrificial fire had to be kept continually in the temple, Lev. VI, 13. John XIV, 16. with which the censer of the heart of Christ was filled, Lev. XVI, v. 12. John I, 17. Whence he pours out upon all flesh from the Spirit given to him, John II, 28. Acts II, 17. baptizing with the Spirit and fire, Matt. III, 11. Luke III, 16. Cf. Psalm XXIX, 3, 7. Psalm LXVIII, 43. Luke XII, v. 49. This fire, therefore, sent into the earth illuminates the minds of preachers, as Primasius says here. Blessed Gerhard seems to understand lightnings and voices as referring both to doctrine and to persecutions: After the Apostles received the fire of the Holy Spirit sent down from heaven by Christ, they began to speak in various tongues, which the voices signify, to thunder with preaching, to flash with miracles, and to shake the whole world with the splendor of miracles and the magnitude of doctrine, Acts II, 4. Psalm 68, 34. Most grievous persecutions also followed, by which the whole world was shaken; finally, heresies followed those. Marloratus has similar things to these. But the former explanation is simpler, preserving the unity of sense. Grotius draws everything to the destruction of the city, but with a twisted neck, as they say, and against chronology.

PART II. CONCERNING THE TRUMPETING OF THE FOUR ANGELS. I. CONCERNING THE FIRST TRUMPETING.

Latin:

Vers. 5.

Καὶ εἴληφεν ὁ Ἄγγελος τὸ λιβανωτόν.] Τὸν λιβανωτὸν, ut jam diximus.

Καὶ ἐγέμισεν αὐτὸν ἐκ τοῦ πυρὸς τοῦ θυσιαστηρίου.] Lege αὐτήν altaris scilicet victimarii, quod ex potissima parte τῶν ὁλοκαυ- τωμάτων dicitur. Ignis, qui in eo altari, iram Dei significat. Vide, quæ diximus ad Marcum IX, 46. Et passim in Prophe- tis ignis est DEI ira.

Καὶ ἔβαλεν εἰς τὴν γῆν.] Nempe ignem illum sive carbo- nes, iram Dei effudit in Judæam. Ita enim γῆ sumitur in hac parte Apocalypseos. Sic ignis in Hierosolyma effundi- tur, Ezech. X, 2.

Καὶ ἐγένοντο φωναὶ καὶ βρονταί.] Id est, φωναὶ βροντῶν, ut supra diximus IV, 5. pro eodem φωνὴ βροντῆς VI, 1.

Καὶ ἀστραπαὶ καὶ σεισμός.] Hæc omnia significant novas à Deo minas venisse, per multa nempe ostenta, quæ memo- rat Josephus, & in Chronico Eusebius, partim etiam Taci- tus. Sic fulmina & tonitrua in minarum sentu etiam supra habuimus IV, 5. Ad ἀστραπὰς recte referas visas in cœlo concurrere acies & arma rutilantia, ut Tacitus loquitur, gladium igneum, ut Josephus, & quod subito igne colluxit templum. Ad βροντὰς & φωνὰς vocem in templo auditam,

μεταβαίνωμεν ἐντεῦθεν, ad terræ motum, quod porta ænea sponte patuit. Vide Josephum VI, 31. & Tacitum Historiæ rum V.

Cur hic aliud altare introducamus, nec retinea- mus illud, quod antea commemoratum? Neque enim Angelus Mediator ignem iræ, sed amoris di- vini, quem odoramentis suis conciliarat, effun- dit, cujus effectus in terra non Judaica tantum, sed universa, quia clangor ad totum mundum perti- net, sequuti sunt, salutares, non exitiosi. Nam Φωναὶ βροντῶν, voces etiam sunt, quæ filiis toni- trui conveniunt, hoc est, Apostolis, ut dicti sunt Jacobus & Johannes ab ipso Christo, Bnehargem Marc. III, 17. ut & fulgura, quibus in terris lucent virtutum splendore, ut Gregorius Nazianz. de Basilio M. Sermo ejus tonitru, vitaque fulgur erat. Etiam Verbum Evangelii fulguri confertur, Matth. XXIV, 27.

Terræ motus autem mysticæ sunt commotiones animorum hominum, qui hactenus terrenis ad- hæserunt, sed convertuntur ad Deum, quibus exi- muntur corda lapidea, & induntur corda earnea, Ezech. XXXVI, 26. ut non ea quærant, quæ in terris sunt, sed quæ supra in cælis, Coloss. III, 2. Ignis ille est Spiritus gratiæ & precum, Zach. XII, v. 10. qui in forma ignis datus est, Act. II, 2. preces nostras accendit, Marc. IX, 49. Job. IV, 24. cælo- que demissus nobiscum semper manet in templo cordis nostri, uti ignis sacrificialis jugiter servari debebat in templo, Lev. VI, 13. Job. XIV, 16. quo impletum est thuribulum cordis Christi, Lev. XVI, v. 12. Job. I, 17. Unde de Spiritu sibi donato effu- dit super omnem carnem, Joh. II, 28. Act. II, 17. ba- ptizans Spiritu & igne, Matth. III, 11. Luc. III, 16. Conf. Psal. XXIX, 3. 7. Psal. LXIIX, 43. Luc. XII, v. 49. Hic itaque ignis missus in terram prædicato- rum mentes illuminat, ut hic Primasius. B. Gerhar- dus fulgura & voces tum de doctrina, tum de per- secutionibus intelligere videtur: Postquam Aposto- li ignem Sp. S. à Christo è cælo demissum acceperunt, cœperunt loqui variis linguis, quod significent vo- ces, tonare prædicatione, fulgurare miraculis, ac orbem universum miraculorum splendore & doctri- næ magnitudine concutere, Act. II, 4. Psalm. 68, 34. secutæ etiam sunt gravissimæ persecutiones, quibus totus orbis commotus fuit, illas demum exceperunt hæreses. Quibus gemina habet Marloratus. Sim- plicior autem est prior explicatio, unitatem sen- sus custodiens. Grotius trahit omnia ad excidium urbis, sed collo, quod dicitur, obtorto, & contra Chronologiam.

PARS II. DE QUATUOR ANGELORUM TUBI- CINIO. I. DE PRIMO TUBICINIO.

## 8:6
Verse 6.

Καὶ οἱ ἑπτὰ ἄγγελοι οἱ ἔχοντες τὰς ἑπτὰ σάλπιγγας, ἡ- τοίμασαν ἑαυτὸς ἵνα σαλπίζωσιν.] So that they might give a sign of God's battle against the Jews.

Indeed, all the Angels prepare themselves here: But only four sound with lesser trumpets in this chapter. The remaining three will sound in ch. IX, with greater trumpets announcing a triple woe.

Latin:

Vers. 6.

Καὶ οἱ ἑπτὰ ἄγγελοι οἱ ἔχοντες τὰς ἑπτὰ σάλπιγγας, ἡ- τοίμασαν ἑαυτὸς ἵνα σαλπίζωσιν.] Ut signum darent pugnæ Dei in Judæos.

Præparant quidem hic sese omnes Angeli: Sed clangunt tantum quatuor cum tubis minoribus in hoc capite. Reliqui tres sonabunt c. IX, tubis ma- joribus triplex væ denunciantibus.

## 8:7
Verse 7.

Καὶ πρῶτος ἐσάλπισε, καὶ ἐγένετο χάλαζα, καὶ πῦρ μεμι- γμένον ἐν αἵματι, καὶ ἐβλήθη εἰς τὴν γῆν.] Just as the first horse above shows the reason why the three other horses follow, so here the first trumpeter explains the cause of the others. The earth here, as we have said, is Judea; into it is sent divinely a hardness of heart and a bloodthirsty wrath, which two things appeared so much in the Jews at that time that they never appeared more in any people. Hail, being hard, signifies the hardening of hearts, and below ch. XI, 19. ch. XVI, 21. Bloody fire signifies bloodthirsty wrath notes [it] quite clearly. In the Manuscript it is μεμιγμένα, so that this may refer to hail no less than to fire. And thus the Latin reads. You have hail with fire in Psalm 18:14 & 105:32 & Exod. 9:22.

The angels here are equal and each trumpet blast brings a unique prophecy. It is the function of a trumpet blast to prepare attention. The prophecy then follows. Therefore, there is no need, as some do, to call the angels evil because heresies are already being proclaimed; much less to establish them as the authors of heresies, or to make the heretics themselves the trumpets of evil angels. For they only perform their duty divinely commanded, when the trumpets are given to them, by announcing to the world the spiritual evils that will occur in the Church. But because angels are designated as heralds of the Word according to the interpretation handed down in Apoc. 1, the angel trumpeters seen in the heavens can signify the heralds and Doctors of the Word, who have filled the world with the voices of evangelical preaching by the merit of the sacrifice of Christ performed on the cross, which some wish to be expressed by the censer filled with fire and incense in this place. Yet you might perhaps not incorrectly understand the heresiarchs by the angels. That name certainly gave an opportunity for thinking that these things were said about heretics, although from the name of the star in v. 11 it might seem that a Doctor of the Word, whose appellation this is, is designated, and thus by parity of reasoning, in the remaining trumpets also, angels who are heralds of the word, but of a false name, or Pseudo-Prophets are insinuated. Where, however, it is not necessary to make the angel the same as the star fallen from heaven: since he who predicts these things and he about whom those things were predicted are quite clearly distinguished. And thus Lyranus, Aureolus, and others, both ancient and modern, think that the four angels who blow their trumpets in this chapter 8 denote four heresiarchs according to the letter: Arius, Macedonius, Pelagius, and Eutyches. I do not find that the first trumpeter indicates only the cause of the others. For a parity of every kind is detected here. However, it is not appropriate to restrict the earth, designated indefinitely and universally, to Judea: and the fulfillment teaches that the fates not only of that [land] but of the entire Church are predicted. Although Marloretus produced a similar Gloss: What is said here about hail and fire can be referred to the Jews, who stubbornly resisted the preaching of the Apostles: Whence, provoking divine vengeance upon themselves for the despised admonition of GOD, they fell into miserable calamities. That which is signified by blood and fire and smoke in Joel C. 2 v. 30. To which also those things which Sophonias has in 1:10 seem to pertain. At the same time, John also alludes to those portents that happened either in the flood, or in Sodom, or even in Egypt, just as scripture is accustomed to allude to such things in other places. And they were cast into the earth. Therefore, not by chance but by divine providence and the just judgment of God do such calamities happen to men on account of the contempt of the Gospel, so that we may learn, as often as GOD speaks to us through His servants, to tremble at His word, lest He, deservedly angered by our ingratitude, send various plagues from His treasuries and utterly destroy the rebels. And the third part of the trees was burned up. He threatens a great calamity that will befall mortals, especially the nation of the Jews, who spurn the counsel of GOD in themselves: showing that they will perish by famine, sword, and pestilence, which are understood by hail, blood, and vapor of smoke in Joel Chapter 2 v. 30.

On the other hand, Thomas, the ordinary Gloss, and Pareus explain [these] not as the evils which the Jews suffered, but which they inflicted; who says: Hail is water frozen in the air by cold, harmful to crops. Fire is contrary to hail. Blood is cruelty. Therefore, with the first trumpet sounding, which began with the preaching of the Apostles at Pentecost, hail, fire, and blood fell upon the Apostles, that is, most grave contradictions, dangers, persecutions, exiles, and slaughters occurred from the obstinate Jews. Let us therefore compare the Calvinists among themselves. And those evils were already fulfilled; therefore they are not predicted here. Others, with Foxe and Cocceius, understand the vengeance of God against the Jews. But this had already preceded in the highest degree. Napier [understands] the tyrant Emperors: some [understand] the ten persecutions: Mede, with Andreas, [understands] the irruptions of the Goths from the year of CHRIST 395. Forbes understands the flames of dissensions between bishops: Crugotius [understands] the pride of Victor the Roman Pope and the ignited heresy of Artemon, who was striving to consume the Deity of Christ. But more correctly, hail and fire mixed with blood can be taken as referring to the passive persecutions of Christians, and to the early heresies of Simon Magus, the Ebionites, and the Cerinthians, as was done by Blessed Luther in his Preface to this place, [and by] Osiander, Winckelmann, Cramer, Hoë, Gerhard, Gravius, Cluverius, Dölingius, and Dürfeld. That which Megalander also applies to Tatian. The properties of hail are opposed to rain, through which the irrigation of saving doctrine is expressed in Psalm 68:10, Isaiah 55:10, Hosea 6:3. Therefore, a pestiferous dogma is like hail and fire mixed with blood, which burns up the earth and deprives it of all recreation and solace, and all green grass, that is, not only men devoted to the earth, who were to be lifted up to heavenly things by the fire of love, but they are burned up and perish by the fire of divine wrath, no differently than those who were struck by fiery serpents, Num. 20, had to perish by a poisonous and deadly strike, 2 Pet. 2:3. The mixture of blood with fire and hail makes for a periphrasis of heresy. For those things are most diverse. It is not unusual for rain with blood and separately rain with fire to be sent from heaven: but for them to be sent together, rain, blood, and fire, is perhaps not found. B. Gerhard explained these symbols thus: Those heretics oppressed the seed of the divine Word in the hearts of men with the hail of their false doctrine; with the hail was mixed fire and blood, because they boasted of peculiar revelations and of the multitude of their martyrs. Hail and fire mixed with blood are three symbols of heretical dogma, by which the crop of orthodox doctrine born in the hearts of men is laid low, burned up, and defiled. Some understand by blood the bloody wars and sheddings of blood stirred up by heretics. To which interpretation, sought from B. Luther and Osiander regarding Tatian and the Encratites, we readily assent, as it is fully approved by the Weimar Paraphrasts. B. Gravius extends this to many more heretics, the Encratites being excepted: Such were not only the remnants from the School of the Nicolaitans and the Pseudo-Apostles, but also those succeeding them, the Saturninians, Basilidians, Carpocratians (who were also called Gnostics), and Valentinians and their disciples, the Cerdonians, Marcionites, and the Manichaeans who followed them, who introduced monstrous prodigies of opinions concerning GOD, concerning Christ, concerning creation, concerning Angels, concerning man, concerning sin, etc., by which a third part of the trees, that is, of men, was burned up, that is, seduced and cast down into destruction, and that from hail, fire, and blood mixed and sent to the earth. For just as hail is harmful to crops, so the pernicious doctrine of these heretics was harmful to the Church. Just as hail is sometimes mixed, as it were, with lightning and fire in horrendous storms, so heretics have mixed their dreams with divine miracles and the principles of their own blind reason. Just as hail is said to be mixed with blood, so this heretical doctrine was intermingled with horrendous vices, and introduced a license for sinning, lusts, and atrocious crimes, which are likened to blood and are called in German Blutschulden, by which the trees and green grass, that is, men both famous and common, were corrupted. But the gloss of those who, in Marloratus, understand these to be the heralds who preached in the time of the former world, the confusion of tongues, and the Sodomites, such as Noah, Lot, and others, is highly inappropriate; for these things have already passed away many centuries ago. Nor is the interpretation of the Papists sufficiently consistent, who interpret these things according to the analogy of the plagues in Egypt in Exodus IX, concerning hail and fire, just as they sound. For there, it is a historical account, in which, however, mixed blood does not occur, and it is deservedly understood according to the letter. Here, however, in the divine visions of prophecy, mystical senses prevail: of prophecy, I say: for the case is different when historical matters intervene. B. Cluverus treats the fulfillment of these prophecies at length, bringing forward in the first place the heresiarchs who emerged from the school of Menander, a follower of Simon Magus: Basilides and Saturninus, and so on to the Gnostics and Nicolaitans, etc., with whom should be compared Danaeus, who, in his notes on Augustine’s *De Haeresibus*, assigns the seminaries of those four heresies to: philosophy wrongly used, along with Epiphanius, *Haer.* XXVI, and Tertullian, *lib. contr. Hermog.* and *contr. Marcion.*; Judaism, pride, and unchastity. 2 Pet. II. 10. seqq. Jud. v. 4. seqq. Regarding heresies, these are to be understood from the analogy of the Angels and the Doctors, of the trumpet and the proclamation, and of the great star and the distinguished Doctor of the Church, of the obscuring of the Sun and the doctrine concerning Christ, of the smoke from the abyss and the destructive and idolatrous doctrine, although of a different kind, which it is possible to gather were fulfilled in both the Anti-Christ under the sixth and seventh trumpet.

And the third part of the earth was burnt up) The third part of those dwelling in Judaea was easily inflamed by that smoke. A synecdoche which is explained below in XIII, 12. There is added in the Manuscript: And the third part of the trees, by error, as I think. And all green grass was burnt up) That which was most green, that is, which ought to have been upright, that also was inflamed. Concerning green in this sense, see Luke XXIII. 31. χλωρὸς sometimes signifies pale, as above in VI. 8, sometimes green. The meanings must be distinguished according to the subject matter. It signifies, however, the Priests, who ought to have preceded the others in modesty and a zeal for peace. And it is a mystical explanation of that which we have in Exodus IX. 24. For there is much allusion here to the plagues of Egypt.

It was not by error that this was added in the Manuscript; most other Codices have it. And not only all green grass, by which Grotius understands Priests, others more correctly the simple and plebeian faithful; but also a third part of the trees, that is, of the Doctors and more distinguished magnates, was consumed; which explanation was approved by most. By trees, says B. Gerhard, are denoted the illustrious and powerful: likewise Doctors of the Church, but by grass the humble and plebeian. No longer trees of righteousness, Is. LXI. 3. and green grass, but unfruitful trees, and withered grass, dead to every good. By the third part is signified a great multitude. At the same time it is also hinted that it is not yet a question of the universal apostasy finally to follow under the Anti-Christ.

II. OF THE SECOND TRUMPETING.

Latin:

Vers. 7.

Καὶ πρῶτος ἐσάλπισε, καὶ ἐγένετο χάλαζα, καὶ πῦρ μεμι- γμένον ἐν αἵματι, καὶ ἐβλήθη εἰς τὴν γῆν.] Sicut primus equus supra causam ostendit, cur tres alii equi sequantur, ita hic primus tubicen causam explicat cæterorum. Terræ hic, ut diximus, est Judæa, in eam immittitur divinitus durities animi, & iracundia sanguinaria, quæ duo ita eo tempore in Judæis apparuere, ut nunquam in ullo populo magis. Grando dura, animorum obdurationem significat, & infra c. XI, 19. c. XVI, 21. Ignis sanguineus iracundiam sangui- nariam satis aperte notat. In Manuscripto est μεμιγμένα, ut hoc ad grandinem non minus quam ad ignem referatur. Et sic legit Latinus. Grandinem cum igne habes Psalm. IIX, 14. & CV, 32. & Exod. IX, 22.

Angeli hic pares sunt & quodque tubicinium singularem affert prophetiam. Tubicinii est attentionem parare. Sequitur deinde prophetia. Proinde non opus est, Angelos malos ideo cum nonnullis dicere, quod hæreses jam pronuncien- tur; nedum hæresium Autores illos constituere, vel hæreticos ipsos tubas facere malorum Ange- lorum. Illi enim solum officio suo divinitus mandato, quando tubæ ipsis datæ sunt, fungun- tur, orbi denunciando futura in Ecclesia mala spiritualia.
