Quia vero Angeli præcones Verbi designatur juxta interpretationem Ap. 1. tradi- tam, significare Angeli tubicines veri in cœlis visi possunt præcones & Doctores Verbi, qui orbem Evangelicæ prædicationis vocibus imple- verunt merito sacrificii Christi in cruce peracti, quod per thuribulum hoc loco igne ac thymia- mate repletum exprimi nonnulli volunt. Per Angelos tamen fortassis non inrecte hæresiarchas intelligas. Nomen certe illud ansam dedit co- gitandi hæc dicta esse de hæreticis, quanquam è nomine stellæ v. 11. videri possit Doctorem Verbi, quorum hæc est appellatio, designatum, & ita ex paritate rationis etiam in reliquis tubis angelos præcones verbi, sed falsi nominis, vel Pseudo- Prophetas insinuari. Ubi vero necessum non est angelum eundem cum sidere de cœlo lapso facere: Siquidem haud obscure distinguantur is qui hæc prædicit, & is, de quo ista prædicta sunt. Atque ita existimant Lyranus, Aureolus, & alii tam veteres, quam recentiores, quatuor Angelos, qui hoc cap. IIX. tubas suas inflant, quatuor hæ- resiarchas secundum literam notare, Arium, Ma- cedonium, Pelagium, & Eutychetem. Primum tubicunem causam tantum cæterorum indicare non invenio. Omnimoda enim hic paritas de- prehenditur. Terram autem indefinite ac uni- versaliter designatam ad Judæam restringere haud convenit: nec illius tantum, sed universæ Eccle- siæ fata prædici complementum docet. Quan- quam similem Glossam prodiderit Marloretus: Quod hic de grandine & igne dicitur, ad Judæos re- ferri potest, Apostolorum prædicationi pertinaciter resistentes: Unde divinam in semetipsos ultionem ob contemptam DEI admonitionem provocantes, in miseras inciderunt calamitates. Id, quod per sanguinem & ignem & fumum in Joële significatur C. II. v. 30. Quo etiam pertinere vi- dentur, quæ habet Sophonias I, d. 10. Simul etiam alludit Johannes ad portenta illa sive in diluvio, sive in Sodomis, sive etiam in Ægypto facta, quemad- modum & aliis locis scriptura solet ad hujusmodi alludere. Projectaque sunt in terram. Ergo non fortuito sed divina providentia & justo Dei ju- dicio hujusmodi calamitates hominibus ob Evan- gelii contemptum accidunt, ut discamus, quoties DEUS nobis per servos suos loquitur, ad illius ser- monem contremiscere, ne ingratitudini nostræ me- rito iratus varias plagas è thesauris suis immittat, ac rebelles penitus conficiat. Et tertia pars arbo- rum concremata est. Grandem calamitatem futu- ram mortalibus, imprimis Judæorum genti consilium DEI in se spernentibus minatur: nimirum fame, gladio, & peste perituros ostendens, quæ per gran- dinem, sanguinem & vaporem fumi accipiuntur apud Joëlem Cap. II. v. 30.

De malis contra, non quæ Judæi passi sunt, sed quæ intulerunt, explicant Thomas, Glossa or- din. Pareus; qui: Grando, inquit, est aqua in aëre frigore congelata, segetibus noxia. Ignis con- trarius grandini. Sanguis sævitia est. Ergo clangente tuba prima, quæ cum prædicatione Apostolorum in Pentecoste cæpit, grando, ignis, sanguis super Apostolos cecidit, hoc est, gravissimæ contradictiones, pericula, persecutiones, exilia, cæ- des evenerunt, à pervicacibus Judæis. Commit- tamus ergo inter se Calvinianos. Et erant jam illa mala adimpleta; non ergo hic prædicuntur. Alii cum Foxo, & Coccejo vindictam Dei contra Judæos intelligunt. Sed hæc jam præcesserat in supremo gradu. Napeirus Tyrannos Imperato- res: Nonnulli decem persecutiones: Medus cum Andrea irruptiones Gothorum ab anno CHRISTI 395. Forbesius dissensionum flammas inter Episco- pos: Crugotius superbiam Victoris P. R. & igni- tam hæresin Artemonis Deitatem Christi con- sumere satagentis intelligunt. Sed rectius grando & ignis admixtus cum sanguine de Chri- stianorum persecutionibus passivis accipi possunt, & de hæresibus primis Simonis Magi, Ebionita- rum & Cerinthianorum, ut factum à B. Luthero in Præfat. in h. l. Osiandro, Winckelmanno, Cræ- mero, Hoë̈o Gerhardo, Gravio, Cluvero, Dölingio, Dürfeld. Id quod etiam Tatiano applicat Me- galander. Grandinis proprietates pluviæ, per quam doctrinæ salutaris irrigatio exprimitur Psalm. LXVIII. vers. 10. Esa. LV. vers. 10. Hoseæ VI. vers. 3. adversantur. Grandinis ergo instar est, & ignis sanguine mixti dogma pestife- rum, quod terram exurit, omnique recreatione ac solatio privat, & viride gramen omne, hoc est, non tantum homines terræ deditos, qui erant igne amoris attollendi ad cœlestia, igne autem iræ divinæ exuruntur, & pereunt, non secus at- que illis, qui à serpentibus ignitis icti erant, Num. XX. venenato ac mortifero ictu pereun- dum fuit, 2. Petr. II. vers. 3. Sanguinis mixtura cum igne & grandine facit ad periphrasin hære- seos. Diversissima enim illa sunt. Pluviam cum sanguine ac seorsim pluviam cum igne demitti cœlitus, non insolens est: sed illa con- junctim dimitti, pluviam, sanguinem & ignem, forte non invenitur. B. Gerhardus hæc sym- bola ita exposuit: Hæretici illi grandine falsæ suæ doctrinæ semen Verbi divini in cordibus homi- num oppressærunt, cum grandine fuit mixtus ignis & sanguis, quia gloriati sunt de peculiaribus revelationibus ac de multitudine suorum marty- rum. Grando ac ignis mixta sanguine sunt tria symbola dogmatis hæretici, quo seges doctrinæ or- thodoxæ in cordibus hominum nata prosternitur, exuritur & fœdatur. Quidam per sanguinem intelligunt bella cruenta & sanguinis effusiones ab hæreticis excitatas. Cui interpretationi è B. Lu- thero, & Osiandro quoad Tatianum & Encrati- tas petitæ à Vinariensibus Paraphrastis ex asse ap- probatæ facile annuimus. Encratistis demptis ad plures hæreticos extendit B. Gravius: Qua- les non tantum fuerunt ex Schola Nicolaitarum & Pseudo-Apostolorum reliquiæ, sed etiam his succe- dentes Saturniniani, Basilidiani, Carpocratiani (qui & Gnostici dicti fuerunt) & Valentiniani eorumque discipuli, Cerdoniani, Marcionitæ, eos- que secuti Manichæi, qui monstrosa opinionum de DEO, de Christo, de creatione, de Angelis, de ho- mine, de peccato, &c. introduxerunt prodigia, qui- bus tertia pars arborum, hoc est, hominum concrema- ta, hoc est, seducta & in exitium præcipitata est, id- que ex grandine, igne & sanguine mixta & in terram missa. Quemadmodum enim grando no- xia est frugibus: Ita perniciosa horum hæreticorum doctrina noxia fuit Ecclesiæ. Sicut grando inter- dum in horrendis tempestatibus fulgure & igne quasi miscetur: Ita hæretici sua somnia miscuerunt cum divinis miraculis, & cæcæ rationis suæ princi- piis. Sicut grando mixta dicitur sanguine: Ita doctrina hæc hæretica permixta fuit horrendis vi- tiis, & peccandi licentiam, libidines &, atrocia scele- ra, quæ sanguini conferuntur, & Germanice Blut- schulden appellantur, introduxit, quibus arbores & fœnum viride, hoc est, homines tam celebres, quam plebeji fuere corrupti. Valde autem inconveni- ens est illorum Glossa, qui apud Marloratum eos Præcones intelligunt, qui tempore prioris mundi, confusionis linguarum & Sodomorum prædicarunt, utpote Noam, Lothum, & alios: Hæc enim a mul- tis seculis jam præterita sunt. Neque satis conve- nit Pontificiorum interpretatio, qui hæc ad analo- giam plagarum in Ægypto Exod. IX. de grandi- ne & igne, prout sonant, interpretantur. Nam illic historica relatio, in qua tamen sanguis admixtus non occurrit, merito secundum literam intelligi- tur. Hic vero in visionibus divinis prophetiæ mystici sensus obtinent: Prophetiæ, inquam: Alia enim ratio est, cum interveniunt historica. Complementum harum prophetiarum exequi- tur prolixe B. Cluverus e Menandri, Simonis Ma- gi sectatoris, schola egressos Hæresiarchas: Basiliden & Saturninum primo loco adducens, & ita porro Gnosticos & Nicolaitas &c. quo cum conferatur Danæus, qui ad Augustin. de hæresib. Seminaria hæresium istarum quatuor assignat male usurpa- tam Philosophiam, cum Epiph. hær. XXVI. & Ter- tull. lib. contr. Hermog. & contr. Marcion. Ju- daismum, superbiam, & impudicitiam. 2. Petr. II. 10. seqq. Jud. v. 4. seqq. De hæresibus autem hæc ac- cipienda ex analogia Angelorum, & Doctorum, tubæ & præconii, & stellæ magnæ ac Doctoris insignis Ecclesiæ, obscurationis Solis & doctrinæ de Christo, fumi ex abysso, & doctrinæ exitiosæ & idololatricæ, licet diversi generis, sub sexta & septi- ma tuba in Anti-Christo utroque impleta colli- gere est.

Καὶ τὸ τρίτον τῆς γῆς κατεκάη) Inflammata fuit eo fumo facile pars tertia in Judæa habitantium. Συνεκδοχὴ quæ ex- plicatur infra XIII, 12. Additur in Manuscripto: Καὶ τὸ τρίτον τῶν δένδρων per errorem, ut puto. Καὶ πᾶς χόρτος χλωρὸς κατεκάη) Quod maxime viride, id est, probum esse debuit, id quoque inflammatum est. De viridi in hoc sensu vide Luc. XXIII. 31. χλωρὸς modo palli- dum significat, ut supra VI. 8. modo virens. Significatio- nes pro materia distinguendæ. Significat autem Sacerdo- tes, qui modestia & pacis studio anteire cæteros debuerant. Et est mystica explicatio ejus, quod habemus Exod. IX. 24. Multa enim hic est ad Ægypti plagas allusio.

Non per errorem id in Manuscripto additum; habent alii Codices plerique. Neque tantum omnem gramen viride, per quod Sacerdotes intel- ligit Grotius, alii rectius fideles rudes & plebe- jos; sed etiam tertia pars arborum, id est, Docto- rum & magnatum insigniorum consumpta; quæ explicatio plerisque probata fuit. Per arbores, inquit B. Gerhardus, notantur illustres ac potentes: item Ecclesiæ Doctores, per gramen vero humiles & plebeji. Non amplius arbores justitiæ, Es. LXI. 3. & viride gramen, sed arbores infrugiferæ, & gramen arefactum, ad omne bonum emortuum. Per ter- tiam partem significatur magna multitudo. Simul etiam innuitur, nondum agi de universali apostasia sub Anti-Christo demum secutura.

II. DE SECUNDO TUBICINIO.

## 8:8
Ver. 8. And the second angel sounded, and as it were a great mountain burning was cast into the sea)

Ὄρος καιόμενον הר שרפ Jer. LI. 25. is the casting of a mountain into the sea, Ps. XLVI. 7. This mountain is the Antonia, a fortress near the temple. For it is common for the Prophets to give the name of mountains to fortresses, Is. XIII. 2, Ezek. XXXVIII. 20, Mic. I. v. 4, c. II. v. 12, c. V. v. 1, Amos VI. v. 1, Obad. I. v. 8, 9. Again, by fortresses are understood those who dwelt in the fortresses, as appears in those same passages. Wherefore, just as by the mountain Antonia is to be understood, so by the Antonia are to be understood the soldiers who were in the Antonia, who all poured forth with great anger upon the Jerusalemite people, who are here called by the name of the sea, as above VII. v. 1, 3. See what is said there, and above IV. v. 6, and Dan. IV. 2. The event which is here predicted is the same as that narrated by Josephus in Antiquities XX. 4, and in Jewish War I. 10.

Καὶ ἐγένετο τὸ τρίτον τῆς θαλάσσης αἷμα) A great part of the people were either slain or wounded.

Latin:

Vers. 8. Καὶ ὁ δεύτερος ἄγγελος ἐσάλπισε, καὶ ὡς ὄρος μέγα καιόμενον ἐβλήθη εἰς τὴν θάλασσαν)

Ὄρος καιόμενον הר שרפ Jer. LI. 25. montis jactus in mare est Ps. XLVI. 7. Mons iste est Antonia arx vicina templo. Nam arcibus dare montium nomen frequens Prophetis, Es. XIII. 2. Ezech. XXXVIII. 20. Mich. I. vers. 4. c. II. vers. 12. c. V. vers. 1. Amos VI. vers. 1. Abd. I. v. 8. 9. Rursus per arces intelliguntur ii, qui in arcibus habitabant, ut iisdem locis apparet. Quare sicut per montem intelligenda Antonia; ita per Antoniam intelligendi milites, qui in Antonia erant, qui omnes magna cum ira effusi in populum Hierosolymitanum, qui hic maris vocatur nomine, ut supra VII. v. 1. 3. Vide ibi dicta, & supra IV. v. 6. & Dan. IV. 2. Res quæ hic prædicitur, eadem narratur a Josepho antiquæ historiæ XX. 4. Belli vero Judaici I. 10.

Καὶ ἐγένετο τὸ τρίτον τῆς θαλάσσης αἷμα) Magna pars populi aut cæsa, aut vulnerata.

## 8:9
Καὶ ἀπέθανε τὸ τρίτον τῶν κτισμάτων ἐν τῇ θαλάσσῃ τὰ ἔχοντα ψυχὰς) Josephus says that twenty thousand men perished, partly by slaughter and partly by the collapse of a tower, but Eusebius says thirty thousand. Add also a huge number of cattle, prepared for sacrifices.

And the third of the ships were destroyed) Understand many vessels of the temple, plundered by the soldiers. Just as the people are the sea, so movable goods are the ships.

Although this Gloss, which is not found in Marloratus, as the preceding one is, may seem specious—for it explains this as the mountain, that is, the Roman kingdom, being cast into the vast sea of the kingdom of Christ and being absorbed by it—it is by no means to be approved. For what was the point of presenting things that had already been fulfilled, wrapped in such riddles, and predicting them as if they were future? And if mountain or citadel is taken literally, why is sea explained figuratively? If sea is the people, why are the ships in the sea taken not from the vessels of the city or the people, but of divine worship or the temple? By the burning mountain, Cocceius understands the Roman war against the Jews under Titus Vespasian and the destruction of the Jewish polity; Wolterus, Napeirus, Medus, Forbesius, and Pezelius understand the fire of the ambition of the Bishops; Crugotius understands the burning heresy of Arius; Pareus understands the Roman Empire raging against the Christians; others understand the devastation of Italy by barbarian nations. We, from the analogy of the remaining trumpets, and especially the third concerning the star or Doctor of great brightness, and the two last concerning both Antichrists, understand these concerning heretics, following the preceding ones under the first trumpeter with most Interpreters and Doctors. Although some of them explain it as Arius, who, because of his pride and great authority in the Church, is compared to a great mountain, and indeed a burning fire, because the fire of this heresy began to have great growth in a short time. Blessed Luther, whom most of our countrymen, Osiander, and Winckelmann [follow]. Hoë, Gerhardus, Gravius, Kromayer; Bullinger, likewise Szegedinus, follow [the interpretation] concerning Cerdon, Marcion, and Lyra, and Blessed Danhauerus concerning Montanus and the Cataphrygians, to whom they add the Peputians, fanatics, Enthusiasts, and Antinomians, who boasted of ecstasies and revelations and were established in great authority, and for that reason are compared to a great mountain; from whom, however, Cluverus departed, explaining it as internal discords and horrendous slaughters from the end of the reign of Alexander Severus up to Aurelian. To not a few of the ancients, such as Ticonius, Primasius, Bede, Anselm, the interlinear Gloss, Thomas, and Viega, that mountain is the Devil himself, great because of pride, burning because of envy, by whose torches he is inflamed, who lay upon the Church through tyrants and strove to oppress it. But it was previously noted that the trumpeting Angels sound heresies, not persecutions, even though persecutions could have been joined to them, just as some say that the persecutions stirred up by the Manichaeans are denoted by blood: which, however, is rather a symbol of heretical dogma infecting the sea of the world with blood, because fish cannot live in a bloody sea, but die. Ships are particular Churches fluctuating in the dangerous sea of the world. The third part is said to be corrupted διεφθάρη, the Vulgate rendered it perished. Which shows the fulfillment of the aforementioned heresies. For many particular Churches, which previously were Christ's little ships, occupied by these heresies, made shipwreck of the faith, 1 Tim. 1:19. Many, who on account of the reputation of their doctrine and holiness stood out among the rest like ships, and in the sea of the Church ought to have sailed into the harbor of salvation, snatched away by the force of the tempest and dashed against the rocks of persecution, made shipwreck of the faith, as blessed Gerhard has it here: For the principal Churches throughout Asia Minor had been infected. Tertullian himself, an excellent Doctor of the primitive Church, was seduced by a Montanist through Paul. See Eusebius, book V, ch. 16. It wandered most widely, as Danaeus teaches, p. 59. The heresy of the Marcionites, and as Epiphanius says, this poison pervaded Rome itself, Italy, Egypt, Thebais, Arabia, Palestine, Cyprus, and finally Persia, a most remote nation. This evil also raged in the Church for a very long time, so much so that it lasted even to our own times. Although indeed the Emperor of the Christians immediately restrained it with the most severe laws, yet it erupted even in the times of Constantine the Great, as Eusebius writes in his life, book 3, and in the time of the Emperor Arcadius, while Theodoret, Bishop of Cyrus, was living, who says that he had seen men of this sect, book 5, Hist. ch. 31, and in his book of heretical fables he commemorates the response of a certain old Marcionite, who washed his hands in the morning with spittle and not with water, so as not to use the things of the Creator. Finally, Epiphanius writes that in his own century there were still some Marcionites born in Rome. As a viper brings forth vipers, so this heresy brought forth many heresies, and its school had very many and most audacious men as successors, among whom these were the first and principal ones: a certain Lucianus, Potitus, Blastus, Synerus, Prepo, Pithon, Hermogenes, Afer, Apelles, and others. Finally, this heresy was at last interpolated with the new name of adversaries of the Law and the Prophets, which kind of men Augustine had as an enemy in his own century.

III. ON THE THIRD TRUMPET-BLAST.

Latin:

Καὶ ἀπέθανε τὸ τρίτον τῶν κτισμάτων ἐν τῇ θαλάσσῃ τὰ ἔχοντα ψυχὰς) Hominum interiisse partim cæde, partim collapsa turri viginti millia, ait Josephus, at Eusebius triginta millia. Adde & pecudum ingentem numerum, paratarum ad sacra.

Καὶ τὸ τρίτον τῶν πλοίων διεφθάρησαν) Intellige multa vasa templi, a militibus direpta. Sicut populus mare, ita res mobiles navigia.

Etsi speciosa videatur hæc Glossa, quæ in Marlvrato non reperitur, ut præcedens: hic enim de monte, id est, regno Romano in mare vastissimum regni Christi præcipitando, & ab eodem absorben do explicat: nullatenus tamen probanda. Quid enim attinebat ea, quæ jam impleta erant, talibus gryphis involuta exhibere, ac ceu futura prædicere? Et si mons vel arx proprie accipitur, cur mare improprie explicatur? Si mare est populus, cur naves in mari de vasis non urbis vel populi, sed cultus divini vel templi accipiuntur? Per montem igneum Alcafar Romanorum bellum contra Judæos sub Tito Vespasiano, politiæ Judaicæ destructionem Coccejus, ignem ambitionis Episcoporum Wolterus, Napeirus, Medus, Forbesius, Pezelius, hæresin Arii ardentem Crugotius, Pareus Rom. Imperium sæviens contra Christianos, alii Italiæ devastationem per gentes barbaras intelligunt. Nos ex analogia reliquarum tubarum, & cumprimis tertiæ de stella vel Doctore magnæ claritatis, & duarum ultimarum de Anti-Christo utroque hæc de hæreticis, præcedentes sub primo tubicinio sequutos cum plerisque Interpp. & Doctoribus intelligimus. Quamvis eorum nonnulli de Ario, qui propter fastum, & autoritatem magnam in Ecclesia magno monti, comparetur, & quidem igne ardenti, quia ignis hærefeos hujus brevi tempore magna cœpit incrementa, explicent. B. Lutherus, quem plerique nostrates, Osiander, Winckelmann. Hoë, Gerhardus, Gravius, Kromayer; Bullinger, item Szegedinus sequuntur, de Cordone, Marcione & Lyra, & B. Danhauerus de Montano & Cataphrigibus, quibus addunt & Peputianos, fanaticos, Enthusiastas, Antinomos, accipiunt, qui ἐκςάσεις & revelationes jactitarunt, & in magna autoritate constituti fuere, atque idcirco magno monti comparantur, a quibus tamen abiit Cluverus, de intestinis discordiis, & horrendis cladibus inde a fine imperii Alexandri Severi ad Aurelianum usque exponens. Non paucis veterum, ut Ticonio, Primafio, Bedæ, Anshelmo, Glossæ interlin. Thomæ, Viegæ mons ille est ipse Diabolus, magnus ob superbiam, ardens ob invidiam, cujus facibus inflammatur, nuncupatus qui per tyrannos Ecclesiæ incubuit, eamque opprimere sategit. Sed Angelos tubicines hæreses clangere, non persecutiones, antea monitum, etsi illis junctæ esse potuerint persecutiones, quomodo nonnulli a Manichæis excitatas persecutiones sanguine denotari ajunt: quod tamen symbolum potius est dogmatis hæretici sanguine mare mundi infici- entis, quia in mari sanguineo vivere nequeunt pisces, sed moriuntur. Naves sunt particulares Ecclesiæ in periculoso mundi mari fluctuantes. Tertia pars dicitur corrupta esse διεφθάρη, Vulg. reddidit interiit. Quod complementum prædi- ctarum hæresium ostendit. Multæ enim Eccle- siæ particulares, quæ prius fuere Christi navicu- læ, per has hæreses occupatæ fidei naufragium fecerunt, 1. Tim. I. 19. Multi, qui propter doctri- næ & sanctitatis opinionem inter cæteros emine- bant instar navium, & in Ecclesiæ mari in portum salutis religios velare debuissent, vi tempestatis abrepti, & ad persecutionis scopulos allisi fidei nau- fragium fecerunt, ut hic habet B. Gerhardus: In- fectæ enim erant per Asiam minorem Ecclesiæ præcipuæ. Tertullianus ipse eximius Ecclesiæ primitivæ Doctor a Paulo Montanista seductus est. Vid. Euseb. l. V. c. 16. Latissime vagata est, docente Danæo p. 59. Marcionitarum hæ- resis, & ut ait Epiphanius Romam ipsam, Italiam, Ægyptum, Thebaida, Arabiam, Palæstinam, Cy- prum, denique Persidem remotissimam gentem per- vasit hoc venenum. Diutissime etiam hoc malum in Ecclesia grassatum est, adeo ut ad nostra usque tempora duraverit. Quanquam vero Imperator Christianorum severissimis legibus statim coërcere- tur, tamen etiam Constantini Magni temporibus erupit, ut in ejus vita libr 3. scribit Euseb. & tem- pore Arcadii Imperatoris, vivente Theodoreto, Cy- ri Episcopo, qui se hujus sectæ homines vidisse ait, lib. 5. Hist. c. 31. & lib. fabul. hæretic. commemo- rat responsum senis cujusdam Marcionitæ, qui ma- ne sputo non autem aqua manus suas abluebat, ne rebus Creatoris uteretur. Denique Epiphanius scribit suo seculo adhuc quosdam Marcionitas Ro- mæ natos fuisse. Multas hæreses uti vipera vipe- ras, sic hæc hæresis peperit, & successores scholæ plu- rimos audacissimosque homines habuit, inter quos bi fuere primi & præcipui. Lucianus quidam, Po- titus, Blastus, Synerus, Prepo, Pithon, Hermogenes, Afer, Apelles & alii. Denique interpolata tan- dem est hæc hæresis novo nomine adversariorum legis & Prophetarum, quod genus hominum suo seculo inimicum habuit Augustinus.

III. DE TERTIO TUBICINIO.

## 8:10
Ver. 10. And the third angel sounded, and there fell from heaven a great star)

Falling stars are often Doctors who have strayed from the truth. Note, however, that Egyptian impostor here, of whom Acts 21:38, in Josephus, Antiquities of the Jews 20.6, Jewish War 2.27, who says that he was considered a prophet by his own people.

Burning as a lamp) In the manner of a conflagration, proceeding far and wide.

And it fell upon the third part of the rivers and the fountains) excluded from the city, he invaded smaller towns and villages, which are thus rivers and fountains, just as a great city is the sea.

Latin:

Vers. 10. Καὶ ὁ τρίτθ Ἄγγελος ἐσάλπισε, καὶ ἔπεσεν ἐκ τῶ ὐρανῶ ἀστὴρ μέγας)

Stellæ cadentes sæpe sunt Doctores a vero devii. Nota- tur autem hic Ægyptius ille impostor, de quo Act. XXI. 38. apud Josephum antiquæ historiæ XX. 6. Belli Judaici II. 27. qui eum a suis Prophetam habitum dicit.

Καιόμενος ὡς λαμπάς) Incendii in modum, longe late- que procedens.

Καὶ ἔπεσεν ἐπὶ τὸ τρίτον τῶν ποταμῶν καὶ τὰς πηγὰς) ex ur- be exclusus minora oppida & vicos invasit, qui sic flumina & fontes, quomodo magna civitas mare.

## 8:11
Ver. 11.

And the name of the star is called Wormwood) perhaps its name was Schibu, which signifies a kind of wormwood in those parts. And I doubt whether it should have been written here ὁ ἀψίνθιΘ: and soon after eis ἀψίνθιον, because ἄψινθος is the name of a city, whence the name of the herb, growing there, is ἀψίνθιον. And the third part of the waters became wormwood) A great part of the Jews began to follow him first, then also to imitate his deeds: who were called assassins. A bitter grape, Deut. 32:32. He has made me drunk with wormwood, Lam. 3:15. It is, however, a Hebrew idiom: it has become into wormwood, that is, it has been turned into wormwood. And many of the men died from the waters, because they were made bitter) Many perished through men, infected by that faction: clearly just as those who drink infected waters are accustomed to perish:

That Egyptian impostor had already perished long before this vision happened to St. John. Concerning an eminent Doctor of the Church, because Doctors are designated by stars, Interpreters commonly explain it, Marloratus concerning heretics in general. Most almost all agree with blessed Luther, Flacius, Osiander, Aegidius Hunnius, Winckelmann, Gerhard, Quistorpius, Cluverus, Dannhauer, Gravius, Dürfeld, Döling, Kromejer, etc., regarding Origen, some regarding Paul of Samosata. Both fit these aptly, especially if Origen paved the way for the Arians by denying or calling into doubt the divine nature of Christ, concerning which, however, there is still a significant controversy among the learned, and elsewhere, namely in the confession of the Martyrs, our opinion has been stated. Origen was certainly a great star from Egypt, ὠγύ- & γέννομαι, son of the Sun, a great Doctor in the Church, on account of his remarkable erudition and manifold writings, whence he was formerly called χαλκέντερΘ Adamantius, and his illustrious fame, which the Hexapla in particular rendered celebrated, concerning whom Jerome says that he wrote as many volumes as no one could read, and the saying is well known: Where Origen is good, no one is better; where he is bad, no one is worse. For he was truly wormwood, and that of a deadly kind, just as Scripture uses this word concerning deadly and fatal bitterness, as in Deut. XXIX. 10, Heb. XII. 5, Prov. V. 4. and in the dogmas of the faith, for example, in the creation of all souls at the beginning of the world and their mission into bodies as a place of punishment, concerning the μετεμψυχώσει and the transition of rational souls even into brute animals, in the denial of the resurrection of this flesh, in the future salvation of demons, for whom Christ would suffer in the air, in free will, in the perfection of good works, and in satisfaction through one's own meritorious works, in election made on account of merits, in certain sins that pass with us to be purged by the torture of fire, in the lack of remaining forgiveness for those who have relapsed after baptism; and in corrupting the meanings of Scripture through various allegories, which Athanasius attributes to him. Whence in the Second Council of Constantinople his books were condemned, though not equally he himself, whether out of reverence for his name and his various merits in the Church, or out of hope for his repentance, or out of the presumption that the Origenian writings had been corrupted and interpolated by others infected with heresy, and that the author was innocent, or for whatever other reason the attendees thought he should be spared, among whom he undoubtedly had many disciples. Other errors of Origen are also recounted, primarily by Jerome. Regarding creation, he attributes this error to him in his Epistle and Apology to Avitus: He asserts that there are innumerable worlds, not, according to Epicurus, many at one time and similar to one another, but that after the end of one world there is the beginning of another, etc. The firmament, that is, the heaven, is hell in comparison to the higher heaven. And against Rufinus: Angels turned into human souls; angels are not only around us, but also within us. Devils, just as the impious, are still to be saved. Concerning the ruin of souls from heaven, according to Jerome to Pammachius, souls existed before bodies and did something, because of which they are bound to gross bodies. See also Augustine, book XI of The City of God, ch. 23. Epiphanius, Vol. II, book 1, concerning this error of his. In the Epistle to Avitus: Souls, after they have attained salvation, will no longer be souls. Theophilus of Alexandria, concerning the providence of God, reports that Origen taught that it does not extend to all creatures, and that God dwells only in the regions of the heavens, which was a denial of divine immensity: he never seems to have understood the power of original sin: whence he attributes to the saints after the fall that same perfection which Adam had before he fell: he established purgatory as the punishment for sins, asserted the possibility of fulfilling the law, as well as the perfection of free will in spiritual matters, and made good works the cause of justification, and attributed the indwelling of God to our merits, he handed down only one penance for more serious offenses; he felt that Baptism would be necessary after the resurrection, he was too superstitious in external exercises, he slept not in a bed, but on the pavement; he endured in cold and nakedness, he abstained from wine and oil, he used one garment without shoes, he admitted no anxiety about the morrow: That he might be a Eunuch, he cut off for himself the member by which we are men: He said that the resurrection of our bodies would be such that they would not have the same members. All of which testify how truly the doctrine of Origen was wormwood, even if he perhaps thought correctly about the Holy Trinity.

is book V. of the History, chapter 35. and the scholastic fountains are twin with the Ecclesiastical streams, Psalm LXVIII. v. 27. John VII. v. 38. Isaiah XI. v. 9. chapter XLIV. v. 30. c. XLIX. v. 10.

IV. CONCERNING THE FOURTH TRUMPET.

Latin:

Vers. 11.

Καὶ τὸ ὄνομα τῶ ἀστέρΘ λέγεται ἄψινθος) forte nomen ei fuit Schibu, quod absinthii genus in illis partibus significat. Et dubito annon hic scriptum fuerit ὁ ἀψίνθιΘ: & mox eis ἀψίνθιον, quia ἄψινθος nomen urbis est, unde nomen her- bæ, ibi provenienti, ἀψίνθιον. Καὶ ἐγένετο τὸ τρίτον τῶν ὑδάτων εἰς ἄψινθιον) Magna pars Judæorum cœpit eum sequi primum, deinde & facta ejus imitari: qui dicti sicarii. Uva amara, Deut. XXXII. 32. Ine- briavit me absinthio. Lam. III. 15. Est autem Ebræa locutio: facta est in absinthium, id est, in absinthium versa est. Καὶ πολλοὶ τῶν ἀνθρώπων ἀπέθανον ἐκ τῶν ὑδάτων, ὅτι ἐπι- κράνθησαν) Multi interiere per homines, illa factione con- tactos: plane sicut perire solent, qui aquas infectas bibunt:

Ægyptius ille impostor jam pridem perie- rat, quum hæc visio S. Johanni contingeret. De Doctore insigni Ecclesiæ, quia stellis desi- gnantur Doctores, communiter Interpretes ex- plicant, Marloratus de hæreticis in genere. Ple- rique fere cum B. Luthero, Flacius, Osiander, Ægidius Hunnius, Winckelmannus, Gerhardus, Quistorpius, Cluverus, Dannhauerus, Gravius, Dürfeld, Döling, Kromejer, &c. de Origene, non- nulli de Paulo Samosateno. Utrique hæc apte conveniunt, imprimis si Origenes Arianis negan- do vel in dubium vocando divinam Christi na- turam prælusit, de quo vero penes eruditos in- signis adhuc est controversia, & alibi, in confessio- ne nempe Martyrum, nostra dicta est sententia. Origenes certe sidus magnum ab Ægypto ὠγύ- & γέννομαι Solis filius, magnus in Ecclesia Doctor fuit, ob insignem eruditionem, scripta multiva- ria, unde χαλκέντερΘ Adamantius antehac di- ctus, & illustrem famam, quem Hexapla impri- mis celebrem reddidere, de quo Hieron. quod tot scripserit volumina, quot nemo legere possit, notumque est diverbium: Origenes ubi bene, ne- mo melius, ubi male, nemo pejus. Vere enim ab- sinthium fuit, idque ferale, uti hac voce Scriptu- ra de ferali ac funesta acerbitate utitur, utpote Deut. XXIX. 10. Ebr. XII. 5. Prov. V. 4. & in dogmatibus fidei, verbi gratia, animarum omni- um sub initium mundi creatione, & in corpora im- missione pœna loco destinata, de μετεμψυχώσει ac transitu animarum rationalium, etiam in bruta animantia, negata carnis hujus resurrectione, de salvatione futura Dæmonum, pro quibus Christus passurus sit in aëre, de libero arbitrio, perfectione bonorum operum, & satisfactione per opera propria meritoria, electione ob merita facta, peccatis quibus- dam nobiscum transituris incendii cruciatu pur- gandis, de non reliqua relapsis post baptismata venia; & in corrumpendis per allegorias varias Scripturæ sententiis, quod Athanasius ei tribuit. Unde in Concilio Constantinopolitano II. libri ejus con- demnati sunt, non æque ipse sive ob nominis reverentiam & varia in Ecclesia merita, sive ob spem pœnitentiæ, sive ob præsumptionem de vitiatis & interpolatis ab aliis hæresi infectis scriptis Origenianis, autorisque innocentia, seu quacunque alia de causa ipsi parcendum duxe- rint Adscessores, in quibus sine dubio multos ha- buit Discipulos. Recensentur & alii errores Origenis imprimis ab Hieronymo. De creatio- ne hunc ei errorem tribuit Epist. & Apolog. Avit. Mundos asserit innumerabiles, non juxta Epi- curum uno tempore plurimos, & sui similes; sed post alterius mundi finem alterius esse principium &c. firmamentum, id est, cælum ad comparationem su- perioris cæli esse inferos. Et adv. Ruffin. Ange- los versos in animas hominum: Angelos non tantum circa nos esse, sed etiam intra nos. Dia- bolos, sicut & impios adhuc salvandos. De anima- rum ruina de cælo teste Hieronymo ad Pamm. ani- mas fuisse ante corpora, & egisse aliquid, quod sint crassis corporibus alligatæ. Vid. & August. l. XI. de Civit. Dei c. 23. Epiphanius T. II. l. 1. de hoc errore ejusdem. In Epist. ad Avit. Animas, posteaquam salutem consecuta fuerint, amplius non futuras animas. Theophil. Alexandr. de provi- dentia Dei Origenem tradit docuisse, eandem non extendere ad omnes creaturas, Deumque in cælo- rum tantum regionibus commorari, quæ fuiset im- mensitatis divinæ negatio : peccati originalis vim nunquam videtur intellexisse : unde lanctis post lapsum eam adhuc perfectionem tribuit , quam Adam habuit, antequam laberetur : pœnam pec- catorum statuit purgatorium, legis implendæ pos- sibilitatem asseruit, ut & liberi arbitrii in spiri- tualibus perfectionem, causamq; justificationis fe- cit bona opera, & inhabitationem Dei nostris me- ritis tribuit, unam tantum pœnitentiam in delictis gravioribus tradidit; Baptismum necessarium fore post resurrectionem sensit , in exercitiis externis nimis superstitiosus fuit, non in lecto, sed in pa- vimento dormiit; in frigore & nuditate duravit, vino oleoq; abstinuit, una usus est veste sine calceis, nihil de crastino solicitudinis admisit : Ut Eunu- chus esset , membrum, quo viri sumus, sibi absci- dit: Resurrectionem corporum nostrorum fic fu- suram dixit, ut eadem membra non habcant. Quæ omnia quam vere absinthium fuerit Origenis do- ctrina, etiansi de SS. Trinitate fortallis recte sen- serit, testantur.

est lib. V. Histor. cap. 35. fontesque scholastici stu- minibus Ecclesiasticis gemini , Psalm. LXVIII. v. 27. Johan. VII. v. 38. Esa. XI. v. 9. cap. XLIV. v. 30. c. XLIX. v. 10.

IV. DE QUARTO TUBICINIO.

## 8:12
Verse 12.

And the fourth Angel sounded, and the third part of the sun was smitten, and the third part of the moon, and the third part of the stars, that the third part of them might be darkened. Just as the earth is said to recede for those sailing; so for those pressed by calamity, the Sun, Moon, and stars are said to set. See what we have said at Matthew XXIV. v. 29. Add the Chaldean Paraphrast on Isaiah XIII. v. 10. & Jeremiah XV. v. 9. The darkness of the Sun, Moon, and stars signifies destruction, Achmet CLXVI. The towns of Galilee and other parts are signified here, captured by Vespasian with the death of very many Jews. The history can be seen in Josephus, book four of the Jewish War. Because a third part of Judea fell into this calamity at that time, therefore the stars are said to have failed by a third part of themselves. For ἵνα σκοτισθῇ in the Manuscript there is ἵνα μὴ φαίνῃ. And the day might not shine for a third part of it. It is a Hebraism for the third part of the day might not shine, that is, the third part of the day was lacking its usual brightness. And the night likewise. The brightness of the night also was less than usual by a third part. The meaning is: In a third part of Judea, both works ceased, and journeys, which were accustomed to be performed more by day, and the latter by night in those places. A lesser evil indeed than in Egypt, Exodus X, 22, yet approaching it.

But concerning Paul of Samosata, it is certain that he denied the pre-eternal existence of the Son of God, and made Christ a mere man, as far as nature is concerned. This was his chief heresy. He wanted to be considered like a great mountain, more a Duke than a Bishop. He was accustomed to walk with a great crowd, and to dictate and read letters in the street out of pure pride of learning, just as he distributed wealth out of affected and proud munificence, in the Pharisaic manner. From that, however, as Danaeus has it on page 111, the Samosatene first deceived himself and others, because, as Theodoret writes, book II. Heretical Fables, being an ambitious and haughty man, but already Bishop of the Church of Antioch, he wanted to win over and curry favor with Zenobia, the most powerful Queen of Arabia, Syria, and Phoenicia, who favored the errors of the Jews concerning Christ, i.e., to serve the Princes and the court, he secretly said that he felt the same about Christ as the Jews, and Zenobia herself, the Prince of the region. Concerning which, although often admonished by neighboring Bishops, he did not hesitate to spread his error. What more? Because out of supreme pride he ordered Psalms composed about his own praises to be sung publicly in the Church in the manner of David. Ejected from the Episcopal see by the Synod of Antioch, and excommunicated, he still did not want to yield, until he was forced to yield by Aurelian. Others also add Novatus, Pelagius, among whom is our B. Gerhard.

According to the analogy of the preceding trumpets, a new heresy, and that a most serious one, is again predicted. Which, although it is understood by some again in a general sense concerning heretics and hypocrites, was specifically that of the Cathars, the Donatists according to most, with Megalandrus leading the way: to whom some, including our B. Gravius, add the Pelagians: of whom the former denied penance to the fallen; the latter attributed too much to the powers of free will, and relied on their own merits in the matter of salvation. Both obscured the Sun of righteousness, Christ, with his righteousness, and obedience, both active and passive, who was made for us by God redemption and righteousness, to a wonderful degree, and by their seduction involved the stars, that is, the chief Doctors of the Church, in a thick fog of errors, or forced them to hide when driven into exile, while they themselves wanted to appear to shine like luminaries, above others, in purity of doctrine and holiness of life, and to many they even seemed to shine. Alcazar takes the fourth trumpet to refer to the blindness and hardening of the Jews, Brightman to the incursions of Genserich and others, Mede to the miserable state of Rome, some to the obscuring of the doctrine concerning Christ and the Gospel through Mahomet and Papal darkness, some to Eutyches, others to Nestorius, and some even to Samosatenus and Arius, along with Flacius, Cramer, Winckelmann, Gerhard, and Döling. Cornelius a Lapide explains it as signs of the final judgment.

Latin:

Vers. 12.

Καὶ ὁ τέταρτο Ἄγγελος ἐσάλπισε, καὶ ἐπλήγη τὸ τρίτον τῶ ἡλίου, καὶ τὸ τρίτον τῆς σελήνης, κὰι τὸ τρίτον τῶν ἀσέρων, ἵνα σκοτισθῇ τὸ τρίτον ἐξ αὐτῶν ) Sicut navigantibus terræ de scedere dicuntur; ita calamitate pressis occidere Sol, Luna, sidera. Vide quæ diximus ad Matth. XXIV.v.29. Adde Pa- raphrasten Chaldæum ad Esa. XIII. v. 10. & Jerem. XV. v. 9. Caligo Solis, Lunæ, siderum interitum significat Achmet CLXVI. Significantur hîc Galilææ & aliarum partium op- pida, capta a Vespasiano cum plurimorum Judæorum in- teritu. Historiam videre est apud Josephum libro belli Ju- daici quarto. Quia tertia serine Judææ pars tunc in hanc calamitatem incidit, ideo sidera dicuntur defecisse tertia sui parte. Pro ἵνα σκοτισθῇ in Manuscripto est ἵνα μὴ φαίνῃ. Καὶ ἡ ἡμέρα μὴ φαίνῃ τὸ τρίτον αὐτῆς ) Est Ebraïsmus pro τὸ τρίτον ἡμέρας μη φαίνῃ, id est, diei tertia pars ad solitum fulgorem aberat. Καὶ ἡ νὺξ ὁμοίως ) Noctis quoque fulgor solito minor par- te tertia. Sensus est : In parte tertia Judææ & opificia cef- sarunt, & itinera, quorum illa de die, hæc de nocte magis in illis locis peragi solebant. Minus quidem malum, quam in Ægypto, Exod. X, 22. attamen eo accedens.

De Paulo Samofateno vero constat, quod Fi- lii Dei præxternam existentiam negarit, Christum- que nudum, quod ad naturam, bominem fecerit. Quæ præcipua ejus hærefis. Magni montis instar haberi voluit Ducenarius magis quam Episcopus. Magna caterva incedere , atque in via dictare consuevit, & legere epistolas ex mero typho eru- ditionis, quemadmodum & ex affectata & super- ba munificentia opes distribuit, more Pharisaico. Ex ea vero, ut habet Danæus pag. 111. primum occafione Samofatenus fese & alios decepit, quod, ut scribit Theodoretus, lib. II. Heret. fabul. Zeno- biam Arabiæ, Syriæ & Phœniciæ Reginam poten- tissimam, & Judæorum erroribus de Christo fa- ventem sibi conciliare & demereri, i. e. Principi- bus & aulæ servire vellet homo ambitiofus & fastuo- sus, sed jam tamen Ecclesiæ Antiochenæ Episcopus, clam idem se de Christo sentire dixit, quod Judæi, & Zenobia ipsa regionis Princeps. De quo a vici- nis Episcopis sæpius admonitus, errorem tamen spar- gere non dubitavit. Quid? quod ex summa super- bia pro Davidicis de suis laudibus compositos Psalmos in Ecclesia publicè cani ordinavit. Sede Episcopali a Synodo Antiochena ejectus, & excom- municatus cedere tamen noluit, donec ab Aure- liano cedere cogeretur. Alii quoque addunt No- vatum, Pelagium, inter quos est B. Gerhardus noster.

Juxta analogiam percedentium tubarum no- va hæresis, eaque gravissima iterum prædicitur. Quæ etsi a nonnullis iterum in genere de hæreticis & hypocritis intelligatur, speciatim Catharorum, Donatistarum juxta plerosque, præeunte Mega- landro fuit : quibus vero nonnulli, etiam B. Gra- vius noster, Pelagianos adjiciunt : quorum illi la- psis pœnitentiam denegabant; hi viribus liberi arbitrii nimium tribuebant, suisque meritis in negotio salutis nitebantur. Utrique Solem justi- tiæ Christum, cum sua justitia, & obedientia cum activa, tum passiva, qui factus nobis a Deo est redemptio, & justitia, mirum quantum ob- scurabant, ac seductione sua stellas, hoc est, Do- ctores Ecclesiæ præcipuos atta errorum caligine involvebant, vel in exilium pulsos latere coge- bant, ipsi vero luminarium instar, præ aliis, do- ctrinæ puritate, ac vitæ sanctitate fulgere videri volebant, multis etiam ita fulgere videbantur. De cæcitate atque induratione Judæorum Alca- sar, de impressionibus Genserici & aliorum Brigt- mannus, de misero Romæ statu Medus, de obscu- ratione doctrinæ de Christo & Evangelica per Ma- homet & Papales tenebras de Eutyche nonnul- li, de Nestorio alii, quidam etiam de Samofateno & Ario, cum Flacio, Cramero, Winckelmanno, Gerhardo, Döling. quartam tubam accipiunt. Cornelius a Lapide de signis extremi judicii ex- plicat.

## 8:13
Verse 13.

And I heard one eagle flying in mid-heaven. Aquila loves corpses, Matt. XXIV. v. 28, Luke XVII. v. 37. Therefore it is apt for predicting slaughters, Ezek. XVII. v. 3. Moreover, that part of the sky in which eagles and birds similar to it fly is called mid-heaven, below c. XIX. v. 17, so far above the lands that they seem no less near to the highest heaven than to the earth. This is what Zechariah says in c. V. v. 9, between heaven and earth. For the same, the Hebrews say ברקיע.

Moreover, many are said to be dead from the waters changed into wormwood, because the most limpid and health-giving fountains of Israel were infected with most bitter poison and became deadly. Furthermore, the heresy was widely propagated, because Arianism was born from it, concerning which Jerome says: The world groaned and marveled that it had become Arian so quickly. It also lasted for a very long time, indeed even now in the Neo-Arians and especially in the Neo-Photinians, or Socinians, and in part also in the Arminians, Nicolaitans, Anabaptists, etc. A great star burning like a torch, John V. v. 35, Matt. V. v. 25, is said to have fallen from heaven, because it slipped from heavenly height and scripture into earthly and dark studies and began to creep on the ground and to savor only carnal things, and at the same time fell from its stellar eminence and brightness, Isa. XIV. v. 12, Lam. II. v. 1. Moreover, it fell upon the third part of the rivers, by which congregations of men, as by seas, are designated, and indeed refreshing and truly wholesome rivers are understood: which similitude is also [found in] Theodoret.

Some read Ἀγγέλε, but older codices have ἀετῶ: and thus Bede, Aretas, Ticonius, and most others read. By the eagle, however, they wish to designate the preachers of the end time announcing threats and punishments to men. B. Cluverus understands that angel as referring to Hosius, Bishop of Cordoba: Whom, however, we do not find to have announced such things.

Saying with a loud voice thrice woe, woe, woe to those who dwell upon the earth from the remaining voices of the three Angels who are about to sound the trumpet)

This is an introduction to the following, which pertain not to some third part, but to the whole of Judea and especially to the capital city. Three woes correspond to three Angels, whom you have at IX.1.14. X.7. XI.11. Of these, the first announces matters shortly before the siege: the second, the siege and the storming: the third, those things which are subsequent to the storming. From this place, as often, the Hebrew מן signifies because of. Thus, ἀπὸ is placed after οὐαὶ at XVIII. 7. These things agree very well with that voice of Jesus son of Ananias, which Josephus recites in Jewish War VI.31. A voice from the east, a voice from the west, a voice from the four winds, a voice against Jerusalem and the temple, a voice against bridegrooms and brides, a voice against all the people. Then: Woe, also to the city, and to the people, and to the temple.

Three Woes denote three kinds of punishments, which are indicated to be still remaining and most severe, and to follow one another in such an order that the first ought to be considered grave compared with the preceding, the second graver, and the third finally most grave. Marloratus understands everything concerning the Anti-Christ. But others more correctly explain the latter two concerning the Eastern and Western Anti-Christ: but they interpret the former concerning Arius, their precursor. By those dwelling on the earth are designated impious men, setting their minds on earthly things, Philip. III. 19. For that Woe does not strike the rest with its wrath. And the Grotius Gloss is too empty and completely foreign. For these concern the whole world, not just the holy city, and they were still to follow, not indeed to have preceded, which is certain concerning the siege of the city.

Latin:

Vers. 13.

Καὶ ἤκουσα ἑνὸς ἀετῶ πετωμένο ἐν μεσουρανήματι ) Aquila amat cadavera, Matth. XXIV. v. 28. Luc. XVII. v.37. Ideo apta prædicendis stragibus, Ezech. XVII. v. 3. Μεσουράνημα autem dicitur ea pars cœli , in qua volant aquilæ, & similes ei volucres, infra c. XIX. v. 17. adeo longe supra terras, ut videantur non minus cælo altissero propinquæ, quam ter- ris. Hoc est quod dicit Zacharias c.V.v.9. inter cælum & ter- ram. Pro eodem dicunt Ebræi ברקיע.

Mortui autem multi dicuntur ex aquis in ab- sinthium mutatis, quia fontes Israelis limpidiffi- mi, salutiflui veneno amarissimo infecti exitiofi facti sunt. Late autem propagata hærefis fuit, quia ex ea enatus Arianismus, de quo Hieronymus : Ingemuit orbis, & se tam cito Arianum factum esse miratus est. Duravit etiam diutissime, imo etiam- num in Neo - Arianis & imprimis in Neo-Photinia- nis, vel Socinistis, ex parte etiam in Arminianis, Nicolai, Anabaptistis, &c. De cœlo stella magna ardens instar faculæ Johan. V. v. 35. Matth. V. v.25. cecidisse dicitur, quia de cœlesti altitudine ac scriptura in terreneæ ac tenebricosa studia prola- psus humi serpere & carnalia tantum sapere cœ- pit, simulque stellari eminentia & fulgore exci- dit, Esa. XIV. v. 12. Thren. II. v. 1. Cecidit autem in tertiam partem fluminum, quibus cougrega- tiones hominum, ut per maria, designantur, & flumina quidem reficientia, ac vere salubria intelliguntur: quæ similitudo etiam Theodoreti

Nonnulli Ἀγγέλε legunt, sed vetustiores codi- ces ἀετῶ habent: atque ita legerunt Beda, Aretas, Ticonius, alii plerique. Per aquilam autem desi- gnari volunt prædicatores extremi temporis com- minationes & supplicia hominibus denunciantes. Angelum illum de Ofio Cordubensi Episcopo intel- ligit B. Cluverus : Quem vero talia prænunciasse non invenimus.

Λέγοντος φωνῇ μεγάλῃ τρὶς οὐαὶ, οὐαὶ, οὐαὶ τοῖς κατοικοῦσιν ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς ἐκ τῶν λοιπῶν φωνῶν τῶν τριῶν Ἀγγέλων τῶν μελλόντων σαλπίζειν)

Hæc est introductio ad sequentia, quæ non ad tertiam aliquam partem, sed ad totam Judæam ac maxime ad ur- bem principem pertinent. Tria væ tribus conveniunt Angelis, quos habes IX.1.14. X.7. XI.11. Ex his primus nun- tiat res paulo ante obsidium: secundus obsidium & expu- gnationem: tertius ea, quæ expugnatione posteriora sunt. Ex hoc loco, ut sæpe מן Ebr. valet propter. Sic ἀπὸ post οὐαὶ ponitur XVIII. 7. Optime hæc conveniunt cum illa voce Jesu filii Ananielis, quam recitat Josephus Belli Judaici VI.31. Φωνὴ ἀπὸ ἀνατολῆς, Φωνὴ ἀπὸ δύσεως, Φωνὴ ἀπὸ τῶν τεσσάρων ἀνέμων, Φωνὴ ἐπὶ Ἱεροσόλυμα, καὶ τὸν ναὸν, Φωνὴ ἐπὶ νυμφίους καὶ νύμφας, Φωνὴ ἐπὶ τὸν λαὸν πάντα. Deinde: Οὐαὶ, καὶ τῇ πόλει, καὶ τῷ λαῷ καὶ τῷ ναῷ.

Tria Væ tria suppliciorum genera notant, quæ gravissima adhuc superesse, atque eo ordine sese consecutura indicatur, ut primum comparate cum præcedentibus grave, secundum gravius, tertium denique gravissimum censeri debeat. Omnia de Anti-Christo intelligit Marloratus. Sed alii rectius posteriora duo de Anti-Christo Orientali & Occidentali explicant: prius autem de Ario, eorum præcursore interpretantur. Per habitantes in terra designantur homines impii, ἐπίγεια φρονῶντες, Philip. III. 19. Nam cæteros ira Væ illa non feriunt. Et jejuna nimis & aliena penitus est Grotiana Glossa. Nam totum orbem hæc, non urbem sanctam tantum concernunt, & sequutura adhuc erant, non vero præcesse- rant, quod de obsidio urbis certum est.

## 9:1 Argument
II. THE THREE GREATER TRUMPETINGS, AND BETWEEN THESE THE FIFTH AND SIXTH. CHAPTER IX.

ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

At the sound of the fifth trumpet, a star was seen fallen from heaven, to which was given the key to the abyss, by which being opened, smoke arises darkening the Sun and the air, and from the smoke locusts like scorpions come forth, which however ought to bring no harm to grass and trees, but only to men not sealed, whom they afflict for 5 months more bitterly than death. The locusts are described with their King. As the sixth Angel sounds, four Angels bound at the Euphrates are simultaneously released to kill a third part of men, of whom a great and horrible army is seen, and power is in their mouth and heads: Yet those not killed by this plague do not overcome, nor indeed do they repent for idolatry and other sins.

There are two parts: I. The visions of the fifth seal opened, the poisonous smoke, and the scorpion-like bites of the locusts, to v. 12. II. The visions of the sixth seal, to v. 21. A huge army for killing a third part of the world.

PART I. CONCERNING THE V. TRUMPETING, CONCERNING THE POISONOUS SMOKE AND THE SCORPION-LIKE BITES OF THE LOCUSTS ARISING THEREFROM.

Vers. 1.

And the fifth angel sounded, and I saw a star fallen from heaven unto the earth)

This false Doctor is Eleazar, son of Ananias, who taught that sacrifices were not to be received from pagan princes, contrary to what had been done even with the authority of Prophets, under Cyrus and Alexander and their successors, and also under Augustus and Tiberius. Josephus II. 30. This is related here later, because the effects that followed from it are later than those mentioned before. Thus historians often follow the series of connected things, not of times. This Gloss concerning Eleazar is foreign, not only by reason of time, but also of the thing itself. Concerning the time, Grotius acknowledges that the antecedents do not follow in order. But he seeks an escape in the order of effects. But in truth, the predictions of the Holy Prophets do not make such leaps, that they observe now the priority of times, now again in the same vision and prophecy, such as this is, for this third vision is still continued, the priority of effects. But what does that dogma concerning the non-reception of victims have to do with such a laborious description of the falling star and also the army of locusts, similar to scorpions? Most understand Arius, and B. Cluverus wishes him to be designated here by the Angel indicated by Peter, Bishop of Alexandria, warning of an imminent new heresy. Arius certainly could have shone like a star by his illustrious erudition, having fallen from heaven or the Church to the earth out of pride—that is, heretical dogmas prevailing on earth outside the Church, such as those of Paul of Samosata and his followers—and he is predicted to stir up a smoke so destructive that a third, that is, a great part of the world is to be darkened and deprived of the light of divine truth. We hinted a little earlier that the event confirmed this with the words of Jerome: The world groaned and marveled to find itself Arian so quickly. Others, with B. Gerhard agreeing, understand the Roman Pope by this star fallen from heaven: because a star falling from heaven is a symbol of a Bishop who casts aside the care of heavenly things and takes up the care of earthly ones, gaping after riches, honors, dignities, and pleasures. For the first Roman Bishops were pious and holy. Although these things are so, the order of times convinces us to understand it rather of Arius, who it is agreed also gaped greatly after earthly things. For those who refer Arius to the preceding trumpet, under which the Novatians and Pelagians are placed, do not seem to observe how different the Arian heresy was from those; nor do they find who the Heresiarch is that conveniently follows the preceding Novatians and Pelagians; or how the third Woe is to be explained by the analogy of the others concerning a false Teacher or Pseudo-Prophet, which must be accepted entirely concerning the Great Anti-Christ and supreme Pseudo-Prophet, the Roman Pontiff, in whom the sink of heresies converges. It cannot be understood of Eleazar. For he was never a star or a distinguished Teacher of the Church of Christ, of whom stars are explained in Apoc. 1. He was never established in the heaven of the Church; therefore, he could not fall from heaven. False Teachers, such as that Eleazar, do not deserve such an excellent title. Fromondus slanders this star falling from heaven as being Luther, who fell from a heavenly and monastic way of life into the lusts of the world and earthly pleasures. The key of the abyss, he says, was given to him, so that he might recall a great host of monstrous locusts, that is, ancient heresies long buried in hell. This he accomplished partly by himself, partly through others born from him—Zwinglians, Calvinists, Anabaptists, Ubiquitarians, new Arians, and almost infinite other heresies. By these, the air and the Sun, that is, the Church and Christ, were darkened. Lutherans are like locusts, a sordid and pot-bellied animal, which sometimes tries to lift itself on high by flight, but always in it cuts back the belly and the earth. The Lutheran sects fly in swarms, without a King, like locusts, having no visible King of sacred things or Pontiff over them, except that the Angel of the abyss rules them invisibly. They have iron breastplates, that is, an incredible obstinacy and hardness of heart. In which, however, the Anabaptists surpass them all. They have a mild face at the beginning, as men do, when they promise that they bring the pure and unadulterated Word of God and sincere truth, but they sting with their tail, like scorpions, when in the end they breathe in deadly poison for honey. But all these things fit more aptly to the Papists. They have no King, because they do not acknowledge God, from whom they diverge in most articles of faith, as King, but they are ruled entirely by the Angel of the abyss, the Father of lies, and the most ancient murderer. Nor does Fromondus trust this gloss of his; nay, he observes against Bellarmine that the first five trumpets refer rather to the times closer to the Anti-Christ, which I would concede regarding the four former, but not regarding the fifth, except as it pertains to the locusts, which it is entirely credible represent the Jesuits, the remnants of the Nestorians, from the time they caused the Nestorian theses of the Crypto-Calvinist Wittenbergers to be reprinted at Ingolstadt. For it must be admitted, to use the words of Fromondus applied to the Papists, that to no heresy of all those hitherto known to the world do those things which are narrated concerning the infernal locusts better apply than to the heresy of the Papists, and especially to the latest excrement of the Pope, the Loyolists, who are clearly Nestorianizing. Lyranus thinks that those ancient Vandals and Lombards, who nourished long hair and beards, are described literally. But since it looks toward times closer to the Anti-Christ, St. John describes some who are like the Lombards, rather than the Lombards themselves, as Fromondus advises ad h. l.

And there was given to him the key of the pit of the abyss, to him, that falling star. His doctrine was not of God, but of Satan, who is said to be shut up in a deep prison, since he cannot do what he wishes, Luke VIII. 31, below XXI. 3. But he who publishes those dogmas, τὰ βάθη τῦ Σατανᾶ, is said to have the key of the deep pit, as may be seen below in the said chapter XX. Φρέαρ τῆς ἀβύσσυ for φρέαρ ἄβυσσον. A Hebrew idiom. Thus, deep and pit are used with equal meaning, Ps. LXIX. 16. Now prisons were accustomed to be in deep places, Jerem. XXXVIII. 6. And those places were sometimes accustomed to be closed and locked, Dan. VI. 17. Thus below in XX. what is first ἄβυσσος, is soon called φυλακὴ, the Hebrews place among the infernal regions באר שחת from Psalm LV. 24. See the book which is called The Cedar of Lebanon.

Latin:

II. TRIA MAJORA TUBICINIA, ET INTER HÆC QUINTUM ET SEXTUM. CAPUT IX.

ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Ad sonitum quintæ tubæ visa est stella de cœlo prolapsa, cui data clavis ad abyssum, qua aperta fumus Solem, & aërem obtenebrans oritur, & e fumo locustæ scorpionum instar prodeunt, quæ tamen gramini & arbori- bus nullum damnum inferre debent, sed solum hominibus non signatis, quos per 5. menses affligunt morte acerbius. Locu- stæ describuntur cum suo Rege. Clangen- te sexto Angelo quatuor Angeli ad Eu- phratem ligati simul liberi ad occidendam tertiam partem hominum dimittuntur, quorum magnus & horribilis exercitus videtur, & virtus est in ore & capitibus: Superant tamen non occisi ab ista plaga, nec vero pro idololatria, aliisque delictis pœnitentes.

Partes sunt duæ: I. Sigilli quinti aperti visa, fumus venenatus, & morsus locustarum scorpioni- ci, ad v. 12. II. Visa Sigilli sexti, ad v. 21. Ingens ad tertiam partem orbis occidendam exercitus.

PARS I. DE V. TUBICINIO, DE FUMO VENENA- TO ET LOCUSTARUM INDE ORIUN- DARUM MORSIBUS SCOR- PIONICIS.

Vers. 1.

Καὶ ὁ πέμπτος ἄγγελος ἐσάλπισε, καὶ εἶδον ἀστέρα ἐκ τοῦ οὐρα- νῶ πεπτωκότα εἰς τὴν γῆν)

Hic falsus Doctor est Eleazarus, Ananiæ filius, qui docuit non esse recipiendas victimas a paganis principi- bus, contra quam factum fuerat auctoribus etiam Prophetis, sub Cyro & Alexandro eorumque successoribus sub Augusto quoque & Tiberio. Josephus II. 30. Serius hoc hic refertur, quod effectus inde secuti seriores sint antedictis. Sic historici saepe rerum connexarum, non temporum, sequuntur seriem. Aliena haec de Eleazaro Glossa est, non solum ratione temporis, sed etiam rei ipsius. De tempore agnoscit Grotius, non sequi ordine antecedentia. Sed effugium quaerit in effectuum ordine. Verumenimvero praedictiones S. Prophetarum non faciunt tales saltus, ut modo prioritatem temporum, modo iterum in eadem visione, ac prophetia, qualis haec est, adhuc enim tertia visio continuatur, prioritatem effectuum observent. Quid vero huc dogma illud de non recipiendis victimis ad tam operosam descriptionem stellae cadentis nec non exercitus locustarum, scorpionibus similium. Arium plerique intelligunt, eumque a Petro Episcopo Alexandrino hic per Angelum indicato, de imminente nova haeresi praemonente designatum vult B. Cluverus. Arius certe sideris instar lucere poterat illustri eruditione sua ex superbia de coelo vel Ecclesia in terram, hoc est, haeretica dogmata in terra extra Ecclesiam obtinentia, qualia Pauli Samosateni erant & asseclarum prolapsus, fumum tam exitiosum praedicitur excitaturus, quo tertia, hoc est, magna, pars orbis obtenebranda, ac luce divinae veritatis privanda sit. Quod eventum comprobasse paulo ante Hieronymi verbis innuimus: Ingemuit orbis, & se tam cito Arianum factum miratus est. Alii, adstipulante B. Gerhardo, per hanc stellam e coelo delapsam Papam Romanum intelligunt: Quod stella e coelo cadens symbolum sit Episcopi, abjicientis curam rerum coelestium, & suscipientis curam terrenarum, inhiantis divitiis, honoribus, dignitatibus, voluptatibus. Primi enim Episcopi Romani pii & sancti fuere. Quanquam vero haec ita se habent: ordo tamen temporum convincit, ut de Ario potius intelligamus, quem terrenis pariter valde inhiaffe constat. Nam qui Arium ad praecedentem tubam, sub qua Novatiani, & Pelagiani locantur, referunt, non videntur observare, quam diversa fuerit ab istis haeresis Ariana; nec inveniunt, quinam Haeresiarcha commode sequatur ad praecedaneos Novatianos & Pelagianos: aut quomodo tertium Vae ad analogiam reliquorum de falso Doctore vel Pseudo-Propheta explicandum sit, quod omnino de Anti-Christo Magno & summo Pseudo-Propheta, Pontifice Romano, in quo concurrit sentina haeresium, accipiendum. De Eleazaro intelligi nequit. Nam is nunquam stella vel Doctor insignis fuit Ecclesiae Christi: de quibus stellae exponuntur, Apoc. 1. Nunquam in coelo Ecclesiae constitutus fuit; de coelo ergo labi non potuit. Falsi Doctores, qualis Eleazarus ille, tam eximium titulum non merentur. Stellam hanc de coelo cadentem calumniatur Fromondus Lutherum esse, a coelesti & monastico vitae genere in seculi libidines & voluptates terrenas prolapsum. Data est, inquit, ei clavis abyssi, ut magnum agmen monstrosarum locustarum, id est, veteres, & in inferno dudum sepultas haereses revocaret. Quod partim per se, partim per alias ex ipso natas Zwinglianorum, Calvinistarum, Anabaptistarum, Ubiquetariorum, novorum Arianorum, & infinitas fere alias haereses praestitit. Quibus aër & Sol, hoc est, Ecclesia & Christus obscuratus est. Lutherani similes sunt locustis, animali sordido & ventricoso, quod quandoque conatur volatu se in altum attollere, sed semper in ventrem & terram recidit. Sectæ Lutheranicæ volant turmatim, sine Rege, sicut locustæ, nullum Regem sacrorum sive Pontificem supra se habentes visibilem, nisi quod Angelus abyssi eos invisibiliter regat. Loricas ferreas, id est, obstinationem & du- ritiem pectoris incredibilem habent. In quo ta- men Anabaptistæ omnes superant. Faciem blandam initio, ut homines gerunt, quando se purum putum Dei Verbum & sinceram veritatem afferre promit- tunt, sed cauda pungunt, ut scorpiones, quando in fi ne venenum pro melle læthiferum inspirant. Sed hæc omnia aptius quadrant in Papistas. Regem nullum habent, quia Deum, a quo in plerisque fi- dei capitibus divarricantur, Regem non agno- scunt, reguntur autem omnino ab Angelo abyssi, Patre mendaciorum, & homicida antiquissimo. Neque fidit huic Glossæ suæ Fromondus, imo contra Bellarminum observat, quinque primas tubas spectare potius ad tempora propinquiora Anti-Christo, quod de quatuor prioribus con- cesserim, non item de quinta, nisi quod ad locu- stas attinet, quas figurare Jesuitas, Nestorianas re- liquias prorsus credibile est, ex quo recudi fece- runt Ingolstadii Crypto-Calvinianorum Wit- tebergensium theses Nestorianas. Fatendum enim est, ut verbis Fromondi utar ad Papales ap- plicatis, nulli ex omnibus hæresibus, mundo hacte- nus notis, melius convenire ea, quæ narrantur de in- fernalibus locustis, quam hæresi Papistarum, & im- primis excremento Papæ novissimo, Lojolitis plane Nestorianizantibus. Lyranus putat ad literam describi veteres illos Wandalos & Longobardos, qui prolixos capillos & barbas alebant. Sed cum ad tempora viciniora Anti-Christo respiciat, potius aliquos similes Longobardis, quam Longobardos de- scribit S. Johannes, ut monet Fromondus adh. l.

Καὶ ἐδόθη αὐτῷ ἡ κλεῖς τῦ φρέατος τῆς ἀβύσσυ) αὐτῷ, illi stellæ cadenti. Ejus doctrina non erat Dei, sed Satanæ, qui dicitur in profundum carcerem includi, cum non possit agere, quæ velit, Luc. VIII. 31. infra XXI. 3. Qui vero ea dogmata vulgat, τὰ βάθη τῦ Σατανᾶ, is dicitur clavem habe- re putei profundi, ut videre est infra dicto capite XX. Φρέαρ τῆς ἀβύσσυ pro φρέαρ ἄβυσσον. Ebraica loquutio. Sic pro- fundum & puteus pari significatu ponuntur, Ps. LXIX. 16. Solebant autem carceres esse in locis profundis, Jerem. XXXVIII. 6. Eaque loca interdum claudi & obserari sole- bant, Dan. VI. 17. Sic infra XX. quod primum ἄβυσσος, mox vocatur φυλακὴ, Ebræi inter infernas regiones po- nunt באר שחת ex Psalmo LV. 24. Vide librum, qui di- citur Cedrus Libani.

## 9:2
V. 2. Καὶ ἤνοιξε τὸ φρέαρ τῆς ἀβύσσυ, καὶ ἀνέβη καπνὸς ἐκ τῦ φρέατος) A seditious doctrine opened itself, that one must not obey the Romans. Added here in the Manuscript: Καπνὸς καμίνυ μεγάλης, where again ὡς is understood. Smoke, such as from a great furnace, Gen. XIX. 28. Exod. XIX. 18. Κάμινος is accustomed to be placed in either the masculine or feminine gender. See Matth. XIII. 42. 50. Job. XLI. 12. Deut. IV. 28. Jerem. XI. 3. Just as immense smoke hinders the sight, so do evil doctrines hinder the mind. He persists, however, in the comparison begun. For smoke takes away the view of the stars.

How the sun and air were darkened by the seditious dogma concerning not obeying the Romans, Grotius does not explain. But by the impious dogma of Arius from the abyss of hell, which after Samosatenus seemed for a time to be shut up in Orcus, and was again recalled, the Sun of righteousness, Christ, is not darkened in respect of Himself, but in respect of us, whose Deity Arius, as much as in him lay, strove to obscure, nay, to take away, so that He might not be acknowledged by the faithful, and shine for their consolation: for when the Deity of Christ is denied, His satisfaction is taken away, and when that is taken away, no light of consolation remains for miserable sinners, no salvation; the air in the Church is darkened, and nothing remains but the darkness of errors and heresies precipitating into outer darkness and the abyss of hell. When the knowledge of Christ, who is the source of all light, is diminished, the whole doctrine of salvation is undermined. Since, therefore, this mystical air is to be understood in this way, it is gathered that the public doctrine of the Church had been infected and corrupted, and that judgment and spiritual joy in men had been obscured. For the light of doctrine illuminates the eyes of the mind and procures true gladness for man. Blessed Gerhard holds it thus: By the Sun is denoted the saving doctrine concerning the person, office, and benefits of Christ: for He Himself is the Sun of righteousness, Mal. IV. 2, under whose wings alone is salvation. Just as the natural life of man consists in the continuous drawing of air: so the spiritual life of man consists in the word of God, which was likewise miserably obscured when traditions and apparitions of souls were introduced into the Church to confirm purgatory. For spiritual life consists in faith, Gal. II. 29, which was likewise obscured, because the hearts of men, previously illuminated by the light of doctrine, lost the purity of doctrine. Furthermore, the pit of the abyss for B. Gerhard is purgatory, which is said to be next to hell, and the Pope is said to hold its key, who boasts that he has the power to liberate souls from the flames of purgatory through indulgences. Sebastian Mejer, along with Bullinger, also interprets this as referring to the Pope. But we have already stated the reason why we do not agree with the most learned interpreter here. B. Gravius rightly says: Arius, a presbyter of the Church of Alexandria, previously held the key of the kingdom of heaven through a legitimate calling, but, inflated by ambition and pride, having abandoned this key, he received from Satan, by the just judgment of God, the key of the pit of the infernal abyss as a punishment for his contempt of the Word, and as if from hell he produced diabolical errors. The pit of the abyss was closed several times, when the impious ravings of Ebion and Cerinthus, Valentinus and Paul of Samosata, had been refuted and rejected by the pious and orthodox Doctors of the Church and by the salutary decrees of councils. But Arius in turn opened that fountain of errors, and tried to force it upon the Church with all his might. And the smoke of the pit of the abyss ascended, as the smoke of a great furnace. By this smoke is understood false and erroneous doctrine, which went forth into the Church of God with great force, and indeed with fiery fervor as if from a furnace, to the greatest ruin of Christians. And the Sun and the air were darkened by the smoke of the pit. Through the pestiferous errors of Arius, not only was the Sun of righteousness, Christ, obscured and hindered in respect of his person and office, but also the air, that is, the faith and operation of the Holy Spirit (by which, as if from air, Christians have spiritual life).

Latin:

V. 2. Καὶ ἤνοιξε τὸ φρέαρ τῆς ἀβύσσυ, καὶ ἀνέβη καπνὸς ἐκ τῦ φρέατος) Aperuit se dogma seditiosum, non est paren- dum Romanis. Additur hic in Manuscripto: Καπνὸς κα- μίνυ μεγάλης, ubi rursum ὡς subauditur. Fumus, qualis e magna fornace, Gen. XIX. 28. Exod. XIX. 18. Κάμινος poni solet vel Masculino vel Fœminino genere. Vide Matth. XIII. 42. 50. Job. XLI. 12. Deut. IV. 28. Jerem. XI. 3. Sicut fumus ingens visum impedit, ita mentem ma- la dogmata. Perstat autem in cœpta comparatione. Nam fumus siderum conspectum adimit.

Quomodo Sol & aër obscuratus fuerit per dogma seditiosum de non parendo Romanis, non explicat Grotius. Per impium autem Arii dogma ex abysso inferni, quod post Samosate- num ad tempus videbatur orco conclusum, ite- rum revocatum non obscuratur ratione sui, sed ratione nostri Sol justitiæ Christus, cujus Deita- tem Arius, quantum in ipso erat, obfuscare, imo tollere satagebat, ne agnoscatur a fidelibus, eo- rumque solatio fulgeat: Negata enim Deitate Christi tollitur ejus satisfactio, qua sublata nulla restat miseris peccatoribus solatii lux, nulla sa- lus; obtenebratur aër in Ecclesia, nec nisi errorum & hæreseon in exteriores tenebras & abyssum in- ferni præcipitantes tenebræ restant. Cum Chri- sti cognitio, qui omnis lucis fons est, minuitur, tota salutis doctrina labefactatur. Cum ergo mysticus aër hic intelligendus sit, colligitur, do- ctrinam publicam Ecclesiæ infectam & corruptam fuiffe, ac judicium & gaudium spirituale in homi- nibus obscuratum. Doctrinæ enim lumen ocu- los mentis illustrat veramque homini lætitiam conciliat. B. Gerhardus ita habet : Per Solem denotatur salutaris doctrina de Christi persona, offi- cio & beneficiis : ipse enim est Sol justitiæ, Mal. IV. 2. sub cujus solius alis salus. Sicut vita naturalis ho- minis consistit in haustu aëris continuo : Sic spiri- tualis hominis vita in Dei verbo, quod itidem mi- sere obscuratum, quando traditiones & apparitio- nes animarum ad confirmandum purgatorium in Ecclesiam introductæ. Consistit enim spiritualis vi- ta in fide, Gal. II. 29. hæc itidem obscurata, quia corda hominum prius luce doctrinæ illuminata pu- ritatem doctrinæ amiserunt. Cæterum puteus abyssi B. Gerhardo est purgatorium, quod infer- no dicitur proximum, clavemque ejus habere di- citur Papa, qui glorietur, quod habeat potestatem per indulgentias ex purgatorii flammis animas li- berandi. De Papa etiam interpretatur Sebastia- nus Mejer, cum Bullingero. Sed cur doctissimo Interpreti hic non annuamus, causam jam dixi- mus. Recte B. Gravius : Habuit ante Arius Pres- byter Ecclesiæ Alexandrinæ per legitimam vocatio- nem clavem regni cælorum, sed ambitione & super- bia inflatus relicta hac clave a Satana justo Dei ju- dicio contemtum Verbi punientis, accepit clavem putei abyssi infernalis, & quasi ex orco diabolicos produxit errores. Conclusus aliquoties erat puteus abyssi, quando per pios & orthodoxos Ecclesiæ Docto- res ac per conciliorum salubria decreta, refutata & rejecta essent impia Ebionis & Cerinthi, Valentini & Pauli Samosateni deliria. Sed Arius fontem illum errorum vicissim aperuit, & Ecclesiæ summis viribus obtrudere conatus est. Et ascendit fumus putei abyssi, sicut fumus fornacis magnæ. Intelli- gitur hic fumus falsa & erronea doctrina, quæ magno impetu, & quidem cum igneo fervore tanquam ex fornace in Ecclesiam Dei egressa est, maxima Chri- stianorum cum pernicie. Et obscuratus est Sol & aër a fumo putei. Per errores Arii pestiferos non tan- tum Sol justitiæ Christus ratione personæ & officii, sed etiam aër, hoc est, fides & operatio Spiritus San- cti (quibus tanquam ex aëre Christiani vitam spi- ritualem habent) obscurata & impedita sunt.

## 9:3
Vers. 3. Καὶ ἐκ τῦ καπνῦ ἐξῆλθον ἀκρίδες εἰς τὴν γῆν )

Kαὶ here means for. He gives the reason why that dogma was mournful, because from it was born the worst faction of the Zealots, who both in Jerusalem and throughout all Judea despoiled others who were lovers of peace, and vexed them in many ways, of whose crimes Josephus writes at length. Plunderers are compared to locusts, because they leave everything behind them empty. Josephus uses this simile in Jewish War IV. 7. Aristophanes, Acharnians: Ὅσοι τὸ χἐπμα παριόντων προσέρχεται: Where the Scholiast says: βόλελαι πολὺ πλῆθος σημαίνουσι, οἷδε δὲ ἀκρίδων οἱ πύργο- πες, rightly, because he says that a multitude is signified by locusts. So also Judges VII. 12. So also Achmes 300. In Joel, the armies of Phul, Tiglath-Pileser, Shalmaneser, and Sennacherib are called caterpillars, locusts, bruchi, and attelabi, as we said there. Here also there is a reference to the plague of Egypt, although in an allegorical sense, as above regarding the hail. See Exodus X. 4. Εἰς τὴν γῆν into Judea, as we have already seen often.

Καὶ ἐδόθη ἀυταῖς ἐξυσία, ὡς ἔχυσιν ἐξυσίαν οἱ σκορπίοι τῆς γῆς)

That they might exhaust the state with a slow evil, as scorpions are wont to do. Pliny II. 25. Proverbs XXIII. 31. See below 5, 10. A scorpion signifies damage and disease. Achmes 285. Ἐξυσία here and below is to be referred to the permission of God.

By the locusts arising from the smoke of false doctrines by the Devil, the Prince of the abyss, are understood the broods of the Arians, Nestorians, Semi-Arians, Aëtians, Eunomians, Photinians, Macedonians, as well as the Acacians. In Africa and Syria larger locusts are born, endowed with stronger wings, which are very destructive to herbs, crops, and trees, and they erode them with their bite and pollute them with their touch, such as were brought into Egypt by the east wind. Ex. X. For just as locusts (according to Pliny, book II, ch. 29) in the autumn season lay dense eggs, which last through the winter under the ground: in the following year at the end of Spring, they emit blackish offspring, and crawling without legs and wings. Thus Origen, Samosatenus, and others, like eggs, brought forth malignant opinions, during a moderate tranquility of the Church, which, enduring through the time of persecutions, with the Ecclesiastical Spring, as soon as the serenity of peace shone forth, created Arius, Euzoius, Eusebius of Nicomedia, Eudoxius, Aëtius, and similar theologasters, in a huge number, small indeed at the beginning and as it were crawling on the ground, but soon strengthened by such kindness: That the mothers of the locusts die when they have laid their eggs, Pliny confirms as certain, with a small worm immediately growing around their throats, which strangles them. And that others, lifted up in swarms by the wind, fall into the seas or ponds. Thus for Arius, Eunomius, Photinus, Nestorius, and others, the birth of heresy was lethal both corporally and spiritually, with divine vengeance following them. And for all other masters of heretical opinions, their birth is their eternal destruction, unless they repent: very often also their whole hosts, by synodal or Caesarean authority, have been expelled from the Churches and utterly extinguished. Conf. the history of Exod. X. 19. They are not born except in flat and cracked places. Nor do heretics arise except in minds that are easy and open to creeping in. Read the history of that Arian priest, who persuaded Constantia, the widow of Licinius, that Arius was unjustly condemned, and who afterwards, through the recommendation of his sister, was esteemed dear to Constantine and made the guardian of his will, and bound Constantius to himself, and by this pact caused Arius to be recalled from exile, and his heresy to be introduced into the Church with full sails, in Rufinus, book 1, Hist. ch. 11, Sozomen, book 2, ch. 26. Locusts fly in swarms, infest fields and gardens, and contaminate them: So also the Arians crept into the Church in swarms in a great host, infested the garden and field of the Church, despoiled them, and defiled them with the perverse poison of their doctrine. Add that the Arians neither fly on high with St. John the Eagle to the heavenly contemplation of the divine nature of Christ; nor do they walk below according to the Canon of the Word of God, but, lifted up by pride, they fall back to the earth, now saying certain sublime things about Christ; soon again they think humbly about him. Locusts traverse immense tracts and cover everything with a dire cloud for the harvests, eroding everything with their bite, whence they seem to be called ἀκρίδες from their sharp erosion. And those heretics, especially the Arians, devastated the Churches of the whole East and West as if they were most fertile fields, which they could not consume and draw to their own opinion, yet they scorched them with their touch. Locusts (says Haymo) do not have straight steps, nor do they fly like birds. Thus heretics do not have the right faith to fly into heaven, nor straight steps to do good works. The same author further says: Locusts leap and gnaw the green things: Thus heretics are lifted up by boasting, and kill souls that are green with faith, when they can. Blessed Gerhard understands the various monastic orders, which, after the doctrine concerning purgatory and other Anti-Christian errors were introduced, prevailed in the Church. For they led men away to the merits of works, to works of supererogation, to their own satisfactions, to Papal indulgences, etc. Likewise the indulgence-sellers, who carried and sold letters of indulgences throughout the whole world. Likewise the Sophists, who defended Papal errors and Anti-Christian doctrine in their writings, they are compared to locusts, because they propagated themselves in great abundance far and wide, and seized and consumed everything for themselves. Which it is permitted, in our judgment, to include in this army of locusts, because Papists, Jesuits, and others are now approaching Nestorianism, denying the communication of idioms, because of the denial of which Nestorius was condemned by the Council of Ephesus.
