Τῦ ἐκπορευομένῦ ἐκ τῶν στομάτων αὐτῶν) quod videbatur ex ore equorum prodire, quia ante ora equorum volabant ista missilia, non secus quam si ex ore prodirent.

Plagæ illæ quomodo ex impuro Mahometi ore procefferint, jam diximus; sulphur libidinum, fu- mus falsarum doctrinarum & ignis bellorum. Qui- dam apud Gravium de machinis bellicis & hor- rendis bombardis, ex quibus ejicitur ignis, fumus & sulphur, quibus Turcæ firmissimas urbes & mu- nitiones expugnant, & sæpe in cineres redigunt, interpretantur.

## 9:19
Verse 19.

For the power of the horses is in their mouth) לפני in their sight: before them.

And in their tails; for their tails are like serpents, having heads) Similar to the amphisbaena, for which the other head serves as a tail. See Nicander, Pliny, and Lucan. Often among the Romans, when a king was in need of haste, a foot-soldier would sit behind the horseman on the same horse, who, when there was need, would dismount from the horse. These foot-soldiers he aptly calls the tail of the horse here.

Καὶ ἐν αὐταῖς ἀδικῦσι) Through those foot soldiers they do no less harm to the enemy than through the horsemen. For the foot soldiers are more effective for an assault. Ἀδικεῖν here means to do harm, as above II. 11. V. 6. VII. 7. and here 4. 10. We have given the reason for this locution elsewhere.

Per potentiam oris equorum Gravius understands the edicts of the Turkish Emperors to be more grievous in their efficacy, others commonly understand them as impious deeds. By these is indicated the faculty and cunning of doing harm, because they fight as if both front and back, deceiving enemies with a serpentine sort of prudence, sometimes even treacherously oppressing Christians when truces have been violated: examples of which occur in the Hungarian and Cypriot wars, as B. Gravius holds here again. For Mahomet, with Arius and Macedonius, denied the divinity of Christ and the Holy Spirit; with Nestorius, he asserted that the Jews did not truly crucify Christ; with Eutyches, he asserted that the son of Mary was made invisible; and thus he breathed out those four most grievous heresies, like a single smoke, from the mouth of the Saracen horses, and destroyed an infinite multitude of men. And indeed under hyacinthine breastplates, or under the specious pretext of defending the sanctuary, because they wish to appear to be defending Scripture itself. Conf. Ex. XXVI. verse 14. ch. XXXVI. 16. The interlinear gloss derives the word from hyacinth, a gem of a smoky color. By tails are understood, according to Is. IX. 15, with Ticonius, Nicolaus, Cramer, Winckelmann, Gerhard, Döling, Dürfeld, Napier, and Cocceius, false teachers and priests, who are like serpents because of their poisonous and pestiferous dogmas, Gen. III. 1. Apoc. XII. 9. Others, with the interlinear gloss, understand by tails the secret deceptions and frauds of the Turks. By heads, the magnates among the Turks, Sultans, Prime Viziers, Pashas, Beys, etc., are indicated, in whom they trust as heads and patrons, and by whose power they inflict the greatest damage.

Latin:

Vers. 19.

Ἡ γὰρ ἐξουσία τῶν ἵππων ἐν τῷ στόματι αὐτῶν ἐστι) לפני in conspectu eorum: ante eos.

Καὶ ἐν ταῖς ὐραῖς αὐτῶν· αἱ γὰρ ὐραὶ αὐτῶν ὅμοιαι ὄφεσιν, ἔχουσαι κεφαλάς) Similes amphisbænæ cui pro cauda est caput alterum. Vide Nicandrum, Plinium & Lucanum. Sæpe apud Romanos ubi festinationis Rex egeret, post equitem sedebat in eodem equo pedes, qui ubi opus erat, descendebat de equo. Eos pedites hic caudam equi appo- site vocat.

Καὶ ἐν αὐταῖς ἀδικῦσι) Per illos pedites hosti non mi- nus quam per equites nocent. Pedites enim ad oppugna- tionem plus valent. Ἀδικεῖν hic est nocere, ut supra II. 11. V. 6. VII. 7. & hic 4. 10. Causam hujus locutionis red- didimus alibi.

Per potentiam oris equorum Gravius edicta Im- peratorum Turcic. efficacia, alii communiter fa- cta impia intelligunt. Hisce indigitatur nocendi facultas & calliditas, quod quasi ante & retro pu- gnent, serpentina quasi prudentia fallant hostes, ali- quando quoŵ, violatis induciis perfide Christianos opprimant: cujus rei exempla in bellis Hungaricis & Cyprico occurrunt, ut hic iterum habet B. Gra- vius. Mahometh enim cum Ario, & Macedonio Christi, & Spiritus S. divinitatem abnegavit, cum Nestorio Judæos non vere Christum crucifixisse, cum Eutyche filium Mariæ invisibilem factum esse asseruit; & sic quatuor illas gravissimas hæreses, tanquam unum fumum equorum Saracenicorum ore proflavit, atque infinitam hominum multi- tudinem perdidit. Et quidem sub hyacinthinis loricis, seu sub specioso sanctuarii defendendi prætextu, quia Scripturam ipsam tueri sese vide- ri volunt. Conf. Ex. XXVI. vers. 14. c. XXXVI. 16. Glossa interlin. ab hyacintho, fumidi coloris gem- ma, vocem deducit. Per caudas intelliguntur juxta Es. IX. 15. cum Ticonio, Nicolai, Cramero, Winckelmanno, Gerharde, Döling, Dürfeld. Na- peiro, Coccejo falsi Doctores, & Sacerdotes, qui serpentibus similes sunt ob venenata & pestifera dogmata, Gen. III. 1. Apoc. XII. 9. Alii cum glossa interlin. per caudas intelligunt occultas deceptio- nes, fraudesque Turcarum. Per capita Magna- tes inter Turcas, Sultani, Primovecier, Bassa, Be- gæ &c. indicantur, quibus ceu capitibus & pa- tronis confidunt, & quorum potentia maxima damna inferunt.

## 9:20
Verse 20.

Καὶ οἱ λοιποὶ τῶν ἀνθρώπων, οἳ ἐκ ἀπεκτάνθησαν, ἐν ταῖς πληγαῖς ταύταις ὐ μετενόησαν ἐκ τῶν ἔργων τῶν χει- ρῶν ἀυτῶν ) From their evil crimes. He gives the reason why God added the final destruction to the plagues of Jerusalem, because the men were not corrected at all. Ἔργα χειρῶν is said of evil deeds. Deut. XXXI. 29. Ps. XXVIII. verse 4. Lam. II. 64. and elsewhere.

Ἵνα μὴ προσκυνήσωσι τὰ δαιμόνια, καὶ τὰ εἴδωλα τὰ χρυ- σᾶ, καὶ τὰ ἀργυρᾶ, καὶ τὰ χαλκᾶ, καὶ τὰ λίθινα, καὶ τὰ ξυλινὰ ἃ ἔτε βλέπειν δύναται, ἔτε ἀκέειν, ἔτε περιπατεῖν ) Just as he said of the Zealots, that they served the same deity that the Romans served, whom they called idolaters: so now he teaches that all the Jerusalemites were also idolaters, namely in the mystical sense, which Paul explains to us, Eph. V. verse 5. Coloss. III. 5. For they served money, gems, and tables, by which, as inanimate things, they could not be saved in danger. Not only were private individuals plundered by private individuals, but even the priests were perishing, defrauded of their food by the chief priests. Nor was greater violence ever seen than when Jerusalem was besieged. See these things explained one by one in Josephus. Battles, treachery, and fires among themselves, says Tacitus. The words concerning idols are taken from Dan. V. 4. Then indeed, and what is usually objected to idols in Ps. CXV. 4, 5, 21, CXXXV. 16, that they are devoid of senses, the same is rightly applied to wealth. A passage of Philo on Monarchy should not be omitted here: Πλάτη γὰρ αἱ περιβόητοι ὗλαι χρυσός καὶ ἄργυρθ• Χθῆτα; πιφύκασιν, αἷς ἀκολθᾶσιν οἱ πολλοὶ τὰ τὸ λεγομένε τυφλᾶ πλκτε μέγα ἢ μάλιςα τῆς ἐυδαιμονίας αἴτια νομίζον- τες, τάδε ἐςιν ἃ φησιν εἴδωλα σκιᾶς ἐοικότα καὶ φάσμασι, ἐδε- νὸς ἐρηρεισμένα ὀχυρῶ καὶ βεβαίω. Thus those who serve riches are said to be θυσιάζον χρυσίῳ Sirach XXX. 17, where gold is also called ξύλον προσκόμματ, that is, an idol.

Latin:

Vers. 20.

Καὶ οἱ λοιποὶ τῶν ἀνθρώπων, οἳ ἐκ ἀπεκτάνθησαν, ἐν ταῖς πληγαῖς ταύταις ὐ μετενόησαν ἐκ τῶν ἔργων τῶν χει- ρῶν ἀυτῶν ) A malis suis facinoribus. Causam reddit, cur ultimum exitium Deus ad plagas Hierosolymorum addi- derit, quia homines nihil erant correcti. Ἔργα χειρῶν de malis factis dicitur. Deut. XXXI. 29. Psal. XXVIII. vers. 4. Lament. II. 64. & alibi.

Ἵνα μὴ προσκυνήσωσι τὰ δαιμόνια, καὶ τὰ εἴδωλα τὰ χρυ- σᾶ, καὶ τὰ ἀργυρᾶ, καὶ τὰ χαλκᾶ, καὶ τὰ λίθινα, καὶ τὰ ξυλινὰ ἃ ἔτε βλέπειν δύναται, ἔτε ἀκέειν, ἔτε περιπατεῖν ) Sicut de Zelotis dixit, eos eidem numini servijsse, quibus servie- bant Romani, quos illi idololatras vocabant: ita nunc do- cet etiam Hierosolymitas omnes fuisse idololatras, nempe sensu mystico, quem nobis explicat Paulus, Eph. V. vers. 5. Coloss. III. 5. Serviebant enim pecuniæ, gemmis, men- sis, a quibus utpote inanimis rebus servari in periculo non poterant. Non privati tantum a privatis expilabantur: sed & Sacerdotes interibant alimentis fraudati per Sacer- dotum principes. Neque unquam major visa est violen- tia quam obsessis Hierosolymis. Vide hæc singulatim ex- plicata apud Josephum. Prælia, dolus, incendia inter ipsos ait Tacitus. Sumpta sunt verba de idolis ex Dan. V. 4. Tum vero & quod idolis objici solet Psal. CXV. 4. 5. 21. CXXXV. 16. destitui illa a sensibus, idem ad opes recte applicatur. Non omittendus hic Philonis locus de Mo- narchia : Πλάτη γὰρ αἱ περιβόητοι ὗλαι χρυσός καὶ ἄργυρθ• Χθῆτα; πιφύκασιν, αἷς ἀκολθᾶσιν οἱ πολλοὶ τὰ τὸ λεγομένε τυφλᾶ πλκτε μέγα ἢ μάλιςα τῆς ἐυδαιμονίας αἴτια νομίζον- τες, τάδε ἐςιν ἃ φησιν εἴδωλα σκιᾶς ἐοικότα καὶ φάσμασι, ἐδε- νὸς ἐρηρεισμένα ὀχυρῶ καὶ βεβαίω. Sic qui divitiis serviunt, di- cuntur θυσιάζον χρυσίῳ Sirach. XXX. 17. ubi etiam aurum dicitur ξύλον προσκόμματ, id est, idolum.

## 9:21
Verse 21.

Καὶ ὐ μετενόησαν ἐκ τῶν φόνων ἀυτῶν ) See Josephus, War V. 1. 27.

Εἴτε ἐκ τῶν φαρμακειῶν ἀυτῶν ) In the same house, some were killing others with poison, so that they might have more food.

Οὔτε ἐκ τῆς πορνείας αὐτῶν) These are what Josephus calls μύση. See Rom. II. 22. and what is said there. A people most prone to lust: Tacitus on the Jews.

Οὔτε ἐκ τῶν κλεμμάτων ἀυτῶν ) They did not even abstain from sacrilege, Josephus V. 33.

Ἔργα τῶν χειρῶν are idols, which can neither see nor hear, Psal. CXV. 4. Psal. CXXXV. v. 16. Es. XLIV. 9. Concerning idols see Exod. XX. 4. Deut. VI. v. 13. c. XXVII. v. 15. Jud. XVIII. v. 24. c. XXII. 29. Idolaters, however, are said to serve demons, Levit. XVII. 7. Deut. XXXII. 17. 1. Reg. XVI. 7. 2. Reg. XIX. 18. c. XXII. 17. Job. XI. 14. Psal. XXIX. 6. Esa. III. 10. LVI. 2. c. LVIII. 13. Jerem. XLIV. vers. 8. Thren. III. 64. Os. XIV. 4. Mich. V. 13. Psal. CVII. vers. 36. 1. Cor. X. 20. The survivors are said not to have repented of their sins according to the first table of the law, such as idolatry: for to this the Papists, whitewashed with the Christian name, are vehemently addicted: nor according to the other table of the law either, regarding the fourth, sixth, and seventh commandments. Οἱ λοιποὶ are the Christians, who, having seen the judgments of God against the impenitence of the Saracens, have not at all repented of their own sins. Others understand those who survived the tyranny of Mahomet, the Papist idolaters in the Second Council of Nicaea. Flacius, Nicolai, Hoë, Winckelm. Gerhardus, Gravius, Döling. Kromejer, Pareus, Napeirus, Medus, Forbesius? Furthermore, concerning sorceries, one may read 2 Macc. 10:13. Φαρμακεία, however, otherwise denotes diabolical illusions and incantations against the first table, Exod. 7:11, ch. 9:12, ch. 22:13, Deut. 18:10, 2 Kings 9:22, 2 Chron. 33:6, Ps. 58:5, Isa. 47:9, 12, Jer. 27:7, Dan. 2:2, Mic. 5:12, Nah. 3:4, Mal. 3:5, Wisd. 12:4, ch. 18:13, Rev. 18:23, ch. 21:8, ch. 22:15. Concerning whoredom, see Acts 15:20, 1 Cor. 6:18, Gen. 6, ch. 19, Deut. 22:17, Prov. 7:5, Isa. 3:16, ch. 9:5, ch. 23:31, 2 Kings 9:30, Ezek. 16:49, Matt. 5:27, 28, ch. 15:19, Mark 6:22, Rom. 13:13, 1 Cor. 6:18, ch. 10:8, Gal. 5:19, Eph. 5:3, 4, 5, Col. 3:5, 1 Thess. 4:3 seqq. 2. 2 Thess. 3:4, 2 Tim. 3:3, Heb. 13:4, 5, Rev. 22:15, Sir. 10:4 seqq., ch. 23:4, 5, ch. 26:12. Concerning thefts and injustice, Hab. 2:6, Zech. 5:8, 1 Cor. 6:10, Eph. 4:28, 1 Tim. 6:8, Lev. 19:11, 13, Isa. 5:8, Jer. 7:9, Hos. 4:2, Mic. 3:1, 2, Prov. 11:1, 29:4, Sir. 27:1, Ezek. 18:13, 17, Prov. 28:8, Exod. 32:8, Deut. 24:14, Ps. 55:12, Jer. 16:13, Isa. 1:23. Now concerning sorceries and magical arts in the Papacy, concerning homicides in persecution and the inquisition, and the burning alive and other various punishments of heretics, as they call them, and wars against the same, concerning thefts, rapines, simonies, penitentiary taxes, the peddling of indulgences, the sales of Episcopal palls, etc. concerning whoredoms, likewise adulteries, brothels, and the profit thence redounding to the Pope, concerning sodomy, which the Archbishop of Benevento, Johannes de Casa, sang in rhythms, what does it matter to speak? Those things are notorious and, by public writings, obvious to everyone. That these idolatries, sorceries, and other sins are the causes why even now, by the judgment of God, the Mahometans retain so many empires and kingdoms taken away from Christians, is here indicated not obscurely, namely Egypt, Palestine, Damascus, Syria, Asia, Cyprus, Thrace, Armenia, Mysia, and in part Hungary, and that they subsequently afflict Christians, who, under the Western Anti-Christ, are given over to and immersed in such sins without repentance.

Εἴτε ἐκ τῶν φαρμακειῶν ἀυτῶν ) In eadem domo alii alios veneno necabant, ut eo plus haberent alimentorum.

Οὔτε ἐκ τῆς πορνείας αὐτῶν) Hæc sunt, quæ μύση vocat Josephus. Vide Rom. II. 22. & ibi dicta. Projectissima in libidinem gens: Tacitus de Judæis.

Οὔτε ἐκ τῶν κλεμμάτων ἀυτῶν ) Ne sacrilegiis quidem abstinebant, Josephus V. 33.

Οἱ λοιποὶ sunt Christiani, qui visis judiciis Dei adversus impœ- nitentiam Saracenorum a suis peccatis haudqua- quam resipuerunt. IX, 30. Ezech. XVI. 49. Matth. V. 27. 28. c. XV. 13. Marc. VI. 22. Rom. XIII. 13. 1. Cor. VI. 18. c. X. 8. Gal. V. v. 22. Eph. V. 3. 4. 5. Col. III. 5. 1. Thesf. IV. 3. seqq. 2. Thesf. III. 4. 2. Tim. III. 31. Ebr. XIII. 4. 5. Apoc. XXII. 8. Sir. X. 4. seqq. c. XXIII. 4. 5. c. XXVI. 12. De furtis & injustitia Hab. II, 6. Zach. V. 8. 1. Cor. VI, 10. Eph. IV. 28. 1. Tim. VI. 8. Lev. XIX. 11. 13. Ef. V. 8. Jer. VII. 9. Of. IV. 2. Mich. III. 1. 2. Prov. XI. 1. XXIX. 4. Sir. XXVII. 1. Ez. XIIX. 13. 17. Prov. XXIIX. 8. Ex. XXXII. 8. Deut. XXIV. 14. Pfal. LV. 12. Jer. XVI. 13. Ef. I. 23. Jam de vene- ficiis, & Magicis artibus in Papatu, de homicidiis in persecutione & inquisitione, ac vivicomburio, aliisque variis suppliciis hæreticorum, quos vo- cant, bellisque adversus eosdem, de furtis, rapi- nis, Simoniis, taxis pœnitentiariis, indulgentiarum nundinationibus, palliorum Episcopalium vendi- tionibus &c. de scortationibus, item adulteriis lu- panaribus & quæstu inde ad Papam redundante, de Sodomia, quam Archi - Episcopus Beneventanus Johannes de Casa rhythmis decantavit, quid atti- net dicere? Notoria illa sunt, publicisque scriptis nemini non obvia. Quæ idololatriæ, veneficia, aliaque peccata causas esse, cur etiamnum Dei judicio Mahometani tot imperia & regna Chri- stianis adempta retineant, haud obscure hic indi- catur, Ægyptum nempe, Palæstinam, Damascum, Syriam, Asiam, Cyprum, Thraciam, Armeniam, Mysiam & ex parte Hungariam, quodque subinde Christianos affligant, sub Anti-Christo Occiden- tali, ejusmodi peccatis citra μετάνοιαν deditos, & immersos.

## 10:1 Argument
PART II. OF THE BOOK, THE SECOND PROPHECY, AND IN IT THE SEVENTH TRUMPET, THE FOURTH VISION, AND ITS PREPARATORY MEMBER. CHAPTER X. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

A preparation for the second prophecy is seen, namely the strong angel with the book, with an oath concerning the end of time, and the book to be devoured. There are two parts: I. The prosopography of the angel, to v. 3. II. The things done by the angel, to v. 11.

PART I. THE PERSON OF THE ANGEL.

V. 1. And I saw a strong angel) An angel who might represent the person of Christ, just as angels were accustomed to represent the person of God under the Old Testament. See above 1:13. Strength is attributed to Christ above v. 12. Coming down from heaven) Thus God is said to descend as often as He is about to do or say something great. Maimonides notes this in the Guide for the Perplexed 1:10.

The angel is described by reason of the individual, or distinction as 'another'; by reason of virtue as 'strong'; by reason of origin, because he came from heaven; by reason of singular attire, because he is clothed with a cloud and his head covered with a rainbow; by reason of appearance and singular vision, because his face is like the sun, his feet like pillars of fire, one seen in the sea, namely the right, the other on the land: his hands holding an open little book, verse 2; finally, his voice like the roaring of a lion, to which are joined seven thunders speaking, but whose voices are to be sealed, verses 3 and 4. But that angel did not only represent the person of Christ, but was Christ himself, to whom the name 'strength' is attributed, as Grotius admits, ch. 5:12, in which most interpreters agree. For Ticonius, Victorinus, Primasius, Beda, Richardus, and most others explain it as the Son of God, as Cluverus admits, as also Albert the Great, who explains it of Christ powerfully commanding the demons, who descends from the heavens clothed in the cloud of his flesh, having the virtue and power of reconciling as a rainbow placed upon his deity as a head, whose assumed humanity shines like the sun, illuminates the minds of men, and inflames them: whose feet are preachers bearing his name, kindled by the Holy Spirit, supporting the building of the Church like pillars. And Blessed Cluverus acknowledges that this is, as it were, the sum of the common gloss of certain ancients, to which Flacius, D. Hoë, Cramerus, Gerhardus, the Weimar Paraphrast, almost all the Calvinists, Bullinger, Napeirus, Forbesius, Coccejus, Crugotius, Cotterius, etc., and among the Papists, Thomas Aquinas, the Gloss, Ludovicus ab Alcafar, etc., give their support. Let us hold, says Pareus, the common opinion that this angel is Christ, the avenger of his Church, because both the description of the person and all his deeds clearly confirm this sense. The scope also requires it. For without Christ, the Church would be little firm in all these consolations. It is added that this strong angel is undoubtedly the same who is Michael standing upon the waters, and swearing by the living God, Dan. 12:7, from whence this part of the vision seems to be taken. But that Michael, the Great Prince standing for the people, was Christ. Although some go in a different direction, and indeed Lyranus concerning the Emperor Justin, Aureolus concerning Justinian, Lambertus Florius, Georg. Nigrinus, Joh. Waltherus concerning the Ministers of the Gospel, and especially Blessed Luther; Blessed Luther himself, Osiander, Heilbrunnerus, Winckelmb. Dürfeld. concerning the Pope; Andreas Cæsar. As also most Papists; Viegas, Ribera, Cornelius a Lapide explain it concerning a created Angel: Other interpreters, however, as being better and more numerous, are deservedly preferred here; because they are supported by reasons (1) that he is called ἄλλος, another, very different from the others, by which name the Son of God was designated Rev. VII. 2. ch. VIII. 3. ch. XVIII. 1. ch. XX. 1. (2) He is described in such a way by reason of his person, that it is certain that the Son of God is signified, inasmuch as he is ἰσχυρὸς. Cf. Is. IX. 6. Rev. V. 5. descending from heaven, because the Son of God is said to descend when he exhibits aid, Ex. III. 8. And there is added in the vision his majestic description, which if it be compared with Dan. X. 5. & Rev. I. 13. having observed, however, apart from the place of Daniel, those things concerning which we have carefully warned in T. IV. Syst. Theol. ch. II. q. XVIII. p. 265, they clearly confirm that the Angel present is none other than the Son of God himself.

Clothed with a cloud) A sign of power. See above I. 7. Thus Ps. CIV. 2. עֹטֶה־אוֹר כַּשַּׂלְמָה Ἀναβαλλόμενος φῶς ὡς ἱμάτιον. A similar expression in Horace concerning Apollo: Nube candentes humeros amictus (Having his shining shoulders wrapped in a cloud).

Ticonius explains the cloud as the Church: But this glorious clothing of the Angel is described, which is proper to God alone, Ps. CIV. 3. A symbol of divine majesty, (whence God often appeared in a cloud in the O. T.) & of grace refreshing and making fruitful the elect, Hos. VI. 4. Others from Augustine tr. XXXIV. in John concerning the human nature, but explain it through the ἐπισκιασμὸν (overshadowing) of the divine Majesty. He is covered by a cloud, not so that the sun may be obscured, but so that it may be tempered.

And a rainbow upon his head] He does not forget his covenant, see above IV. 3. In the Manuscript: The rainbow upon his head.

Whose covenant was it? Was it not GOD'S own? It is GOD, therefore, who appears here: And this is held to be another sign of Majesty, Ez. 1, 28. Sir. 23, 12. as also of grace, favor, and serenity, Gen. 9, 8.

And his face as the sun] A sign of Majesty, see above I, 16.

Grotius himself acknowledges this as a sign of Majesty. Christ shines with glory, both by reason of his divine nature as the character of the hypostasis of GOD and the brightness of his glory, Heb. 1, 2. and by reason of his human nature, whence his whole body shone with the brightness of the sun; Matt. 17, 1. and by reason of his efficacy, because as the sun of righteousness he scatters the rays of his splendor and light upon us, so that he may illuminate, kindle, inflame, and vivify. Compare Dan. X. 5. et seqq. where the Son of GOD is seen not dissimilarly, where his face is as the appearance of lightning, and his eyes as a burning lamp, and his body as chrysolite.

And his feet as pillars of fire] Feet, actions as above 1, 15. Pillars designate firmness, fire designates efficacy.

Pillars on account of the strength by which Christ sustains all things, Heb. 1, 3. fire both on account of his wrath against the impious and enemies, and on account of his grace toward the faithful in the word and the fiery efficacy of the Spirit. Compare Apoc. 1, 15. 16. Feet as pillars of fire are the Ministers of the Word according to Ticonius, the Ordinary Gloss, Thomas, Chytraeus, Cramer, Höë, Döling.

Latin:

PARS II. LIBRI PROPHETIA SECUNDA, ET IN EA SEPTIMUM TUBICINIUM VISIO QUARTA EJUSQUE MEMBRUM PRÆPARATORIUM. CAPUT X. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Parasceve ad alteram prophetiam videtur, nempe Angelus fortis cum libro cum jura- mento de temporis desitione, ac libri ad devo- randum. Partes duæ sunt I. Angeli Prosopographia, ad v. 3. II. Angeli τὰ πραχθέντα, ad v. 11.

PARS I. ANGELI PERSONA.

V. 1. Καὶ εἶδον ἄγγελον ἰσχυρὸν) Angelum qui Christi per- sonam referret, sicut Angeli solebant Dei personam referre sub V. T. Vide supra I. 13. ἰσχὺς Christo tribuitur supra V. 12. Καταβαίνοντα ἐκ τῦ ὄρανῦ) Sic Deus dicitur descendere, quoties aliquid magni aut acturus aut dicturus est. Notan- dum id Maimonidæ Duce dubitantium I. 10.

Describitur Angelus ratione individui, vel di- stinctionis ceu ἄλλον, ratione virtutis ceu fortis; ratione originis, quod de cœlo venerit; ratione vestitus singularis, quod nube amictus, & iride caput tectus; ratione speciei & singularis visionis, quod facies instar Solis, pedes veluti columnæ ignis, alter in mari, videl. dexter, alter in terra visus: manus libellum apertum tenentes vers. 2. vox denique instar rugitus leonis, cui adjuncta septem tonitrua loquentia, sed quorum voces obsignandæ, vers. 3. & 4. Angelus autem ille non referebat tantum personam Christi, sed erat ipse Christus, cui nomen ἰσχύς fatente Grotio tribuitur, c. V. 12. in quo plerique Interpp. consentiunt. De Filio enim Dei explicant Ticonius, Victorinus, Primasius, Beda, Richardus & plerique alii, fatente Cluvero, ut & Albertus M. qui de Christo fortiter Dæmonibus imperante exponit, qui e cœlis descendat nube carnis suæ amictus, virtutem & potentiam reconciliandi tanquam iridem in Deitate sua velut capite repositam habens, cujus assumpta humanitas instar Solis luceat, mentes hominum illuminet, atque inflammet: Cujus pedes sint prædicatores nomen ejus portantes Spiritu S. accensi, ædificium Ecclesiæ tanquam columnæ sustinentes. Et hanc quasi summam communis veterum quorundam glossæ esse, agnoscit B. Cluverus, quibus suffragantur Flacius, D. Hoë, Cramerus, Gerhardus, Paraphraste Vinariens. Calviniani plerique omnes Bullinger, Napeirus, Forbesius, Coccejus, Crugotius, Cotterius &c. & e Pontificiis Thomas Ang. Glossa, Ludovicus ab Alcafar, &c. Teneamus, inquit Pareus, communem sententiam Angelum hunc esse Christum Ecclesiæ suæ vindicem, quia hunc sensum & personæ descriptio & gesta omnia perspicue confirmant. Scopus etiam requirit. Sine Christo enim parum firma esset Ecclesia in his omnibus consolatio. Accedit quod hic Angelus fortis idem haud dubio est, qui Michaël stans super aquis, & jurans per Deum viventem, Dan. XII. 7. unde hæc pars visionis desumpta videtur. Michaël vero ille Princeps Magnus stans pro populo fuit Christus. Quanquam vero nonnulli in diversum abeant, & Lyranus quidem de Justino Imperatore, Aureolus de Justiniano, Lambertus Florius, Georg. Nigrinus, Joh. Waltherus de Evangelii Ministris, & imprimis B. Luthero; ipse B. Lutherus, Osiander, Heilbrunnerus, Winckelmb. Dürfeld. de Papa; Andreas Cæsar. ut & Pontificii pleriq; Viegas, Ribera, Cornelius a Lapide de Angelo creato explicent: Alii tamen Interpretes ceu potiores ac plures hic merito præferuntur; quia rationibus stipati sunt (1) quod dicatur ἄλλος alius multum a cæteris diversus, quo nomine Filius Dei designatus fuit Apoc. VII. 2. c. IIX. 3. c. XIIX. 1. c. XX. 1. (2) Describitur ita ratione personæ, ut constet, Filium Dei significari, utpote quod sit ἰσχυρὸς. Conf. Es. IX. 6. Ap. V. 5. descendens de cœlo, quia Filius Dei descendere dicitur, cum auxilium exhibet, Ex. III. 8. Additurque in visione Majestatica ejus descriptio, quæ si conferatur cum Dan. X. 5. & Ap. I. 13. observatis tamen citra locum Danielis iis, de quibus T. IV. Syst. Theol. c. II. q. XIIX. p. 265. cum cura monuimus, luculenter confirmant Angelum præsentem nullum alium esse, quam ipsummet Filium Dei.

Περιβεβλημένον νεφέλην) Signum potentiæ. Vide supra I. 7. Sic Psal. CII 2. עֹטֶה־אוֹר כַּשַּׂלְמָה Ἀναβαλλόμενος φῶς ὡς ἱμάτιον. Par locutio apud Horatium de Apolline: Nube candentes humeros amictus.

Nubem de Ecclesia exponit Ticonius: Sed vestitus hic gloriosus Angeli describitur, qui soli Deo proprius est, Ps. CIV. 3. Symbolum Majestatis divinæ, (unde in nube sæpe apparuit Deus in V. T.) & gratiæ refocillantis ac fœcundantis electos, Os. VI. 4. Alii ex Augustino tr. XXXIV. in Job. de humana natura, sed per ἐπισκιασμὸν divinæ Majestatis ex- plicant. Nube tegitur, non ut obscuretur sol, sed ut temperetur.

Καὶ ἶρις ἐπὶ τῆς κεφαλῆς αὐτῦ] fœderis sui non oblivisci- tur, supra IV. 3. In Manuscripto: Ἡ ἶρις ἐπὶ τὴν κεφα- λὴν αὐτῦ.

Cujus fœdus erat? Annon ipsius DEI? DE- US ergo est, qui hic apparet: Idque iterum Ma- jestatis signum habetur, Ez. 1, 28. Sir. 23, 12. ut & gratiæ, favoris, & serenitatis, Gen. 9, 8.

Καὶ τὸ πρόσωπον αὐτῦ ὡς ἥλιος] Majestatis signum su- pra I, 16.

Hic Majestatis signum agnoscit ipse Grotius. Splendet Christus gloria, tum ratione divinæ na- turæ ceu character hypostaseos DEI & splendor glo- riæ ejus, Ebr. 1, 2. tum ratione humanæ naturæ, unde corpus ejus totum instar solis claritate ful- sit; Matth. 17, 1. tum ratione efficaciæ, quia ceu sol justitiæ radios fulgoris & lucis suæ in nos spar- git, ut illuminet, accendat, inflammet ac vivificet. Conf. Dan. X. 5. seqq. ubi non absimiliter Filius DEI videtur, qua facies ejus est velut species ful- guris, & oculi ejus, ut lampas ardens, & corpus ejus, quasi chrysolitus.

Καὶ οἱ πόδες αὐτῦ ὡς σύλοι πυρὸς] Pedes, actiones ut supra 1, 15. Columnæ firmitatem, ignis efficaciam de- signat.

Columnæ ob robur, quo sustentat Christus o- mnia, Ebr. 1, 3. ignis cum ob iram adversus im- pios, & hostes, tum ob gratiam erga fideles in verbo & efficacia Spiritus ignea. Conf. Apoc. 1, 15. 16. Pedes ut columnæ ignis Verbi Ministri sunt Ticonio, Glossæ Ordin. Thomæ, Chytreo, Cra- mero, Höëο, Döling.

## 10:2
Verse 2. And he had in his hand a little book opened] that is, a sentence about to be pronounced. The Hebrews call every writing ספר, such as an instrument of divorce, of purchase, and others. Decrees, the execution of which is suspended, are accustomed to be sealed, as we have seen above. But sentences about to be pronounced ought to be open. Now this sentence contained the causes of the destruction of the city of Jerusalem and of the temple and of the city for the most part. In Ezekiel for little book there is מגלה III. 1. and following.

He has that book open, which in chapter 5 he received closed from the hand of the one sitting on the throne, and in chapter 6 began to open. The seventh seal is now opened, and therefore the whole book is now open, as being sealed with seven seals, Apoc. 8, 1. Christ is therefore presented here as the supreme Author of the revelation, so that before the sounding of the seventh most horrible trumpet concerning the Anti-Christ, the faithful may have comfort, which his gracious manifestation with the rainbow on his head provides for them most solidly.

And he set his right foot upon the sea] To set a foot signifies dominion. Thus also the Latins say, to have under one's feet. Christ, through the Romans as the satellites of his tribunal, subdued the Jerusalemites. Christ himself dictates this meaning to us in Matt. XXII. verse 7. The sea in this part of the Apocalypse is that multitude of Jews which is at Jerusalem, see above V. 13. VII. 1. 2. 3. VIII. 8. The right foot is the greater part of the citizens.

For what Angel, indeed, has universal dominion both in the sea and on the land besides Christ, the Angel of the covenant, to whom all things are subjected even in the sea, Ps. 8, Heb. 2? He has his right foot in the sea, because Satan, that strong man armed, is consigned to the abyss of the sea, Luke 11, verse 21, Matt. 8, 32, Apoc. 20, 2; his left foot on the land, to which the Princes of the earth pertain, for He is King and Prince of the Kings on earth, Apoc. 1, v. 5, 17, v. 14, and 19, 16. To set a foot somewhere implies ownership, by a Hebrew idiom; Deut. 11, v. 24, Jos. 1, 3, Ps. 10, 10, Ps. 89, 26, Ps. 108, verse 10. A strange gloss that the right foot is the greater part of the citizens, and the sea is the multitude of the Jews. To set the right foot in the sea, therefore, is to set the greater part of the citizens into the multitude of the Jews. Who understands these things?

Τὸν δὲ εὐώνυμον ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς] He also held the whole land of Judea by means of Roman garrisons and stations.

Who is he that held the whole land of Judea through Roman garrisons? The discourse is of the strong Angel, Christ: who holds not only the land of Judea, but the whole world, not by foreign garrisons, but by His own power. For He upholds all things by the word of His power, Heb. I. 3, and by that placing of both feet His omnipresence is signified, and the whole earth is constituted the footstool of His feet, which is an argument of divine potency, authority, and dominion, Es. LXVI. 1, Psal. CX, 1, the propagation of the Gospel and of the kingdom of Christ throughout the whole world being especially noted. And because two beasts proceed in c. XIII, one from the sea, the other from the earth, it is intimated that Christ, being more powerful, will trample them under both feet and supplant them, so that they may not be able, as they would wish, to harm the Church, against which, on account of His protection, not even the gates of hell can prevail, Matth. XVI. 18. And this Prophecy constrains the sea, that is, the tumultuous multitude of nations, subject to perpetual agitations and waves. And the earth, that is, the foundation and support of this sea, by which it is contained, namely the wisdom and prudence of this age. For we are moved to accept the sea and the earth in this place in this way by the harmony of the following passages, since in chapter XII. 12. the inhabitants of heaven are distinguished from the inhabitants of the earth and the sea, and that for the same reason that in chapter XI. 18. the dead, the nations, and the destroyers of the earth are opposed to the servants of God, the Prophets, the Saints, and those who fear his name, both great and small. For just as the inhabitants of heaven in chapter XII. are commanded to rejoice and exult; so in chapter XI. a reward is predicted to be given to them, and on the contrary, the destroyers of the earth are to be judged and destroyed. Similarly, in this place, the Angel places his fiery feet upon the inhabitants of the earth and the sea, and bellows over them with a great voice. He places the right [hand/side] upon the sea, because it requires greater restraint; the left upon the land, because it requires less.

Latin:

Vers. 2. Καὶ εἶχεν ἐν τῇ χειρὶ αὑτῦ βιβλιδάριον ἀνεῳγμένον] id est, sententiam jamjam pronuntiandam. Ebræi omne scriptum vocant ספר, ut instrumentum divortii, empti- onis & alia. Decreta, quorum executio suspenditur, ob- signari solent, ut supra vidimus. At sententiæ jamjam pro- nuntiandæ parere debent. Erat autem hæc sententia causas continens excidii urbis Hierosolymorum & templi & civita- tis ex maxima parte. In Ezechiele pro βιβλιδάριον est מגלה III. 1. & sequentibus.

Librum illum habet apertum, quem c. 5. acce- pit clausum ex manu sedentis in throno, & c. 6. aperire cœpit. Septimum sigillum jam aper- tum, ideoque totus liber jam apertus, utpote septem sigillis obsignatus Apoc. 8, 1. Christus er- go ceu supremus Autor revelationis hic sistitur, ut ante sonitum tubæ septimæ maxime horrendæ de Anti-Christo solatium habeant fideles, quod gra- tiosa ej9 manifestatio cum iride in capite ipsis præ- bet solidissimum.

Καὶ ἔθηκε τὸν πόδα αὑτῦ τὸν δεξιὸν ἐπὶ τῆς θαλάσσης] Pedem ponere dominium significat. Sic & Latini dicunt, habere sub pedibus. Christus per Romanos tanquam tri- bunalis sui satellites Hierosolymitas subegit. Hunc sensum nobis dictat Christus ipse Matth. XXII. vers. 7. Mare in hac parte Apocalypseos est multitudo Judæorum illa, quæ Hierosolymis, vide supra V. 13. VII. 1.2.3. VIII. 8. Pes de- xter major pars civium.

Ecquisnam vero Angelus dominium & in ma- ri & in terra universale habet præter Christum, Angelum fœderis, cui omnia etiam in mari subdita sunt, Psal. 8. Ebr. 2. In mari dextrum pedem ha- bet, quia ad abyssum maris refertur Satanas, fortis ille armatus, Luc. 11, vers. 21. Matth. 8, 32. Apoc. 20, 2. in terra sinistrum, ad quam Principes terræ pertinent, est enim Rex, & Princeps Re- gum in terra, Apoc. 1, v. 5. 17, v. 14. & 19, 26. Pe- dem aliquo ponere infert dominum, phrasi Ebræa; Deut. 11, v. 24. Jos. 1. 3. Psal. 10, 10. Ps. 89, 26. Ps. 108, vers. 10. Mira glossa dextrum pedem esse ma- jorem partem civium, mare multitudinem esse Judæorum. Ponere ergo pedem dextrum in mare est ponere majorem partem civium in multitudinem Judæorum. Quis hæc intelligit?

Τὸν δὲ εὐώνυμον ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς] Tenebat etiam per Romana præsidia & stationes totam terram Judæam.

Quis ille, qui tenebat totam terram Judæam per præsidia Romana? De Angelo forti, Christo, sermo est: qui non tantum terram Judæam, sed totum orbem tenet, non per præsidia aliena, sed virtute propria. Omnia enim portat verbo virtutis suæ Ebr. I. 3. & positu illo pedis utriusque omnipræsentia ejus significatur, ac terra tota scabellum pedum ejus constituitur, quod est argumentum divinæ potentiæ, potestatis ac dominii, Es. LXVI. 1. Psal. CX, 1. Evangelii imprimis & regni Christi per totum orbem propagatio notata. Et quia duæ bestiæ procedunt c. XIII. una è mari, altera de terra, Christum potentiorem eas utroque pede conculcaturum innuitur & supplantaturum, ne possint, ut vellent, nocere Ecclesiæ, adversus quam, ob ejusdem præsidium, nec portæ inferiorum prævalere possunt, Matth. XVI. 18. Et mare stringit hæc Prophetia, hoc est, multitudinem gentium tumultuosam, perpetuisque agitationibus & fluctibus obnoxiam. Et terram hoc est pedamentum & sustentamen hujus maris, quo continetur, sapientiam nimirum & prudentiam hujus seculi. Sic enim accipere hoc loco mare & terram, sequentium harmonia movemur, cum cap. XII. 12. cæli habitatores incolis terræ marisque contradistinguantur, idque eadem ratione, qua cap. XI. 18. mortui, gentes & corruptores terræ opponuntur servis Dei, Prophetis, Sanctis, & timentibus nomen ejus magnis & parvis. Etenim sicut cælicolæ cap. XII. jubentur lætari & exultare; sic cap. XI. illis merces danda prædicitur, & contra judicandi perdendique corruptores terræ. Similiter hoc loco Angelus terræ marisque inquilinis igneos suos pedes imponit, magnaque super eos voce mugit. Dexterum autem mari imponit, quod majori coërcitione; sinistrum terræ, quod minori illa indiget.

## 10:3
Vers. 3. Καὶ ἔκραξε φωνῇ μεγάλῃ ὥσπερ λέων μυκᾶται] For Christ is the Lion from the tribe of Judah, see V. 5. The words of an angry GOD are compared to the roaring of a Lion, Is. XXXI. verse 4, likewise Amos III. 8, where in Hebrew it is שאג, which is translated there, as also in Hos. XI. verse 10, by ἐρυύγεσθαι, elsewhere by ὠρύεσθαι, as also in 1 Pet. V. 8, which Apollonius in his Argonautica also attributes to the Lion. But as the Scholiast notes there, the customary word for this is βρυχᾶν, which Pollux, however, notes is also said of the bear and the panther. Μυκᾶσθαι belongs to oxen, but it is accustomed to be transferred to the lion, and elsewhere to thunder.

It must therefore be acknowledged that it was Christ, not an Angel, who appeared in the person of Christ. The efficacy of the Word of GOD, which is the voice of Christ, 1 Pet. 1:11, Ps. 95:8, is designated by this great voice, concerning which Dan. 10:6, Apoc. 1:15, "His voice as the voice of a multitude." A horrible voice can also be noted by the roaring of a lion, because the roaring of a lion is a symbol of horror and cruelty, to indicate the horrible judgments of GOD, Is. 5:29, Hos. 11:10, Amos 3, et seqq. However, the Τὸ μυκᾶν is attributed to the lion, with Cluverus as authority, it seems, so that it may be intimated that the lion's wrath will be joined with the patience and moderation of an ox. Conf. Jer. 25:30, Joel 3:16, Am. 1:2, and ch. 14:2, ch. 16:17, ch. 19:6.

Καὶ ὅτε ἔκραξεν] He called out the thunders. Ἐλάλησαν αἱ ἑπτὰ βρονταὶ τὰς ἑαυτῶν φωνὰς] That voice was so great that it could be heard amidst the seven thunders. Thunders signify dreadful things: seven, however, a complete number. Just as thunders occurred before the war, above in chapter 8, verse 5, so now at the end of the war. Φωνὴ properly belongs to living creatures: But it is accustomed to be transferred to other things, and specifically to thunders, as Ps. 77, vers. 19. 104, vers. 7. But here we must take φωνὰς properly, because it says τὰς ἑαυτῶν φωνὰς, that is, articulate and distinct, such as are human voices, which can be written. See below 11, 25. You may rightly adapt here that of Job 26, 14.

Latin:

Vers. 3. Καὶ ἔκραξε φωνῇ μεγάλῃ ὥσπερ λέων μυκᾶται] Quippe Christus est Leo ex stirpe Juda supra V. 5. DEI irati verba Leonis mugitui comparantur, Es. XXXI. vers. 4. item Amos III. 8. ubi in Ebræo שאג, quod ibi ut & Os. XI. vers. 10. per ἐρυύγεσθαι vertitur, alibi per ὠρύεσθαι, ut & 1. Petr. V. 8. quod & Apollonius in Argonauticis dat Leoni. Sed ut ibi Scholiastes notat, usitata vox huic rei est βρυχᾶν, quam tamen & de urso & de Panthera dici Pollux notat. Μυκᾶσθαι est boum, sed transferri solet ad leonem, alibi ad tonitrua.

Christum ergo, non Angelum in persona Christi apparuisse agnoscendum. Verbi DEI, quæ vox Christi est, 1. Petr. I. 11. Ps. 95, v. 8. efficacia per hanc vocem magnam designatur, de qua Dan. 10, 6. Apoc. 1, 15. Vox sermonem ejus ut vox multitudinis. Potest & notari per rugitum leonis vox horribilis, quia leonis rugitus horroris & crudelitatis symbolum est, ad indicanda judicia DEI horribilia, Es. 5, 29. Os. 11, 10. Amos 3, seqq. Τὸ μυκᾶν autem leoni tribui, Cluvero autore, videtur, ut leonis iram cum bovis patientia & moderatione conjunctam fore innuatur. Conf. Jerem. 25, 30. Joël. 3, 16. Am. 1, 2. & cap. 14, 2. cap. 16, 17. cap. 19, 6.

Καὶ ὅτε ἔκραξεν] Vocavit tonitrua. Ἐλάλησαν αἱ ἑπτὰ βρονταὶ τὰς ἑαυτῶν φωνὰς] Vox illa tanta erat, ut inter septena tonitrua exaudiri posset. Tonitrua res horrendas significant: septem vero, numerum completum. Sicut ante bellum facta tonitrua, su- pra 8, vers. 5. ita nunc in belli exitu. Φωνὴ proprie est ani- mantium : Sed solet & ad res alias transferri, & nomina- tim ad tonitrua, ut Psal. 77. vers. 19. 104, vers. 7. Verum hic proprie φωνὰς sumere debemus, quia dicit τὰς ἑαυτῶν φωνὰς, id est, ἐνάρθρους atque distinctas, quales sunt vo- ces humanae, quae scribi possunt. Vide infra 11,25. Recte huc aptes illud Jobi 26, 14.

## 10:4
Vers. 4.

Καὶ ὅτε ἐλάλησαν αἱ ἑπτὰ βρονταὶ ἔμελλον γράφειν] I had been about to write down those voices which had thundered, just as I had written down what I had heard. These thunders were more serious and more numerous than those above 8, 5. Καὶ ἤκουσα φωνὴν ἐκ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ λέγουσάν, σφράγισον ἃ ἐλά- λησαν αἱ ἑπτὰ βρονταὶ, καὶ μετὰ ταῦτα γράψεις] Others better: Μὴ ταῦτα γράφῃς. And σφράγισον here is conceal, by Metonymy. Because we are accustomed to seal up things which we wish to be hidden from others, such as mystical testaments, and that in Is. 29, v. 11. In Daniel 8, vers. 26. and 12, v. 4. סתם is put for the same. The Greeks in the former place have σφράγισον as here: in the latter ἔμ- φραξον, which is an interpretation of that σφράγισον. GOD means this, that those evils which were to follow the storming of the city are so serious that they cannot be described according to their dignity; but can only be conceived in the mind under the appearance of all the horrible things that are read of anywhere.

Something similar concerning the thunders joined to the roaring of the Lord is held in Jerem. XXV. 30. and there proceed in Apoc. IV. 5. from the throne of GOD thunders and voices, namely of divine judgments. Therefore, the strong and clear proclamations of the Majesty and Justice of God are noted, and the thunders of the zealots who have opposed themselves to the Anti-Christ, Mark III, 17, just as lion-like preachers and sons of thunder are called those who effectively proclaim the magnificence and judgments of GOD, Apoc. VI, 1. St. John had a command to write those things which he saw c. I, 11. Therefore he wished to obey here also in recording the voices of the thunders; but he is ordered to seal them, not to write them: and therefore he communicated them neither by living voice nor by traditions, otherwise they would not have remained sealed. But without doubt he is said to seal them by the voice of GOD himself. For it was the same one's task to say so, whose task it was to command in Ap. I. 11. Some make it the voice of an Angel. But he is distinguished from him whose voice is perceived in this place v. 8. So also Paul heard ἄῤῥητα ῥήματα, which it was not permitted to speak on earth, even though he could understand them in heaven 2. Cor. XII, 4. so that it is established that our knowledge, however small it may be, is imperfect, 1. Cor. XIII. 9. and that something is granted to the Prophets above others, as those in whom the sufferings of Christ also abounded, 2. Cor. I. 5. Marloratus thinks: That it is signified that many preachers of the word were raised up, who with invincible constancy would argue against Kings and Princes, convince the people of unbelief, and announce the horrible judgment of GOD to all, as well great as small, unless all should maturely repent. For thunder signifies judgment, rebuke, and terror, Ps. XVIII. v. 14. and XXIX. v. 3. and Is. XXIX. v. 6. But John seems in this place to indicate (although more secretly) the destruction of the Roman Empire, which then held power: in whose place the Mahometan and Papistical impiety was to succeed. That which is signified by that little horn in Dan. VII. But he did not wish to write those things more openly then: just as the Apostle writes about this matter more obscurely and as it were sphinx-like in the judgment of many 2. Thess. II. 3. Lactantius, however, in book 7, ch. 15 of the Divine Institutions, writes in express words of the defection of that Empire. That which we see has happened today, and time, the most certain revealer of all future things, has brought this truth into the light: Which we leave in its own place: Which GOD himself has sealed, who could seal it?

PART II. The deeds and words of the Angel.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

Καὶ ὅτε ἐλάλησαν αἱ ἑπτὰ βρονταὶ ἔμελλον γράφειν] Per- scripturus fueram voces illas quae intonuerant, sicut audita perscripseram. Graviora & plura erant haec tonitrua quam illa supra 8, 5. Καὶ ἤκουσα φωνὴν ἐκ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ λέγουσάν, σφράγισον ἃ ἐλά- λησαν αἱ ἑπτὰ βρονταὶ, καὶ μετὰ ταῦτα γράψεις] Melius a- lii : Μὴ ταῦτα γράφῃς. Et σφράγισον hic est occule, per Metonymiam. Quia quae celata alios volumus, solemus ob- signare, ut testamenta μυστικὰ, & illa Es. 29, v. 11. Apud Danielem 8, vers. 26. & 12, v. 4. pro eodem ponitur סתם. Graeci priore loco habent σφράγισον ut hic: posteriore ἔμ- φραξον, quod est interpretamentum illius σφράγισον. Hoc vult DEUS, ea mala quae expugnationem urbis sunt secutu- ra, adeo sunt gravia, ut pro dignitate describi non possint; sed non aliter, quam sub specie omnium quae usquam legun- tur horribilium, animo concipi.

Simile quid de junctis rugitui Domini tonitri- bus habetur Jerem. XXV. 30. & prodeunt Apoc. IV. 5. e throno DEI tonitrua & voces judicio- rum nempe divinorum. Notantur ergo valida & clara Majestatis & Justitiae divino praeconia & zelotarum, qui se Anti-Christo oppositi sunt, tonitrua, Marc. III, 17. quemadmodum & leo- nini praedicatores ac tonitruum filii dicuntur, qui efficaciter DEI magnificentiam & judicia pro- clamant, Apoc. VI, 1. Scribendi mandatum ha- bebat S. Johannes ea, quae vidit c. I, 11. Illi er- go etiam hic in consignandis vocibus tonitruum parere voluit; sed obsignare eas jubetur, non scribere: ideoque nec viva voce nec per traditio- nes eas communicavit, alias non mansissent obsi- gnatae. Sine dubio autem ipsius DEI voce per- hibetur easdem consignare. Nam ejusdem erat perhibere, cujus Ap. I. 11. erat jubere. Angeli vocem nonnulli faciunt. Sed ille distinguitur ab eo, cujus vox percipitur hoc loco v. 8. Sic & Paulo ἄῤῥητα ῥήματα audivit, quae non licuit in ter- ris proloqui, etsi ea in coelo intelligere potue- rit 2. Cor. XII, 4. ut constet, cognitionem nostra quantulacunque sit, imperfectam esse, 1. Cor, XIII. 9. ac Prophetis aliquid prae aliis conceda- tur, utpote in quibus etiam passiones Christi ab- undarunt, 2. Cor. I. 5. Marloratus putat: Signi- ficari multos verbi praecones excitatos fuisse, qui invicta constantia Reges & Principes arguerent, populum incredulitatis convincerent, & omnibus tam magnis, quam parvis, horrendum DEI judi- cium annuntiarent, nisi omnes mature resipiscerent. Nam tonitru judicium, increpationem & terro- rem significat, Psal. XVIII. v. 14. & XXIX. v. 3. & Es. XXIX. v. 6. Videtur autem Johannes hoc loco indicare, (quamvis occultius) Romani Imperii, quod tum rerum potiebatur, interitum: in cujus locum successura erat Mahumetana & Papistica impietas. Id quod per parvum illud cornu apud Dan. VII. significatur. Noluit autem ista tum apertius scribere: sicut Apostolus hac de re obscu- rius & quasi sphingicῶς multorum judicio scribit 2. Thess. II. 3. Lactantius tamen divinarum insti- tutionum lib. 7. c. 15. disertis verbis ejus Imperii de- fectionem scribit. Id quod hodie factum videmus, & tempus, omnium futurorum revelator certis- simus, hanc veritatem in lucem produxit: Quae nos suo loco relinquimus: Quae obsignavit ipse DEUS, ecquis obsignare possit?

PARS II. Angeli facta, & dicta.

## 10:5-6
Vers. 5. 6.

Καὶ ὁ Ἄγγελος ὃν εἶδον ἑστῶτα ἐπὶ τῆς θαλάσσης καὶ τῆς γῆς, ᾖρε τὴν χεῖρα αὑτοῦ τὴν δεξιὰν εἰς τὸν οὐρανὸν καὶ ὤμο- σεν ἐν τῷ ζῶντι εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων] Christ would not swear, unless he were promising some great good to the Church, Heb. 6, vers. 17. 7, vers. 21. Nor does he only swear, but he swears with a most solemn gesture, Gen. 14, 22. Deut. 32, 40. Ex. 6, 8. Num. 14, 30. Ezech. 20, 6. And he uses the same formula as the Angel in Daniel 12, 7, where it treats of the liberation from the evils brought by Antiochus.

Latin:

Verf. 5. 6.

Καὶ ὁ Ἄγγελος ὃν εἶδον ἑστῶτα ἐπὶ τῆς θαλάσσης καὶ τῆς γῆς, ᾖρε τὴν χεῖρα αὑτοῦ τὴν δεξιὰν εἰς τὸν οὐρανὸν καὶ ὤμο- σεν ἐν τῷ ζῶντι εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων] Non juraret Christus, nisi magnum aliquod bonum Ecclesiæ promitte- ret, Ebr. 6, vers. 17. 7, vers. 21. Neque jurat tantum, sed jurat gestu maxime solenni, Gen. 14, 22. Deut. 32, 40. Ex. 6, 8. Num. 14, 30. Ezech. 20, 6. Et utitur eadem formula qua apud Danielem Angelus 12, 7. ubi de liberatione ab illa- tis per Antiochum malis agitur.

## 10:6
Ὅς ἔκτισε τὸν οὐρανὸν καὶ τὰ ἐν αὐτῷ καὶ τὴν γῆν καὶ τὴν θάλασσαν καὶ τὰ ἐν αὐτῇ] taken from Nehem. X. 6. But that καὶ τὴν γῆν and the following are missing in the Manuscript.

Latin:

Ὅς ἔκτισε τὸν οὐρανὸν καὶ τὰ ἐν αὐτῷ καὶ τὴν γῆν καὶ τὴν θάλασσαν καὶ τὰ ἐν αὐτῇ] sumpta ex Nehem. X. 6. Sed illa καὶ τὴν γῆν & sequentia desunt in Manuscripto.

## 10:7
Vers. 7.

Ὅτι χρόνος οὐκ ἔσται, ἀλλὰ ἐν ταῖς ἡμέραις τῆς φωνῆς τῆς ἑβδόμης Ἀγγέλου, ὅταν μέλλῃ σαλπίζειν, τελεσθῇ τὸ μυστή- ριον τοῦ Θεοῦ.] It will not be long before the mystery of God is completed. For χρόνος οὐκέτι ἔσται signifies, that the matter would not be delayed any longer. Thus Is. 13, v. 22. ימיה לא ימשכו his days shall not be prolonged. It is the same as that it shall not delay, Hab. 2, vers. 7. and χρονιεῖ Sir. 7, 17. 12, 12. But that mystery of God which is said not to be delayed any longer is no other than that which is praised and celebrated after the sounding of the seventh trumpet below 11, 15. This indeed is what was permitted to Christians by Hadrian at Jerusalem, namely, residence and free worship of God and Christ there, with all remnants of the Jews expelled from thence: whence it came to pass that, with no Jews approaching that Church any further, after that the Bishop there was from the Gentiles, and if there were Jews elsewhere who had believed in Christ, they became an accession to the believers from the Gentiles. Which, just as it was the supreme victory of Christ over the contumacious Jews and a consolation to the pious: so it is the limit of the Apocalypse concerning Jewish affairs. You have the word Μυστηρίκ in a similar sense in 1 Corinthians 15, verse 51, and often in the Greek in Daniel. Furthermore, in the Manuscript it is: ὅταν μέλλῃ σαλπίζειν καὶ ἐτελέσθη, so that the conjunction is redundant and indefinite for the future prophetically. Reference is made to that of Daniel עד צור קץ.

Which he announced as good news to his servants the prophets] From the verb εὐαγγελίσατο you see that it deals with a joyful matter, as we have said. Moreover, εὐαγγελίζειν is accustomed to govern after itself sometimes the Dative of the person to whom the message is, sometimes the Accusative, as here and Luke 3, verse 18, Acts 8, verse 40, chapter 13, verse 32, chapter 14, verses 15, 21. Understand, however, the prophets here as those of the New Testament, and indeed from the Jerusalem Presbyteries, who are indicated above 5, 5 and 7, 13.

To the deeds of this Angel pertains the extension of the hand into heaven; which rite was that of those swearing, which phrase even GOD himself uses anthropopathically, as is clear from the passages adduced by Grotius. For even GOD himself has not rarely sworn; which Blessed Cluverus indeed denies concerning Christ, but the passages are clear, Gen. XXII. 16, Ez. XXXIII. 11, as also Dan. XII. 7, Heb. VI. 13. Concerning GOD the Father, Psalm CX. v. 4, Psalm CXXXII. 11, Ezech. XXXIII. verse 11. And the passage in Dan. XII. is entirely parallel, not dealing with liberation from evils brought in by Antiochus, but by the Anti-Christ. The oath and the command concerning receiving and eating the little book have been spoken of, as also the interpretation of this symbol, that he ought to prophesy AGAIN or openly announce to peoples and nations and tongues those things which were consigned in that book, that is, he ought to announce the divine decrees and judgments. The oath is concerning the end of times, or the consummation of the age in the 1st verse in express words. For with the heaven perishing, which Christ predicted Luke XXI. 33, and the stars about to perish. Therefore, there will be no more times, which arise from the luminaries out of the motion of the heaven, Gen. I. 14. No time, namely, of persecution, is what Ticonius, Thomas, Ribera, Cornelius a Lap., Fox, Piscator, Pareus, Flacius, Chytræus, Hoë, Cramer, Gerhard, Grave, Döling, Kromejer judge there will be. Lyra restricts it to the Arian heresy. But the subsequent visions declare that there will as yet be no end to the persecutions. Why, indeed, do we wish to depart from the literal meaning of the words, when no cause compels us, which implies that there will be no more time, and not that the matter will not be delayed any longer, χρόνον ὀυκ ἔσται. Cf. Ps. LXXII. 5, 7, 2. The consummation of the age is indicated κατὰ διάνοιαν, when the mystery of GOD shall be finished, as He has declared to His servants the prophets, through the Spirit, which they in turn have announced in writing to the whole world. For when all things that have been predicted have been fulfilled, then there will be an end. What of the fact that the very consummation of the age is also predicted, and the ceasing of the sun and moon, the destruction of heaven and earth, and the cessation of days and nights and consequently of times; therefore, those things are not fulfilled until there will be no more time, but mere eternity will follow, and the eternal blessedness of the faithful, which itself has likewise been predicted by the servants of GOD, the prophets, Is. LXVI. 23, Ezech. XXXIX. 2. Dan. II. 44. cap. VII. v. 26. 27. cap. XII. 1. 2. 2 Petr. III. 13. &c. There shall be time no longer, which time, as Fromondus says, by which the vicissitudes of the lower world are governed, shall cease, when the motion of the heavens, in which time flows, ceases. For immediately upon the completion of the universal judgment, the sun, moon, and all the stars, together with their heavens, shall stand still, because they will then have finished the task of their work, for which they were created. For they are moved only so long as the number of the Elect is being fulfilled, so that through the vicissitudes of day and night, summer and winter, and others, sustenance and necessities may be provided for mortals, which will be superfluous when all are to be immortal. The prophets likewise are to be understood literally, because the discourse is concerning the mysteries themselves being revealed, and the fulfillment of their prophecies. Whence, therefore, will it be taught that the Jerusalemite Presbyters were such as to have predicted such things, or to have announced them προφητικῶς, as that excellent name occurs in the Scriptures? Grotius trifles rashly concerning the end of Jewish affairs as designated in the Apocalypse. For the end of them, both of the synagogue with its divine worship and sacrifices and of the polity, had already arrived before St. John was relegated to Patmos, in which place he had these visions. But how will it be convinced that the free worship of GOD, after the Jews were expelled, which Hadrian conceded, is designated in this passage? For there is nothing of the sort in the text: nor does the matter seem to have been of such importance that a divine oath was necessary, especially because it could have been established from the Prophetic oracles of the Old Testament and the command of Christ when He sent forth the Apostles, concerning the propagation of the Gospel through the whole world: indeed, from the notoriety of the thing. Brightman understands the mystery concerning the conversion of the Jews toward the end of the world in a very significant way from Rom. XI. 25. But that there is another sense of this passage, we have shown in the same place. Moreover, the manifestation of the Anti-Christ is called a mystery, 2 Thess. II. 7, Apoc. XVII. 5, 8, as is also the resurrection of the dead joined with the transformation of the living, 1 Cor. XV. 51, not to mention anything of the other things predicted here.

Latin:

Vers. 7.

Ὅτι χρόνος οὐκ ἔσται, ἀλλὰ ἐν ταῖς ἡμέραις τῆς φωνῆς τῆς ἑβδόμης Ἀγγέλου, ὅταν μέλλῃ σαλπίζειν, τελεσθῇ τὸ μυστή- ριον τοῦ Θεοῦ.] Non diu erit quin arcanum Dei compleatur. Nam χρόνος ἐκέτι ἔσται significat, non diutius res omere- tur. Sic Esa. 13, v. 22. ימיה לא ימשכו ἡμέραι αὐτοῦ ὲ μὴ ἐφελκυσθῶσιν. Idem est quod ὲ μὴ χρονίσῃ, Ab. 2, vers. 7. & χρονιεῖ Sir. 7, 17. 12, 12. Arcanum autem illud Dei quod non diutius differendum dicitur, non aliud est ab eo quod post cantum tubæ septimæ laudatur, & celebratur infra 11, 15. Id vero est quod Christianis per Adrianum Hierosolymos rum habitatio & liber ibi cultus Dei & Christi permissus est, expulsis inde omnibus Judæorum reliquiis: unde factum est, ut nullis ultra Judæis ad illam Ecclesiam accedentibus, post id Episcopus ibi esset ex gentibus, & si qui alibi essent Ju- dæi, qui in Christum crediderant, ii fierent accessio cre- dentium ex gentibus. Quæ sicut summa fuit Christi de contumacibus Judæis victoria & piorum consolatio: ita terminus est Apocalypseos de rebus Judaicis. Μυστηρίκ vocem pari sensu habes 1. Corinth. 15, vers. 51. & apud Da- nielem in Græco sæpe. Deinde in Manuscripto est: ὅταν μέλλῃ σαλπίζειν καὶ ἐτελέσθη, ut sit copula παρέλκουσα & ἀόριστος pro futuro προφητικῶς. Respicitur illud Danielis עד צור קץ.

Ὃ εὐηγγελίσατο τοῖς δούλοις αὑτοῦ τοῖς προφήταις] Ex ver- bo εὐαγγελίσατο vides de re læta agi, ut dixunus. Solet autem εὐαγγελίζειν modo post se regere Dativum personæ, cui sit nuntius, modo accusativum, ut hic & Luc. 3, vers. 18. Actorum 8, vers. 40. cap. 13, vers. 32. cap. 14, vers. 15. 21. Prophetas autem hic intellige Novi Testamenti, & quidem ex Presbyteriis Hierosolymitanis, qui indicantur su- pra 5, 5. & 7, 13.

Ad Angeli hujus facta pertinet manus exten- sio in cælum; qui ritus erat jurantium, qua phrasi etiam DEUS ipse ἀνθρωποπαθῶς utitur, ut ex locis à Grotio adductis patet. Nam & ipse DEUS non raro juravit; quod de Chri- sto quidem negat B. Cluverus, sed loca lucu- lenta sunt, Gen. XXII. 16. Ez. XXXIII. 11. ut & Dan. XII. 7. Ebr. VI. 13. De DEO Patre Psal. CX. v. 4. Psal. CXXXII. 11. Ezech. XXXIII. vers. 11. Et parallelus omnino est locus Dan. XII. non de liberatione à malis agens per Antiochum illatis, sed per Anti-Christum. Dicta sunt juramentum, & mandatum de accipiendo, & comedendo li- bello, ut & interpretamentum hujus symboli, quod ITERUM prophetare vel illa populis & gentibus & linguis palam prænuntiare debeat, quæ libro isto consignata, hoc est, divina de- creta & judicia annunciare debeat. Juramen- tum est de fine temporum, seu consummatione seculi 1. verbis expressis. Cælo enim intereun- te, quod prædixit Christus Luc. XXI. 33. & astra interitura. Nulla ergo tempora, quæ à lumi- naribus oriuntur è motu cæli, Gen. I. 14. am- plius erunt. Nullum tempus, scil. persecutionis, fore censent Ticonius, Thomas, Ribera, Corne- lius a Lap. Foxus, Piscator, Pareus, Flacius, Chytræus, Hoë, Cramerus, Gerhardus, Grave, Döling, Kromejer. Ad hærefin Arianam restrin- git Lyra. Sed persecutionum adhuc nullum fo- re finem subsequentes visiones declarant. Cur vero à proprietate verborum discedere volumus, causa nulla cogente, quæ infert, non fore ampli- us tempus, non autem non diutius rem dilatum iri, χρόνον ὀυκ ἔτι ἔσαι. Conf. Psal. LXXII. 5. 7, 2. Indicatur consummatio seculi κατὰ διάνοιαν, cum consummabitur mysterium DEI, ut annunciavit Prophetis servis suis, per Spiritum, quod ipsi vi- cissim scriptotenus orbi toti annunciarunt. Cum enim omnia, quæ prædicta sunt, impleta fuerint, tunc finis erit. Quid? quod prædicta etiam sit ipsa seculi consummatio, & solis ac lunæ desitio, cœli terræque interitus, dierum & noctium adeo- que temporum cessatio, non ergo implentur il- la, nisi cum non amplius tempus erit, sed mera se- quetur æternitat, & beatitudo æterna fidelium, quæ ipsa itidem à servis DEI Prophetis est præ- dicta Es. LXVI. 23. Ezech. XXXIX. 2. Dan. II. 44. cap. VII. v. 26. 27. cap. XII. 1. 2. Petr. III. 13. &c. Tempus non erit amplius, quod tempus, di- cente Fromondo, quo mundi inferioris vicissitudi- nes gubernantur, cessabit, cessante cœli motu, in quo tempus fluit. Statim enim peracto judicio universali sol luna & universa sidera cum cœlis suis stabunt, quia tunc operis sui pensum, propter quod creata sunt, absolverint. Tamdiu enim so- lum moventur, donec adimpleatur numerus Ele- ctorum, ut per diei & noctis, æstatis & hyemis, cæ- terasque vicissitudines, alimenta & necessaria mor- talibus provideatur, quæ superflua erunt, quando omnes futuri sunt immortales. Prophetæ itidem proprie intelligendi sunt, quia de mysteriis ipsis patefactis, & vaticiniis eorum adimplendis ser- mo est. Cur ergo Presbyteros Hierosolymita- nos, quales talia prædixisse, aut προφητικῶς uti no- men illud ἐξαίρετον in scripturis occurrit, prænun- ciasse, unde docebitur? De fine rerum Judaica- rum in Apocalypsi designato temere nugatur Grotius. Finis enim earum, tum synagogæ cum cultu divino & sacrificiis tum politiæ jam adve- nerat, antequam in Patmum relegaretur S. Jo- hannes, in quo has visiones habuit. Liberum autem cultum DEI, expulsis Judæis, quem con- cessit Adrianus, hoc loco designari, quomodo convincetur? Nihil enim tale in textu: nec res tanti videtur fuisse, ut juramento divino opus fuerit, maxime quia de propagatione Evangelii per totum orbem ex vaticiniis Propheticis Vet. Test. & mandato Christi, cum emitteret Apo- stolos, constare poterat: imo ex notorietate rei. Brightmannus mysterium de conversione Judæorum sub finem mundi valde insigni intelligit è Rom. XI. 25. Sed alium istius loci sensum esse, ibidem do- cuimus. Vocatur autem & Anti-Christi mani- festatio mysterium, 2. Thess. II. 7. Apoc. XVII. 5. 8. ut & resurrectio mortuorum cum immutatione vi- ventium conjuncta, 1. Cor. XV. 51. ne de aliis hic prædictis quicquam dicamus.

## 10:8
Vers. 8. καὶ ἡ φωνὴ, ἣν ἤκουσα ἐκ τῶ ὀυρανῶ] Above 4. πάλιν λαλῶσα μετ᾿ ἐμῶ] Supply ἦν. καὶ λέγουσα, ὕπαγε] Approach that great Angel. λάβε τὸ βιβλαρίδιον τὸ ἀνεῳγμένον ἐν τῇ χειρὶ τῶ Ἀγγέλω τῶ ἑςῶτος ἐπὶ τῆς θαλάσσης, καὶ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς] The causes of that severe judgment against the inhabitants of Jerusalem.

We are nowhere taught the causes of the destruction of Jerusalem written in that book; and not even a single jot occurs from which that could be gathered. Let us therefore dismiss those inventions of the Grotian brain.

Latin:

Vers. 8. καὶ ἡ φωνὴ, ἣν ἤκουσα τῶ ὀυρανῶ] Supra 4. πάλιν λαλῶσα μετ᾿ ἐμῶ] Supple ἦν. καὶ λέγουσα, ὕπαγε) Accede ad Angelum istum ma- gnum. λάβε τὸ βιβλαρίδιον τὸ ἀνεῳγμένον ἐν τῇ χειρὶ τῶ Ἀγγέλω τῶ ἑςῶτος ἐπὶ τῆς θαλάσσης, καὶ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς] Causas istius se- veri judicii in Hierosolymitas.

Causas excidii Hierosolymitani in libro illo scri- ptas, nuspiam docemur; ac ne apex quidem occurrit, ex quo id colligi queat. Mittamus er- go commenta illa cerebri Grotiani.

## 10:9
Vers. 9. καὶ ἀπῆλθον πρὸς τὸν Ἄγγελον, λέγων αὐτῷ, δὸς μοι τὸ βιβλαρίδιον] Namely, that I may read and learn those causes in the manuscript: λέγων αὐτῷ δῦναι μοι τὸ βιβλάριον, which I think is correct. For βιβλάριον is the first diminutive, βιβλαρίδιον the second: such as are pauxillum and puellulus among the Latins.

And he says to me, take and eat it] As was once commanded to Ezekiel III. 1. Now the eating signifies enigmatically, as Philo says in his allegories, the taking up, the comprehension, which is followed by meditation, as a kind of digestion. Thus, those things which we learn well, we are said to turn into juice and blood. Add Jeremiah XV. 16.

καὶ πικρανεῖ τὴν κοιλίαν) he says κοιλίαν, which elsewhere are called τὰ σπλάγχνα, unless perhaps with the Manuscript we prefer to read καρδίαν. The sense is: You will not be able to think of these things without being moved by a certain compassion. Concerning the destruction of so many fellow countrymen; among whom there will be both those well known to you and kinsmen. Thus Hezekiah says he passed his life in bitterness on account of the sadness of his heart, Isa. 38:15. πικραίνειν is חמר in Job 27:2 and elsewhere.

ἀλλ᾽ ἐν τῷ ςόματί σου ἔςαι γλυκὺ ὡς μέλι] You are compelled to admit that nothing happened to them which they did not deserve, which Josephus often acknowledges. You will approve of the justice of Christ, and this from Ezekiel III. 3.

B. Gerhard writes thus concerning these things: This little book was sweet as honey in the mouth of John, that is, the knowledge of those mysteries concerning future things delighted him; Ps. CXIX. 103; Jer. XV. 16; but on account of the foreseen calamities of the Church he was cast into grievous sadness. The pleasure of the mouth is a symbol of the pleasure which the pious perceive from the revelation of divine mysteries, before they fully perceive the same. The pain of the belly is a symbol of the pain which they conceive from the consideration of the persecution which will be described in the following prophecy, and which the Anti-Christ will exercise against the Church at the end of the age. Furthermore, the judgments of GOD are not ill called bitter on account of συμ- πάθειαν and commiseration, which among the Hebrews has its name from the womb: but they are called sweet on account of divine justice, vengeance against the enemies of the Church, and divine truth. Primasius: When you have perceived it, you will be delighted by the sweetness of the divine eloquence (Ps. XIX. 15.) and the hope of the promised salvation, and the sweetness of divine justice. But you will surely feel bitterness when this must be preached to the devout and the undevout; Conf. Jer. XV. 15. Rom. IX. 1. 2. But these things are not rightly snatched away to judgments either already past or still future against the Jews; since the seventh trumpet does not sound concerning the Jews, but concerning the great Anti-Christ; and Grotius himself is subsequently to admit at ch. XIII. 1. that the prophecies contained in this second prophecy extend to all lands within the Roman Empire.

Latin:

Vers. 9. καὶ ἀπῆλθον πρὸς τὸν Ἄγγελον, λέγων αὐτῷ, δὸς μοι τὸ βιβλαρίδιον] Nempe ut legam, & causas illas cognoscam in Manuscripto: λέγων αὐτῷ δῦναι μοι τὸ βιβλάριον quod rectum puto. Nam βιβλάριον est primus diminutivus : βιβλαρίδιον secundus : quale est apud Latinos pauxillum, puellulus.

καὶ λέγει μοι λάβε καὶ κατάφαγε αὐτὸ] Ut quondam Ezechieli imperatum III. 1. Comestio autem αἰνιγματικῶς significat, ut Philo in allegoriis ait τὴν ἀνάληψιν, comprehensionem, quam sequitur meditatio, quasi concoctio quædam. Sic quæ bene discimus, ea dicimur in succum & sanguinem vertere. Adde Jerem. XV. 16.

καὶ πικρανεῖ τὴν κοιλίαν) κοιλίαν dicit quæ alibi vocantur τὰ σπλάγχνα, nisi forte cum Manuscripto malimus legere καρδίαν. Sensus est : Non poteris ista cogitare, ut non miseratione quadam movearis. Super interitu tot popularium; inter quos erunt & bene noti tibi & consanguinei. Sic Ezechias amarum se dicit obiisse præ cordis mœstitia III. 14. πικραίνειν est חמר Job. XXVII. 2. & alibi.

ἀλλ᾽ ἐν τῷ ςόματί σου ἔςαι γλυκὺ ὡς μέλι] Cogeris fateri nihil eis evenisse quod non mererentur, quod sæpe agnoscit Josephus. Approbabis Christi justitiam, & hoc ex Fzechiele III. 3.

B. Gerhardus de his ita : Mellis instar dulcis fuit hic libellus in ore Johannis, hoc est, mysteriorum istorum de futuris rebus cognitio illum oblectavit; Psal. CXIX. 103. Jer. XV. 16. sed ob prævisas Ecclesiæ calamitates in gravem conjectus fuit mœstitiam. Voluptas oris symbolum est voluptatis, quam pii percipiunt ex mysteriorum divinorum revelatione, antequam eadem plene percipiunt. Dolor ventris est symbolum doloris, quem concipiunt ex consideratione persecutionis, quæ in seq. prophetia describetur, quamque Anti-Christus in fine seculi adversus Ecclesiam exercebit. Cæterum judicia DEI amara non male ob συμ- πάθειαν & commiserationem, quæ Ebræis ab utero nomen habet: Dulcia vero ob divinam justitiam, vindictam adversus hostes Ecclesiæ, & veritatem divinam dicuntur. Primasius: Cum perceperis, oblectaberis divini eloquii dulcedine (Psal. XIX. 15.) & spe salutis promissæ, & divinæ suavitate justitiæ. Sed amaritudinem profeĉto senties, cum hoc devotis & indevotis prædicandum erit; Conf. Jer. XV. 15. Rom. IX. 1. 2. At non recte hæc ad judicia vel jam præterita, vel adhuc futura adversus Judæos abripiuntur; quum tuba septima non de Judæis clangat, sed de Anti-Christo magno; & Grotius ipse deinde fassurus sit ad c. XIII. 1. vaticinia in hac altera prophetia contenta, ad terras omnes in Romano Imperio se porrigere.

## 10:10
Verse 10.

And I took the little book out of the angel's hand and ate it up] I ate as I had been commanded symbolically, and at the same time I grasped that very thing which was signified by that symbol; signs instituted by God have their own realities as companions:

And it was in my mouth as sweet honey] A proverbial expression. Theocritus: May it become as sweet as honey in my throat. The meaning is: I could not but approve of what Christ had done, especially once the reasons were known.

And when I had eaten it, my heart was made bitter] When I began to think how many men were to perish there, how many were to go into captivity, I could not restrain myself from being moved with grief again.

-- Who in speaking of such things could refrain from tears.

Andreas, Cluverus, Quistorpius, Gerhardus, Grave, Danhawerus, Piscator, Junius, Pareus, Medus, Crugotius, Coccejus, Ribera, and Cornelius à Lapide say that the Apocalypse became bitter to St. John on account of the Woes of the Anti-Christ. But Ticonius, Primasius, Chytræus, Flacius, Cramerus, Woltherus, Riccardus, Szegedinus, and Cotterius apply it to the Word of God, which is bitter to our flesh.

Latin:

Vers. 10.

καὶ ἔλαβον τὸ βιβλαρίδιον ἐκ τῆς χειρὸς τῶ Ἀγγέλε καὶ κατέφαγον αὐτὸ] Edi ut jussus eram συμβολικῶς & simul comprehendi id ipsum, quod significatum erat illo συμβόλῳ, signa à Deo instituta res suas habent comites:

καὶ ἦν ἐν τῷ ςόματί με ὡς μέλι γλυκὺ] Proverbiale. Theocritus: ὡς μέλι μοι γλυκὺ κατὰ βρόχθοιο γένοιτο. Sensus est: non potui non approbare, quod Christus fecerat, cognitis præsertim causis.

καὶ ὅτε ἔφαγον αὐτὸ, ἐπικράνθη ἡ καρδία με] Ubi cogitare cœpi, quot ibi homines essent perituri, quot in captivitatem ituri, non potui me continere, quin dolore iterum commoverer.

-- Quis talia fando Temperet a lacrymis.

Apocalypsin S. Johanni in fine amaram evasisse ob Væ Anti-Christi, Andreas, Cluverus, Quistorpius, Gerhardus, Grave, Danhawerus, Piscator, Junius, Pareus, Medus, Crugotius, Coccejus, Ribera, Cornelius à Lapide ajunt. Ticonius vero, Primasius, Chytræus, Flacius, Cramerus, Woltherus, Riccardus, Szegedinus, Cotterius. Verbo DEI carni nostræ amaro applicant.

## 10:11
Verf. 11. And he says to me] That angel representing Christ. In the Manuscript: they say to me, namely the voice from heaven and the Angel, that is, God the Father and Christ. You must prophesy again] You think you have already seen the catastrophe of the Jewish tragedy: But the matter stands otherwise: And there will be other wars, and greater slaughters, and more widely spread. A similar expression to Ezekiel II. 3. upon peoples] Concerning the Jews, not only those who will be survivors in Judea, but also those who are in Africa, Egypt, Greece, and Cyprus. I interpret 'upon' here according to the Hebrew custom, as in 'upon peoples', just as 'upon Pharaoh', Ezech. XXXII. 2. and upon nations] The Romans. and tongues] The allies of the Romans, who are as varied in languages, habit, as in dress and arms. and many kings] Concerning the Emperor Aelius Hadrian, concerning Martius Turbo, concerning Turannius Rufus, concerning Julius Severus, his commanders. For we said above VI. 15 that such are also called kings by the Hebrews, but by us kings. But also to Hadrian many kings had sent auxiliaries, such as Cosroes of the Parthians, Pharasmanes of the Alans, other kings of the Bactrians, Albanians, Iberians, and other nations. Many also were toparchs. See Aelius Spartianus.

He does violence to the letter, when those things which are said about peoples, nations, and tongues from the nature of an indefinite expression, the custom of scripture, the analogy of Dan. VII. and the Apocalypse, and the parallelism of chap. VII. v. 9, XIV. v. 6, concerning all the peoples of the earth, but especially from the condition of the prophecies themselves, are twisted to the Jews alone, and snatched away to a few commanders; when nevertheless there is a very great difference between commanders and kings, or Emperors, and they are not to be confused rashly. That the people of the Jews are dispersed among others does not make one people into many, just as to make one Roman nation and their allies from diverse nations and tongues, or even kings who had sent auxiliaries, is nothing other than to pervert scripture.

Moreover, this new investiture, as it were, of John and the designation of the prophecy 'you must prophesy AGAIN', you must prophesy AGAIN to peoples and nations and tongues, indicates that this which follows is a universal prophecy, and that it equally looked to the universal judgments of God which excels: furthermore, that a new prophecy and another vision begins here, to which this was a certain investiture and preparation: Finally, that the antecedents and consequences properly concern not history, but prophecy, not things past, but things still yet to be, which are revealed for the good of the Church from the secret treasures of Divine wisdom. Whence from the fact that a new Prophecy is entrusted to John to be proposed to the peoples, it is rightly gathered that he must have been freed from the Mines or from Patmos to deliver this Apocalypse to the Churches.

THE SECOND SECTION OF THE FOURTH VISION, NARRATIVE.

Latin:

Verf. 11. καὶ λέγει μοι] Angelus ille Christum referens. In Manuscripto: λέγουσι μοι nempe vox è cœlo & Angelus, id est, Deus Pater & Christus. δεῖ σε πάλιν προφητεῦσαι] Putas te jam catastrophen vidis- se Judaicæ tragœdiæ: Sed aliter se res habet: Et erunt etiam altera bella, & strages majores, latiusque fusæ. Similis loquutio ad E- zechielem II. 3. ἐπὶ λαοῖς] De Judæis, non tantum qui in Judæa super- stites erunt, sed & iis qui in Africa, Ægypto, Græcia & Cy- pro. ἐπὶ hic interpretor de more Ebræo על-לאמים sicut. על-פרעה. Ezech. XXXII. 2. καὶ ἐπὶ ἔθνεσι] Romanis. καὶ γλώσσαις] Sociis Romanorum, qui Tam varii linguis, habitu quam vestis & armis. καὶ βασιλεῦσι πολλοῖς] De Ælio Adriano Imperatore, de Martio Turbano, de Turannio Rufo, de Julio Severo, du- cibus ejus. Nam & tales vocari Ebræis מלכים nostris vero βασιλέας diximus supra VI. 15. Sed & Adriano multi Reges auxilia miserant, ut Cosroes Parthorum, Pharasma- nes Alanorum, alii Reges Bactrianorum, Albanorum, Ibe- rorum & aliarum gentium. Multi & Toparchæ. Vide Æ- lianum Spartianum.

Vim facit literæ, cum quæ de populis, gen- tibus, & linguis dicta sunt ex indefinitæ loquu- tionis ratione, more scripturæ, Dan. VII. & Apo- calypseos analogia, ac parallelismo cap. VII. v. 9. XIV. v. 6. de omnibus terræ populis, inprimis vero è conditione ipsorummet vaticiniorum col- ligenda ad solos Judæos detorquentur, ad paucos Duces abripiuntur; quum tamen inter Duces ac Reges, vel Imperatores maxima sit differentia nec temere illi confundendi sint. Quod populus Judæorum inter alios dispersus sit non facit è po- pulo uno plures, licuti ex gentibus & linguis di- versis gentem unam Romanam, & socios eorum facere, vel etiam Reges, qui auxilia miserant, ni- hil aliud est, quam scripturam pervertere?

Nova autem hæc velut investitura Johannis & designatio prophetiæ δεῖ σε πάλιν προφητεῦσαι, oportet te ITERUM prophetare populis & gen- tibus & linguis, universalem hanc esse prophe- tiam, quæ sequitur, eamque quæ præcellit pariter ad universalia Dei judicia spectasse indicat: ad- hæc novam hic prophetiam: & visionem aliam in- cipere, ad quam hæc investitura quædam fuit & præparatio: Denique antecedentia, & conse- quentia proprie concernere non historiam, sed prophetiam, non præterita, sed adhuc demum fu- tura, quæ Ecclesiæ bono ex arcanis sapientiæ Divinæ thesauris adaperiuntur. Unde ex eo, quod nova Prophetia Johanni commendatur populis proponenda, recte colligitur, quod à Metallis, vel à Pathmo liberandus Apocalypsin hanc tradere debuerit Ecclesiis.

VISIONIS QUARTÆ ALTERA SECTIO ΔΙΗΓΗΤΙΚΗ.

## 11:1 Argument
CHAPTER XI. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

The temple with the altar is measured with a reed, and the choir of the temple is to be cast out, and the holy city is predicted to be trampled for 42 months, two witnesses of the Lord are delivered to prophesy for 1260 days with a fiery mouth, with power over rains and other plagues, and to be killed by the beast arising from the earth, but to be resurrected after 3 ½ days, and to be carried into heaven with glory, with others prostrated by a great earthquake, and others giving honor to God with fear. But with the seventh Angel sounding the trumpet, celestial Music and Eucharist are heard, and the ark of the testament is seen. There are three parts: I. The dimension of the temple to v. 2. II. The killing of the two witnesses, and the congratulation of those dwelling on the earth, and the exultation of that one with the terror of others to v. 15. III. A summary representation of the seventh trumpet-blast to v. 17.

PART I. The dimension of the temple, and the devastation in the days of the Anti-Christ.

Verf. 1. And there was given to me a reed like a rod] After I had already seen the destruction of the temple in the Prophecy, as Ezekiel once did, there was given to me, as once to Ezekiel, a measuring rod or ten-foot pole made of reed, such as land-surveyors were accustomed to use. In Ezekiel it is called 'measuring reed', 'reed of measure'. A measuring line was not given to John, because the temple was not to be restored, but to be measured for another reason. And the angel stood saying: Arise and measure the temple of God] All these things are metonymical. The temple is called that ark in which the sanctuary and the basilica had stood, the 'hekal' and 'debir'. [Similar expression: Every man smokes Neptunian Troy], and the altar] The place of the sacrificial altar, which is accustomed to be called that of burnt offerings, and those who worship in it] That is, the place in which the people were accustomed to worship God, the Court of the Israelites. But John is ordered to measure this space, because God was going to keep it untouched by the Gentiles in memory of its ancient sanctity. Between the destruction and the times of Hadrian, nothing worth mentioning had happened in Jerusalem. A few towers had been made by Titus as a monument to victory, near which first tents, then also some houses began to be built.

Latin:

CAPUT XI. ARGUMENTUM ET PAR- TITIO.

Calamo templum cum altari, & illic adoranti- bus dimetitur chorus templi interior eji- ciendus, & sancta civitas conculcanda per 42. menses, prædicitur, bini testes Domini vaticinaturi per 1260. dies ore igneo, tra- duntur, cum potestate pluviarum, & pla- garum aliarum, & à bestia è terra oriunda occidendi, sed post 3 ½. dies resuscitandi, & cum gloria in cælum evehendi, aliis terra motu ingenti prostratis, aliis cum timore Deo honorem deferentibus. Septimo au- tem Angelo tuba clangente, Musica & Eucharistia cœlestis auditur, & arca testa- menti videtur. Partes tres sunt: I. Templi dimensio ad verf. 2. II. Duorum testium occisio, inque terra habitantium congratulatio, istiusque cum terrore aliorum exultatio ad v. 15. III. Septimi tubicinii summaria repræsentatio. ad v. 17.

PARS I. Templi dimensio, & in diebus Anti-Christi devastatio.

Verf. 1. Καὶ ἐδόθη μοι κάλαμος ὅμοιος ῥάβδῳ] Post- quam videram jam in Prophetia templi excidium, ut olim Ezechiel, data est mihi, ut olim Ezechieli, fin manur pertica five decempeda ex arundine, qualibus uti solebant agrimen- fores. Ea in Ezechiele dicitur קנה המדה, κάλαμος μέτρου.
