There follows Cardinal Julian, more an armor-bearer than a key-bearer, who took the name of Julius II. He stripped Borgia, who deserved a thousand deaths, of his troops, cities, and all dignity, and dismissed him on the condition that he might recover the fortresses of Cesena and Forlì fortified by his protection. Julius, desirous not only to recover the Ecclesiastical territory but also to extend it further, drives Bentivoglio from Bologna; he strikes a treaty at Cambrai in the Netherlands for the destruction of the Venetian name with Caesar, the Kings of Spain and France, and also with the Dukes of Ferrara and Mantua. Soon, at the instigation of Julius, the treaty between Caesar and the Gaul is broken. The French King, having been proscribed by the hostile Pontiff, when he was again seeking Milan with a renewed army under the leadership of Duke Louis de la Trémoille, was defeated by the Swiss in a bloody battle at Novara and excluded from almost all of Italy. The fathers of the Council, begun at Pisa and renewed with little success at Milan, terrified by fear of the Swiss, had transferred themselves to Lyon, cursing Julius. But he, having driven the Bentivogli from Bologna and recovered Ravenna, adds Parma and Piacenza to his dominion. Concerning his successor Leo X. He is said to have once thrown the keys into the Tiber, adding that the sword of Paul would be effective when the keys of Peter could do nothing. Ulrich von Hutten wrote about him, among many things, also this:

The merchant Julius takes the whole world by fraud, / For he sells the heavens, yet possesses them not himself.

Louis, King of the Franks, inscribed on his gold coins: I shall destroy the name of Babylon. And further: The delicate Pontiff, most thirsty for gold in the ancestral manner (as the monk of Citiz, P. Langius, says), joining Florentine avarice to Roman, having everything for sale for money, building the Basilica of St. Peter begun by Julius: so holy that, among wines and luxuries, he would mock the Gospel of Christ as a profitable fable for himself and his own. Most desirous of rest and leisure, he obtained from Louis XII that, omitting the reformation of the Church, he would subscribe to the Lateran Council. He was draining the purses of the common people under the shadow of a Turkish expedition, etc. I pass over other things. For there are countless things: which are not to be imputed so much to the empire as to the Pontiff, who, when they are powerful in courts, adorns them through the clergy, cardinals, apostolic nuncios (as he calls them), archbishops, bishops, prelates, monks, and Jesuits, who are the private confessors, whether secretly or openly, whether directly or through an indirect scene, where they serve themselves and the reason of their state. The Romans used those wild beasts in punishing the Christians, by whom their empire is described, if we may say so; that was done without doubt so that the empire might be recognized, which that wild beast with iron teeth points to, with which it crushes most things, trampling the rest with its feet, Dan. 7, 7. But it is compared to the leopard not so much because of the variety of religions as because of the cunning and the speed of its victories, according to that saying of Caesar: I came, I saw, I conquered: just as immediately following the second Punic war, as Florus says in book II, chapter 7, the African nations, Macedonia, Greece, Syria, and all other things [were conquered] by a kind of tide and torrent of fortune.

But to return to Grotius, those kings never wore diadems, nor are they all called kings by Grotius except equivocally. For these were subject and subordinate to the Roman Empire, as Grotius says: Nor were they all addicted to idolatry. Herod certainly and his successors were devoted to the religion of the Hebrews. Abgarus, King of Edessa in Syria, was devoted to the Christian religion, of whom Eusebius speaks in book I, chapter 13. Nor did idolatry rise so much at that time as it began to be sown through the proclamation of the Gospel in the world. What if for Grotius the ten horns are ten provinces under Roman senators, who to Cineas, the legate of Pyrrhus, seemed to be kings and in a way held a diadem: even if a finite number can be said to be used for an infinite, as in Gen. 31, 7; 1 Sam. 1, 8; Job 19, 3; Eccl. 7, 19. But Roman idolatry is not distinguished well enough from the Greek, Egyptian, and Phrygian: since Rome once assumed the various religions and superstitions of all peoples, and having led the foreign gods away in triumph, set up cushions and altars, and even by a magic spell evoked the gods of besieged cities, as if promising them worship if they would cross over to their side: We have received into our Roman rites your Isis and the semi-gods, the dogs, and the sistra commanding mourning, and the man whom you, weeping, attest is Osiris, sings Lucan.

In the previous treatment of these things which we have examined so far, Grotius has it thus:

Having ten horns) Having many minister-kings; not indeed those who were to exist some centuries later, and are designated below in chapter 17, 12, but yet many and powerful, such as were the kings of Armenia, Thrace, Galatia, Pontus, Judea, Arabia, Adiabene, the Suebi, the Cottian Alps, and the Idionni Alps.

And seven heads) Heads have two meanings, of emperors and of mountains, as is evident below in chapter 17, 19. Here mountains are signified more, that is, the principal seat and origin of that idolatry, not Phrygian, not Egyptian, not Greek, but Roman.

And upon his ten horns ten diadems) So that the power of the empire sustaining that idolatry may be better understood, an explanation is added, by which it is understood that those who are designated by the name of horns were kings by supreme right, and yet in obedience and reverence to the Roman empire, such as Herod and his successors, and other kings. Other successors were not content with the name of prefects; when they took the diadem with the royal name. Diodorus Siculus is a witness in book 20. Tertullian against Marcion, book 1. What now if the supreme, the great, cannot be seen even among kings in many ways, but only the one and singular, namely, in him who is received as King of Kings because of the summit of his greatness and the subjection of other ranks, as the pinnacle of dominion.

And upon his heads names of blasphemy, & upon his heads names of blasphemy.) Mountains or the city of Rome are the same. That city called itself eternal, which in reality was impious. See what we shall say at chapter XVII.

Magnates, as we have already hinted in the aforementioned, he transforms into Kings, and in place of ten, which is a finite number, he substitutes more at will; he holds the royal diadems as insignias of no place, lest he be forced to admit Kings whom he cannot find: but he interprets the Beast with an unheard-of commentary on idolatry, so that he may finally adorn some sense not adverse to the Roman beast. And thus he believes he has conducted the cause of the Anti-Christ excellently. Behold a distinguished Interpreter of Scripture!

Latin:

CAPUT XIII. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Videntur duæ bestiæ, altera e mari 7. capitum & coronarum nominibus maledicis insi- gnium, 10. cornuum, similis pardo, urso, leo- ni, uno capite læso, sed cum admiratione to- tius terræ sanato, sancto, vincente sub Dra- cone, & adorata ab orbe, sed itidem gla- dio ferienda; altera e terra ascendente duobus cornibus, ceu agninis, & Draconis lingua, priori imagini animatæ veneratio- nem conciliante, per miracula, & assum- ptionem characteris ejus.

Dispescitur ergo in duas partes, I. de marina, ad v. 10. II. de terrestri bestia ad v. 18.

PARS I. DE BESTIA MARINA.

Vers. 1.

Καὶ εἶδον) Nova ὀπτασία, non jam ut dixi, ad Romanos solos, sed ad omnes terras Romani Imperii se extendens. Εἶδον מַרְאֶה Ezech. 1, 1. Dan. 8, 14. c. 10, 4.

Ἐκ τῆς θαλάσσης) Ex populo Romano. Nam aquæ po- pulus: mare populus ingens. Sic & Dan. 5. vers. 3. Ezech. 26, 3.

Θηρίον) feram. Lactantius belluam dixit V. Nemo tanta hujus belluæ immanitatem potest pro meritis describere, quæ uno loco recubans per totum orbem dentibus ferreis sævit, & non tantum artus hominum dissipat, sed & ossa ipsa com- minuit & in cineres furit. Apud Danielem Jacchiades di- cit ferarum nomine designari regna idololatrica, quia sci- licet intellectum earum rerum quæ maxime cognitu sunt necessariæ, non habent. Hic vero ipsa potius idololatria, sive falsa religio significatur, sicut solent in figuris Propheti- cis concreta & abstracta inter se permisceri.

Non hic tantum, sed & in præcedentibus etiam de populo Romano non Roma sola actum. Fe- rarum nomine in genere regna citra respectum idolatriæ designari e Daniele constat; multo mi- nus idololatriam in abstracto illa significant. A ro- bore, crudelitate, aliisque qualitatibus & imperio- rum & bestiarum Metaphora petita, non a religio- ne, quæ indifferenter se ad illas habet & abunde determinanda est. Conf. hic Dan. 5, 27. c. 7, 7. Tra- ctarat Grotius hoc caput antea in gratiam Pontifi- cis Romani, ne ille amplius crederetur bestia hic visa. Ea ergo repetere, ne forte ab aliquo deside- rentur, & ne intacta, & indiscussa maneant, si ali- quid diversi ab hisce exhibeant, placet, lineis con- tractioribus hic inclusa:

Vers. 1. Καὶ εἶδον ἐκ τῆς θαλάσσης θηρίον ἀναβαῖνον, & vidi de mari bestiam ascendentem) Illud εἶδον vidi Ebraice מַרְאֶה est vox frequens Prophetis Ezech 1, 1. Dan. 8, 2. c. 10, 4. & alibi. Θηρίον bestia hoc loco est idololatria ferino more sæviens. Ἀναβαῖνον ascendentem, significat vi- res acquirere, Dan. 4, 8. & cap. 8. 8. Ex mari, id est, non ex seditione populari, sed ex vi ac potestate imperii. Nam sicut aquæ populos significant infra c. 17, 15. Ita mare est vis illa sive potestas congregata ex populorum obsequio.

Si aquæ sunt populi, mare non erit vis & potestas ex populorum obsequio congregata: Sed aquarum, id est, populorum congregatio. Hoc importat ista maris definitio. Sed Grotius pervertit omnia.

Ἀναβαῖνον) ortum habens. Ascendere, oriri Ebræis Es 55, 17. Marc. 4, 7. Sic Daniel 7, 3. de feris סָלְקָן ἀνέβαινον. Fuerat idololatria Romæ semper, sed velut nova surrexerat additis ad Deos Cæsaribus defunctis. Claudianus: Et si quos Roma recepit Aut dedit ipsa Deos.

Ἔχον κέρατα δέκα) Plurimos habens Reges, exem- plum illud sequentes. Et quid mirum, quando & Ju- dæi Reges in Cæsarum gratiam ἐξέπεσον τῶν πατρίων ἐθῶν, ut Josephus loquitur institutis in ipsa Judæa agonibus athleticis, theatris, amphitheatris, ludis, gymnicis, Mu- ficis, Thymelicis, extra vero Judaicum solum etiam templis in honorem Cæsarum structis. His jam adde Reges Ara- bum, Itureæ, Comagenorum, Ponti Polemoniaci, Arme- niæ, Thraciæ, Galatiæ, Adiabenæ, Suevorum, Alpium. Non eadem per omnia res est, quæ hic & quæ infra c 17. no- tatur. Hic decem Reges significantur Romana sacra se- ctantes: Hi decem Reges multo posterius exorti, quibus Deus usurus sit ad dilacerandum imperium Romanum.

Καὶ κεφαλὰς ἑπτὰ) id est, septem montes, ut intelliga- mus hic designari idololatriam, non Phrygiam, non Ægy- ptiam, non Chaldaicam, sed proprie Romanam, Romanis legibus receptam. Præterea septem capita, ut infra disci- mus, & aliud significant, Principes nempe septem, quorum jam non nomina, sed res in præcedentibus præsignificatas habuimus. Ii sunt Claudius, Nero, Galba, Otho, Vitel- lius, Vespasianus & Titus. A Claudio incipi debuit, quia is primus exilia decrevit in Doctores Christianismi, quod Tiberius non fecerat.

Καὶ ἐπὶ τῶν κεράτων αὐτῶ δέκα διαδήματα) Diademata significant jus plenum in subditos, quale habebant Reges illi, quanquam in fide erant & reverentia Romani imperii. Itaque Augustus dixit Herodi Magno, posse eum de filio suo constituere, & ut patrem & ut Regem: Et Antonius, ini- quum esse Herodem vocari ad rationes reddendas de iis, quæ ut Rex fecerat. Ita enim nec Regem fore. Diadema insigne Regium, 1. Macc. 1, 10. c. 11, 13. c. 13, 32. Διάδημα צניף Esa. 62, 3.

Καὶ ἐπὶ τὰς κεφαλάς αὐτῶ) Super montes, id est, super ipsam urbem, quæ per montes septem non ambigue designa- tur. Vide Festum in voce Septimontium. Horatius: Di quibus septem placuere colles. Propertius de Roma: Septem urbs alta jugis &c. Vide & supra c. 12, 3. & c. 17, 7. 9.

Ὀνόματα βλασφημίας) multi libri ὄνομα βλασφημίας, id vero est, urbs æterna. Ita Hieronymus explicat quæ- stione undecima ad Algasiam. Prosper: Quis non intelligat, quam dicit Apocalypsin ferentem poculum plenum execratio- nibus immunditiæ ac fornicationis terræ? Æterna cum di- citur, quæ temporalis est, nomen est blasphemiæ. Cæsar di- cebat decem legiones habere populum Romanum, quæ etiam cœlum diruere possent.

Nova omnino surrexit idololatria, quam conci- liavit ferarum altera, per quam Anti-Christus intel- ligendus, vel imperium ejusdem καισαροπαπία, das Kayserliche Pabstthum, quemadmodum per priorem designatur παποκαισαρία, das Pabstische Kayserthum, hoc est, imperium Romanum qui- dem, sed qua Papæ obnoxium. Utriusque ratio e descriptione liquet: Et quidem quod Romanum imperium, quia bestiæ imperia notant, in locis Pro- pheticis designetur, ex illa feræ figura: quod septem capitum & coronarum, decem cornuum fuerit, & conspecta sub specie diversorum animalium sit, quæ concurrunt unice in imperio Romano: ob mixturam cæteris analogis habet de primo impe- rio Babylonio nempe os leoninum, quod fortitudi- nis, avaritiæ, superbiæ, & blasphemiæ, quæ ore se produnt, & edictis Papalibus: de secundo Persico ursinæ calliditatis, quod ad pedes in regna irrum- pendi, opes corradendi; Vid. Lactant. V. c. 11. de tertio Græco scil. velocitatis & varietatis, Jer. 5, 6. Hab. 1, 8. quæ in Alexandr. M. apparuit: Deditque huic Draco, non qua imperium, sed qua Papæ obno- xium est potestatem ferinæ crudelitatis &c. Pote- stas enim imperialis cæteroquin & qua talis a Deo est, Dan. 2, 11. Rom. 13, 1. Prov. 8, 16. Crudelitas, bla- sphemia, persecutio sanctorum, & admissio cultus re- ligiosi a Dracone, Matth. 4, 9. Joh. 8, 44. Apoc. 12, 9. Per capita septem montes Romæ, quæ septicollis dici- tur juxta communem Interpretum explicationem e cap. 17, 9. depromptam, designant:

Septem urbs alta jugis toti quæ præsidet orbi. ait Propertius l. III. Eleg. de Roma, quales sunt Pa- latinus, Capitolii, Aventinus, Exquilinus, Cœlius, Viminalis, Quirinalis. Septem Ecclesiæ persequutio- nes designari putat Galatinus, quas ipse recenset.

Lessius, qui hic singularis est, Diabolum mundo regnantem per bestiam intelligit. Septem sunt Re- ges impii septem ætatum mundi. Sed figura bestiæ docet, imperium Romanum describi, & Draco aper- te a bestia distinguitur. Alii apud Gerhardum se- ptem præcipuas Romani imperii urbes designari per septem capita volunt 1. Romam in Italia, 2. Con- stantinopolim in Thracia, 3. Antiochiam in Asia, 4. Alexandriam in Ægypto, 5. Hierosolymam in Sy- ria, 6. Carthaginem in Africa, 7. Toletum in Hispa- nia, quæ omnes a vera fide ad impia Anti-Christi utriusq; Muhammedici & Papistici dogmata transie- runt. Sed hæ rectius referuntur ad septem coronas vel Reges Apoc. 17, 9. Fuerunt enim Reginæ quasi coronatæ cæterarum urbium. Formas septem regi- minis cum Jacobo Rege M. Brit. Maresius intelligit Cornua diadematibus coronata decem totidem præ- cipua regna sunt, Syria & Assyria, Ægyptus, Asia minor, Græcia, Italia, Gallia, Hispania, Africa, Ger- mania, Anglia cum Scotia, Hybernia & vicinis re- gnis septentrionalibus, vel insulis continenti adjectis & provinciis minoribus omissis, Hungaria, Bulga- ria; &c. Antiquum Roman. Imperium, sub Ethni- cis Imperatoribus e persecutionibus & idolola- tria bestiæ præsumit cum plerisque aliis B. Ger- hardus. Sed malumus de Papali imperio intelligere ob seriem visionum, quæ turbanda haud videtur.

Caput vulneratum Osiand. & Joh. Christ. Arto- pœus de Julio Cæsare inde ita nominato, Bullinge- rus, Piscator, Junius, Szegedinus, Vinarienses, Alca- zar de Nerone, in quo Julii Cæsaris familia interiit, sanatio autem facta R. I. per Flav. Vespas. Coccejus de Græcia vulnerata per Julianum, Medus imperium Ethnicum vulneratum in prælio cum Michaele, Flacius imperium Constantinopolitanum nunc mu- tatum in Turcicum, Beda, Primasius, Anshelmus, Richardus, Ansbertus, Haymo, Glossa, Thomas, Bel- larm. Anti-Christum denotari autumant, quibus annuunt Cornelius, Tirinus alii. Pareus explicat de Pontificibus anno 1378. ad ann. 1414. Ribera & Suarez de præcipuo Regum Anti-Christo adhæ- rentium, B. Phil. Nicolai de Hispania per 700. an- nos saucia inde ab anno Christi 720. per victorias adversus Saracenos a Ferdinando V. sanata. Al- phonsus Mantuan. apud Pareum, Danhauer & Döling. de Rom. Imperio per Lutherum quasi vul- nerato in Gallia, Anglia, Ungaria, Polonia, per Pontificios, imprimis vero Jesuitas iterum restitu- to. Sed rectius alii per primum & præcipuum bestiæ caput Romam vel Italiam per barbarorum incur- siones sauciatam intelligunt, utpote Foxus, Brigt- mannus, Colladon, Hoë, Dürfeld, cui alii cum Napei- ro, Forbesio, Hopfnero, Cluvero & Richtero septimum caput seu R. I. Christianum addunt ab anno Chri- sti 400. ad mortem usque vulneratum per Attilam, Totilam, Gensericum, Hunnericum, Odoacrum, A- dolphum, ut & in Oriente per Saracenos, Persas, Ma- hometh, & Turcas, Roma ipsa sexies devastata, Italia a Longobardis per 77. annos, a Gothis per 206. annos occupata, unde annis 324. nullus in Occidente Impe- rator obtinuit, usque ad Romyllum vel Augustulum, & Carolum M. a quo sanatum est Romanum Im- perium, qui adjutus opera Leonis III. ut legere est apud Centur. Magdeb. Cent. IIX. f. 752. 340. ad Germanos devenit imperium, postquam hic accu- satus, quod sibi Romam subjicere vellet, & captiva- tus e captivitate elapsus ad Carolum se receperat, cum exercitu ejus Romam remissus: Carolus au- tem eo perveniens cum honore exceptus esset, & se de criminibus intentatis juramento purgasset, populoq; Romano consilium de Carolo in Roma- num Imperatorem eligendo dedisset: Qui etiam in Basilica S. Petri anno 800. æræ Christianæ ipso na- tivitatis Christi festo eundem Imperatorem Roma- num proclamavit,unxit, & coronavit. Quam impe- rii translationem a Papa factam Cardinalis Bellar- minus peculiari scripto sustentare voluit, neque id diffitetur B. Lutherus præfat. in Apoc. & in c. 12. necnon gloss. Margin. Dan. 2, 41. non tamen alio sensu id concessit vel concedendum est, quam quod suasu & consilio Pontificis id factum, qui non habebat id in manu sua, sub Longobardorum po- testate Roma per 200. annos cum Episcopo detenta, & imperio Romano ejusq; nomine in Oriente pe- nes Imperatores etiam post Carolum M. superstite; quod autem Carolum unxerit & coronarit, id ex concessione populi non tanquam Pontifex, sed ceu Episcopus Romanus fecit, ubi hodie Romani Impe- ratores ab Archi-Episcopo Moguntino, Rex Daniæ ab Haffniensi, Sueciæ ab Upsaliensi ungitur & co- ronatur citra Papalis dignitatis vel OecumeniciE- piscopatus axioma. Neque terrarum quicquam in Italia a Pontifice Rom. consequutus est Carolus, qui ut Patritius Romanus Dominus in Italia & Ro- mæ fuit, antequam Rex vel Imperator Romanor. renunciaretur, ad quam dignitatem a proceribus imperii & populo Romano proprie evectus est, non ab Episcopo, nedum a Papa Romano, qua ta- li. Quo de legatur B. Lutherus tr. Dass das Pabst- thum zu Rom vom Teuffel gestifftet sey. Anno 1545. adornato part. III. Romam intrat Carolus, in- quit Cluverus epit. Hist. p. m. 682. extremo anni 94. die (juxta illos, qui festo nativitatis novum ordie- bantur annum) largitione & promissis corruptus, ne a spurcissimo Pontifice pœnas scelerum exige- ret. Inauguratur ibi regno Siculo, exhaustoq; opi- bus regno Neapolitano præsidia ei imponit. An urbs æterna nomen blasphemiæ, quod hic occurrit, sit, viderint Philologi. Quo de etiam Prosper in dim. temp. l. 7. Æterna quum dicitur, quæ tempora- lis est, nomen est blasphemiæ. Appellabant eam & Deam, ut in Martiali videre est, Terrarum Dea gen- tiumq; luna. Erexerunt ei templum, quod a Smyr- nensibus factum, teste Tacito Annal. IV. Cæsares vocari Dii, Divi & Augusti non renuerunt cum mortales, inquit iterum Prosper l. c. licet Reges in ea dicantur, eique supplices dicant Numini vestro, al- taribus vestris perennitati vestræ &c. quæ vanitas non veritas tradidit, eáq; execrabilia sunt. Hæc enim æterno Deo debentur. Sed quid hoc ad idololatriam quam intelligi vult Grotius non urbem ipsam, quod Roma urbs æterna dicta? Etsi autem vetus Ro- ma istam formam maxime quoad omnia expresse- rit, sufficit tamen, quod hisce indiciis Roma ipsa & Romanum Imperium Papale satis prodatur. Con- tigit sane Romani Imperii eversio tempore Augu- stuli, adeoq; ut Tertullianus loquitur abscessio ejus in decem Reges, seu dissipatio in plura regna, ejus tamen formam imitatur quodammodo hodiernum im- perium Germanicum, unde imago ejus dicitur. Blasphemiarum adhuc satis in urbe, quæ notoriæ non solum veteri, sed & nova. Blasphematur Deus, Divina potentia, Christus, quem sacrificuli quoti- die creare queant, regnum & populus Christi, lex Di- vina, quæ imperfecta creditur & Pharisæico more corrupta Romæ, & quid non? Mariam vocant Do- minam in Psalterio Mariano Bonaventuræ etiam in illis locis, ubi nomen יהוה adhibetur, ut Ps. 30. In te Domina speravi, Psal. 50. Miserere mei Domi- na: Quod Psalterium a Sixto IV. & Innocentio VIII. confirmatum; dicunt ei ab Angelis τρισάγιον ac- clamatum Anton. part. IV. Tit. 15. c. 44. throno Dei

Majorem Osorius T. III. p. 139. applicant ei, quod de æterna generatione sapientiæ hypostaticæ di- ctum, idem Osorius & Blasius Viegas, in Apoc. 12. Scio, inquiunt, in Antidotario animæ, quia potes omnia, quæ vis, ipsa misericordia; turris fortissima, inquit Bernardin. de Busto in Mariali ad Alexandr. VI. nomen Dominæ, ad ipsam confugiet peccator, & salvabitur: & in Marial. l. II. part. 1. c. 24. Si Ma- ria pro nobis, quis contra nos? Si ipsa justificat; quis condemnabit? Velocior nonnunquam est salus me- morato nomine Mariæ, quam invocato nomine Jesu, ut habetur libr. de excell. Virg. Anshelmi & in the- saur. præcon. Deipar. Anno 1539. Blasius de Viegas in Apoc. p. 543. non dubitavit illud Gersonis lauda- re: Deum dedisse dimidium regni sui Virgini Ma- riæ, potestate Deo remanente cessisse quodammodo mi- sericordiam Dei matri sponsæque regnanti: Ideoque, Vir- ginem habere divisum cum Deo imperium. Vincen- tius Pimpinella Archi - Episc. Tholosanus nuncius Apostol. ad Ferdin. Reg. Hungariæ & Bohemiæ: Tu Claviger (Petre) aperi corda Principum & ho- minum quorumcunque dura, & marmorea. Tu En- sifer, Electionis vas (Paule) incide, separa, discute a pectoribus mortalium duritiem inauditam: venite in nubibus cæli, dissipate gentes, quæ contra Christia- nos bella volunt; utrique Simones Magos, Attilas & Totilas, quotquot sunt, convertite, & ad pristinam Christi fidem revocate. Quid? quod luculenta fit Papæorum idololatria & blasphemia in breviariis, Rosariis, cursibus horariis, Antidotariis, Antipho- nis, Collectis, Marialibus, Processionalibus, Missa libus, Ritualibus & similibus Scriptis publicis au- toritate Papali, Brevibus Apostolicis, & Bullis Papa- libus sancitis; quorum proinde denominationem adeo ferre non poterant in Colloquio Thoruniensi Romano-Catholici, cum illa in usum vocarem ad principia liquidandi doctrinam Romano-Catholi- cam, quod evidenter inde convinci possent ab ipsa praxi quotidiana Romano-Catholicæ Ecclesiæ de superstitionibus, idololatriis, & blasphemiis publi- cis, ut inde etiam arripuerint occasionem abrum- pendi colloquium, ne scilicet verenda ipsorum pa- lam detegerentur, quomodo nempe haud vere- antur a Maria & Sanctis petere remissionem pecca- torum, cum Deo reconciliationem, gratiæ & dono- rum per gratiam etiam spiritualium largitionem, mentium illuminationem, Scripturæ intelligentiam, ab inimicis defensionem, a potestate Satanæ liberatio- nem, & auxilium in hora mortis. In Missali Eccle- siæ Tullensis hæc leguntur: O felix puerpera nostra piare scelera, jure Matris impera Redemptori &c.

Quomodo & quam sæpe Romano Papistico im- perio comes fuerit sævitia, ac leonum & ursorum indoles, a quibus etiam nomina habuere, qui præ- fuerunt, nemini facile ignotum est. Nam & in pro- pria sævierunt viscera. Sergius III. antecessorem Christophorum arctiori custodia revinxit, & For- mosi facta improbavit, adeo, ut cadaver ejus inve- stigatum capitali juberet supplicio affici, iterumque in Tiberim projici: Quod deinde repertum a Piscatoribus ferunt Basilicæ Apostolorum illatum, &, si credere fas est, ab imaginibus Sanctorum ve- nerabunda capitum demissione exceptum Sergius hic e Marozia scorto Johannem XI. Papam genuit, teste Luitprando. Sic sævientibus in se invicem Christianæ legis Antesignanis Hungari a Deo ul- tores immissi sunt. Illi enim Ticinum prædando delati Berengarium tunc Italiæ Regem immensis subnixum copiis ad Bremam fl. ingenti strage ce- ciderunt: Pars Italiam, pars Germaniam effusissi- me devastarunt. Legatur epit. Cluv. in Epit. Hi- st ftor. p. 465. Ita Romanus I. teste Platina præde- cessoris sui Stephani acta improbavit, Theodorus successor Romani Johannes IX. Formosi acta tu- tando eam excitavit seditionem, ut paulum admo- dum ab justo prælio abfuerit, Ravennam profe- ctus in concilio sanctiones Stephani rescidit; qua- lia innumera suggerunt Historici. Nec minus de impietate ac fraudibus Pontificum testimonia per- hibent, Hildebrandum Simoniacis artibus Papatum conscendisse, sed corpore Dominico sumpto sibi mortem subitaneam ascivisse, si eo modo ad Papa- tum pervenit, denique ExPapam ante mortem sce- lera sua confessum esse, ut ex Sigeberto & Brennone Cardin. annotavit B. Cluverus. De Paschali: Ni- hil, inquit, in Henricum decessoribus suis mitior, cu- rat persuaderi ejus filio Henrico Juniori, ut Ecclefiæ quam vocabant, obedientiam subjectioni Patri jura- tæ preferat, parum memor quam nulla legis Divinæ sanctio filium culpæ Patris vindicem constituat. Ex- armato fortissimo Principi institit Legatus Pontifi- cius, ut fateretur, injuste abs se Hildebrandum & Pontificiam Majestatem esse violatam. De Alexan- dro VI. Hieronymum Savanarolam Florentini in cineres redigere cum sociis Pontificis instinctu, cu- jus horrenda flagitia carpebat & tyrannidem. Viro sanctitate vitæ & prædictionibus clara imputata est dissidii excitatio in Rep. crimen Apostolis aliisŕ, testi- bus Christi solitum impingi. Neǵ vero melior Cai- pha Alexander VI. Pontificiis historiographis testibus (Guic. lib. 1. Volater. l. 23. Anthr. Onuphrio) Pri- mum Cardinales, a quibus Pontificatum emerat, va- rie ab eo damnati, debitas, ut ait Onuphrius, scelerati studii venalisǵ suffragii pœnas dedere. Tum Ursi- nos bello persecutus æstate una, cũ nihil inde præter dedecus reportaret, in gratiam eos recepit. Spurios deinde suos, Innocentii exemplo palam jactare, solu- taǵ omni disciplina honoribus & divitiis cumulare unice studuit. Lucretiam filiam Hispano, cui nupse- rat, ademptam tribus Principibus, primum Johanni Sfortiæ Pisauriensi, deinde Aloisio Aragoni, tertio Alfonso Estensi Ferrariæ Duci contra jus fasǵ eloca- vit, simul ipse eam in amoribus deliciisǵ habuit, filiis rivalibus patris: Unde Pontanus & Sanazarius versibus in hæc facinora lusere. Pontanus:

Hoc jacet in tumulo Lucretia nomine, sed re Thais, Alexandri filia, sponsa, nurus.

Actius Sanazarius:

Pollicitus cœlum Romanus & astra Sacerdos Per scelera & cædes ad styga pandit iter.

Et in Lucretiam idem:

Ergo te semper cupiet Lucretia Sextus! O fatum diri Numinis, hic Pater est.

E nothis minimum Principem regni Siciliæ; medium, Cæsarem Borgiam, Cardinalem; maximum Candiæ Ducem in Hispania fecit. Sed hunc Cardinalis noctu vagantem per insidias occidi, projiciǵ in Tiberim jus- sit. Post cujus mortem spreto sacerdotio cupidus dominandi se in Galliam cum magna vi auri ac su- pellectilis contulit. Dici paucis nequit, quantum doli necisque patraverint Pontifex ejusque filius, ut execrandas cupiditates adimplerent. Volate- ranus, Guicciardinus, Jovius & ex illis Onuphrius idonei testes sunto. Sequitur Julianus Cardina- lis, armiger magis quam claviger, qui Julii II. no- men sumpsit. Borgiam mille neces meritum co- piis urbibusque ac omni dignitati exutum ea dimisit conditione, ut Cæsenæ & Forolivii arces ejus præsidio munitas reciperet. Julius Ecclesiasticam ditionem non tantum recuperare, sed & latius pro- ferre cupidus, Bentivolum Bononia pellit; ad Veneti nominis excidium cum Cæsare, Hispaniæque, & Galliæ Regibus, cum Ducibus quoque, Ferrariæ & Mantuæ, Cameraci in Belgis fœdus percutit. Mox autore Ju- lio inter Cæsarem & Gallum fœdus rumpitur. Rex Francus ab infesto Pontifice proscriptus cum redinte- grato exercitu rursus Mediolanum Duce Ludovico Tremollio repeteret, ab Helvetiis sanguinario ad No- varam prælio victus, totâque fere Italia exclusus est. Concilii Pisis inchoati & Mediolani parum prospere renovati patres Helvetiorum timore perterriti Lug- dunum se transtulerant, Julium execrantes. At ille, pulsis Bononia Bentivolis, Ravennâque recepta, Par- mam & Placentiam suo adjicit dominio. De succes- sore Leone X. Claves hic in Tiberim projecisse fer- tur aliquando, addens, valiturum Pauli gladium, cum claves Petri nihil possent. Ulricus Huttenus in illum, ut multa ita & illud:

Fraude capit totum Mercator Julius orbem, Vendit enim cælos, non habet ipse tamen.

Ludovicus Francorum Rex nummis inscripsit au- reis: Perdam Babylonis nomen. Et porro: Delica- tulus Pontifex auri patrio more (ut ait Monachus Citizensis P. Langius) sitientissimus, Romanæ Flo- rentinam jungens avaritiam cuncta pecuniis venalia habens Basilicam D. Petri a Julio inchoatam extru- ens: Sanctus adeo, ut inter vina & lautitias Evange- lium Christi ut quæstuosam sibi suisque fabulam irri- deret. Quietis & otii cupidissimus apud Ludovicum XII. obtinuit, ut omissa Ecclesiæ reformatione Latera- nensi Concilio subscriberet. Emungebat sub umbra Turcicæ expeditionis crumenas vulgi &c. Taceo alia. Sunt enim innumera: quæ non tam imperio censentur imputanda, quam Pontifici per Clerum, Cardinales, Nuncios Apostolicos, quos vocat, Archi- Episcopos, Episcopos, Prælatos, Monachos, Jesuitas, quum in aulis valent imprimis, qui a confessioni- bus privatis sunt, seu clam seu palam, seu directe seu per indirectam scenam, ubi sibi & rationi sta- tus sui inserviunt, adornanti. Usi sunt feris illis in puniendis Christianis Romani, a quibus eorum imperium describitur, per nos licet; Factum id sine dubio, ut agnosceretur imperium, quod indigitat fera illa cum dentibus ferreis, quibus pleraque com- minuit, cætera conculcans pedibus, Dan. 7, 7. Par- do autem comparatur non tam propter religionum varietatem, quam propter calliditatem, & victoria- rum celeritatem, juxta illud Cæsaris: Veni, vidi, vi- ci: quemadmodum post secundum bellum Puni- cum sequutæ statim, Floro l. II. c. 7. dicente, Afri- canæ gentes, Macedonia, Græcia, Syria, cæteraque omnia quodam quasi æstu & torrente fortunæ.

Sed ut ad Grotium revertamur, Reges illi nun- quam diademata gestarunt, nec nisi æquivoce a Grotio Reges dicuntur omnes. Hi enim obnoxii & subditi fuere Romano Imperio, dicente Grotio: Nec illi omnes idololatriæ addicti. Herodes certe & successores Ebræorum religioni dediti fuere. Rex Edesse in Syria Abgarus Christiana, de quo Eu- seb. l. I, c. 13. Neque tam ascendit idololatria isto tem- pore, quam seminari cœpit per Evangelii in orbe præconium. Quid quod Grotio decem cornua decem provinciæ sint sub Senatoribus Romanis, qui Cyniæ Pyrrhi Legato Reges videbantur, & diadema quodammodo obtinebant: etsi numerus finitus pro infinito adhibitus dici possit, ut Genes. 31, 7. 1. Sam. 1, 8. Job. 19, 3. Eccl. 7, 19. Non autem satis bene Romana idololatria a Graeca, Aegyptia & Phry- gia distinguitur : Siquidem Roma olim omnium populorum varias religiones & superstitiones as- sumpserit, & Diis peregrinis in triumphum abdu- ctis pulvinaria & aras statuerit, ac carmine etiam Magico obsessarum urbium Deos, tanquam cul- tum ipsis, si in partes suas transire vellent, promit- tendo, evocarint: Nos in sacra tuam Romana recepimus Isim Semi-Deosq; canes, & sistra jubentia luctus Et quem tu plangens hominem testaris Osirim, canit Lucanus.

In tractatione priori de his, quae hactenus evol- vimus, ita habet Grotius:

Ἔχον κέρατα δέκα, habentem cornua decem) Haben- tem Ministros Reges multos; non quidem illos, qui aliquot post seculis erant extituri, & infra desi- gnantur c. 17, 12. sed tamen multos ac potentes, qua- les erant Reges Armeniae, Thraciae, Galatiae, Ponti, Judaeae, Arabiae, Adiabenae, Suevorum, Alpium Cot- tiarum, Alpium Idionni.

Καὶ κεφαλὰς ἑπτὰ, & capita septem) Capita duas si- gnificationes habent Imperatorum & montium, ut pa- tet infra c. 17, 19. Hic montes magis significantur, id est, idololatriae illius non Phrygiae, non Aegyptiae, non Graecae, sed Romanae sedes praecipua & origo.

Καὶ ἐπὶ τῶν κεράτων ἀυτῶ δέκα διαδήματα, & super cornua ejus decem diademata) Ut magis intelligatur vis imperii idololatriam illam sustinentis, explicatio ad- ditur, qua intelligatur illos, qui cornuum nomine de- signati sunt, summo jure fuisse Reges,& tamen in obse- quio & reverentia Romani imperii, qualis Herodes & ejus successores, aliique Reges. Alii successores ubi praefectorum nomine contenti non fuere; cum Regio nomine sumpsere diadema. Testis Diodorus Siculus lib. 20. Tertullianus adversus Marc. 1. Quid nunc si nec inter Reges videri potest plurifariam summum, ma- gnum, sed unicum & singularis, apud eum scilicet, qui Rex Regum ob summitatem magnitudinis, & subjectionem ca- terorum graduum, quasi culmen dominationis excipitur.

Καὶ ἐπὶ τὰς κεφαλὰς ἀυτῶ ὀνόματα βλασφημίας, & super capita ejus nomina blasphemiae.) Montes aut urbs Roma idem sunt. Ea urbs se vocabat aeternam, quod re ipsa impium erat. Vide quae dicemus ad caput XVII.

Magnates, ut in antedictis jam innuimus, trans- mutat in Reges, & loco decem, qui numerus fini- tus est, plures sufficit pro lubitu, diademata Regia insignia nullo loco habet, ne Reges, quos inveni- re nequit, admittere cogatur: Bestiam vero inau- dito commentario de idololatria interpretatur, ut tandem exornet sensum aliquem non adversum bestiae Romanae. Atque ita sese egregie causam Anti-Christi egisse credit. Hem praeclarum Scri- pturae Interpretem!

## 13:2
Vers. 2.

And the beast, which I saw, was like a leopard, and his feet as a bear's, and his mouth as the mouth of a lion.) Just as the Apocalypse previously distinguished the forms of the four animals in the Old Testament combined into one: so now, conversely, it draws together the distinct forms of the beasts in Daniel 7 into one. The leopard is variegated, Jer. 13, 23. For the Greeks seem to understand by the name of pardalis the same animal which the Latins call a panther, or even a 'Varius', as Pliny has handed down. Such was Claudius, now mild, now savage. The bear tramples what it meets with its foot. Ovid: 'And bears with armed claws.' But Anacreon says that a 'chasm of teeth' is given to the lion. That mouth of the beast is Domitian himself below v. 4. Therefore, as the more important part, the name of the beast is given to him below c. 17, 11. For the persecution of Domitian, being the most severe, had to be repeated, like that of Antiochus in Daniel, and all the more so because the outcome of Domitian's idolatry prefigured the outcome, as we shall say there. These feet and this mouth therefore show that cruelty will often be a companion of idolatry, sometimes even using lions and bears against Christians, as is known from the martyrdom of Ignatius and that saying in Tertullian, 'The Christians to the lion.'

And the Dragon gave him his power, and his throne, and his authority) Just as a serpent has great power to harm, so does the Devil. Added to this is the permission of God, who often does not hinder him. This is called authority here, as also in Luke 22:33. From both follows a certain great kingdom over the minds of men, which is signified by the name of throne. This the Demon presiding over the Roman empire bestows upon the Roman idolatry to be exercised as if in his stead, breathing his own affections and efficacy into the superstition.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

Καὶ τὸ θηρίον, ὃ εἶδον, ἦν ὅμοιον παρδάλει, καὶ οἱ πόδες ἀυτῶ ὡς ἄρκτε, καὶ τὸ ςόμα ἀυτῶ ὡς ςόμα λέοντος.) Sicut ante Apocalypsis quatuor animalium formas in Vetere Testa- mento in unum compositas distinxit: ita nunc contra res distinctas apud Danielem 7. ferarum formas in unum con- trahit. Pardalis varia Jer. 13, 23. Videntur enim Graeci παρδάλεως nomine idem animal intelligere, quod Latini panthera vocant, aut etiam Variam, ut Plinius tradidit. Talis Claudius, nunc mitis nunc saevus. Ursus pede obvia proterit. Ovidius: Armatuq; unguibus ursos. At λέοντι χάσμ᾽ ὀδόντων datum ait Anacreon. Id os ferae est Do- mitianus ipse infra v. 4. Ideo ipsi tanquam potiori parti datur nomen θηρία infra c. 17, 11. Domitiani enim perse- cutio, upote gravissima repeti debuit, ut illa Antiochi apud Danielem, eoque magis, quod eventus Domitiani idolola- triae eventum praefigurabat, ut ibi dicemus. Ostendunt ergo hi pedes & hoc os idololatriae saepe comitem fore saevi- tiam, nonnunquam etiam leonibus & ursis usurarn in Chri- stianos, ut notum ex Ignatii martyrio & dicto illo apud Tertullianum, Christianos ad leonem.

Καὶ ἔδωκεν αὐτῷ ὁ Δράκων τὴν δύναμιν αὐτοῦ , καὶ τὸν θρόνον αὐτοῦ , καὶ τὴν ἐξουσίαν αὐτοῦ) Sicut ferpens magnam vim ad nocendum habet, ita & Diabolus. Accedit Dei permissus eum saepe non impedientis. Id ἐξουσία dicitur hic, ut & Luc. 22, 33. Ex utroque sequitur magnum quod- dam regnum in animos hominum, quod θρόνος nomine si- gnificatur. Haec Daemon Romano imperio praesidens ido- lolatriae Romanae quasi vice sua exercenda tribuit, affectus suos & efficaciam superstitoni exspirans.

## 13:2
Verse 2.

And the beast, which I saw, was like unto a leopard) The cruelty of Roman idolatry, such as it was after Nero, could not be sufficiently expressed under the image of a single wild beast, and therefore several had to be assumed. And the Prophet names those especially whose ministry the Romans used for the punishment of Christians. The leopard is an animal of varied color; thus Roman idolatry had gods male, female, hermaphrodite, greatest, middle, least, good, evil, intermediate, with varied countenance, varied habit, varied power.

And his feet as the feet of a bear) And bears armed with claws. Ovid, Metamorphoses X.

And his mouth as the mouth of a lion) Anacreon: Nature gave horns to bulls, hooves to horses, swiftness to hares, a chasm of teeth to lions. Creative Nature gives the strength of hooves to horses, both horns to bulls, speed to little hares, and teeth to lions. Lactantius, book V, ch. 11: No one can describe according to their deserts the inhumanity of this great beast, which, though resting in one place, nevertheless rages throughout the whole world with iron teeth, and not only dissipates the limbs of men, but also crushes the very bones, and rages into ashes.

And the Dragon gave him his power) That Dragon named above in ch. 12:3. The Devil, without doubt, the ancient serpent, above in ch. 12:9, as also the Hebrews [call him] נחש הקדנמי, whom Moses designated under the image of a serpent, Gen. 3:1. In the name of the Dragon there is indeed something of a serpent, but with the addition of flight, that is, the speed of acting. The Devil used the name of false gods so that he might detract from the worship of God. And whatever strength he had, God permitting, he turned to that end. Whence so many prodigies are recorded in Roman histories; see what is below in ch. 13:13. Add 2 Thess. 2:9.

And his throne) The Devil had willed that the empire, which he himself, God providently permitting, had established at Rome in the name of Mars, with auspices, auguries, and prodigies, should all serve idols.

And great power) The greatest majesty, by which that empire was strong even among foreign nations, among whom temples, altars, and priesthoods were built everywhere in honor of Rome, Augustus, and Tiberius.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

Καὶ τὸ θηρίον, ὃ εἶδον, ἦν ὅμοιον παρδάλει, & bestia, quam vidi, similis erat pardali) Non potuit satis cru- delitas Romanae idololatriae, qualis post Neronem fuit, exprimi sub unius ferae imagine, itaque plures fuere assumendae. Et eas maxime nominat Prophe- ta, quarum ministerio Romani uti in poenas Chri- stianorum. Pardalis varii coloris animal, sic idolola- tria Romana Deos habebat mares, foeminas, mari- foeminas, maximos, medioxumos, minimos, bo- nos, malos, medios, vario vultu, vario habitu, varia potestate.

Καὶ οἱ πόδες αὐτοῦ ὡς ἄρκτου) & pedes ejus sicut pedes ursi. Armatosq; unguibus ursos. Ovidius X. Metamorphoseos.

Καὶ τὸ στόμα αὐτοῦ ὡς στόμα λέοντος, & os ejus sicut os leonis) Anacreon, Φύσις κέρατα ταύροις Ὁπλὰς δ' ἔδωκεν ἵπποις Ποδωκίην λαγωοῖς, Λέουσι χάσμ' ὀδόντων. Equis dat ungularum Natura vim creatrix, Tauris utrumq; cornu Lepusculisq; cursum Leonibusq; dentes. Lactantius libr. V. c. 11. Nemo hujus tantae belluae im- manitatem potest pro meritis describere, qua uno loco re- cubans tamen per totum orbem dentibus ferreis saevit, & non tantum artus hominum dissipat, sed & ossa ipsa com- minuit, & in cineres furit.

Καὶ ἔδωκεν αὐτῷ ὁ Δράκων τὴν δύναμιν αὐτοῦ, & dedit illi Draco virtutem suam) Draco ille nominatus supra c. 12, 3. Diabolus haud dubie ὅφις ὁ ἀρχαῖος serpens anti- quus supra c. 12, 9. ut & Ebraei נחש הקדנמי, quem sub serpentis imagine Moses designavit, Gen. 3. v. 1. In Draconis nomine est quidem aliquid serpentis, sed ad- juncto volatu, id est agendi celeritate. Diabolus fal- sorum Deorum nomine utebatur, ut Deo cultum de- traheret. Et quicquid habebat, Deo sinente, virium, eo convertebat. Unde tot prodigia Romanis historiis memorata; vide quae infra c. 13, 13. Adde 2. Thess. 2, 9.

Καὶ τὸν θρόνον αὐτοῦ, & thronum suum) Diabolus imperium, quod ipse, Deo provide sinente, constituerat Romae Martis nomine, auspiciis, auguriis, prodigiis, id totum voluerat servire idolis.

Καὶ ἐξουσίαν μεγάλην, & potestatem magnam) Maje- statem maximam, qua imperium illud etiam apud ex- teras gentes valebat, apud quas passim structa templa, arae, sacerdotia in honorem Romae, Augusti, Tiberii.

## 13:3
Vers. 3.

And one of his heads as it were wounded to death) Some of the ancients have referred this to Nero. I refer it to the fall of the Capitol, which happened while the Vitellians and Flavians were fighting among themselves at Rome. For we are taught below that mountains are also signified by the name of heads. Among those mountains, however, the Capitol stands out, both as a citadel and the chief temple of Rome. It is common for the Prophets to call temples situated on mountains by the name of mountains, whence the Jerusalem temple is called the mountain of the Lord. But we have also heard above that citadels situated on high ground are called mountains, VIII. 8. Now when such citadels are overturned, then the mountains themselves are said to fall by a certain poetic locution, as in Ezek. 38:20, Jer. 51:25. But here, because the mountains are described under the figure of heads, a wound is said to have been inflicted upon the mountain as if it were lethal, that is, one which seemed lethal. Many nations had believed that with the collapse of the Capitol an end was imminent for Roman affairs, as we learn from Tacitus, Histories V, because the fate of the city was believed to be contained in that most august of all temples, as can be seen in Livy, book V; hence Virgil in the ninth Aeneid:

While the house of Aeneas shall inhabit the immovable rock of the Capitol, and the Roman father shall hold the empire.

And Horace:

--- --- while the Pontiff shall ascend the Capitol with the silent virgin.

And his deadly wound was healed) Vespasian, which was thought least likely to happen, restored both the city, and the empire, and the Capitol, whence on his coins was added: Roma resurges: With what pomp of idolatry the Capitol was restored can be read in Tacitus, Histories IV.

And the whole earth wondered after the beast) Men of all lands, who had begun to think ill of the Roman gods, with the Capitol so magnificently restored, changed their opinion and became more obstinate in Roman idolatry, as if astonished by so unexpected an event. And it is a brief locution, wondered after the beast, for wondered walking after the beast, which full locution stands in Luke 21:18, 2 Pet. 2:10. In like manner Acts 7:9, they sold into Egypt for they sold to be brought into Egypt.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

Καὶ μίαν ἐκ τῶν κεφαλῶν αὐτοῦ ὡσεὶ ἐσφαγμένην εἰς θάνα- τον) Id veterum quidam ad Neronem traxere. Ego ad lapsum Capitolii, qui evenit Vitellianis & Flavianis Romae inter se pugnantibus. Nam capitum nomine etiam montes significari etiam infra docemur. Inter eos autem montes eminet Capitolium & arx & templum praecipuum Romae. Frequens autem Prophetis templa in montibus sita sic ap- pellare montium nomine, unde templum Hierosolymita- num dicitur mons Domini. Sed & arces in arduo sitas montes dici jam supra audivimus VIII. 8. Ubi autem ta- les arces evertuntur, tunc ipsi montes, Poetica quadam lo- cutione dicuntur cadere, ut Ezech. 38, 20. Jerem. 51, 25. Sed hic quia montes describuntur sub figura capitum, dicitur inflicta monti plaga quasi lethalis, id est, quae lethalis vide- batur. Crediderant multae gentes collapso capitolio fi- nem imminere rebus Romanis, ut ex Tacito discimus Hi- storiarum V. quia fatum urbis illo templo omnium augu- stissimo contineri credebatur, ut videre est apud Livium li- bro V. inde Virgilius Aeneidos nono:

Dum domus Aeneae Capitoli immobile saxum Incolet, imperiumque pater Romanus habebit.

Et Horatius:

--- --- dum Capitolium Scandet cum tacita virgine Pontifex.

Καὶ ἡ πληγὴ τοῦ θανάτου αὐτοῦ ἐθεραπεύθη) Vespasianus quod minime futurum putabatur, & urbem, & imperium, & capitolium restituit, unde nummis ejus additum : Roma resurges: Quanta cum idololatriae pompa restitutum sit Ca- pitolium, legi potest apud Tacitum historiarum IV.

Καὶ ἐθαύμασεν ὅλη ἡ γῆ ὀπίσω τοῦ θηρίου) Homines terra- rum omnium, qui male existimare coeperunt de Diis Roma- nis, Capitolio tam magnifice restituto mutavere sententiam rursumque in idololatria Romana facti sunt obstinatiores, tam inopinato eventu veluti attoniti. Et est brevis locutio ἐθάυμασεν ὀπίσω τοῦ θηρίου, pro ἐθαύμασεν πορευομένη ὀπίσω τοῦ θηρίου, quae locutio plena extat Luc. 21, 18. 2. Petr. 2, 10. Pari modo Act. 7, 9. ἀπέδοντο εἰς Αἴγυπτον pro ἀπέδοντο κο- μισόμενον εἰς Αἴγυπτον.

## 13:3
Verse 3.

And I saw one of his heads, as it were wounded to death) The Capitol, the most august temple of Rome and of the whole Roman empire on one of the seven hills, called for that reason the Capitoline, was burned while the Vitellians and Flavians were fighting among themselves: which omen all nations believed to be the most certain sign of the falling Roman empire. From that, the boldness of the Jews to rebel was increased. Germany, however, and all the Gauls were raised in the hope of partly preserving and partly recovering their liberty. Tacitus, Histories IV: Nothing had impelled them so much to believe that the end was at hand as the burning of the Capitol. The city had been captured once by the Gauls, but the empire had remained because the seat of Jupiter was intact. Now by a fatal fire, a sign of heavenly wrath was given, and the possession of human affairs was portended to the Transalpine nations. Camillus in Livy, Book V. This is the Capitol, where once, upon a human head being found, it was answered that in that place would be the head and sum of the empire: here, when the Capitol was being cleared by augury, Juventas and Terminus, to the great joy of our fathers, did not allow themselves to be moved, nor did the Ancilia sent down from heaven, here all the gods are propitious while you remain. From the same opinion come those things in the poets: 'The immovable rock of the Capitol,' and 'while the Pontifex shall climb the Capitol with the silent virgin,' and many similar things, which are obvious to those reading them.

And his deadly wound was healed, and his deadly wound was healed) For Vespasian, who also restored the Roman empire, restored the same Capitol, and indeed with great pomp of idolatry. Tacitus, Histories IV. He confers the care of restoring the Capitol upon L. Vestinus, a man of the equestrian order, but of authority and fame among the nobles. The soothsayers gathered by him advised that the remains of the former temple should be the marshes were to be drained, the temple was to be set upon the same foundations, the gods were unwilling that the ancient form be changed. On the eleventh day before the Kalends of July, in clear light, the whole space which was dedicated to the temple was bound with fillets and garlands. Soldiers entered, to whom were given auspicious names, with lucky branches. Then the Vestal Virgins, with boys and girls whose parents were still living, washed the area with water drawn from streams, springs, and rivers. Then Helvidius Priscus the Praetor, with Plautius Aelianus the Pontiff leading the way, having purified the area with the sacrifice of a pig, a sheep, and a bull, and having offered the entrails upon the turf, prayed to Jupiter, Juno, Minerva, and the guardian gods of the Empire that they would prosper the undertakings and raise up their own seats, begun by the piety of men, with Divine aid; he touched the fillets with which the stone was bound and to which the ropes were attached; at the same time the other Magistrates, the Priests, the Senate, the knights, and a great part of the people, with zeal and joy, pulled the huge stone together, and here and there were cast into the foundations silver and gold coins and the first fruits of metals, untouched by any furnaces, but as they are produced. The soothsayers foretold that the work should not be violated by stone or gold destined for any other purpose. On the coins of Vespasian we find: You shall rise again, Rome.

And the whole earth wondered after the beast) There is 'emprosis' for 'wondered walking after the beast', as in Luke 21:8 and 2 Peter 2:10. Thus also 'to come', 'to follow after someone', is frequent in the sacred books. The sense is, when those who had despaired of the Roman gods and the Roman empire saw both these and those restored in their ancient seat, they followed the Roman sacred rites and customs all the more with a certain astonished stupor because of so unexpected an event.

And they worshipped the Dragon who gave the power to the beast) Not directly indeed, but by consequence, they unknowingly rendered all that cult of religion to the Devil and his satellites, 1 Cor. 10:20, 21, above c. 9:20.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

Καὶ εἶδον μίαν ἐκ τῶν κεφαλῶν αὐτοῦ, ὡς ἐσφαγμένην εἰς θάνατον, & vidi unum de capitibus suis, quasi occisum in mortem.) Capitolium templum Romae Romanique totius imperii augustissimum in uno septem montium, dicto ob id Capitolino, exustum bellantibus inter se Vitellianis & Flavianis: quod omen cunctae gentes certissimum credidere ruituri imperii Romani. Inde aucta Judaeis ad rebellandum audacia. Germania au- tem, Galliaeque omnis erecta in spem partim servandae partim recuperandae libertatis. Tacitus Histor. IV. Nihil aeque, quam incendium Capitolii, ut finem adesse crederent, impulerat. Captam olim a Gallis urbem, sed integra Jovis sede mansisse imperium. Fatali nunc igne, caelestis irae signum datum, & possessionem rerum huma- narum Transalpinis gentibus portendi. Camillus apud Livium libro V. Hic Capitolium est, ubi quondam hu- mano capite invento responsum est eo loco caput rerum summamq; imperii fore: hic cum augurato liberaretur Capitolium, Juventas Terminusq; maximo gaudio patrum nostrorum moveri se non passi, nec Ancilia caelo dimissa, hic omnes propitii manentibus vobis Dii. Ex eadem opi- nione ista apud Poetas: Capitoli immobile saxum, & - - - dum Capitolium Scandet cum tacita virgine Pontifex multaque similia, quae obvia eos legentibus.

Καὶ ἡ πληγὴ τοῦ θανάτου αὐτοῦ ἐθεραπεύθη, & plaga mortis ejus curata est) Restituit enim Capitolium idem, qui & imperium Romanum Vespasianus & magna qui- dem idolatriae pompa. Tacit. hist. IV. Curam re- stituendi Capitolii in L. Vestinum confert, equestris ordinis virum, sed autoritate famaq; inter proceres. Ab eo con- tracti haruspices monuere, ut reliquiae prioris delubri in paludes aveherentur, templum iisdem vestigiis sisteretur, nolle Deos mutari veterem formam. Undecimo Calendas Julias serena luce spatium omne quod templo dicabatur evinctum vittis coronisq; Ingressi milites quibus fausta nomina felici- bus ramis. Dein Virgines Vestales cum pueris puellisq; pa- trimis matrimisq; aqua, rivis & fontibus amnibusq; hau- sta, perluere. Tum Helvidius Priscus Prætor, præeunte Plau- tio Æliano Pontifice, lustrata suove taurilibus area, & super cespitem redditis extis, Jovem, Junonem, Minervam, præsi- desq; Imperii Deos precatus uti cœpta prosperarent, sedesq; suas pietate hominum inchoatas Divina ope attollerent, vit- tas quibus ligatus lapis, innexiq; funes erant, contigit, simul cæteri Magistratus & Sacerdotes & Senatus & eques, & magna pars populi studio lætitiaq; connixi saxum ingens traxere, passimq; injectæ fundamentis argenti aurig; stipes & metallorum primitiæ, nullis fornacibus victæ, sed ut gignun- tur. Prædixere haruspices, ne temeraretur opus saxo aurove in aliud destinato. In nummis Vespasiani reperimus : Romæ resurges.

Καὶ ἐθαύμασεν ὅλη ἡ γῆ ὀπίσω τῦ θηρίε, & admira- ta est universa terra post bestiam) Est ἔμπροσις pro ἐθαύ- μασε πορευομένη ὀπίσω τῦ θηρίε, admirata est incedens post bestiam, ut Luc, 21, 8. & 2. Petr. 2, 10. Sic & ἴεχεσθαι, ἀκο- λυθεῖν ὀπίσω τινὸς, venire sequi post aliquem, frequentia in sacris libris. Sensus est, cum ii, qui de Diis Romanis imperioque Romano desperaverant, viderent & hos & illos in veteri sede restitutos, eo magis sectati sunt sa- cra ritusque Romanos cum attonito quodam stupore ob adeo inexpectatum eventum.

Καὶ προσσκύνησαν τῷ δράκοντι τῷ δεδωκότι τὴν ἐξυ- σίαν τῷ θηρίῳ, & adoraverunt Draconem, qui dedit pote- statem bestiæ) Non directè quidem, sed per consequen- tiam ignari omnem illum cultum religionis Diabolo detulerunt, & ejus satellitibus, 1. Cor. 10, 20. 21. supra c. 9, 20.

## 13:4
Vers. 4.

Καὶ προσεκύνησαν τῷ δράκοντι, τῷ δεδωκότι τὴν ἐξουσίαν τῷ θηρίῳ) That is, they served the Devil. For it is a metonymy, because those who serve someone are accustomed to prostrate themselves before him. The same expression is found in Gen. 27, 29; c. 49, 8; Is. 45. Therefore προσκυνεῖν is expressly explained by being subjected, Gen. 37, 7, 8. But they truly serve the Devil who worship idols: for they promote his dominion even while unaware, 1 Cor. 10, 20. In the manuscript: Ὅτι ἔδωκε τὴν ἐξουσίαν.

And they worshipped the beast) that is, they served the Roman idolatry: they followed Roman rites.

Saying, Who is like unto the beast) What religion is equal to the Roman?

Who is able to make war with him?) Who could resist him with impunity? As if they were saying: the things which the Christians are attempting are foolish. These things, however, are taken from the words of Rabshakeh, 2 Kings 18:35. Similar words in Dan. 8:4, 7. In the Manuscript it is καὶ τίς, just as the Latin also reads.

In the previous treatment these things are as follows:

Latin:

Vers. 4.

Καὶ προσεκύνησαν τῷ δράκοντι, τῷ δεδωκότι τὴν ἐξουσίαν τῷ θηρίῳ) Id est, servierunt Diabolo. Est enim Metony- mia, quia, qui alicui serviunt, coram eo prosterni solent. Eadem locutio Gen. 27, 29. c. 49, 8. Es. 45. Ideo προσκυνεῖν ex止めresse explicatur per subjici, Gen 37,7.8. Vere autem Dia- bolo serviunt, qui colunt idola : ipsius enim imperium etiam nescientes promovent, 1. Cor. 10, 20. In Manuscripto : Ὅτι ἔδωκε τὴν ἐξουσίαν.

Καὶ προσεκύνησαν τῷ θηρίῳ) id est idololatriae Romanae inservierunt: sectati sunt ritus Romanos.

Λέγοντες, Τίς ὅμοιος τῷ θηρίῳ) Quae religio par Romanae?

Τίς δύναται πολεμῆσαι μετ' αὐτοῦ ;) Quis impune ei posset obsistere? Quasi dicerent: stulta sunt, quae moliuntur Christiani. Desumpta autem haec ex verbis Rabsacis, 2. Reg. 18, 35. Similia verba Dan. 8, 4. 7. In Manuscripto est καὶ τίς quomodo legit & Latinus.

In priori tractatione haec ita habent:

## 13:4
Verse 4.

And they worshipped the beast) To the multitude of Roman gods, which one can find named everywhere in histories, and among Christians, Arnobius, Lactantius, Augustine. Ovid has the chief of these at the end of his Metamorphoses: Ye gods, I pray, companions of Aeneas, to whom sword and fire yielded, and ye native gods, and thou Father Quirinus of the City, and thou Father Gradivus, sire of the invincible Quirinus, and Vesta, consecrated among the Caesarean Penates, and with Caesarean Vesta, thou domestic Phoebus. And thou, Jupiter, who holdest the high Tarpeian heights.

Saying: Who is like the beast, and who will be able to fight with it? These are almost the very words of Rabshakeh, 2 Kings, as the Hebrews call the books, chapter XVIII, at the end.

Since Grotius, who understands Roman idolatry well, knows it does not suffice for the sense of St. John, he adds cruelty as a companion, so that idolatry may correspond to savage beasts. But although this, even if most abominable, flourished not so much in ancient superstition as in Roman Anti-Christianity; yet it does nothing here to the point, where the beast, in the prophetic manner of Scripture, is to be understood not of idolatry, but of an empire or kingdom. The tuneful trifles about the Capitol burned down, and its death-wound cured by Vespasian in the destruction of the city, deserve indignation rather than refutation. He turns a mountain into the Capitol, a fire into a slaughter unto death, extermination into healing, an enemy into a friend, the restoration of Divine (pagan) worship into the curing of a deadly wound, the veneration of the Devil into religion: What is this other than changing squares into rounds? Almost everyone understands it of the Anti-Christ: Irenaeus, book V, c. 28; Tertullian, de resurr., c. 25; Hippolytus, Ephrem Syrus, Prudentius, Gregory the Great, etc. Idolatry of the Roman Papal empire also shows itself with a varied countenance, with varied habit, with varied power, whether you look at the adornment, or the mode of worshipping, or the various deities and objects of worship, through the veneration of statues and images, through angel-worship, saint-worship, Mary-worship, bread-worship, cross-worship, shroud-worship (holy Shroud pray for us), demon-worship, if it appears in the form of a Deity. And why, I ask, does he try to intrude Domitian here, which he previously accepted concerning idolatry? So certain and constant is the man's opinion! The beast is said to be worshipped; that does not fit idolatry so well: for even if an idol is worshipped, yet idolatry is not usually said to be worshipped. And who will admit, to answer the appendix at the same time, that idolatry is worshipped because men worshipping idols worship and adore the Devil in them? In what place of Scripture will it be taught that professors of idolatry, or the idolatry of the Gospel opposed to it, are called the Gospel? By what right, likewise, does he drag what he had said about idolatry immediately to Domitian? Did the beast finally have leonine teeth for tearing and ursine feet for crushing under Domitian, or only under him? To say nothing of the fact that Domitian's persecution did not last 3 1/2 years; but if one trusts Baronius, five years: for he teaches that it began in the year of Christ 93 and ended in 98, during which there were certainly far more serious ones, under Trajan, Diocletian, Nero, and others. Tertullian, Apol. c. 5. What Maresius has about those 1260 years in his dissertation on Apoc. XIII against Grotius, p. 126, we do not make our own: how, for instance, in the year 1260 from the ascension of Christ. Satan, about to drown the woman from his mouth, sent forth Boniface VIII and his Decretals, in which he surpassed all his predecessors in shamelessness and blasphemies. For even if the prophecy was not fulfilled on that day, looking not to past but to future times, the Holy Spirit could have hinted that the tyranny of the Anti-Christ would last as long as the empire itself lasted. For those doubled years make 1520, which have long since passed, while the Anti-Christ still endures, even though in that year such a one was openly declared the Roman Pontiff by Blessed Luther, and his power has not been a little diminished since then. Finally, those things which are said about the beast in general are restricted by Grotius to Domitian alone only rashly; but the name of blasphemy, as it is sometimes taken more generally elsewhere, when it signifies insults not only directed against the name of God, that is, God himself, but also against the tabernacle of God, the Church, and the saints in heaven or in the Church, the saints and the faithful, to which persecutions are joined, because the wild beast speaks blasphemous and great or horrible things, when it opens its mouth, with the witness of Papal bulls, which it makes its own by promulgating and executing them, the Empire itself. But when a mouth speaking great and blasphemous things is attributed to this beast, from the likeness of Dan. 7, 8, that is, swollen and proud no less than blasphemous, that certainly (I speak of the mouth) is not idolatry, but of a man worshipping an idol. Indeed, that law of the XII tables was already in exile before the Capitol was restored.

Moreover, all these things are to be applied more explicitly to the Roman Papal empire. It had bear-like feet, because this beast was so powerful that it subjugated the East to itself through Lucullus, Pompey, and Crassus, Macedonia and all Greece through Paulus Aemilius, the good part of Africa through Scipio and Marius, and Egypt through Octavian Augustus. Its power decreased and began to wane when it was ravaged here and there by the Goths, Vandals, and other barbarian nations; it decreased when it was wounded several times by a lethal blow, soon with two Augusti existing and contending with each other, namely Antoninus the Philosopher and Lucius Aurelius Verus, soon under Gallus and Volusianus, etc. Nor are only the increases and decreases to be urged; but the attributes of the Babylonian harlot, which fit no one more aptly than Papal Rome: Which 1. besides Christ the bridegroom admits other lovers, and prostitutes its bed greatly. For it calls the Roman Pontiff its Bridegroom in C. quoniam de immunit. in 6. Bellarm. praefat. de Pontif. God C. inter corporalia de translat. Praelat.

Bald. in l. ult. C. sentent. rescind. Decius in c. 1. de constit. Dominum Dominantium. Bald. in C. Eccles. ut lit. pend. they even name the typical Jesus Francis, other saints, Mary, relics, images &c. 2. The golden cup of fornication is because of the splendid appearance of the faith, doctrine, and Christian religion, but it is full of abomination and uncleanness, because of the abomination of manifold idolatries, and the uncleanness of fornications and of Papal dogmas and decrees for concubines, incests, Sodomy, and other most impure flagitious acts. 3. St. Bernard complained of its pride and luxury in l. 15. de consider. to Pope Eugenius: Histrionic attire, Royal apparatus, gold on bridles, on saddles, and spurs, and spurs shine more than altars, thence splendid tables and foods and cups, thence banquetings and drunkenness &c. Thence the purses are stuffed, and for this sort of thing the Provosts of Churches, Deans, Archdeacons, Bishops, and Archbishops wish to be, and are. For these do not yield to that business which walketh in darkness, for he himself is the Anti-Christ. 4. She is drunk with the blood of the saints, and of the martyrs of Jesus. No wonder: for they are numbered at more than thirty-two times ten million eighty-five hundred thousand 328500000 cruelly slaughtered by the will of the Roman Pontiff. The Jesuit Franc. Ribera must also be heard concerning this, who in Ap. p. 328 says: This fits no city as well as it fits Rome, in which innumerable martyrs have been killed. Although she is said to be drunk not only because of the blood shed in her, but also because of the blood which, by her command and power, was shed in other cities, for she herself shed this also. Nor does he speak only of the blood shed up to the times of John, but also of that which was to be shed afterwards. She is called drunken, so that the shedding of much blood may be indicated. For drunkenness is accustomed to signify a great abundance. 5. The wounded beast is said to have returned from the Roman Empire through the incursions of the barbarians, who for over three centuries wounded, devastated, and occupied Rome, so that for all that time there was no Western Emperor. Likewise by the medical aid of Charlemagne and Leo III. 6. To whom are blasphemies more proper than to the Roman beast, which belches forth nothing but words of blasphemy, blasphemous against God, blasphemous against the tabernacle of the Church, blasphemous against the heavenly saints. For they do not redound to the praise of the saints when they are adorned with praises that derogate from the Divine glory: for in the same, the very name of God is then blasphemed, inasmuch as the saints and the Roman Church itself, or the Pontiff who is held to be the representative Church, are slaughtered with Divine eulogies: such as, for example, are those when every power in heaven and on earth is said to be given to him, as if he were worshipped as God C. Satis dist. XCVI. It is sufficiently evident that the Pontiff was called God by Constantine, Felinus in C. Ego. XI. de jurejur. The Pope is our Lord God. Ludov. Gomesius in reg. Cancell. The Pope is a certain visible Deity, bearing a certain God before him. In the Lateran Council, the Fathers acclaimed the Pope, not without blasphemy: Thou art all, and above all, all power is given to thee in heaven and on earth. In the Council of Cologne, sess. IX, it was said of the same: The sight of thy Divine Majesty. Paulus Jovius in Phil. III. observes that the Orators sent to the Pontiffs, prostrate at his feet, saluted him as Christ himself, the Lamb of God, with this invocation repeated three times: Thou that takest away the sins of the world, have mercy upon us. Who does not acknowledge these to be blasphemous? How great a blasphemy it is that the whole Psalter, nay, the whole Bible, has been applied to Mary the Mother of God, is known at the crossroads. Panormitanus C. Quanto extra de translatione Prælati, from Hostiensis, brings forward these things: The Pope and Christ make one Consistory, so that, sin excepted, the Pope can do almost everything that God does. Alvarus Pelagius, *de planct. Eccles.*, lib. 1, art. 3. The Pope participates in both natures of Christ. Glossa in C. *Quinto* de transl. The Pope can make something out of nothing.

These things, therefore, cannot be snatched away to Pagan Rome. For that city, even though it permitted any religion whatsoever, nevertheless compelled no one to religion: nor does it cause any scruple that St. John marveled on account of this vision. For that deserves no common admiration, that a woman who boasts of the highest sanctity, who ought to have cherished the faithful in her bosom like a mother, pursues the same with hatred and persecutes them even unto blood. And from these and similar characters, Doctors, Pontiffs themselves, Bishops, Emperors, etc., have long since concluded that the Pontiff is the Anti-Christ; Gregory the Great, l. VI. Ep. 30. to Maurice Augustus, circa the year 858. Günther and Tetgaud, Bishops of Cologne and Trier, to Nicholas I, in Aventinus, l. 4. ann. p. 255. In the year 991, Arnulf, Bishop of Orléans, in the Synod of Reims, as also in Platina, f. 229. Rupert, Abbot of Deutz, in the year 1124, l. VIII. in Apoc. John of Salisbury, Bishop, in the year 1157. Eberhard, Archbishop of Salzburg, in Aventinus, book 7, year 420; in the year 1240, William of Saint-Amour; in the year 1240, William Aurifex; in the year 1253, Rupert Capito; in the year 1306, Peter John of Olivi; Emperor Frederick II to the estates of the Empire, and his Chancellor Peter de Vinea, book 1, epistle 31; Emperor Louis IV at Regensburg, year 1324; the Emperor with the estates of the Roman Empire, year 1338, etc.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

Καὶ προσσκύνησαν τῷ θηρίῳ, & adoraverunt bestiam) Multitudini Deorum Romanorum, quos passim nomi- natos reperire est in historiis, & apud Christianos, Ar- nobium, Lactantium, Augustinum. Horum præcipuos habet Ovidius fine Metamorphoseos: Di precor, Æneæ comites quibus ensis & ignis Cesserunt, diq; indigetes, Genitorq; Quirine Urbis, & invicti Genitor Gradive Quirini, Vestaq; Cæsareos inter sacrata Penates, Et cum Cæsarea tu Phœbe domestica Vesta. Quiq; tenes altas Tarpejas Jupiter arces.

Λέγοντες· τίς ὅμοιος τῷ θηρίῳ, τίς δύναται πολεμῆσαι μετ' ἀυτῦ; dicentes: Quis similis bestiæ, & quis poterit pu- gnare cum ea? Sunt ipsa prope verba Rabsacis, Regum II. ut Ebræi libros appellant, cap. XVIII. in fine.

Quum haud sufficere sensui S. Johannis idolola- triam Romanam probe intelligat Grotius, comi- tem addit crudelitatem, ut feris truculentis respon- deat idololatria. Quæ vero etsi maxime abomina- bilis, non tam in veteri superstitione, quam in Ro- mana Anti-Christiana viguerit; nihil tamen hic ad Rhombum facit, ubi bestia Prophetico Scripturæ more non de idololatria, sed de imperio, vel regno intelligenda venit. Nugæ canoræ de Capitolio ex- usto, & plaga mortis ejus per Vespasianum in urbis de- structione curata indignationem potius, quam re- futationem merentur. Convertit montem in Capi- tolium, incendium in mactationem ad mortem, ex- terminium in sanationem, hostem in amicum, cultus Divini (pagani) restitutionem in plagæ mortiferæ curationem, venerationem Diaboli in religionem: Quod quid aliud est, quam mutare quadrata ro- tundis? De Anti-Christo plerique omnes intelli- gunt Irenæus l. V. c. 28. Tertullianus de resurr. c. 25. Hippolytus, Ephrem Syrus, Prudentius, Gregorius M. &c. Vario etiam vultu idololatria Romani Papistici imperii se ostentat, vario habitu, varia po- testate, sive ornatum, sive modum colendi, sive nu- mina & σεβάσματα varia respicias, per statuarum & imaginum venerationem, per Angelolatriam, Hagiolatriam, Mariolatriam, artolatriam, stauro- latriam, sudarilatriam, (sancte Sudari ora pro nobis) Dæmoniolatriam, si appareat in forma Numinis. Et cur quæso intrudere hic Domitianum conatur, quod antea de idololatria accepit? Tam certa & constans est viri sententia! Bestia dicitur adorari, id non adeo convenit idololatriæ: nam etsi ido- lum adoretur, non tamen idololatria adorari dici solet. Et quis admittet, ut ad appendicem si- mul respondeam, ideo adorari idololatriam, quia homines adorantes idola in illis Diabolum colunt & adorant. Quo scripturæ loco docebitur, profes- sores idololatriæ, aut illi oppositi Evangelii idolola- triam, vel Evangelium dici? Quo item jure id, quod de idololatria dixerat, mox trahit ad Domitianum? An demum sub Domitiano, aut solum sub ilio sue- re illi bestiæ dentes leonini ad laniandum, pedes ursini ad atterendum? Ut taceam, quod Domitiani persecutio non 3½. annos durarit; sed si Baronio fi- des, quinquennium: Cœpisse enim anno Christi 93. docet, desiisse anno 98. qua longe profecto gravio- res aliæ fuere, sub Trajano, Diocletiano, Nerone, aliis. Tertull. apol. c. 5. Quæ de annis illis 1260. Maresius habet in dissert. ad Ap. XIII. adv. Grot. p. 126. ea nostra non facimus: quomodo scil. anno ab ascensione Christi 1260. Satan ex ore suo sub- mersurus mulierem, Bonifacium VIII. ejusque De- cretalia, in quibus omnes Prædecessores suos im- pudicitia & blasphemiis superavit, emiserit. Etsi enim eo die impleta non sit prophetia, non præte- rita sed futura spectans tempora, innuere potuit Spiritus sanctus tam diu duraturam tyrannidem An- ti-Christi, quamdiu durarat ipsummet imperium. Anni enim illi geminati 1520. efficiunt, qui jam pridem transierunt, durante adhuc Anti-Christo, utut illo anno talis a B. Luthero declaratus palam Romanus Pontifex fuerit, nec parum imperium ejus exinde imminutum sit. Denique nonnisi temere quæ de bestia in genere dicuntur, a Grotio ad unum Domitianum restringuntur; Blasphemiæ autem nomen ut quandoque alias generalius sumptum, quum non adversus nomen Dei, hoc est, ipsum Deum tantum directa, sed adversus tabernaculum etiam Dei Ecclesiam, & sanctos in cœlo vel Eccle- sia, sanctos & fideles contumelias in eos significat, quibus conjunctæ persecutiones, quia loquitur fera & blasphema & magna vel horrenda, cum os suum aperit, testibus bullis Papalibus, quas suas facit pro- mulgando, & exequendo ipsummet Imperium. Quando autem huic bestiæ tribuitur os loquens ma- gna & blasphema e simili Dan. 7, 8. tumida scilicet & superba non minus quam blasphema, illud certe (de ore loquor) non idololatria est, sed hominis ido- lum colentis. Lex vero illa XII. tabularum exulabat jam ante Capitolium restauratum.

Cæterum hæc omnia explicatius Romano Papi- stico imperio applicanda. Pedes habuit ursinos, quia tam potens fuit hæc bestia, ut sibi Orientem per Lu- cullum Pompejum, & Crassum, Macedoniam vero totamq; Græciam per Paulum Æmilium, Africabo- nam partem per Scipionem & Marium, Ægyptum per Octavianum Augustum subjugaverit. Decre- vit autem & imminui cœpit ejus potestas, cum a Gothis, Vandalis & aliis barbaris gentibus hinc inde vastaretur, decrevit, cum plaga lethali aliquoties vulneraretur, mox duobus Augustis existentibus & invicem contendentibus, Antonino videl. Philo- sopho, & Lucio Aurelio Vero, mox sub Gallo & Velu- siano, &c. Nec tantum incrementa & decrementa urgenda; Sed προσκείμενα meretricis Babylonicæ, nulli aptius quam Romæ Papali convenientia: Quæ 1. præter Christum sponsum alios Amasios admittit, thorumque suum valde prostituit. Pon- tificem enim Romanum Sponsum suum vocat in C. quoniam de immunit. in 6. Bellarm. præfat. de Pontif. Deum C. inter corporalia de translat. Prælat.

Bald. in l. ult. C. sentent. rescind. Decius in c. 1. de constit. Dominum Dominantium. Bald. in C. Ec- cles. ut lit. pend. Franciscum etiam Jesum typicum, sanctos alios, Mariam, reliquias, imagines &c. nuncupant. 2. Poculum fornicationis aureum est ob splendidam fidei doctrinæ & religionis Christianæ speciem, at plenam abominatione, ac immunditia, ob abominationem idololatrias mul- tivariæ, & immunditiam fornicationum & do- gmatum ac decretorum Papalium pro concubinis, incestibus, Sodomia & flagitiis aliis impurissimis. 3. De fastu & luxu ejus questus est S. Bernardus l. 15. de consider. ad Papam Eugenium: Histrioni- cus habitus, Regius apparatus, aurum in frenis, in sel- lis, & calcaribus, & plus calcaria quam altaria ful- gent, inde splendide mensæ & cibi & scyphi, inde co- messationes & ebrietates &c. inde referta marsupia, pro hujusmodi volunt esse & sunt Ecclesiarum Præ- positi, Decani, Archi-Decani, Episcopi, Archi-Episco- pi. Nec enim hæc cedunt illi negotio, quod perambu- lat in tenebris, ipse enim est Anti- Christus. 4. Ebria est de sanguine sanctorum, & martyrum Jesu. Non mirum: Numerantur enim ultra tricies & bis mil- lia millium octuagies quinquies centena millia 328500000. de voluntate Pontificis Romani cru- deliter trucidatorum. Audiendus etiam de eo Je- suita Franc. Ribera, qui in Ap. p. 328. Hoc in nullam urbem, inquit, æque convenit, ac in Romam, in qua innumerabiles Martyres occisi sunt. Quamvis non ebria tantum dicatur propter sanguinem in ea fu- sum, sed etiam propter sanguinem, qui ejus jussu & potestate in aliis urbibus effusus est, nam hunc etiam ipsa fudit. Nec de sanguine usq; ad Johannis tempora effuso tantum loquitur, verum & de eo, qui erat postea effundendus. Ebria dicitur, ut plu- rimum sanguinis fusum indicetur. Ebrietas enim copiam magnam solet significare. 5. Bestia sau- ciata rediisse de Imperio Romano per barbaro- rum incursiones, qui Romam ultra tria secula vul- nerarunt vastaruntque & occuparunt, ut nullus to- to isto tempore Imperator Occidentalis fuerit. Satana item ope medica Caroli M. & Leonis III. 6. Cui magis propriæ sunt blasphemiæ, quam Roma- næ bestiæ, quæ nihil nisi verba blasphemiæ eru- ctat, blasphema in Deum, blasphema in tabernacu- lum Ecclesiæ, blasphema in sanctos cœlites. Non enim laudi sanctorum cedunt, quando ornantur laudibus Divinæ gloriæ derogantibus: in iisdem enim tum blasphematur ipsummet nomen Dei, ut- pote cum mactantur elogiis Divinis Sancti & Ec- clesia ipsa Romana, vel Pontifex qui habetur Ec- clesia repræsentativa: qualia v.g. sunt,cum utDeus colitur omnis potestas in cœlo & in terra ipsi data dicitur C. Satis dist. XCVI. Satis constat Pontificem a Constantino Deum appellatum Felinus in C. Ego. XI. de jurejur. Papa Dominus Deus noster. Lu- dov. Gomesius in reg. Cancell. Papa est quoddam Numen visibile, quendam Deum præ se ferens. In Concilio Lateranensi Papæ acclamabant Patres non absque blasphemia: Tu es omnia, & supra omnia, omnis potestas tibi data in cœlo & in terra. In Con- cil. Colon. sess. IX. de eodem dicebatur: Majesta- tis tuæ Divinæ conspectus. Paulus Jovius in Phil. III. observat, Oratores ad Pontifices missos ad pedes illius stratos ipsum Christum Agnum Dei salutasse, cum hac invocatione trina vice repetita: Qui tollis peccata mundi miserere nostri. Quis non agnoscit hæc esse blasphema? Quanta blasphemia totum Psalterium, imo tota Biblia ad Mariam Deiparam applicata sint, in trivio notum est. Panormitanus C. Quanto extra de translatione Prælati ex Hosti- ensi hæc affert: Papa & Christus faciunt unum Consistorium, ita quod excepto peccato potest Papa quasi omnia facere, quæ facit Deus. Alvarus Pela- gius de planct. Eccles. l. 1. art. 3. Papa participat utramque naturam Christi. Glossa in C. Quinto de transl. Papa potest de nihilo aliquid facere.

Hæc itaque ad Romam Ethnicam abripi non possunt. Illa enim etsi religionem quamvis permi- sit; neminem tamen ad religionem coëgit: neque scrupulum movet,quod ob hanc visionem miratus sit S. Johannes. Id enim admirationem non vul- garem meretur, quod ea mulier, quæ sanctitatem summam jactat, quæ fideles in gremio suo matris instar fovere debebat,eosdem odio prosequitur,& ad sanguinem usque persequitur. Et ex his simi- libusque characteribus concluserunt jam pridem Doctores, Pontifices ipsi, Episcopi, Imperatores, &c. Pontificem esse Anti-Christum; Gregorius M. l. VI. Ep. 30. ad Maurit. August. circa ann. 858. Güntherus & Tetgaudus Colonienf. & Trevirenf. Episcopi ad Nicol. I. apud Aventin. l. 4. ann. p. 255. Ann. 991. Arnulphus Aurelian. Episc. in Synodo Remensi, ut & apud Platin. f. 229. Rupertus Abbas Tuit. Ann. 1124. l. VIII. in Apoc. Johannes Sarisbu- riens. Episc. Anno 1157. Eberhardus Archi-Episc. Salisburg. apud Avent. l. 7. ann. 420. anno 1240. Guilhelmus de S. Amore, anno 1240. Guilhelmus Aurifex Anno 1250. Rupertus Capito, Ann. 1253. Petrus Johannis Biranensis Ann. 1306. Fridericus II. Imperator ad status Imper. ejusque Cancellarius Petrus de Vineis l. 1. ep. 31. Ludovicus IV. Impera- tor Reginoburgi Ann. 1324. Imperator cum statibus Rom. Imp. Anno 1338. &c.

## 13:5
Verse 5.

(Καὶ ἐδόθη αὐτῷ στόμα λαλῶν μεγάλα) This mouth is Domitian himself, whence below in c. 17 he is called τὸ θηρίον as his principal part. It was the mouth of idolatry both by speaking and by grinding with the teeth. The words of this passage are taken from Dan. 7, 8. 11. where it treats of Antiochus.

Καὶ βλασφημίαν) Because he himself first wished to be called Lord and God, as Suetonius and Martial teach us. Before, that honor was not held except by the dead.
