The word βλασφημίας is accustomed to be used especially concerning new inventions of idolatry, 2 Macc. 8, 21. It corresponds to the Hebrew חרוף in Ps. 69, 10, likewise נאצה in Ezek. 35, 12. In the Manuscript καὶ βλάσφημα is not bad.

And authority was given to him to act for forty-two months) Thus also the Manuscript without the word πόλεμον; which follows shortly. Ποιῆσαι is an added note of time to persevere in an act, as in James 4:13, where we spoke about this locution, namely, to act against the Christians. For Domitian began the persecution against the Christians in the thirteenth year of his reign. He himself, however, was killed in the sixteenth year of his principate. Behold those very years, three and a half or 42 months, which are prefigured here. Thus Josephus elsewhere described the persecution of Antiochus as 42 months, elsewhere as three and a half years. Concerning this Domitianic persecution, see Augustine, De Civitate Dei XVIII. 52, and Orosius VII. 10.

Regarding those, Grotius had previously handed down these things:

Ver. 5.

And there was given to him a mouth speaking great things) The Romans, elated by the successes of their idolatry, despised others in comparison to their own gods. Hence, laws were so often made against foreign rites. Cicero, Book II of the Laws: Let no one have gods separately, neither new ones, nor foreign ones, unless publicly admitted; let them be worshipped privately. The words are from Dan. 7, verses 8, 11, 20, where it treats of Antiochus.

And blasphemies & blasphemy) Against the true GOD, the maker of the world. Cicero for L. Flaccus: 'Every city has its own religion, Laelius, and we have ours.' While Jerusalem stood and the Jews were at peace, yet the religion of those sacred rites was abhorrent to the splendor of this empire, the gravity of our name, and the institutions of our ancestors: but now all the more so, because that nation showed by arms what it felt about our empire: it taught how dear it was to the immortal gods by the fact that it was conquered, that it was sold, that it is in servitude. Suetonius on Augustus: 'He praised his grandson Gaius because, when passing by Judea, he had not offered prayers at Jerusalem.' Add the horrible words of the Prince Gaius against the true God in the embassy of Philo, and the lies of Tacitus and others.

And power was given to him to act for forty-two months.) The word πόλεμον, which some books have before ποιῆσαι, many and the best do not have. Nor is it necessary, since the word πολέμου follows immediately. Ποιῶν χρόνον τινὰ means to endure. XLII months are three years and a half. Therefore, by the wonderful providence of God, the cruelty against Christians under Domitian lasted for the same amount of time, from the moment it had begun to rage until his death, as the vexation of the Jews had lasted under Antiochus, predicted in Daniel 7:24, whose prophecy you will find excellently explained in Josephus, who puts for three years and a half, as here, XLII months, but elsewhere three years and six months. Concerning this cruelty of Domitian against the Christians, see Tertullian in his Apologetic, Eusebius in his Ecclesiastical History book III, ch. XIII, and in his Chronicle, Sulpicius Severus in book II, Augustine in The City of God book XVIII, ch. III, and Orosius in book VII. c. 10.

He finds that three-year period with the half-year barely, if at all, in history, and yet he needs a crab-like gait to attain it, whereas, contrary to John, it is not to cover the history of past things, but to bring the prophecy of future things into the light, placed on a sun-disk.

Latin:

Vers. 5.

Καὶ ἐδόθη αὐτῷ σόμα λαλῶν μεγάλα) Hoc os est ipse Do- mitianus, unde infra c. 17. dicitur τὸ θηρίον tanquam pars ejus præcipua. Os fuit is idololatriæ & loquendo & com- minuendo dentibus. Sumpta verba hujus loci e Dan.7, 8. 11. ubi de Antiocho.

Καὶ βλασφημίαν) Quia semet ipse primus Dominum ac Deum vocari voluit, ut Suetonius & Martialis nos do- cent. Ante is honor non habitus nisi mortuis. Solet vox βλασφημίας eximie usurpari de commentis idololatriæ no- vis, 2. Macc. 8, 21. Respondet Ebræo חרוף Psal. 69, 10. item נאצה Ezech. 35, 12. In Manuscripto καὶ βλάσφημα non male.

Καὶ ἐδόθη αὐτῷ ἐξουσία ποιῆσαι μῆνας τεσσαράκοντα δύο) Sic & Manuscriptus sine voce πόλεμον; quæ mox seque- tur. Ποιῆσαι addita temporis nota est in actu perseverare, ut Jac. 4, 19. ubi de hac loquutione diximus, ποιῆσαι nempe contra Christianos. Incepit enim Domitianus persecutio- nem adversus Christianos anno imperii sui decimo & tertio. Ipse autem interfectus est anno sui principatus sexto & decimo. Ecce ipsi anni, tres cum dimidio sive menses XLII. qui hic præfiguricantur. Sic Antiochi persecutionem Josephus alibi descripsit mensibus XLII. alibi tribus an- nis & dimidio. De hac Domitianea persecutione vi- de Augustinum de Civitate Dei XVIII. 52. Orosium VII. 10.

De illis prius hæc tradiderat Grotius:

Vers. 5.

Καὶ ἐδόθη αὐτῷ σόμα λαλῶν μεγάλα, & datum est ei os loquens magna) Romani idololatriæ successi- bus elati præ suis Diis alios spernebant. Inde toties leges factæ contra sacra peregrina. Cicero 11. de le- gibus: Separatim nemo habessit Deos, nebę novas, sed nec advenas, nisi publice adscitos, privatim colunto. Ver- ba sunt ex Dan. 7. vers. 8. 11. 20. ubi de Antiocho agitur.

Καὶ βλασφημίας & blasphemiam) Contra verum DEUM mundi opificem. Cicero pro L. Flacco: Sua cuique civitati religio, Læli, est, nostra nobis. Stantibus Hierosolymis pacatisq́; Judæis tamen istorum religio Sacrorum a splendore hujus imperii, gravitate nominis nostri, majorum institutis abhorrebat: nunc vero hoc magis, quod illa gens, quid de imperio nostro senti- ret, ostendit armis: quam chara Diis immortalibus esset, docuit, quod est victa, quod elocata, quod servit. Sue- tonius de Augusto: Cajum nepotem, quod Judæam præ- tervehens apud Hierosolymam non supplicasset, collauda- vit. Adde horrenda Caji Principis in verum Deum dicta in legatione Philonis, & mendacia Taciti, alio- rumque.

Καὶ ἐδόθη αὐτῷ ἐξουσία ποιῆσαι μῆνας τεσσαράκοντα δύο, & data est ei potestas facere menses quadraginta duos.) Vocem πόλεμον, quam ante ποιῆσαι habent libri nonnulli, multi & optimi non habent. Neque id opus, cum jam mox πολέμου vox sequatur. Ποιῶν χρόνον τινὰ est durare. Menses XLII. sunt anni tres cum dimidio. Mira ergo Dei providentia, tantundem temporis duravit sævitia in Christianos sub Domitia- no, ex quo scilicet sævire cœperat, ad mortem usque, quantum durarat Judæorum vexatio sub Antiocho, prædicta Danieli VII. 24. cujus vaticinium optime explicatum reperies apud Josephum, qui pro tribus annis & dimidio ponit, ut hic, menses XLII. alibi vero tres annos menses sex. De hac Domitiani in Christianos sævitia vide Tertullianum Apologetico, Eusebium historiarum III. c. XIII. & in Chronico Se- verum Sulpitium libro II. Augustinum de Civitate Dei libro XVIII. cap. III. Orosium libr. VII. c. 10.

Triennium illud cum Semestri vix ac ne vix invenit in historia, & opus tamen habet can- crino incessu ad illud assequendum, cum con- tra Johannem non historiam præteritorum tegere, sed prophetiam futurorum in apricum proferre, in solis disco positum sit.

## 13:6
Verse 6.

And he opened his mouth for blasphemy against God) Idolatry treated God contumeliously through Domitian, saying among other things when it thundered, 'Let him strike whom he wishes.' Manuscript: 'And he opened his name for blasphemies,' not badly, so that 'the Beast' is understood. A similar locution in Matthew 13, verse 36, and the Latin reads no differently here.

To blaspheme his name) Dan. 7:25. 'He shall speak words against the Most High' ch. 7:25.

And his tabernacle) מִשְׁכָּנוֹ, the Church. Thus God calls the ancient Jerusalemites אָהֳלִי בָהּ Ezekiel 23. For the saints are called the temple of God: But here rather a tabernacle because of uncertain seats, just as once in the desert.

And those who dwell in heaven) The individual Christians, whose 'citizenship is in heaven' Philippians 3:20. See what is above in chapter 4:34. Thus the Hebrews are called by Daniel גבה שמים ch. 8:10, as Aben-Ezra explains there. Idolaters called Christians atheists and the causes of all evils in the empire.

We append to these the former commentary:

Verse 6.

And he opened his mouth for blasphemy against God) and he opened his mouth in blasphemies against God. Suetonius on Domitian: 'With equal arrogance, when he dictated a letter in the name of his procurators, he began thus: Our Lord and God commands that this be done. Whence it was established thereafter that he should not be addressed otherwise, even in writing or speech. He permitted no statues of himself to be placed in the Capitol except those of gold and silver and of a certain weight.' Then: 'For eight continuous months so many lightning bolts were reported and announced that he exclaimed: Let him strike now whom he wishes.'

And his tabernacle) The Church is the mystical temple of God 1 Cor. 3:16, 17; ch. 6:19; 2 Cor. 6:16. Why therefore here rather a tent? So that it may be understood that the Church in those times was wandering and erratic, just as the tent of God had been before the temple was built. Thus God calls the Jerusalemites אהלי בה Ezekiel 23.

And those dwelling in heaven, &c. (those who dwell in heaven) He was most hostile to the universal Church as well as to its individual members. The expression is taken from Dan. 8:10, where the Hebrews are called צבא השמים. Philip. 3:20, 'Our citizenship exists in heaven,' our conversation is in the heavens. For where the treasure is, there is the heart, Matth. 6:21. Domitian was so cruel to the Christians that he did not spare even women, and indeed those most closely related to himself. See the writing of Erycius Puteanus concerning Flavia Domitilla, and Eusebius, History III. 14.

What do the times of Domitian, which had already passed, have to do with this? What of the erratic Church? Could those who were hiding in secret, in crypts and caverns, or wandering in the woods, become subject to blasphemy and persecution, and if so, how? Although this is not so much about persecution as it is about the slanders and accusations of the saints, from which, however, that arose: yet it is not under Domitian but under the Roman Anti-Christ, and the beast addicted to him.

Latin:

Vers. 6.

Καὶ ἤνοιξε τὸ ςόμα αὐτῦ βλασφημίαν πρὸς τὸν Θεὸν) Idololatria per Domitianum contumeliose Deum tracta- vit, dicens inter alia cum fulguraret, feriat quem volet. Manuscriptus: Καὶ ἤνοιξε τὸ ὄνομα ἀυτῦ εἰς βλασφημίας, non male ut subintelligatur τὸ Ἐνεῖον. Similis locutio Matth. 13. vers. 36. nec aliter hic legit Latinus.

Βλασφημῆσαι τὸ ὄνομα ἀυτῦ) Dan. 7, 25. Λόγους πρὸς τὸν ὕψιστον λαλήσει c. 7, 25.

Καὶ τὴν σκηνὴν ἀυτῦ) מִשְׁכָּנוֹ, Ecclesiam. Sic Hieroso- lymitas veteres Deus vocat אָהֳלִי בָהּ Ezech. XXIII. San- cti enim templum Dei dicuntur: Sed hic potius taberna- culum propter incertas sedes, sicut olim in deserto.

Καὶ τὲς ἐν τῷ ὀρανῷ σκηνῦντας) Singulos Christianos, quo- rum πολίτευμα ἐν ὀρανῷ Philipp. 3, 20. Vide quæ supra cap. 4, 34. Sic Ebræi a Daniele vocantur גבה שמים c. 8, 10. ut ibi exponit Aben-Esdra. Vocabant idololatræ Christianos ἀθέως & causas omnium in imperio malorum.

Subjicimus hisce commentarium priorem:

Vers. 6.

Καὶ ἤνοιξε τὸ ςόμα ἀυτῦ εἰς βλασφημίαν πρὸς τὸν Θεὸν) & aperuit os suum in blasphemias ad Deum. Sue- tonius de Domitiano: Pari arrogantia cum procurato- rum suorum nomine dictaret Epistolam, sic cœpit: Domi- nus & Deus noster sic fieri jubet. Unde institutum posthac, ut ne scripto quidem ac sermone cujusquam appellare- tur aliter. Statuas sibi non nisi aureas in Capitolio & ar- genteas poni permisit ac ponderis certi. Deinde: Con- tinuis octo mensibus tot fulgura facta nuntiataq́; sunt, ut exclamaverit: feriat jam quem volet.

Καὶ τὴν σκηνὴν ἀυτῦ, & tabernaculum ejus) Ecclesia templum Dei mysticum 1. Cor. 3, 16. 17. c. 6, 19. 2. Cor. 6, 16. Cur igitur hic potius tentorium? Ut intelli- gatur Ecclesia illis temporibus fuisse vaga & erratica, sicut fuerat tentorium Dei, antequam templum strueretur. Sic Deus Hierosolymitas vocat אהלי בה Ezech. 23.

Καὶ τὲς ἐν ὀρανῷ σκηνῦντας, &c. eos, qui in cælo habi- tant) Ut Ecclesiæ universæ ita & singulis ejus mem- bris fuit infestissimus. Locutio ex Dan. 8,10. desumpta, ubi Ebræi vocantur צבא השמים. Philip. 3, 20. Ἡμῶν δὲ τὸ πολίτευμα ἐν ὀρανῷ ὑπάρχει, nostra autem con- versatio in cælis est. Ubi enim thesaurus, ibi eor, Matth. 6, 21. Fuit autem adeo crudelis in Christianos Domi- tianus, ut nec fœminis, & sibi quidem conjun&iffimis parceret. Vide de Flavia Domitilla scriptum Erycii Puteani, & Eusebium historiæ III. 14.

Quid huc faciunt tempora Domitiani, quæ jam transierant? Quid Ecclesia erratica? Num & quo- modo illæ, quæ in abscondito, in cryptis & caver- nis latitabant, vel in sylvis oberrabant blasphemiæ & persequationi obnoxia fieri poterant? Quam- vis non tam de persecutione, quam de calumniis & criminationibus sanctorum, e quibus tamen illa oriebatur, hic agatur: at non sub Domitiano sed sub Anti-Christo Romano, eique addicta bestia.

## 13:7
Vers. 7.

And it was given to him to make war with the saints) 'It was given' signifies the permission of God, as above c. 6:2, 4, 8; c. 9:3, 5. 'To make war' here is to treat hostiley, although they were not resisting, as above c. 11:7; c. 12:17. Similar to Dan. 11:33.

And to overcome them) That is, to deliver to death or exile, as in the aforementioned place c. 11:7. These and the preceding words of this verse are absent in the Manuscript. And they are sufficiently comprehended in the words placed before.

And it was given to him authority over every tribe and tongue and nation) To him, namely, to the beast. Idolatry was propagated more widely by Domitian than before, with the Dacians, Chatti, and Sarmatians conquered. In the Manuscript, 'tribe and people and tongue and nation,' as the Latin also reads. Concerning this distribution of the human race, see above chapter 5:9; c. 11:9; and below c. 14:6.

This prior treatment presented it thus:

Vers. 7.

And it was given to him to make war with the saints, and it was given to him to make war with the Saints) 'It was given' signifies the permission of God. 'War' as also above c. 11:7. This is to be understood as the most savage slaughter, which is the only kind of war that can exist against those who had learned only to suffer, and not also to resist.

And to overcome them) By killing, by driving into exile, into prisons, with God giving them into the hands of the Tyrant.

And it was given to him authority over every tribe and people, and tongue, and nation) See what is below chapter 17:15. This means that by the example of the Emperor and the Roman people, almost all peoples were drawn to both practice idolatry more impudently and to use every kind of cruelty against the Christians.

Now follow the persecutions, and indeed bloody ones under the Roman empire; but when the Babylonian harlot sat upon it, that is, in the time of the Roman Anti-Christ, which the Prophet was later to explain more fully and clearly. But how can it be gathered from this phrase that the peoples were thus drawn to practice idolatry more impudently: They can be moved by the example of others, even if those who received the power are those who are incited by their example. And concerning Domitian the matter is doubtful, since his pride, tyranny, and wickedness made him hated everywhere rather than drawing others to imitation.

Latin:

Vers. 7.

Καὶ ἐδόθη ἀυτῷ ποιῆσαι πόλεμον μετὰ τῶν ἁγίων) ἐδόθη Dei permissum significat, ut supra c. 6,2.4.8. c. 9,3. 5. ποιῆσαι πόλεμον est hic hostiliter tractare, quamvis non resistentes, ut supra c. 11,7. c. 12,17. Simile Dan. 11,33.

Καὶ νικῆσαι ἀυτούς) Id est, morti aut exilio tradere, ut di- cto loco c. 11,7. Absunt in Manuscripto hac & hujus com- matis præcedentia. Et satis comprehenduntur in verbis ante positis.

Καὶ ἐδόθη ἀυτῷ ἐξουσία ἐπὶ πᾶσαν φυλὴν καὶ γλῶσσαν καὶ ἔθνος) Ἀυτῷ nempe τῷ θηρίῳ. Idololatria per Domitia- num latius quam ante propagata est, victis Dacis, Cattis, Sarmatis. In Manuscripto, φυλὴν καὶ λαὸν καὶ γλῶσσαν καὶ ἔθνος, quomodo legit & Latinus. De hac distributione humani generis vide supra cap. 5,9. c. 11,9. & infra c. 14,6.

Hæc prior tractatio sic exhibuit:

Vers. 7.

Καὶ ἐδόθη ἀυτῷ ποιῆσαι πόλεμον μετὰ τῶν ἁγίων, & datum est illi bellum facere cum Sanctis) Ἐδόθη datum est, Dei permissionem significat. Πόλεμος bellum ut & supra c. 11, 7. Intelligenda sævissima laniena, quod so- lum belli genus esse potest adversus eos, qui pati tan- tum, non & resistere didicerant.

Καὶ νικῆσαι ἀυτὸς, & vincere eos) Interficiendo, in exilium, in carceres agendo, Deo ipsos in Tyranni ma- nus dante.

Καὶ ἐδόθη ἀυτῷ ἐξουσία ἐπὶ πᾶσαν φυλὴν καὶ γλῶσσαν, καὶ ἔθνος, & data est illi potestas in omnem tribum & po- pulum, & linguam, & gentem) Vide quæ infra cap. 17, 15. Hoc vult exemplo Imperatoris populiqne Romani tra- ctos fuisse populos ferme omnes, ut & idololatriam im- pudentius exercerent, & omni sævitia genere in Chri- stianos uterentur.

Jam sequuntur persecutiones, eaq́; cruentæ sub imperio Romano; sed cum insidebat ei meretrix Babylonica, hoc est, tempore Romani Anti-Christi, quas postmodum specRoundelius & disertius expositu- rus erat Propheta. Quomodo vero ex hac phrasi colligetur ita tractos populos ad idololatriam im- pudentius exercendam: Moveri possunt exmplo aliorum, etsi illi quæ acceperint potestatem in eos, qui excitantur ipsorum exemplo. Et de Domitia- no res dubia est, quum superbia, tyrannis & impro- bitas ejus passim invisum ipsum magis reddiderint, quam alios ad imitationem traxerint.

## 13:8
Verse 8.

Καὶ προσκυνήσουσιν ἀυτῷ πάντες οἱ κατοικοῦντες ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς) that is, ἵνα προσκυνήσωσιν, that all who are in the Roman empire may serve idolatry, because here γῆ [earth] is as above in chapter 12, 12. just as ὀικυμένη [inhabited world] in Luke 2, 1.

Ων ὐ γέγραπταιτὸ ὄνομα ἐν βίβλῳ τῆς ζωῆς τῷ ἀρνίω τᾶ ἐσφαγμένε ἀπὸ καταβολῆς κόσμε) Supply γεγραμμένῳ [written]. For these last words are to be referred to the book, not to the Lamb, as Arethas and others rightly saw from the passage which is below in chapter 17, 8. You have similar transpositions of words in 2 Corinthians 2, verse 7, chapter 12, verse 2, and elsewhere. Just as in Athens and in other cities there were books, in which the names of citizens and of those born, and of those advanced to man's estate, were written, and the dishonored were erased. For this book is conceived in such a way that whoever is righteous, at whatever time he is inscribed in it, and whoever ceases to be so is taken away. In the Constitutions of Clement: As the Lord himself somewhere instructing us shows, saying, Do not rejoice that the spirits obey you, but rejoice that your names are written in heaven; since the former happens by his power, the latter by our intention and zeal, it is clear that we are helped by him. The same Clement to the Corinthians: Let us therefore strive to be found in the number of those who wait for him, so that we may receive the promised gifts; but how will this be, beloved? If our service is established through faith toward God, if we seek out the things that are pleasing and acceptable to him, if we perform the things that belong to his blameless will, and follow the way of truth, casting off from ourselves injustice and lawlessness, greed, strife, malice and deceit, whisperings and backbitings, hatred of God, pride and arrogance, vainglory and love of money. Chrysostom in the second [homily] against the Jews, explaining that passage of Daniel 12:1, 'he who is found written in the book,' says, that is, those who are worthy of salvation. See what is said on Luke 10:20 and here above 3:5. From the beginning of the world it is so stated, as 'from the blood of Abel the righteous,' Matt. 23:35. But that life, from which that book has its name, is rightly called the life of the slain Lamb, because the slain Lamb was the first of all to attain to that life. See above 1:5, 8; 2:8; 5:9.

Concerning them he had previously handed down these things:

v. 8. 'And all who dwell on the earth will worship him.' They will imitate that custom, not only those who will be part of the Roman empire, but wherever the name and fame of that empire will reach. 'Whose name is not written in the book of life of the Lamb who was slain from the foundation of the world,' whose names are not written in the book of the life of the Lamb who was slain from the origin of the world. It seems that Christ is here called the Lamb slaughtered before the foundations of the world were laid, by divine decree, of course, in which sense the same Christ is called 'foreknown before the foundation of the world,' 1 Pet. 1:20. But if anyone has well compared the place similar to this book in 17:8, he will find that there is a transposition of words here, and that the book itself is said to be written 'from the foundation of the world,' with the likeness taken from well-ordered cities, where from the beginning of the city's founding there exist perpetual monuments which contain the names of the citizens. Deservedly, however, this book received its name from him who was destined from eternity to be the head of all the Saints, among whom the martyrs are preeminent. See Heb. 11:40. Examples of those who have suffered in every age commend patience to us, Matt. 5:12, 23:35. But they are much mistaken who, from this figurative expression, invent for us divine decrees about saving men without any condition, without regard for any act or quality. The ancient writer of the books which are commonly called the Constitutions of Clement: 'As the Lord himself somewhere instructing us shows, saying, Do not rejoice that the spirits obey you, but rejoice that your names are written in heaven; since the former happens by his power, the latter by our intention and zeal, it is clear that we are helped by him.' As the Lord himself somewhere instructing us shows, saying: Do not rejoice that the spirits obey you, but rejoice that your names are written in heaven: because the former is done by his power, but the latter by our good will and zeal, being helped, that is, by him. Chrysostom in the second [homily] against the Hebrews, interpreting that passage of Daniel 12:1: 'He who is found written in the book,' says thus: 'that is, those who are worthy of salvation.' Josephus Jachiades on the same passage of Daniel: 'Everyone who is found written in the book of life for his righteousness.' To pay the highest honors to the empire, if that is what it means to worship here, is not to imitate the ways of an idol. If, however, the beast that obeys the Anti-Christ and submits itself to him is marked, it must be understood universally of all, not only of some. For the universal particle 'all,' and the designation of the inhabitants on the earth made without restriction, and the contrast of those whose names are written in the book of life of the Lamb [confirm this]. For these exhaust the whole world: the worshippers of the beast, which is the Papal one, whose names are not written, and those whose names are written in this book. Therefore, worship is not indifferent to others for salvation, as the Calixtines suppose: for those who worship the beast, insofar as it obeys the Anti-Christ and is ruled by him, are not found in the book of life. But nothing is written in that book of life for one's own righteousness, but all who are written are written in it for the righteousness and obedience of one, since we are not inscribed in it except by the blood of the Lamb, whom those who reject through unbelief have no place in the book of life. For 'he who does not believe will be condemned,' Mark 16:16; indeed, 'he is already judged, because he does not believe in the name of the only-begotten Son of God,' John 3:18. But others rightly explain it without transposition, whether 'from' is before, or 'from the foundations of the world'; because the inscription was made before those things from eternity, Eph. 1:4, 2 Tim. 1:9. But the inscription was made by the blood of the Lamb, that is, by the power of his merit, by reason of eternal foresight; therefore the mention of the slain Lamb was added, cf. Luke 10:20, Matt. 25:34, John 8:56, 1 Cor. 10:3, Heb. 13:8, Rev. 17:8, Eph. 3:9. The inscription was therefore not made without regard for the righteousness of Christ, even if it was not at all supported by the foresight of our righteousness or our merits. Rom. 9:11. The trifles of the Rabbis prove nothing, nor do the Clementines, as they are spurious. Chrysostom is to be understood concerning the worthiness by which Christ renders us worthy. But the book of life is not called the Lamb's only because he was the first to attain to that life; but because he was written in the highest and first place (in order of nature and dignity), 1. Pet. I. 19. And because on account of him and his merit the others are inscribed, who without him will be able to be inscribed by no one, and because that book is his, written by him no less than by the Father and the Holy Spirit—for these three are one; and no less to him, as regards his divine nature, and add also as regards his human nature, to which, through the grace of hypostatic union, if I may so say, it is appropriated, or so granted, that it is considered his own, so that the Book or catalogue of divine election and predestination is not to be sought from elsewhere. For he has it in his hand, just as he has consigned the elect themselves in his hand, Is. XLIX, 16, and possesses them providentially, Joh. X, 28. Dan. XII. 1. Phil. IV, 3.

Latin:

Vers. 8.

Καὶ προσκυνήσουσιν ἀυτῷ πάντες οἱ κατοικοῦντες ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς) id est, ἵνα προσκυνήσωσιν, ut serviant idololatriz omnes, qui in Romano sunt imperio, quod hic γῆ ut supra c. 12,12. sicut ὀικυμένη Luc. 2, 1.

Ων ὐ γέγραπταιτὸ ὄνομα ἐν βίβλῳ τῆς ζωῆς τῷ ἀρνίω τᾶ ἐσφαγμένε ἀπὸ καταβολῆς κόσμε) Supple γεγραμμέ- νῳ. Nam hæc postrema referenda ad librum non ad Agnum recte vidit Arethias, & alii ex loco, qui infra cap. 17, 8. Similes trajectiones vocum habes 2. Corinth. 2. vers. 7. cap. 12. vers. 2. & alibi. Sicut Athenis & in aliis ci- vitatibus erant libri, in quibus civium & natorum, & ad ætatem virilem provectorum, scribebantur nomina, & e- radebantur οἱ ἄτιμοι. Concipitur enim hic liber ad eum mo- dum, ut qui justus est, quoquo tempore ei inscribatur, qui esse desinit auferatur. In Constitutionibus Clementis. Κα- θὼς αὐτὸς πω παιδεύων ἡμᾶς ὁ Κύριος δείκνυσι, λέγων, μὴ χαίρετε, ὅτι τὰ πνεύματα ὑμῖν ὑπακούουσι, ἀλλὰ χαίρετε, ὅτι τὰ ὀνόματα ὑμῶν γέγραπται ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ· ἐπειδὰν τὸ μὲν αὐτῷ δυνάμει γίνεται, τὸ δὲ ἡμετέρᾳ ἐννοίᾳ καὶ σπουδῇ, δῆ- λον ὅτι βοηθουμένοις ὑπ’ αὐτῷ. Idem Clemens ad Corinthi- os: Ἡμεῖς οὖν ἀγωνισώμεθα εὑρεθῆναι ἐν τῷ ἀριθμῷ τῶν ὑπομε- νόντων αὐτὸν, ὅπως ἀπολάβωμεν τῶν ἐπαγγελμένων δωρεῶν· πῶς δὲ ἔσται τοῦτο ἀγαπητοί; ἐὰν ἐστηριγμένη ἡ διακονία ἡ- μῶν διὰ πίστεως πρὸς τὸν Θεὸν, ἐὰν ἐκζητῶμεν, τὰ εὐάρεστα καὶ εὐπρόσδεκτα αὐτῷ, ἐὰν ἐπιτελέσωμεν τὰ ἀνήκοντα τῇ ἀμώμῳ βουλήσει αὐτοῦ, καὶ ἀκολουθήσωμεν τῇ ὁδῷ τῆς ἀληθεί- ας, ἀποῤῥίψαντες ἀφ’ ἑαυτῶν ἀδικίαν καὶ ἀνομίαν, πλεονε- ξίαν, ἔρεις, κακοηθείας τε καὶ δόλους, ψιθυρισμούς τε καὶ κα- ταλαλιὰς, θεοστυγίαν ὑπερηφανίαν τε καὶ ἀλαζονείαν, κενο- δοξίαν καὶ φιλαργυρίαν. Chrysostomus in secundo adversus Judæos explicans illud Danielis XII. 1. ὁ εὑρεθεὶς γεγραμ- μένος ἐν τῷ βιβλίῳ, ait, τουτέστιν οἱ σωτηρίας ὄντες ἄξιοι. Vide quæ dicta ad Lucam X. vers. 20. & hic supra III. 5. A principio mundi ita dictum, ut ἀπὸ τοῦ αἵματος τοῦ Ἀβὲλ τοῦ δικαίου, Matth. XXIII. 35. Vita autem illa, unde liber ille nomen habet, recte dicitur vita agni occisi, quia Agnus occisus primus omnium ad eam vitam pervenit. Vide supra I. 5. 8. II. 8. V. 9.

De illis prius hæc tradiderat:

v. 8. Καὶ προσκυνήσουσιν αὐτῷ πάντες οἱ κατοικοῦντες ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς, & adorabunt eum omnes, qui inhabitant ter- ram]. Morem illum imitabuntur, non tantum qui pars erunt Romani imperii, sed quocunque nomen & fama ejus imperii perveniet. Ὧν οὐ γέγραπται τὸ ὄνομα ἐν τῷ βιβλίῳ τῆς ζωῆς τοῦ ἀρ- νίου τοῦ ἐσφαγμένου ἀπὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου, quorum non sunt scripta nomina in libro vitæ Agni, qui occisus est ab origine mundi.] Videtur hic Christus dici Agnus mactatus ante jacta mundi fundamenta, decreto scilicet divino, quo sensu idem Christus dicitur προεγνωσμένος πρὸ καταβο- λῆς κόσμου, præcognitus ante mundi constitutionem, 1. Petr. I. 20. Sed si quis bene contulerit locum hujus libri simi- lem XVII. 8. inveniet trajectionem hic esse vocum, & i- psum librum dici ἀπὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου ab origine mundi conscriptum scilicet, similitudine sumpta à bene mora- tis civitatibus, ubi ab initio conditæ urbis exstant per- petua monumenta, quæ civium nomina continent. Me- rito autem hic liber ab eo nomen accepit, qui ab æterno erat destinatus, ut omnium Sanctorum, inter quos emi- nent martyres, caput esset. Vide Ebr. XI. 40. Com- mendant nobis patientiam exempla ab omni ævo passo- rum similia, Matth. V. 12. XXIII. 35. Multum autem falluntur, qui ex hac figurata locutione decreta nobis di- vina fingunt de hominibus sine ulla conditione, fine ul lius actus aut qualitatis intuitu servandis. Scriptor ve- tus librorum, qui vulgo constitutiones Clementis dicun- tur: Καθὼς αὐτὸς που παιδεύων ἡμᾶς ὁ Κύριος δείκνυσι, λέ- γων μὴ χαίρετε, ὅτι τὰ πνεύματα ὑμῖν ὑπακούουσι, ἀλλὰ χαίρετε, ὅτι τὰ ὀνόματα ὑμῶν γέγραπται ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ ἐ- πειδὰν τὸ μὲν αὐτῷ δυνάμει γίνεται, τὸ δὲ ἡμετέρᾳ ἐννοίᾳ καὶ σπουδῇ, δῆλον ὅτι βοηθουμένοις ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ. Sicut ipse nos alicubi instituens Dominus ostendit, dicens: Ne gaudete, quod Spiritus vobis obediunt, sed gaudete, quod nomina ve- stra scripta sunt in cælo: quia illud ipsius virtute fit, hoc vero nostra bona voluntate ac studio, ab ipso scilicet adjun tis. Chrysostomus in secundo adversus Ebræos illud Da- nielis XII. 1. interpretans: Ὁ εὑρεθεὶς γεγραμμένος ἐν τῷ βιβλίῳ, qui inventus fuerit scriptus in libro sic ait: τε- τέστιν οἱ σωτηρίας ὄντες ἄξιοι, id est, qui salute digni sunt. Josephus Jachiades ad eundem Danielis locum כל הנמצא כתוב בספר החיים לצדקתו Omnis qui invenitur scriptus in libro vitæ pro justitia sua. Summos imperio honores deferre, si id hic est ad- orare, non est idoli mores imitari. Si tamen bestia quæ Anti-Christo paret, seque submittit, notatur, in universum de omnibus est intelligendum, non de quibusdam tantum. Nam id particula univer- salis πάντες, & designatio inhabitatorum in terra sine restrictione facta, & ἀντίθεσις eorum, quo- rum nomina in libro vitæ Agni scripta. Hi enim exhauriunt totum orbem, adoratores bestiæ, quæ Papalis, quorum nomina non scripta sunt, & illi quorum in hoc libro scripta sunt nomina. Non ergo adoratio aliis ad salutem indifferens est, ut Ca- lixtini autumant: nam in libro vitæ non inveniun- tur, qui bestiam adorant, quatenus AntiChristo paret & ab eodem regitur. Non autem pro justitia sua quicquam in illo vitæ libro scribitur, sed o- mnes qui scribuntur pro justitia & obedientia uni- us scribuntur in eodem, siquidem nonnisi Agni sanguine eidem inscribamur, quem qui per ἀπι- στίαν reprobant, in libro vitæ locum non habent. Qui enim non crediderit, condemnabitur, Marc. XVI. 16. imo jam judicatus est, quod non credat in nomen Filii Dei unigeniti, Joh. III. 18. Recte autem alii citra trajectionem explicant, sive ἀπὸ sit ante, sive á jactis mundi fundamentis; quia ante illa inscriptio facta ab æterno Ephes. I. 4. 2. Tim. I. 9. Sanguine autem Agni, id est, vi meriti ejus, facta inscriptio ratione æterni intuitus, ideo addi- ta Agni occisi mentio, conf. Luc. X, 20. Matth. XXV, 34. Joh. VIII, 56. 1. Cor. X, 3. Ebr. XIII, 8. Apoc. XVII, 8. Ephes. III. 9. Non ergo fine in- tuitu justitiæ Christi facta inscriptio, etsi nostræ justitiæ aut meritorum nostrorum prævisione mi- nime fulta. Rom. IX, 11. Rabbinorum nugæ nil probant, nec Clementina, utpote notha. Chry- sostomus de ἀξιότητι intelligendus est, qua nos di- gnos reddit Christus. Non autem Agni liber vitæ tantum dicitur, quod is primum ad eà vitam per- venerit; sed quod is summo & primo (ordine na- turæ & dignitatis) loco scriptus sit, 1. Pet. I. 19. quodque ob ipsum & meritum ejus inscripti cæte- ri, qui sine ipso inscribi nulli poterunt, & quod liber ille ejus sit ab ipso non minus quam Patre & Spiritu S. hi enim tres unum sunt, scriptus; nec minus ipsi, quod ad divinam naturam proprius, adde & quoad humanam, cui per communicatio- nis hypostaticæ gratiam, ut ita dicam, appropria- tus, vel ita concessus, ut proprius censeatur, non aliunde petendus sit Liber vel catalogus electio- nis & prædestinationis divinæ. Habet enim eum in manu sua, ut electos ipsos, quos in manu sua consignavit, Es. XLIX, 16. provideque possi- det, Joh. X, 28. Dan. XII. 1. Phil. IV, 3.

## 13:9
Verse 9.

If anyone has ears, let him hear] Concerning this formula for exciting an audience, see above II. 7. 11. 17. 29.

If anyone gathers captivity] In the manuscript it is, if anyone into captivity, into captivity goes, which I do not disapprove of, so that in the former member one may understand 'leads' from the following 'goes'. The sense is: Bear this patiently, Christians, vengeance will not be lacking. Rome, which leads you captive, will be captured by the Vandals and Goths more than once. The punishments of states are later than those of individual men. For the life of states is also longer.

Latin:

Vers. 9.

Ἔι τις ἔχει ὖς ἀκουσάτω] De hac formula audientiam exci- tantis vide supra II. 7. 11. 17. 29.

Ἔι τις αἰχμαλωσίαν συνάγει] In Manuscripto est, εἴτις εἰς αἰχμαλωσίαν, εἰς αἰχμαλωσίαν ὑπάγει, quod non impro- bo, ut in priore membro subaudiatur ἄγει ex sequente ὑπά- γει. Sensus est: Patienter hoc ferte Christiani, non deerit ultio. Roma quæ vos captivos agit, capietur à Wandalis & Gothis non semel. Pœnæ civitatum seriores sunt, quam hominum singulorum. Nam & vita civitatum est longior.

## 13:9
Verse 9.

If anyone has ears, let him hear] A solemn preface to a great matter that must be diligently observed, Matth. 11, v. 15. 13, 9. and 43. Mark 4, 9. 27. 7, 16. 8, 18. Luke 8, 8. 14, 35. above 11, v. 7. 11. 17. 29.

Latin:

Vers. 9.

Ἔι τις ἔχει ὖς ἀκουσάτω, si quis habet aures audiat] Sole- mnis præfatio magnæ diligenterque observandæ rei, Matth. 11, v. 15. 13, 9. & 43. Marci 4, 9. 27. 7, 16. 8, 18. Luc. 8, 8. 14, 35. supra 11, v. 7. 11. 17. 29.

## 13:10
If anyone shall kill with the sword] Through injury, as Domitian did the Christians.

He must be killed with the sword] He himself will perish by the sword, as Domitian did by the sword of his household, and that after God had given many pre-significations of that event. See our annotations to book I of 'On the Law of War and Peace' IV. 5. Suetonius and Dio on Domitian, and Philostratus on Apollonius VIII. 11. It was the law of Rhadamanthus:

If one should suffer what he did, justice would be straight.

The treatment of this special passage was of almost the same tenor.

Latin:

Ἔι τις ἐν μαχαίρᾳ ἀποκτενεῖ] Per injuriam, ut Christianos Domitianus.

Δεῖ ἀυτὸν ἐν μαχαίρᾳ ἀποκτανθῆναι] Is ipse gladio peribit, ut Domitianus domesticorum gladio, idque postquam mul- tas ejus rei Deus dederat præsignificationes. Vide annotata nostra ad librum I. de jure belli & pacis IV. 5. Suetonium ac Dionem Domitiano & Philostratum de Apollonio VIII.11. Jus erat Radamantii:

Εἴκε πάθοι τὰ κ᾽ ἔρεξε, δίκη ἰθεῖα γένοιτο.

Ejusdem fere tenoris erat specialis loci hujus tractatio.

## 13:10
Verse 10.

If anyone gathers captivity, into captivity he goes: he who shall have led into captivity, into captivity he shall go.] Rome, which had made Christians captive, itself became captive to the Goths and Vandals.

Ἔι τις ἐν μαχαίρᾳ ἀποκτενεῖ, δεῖ ἀυτὸν ἐν μαχαίρᾳ ἀπο- κτανθῆναι, he who kills with the sword must be killed with the sword] Domitian, who had killed so many Christians with the sword, was himself also killed by the sword, and indeed by his own household. he was killed, by this divine decree, pre-signified by many and those most clear indications. See Suetonius, Dio, and Philostratus, book VIII, ch. 10. That this does not refer only to the captivity of the Goths and the sword of Domitian, and how the τὸ ἀντιπεπονθὸς (retaliation) is to be rendered to Rome, the Angel will teach more expressly hereafter, namely, with interest, not a simple, but a double ἀποδόσει (repayment), Apoc. XIII. 6. ἀπόδοτε αὐτῇ, ὡς καὶ αὐτὴ ἀπέδωκεν ὑμῖν, καὶ διπλώσατε αὐτῇ διπλᾶ κατὰ τὰ ἔργα ἀυτῆς (repay her, even as she repaid you, and double unto her double according to her works). But the beast referred to here is not the marine one but the terrestrial one, which greatly stimulates that one to the oppression of the faithful, and therefore it deserves, by the power of divine justice, a double punishment for both itself and the seduction of the other beast, which is to be paid more certainly than certain. Ὧδέ ἐστιν ἡ ὑπομονὴ, καὶ ἡ πίστις τῶν ἁγίων (Here is the patience and the faith of the saints)] ὧδε (here), that is, in this matter: just as we say, unde discerem (from where I might learn), for, de quo discerem (from whom I might learn). A similar locution is below, ch. IV, verse 12, XVII, v. 9. But this ὧδε (here) is referred to the preceding, ἡ ὑπομονὴ καὶ ἡ πίστις (the patience and the faith), that is, ὑπομονὴ διὰ τῆς πίσεως (patience through faith): because we believe that God will be the avenger, therefore we easily tolerate adversities. Ἅγιοι (saints) here are Christians, as above V, v. 8, VIII, v. 3, 4, here above 7. A similar exhortation is in Dan. XII. 11. So also the former treatise has it. Ὧδέ ἐστιν ἡ ὑπομονὴ καὶ ἡ πίστις τῶν ἁγίων, bis est patientia & fides sanctorum (Here is the patience and the faith of the saints, twice is the patience and faith of the saints)] Tertullian in his book on patience: It is that very thing which both follows and precedes faith. Then concerning Abraham: Deservedly therefore blessed, because also faithful; deservedly faithful, because also patient; thus faith illuminated by patience, and what follows. The sense is, that the patience and faith of Christians are confirmed, because they know that God will be the avenger of his own injuries. That same Tertullian in the same book: If you have deposited an injury with him, he is the avenger. How much is allowed to patience, that it may have God as a debtor? Patience, or perseverance and faith, is needed, so that we do not deny the truth, whether led by fear or by the flatteries of the Anti-Christ, and precipitate ourselves into eternal destruction, 2. Petr. II. Ap. XIV.

PART II. OF CHAPTER XIII. CONCERNING THE TERRESTRIAL BEAST.

Latin:

Vers. 10.

Ἕι τις αἰχμαλωσίαν συνάγει, εἰς αἰχμαλωσίαν ὑπάγει qui in captivitatem duxerit: in captivitatem vadet.] Roma quæ Christianos captivos fecerat, ipsa facta est captiva Gotho- rum & Wandalorum.

Ἔι τις ἐν μαχαίρᾳ ἀποκτενεῖ, δεῖ ἀυτὸν ἐν μαχαίρᾳ ἀπο- κτανθῆναι, qui in gladio occiderit, oportet eum gladio occidi] Domitianus qui tot Christianos gladio interfecerat, ipse quoque gladio, & quidem domesticorum suorum interfectus est, divino hoc decreto, multis iisque clarissimis indiciis præsignificato. Vide Suetonium, Dionem & Phi- lostratum lib. VIII. c. 10. Non ad solam captivitatem Gothorum & gla- dium Domitiani hic respici, & quomodo τὸ ἀντι- πεπονθὸς Romæ reddendum sit, expressius dein- ceps docebit Angelus, nimirum, cum fænore, non fimplici, sed duplici ἀποδόσει, Apoc. XIII. 6. ἀπόδοτε αὐτῇ, ὡς καὶ αὐτὴ ἀπέδωκεν ὑμῖν, καὶ δι- πλώσατε αὐτῇ διπλᾶ κατὰ τὰ ἔργα ἀυτῆς. Respi- citur autem hic bestia non marina sed terrena,quæ illam maximé extimulat ad oppresfionem fideli- um, ideoque duplex & sui & seductionis alterius bestiæ causa promeretur vi divinæ justitiæ suppli- cium, certo certius exsolvendum. Ὧδέ ἐστιν ἡ ὑπομονὴ, καὶ ἡ πίστις τῶν ἁγίων] ὧδε, id est in hac re: sicut dicimus, unde discerem, pro, de quo disce- rem. Similis loquutio infra IV. vers. 12. XVII. v. 9. Re- fertur autem hoc ὧδε ad præcedentia, ἡ ὑπομονὴ καὶ ἡ πίστις, id est, ὑπομονὴ διὰ τῆς πίσεως: quia credimus Deum ultorem fore, ideo facile toleramus adversa. Ἅγιοι hic sunt Christi- ani, ut supra V. v. 8. VIII. v. 3. 4. hic supra 7. Similis ex- hortatio Dan. XII. 11. Sic etiam prior habet tractatus. Ὧδέ ἐστιν ἡ ὑπομονὴ καὶ ἡ πίστις τῶν ἁγίων, bis est patien- tia & fides sanctorum] Tertullianus libro de patientia: Ipsa adeo est, quæ fidem & subsequitur & antecedit. Dein- de de Abrahamo: Merito ergo benedictus, quia & fide- lis; merito fidelis, quia & patiens; ita fides patientia illu- minata, & quæ sequuntur. Sensus est, confirmari Chri- stianorum patientiam & fidem, quod nôrint Deum inju- riarum suarum fore vindicem. Idem ille eodem libroTer- tullianus:Si injuriam apud eum deposueris,ultor est. Quan- tum patientiæ licet, ut Deum babeat debitorem? Patientia, vel perseverantia & fide opus est, ut ne veritatem abnegemus, sive metu sive blandi- tiis Anti-Christi adducti, nosque in æternum exi- tium præcipitemus, 2. Petr. II. Ap. XIV.

PARS II. CAPITIS XIII. DE BESTIA TERRENA.

## 13:11
Vers. 11.

Καὶ εἶδον ἄλλο θηρίον (And I saw another beast)] What is predicted here is later than what has already been said. What the form of this θηρίου (beast) was is not said. I believe it was the form of a viper, because among those born from the earth, it claims this name for itself by an exceptional right. See Acts XXVIII, v. 4, 5. And Erictho, working with magic rites, is thus described in Lucan: And she vomits, the horrid one is girded with viperous wreaths. Ἀναβαῖνον ἐκ τῆς γῆς (Coming up out of the earth)] This beast is magic, which at that time, of which it is treated here, being openly practiced by the Pythagoreans, raised up the falling idolatry, especially through Apollonius of Tyana, whom the men of that time dared to oppose to Christ, as appears from the book of Hierocles, to which Eusebius responded. But magic is rightly said to ascend from the earth, because the magi spoke from the earth, that is, from caves, Is. XXIX, verse 4, XLV, verse 32, XLVIII, verse 18, and raised up shadows from the earth, 1. Sam. XXVIII, 13. Seneca in Oedipus: Suddenly the earth gapes, and loosened with an immense gulf it lay open: I myself saw the pale gods among the shades. These are those ἄδυλα ἄβατα καὶ φοβερά (inaccessible, untrodden, and fearful things), about which Nazianzen speaks in his second oration against Julian. Καὶ εἶχε κέρατα δύο ὅμοια ἀρνίῳ (And it had two horns like a lamb)] The magi had two semblances of virtues, similar to Christian virtues, temperance in food, and abstinence from Venus. Clement of Alexandria, Strom. III. ἀμέλει διὰ φροντίδος ἐστὶ κἀγ τοῖς μάγοις ὅ,τε τε ὀψὲ καὶ ἐμψύχων καὶ ἀφροδισίων ἀπέχεσθαι (Indeed, it is a matter of concern even among the magi to abstain from both meat and living things and sexual pleasures). Theodoret has the same in his third sermon. Philostratus I. 10 reports this specifically about Apollonius of Tyana. The horns of the lamb are Christian virtues. Ἀρνίῳ (lamb) here for τῷ ἀρνίῳ (the lamb) just as that δεάκων (dragon) for ὁ δεάκων (the dragon). Such omission of articles is frequent among all authors.

The other commentary was as follows:

Vers. 11.

Καὶ εἶδον ἄλλο θηρίον (And I saw another beast)] Magic. Ἀναβαῖνον ἐκ τῆς γῆς (Ascending out of the earth)] To which the origin is private, not public. It is the custom of the Hebrews to call τὰς ἰδιώτας (the common people) the people of the earth: it is opposed to that which was said above about the former beast, that it arose from the sea. Καὶ εἶχε κέρατα δύο, ὅμοια ἀρνίῳ (And it had two horns, like a lamb)] Abstinence in food and chastity, virtues similar to the virtues of Christians, through which the Magi rendered themselves venerable. See Philostratus concerning Apollonius of Tyana, who is especially denoted here, lib. I, cap. 10. Theodoret notes both in his third sermon. He makes the former beast the idolatry of Domitian; this one, the magic of Apollonius of Tyana. But what is this other than to pervert Scripture significantly, while from an ἀποκαλύψει (revelation) of future things, he constructs a history of past things, and from the Apostles, prophets only of things already done. But at this time in the Roman empire, magic had flourished so much that it may deservedly be said to have emerged or ascended, and that after Apollonius had withdrawn himself from the Emperor's punishment by magical arts: although it may also be doubted concerning his magic from Justin Martyr, quest. 24 to the Orthodox; it could not yet be taught; nor can the Magi, much less magic in the abstract, be designated in the Holy Scriptures by a beast. By this beast, a certain notable impostor is wrongly understood by Tertullian, Ambrose, Arethas, Andreas, Ribera, Viega, Cornelius à Lapide, and the armor-bearer of the Anti-Christ by Irenaeus, when according to the idiom and prophetic style it is likewise an empire, and thus the Papal empire is understood in this place, which is truly σιδηρόξυλον (iron-wood), according to the phrase of the Holy Scripture, Matth. XX. 26. Certainly most interpreters, and more correctly, understand the Roman Pontiff to be that great Western Anti-Christ, which Bernard does not deny in epistle CXXVI. That beast from the Apocalypse, to which was given a mouth speaking blasphemies, and to wage war with the saints, occupies the chair of Peter like a lion prepared for prey. You may see this passage of the Holy Abbot vindicated in the Conf. Cathol. of B. Gerhard, in his book on the Anti-Christ, and in the epistle of Jerome to Paul, c. 1. Lyranus, Aureolus, and Dom. Soto in IV. sent. dist. 49. q. 1. art. 2. understand by the former beast Sinochius, Siroes, or Sirus, the son of Cosroes, but by this one Mahomet, in which the latter is followed by Joh. Annius and Hentenius in the prologue to the commentary of Arethas. But Suarez, in his treatise on the Anti-Christ, and Pererius deny that it is the Anti-Christ. Alcafar, with whose heifer Grotius has plowed much, explained it concerning the Roman Empire, attacking the Church of Christ, so that by the beast of the sea, according to him, the amplitude of the Roman Empire, the majesty of the earth, and the unbridled affection for earthly desires are understood. The two horns, however, are his threat and severity, and secondarily two magicians, Simon and Apollonius. But more correctly, in the judgment of Cornelius, Gregory in book XXXIII of the Morals, c. 20, Arethas, Rupert, Haymo, and Pannonius understand all the ministers of the Anti-Christ: which Jesuit (Alcafar) says that Ambrose and others previously cited understand some notable impostor, a precursor as it were of the Anti-Christ: concerning whom, however, he has nothing to say, except that he impiously brings in here the mystery of the Holy Trinity, which the Anti-Christ is to imitate, namely that the Dragon is the Father, he himself is the Son, and this impostor and his herald is like the Holy Spirit. For just as Christ defers to the Father, and the Holy Spirit glorifies Christ: so the Anti-Christ will worship the Devil as his father, and this False Prophet will preach and ennoble the Anti-Christ with great signs: which he praises from Joseph Acosta, book II, on the latest times. c. 17. he praises, and which he also relates in chapter 11, an example of a certain precursor of the Anti-Christ seen by him in Peru, who, when he was a Doctor of Theology and was considered as the oracle of that place, deceived by a little woman, said that he was the Redeemer of the world by efficacy, but that Christ was so only by sufficiency. This second beast is said to ascend not from the sea like the former, but from the earth, with Maresius, p. 137, dissert., explaining it as much as without, the Popes were finally to arrive at that authority with much noise and especially clandestine counsels, both because the beginnings of that dignity were very abject and vile, and also because many sons of the earth and men of the lowest sort were to attain this authority. Sixtus V was born of a cowherd father, Benedict XII of a baker, Urban IV of a cobbler; many were so obscure that their surnames and fatherland did not become known on account of the ignobility of their birth, so that not undeservedly the stercorary seat is used in the inauguration of the Popes to shadow forth this thing, because this second beast truly ascended from dust and dung. But that there is some indication of Magic in the fact that the Roman Popes were born from the earth by those devoted to Magic, and were raised to the Papacy through Magic, is abundantly evident from histories, even Papal ones. Thus Baronius, concerning the life and deeds of Hildebrand, teaches that five Popes consecrated themselves entirely to Satan: Sylvester II, Benedict IX, John XX, John XXI, and Gregory VII. The Abbot of Ursperg and also Sigebert, Hermannus Contractus, and Martinus Polonus report the same concerning Gregory VII, namely that he was a necromancer; Platina also, and Antoninus, Aretinus from the Florilegium, Arnoldus, Albertus, and the author of the Oneris Ecclesiae, report that he arrived at such a dignity through Diabolical frauds and magical arts.

The description of the Anti-Christ and his attributes, collected from this chapter by Cornelius à Lapide, certainly fits the Roman Pontiff very well, inasmuch as he is most powerful, savage, about to receive power from the Devil, will pretend that he has risen from the dead, will be worshipped by men, will be blasphemous against God, the Church, and the Saints, will war against the Saints, will subject all nations to himself, will be a monarch of the whole world, will perform wondrous deeds, will order all to be killed who will not worship the image of the Anti-Christ, will force all to bear the character of the Anti-Christ, and will decree that no one can buy or sell without it, and that his name expressed in numbers contains it: all of which are notorious and obvious to everyone, if perhaps you except the last point about the name, which Irenaeus indeed very rightly expressed long ago through the name Λατεῖνος. The rest of the things brought forward there are either doubtful, whether they are assigned to the Anti-Christ, or they can nevertheless be applied to the Roman Pontiff, even if they are not so obvious. We say they are doubtful, because he will pretend that he will rise from the dead and because he will order the image of the Anti-Christ to be painted everywhere, as if rising from the dead. It is not said in this place about the Anti-Christ, at least it is said, and that about the first beast, that its lethal wound is to be healed, and that it is to live. And that it was given to the Anti-Christ to give spirit to the image of the beast: concerning the meaning of which [we speak] at verses 14 and 15. About the painting, not even a jot occurs in the text. It is doubtful that he will have a Pseudo-Prophet as a precursor, whom it will be taught subsequently is not a precursor, but the Anti-Christ himself. The difficulty about the name has already been settled by the interpretation of Irenaeus. Concerning the three years and a half of his reign, it has already been treated above.

As for the two horns of the Lamb, according to Primasius, Ticonius, and the Glossa Ordinaria, they are the two Testaments; to Ribera, they are gentle sermons and miracles; to Danhawer, the horn of fraud and violence; to Philipp Nicolai, Gravius, and Heilbrunner, Italy and Spain; to Mede, the power of binding and loosing; to Cotterius, the power of saving and destroying; to Dürfeld, the earthly and heavenly kingdom; to Joseph Acosta, the two horns are the insignia of the episcopal dignity, the miter or the infula (for this is two-horned): to many others, the double power of the Pope, ecclesiastical and secular. According to Grotius, these two horns are Simon Magus and Apollonius, likewise threat and severity. But these are not like the Lamb, but as Cornelius himself praises from Gregory the Great: To ascend from the earth is to be proud of earthly glory: which is most proper to the Roman Anti-Christ, who puffs himself up to an excessive degree with secular power, even if only usurped over Emperors themselves and Kings, as is evident even from the example of Frederick Barbarossa, trampling them with his feet, impiously applying the Davidic oracle concerning the asp and the basilisk, which speaks of those walking in his way. But is this the way of the Popes, to rule over Emperors and trample them with their feet? Surely according to that saying of Christ: But you are not so. Luke 22. The beast, which has two horns like the Lamb, because through the hypocrisy of holiness he lies that he possesses the singular wisdom and life which the Lord truly had in Himself. But because under the appearance of a Lamb he pours the serpentine virus into his reprobate listeners, it is rightly added, and he spoke as a Dragon. These are the words of Gregory the Great. Now, concerning the imitation of the wisdom and words of the Lord, as well as the Papal life and holiness, the hypocritical matter is in the open. For many examples teach that that saying of Irenaeus is true concerning the Roman Pontiffs and Papal writers, ὅμοια μὲν λαλῦσιν, ἀνόμοια δὲ φρονῦσι, some of which we have given in the Fratres Walenburgenses and in Grotius himself in the article on justification, good works, and merits in the Exegesis of the Augsburg Confession. The whole world complains about the Papal humility and holiness of the servant of servants and our most holy Lord, as the Roman Pontiffs love to be called and call themselves. Concerning John XII, certainly Baronius himself, in the Ecclesiastical Roman [Annals]. The principal Cardinal, at the year 955, no. 2; 963, no. 13; 964, no. 1, etc., commemorates that he not only ordained deacons in a horse stable, created bishops for a price, and those sometimes ten years old, committed many sacrileges, incests, rapes, and adulteries with impunity, deprived his own chamberlain of his eyes and life, killed Cardinals after their genitals were amputated, walked about dressed in a breastplate and sword, stirred up seditions and arms against the Emperor Otto, mutilated others with his hand, tongue, fingers, and hands, and was the author of shedding Roman blood copiously; but also that he drank wine in the love of the Devil, and in a game of dice asked for the help of Jupiter, Venus, and the other Demons. The bishops in the Council of Brixen, as reported by the Abbot of Ursperg in his Chronicle for the year 1180, condemned Gregory VII as a worshiper of divinations and dreams, a necromancer, and one endowed with a Pythonic spirit. The Gloss on Chapter Sancta Romana in the Extravagantes of John XXII, title concerning religious houses, does not deny that Boniface VIII defiled the Church with dishonest exactions, simonies, and foul language. William of Ockham, chapter 124 of his Work of Ninety Days, deserves to be heard here also: Concerning many Pontiffs, he says, the Church erred, considering them holy men; whence it is said in the Chronicles around the 27th that those called Roman Bishops, after the Church was endowed with temporal riches, were such that, after they were assumed to the Papacy, or in the very assumption to the Papacy, they were ensnared, namely, in the crime of heresy, idolatry, heretical depravity, blasphemy, fornication, and were involved in many other enormous crimes. Antoninus of Florence, part III, summary, title 22, chapter 7. The Pope can engage in necromancy, as is held in the Chronicles concerning a certain Pope Sylvester the Magician, but he repented: And he can be involved in rapine, as Damianus narrates concerning Pope Benedict; he can even be given to luxuries, as is narrated in the Chronicles concerning John XI, who, while he was enjoying himself in adultery, was suddenly struck down by the Devil, and he can commit whatever other flagrant crimes. If anyone desires more recent witnesses, even the Jesuits, who know how to palliate and excuse everything, behold Stapleton, who in his Relectio principiorum fidei confesses that the shameful deeds of the Roman Pontiffs were enormous and horrible; indeed, that there was hardly any sin, with the sole exception of heresy, by which that see was not foully stained, especially from the year 800 and thereafter. Behold also another Cardinal, Bellarmine, who in the preface to his book on the Roman Pontiff writes as follows: God finally permitted that even some not very upright Pontiffs should sometimes hold and rule this see, such as were indeed Stephen VI, Leo V, Christopher I, Sergius III, John XII, and NOT A FEW others, if what is read in the historians of their times concerning their life and deeds is true: yet he adds afterwards categorically: We acknowledge and confess that the vices of the Pontiffs in this were not few. And indeed, not only were the Pontiffs not very upright, but they were even most wicked and stained with heresy. Clement, favoring Nicolaitanism, Epist. V. (unit. Gratian. C. de lectissimis MS. 12. q. 1.), according to Junius; Marcellinus, an idolater, in the Pontifical of Damasus and Epist. Nicol. 1. C. nunc autem dist. 21.; Liberius, not denying the Arian heresy, according to Ockham and Benno in his epistle on the life of Hildebrand around the year 1076 and Platina in his life; Zepherinus, Montanizing, according to B. Rhenanus in the argument of book 12 of Tertullian, c. Prax.; Alexander II, Arianizing, as Bellarmine does not deny, book IV de Rom. Pont. c. 7; Anastasius II favored the Nestorians, as Alfonso de Castro admits in book 1 adv. hær. c. 4, and the Eutychians, according to the laws in Bellarmine, book IV de Rom. Pontif. c. 10; but Hircanus I was addicted to the Monothelites, according to Melchior Cano, c. VI, loc. c. ult., and the Sixth Synod, by which he was condemned, with the consent of Leo II in his epistle. Confirmed by the Synod, which Bellarmine could not deny, c. 11. Hadrian, around the year 772, asserted the religious veneration of images, which had been condemned by Charlemagne at the Synod of Frankfurt in the year 794, by the approval of the Acts of the Second Council of Nicaea. Compare his Epistles to the Emperor and to Tarasius. John XXII, according to the Council of Constance, Sess. II, stubbornly dogmatized, at the devil's persuasion, that the life and soul of man dies with the human body and is extinguished like that of brute animals, etc.

But to return to Grotius: The two horns like a Lamb are not so much abstinence in diet and chastity as holiness or purity and patience. For lambs are pure and patient, a figure of that immaculate Lamb of God, who is also most meek and patient, 2 Pet. 1:19, Isa. 53:9, 1 Pet. 2:23. To make the power of the first beast is very ineptly explained as celebrating sacrifices. For it is not the role of an Empire or an Emperor to sacrifice, but to command and exercise his power. Nor is 'in the sight of the beast' the same as 'in honor of idols.' That beast, as such, or apart from communion with the sea beast, does not serve idols. Regarding this second beast, Forbes is not wrong: The vision of the second beast is offered merely for a clearer explanation of that last mark with which the first beast is distinguished regarding the healing of the wounded head, if the exclusive is omitted. For this is not the only cause, but a declaration of the mutual power of both beasts, and their designation through certain characters or marks.

And he spoke as a dragon] He spoke such things as the Dragon had spoken through Simon, whose presence was according to the working of Satan, 2 Thess. 2:9. Origen reports the same concerning Apollonius in his sixth book against Celsus, Lactantius in the aforementioned place, and Cedrenus in his compendium.

In his previous commentary, Grotius had proposed these things as follows:

And he spoke as a dragon] The things which the Magi taught did not in truth pertain to the honor of God, but to that of the Devil. See Origen on Apollonius in his sixth book against Celsus, Lactantius V. 3, and Cedrenus in his compendium of history: Thus the presence of Simon Magus was according to the working of Satan, 2 Thess. 2:9. Concerning the Jews, the worshippers of one God, see how contemptuously Apollonius spoke in Philostratus, book V, v. 11: 'They have long since cut themselves off not only from the Romans, but from all men.'

The Dragon was described by his notable strength and ferocity: and the first beast spoke great things, by the authority of B. Gravius; this beast speaks great things, for it extols the Pontiffs not only above all Bishops and the whole Church and all Councils, but even above all Kings and the Emperor. 1. It speaks blasphemies against God, by transferring the glory of God and the benefits of Christ to dead saints, to idols, and to the merits of one's own works. 2. Against the tabernacle of God, not that of the Old Testament, which exhibits the benefits of Christ prefigured in the Israelite tabernacle. 3. And against those who dwell in heaven, that is, in the ecclesiastical heaven, and are true members of the Evangelical Church, whom the Roman Pope with his followers blasphemes and traduces through his sycophants as heretics and pseudo-Christians. He gave power to the beast, etc. by the same author, it can be understood of the civil adoration and celebration of the old Roman empire, which, with Satan directing it, transferred all its glory and Majesty still remaining into the Hierarchy of the Roman Pontiff and renewed it therein. They also adored the beast itself, that is, they venerated the Antichrist himself and, fascinated by blind superstition, extolled his power both in spiritual and political matters, saying: Who is like the beast and who can fight with it? For emperors, Kings, Princes, and all who refused to obey his decrees experienced the strength and efficacy of Papal omnipotence to their great detriment. Many documents exist concerning the power and fraudulence of the Anti-Christian Magnates, exercised even against Emperors, Kings, and Princes. Cardinal Bertrand teaches this in his treatise on the origin and use of jurisdiction, p. 4. Because Jesus Christ while he was in this world, and from eternity was the natural Lord, and by natural right could have passed sentences of deposition and condemnation and any others whatsoever against Emperors and whosoever else, as being against persons whom he had created and had endowed with natural and gratuitous gifts, and was even preserving, and for the same reason his vicar can. For the Lord would not seem to have been discreet (to speak with reverence) unless he had left behind him such a unique Vicar, who could do all these things. Augustinus Steuchus in his book on the Donation of Constantine asserts that all Kings are vassals of the Pope. Alexander Pesantius in his Roman book on the immunity of the Church and the power of the Pontiff says: The Supreme Pontiff by divine right has the fullest power over the whole orb of the earth, both in Ecclesiastical matters and in Political, he is to be called Lord of the world by divine right. Thomas Bozius in the dedication of his book on the temples of the Church. A monk strives to show from the Fathers, Theologians, and Casuists that the Pontiff has power over all temporal things which fall into human use. But with what ferocity and cunning they have used this power assumed for themselves, examples teach, which there is no time to adduce here now. That has been done elsewhere. Maresius reports some draconian utterances: of Siricius concerning those honestly married: Those who are in the flesh cannot please God: of Alexander III, pressing the neck of Frederick with a proud foot: You shall walk upon the asp and the basilisk: of Julius II, going forth into battle and throwing the keys of Peter into the Tiber: Because the key of Saint Peter is no longer of value, let now the sword of St. Paul prevail. [regarding] Leo X proposing to Cardinal Bembo something from the Gospel, how much this fable about Christ has profited us and our assembly is known enough to all centuries: what kind of men were Boniface VIII and Gregory VII, who arrogated to themselves all right over Kings and Princes, what kind of impious, proud, and to Christ insulting dogmas [are held] in general by the Roman Pontiff, who is accustomed to boast of the fullness of power, the authority of giving or taking away kingdoms to whom he wishes—which the Demon attributed to himself in the temptation of Christ—and that all divine and human law is enclosed in the cabinet of his breast: indeed, a most foul book came forth from Italy, published as if under the very eyes of the Pope, concerning the three impostors, Moses, Christ, and Mahomet, which the Italian monk Campanella ascribes to Poggio the Florentine, and he brands a similar impiety in Boccaccio, of the same nation. Since Grotius has replied to these things in an appendix, one must also look into those. Grotius said that the epistle of Siricius is supposititious, but Cardinal Baronius—no less superior to Grotius in faith than in authority—says that most people accept it, at the year 386, no. 11; indeed, Pope Innocent himself [says so] in an epistle to Victricius. Furthermore, Grotius says that the book about the three impostors is a fable, and he does not wish it to be attributed to the Pope, nor was it attributed to him; yet the voice of Leo X to Cardinal Bembo was not foreign: 'How much this fable about Christ has profited us and our assembly,' which is known to all centuries now. The words 'And he exercised all the power of the first beast in his sight' are distorted by Grotius to refer to sacrifices celebrated by the Magi in honor of idols; nor is the first beast idolatry, much less an idol, but the Roman Empire, such as it is under the Papists: nor does the force of idolatry lie in sacrifices, which Apollonius shunned as bloody, and where ποιεῖν is the same as to sacrifice, and προσκυνῆσαι ἐνώπιόν τινος [is] to exercise the power or authority of another in his presence. Rightly, therefore, does Maresius understand this of the Roman Pontiff: 'Who, having risen from very humble and obscure beginnings, gradually seized for himself all the authority of the first beast, that is, of the Roman Empire, which he insolently exerts and exercises, not only in the presence of those very men who are called Roman Caesars and Emperors in title only, but also over them.' He even seized for himself all the insignia of the Emperors, namely the purple cloak, concerning which Ambrose [wrote] to Theodosius: 'Purple makes an Emperor, not a Priest,' the purple shoes, the name and adoration of a deity, the kissing of the feet, the tax from harlots, the right of apotheosis, the supreme Pontificate, and what not? So that it is no wonder that Grotius opposes this, because he could not do otherwise; it is certain to us that this very Rome, namely the modern one under the Pontiff, the Papal one which we have spoken of, both was and is the sacred empire within it, like an anchor to a long-fluctuating Europe. Because if it were not Papal, the Imperial authority itself would not exist: which the Roman Pontiff can blow away with bulls, in his own opinion. But he could not do so regarding the Peace of Osnabrück. But indeed, when he attempted that, is he to be judged as having been like an anchor to a fluctuating Europe? Let what Hornbeck [wrote] about that bull be read; let others be read. v. 12. And he exercises all the power of the first beast] Magic will harm Christians by God's permission, just as idolatry, sustained by the power of the Caesars, had harmed them before. Concerning the word ἐξουσίας, see above 2. In his sight] in honor of the Roman religion.

The former commentary has it thus:

Latin:

Vers. 11.

Καὶ εἶδον ἄλλο θηρίον] Quod hic prædicitur, posterius est jam dictis. Qualis forma fuerit hujus θηρίου non dicitur. Credo fuisse formam viperæ, quia inter è terra nata, illa exi- mio jure hoc nomen sibi vindicat. Vid. Act. XXVIII. v. 4. 5. Et Ericheho magicis operans sacris apud Lucanum sic describitur: Et vomat vipercis subfringitur horrida sertis. Ἀναβαῖνον ἐκ τῆς γῆς] Hæc bestia est magia, quæ à Pytha- goristis illo tempore, de quo hic agitur aperte exercita laban- tem idololatriam erexit, maxime per Apollonium Tyanæum, quem ejus temporis homines Christo ausi sunt opponere, ut ex Hieroclis libro apparet, cui respondit Eusebius. Magia autem recte dicitur è terra afcendere, quia magi ex terra, id est, ex antris loquebantur, Es. XXIX. vers. 4. XLV. verf. 32. XLVIII. vers. 18. & umbras fuscitabant ex terra 1. Sam. XXVIII. 13. Seneca Oedipode: Subito debiscit terra, & immenso sinu Laxata patuit: ipse pallentes Deos Vidi inter umbras. Hæc sunt illa ἄδυλα ἄβατα καὶ φοβερά, de quibus Nazian- zenus oratione secunda in Julianum. Καὶ εἶχε κέρατα δύο ὅμοια ἀρνίῳ] Magi duo habebant vir- tutum simulachra, virtutibus Christianis similia, temperan- tiam in victu, & à Venere abstinentiam. Clemens Ale- xandrinus Strom. III. ἀμέλει διὰ φροντίδος ἐστὶ κἀγ τοῖς μάγοις ὅ,τε τε ὀψὲ καὶ ἐμψύχων καὶ ἀφροδισίων ἀπέχεσθαι. Idem ha- bet Theodoretes sermone tertio. Speciatim de Apollonio Tyanæo id refert Philostratus I. 10. Cornua agni sunt vir- tutes Christianæ. Ἀρνίῳ hic pro τῷ ἀρνίῳ ut jam illud δεά- και pro ὁ δεάκων. Frequens talis articulorum omissio apud omnes Autores.

Altera commentatio talis fuit:

Vers. 11.

Καὶ εἶδον ἄλλο θηρίον, & vidi aliam bestiam] Magiam. Ἀναβαῖνον ἐκ τῆς γῆς asfendentem de terra] Cui origo privata non publica. Mos est Ebræorum vocare τὰς ἰδιώ- τας populum terræ: opponitur ei, quod de priore bestia supra dictum, ex mari eam ortam. Καὶ εἶχε κέρατα δύο, ὅμοια ἀρνίῳ habebat, & duo cornua similia Agni) Abstinentiam in victu & castitatem virtu- tes Christianorum virtutibus similes, per quas Magi se red- debant venerabiles. Vide Philostratum de ApollonioTy- anæo, qui præcipue hic denotatur lib. I. cap. 10. Utrum- que notat Theodoretus sermone tertio. Ut priorem feram Domitiani idololatriam; ita hanc Apollonii Tyanæi magiam facit. Sed quid hoc aliud est, quam Scripturam insigniter perver- tere, dum ex ἀποκαλύψει futurorum, præterito- rum historiam, ex Apostolis rerum jam factarum duntaxat Prophetas extruit. Hoc autem tempore in imperio Romano Magiam adeo viguisse, ut emer- sisse vel ascendisse merito dicatur, idque postquam Apollonius Magicis artibus se Imperatoris pœnæ subtraxerat: quanquam etiam de Magia illius è Justino Martyre quæst. 24. ad Orthod. dubitari possit; nondum doceri potuit; neque per feram Magos, nedum magiam in abstracto in S. literis de- signari. Per hanc bestiam perperam insignis qui- dam Impostor a Tertulliano, Ambrosio, Areta, An- drea, Ribera, Viega, Cornelio à Lapide, armiger Anti-Christi ab Irenæo intelligitur, quum juxta idiotismum & stylum Propheticum ea itidem im- perium sit, adeoque Papale imperium, hoc loco intelligatur,quod vero est σιδηρόξυλον, juxta phra- sin Scripturæ sacræ Matth. XX. 26. Pontificem certe Romanum plerique omnes Interpretes &re- ctius intelligunt Anti-Christum illum Occidenta- lem Magnum non abnuente Bernardo epist. CXXVI. Bestia illa de Apocalypsi, cui datum est os loquens blasphemias, & bellum gerere cum sanctis, Petri cathedram occupat tanquam Leo paratus ad prædam. Quem S. Abbatis locum vindicatum vi- de sis in Conf. Cathol. B. Gerhard. l. de Anti- Christo & Hier. epist. ad Paul. c. 1. Lyranus, An- reolus, & Dom. Soto in IV. sent. dist. 49. q. 1. art. 2. per priorem bestiam Sinochium, Siroem vel Sirum Cosroæ filium, per hanc vero Mahomethen intelli- gunt, in quo posteriori Joh. Annius & Hentenius in prologo comment. Aretæ. Quam vero (bestiam) Suarez tr. de AntiChr. & Pererius negant esse An- ti-Christum. Alcafar, cujus vitulo multum aravit Grotius, de Romano imperio, Christi Ecclesiam im- pugnante exposuit, ut per bestiam maris Romani Imperii amplitudo, Majestas terræ, cupiditatum terrenarum effrenatus affectus secundnm ipsum intelligatur. Duo cornua vero sunt ipsi commina- tio, ac feveritas, & secundario duo magi, Simon, & Apollonius. Rectius autem, Cornelis judicio, Gregorius l. XXXIII. Moral. c. 20. Aretas, Ru- pertus, Haymo & Pannonius universos Anti-Chri- sti Ministros intelligunt: Qui Jesuita (Alcafar) Optime Ambrosium & alios antea adductos insi- gnem aliquem impostorem, præcursorem quasi Anti-Christi, intelligere, ait: De quo tamen nihil habet, quod dicat, quam quod impie huc addu- cat mysterium S. Trinitatis, quod imitaturus sitAn- ti-Christus, scilicet ut Draco sit Pater, ipse sit Filius, hic vero impostor ejusque Præco sit instar Spiritus Sancti. Sicut enim Patri Christus defert, & Chri- stum Spiritus Sanctus clarificat: Ita Diabolum ut Patrem suum colet Anti-Christus, Anti-Christum Pseudo-Propheta bic signis magnis prædicabit & no- bilitabit: Quod è Josepho Acosta l. II. de tempor. noviss. c. 17. laudat, quod & cap. 11. mirum cujus- dam præcursoris Anti-Christi in Peru à se visi re- ferat exemplum, qui cum esset Doctor Theolo- gus, & quasi oraculum illius loci haberetur, à mu- liercula deceptus se dicebat esse Redemptorem mundi per efficaciam, Christum vero fuisse tan- tum per sufficientiam. Dicitur altera hæc bestia non è mari ut prior, sed ex terra afcendere, Ma- resio p. 137. differs. exponente, tam quod absque, „ multo strepitu & clanculariis potissimum consiliis ad eam autoritatem Pontifices tandem erant de- venturi, tum quod abjecta & vilia admodum fue- rint illius dignitatis exordia, tum etiam quod ple- rique terræ filii & infimæ sortis homines hanc au- toritatem adepturi erant. Bubulco patre Six- „ tus V. ortus fuit, Benedictus XII. pistore, sutore Urbanus IV. multi tam obscuri, ut eorum cogno- mina & patria propter generis ignobilitatem non innotuerint, ut non immerito stercoraria sedes huic rei adumbrandæ, eo quod revera ex pulve- re & stercore ascenderit secunda hæc bestia, in „ Pontificum inauguratione adhibeatur. Quod si Magici indicium aliquod sit ortus ex terra per Ma- giæ deditos, & per Magiam ad Papatum evectos Pontifices Romanos fuisse, ex historiis, etiam Pon- tificiis, abunde constat. Ita Baron. de vita & rebus gestis Hildebrandi docet, quinque Papas se totos Satanæ consecrasse, Sylvestrum II. Benedictum IX. Johannem XX. Johannem XXI. & Gregorium VII. Idem de Gregorio VII. tradit Abbas Usperg. nec- non Sigebertus, Hermannus Contractus, Martinus Polonus, quod nempe necromantes is fuerit, Pla- tina etiam Antonin. Aret. ex Floril. Arnold. Al- bert. Autor. oneris Eccl. quod fraudibus Diabolicis & artibus magicis ad tantã dignitatem pervenerit.

Descriptio certe Anti-Christi & προσκείμενα ejus ex hoc capite collecta à Cornelio à Lapide, optime Pontifici Romano conveniunt, utpote quod potentissimus, quod sævus, quod à Diabolo potestatem accepturus, quod finget se a mortuis re- surrexiise, quod adorabitur ab hominibus, quod bla- sphemus erit in Deum, Ecclesiam, & Sanctos, quod bellabit contra Sanctos, quod omnes gentes, sibi subi- get, totiusque orbis Monarcha erit, quod faciet facta miranda, quod jubebit occidi omnes, qui nolent ado- rare imaginem Anti-Christi, quod coget omnes ge- stare Anti-Christi characterem, statuetque ut ne- mo sine eo quid emere aut vendere possit, quod nomen ejus numeris expressum contineat: Quæ no- toria omnia sunt, & omnibus obvia, si forte po- stremum de nomine excipias, quod vero jam Ire- næus rectissime per nomen Λατεῖνος expressit. Cæ- tera illic adducta aut dubia sunt, an Anti-Christo assignata, aut applicari tamen Romano Pontifici possunt, etsi non ita obvia sint. Dubia dicimus, quod finget se resurgere à mortuis & quod jubebit passim pingi imaginem Anti-Christi, quasi resurgen- tis à morte. Non id dicitur hoc loco de Anti- Christo, saltim dicitur, idque de fera prima, quod sananda sit plaga ejus lethalis, eademque victura sit. Et quod Anti-Christo datum sit, dare spiritum imagini bestiæ: de quorum sensu ad v. 14. 15. De pictura in textu ne gry quidem occurrit. Du- bium, quod præcursorem habiturus sit Pseudo- Prophetam, quem non præcursorem esse, sed ipsummet AntiChristum, deinceps docebitur. Difficultas de nomine jam expedita est Irenæi in- terpretatione. De triennio & semestri regni ejus supra jam tractatum.

Quod ad cornua duo Agni, Primasio, Ticonio, Glossa ordin. illa sunt duo Te- stamenta, Riberæ sermones mansueti & miracula, Danhawero cornu fraudulentie & violentiæ, Phi- lippo Nicolai, Gravio, & Heilbrunnero Italia & Hispania, Medo potestas ligandi & solvendi, Cot- terio potestas servandi & perdendi, Dürfeldio re- gnum terrestre, & cæleste, Josepho Acostæ duo cor- nua Episcopalis dignitatis mitræ sive insulæ (hæc enim bicornis est) insigne: Multis aliis Papæ po- testas gemina Ecclesiastica & secularis. Juxta Gro- tium hæc duo cornua sunt Simon Magus, & Apol- lonius, item comminatio ac severitas. Verum hæc agni non similia sunt, sed ut Cornelius ipse è Gre- gorio M. laudat : De terra ascendere est deterren- gloria superbire : Quod maxime proprium Anti- Christo Romano, nimium quantum se potestate seculari etsi usurpata tantum in Imperatores ipsos & Reges efferente, ut vel exemplo Friderici Bar- barossæ constat, pedibus cum oraculo Davidico super aspidem & Basiliscum impie adducto, con- culcante, quod de ambulantibus in via sua lo- quitur. Num vero hæc viaPontificum est impera- re super Imperatores, eosque pedibus calcare? Scilicet juxta illud Christi : Vos autem non sic. Luc. XXII. Bestia, quæ habet duo cornua Agni similia, quia per hypocrisin sanctitatis eam, quam in se ve- raciter Dominus habuit, singularem sibi inesse sa- pientiam mentitur, & vitam. Sed quia sub Agni specie auditoribus reprobis serpentinum virus in- fundit, recte subditur, & loquebatur ut Draco. Hæc Gregorius M. Jam de imitatione sapientiæ & verborum Domini nec non vitæ & sanctitatis Pa- pali, sed hypocritica res in aprico est. Nam & de Pontificibus Romanis & Pontificiis Scriptoribus verum esse illud Irenæi,ὅμοια μὲν λαλῦσιν,ἀνόμοια δὲ φρονῦσι, plurima docent exempla, quorum nonnulla dedimus in Fratrib. Walenburg. & Gro- tio ipso in articulo de justificatione, Bonis operibus & meritis in Exeg. Aug. Confess. De Pontificia hu- militate ac sanctitate servi servorum & sanctissimi Domini nostri, uti vocari amant, & se vocant Pontifices Romani, totus orbis queritur. De Jo- hanne XII. certe Baronius ipse Eccl. Rom. Cardi- nalis præcipuus ad ann. 955. n. 2. 963. n. 13. 964. n. 1. sqq. commemorat, quod non solum Diaco- nos in equorum stabulo ordinarit, Episcopos pretio creaverit, & eos quidem interdum decem annorum, sacrilegia, incestus, stupra, & adulteria plurima impune commiserit, commissarium suum oculis & vita privarit, Cardinales virilibus eis am- putatis occiderit, lorica & gala is indutus incesse- rit, seditiones & arma contra Imperatorem Ot- thonem commoverit, alios manu, lingua, digitis, manibusque mutilarit, Romanum sanguinem co- piose effundendi autor fuerit; sed etiam in Dia- boli amorem vinum biberit in ludo aleæ, Jovis, Venerisque cæterorumque Dæmonum auxilium poposcerit. Episcopi in Concilio Brixiensi, refe- rente Abbate Urspergensi in Chron. Ann. 1180. Gregorium VII. ut Divinationum & somniorum cultorem, necromanticum, & Spiritu Pythonico præditum condemnarunt. Glossa C. Sancta Ro- mana in Extr. Joh. XXII. tit. de domib. relig. Bo- nifacium IIX. exactionibus improbis, Simoniis, & turpiloquiis Ecclesiam fœdasse non abnuit. Guilh. Occam c. 124. operis 94. dierum hic etiam audiri meretur: De multis, inquit, Pontificibus Ecclesia, reputans eos sanctos viros, erravit, unde dicitur in Chronicis circa 27. vocatos Romanos Epi- scopos, postquam Ecclesia extitit temporalibus divi- tiis dotata, fuisse, qui sceleribus maxime publicis & notoriis postquam fuerunt ad Papatum assumpti, vel in ipsa assumptione ad Papatum irretiti feil. crimi- ne hæresis idololatriæ pravitatis hereticæ, blasphemiæ, fornicationis, & aliis multis enormibus criminibus involuti fuerunt. Antoninus Florentinus part. III. summ. tit. 22. c. 7.
