Papa potest necromantiæ inten- dere, sicut in Chronicis habetur de quodam Sylvestro Papa Mago, sed pœnituit: Et rapinis involvi, sicut de Benedicto Papa narrat Damianus; etiam luxu- riis vacare, sicut de Johanne XI. narratur in Chro- nicis, qui cum in adulterio, oblectaretur, à Diabolo subito percussus est & quæcunque alia flagitia ad- mittere potest. Si recentiores quis desiderat testes, Jesuitas etiam, qui omnia palliare & excusare norunt, en Stapletonum, qui relect. principior fid. fatetur, enormia & horrenda fuisse Pontificum Romanorum flagitia, imo vix ullum peccatum, sola hæresi exce- pta, quo illa sedes turpiter maculata non fuerit, maxime ab anno 800. & infra. En & Cardinalem alterum, Bellarminum, qui in præfat. libr. de Rom. Pontif. quidem ita scribit: Permisit ad extremum Deus, ut etiam quidam parum probi Pontifices aliquando hanc sedem tenerent & regerent, qua- les sane fuerunt Stephanus VI. Leo V. Christo- phorus I. Sergius III. Johannes XII. aliique NON PAUCI, si vera sunt, quæ de eorum vita & rebus gestis apud Historicos eorum temporum scripta leguntur: Addit tamen postmodum Categorice: Nos agnoscimus & fatemur, vitia Pontificum hac fuiffe non pauca. Nec vero solum Pontifices non parum probi, imo maxime improbi fuere, sed etiam hæresi commaculati. Clemens Nicolaismo favens epist. V. (unit. Gratian. C. de lectissimis MS. 12. q. 1.) teste Junio, Marcellinus idololatra, Pontificali Damasi & Epist. Nicol. 1. C. nunc au- tem dist. 21. Liberius Arianæ hæresi non abnuens, teste Occamo & Bennone in epist. de vita Hilde- brandi circa ann. 1076. & Platina in ejus vita. Ze- pherinus Montanizans, teste B. Rhenan. in arg. l. 12. Tertull. c. Prax. Alex. II. Arianizans, non diffitente Ballarm. l. IV. de Rom. Pont. c. 7. Ana- stasius II. favit Nestorianis, Alphonso de Castro l. 1. adv. hær. c. 4. fatente, Eutychianis legibus apud Bellarm. l. IV. de Rom. Pontif. c. 10. Monotheletis vero addictus fuit Hircanus I. teste Melch. Cano, c. VI. loc. c. ult. & Synodo VI. à qua condemna- tus, consentiente Leone II. in epist. Synodi con- firmatum, quod negare non potuit Bell. c. 11. A- drianus circa ann. 772. religiosam imaginum venera- tionem à Carolo M. Synodo Francof. anno 794. da- mnatam approbatione Actorum Synodi Nicenæ II. adseruit. Conf. Epistolæ ejus ad Imper. & Ta- masium Joh. XXII. teste Concilio Constant. Sess. II. pertinaciter Diabolo suadente dogmatizavit, vitam animam hominis cum corpore humano mori & ad instar animalium brutorum extingui, &c.

Verum ut ad Grotium redeamus: Duo cornua similia Agni non tam abstinentia in victu & castitas, quam sanctimonia vel puritas & patientia sunt. Agni enim puri sunt, & patientes, immaculati il- lius Agni Dei ejusdemque mansuetissimi & pa- tientissimi figura, 2. Petr. I. 19. Es. LIII. 9. 1. Petr. II. 23. Potestatem prioris bestiæ facere perquam in- eptè exponitur sacrificia celebrare. Non enim Imperii vel Imperatoris est sacrificare, sed impe- rare ac potestatem suam exercere. Nec in conspectu bestiæ idem est, quod in honorem idolorum. Be- stia illa, qua talis, vel citra communionem cum bestia marina non servit idolis. De hac posterio- ri bestia non male Forbesius: Visio secunda bestiæ of- fertur ad clariorem duntaxat explicationem ultimæ illius notæ, qua prior bestia insignita est de curatio- ne capitis vulnerati, si exclusiva omittatur. Non enim hæc unica tantum est causa, sed declaratio potesta- tis bestiæ utriusque mutua, earumque per certos characteres vel γνωρίσματα designatio.

Καὶ ἐλάλει ὡς δράκων] Loquebatur qualia Draco per Si- monem loquutus fuerat, cujus παρουσία fuit κατ᾽ ἐνέργειαν τοῦ Σατανᾶ 2. Thess. II. vers. 9. Idem de Apollonio tradit Orige- nes sexto contra Celsum, Lactantius dicto loco, Cedrenus in compendio.

In priori commentatione hæc ita proposuerat Grotius:

Καὶ ἐλάλει ὡς δράκων, & loquebatur sicut Draco] Ea quæ docebant Magi, non ad Dei, sed ad Diaboli honorem revera pertinebant. Vide de Apollonio Origenem sexto contra Celsum, Lactantium V. 3. Cedernum in historiæ compendio: Sic Simonis Magi παρουσία κατ' ἐνέργειαν τῦ Σατανᾶ, adventus secundum operationem Satanæ, 2. Thess. II. 9. De Judæis unius Dei cultoribus vide quam con- temptim loquutus sit Apollonius Philostrati libro V. v. 11. Ἐκεῖνοι πάλαι ἀφιστᾶσιν ὀ μόνον Ῥωμαίων, ἀλλὰ καὶ πάντων ἀνθρώπων: illi jam olim se absciderunt non à Romanis tan- tum, sed & ab hominibus omnibus.

Descriptus Draco erat ab insigni robore ac fe- rocia: & prior bestia loquebatur magna, B. Gra- vio autore; magna loquitur hæc bestia, extollit enim Pontifices non super omnes Episcopos tantum & to- tam Ecclesiam & Concilia omnia, sed etiam super Reges omnes & Imperatorem. Blasphemias 1. in Deum loquitur, transferendo gloriam Dei & benefi- ciorum Christi in sanctos demortuos, in idola, & in propria operum merita. 2. In tabernaculum Dei non illud Veteris Testamenti, quæ exhibet Christi be- neficia in tabernaculo Israëlítico præfigurata. 3. Et eos, qui in cœlo habitant, hoc est in cœlo Ecclesiasti- co, & sunt vera Ecclesiæ Evangelicæ membra, quos Papa Romanus cum suis asseclis blasphemat, & tan- quam hæreticos & Pseudo Christianos per suos gna- thones traducit. Dedit potestatem bestiæ &c. eo- dem Autore, De civili intelligi potest adoratione & celebratione veteris Romani imperii, quod dirigente Satana omnem suam gloriam & Majestatem adhuc reliquam in Pontificis Romani Hierarchiam trans- tulit & in ea renovavit. Adorarunt quoque bestiam ipsam, hoc est, Antichristum ipsum venerati sunt & fascinati cæca superstitione extulerunt ejus poten- tiam tam in spiritualibus quam in politicis dicentes: Quis similis bestiæ & quis potest pugnare cum ea? Omnipotentiæ enim Papalis robur & efficaciam ma- gno suo cum damno experti sunt imperatores, Reges, Principes & omnes, qui ejus decretis obedire recu- sarunt. De Anti-Christi Magnatum potentia & fraudulentia multa extant documenta, etiam in Imperatores, Reges & Principes exercita. Id do- cet Cardin. Bertrandus in tr. de orig. & usu jurisd. p. 4. Quia Jesus Christus dum fuit in hoc mundo, & ab æterno naturalis Dominus fuit, & de jure natu- rali in Imperatores & quoscunque alios depositionis sententias ferre potuisset, & damnationis & quas- cunque alias utpote in personas, quas creaverat, & donis naturalibus & gratuitis donaverat, & etiam conservabat & eadem ratione ejus vicarius potest. Nam Dominus non videretur fuisse discretus (ut cum reverentia loquar) nisi unicum post se talem Vi- carium reliquisset, qui hæc omnia posset. August. Steuchus l. de donat. Constant. adstruit, omnes Reges esse Papæ Vasallos. Alexander Pesantius Rom. libr. de immunit. Eccl. & potest. Pontif. Summus, inquit, Pontifex divino jure habet plenis- simam potestatem in universum terrarum orbem, tum in rebus Ecclesiasticis, tum in Politicis, est di- cendus Dominus orbis jure divino. Thom. Boz. in ded. l. de templ. Eccl. Monach. ex Patribus, Theologis & Casuistis ostendere nititur, Pontificem habere potestatem circa temporalia omnia, quæ ca- dunt in usum humanum. Quanta vero ferocia & versutia hac sibi assumpta potestate usi sint, exem- pla docent, quæ hic adducere jam non vacat. Fa- ctum id alias. Draconias voces nonnullas refert Maresius: Syricii de honeste conjugatis: Qui sunt in carne, non possunt placere Deo: Alexandri III, Friderici collum pede superbo prementis, super aspi- dem & basiliscum ambulabis: Julii II. in pugnam prodeuntis, & claves Petri projicientis in Tiberim: Quia clavis sancti Petri non amplius valet, valeat nunc gladius S. Pauli Leonis X. ad Cardinalem Bembum aliquid ex Evangelio proponentem, quan- tum nobis profuerit ac nostro cœtui hæc de Christo fabula, satis est seculis omnibus notum: Quales Bonifacii VIII. & Gregorii VII. omne jus sibi in Reges & Principes arrogantium, quales in genere impia, superba & Christo coutumeliosa dogmata plurima Pontificis Romani, qui plenitudinem po- testatis, authoritatem regna dandi vel auferendi, quibus voluerit, quod Dæmon sibi tribuit in tenta- tione Christi, & omne jus divinum & humanum scrinio pectoris sui inclusum jactare solet: quin ex Italia prodiit teterrimus liber, quasi sub ipsius Papæ oculis editus, de tribus impostoribus Mose, Christo, & Mahomete, quem Campanella Monachus Italus adscribit Poggio Florentino, & similem suggillat impietatem in Bocario, ejusdem nationis. Ad quæ quum reposuerit nonnulla in appendice Grotius, de illis etiam dispiciendum. Dixit Grotius episto- lam Syricii supposititiam esse, at plerosque eam re- cipere, ait Cardin. Baronius, Grotio fide non mi- nus quam autoritate superior ad ann. 386. n. 11. imo Papa ipse Innocentius in Epist. ad Victr. Porro librũ de tribus impostoribus fabulam esse dicit Grotius, nec Papæ tribui vult, sed nec illi tributus fuit; non aliena tamen vox Leonis X. ad Card. Bembum fuit: Quantum nobis profuerit ac nostro cœtui hæc de Christo fabula, quæ omnibus jam seculis nota. Verba & potestatem prioris bestiæ omnem exercebat in con- spectu ejus, detorquentur à Grotio ad sacrificia per Magos celebrata in honorem idolorum, nec n. pri- or bestia idololatria, nedum idolum est, sed Rom. im- per. quale sub Papistis: nec vis idololatriæ in sacri- ficiis sita, quæ cruenta aversatus fuit Apollonius, & ubi ποιεῖν est idem quod sacrificare, & προσκυνῆσαι ἐνώπιόν τινος, alterius potestatem facere vel autori- tatem exercere coram ipso. Rectè ergo id de Pon- " tifice Romano intelligit Maresius: Qui ex tenuibus & obscuris admodum initiis ortus, omnem paula- tim ad se prioris bestiæ, id est Rom. imperii auto- ritatem rapuit, quam proterve exerit atque excer- cet, non modo coram illis ipsis, qui Cæsares & Im- peratores Romani titulotenus dicuntur, sed & in eos. Ipsa etiam Imperatorum insignia omnia ad " se rapuit, paludamentum nempe purpureum, de quo Ambrosius ad Theodosium: Purpura Impe- ratorem non Sacerdotem facit, calceos purpure- os, numinis & nomen & adorationem, pedum osculum, vectigal ex Meretricibus, jus ἀπο- " θεώσεως, summum Pontificatum, & quid non? Ut non mirum, Grotium id opponere, quia ali- ter non potuit; Nobis constat, hanc ipsam Ro- mam, hodiernam scilicet sub Pontifice, Papalem quam diximus, & sacrum in ea imperium fuisse & esse velut Anchoram fluctuenti diu Europæ. Quia si non esset Papalis, ne esset Imperatoria ipsa auto- ritas: Quam difflare bullis potest Pontifex Ro- manus, sua opinione. Non potuit autem circa pa- cem Osnabrugensem. An vero, cum id tentaret, fluctuanti Europæ velut Anchora fuisse censendus est? Legatur quæ de ea bulla Hornbeck. legatur alii. v. 12. Καὶ τὴν ἐξουσίαν τῦ πρώτου θηρίου πᾶσαν ποιεῖ] Nocebit Christianis magia Dei permissu, sicut ante nocuerat idolola- tria vi Cæsarum sustentata. De voce ἐξουσίας vide supra 2. Ἐνώπιον ἀυτῶ] in honorem Romanæ religionis.

Prior commentatio sic habet:

## 13:12
And he exercised all the power of the first beast) They celebrated sacrifices, and the Magi commanded them to be celebrated. In his sight,] in honor of the idols; thus this phrase is taken in Luke 4:7 and elsewhere.

How much more fittingly is this explained concerning the power of the Roman Pontiff, given by the Dragon himself in honor of Roman idolatry and apostasy and heresy,

and usurped by the Roman Pontiff? Or also 'in his sight' (of the first beast), because the Caesarean power is exercised by the Pope in the sight of the first beast of the Papal Caesars, who are confirmed by the Pope, venerate and defend the Pope's authority, execute Papal decrees, bulls, and Briefs, and are advocates of the Romano-Papal Church, in whose courts the Pope dominates the Emperors themselves—who are his counselors—through his own sworn, unique Apostolic [agents], Cardinals, Archbishops, Bishops, Abbots, Priors, Canons and Prelates, Jesuits, and other monks, confessors, mass-priests, and the remaining Orders, and the professed, and whosoever else is bound by the religion of an oath to the profession of the Roman Catholic Tridentine faith. For the things which he does and executes, the second or earthly beast, the Pope, performs not secretly but with such [people] aware, and in the sight of the Papal empire itself, affecting Caesarean power, whether direct or indirect, over secular matters: so that indeed two beasts appear to act, one through itself, the other through those subject to it, the marine [beast] through the earthly, and the earthly in the sight of the marine: yet in reality only one beast acts properly, according to that [principle]: what one does through another, he is considered to have done himself. The bulls are also different, namely, [from] the Imperial Edicts, even if the Pontifical clergy dominates in the certain rationale of both: whence they often aim at the same goal, animated and agitated by the same spirit: for the earthly beast puts the spirit of the marine beast into the image, so that it may speak, namely in its own manner, by promulgating Papal decrees, bulls, and briefs: by which a great part is ruled by the Canon law already sanctioned and received: from which the image of the beast obtained its form in a certain way and therefore its spirit more truly than the beast, that is, it seemed more a shadow of an empire than an empire, before it was informed by that spirit and obtained a certain rationale and form of state, which for the most part exerts itself in the work itself: and by right, prescribed by the Roman Pontiff, it always ought to exert itself. Which even the Papal Bull of Innocent X against the Peace of Münster can testify. Nor undeservedly [does] Lipsius [say] in the preface to the Miracles, whatever remains of the empire is exercised and held by the Pope as a Roman Dictator, which he concludes from the purple Senate of Cardinals, the tributes, the embassies to foreigners, and the submissions of Princes and Kings toward this see.

Καὶ ποιεῖ τὴν γῆν καὶ τὰς ἐν ἀυτῇ κατοικοῦντας, ἵνα προσκυνήσωσι τὸ θηρίον τὸ πρῶτον] This is a locution such as above III. v. 9. The natural expression would have been, ποιεῖ ἵνα ἡ γῆ τετέσιν οἱ κατοικοῦντες ἐν ἀυτῇ προσκυνήσωσι. Here I explain that καὶ as τετέσιν, for it is explanatory of the former. And προσκυνεῖν τὸ θηρίον τὸ πρῶτον is to serve the Roman religion, in the way that προσκυνεῖν is used also above 3. Πρῶτον for πρότερον is not rare among the Greeks. See John I. 30. Οἱ κατοικοῦντες ἐπὶ τῇ γῇ are the men of the Roman dominion. They did this by magic, by authority, and by example; as Apollonius did before the Sun, Jupiter, the Dodonaean, the Pythian Apollo, Amphiaraus, Trophonius, the Muses, and Aesculapius, all of which you have in Philostratus.

Or as the former treatment has it:

Καὶ ποιεῖ τὴν γῆν καὶ τὰς ἐν ἀυτῇ κατοικοῦντας, ἵνα προσκυνήσωσι τὸ θηρίον τὸ πρῶτον, & he made the earth and those dwelling in it worship the first beast] By their own authority and doctrine they brought it about that both the peoples as a whole publicly and individual men privately should persevere in the worship of false gods.

The Pontiff does this by his own authority, which he assumed for himself, so that the former beast, in the decrees which he promulgates for the benefit of the Papal kingdom, might be heard reverently throughout the whole empire and be religiously honored, nay, be adored like God, just as it was acclaimed to Paul V as Vice-God, in letters not without fate expressing the number of the beast, DCLVVVI.

But what shall we say concerning the immense pride of the beast? Pope Adrian IV was angry with Frederick Barbarossa by letter because he had placed his own name before the Papal one, to whom the Emperor therefore replied manfully: Is it recognized that in the time of Constantine Sylvester had any royal power? But by the concession of his piety, liberty was given to the Church, peace was restored, and whatever royal power it is recognized that your Papacy has, was given by the generosity of Princes, whence when we write back to the Roman Pontiff, we place our name first by ancient right. See Nauclerus, generation 39, vol. 2. Regarding the plots and insolence of the Roman Pontiff, the following is held in Nauclerus at the year 1212: Otto the Saxon, excommunicated, deposed, and removed from the empire, nevertheless conducted himself as Emperor, and in the Nuremberg assembly of Princes, he exposed the manifold cunning of the Roman Pontiff shown against him: We confess, he said, that it is of your right, not the Roman Pontiff's, to create and depose an Emperor at the same time. How Frederick II decided the insolence of the Pontiff should be checked, Aventinus records in book 7. Annals, page 541. How Innocent III arrogated to himself authority over the Emperor Baldwin of Constantinople, and when he alleged the Petrine admonition 'be subject to every human creature for God's sake, or to the King, etc.', gave him the reply that this is not a precept of law, but a counsel of humanity, can be read in C. solita, title on obedience and major authority. John XXII did not doubt that it was best for Christian affairs to write to the Emperor Louis the Bavarian himself in the year of Christ 1327, when the Roman Pontiff moderates both dignities at his own discretion, dominates the Church (which, according to Pontifical nomenclature and their ultimate analysis, is the Roman Pontiff himself), by his law and command every power is chosen, and the Emperor is bound by the religion of an oath to him who, by presiding over the earth, performs the role of the heavenly Emperor. He commanded then in the same public letters that Louis should within three months abdicate the royal name, government, and public functions, abstain entirely from managing affairs, rescind what he had done up to that point, and not resume power after this except by his order and mandate. Nor did Louis argue without cause against the Pontiff, by a public decree fortified by the votes of the nobles, that those excellent Pastors and gods of the earth and of men wish not only to be called, but also to be believed to be, those who drive the Caesar out of Italy and Rome, but especially that the Emperor and the Pastor, the Lord and the servant, are diverse and repugnant, and that the many-headed beast (behold the seven-headed beast denounced by the decree of the empire) and the two-headed monster are Augustus and the Supreme Pontiff. It is known among the common people that Boniface VIII proclaimed himself lord not only of France, but of the world, to whom Philip the Fair replied beautifully and manfully: Philip, by the grace of God, King of the Franks, to Boniface, acting as Supreme Pontiff, little or no greeting: Let your great foolishness know that we are not subject to anyone in temporal matters, and that the collation of churches and prebends pertains to us by royal right. This response the Parisian School did not disapprove, but confirmed with its own vote, as witnessed by Stephanus Aufrerius in his repetition of Clement I, on the office of the ordinary, no. 57. Julius II did not fear to threaten Louis XII, King of France, with deposition, to whom indeed the Council of Tours opposed itself in this way: That it is not lawful for the Roman Pontiff to pursue temporal Princes with arms outside the dominion of the Church, and if he attempts to vex anyone, it is lawful for that Prince to invade the lands of the Church to repel this injury; see John Serranus in his historical inventory. During the reign of Pius IV, excommunication was fulminated against the Queen of Navarre with a decree by which she was stripped of the kingdom of Navarre. Sixtus V and Gregory XIII excommunicated Henry IV of Navarre and subjected the ecclesiastics and other nobles of the kingdom to an interdict. Many other things of this kind we have involved in deliberate silence. And yet Grotius, playing the Pope, has tried to persuade

that the Popes and Roman Magistrates were under the faith and legitimate rule of the Ottos, and that Charlemagne was not declared Emperor by Pontifical authority, but by the Senate and the Roman people. How this may please the Pope, let those see who might happen to want to patronize Grotius.

whose deadly wound was healed) Again a Hebrew idiom, in which 'his' abounds. A grave wound had been inflicted on idolatry by the fall of the Capitol: add also the free preaching under Vespasian and Nerva. But Pythagorean magic brought some medicine to the wound. In the Manuscript: 'His wound'.

And before.

Whose deadly wound was healed) Many had believed that with the fall of the Capitol, all idolatry, of which it had been the principal seat, would collapse at the same time; but it happened far otherwise. For both the Capitol was restored, and at that very time Apollonius began to be known.

Maresius replies to the trifles of Grotius: Although Apollonius had begun to be known only after the Capitol was restored, as the Commentator falsely notes, yet neither he nor his magic directly brought any delay to the Gospel (unless perhaps because he caused by his tricks that Christ and the Apostles were slandered among some as having used magic in their miracles) or added any weight to Ethnic idolatry; since to the more sensible he was a subject of contempt and ridicule as an impostor and a wanderer, especially to Domitian, who had his hair and beard insultingly shaved off: Much less is he to be believed to have caused the Roman empire to be pursued with greater worship by the people than before, since no one was more insolent in that whole age toward the Caesars, as was also observed by Eusebius in his work against Hierocles. It is also false that Apollonius became known only at the time when the Capitol was restored. For Philostratus in book 4 testifies that he came to Rome under Nero in the consulship of Telesinus, and that his fame and name had already long been flying through the mouths of men. Baronius conjectures the consulship of Telesinus to be in the year of Christ 68, the 12th of Nero. Indeed, the same Philostratus in book 5 relates how he was sought out by Vespasian in Egypt and humbly asked to make himself King; which altogether preceded both the reign of Vespasian and the restoration of the Capitol by him. If also the first beast is established as idolatry, did not the Pontiff bring it about that it was worshipped everywhere, even by the admission of the Pontificians themselves, who trace the imitation of the paganism of the Gentile gods, images, festivals, and sacred processions of the Ambarvalia and all their rites: concerning which B. Nic. Hunnius is to be read in his Apostasy of the Roman Church, regarding Polydorus Vergilius. Not concerning the feigned death and resurrection of the Anti-Christ. c. 15. but concerning a wound to the head of one of the ten Kings who are members of the Anti-Christ, as Ribera wishes in that place. Alcasar judges that this is true of both, both of the Anti-Christ and of his members.

Latin:

Καὶ τὴν ἐξουσίαν τῦ πρώτου θηρίου πᾶσαν ποιεῖ, & potesta- tem prioris bestiæ omnem faciebat) Sacrificia celebrabant, & celebrari præcipiebant Magi. Ἐνώπιον ἀυτῶ, in conspectu ejus.] In honorem idolo- rum, ita hæc loquutio sumitur Luc. IV, 7. & alibi.

Quanto convenientius hoc de potestate Rom. Pontificis in honorem Romanæ idololatriæ & a- postaseos atque hærefeos, ab ipso Dracone datæ,

& à Rom. Pontifice ufurpatæ explicatur? aut et- iam ἐνώπιον ἀυτῶ (τᾶ πρώτω θηρίκ) quod pote- stas Cæsarea Papæ in conspectu prioris bestiæ Cæ- sarum Papalium, qui à Papa confirmantur, Papæ autoritatem venerantur & tuentur, Papalia decre- ta, bullas & Brevia exquuntur, & Ecclesiæ Roma- no-Papalis Advocati sunt, in quorum aulis Papa per suos juratos unicos Apostolicos, Cardinales, Archi-Episcopos, Episcopos, Abbates, Priores, Canonicos & Prælatos, Jesuitas, aliosque Mona- chos, Confessionarios, Sacrificulos, & reliquos Ordines, ac professos & quoscunque alios, juris- jurandi religione ad professionem fidei Romano- Catholicæ Tridentinæ adstrictos, ipsosque Con- siliarios Imperatores dominatur, exerceatur. Ea enim, quæ agit, & exequitur, non clam sed con- sciis talibus, & in conspectu ipsius imperii Papalis peragit bestia secunda vel terrestris Papa, Cæsare- am potestatem sive directam sive indirectam in se- cularia affectans: ut videantur quidem duæ bestiæ agere, altera per se, altera per sibi obnoxios, ma- rina per terrestrem, & terrena in conspectu ma- rinæ: revera tamen una tantum bestia proprie a- gat juxta illud: quod quis per alterum facit, ipse cen- setur fecisse. Bullæ etiam diversæ sunt Papales nem- pe, atque Edicta Cæsarea, etsi in utriusque certa ra- tione dominetur clerus Pontificius: unde sæpe ad eundem collimant scopum, ab eodem animatæ & agitatæ spiritu: Indit n. spiritum bestiæ marinæ ima- gini terrestris bestia, ut loquatur, more nempe suo, decreta, bullas, & brevia Papalia promulgando: quibus magnam partem regitur jure Canonico jam sancito, & recepto: à quo veluti formam certa ra- tione adeoq; spiritum nacta est imago bestiæ verius, quam bestia hoc est, umbra imperii magis, quam im- perium visa, antequam spiritu illo informaretur, & certam status rationem atque formam adipiscere- tur, quæ ut plurimum sese opere ipso exerit: ac de jure, á Pontifice Romano præscripto, semper sese exerere debebat. Quod vel Bulla Papalis Innocen- tii X. adversus pacem Monasteriensem testari potest. Nec immerito Lipsius ad mir. præfat. quicquid ex imperio restat, à Papa ceu Dictatore Romano exerce- ri & teneri, quod ex Cardinalium Senatu purpureo, tributis, legationibus ad exteros, Principum & Re- gum submissionibus erga sedem hanc concludit.

Καὶ ποιεῖ τὴν γῆν καὶ τὰς ἐν ἀυτῇ κατοικοῦντας, ἵνα προσκυ- νήσωσι τὸ θηρίον τὸ πρῶτον] Est locutio qualis supra III. v. 9. Naturalis elocutio fuerat, ποιεῖ ἵνα ἡ γῆ τετέσιν οἱ κατοικοῦν- τες ἐν ἀυτῇ προσκυνήσωσι. Hic καὶ illud per τετέσιν expono, est enim ἐξηγητικὸν prioris. Et προσκυνεῖν τὸ θηρίον τὸ πρῶ- τον est religioni Romanæ inservire, quomodo προσκυνεῖν su- mitur & supra 3. Πρῶτον pro πρότερον non rarum Græcis. Vide Joh. I. 30. Οἱ κατοικοῦντες ἐπὶ τῇ γῇ homines ditionis Romanæ. Faciebant hoc magi autoritate & exemplo; ut Apollonius apud Solem. Jovem, Dodonæum, Apollinem Py- thium, Amphiaraum, Trophonium, Musas, Æsculapium, quæ omnia habes apud Philostratum.

Vel ut prior habet tractatio:

Καὶ ποιεῖ τὴν γῆν καὶ τὰς ἐν ἀυτῇ κατοικοῦντας, ἵνα προσ- κυνήσωσι τὸ θηρίον τὸ πρῶτον, & fecit terram & habitantes in ea adorare bestiam primam] Sua autoritate & doctri- na efficiebant, ut & populi universi publice & homines singuli privatim in cultu falsorum Deorum persevera- rent.

Facit id Pontifex pro autoritate sua, quam ipse sibi sumpsit, ut prior bestia in decretis, quæ in gratiam regni Papalis promulgat, reverenter in toto imperio audiatur, atque religiose honoretur, imo instar Dei adoretur, quemadmodum PaV- Lo V. VICe Deo acclamatum fuit, literis non absque fato numerum bestiæ DCLVVVI. expri- mentibus.

Quid vero de immenso fastu bestiæ dicemus? A- drianus IV. Pontifex Frider. Barbarossæ per literas succensuit, quod nomen suum Papali præposuerit, cui proinde Imperator mascule respondit: Num- quid tempore Constantini Sylvester Regalis aliquid habere dignoscitur? Sed ejus pietatis concessione li- bertas data Ecclesiae, pax restituta, & quicquid Re- galis Papatus vester habere dignoscitur, largitione Principum donatum, unde cum Romano Pontifici rescribimus, jure ex antiquo nomen nostrum praepo- nimus. Vid. Naucler. gener. 39. vol. 2. De insidiis & insolentia Pontificis Romani apud Naucler. ad ann. 1212. ista habentur: Otto Saxo excommunica- tus, depositus & ab imperio abrogatus nihilominus pro Imperatore se gessit, & in conventu Noribergen- si Principum multiplices Rom. Pontificis contra se ostensas calliditates exposuit: Vestri, inquiens, ju- ris esse fatemur, non Romani Pontificis, Imperato- rem creare simul & destituere. Quomodo insolen- tiam Pontificis compefcendam statuerit Fridericus II. commemorat Aventinus l. 7. Annal. pag. 541. Quomodo Innocentius III. inBalduinum Imperato- rem Constantin. sibi jus arrogarit, eiq; Petrinum monitum alleganti subditi estote omni humana crea- turae propter Deum sive Regi &c. id responsi dederit, quod id non sit praeceptum juris, sed consilium huma- nitatis, legere est C. solita tit. de obedient. & major. Optime rebus Christianis consultum tum fore non dubitavit Johannes XXII. ad Imperatorem ipsum Ludovicum Bavarum Ann. Christi 1327. perscribe- re, quando Pontifex Rom. dignitatem utramque suo arbitratu moderatur, Ecclesia dominatur (quae jux- ta nomenclaturam Pontificiam, ultimamque eo- rum analysin est Pontifex ipse Romanus) ejus lege atque imperio omnis potestas eligitur, & Impera- tor religione sacramenti ei, qui terris praesidendo vi- cem caelestis Imperatoris perfungitur, addictus est. Praecepit inde iisdem literis publicis, ut Ludovicus intra menses tres sese abdicet a Regio nomine, guberna- tione, functionibus publicis, rebus gerendis penitus abstineat, a se hactenus acta rescindat, nec post hac nisi jussu & mandato suo potestatem refumat. Nec abs re arguit Ludovicus Pontificem decreto publi- co procerum suffragiis munito, quod Caesarem Ita- lia Rome extrudere egregii illi Pastores Deosque ter- rarum hominumque se non solum dici, sed etiam cre- di velint, maxime autem diversa sint, & repugnent Imperator & Pastor, Dominus & servus, bellua multorum capitum (en bestiam septicipitem ex de- creto imperii denunciatam) & monstrum biceps sit Augustus & Pontifex Maximus. In vulgo notum est, Bonifacium VIII. non solum Gallia, sed mundi Dominum se predicasse, cui Philippus Pulcer pulcre & mascule rescripsit: Philippus Dei gratia, Fran- corum Rex Bonifacio se gerenti pro summo Pontifice salutem modicam sive nullam: Sciat tua maxima fatuitas in temporalibus nos alicui non subesse, Eccle- siarum & praebendarum collationem ad nos jure Re- gio pertinere. Quod responsum non improbavit Schola Parisiensis, sed calculo suo confirmavit teste Stephano Aufrerio in repetit. Clement. I. de offic. or- dinar. n. 57. Julius II. Ludovico XII. Gallia Rege non veritus est exautoratiouem minitari, cui vero Turonense Concilium se hoc modo opposuit: Non licere Pontifici Romano armis prosequi Principes temporales extra dominium Ecclesiae, & si quem ve- xare attentet, licere ei Principi ad hanc propulsan- dam injuriam invadere terras Ecclesiae; vid. Joh. Serranus in invent. hist. Gal. Pio IV. sedente ex- communicatio fulminata est in Reginam Navarra cum decreto, quo regno Navarrae exuebatur. Six- tus V. & Gregorius XIII. Henricum IV. Navarræum excommunicavit, & interdicto subjecit Ecclesia- sticos aliosque regni Proceres. Alia ejus generis plurima consulto silentio involvimus. Et persua- dere tamen adhuc Grotius Papizans conatus est,

Papas & Magist. Romanos sub fide & imperio legi- timo Ottonum fuisse, Carolumque M. non Pontificia autoritate,sed a Senatu & populo Romano Imperatore renunciatum fuisse. Quod quomodo Papæ placitu- rů sit, viderint, quiGrotio forte patrocinari velint.

ὃυ ἐθεραπεύθη πληγὴ τῦ θανάτε ἀυτῦ) Rursus Ebraica lo- quutio, in qua abundat ἀυτῦ. Idololatriæ grave vulnus infli- ctum fuerat lapsu Capitolii: adde & libera prædicatione sub Vespasiano & Nerva. Sed vulneri medicamen aliquod attu- lit magia Pythagorica. In Manuscripto: Ἡ πληγὴ ἀυτῦ.

Et antea.

Ὅυ ἐθεραπεύθη ἡ πληγὴ τῦ θανάτυ ἀυτῦ, cujus curata est plaga mortis) LapsoCapitolio futurum multi crediderant, ut tota simul idololatria, cujus ibi præcipua sedes fuerat, corrueret; sed longe aliter evenit. Nam & Capitolium restitutum fuit, & eo ipso tempore nosci cœpit Apollon.

Ad nugas Grotii respondet Maresius: Etsi Apol- lonius innotescere cæpisset demum post Capitolium restitutum, ut Commentator falso notat, tamen nec ipse nec ipsius magia direct̄e ullam remoram attulit Evangelio, (nisi forte quod præstigiis suis effecit, ut Christus & Apostoli traducerentur apud nonnullos, tanquam usi magia in miraculis suis) aut idololatria Ethnica ullum adjecit pondus; cum cordatioribus tanquam impostor & erro contemtui & deridiculo fuerit, Domitiano præsertim, qui illi comam & bar- bam contumeliose abradi fecit: Multo minus effecisse credendus, ut imperium Roman.majori quam antea cultu populi prosequerentur, cum nemo procacior to- to illo ævo in Cæsares fuerit, ut etiam ab Eusebio in Hieroclem observatum est. Id quoque falsum est,eo de- mum tempore, quo Capitolium restitutum est, Apollo- nium innotuisse. Nam Philostratus l. 4. testatur, eum sub Nerone venisse Romam Telesino Cos. & jam antea diu ejus famam nomenque per ora virum volitasse. Consulatum vero Telesini conjicit Baronius in annum Chr. 68. 12. Neronis. Imo & idem Philostratus l. 5. refert,quo pacto a Vespasiano in Ægypto quæsitus fue- rit, & suppliciter rogatus, ut Regem se faceret; quod omnino præcessit & Vespasiani imperium & Capitolii per ipsum restitutionẽ. Si etiam prior bestia idololatria statuatur, annon effecit Pontifex, ut ea passim adora- retur,vel ipsismet Pontificiis fatentib.gentilium divo- rum, simulacrorum, festorum, pomparum sacrarum Ambarvalium Rituum omnium suorum in paganismů κακοζηλίαν referentibus: Quo de è Polydoro Virgilio legendus B.Nic.Hunnius in Apost. Ecclesiæ Rom.Non de Anti-Christi ficta morte et resurrectione. Hoc etiam Bellarm.placuit l. III. de Rom. pontif. c. 15. sed de vul- nere capiti alicujus è decẽ Regibus Anti-Christi mem- bris,ut Ribera in b.l. vult. Alcasar de utroque id esse verum judicat,& de Anti-Christo & de ejus membris.

## 13:12
v. 12. And he performs great signs) As that Simon the Samaritan did before. See what was said at 2 Thess. 2:9. A tree spoke to Apollonius. An Empusa was put to flight by him. A pestilence walking about in the guise of a beggar was suppressed at Ephesus. A leg was drawn out of a fetter. He himself suddenly disappeared from the place of judgment. He predicted many things. Among other things, he signified the murder of Domitian at Ephesus at the very time that that event was being carried out at Rome. Concerning all these and many other truly stupendous things, see Philostratus and Lactantius at the cited place. Here below he is called the False Prophet, ch. 16:13, 19:20, 20:10.

And that he should make fire come down from heaven onto the earth in the sight of men] That was done both when Apollonius was born, and when he had raised the image of Achilles.

Latin:

v. 12. Καὶ ποιεῖ σημεῖα μεγάλα, & fecit signa magna) Ut ante Simon ille Samarita. Vide quae dicta ad 2. Thes. 2, 9. Arbor loquuta Apollonio. Empusa ab eo fugata Pestilentia sub habitu mendici obambulans oppressa Ephesi. Crus e compede eductum. Ipse ex judicii loco subito disparuit. Praedixit multa. Inter caetera caedem Domitiani significavit Ephesi eo ipso tempore, quo Ro- mae ea res peragebatur. De quibus omnibus aliisque mul- tis sane stupendis vide Philostratum & Lactantium dicto loc. Hic infra Pseudo-Proph. dicitur, c. 16, 13. c. 19, 20. c. 20, 10.

Καὶ πῦρ ἵνα ἐκ τῦ ὐρανῦ καταβαίνῃ ἐπὶ τὴν γῆν ἐνώπιον τῶν ἀνθρώπων, ut etiam ignem faceret de caelo descendere in ter- ram in conspectu hominum] Id factum & cum Apolloni- us nasceretur, & cum simulachrum Achillis excitasset.

## 13:13
v. 13. And he doeth great wonders) Such as Simon Magus had done: concerning whom see what is said in 2 Thess. II, 9.

And that he should make fire come down from heaven upon the earth) Magicians are said to do what Demons do at their invocation. Thus they call down fires from heaven, as Apollonius does in Philostratus V, 5. Thus they imitate Elijah, just as Jannes and Mambres imitated Moses. And it is a transposition, with 'that' (ἵνα) placed after the noun, as in John XIII, 20; Rom. XI, 31.

Latin:

v. 13. Καὶ ποιῇ σημεῖα μεγάλα) Qualia fecerat Simon Magus: de quo vide, quæ dicta 2. Thess. II, 9.

Καὶ πῦρ ἵνα ἐκ τῦ ὐρανῦ καταβαίνῃ ἐπὶ τὴν γῆν) Facere di- cuntur magi, quod ad eorum invocationem faciunt Demo- nes. Sic ignes cœlo devocant, ut Apollonius apud Philo- stratum V, 5. Ita Eliam imitantur, quomodo Jannes & Mambres Mosem. Et est trajectio ἵνα post nomen posito, ut Joh. XIII, 20. Rom. XI, 31.

## 13:14
v. 14. And deceiveth them that dwell on the earth by the means of those miracles which he had power to do in the sight of the beast) Explain 'in the sight of' as above in 12. Such are those in the history of Apollonius: a tree that spoke, an Empusa put to flight, a pestilence walking about in the guise of a beggar suppressed at Ephesus, a leg drawn out of a shackle: his own invisible departure from the place of judgment: the murder of Domitian predicted at the time it was happening.

Saying to them that dwell on the earth, that they should make an image to the beast, which had the wound by a sword, and did live.) This can be taken concerning the shade of Achilles, if you interpret 'saying to make' as 'saying that he had made'. Philostratus calls it the 'Vision of Achilles' in IV, 1, and adds that after that event the Thessalians were warned by Apollonius to perform sacrifices to Achilles. It should be known, however, that in many places of the Roman Empire the cult of Achilles existed, as among the Ibians, according to Athenagoras; at the straits of Maeotis, as Strabo teaches in book XI; in Leuconotus, as the Periplus has it; in the island of his own name and elsewhere, as Philostratus in his Heroicus and Pliny V, 3 and X, 29 have it. Eusebius, writing against Hierocles, acknowledges this history about the shade of Achilles speaking through Apollonius to be true. But also other deeds of this kind by Apollonius are recorded by Vopiscus in these words: he restored life to the dead. But if you wish to translate λόγων ποιῆσαι, commanding it to be done, you will be able to interpret it concerning the disciples of the magician Apollonius, who ordered an image to be made for Apollonius, through which a demon uttered oracles. For the writer of the responses to the orthodox openly testifies to this. And Vopiscus explicitly says that Apollonius was held as a god. Lactantius, however, V. 3. That his image, set up under the name of Hercules Alexiacus, remained among the Ephesians until his own time. But both the raising of a shade and those images uttering a voice are rightly said to be done τῷ θηρίῳ, that is, for the use and honor of the Roman religion. And it had been wounded by the sword, that is, by the preaching of the Gospel under Nerva. But it recovered its strength through magical arts: which here is ἔζησε for ἀνέζησε, the simple for the compound, in the Hebrew manner. And it is an elegant comparison of the sign and the thing signified. A dead or lifeless man seen as living. So too with idolatry. The statue pleased Nebuchadnezzar. But Daniel saw that it was nothing other than a troop of wild beasts.

Latin:

v. 14. Καὶ πλανᾷ τὺς κατοικῦντας ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς διὰ τά ση- μεῖα, ἃ ἐδόθη αὐτῷ ποιῆσαι ἐνώπιον τῦ θηρίυ) ἐνώπιον expone ut supra 12. Talia sunt in Apollonii historia, locuta arbos, fugata Empusa, pestilentia sub habitu mendici obambulans oppressa Ephesi, crus e compede eductum: ipsius ex judicii loco inconspicuus abitus: prædicta, quo tempore fiebat, Domitiani cædes.

Λέγων τοῖς κατοικῦσιν ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς,εἰκόνα ποιῆσαι τῷ θηρίῳ, ὃ εἶχε τὴν πληγὴν τῆς μαχαίρας κὼ ἔζησε.) Potest hoc de umbra Achillis sumi, si λέγων ποιῆσαι interpreteris dicens se fecisse. Εἶδον Ἀχιλλέως vocat Philostratus IV, 1. additque post id fa- ctum monitos ab Apollonio Thessalos, ut Achilli sacra fa- cerent. Sciendum autem multis in locis Romani imperii cultum fuisse Achillis, ut apud Ibium teste Athenagora, apud angustias Mœotidis docente Strabone XI. in Leu- conoto, ut habet Periplus in sui nominis insula & alibi, ut habent PhilostratusHeroicis, Plinius V,3. X, 29. Historiam autem hanc de umbra Achillis per Apollonium locuta, ve- ram agnoscit Eusebius contra Hieroclem scribens. Sed & alia alia hujusmodi facta ab Apollonio memorat Vopiscus his ver- bis: ille mortuis reddidit vitam. Quod si velis λόγων ποι- ῆσαι vertere, jubens fieri, interpretari poteris de magis Apol- lonii discipulis, qui Apollonio simulachrum fieri jussere, per quod Daemon oracula edidit. Aperte enim id testatur scri- ptor responsionum ad orthodoxos. Et pro Deo habitum A- pollonium diserte ait Vopiscus. Lactantius vero V. 3. Si- mulacrum ejus sub Herculis Alexiaci nomine constitutum ab Ephesiis mansisse ad sua tempora. Tam autem umbrae exci- tatio, quam simulacra ista vocem edentia, recte dicuntur fa- cta τῷ θηρίῳ, id est, in usum honoremque Romanae religio- nis. Et vulnerata fuerat gladio, hoc est praedicatione Evan- gelii sub Nerva. Sed per magicas artes vires recuperavit: quod hic est ἔζησε pro ἀνέζησε simplex pro composito, more Hebraeo. Et est elegans comparatio signi & rei signatae. Ho- mo mortuus aut exanimis imago visa vivere. Sic & idolola- tria. Statua placebat Nabuchodonosoro. At Daniel vidit eam nihil esse aliud quam ferarum agmen.

## 13:14
v. 14. And he deceives those dwelling on the earth because of the signs which were given to him to perform in the sight of the beast] Ἐνώπιον in the sight of here is in honor of, as also above. Those signs tended toward restoring strength to the failing idolatry. By his own example, he led the way to sacrificing to the Sun, to Jupiter Dodonaeus, to Apollo Pythius, to Amphiaraus, to Trophonius, to the Muses, to Aesculapius.

saying to those dwelling on the earth, that they should make an image to the beast] I interpret Λέγων saying as preaching, and ποιῆσαι as not about the inhabitants of the earth, but about himself. He boasted that the image was raised by him, so that by that argument men would believe that honor should be given to the gods, contrary to what the Christians were teaching. That εἰκὼν image was the εἶδος of Achilles himself, as Philostratus speaks, whom see IV. 5. That image wished to explicitly warn the Thessalians to restore the interrupted sacrifices to Achilles. O'ς ἔχει τὴν πληγὴν τῆς μαχαίρας καὶ ἔζησε, which has the wound of the sword, and lived] That sword is the announcement of the Gospel throughout the whole world, Heb. 4:12; by it, idolatry had received such a wound that it seemed about to perish: but it revived, primarily by the authority of magic.

Latin:

v. 14. Καὶ πλανᾷ τὺς λαὺς τὺς κατοικῦντας ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς διὰ σημεῖα ἃ ἐδόθη αὐτῷ ποιῆσαι ἐνώπιον τῦ θηρίυ] Et se- duxit habitantes in terra propter signa quae data sunt illi facere in conspectu bestiae] Ἐνώπιον in conspectu hic est in honorem, ut & supra. Eo illa signa tendebant, ut i- dololatriae labascenti vires restituerentur. Exemplo ipse suo praeivit ad sacrificandum Soli, Jovi, Dodonaeo, Apolli- ni Pythio, Amphiarao, Trophonio, Musis, Aesculapio.

Λέγων τοῖς κατοικῦσιν ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς, εἰκόνα ποιῆσαι τῷ θη- ρίῳ, dicens habitantibus in terra, fecisse se imaginem bestiae] Λέγων dicens interpretor praedicans, & ποιῆσαι fumo non de habitatoribus terrae, sed de ipso. Jactavit a se excitatum simulachrum, ut eo argumento crederent homines Diis habendum honorem, contra quam Christiani docebant. Ea εἰκὼν imago fuit ipsius Achillis εἶδος, ut loquitur Philo- stratus, quem vide IV. 5. Id simulachrum voluit diserte monere Thessalos, ut intermissa sacra Achilli instaurarent* O'ς ἔχει τὴν πληγὴν τῆς μαχαίρας καὶ ἔζησε, quæ habet gla- dii plagam, & vixit] Machæra ista est Evangelii annunti- atio per totum orbem Ebr. 4, 12. per eam idololatria vul- nus tantum acceperat, ut peritura videretur: sed revixit magiæ imprimis autoritate.

## 13:15
v. 15. And it was given to him to give spirit to the image of the beast] Magic gave spirit or voice, whether to a shade or to an image. But this genitive τῦ θηρίου here is indicative of possession, because these things served idolatry. The voice is called Spirit, because it is accustomed to be the judgment of life, which is called רוח.

And that the image of the beast should speak] And this is true whether you take it of a shade or of a statue. That images speak is a wonderful thing, yet not incredible. You have this in Roman histories, and in Valerius Maximus concerning the images of Juno Moneta, Fortuna, Muliebris, and Silvanus: And Moses Maimonides in part III, ch. 24 of the Guide for the Perplexed says that he had read two books about speaking images. That ἵνα is governed by ἐδόθη αὐτῷ which preceded it.

And should cause those who do not worship the image of the beast, that they should be killed] Philostratus says it is believed by most that Apollonius lived beyond his hundredth year. The same says he was a friend of Nerva. Wherefore we rightly conclude that he was also a friend of Trajan, and that the persecution stirred up against the Christians was at the persuasion of Apollonius and other magicians: Just as Iamblichus, being both a Pythagorean and a magician, was the author for Julian of abandoning Christianity. Moreover, the article here in τῇ εἰκόνι is placed for the genus of images itself, in the way Proclus teaches in Plato's Republic that the article is often placed, and thus ἄνθρωπος is said for the human race. Examples of this usage are not rare in our own books also, as Gen. 3:8, Exod. 8:6, 10:12, Judg. 2:14, Sirach 43:21, Matt. 19:10, Mark 2:27, 3:26, 7:23, John 2:25, 7:51, Rom. 4:6, Jas. 1:7. See also Eph. 16:1, and what is said there, and ch. 21:7, 25:3, and Jer. 5:25, and ch. 32:43, Ezek. 6:7. Understand that they were to be killed as referring to the Bishops and Presbyters. For the common people were deprived of trade, as we shall now say. From this edict of Trajan, Bishops were affected with the punishment of death: Anacletus of the Roman Church, Simon the son of Cleopas of the Jerusalem Church, Ignatius of Antioch, Onesimus of Ephesus.

Latin:

v. 15. Καὶ ἐδόθη αὐτῷ πνεῦμα δοῦναι τῇ εἰκόνι τοῦ θηρίου] Spi- ritum sive vocem dedit magia, sive umbrae sive simulacro. Iste autem Genitivus τῦ θηρίου hic est significativus dominii, quia res istae serviebant idololatriae. Vox dicitur Spiritus, quia solet judicium esse vitae, quae dicitur רוח.

Καὶ ἵνα λαλήσῃ ἡ εἰκὼν τῦ θηρίου] Et hoc verum sive de um- bra accipias, sive de statua. Imagines loqui res mira, non tamen incredibilis. Habes id in historiis Romanis, & Va- lerio Maximo de simulachris Junonis Monetae, Fortunae, Muliebris, Silvani: Et Moses Maimonides parte III. c. 24. Ductoris dubitantium, duos sibi libros lectos ait de imagini- bus loquutis. Illud ἵνα regitur ab ἐδόθη αὐτῷ quod prae- cessit.

Καὶ ποιήσῃ τὺς μὴ προσκυνῦντας τῇ εἰκόνι τῦ θηρίου, ἵνα ἀπο- κτανθῶσι] Ait Philostratus a plerisque credi ultra centesi- mum annum vixisse Apollonium. Idem ait Nervae fuisse amicum. Quare & Trajano fuisse amicum recte colligimus, & persecutionem in Christianos excitatam suadente Apollo- nio & magis aliis: Sicut Jamblichus pariter & Pythagoricus & magus Juliano autor fuit deserendi Christianismi. Est autem hic articulus in τῇ εἰκόνι positus pro genere ipso imaginum, quomodo articulum saepe poni docet Proclus in Republica Platonis, ac ita dici ἄνθρωπος pro humano genere. Exempla ejus loquutionis in nostris quoque libris non rara, ut Gen. III. 8. Exod. VIII. 6. X. 12. Jud. II. 14. Sirach. 43, 21. Matth. 19, 10. Marc. 2, 27. c. 3, 26. c. 7, 23. Joh. 2, 25. c. 7, 51. Rom. 4, 6. Jac. 1, 7. Vide & Ef. 16, 1. & ibi dicta, & c. 21, 7. c. 25, 3. & Jer. 5, 25. & c. 32, 43. Ezech. 6, v. 7. Ut occiderentur intellige de Episcopis & Presbyteris. Nam plebejus commercia adimebantur, ut jam dicemus. Ex hoc Trajani edicto supplicio mortis affecti Episcopi, Romanae Ec- clesiae Anacletus, Hierosolymitanae Simon Cleopae filius, An- tioch. Ignatius, Ephesinae Onesimus.

## 13:15
v. 15. And it was given to him to give spirit to the image of the beast, & datum est illi, ut daret Spiritum imagini bestiæ] Given to him by the Devil, God permitting, so that that image might seem to live. It is a locution κατὰ φάσιν according to that which appeared, as 1 Sam. XXVIII. 14. Moreover, it is called εἰκὼν τῦ θηρίε the image of the beast, because it served to commend idolatry.

And that the image of the beast might speak] The very words are in Philostratus; but he himself, Apollonius, was worshipped as a god on account of these deeds, as Vopiscus teaches us from Aurelian, and Lactantius, and his image also spoke by the power of a Demon. The writer of the responses to the orthodox: Αὐτὸν δὲ τὸν Δαίμονα ἐν τῷ ἐκείνε ἀγάλματι ἱδρυνόμενον τὸν ἐκ ταῖς μαντείαις ἀπατήσαντα τὲς ἀνθρώπες ὡς Θεὸν σέβειν κῷ τιμᾷν τὸν Ἀπολλώνιον, ἐφίμωσε καταργήσας ἀυτῦ τὰς μαν- τείας; he made the Demon himself, who was dwelling in his statue and deceiving men through prophecies so that they would worship and venerate Apollonius as a God, fall silent, destroying his prophecies; namely Christ, of whom the discourse is there.

And that he might cause those who do not worship the image of the beast, that they should be killed.] Εἰκόνι image here for any idol, the singular for the plural. Since Apollonius was a friend of Nerva, and lived on to the times of Trajan, and indeed even enjoyed the friendship of Trajan, it should not be doubted. And Trajan, confirmed in the worship of idols by authority, wished to compel Christians to the same worship by the fear of the most severe punishments: clearly as Julian had Iamblichus, not unlike Apollonius, as an advisor to wicked things: whom Spartianus also notes to have accomplished many things through magicians.

To these things we add nothing else than what Maresius has in his dissertation, to which Grotius attempted to respond in the Appendix, so that those things may be compared: That the bringing down of fire from heaven is attributed to Apollonius by the Commentator, because lightning is said to have fallen at his very birth, Philostr. book 1, and also because the image of Achilles, having been awakened by him, departed after the conversation was finished, with a moderate flash of lightning emitted, as Philostr. has it, book 4, does not make to the point. For besides the fact that faith is not to be rashly placed in these matters in the most lying Philostratus, who is rhetorizing everywhere, whom Eusebius expressly accused of vanity, certainly it cannot be attributed to the nascent Apollonius, and what others are reported by historians to have been born in the past with the sky thundering and lightning as an omen of a future life, whom nevertheless no sane person would say for that reason brought fire from heaven to earth ἐνώπιον τῶν ἀνθρώπων, in the sight of men. But the latter deed was done secretly without any witness, not by Apollonius himself, but by a summoned Demon, nor did it rest on anything else than the report of the Impostor himself. But these miracles and prodigies are conspicuous in the Roman Antichrist, who once terrified the whole world with the brute thunderbolts of his excommunications, and whose Ministers and Quaestors, in the memory of our fathers, used to avenge neglected indulgences or relics with the sacred fire of Anthony sent from heaven: not to mention what exists in Benno concerning Gregory VII. That he shook sparks of fire from his sleeves by magical arts. The words of Benno are: When he wished this, he would shake his sleeves, and it would fly apart in the manner of sparks of fire: and with these miracles he would deceive the eyes of the simple as if it were a sign of holiness. Concerning Zacharias, Ranulph reports in Pol. book V. ch. 25. that he made fiery clouds precede him in the night time; and Anonymous, that flashes of lightning accompanied the image of Clement through the whole space. Furthermore, concerning the miracle of the fire descending from heaven, some observe that it is not necessary that those things which occur in the Apocalypse, as being mystical, should be explained according to the letter: Thus Piscator, Pareus, Mede, Cotterius, Gerhard: But concerning the heavenly fire, the Holy Spirit, which the Pope boasts of, B. Nicolai, B. Grave, and Artopæus understand, as also B. Hœ, Cluverus, Bullingerus, Pareus. Concerning the lightning of Papal excommunication take it B. Cramerus, B. Winckelmannus, Döling, Dürfeld, Hoë, Heilbrunnerus, Szegedinus, Napeir, as also Pareus, Crugotius; concerning Ignatius Loyola, Danhawer. There are not lacking, however, those who bring forward Papal examples concerning physical fire produced through magical prestidigitations, Napeirus, Hoëus, B. Hülsemann. Brev. p. 458. Lyra wishes the angel Gabriel to be signified by fire interpreted concerning Mahomet, and the moon, a part of which he pretended to hold in his hand.

These things cannot be accepted concerning the hands of Achilles, evoked by Apollonius: for he can be called neither the former nor the latter beast, nor magic, nor idolatry, or an idol in the Roman empire or among the Roman Emperors: who, tracing their origin to Trajan, were far removed from Achilles. More correctly, the battle is understood through the sword of the Vitellians and the Flavians. What was done here by Apollonius was done secretly from everyone: nor is it entirely undoubted, nor is the image of the beast or of idolatry conveniently enough called that which serves to commend it, because an image receives its denomination not from the use to which it is destined, but from its archetype, or it can be taught that Apollonius was worshipped as a God because he gave life to an image: Nor does Justin at least say that Christ destroyed the prophecies concerning him, and as it were imposed silence upon Satan dwelling in his image. Whence more conveniently Maresius: It was granted to the Pontiff by divine providence to give life to the image of the former beast excited in himself, that is, to procure efficacy and authority for his Hierarchical domination, and at the same time to be able to speak, that is, to establish laws, to promulgate diplomas, edicts, and decrees, and thus to attain a Dictatorial authority as if not dissimilar. To which matter also various miracles and prodigies of images served, namely of those sweating or shedding blood, or even speaking, as if they had been living and animated. Examples are obvious to anyone, if there is faith in the storytellers, which is owed to them no less than to the commentator Philostratus. It is known what the image of the Crucifix said to Thomas: You have written well of me, Thomas, what reward will you receive? To say nothing of the magical image of Sylvester II made of bronze, which, when consulted in doubtful matters, answered him, he acknowledges in the Appendix. Grotius, that magic was among the forbidden things at Rome: How then did it arrive at such authority there, especially under Domitian and Trajan, whom he by no means shows to have been devoted to magic, when Suetonius and Philostratus testify rather the contrary concerning the former, an open enemy of Apollonius, about whom Jerome doubts whether he was a Magus, Suidas denies it, Eusebius leaves in the middle whether the things narrated about him are true or fabulous; so that he might sustain and restore the faltering idolatry, and heal the wound inflicted upon it by the preaching of the Gospel? Nor does it contribute anything to the matter or to the times of Domitian or Trajan that Hierocles equated Apollonius to Christ at the time of Constantine. And ought there not to have been an agreement between Apollonius and Domitian, if the first beast was Domitian, and Apollonius the same Pseudo-Prophet as Aquibas Barchocheba, concerning whom he had dealt at Matthew XXIV. 24.

But how is magic best said to have risen from the earth in those times, because those addicted to it were neither powerful nor noble, unless the same must be said of the Christian religion 1 Cor. I. 26. The phrase 'ascends from the earth' is explained by Ribera, it was similar to those which are seen on the earth in no terrible form, as sea monsters are wont to be, because at that time, or even to Apollonius himself, abstinence from Venus and a softer vice was proper, it is not sufficiently established by any witness. Whatever Apollonius also did, it pertained to the times of Nero. And it truly contributes little to this that it is reported that at the birth of Apollonius a lightning bolt fell from heaven to earth, which Eusebius also held for a fable, or that he departed from Apollonius secretly, not without some faint lightning, and it is predicted here what was still to be, not what had already been done long ago. But the Gloss interlinear interprets those words λέγων ποιῆσαι beyond the intention of others as enunciative, saying 'it renders' [meaning] 'commanding', and when St. John had spoken about the power received, it was more appropriate to follow up what he commanded for it. Furthermore, without cause the singular is put for the plural, indeed against the series of the context and the article demonstrating the image of which there is speech. Suidas, however, clearly teaches that Apollonius died under Nerva, Eusebius l. 4. c. 2. that the doctrine of the Gospel flourished most under Trajan; which in no way agree with the prophecy of the Apostle, nor do they square with the Grotian opinion concerning the healing of the wound. But concerning the Antichristian ones, B. Cluver brought these forward: Laurent. Valla in his oration on the donation of Constantine: Our storytellers, he says, everywhere introduce speaking idols. Luitprandus l. 1. c. 8. writes concerning the affairs of Europe: When the body of Formosus was brought into the church of Peter, the sacred images greeted it venerably. John Foxe in the Martyrology p. 1188 reports that in the time of Henry VIII there was a certain idol in England called the image of 'grace', elaborated with wheels and weights in such a way that someone occupying its cavity could move the individual parts of the idol, the mouth, hands, eyes, lips, and that it reached out a hand to those bringing gifts, and looked with a sad countenance upon those giving little, and with a cheerful one upon those giving much. Stumpffius lib. 13. Chron. Helvet. c. 34. notes that certain statues of the Saints, with their heads excavated and oil poured in, were seen to weep. And in the Apology of the Augsburg Confession, chapter on the invocation of Saints, the Confessors testify that they saw in a certain monastery an image of the Blessed Virgin, which, as if it were an automaton moved by bronze, could either turn away from those petitioning or nod in agreement. And that such an image existed at Constantinople, Evagrius writes in Book V of his Ecclesiastical History, chapter 8, which, when the captive Anatolius wished to venerate, it turned away from him. Nor, however, is the same person entirely alien to our explanation proposed earlier: wherever the Pope had once placed some idol of his own dominion, he gradually animated it through his apostles in such a way that he finally compelled the peoples to receive it as both divine and sacrosanct. For he fashioned a forum for himself in Europe and elsewhere, and converted ecclesiastical functions into powerful satrapies, with the chief authority of kingdoms transferred to them, so that nothing was held to be ratified and valid any longer without bishops, abbots, and priests sworn to him.

Finally, that Apollonius extended his days until the times of Trajan is hardly credible, nor is it certain that he would have induced Trajan to persecute Christians if he had been intimate with him: whose persecution was slow and mild, even if long-lasting, not as bitter as that which is predicted here, which, as Anti-Christian, is most fitting for the Roman Pontiff. Hence the saying 'more fortunate than Augustus, better than Trajan' in Curtius, book 8. To whom the ancients were even so inclined that they said the soul of Trajan was recalled from the underworld by the prayers of Gregory. See Origen, Mechtild's revelations. Therefore, neither the Capitol, nor Apollonius, nor Simon the Samaritan have anything to do with this. Regarding the healing of the wound of the empire, and regarding miracles, whether true or fictitious, since these pertain to the times of the Anti-Christ, the discussion is about that, not about the time of the Apostles; Grotius perverts everything according to his custom, so that the Anti-Christ may remain hidden.

That they might give them marks on their right hand, or on their foreheads] The Magi were the authors to Trajan that he should forbid hetaeriae, that is, sodalities or all colleges, as can be seen in Pliny, book 10, epistle 97, with the exception of those which gathered in the name of religion, namely pagan, L. 1. §. Sed religionis D. de collegiis. But since men by nature love associations, it happened from this that there was no one in the Roman Empire who did not give his name to an association dedicated to some one of the gods, whence names of colleges, which can be seen in Gruter's Inscriptions. Those who were enrolled in these colleges at the same time received on their body some χάραγμα, that is, a sign of a god, or an explicit name of a god, or one disguised by numbers, which two things are to be understood here from what follows. Prudentius: When the one to be consecrated receives the seal, they bring small needles to the furnaces, with these they proceed to burn the limbs, and as they have become fiery, whatever part of the body the burning mark has branded, they declare him thus consecrated. Philo, explaining the same thing, says: 'Of those who enslave themselves to things made by hand with a heated iron.' The most frequent parts of the body on which letters, or signs, or numbers were imprinted were the forehead and that joint between the hand and the arm. The custom of marking the forehead is from the East, where slaves carried the names of their masters on their forehead so that they could be recognized. We showed this above VII. 3. See also IX. 4. and Plutarch, Nicias at the end: where there is 'horses branded on the forehead.' Now gods are the masters of those serving them, whence the name בעלים; concerning the other part, there is testimony in Lucian, on the Syrian Goddess, where he says the Assyrians are 'branded on the wrists.' This custom was derived from soldiers. For 'the brands are of those serving in the armies on their hands,' says Julian: Vegetius, book 8, says soldiers were written with points of signs. Chrysostom, on Romans IV. 11, calls the same thing 'the seal of the soldier.' In imitation of the soldiers, the arms-manufacturers were marked. Stigmata, that is, a public mark, are inflicted on the arms of the arms-manufacturers in imitation of recruits, say the Emperors, L. Stigmata C. de Fabricensibus. Both the water-men and the keepers of the waters, whom they call hydrophylaces, who have been appointed as keepers of all the aqueducts of this royal city, are marked, and we decree that they be marked on their individual hands with the auspicious name of our piety imprinted. L. Decernimus C. de Aquæductu. But it is the same thing to have the arms marked or the hands: because the sign was imprinted on that part which is between the hand and the arm, τῷ καρπῷ, as we have already said. Both methods of marking remained in Africa and the East. See Leo Africanus, book IV, where he speaks of the Broscha.

And in the previous treatise: Verse 16.

And he makes all the small, and the great, and the rich, and the poor, and the free, and the slaves, to have a character] Magic also achieved this by its own example, that there were associations of nobles, knights, plebeians, freedmen, and slaves in Rome, in the provinces, in the colonies and municipalities, which associations had their own peculiar mark. Let the Dendrophori of Carthage be an example from such a mark or gentile profession, as law XX C. Theod. de Paganis, sacrificiis & templis speaks. Such existed also in Rome, Como, Verona, and elsewhere, as the inscriptions show, among those which Gruter published p. 14, 175, 261, 350, 438, 494. A certain Trajan forbade guilds by edict, as can be seen in Pliny, book X, epistle 97, but colleges which gathered for the sake of religion, namely pagan, were excepted from the same edict, l. 1. §. sed religionis D. de collegiis. Of such colleges, and indeed around these times especially, there is much mention in the Gruterian inscriptions: see chapter 4 of the index; one must read here ἀυτοῖς, that is, to themselves, or take ἀυτοῖς in that sense. Ancient books did not have aspirations written in. And thus Arethas explains this passage. 'On their right hand,' in their right hand] in imitation of soldiers: 'The brands are of those serving in the armies on their hands,' says Aelian. Chrysostom, on Romans IV, verse 11, calls this very thing 'the seal of the soldier.' Vegetius said soldiers were written with points. Thus also stigmata, that is, public marks, were inflicted on the arms of the arms-manufacturers in imitation of recruits, L. stigmata C. de fabricensibus. Thus also Emperor Zeno wished the keepers of the waters to be marked with his name imprinted on their hands, so that by that sign they might be in some way associated with the military, L. decernimus. C. de Aquæductu. 'Or on their foreheads,' or in their foreheads] I think that was done especially in the East, where the custom was for slaves to be marked on the forehead, not for the sake of punishment, as among the Romans, but so that their masters might be known. See Hesychius on the Babylonians under the word ἱεράνια and Σαμίων δῆμῷ. Ezekiel 9:4 alludes to that custom. In that manner, those who were incorporated inscribed some one of the gods as a master for themselves, like slaves. Philo mentions in I de Monarchia 'of those who enslave themselves to things made by hand with a heated iron'

of those who were marked and bound themselves to the works of human hands with a heated iron.

But were there not also before Apollonius and the rise of magic such associations in Rome as were noted by Philo? Thomas says the character of the beast can be understood as the profession of an illicit cult, q. 63, art. 3, which is notorious in the Papacy, even with certain explicit marks, the sign of the cross, the chrism of confirmation, which is imprinted on the forehead, the anointing of the priests on the right hand, or the indelible character with the tonsure, without which no commerce can be had with the beast, whether of sacred offices or of benefices. And in this way also Augustine, book 20, de C. D. c. 9, Primasius, Ticonius, Lyra, Thomas, B. Nicolai, B. Winckelmannus, B. Cluverus, Pareus, Ribera explain the character in the hand, so that it is an operation; but the character in the forehead, so that it is a profession; the former is the circular Pater Noster on a chain, the latter is the priestly chrism or that of confirmation. But who would desire sodalities and associations, where everything is full of cloisters and monasteries and confraternities? Yet Christians were not proscribed in former times, as many as had not given their name to some sacred sodality; nor is a prescription expressed anywhere by a denied ability to buy or sell. It is known, however, that in the Papacy all are excommunicated by the Bull In Coena Domini who have any commerce, even in matters pertaining to war, with heretics: nor is it safe to trade in Spain and Italy, because of the cruelty of the inquisition, nor did Mechtild, Queen of England, permit this to those not addicted to the Roman Pontiff, as Berthold testifies. To whom also (commerce) with the East Clement V and VIII. and John XXII forbade, and Martin V by a peculiar constitution prohibited holding domiciles, entering into contracts, exercising any negotiations whatsoever, or having the comforts of humanity with the faithful of Christ: although the stigma itself proves that the discourse is clearly about the peculiar law of Babylon, c. 18, 3. 11. 13. 15, such as it is, that benefits and prebends are bought and sold in turn to others, Canonries, episcopal palls, indulgences, penitentiary taxes, revenues of brothels, and dispensations: for the sweet odor of gain from any matter, even if filthy, is to the Pontiff, that I may pass over other things dry-shod. And it contributes to this image of the beast and his character, that Archbishops, Bishops, Cardinals, Abbots, Doctors and Professors are compelled to receive the character in their hand, that is, to bind themselves by oath, even those who are seduced to the Roman Church, to whom it must be sworn that for such or such a number of years they have adhered to the heretical, impious and damned doctrine of Luther, and that this must be confessed to the B. Virgin Mary, and to all the Saints, etc.

Latin:

v. 15. Καὶ ἐδόθη ἀυτῷ πνεῦμα δῦναι τῇ εἰκόνι τῦ θηρίε, & datum est illi, ut daret Spiritum imagini bestiæ] Datum illi à Diabolo, Deo sinente, ut videretur vivere istud simula- crum. Est loquutio κατὰ φάσιν secundum id quod videba- tur, ut 1.Sam.XXVIII. 14. Vocatur autem εἰκὼν τῦ θηρίω imago bestiæ, quia idololatriæ commendandæ inserviebat.

Καὶ ἵνα λαλήσῃ εἰκὼν τῦ θηρίε, & ut loquatur imago be- stiæ] Ipsa verba sunt apud Philostratum; sed & ipse Apol- lon. ob hæc facta pro Deo cultus, ut Vopiscus ex Aureliano nos docet, & Lactantius, & ejus quoque imago vi Dæ- monis locuta. Scriptor responsionum ad orthodoxos: Αὐτὸν δὲ τὸν Δαίμονα ἐν τῷ ἐκείνε ἀγάλματι ἱδρυνόμενον τὸν ἐκ ταῖς μαντείαις ἀπατήσαντα τὲς ἀνθρώπες ὡς Θεὸν σέβειν κῷ τιμᾷν τὸν Ἀπολλώνιον, ἐφίμωσε καταργήσας ἀυτῦ τὰς μαν- τείας; ipsum Dæmonem in ipsius habitantem imagine & per vaticinia imponentem hominibus, ut Apollonium pro Deo colerent atque venerarentur, silere fecit, vaticinia ipsi- us destruens. Christus scilicet, de quo ibi sermo.

Καὶ ποιήσῃ τὲς μὴ προσκυνῶντας τῇ εἰκόνι τῦ θηρίε, ἵνα ἀποκτανθῶσι: Et faciat,ut quicunque non adoraverint ima- ginem bestiæ, occidantur.] Εἰκόνι imaginem hic pro quovis simulachro singulare pro plurali. Apollonius Nervæ a- micus quum fuerit, & ad Trajani tempora provixerit, quin etiam Trajani usus sit amicitia, dubitari non debet. Et autoritate confirmatus in idolorum cultu Trajanus Chri- stianos ad eundem cultum gravissimarum pœnarum metu cogere voluit: plane ut Julianus Jamblichum Apollonio non disparem habuit ad prava suasorem: quem multa per magos effecisse notat & Spartianus.

Ad hæc nihil aliud addimus, quam quæ Mare- sius habet in dissert. ad quæ respondere conatus est Grotius in Appendice, ut conferri illa possint: Quod ignis e cælo eductio Apollonio tribuitur a Commenta- tore, quia fulgur dicitur decidisse in ipsig nativitate, Philostr. l. 1. nec non quia Achillis excitatum simula- chrum, ab eo, post finitum colloquium, mediocri ful- gure emisso discessit, ut habet Philostr. l. 4. non facit ad rhombum. Nam præterquam quod mendacissimo Philostr. passim rhetoricanti fides in istis non sit teme- re adhibenda, quem vanitatis ex professo Eusebius insimulavit, certe prius non potest nascenti Apollo- nio deputari, & quod alii olim cælo tonante & fulgu- rante in omen futuræ vitæ ab Historicis nati referun- tur, quos tamen ideo nemo sanus dixerit cælo ignem in terram deduxisse ἐνώπιον τῶν ἀνθρώπων, in conspectu hominum. Posterius vero factum fuit clam omni te- ste, non ab ipso Apollonio, sed a Dæmone evocato, nec de eo aliunde, quam ex ipsius Impostoris relatione con- stitit. Hæc vero miracula & prodigia in Antichristo Rom. conspicua, qui brutis excommunicationu suaru fulminibus totum olim terretavit orbe, cujusve Mi- nistri & Quæstores, Patrum nostrorum memoria ne- glectas indulgentias vel reliquias igne sacro Antonii cælitus immisso vindicabant: ut taceam quod extat apud Bennonem de Gregorio VII. Eum magicis ar- tibus scintillas ignis de manicis suis excussisse. Verba Bennonis sunt: Hic cum vellet manicas suas discu- tiebat, atque in modum scintillarum ignis dissiliebat: atque his miraculis simplicium oculos velut sanctita- tis signo ludificabat. De Zacharia refert. Ranulph. in Pol. l.V. c.25. quod nocturno tempore igneas nubes se præcedere fecerit; & Anonym. quod Clementis ima- ginem coruscationes per totum spatium comitatæ sint. Cæterum de miraculo ignis de cælo descendentis nonnulli observant, non necessum esse, ut κάτ τὸ ῥητὸν explicentur, quæ in Apocalypsi utpote mystica occurrunt: Ita Piscator, Pareus, Medus, Cotterius, Gerhardus: De igne autem cœlesti, Spi- ritu S. quem jactat Papa, intelligunt B. Nicolai, B. Grave, & Artopæus, ut & B. Hœ, Cluverus, Bul- lingerus, Pareus. De fulmine excommunicatio- nis Papalis accipiunt B. Cramerus, B. Winckel- mannus, Döling, Dürfeld, Hoë, Heilbrunnerus, Szegedinus, Napeir. ut & Pareus, Crugotius: De Ignatio Lojola Danhawer. Non desunt tamen qui de igne physico per prestigias Magicas producto exempla adducant Papalia, Napeirus, Hoëus, B. Hülsemann. Brev. p. 458. Lyra de Mahomete in- terpretatus per ignem Angelum Gabrielem designa- ri vult, & lunam, cujus partem manu sua se tenere mentiebatur.

De manibus Achillis, ab Apollonio evocatis hæc accipi non possunt: nam is nec prior, nec posterior bestia, nec magia, nec idololatria, aut idolum in Rom. imperio aut Imperatoribus Romanis dici potest: qui originem ad Trajanum referentes ab Achille procul fuere. Rectius per gladium Vitel- lianorum & Flavianorum pugna intelligitur. Quod hic ab Apollonio factum, clam omnibus factum: neque omnino indubitatum est, nec commode satis imago bestiæ vel idololatriæ dici- tur, quod ei commendandæ inservit, quia imago denominationem accipit non ab usu cui destina- tur, sed ab archetypo suo, aut doceri potest, pro- pterea Apollonium pro Deo cultum fuisse, quod imagini vitam dederit: Neque de eo Justinus sal- tim Christum dicit destruxisse vaticinia, & quasi silentium imposuisse Satanæ in sua imagine habi- tanti. Unde convenientius Maresius: Pontifici divina providentia concessum,ut vitam daret ima- gini prioris bestiæ in se excitatæ, hoc est, Hierar- chicæ suæ dominationi efficaciam & autoritatem conciliaret, & simul posse loqui, id est, leges con- dere, diplomata, edicta & decreta promulgare, & sic Dictatoriam autoritatem veluti haud absimi- lem consequi. Cui rei inservierunt etiam miracu- la & prodigia varia imaginum nominatim vel su- dantium vel sanguinem mittentium, vel etiam lo- quentium, ac si vivæ & animatæ fuissent. Exem- pla sunt cuivis obvia, si fabulonibus fides, quæ il- lis non minus debetur,quam Commentatoris Phi- lostrato. Notum quid dixerit imago Crucifixi ad Thomam: Bene scripsisti de me Thoma, quam mercedem reportabis? Ut taceam magicam Syl- vestri II. imaginem ex ære, quæ consulta in dubiis ipsi respondebat, Agnoscit in Append. Grotius, magiam Romæ inter vetita fuisse: Quomodo ergo ad tantam ibi pervenit autoritatem, imprimis sub Domitiano & Trajano, quos Magiæ deditos fuisse minime ostendit, quum de illo contrarium potius testentur Suetonius, & Philostratus, hoste Apollo- nii aperto, de quo Hieronymus, anne Magus ille fuerit, dubitat, Suidas id negat, Eusebius verane an fabulosa sint, quæ de illo narrantur, in medio relinquit; ut idololatriam labascentem sustineret, ac restitueret, eique inflictum vulnus Evangelii præconio sanaret? Nec ad rem quicquam facit aut ad Domitiani vel Trajani tempora, quod Hiero- clem tempori Constantini, Apollonium Christi æquarit. Et annon inter Apollonium & Domitia- num convenire debuit, si prima bestia Domitia- nus fuit, & Apollonius Pseudo-Propheta idem, quod Aquibas Barchocheba, quo de ad Matth. XXIV. 24. egerat.

Quomodo autem optime illis temporibus ma- gia ex terra orta dicitur, quod ei addicti neque po- tentes neque nobiles fuerint, nisi idem de Christiana religione dicendum 1. Cor. I. 26. Ribera phrasis ascendit ex terra explicatur, similis fuit illis, quæ vi- dentur in terra non terribili forma, ut solent esse monstra marina, quod isto tempore, aut ipsi Apollo- nio etiam abstinentia à Venere, & vitio molliori propria fuerit, nullo teste sufficienter constat. Quicquid etiam fecit Apollonius, ad Neronis per- tinuit tempora. Et parum profecto huc facit, quod sub Apollonii nativitatem fulgur e cælo in terram decidisse referatur, quod pro fabula quoque habuit Eusebius, aut quod spatium clam, non sine tenui aliquo fulgure, ab Apollonio discessit, ac præ- dicitur hic, quod futurum adhuc erat, non quod pridem jam factum. Verba autem illa λέγων ποιῆ- σαι præter mentem aliorum enunciative interpre- tatur Glossa interlin. dicens reddit præcipiens, & quum de potestate accepta loquutus esset S. Johannes, magis conveniens erat, quid pro illa mandaverit pro- sequi. Porro citra causam singulare pro plurali po- nitur, imo contra seriem contextus & articulum de- monstrantem imaginem, de qua sermo. Suidas vero diserte docet, Apollonium sub Nerva mortuum, Eu- sebius l. 4. c. 2. doctrinam Evangelii maxime floru- isse sub Trajano; quæ cum Apostoli prophetia nullatenus conveniunt, neque sententiæ Grotianæ quadrant de plagæ sanatione. De Antichristianis vero B. Cluver. hæc adduxit: Laurent. Valla orat. de donatione Constantini: Nostri, inquit, fabula- tores passim inducunt idola loquentia. Luitpran- dus l. 1. c. 8. de rebus Europæ scribit: Cum For- mosi corpus in ædem Petri sit illatum, imagines sa- cras illud venerabiliter salutasse. Joh. Foxus in Martyrologio p. 1188 refert, tempore Henrici VIII. idolum quoddam fuisse in Anglia dictum imago " gratiæ, rotis & ponderibus ita elaboratum, ut aliquis concavitatem ejus occupans, singulas ido- li partes, os, manus, oculos, labra potuerit mo- vere, idque dona afferentibus manum porrexisse, parum dantes tristi, multum hilari vultu adspexis- se. Stumpffius lib. 13. Chron. Helvet. c. 34. annotat, quasdam Sanctorum statuas, excavatis earum capitibus, infusoque oleo flere fuisse visas. Atque in Apol. Aug. Conf. cap. de Sanctorum invocatio- ne testantur Confessores, se vidisse in quodam mo- nasterio simulachrum B. Virginis, quod quasi αὐ- τόματον ære motum vel avertiari potuerit peten- tes vel annuere. Ac talem imaginem Constantino- poli fuisse, scribit Evagrius l. V. Hist. Eccl. c. 8. quam cum venerari vellet Anatolius captivus, a- " versata sit eum.,, Nec tamen idem a nostra explica- tione antea proposita alienus omnino est: Papa ubicunque idolum aliquod dominationis suæ se- mel posuerat, paulatim ita eam animavit per Apo- stolos suos, ut tandem & divina & sacrosancta eam " recipere cogeret populos. Forum enim sibi fin- xit in Europa & alibi, & Ecclesiasticas functio- nes in potentes satrapias convertit, præcipua re- gnorum autoritate in ipsas translata, ut absque ju- ratis sibi Episcopis, Abbatibus & Sacerdotibus nihil ratum validumque haberetur amplius.

Denique Apollonium dies suos usque in Trajani tempora produxisse, vix credibile est, neque certum, eum inducturum fuisse Trajanum ad persequen- dos Christianos, si ipsi familiaris fuisset: cujus persecutio lenta fuit, & mollis etsi diuturna, non tam acerba, ut quæ hic prædicitur, quæ ceu An- ti-Christiana maxime Romano Pontifici convenit. Unde dictum felicior Augusto, melior Trajano, apud Curtium l. 8. Cui veteres eo usque etiam propensi fuere, ut animam Trajani ab inferis precibus Gre- gorii revocatam dixerint. V. Origenem, Mechtild. revelat. Nihil ergo huc vel Capitolium, vel Apollo- nius, vel Simon Samarita. De curanda imperii pla- ga, deque miraculis seu veris seu fictis, quum ad Anti-Christi hæc pertineant tempora, sermo est, non de tempore Apostolorum; pervertit omnia pro more suo Grotius, ut lateat AntiChristus.

"Ινα δῶσιν αὐτοῖς χαράγματα ἐπὶ τῆς χειρὸς αὐτῶν τῆς δεξι- ᾶς, ἢ ἐπὶ τῶν μετώπων αὐτῶν] Magi autores fuere Trajano, ut hæterias, id est, sodalitates, sive collegia omnia vetaret, ut videre est apud Plinium lib. X. epist. 97. exceptis quæ religio- nis nomine, Paganicæ scilicet, coibant, L. 1. §. Sed re- ligionis D. de collegiis. Cum vero homines natura ament sodalitates, factum inde, ut nemo esset in imperio R. qui non in sodalitatem Deorum alicui dicatam, nomen daret, un- de circa hoc tempus tot collegiorum vocabula, quæ videri possunt in Gruteri Inscriptionibus. Qui in ista collegia ad- scribebantur, simul accipiebant in corpore suo χάραγμα aliquod, id est, Dei signum, aut exertum Dei nomen, aut per numeros dissimulatum, quæ duo hic ex sequentibus sub- audienda sunt. Prudentius: Quod cum sacrandus accipit sphragitida Acus minutas ingerunt fornacibus, His membra pergunt urere, utque igniverint, Quamcunque partem corporis fervens nota Signarit, hunc sic consecratum prædicant.
