Phrasis autem illa nemo potuit ingredi in templum, inaccessam gloriam Divi- nam & incognitam revelationem indicat; donec scil. deinceps explicaretur ab ipso Deo.

## 16:1 Argument
CHAPTER XVI. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

The Angels are commanded to pour out the vials upon the earth, and they pour out all seven of them in order, and what followed is explained.

There are two parts: I. The pouring out of the seven vials done in order. II. The consequence or effect, at a great earthquake, the ruin of Babylon and its cities, and a plague of hail so pressing them that they break out into blasphemies, to verse 21.

PART I. THE ORDERED POURING OUT OF THE SEVEN VIALS.

Ver. 1. And I heard a great voice out of the temple) A voice from the inner sanctuary of God. See above XIV. 13.

Saying to the seven angels, go) Thus 'go' above X. verse 8.

Pour out the vials of the wrath of God into the earth) Vials full of fire, signifying the wrath of God upon idolaters. Into the earth, that is, into the Roman Empire, as the series of events teaches that the word 'earth' is to be taken here. In the Manuscript 'the seven vials', as the Latin also reads.

They pour out into the earth, or earthly men, Apoc. XIV. But into the whole earth. For the text is not to be restricted, with the blessed Cluver and the blessed Gravius, where the Holy Spirit does not restrict it. Yet we understand the Empire of the Roman Anti-Christ. But he arrogates to himself authority over the whole earth and every human creature, creating bishops in those places which were never subject to him, in America, India, etc. And thus the series of events, but truly explained, teaches that the word 'earth' is to be taken. By Angels, however, we understand celestial Spirits, who primarily come under this name. The blessed Gravius thinks that the Ministers of the Word are signified by them, although he does not deny that the Angel seen was of a spiritual nature: nor does he deny that the harvest concerning the ruin of Anti-Christian tyranny, with which the harvest of the last day is conjoined, is designated there. But there are seven, because this revelation loves the number seven, and the seventh plague is finished with the apparatus of the final judgment. But the Angels do not pour out the vials before it is commanded to them, nor in any other than the commanded order: because no evil befalls us without the will of God, Am. III. 6.

Latin:

CAPUT XVI. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Jubentur Angeli effundere phialas in terram, & effundunt ordine easdem omnes septem, & quæ consequuta sint, exponitur.

Partes sunt duæ I. Septem phialarum effusio ordine facta. II. Consequens vel effectum, ad ter- ræ motum ingentem, Babylonis & civitatum ejus ruina, & plaga grando ita eos premens, ut in blasphemias erumpant, ad v. 21.

PARS I. SEPTEM PHIALARUM ORDINATA EFFUSIO.

Vers. 1. Καὶ ἤκουσα φωνῆς μεγάλης ἐκ τοῦ ναοῦ) Ex adyto Dei vocem. Vide supra XIV. 13.

Λεγούσης τοῖς ἑπτὰ ἀγγέλοις, ὑπάγετε) Sic ὕπαγε supra X. vers. 8.

Ἐκχέετε τὰς φιάλας τοῦ θυμοῦ τοῦ Θεοῦ εἰς τὴν γῆν) Phialas igne plenas, iram Dei in idololatras significante. In ter- ram, id est, in Imperium Romanum, quomodo vocem ter- ræ hic sumendam docet rerum series. In Manuscripto τὰς ἑπτὰ φιάλας, quomodo legit & Latinus.

Effundunt in terram, vel homines terrenos Apoc. XIV. In terram autem universam. Non enim restringendus cum B. Cluvero & B. Gravio textus, ubi Spiritus sanctus non restringit. Imperium ta- men Romani Anti-Christi intelligimus. Sed is in universam terram, & omnem creaturam humanam imperium sibi arrogat, Episcopos creans, in illis locis, quæ nunquam ei subjecta fuere, in America, India, &c. Atq; ita vocem terræ accipiendam esse, omni- no rerum series, sed vere explicata, docet. Per An- gelos autem intelligimus cœlestes Spiritus, qui πρώ- τως hoc nomine veniunt. Significari autem per eos- dem Verbi Ministros B. Gravius existimat, etsi vi- sum Angelum spiritualis naturæ non neget: neque diffitetur messem de tyrannidis Anti-Christiane ruina, qua cum conjuncta est messis novissimæ diei illic designari. Septem autem sunt, quia amat hæc ἀποκάλυψις septenarium numerum, & septima pla- ga finitur extremi judicii apparatu. Non effundunt autem Angeli prius phialas, antequam id ipsis de- mandetur, nec alio, quam demandato ordine: quia nihil mali absque Dei voluntate nobis obtingit Am. III. 6.

## 16:2
Ver 2. And the first went, and poured out his vial into the earth. And there was a noisome and grievous sore upon the men which had the mark of the beast) There were various fires in the vials, and various effects. A noisome and grievous sore, שחין רע Deut. XXVIII. 35. Job II. 7. In the Manuscript: Upon the men, not badly. This plague and the two following allude to the plagues of Egypt, yet not with the exact same meaning. By the name שחין the Hebrews say all evils are signified which arise from heat. And certainly to the Arabs שחן is to heat. Therefore, all sultry diseases are signified here, in which the plague is the chief. But it very often invaded the Roman world between the times of Trajan and Constantine, as under Commodus greater than any before, so that in the city two thousand men died daily, and very many also elsewhere, as Dio and Herodian testify. Another was no less under Gallus and Volusianus, as Zosimus reports, and again under Gallienus, by the same witness. There was also another after Decius, of which Eusebius makes mention VIII. 17, Trebellius, Gallienus, Orosius VII. 15, Jerome in his Chronicle in the 257th Olympiad, on the occasion of which Cyprian wrote his book on mortality. Another under Gallienus, which is mentioned in the Martyrologies, and under Claudius, who succeeded Gallienus, as Trebellius records. Another under Diocletian, in Eusebius VII. 2.

There was a command concerning the pouring out of the vials upon the earth v. 1 & 2. There follows the obedience of the Angels in the pouring out of the vials according to the order commanded v. 3 seqq. By the plague of the first vial Grotius understands a pestilence, and indeed one which was introduced between the times of Trajan and Constantine under Commodus, and which under Gallus and Volusianus, which under Gallienus, which after Decius, which under Claudius, which under Gallienus, as he recounts them quite confusedly. But why the light of pestilence? Why introduced in those times which he recounts? Not in others. For a plague, and no lighter one, afflicted many other times. Before Gallus, 30,000 funerals came into the accounts of Libitina, consumed by pestilential diseases under the consuls Plautius Hypsaeus and Flavius; after the horrendous devastations of locusts, such a plague pervaded Africa that in Numidia alone 800,000 people are reported to have been consumed, 200,000 near the maritime coast, 30,000 near Utica, and 1,500 corpses were carried out from the Utican gate in one day. Raging for a full 15 years, it devastated Rome under Gallus and Volusianus: under Justinian it so infested Constantinople that 10,000 came into the accounts of Libitina daily. Under Charles: the year 1348 is so distinguished by earthquakes and contagions that Albert of Strasbourg thinks that such a force of diseases and deaths had not reigned since the flood. Certain provinces were completely evacuated of people. Clement VI, shut up in a chamber having continuous fires, admitted no one to himself, visited no one. This evil did not rage for one year only. In the forty-ninth year it consumed very many Princes, among these the Queen of Hungary, the daughter of the Emperor, and his sister, the wife of John, King of France; Strasbourg alone gave 16,000 to Libitina in that year. The Jews, accused everywhere of poisoning and corrupting the fountains, perished in fires at the clamor of the mob, as Cluverus reports in his Epitome. Grotius does not provide the cause. He himself said it. It is not for us to divine it. Others interpret it as the anguish of conscience in those who have become participants in Papal idolatry: because human doctrines and traditions cannot tranquilize the conscience. There are not lacking, however, those who understand it as the French disease, which is very familiar to the priests of Italy and others indulging in whoredoms. But the former explanation is more suitable and more congruent to the text and the scope.

Latin:

Vers 2. Καὶ ἐξῆλθεν ὁ πρῶτος, καὶ ἐξέχεε τὴν φιάλην αὑτοῦ εἰς τὴν γῆν. Καὶ ἐγένετο ἕλκος κακὸν καὶ πονηρὸν εἰς τοὺς ἀν- θρώπους, τοὺς ἔχοντας χάραγμα τοῦ θηρίου) Varii ignes erant in phialis, varii & effectus. Ἕλκος κακὸν καὶ πονηρὸν שחין רע Deut. XXVIII. 35. Job. II. 7. In Manuscripto: Ἐπὶ τοὺς ἀνθρώπους, non male. Hæc plaga & duæ sequentes alludunt ad plagas Ægypti, significatu tamen non plane eodem. Nomine שחין ajunt Ebræi significari omnia ma- la, quæ ex calore oriuntur. Et certe Arabibus שחן est ca- lefacere. Significantur ergo hic omnes morbi æstuosi, in quibus præcipua est pestilentia. Ea autem sæpissime orbem Romanum invasit inter Trajani & Constantini tempora, ut sub Commodo major quam ulla ante, ita ut in urbe morerentur quotidie bis mille homines, plurimi etiam alibi, testibus Dione & Herodiano. Non minor alia sub Gallo & Volusiano, Zosimo referente, rursum sub Gal- lieno, eodem teste. Fuit & alia post Decium, cujus meminit Eusebius VIII. 17. Trebellius, Gallienus, Orosius VII. 15. Hieronymus in Chronico Olympiade CCLVII. cujus occa- sione librum de mortalitate scripsit Cyprianus. Alia sub Gallieno, cujus mentio in Martyrologiis, & sub Claudio, qui Gallieno successit, memorante Trebellio. Alia sub Dio- cletiano, apud Eusebium VII. 2.

Fuit mandatum de effundendis phialis in terram v. 1. & 2. Sequitur Angelorum obsequium in effu- sione phialarum secundum ordinem demandatum v. 3. seqq. Per plagam primæ phialæ Grotius intel- ligit pestilentiam & quidem quæ inter Trajani & Constantini tempora sub Commodo immissa est, & quæ sub Gallo & Volusiano, quæ sub Gallie- no, quæ post Decium, quæ sub Claudio, quæ sub Gallieno, uti eas satis consusè recenset. Sed cur lucem pestilentiæ? Cur illis, quæ recenset, temporibus immissam? Non aliis. Multa enim alia tempora lues, nec illa levior, afflixit. Ante Gal- lum 30000. funerum in rationem Libitinæ vene- runt, pestilentibus morbis absumpta Plautio Hy- psæo, & Flavio Coss. post horrendas locustarum po- pulationes tanta Africam lues pervasit, ut in sola Numidia octingenta millia hominum circa mariti- mam oram ducenta millia apud Uticam 30000. consumpta tradantur, ex porta Uticensi uno die M. D. cadavera elata. Ea totos XV. annos sæviens sub Gallo & Volusiano Romam vastavit: Sub Justi- niano Constantinopolin sic infestavit, ut 10000. quo- tidie in rationes Libitinæ venirent. Sub Carolo: An- nus 1348. terræ motibus & contagiis adeo est nobili- tatus, ut Albertus Argentinensis inde a diluvio haud regnasse tantam vim morborum & mortium putet. Quædam provinciæ hominibus plane evacuatæ. Cle- mens VI. camera inclusus continuos habenti ignes, neminem ad se admisit, neminem visitavit. Non uno anno hoc malum grassabatur. Quadragesimo no- no plurimos Principes absumpsit, in his Reginam Hungariæ, Cæsaris filiam, ejusdemque sororem Jo- hann. Franci Regis conjugem; sola Argentina eo anno XVI. millia Libitinæ dedit. Judæi passim venefi- cii corruptorumque fontium accusati incendiis ad cla- morem vulgi periere, ut refert in Epitom. Cluverus. Causam non reddit Grotius. Αὐτὸς ἔφα. Divinare eam nostrum non est. Alii interpretantur de ango- re conscientiæ in illis, qui idololatricæ Papalis facti sunt participes: quia humanæ doctrinæ & traditio- nes non possunt tranquillare conscientiam. Non desunt tamen, qui de lue Gallica, quæ sacrificulis Italiæ, aliisque scortationibus indulgentibus valde familiaris sit, intelligant. Sed prior explicatio con- venientior & textui, ac scopo magis congrua est.

## 16:3
Vers. 3. And the second angel poured out his vial into the sea) The sea in this part of the Apocalypse is simply placed for the multitude of people in the city of Rome. See above XIII. 1.

And it became blood as of a dead man) As of a man wounded to death. See above XIV. 13.

And every living soul died in the sea) It is a hyperbole. For every soul signifies a very great many. Great slaughters were produced in Rome in the said space of time, as in the times of Commodus, by the cruelty of Commodus, by sedition, by fire: And when the Emperor Pertinax was killed, and Plautianus the prefect of the praetorium.

Which plague can be understood of bloody wars, because seas denote peoples. For how under Severus there was so much blood that it flowed into the rivers; under Julian such gore was seen that it flowed in the manner of rivers. In the time of Henry IV so much blood was shed that it reached to the knees of horses. Under Constans II such a slaughter of the Romans was made that the sea was reddened with their blood, which example especially pertains here.

Latin:

Vers. 3. Καὶ ὁ δεύτερος ἄγγελος ἐξέχεε τὴν φιάλην αὑτῶ εἰς τὴν θάλασσαν) Mare in hac parte Apocalypseos simplici- ter positum est multitudo hominum in urbe Roma. Vide supra XIII. 1.

Καὶ ἐγένετο ἅιμα ὡς νεκρῶ) Ut hominis ad mortem vulne- rati. Vide supra XIV. 13.

Καὶ πᾶσα ψυχὴ ἡ ζῶσα ἀπέθανεν ἐν τῇ θαλάσσῃ) Est ὑπερβολή. Nam πᾶσα ψυχὴ valde multos significat. Magnæ strages dicto temporis spatio editæ sunt Romæ, ut Commo- di temporibus, sævitia Commodi, seditione, incendio: Et cum interfectus Pertinax Imperator, & Plautianus præfe- ctus prætorio.

Quæ plaga de bellis cruentis, quia maria populos notant, intelligi potest. Nam quomodo sub Seve- ro tantum est sanguinis ut in fluvios influeret; sub Juliano tantus cruor visus, ut flueret more flumi- num. Tempore Henrici IV. tantum sanguinis fu- sum, ut ad equorum genua pertingeret. Sub Con- stante II. tanta Romanorum cædes facta, ut mare eorum sanguine purpurasceret, quod exemplum imprimis huc facit.

## 16:4
Vers. 4. And the third angel poured out his vial into the rivers and the fountains of waters) Into the cities outside Rome, and into the villages. The same enigmatic locution as above VIII. 10.

And it became blood) Huge slaughters produced through the provinces by the war of Albinus, Niger, Tetricus, Zenobia, Carausius, Allectus, and the uprisings of the Bagaudae and the Carpi.

This can be accepted concerning miraculous blood, how in Rome in the year 1220 a cloud rained dust mixed with blood; under Ferdinand II waters were seen frozen with gore in ponds, likewise drops of blood dripping from beams, bread, tables, and boots sweating blood, historians report.

Latin:

Vers. 4. Καὶ ὁ τρίτος ἄγγελος ἐξέχεε τὴν φιάλην αὑτῶ εἰς τὲς ποταμὲς καὶ τὰς πηγὰς τῶν ὑδάτων) In urbes extra Romam, & in vicos. Eadem ænigmatica loquutio supra VIII. 10.

Καὶ ἐγένετο ἅιμα) Ingentes strages editæ per provincias bello Albini, Nigri, Tetrici, Zenobiæ, Carausi, Alacti, & motibus Bacaudarum & Carporum.

Id accipi potest de sanguine miraculoso quomo- do Romæ an. 1220. mixtum sanguine pulverem nu- bes pluvisse; sub Ferdinando II. visas aquas cruore congelatas in stagnis, guttas item sanguinis e tra- bibus destillantes, panes, mensas, ocreas, sangui- nem sudantes referunt Historici.

## 16:5
Ver. 5. And I heard the Angel of the waters saying) This third Angel is called the Angel of the waters, because he poured his vial into the waters. Thus certain Angels are called of fire, of air, of dust among the Rabbis.

I do not know whether the Rabbis also imagine watery Angels, as they do fiery ones of fire, in which matter they have Grotius as one who does not deny it.

Righteous art thou, who art, and who wast) Concerning this locution see above I. 8. IV. 8. XI. 17. He does not add here 'who art to come', because he only means this, that God is acting as justly now with the men of the Roman empire as he did formerly with the Egyptians, Assyrians, Babylonians, and Antiochus.

the holy one) So also above XV. 4. For 'holy' some Codices have 'saintly'. But 'holy' is correct, חסיד merciful. For that punishment of the Roman empire was a liberation of the Christians.

Because thou hast judged these things) These things, namely the judgments or the righteous acts, משפטים.

Latin:

Vers. 5. Καὶ ἤκουσα τοῦ Ἀγγέλου τῶν ὑδάτων λέγοντος) Angelus hic tertius vocatur Angelus aquarum, quia in aquas immisit phialam. Sic Angeli quidam dicuntur ignis, aëris, pulveris apud Rabbinos.

Angelos Aquarum nescio an Rabbini etiam aqueos fingant, ut ignis igneos, in quo non habent abnuentem Grotium.

Δίκαιος εἶ ὁ ὢν, καὶ ὁ ἦν) De hac loquutione vide supra I. 8. IV. 8. XI. 17. non addit hic ἐσόμενος, quia hoc tantum vult, Deum tam juste nunc agere cum Romani imperii hominibus, quam olim cum Aegyptiis, Assyriis, Babyloniis, Antiocho.

ὁ ὅσιος) Sic & supra XV. 4. Pro ὅσιος quidam Codices habent ἅγιος. Sed rectum est ὅσιος חסיד misericors. Punitio enim ista Romani imperii liberatio erat Christianorum.

Ὅτι ταῦτα ἔκρινας) Ταῦτα nempe τὰ κρίματα sive τὰ δικαιώματα משפטים.

## 16:6
Ver. 6. For they have shed the blood of saints and prophets) The magistrates and provincial peoples killed many Christians, among whom some were also distinguished by prophetic gifts; below in XVIII. 20 they are named saints and Apostles and Prophets.

And thou hast given them blood to drink) 'And' here signifies 'therefore'. You have returned like for like. They are said to drink blood who are filled with grief on account of slain parents, children, kinsmen, relatives, friends, and fellow-citizens. Taken from Obadiah 16.

They are worthy) They have deserved this. Thus 'worthy of death' Rom. I. 32. Thus Cyrus's head was put into a skin full of blood.

God is celebrated as just everywhere, both in the remaining Scriptures and in this prophecy. The periphrasis of eternity, which we saw in Apoc. I, repeated also in chapter XI, is rashly restricted to certain times.

Latin:

Vers. 6. Ὅτι αἷμα ἁγίων καὶ προφητῶν ἐξέχεον) Magistratus & populi provinciales multos occiderunt Christianos, inter quos nonnulli & propheticis donis clarebant, infra XVIII. 20. nominantur sancti & Apostoli ac Prophetae.

Καὶ αἷμα αὐτοῖς ἔδωκας πιεῖν) Καὶ hic valet propterea. Par pari retulisti. Bibere dicuntur sanguinem, qui moerore implentur ob interfectos parentes, liberos, cognatos, affines, amicos, populares. Desumptum ex Abdia. 16.

Ἄξιοί εἰσι) Hoc meruere. Sic ἄξιοι θανάτου Rom. I. 32. Sic Cyri caput demissum in utrem plenum sanguinis.

Justus passim celebratur Deus, tum in reliquis Scripturis, tum in hac prophetia. Periphrasis æternitatis, quam Apoc. I. vidimus, repetita etiam cap. XI. temere ad certa tempora restringitur.

## 16:7
Ver. 7. And I heard from the altar saying) I heard another saying, namely the Angel who guards the spirits of the martyrs. For they are under the altar, above VI. 9.

Yea, Lord God Almighty) יהוה אל צבאות above IV. 18. XI. 17.

True and righteous are thy judgments) The sense is the same as above XV. 3 and Psalm XIX. 10.

The angel from the censer (perhaps Christ, ch. VIII.) proclaims both the omnipotence, and the justice, and the truth of the judgment or the threatening of God.

Latin:

Vers. 7. Καὶ ἤκουσα ἐκ τοῦ θυσιαστηρίου λέγοντος) Audivi alium dicentem, nempe Angelum, qui Spiritus martyrum custodit. Ii enim sub altari, supra VI. 9.

Ναὶ Κύριε ὁ Θεὸς ὁ παντοκράτωρ) יהוה אל צבאות supra IV. 18. XI. 17.

Ἀληθιναὶ καὶ δίκαιαι αἱ κρίσεις σου) Sensus idem qui supra XV. 3. & Psal. XIX. 10.

Angelus e thuribulo (forte Christus cap. VIII.) & omnipotentiam, & justitiam, & veritatem judicii vel comminationem Dei prædicat.

## 16:8
Ver. 8. And the fourth angel poured out his vial upon the sun, and it was given unto him to scorch men) From this heat of the sun comes sterility and the famine following it. See Matt. XIII. 6. Mark IV. 6. Famine burns, therefore it is not inappropriately called by the name of fire. A huge famine under Commodus is in Herodian.

Latin:

Vers. 8. Καὶ ὁ τέταρτος Ἄγγελος ἐξέχεε τὴν φιάλην αὑτοῦ ἐπὶ τὸν ἥλιον, καὶ ἐδόθη αὐτῷ καυματίσαι τοὺς ἀνθρώπους) Ex hoc æstu solis sterilitas & eam sequens fames. Vide Matth. XIII. 6. Marc. IV. 6. Fames urit, ideo ignis nomine non male appellatur. Fames ingens sub Commodo est apud Herodianum.

## 16:9
Ver. 9. And men were scorched with great heat) Their bowels were scorched for them by famine.

And men blasphemed the name of God who has power over these plagues) In the Manuscript: They blasphemed before God. Thus for the Hebrews אל פני is sometimes 'against'. They said that these evils happen because of the Christians, the worshippers of one God. They used to say that after the Christian race began in the world, the orb of the earth perished, and the human race was afflicted with multiform evils. Thus Arnobius lib. X. and he specifically enumerates pestilences, droughts, wars, and the lack of crops. Cyprian to Demetrianus: 'But indeed when you say that very many complain that wars arise more frequently, that plagues, that famines rage, and that the rains and long-continued showers suspend, that it is imputed to us.' See also Ambrose and Prudentius against Symmachus and Augustine in the first five books of The City of God and Orosius in book VII.

And they did not repent to give him glory) That is, εἰς τὸ δοῦναι.

The vial poured into the sun (of justice, as it is preached through the Word of the Gospel; for Primasius, Winckelmann, Danhauer, Gravius, Dürfeld, Pareus, Forbes, Coccejus, and Dieslius understand this), that is, into Holy Scripture or by metonymy into the Church, whence those burning with fire (consciences) driven by torments and the fire and flames of Divine wrath as if into madness, with no remaining comfort or refreshment of Holy Scripture, began to blaspheme the name of God without repentance, which experience confirms remarkably in the Romanists devoted to the great Anti-Christ.

Latin:

Vers. 9. Καὶ ἐκαυματίσθησαν οἱ ἄνθρωποι καῦμα μέγα) Adusta sunt illis viscera pre fame.

Καὶ ἐβλασφήμησαν οἱ ἄνθρωποι τὸ ὄνομα τοῦ Θεοῦ τοῦ ἔχοντος τὴν ἐξουσίαν ἐπὶ τὰς πληγὰς ταύτας) In Manuscripto: Ἐβλασφήμησαν ἐνώπιον τοῦ Θεοῦ. Sic Ebræis אל פני interdum est contra. Dixerunt ista mala evenire ob Christianos unius Dei cultores. Dicebant, postquam in mundo Christiana gens cœpit, terrarum orbem periisse, multiformibus malis affectum esse genus humanum. Ita Arnobius lib. X. & speciatim enumerat pestilentias, siccitates, bella, frugum inopiam. Cyprianus ad Demetrianum: Sed enim cum dicas plurimos conqueri, quod bella crebrius surgant, quod lues, quod fames sæviant, quodque imbres & pluvia seria longa suspendant nobis imputari. Vide & Ambrosium & Prudentium contra Symmachum & Augustinum libris quinque primis de civitate Dei & Orosium libro VII.

Καὶ ὀὐ μετενόησαν δοῦναι αὐτῷ δόξαν) Id est, εἰς τὸ δοῦναι.

Phiala in solem (justitiæ, prout per Verbum Evangelii prædicatur; hunc enim intelligunt Primasius, Winckelmannus, Danhauerus, Gravius, Dürfeld, Pareus, Forbesius, Coccejus, Dieslius) hoc est in Scripturam sacram vel per Metonymiam in Ecclesiam effusa, unde igne æstuantes (conscientiæ) tormentis & igne ac flammis iræ Divinæ velut in rabiem nullo reliquo Scripturæ S. solatio vel refrigerio adacti blasphemare cœperunt nomen Dei sine μετανοίᾳ vel pœnitentia, quod insigniter in Romanensibus Anti-Christo magno deditis confirmat experientia.

## 16:10
Ver. 10. And the fifth angel poured out his vial upon the throne of the beast) Not upon individuals, but upon the empire itself, through which idolatry was sustained.

And his kingdom became darkened) The Roman dominion lost much of its pristine splendor, having been attacked, devastated, and partly even occupied by barbarians, Persians, Borani, Goths, Burgundians, Alemanni, Marcomanni, Scythians, and Sarmatians under Alexander, Valerian, Gallienus, Claudius, and others. See Herodian and the Latins who wrote the lives of the Caesars and the Chronicles. There is an allusion to the darkness of Egypt. In a similar sense Isaiah VIII. 22 has מענף and חשכה. And they gnawed their tongues for pain) Aristophanes in the Wasps: 'Eating his bile from anger,' where the scholiast says 'instead of his lips, for those who are angry bite their lips.' Thus those who are angry and cannot avenge themselves are accustomed to do. Ver. 11. And they blasphemed the God of heaven because of their pains, and because of their sores) He joins the vials, the second, third, and fourth with the first. ἐκ here signifies the moving cause, as מן often does among the Hebrews. They called the Christians 'atheists' because they worshipped one God, the creator of the world. And they did not repent of their works) they did not desist from idolatry. Nay, they even added new sacred rites, Criobolia, Taurobolia.

This plague now strikes the throne and Papal seat itself, the vial of wrath and condemnatory sentence having been poured out by the great man Luther and his faithful followers. It became darkened, because such a Pontifical kingdom is revealed; since things are said to be done in sacred matters when they are revealed; because the darkness of the Papacy is also added to those things made manifest, how, deprived of the spiritual light of the Gospel, it wanders in the darkness of ignorance, errors, sin, and damnation, nevertheless the Papal throne with its Anti-Christian kingdom was not brought to repentance. For such as the throne is, such also is the light and the darkness, concerning which spiritual darkness see Isaiah LX. 1, 2, Eph. V. 8, 14, 1 Thess. V. 4, 5, 2 Cor. VI. 14. In which sense the Caesarean also explained that the manifestation of darkness is denoted, by which the government of the Anti-Christ is demonstrated as ἀφεγγὴς τῷ τῆς δικαιοσύνης ἡλίῳ, which in place of conversion has wrought a greater blasphemy of the Anti-Christians through an accident, just as the light of the Gospel is said to blind, and the Gospel is the odor of death unto death 2 Cor. II. Others prefer to interpret it concerning the grief of the Anti-Christian kingdom, because light denotes joy, and darkness denotes sadness, 2 Sam. XXII. 29, 30, Job XXX. 30, Jer. XIV. 2, Lam. IV. 16, Jer. XIII. 16 (which the blessed Cluverus made especially parallel to ours, adding his vote to this opinion with Aretius), Mic. VII. 8. Although the Papists may perhaps be little concerned about spiritual darkness; yet they do not bear without pain the fact that unarmed champions attack, besiege, and storm the seat of their King; and that Princes oppose themselves to the supreme Pontiff, to Cardinals and Archbishops, who do not hesitate to compare themselves, nay, to prefer themselves to Kings themselves; therefore they gnaw their tongues for pain, or out of vexation: to which perhaps ulcers are joined, so that it may be intimated that the first plague is not yet finished, but rather increased. How many blasphemies they have vomited forth out of anger and fury, even in written books, is now manifest to the world. Concerning which, just as the Psalter once could, so now the Bibles can testify, drawing to the praise of Mary most of the eulogies which were attributed to God, not without the highest blasphemy and idolatry: which have appeared in this century. This, forsooth, is their repentance from the manifested darkness of errors, more than Cimmerian, or rather Egyptian, and in the sun, as the saying is, exposed. The darkness of the Papacy is certainly now so manifested that in Italy itself the illustrious Republic of Venice has begun to hold the Pontifical throne in contempt, and has forced the supreme Pontiff Paul V to revoke the thunderbolt of excommunication, and has driven the Jesuits, the assistants and chief defenders of the Anti-Christ, from its territories, with this prosemptic: Soon, far, slowly, (or never) yield, withdraw, return. In France, however, Henry IV, and in Germany Ferdinand III, [granted] peace to the adversaries of the Papal throne granted. What torments of soul followed the eating of that vial and the plague of tongues, the Bull of Innocent X, among other things, will teach. The Roman see experienced similar fates in England, Scotland, and Ireland under James VI. In Poland, it was admitted and sanctioned by a confederation as if it were a fundamental law of the three religions, and thus of the Evangelical; in Hungary, Transylvania, and, though for a brief time, in Bohemia, Austria itself, and other Austrian provinces. In Sweden, when it meditated the propagation of its kingdom through Sigismund—if history is to be believed—under Charles; in Belgium, when it abdicated the government most devoted to the Antichrist, the Spanish one. In the Duchies of Jülich, Cleves, and Berg, not without pain, indignation, and blasphemy. To say nothing of the fact that the Pope’s indirect power in secular matters, and the works of Bellarmine, the greatest champion of that same power, were both burned in Rome itself and condemned and adjudged to the fire in France, although by the intercession of the Jesuits with the Queen, grace was granted to them, who were nevertheless ordered to depart themselves in the year 1611: such as these were the points: that the Pope ought not to command Kings, nor have the power of excommunicating a King and stripping him of his kingdoms, nor be above a council, and that the clergy are indeed subject to the jurisdiction of the Magistrate, etc. This vial was certainly poured out upon the empire itself and the very Papal beast sustaining idolatry, not upon Pagan Rome, as Grotius perverts it: whose gloss concerning the time of the darkening in no way agrees with the series of the Apocalyptic vials. And do not the Anti-Christians consider Catholics to be atheists because they worship the one God, the maker of the world, and do not allow anyone to be joined or coordinated with Him in the religious worship of the first table?

Latin:

Vers. 10. Καὶ ὁ πέμπτος Ἄγγελος ἐξέχεε τὴν φιάλην αὑτοῦ ἐπὶ τὸν θρόνον τοῦ θηρίου) Non in singulos, sed in ipsum imperium, per quod idololatria sustentabatur.

Καὶ ἐγένετο ἡ βασιλεία αὐτοῦ ἐσκοτωμένη) Romana Do- minatio multum amifit fplendoris pristini, incursatum, va- statum, partim & insessum a barbaris, Persis, Boramis, Go- this, Burgundis, Alemannis, Marcomannis, Scythis, Sar- matis sub Alexandro, Valeriano, Gallieno, Claudio & aliis. Vide Herodianum & Latinos, qui vitas Cæsarum scripsere & Chronica. Alluditur ad tenebras Ægypti. Pari sensu מענף & חשכה habet Ef. VIII. 22. Καὶ ἐμασσῶντο τὰς γλώσσας αὑτῶν ἐκ τῶ πόνε) Aristo- phanes Vespis : Ὑπὸ ὀργῆς τὴν χολήνην ἐσθίων, ubi Scholia- stes ἀντὶ τῶ τὰ χείλη, ὦ γὰρ ὀργιζόμενοι ὀιδάκνεσι τὰ χείλη. Ita solent, qui irascuntur, nec vindicare se possunt. Vers. 11. Καὶ ἐβλασφήμησαν τὸν Θεὸν τᾶ ὐρανᾶ ἐκ τῶν πό- νων αὑτῶν, καὶ ἐκ τῶν ἑλκῶν αὑτῶν) Conjungit phialas, se- cundam, tertiam, quartam cum prima. ἐκ significat hic causam moventem ut מן sæpe apud Ebræos. Christia- nos, quod unum Deum mundi opificem colerent, voca- bant ἀθέες. Καὶ ἐ μετενόησαν ἐκ τῶν ἔργων αὑτῶν) non destiterunt ab idololatria. Imo & nova sacra addiderunt, Criabolia, Taurobolia.

Hæc plaga jam ipsum thronum & sedem Papa- lem ferit, effusa phiala iræ & sententiæ condemna- toriæ per Megalandrum Lutherum, ejusque fideles sectatores. Tenebrosum factum est, quod pate- factum tale sit regnum Pontificium; quum res tum fieri in sacris dicantur, quum patefiunt; quia addi- tur etiam manifestatis tenebris Papatus, quomodo luce spirituali Evangelii destitutus in tenebris ignorantiæ errorum peccati & damnationis verse- tur, nihilo secius ad μετάνοιαν reductus fuerit thro- nus Papalis cum regno suo Anti-Christiano. Qualis enim thronus, talis etiam lux & tenebricositas, de quibus spiritualibus tenebris Ef. LX. 1. 2. Eph. V. 8. 14. 1. Thes. V. 4. 5. 2. Cor. VI. 14. Quo sensu etiam ex- posuit Cæsariensis patefactionem tenebrarum de- notari, qua demonstrata Anti-Christi gubernatio ἀφεγγὴς τῷ τῆς δικαιοσύνης ἡλίῳ, quæ loco conver- sionis majorem blasphemiam Anti-Christianorum operata est per Accidens, ut Evangelii lux excæ- care dicitur, & Evangelium sit odor mortis ad mor- tem 2. Cor. II. Alii de dolore regni Anti-Christiani, quia lux gaudium, tenebræ tristitiam denotant, 2. Sam. XXII. 29. 30, Job. XXX. 30. Jer. XIV. 2. Thr. IV. 16. Jer. XIII. 16. (quem imprimis nostro pa- rallelum fecit B. Cluverus, huic sententiæ cum Are- ta calculum adjiciens) Mich. VII. 8. interpretari malunt. Etsi vero de tenebris spiritualibus parum soliciti sint forte Papales; id tamen sine dolore non ferunt, quod sedem Regis sui aggrediantur inermes Agonistæ, & oppugnent, & expugnent; quodque opponant sese Principes Pontifici summo, Cardina- libus & Archi-Episcopis, qui ipsis Regibus se com- parare imo præferre non dubitant; ideo comman- ducant linguas suas præ dolore, vel ex molestia: Cui forte junguntur ulcera, ut nondum finitam esse plagam primam, sed auctam potius innuatur. Quantas, libris etiam scriptis, præ ira & furore evo- muerint blasphemias, orbi jam patefactum est. De quibus uti quondam Psalterium, ita nunc testari possunt Biblia in Mariæ laudem trahentia pleraque elogia, quæ Deo tributa, non absque summa blas- phemia & idololatria: quæ hoc seculo prodierunt. Hæc scilicet est ipsorum resipiscentia a manifesta- tis tenebris errorum, plus quam Cimmeriis, vel po- tius Ægyptiacis, & in solis, quod dicitur, disco ex- positione. Tenebræ certe Papatus ita jam pate- factæ, ut in ipsa Italia illustris Resp. Veneta thronum Pontificium contemptui habere cœperit, & Pon- tificem summum Paulum V. ad fulmen excommu- nicationis abrogandum adegerit, ac Jesuitas para- statas & propugnatores Anti-Christi præcipuos di- tionibus suis exegerit, cum hoc prosemptico: Mox, longe, tarde, (vel nunquam) cede, recede, redi. In Gallis vero Henricus IV. in Germania Ferdinandus III. pacem adversariis throni Papalis concesserit. Quæ autem ad illam phialam & pla- gam linguarum manducationes, qui animi crucia- tus sequuti sint, inter alia Bulla Innocentii X. doce- bit. Similia fata experta est sedes Romana in An- glia, Scotia, Hybernia, sub Jacobo VI. In Polonia ad- missa & ceu lege fundamentali trium religionum adeoque Evangelicæ sancita confœderatione, in Hungaria, Transylvania, &, ad breve licet tempus, in Bohemia, Austria ipsa, & provinciis aliis Austria- cis. In Suecia cum meditaretur per Sigismundum, si historiæ fides habenda, regni sui propagationem sub Carolo, in Belgio cum abdicavit regimen Anti- Christo cum maxime devotum Hispanicum. In Ducatibus Juliacensi, Clivensi & Montium non absque dolore, indignatione, ac blasphemia. Ut ta- ceam, quod Papæ etiam indirecta potestas in secu- laribus, & Bellarmini ejusdem Propugnatoris ma- ximi opera tum in ipsa Roma cremanda fuerint, tum in Gallia damnata, & igni adjudicata sint, etsi intervenientibus penes Reginam Jesuitis gratia fa- cta, qui tamen ipsi cedere Anno 1611. jussi sunt: quales erant: Papam non debere Regibus imperare, nec habere potestatem Regis excommunicandi, & re- gnis suis exuendi, neque supra concilium, clerum ve- ro jurisdictioni Magistratus subjectum esse, &c. In ipsum certe imperium bestiamque ipsam Papalam idololatriam sustentantem hæc phiala effusa, non in Romam Ethnicam, ut pervertit Grotius: cu- jus glossa de obscurationis tempore nullatenus convenit seriei phialarum Apocalypticæ. Et annon Anti-Christiani Catholicos, quod unum Deum mundi opificem colant, nec ei quenquam in cultu religioso primæ tabulæ sub-vel coordinari pa- tiantur, pro atheis habent?

## 16:12
Verse 12. And the sixth angel poured out his vial upon the great river Euphrates) He continues to speak enigmatically. For just as he calls Rome not Rome, but Babylon: so he calls the Tiber not the Tiber, but the Euphrates.

And its water was dried up) That is, through the bridge he provided a way no less than if it were dry. There is an allusion to the history of Cyrus, Jerem. 51:20, 30, 31. See what is said there.

That the way of the kings from the east of the sun might be prepared) By the east he signifies Christ, as above VIII. 2, where see what was said. Kings to our writer are not only Emperors, but also Presidents and Dukes, as we said above VI. 15. Constantine is understood here with his sons and Dukes. The history is in Zosimus and Eusebius. These are the Kings whom those magi from the east had once prefigured, Matt. II.

Latin:

Vers. 12. Καὶ ὁ ἕκτος Ἄγγελος ἐξέχεε τὴν φιάλην αὑτοῦ ἐπὶ τὸν ποταμὸν τὸν μέγαν Εὐφράτην) Pergit αἰνίττεσθαι. Nam sicut Romam, non Romam vocat, sed Babylonem: Ita Ty- berim, non Tyberim, sed Euphraten.

Καὶ ἐξηράνθη τὸ ὕδωρ αὐτοῦ) Id est per pontem viam præ- buit non minus quam si siccus esset. Alluditur ad historiam Cyri Jerem. LI. 20. 30. 31. Vide quæ ibi dicta.

Ἵνα ἑτοιμασθῇ ἡ ὁδὸς τῶν βασιλέων ἀπ’ ἀνατολῶν ἡλίου) Per orientem significat Christum, ut supra VIII. 2. ubi dicta vi- de. Βασιλεῖς nostro Scriptori sunt non Imperatores tantum, sed & Præsides & Duces, ut diximus supra VI. 15. Intelli- gitur hic Constantinus cum filiis suis & Ducibus. Historia est apud Zosimum & Eusebium. Hi sunt Reges quos olim fi- guraverant magi illi ἀπ’ ἀνατολῶν, Matth. II.

## 16:13
Verse 13. And I saw out of the mouth of the dragon, and out of the mouth of the beast) From the Devil, and Roman idolatry, which is the former beast, from the sea.

And out of the mouth of the false prophet) The false prophet is the same as the terrestrial beast: Just as the two Prophets above XI. 11 signify a gathering of Prophets, so here the False Prophet, by enallage, signifies a multitude of Prophets. Thus the image is a multitude of idols, as we observed above.

Three unclean spirits like frogs) And here there is an allusion to the frogs of Egypt, but enigmatically. Frogs are both impure, and they dwell in the mud, and they croak to no profit. Schemos Rabba also compares those ignorant of the law to dogs. Those three spirits, which are compared to frogs, are the inspection of entrails, augury, and the Sibylline books, in which Maxentius trusted. See Zosimus, book II. In the manuscript, 'three' is absent.

Latin:

Vers. 13. Καὶ εἶδον ἐκ τοῦ στόματος τοῦ δράκοντος, καὶ ἐκ τοῦ στόματος τοῦ θηρίου) Ex Diabolo, & idolatria Romana, quæ fera prior est, ex mari.

Καὶ ἐκ τοῦ στόματος τοῦ ψευδοπροφήτου) Idem est ὁ ψευδο- προφήτης, & fera terrestris: Sicut duo Prophetæ supra XI. 11. significant cœtus Prophetarum, ita hic Pseudo-Prophe- ta per ἐναλλαγὴν multitudinem Prophetarum. Sic ἡ εἰκὼν multitudo simulacrorum, ut supra observavimus.

Πνεύματα τρία ἀκάθαρτα ὡς βάτραχοι) Et hic allusio est ad ranas Ægypti, sed αἰνιγματωδῶς. Ranæ & impuræ sunt, & in cœno versantur, & coaxant nullo cum fructu. Ignaros le- gis canis comparat etiam Schemos Rabba. Tres isti Spiri- tus, qui ranis comparantur, sunt exstispicium, auspicium & libri Sibyllini, quibus fidebat Maxentius. Vide Zosimum libro II. In Manuscripto abest τρία.

## 16:14
For they are spirits of demons performing miracles) They sometimes speak the truth, by the instinct and work of the Demon, God permitting it.

(Which go forth unto the kings of the whole world) They deceive Maxentius and the nobles who are with him.

To gather them to the war of that great day of God the Almighty) That great day is the one on which Constantine took Rome.

More correctly concerning the empire of the East, abstracted from the Western, no longer acknowledging the Papal Dominion. These words, says B. Gravius, are not to be understood literally concerning the coming of the Turks, who do not require the drying up of the Euphrates, but figuratively. The Euphrates signifies the principal defenses of Babylon, which were the huge treasures, the revenues of bishoprics derived from all the Western Provinces to the Roman see, palls, annates, tithes, first fruits, taxes, indulgences, reservations, dispensations, vacancies, commendams, etc. These waters are dried up by the benefit of the reformation instituted by B. Luther, and a huge decrease occurs daily, by the defection and desolation of so many Papal bishoprics, colleges, and cloisters. The Kings coming from the East will seize this opportunity, and perceiving that the powers of the Papal see have been weakened, they will capture and desolate the Anti-Christian Babylon. The type of this matter is taken from the history of the capture of Babylon by Cyrus from Herod. book 1 and Xenoph. book 7 of the Cyropaedia. Babylon had two notable defenses: 1. walls 50 royal cubits thick and 200 royal cubits high. 2. The Euphrates flowing through the city itself with such depth that two men standing upon one another would not emerge from the waters. For the assault of that most fortified city came the Kings from the East, Darius the Mede and Cyrus the Persian, Jer. 51:28. Despairing of the storming of the walls, a plan was initiated for diverting the Euphrates. Therefore, with very many and very deep trenches prepared, the waters of the Euphrates were led into the trenches and provided the Persians with a dry passage into the city. Soon the palace was stormed, King Belshazzar, who was passing his time securely at banquets, was slaughtered, and Babylon with the entire Monarchy was captured, Dan. 5:30. The matter corresponds most excellently to this type: 1. The Anti-Christian Babylon is fortified with two most strong defenses. It had 1. for walls, Emperors, Kings, Princes, Bishops, Prelates, and robust peoples, demented by superstition, drawing their weapons for Babylon. It had 2. the Euphrates, rolling the treasures of the world to Rome in a most deep channel, so that the treasury of the Church might exceed the wealth of all Kings by a great distance. Therefore, just as Babylon prides itself on most deep waters, so Rome prides itself on inexhaustible treasures. But just as the Euphrates, led into trenches and dried up, provided an easy passage for the Kings of the Medes from the East so that the old Babylon might be captured, so with the Papal riches diminished, the way will be easy for the Kings destined by GOD to capture and destroy the new Anti-Christian Babylon. They are called Kings of the East because they adhere to Christ, who is the Dayspring from on high, Luke 1, and are sent Divinely to attack the Anti-Christ. Just as once the Kings of the Medes and Persians were sent from the East by Divine command for the desolation of Babylon. However, we admit that concerning the adherence to Christ not so much in doctrine as in the battle against the Anti-Christ: Although from the mouth of the Dragon there proceeded Monks of various orders for the sake of strengthening him, and religious men so called by antiphrasis, especially the Jesuits, similar to croaking frogs, as we said at chapter 9, however much the writings of our people—B. Chemnitz, B. Gerhard, B. Hunnius, Heilbrunner, Zeemann, Brochmand, and others, as also Dan. Chamier’s Panstratia, Rivet’s Catholicus Orthodoxus, Voetius’s Desperata Causa Papatus, Maresius’s Anti-Tirinus and Anti-Christus Revelatus—have demonstrated that they croak to no fruit. But these things depict primarily the Jesuits and the demons of other orders, insinuating themselves by false miracles into the courts of Kings for the sake of propagating Papism throughout the world, for which end the Spanish League was initiated. The place of punishment is called Harmageddon according to B. Luther, that is, the ill-omened and execrable League, looking back to the city of the tribe of Simeon, Hormah, Num. 21:3, at which the Israelites first cursed the Canaanites. But what do those three impure spirits similar to frogs signify more correctly than the Jesuits, belched forth from the impure mouth of the two-horned beast, similar to croaking frogs, especially those which penetrated into the court of Pharaoh, impure not only by reason of superstition and impure doctrine, which the Casuists and Moralists attest, but especially by reason of the definitions, decisions, and disputations, by which they foster and defend impure marriages, incests, sodomies, and concubinage, as well as by reason of an impious and unclean life. The number three is one of perfection and is especially suited to that manifold variety. For the Pope considers his kingdom perfect and blessed in this respect as well. Concerning the Sibylline books, which not a few judge to have been edited not for the sake of idolatry, which they do not champion, but for the sake of a purer Theology, to which they sometimes bear witness, see what has been said in the Isagoge.

Verse 14. And behold I come as a thief) These things and what follows up to what he gathered are to be read as a parenthesis, and they are the words of Christ. See above III.3. Christ says that he will come upon the idolaters unexpectedly.

Latin:

Εἰσὶ γὰρ πνεύματα δαιμόνων ποιοῦντα σημεῖα) Vera inter- dum dicunt, Dæmonis instinctu atque opera, Deo id sinente.

Ἃ ἐκπορεύεται ἐπὶ τοὺς βασιλεῖς τῆς οἰκουμένης ὅλης) Deci- pient Maxentium & proceres qui cum eo.

Συναγαγεῖν αὐτοὺς εἰς πόλεμον τῆς ἡμέρας ἐκείνης τῆς μεγά- λης τοῦ Θεοῦ τοῦ παντοκράτορος) Dies illa magna est, qua Con- stantinus Romam cœpit.

Rectius de Orientis imperio abstracto ab Occi- dentali non amplius Dominatum Papalem agno- scente. Hæc verba, inquit B. Gravius, non literali- ter de adventu Turcarum, qui exsiccatione Euphra- tis non indigent, sed figurate intelligenda sunt. Eu- phrates significat præcipua Babylonis præsidia, quæ fuerunt ingentes thesauri, ex omnibus Provinciis Oc- cidentalibus ad sedem Romanam derivati proven- tus Episcopatuum, pallia, annata, decimæ, primitiæ, taxæ, indulgentiæ, reservata, dispensationes, vacan- tiæ, commendæ, &c. Hæ aquæ exsiccantur beneficio reformationis a B. Luthero institutæ, & ingens quo- tidie fit decrementum, defectione & desolatione tot Episcopatuum, collegiorum & claustrorum Papalium. Hanc occasionem arripient Reges ab Oriente ve- nientes & cernentes, labefactatas esse sedis Papalis vires, Babylonem Anti-Christianam capient & deso- labunt. Typus hujus rei desumitur ex historia captæ Babylonis per Cyrum ex Herod. lib. 1. & Xenoph. lib. 7. Pæd. Habuit Babylon duo insignia præsidia 1. mu- ros crassos 50. cubitos & altos 200. cubitos Regios. 2. Euphratem urbem ipsam interlabentem tanta pro- funditate, ut duo viri sibi insistentes aquis non emine- rent. Ad oppugnationem urbis illius munitissimæ ve- nerunt Reges ab Oriente, Darius Medus & Cyrus Persa Jer. LI. 28. Desperata murorum expugnatio- ne consilium initum fuit de Euphrate divertendo. Fossis igitur plurimis profundissimisq́; paratis aquæ Euphratis in fossas deductæ siccum Persis in urbem transitum præbuerunt. Mox Regia expugnata, Rex Belsasar convivia securus agens trucidatus, & Ba- bylon cum universa Monarchia capta fuit. Dan. V. 30. Huic typo res optime respondet 1. Babylon Anti- Christiana duobus munita est præsidiis fortissimis. Habuit 1. pro muris Imperatores, Reges, Principes, Episcopos, Prælatos & populos robustos, superstitione dementatos pro Babylone arma stringentes. Habuit 2. Euphratem alveo profundissimo mundi thesauros Romam advolventem, ut fiscus Ecclesiæ omnium Re- gum gazas longissime excederet. Ut igitur Babylon aquis profundissimis: Ita Roma thesauris inexhau- stis superbit. Sicut vero Euphrates in fossas deductus & exsiccatus Regibus Madai ab ortu transitum faci- lem præbuit, ut Babylon vetus caperetur: Sic opibus Papalibus diminutis Regibus a DEO destinatis via facilis erit, ut Babylonem novam Anti-Christianam capiant atque destruant. Dicuntur Reges Orientis, quia adhærent Christo, qui est Oriens ex alto Luc. I. & Divinitus ad oppugnandum Anti-Christum mit- tuntur. Quemadmodum olim Reges Medorum & Persarum ab oriente ad desolationem Babylonis Di- vinitus ablegati fuerunt. Illud autem de adhæsione Christi non tam in doctrina quam pugna contra Anti-Christum admittimus: Licet ex Draconis ore prodierint illius firmandi causa varii ordinis Mo- nachi, & religiosi κατ' ἀντίφρασιν ita dicti, imprimis Jesuitæ, ranis coaxantibus gemini, ut ad IX, cap. di- ximus, utut nullo fructu eosdem coaxare nostra- tium scripta, B. Chemnitii, B. Gerhardi, B. Hunnio- rum, Heilbrunneri, Zeæmanni, Brochmandi, & alio- rum, ut & Dan. Chamieri Panstratia, Riveti Catho- licus Orthodoxus, Voëtii desperata causa Papatus, Maresii Anti-Tirinus & Anti-Christus Revelatus demonstrarunt. Hæc autem apprime depingunt Jesuitas aliorumque ordinum Dæmonas, falsis mi- raculis se insinuantes in Regum aulis ad Papismum per orbem terrarum propagandum, quo fine Liga Hispanica inita est. Pœnæ locus Harmageddon se- cundum B. Lutherum dicitur, id est, infausta & exe- cranda Liga, civitatem tribus Simeon Horma respi- ciens, Num. XXI. 3. ad quam Israëlitæ Cananæos pri- mum execrati sunt. Tres vero illi Spiritus impuri ra- nis similes quid rectius innuunt, quam Jesuitas, ex impuro bestiæ bicornis ore eructatos ranis coa- xantibus similes, imprimis illis, quæ in aulam Pha- raonis penetrarunt, impuros non tantum ratione superstitionis & impuræ doctrinæ, quam testantur Casuales & Moralistæ, sed imprimis ratione defini- tionum, decisionum, & disputationum, quibus impu- ra conjugia, incestus, sodamias, concubinatus fovent ac defendunt, necnon ratione impie, & immunde vite. Numerus ternarius perfectionis est & mul- tiplici illi varietati apprime convenit. Regnum enim suum hac quoque parte Pontifex perfectum & beatum æstimat. De libris Sibyllinis, quos in gra- tiam non idololatriæ quam non propugnant, sed purioris Theologiæ, cui quandoque testimonium perhibent, editos, non pauci censent, vid. quæ in Isagog. dicta.

Vers. 14. Καὶ ἰδὲ ἔρχομαι ὡς κλέπτης) Hæc & quæ sequun- tur usque ad quæ συνήγαγεν legenda per παρένθεσιν, & sunt verba Christi. Vide supra III.3. Ait Christus de improviso se superventurum idololatris.

## 16:15
Blessed is he that watcheth) It is an admonition to Christians as above III. 2. 3.

And keepeth his garments) He who persists in the pursuit of good works, below XIX. 8.

Lest he walk naked) Like him of whom above III. 17.

And they see his shame) And here is an active plural for a passive singular. And let those things appear which ought to be covered, nakedness, shame, nakedness, etc., above. We have said, however, that the former crimes are signified, which present themselves to be seen by God, unless they are covered by a better life.

Latin:

Μακάριος ὁ γρηγορῶν) Admonitio est ad Christianos ut supra III. 2. 3.

Καὶ τηρῶν τὰ ἱμάτια αὑτῦ) Qui perstat in bonorum ope- rum studio, infra XIX. 8.

Ἵνα μὴ γυμνὸς περιπατῇ) Ut ille de quo supra III. 17.

Καὶ βλέπωσι τὴν ἀισχημοσύνην ἀυτᾶ) Et hic est activum plurale pro passivo singulari. Et appareant ea, quæ tegi de- bent ערוה αἰσχύνη γυμνότης &c. supra. Diximus autem si- gnificari priora crimina, quæ Deo conspicienda se præbent, nisi obtegantur per vitam meliorem.

## 16:16
Verse 16. And he gathered them) Namely, those three spirits drew together the idolatrous Kings and Leaders into one: they caused them to assemble.

Into a place called in the Hebrew tongue Armageddon) On the Janiculum, which from that assembly could rightly be called the mount of the congregation. For that is Har-Magedon. For there gathered into that place on the side of Constantine ninety thousand foot soldiers, eight thousand horsemen, mostly from the Germans, and Gauls, and Britons. On the side of Maxentius one hundred and seventy thousand foot soldiers, eighteen thousand horsemen from the Romans, Italians, Tuscans, Sicilians, and Carthaginians. For so Zosimus says. Magedo was the name of the plain where Josiah perished 1 Kings 23:29, 2 Chronicles 35:22, Zechariah 12:11. But that history is not referred to here, but rather the slaughter dealt by Barak to the Canaanites at the waters of Megiddo, Judges 5:19. Waters are usually in mountainous places. The Hebrew Har is usually translated by mountain. Thus Argarizin in Eusebius in the Praeparatio. Har-Gerizim. Thus Arsamosata in Pliny and Tacitus, Har-Shemesh, that is, the mount of the sun, Sinai. Doubtless the pronunciation of the letter Heth was so faint that it was not heard. And the letter He itself [is] E to the Greeks.

From the throne) That is, from that place of the sanctuary in which God sat magnificently above the Cherubim, setting his feet upon the floor. For in that figure the seat of God was conceived among the Hebrews.

Saying, It is done) It was Rome. A similar expression below XXI. 6.

Latin:

Vers. 16. Καὶ συνήγαγεν ἀυτὸς) Nempe illa τρία πνεύματα in unum contraxere Reges ac Duces idololatras: fecere ut convenirent.

Εἰς τόπον τὸν καλύμενον Ἑβραϊτὶ Ἀρμαγεδών) In Janiculo qui ex illo conventu recte dici posset mons congregationis. Id enim הר מגרגו . Coire enim in eum locum ex parte Constantini nonaginta millia peditum, octo millia equi- tum, ex Germanis maxime, & Gallis & Britannis. Ex parte Maxentii centum & septuaginta peditum millia, octodecim equitum millia ex Romanis, Italis, Thuscis, Siculis, Cartha- ginensibus. Ita enim Zosimus. Magedo vocata fuit plani- ties, ubi Josias periit 1. Reg. XXIII.29 2. Paral. XXXV. 22. Zach. XII. 11. Verum ea historia hic non respicitur, sed po- tius strages a Baraco in Cananzos edita, ad aquas Mageddo Jud.V. 9. Aquæ solent esse in montanis locis. הר Ebræum solet verti per ὄς. Sic Ἀργαριζὶν apud Eusebium in Præ- paratione. הר גריזין. Sic Arsamosata apud Plinium & Tacitum הר שמשת id est mons solis Syna. Nimirum literæ ח pronunciatio erat ita tenuis, ut non audiretur. Et ipsa litera ה Græcis E.

Ἀπὸ τῶ θρόνε) Id est ab illo adyti loco, in quo magnifice Deus sedit supra Cherubinos pedes imprimens areæ. Ea enim figura Dei sedes concipiebatur apud Ebræos.

Λέγεσα, γέγονε) Fuit Roma. Similis locutio infra XXI. 6.

## 16:17
Verse 17. And the seventh Angel poured out his vial into the air) That is, into the mid-heaven, as above VIII. 13, XIV. 6. Why this? Because these evils were to be scattered widely into the sea, the rivers, the earth, that is, the people of the city into smaller cities or towns, and into all parts of the Roman dominion.

With all respect to the judgment of others, says the blessed Gravius, I think that the dissensions between the Kings and Princes themselves that arose in the Pontifical kingdom are to be understood here. For the King of the Gauls, although attached to the Pontifical religion, 'And a great voice came out of the temple of heaven') From the heavenly sanctuary. A huge secret is revealed, that Rome is mortal. In the Manuscript 'out of the temple' without those words 'of heaven.' And so the Latin.

attacks the two-horned beast, that is, the Spaniard with his League. The Roman Pontiff himself, having followed the party of the King of France for some time, defected to the Leaguers. The modern Pope is plotting a new war distinct from the rest, the King of Portugal, having shaken off the Spanish yoke, has passed over to the French, Swedish, and confederate camps: Some wish to be called Neutrals. Which we leave in their own place.

Latin:

Vers. 17. Καὶ ὁ ἕβδομ@ Ἄγγελος ἐξέχεε τὴν φιάλην ἀυτῶ εἰς τὸν ἀέρα) Id est εἰς τὸ μεσράνημα, ut supra VIII, 13. XIV. 6. Quare hoc? Quia hæc mala late erant spargenda in mare, amnes, terram, id est, populum urbis in urbes aut oppida minora, & in omnes partes ditionis Romanæ.

Salvo aliorum judicio, inquit B. Gravius, in- telligi hic existimo dissensiones inter ipsos Re- ges & Principes in regno Pontificio ortas. Rex enim Galliarum Pontificiæ quamvis religioni addi- Καὶ ἐξῆλθε φωνὴ μεγάλη ἀπὸ τῶ ναῦ τῶ ἐρανᾶ) Abadyto cœlesti. Ingens arcanum patefit, Romam esse mortalem. In Manuscripto ἐκ τῶ ναῦ sine illis τῶ ἐρανᾶ. Et sic Latinus.

ctus oppugnat bestiam bicornem, hoc est, Hispanum cum sua Liga. Pontifex Romanus ipse, aliquandiu sequutus partes Regis Galliarum, defecit ad Ligistas. Modernus Papa novum molitur bellum a reliquis distinctum, Rex Portugalliæ, excusso jugo Hispanico transiit ad castra Gallica, Svecica & confœderato- rum: Quidam Neutrales dici volunt. Quæ nos suo loco relinquimus.

## 16:18
Verse 18. And there were lightnings and thunders and voices) That is, voices of thunders. Thus also above IV. 5, VIII. 5, for which we have voices of thunder above VI. 1.

And there was a great earthquake, such as there was not, since men were upon the earth, such a great earthquake) The earthquake in this place is a huge change of affairs, see above XI. 13. Psalm XVIII. 8. and often among the ancient Prophets. Those words 'such as there was not, such a great earthquake' are explanatory of what preceded, 'such as there was not,' namely so great, and therefore admirable. This earthquake is the dominion of the Ostrogoths in Italy, the Queen of nations, and indeed in the very city of Rome. In the Manuscript: 'Since men were,' etc., by hypallage, of which we have just spoken. Daniel said for this: 'Such as has not been since a nation was upon the earth.'

Not the dominion of the Ostrogoths, but the movement of the attackers of the Western Anti-Christ, (which will be as it were of the whole earth because of the huge army against Italy and the patrimony falsely so-called of Peter, and the gift of Constantine, and Rome, where that Queen sat, the harlot, formerly whoring with all the Kings of the earth, the great city, nay, greatest in power, authority, and empire, but divided into three parts. Whether this fire by which it was consumed is the heavenly fire of truth and spiritual overthrow, or whether it is to be understood as bodily, Interpreters still dispute, and the definition is difficult before the prophecy is converted into history, the prediction into fulfillment. The beginning of this storm, if you listen to the blessed Gravius, who wished to be singular here, is to be placed in the year of Christ 1630, in which, through the arrival and glorious victories of the Northern Lion, a notable and previously unheard-of commotion of the whole Roman empire, Kingdoms, and Dominions in the West arose. Divinely directed indeed against Babylon, but by the just judgment of God punishing the security, hypocrisy, ingratitude, and other horrible sins of the Evangelicals, it was turned against all the inhabitants of Germany and certain neighboring Regions, myriads of whom perished in this most disastrous and still-continuing war. Our opinion is more consistent with the continuity of the visions.

These things can be admitted, whether the words of Christ are read in a parenthesis, which is not necessary, or without a parenthesis, since they cohere with the following things that denounce the final judgment under the pouring out of the last vial. We had similar words of Christ in Revelation III, and concerning the coming of Christ in 1 Thessalonians V. But that the congregation prior to the final judgment, such as that was not under Constantine, but which is yet to be in the future under Gog and Magog, is to be understood, after the Dragon, as far as pagan persecutions and those who were outside the Church were concerned, rested for a thousand years from Constantine the Great, will be evident around chapter XX. The blessed Gravius interprets this vial a little differently: After the reformation made by the ministry of the blessed Luther, although among the Israelites, that is, in the Evangelical Church, the brightness of truth enlightened many: Nevertheless, the majesty of the Roman Pontiff and his kingdom was obscured day by day more and more, deserted by many: kitchens grow cold, authority becomes cheap not only among the Evangelicals, but also among the Pontifical Princes themselves, who value his omnipotence, sales of indulgences, and brute thunderbolts little. And certainly, a much greater obscuration will follow in the progress of time before his total ruin.

Latin:

Vers.18. Καὶ ἐγένοντο ἀςραπαὶ καὶ βρονταὶ καὶ φωναὶ) Id est Φωναὶ βροντῶν. Sic & supra IV. 5. VIII. 5. pro quo φωναὶ βροντῆς habemus supra VI. 1.

Καὶ σεισμὸς ἐγένετο μέγας, διῖ©- ἐκ ἐγένετο, ἀφ᾿ ὗ οἱ ἄν- θρωποι ἐγένοντο τηλικᾶτ@- σεισμὸς ὅτω μέγας) Terræ mo- tus hoc loco est ingens rerum mutatio, supra XI. 13. Psal. XVIII. 8. & apud Prophetas veteres sæpe. Illa τοιῦτ@- ὅτω μέγας sunt ἐξηγητικὰ ejus quod præcessit διῶ, qualis non fuit, nempe tantus, ideoque admirabilis. Is terræ motus est Ostrogothorum dominatus in Italia gentium Regina, adeoque in ipsa urbe Roma. In Manuscripto: Ἀφ᾽ ὗ ἄνθρωπ@- ἐγένετο, &c. per ὑπαλλαγὴν, de qua modo diximus. Daniel pro eo dixit: Οἵα ἐγέγονεν ἀφ᾽ ὗ ἐγενήθη ἔθν©- ἐν τῇ γῇ.

Non Ostrogothorum dominatus, sed oppugnato- rum Anti-Christi occidentalis motus, (qui erit terræ veluti universæ ob ingentem exercitum adversus Italiam & Petri ψευδωνύμως nuncupati patrimoni- um, ac Constantini donum, & Romam, ubi sedem si- xit Regina illa, meretrix, scortans quondam cum uni- versis Regibus terræ, civitas magna, imo potentia, autoritate & imperio maxima, sed in tres partes discerpta. Ignis hic quo exhausta, an sit ignis cælestis veritatis & eversio spiritualis,an vero corporalis in- telligatur,disquirunt adhuc Interpretes,& difficilis est definitio, antequam prophetia convertatur in historiam, vaticinium in complementum. Initium hujus tempestatis, si B. Gravium audias, qui hic sin- gularis esse voluit, collocandum in A. C. 1630. quo per adventum & gloriosas victorias Leonis septen- trionalis insignis & antea non audita orta est totius imperii Romani Regnorum & Dominiorum in Occi- dente commotio. Divinitus quidem directa contra Babylonem, sed justo Dei judicio securitatem, hypo- crisin, ingratitudinem, aliaque horrenda Evangeli- corum peccata puniente, in omnes Germaniæ & vici- narum quarundam Regionum incolas versa, quorum infinitæ myriades funestissimo hoc & adhuc durante bello perierunt. Nostra sententia e συνεχεία visio- num magis consentanea est.

Admitti hæc possunt, ut verba Christi sive in pa- renthesi leguntur, quod necessum non est, sive ἄνευ παρενθέσεως quum cohæreant cum consequenti- bus judicium novissimum sub ultimæ phialæ effu- sione denunciantibus. Similia Christi verba ha- buimus Apoc. III. & de adventu Christi 1. Thess.V. Congregationem autem judicio novissimo præ- viam, qualis illa sub Constantino non erat, sed quæ adhuc futura demum est sub Gogo & Magogo in- telligi, postquam inde a Constantino M. per mil- le annos Draco, quantum ad persecutiones pa- ganas & eorum, qui extra Ecclesiam fuerant, quievit, circa c. XX. patebit. B. Gravius hanc phia- lam paulo aliter interpretatur: Post reformatio- nem ministerio B. Lutheri factam, quamvis apud Israëlitas, hoc est, in Ecclesia Evangelica fulgor veri- tatis multos illustraret: Tamen Pontificis Romani, ejusque regni Majestas fuit indies magis magisque ob- scurata, deserta a pluribus: frigent culinæ, vilescit autoritas non modo apud Evangelicos, sed ipsos quo- que Principes Pontificios, qui ipsius omnipotentiam, nundinationes, & bruta fulmina parvi pendant. Et certe multo major ante totalem ejus ruinam temporis progressu obtencbratio sequetur.

## 16:19
Verse 19. 'And the great city became' (So also XVII. 18 below, they call Rome the 'great city,' indicating Tatian, Porphyry, and other Greeks.)

Into three parts) Taken from Ezekiel VI. 2, from which place you will understand the third part of Rome burned by fire, the other two parts exhausted and deserted. That was done by Totila, who destroyed the third part of the walls. The matter itself is narrated, so that it clearly agrees with these words in Procopius, Gothic Wars III and IV.

And the cities of the nations fell) Many cities in Italy and in the provinces were overthrown by the Goths. He says 'fell,' because up to the times of Honorius a great multitude of the common people and many Senators remained, as we shall say below XVII. 16.

And Babylon the great was remembered before God, to give unto her the cup of the wine of the fierceness of his wrath) That 'and' here is 'so': And 'was remembered' is passive, as Acts X. 31. God is said to remember evil actions when he avenges them, as Hosea VII. 2, VIII. 13. Those words 'Babylon the great' are taken from Daniel IV. 17. God shows by that event that he has not forgotten the crimes of Rome. 'Of the wine of the fierceness,' that is, of the poisoned wine, as we said above XIV. 8, 10. 'Of the wrath,' that is, which comes from the wrath of God, as in the said place XIV. 10. What this is will be explained more fully in the following chapter.

And every island fled, and the mountains were not found) Many maritime towns were overthrown, which are 'iyyim to the Hebrews, 'islands' to the Interpreters: Many fortresses also in the middle of the lands. For we said above VIII. 8 that the name of mountains is given to fortresses. And the allegory is elegant, because we said above VI. 14 that both mountains and islands are accustomed to be moved by earthquakes.

Latin:

Vers. 19. Καὶ ἐγένετο ἡ πόλις ἡ μεγάλη) Sic & XVII. 18. infra μεγάλην πόλιν dicunt Romam indicantes Tatianus, Porphyrius, Græcorumque alii.

Εἰς τρία μέρη) Sumptum ex Ezechiele VI. 2. ex quo lo- co intelliges Romæ partem tertiam igne exustam, partes duas alias exhaustas atque desertas. Id factum a Totila, qui partem tertiam mœnium destruxit. Narratur res ipsa, plane ut his verbis conveniat apud Procopium Gothicorum III. & IV.

Καὶ αἱ πόλεις τῶν ἐθνῶν ἔπεσον) Multæ urbes in Italiâ & in provinciis a Gothis eversæ. Ἔπεσον dicit, quia ad tem- pora Honorii plebs plurima & Senatores multi manebant, ut dicemus infra XVII. 16.

Καὶ Βαβυλὼν ἡ μεγάλη ἐμνήσθη ἐνώπιον τῦ Θεῦ, δῆναι ἀυτῇ τὸ ποτήριον τῶ δινα θυμᾶ τῆς ὀργῆς ἀυτᾶ) Illudκὴ hic est sic: Et ἐμνήσθη passivum, ut Act. X. 31. Meminisse Deus malarum actionum dicitur, cum eas ulciscitur, ut Of. VII. 2. VIII. 13. Illa verba Βαβυλὼν ἡ μεγάλη sumpta ex Dan. IV. 17. Deus ostendit illo evento, se non oblitum criminum Romæ. Τῷ ὄινε τῶ θυμᾶ, id est venenati vini, us diximus supra XIV. 8.10. Τῆς ὀργῆς, id est, quod venit ab ira Dei, ut dicto loco XIV. 10. Hoc quid sit, amplius expli- cabitur capite sequenti.

Καὶ πᾶσα νῆσ@- ἔφυγε, καὶ ὄρη ἕχ εὑρέθησαν) Eversæ sunt multa oppida maritima, quæ איים Ebræis, Νῆσοι In- terpretibus: Multæ etiam arces in mediis terris. Arcibus enim dari montium nomen diximus supra VIII. 8. Et ele- gans est ἀλληγορία, quia per terræ motus transmoveri solere & montes & insulas diximus supra VI. 14.

## 16:20
Vers. 20. And a great hail as of a talent weight cometh down from heaven unto men) A huge judgment of hardening upon the remnants of the idolaters, above VIII. 7. XI. 19. Nor did he poorly preserve the propriety of the comparison. For histories of many regions and times relate that hail of the size of huge stones has sometimes fallen. Everything that is heavy is called by the Greeks talent-weight, or talent-like, as in the case of talent-weight diseases in Alcaeus. But this is an application of the allegorical history, which is in Exod. IX, 24.

Latin:

Vers. 20. Καὶ χάλαζα μεγάλη ὡς ταλαντιαία καταβαίνει ἐκ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ πρὸς τοὺς ἀνθρώπους) Ingens obdurationis judicium in reliquias idololatrarum, supra VIII. 7. XI. 19. Nec male servavit τὸ πρέπον comparationis. Nam & grandinem in- gentium saxorum magnitudine interdum cecidisse narrant complurium regionum ac temporum historiæ. Omne quod grave est, Græcis dicitur ταλαντιαῖον, vel ταλαντιαῖον, ut νοσημάτων ταλαντιαίων apud Alcæum. Est autem hic appli- catio Allegoricæ historiæ, quæ in Exod. IX, 24.

## 16:21
And men blasphemed God because of the plague of the hail, for the plague thereof is exceeding great) So great was the hardening of their hearts, that the remnants of the idolaters in the Roman Empire cursed the Christians more and more, as if their religion were the cause of all these evils. This was the last gasp of dying idolatry. But by these are to be understood especially the Roman Senators, who, scattered through Italy, were killed by the Goths, some here, some there.

The interpretation is not incorrect, provided that one substitutes Christian or rather Anti-Christian Rome in the place of Pagan or Ethnic Rome, the Roman Pontiff in the place of the Gentile Roman Emperor, and the Roman Cardinals in the place of the Senators, and understands the last gasp and attempt of Papal idolatry, now about to be exterminated with the coming of Christ and punished with hellfire.

It is helpful now to repeat by way of recapitulation, and to summarize those things which have been said concerning the seven Apocalyptic vials, as they have been a crux for more than one interpreter. But having weighed everything, this is our opinion concerning them: That indeed by the first Angel, by the sores protruding upon those who have the mark of the beast, is indicated the sore of conscience, which will be wounded from the fact that they are not permitted to be certain of the grace of God. For this is a path near to despair, Mark IX. 46. Is. XLVI. 24. Therefore they are said to have a cauterized conscience, 1 Tim. IV. 2; an evil conscience, Heb. X. 22.

The second Angel will pour out the vial in the very last times into the sea, from which will overflow blood like that of a dead man, who had recently died: for blood rarely tends to come out naturally red from a dead body, whence the living creatures in the sea will necessarily perish v. 3.

The third will pour the third vial into the rivers and fountains of waters, whence blood will arise. Which being done, the divine justice will be proclaimed by another Angel saying, Thou art just, O Lord, who art, and who wast, and holy, because thou hast judged these things. Because they have poured out the blood of saints and Prophets, and thou hast given them blood to drink: for they are worthy. And another voice was heard from the altar, overlaid with gold, saying: Verily, Lord God Almighty, true and just are thy judgments. By the sea is understood a collection of waters, a notable multitude of peoples. Therefore, entire peoples, regions, and kingdoms are denoted, the Holy Spirit himself being the interpreter. Apoc. XVII. 15. The waters which thou sawest, upon which the harlot sitteth, are peoples, and armies, and nations, and tongues. But the rivers and fountains, as if smaller, are cities, and towns, or villages; or if you prefer, you will be able to understand magnates and Magistrates, as well as those of lower order, and commoners, as also subjects; the harlot will infect all these with her fornications by the just judgment of God, whence the biting worm of conscience will arise in their souls, consuming them forever.

The fourth Angel is occupied in the pouring out of the fourth vial, which is poured out upon the sun; to which it is given to scorch men with fire, and they shall be scorched with a great flame, and they have power to blaspheme the name of God over these plagues: and yet they are not about to give glory to God through repentance. The sun mystically is Christ, who is called the sun of righteousness Mal. IV. 1. Jehovah our righteousness, Jer. XXIII. 6. and has been made righteousness for us by God, that we may glory in him alone, and in his righteousness alone Jer. IX. 24. 1. Cor. I. 30. 31. therefore the Church is said to be περιβεβλημένη τὸν ἥλιον, because she puts on the righteousness of Christ Gal. III. 27. and the garment of this righteousness of her priest, and is adorned with it as the most beautiful habit of her bridegroom, the priestly stole of righteousness Is. LXI. 10. and she rejoices in this her Lord in such a distinguished garment, as a royal bride in her most beautiful adornment Ps. XLV. 8. adorned with embroidered garments v. 15. adorned with the garments of solemn feast days Zech. III. 5. of which one may also read Matt. XVII. 12. Rev. III. 18. c. XIV. 15. c. XIX. 8. 9. He who is destitute of these, it is necessary that he be eternally exiled, and excluded from the marriage of the lamb Rev. XIX. 7. Matt. XXII. 12. The earth there (in βασιλείᾳ ἐσκοτωμένῃ) is dark and obscure, because it is obscured both by smoke and by the mists of stench. The land of oblivion, because, just as they themselves have forgotten God, so God forgets to have mercy on them, as Anselm has it, l. 4. de imag. mundi c. II. Then they will be forcibly cast into the outer darkness, who now voluntarily delight in the inner ones, as Gregory the Great says, l. XXV. moral. c. cent. The fire will shine for the miserable not for the object of consolation, but for the increase of misery, that they may discern whence they suffer by divine power, according to Basil the Great in Ps. 28. Fire will be prepared by its scorching power: the brightness will yield to the joy of the saints, the scorching part to the torment of the damned. The flame of fire designates the wrath of God and hellfire, burning even into hell, Deut. 32, 22. Ps. 97, 10. 2. Thess. 5, 8. 9. 2. Pet. III. 11. never to fail, Is. 66, 24. Mark 9, 44. Rev. 14, 10. 11. c. 18, 7. c. 17, 4. c. 20, 10. Whence God, because of infinite and eternal wrath, is called a consuming fire πῦρ καταναλίσκον Heb. 12, 29. Deut. 4, 24.

The fifth vial is to be poured out upon the very throne of the beast, and from thence his kingdom will be greatly darkened, and they shall gnaw their tongues for pain. By which are foreshadowed the most exquisite hellish torments, to be kindled by the fiery river, because of the extreme magnitude of which the reprobate shall gnaw their teeth, Is. 30, 33. c. 22, 13. of which also see Rev. 17, 16. Luke 16, 23. 24. 25. because of which most grievous hellish pains the damned in those outer darknesses, as they are called Matt. 8, 22. c. 22, 13. 1. Pet. 2, 4. 6. 7. 8. will more vehemently blaspheme the most holy name of the Lord, together with the Devil, and his damned angels; whence their torments will be increased more and more, and they shall have no end ever, they shall leave them no rest, no interval, they shall never cease to be tormented, because they shall never cease to blaspheme and accuse the name of the Lord. As the ulcer pertains to the worm of conscience that will not die, so heat and flame pertain to the inextinguishable fire, by both of which hellish torments, both internal and external, are designated. But there is no place in hell for repentance, none for the remission or rest of punishments, no end, or limit. For the damned shall indeed seek death, and shall not find it, Rev. 9, 6. They shall be tormented in the flesh without intermission by fire, in the soul by the worm of conscience: Thus they shall die, so that they always live, thus they shall live, so that they always die, as Bernard says in his Meditations. As long as God shall live, the elect shall live: as long as the elect shall live, the reprobate shall die, i.e., for ages of ages. There will not be men there before death, and after death, but always in death, says Augustine, XIII. de C. D. c. 11. and by this, never living, never dead, but dying without end. For it will never be worse for man in death, than where death itself will be without death, as the distinguished theologian speaks. Thus fire burns, says Bernard (med. mort. c. 3), so that it may always preserve, thus torments are conducted, so that they may always be renewed: and as Paulinus sings mournfully of the death of Celsus out of human compassion: Life for them will be to die without end, and death to live in punishments, and while it lasts to feed crosses with its own flesh. produces his own executioners from his own body, and will be food for his own worms. For the mind, as Isidore has it in his meditations, will be burned by sadness, the body by flame. There will be weeping from pain, as Bernard says in sermon VIII on the Psalm: He who dwells: Gnashing of teeth from fury. For if, to repeat this from Augustine (l. VI. de C. D. c. 6), the soul lives in eternal punishments, that death is rather to be called eternal than life: for there is no greater and worse death than where death does not die. Nor is the reason for such a judgment lacking, for (as Gregory suggests in his Morals) it pertains to the sentence of strict judgment that they should never lack punishment, whose mind in this life never wished to lack sin.

In the sixth place, the Angel is described with a vial, which he himself will pour out into the Euphrates, the river passing through Assyria (Gen. II. 14), so that it may be dried up, and a way may be prepared for the Kings from the rising of the sun, with the accompanying vision of three frogs. Just as Babylon, says B. Gerhard (p. 121), collected such great riches by the benefit of the Euphrates flowing past it: so the Roman Anti-Christ had his financial nets, namely, the greatest revenues from indulgences, palls, annates, bulls, etc. He thinks the sixth Angel censured these methods of acquiring. But the punishments of Babylon are recounted here, designated by the pouring out of the vials, not the faults; the torments, not the crimes. But the same author more correctly says further that the Euphrates is a symbol of the wealth by which mystical Babylon, i.e., Rome, is fortified: just as ancient Babylon was once fortified by the Euphrates. Cyrus, attacking Babylon, diverted the Euphrates and the rivers near the city elsewhere, so that he might prepare a way for himself into the city (Jer. LI. 31); thus in this place it is predicted that God will prepare a way for the Kings coming from the rising of the sun, so that they may be able to destroy the kingdom of the Anti-Christ, which is mystical Babylon. Historians, praised by Ussher in his Chronology (p. 144), report these things about Cyrus: Cyrus, opening the mouths of the trenches dug by him around the city wall, having diverted the water of the river there, rendered its former channel (stretching through the city with a width of two stadia) passable for men (Herodot. l. 1. c. 190. 191. Xenoph. Instit. l. III. with Jeremiah c. L. 38. & LI. 32. 36.). But Cyrus, crossing the river, now fordable, with his army, having observed all the small gates that led to the river, and having climbed the embankments, invaded the city (Babylon) while they were celebrating feasts on a holiday (Jer. LI. 39. 57.). And such was the magnitude of the city that (as the inhabitants narrated) when those who lived in the outermost parts of the city had already been captured, those who lived in the middle part had not noticed it (Herodot. l. 1. c. 19.). To this point also those words of the prophet Jer. LI. 31: Runner will run to meet runner, and messenger to meet messenger, to indicate to the King of Babylon that his city is captured at the extremity. Conf. Dan. V. 2. 3. 10. 30. Xenoph. Instit. l. 7. Es. 13. 14. 21. 43. 46. 47. Hab. 2. Jer. 25. 50. 51. Dan. 5, 21. c. 5, 8. 12. 15. Others, with Szegedinus, Dölino, Dürf. Franz, Kromeicro, accept these as referring to the drying up of great revenues, which was done through the preaching of the Gospel in Sweden, Denmark, Pomerania, etc. Although, however, these things are contrary neither to the faith nor to the analogy of prophecy, the order of the prophecy nevertheless demands another sense; therefore, since the Turks have no need of a crossing of the Euphrates, seeing that they have long since fixed their seat in Hungary and Transylvania, the metaphorical interpretation, from the comparison of the crossing of the Persian King, B. Gerhard's explanation, can be admitted more easily even in judgment: because those things which are observed from our text concerning the Kings arriving from the rising of the sun, along with some others around this place—namely, that hostile kings are understood, such as were once Darius, King of the Medes, and Cyrus, King of the Persians—are more correctly understood in general as pious Kings and Princes who, having rejected Anti-Christian errors, receive the light of the Gospel, inasmuch as the rising of the sun is a symbol of a good and auspicious thing (Apoc. VII. 2.), and the doctrine of the Gospel is the doctrine concerning Christ, who is the rising from on high (Luc. I. 78.). Richter, Gerhard, Cluver, Erasm. Schmid, and Pareus accept these things, therefore, concerning the devastation and final punishment of Babylon.
