Fourthly, because here in v. 12 and 13 these ten Kings are said to have received power after the beast, and to have delivered their power to the beast, that is, to the Anti-Christ, and then it is added concerning the same in verse 16: These shall hate the whore, and shall burn her with fire. Fifthly, because in the preceding chapter in the vial of the seventh Angel John says: And great Babylon came in remembrance before God, to give unto her the cup of the wine of the fierceness of his wrath. And in this chapter XVII he begins to describe this cup. Therefore it clearly signifies that this destruction of Babylon will be after the seven vials and the last plagues. For this is aptly reserved as if in the last place, because it will be general, and it will be as if a plague of the whole world, in that it itself will be the Mistress of the world, and consequently, with it cut off, the world will seem to be cut off. It is confirmed because this will greatly suit the genius and scope of the Anti-Christ, so that, namely, he himself, as King of Jerusalem and of the Jews fighting against Christ, may overturn the metropolis of His kingdom and Church, to wit, Rome. For he himself will desire this with the highest wishes, so that he may seem to have destroyed the kingdom of Christ. Just as, therefore, the Anti-Christ is opposed to Christ, the Jews to the Christians, and Jerusalem to Rome: so the Anti-Christ will take pains to abolish Christ, the Christians, Rome, and its Pontificate, just as his forerunners, the Calvinists and other heretics, are already taking pains to do. Sixthly, the Fathers teach this. Tertullian, book to Scapula, chapter 2. A Christian, he says, is an enemy to no one, much less to the Emperor, whom he knows to be appointed by his GOD, and it is necessary that he should both love, and revere, and honor him, and wish him well together with the whole Roman Empire, as long as the age shall stand, for it will stand for that long. Theodoret in Dan. VII teaches that the Anti-Christ will emerge from the Roman Empire and will fight against it. St. Jerome in Dan. II speaks thus concerning the Anti-Christ: And the arms of the fighting Roman people shall be overcome by him and crushed. Lactantius, Book VII, Chapters 15 and 25, teaches that the Anti-Christ will overturn the Roman Empire and will transfer it from the West to Asia. At whose destruction, he says, the world itself is about to fall. Again, he says: The thing itself declares that the fall and ruin will be shortly, except that while the city of Rome is safe, nothing seems to be feared from these things. But truly when that head of the world shall have fallen, and shall have begun to be ῥύμη, (which they say is of the Sibyls) who would doubt that the end has now come for human affairs and for the orb of the earth. St. Chrysostom hom. 4. on the 2nd Epistle to the Thessalonians. Just as, he says, the kingdom of the Medes was destroyed by the Babylonians, that of the Babylonians by the Persians, that of the Persians by the Macedonians, that of the Macedonians by the Romans: so also the kingdom of the Romans by the Anti-Christ. In these arguments, even if not all are equally firm, we easily acquiesce. But what is inferred from that: that Beza and others err fraudulently, while they teach that the Roman empire has failed, so that from it they may prove that the Anti-Christ has already come, and that he is the Roman Pontiff, that is also an ἀνακόλουθον, in the judgment of Alcazar the Jesuit himself, nor does it agree with other Papist fabrications about the Anti-Christ being destroyed before the end of the world, not to mention the prophecy of Malachy, that the Roman Pontiff at the time of the Anti-Christ will be Peter the Roman, and that the final judgment will succeed him. But what is to be thought of the Cornelian narrative: the Anti-Christ, gradually growing in strength and number, will defeat three Kings out of ten, who will then be in the world. Soon the remaining ten and all the nations, struck with fear, will send embassies to him, and will submit themselves to him, just as they did to Alexander the Great when Darius was defeated, whence he himself then immediately became Monarch. The Anti-Christ then [will pour] all his venom against Christ and Harassing Christians, and strengthening and propagating the Roman empire, then because it was and will be a rival to the empire, then because it was the seat of the Pontiffs of Christ, he will take care that it be besieged and overturned, and will commit the matter to ten Kings, that is, some of those who will be more powerful and nearer to Rome, the others nevertheless favoring, and assisting with money, provisions, and other means. For there will be no need to gather the armies of ten Kings, that is, of the whole world, for the sake of destroying one city: nor will the time of the kingdom of the Anti-Christ (which will be of three years and a half) suffer such long delays, that Kings from the extreme East, as is said in Chap. XVI, 14, should come to him at Armageddon. For these things require many years. Some Kings, therefore, nearer to Rome will overturn and burn it. Then he will summon the enemy to Armageddon, just as he had already summoned those from the East in Chap. XVI, 14, and other nations from the four corners of the earth together with Gog and Magog. Therefore all these will gather to the Anti-Christ in Judea, so that they may everywhere destroy the name of Christ and of Christians, and their army will be innumerable. Soon Christ will finish off all those gathered, and will kill them with fire sent down upon them from heaven? These are melodious trifles, Jesuitical dreams, which vanish of their own accord into thin air. Because the Anti-Christ of three years is a Utopian Jew from the tribe of Dan, and Utopic, nor does Scripture know any other Anti-Christ than the Roman Pontiff himself.

They will eat her flesh, that is, by the received phrase of Scripture, they will slaughter her members and citizens with a certain pleasure, just as has been done to Evangelical Christians by Roman Catholics, Job XIX, 21. Chap. XXXI, 31. Eccl. IV, 3. Isa. IX, 20, 21. Chap. X, 18. Dan. V, 1, 5. Zech. XI, 9. Although indeed some of these Kings by reason of Persons still adhere to the Pontifical religion, they nevertheless permit the free exercise of the Evangelical religion, and no longer care for the Pope's brute thunderbolts. But finally, when the time divinely predetermined has elapsed, God the Best and Greatest will stir up in these very kingdoms such Kings who will pursue the Anti-Christian beast with hatred, will attack it, and will make it desolate, i.e., they will no longer contribute their treasures to the expanding of the Papacy, but will strip it. Indeed, they will devour her flesh, i.e., the ecclesiastical benefices, revenues, and prebends of the little priests and Monks, and will convert them to the use of Evangelical Churches and Schools, as the Blessed Gravius holds here.

Latin:

Vers. 16.

Καὶ τὰ δέκα κέρατα ἃ εἶδες καὶ τὸ θηρίον.] Ἐπὶ τὸ θηρίον, habet Arethas & multi libri, nec aliter legit Latinus. Οὗτοι μισήσουσι τὴν πόρνην.] Suo tempore insurgent ho- stiliter in dominationem Romanam. Hoc maxime con- spectum Honorii temporibus, ut videre est apud Proco- pium & Historicos alios. Hæc est Romani status abscessio in decem Reges apud Tertullianum: Regni Romani defe- ctio apud Ambrosium: Discessio gentium à Romano im- perio apud Hieron. εἰς δέκα βασιλέας διηρῆσθαι τὴν οἰκουμένην, ait Arethas. Καὶ ἠρημωμένην ποιήσουσιν αὐτήν.] Magis afficient cladi- bus : Τάς τε ἀνθρώπους ἅπαντας ἔκτεινον, ὅσοι ἐγένοντο ἐν πᾶσιν ὁμοίως μὲν πρεσβύτας, ὁμοίως δὲ νέυς, ὔτε γυναικῶν, ὔτε παίδων φειδόμενοι. Καὶ γυμνὴν ποιήσουσιν αὐτήν.] Abstrahent aurum, lapi- des, uniones. Hoc factum est per Alaricum Gothum, & per Genzericum Wandalum. De illo Procopius: Ἐν ῥώμῃ τῶν τε δημοσίων καὶ τῶν ἰδίων ὀδοτιῶν ἀπολιπόντων. De altero vero: χρυσᾶ τε καὶ ἀργύρου καὶ τῶν ἄλλων βασιλέως κτημάτων πολύ τι χρῆμα ἐν ταῖς ναυσὶν ἐνθέμενοι εἰς Καρχηδόνα ἔπλει ἐσύλησε δὲ καὶ Διὸς τοῦ Καπιτωλίου ναόν.

Καὶ τὰς σάρκας αὐτῆς φάγονται.] Provincias in suos usus vertent, spreta Romanorum amicitia. Sic Daciam, Panno- niam, Thraciam, Illyricum modo hi, modo illi populi inva- sere: præterea Galliam Gothi utrique, Burgundiones, Franci: Hispaniam Wandali primum, deinde Wisigothi, Africam Wandali, Britanniam Anglosaxones: Italiam ipsam cum Dalmatis, Alpibus, Norico-Ostrogothi, deinde Longobardi. Loquutio sumpta ex Esa. X, 18. & XLIV, 16.

Καὶ αὐτὴν κατακαύσουσιν ἐν πυρὶ.) Ipsam Babylonem ipsam meretricem comburent, nempe τρίτον μέρος, quod subintelligendum ex fuperioribus XVI, 19. Est talis συνεκ- δοχὴ etiam Historicis frequens. Sic 1. Macc. I, 33. ab Antio- chi hominibus exusta Hierosolyma, quod de pulcherrimis quibusdam ædificiis interpretatur Josephus, & consequens in utroque Macchabaico historia ostendit. Prophetis autem frequentissima talis loquutio, ut Ezech. XXIX, 12. & alibi sæpe. Fuit vetus traditio apud Judæos, fore ut Roma incen- deretur. Habes ejus indicia apud Bachajum & apud Jona- thanem 1. Sam. II, 5. Ezech. XXXIX, 16. Eam Johannes hic approbat, ut & alia ejus generis non pauca. Impletum hoc per Ostrogothos sub Totila. Procopius Gothicorum IX. Ἐτύγχανε γὰρ Τωτίλας πολλὰς μὲν ἐμπρησάμενος τὰς τῆς πό- λεως οἰκοδομίας. Nec est, quod quisquam opponat, tunc Romam fuisse Christianam. Contra enim verum est etiam postquam Imperatores facti erant Christiani, Romæ mansisse idololatriam tum in Senatu, tum in plebe. Nec in Senatu tantum erant pagani, sed & consulatus adipiscebantur, ut Symmachus, cujus oratio exstat pro sacris paganicis. Hiero- nymus ad Esa. LVII. de fuis temporibus agens: Ipsaque Ro- mæ orbis Domina in singulis insulis Domibusque tutelæ simu- lachrum cereis venerans ac lucernis, quam ad tuitionem cedium isto appellant nomine, ut tam intrantes, quam ex- euntes domum suam semper insoliti admoneantur erroris. Et hæc est causa, cur idem Hieronymus, cum Romæ viveret, se purpuratæ meretricis colonum fuisse dicit in Prologo ad Didymum. Cum Totilas urbem invasit, jam plerique ci- ves effugerant, multi fame extincti, multi trucidati, ita, ut de plebe ægre restarent quingenti. Ad hæc cum sequutum est multarum ædium Romæ incendium, portæ dirutæ, mœni- um pars tertia disjecta, noluerunt Romani redire Senatores, & alii, qui exierant paganismo contacti. Sunt, quæ hic sunt verba, sumpta ex loco Dan. VII, 11. In pari causa par even- tus. Vide quanta fuerit Dei patientia in expetenda idolo- latrarum conversione.

Hæc in priori commentatione ita tradiderat Grotius.

Vers. 16.

Καὶ τὰ δέκα κέρατα ἃ εἶδες καὶ τὸ θηρίον, & decem cornua, quæ vidisti in bestia.) Rectius alii libri κατὰ τὸ θηρίον. Solet enim Præpositio cum Accusativo usurpari, ubi aliquid præce- dit, quod rei insit, aut circa rem sit. Οὗτοι μισήσουσι τὴν πόρνην, bi odient fornicariam.) Qui fœderati fuerant populi ac Reges, iidem hostes fient. Quod fieri cœptum Honorii temporibus. Vide Procopium Vanda- licorum I. & adde cæteros, qui Romanam historiam aut Chronica illorum temporum Græce Latineque scripserunt. Irenæus: Decem Regibus, in quod dividetur, quod nunc regnat imperium. Tertullianus, quod hic prædicatur, vocat Roma- ni status abscessionem in decem Reges dispersam. Expectan- dam Romani Regni defectionem vere dixit Ambrosius. Hie- ronymus discessionem gentium à Regno Romano id ipsum appellat. Arethas ex antiquioribus, εἰς δέκα βασιλείας διη- ρῆσθαι τὴν οἰκουμένην. Καὶ ἠρημωμένην ποιήσουσιν αὐτὴν, & desolatam facient il- lam.) Magnis cladibus atterent exhaurientque Romanum imperium, ita, ut vastitas futura sit plurimis in locis. Pro- copius Vandal. I. Τούς τε ἀνθρώπους ἅπαντας ἔκτεινον, ὅσοι ἐγένοντο ἐν ποσὶν, ὁμοίως μὲν πρεσβύτας, ὁμοίως δὲ νέους, ὔτε γυναικῶν, ὔτε παίδων φειδόμενοι: Homines omnes quos repere- rant, occidebant, pariter senes, pariter juvenes, ne mulieribus quidem parcentes aut pueris. Καὶ γυμνὴν ποιήσουσιν αὐτὴν, & nudam facient illam.) Di- vitiis ornamentisque spoliabunt, ut Alaricus Gothus, Gen- zerichus Vandaius. De illo Procopius: Ἐν ῥώμῃ τῶν τε δη- μοσίων καὶ τῶν ἰδίων ὀδοτιῶν ἀπολιπόντες, nihil Romæ relinque- bant publicarum privatarumve rerum. De hoc vero in hunc modum: Χρυσᾶ τε καὶ ἀργύρεα, καὶ τῶν ἄλλων βασιλέως κτη- μάτων πολύ τι χρῆμα ἐν ταῖς ναυσὶν ἐνθέμενοι, ἐς Καρχηδό- να ἔπλεον. Ἐσύλησε δὲ καὶ τὸ τοῦ Διὸς τοῦ καπιτωλίου νεών. Cum ingentem vim auri argentique rerum aliarum ad Imperatorem pertinentium imposuisset navibus, Carthaginem navigavit: Et- iam templum Jovis Capitolini spoliavit.

Καὶ τὰς σάρκας αὐτῆς φάγονται, & carnem ejus manduca- bunt.) Provincias suas facient, ut Daciam, Pannoniam, Thra- ciam, Illyricum, plerique eorum, quos diximus populorum, præterea Galliam Franci, Burgundiones, Gothi utrique Hi- spaniam Vandali primum, inde Visigothi, Africam Vandali, Britanniam Anglo-Saxones, Italiam ipsam cum Dalmatis, Al- pibus, Norico-Ostrogothi, deinde Longobardi.

Καὶ αὐτὴν κατακαύσουσιν ἐν πυρὶ, & ipsam igni cremabunt.) Id factum à Totila, non quidem toti urbi (neque id necesse est, ut impletum sit hoc vaticinium) sed parti ejus, quo tem- pore Romam primum cepit, & quo minus totam incenderet, Belisarii dedit monitis. At portæ incensæ, ædificiaque non pauca. Procopius III. Gothicorum, ubi secundum in Ro- mam introitum narrat, καὶ ἀνοικοδομεῖται, ὅτι τάχιστα πάντα ἐκέλευεν, ὅσα καθελών τε καὶ πυρπολήσας αὐτὸς ἔτυχεν ἡνίκα ῥώμην τὸ πρότερον εἷλε, statim ædificari iterum jussit, quæ ipse dejecerat cremaveratque, cum ante Romam ingressus esset. Idem Gothicorum IV. Ἐτύγχανε δὲ Τωτίλας πολλὰς μὲν ἐμπρησά- μενος τὰς τῆς πόλεως οἰκοδομίας, multa urbis ædificia Totilas incenderat. De tertia mœnium parte diruta vide quæ eo- dem libro in priore Totilæ introitu habet idem Procopius. Vide itidem, quæ mox sequuntur de miserabili urbis con- spectu, portisque à Belisario repositis. Ex quibus optime intelligas ea, quæ hic breviter, latius autem capite sequenti prædicantur.

Videtur Commentator legisse καὶ τὸ θηρίον, pro quo reponendum putat κατὰ τὸ θηρίον, cum tamen emendatissimi Codices plerique omnes, Ste- phanorum nominatim habeant ἐπὶ. Odium me- retricis & illius ruinam dicit tum contigisse, cum fœderati illi populi ac Reges cœperunt fieri ho- stes imperii. Perperam, quia Reges non sunt facti, nec regna constituerunt, nisi post eversum imperium, quæ fuit illa Tertulliano dicta Roma- ni imperii abscessio in decem Reges, Anti-Chri- stum superductura; una enim cum hac poste- riori bestia regnum capessiverunt. Et mirum est, Commentatorem, qui illam Tertulliani sen- tentiam videbatur rejecisse ad cap. XIII. sub finem p. 46. eam huc detorquere: Neque etiam illa, quam putat, abscessio per Gothos primum cœpit sub Honorio, uti vult; nam multo antea nempe anno Christi 254. cœperant irrumpere in Impe- rium, adversus quos pugnans Decius à Trebonia- no Gallo proditus occubuit. Et cum Honorio im- perante passim actum esset de idolatria Ethni- ca, omnibus ejus templis eversis, ut notat Baro- nius ad ann. 399. n. 9. qua ratione potuisset eo tempore Roma, imperiumve Rom. ubique fer- me Christianum πόρνης & fornicariæ nomen re- tinere? Quare illud decem Regum una cum bestia exortorum in illam, quæ & purpurata procul du- bio meretrix odium, longe posterius esse debet hac abscessione, & pertinere ad Pontificis Ro- mani ruinam gradatim peragendam per eosdem Reges, qui ipsi antea tantopere favisse visi fue- rant: quod ex parte cœptum, & porro, dante Deo, fiet, sic ut Roma tandem remaneat omni destituta autoritate, opibus suis plene nudata, iisque privata provinciis, & regnis, quæ antea tanquam feuda Ecclesiæ & patrimonium Petri, ut Anglia quondam, ei fuerint obnoxia. Ne- que hoc vaticinium de urbe exurenda pertinet ad Totilæ incendium, quod totale non fuit. Longe gravius malum Pontificii ipsi hoc Ro- mæ minantur, ut Ribera in excidio supre- mo Anti-Christi, quod expressius describitur capite sequenti. Hæc Maresius. Franciscus Suarez. 3. p. tomo 2. disp. 59. art. 6. sect. 2. censet incertum esse, an Romanum imperium & multo magis an Romana urbs evertenda sit ante Anti- Christum, an per ipsum Anti-Christum. Ribera & Viegas hic censent ante Anti Christum ever tenda, idque putant se demonstrare ex eo, quod Roma hic dicatur evertenda à decem Regibus, ergo ante Anti-Christum. Nam Anti-Christus veniens statim debellabit tres Reges & oc- cidet, ut tantum septem restent, qui sponte ei se subdent. Cum ergo sub Anti-Christo tantum fururi sint septem Reges, sequitur tunc Romam non esse evertendam, sed ante, cum nimirum in orbe erunt decem Reges. Hæc sententia, in- quit Cornelius, est probabilis, eamque sequutus sum 2. Thess. II, 9. eique favere videtur S. Hieronymus in Dan. VII. Contrarium, à seipso discedens 2. Thess. II. jam amplectitur: nimirum Romam & Romanum Imperium evertenda esse non ante An- ti-Christum, sed ab Anti-Christo per decem Reges ei jam subjectos. Probatur primo quia Daniel c. 7. recensens seriem Monarchiarum docet, quod sicut Chaldæorum monarchia eversa est à Persis, Persarum à Græcis, Græcorum à Romanis, ita Ro- manorum imperium evertetur ab ipso Anti-Chri- sto. Secundo quia communis Doctorum senten- tia est, Romanum imperium esse ultimum & du- raturum usque ad finem mundi, nec tantum Do- ctorum recentiorum, sed & Patrum communis, teste S. Hieronymo in Dan. c. IX. hæc est traditio, eaque ut videtur Apostolica. Non ergo à decem Regibus sed ab Anti-Christo in fine mundi evertetur. Con- firmatur quia Dan. II. v. 8. & 24. vidit cornu par- vulum, quod designat Anti-Christum inter decem cornua, id est, decem Reges oriri ex bestia, qua de- signat Romanum imperium. Ergo orietur Anti- Christus ex Romano imperio. Stabit ergo illud usque ad ejus adventum, & ab eo evertetur. Rur- sum cum hoc loco mulier, id est, Roma dicatur in- sidere eidem bestiæ, habenti hæc cornua decem, se- quitur, Romam dominaturam Romano impe- rio & decem Regibus, donec à cornu parvulo, id est Anti-Christo ex eo oriente per decem Reges ei re- bellantes evertatur & concremetur, ut dicitur hic v. 16. Tertio, quia id exigit acoluthia Apocaly- pseos: Hæc enim dividitur in duas partes: prior usque ad caput undecimum continet & enarrat se- ptem sigilla libri signati: posterior à capite undeci- mo usque ad finem continet contenta ipsius libri. Jam sigilla continent ea, quæ præire debent tempus Anti-Christi, liber vero continet illa, quæ fient tempore Anti-Christi. Ergo cum hæc duo capita XVII. & XVIII. contineantur in ipso libro signato, sequitur ea spectare ad Anti-Christum ipsum ejus- que tempus. Respondet Ribera esse hysterologiam sive perturbatum ordinem. Hæc enim duo capita, sive hoc Babylonis, id est, Romæ excidium recto or- dine ponendum esse anterius, nimirum cap. IX, 13. in tuba sexti Angeli. Verum hæc hysterologia ni- mis dura est & præpostera; perturbat enim totum Apocalypseos ordinem. Adde sic ipsa sigilla libri fore longe majora & copiosiora ipso libro: deme hæc duo capita, & alia, quæ eodem spectant, relin- ques exiguam libri materiam. Ita, ut in acoluthia Apocalypseos evitemus hanc hysterologiam, & hæc incommoda non parva, dicendum est, hæc, uti & præcedenti à cap. undecimo & deinceps specta- re ad ipsum librum signatum & consequenter ad tempora Anti-Christi. Sic enim plana evadit to- ta series Apocalypseos. Confirmatur, quia Angelus unus ex iis, qui capite præcedenti visi sunt Johanni habere phialas & plagas novissimas, hæc de Babylo- nis excidio revelavit Johanni; ergo hoc ipsum per- tinet ad plagas orbis ultimas. Quarto quia hic v. 12. & 13. dicuntur hi decem Reges potestatem acce- pisse post bestiam, & potestatem suam bestiæ, id est, Anti-Christo tradidisse, ac deinde de iisdem subdi- tur vers. 16. Hi odient fornicariam, & ipsam igne concremabunt. Quinto quia capite præcedenti in phiala septimi Angeli ait Johannes: Et Baby- lon magna venit in memoriam ante Deum, dare il- li calicem vini indignationis iræ ejus. Et hoc ca- pite XVII. calicem hunc enarrare incipit. Ergo plane significat post septem phialas & plagas novis- simas fore hoc Babylonis excidium. Hoc enim apte ultimo quasi loco servatur, quia erit generale, eritque quasi plaga totius orbis, eo quod ipsa erit or- bis Domina, ac proinde ea excisa orbis excisus vi- debitur. Confirmatur quia id valde congruet genio & scopo Anti-Christi, ut nimirum ipse Rex Hiero- solymæ & Judæorum pugnans contra Christum, regni & Ecclesiæ, ejus metropolim, puta Romam, evertat. Hoc enim ipse summis votis optabit, ut re- gnum Christi delevisse videatur. Sicut ergo Anti- Christus Christo, Judæi Christianis, Hierosolyma Romæ opponitur: Ita Anti-Christus Christum, Christianos, Romam, ejusque Pontificatum abole- re sataget, ut jam satagunt ejus prodromi Calvini- stæ aliique hæretici. Sexto id docent Patres. Tertul- lianus l. ad Scapulam cap. 2. Christianus ait nullius est hostis, nedum Imperatoris, quem sciens à DEO suo constitui, necesse est, ut & ipsum diligat, & re- vereatur, & honoret, & salvum velit cum toto Romano imperio, quousque seculum stabit, tam diu enim stabit. Theodor. in Dan. VII. docet An- ti-Christum ex Romano imperio proditurum & contra ipsum pugnaturum. S. Hieronymus in Dan. II. sic ait de Anti-Christo: Et brachia pugnan- tis populi Romani expugnabuntur ab eo & con- terentur. Lactantius Libr. VII. Cap. 15. & 25. docet, Anti-Christum imperium Romanum ever- surum, illudque ab Occidente in Asiam translatu- rum. Cujus, inquit, interitu mundus ipse lapsu- rus est. Rursum: Res, inquit, ipsa declarat, lapsum ruinamque brevi fore, nisi quod incolumi urbe Ro- ma nihil istis videtur esse metuendum. At ve- ro cum caput illud orbis ceciderit, & ῥύμη esse cœ- perit, (quod Sibyllæ esse ajunt) quis dubitet jam venisse finem rebus humanis orbique terrarum. S. Chrysostomus hom. 4. in Epist. 2. ad Thessal. Sicut, ait, regnum Medorum à Babylonis destructum est, Babyloniorum à Persis, Persarum à Macedoni- bus, Macedonum à Romanis: ita & regnum Ro- manorum ab Anti-Christo. Quibus argumen- tis, etsi non omnia æque firma sint, facile ac- quiescimus. Sed quod inde infertur: Bezam aliosque fraudulenter errare, dum docent defecisse Romanum imperium, ut ex eo probent, venisse jam Anti-Christum, eumque esse Romanum Ponti- ficem, id & ἀνακόλουθον est, judice ipso Alcasare Jesuita, nec cum aliis Papistarum commentis de Anti-Christo ante finem mundi exscindendo conveniunt, ut Malachiæ jam taceam vaticinium, Romanum Pontificem tempore Anti-Christi fo- re Petrum Romanum, eique successurum extre- mum judicium. Quid vero de Corneliana narra- tione habendum: Anti-Christus sensim viribus & numero crescens, debellabit tres Reges ex decem, qui tum erunt in orbe. Mox reliqui decem omnesque gentes perculsæ ad eum legationes mittent, eiq́; se sub- dent, uti fecerunt Alexandro Magno devicto Da- rio, unde ipse tunc statim factus est Monarcha. An- ti-Christus deinde omne suum virus in Christum & Christianos exerens, ac imperium firmans & pro- pagans Romam, tum quia imperii fuit eritque æmula, tum quia sedes fuit Pontificum Christi, ob- sideri & everti curabit, remque committet decem Regibus, id est, aliquot ex iis, qui potentiores & Romæ viciniores erunt, cæteris tamen faventibus, & pecunia, commeatu aliisque modis adjuvanti- bus. Nec enim opus erit pro una urbe exscin- denda exercitus decem Regum, id est; totius mundi congregare: nec etiam tempus regni Anti-Christi (quod erit trium annorum cum medio) tam lon- gas moras patietur, ut ex extremo Oriente, ut dici- tur Cap. XVI, 14. Reges ad eum veniant in Arma- gedon. Hæc enim plures annos requirunt. Ali- quot ergo Reges Romæ viciniores eam evertent & comburent. Hoste deinde in Armagedon evoca- bit, uti jam evocarat illos ex Oriente Cap. XVI, 14. aliasque gentes ex quatuor plagis terræ una cum Gog & Magog. Hi ergo omnes ad Anti-Christum in Judæa convenient, ut Christi & Christianorum nomen ubique deleant, eritque exercitus eorum innumerabilis. Mox Christus omnes congrega- tos conficiet, & occidet igne de cælo in eos immisso? Nugæ sunt canoræ, somnia Jesuitica, quæ sponte sua evanescunt in auras. Quia Anti-Christus trium annorum Judæus è tribu Dan Utopicus est, & Utic, nec alium novit Scriptura Anti-Christum, quam ipsum Pontificem Romanum.

Carnes ejus comedent, hoc est Phrasi Scripturæ recepta, membra & cives ejus cum voluptate quadam trucidabunt, quemadmodum Christia- nis Evangelicis à Romano Catholicis factum, Job. XIX, 21. Cap. XXXI, 31. Eccl, IV, 3. Esa. IX, 20. 21. Cap. X, 18. Dan. V, 1. 5. Zach. XI, 9. Quam- vis vero quidam horum Regum ratione Personarum adhuc adhæreant Pontificiæ religioni, liberum tamen permittunt Evangelicæ religionis exerci- tium, nec bruta Papæ fulmina curant amplius. Tandem vero evoluto tempore Divinitus præfini- to in his ipsis regnis Deus Optim. Max. tales exci- tabit Reges, qui odio persequentur bestiam Anti- Christianam, eam oppugnabunt & desolatam fa- cient, h. e. non amplius suos thesauros conferent ad ampliansum Papatum, sed deferent eum. Imo carnes ejus, h. e. beneficia Ecclesiastica, reditus & præbendas sacrificulorum & Monachorum devo- rabunt, & in Ecclesiarum & Scholarum Evan- gelicarum usum convertent, ut hic habet Beatus Gravius.

## 17:17
Vers. 17.

For God gave into their hearts to do his will, and to do one will.) He speaks as if he were living in the time of those ten Kings. God had used those Kings, both to increase and to undermine the Roman empire. Those words 'and to do one will' are absent from the Manuscript, as also from the Latin.

And to give their kingdom to the beast.) So that they would no longer obey Rome, and at the same time Roman idolatry, than it seemed good to GOD. The 'words of GOD' here are the decrees of God; namely, those concerning the dismembering of the Roman empire into many Kings. The decrees of GOD among the Hebrews are called words, as are also the thoughts of men. There is also a Hebraism in it, that he said 'the words of GOD', when he could have said 'his'. For God had preceded. These things thus previously.

Vers. 17.

For God.) The avenger of both the false worship and the cruelty which the Romans had used against Christians. Many idolaters were still living at that time, partly open, partly hidden in Rome, even in the Senate.

He had given into their hearts.) Not only by that common mode of providence by which God is said to do what He allows to happen, as noted by Maimonides, but also by visions and omens, such as those by which God had also given courage to Vespasian to seize the empire and to subdue the Jews with all evils.

To do what is pleasing to Him.) So that they might execute His judgments upon Rome, although they did not look to Him any more than Nebuchadnezzar, who was likewise chosen by God to execute His judgments upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem. And to give their kingdom to the beast.) A return, so that we may know that they both defected from the Roman society, and had once assumed the Roman society, and remained in it, with God dispensing all these things in a singular way. Until the words of God shall be finished.) The 'words of God' here are the decrees of GOD, just as God is said everywhere to have said within Himself what He has decreed. By metaleipsis, however, those times appointed by God for preserving and dismembering the Roman empire ought to be understood here. That is indeed deservedly cast back upon God, the avenger of both the false worship and the cruelty which the Romans had used against Christians. But since Rome was Christian in the time of Totila, and had fully and plainly admitted the worship of the true GOD, and had taken the temples of idols away from piety and consecrated them to the true religion, whether it was consistent with Divine justice that the city, then innocent and Christian, should be destroyed because of the hatred and persecutions of its former citizens against Christians, and because perhaps a few idolaters, as the Commentator suspects, still lurked there favoring the old errors, let the Jesuits examine. I certainly, says Maresius, as I believe that the plundering of the city by the Goths, and the ruin of the empire brought on by other peoples, which was already collapsing under its own weight, did not happen without the Divine Will: So I am persuaded that there was a sufficiently ample crop of personal and public vices in the empire and the city, which would provoke Divine wrath, even without any special regard for any Christian blood previously shed there, to such an extent that that devastation by Totila was a warning to Rome of greater evils, which it would have to expect, unless it should remit from its arrogance, and check that impetus with which it was rushing headlong into Anti-Christianism.

Latin:

Vers. 17.

ὁ γὰρ Θεὸς ἔδωκεν εἰς τὰς καρδίας αὐτῶν ποιῆσαι τὴν γνώ- μην αὐτῦ, καὶ ποιῆσαι γνώμην μίαν.) Loquitur, tanquam vi- veret tempore illorum decem Regum. Deus illis Regibus usus erat, tum ad augendum, tum ad labefactandum Roma- num imperium. Illa καὶ ποιῆσαι γνώμην μίαν, absunt à Manu- scripto, ut & à Latino.

Καὶ δῦναι τὴν βασιλείαν αὐτῶν τῷ θηρίῳ.) Ut non diutius obedirent Romæ, & simul Romanæ idololatriæ, quam id DEO videretur. Λόγοι Θεῦ hic sunt Dei decreta; nem- pe illa de discerpendo in multos Reges imperio Romano. DEI decreta apud Ebræos vocantur verba, ut & hominum cogitata. Est & in eo Ebraismus, quod dixit οἱ λόγοι τῦ Θεῦ, cum potuisset dicere αὐτῦ. Nam Θεὸς præcesserat. Hæc ita prius.

Vers. 17.

ὁ Θεὸς γὰρ, Deus enim.) Ultor & falsi cultus & sævitiæ, qua in Christianos usi Romani fuerant. Vivebant tunc ad- huc multi idololatræ partim aperti, partim tecti Romæ, etiam in Senatu.

Ἔδωκεν εἰς τὰς καρδίας αὐτῶν, dederat in corda eorum.) Non communi tantum illo providentiæ modo, quo Deus fa- cere dicitur, quæ fieri sinit, ut notatum Maimonidæ, sed vi- sis quoque & ostentis, qualibus & Vespasiano Deus addiderat animos, ad capessendum imperium, domandosque omnibus malis Judæos.

Ποιῆσαι τὴν γνώμην ἀυτ̃ε, ut facerent quod placitum est illi.) Ut judicia ipsius in Romam exsequerentur, quanquam id non magis ipsi spectabant, quam olim Nabuchodonosor à Deo iti- dem ad judicia ejus in Hierosolymitas exercenda delectus. Καὶ δῦναι τὴν βασιλείαν ἀυτῶν τῷ θηρίῳ, ut darent regnum suum bestiæ.) Ἐπ́ανοδὸς, ut sciamus & desciivisse eos à socie- tate Romana, & societatem Romanam induisse olim, in ea- que mansisse, Deo hæc omnia singulari modo dispensante. Ἄχρις τελεσθῆσονται οἱ λόγοι τῦ Θεῦ, donec consummarentur verba Dei.) Λόγοι Θεῦ verba Dei hic sunt DEI decreta, sicut Deus passim dixisse apud se dicitur, quod decrevit. Per μετά- ληψιν transsumptionem autem intelligi hic debent tempora illa ad conservandum discerpendumque imperium Romanum à Deo constituta. Id quidem merito rejicitur in Deum ultorem & falsi cultus & sævitiæ, qua in Christianos Ro- mani usi fuerant. Sed cum Roma esset Christia- na tempore Totilæ, plene & plane admisisset cul- tum veri DEI, idolorumque templa pietati adem- pta, veræ religioni consecrasset, an consentaneum fuerit justitiæ Divinæ, urbem tum insontem & Christianam propter civium quondam suorum in Christianos odium & persecutiones, & quod for- te adhuc pauci, ut suspicatur Commentator, illic laterent idololatræ veteribus faventes erroribus Jesuitæ dispiciant. Ego certe, inquit Maresius, ut credo sine Numine non factam à Gothis urbis direptionem, & ab aliis populis invectam imperii ruinam, quod mole jam sua ruebat: Ita persua- deor satis amplam fuisse in imperio & urbe vitio- rum personalium ac publicorum segetem, quæ iram Divinam provocaret, etiam citra ullum sangui- nis Christiani antea illic effusi specialem respectum, adeo, ut illa Totilæ vastatio fuerit Romæ commina- tio majorum malorum, quæ expectanda haberet, nisi de supercilio suo remitteret, & impetum illum, quo ruebat præceps in Anti-Christianismum, suffla- minaret.

## 17:18
Verse 18.

Καὶ ἡ γυνὴ ἣν εἶδες.] Whose figure you saw. Ἔστιν ἡ πόλις ἡ μεγάλη.) Above XVI, 19, and in this chapter I, 5. Thus later prophecies are accustomed to declare more clearly by certain degrees that which earlier ones had said more obscurely. Ἡ ἔχυσα βασιλείαν ἐπὶ τῶν βασιλέων τῆς γῆς.) After the description from the seven mountains, no other clearer [description] could be brought forward than this one. See above 12. Under the figure of the woman is understood not only the city, but the dominion having its seat in that city, as we have already said.

Grotius concludes the former treatment thus:

Verse 18.

Καὶ ἡ γυνὴ ἣν εἶδες, ἔστιν ἡ πόλις ἡ μεγάλη, & the woman, whom you saw, is the great city.) Porphyry in his work On Abstinence called Rome the great city. Tatian and many other Greeks [did the same]. Ἡ ἔχυσα βασιλείαν ἐπὶ τὺς βασιλέας τ̃ γῆς, which has kingdom over the Kings of the earth.) Besides the mark placed just now from its location, he sets another no less illustrious one concerning its empire over Kings. Lucan: And all the purple which serves the Latin sword. Antiochus in Tacitus, Histories II: the richest of the serving Kings. Tertullian in Against Marcion III teaches us that Babylon, of which there is mention in the following chapter, is Rome itself. See also the comparison of Babylon with Rome, which is in Orosius, Book II, chapter 2. As for the fact that that woman, who is treated in this place, is said above at IV, 3 to have the name of blasphemy inscribed [on her], Jerome well interprets it in the 6th question to Algasia, that it was said because Rome was called the Eternal City. Following him, Prosper: When that which is temporal is called eternal, it is certainly a name of blasphemy. To which you might not absurdly refer that boast of Caesar the Dictator, which is in Hirtius, that the Roman people have ten legions, with which they could even tear down the sky. These things, as Maresius teaches in this place, apply especially to the present Rome, which arrogates to itself empire over all the Kings of the earth, and often exercised it in fact according to Hildebrandine and Bonifacian Theology, and it is established that it is taught or believed no otherwise in the city according to Santarelli That the Jesuits' writings, not long ago published there and publicly burned by the hand of the executioner in Paris, are consistent with Bellarmine's controversies, is consistent with the common opinion of all Canonists and Theologians truly of the Roman communion. What authority the Pontiff formerly exercised in England, what he claims to belong to himself in Sicily, no one is ignorant. That he transferred the kingdom of Navarre, taken from its legitimate Lord, to the Spaniard: That the Spaniard defends his right to both Indies by the title of a Pontifical donation, that the Roman see has often subjected the various kingdoms of Europe to an interdict, and has granted them to the first occupant after deposing their legitimate Kings, is known to everyone; it is so evident that in truth that son of perdition sits in this City, who, according to Paul, exalts himself above every Deity and dares to apply to himself the prophecies, Jer. XVII, 8. Dan. VII, 27. Isa. XLIX, 23. This can be seen in that proud effigy of Paul V, prefixed to very many books published at Rome and Bologna and dedicated to him himself (just as the most illustrious Plessis took care to have a copy of it added to the Mystery of Iniquity for the perpetual memory of the matter) with this inscription: To Paul V, Vice-God, most invincible Monarch of the Christian Republic, and most fierce Conservator of Pontifical omnipotence.

Latin:

Vers. 18.

Καὶ ἡ γυνὴ ἣν εἶδες.] Cujus vidisti figuram. Ἔστιν ἡ πόλις ἡ μεγάλη.) Supra XVI, 19. & hoc capite I, 5. Sic solent prophetiæ posteriores per gradus quosdam clarius eloqui id, quod priores dixerant occultius. Ἡ ἔχυσα βασιλείαν ἐπὶ τῶν βασιλέων τῆς γῆς.) Post de- scriptionem ex septeni montibus non poterat afferri altera clarior quam ista. Vide supra 12. Intelligitur sub figura mu- lieris non sola urbs, sed dominatio in ea urbe sedem habens, ut jam diximus.

Tractationem priorem ita concludit Grotius:

Vers. 18.

Καὶ ἡ γυνὴ ἣν εἶδες, ἔστιν ἡ πόλις ἡ μεγάλη, & mulier, quam vidisti, est civitas magna.) Μεγάλην πόλιν magnam urbem pro Roma dixit Porphyrius περὶ ἀποχῆς. Tatianus & alii Græ- corum multi. Ἡ ἔχυσα βασιλείαν ἐπὶ τὺς βασιλέας τ̃ γῆς, quæ habet re- gnum super Reges terræ.) Præter notam à situ modo posi- tam alteram ponit non minus illustrem de imperio in Reges. Lucanus: Atque omnis Latio quæ servit purpura ferro. Antiochus Tacito Historiarum II. inservientium Regum di- tissimus. Babylonem, cujus capite sequenti mentio, ipsam esse Romam docet nos Tertullianus adversus Marcionem III. Vide & comparationem Babylonis cum Roma, quæ apud O- rosium est Libr. II. cap. 2. Quod autem mulier illa, de qua hoc loco agitur supra IV, 3. dicitur inscriptum habere nomen blasphemiæ, bene interpretatur Hieronymus VI. quæstione ad Algasiam, ideo dictum, quod Roma Urbs æterna dicere- tur. Quem sequens Prosper: Æterna cum dicitur, quæ tem- poralis est, utique nomen est blasphemiæ. Quo & illam Cæ- saris Dictatoris jactationem, quæ apud Hirtium est, non ab- surde referas, decem legiones habere Romanum populum, qua etiam cœlum diruere possint. Apprime hæc, ut docet hoc loco Maresi- us, Romæ præsenti conveniunt, quæ sibi arro- gat imperium in omnes Reges terræ, illudque de facto sæpe exercuit ex Hildebrandina & Bonifaciana Theologia, nec aliter in ur- be doceri aut credi constat ex Santarelli Jesuitae scriptis, non ita pridem illic editis & Lutetiae lictoris manu publice crematis constat ex Bellarmini controversiis, constat ex omnium Canonistarum & Theologorum vere communionis Romanae communi sententia. Quam autoritatem Pontifex in Anglia olim exercuerit, quam pertendat sibi in Siciliam competere, nemo nescit. Ut Navarrae regnum legi- timo Domino ablatum in Hispanum transtulerit: Ut Hispanus jus suum in Indiam utramque, donationis Pon- tificiae titulo tueatur, ut sedes Romana varia Euro- pae regna interdicto saepe subjecerit, exautoratisque legitimus Regibus illa primo occupanti concefferit, cuivis notum, adeo constat revera hanc Urbem in- sidere filium illum perditionis, qui se apud Paulum supra omne Numen effert & sibi audet applicare vaticinia, Jerem. XVII, 8. Dan. VII, 27. Esa. XLIX, 23. Id videre est in superba illa Pauli V. effigie, plurimis libris Romae & Bononiae editis ipsique di- catis praefixa (prout illius exemplar Illustrissimus Plessaeus mysterio iniquitatis ad perpetuam rei me- moriam addi curavit) cum hac inscriptione: Pau- lo V. Vice-Deo, Christianae Reipublicae Monarchae invictissimo, & Pontificiae omnipotentiae Conservatori acerrimo.

## 18:1 Argument
CHAPTER XVIII. ARGUMENT AND DIVISION.

An angel of great power, illuminating the earth with his glory, announces the fall of Babylon, and its cause, whoredom, and therefore commands the faithful to flee from it, to which retribution is to be made according to its works: and its pride is to be punished: Which most orders of the earth mourn, but the heavens and the saints rejoice because of its ruin: and the just judgment of God, in which no joy will be found any longer.

There are two parts: I. The ruin of Babylon up to verse 8. II. The sadness of its accomplices and the joy of the faithful arising from thence, up to verse 24.

PART I. THE RUIN OF BABYLON.

Ver. 1.

And after these things I saw another angel coming down from heaven having great power.] That Angel announces the burning of Rome as a consequence, with a certain explanation of the things said before. Just as the devastation of ancient Babylon is predicted not once, but often in Isaiah and Jeremiah, sometimes with those poetic colors, so that the reader, as if brought into the present matter, looks upon the corpse of the city, so also it had to be done concerning the other Babylon. Wherefore what had been indicated in few words, above XVI, 9. and XVII, 6. that is now placed before the eyes as if in a picture. This is the angel who had received from God a truly great power of showing the world that Rome is neither eternal nor invincible. Therefore, that angel seemed to descend from heaven to exercise that power, indeed, שַׂר גָּדוֹל Dan. 12.

And the earth was lightened with his glory.] Words from Ezekiel XLIII, 2. Δόξα here, as כָּבוֹד for the Hebrews, signifies brightness, Exodus XL, 32. Num. XIV, 10. 2. Corinthians III, 7. This splendor signified that it would come to pass that through him men would learn what they were ignorant of, that Rome, as I said, is not eternal.

We understand this of Christ, whose power is truly great, Matt. XXIX, 18. He illuminates the whole world with the splendor of his Majesty and grace, Heb. I, 3. Mal. IV, 1. Others understand a certain excellent Doctor, B. Phil. Nicolai and B. Hoe, B. Luther in particular, who illuminated the world with the splendor of the Gospel. But the voice concerning the ruin of Babylon is attributed to the second angel in chapter XIV, not the first.

Latin:

CAPUT XVIII. ARGUMENTUM ET PAR- TITIO.

Angelus magnae potestatis terram gloria sua illustrans casum Babylonis annuntiat, ejus- que causam, scortationem, ideoque fugere ex eadem jubet fideles, cui retribuendum secundum opera: & fastus puniendus: Quam lugent plerique terrae ordines, gau- dent vero caeli, & sancti ob ejus ruinam: & justum Dei judicium, in qua nullum amplius gaudium invenietur.

Partes duae sunt: I. Ruina Babylonis ad vers. 8. II. Inde orta & tristitia complicum, & laetitia fidelium, ad vers. 24.

PARS I. RUINA BABYLONIS.

Vers. 1.

Καὶ μετὰ ταῦτα εἶδον ἄλλον ἄγγελον καταβαίνοντα ἐκ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ ἔχοντα ἐξουσίαν μεγάλην.] Ille Angelus consequentia incendium Romae nuntiat, cum quadam antedictorum ex- plicatione. Sicut Babylonis veteris devastatio, non semel, sed saepius praedicitur apud Esaiam & Jeremiam, interdum cum iis poeticis coloribus, ut lector velut in rem praesentem ad- ductus cadaver urbis aspiciat, ita & de altera Babylone faci- endum fuit. Quare quod paucis verbis indicatum fuerat, supra XVI, 9. & XVII, 6. id nunc tanquam in pictura subji- citur oculis. Angelus hic est, qui a Deo potestatem acceperat sane magnam, ostendendi mundo Romam nec aeternam esse, nec invictam. Descendere ergo ex caelo visus est is Angelus ad exercendam scilicet illam potestatem, שַׂר גָּדוֹל Dan. 12.

Καὶ ἡ γῆ ἐφωτίσθη ἐκ τῆς δόξης αὐτοῦ.] Verba ex Ezechiele XLIII, 2. Δόξα hic ut כָּבוֹד Hebraeis fulgorem significat Exodi XL, 32. Num. XIV, 10. 2. Corinth. III, 7. Hic splendor significabat fore, ut per eum discerent homines, quod ignora- bant, Romam, ut dixi, non esse aeternam.

De Christo intelligimus, cujus potestas vere magna, Matth. XXIX, 18. Hic splendore Majesta- tis, & gratiae suae totum illustrat orbem, Ebr. I, 3. Mal. IV, 1. Alii excellentem quendam Doctorem, B. Phil. Nicolai & B. Hoe B. Lutherum peculiariter intelligunt, qui splendore Evangelii orbem illu- stravit. Sed vox de ruina Babylonis c. XIV. secun- do, non primo Angelo tributa.

## 18:2
And he cried with a strong voice.] He signified a great matter with a great shout.

Saying, Babylon the great is fallen, is fallen.] The aorist is here for the present. For the matter is shown as if it were present. Behold, Rome is falling. The words are taken from Isa. XXI, 9. and Jer. LI, 8. as we said above XIV, 8. This is that day which Scipio imagined for himself with tears while Carthage was burning. See Polybius and Plutarch.

But what does the imagination of Scipio have to do with this, with Carthage burning? Some understand this of a spiritual fall, but most understand it of a bodily ruin, which the literal sense demands, and which should by no means be abandoned without cause. And the punishment of Babylon is described here. That spiritual ruin, however, or the manifestation of it, is to be considered a benefit. Babylon has fallen, with regard to the public manifestation of its ruin and the decline of its authority, in the case of Emperor Frederick II, whom many Romanists declared to be the Antichrist. It fell in the case of Philip, King of the French, who wrote to Boniface VIII in this manner: Philip, by the grace of God, King of the French, to Boniface, who poses as the Supreme Pontiff, little or no greetings! Let your great stupidity know that in temporal matters we are subject to no one: that the collation of churches and prebends belongs to us by Royal right, etc. But we consider those who believe otherwise to be fools and senseless. It fell in the case of Emperor Louis IV, who publicly declared the Roman Pontiff to be the Antichrist. It fell in the case of the Eastern Churches, which answered the Roman Pontiff when he demanded obedience thus: We firmly believe in your supreme power over your subjects; we cannot tolerate your supreme pride, we cannot satisfy your supreme avarice, the Devil be with you, because the Lord is with us. What of the fact that even today the Greek Church of the West publicly excommunicates the Roman Pontiff every year on the first Sunday of Lent as a heretic.

And it has become a dwelling place of demons.] The Greeks translate שְׂעִירִים, which is about Babylon, Isa. 13:21, as demons, and in the manuscript at this place it is of demons. Now שְׂעִירִים are goat-shaped demons, as we said at Leviticus 17:7. Certain kinds of demons are accustomed to delight in desert places, Matthew 12:43. Cyril and Procopius affirm the same regarding Isaiah. See also Cassian, Collation 7, 23.

And a cage of every unclean spirit.] This 'and' is explanatory of what preceded. For demons are unclean spirits, Matthew 10:1, Mark 1:23, 26, 27, 3:11, 30, 5:8, 13, 6:7, 25, 9:25, Luke 4:33, 36, 6:18, 29, 9:42, 11:29, Acts 5:16, 8:7. A cage is a station, a military term, Baruch 3:22.

And a cage of every unclean bird.] Of birds of prey, which feed on corpses, such as Isaiah designates in the aforementioned place 13:21, and 14:23, and 34:11, and Zephaniah 2:4. Such are אִיִּים צִיִּים and the like.

Of demons, that is, the eternal habitation of devils is designated here, Rev. 19:20. These are figures of the Babylonian demons bringing in rapacity and destruction because of their terrible appearance.

Latin:

Καὶ ἔκραξεν ἐν ἰσχυρᾷ φωνῇ.] Rem magnam, magno cla- more significavit.

Λέγων Ἔπεσεν, ἔπεσε Βαβυλὼν ἡ μεγάλη.] Est ἀόριστος hic pro præsenti. Nam res velut præsens ostenditur. En ca- dit Roma. Verba desumpta ex Esa. XXI, 9. & Jerem. LI, 8. ut diximus supra XIV, 8. Hæc est illa dies, quam sibi cum la- crymis imaginabatur Scipio ardente Carthagine. Vide Poly- bium & Plutarchum.

Quid vero huc Scipionis imaginatio ardente Carthagine? De casu spirituali nonnulli, at ple- rique de corporali ruina, quam τὸ ῥητὸν postulat, citra causam minime deserendum, intelligunt. Et describitur hic pœna Babylonis. Illa vero spi- ritualis ruina vel ejusdem manifestatio pro be- neficio habenda. Cecidit Babylon, quod ad ma- nifestationem ruinæ publicam, & occasum autori- tatis, apud Fridericum II. Imperatorem, quem Anti-Christus multis Romanensibus inesse decla- ravit. Cecidit penes Philippum Regem Gallia- rum, qui ad Bonifacium IIX. hunc in modum scripsit: Philippus, Dei gratia, Francorum Rex Bonifacio gerenti se pro summo Pontifice salutem modicam, sive nullam! Sciat tua maxima fatui- tas, in temporalibus nos alicui non subesse: Ecclesia- rum & præbendarum collationem ad nos jure Re- gio pertinere &c. Secus autem credentes fatuos & insipientes reputamus. Cecidit apud Ludovi- cum IV. Imperatorem, qui Pontificem Rom. pro Anti-Christo publice declaravit. Cecidit apud Ecclesias Orientales, quæ Pontifici Rom. obedien- tiam exigenti sic responderunt: Potentiam tu- am summam erga subditos tuos firmiter credi- mus; superbiam tuam summam tolerare non pos- sumus, avaritiam tuam summam satiare non va- lemus, Diabolus tecum, quia Dominus nobiscum. Quid? quod hodieque Ecclesia Græca Occidenta- lis Dominica Quadragesima Pontificem Roma- num ceu hæreticum quotannis publice excom- municet.

Καὶ ἐγένετο κατοικητήριον δαιμόνων.] Græci שְׂעִירִים, quod est de Babylone, Esa. 13, 21. vertunt δαιμόνια, & in Manuscri- pto hoc loco est δαιμονίων. Sunt autem שְׂעִירִים δαιμόνια τραγόμορφα, ut diximus ad Levit. 17, 7. Solent autem quæ- dam Dæmonum genera delectari locis desertis, Matth. 12, 43. Idem affirmant ad Esaiam Cyrillus & Procopius. Vide & Cas- sianum Coloff. 7, 23.

Καὶ φυλακὴ παντὸς πνεύματος ἀκαθάρτου.] Hoc καὶ est ἐξηγητικὸν ejus quod præcessit. Nam δαιμόνια sunt πνεύματα ἀκάθαρτα, Matth. X, 1. Marc. I, 23. 26. 27. III, 11. 30. V, 8. 13. VI, 7 25. IX, 25. Luc. IV, 33. 36. VI, 18. 29. IX, 42. XI, 29. Act. V, 16. IIX, 7. Φυλακὴ est statio, vox militaris, Baruch. III, 22.

Καὶ φυλακὴ παντὸς ὀρνέου ἀκαθάρτου.) Avium rapacium, quæ cadaveribus pascuntur, quales designat Esaias dicto loco XIII, 21. & XIV, 23. & XXXIV, 11. & Sophon. II, 4. Talia sunt אִיִּים צִיִּים & similia.

Dæmonum, id est, Diabolorum æterna habitatio hic designata, Apoc. XIX, 20. Dæmonia illa Baby- lonia inferentium ob conspectum terribilem ra- pacitatem ac perditionem figuræ.

## 18:3
Verse 3.

For all nations have drunk of the wrath of the wine of her fornication.) Wrath here is again poison, as also above 14:8, where we dealt with that meaning of the word. In the manuscript: all nations have drunk, and thus the Latin reads.

And the kings of the earth have committed fornication with her.) They followed her example, nay, they even worshipped her. See above 17:2, where the words are the same.

And the merchants of the earth have grown rich from the power of her luxury. The sense is equal to Isaiah 46:15, and below 23. Luxury is Roman excess, about which many learned men have written books. But power is wealth, providing for such great luxury.

For the exercise and adornment of Papistical cults, for the splendor of ceremonies, and likewise for pomp, pride, delights, and luxurious futility, various wares are required, by the selling of which the merchants of the earth grow rich. D. Winckelm. in h. l. A book appeared in the year 1534 in the Gauls, as Sleidanus reports in book 9, in which that trade is wittily described: These alone sell, resell, exchange, and indeed at all times. For other merchants cease entirely on feast days, especially the more celebrated ones; but these intermit no time of the year, and they handle wares of every kind, and there is nothing that escapes their hands, not men, not women, not infants, whether born or yet to be born. For they make profit from all things whatsoever. Heaven, hell, the earth, time itself, and all creatures whatsoever, both animate and inanimate, serve their greed: wine, bread, oil, flax, milk, butter, cheese, water, salt, fire, fumigations. From these things, I say, they know how to elicit gold and silver, indeed even from the very sight of the thing sold, which is usually free for others. Furthermore, the price is even increased by the merchant's attire. For what an Abbot or Bishop chants costs much more than the mass of some monk or vicar. In this matter, they differ in no way from harlots. For the more ornate the attire of these women, the more dearly they sell their shame. Nor do they need precious material to make a profit: they make even a particle of wax fruitful for themselves, the lesser ones at least. But the greater ones are exercised in letters and diplomas, of the sort that are commonly called officials, copyists, seal-bearers, dataries, and others of that kind. But that magnificent one, who excels all the others and assumes the most holy name for himself, does not indeed use wax, but by a certain wondrous artifice converts lead into gold. And what is most unworthy, other merchants compel no one to the purchase of their wares; but these force the unwilling to buy, and if anyone refuses, they clamor that he is a heretic. And what, finally, is more unjust than to sell a thing not one's own, nay, to sell it to those to whom it properly belongs, and indeed one thing to many? Examples are in bells, the areas of the temple, cemeteries, baptisms, and the like. Which, although they are the property of the Churches, yet they sell them, and often one to many. Those wares can be distributed into certain classes of riches, luxury, clothing, utensils, victuals, retinue, and spiritual tyranny.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

Ὅτι ἐκ τοῦ θυμοῦ τοῦ οἴνου τῆς πορνείας αὐτῆς πεπότικε πάντα τὰ ἔθνη.) Θυμὸς iterum hic est venenum, ut & supra XIV, 8. ubi de isto vocis illius significatu egimus. In Manuscripto: πέπωκε πάντα τὰ ἔθνη & sic legit Latinus.

Καὶ οἱ βασιλεῖς τῆς γῆς μετ' αὐτῆς ἐπόρνευσαν.) Ejus exem- plum sequuti sunt, imo & ipsam coluere. Vide supra XVII, 2. ubi verba eadem.

Καὶ οἱ ἔμποροι τῆς γῆς ἐκ τῆς δυνάμεως τοῦ σρήνους αὐτῆς ἐπλούτησαν. Sensus par Esa. XLVI, 15. & infra 23. Στρῆνος est luxus Romanus, de quo complures viri eruditi libros conscripsere. Δύναμις vero חַיִל divitiæ, ad tantum luxum suppetentes.

Ad exercitium & ornatum cultuum Papistico- rum, ad splendorem ceremoniarum, ad pompas item, fastum, delicias, luxuriosamque futilitatem explendam variæ merces requiruntur, quibus vendendis mer- catores terræ ditescunt. D. Winckelm. in h. l. Pro- diit an. 1534. in Galliis liber, referente Sleidano l. 9. in quo ista mercatura facete describitur: Hi soli vendunt, revendunt, permutant, & quidem omni tem- pore. Nam cæteri mercatores diebus festis, præsertim celebrioribus plane cessant; hi vero nullum anni tem- pus intermittunt, & omnis generis merces tractant, ni- hilque est, quod ipsorum manus effugiat, non viri, non mulieres, non infantes tam nati quam nascituri. Quæ- stum enim faciunt ex omnibus rebus in universum. Servit ipsorum cupiditati cælum, infernus, terra, tem- pus ipsum, & omnes plane creaturæ tum animatæ, tum inanimes vinum, panis, oleum, linum, lac, butyrum, caseus, aqua, sal, ignis, fumigationes. Ex his inquam rebus norunt elicere aurum & argentum, imo ex ipso rei venditæ aspectu, qui solet aliis esse gratuitus. Quin mercatoris etiam vestitu augetur pretium. Quam enim Abbas decantat aut Episcopus, multo constat majoris, quam alicujus monachi aut vicarii missa. Quæ quidem in re nihil differunt a meretricibus. Nam hæ quo sunt ornatiori cultu, eo carius turpitudi- nem suam vendunt. Nec illis ad quæstum faciendum, pretiosa opus est materia: vel ceræ particulam sibi fru- ctuosam faciunt tenuiores quidem. Majores autem in literis atque diplomatis exercentur, cujusmodi sunt, qui vulgo dicuntur officiales, copistæ, sigilliferi, datarii, & id genus alii. Magnificus autem ille, qui cæteris omnibus præstat, & sanctissimum nomen sibi sumit, non quidem utitur cera, sed mirabili quodam artificio plumbum convertit in aurum. Et quod indignissi- mum, negotiatores reliqui neminem adigunt ad sua- rum mercium emtionem; hi vero cogunt invitos ut emant, & si quis recuset, hæreticum esse clamitant. Et quid tandem iniquius, quam rem vendere non suam, imò vendere iis, ad quos proprie pertinet, & quidem compluribus rem unam? Exempla sunt in campanis, areis templi, cæmeteriis, baptizmis & similibus. Quæ cum Ecclesiarum sint propria, tamen illi vendunt, & sæpe unum pluribus. Possunt merces illæ in certas classes distribui divitiarum, luxus, vestitus, utensilium, victus, sa- tellitii, tyrannidis spiritualis.

## 18:4
Vers. 4.

And I heard another voice from heaven saying.] This is inserted as if by a parenthesis. For the discourse begun is resumed there: ὅτι ἐκολλήθησαν. Come out of her, my people.] By this voice it is shown that God had so exercised his judgments upon Rome that he saved the pious from the common evil. You, my people, that is, you who neither worship idols nor limp, but are Christians by sincere faith, where the army of Totila shall appear, go out to the basilicas of the Apostles outside the city, where I shall render you safe, just as I rendered you safe in the same way in the times of Alaric. The words are taken from Isa. XLVIII, 20, and Jerem. L, 8, LI, 6, 45, Zach. II, 7. Thus, when Jerusalem was being captured by Nebuchadnezzar, God had saved the observers of the law, and before Titus captured the same city, he had led out the Christians, just as once Lot from Sodom. What does the army of Totila have to do here? What do the Basilicas of the Apostles? Where concerning the army of the Anti-Christ, and of Magog, and also of the Kings who are about to attack the Anti-Christ most recently a little before the final judgment, and concerning the temple of the heavenly Jerusalem about to receive the Elect shortly. That you may not share in her sins, and that you may not receive of her plagues.] Here also the latter member serves to explain the former. For he had called ἁμαρτίας the punishments or calamities of the Hebrews. Cf. Gen. XIX, 3, and Matth. XXIV, 15, 16, 17.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

Καὶ ἤκουσα ἄλλην φωνὴν ἐκ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ λέγουσαν.] Hoc vel- ut per parenthesin interjicitur. Nam ceptus sermo resumi- tur ibi: ὅτι ἐκολλήθησαν. Ἐξέλθετε ἐξ αὐτῆς ὁ λαός μου.] Hac voce ostenditur, De- um ita sua in Romam judicia exercuisse, ut pios de communi malo servaverit. Tu popule mi, id est vos, qui nec idola co- litis, nec claudicatis, sed sincera fide estis Christiani, ubi Totilæ apparuerit exercitus, exite ad basilicas Apostolorum extra urbem, ubi ego vos tutos præstabo, sicut tutos vos præstiti eodem modo Alarici temporibus. Sumpta verba ex Esa. XLVIII, 20. & Jerem. L, 8. LI, 6. 45. Zach. II, 7. Sic cum Hierosolyma à Nabuchodonosoro caperetur, legis obser- vatores servaverat Deus, & priusquam eandem urbem Titus caperet, eduxerat Christianos, ita ut olim Lothum è Sodomis. Quid huc Totilæ exercitus? Quid Basilicæ Apo- stolorum? Ubi de exercitu Anti-Christi, & Magogi, nec non Regum, qui Anti-Christi oppugnaturi sunt novissime paulo ante extremum judicium, & de cœlestis Hierosolyma templo propediem Electos suscepturo. Ἵνα μὴ συγκοινωνήσατε ταῖς ἁμαρτίαις αὐτῶν, καὶ ἐκ τῶν πληγῶν αὐτῆς ἵνα μὴ λάβητε.] Hic quoque membrum po- sterius servit priori explicando. Nam ἁμαρτίας vocarat Ebræorum pœnas sive calamitates. Conf. Genes. XIX, 3. & Matth. XXIV, 15. 16. 17.

## 18:5
Vers. 5.

That her sins have reached unto heaven.] With that heavenly voice finished, the Angel continues to speak and to explain the causes and the manner of the Roman devastation. Ἐκολλήθησαν here by a certain catachresis means 'have been heaped up.' That was said once of Sodom, Gen. XVIII, 20, and of Nineveh, Jon. I, 2. / Thus also Homer: 'Their insolence and violence reached the iron heaven.' And God remembered her injustices.] That former αὐτῆς is absent from many Codices, and in Arethas. The sense is as above XIX, 17. God is said to remember crimes when he punishes them.

Latin:

Vers. 5.

Ἵνα ἐκολλήθησαν αὐτῆς αἱ ἁμαρτίαι ἄχρι τοῦ οὐρανοῦ.] Ab- soluta illa voce cœlesti pergit Angelus loqui & causas mo- dumque vastitatis Romanæ explicare. Ἐκολλήθησαν hic per κατάχρησιν quandam valet coacervata sunt. Dictum id olim de Sodomis, Genes. XVIII, 20. & de Ninive Jon. I, 2. / Sic & Homerus : Τῶν ὕβρις τε βίητε σιδήρεον ὠρανὸν ἷκε. Καὶ ἐμνημόνευσεν αὐτῆς ὁ Θεὸς τὰ ἀδικήματα αὐτῆς. ] Prius illud αὐτῆς abest à Codicibus multis, & apud Aretham. Sensus qui supra XIX, 17. Dicitur Deus recordari crimi- num, ubi ea punit.

## 18:6
Vers. 6.

Render to her.] You Goths. Thus God addresses the Medes in Isa. L, 14, and following. As she also rendered to you.] Just as she treated all peoples: Just as she had cut down Corinth, Numantia, Carthage, and so many other cities. But ὑμῖν is absent in the Manuscript, not wrongly. See Jerem. L, 15, LI, 24, 49, and Psalm CXXXVII, 8. And double to her double according to her works.] To render double is said also in a good sense, as Zachar. IX, 12, Isa. XXXI, 7, and in a bad sense Jerem. XVI, 18. There is nothing unjust in this matter. 'It is not just if someone has gouged out the eye of someone that he should only have his own gouged out, but that he should suffer more,' says Aristotle. See our book II on the law of war and peace II. 20. Mithridates had once said that unless the forest were cut down, the wolves would never be quiet. In the cup in which she mixed, mix for her double.] The cup has a double meaning both in this book and elsewhere. Sometimes it pertains to vices, here to calamities. See above XIV, 10, XVI, 9.

Latin:

Vers. 6.

Ἀπόδοτε αὐτῇ. ] Vos Gothi. Sic Medos alloquitur Deus Es. L, 14. & sequentibus. Ὡς καὶ αὐτὴ ἀπέδωκεν ὑμῖν. ] Sicut ipsa tractavit omnes populos : Sicut ipsa exciderat Corinthum , Numantiam, Carthaginem , tot urbes alias. Sed ὑμῖν abest in Manu- scripto non male. Vide Jerem. L, 15. LI, 24. 49. & Psalm. CXXXVII, 8. Καὶ διπλώσατε αὐτῇ διπλᾶ κατὰ τὰ ἔργα αὐτῆς. ] Du- plum reddere , & in bonam partem dicitur, ut Zachar. IX, 12. Esa. XXXI, 7. & in malam Jerem. XVI, 18. Nihil in hac re iniqui est. Οὐ δίκαιον εἴτις τὸν ὀφθαλμὸν ἐξέκοψέ τινος ἀντεκκοπῆναι μόνον, ἀλλὰ πλείονα παθεῖν, ait Ari- stoteles. Vide nostra lib. II. de jure belli & pacis II. 20. dixerat olim Mithridates, nisi sylva excisa nunquam quietu- ros lupos. Ἐν τῷ ποτηρίῳ ᾧ ἐκέρασε, κεράσατε αὐτῇ διπλῶν. ] Po- culi duplex significatio est & in hoc libro & alibi. Inter- dum ad vitia, hic ad calamitates pertinet. Vide supra XIV, 10. XVI, 9.

## 18:7
Vers. 7.

Ὅσα ἐδόξασεν ἑαυτὴν καὶ ὅσα ἐστρηνίασε. ] How much she glorified herself and how much she lived luxuriously. Regarding the word στρηνιάζειν see 1 Tim. V, 11. The sense is the same in Prov. XVI, 18. Τοσοῦτον δότε αὐτῇ βασανισμὸν. ] Βασανισμὸς is called every vexation, as above IX, 5. In certain Codices Βασανισμὸν καὶ πένθος. תאניה ואניה Lam. II, 5.

Causæ devastandæ Babylonis potiores sunt 1. Avarice, because her merchants were Princes, that is, Cardinals, Archbishops, Bishops, Prelates, etc., who collected huge treasures by their trading, dealt in merchandise of the greatest importance, and were entirely given over to avarice and injustice. 2. Sorceries. Because they ensnared an innumerable crowd of men with false doctrine, idolatry, superstitions, and abominations, and cast them into the abyss.

3. Tyrannical force, because the blood of the Prophets and Saints was found in her: The blood of the Doctors of the Church shed in her cries out to heaven and demands vengeance. Libertus Fromondus wishes this devastation of the city to be imminent not for Rome, but for Constantinople as a new Rome, led by no other argument than that it was filled with such a great frequency of goods, merchants, and all kinds of men that by the consensus of all it far surpasses ancient Rome. But most acknowledge that these things must be understood mystically regarding the merchants, which has already been shown to fit the merchandise of Anti-Christian Rome perfectly. Constantinople certainly does not compare with the same in these matters. Ὅτι ἐν καρδίᾳ αὐτῆς λέγει. ] She thought, that nothing of the sort would happen to her. Claudian: He rages with a similar crime, whoever aspires to the spoils of Rome or alone possesses them. Ὅτι κάθημαι βασίλισσα. ] This present tense must be taken for all time, as if she were saying: I reign forever. Est ex- plicatio verborum Babylonis apud Esaiam ἐγώ εἰμι καὶ ὐκ ἔσιν ἑτέρα, which you have in Zephaniah II. 5.

Verbum sedere cum emphasi adhibetur, the word 'to sit' is used with emphasis, quite solemn for the Pontiff. Κάθημαι βασίλισσα she says, I SIT A QUEEN. The harlot boasts thus of her rule. I sit, that is, I command as Queen and Lady not only regarding ecclesiastical, but also regarding political rule: which she has taken upon herself not only in the territories donated by Constantine the Great, and in the patrimony of Peter, which she calls her own (they call it STATO DE CHIESA of the whole and of Calabria or the kingdom of Naples as a fief of the King of the Spains, the dominion pre- tending) but throughout the whole world he uses that fraudulently, this violently. Concerning the fictitious donation of Constantine, which the Pope fraudulently boasts of, E. K. de Repkav, Glosses of Saxon Law, A.D. 1160, book 3, art. 63, have dealt with sufficiently. He says thence, that such a given gift by law is not long-lasting, and is not valid for him. Dante Alighieri, book on Monarchy, A.D. 1321: Constantine could not alienate the dignities of the empire. Laurentius Valla, A.D. 1411: They claim the city of Rome is theirs, their kingdom of Sicily and Naples, their whole of Italy, the Gauls, the Spaniards, the Germans, the Britons, and finally their West. For all these things are contained in the very page of the donation. Therefore, are all these things yours, Supreme Pontiff? Is it your intention to recover everything? To despoil all Kings and Princes of their cities? &c. But I, on the contrary, think it is more just that it is permitted to Princes to despoil you of all the empire which you hold. I will not show that that donation, from which they wish the supreme right of the Supreme Pontiff to have been born, was equally unknown to Sylvester and Constantine. Which page of the donation is the patronage of all those things, so that it is not only false, but also stupid. See Fasciculus rerum expetendarum, A.D. 1535; Jacobus Spigelius in his commentary on the verse of Günther; Nicolaus Cusanus, Cardinal, book III, Concordantia Catholica, ch. 2; Hieronymus Paulus Cathalanus; Aeneas Sylvius, Cardinal; Filinus in C. Solitae at the end, from the treatise on ministers and obedience; Alcuisius in the authentic [text] 'How bishops ought' &c.; Petrus de Bella Pertica in the rubrics of the proemium of the Institutes, n. 11; Bartholus in the proemium of the Digest; Alexander in Consilia, n. 23, book 5; Johannes Aventinus, book II, Annals: 'The things which are proclaimed concerning Sylvester and the donation of Constantine are fictitious, false, inept, and contradictory.' I wonder that there exist such stupid people who believe [them], and such impudent people who dare to defend them, especially since even Pius II Pontifex Maximus, laughs at them as old wives' tales and an empty fable. Cranzius in History of Saxony; Franciscus Guicciardinus, book IV, History, p. 156, says that this fable has been refuted by the most serious writers and by the facts themselves. Baronius himself admits that that instrument of donation is false and fabricated, and devised in bad faith, with deceit and fraud, and written by some impostor &c., book III, A.D. 324, n. 118. Among other things, the signs of falsity are the variations: For when C. Futuram 12, q. 1, Melchiades mentions the donation as having been made in his own time, C. Constantinus dist. 96 says it was finally made under Sylvester. When C. Constantinus says the city of Rome and all Italy together with the empire of the West were donated to Sylvester, C. fundamentum in the Decretals, book 1, tit. 9, on Elections, in the Sixth [Book], makes mention only of the City. Whence Otto III Emperor, openly contradicted this donation as being fictitious: Which also conflicts with the division of the empire made by Constantine the Great (Eusebius, book IV, on the life of Constantine; Socrates, book II, last chapter) and with the preservation of Italy under the successors of Constantine for 140 years, and with the testimonies of the Papists, who assert that the Papal Exarchate had its beginning around A.D. 800 from the donation of Pepin and Charles II, such as Platina, Volaterranus, Sabellicus, Ennead 8, book 8, and of the Pontiffs themselves, who refer that donation to Louis the Pious, son of Charles the Great, not to mention that Constantinople did not even exist then, and yet it is feigned that the Principality of the Pope was bestowed upon it. See on these things at length B. D. Hoë, Vol. 3, p. 206, seq. And no less does this Queen also boast of empire over the whole world, with Boniface VIII so decreeing in C. Unam sanctam, on Majorities and Obedience, in the Sixth [Book]: 'We declare, command, define, and pronounce that it is of necessity for salvation to be subject to the Roman Pontiff for every human creature': Whereas on the contrary

Pelagius I, Exul. 16, to Childeric, King of the Franks, A.D. 555, rightly wrote: 'The Holy Scriptures command that we (bishops) be subject to Kings,' and Hadrian IV, in the presence of Frederick I Barbarossa, pretending that the empire was a benefit received from the Roman Church, made it known by circular letters that his empire was from God alone through the election of the Princes, and 'whoever says that we received the Imperial crown as a benefit from the Lord Pope is contrary to divine institution and the doctrine of Peter, and will be guilty of a lie.' To this contribute the eulogies of Papal flatterers, Augustinus de Ancona in his Summa on Ecclesiastical Power, q. 1, art. 7, that the Pope has all Royal and imperial power in this world, that he can command Kings as vassals subject to his power, and can both depose and institute them; q. 46, that he also has jurisdiction over the Kings of the Turks, Pagans, and infidels; q. 32, and since Christ merited all supreme power over every creature through his passion, therefore he gave and left it to the Pope. C. 23, that Christ occupied all the empires and kingdoms of the world at his exaltation and took them away from Caesar, Kings, and other Princes through his soldiers, the Apostles, and conferred them upon the Roman Pontiff: As Jodocus de Titano, chamberlain of Urban VI, has it in his treatise on Monarchy. Whence it is without doubt that he also assigns and distributes bishoprics in the lands of the Turks and Kings to his own Roman Pontiffs, as he pleases.

And I am no widow] in Isaiah: I shall not sit as a widow. I shall always be the seat of those who reign.

And I shall not see mourning.] This is placed for those words of Isaiah: Neither shall I know bereavement. I shall not be deprived of offspring, that is, of people. See Matthew 23:17. 'To see' is frequent among the Hebrews for 'to experience'.

Latin:

Vers. 7.

Ὅσα ἐδόξασεν ἑαυτὴν καὶ ὅσα ἐστρηνίασε. ] Quantum se jactavit & luxuriata est. De voce στρηνιάζειν vide 1.Tim.V, 11. Sensus idem Prov. XVI, 18. Τοσοῦτον δότε αὐτῇ βασανισμὸν. ] Βασανισμὸς dicitur omnis vexatio, ut supra IX, 5. In quibusdam Codicibus Βασανισμὸν καὶ πένθος. תאניה ואניה Lam. II, 5.

Causæ devastandæ Babylonis potiores sunt 1. Ava- ritia, quia Mercatores ejus fuerunt Principes, h. e. Cardinales, Archi- Episcopi, Episcopi, Prælati &c. nundinationibus suis ingentes collegerunt thesau- ros , mercimonia tractarunt maximi momenti, avaritiæ & injustitiæ prorsus dediti. 2. Veneficia. Quia falsa doctrina , idololatria , superstitionibus & abominationibus innumeram hominum tur- bam inescarunt , & in barathrum præcipitarunt.

3. Vis tyrannica, quia sanguis Prophetarum & San- ctorum inventus est in ea : Sanguis in illa effusus Doctorum Ecclesiæ in cælum clamat, & vindi- ctam postulat. Libertus Fromondus hanc urbis de- vastationem non Romæ, sed Constantinopoli ceu novæ Romæ imminere vult, nullo alio ductus ar- gumento, quam quod illa tanta mercium, merca- torum & omnium hominum frequentia repleta fuerit, ut omnium consensu Romam veterem lon- ge superet. At mystice hæc de mercatoribus in- telligenda esse plerique agnoscunt, quæ optime mercimoniis Romæ Anti- Christianæ convenire jam ostensum est. Paria certe cum eadem non facit in hisce Constantinopolis. Ὅτι ἐν καρδίᾳ αὐτῆς λέγει. ] Cogitavit, nihil tale sibi even- turum. Claudianus : Simili bacchatur crimine, quisquis Adspirat Romæ spoliis aut solus habentis. Ὅτι κάθημαι βασίλισσα. ] Præsens hoc sumendum pro omni tempore, quasi dicat : Regno in perpetuum. Est ex- plicatio verborum Babylonis apud Esaiam ἐγώ εἰμι καὶ ὐκ ἔσιν ἑτέρα, quæ habes apud Sophoniam II. 5.

Verbum sedere cum emphasi adhibetur, Ponti- fici admodum solemne. Κάθημαι βασίλισσα in- quit, SEDEO REGINA. De regimine suo ita gloriatur meretrix. Sedeo, id est, inpero Re- gina, & Domina non tantum quoad Ecclesia- sticum, sed etiam quod ad Politicum regimen: quod non tantum in ditionibus à Constan- tino Magno donatis , & in patrimonio Petri, quod vocat sibi sumpsit ( vocant STATO DE CHIESA totius & Calabriæ seu regni Neapolitani ceu feudum Regis Hispaniarum dominium præ- tendentes) sed per universum mundum usurpat illud fraudulenter, hoc violenter. De fictitia Constantini donatione, quam fraudulenter jacti- tat Papa, affatim egerunt EK de Repkav, Juris Saxonici Glossor A. 1160. l. 3. art. 63. Sagen dan- nenhero, dass so gethane Gabe durch Recht nicht lange, und nicht taug um ihn. Dantes Aligerius l. de Monarch. An. 1321. Constantinus non potuit alienare imperii dignitates. Laurent. Valla An. 1411. Suam esse agunt urbem Romam, suum regnum Siciliæ Neapolitanumque, suam universam Italiam, Galli- as, Hispanos, Germanos, Britannos, suum denique occidentem. Hæc enim cuncta in ipsa donationis pagina contineri. Ergo hæc omnia tua sunt, summe Pontifex? Omnia tibi in animo est recuperare? O- mnes Reges ac Principes spoliare urbibus? &c. At ego contra existimo, justius licere Principibus, spolia- re Te imperio omni, quod detines. Non ostendam, quod donatio illa, unde natum esse jus summum sum- mi Pontificis volunt, Sylvestro pariter & Constantino fuerit incognita. Quæ donationis pagina est isto- rum omnium patrocinium, ut non modo falsum, ve- rum & stolidum. Vid. Fasciculus rerum expetendar. An. 1535. Jacob. Spigelius in comment. sup. vers. Günther. Nicol. Cusanus Cardin, l. III. Concord. Cath. c. 2. Hieronymus Paulus Cathalanus, Æn. Sylvius Cardin. Filinus in C. Solitæ in fin. ex tr. de ministr. & obed. Alcuisius in authent. Quomo- do oporteat Episcopos &c. Petrus de Bella Perti- ca in rubris. proœm. instit. n. 11. Bartholus in pro- œm. ff. Alexander in Consil. n. 23. l. 5. Joh. Aven- tinus l. II. Annal. Quæ de Sylvestro & donatione Constantini prædicantur, ficta, salsa, inepta, pugnan- tiaque sunt. Miror extare tam stolidos, qui cre- dant, & tam impudentes, qui defendere audeant, præ- cipue cum etiam Pius II. Pontifex Max. ut commen- ta anilia, fabulamque inanem rideat. Cranzius in Hist. Sax. Franciscus Gvicciardinus l. IV. Hist. p. 156. Fabulam hanc à Scriptoribus gravissimis rebus- que ipsis refutatam esse dicit. Baronius ipse fate- tur, instrumentum illud donationis esse falsum, & commentitium, & mala fide, dolo, & fraude excogi- tatum, ab impostore aliquo scriptum &c. l. III. A. 324. n. 118. Falsitatis indicia inter alia sunt varia- tiones: Quum enim C. Futuram 12. q. 1. Melchia- des quasi suo tempore factam donationem com- memoret, C. Constantinus dist. 96. sub Sylvestro demum factam ait. Quum C. Constantinus Roma- næ urbs & tota Italia una cum imperio Occidentis Sylvestro donata dicatur, C. fundamentum in de- cretal. l. 1. tit. 9. de Election, in VI. Urbis tantum mentionem facit. Unde Ottho III. Imperator pa- lam huic donationi, ceu fictæ, contradixit: Quæ re- pugnat etiam divisioni imperii à Constantino M. fa- ctæ Euseb. l. IV. de vit. Const. Socr. l. II. c. ult. & conservationi Italiæ penes successores Constant. per 140. annos, ac testimoniis Papistarum, qui Exarcha- tum Papalem circa A. 800. ex donatione Pipini & Caroli II. initium habuisse asserunt, utpote Plati- na, Volaterr. Sabell. Enn. 8. l. 8. & Pontificum ipsorum, qui eam donationem ad Ludovicum Pi- um Caroli M. filium referunt, ut taceam quod tum ne extiterit quidem Constantinopolis, & fin- gatur tamen super eam Principatum Papæ tribu- tum fuisse. Vid. de his prolixe B. D. Hoë Tom. 3. p. 206. seq. Nec minus quoque Regina hæc glo- riatur de imperio in totum orbem, ita decernente Bonifacio IIX. C. Unam sanctam de Major: & obed. in VI. subesse Romano Pontif. omni humanæ creatu- ræ declaramus, præcipimus, definimus & pronun- tiamus de necessitate salutis: Quum ex adverso

Pelagius I. Exul. 16. ad Childeric. Franc. Reg. An. 555. merito scripserit: Regibus nos (Episco- pos) subditos esse Scriptura S. præcipiunt, & Adria- no IV. apud Frideric. I. Barbaross. prætendente, imperium esse beneficium à Romana Ecclesia ac- ceptum, literis circularibus testatum fecerit, à Deo solo per Electionem Principum imperium suum esse, & quicunque nos Imperialem coronam ex bene- ficio à Domino Papa suscepisse dicit, divina institutio- ni ac doctrinæ Petri contrarius est, & mendacii reus erit. Quo faciunt elogia adulatorum Papalium Augustini de Ancon. in summa de Eccl. potest. q. 1. art. 7. quod Papa omnem Regalem & imperialem potestatem habeat in hoc mundo, quod Regibus tanquam Vasallis sua potestati subjectis imperare, eosque & destituere & instituere possit, q. 46. quod etiam in Turcarum, Paganorum & infidelium Re- ges jurisdictionem habeat, q. 32. cumque Christus omnem potestatem summam in omnem creaturam per passionem suam meruerit, idcirco ille eam Papæ dederit & reliquerit. C. 23. quod Christus omnia imperia & regna mundi in exaltatione sua occupa- rit & à Cæsare, Regibus, aliisque Principibus per milites suos Apostolos abstulerit & Pontifici Romano contulerit: Ut habet Jodocus de Titano Urban. VI. cubicularius tract. Monarchial. Unde sine dubio est, quod Episcopatus etiam in terris Turca- rum & Regnorum R. P. suis assignet ac distribuat, prouti lubet.

Καὶ χήρα ὂυκ εἰμι] in Esaia: Οὐ καθιῶ χήρα. Ero sem- per regnantium sedes.

Καὶ πένθος ὐ μὴ ἴδω.] Hoc positum pro illis Esaiæ: Οὐδὲ γνώσομαι ὀρφανίαν. Non orbabor prole, id est, po- pulo. Vid. Matth. XXIII, 17. Videre apud Ebræos fre- quens pro experiri.

## 18:8
Verse 8.

Therefore in one day shall her plagues come.] The sense is equal to that which is in Isaiah 46:9. 'In one day' here is 'suddenly' in Hebrew idiom, which also occurs below.

Death.] Pestilence, as we said above 6:8, Matthew 24:7. Concerning the huge pestilence throughout the Roman world in the time of Justinian, see Procopius, book two of the Persian Wars. That in Isaiah 47:11 is מות.

Καὶ πένθος.] Mourning for those killed by the Goths. This is the word רעה in the cited passage of Isaiah.

Καὶ λιμὸς.] This is that famine of Rome which Procopius describes in Gothic War III, where he says that grain and bran were bought with patrimonies: that he was considered blessed who could obtain an animal that had died of disease, that the common people had fed on nettles for some time: where those had failed, bodies were consumed by emaciation. That some had eaten dung: many had killed themselves because of hunger: many were consumed by famine: a father with five children had thrown himself into the Tiber on account of it. Famine is שוא in the cited passage of Isaiah, which is explained here.

Vidua non sum, luctum non videbo, he says, that is to say, I am the spouse of Christ, whom He cannot desert, therefore I shall be able neither to err in the faith, nor to be conquered in any way, as the Pope rashly boasts from Matt. XVI. Bellarmine makes temporal happiness a mark of the Church. B. Glassius: I am not a widow, that is, I am very populous. Adverbs of negation are sometimes augmentative.

Καὶ ἐν πυρὶ κατακαυθήσεται.] Namely, by a third part of itself, as we said above XVI, 19. XVII, 16. with all the gates moreover burned.

The fire is understood not as one of grace, as Alcafar foolishly claims, but of wrath, inasmuch as by it Babylon is not to be blessed, but horribly burned.

Ὅτι ἰσχυρὸς Κύριος ὁ Θεὸς ὁ κρίνας ἀυτὴν.] That is, having condemned. God, who condemned Rome to these evils, most easily executes His decrees. All creatures obey Him. See Jer. LI, 6. concerning Babylon.

Latin:

Vers. 8.

Διὰ τῦτο ἐν μίᾳ ἡμέρᾳ ἥξουσιν αἱ πληγαὶ ἀυτῆς.] Sen- sus par ei, qui apud Esaiam XLVI, 9. Ἐν μίᾳ ἡμέρᾳ hic est subito loquutione Ebræa, quæ & infra oc- currat.

Θάνατος.] Pestilentia, ut diximus supra VI, 8. Matth. XXIV, 7. De ingenti pestilentia per orbem Romanum Ju- stiniani tempore vide Procopium Persicorum secundo. Id Esa. XLVII, 11. est מות.

Καὶ πένθος.] Luctus ob interfectos à Gothis. Id dicto Esaiæ loco est רעה.

Καὶ λιμὸς.] Hæc est illa fames Romæ, quam describit Procopius Gothicorum III. ubi leges patrimoniis emptum frumentum & furfurem: pro beato habitum qui animal morbo emortuum adipisci posset, urticis pastum fuisse ali- quandiu plebem: ubi eæ defecerant, macie confecta corpo- ra.
