Quosdam stercus esitasse: multos se ob famem inter- fecisse: multos fame consumptos: patrem cum quinis libe- ris ob id se jecisse in Tiberim. Fames est שוא dicto E- saiæ loco, qui hic explicatur.

Vidua non sum, luctum non videbo, inquit, q. d. Sponsa Christi sum, quam deserere nequit, ideo nec errare in fide, nec ullo modo expugnari potero, ut è Matth. XVI. temere jactitat Papa. Felicitatem temporalem Bellarminus notam facit Ecclesiæ. B. Glassius: Vidua non sum, id est, populosa admodum sum. Adverbia negandi quandoque ἀυξητικὰ sunt.

Καὶ ἐν πυρὶ κατακαυθήσεται.] Nempe tertia sui parte, ut diximus supra XVI, 19. XVII, 16. portis insuper omni- bus incensis.

Ignis non gratiæ, ut ineptit Alcafar, sed iræ in- telligitur, utpote, quo Babylon non beanda, sed horribiliter concremanda.

Ὅτι ἰσχυρὸς Κύριος ὁ Θεὸς ὁ κρίνας ἀυτὴν.] Id est κατακρί- νας. Deus qui Romam in hæc mala damnavit, facillime de- creta sua exequitur. Parent illi creaturæ omnes. Vide Je- rem. LI, 6. de Babylone.

## 18:9
Vers. 9.

Καὶ κλαύσουσι καὶ κόψονται ἐπ᾿ ἀυτὴν.] They will testify to their sorrow with weeping and wailing. See above I, 7. Matt. XI, 17.

ANNOTATIONS ON THE APOCALYPSE

Οἱ βασιλεῖς τῆς γῆς [The kings of the earth]. Namely those who did not fail. Under the name of Kings are comprehended both Senators and Prefects.

Οἱ μετ᾽ αὐτῆς πορνεύσαντες [They who committed fornication with her]. Those who were idolaters either openly or secretly.

Καὶ στρηνιάσαντες [And lived luxuriously]. Those who had set no limit to their expenses.

Ὅταν βλέπωσι τὸν καπνὸν τῆς πυρώσεως αὐτῆς [When they see the smoke of her burning]. Such is that: Every man smokes for Neptunian Troy. Seneca on the same matter: The Trojans will see their fatherland by this sign.

Latin:

Vers. 9.

Καὶ κλαύσουσι καὶ κόψονται ἐπ᾿ ἀυτὴν.] Fletu & plan- ctu mœrorem suum testabuntur. Vide supra I, 7. Matth. XI, 17.

ANNOTATA AD APOCALYPSI

Οἱ βασιλεῖς τῆς γῆς.] Nempe qui non defecerunt. Sub Regum nomine comprehenduntur & Senatores & Præfecti.

Οἱ μετ᾽ αὐτῆς πορνεύσαντες.] Qui aut palam aut clam erant idololatræ.

Καὶ στρηνιάσαντες.] Qui nullum sumptibus modum fe- cerant.

Ὅταν βλέπωσι τὸν καπνὸν τῆς πυρώσεως αὐτῆς.] Tale illud: Omnis homo fumat Neptunia Troja. Seneca de eadem re: Troës hoc signo patriam videbunt.

## 18:10
Vers. 10.

Ἀπὸ μακρόθεν ἑστηκότες [Standing afar off]. So also below 15. 17. Those who do not wish to be recognized as friends of the miserable are accustomed to stand far off, Matt. XXVI, 53. XXVII, 55.

Διὰ τὸν φόβον τῦ βασανισμῦ αὐτῆς [For the fear of her torment]. From fear lest they fall into the same evil. See above 7.

Λέγοντες, Οὐαὶ ὐαὶ ἡ πόλις ἡ μεγάλη Βαβυλὼν [Saying, Woe, woe, the great city Babylon]. 'Woe' is sometimes of one threatening, sometimes of one grieving: Mantua, alas, too miserable a neighbor to Cremona. Concerning the epithet 'great' see above XVI, 18. and Dan. IV, 27.

Ἡ πόλις ἡ ἰσχυρά [The strong city]. עיר מבצר Jerem. I, 18.

Ὅτι μιᾷ ὥρᾳ ἦλθεν ἡ κρίσις σε [For in one hour thy judgment is come]. Thy punishment; μιᾷ ὥρᾳ [in one hour] within a short time. See above XVII, 12.

From that which is said, 'The Lord will judge her,' some gather that Rome will be burned from heaven. Others object that in chapter XVII, 16, this is expressly attributed to the Kings. But both can concur, with heaven cooperating with the Kings for the destruction of Rome, as once happened to the thundering legion. THEY SHALL STAND afar off: The fear of judgment described will render them anxious. They will stand in such consternation that they will not even be able to think of arms or aid.

Latin:

Vers. 10.

Ἀπὸ μακρόθεν ἑστηκότες.] Sic & infra 15. 17. Longe sta- te solent, qui nolunt agnosci pro amicis miserorum, Matth. XXVI, 53. XXVII, 55.

Διὰ τὸν φόβον τῦ βασανισμῦ αὐτῆς.] Metu ne in eadem male incidant. Vide supra 7.

Λέγοντες, Οὐαὶ ὐαὶ ἡ πόλις ἡ μεγάλη Βαβυλὼν.] Væ in- terdum minantis est, interdum condolentis: Mantua væ misera nimium vicina Cremonæ. De cognomine magnæ vide supra XVI, 18. & Dan. IV, 27.

Ἡ πόλις ἡ ἰσχυρά.] עיר מבצר Jerem. I, 18.

Ὅτι μιᾷ ὥρᾳ ἦλθεν ἡ κρίσις σε.] Pœna tua; μιᾷ ὥρᾳ in- tra breve tempus. Vide supra XVII, 12.

Ex illo, quod dicitur, Dominus judicabit illam, quidam colligunt Romam cœlitus conflagratu- ram. Alii opponunt quod cap. XVII, 16. ex- presse id Regibus tribuatur. Sed utrumque con- currere poterit, cœlo cooperante Regibus ad in- teritum Romæ, ut legioni fulminatrici quondam accidit. STABUNT longè: Metus judicii descri- ptus solicitos reddet. Tanta stabunt consterna- tione, ut de armis vel auxilio ne cogitare quidem possint.

## 18:11
Verse 11.

And the merchants of the earth weep and mourn over her.] He compares Rome not only openly to Babylon but also tacitly to Tyre, on account of its immense commerce with the whole world. This is taken from Ezek. XXVII, 36, and what follows is from the same chapter.

For no one buys their cargo anymore.] Γόμος is called משא, which is carried by beasts of burden, Exod. XXIII, 5, but also what is carried by ships. In the Glossary, γόμος is a burden.

Latin:

Vers. 11.

Καὶ οἱ ἔμποροι τῆς γῆς κλαίυσι καὶ πενθῦσιν ἐπ᾽ αὐτῇ.] Non tantùm Babyloni aperte sed & tacite Tyro Romam comparat ob ingentia ejus cum toto orbe commercia. De- sumpta hæc ex Ezech. XXVII, 36. & quæ sequuntur ex eo- dem capite.

Ὅτι τὸν γόμον αὐτῶν ὐδεὶς ἀγοράζει ὐκέτι.] Γόμος משא dicitur quod jumentis fertur, Exod. XXIII, 5. sed & quod navibus. In Glossario γόμος onus.

## 18:12
Verse 12.

Cargo of gold and silver and precious stone and pearl.] See above XVII, 4. Ezekiel XXVII, 12, 22. XXVIII, 4, 13.

And fine linen and purple and silk and scarlet.] See above XVII, 4. Byssus is the finest and most excellent kind of flax. Silk is named from the Seres, that is, from the Chinese, because worms spin it. Justinian arranged for these things, which were once sought from the ends of the earth, to be produced within the Roman Empire. Procopius in his Persian Wars calls it metaxa. Suidas: Seric is silk. Petronius in his description of Roman luxury: 'Here the Numidians their crusts, there the Seres their fleeces.' See Ezek. XXVII, 16, 24.

And all thyine wood.] The Latin translates it 'thyina,' where in Hebrew it is אלגומים, or with transposed letters אלמוגים. The Septuagint in 1 Kings X, 11, 12, translates it 'unhewn.' But Theodotion, whose version is accepted in the Chronicles, 2 Chron. II, 19, IX, 10, 11, translates it 'pine,' as does Josephus 'pines.' I think it is an Arabic word, and 'al' is the article, meaning 'undulating wood,' from גום, which for the Arabs means to fluctuate. Here, however, it is signified under a general name, the citron wood, from which the tables of wealthy Romans were made, as Martial teaches us in many places, and Pliny XIII, 15, who says the same is called Thyam and Thyon. It was sought especially from Mauritania, Ezek. XXVII, 5, 6. In the manuscript it is 'thyine vessel,' that is, tables.

And all ivory vessel.] Such as beds made of ivory, which Varro in his 'De Lingua Latina' teaches us were already in use in his own age. Labeo also mentions it in 'On Bequeathed Furniture,' Ezekiel XXVII, 15.

And all vessel.] By this name all furniture and equipment is understood. כלי. See what we said in Acts IX, 15, X, 19. See Ezek. XXVII, 9.

Of most precious wood.] Such as boxwood, whence the name 'pyxis' (box), or ebony, Ezek. XXVII, 15.

And brass.] Whence cauldrons, Ezek. XXVII, 13.

And iron.] Whence weapons for war, hunting, and cooking, Ezek. XXVII, 12, 19.

Καὶ μαρμάρου.) Of Parian or Laconian marble, whence columns and statues.

Latin:

Vers. 12.

Γόμον χρυσῦ καὶ ἀργυρῦ καὶ λίθυ τιμίυ καὶ μαργαρίτυ.] Vide supra XVII, 4. Ezechiel. XXVII, 12. 22. XXVIII, 4. 13.

Καὶ βυσσῦ καὶ πορφυρῦ καὶ σηρικῦ καὶ κοκκίνε.] Vide su- pra XVII, 4. Byssus est tenuissimum ac præstantissimum li- ni genus. Sericum est à Seribus dictum, id est à Sinensibus, quod vermes nent. Hæc olim ab ultimo orbe petita Justi- nianus curavit, ut in imperio Romano fierent. Metaxam vocat Procopius Persicorum l. Suidas: Σερικὴ ἡ μεταξά ἐστι. Petronius in descriptione luxus Romani: Hinc Numidæ crustas, illinc sua vellera Seres. Vide Ezech. XXVII, 16. 24.

Καὶ πᾶν ξύλον θύινον.] Thyina vertit Latinus, ubi in Ebræo אלגומים, aut transpositis literis אלמוגים. Septuaginta 1. Reg. X, 11. 12. vertunt ἀπελέκητα. At Theo- dotion, cujus versio in Paralipomenis recepta est 2. Paral. II, 19. IX, 10. 11. πεύκινα quomodo & Josephus πεύκας. Puto esse vocem Abrabicam, & אל esse articulum, ligna un- dulata, à גום, quod Arabibus est fluctuare. Hic vero sub nomine generali significari citra, unde erant divitum Roma- norum mensæ, ut Martialis compluribus locis nos docet, & Plinius XIII, 15. qui idem ait Thyam & Thyon appellari. Petebatur maxime ex Mauritania, Ezech. XXVII, 5. 6. In manuscripto σκεῦος θύινον, id est mensas.

Καὶ πᾶν σκεῦος ἐλεφάντινον.] Ut lectos ex ebore, quos jam sua ætate usitatos nos docet Varro de lingua Latina. Meminit & Celsus l. Labeo de Supellectile legata, Ezechiel. XXVII, 15.

Καὶ πᾶν σκεῦος.] Hoc nomine omnis supellex atque instrumentum intelligitur. כלי. Vide quæ diximus Actor. IX, 15. X, 19. Vid. Ezech. XXVII, 9.

Ἐκ ξύλε τιμιωτάτε.] Uti ex buxo, unde nomen πυξίδων, ex ebeno, Ezech. XXVII, 15.

Καὶ χαλκῦ.] Unde lebetes Ezech. XXVII, 13.

Καὶ σιδήρου.) Unde arma bellica, venatoria, culinaria, Ezech. XXVII, 12. 19.

Καὶ μαρμάρου.) Marmoris Parii aut Laconici, unde co- lumnæ & statuæ.

## 18:13
Vers. 13.

Καὶ κινάμωμον.) See what we said in Exod. XXX, 23. In Hebrew it is written קנמון, and that word exists in Prov. VII, 17, Cant. IV, 14. The price was one thousand five hundred denarii per pound, according to Pliny XII, 14. They are mistaken who think it is what we call cinnamon [canella]. For that is a species of cassia. In the Manuscript, καὶ ἄμωμον is added here.

Καὶ θυμιάματα.) קטורת. Incense, not only in the use of sacred rites, but also in luxuries. See Proverb. VII, 17, Ezech. XXVII, 19, 22.

Καὶ μῦρον.) For they used to drink while anointed.

Καὶ λίβανον.) Frankincense, both in the use of sacred rites and mixed into drink. It also has great use against ulcers and wounds, according to Dioscorides I. 81.

Καὶ οἶνον καὶ ἔλαιον.) Things more pleasant than necessary. See above VI, 6. Much oil is needed for the wrestling school. Wines were brought even from Meroë, Ezech. XXVII, 17, 18.

Καὶ σεμίδαλιν.) Which is simila or similago to the Latins. To the Hebrews סלת. From it cakes were made.

Καὶ σῖτον.) Grain from Africa and Egypt. Thus also Ezech. XXVII, 17.

Καὶ κτήνη.) Here the LXX translate the word בהמה, by which all animals walking on feet are comprehended, whether they be wild or tame. Both had use in banquets: wild ones also for hunting spectacles: The wild beast is sought in the forests of the Moors, and the furthest Ammon of the Africans is searched.

Καὶ πρόβατα.) Not only for banquets and clothing, but also for milk in which women would bathe, Ezechiel XXVII, 18, 21.

Καὶ ἵππων.) Whose use is not only for wars and journeys, but also for the Circensian games. The genitive here and the following ones have ἕνεκα before them. For πλήθους is understood. A similar construction is in Exod. XX, 17. You have horses also in Ezech. XXVII, 14.

Καὶ ῥεδῶν.) Other books have ῥεδῶν. It is the same, whichever way you write it. For it is a Gallic word, as Quintilian teaches us in I. 9, from rheiden, that is, to be carried. The Latins lengthen the first syllable, as Horace: —— Whom he would wish to lift in a carriage (rheda). Cicero says he wrote a letter in a carriage when he was setting out for the camp.

Καὶ σωμάτων.) Understand free men who prostituted themselves for money, both males and females; indeed, males even hired themselves out into the arena; Pollux says σώματα δι' ἁπλῶς ἐκ ἂν δῶλα σώματα. Thus Virgil: Excepto Laurentis corpore Turni.

Καὶ ψυχὰς ἀνθρώπων.) This, but also many preceding things, are from Ezekiel concerning Tyre XXVII, 13, where what is in Hebrew בנפש אדם, the Seventy translate as ἐν ψυχαῖς ἀνθρώπων. Jerome learnedly [translates it as] slaves. Thus also later Greece called slaves ψυχάρια; the body is the master's, they have only their own soul. Servitude descends into the whole soul, says Seneca.

Latin:

Vers. 13.

Καὶ κινάμωμον.) Vide quæ diximus Exod. XXX, 23. E- braice scribitur קנמון, extatque ea vox Prov. VII, 17. Cant. IV, 14. Pretium erat in libras denariùm mille & quingen- torum, teste Plinio XII, 14. Falluntur qui esse putant quam canellam dicimus. Ea enim cassiæ est species. In Manu- scripto hic additur καὶ ἄμωμον.

Καὶ θυμιάματα.) קטורת. Suffitus non tantum in sacrorum usu, sed & in deliciis. Vid. Proverb. VII, 17. Ezech. XXVII, 19. 22.

Καὶ μῦρον.) Potabant enim unguentati.

Καὶ λίβανον.) Thus & in sacrorum usu, & potui misceba- tur. Magnus etiam ejus usus adversus ulcera, vulnerave, teste Dioscoride I. 81.

Καὶ οἶνον καὶ ἔλαιον.) Res jucundæ magis quam neces- sariæ. Vide supra VI, 6. Oleo multo opus est ad palæ- stram. Vina portabantur usque à Meroë, Ezech. XXVII, 17. 18.

Καὶ σεμίδαλιν.) Quæ Latinis simila, vel similago. Ebræis סלת. Inde fiebant placentæ.

Καὶ σῖτον.) Frumentum ab Africa & Ægypto. Sic & Ezech. XXVII, 17.

Καὶ κτήνη.) Hic vertunt LXX. vocem בהמה, qua comprehenduntur animalia omnia pedibus gradientia, sive ea fera sint, sive mansueta. Utraque usum habebant in epu- lis : feræ etiam ad editiones venatorias : Quæritur in sylvis Mauri fera, & ultimus Ammon Af了两rum excutitur.

Καὶ πρόβατα.) Non ad epulas tantum & vestes, sed & ad lac in quo fœminæ lavarentur, Ezechiel. XXVII, 18. 21.

Καὶ ἵππων.) Quorum usus non tantum ad bella & iti- nera, sed & ad ludos Circenses. Genitivus hic & sequen- tes ἕνεκα ante se habent. Subauditur enim πλήθους. Si- milis constructio Exod. XX, 17. Habes eques & apud E- zech. XXVII, 14.

Καὶ ῥεδῶν.) Alii libri ῥεδῶν. Perinde est, utro! modo scribas. Est enim vox Gallica, ut Quintilianus nos docet I. 9. à rheiden scilicet, quod est vehi. Latini priorem pre- ducunt, ut Horatius : —— Quem tollere rheda Vellet. Cicero epistolam se scripsisse ait in rheda cum ad castra pro- ficisceretur.

Καὶ σωμάτων.) Intellige homines liberos, qui pro pecu- nia se prostituebant, tam mares quam fœminæ, mares vero etiam in arenam se auctorabant, σώματα δι' ἁπλῶς ἐκ ἂν δῶ- λα σώματα ait Pollux. Sic Virgilius : Excepto Laurentis corpore Turni.

Καὶ ψυχὰς ἀνθρώπων.) Hoc, sed & multa præceden- tia ex Ezechiele de Tyro XXVII, 13. ubi quod in Ebræo est בנפש אדם septuaginta vertunt ἐν ψυχαῖς ἀνθρώπων. Hieronymus erudite mancipia. Sic & Græcia posterior ser- vos appellavit ψυχαρίa, corpus est Domini, animum tantum habent suum Servitus in totum animum descendit, ait Se- neca.

## 18:14
Vers. 14.

Καὶ ἡ ὀπώρα τῆς ἐπιθυμίας τῆ ψυχῆ συ ἀπῆλθεν ἀπό συ.) There is in these words and the following ones, up to those [words] οἱ ἔμποροι, an address of the Kings to Rome, such as the Greeks call an apostrophe. You have a parallel in Ezekiel XXVII, 39. Ὀπώρα signifies autumn: but by catachresis in this place, the time of enjoying: just as the Latins say to pluck the fruits of Venus. The sense is: You will no longer be able to indulge in loves.

Καὶ πάντα τὰ λιπαρά.) Sumptuous. This pertains to feasts. Καὶ τὰ λαμπρὰ ἀπώλετο ἀπό συ.) Splendid, this pertains to clothes.

Καὶ ἐκέτι ὐ μὴ εὑρήσοις ἀυτά.) So those Kings believed. And certainly, the Empire never returned to Rome afterwards. The Emperors who were called Roman, whether Greek or German, had their seat elsewhere. A manner of speaking, such as above XII, 8, XVI, 20. In the Manuscript: Οὐ μὴ ἀυτὰ εὑρήσουσι.

Regar…ding merchandise, Platina in Sylvest. [writes]: Revenues came to the same basilica from Tarsus of Cilicia: From the possession of Tyre comes oil, come aromatics and cassia: Balsam comes from places bearing the same things here, comes saffron, salt, pepper, cinnamon, etc. The Spaniards especially carry to Rome gold, silver, pearls, precious stones. Italy [carries] cinnamon, frankincense, ointments, wine, oil: Sicily, Sardinia, Corsica, fine flour, wheat, the Germans [supply] beasts of burden. The English [supply] sheep, cloth, the French [supply] carriages & horses: the Swiss [supply] bodies & bodyguards: finally, all of them commonly [supply] the souls of men. But this trafficking will cease in the desolation of mystical Babylon. And therefore the merchants, not only civil, but especially Ecclesiastical, Cardinals, Apostolic Legates, Bishops, Abbots, Canons, Priests, mass-priests, Monks, Nuns, will greatly lament that this Ecclesiastical-Political trade, with its immense profit, has so suddenly vanished and been reduced to nothing. They, therefore, will remain, to be overcome at last in the final battle of Apoc. XIX. The Princes of Germany in their former grievances calculated that the Roman Pontiff from the annates of the Bishoprics of Germany alone collects 119,533 florins. The Parisian Senate under Louis XI complained that from France alone within three years 27 and a half tons of gold had been carried off to Rome. Sebastian Münster in his Cosmographia, in the description of Spain, writes: In Spain alone from Bishoprics and Archbishoprics there is collected annually for the Pope 480,800 crowns or nine tons of gold and 61,600 florins. It is said that the Roman Pontiff up to the year of Christ 1609 had acquired by his trafficking at the minimum 3,660,844 tons of gold, or 366,084 millions of gold. This is B. Gravius: All thyine wood, that is, scented [wood], such as Cypress, Cedar, from which they make altars, idols, crosses, etc., vessels of ivory or of precious wood (Ebony, Branlian), or prepared from bronze, iron, and marble, so that in them the relics of saints, the bodies of martyrs or canonized Divines, or even idolatrous images, ointments, oils, transubstantiated breads, etc., may be kept. Cinnamon, incense, ointment, which are used for the fumigation and scenting of temples, and for the anointing of Pontiffs, Cardinals, Emperors, and Kings. Wine which serves the delights of the Pontifical and Roman Clergy. Oil with which lamps are filled, illuminating the temples and chapels of the Papists, and which comes into use in extreme unction. Fine flour and wheat, from which the most delicate breads are baked for the clergy, beasts of burden and sheep for trade on account of the most ample revenues of the clergy and more solemn processions, horses and carriages for journeys and pilgrimages to the places of saints or jubilees. Human bodies which serve as bodyguards and keepers to the Roman Pontiff and his cardinals; likewise the bodies and relics of saints, which promote the trafficking of the Pontiff, and the liberation of human souls from purgatory, which, being persuaded to the common people and even to the nobles and highest heads, procures great profit for the mass-priests and immense riches for the Roman Church.

The fruits of desire refer to the most pleasant gardens of the Pontiff and the Cardinals, all things fat and excellent, the luxuries and variety of dishes with which they are accustomed to load their tables. Cf. 2 Pet. II, 2 seqq.

Latin:

Vers. 14.

Καὶ ἡ ὀπώρα τῆς ἐπιθυμίας τῆ ψυχῆ συ ἀπῆλθεν ἀπό συ.) Est in his verbis & sequentibus usque ad illa οἱ ἔμποροι al- loquutio Regum ad Romam, qualem Græci ἀποστροφὴν vo- cant. Habes parem Ezech. XXVII, 39. Ὀπώρα, autumnum significat: per κατάχρησιν vero hoc loco tempus fruendi: Sicut Veneris fructus carpere dicunt Latini. Sensus est : Non ultra poteris indulgere amoribus.

Καὶ πάντα τὰ λιπαρά.) Lauta. Hoc ad epulas pertinet. Καὶ τὰ λαμπρὰ ἀπώλετο ἀπό συ.) Splendida, hoc ad ve- stes.

Καὶ ἐκέτι ὐ μὴ εὑρήσοις ἀυτά.) Ita illi Reges credebant. Et certe Imperium nunquam postea ad Romam rediit. Qui Imperatores Romani dicti sunt sive Græci sive Germani, ali- bi sedem habuere. Loquendi genus, quale supra XII, 8. XVI, 20. In Manuscripto : Οὐ μὴ ἀυτὰ εὑρήσουσι.

De mercibus Platina in Sylvest. Venere proven- tus ad eandem basilicam ex Tarso Ciliciæ: Ex possef- sione Tyri venit oleum, venere aromata & cassia: Venit balsamum ex locis huc eadem ferentibus, venit crocum, sal, piper, cinama &c. Hispani præcipue Ro- mam vehunt aurum, argentum, margaritas, lapi- des pretiosos. Italia cinamomum, thus, unguenta, vinum, oleum: Sicilia, Sardinia, Corsica, similam, triticum, Germani jumenta. Angli oves, pannum, Galli rhedas & equos: Helvetii corpora & stipatores: Animas denique hominum communiter omnes. Hæc autem nundinatio cessabit in desolatione Babylonis mysticæ. Ideoque mercatores non tantum civiles, sed cumprimis Ecclesiastici, Cardinales, Legati Apostolici, Episcopi, Abbates, Canonici, Sacerdotes, sacrificuli, Monachi, Moniales, summopere deplorabunt, merca- turam hanc Ecclesiastico-Politicam, cum immenso lu- cro tam subito evanuisse & in nihilum redactam esse. Illi ergo supererunt, tandem in ultimo prælio A- poc. XIX. superandi. Principes Germaniæ in suis olim gravaminibus computarunt, Pontificem Roma- num ex solis annatis ex Episcopatibus Germaniæ col- ligere 119533. florenos. Senatus Parisiensis sub Lu- dov. XI. conquestus est, ex sola Gallia intra trienni- um 27. auri tonnas & dimidiam Romam deportatas esse. Sebastian. Münster. in Cosmograph. in descript. Hispan. scribit: In sola Hispania ex Episcopatibus & Archi-Episcopatibus pro Papa colligi quotannis 480800. cor. seu tonnas auri novem & florenos 61600. Dicitur Pontifex Romanus ad annum usque Christi 1609, nundinationibus suis acquisivisse ad minimum tonnas auri 3660844, vel milliones auri 366084. Hæc B. Gravius: Omne lignum thyinum, hoc est, odora- tum, ut Cupressi, Cedri, ex quibus altaria, idola cru- ces &c. conficiunt, vasa eburnea vel ex ligno pretioso (Ebeno, Branliano,) vel ex ære, ferro & marmore præparata, ut in eis sanctorum reliquiæ, corpora mar- tyrum vel canonizatorum Divorum, vel etiam imagi- nes idolatricæ, unguenta, olea, panes transsubstan- tiati &c. asserventur. Cinamomum, thus, unguen- tum, quæ ad suffitum & odoramentum templo- rum, & ad unctionem Pontificum, Cardinalium Imperatorum & Regum adhibentur. Vinum quod deliciis Pontificiis & Cleri Romani inservit. Oleum quo replentur lampades, templa & facella Pontificiorum illuminantes, quodque in extrema unctione in usum venit. Simila & triticum, ex quibus panes delicatissimi pro clero pinsuntur, jumenta & oves ad mercaturam ob reditus cleri amplissimos & processiones solenniores, equi & rhedæ ad itinera & peregrinationes ad loca san- ctorum vel jubilæa. Corpora humana quæ tan- quam stipatores & custodes Pontifici Rom. ejus- que purpuratis inserviunt; corpora item & reliquiæ sanctorum, quæ nundinationes Pontif. promo- vent, animæque humanæ è purgatorio liberatio, quæ vulgo imo proceribus & capitibus summis persuasa magnum sacrificulis lucrum, & immen- sas divitias Ecclesiæ Romanæ conciliat.

Poma desiderii respiciunt amœnissimos Ponti- ficis & Purpuratorum hortos, pinguia & præcla- ra omnia, lautitias & varietatem ferculorum, quibus mensas onerare solent. Conf. 2. Petr. II, 2. seqq.

## 18:15
Vers. 15.

Οἱ ἔμποροι τούτων.] It comes from the Kings to the merchants: then it is about to come to the sailors, as in Ezekiel. Τούτων, that is, of all those wares which have already been indicated.

Οἱ πλουτήσαντες ἀπ’ αὐτῆς.] See above 3. Ezekiel XXVII, 33.

Ἀπὸ μακρόθεν στήσονται κατὰ τὸν φόβον τοῦ βασανισμοῦ αὐτῆς.] As above 10. They will stand, namely where they will learn of the matter: for they will be far off.

Κλαίοντες καὶ πενθοῦντες] πενθοῦντες here, which is above κόψονται.

Latin:

Vers. 15.

Οἱ ἔμποροι τούτων.] A Regibus venit ad mercatores: Dein- de ad nautas venturus, ut Ezechiel. Τούτων, id est omnium istarum mercium, quæ jam indicatæ sunt.

Οἱ πλουτήσαντες ἀπ’ αὐτῆς.] Vide supra 3. Ezechiel. XXVII, 33.

Ἀπὸ μακρόθεν στήσονται κατὰ τὸν φόβον τοῦ βασανισμοῦ αὐ- τῆς.] Ut supra 10. Stabunt, nempe ubi rem cognoscent: aberunt enim.

Κλαίοντες καὶ πενθοῦντες] πενθοῦντες hic, quod supra κό- ψονται.

## 18:16
Vers. 16.

Καὶ λέγοντες; Οὐαὶ πόλις ἡ μεγάλη, ἡ περιβεβλημένη βύσσινον καὶ πορφυροῦν καὶ κόκκινον, καὶ κεχρυσωμένη ἐν χρυσῷ καὶ λίθῳ τιμίῳ καὶ μαργαρίταις.] Above XVII, 4. But there is a syllepsis here: as we also said above. For κεχρυσωμένη is correctly referred to gold, although by a certain pleonasm; but to stones and pearls it is referred improperly. Such are those:

— — — Danaos & pinea furtim Luxat claustra Sinon. And: Quem febire plagis saltum canibusque ciere. The Scholiast of Sophocles on the Electra on the word ἀπερίστροφοι says thus: Πολλάκις τὸ κατὰ κοινῆ λαμβανόμενον διαφόρως νοεῖται, καὶ ἕμπαλιν. Εἰθ᾽ ἑλέτην δίφροντε καὶ αἱρέο δῆμον ἀρίστω. Τὸ ἑλέτην κατὰ κοινῆ ἐστι, ἀλλ᾽ ἐπὶ μὲν τῶ δίφρω ἀντὶ τῶ ἔλαβον, ἐπὶ δὲ τῶν ἀνδρῶν ἀντὶ τῶ ἐφόνευσαν. Ὅτι μιᾷ ὥρᾳ ἠρημώθη ὁ τοσοῦτος πλοῦτος.] Μιᾷ ὥρᾳ as above 10. There is an hypallage here, for if we speak properly, the city has been desolated of its riches. Similar to Ezek. XXXII, 15. Καὶ ἠρημώθη ἡ γῆ σὺν τῷ πληρώματι, but there is a syllepsis there, such as we have already noted.

The significant trade of the Roman Pontiffs and the riches of the Roman see can testify most clearly: whence there are not wanting those who, among the Canonists, charge them with insatiable avarice and rapacity, see the Gloss on C. fundamenta de Elect. in VI. Where Johannes Monachus says that Rome, founded by robbers, still retains the character of its beginnings. It is hardly possible to recount the individual species of those exactions. These, however, are almost the principal ones: tribute from annates, or vacancies, tribute from preventions, resignations in favor, commendations, dispensations of age, of order, of irregularity, of bodily defect. Likewise from graces, expectatives from devolutions, from benefices about to be vacant, from privileges, exemptions from being visited, homologations of concordats, transactions made under the good pleasure of the Pope, exchanges of benefices with dispensation, Episcopal mandates, expeditions in the formation of a suitable portion, creating protonotaries and Apostolic notaries, with coadjutors by letters of either greater or lesser justice, secular dignities, new Ecclesiastical foundations, or the alteration of old ones, or the reduction of regular monasteries into a secular state, or restitution in full for fruits to be received in absence, for legitimations, for non-obstantes, for indults of secular clerics, for revocations and reductions, for toleramus or tolerations of concubines, for those proscribed for lawsuits, etc. all of which, and countless other headings of barbaric titles pertaining to the arts of the Roman Quaestor—for we have not yet said anything about the penitentiary tax, about Episcopal palls, about Cardinalitial hats, about indulgences, about private Masses, and other methods of milking of that kind—teach how great a force of money it gathers at Rome. For how could the Pope exercise trade with his clergy, and acquire for himself those things which are named here, if he were without these faculties, the sinew of things to be done? It is reported of France alone that in a three-year period it contributed to the Roman Pope nine hundred and forty-six thousand six hundred and sixty-six crowns, and in addition two-thirds of one crown, that is, two million eight hundred and forty thousand crowns, or three million gold [crowns] minus one hundred and sixty thousand, or as the Germans say, nearly twenty-eight tons of gold, as the Parisian Senate complained before King Louis XI. Concerning Pope John XXII, Francesco Petrarca reports that he left to his heirs twenty-five thousand thousand gold pieces, that is, twenty-five millions, or 250 tons of gold. Not therefore less truly than wittily did Franc. Petrarca say in his Dialogue on the Roman Curia that Simon had revived at Rome with his spouse Simonia. Marsilius of Padua, Defens. Par. p. 2. C. 24. says that Rome is a gathering place for simoniacs from everywhere: for there heaven is sold, all the elements are sold, earth, as often as the bodies of the deceased must be committed to the earth, water, which they call holy, air and the sound of bells, fire, the candelabrum. The merits of the living as well as of the dead are sold, taxes are exacted not only from the living, but also from the dead; chants, sacraments, priesthoods are sold, and finally the remission of sins itself is sold. Cf. Dan. XI, 36. 38.

Latin:

Vers. 16.

Καὶ λέγοντες; Οὐαὶ πόλις ἡ μεγάλη, ἡ περιβεβλημένη βύσσινον καὶ πορφυροῦν καὶ κόκκινον, καὶ κεχρυσωμένη ἐν χρυσῷ καὶ λίθῳ τιμίῳ καὶ μαργαρίταις.] Supra XVII, 4. Est au- tem hic σύλληψις: ut & supra diximus. Nam κεχρυσωμένη ad aurum recte refertur, quanquam κατὰ πλεονασμόν τινα; ad lapides vero & margaritas improprie. Talia illa:

— — — Danaos & pinea furtim Luxat claustra Sinon. Et: Quem febire plagis saltum canibusque ciere. Scholiastes Sophoclis ad Electram voce ἀπερίστροφοι sic ait: Πολλάκις τὸ κατὰ κοινῆ λαμβανόμενον διαφόρως νοεῖται, καὶ ἕμπαλιν. Εἰθ᾽ ἑλέτην δίφροντε καὶ αἱρέο δῆμον ἀρίστω. Τὸ ἑλέτην κα- τὰ κοινῆ ἐστι, ἀλλ᾽ ἐπὶ μὲν τῶ δίφρω ἀντὶ τῶ ἔλαβον, ἐπὶ δὲ τῶν ἀνδρῶν ἀντὶ τῶ ἐφόνευσαν. Ὅτι μιᾷ ὥρᾳ ἠρημώθη ὁ τοσοῦτος πλοῦτος.] Μιᾷ ὥρᾳ ut supra 10. Est hic ὑπαλλαγὴ proprie enim si loquamur, urbs ἠρημῶται à divitiis. Simile Ezech. XXXII, 15. Καὶ ἠρημώ- θη ἡ γῆ σὺν τῷ πληρώματι, sed ibi σύλληψις est, qualem jam annotavimus.

De mercatura insigni Romanorum Pontificum proventus & divitiæ sedis Romanæ testari possunt luculentissime: unde non desunt, qui inter Cano- nistas ipsis insatiabilem avaritiam & rapacitatem objiciant, vid. Gloss. in C. fundamenta de Elect. in VI. Ubi Johannes Monachus ait, Romam à prædoni- bus fundatam adhuc de suis primordiis retinere. Spe- cies singulas æruscationum illarum recensere vix possibile est. Hæ autem præcipuæ fere sunt: Tri- butum ex annatis, sive vacantiis, tributum ex præ- ventionibus, resignationibus in favorem, commenda- tionibus, dispensationibus ætatis, ordinis, irregularita- tis, vitii corporalis. Item ex gratiis, expectativis ex devolutionibus, ex beneficiis vacaturis, ex privilegiis, exemptionibus non visitandi, homologationibus con- cordatorum, transactionibus sub beneplacito Papæ factis, permutationibus beneficiorum cum dispensa- tione, mandatis Episcopalibus, expeditionibus in for- maratione congrui, creandis protonotariis & notariis Apostolicis, cum coadjutoribus literis vel majoris vel minoris justitiæ, dignitatibus secularibus, Ecclesiasti- cis novis fundationibus, vel immutatione antiqua- rum, vel reductione regularium monasteriorum in se- cularem statum, vel restitutione in integrum pro fru- ctibus percipiendis in absentia, pro legitimationibus, pro non obstantiis, pro indultis clericorum secularium, pro revocationibus & reductionibus, pro toleramus si- ve tolerantiis concubinarum, proscriptis ad lites &c. quæ omnia & innumera alia barbarorum titulo- rum capita ad artes Quæstoris Romani facientia, nam nondum quicquam de taxa pænitentiaria, de palliis Episcopalibus, de galeris Cardinalitiis, de in- dulgentiis, de Missis privatis, & id genus aliis emun- gendi modis diximus, quantam Romæ nummo- rum vim conflet, edocent. Quomodo enim Pa- pa cum clero suo mercaturam exercere, & ea quæ hic nominantur, sibi acquirere posset, si absque hisce facultatibus nervo rerum gerendarum esset? De sola Gallia fertur, quod triennali spatio ad no- vies centena sex & quadraginta millia sexcentos sex & sexaginta coronatos, & insuper unius coronati bes- sem, hoc est, duodetricies centenum & quadragenum millium coronatorum sive trium auri millionum mi- nus centum sexaginta millibus, sive ut Germani loquuntur, ad octo fere & viginti auri tonnas Pa- pæ Romano tribuerit, ut Senatus Parisiensis co- ram Rege Ludovico XI. conquestus est. De Papa Johanne XXII. perhibet Franciscus Petrar- cha, quod reliquerit hæredibus vicies quinquies millena aureorum millia h. e. viginti quinque mil- liones, sive 250. tonnas auri. Non ergo vere mi- nus quam festive Franc. Petrarcha in Dial. de Rom. currit. Romæ Simonem dixit cum conjuge sua Simonia revixisse. Marsilius Patavin. Defens. Par. p. 2. C. 24. Romam Simoniacorum esse concursum undique ait: ibi siquidem venditur cælum, vendun- tur omnia elementa, terra, quoties defunctorum cor- pora terræ mandanda sunt, aqua, quam vocant lu- stralem, aër & sonitus tintinnabulorum, ignis, can- delabrum. Venduntur merita tam vivorum quam mortuorum, exiguntur vectigalia non à vivis tantum, sed etiam à mortuis; venduntur cantilenæ, sacramen- ta, sacerdotia, ipsa denique venditur remissio peccato- rum. Conf. Dan. XI, 36. 38.

## 18:17
Vers. 17.

And every shipmaster, and all the company in ships, and as many as trade by sea.) Shipmasters, passengers & rowers: taken from Ezech. XXVII, 26. 27. 28. In the Manuscript: Πᾶς ὁ ἐπὶ τόπον πλέων supply τῆτον; because he sails to those places: whence the Latin version is to be corrected: All who sail to the place, not to the lake. Ποιοῦντες ἐργασίας ἐν ὕδασι πολλοῖς we have in Ps. CVI, 23. But also ἐργάζεσθαι θάλασσαν is an elegant expression for τὴν θαλασσικὴν, just as the Greeks say ἐργάζεσθαι χρυσοχοϊκὴν & similar things. Some Codices here after πλέων have, καὶ ταῦταν, but there is no need.

Standing afar off.) He uses the aorist in place of the present. For the sailors were near both to Ostia and to the place which was called the port. See Procopius, Gothic War III.

Latin:

Vers. 17.

Καὶ πᾶς κυβερνήτης, κὰι πᾶς ὁ ἐπὶ τῶν πλοίων πλέων, κὰι ὅσοι τὴν θάλασσαν ἐργάζονται.) Naucleri, vectores & remi- ges: desumptum ex Ezech. XXVII, 26. 27. 28. In Manu- scripto: Πᾶς ὁ ἐπὶ τόπον πλέων supple τῆτον; quia ad ista loca navigat: unde corrigenda versio Latina: Omnes qui in locum navigant, non in lacum. Ποιοῦντες ἐργασίας ἐν ὕδασι πολλοῖς habemus Ps. CVI, 23. Sed & ἐργάζεσθαι θάλασσαν ele- gans locutio pro τὴν θαλασσικὴν, sicut dicunt Græci ἐργάζε- σθαι χρυσοχοϊκὴν & similia. Quidam Codices hic post πλέων habent, καὶ ταῦταν, sed nihil opus.

Ἀπὸ μακρόθεν ἔστησαν.) Utitur ἀορίσῳ vice præsentis. E- rant enim nautæ propinqui tum ad Ostiam tum ad locum, qui portus dicebatur. Vide Procopium Gothicorum III.

## 18:18
And cried, when they saw the smoke of her burning.) above 9. But in the Manuscript: the place of her burning. And thus the Latin reads. Such is that: And the fields where Troy was.

Saying: What city is like unto this great city.) Supply, was. But now all is false.

Latin:

Καὶ ἔκραζον, βλέποντες τὸν καπνὸν τῆς πυρώσεως αὐτῆς.) supra 9. At in Manuscripto: τὸν τόπον τῆς πυρώσεως. Et sic legit Latinus. Tale illud: Et campos ubi Troja fuit.

Λέγοντες· Τίς ὁμοία τῇ πόλει τῇ μεγάλῃ.) Supple, fuit. At nunc φεῦδα πάντα.

## 18:19
Vers. 19.

And cast dust on their heads.) Namely the sailors from Syria & Egypt: For it was the custom for those to testify grief in that manner, Job II, 12. 1 Sam. IV, 12. Jerem. XXV, 34. Ezech. XXVII, 30.

And cried, weeping and wailing, and saying.) above 15. In the Manuscript here, weeping and wailing is absent.

Alas, alas that great city.) Above 10.

In which were made rich all that had ships in the sea by reason of her costliness.) An Hebraism for from whose costliness. By whose excellence. This word is of that time, concerning which this prediction is.

for in one hour she is made desolate.) ὅτι here is interrogative, as in Mark IX, 17. לָמָה.

Sailors, not only those properly so called, but also spiritual ones in the ship of the Church: governors, lower ship-owners, sailors and laborers, Pontiffs and the entire clergy. Nor is it inappropriate that merchants and sailors are understood mystically, as most things in this book are mystical. This is what the painting proposed to the laity in the Papacy does: Namely, they exhibited a great trireme moving over the waves of the sea, inscribed with the name Holy Christian Church. In the prow sat only the Pope with the Cardinals and Bishops, with an image of the Holy Spirit erected: as if He assisted only them. Priests and other Monks sat at the sides, or rowing benches, holding oars and directing the course to the course. But the laity were tossed here through storms and waves outside the ship, and all those to whom the Clerics did not offer help, so as to pull them out of the sea either with their hands or by throwing out ropes, perished in the waters. For a few, having seized the ropes which the Holy Fathers themselves threw out, and helped by their grace and the liberal communication of their good works, climbed onto the ship and by their merits arrived at the port or heaven. We do not deny, however, that other things favor the literal sense, which we have not without reason said should be accepted according to the letter in this chapter.

Latin:

Vers. 19.

Καὶ ἔβαλον χνῦν ἐπὶ τὰς κεφαλὰς αὐτῶν.) Nempe nautæ ex Syria & Ægypto: Nam istis mos erat eo modo mœrorem testari, Job. II, 12. 1. Sam. IV, 12. Jerem. XXV, 34. Ezech. XXVII, 30.

Καὶ ἔκραζον κλαίοντες κὰι πενθοῦντες, κὰι λέγοντες.) supra 15. In Manuscripto hic abest κλαίοντες κὰι πενθοῦντες.

Οὐαὶ, Ὀαὶ ἡ πόλις μεγάλη.) Supra 10.

Ἐν ᾗ ἐπλύτησαν πάντες οἱ ἔχοντες τὰ πλοῖα ἐν τῇ θαλάσ- σῃ ἐκ τῆς τιμιότητος αὐτῆς.) Ebraïsmo pro ἐξ ἧς τῆς τιμιό- τητος. Per cujus excellentiam. Est hoc vocabulum ejus temporis, de quo hæc prædictio est.

ὅτι μία ὥρᾳ ἠρημώθη.) ὅτι hic est interrogativum, ut Marc. IX, 17. לָמָה.

Nautæ non tantum proprie ita dicti, sed etiam spirituales in navi Ecclesiæ, gubernatores, navicu- larii inferiores, nautæ & operarii, Pontifices & universus clerus. Nec incommode mercatores & nautæ μυσικῶς intelliguntur, ut sunt in hoc li- bro pleraque mystica. Quod facit pictura in Pa- patu Laicis proposita : Nimirum triremem ma- gnam super fluctibus maris incedentem exhibe- bant, cui nomen S. Ecclesia Christiana inscriptum. In prora residebat tantum Papa cum Cardinali- bus & Episcopis; cum erecto Spiritus Sancti si- mulachro: quasi ipsis solis assisteret. Sacerdotes & Monachi alii sedebant ad latera, seu transtra, te- nentes remos dirigentes cursum ad cursum.. Laici vero hinc per procellas & fluctus jactabantur ex- tra navem, omnesque quibus Clerici opem non ferebant, ut vel manibus vel ejectis funibus ipsos mari extraherent, peribant in aquis. Pauci enim arreptis funibus, quos ipsi S. Patres ejiciebant, q. ex gratia, & bonorum operum suorum commu- nicatione liberali adjuti, navem conscendebant eorumque meritis in portum vel cœlum perve- niebant. Non diffitemur tamen, literali sensui favere alia, quæ secundùm literam in hoc capite accipienda esse, non abs re diximus.

## 18:20
Verse 20.

Rejoice over her, O heaven.) The Angel, after the recorded devastation of Rome and the admiration and grief of those who had received benefits from that city, proceeds to stir up the pious to approve and praise this judgment of God. He addresses heaven here as above in XII, 12. Jeremiah also predicts the joy of the heavens from the fall of Babylon in LI, 48.

And the saints.) Namely, the perfected, Heb. XII, 23.

And the Apostles, that is, the Spirit of the Apostles. See above XIV, 3. XV, 7. It is customary for the name of men to be given to Spirits, as in Luke XVI, 23, where see the remarks.

And prophets.) You who foretold these things and have departed from this life.

for God has judged your judgment from her.) He has taken vengeance on this Babylon for the death and injuries inflicted upon you. The judgment of the injured is called retaliation, which satisfies the injured, Psalm IX, 5. XVII, 2. Micah VII, 9. It is said to judge a judgment in this way, just as to die a death, to serve a servitude.

Heaven, both Ecclesiastical and glorious, the Church both militant and triumphant in the heavens. An Angel so robust, who could with one hand lift a millstone, and that a huge one, without any difficulty and cast it into the sea with force. His immense strength is thus noted. Compare Jeremiah V, last verse. What prevents us from understanding the uncreated Angel? Moreover, the total and final ruin of Babylon is designated, and by Prophetic words the perpetual devastation of the city is insinuated.

Latin:

Vers. 20.

Εὐφραίνο ἐπ’ αὐτῇ ὀυρανὲ.) Angelus post adscriptam Ro- mæ vastitiem & admirationem doloremque eorum, qui ex ea urbe commoda perceperant, pergit excitare pios ad ap- probandum laudandumque hoc Dei judicium. Alloquitur hic cœlum ut supra XII, 12. Cœli lætitiam ex lapsu Baby- lonis etiam Jeremias prædicat LI, 48.

Καὶ οἱ ἅγιοι.) Nempe τετελειωμένοι Ebr. XII, 23.

Καὶ οἱ Ἀπόστολοι, id est, Apostolorum Spiritus. Vide supra XIV, 3. XV, 7. Solet Spiritibus dari hominum nomen, ut Luc. XVI, 23. ubi dicta vide.

Καὶ προφῆται.) Qui hæc prædixistis & abiistis ex hac vita.

ὅτι ἔκρινεν ὁ Θεὸς τὸ κρῖμα ὑμῶν ἐξ αὐτῆς.) Vindictam ob mortem injuriasque vobis illatas sumpsit de hac Babylo- ne. Judicium læsi vocatur talio, quæ læso satisfacit, Psalm. IX, 5. XVII, 2. Mich. VII, 9. Judicium judicare sic dicitur, sicut mori mortem, servitutem servire.

Cœlum tum Ecclesiasticum tum gloriosum, Eccle- sia & militans & in cælis triumphans. Angelus tam robustus, qui una manu lapidem molarem eumque ingentem absque ulla difficultate sublatum in mare cum impetu præcipitare potuerit. Notatur ita im- mensum ejus robur. Conf. Jerem. V. v. ult. Quid obstat, quo minus Angelum increatum intelliga- mus? Designatur autem totalis & finalis ruina Ba- bylonis, & verbis Propheticis perpetua urbis va- stitas insinuatur.

## 18:21
Verse 21.

And one strong angel took up.) Another from the one who spoke. He will explain the duration of the evils after the burning of the city.

A stone like a great millstone, and cast it into the sea, saying, Thus with violence shall Babylon the great city be thrown down, and shall be found no more.) In the Manuscript, as a great millstone, not badly. Thus a millstone in Mark II, 7. Whether it is an adjective from the noun mill, either mill-like or mill-stone, both are according to analogy, shadowed forth from Jeremiah LI, 63, where by a stone cast into the Euphrates it is signified that Babylon will not rise again for a long time. For the likeness of a stone cast into the sea, or a very great river, is well adapted to this. Horace: But let us swear to these things, as soon as rocks have swum up from the lowest depths, lifted, let it not be a sin to return.

Which is taken from the history of the Phocaeans, which is in Herodotus, except that there, instead of a stone, there is a leaden mass. A similar likeness in Nehemiah IX, 11. Rome lay deserted for a long time or was inhabited by few, it never rose again to its ancient greatness. It was never the seat of empire after that. Βληθήσεται השקע Jeremiah LI, 64. ὀ μὴ ἑυρεθῇ ἔτι, as above IX, 6. XII, 8. XVI, 20. Thus above 14. Jeremiah says for it לא תקום in the said place LI, 64.

Latin:

Vers. 21.

Καὶ ἦρεν εἷς ἄγγελος ἰσχυρὸς.) Alius ab illo qui loquu- tus est. Is diuturnitatem explicabit malorum post incen- dium urbis.

Λίθον ὡς μύλον μέγαν, καὶ ἔβαλεν εἰς τὴν θάλασσαν λέγων, ὅτως ὠρήμματι βληθήσεται Βαβυλὼν ἡ μεγάλη πόλις, καὶ ὐ μὴ ἑυρεθῆ ἔτι.) In Manuscripto, ὡς μυλικὸν μέγαν non ma- le. Sic λίθος μυλικὸς Marc. II, 7. A nomine μύλη adjecti- vum sit, aut μυλικὸς aut μυλινὸς, utrumque est secundum ἀναλογίαν adumbratum ex Jeremia LI, 63. ubi lapide ja- cto in Euphratem significatur sic Babylonem in longo tem- pore non resurrecturam. Est enim similitudo lapidis in ma- re jacti, aut magnum amnem valde ad hoc accommodata. Horatius: Sed juremus in hæc, simul imis saxa renarint Vadis levata, ne redire sit nefas.

Quod desumptum de historia Phocæorum, quæ est apud He- rodotum, nisi quod ibi pro lapide est massa plumbea. Par similitudo Nehem. IX, 11. Roma diu jacuit deserta aut à paucis habitata, nunquam resurrexit ad veterem magnitu- dinem. Nunquam sedes imperii post id fuit. Βληθήσεται השקע Jerem. LI, 64. ὀ μὴ ἑυρεθῇ ἔτι, ut supra IX, 6. XII, 8. XVI, 20. Sic supra 14. Jeremias pro eo dicit לא תקום dicto loco LI, 64.

## 18:22
Verse 22.

And the voice of harpers and musicians and flute players and trumpeters, shall not be heard in you anymore.) Again an apostrophe to the city, such as above 14. Such a transition from the third person to the second and vice versa is frequent among the Prophets. He explains more broadly through its species what Jeremiah is accustomed to say, that the voice of joy and gladness will perish VII, 34. XVI, 9. XXV, 10. Isaiah indeed in the same sense mentions both timbrels and the harp and joyful melodies.

And every craftsman of every craft shall not be found in you anymore.] So many workshops and shops will cease. See Jer. XXII, 1. XXIX, 2. Πάσης τέχνης is missing in the Manuscript.

And the voice of the mill shall not be heard in you anymore.) The noise of so many mills to feed so many thousands of people. From Jeremiah XXV, 10.

But all those things are symbolic. The stone implies hardness, the millstone that which is difficult to move, the strong Angel a swift casting, the sea into which it is cast, a denied emergence. Jeremiah LI, 63. But to which city would all these things be more rightly applied than to Rome? Papists acknowledge this, but they refer it to their Utopian Anti-Christ; but against the will of Scripture, which does not know an Anti-Christ who is to come only at the end of the world and to reign for only three years and a half: But it attributes to him 1260 mystical days, that is, as many years, as shown before. Perpetual desolation, the lack of the joy of the voice of the bridegroom and the bride, without which a city cannot consist, of craftsmen, who are all necessary to a city, of mills, which cities cannot lack, of the light of a lamp, which brings mere darkness, where there are no weddings, there human society must finally cease.

Latin:

Vers. 22.

Καὶ φωνὴ κιθαρῳδῶν καὶ μυσικῶν καὶ ἀυλητῶν καὶ σαλπιστῶν, ὀ μὴ ἀκυσθῇ ἐν σοι ἔτι.) Rursus ἀποστροφὴ ad urbem, qua- lis supra 14. Frequens apud Prophetas talis transitio à ter- tia persona ad secundam & contra. Latius per species suas explicat, quod Jeremias solet dicere perituram vocem gau- dii ac lætitiæ VII, 34. XVI, 9. XXV, 10. Esaias vero in eodem sensu & tympana & citharam & modos lætos me- morat.

Καὶ πᾶς τεχνίτης πάσης τέχνης ὀ μὴ ἑυρεθῇ ἐν σοι ἔτι.] Cessabunt tot officinæ & tabernæ. Vide Jer. XXII, 1. XXIX, 2. Πάσης τέχνης deest in Manuscripto.

Καὶ φωνὴ μύλε ὀ μὴ ἀκυσθῇ ἐν σοι ἔτι.) Strepitus tot molarum ad alenda tot hominum millia. Ex Jerem. XXV, 10.

Omnia autem illa symbolica sunt. Lapis duri- tiem, molaris difficulter mobilem, Angelus for- tis celerem projectionem, mare in quod projici- tur, negatam emersionem infert. Jerem. LI, 63. Cui vero urbi hæc omnia rectius applicarentur, quàm Romæ? Agnoscunt id Papistæ, sed ad suum Anti - Christum Utopicum referunt; sed invita scriptura, quæ non novit Anti-Christum, in fine mundi demum venturum, & per tres annos cum dimidio tantum regnaturum: Sed tribuit ei dies mysticos 1260. hoc est, totidem annos, ut ante ostensum. Perpetuam vastitatem defectus læti- tiæ vocis sponsi & sponsæ, fine qua consistere ne- quit civitas, artificum, qui omnes civitati ne- cessarii sunt, molarum, quibus carere nequeunt urbes, lucis lucernæ, qui meras tenebras infert, ubi nullæ nuptiæ, ibi cessare tandem oportet so- cietatem humanam.

## 18:23
Verse 23.

And the light of a lamp shall not shine in you anymore.) Taken from the same place. Explain from that of Lucretius: If golden statues of youths do not stand through the houses holding fire-bearing lamps in their right hands. And the voice of the bridegroom and of the bride shall be heard no more in thee.] Solemn songs for the bridal chamber. From Jeremiah VII, 34. XVI, 9. XXV, 10. He calls the voice of the bridegroom and bride the songs about the bridegroom and bride. Thus the genitive is often taken objectively. By contrary words, joyful times are signified. Isa. LXII, 5. Jerem. XXXIII, 11.

For thy merchants were the great men of the earth.] He gives three causes for this Divine judgment: extreme luxury, extreme idolatry, and extreme cruelty. He indicates the luxury by the fact that not only Senators and Magistrates, but also peddlers lived there like Princes. Taken from Isa. XXIII, 8, concerning the Tyrians. Concerning the word μεγιστάνων we spoke above at VI, 15. A similar cause for the destruction of the Moabites is in Zephaniah II, 10.

For by thy sorcery were all nations deceived.] The sense is the same as above at XIII, 14. Φαρμακεία here is the same as οἶνος θυμοῦ at XIV, 8. XVIII, 3, because whatever corrupts souls is rightly compared to poison. Thus Isaiah XLVII, 9 speaks of כשפיך to Babylon. And Babylon the corrupter, Jerem. LI, 25.

And in her was found the blood of Prophets and of saints.] That is, she was contaminated with the blood of Christians, among whom some were also conspicuous for Prophetic gifts. The expression is taken from Jeremiah II, 34. The sense is also in Jeremiah LI, 35.

And of all those who were slain upon the earth.] Of others also killed through unjust wars. Slain in the earth, that is, slain and cast down to the earth, Jerem. LI, 49.

Papal Prelates [are] Merchants both in their Principalities and in the sale of indulgences, the purchase of Episcopal palls, etc.

Latin:

Vers. 23.

Καὶ φῶς λύχνε ὀ μὴ φανῇ ἐν σοι ἔτι.) Sumptum indidem Explica ex illo Lucretii: Si non aurea stant juvenum simulachra per ædes Lampadas igniferas manibus retinentia dextris. Καὶ φωνὴ νυμφίου καὶ νύμφης ὐ μὴ ἀκουστῆ͂ ἐν σοὶ ἔτι.] So- lennes cantus ad thalamum. Ex Jeremia VII, 34. XVI, 9. XXV, 10. Vocem sponsi & sponsæ vocat carmina de sponso & sponsa. Sic Genitivus sæpe sumitur objective. Contra- riis verbis læta significantur tempora. Esa. LXII, 5. Jerem. XXXIII, 11.

Ὅτι οἱ ἔμποροί σου ἦσαν οἱ μεγιστᾶνες τῆς γῆς.] Causas hu- jus judicii Divini reddit tres, luxum summum, idololatri- am summam, summamque sævitiam. Luxum eo indicat, quod non Senatores tantum & Magistratus, sed & instito- res velut Principes ibi viverent. Sumptum ex Esa. XXIII, 8. de Tyriis. De voce μεγιστάνων diximus supra VI, 15. Par cau- sa excidii Moabitarum est apud Sophoniam II, 10.

Ὅτι ἐν τῆ͂ φαρμακείᾳ σου ἐπλανήθησαν πάντα τὰ ἔθνη.] Sen- sus idem, qui supra XIII, 14. Φαρμακεία hic idem est, quod οἶνος θυμοῦ XIV, 8. XVIII, 3. quia veneno recte comparatur, quicquid corrumpit animos. Sic כשפיך ad Babylonem di- cit Esaias XLVII, 9. Et Babylon corruptrix Jerem. LI, 25.

Καὶ ἐν αὐτῆ͂ αἵματα Προφητῶν καὶ ἁγίων εὑρέθη.] Id est, contaminata fuit sanguine Christianorum, inter quos non- nulli erant etiam Propheticis donis conspicui. Locutio sum- pta de Jeremia II, 34. Sensus etiam apud Jeremiam LI, 35.

Καὶ πάντων τῶν ἐσφαγμένων ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς.] Aliorum eti- am occisorum per bella injusta. Occisi in terra, id est, occisi & in terram dejecti, Jerem. LI, 49.

Praelati Papales Mercatores tum in Principati- bus suis, tum in venditione indulgentiarum, em- ptione palliorum Episcopalium &c.

## 19:1 Argument
CHAPTER XIX. ARGUMENT AND DIVISION.

A doxology on account of the judgment with the applause of the animals and elders, an exhortation to the celebration of GOD, and exultation on account of the marriage of the lamb, whose Bride's adornment, and the bridegroom's (the Lamb's) face, clothing, and names are described, with an added invitation to the birds to devour the flesh of the beast and its accomplices.

There are three parts: I. The celebration of GOD on account of the judgment, to v. 10. II. The description of the Bride and Bridegroom, to v. 16. III. The invitation of the birds to the feast, to v. 21.

PART I. THE CELEBRATION OF GOD ON ACCOUNT OF THE JUDGMENT.

Vers. 1. And after these things.] At another time. He had shown the vision of chapter XVII, both the woman and the beast. He explained what was to happen to the woman, that is, to the city and the Roman Dominion, how that city, having been weakened by certain degrees, was finally to fall. Now he shows the same thing concerning the beast, that is, concerning idolatry. Wherefore it is no wonder if he recurs here to the times that preceded the ruin of the city. For the series of events demanded that first all things pertaining to the city should be told: then those pertaining to Idolatry. Thus Polybius, thus Tacitus often neglect the order of times, in order to weave together those things which cohere with the events.

I heard as it were the great voice of a great multitude in heaven.] It signifies the huge increases of the Christian people over three hundred years. The Church is said to be in heaven because it cares for and thinks of heavenly things. Above IV, 4. XIII, 6.

Λεγόντων Ἀλληλούϊα.] As if he were saying, singing in honor of GOD similar to those twenty Psalms, in which there is the joyful exclamation הללו יה. We have that word four times in this chapter: and Tob. XIII, 20 in the Greek. The destruction of the wicked is the most just cause of τοῦ ἀλληλούϊα Ps. CIV, 35, where Kimchi noted it: in which there is ἀλληλούϊα, it is called by excellence שיר or שירה. And Christians were accustomed to use such things between Easter and Pentecost.

ἡ σωτηρία.] Praise for salvation received, as above VII, 10, XII, 10.

Καὶ ἡ δύναμις καὶ ἡ δόξα τῶ͂ Θεῶ͂ ἡμῶν.] They are His, they belong to Him. Above IV, 11, VII, 12.

Ὅτι ἀληθιναὶ κ̀ͅ δίκαιαι αἱ κρίσεις αὐτοῦ.] Above XV, 3, XVI, 7.

Ὅτι ἔκρινε τὴν πόρνην την μεγάλην, ἥτις διέφθειρε τὴν γῆν ἐν τῇ πορνείᾳ αὐτῆς.] It is not a question here of all of God's judgments against the woman, but of those first five of the vials. And the word διέφθειρε is excellently placed here, which he uses when dealing with Babylon in Jerem. LI, 25. He explains more clearly that which had been said figuratively about the poisoned cup.

Καὶ ἐξεδίκησε τὸ αἷμα τῶν δούλων αὐτοῦ ἐκ τῆς χειρὸς αὐτῆς.]

Namely, of those who were killed under Nero, Domitian, Trajan, and thereafter. But under those first three persecutions, similar others are to be understood, as we have said. The words are taken from Deut. XXXII, 43.

Latin:

CAPUT XIX. ARGUMENTUM ET PAR- TITIO.

Doxologia ob judicium cum applausu anima- lium & seniorum, adhortatio ad cele- brationem DEI, ac exultatio ob nuptias agni, cujus Sponsæ ornatus, & sponsi (Agni) facies, vestitus, nomina, describuntur, addita invitatio- ne avium, ad devorandum carnes feræ, & com- plicum.

Partes sunt tres: I. DEI ob judicium celebratio, ad v. 10. II. Sponsæ & Sponsi descriptio, ad v. 16. III. Avium ad convivium invitatio, ad v. 21.

PARS I. DEI OB JUDICIUM CELEBRATIO.

Vers. 1. Καὶ μετὰ ταῦτα.] Alio tempore. Visum capitis XVII. & mulierem ostenderat, & feram. Explicavit quid mu- lieri, id est, urbi, Dominationique Romanæ eventurum esset, quomodo ea urbs per gradus quosdam labefactata, tandem ruitura esset. Nunc idem de fera, id est, de idololatria osten- dit. Quare non mirum est, si hic recurritur ad tempora, quæ ruinam urbis præcessere. Exigebat enim rerum series, ut primum omnia, quæ ad urbem pertinent, dicerentur: deinde ea quæ ad Idololatriam. Sic Polybius, sic Tacitus sæpe tem- porum ordinem negligunt, ut contexant ea, quæ rebus co- hærent.

Ἤκουσα ὡς φωνὴν ὄχλου πολλοῦ μεγάλην ἐν τῶ͂ οὐρανῶ͂.] Si- gnificat ingentia incrementa Christianæ plebis per annos tre- centos. Ecclesia in cœlo esse dicitur, quia cœlestia curat ac cogitat. Supra IV, 4. XIII, 6.

Λεγόντων Ἀλληλούϊα.] Quasi dicat canentes in honorem DEI similia viginti illis Psalmis, in quibus est læta exclama- tio הללו יה. Habemus eam vocem quater hoc capite: & Tob. XIII, 20. in Græco. Perditio impiorum causa justissi- ma τοῦ ἀλληλούϊα Ps. CIV, 35. ubi id notavit Kimchi: in quo est ἀλληλούϊα, per excellentiam dicitur שיר vel שירה. Et talibus uti solebant Christiani inter Pascha, & Pentecosten.

ἡ σωτηρία.] Laus ob acceptam salutem, ut supra VII, 10. XII, 10.

Καὶ ἡ δύναμις καὶ ἡ δόξα τῶ͂ Θεῶ͂ ἡμῶν.] Ejus sunt, ad eum pertinent. Supra IV, 11. VII, 12.

Ὅτι ἀληθιναὶ κ̀ͅ δίκαιαι αἱ κρίσεις αὐτοῦ.] Supra XV, 3. XVI, 7.

Ὅτι ἔκρινε τὴν πόρνην την μεγάλην, ἥτις διέφθειρε τὴν γῆν ἐν τῇ πορνείᾳ αὐτῆς.] Agitur hic non de omnibus Dei judiciis in mulierem, sed de primis illis quinque phialarum. Et egre- giè ponitur hic vox διέφθειρε, qua de Babylone agens utitur Jerem. LI, 25. Clarius id explicat, quod figuratè dictum erat de poculo venenato.

Καὶ ἐξεδίκησε τὸ αἷμα τῶν δούλων αὐτοῦ ἐκ τῆς χειρὸς αὐτῆς.]

Nempe illorum, qui interfecti sunt sub Nerone, Domitiano, Trajano ac deinceps. Sed sub primis illis tribus persecutio- nibus intelligendæ similes cæteræ, ut diximus. Sumta ver- ba de Deut. XXXII, 43.

## 19:3
Vers. 3. Καὶ δεύτερον εἴρηκαν ἀλληλούϊα.) Namely, because of the ruin of the city anticipated in their minds from the prophecies.

Καὶ ὁ καπνὸς αὐτῆς ἀναβαίνει εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας.) Present for future in the prophetic manner. Therefore the Latin correctly translates it 'will ascend'. Christians believed that Rome would fall, and that that time was not far off, as appears from Tertullian, Lactantius, and others; εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας among the Prophets, and especially where it deals with the destruction of cities, often signifies a long time. See Is. XXXIV, 4.

Latin:

Vers. 3. Καὶ δεύτερον εἴρηκαν ἀλληλούϊα.) Nempe ob anti- cipatam animo ex vaticiniis ruinam urbis.

Καὶ ὁ καπνὸς αὐτῆς ἀναβαίνει εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας.) Præsens pro futuro more prophetico. Ideo Latinus rectè vertit ascendet. Casuram Romam, neque longè id tempus abesse credebant Christiani, ut ex Tertulliano, Lanctatio & aliis apparet, εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας apud Prophetas, & maximè ubi de excidiis urbium agitur, sæpè significat diu. Vide Es. XXXIV, 4.

## 19:4
Vers. 4. Καὶ ἐπέπεσον οἱ πρεσβύτεροι οἱ εἰκοσιτέσσαρες.) The elders of that Church which was in Aelia or Jerusalem after Hadrian.

Καὶ τὰ τέσσαρα ζῶα.) The spirits of the four men who first had ruled the Jerusalem Church by Apostolic authority.

Καὶ προσεκύνησαν τῷ Θεῷ καθημένῳ ἐπὶ τῷ θρόνῳ.) Thus above IV, 10, V, 14.

Saying: Amen. Alleluia.) Amen, that is, certainly it comes to pass, what the Prophets foretold to us. You have Amen & Alleluia together in Psalm CVI, 48.

Latin:

Vers. 4. Καὶ ἐπέπεσον οἱ πρεσβύτεροι οἱ εἰκοσιτέσσαρες.) Presbyteri ejus Ecclesiæ quæ erat Æliæ sive Hierosolymis post Adrianum.

Καὶ τὰ τέσσαρα ζῶα.) Spiritus quatuor-virûm, qui primi auctoritate Apostolica Ecclesiam Hierosolymitanam rexe- rant.

Καὶ προσεκύνησαν τῷ Θεῷ καθημένῳ ἐπὶ τῷ θρόνῳ.) Sic supra IV, 10. V, 14.

Λέγοντες· Ἀμήν. Ἀλληλούϊα.) Amen, id est certo id eve- niet, quod Prophetæ nobis prædixere. Amen & Alleluja si- mul habes Psalm. CVI, 48.

## 19:5
Verse 5. And a voice came out of the throne.) The voice of Christ to Constantine, through which he was converted. The narrative is in Eusebius.

Praise our God, all ye his servants, and ye that fear him, both small and great.) Aptly to the matter. I wish, says Christ, that not only the common people, but also the highest men, such as Constantine and those who were with him, should worship God, and that according to my prescription. Part of the words is from Ps. CXXXIV, 1. and CXXXV, 1. The other part from Ps. CXV, 13.

Latin:

Vers. 5. Καὶ φωνὴ ἐκ τοῦ θρόνου ἐξῆλθε.) Vox Christi ad Constantinum, per quam conversus est. Narratio est apud Eusebium.

Αἰνεῖτε τὸν Θεὸν ἡμῶν πάντες οἱ δοῦλοι αὐτοῦ, καὶ οἱ φοβούμενοι αὐτὸν, οἱ μικροὶ, καὶ οἱ μεγάλοι.) Apposite ad rem. Volo, ait Christus, ut non plebs tantum, sed & viri summi, quales Constantinus, & qui ei aderant, Deum colant, idque ex meo præscripto. Pars verborum est ex Ps. CXXXIV, 1. & CXXXV, 1. Pars altera ex Ps. CXV, 13.

## 19:6
Verse 6. And I heard as it were the voice of a great multitude, and as the voice of many waters, and as the voice of mighty thunderings, saying Alleluia. Not of the common people only as above 1. but also of many peoples (above XVII, 15. Ezech. XLIII, 1.) and of men speaking effectively, such as are called sons of thunder in Mark III, 17. The conversion of Constantine immensely increased the number of Christians, so that in a short time whole provinces, and most learned and eloquent men, professed the Christian religion. The words are almost taken from Ezech. I, 24.

For the Lord God omnipotent reigneth.) That is, he began to reign over the Kings themselves. He rightly adds omnipotent, as above l. 8. IV, 8. XI, 17. XV, 3. XVI, 4. 14. Below XXI, 22. For it is a huge sign of omnipotence to subdue the heads of that Empire, so long accustomed to idolatry, and fostering idolatry. God has reigned always in the Psalms signifies something great, as XLVII, 9. XCIII, 1, XCVI, 10. XCVII, 1. XCIX, 1.

Let us be glad and rejoice, and give glory to God.) Great joy is signified. Thus rejoice and be exceeding glad Matt. V, 12. to rejoice with joy 1 Pet. I, 8. rejoice with joy 1 Pet. IV, 13. joy and gladness Luke I, 14. to rejoice גיל is to show joy in every way, as Is. XXV, 9. Give glory to God, as Luke XVII, 18. is to give thanks to God for benefits.

Latin:

Vers. 6. Καὶ ἤκουσα ὡς φωνὴν ὄχλου πολλοῦ, καὶ ὡς φωνὴν ὑδά- των πολλῶν, καὶ ὡς φωνὴν βροντῶν ἰσχυρῶν, λεγόντων Ἀλληλού- ϊα. Non plebis tantum ut supra 1. sed & multorum popu- lorum (supra XVII, 15. Ezech. XLIII, 1.) & virorum effica- citer loquentium, quales dicuntur υἱοὶ βροντῆς Marci III, 17. Conversio Constantini immensum auxit Christianorum nu- merum, ita, ut brevi provinciæ totæ, & viri doctissimi, & eloquentissimi Christianam religionem profiterentur. Verba fermè sumpta sunt ex Ezech. I, 24.

Ὅτι ἐβασίλευσε κύριος ὁ Θεὸς ἡμῶν ὁ παντοκράτωρ.) Id est, regnare incepit in ipsos Reges. Rectè addit παντοκρά- τωρ, ut supra l. 8. IV, 8. XI, 17. XV, 3. XVI, 4. 14. Infra XXI, 22. Ingens enim omnipotentiæ fignum subigere capita Im- perii illius, tanto tempore affueti idololatriæ, & idolola- triam foventes. Deus regnavit semper in Psalmis magnum ali- quid significat, ut XLVII, 9. XCIII, 1, XCVI, 10. XCVII, 1. XCIX, 1.

Χαίρωμεν καὶ ἀγαλλιώμεθα, καὶ δῶμεν τὴν δόξαν τῷ Θεῷ.) Significatur magnum gaudium. Sic χαίρετε καὶ ἀγαλλιᾶσθε Matth. V, 12. ἀγαλλιᾶσθαι χαρᾷ. 1. Petr. I, 8. χαρῆτε ἀγαλλι- ώμενοι. 1. Petr. IV, 13. χαρὰ καὶ ἀγαλλίασις. Luc. I, 14. ἀγαλ- λιᾶσθαι גיל est omni modo gaudium oftendere, ut Es. XXV, 9. Date gloriam Deo, ut Luc. XVII, 18. est Deo gratias age- re pro beneficiis.

## 19:7
Verse 7. For the marriage of the Lamb is come, and his wife hath made herself ready.) Every Church of Christ is a bride Matt. XXII, 2. and following, 2 Cor. XI, 2. Eph. V, 32. which places flow from the Old Prophecy, Hosea II, 19. Isa. LIV, 6. 7. 8. But here is specially understood the Church gathered from the house and retinue of Constantine the Great. Under one, however, other similar things are to be understood, i.e., the conversions of other kings as well.

That the order of times is neglected by St. John is asserted without cause. Which stain is not to be rashly affixed to the Holy Spirit in such ordered and definitely restricted divine visions. God is the author of order, not of confusion. 1 Cor. XIV, 33.

That great voice of the triumphant heavenly Elect because of salvation exhibited by the Lord in the final liberation to the faithful, whom they congratulate and with whom they sing in unison. They celebrate the judgments of God as true because of the fulfillment of promises, and just because of the execution of the deserved judgment both through the corruption of the …earth in whoredom, and through the shedding of innocent blood; Alleluia is also repeated because of the eternity of the fire by which the Anti-Christ is tormented: And it is confirmed by the Amen of the living creatures and the elders, because of the testimony of the consensus and συμφωνίας of the militant and triumphant Church. For the living creatures together with the Elders represent the Church offering sacrifice. The voice from the Throne of God is received by the servants of God from the Angels surrounding the Throne of God, so that they may praise God, as a people copious like many waters and sonorous like thunders; the word is made deed, Hallelujah, it is sung to the honor of the divine empire and omnipotence. Smoke properly befits a city, or the smoke of the torments of the harlot is to be understood with Osiander. The bride is described 1. by the bridegroom, who is the Lamb. The related terms explain each other. 2. By her state. She is called a woman, because she is about to celebrate the nuptials, to be joined eternally to the bridegroom. It is therefore an amplification of state when she is called a bride. 3. By her clothing, form, and splendid and pure habit: because she washed her robe in the blood of the Lamb, Apoc. VII, 14. 4. By the material of the clothing; fine linen. For the Lamb made us Kings, Apoc. I, 10. And that royal adornment is explained as being the righteousness of the King and Priest himself, Is. LXI, 10. 5. From the blessedness on account of the calling to the nuptials joined with a partition, v. 9. 6. From the Angelic condition. For Angels are fellow-servants of the elect even in the heavens, serving God day and night; they themselves are like the Angels, equal to the angels. Marriage is the time of the nuptials in this place, in which the spiritual bride of Christ, the Church, in the joy of the heavenly Bridegroom, will be admitted to the communion of honors, goods, and delights, or it denotes the nuptials themselves; the bride prepared herself, but she was first betrothed to Christ through faith, 2 Cor. XI, 2, and having received the earnest of the Holy Spirit from him, 2 Cor. I, by whose power she puts on the garments of holiness and righteousness, Coloss. III, so that she may appear more adorned, and that she may not be deprived of the priestly garments given to her by her own fault. For where the Papacy falls, there men are betrothed to Christ through faith by the sincere preaching of the Gospel. And they prepare themselves for the coming of their Bridegroom Christ, by a pious and holy conversation according to the admonition of Peter, 2 Epist. III, 15, as here B. Osiander. The betrothal of the mystical bride, the Church, requires the consent of the contracting parties, 2 Cor. XI, 2, and the reciprocal donation of an earnest, 2 Cor. I, 22. But the nuptials require 1. a sumptuous preparation, Matt. XXII, 4. 2. The invitation of guests, I, 3. 3. The solemn copulation of the bridegroom and bride, Hos. II, 19, 20. 4. A splendid treatment regarding food and drink, Prov. IX, 2, sqq. Is. LV, 1, sqq. Matt. XXII, 4. 5. Cant. V, 2. 5. The recreation of the guests, Psalm XXXVI, 9. Ps. XXIII, 5. 6. The adornment of nuptial garments, Ps. XLV, 10. Is. LXI, 10. Matt. XXII, 12. Apoc. XIX, 7, 8. But why would the Church gathered in the house of Constantine the Great be specifically designated here? It is a general vision. The bride are the just and the holy ones of the whole world, to whom the righteous acts of the bridegroom have been given. All who have come out of tribulations are clothed in pure fine linen. But do not the just come into tribulations? No one is excepted here, as the Apostle testifies, 2 Tim. III, 12. Acts XIV, 12. Cf. Ap. VII, 13, 14. Moreover, Christ is our adornment not only as a gift and merit, but also as an example, Rom. VIII, 32. Matt. XI, 29, which Corn. Jansenius, Joh. Maldonatus, and Sebast. Barradius, along with Alphonso Salmerone who acknowledge the truth, rashly oppose to themselves, as does Jacobus Faber Stapul. in Matt. XXII. The nuptial garment is the faith of Christ, and it is pure by the regeneration of faith, as also Joh. Ferus in Matt. I, 5. The nuptial garment is Christ: He is put on in two ways: Internally through faith, when with your sins you put on the righteousness of Christ, with your demerits his merits, with your disobedience his obedience: then when externally you emulate his charity. See also Blasius de Viegas in Apoc. p. 243.

Latin:

Vers. 7. Ὅτι ἦλθεν ὁ γάμος τοῦ ἀρνίου, καὶ ἡ γυνὴ αὐτοῦ ἡτοί- μασεν ἑαυτήν.) Omnis Ecclesia Christi sponsa Matth. XXII, 2. & sequentibus, 2. Corinth. XI, 2. Ephes. V, 32. quæ loca ma- nant ex Vetere Prophetia, Oseæ II, 19. Esa. LIV, 6. 7. 8. Sed hic specialiter intelligitur Ecclesia collecta ex domo & comi- tatu Constantini Magni. Sub uno autem intelligenda similia alia, i. e. aliorum quoque regum conversiones.

Ordinem temporum à S. Johanne negligi citrà causam asseritur. Quæ macula Spiritui S. temerè non est affricanda in tàm ordinatis & ad tempora definitè adstrictis divinis visionibus. Deus ordinis autor est, non confusionis. 1. Cor. XIV, 33.

Vox illa magna cœlitum Electorum triumphan- tium ob salutem in finali liberatione fidelibus, quibus congratulantur & concinunt, à Domino exhibitam. Celebrant autem judicia Dei ceu ve- ra ob promissionum impletionem, & justa ob judi- cii promeriti executionem tùm per terræ in scor- tatione corruptionem, tùm per sanguinis inno- cui effusionem; iteratur etiam Allelujah ob ignis, quo cruciatur Anti - Christus, perennitatem: Et confirmatur per Amen animantium & senio- rum, ob consensus & συμφωνίας Ecclesiæ mili- tantis & triumphantis testificationem. Animalia enim cum Senioribus repræsentant Ecclesiam mi- litantem. Vox e Throno Dei ab Angelis Thronum Dei stipantibus ad servos Dei, ut laudent Deum a populo instar multarum aquarum copioso & in- star tonitruum sonoro accipitur, dictum factum, Allelujah, cantatur honori imperii & omnipoten- tiae divinae. Καπνoς proprie civitati convenit, vel intelligendus fumus de tormentis meretricis cum Osi- andro. Describitur sponsa 1. a sponso, qui est Agnus. Relata se mutuo explicant. 2. A statu. Mulier dici- tur, quia jamjam nuptias celebratura aeternum so- cianda sponso. Ampliationis status ergo est, cum sponsa dicitur. 3. A vestitu, forma & habitu splen- dido ac puro: quia lavit stolam sanguine Agni Apo- cal. VII, 1.6. 4. A materia vestitus; byssino. Fecit enim Agnus nos Reges Apoc. I, 10. Et explicatur or- natus ille Regius, quod sit justitia Regis, & Sacerdo- tis ipsius propria, Es. LXI, 10. 5. A beatitudine ob vo- cationem ad nuptias cum partitione conjunctam, v. 9. 6. A conditione Angelica. Angeli enim συνδουλοι sunt electorum etiam in coelis, Deo serviendo di- es ac noctes; ipsi Angelis similes sunt ισαγγελοι. Γαμος tempus nuptiarum hoc loco, quo spiritua- lis Christi sponsa Ecclesia in gaudio coelestis Spon- si, ad communionem honorum, bonorum, delicia- rum admittetur, vel nuptias ipsas notat, seipsum praeparavit sponsa, sed Christo per fidem prius de- sponsata, 2. Corinth. XI, 2. arrhaque Spiritus San- cti ab ipso accepta 2. Cor. I. cujus virtute induit vestes sanctitatis & justitiae Coloss. III. ut ornatior compareat, neve vestibus Sacerdotalibus sibi do- natis propria culpa privetur. Ubi enim corruit Pa- patus, ibi homines per sinceram Evangelii praedicatio- nem Christo per fidem desponsantur. Et illi ad Christi Sponsi sui adventum sese praeparant, pia & sancta con- versatione juxta admonitionem Petri, 2. Epist. III, 15. ut hic B. Osiander. Sponsalia mysticae sponsae Ec- clesiae requirunt consensum partium contrahentium 2. Cor. XI, 2. & arrhae donationem reciprocam, 2. Cor. I, 22. Nuptiae vero 1. lautam praeparationem Matth. XXII, 4. 2. Convivarum invitationem I, 3. 3. Sponsi & sponsae solennem copulationem, Hos. II, 19. 20. 4 Splendidam, quoad cibum & potum, tractatio- nem, Prov. IX, 2. sqq. Es. LV, 1. sqq. Matth. XXII, 4. 5. Cant. V, 2. 5. Convivarum recreationem Psalm. XXXVI, 9. Ps. XXIII, 5. 6. Vestimentorum nuptia- lium exornationem Ps. XLV, 10. Es. LXI, 10. Matth. XXII, 12. Apoc. XIX, 7. 8. Cur vero specialiter Ecclesia in domo Constanti- ni M. collecta hic designaretur? Visio generalis est. Sponsa sunt justi & sancti universi, quibus data τα δικαιωματα sponsi. Vestiti sunt omnes qui e tri- bulationibus venerunt byssino puro. At qui justi non veniunt in tribulationes? Nemo hic excipitur, teste Apostolo, 2. Tim. III, 12. Act, XIV, 12. Conf. Ap. VII, 13. 14. Est autem Christus ornatus noster non ut donum tantum & meritum, sed etiam ut ex- emplum, Rom. IIX, 32. Matth. XI, 29. quae temere si- bi opponunt Corn. Jansenius Joh. Maldonatus, Se- bast. Barradius cum Alphonso Salmerone veritatem agnoscentibus, Jacobo Fabro Stapul. in Matth. XXII. Vestis nuptialis fides Christi est, & pura est fidei rege- neratione innocentia, ut & Joh. Fero in Matth. I, 5. Vestis nuptialis est Christus: Ea dupliciter induitur: Interne per fidem cum tuis peccatis superinduis Chri- sti justitiam, tuis demeritis ipsius merita, tua inobe- dientiae ipsius obedientiam: deinde cum externe ejus charitatem amularis. Videatur etiam Blasius de Viegas in Apoc. p. 243.

## 19:8
Vers. 8.

And it was given to her that she should be clothed in fine linen, bright and pure.) Before this, Christians were in a common cloak, now also in a courtly habit. For in the retinue of kings who live, they are accustomed to be dressed splendidly, Matt. XI, 8. Among splendid garments, the first are fine linens, above XVIII, 16. Gen. XLI, 22. 1 Paral. XV, 27. Esther VI, 8. VIII, 15. Prov. XXXI, 22. Ezek. XVI, 11, 13. The passage of Isaiah LII, 1 is referred to. Fine linen is in Hebrew בוץ. You see here a grave attire like a matron's, not pompous, such as was described before of the harlot.

For the fine linen is the righteous acts of the saints.] They are worthy to be so clothed. For their actions correspond to their attire. For they are both splendid and pure like fine linen. There were among the nobles of the court of Constantine men of great virtues. See Eusebius. The precepts of God are called righteous acts, Luke I, 6. Here, however, by metonymy, they are the acts of God conforming to the precepts.

Whence is that adornment explained? From the bridegroom. Is. LXI, 10. Hos. II, 19. Galat. III, 27. Ephes. V, 26. Apoc. III, 18. The righteous acts are righteousness both imputed, Rom. IV, 6, and inherent and therefore proper, Ephes. IV, 24, which is here begun, there consummated, chap. V, 27. Imputation will not cease there, as it is an internal and eternal act of God: therefore neither will imputed righteousness. For those things which are in God are eternal and immutable, as God himself is: even if faith, the medium of acceptance, were perhaps to cease. Once apprehended through faith, it will be ours eternally, by divine reckoning. The sun of righteousness will irradiate us with its eternal light and splendor, Apoc. XXII, 5. But I shall appear in righteousness (I shall see your face), I shall be satisfied when I have been awakened, with your image, as the Osiandrine paraphrase has it on Psalm XVII, last verse.

PART II. DESCRIPTION OF THE BRIDE AND BRIDEGROOM.

Latin:

Vers. 8.

Και εδοθη αυτη ινα περιβαληται βυσσινον λαμπρον και κα- θαρον.) Antehac Christiani erant in palliolo plebejo, nunc etiam in aulico habitu. Nam in comitatu Regum qui vi- vunt, solent splendidi vestiri, Matth. XI, 8. Inter splen- didos vestitus prima sunt byssina supra XVIII, 16. Genes. XLI, 22. 1. Paral. XV, 27. Esther. VI, 8. VIII, 15. Proverb. XXXI, 22. Ezech. XVI, 11. 13. Respicitur locus Esaiæ LII, 1. Byssus Ebræis בוץ. Vides hic cultum gravem ut matronæ, non pompaticum, qualis meretricis ante descriptus.

Τὸ γὰρ βύσσινον, τὰ δικαιώματα τῶν ἁγίων ἐσὶ.] Digni sunt, qui sic vestiantur. Actiones enim eorum vestitui respon- dent. Sunt enim & splendidæ & puræ ut byssina. Erant inter proceres aulæ Constantini viri magnarum virtutum. Vide Eusebium. Δικαιώματα vocantur Dei præcepta, Luc. I, 6. Hic vero per Metonymiam actus Dei præceptis con- gruentes.

Unde ille ornatus, explicatur? A sponso. Es. LXI, 10. Os. II, 19. Galat. III, 27. Ephes. V, 26. Apoc. III, 18. Τὰ δικαιώματα justitia cum imputata, Rom. IV, 6. tum inhærens adeoque propria, Ephes. IV, 24. quæ hic inchoata, ibi consummata, cap. V, 27. Non desinet illic imputatio, actus Dei internus & æternus: Ideo nec imputata justitia. Quæ enim in Deo sunt, æterna sunt & immutabi- lia, ut ipse Deus: Etsi desitura forte fides, me- dium acceptationis. Semel apprehensa per fi- dem imputata nobis æternum, nostra erit, λογι- σμῷ divino. Irradiabit nos sol justitiæ luce ac splendore suo æterno, Apocal. XXII, 5. Ego au- tem in justitia apparebo (videbo faciem tu- am) satiabor, cum excitatus fuero, imagine tua, ut habet paraphrasis Osiandrina ad Psalm. XVII, v. ult.

PARS II. SPONSÆ ET SPONSI DE- SCRIPTIO.

## 19:9
Vers. 9.

And he says to me, write.] It is a great matter, and to be committed to memory for posterity. Thus above I, 11, 16. XIV, 13, he says, namely the Angel. For that name is understood from the passage above I, 1, and many others.

Blessed.] Happy above the rest are they, above I, 3. XIV, 13. Dan. XII, 12.

Those called to the marriage supper of the Lamb.] Who will be spectators of that most wonderful change. Weddings were celebrated with a feast, Gen. XXIX, 17. Judg. XIV, 10. Esther II, 18.

The faithful, as many as in the persecution of the Anti-Christ kept their faith to Christ, marked by the name of the bride, are proclaimed and written blessed, having been called formerly to the nuptial feast by the invitation of the ministry made more than once, Luke XIV, 15, 16, but now to be gathered by the trumpet of the Archangel for the sake of the same.

And he says to me.] The Angel, who is understood as above.

These are the true words of God.] It will altogether come to pass that Emperors, Dukes, and Counts will become Christians. Such is the affirmation also below XII, 6.

Latin:

Vers. 9.

Καὶ λέγει μοι γράψον.] Res magna est, & memoriæ ad posteros mandanda. Sic supra I, 11. 16. XIV, 13. dicit, nempe Angelus. Id enim nomen intelligitur ex loco supra I, 1. & multis aliis.

Μακάριοι.] Supra cæteros felices illi supra I, 3. XIV, 13. Dan. XII, 12.

Οἱ εἰς τὸ δεῖπνον τῦ γάμου τῦ ἀρνίου κεκλημένοι.] Qui spectatores erunt illius tam admirandæ mutationis. Nuptiæ cum convivio celebrabantur, Genes. XXIX, 17. Judic. XIV, 10. Esther. II, 18.

Fideles, quotquot in persecutione Anti-Chri- sti fidem Christo servarunt, sponsæ nomine in- signiti, beati prædicantur & scribuntur, vocati olim ad convivium nuptiale invitatione ministri- rii plus vice simplici facta, Luc. XIV, 15. 16. nunc autem buccina Arch-Angeli congregandi ejus- dem gratia.

Καὶ λέγει μοι.] Angelus, qui subintellectus & supra.

Οὗτοι οἱ λόγοι ἀληθινοί εἰσι τῦ Θεῦ.] Omnino futurum, ut Imperatores, Duces & Comites Christiani fiant. Talia affirmatio & infra XII, 6.

## 19:10
Vers. 10.

And I fell before his feet.] Namely, treating the messenger of such a great matter with the highest honor, just as also below XXII, 8. To approach the feet was an honor which was shown to Kings and the highest men in the parts of the Orient. 'They fall on their knees before the king, revering the law of their home,' say the Phoenician women to the son of the King in Euripides. Livy, speaking of the Carthaginian envoys, adds that they prostrated themselves in the manner of those adoring, having received the rite, I believe, from that region whence they were sprung, that is, from Phoenicia. The writer of the life of Conon: To venerate the King, which they themselves call προσκυνεῖν. We have brought forward more on this rite in our larger commentary on the Decalogue. The saints of ancient times were accustomed in a similar way to adore Angels sent concerning great matters, as Satraps of the heavenly kingdom. You have examples in Gen. XVII, 17. Judg. XIII, 20.

And he says to me, see that you do not.] So also below XXII, 8. Beware of doing it; ὁρᾶν means to beware, 1 Thess. V, 15, and elsewhere.

I am your fellow-servant and of your brethren, who have the testimony of Jesus.] That honor is accustomed to be shown to much greater ones. We are equals among ourselves, envoys of the same King. By brethren having or keeping the testimony here, understand the Apostles and others endowed with Apostolic gifts. That is manifest from a similar passage below XXII, 8. Philo calls Abraham the fellow-servant of the Angels in his book on Abraham.

Worship God.) He does not say that worship is lawfully exhibited to God alone, for the whole of ancient history contradicts this, and those things which we have said at Matt. VIII, 2. But he acts kindly, as if a colleague were to say to a colleague: Keep this honor for the King.
