Universa scili- cet civitas Christi ab universa civitate Diaboli, quantacunq; utraque erit super terram Gog. Si ba videtur Chami abnepos, primus in Arabia felici Princeps, quia Mahometh inde oriundus erat, aliis a tecto ita dictus: quod Scythæ ἁμαξόβιοι sint, Tur- cis autem Septentrionalibus Tartaros adhærere no- tum est. Turcæ Arabiam totam & magnam Africæ partem, quæ sub nomine Æthiopiæ, & Lybiæ indi- gitatur, ad se transtulerunt. Excipiuntur autem po- puli quidam, quos Turcæ subjugare nequiverunt v. 41. Hæ autem solæ salvabuntur de manu ejus, Edom, & Moab, & primitiæ filiorum Ammon. Per Edom intelliguntur Latini, in occidentali Imperii veteris Romani parte; Per Moabitas Moscovitæ. Per primitias filiorum Ammon Abyssini. Hi liberi in hunc usq; diem a tyrannide Turcica manserunt:

Quo de Dan. 11, 42. 43. Terra Ægypti non effugiet, & dominabitur thesauris auri & argenti, & in omnibus pretiosis Ægypti, per Lybiam & Æthiopiam transibit. Quod refert B. Gravius ad annum 1516. quo Selimus Turcarum Imperator vicit Campso- nem Gaurium Ægypti Sultanum, eumq; in prælio occidit, totaq; Syria & Ægypto occupatis, successo- rem Campsonis Tornumbejum ultimum ex Mam- luchis Sultanum omnibus tormentis ac contume- liis vexatum ante Regiam suspendit. Anno 1453. Mahumethes II. Constantinopolin occupavit edi- ta infinita Christianorum strage. Ab eo tempore Occidentales Christiani orbis provincias terra marique Turcæ miserrime afflixerunt. Quamvis enim Papa & Principes Pontificii feliciter inter- dum cum Turcis pugnarunt, sæpius tamen non si- ne insigni clade & regionum jactura repulsi fue- runt. Anno 1522. Solymannus ingenti classe Rho- dum oppugnavit & occupavit. Non multo post Ungariam infestavit, & Sirmiensem Episcopatum occupavit. Ann. 1526. vicit Ludovicum Regem ingenti prælio, in quo Ludovicus interiit. Ann. 1529. ingenti exercitu Viennam Austriæ frustra obsedit. Ann. 1570. Selymus Cyprum horrendo bello fati- gavit, & imperio Turcico subjecit. Quomodo in Ungaria Neuhåusel, quomodo alias civitates in suam potestatem redegerit in recenti omnium est memoria. Terram præstantem indigitat Propheta imperium Orientale, quod cum suis sibi subjectis regionibus propter Majestatem & potentiam cum- primis innumeras Ecclesias ab ipsis Apostolis eo- rumque discipulis fundatas toto orbe fuit cele- berrimum.

Nonnulli audent tempus prælii definire, sed hæc est mera temeritas. Sunt qui annum 1621. quo Polo- niæ Rex Sigismundus III. & Princeps Wladislaus insignem Dei munere de Turcis reportarunt vi- ctoriam, determinant, quia millesimus ille ab anno 620. est, a quo Turcæ Mahom. suæque sectæ annos numerant, & Hegiram suam ordiuntur. Aliis placet annus 1630, quia Christiani ab anno 630. ini- tium regni & sectæ Mach. deducunt, quo mortuus est Mahometh, ut, Theophanes, Cedrenus, Baronius, Bzovius, Spondanus, alii.

De loco etiam stragis Gogicæ vaticinantur non- nulli, sed mere incerta. Locus sepulturæ, inquit Gra- vius, additur civitas HAMONA, hoc est, multi- tudo, a multitudine sepultorum, quod explicatur v. eod. per vallem multitudinis, & quidem ad Orien- tem maris. Respicit ad strages Ammonitarum ad mare mortuum, quod Orientale dicitur Jos. 12, 3. D. Phil. Nicolai locum ponit ad Constantinopolin. Sed quia terminus ad quem irruptionis Gogiticæ præ- cipue erit Germania & montes Israëlis, hoc est, re- giones Evangelicæ, ex quibus ultimis temporibus Verbum Dei tanquam ad Sionem prodiit: Videtur indigitari civitas seu locus aliquis in Saxonia ad mare Balthicum, quod mare Orientale dic Ost-See vulgo dicitur. Forsan inter Lubecam & Hambur- gum ultima fiet & maxima Gogitarum strages & in- ternecio. Agnoscit tamen ipse incertitudinem, ideo addit: Sed hæc incerta divinæ dispositioni & omni- scientiæ committenda. De combustione armorum hostilium ista habet: Exaggeratur prælii hujus ma- gnitudo. Hominum enim post hoc prælium in multis locis stupenda erit paucitas, ita ut ligna ex hostium occisorum armis & curribus reliqua ad 7. annos suffi- cere possint.

PARS II. DIABOLI ET CULTORUM EJUS IN LACUM IGNIS PROJECTIO.

Καὶ κατέβη πῦρ ἐκ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ ἀπὸ τοῦ Θεοῦ, καὶ κατέφαγεν αὐτούς) Sumptum ex loco Ezech. 38, 21. & 39, 6. Solent Prophetæ ignis voce uti, cum celerem designant exitum, ut de Senacheribi clade, Esaias 9, 5. 10, 6. 26, 11. Cum hæc res nondum evenerit, exspectandus erit Turcico regno exi- tus non dissimilis ei, quem habuere exercitus Senacheribi, aut Antiochi Illustris.

## 20:10
V. 10. And the devil that deceived them into the lake of fire and brimstone) Where his ministers had gone before, he himself will go, nor will his power be restrained by chains any longer, but it will be plainly taken away with no remnants remaining. See what was said above at XIX. 20. That the sinning angels are sent by God into the pool of fire is in Echa Rabtha. 'The one deceiving them,' he who had incited Gog and Magog against the Christians. See above 2 and 7. Concerning the sulphur, it was said above at XIX. 20.

Where also the beast, and the false prophet) See above at the said place XIX. 20.

And they shall be tormented day and night for ever and ever) With the torments of an evil conscience, as above at XIV. 10, and besides by the punishments which God shall render. See what was said by us at Matt. 25, 46. Thus the Hebrews say that the mockers of God and the eternal law will feel punishments. They will be tormented, namely the Devil, Gog, and Magog.

Latin:

V. 10. Καὶ ὁ Διάβολος ὁ πλανῶν αὐτοὺς εἰς τὴν λίμνην τοῦ πυρὸς καὶ θείου) Quo ministeria ejus præcesserant, ibit ipse, nec jam vinculis coercebitur ejus potestas, sed plane aussere- tur nullis manentibus reliquiis. Vide quæ dicta supra XIX. 20. Angelos peccantes mitti a Deo in stagnum ignis est in Echa Rabtha. Ὁ πλανῶν αὐτούς, is qui Gogum & Magogum contra Christianos incitaverat. Vide supra 2. & 7. De sul- phure dictum supra XIX. 20.

Ὅπου καὶ τὸ θηρίον, καὶ ὁ ψευδοπροφήτης) Vide supra dicto loco XIX. 20.

Καὶ βασανισθήσονται ἡμέρας καὶ νυκτὸς εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων) Tormentis malæ conscientiæ, ut supra XIV. 10. & præterea pœnis quas Deus reddiderit. Vide quæ dicta a nobis ad Matth. 25, 46. Sic irrisores Dei ac legis æternæ sensuros supplicia ajunt Ebræi. Torquebuntur, nempe Diabolus Gog & Magog.

## 20:11
V. 11. And I saw a great white throne and him who sat upon it.) Christ, to whom God has handed over this judgment, John 5:22, Acts 17:31. Understand white here as splendid with majesty. See above III.4, 5, 18, IV.4. Therefore, the punishment of some will precede that judgment, just as the glory of the martyrs precedes the same judgment. See what was brought forward at Matthew 25:32.

From whose face the heaven and the earth fled away) This old condition of things has passed away. See what was said at Romans 8:22, 2 Peter 3:7.

And no place was found for them) From the Greek of Daniel concerning the statue 2:35. A similar expression 12:8.

Latin:

V. 11. Καὶ εἶδον θρόνον μέγαν λευκὸν καὶ τὸν καθήμενον ἐπ᾽ αὐτοῦ.) Christum, cui hoc judicium Deus tradidit, Joh. 5,22. Act.17, 31. Λευκὸν hic intellige splendidum cum majestate. Vide supra III.4. 5. 18. IV. 4. Quorundam ergo pœna judi- cium illud ultimum antecedet, sicut martyrum gloria ante- cedit idem judicium. Vide quæ allata ad Matth. 25,32.

Οὗ ἀπὸ προσώπου ἔφυγεν ὁ οὐρανὸς καὶ ἡ γῆ) Abiit hæc vetus rerum conditio. Vide quæ dicta ad Romanos 8, 22. 2.Petr.3,7.

Καὶ τόπος οὐχ εὑρέθη αὐτοῖς) Ex Græco Danielis de statua 2,35. Similis loquutio 12, 8.

## 20:12
V. 12. And I saw the dead, the great and the small, standing before the throne) Christians, to be judged, of course, according to the laws of the Gospel, Rom. 2:16.

And books were opened) From Daniel 7:10. By books, understand the records of the lawsuit. By the records of the lawsuit, however, the thoughts, words, and deeds of men. From these it will appear how rightly some were written in the book of life, others not written or erased. Thus kings were accustomed to have commentaries of things done, Esth. 6:1, Mal. 3:16. The passage of Isaiah 65:6 looks to the same thing. There are many things said similarly among the nations, not because one took from another, but because similar thoughts occur to many. The Greeks used to say that misdeeds were written in the folds of Zeus's tablets. We learn that from Theodectes.

And another book was opened, which is the book of life) This book is like a register of the citizens of the heavenly kingdom, from which the names of those who remained written in that register until death will be read. No account will be taken of those erased, because they lost the right which they had had.

And the dead were judged from the things written in the books according to their works) that is, the judgment written in the book of life is pronounced concerning them, and it appears from the records that this judgment is consistent with their own external and internal works.

Latin:

V. 12. Καὶ εἶδον τοὺς νεκροὺς τοὺς μεγάλους καὶ τοὺς μικροὺς ἑστῶτας ἐνώπιον τοῦ θρόνου) Christianos, judicandos scilicet secundum Evangelii leges, Rom.2,16.

Καὶ βιβλία ἀνεῴχθησαν) Ex Daniele 7,10. Per libellos in- telligi acta litis. Per acta autem litis, hominum cogitata, dicta, facta. Ex his apparebit quam recte alii libro vitæ inscripti fuerint, alii non scripti aut deleti. Sic Reges com- mentarios habere solebant rerum gestarum, Esth. 6, 1. Malach. 3, 16. Eodem respicit locus Esaiæ 65, 6. Multa sunt apud gentes dictutas similiter dicta, non quod alius ab alio sumpserit, sed quod cogitata similia multis incidant. Græci dicebant ἀδικήματα γράφεσθαι ἐν Διὸς δέλτω πτυχαῖς. Discimus id ex Theodecte.

Καὶ ἄλλο βιβλίον ἀνεῴχθη, ὅ ἐστι τῆς ζωῆς) Hic liber est velut matricula civium regni cœlestis, unde nomina legentur eo- rum, qui ad mortem usque in ea matricula scripti perman- serint. Deletorum nulla habebitur ratio, quia jus, quod habuerant, amisere.

Καὶ ἐκρίθησαν οἱ νεκροὶ ἐκ τῶν γεγραμμένων ἐν τοῖς βιβλίοις κατὰ τὰ ἔργα αὐτῶν) id est, judicium perscriptum in libro vitæ de eis pronuntiatur, apparereque ex actis id judicium operibus ipsorum externis & internis esse congruens.

## 20:13
V. 13. And the sea gave up the dead who were in it) This gave up is pluperfect, such as we also noted above XIX.19. All parts of nature will exhibit their deposits. The scholiasts on Homer note that the ancients shuddered at the death of shipwreck, because they believed that souls, being fiery, were extinguished by the force of moisture. This is nothing: All things are in the hand of Christ. Nor does it matter where we have met death, but what kind we were.

Latin:

V. 13. Καὶ ἔδωκεν ἡ θάλασσα τοὺς ἐν αὐτῇ νεκρούς) Hic ἔδωκεν est plusquam perfectum, quale & supra notavimus XIX. 19. Omnes partes naturæ sua deposita exhibebunt. Notant Scholiastæ ad Homerum veteres exhorruisse naufragii mor- tem, quod animas, utpote igneas, a vi humoris crederent exstingui. Nihil hoc est: Omnia in Christi sunt manu. Nec refert ubi mortem obierimus, sed quales.

## 20:13
Καὶ ἐκρίθησαν ἕκαστος κατὰ τὰ ἔργα αὐτῶν) without any distinction of the fate by which they had lost this life.

Latin:

Καὶ ἐκρίθησαν ἕκαστος κατὰ τὰ ἔργα αὐτῶν) nullo discri- mine fati, quo vitam hanc amiserant.

## 20:14
V. 14. And death) Those who will have died by disease will likewise rise again. Death is accustomed to be taken in this way, the genus in the sense of the species. We spoke about it above VI.8.

And Hades) This includes all the other dead, who will have died either by violent fate or by old age. And by personification, the sea, death, and Hades are shown as if they were debtors of a deposit. You have death and Hades depicted in the manner of persons also in Is. 28:15 and 38:18.

Ἕδωκαν τοὺς ἑαυτῶν νεκροὺς) they gave up their dead, that is, those to whom they themselves had given the cause of death. Marcellus Eprius used to say: What have you to do with those dead?

Latin:

V.14. Καὶ ὁ θάνατος) Qui morbo erunt mortui, itidem exsurgent. Θάνατος ita sumi solet, genus in sensu speciei. Diximus de eo supra VI. 8.

Καὶ ὁ ᾅδης) Hoc cæteros omnes mortuos complectitur, qui aut violento fato aut senectute obierint. Et per προσω- ποποιΐαν ostenduntur mare, mors, ᾅδης quasi debitores depo- siti. Habes mortem & ᾅδην in personarum modum depi- ctas & Es.28,15. & 38, 18.

Ἕδωκαν τοὺς ἑαυτῶν νεκροὺς) ἔδωκαν exhibuerant suos mortuos, id est, quibus illa ipsa causam dederant mortis. Marcellus Eprius dicebat: Quid tibi cum eis mortuis?

## 20:14
Καὶ ὁ θάνατος καὶ ὁ ᾅδης ἐβλήθησαν εἰς τὴν λίμνην τοῦ πυρός) He continues the personification, and it signifies that after the judgment there will be no power of either diseases or death against those concerning whom the lawsuit was given. Which is said of Christ in Heb. 7:28, Rom. 6:9. Add a passage very similar to this, 1 Cor. 15:54.

Οὗτός ἐστιν ὁ θάνατος ὁ δεύτερος, ἡ λίμνη τοῦ πυρός) See above 6 and what is said there.

Latin:

Καὶ ὁ θάνατος καὶ ὁ ᾅδης ἐβλήθησαν εἰς τὴν λίμνην τοῦ πυρός) Pertexit προσωποποιΐαν, & significat, post judicium nullam in eos secundum quos lis erat data, fore vim aut morborum aut mortis. Quod de Christo dicitur Ebr. 7, 28. Rom. 6, 9. Adde locum huic persimilem 1. Cor. 15, 54.

Οὗτός ἐστιν ὁ θάνατος ὁ δεύτερος, ἡ λίμνη τοῦ πυρός) Vide supra 6. & ibi dicta.

## 20:15
Vers. 15. Καὶ εἴ τις οὐχ εὑρέθη ἐν τῇ βίβλῳ τῆς ζωῆς γεγραμ- μένος, ἐβλήθη εἰς τὴν λίμνην τοῦ πυρός) Whoever has not died in Christ will not escape the second death. It is not enough to have been written at some time in the book of life: it is necessary that one be found written there at the time of judgment. By lake here and above is understood a certain great capacity. See Zech. 9:11, where in Hebrew it is בור, in Greek λάκκος, in Latin lacus. See also Gen. 37:19, where in Latin the name cisterna is used no less improperly.

He makes the outcome of the Gogitic battle, according to the explanation of most interpreters, the corporal destruction of Rome. To strengthen this opinion, one may observe these things: 1. The primary rule of interpretation: One must not depart from the literal sense without necessity. But none appears here. 2. The emphasis of the words, such as that fire first fell from heaven, as in the destruction of Sodom, whose name was given to this city in ch. XI; second, that the enemies surrounded the city. third, that for this reason a great multitude was gathered; fourth, that they ascended; fifth, over the breadth of the earth; which teach that a war was undertaken, the city besieged, that the enemies are designated not as spiritual but as corporal; that a certain city is indicated, for whose sake it was necessary to ascend, the army, the leader and his heads, the provinces and nations from which it was gathered, the weapons, the signal for the place of gathering, the spoils, the land which it attacks, the time, the horrible sight of the city, the ruin, the slaughter of rain sent down from heaven, the fire cast by the Lord, the burning of weapons, the burial and the valley, the months of burial, etc. Although the Holy Spirit describes it somewhat prolixly in Ezek. ch. 38, 39, he nevertheless leaves no indication that these things are to be understood figuratively and improperly. 6. Those plagues, when they are joined in the sacred writings—famine, pestilence, fire—are accustomed to be understood literally. 7. The kings who lament the city are kings properly so called. 8. Mention is made of smoke from the burning of the city in ch. XVIII:10. 9. Mourning because of the removed merchandise of gems, vessels, wine, wheat, etc., argues that the city was devastated and reduced to a wilderness. 10. It is said to be devastated in one hour, and that with astonishment. These things do not thus agree with a spiritual destruction. 11. A millstone cast into the sea signifies that the city is to be submerged, so that no place for it is found. 12. The fall seems distinct, as announced by another angel from the former one, about which in Rev. XIV:8. 13. The cessation of the propagation of the human race, which is hinted at by the cessation of the joy of the bridegroom and bride in this city, what else do they designate than the total destruction and perpetual desolation of the city? There are not lacking, however, those who prefer that the spiritual ruin of Rome or the Papacy is indicated. But since that is materially the conversion itself, but here there is a prophecy concerning the judgment and punishment of Rome, and neither do sufficiently compelling arguments for the literal sense being deferred occur, nor the authorities of great interpreters, and the agreement of other prophecies which are asserted brings about the properly called destruction, I do not see how I ought to render uncertain the conflagration of the city described so clearly. Since in mysteries, oracles, and prophecies, unless the Holy Spirit expressly commands somewhere that they be understood improperly, one must not depart from the propriety of the letter: otherwise nothing certain will be had. And since the event is the best interpreter of prophecies, but that is still awaited and has been revealed to no one, who would dare to prejudice such a manifest prediction with his own private interpretation, or to bend it with uncertain and doubtful tropes, and to invert things which according to the letter carry no absurdity with them? The Sibylline prophecy is known: ῢώμη μὲν ῥύμη ἔσαι, δήλη δὲ ἄδηλ: which Blessed Luther in his preface to Micah seems to have rendered: Rome, you shall become a space, and well cleared out. Some also bring forward a prophecy of a very ancient manuscript codex about a King who would subjugate the islanders, Spaniards, and Italians in about forty years, would destroy Rome and Florence, and burn them with fire, would strike the supreme clerics who have invaded the seat of Peter, would be named King of the Greeks, would subject the Turks and barbarians to himself, and would make an edict of this kind: Whoever has not adored the crucifix shall die the death. Nicolaus Clemang. (circa Ann. 1416.) urges that [passage] in his commentary on this entire place of the Apocalypse: Revolve, he says, the whole canonical history, you will not find that the Lord has exercised vengeance upon any Babylonian congregation of wicked men without first consulting the just, if it happened that any were there, and separating them from the iniquitous not only by vow but also by place, lest if they were covered in a common dwelling with the wicked, they might also be destroyed in a common extermination. While the whole world was to be destroyed by the inundation of the cataclysm because all flesh had corrupted its ways with foul crimes, Noah with his few is commanded above all things, once the ark was built, to be separated from the drowning sinners, and thus to be saved. Lot is led out by angelic ministry from Sodom, which was to be burned by heavenly fire and brimstone, before that fiery rain broke forth, so that he might not perish with the most wicked; to whom it is also pointedly said by the Angel, make haste, and save thyself in the mountain, because I cannot do anything until thou be come thither. Before the earth, opening its most vast chasm, swallowed up Dathan and Abiram and the accomplices of their sedition, Moses speaks thus to the remaining innocent crowd according to the words of the Lord: Depart from the tents of the wicked men, and touch nothing of theirs, lest you be involved in their sins. When Saul, by the command of the Lord, was to overcome Amalek, the ancient enemy of the people of Israel, even to extermination, and the Kenite, a friend of the same people, was dwelling among the Amalekites, Saul said to the same Kenite: Depart, get you down, and go away from Amalek, lest perhaps I involve you with him. Do not, therefore, so translate those things which are reported in the Holy Scriptures as having been done, or are commanded to be done, into a mystical understanding, that you would wish to deem them void and empty as far as historical imitation is concerned. For although something of Babylon happens everywhere, yet that Babylon is not everywhere, the mother of the fornications and abominations of the earth, whose judgment has reached even to heaven, who has made all drunk with the wine of her prostitution, and who compels all her inhabitants to commit fornication, to blaspheme, to eat things sacrificed to idols, to adore the Dragon. Conf. Is. 48, 10. Jer. 51, 45. Matt. 21, 15. Job 14, 9. One must therefore depart, as the same Author warns, not only in life and morals, but also in way and steps. Concerning the desolation Is. 13, 20. c. 34, 11. Jer. 50, 39.

Yet these could (which pleased others, even B. Kromayer) be understood as described concerning the defection from the Anti-Christian kingdom according to the degrees of repentance, without absurdity: 1. By desolation, with kingdoms and provinces withdrawn from its subjection. 2. By the deprivation of gold, pearls, etc., by denying indulgences, annates, palls, and Peter's pence in those places. 3. By the evacuation of the kitchen, so that they may have need to eat their own flesh somewhere, especially if they wish to seek their former seats.

Latin:

Vers. 15. Καὶ εἴ τις οὐχ εὑρέθη ἐν τῇ βίβλῳ τῆς ζωῆς γεγραμ- μένος, ἐβλήθη εἰς τὴν λίμνην τοῦ πυρός) Qui in Christo diem non obierit, is mortem secundam non evadet. Non sufficit scriptum fuisse aliquando in vitæ libro: opus est, ut scriptus ibi quis reperiatur judicii tempore. Per λίμνην hic & supra intelligitur magna quædam capacitas. Vide Zachar. 9, 11. ubi in Ebræo בור in Græco λάκκος, in Latino lacus. Vide & Genes. 37, 19. ubi in Latino non minus improprie ponitur nomen, cisterna.

Exitum prælii Gogiticii facit, juxta plerorumque Interpretum explicationem, corporale Romæ exi- tium. Cui sententiæ firmandæ hæc observare licet? 1. Regulam interpretationis primariam: A litera non est discedendum citra necessitatem. Ea vero hic nulla apparet. 2. Emphasin verborum, utpote quod primo ignis de cœlo deciderit, sicut in exitio Sodomæ, cujus nomen huic civitati datum c. XI. secundo quod hostes civitatem circumdederint. tertio quod ideo magna multitudo congregata fuerit: quarto quod ascenderint: quinto super latitudinem terræ; quæ docent bellum fuisse su- sceptum, urbem obsessam, hostes non spirituales sed corporales designari; civitatem certam in- dicari, cujus gratia adscendendum fuerit, exerci- tum, Ducem & capita ejus, provincias & natio- nes, e quibus congregatus, arma, classicum lo- cum congregationis, spolia, terram, quam aggre- ditur, tempus, horribilem conspectum civitatis, ruinam, pluviam cœlitus demissam stragem, ignem a Domino projectum, armorum combustionem, sepulturam & vallem, menses sepulturæ &c. etsi prolixiuscule apud Ezech. c. 38. 39. describat Spi- ritus sanctus, nullum tamen indicium relinquit, ea esse figurate & improprie intelligenda. 6. Plagæ illæ cum conjunguntur in sacris, fames, pestis, ignis, solent proprie intelligi. 7. Reges, qui Urbem de- plorant, sunt Reges proprie dicti. 8. Mentio fit fumi ex incendio urbis c. XVIII. 10. 9. Luctus ob merci- monia sublata gemmarum, vasorum, vini, tritici &c. urbem devastatam & in solitudinem redactam arguit. 10. Una hora dicitur vastata, idque cum ad- miratione. Quæ ita non conveniunt spirituali destructioni. 11. Lapis molaris in mare projectus civitatem submergendam, ut locus ejus nullus in- veniatur. 12. Casus videtur distinctus, uti ab alio Angelo annunciatus a priori, de quo Ap. XIV. 8. 13. Cessatio propagationis generis humani, quæ cessa- tione gaudii sponsi & sponsæ in hac Urbe innuitur, quid aliud designant, quam totale excidium, & per- petuam vastitatem Urbis? Non desunt tamen, qui spiritualem Romæ vel Papatus ruinam indicari ma- lint. Sed quum ea materialiter sit ipsa conversio, hic vero de judicio, & supplicio Romæ vaticinium habeatur, nec argumenta satis stringentia deferen- dæ literæ, & autoritates magnorum Interpretum occurrant, συμφωνία vero aliorum, quæ asserun- tur, vaticiniorum proprie dictam destructionem inferat, non video, qui tam luculenter descriptam urbis conflagrationem incertam reddere debeam? Siquidem in mysteriis, oraculis & vaticiniis, nisi diserte Spiritus sanctus alicubi jubeat ea impro- prie intelligi, non sit a proprietate literæ disceden- dum: alioquin nihil certi habebitur. Et quum eventus vaticiniorum optimus interpres sit, is vero adhuc expectetur, neminique revelatus sit, ecquis præjudicare tam manifestæ prædictioni ausit idiα ἐπιλύσῇ, aut inflectere tropis incertis, atq; dubiis invertere, quæ κατὰ τὸ ῥητὸν nullam secum vehunt absurditatem. Notum est vaticinium Sibyllinum: ῢώμη μὲν ῥύμη ἔσαι, δήλη δὲ ἄδηλ: quod B. Lutherus præfat. in Mich. reddisse videtur Roma du sollt ein Raum werden, und wohl ausgeraumet. Proferunt etiam nonnulli prophetiam MS. Codicis perantiqui de Rege quadraginta circiter annis Insulanos, Hispanos & Italos subjugaturo, Romam & Florentiam destructuro, & igne combusturo, supremos Clericos, qui Petri sedem invaserunt, percussuro, Rege Græcorum nominando, Turcas & Barbaros sibi subjecturo, & edictum ejusmodi facturo: Quicunque crucifixum non adoraverit, morte morietur. Nicolaus Clemang. (circa Ann. 1416.) urget illud recedet in commentario super integrum hunc Apocalyseos locum: Revolve, inquit, totam Canoniciam historiam, non invenies in aliquam impiorum hominum Babylonicam congregationem, aliquam Dominum exercuisse ultionem, quin justis, si quos ibi esse contingeret, antea consulendo, ipsos ab iniquis non solum voto, verum & loco secerneret, ne si communi cum sceleratis tegerentur habitaculo, communi etiam contererentur exterminio. Dum fœdis omni carne corrupta sceleribus cataclysmi inundatione totus esset delendus mundus, jubetur ante omnia Noë cum paucis suis, arca fabricata, a mergendis peccatoribus segregari, sicque salvari. Loth a Sodomis cælesti igne ac sulphure concremandis, antequam imber ille igneus erumperet, Angelico ministerio, ne cum pessimis periret, educitur, cui etiam per Angelum signanter dicitur, festina, & in monte salvare, quia non potero facere quicquam, donec ingrediaris illuc. Antequam Dathan & Abiran, complicesque seditionis sua illa vastissima voragine terra dehiscens absorberet, Moses ita ex Domini verbis ad reliquam turbam innocuam loquitur: Recedite a tabernaculis hominum impiorum, & nolite tangere, quæ ad eos pertinent, ne involvamini in peccatis eorum. Cum Saul Domini imperio Amalech antiquum hostem populi Israel usque ad internecionem expugnare deberet, Cineusque amicus ejusdem populi inter Amalekitas habitaret, dixit Saul ad eundem Cinæum: Abite, recedite atque discedite ab Amalech, ne forsan te involvam cum eo. Noli itaque ea, quæ in sacris literis aut gesta referuntur, aut geri mandantur, sic ad mysticum traducere intellectum, ut quantum ad historicam imitationem cassa velis & inania deputare. Nam licet aliquid Babylonis ubique fiat, non tamen ubique est illa Babylon, mater fornicationum & abominationum terræ, cujus usque ad cælum pervenit judicium, quæ a vino suæ prostitutionis omnes inebriavit, & quæ omnes suos cogit incolas fornicari, blasphemare, idolothyta manducare, Draconem adorare. Conf. Es. 48, 10. Jer. 51, 45. Matth. 21, 15. Job. 14, 9. Exeundum ergo, monente eodem Autore, non solum vita ac moribus, sed etiam via & gressibus. De vastitate Es. 13, 20. c. 34, 11. Jer. 50, 39.

Possent tamen (quod aliis, etiam B. Kromajero placuit) hæc de defectione ab Anti-Christiano regno secundum gradus resipiscentiæ descripta intelligi, citra absurdum 1. per desolationem abstractis ab ejus subjectione regnis & provinciis. 2. Per auri, margaritarum &c. privationem indulgentias, annatas, pallia, Petri donaria in illis denegando. 3. Per Culinarium evacuationem, ut vel proprias carnes opus habeant alicubi comedere, maxime si pristinas sedes repetere velint.

## 21:1 Argument
SEVENTH VISION CHAPTER XXI. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

He sees a new heaven and a new earth, as the old ones had passed away, the tabernacle of God and of men, the bride of the Lamb, the new Jerusalem, whose golden and gem-like splendor is depicted, along with its foundations, gates, walls, streets, temple, and citizens.

There are two parts. I. The showing of the new Jerusalem made by the Angel to v. 10. II. Its splendid description to v. 27.

PART I. THE SHOWING OF THE NEW JERUSALEM.

V. 1. Καὶ εἶδον ὀυρανὸν καινὸν, καὶ γῆν καινήν ) This is another vision, but one which took its occasion from the previous vision. So that you may the more believe in that supreme happiness of the future age, God gave us some image of it in the most flourishing state of the Church, which existed from the times of Constantine down to the times of Justinian. There was indeed great piety, holiness, and constancy among Christians in the first three centuries. But the virtues of many were hidden by those very shelters by which the Church itself was hidden. But after the protection of Princes was added to the Church, according to the old prophecies, the virtues of Christians were very illustrious and conspicuous: to piety was added the learning and eloquence of many Bishops: a more certain form of government and of consonant rites was established by the decrees of Universal Councils. Finally, such a great change was made that it could rightly be called by the prophetic name of a new heaven and a new earth. For Isaiah also had used the same words to describe that happy state of the Jewish people after the forces of Antiochus were defeated, 65.17, which is clearer when the passage of the same Prophet 66.22 is compared. Heaven itself favored the human race on account of the flourishing Church, just as it was said of Theodosius the Great: O too beloved of God, for whom the ether fights, And the winds come sworn to the standards. The earth was no longer defiled by the blood of the innocent and the pious. Scripture often marks principal things and the omens of principal things with similar names.

There is no evidence that this is about the most flourishing state of the Church. The continuity of the Apocalypse rather dictates the opposite. For it had already predicted the persecution of the witnesses of the truth. And now it is occupied with depicting the rewards of them and of all the faithful. Nor does History agree. Namely, that the state of the Church was most flourishing from the time of Constantine the Great until Justinian. For how sad was the lot of the Church under the very sons of Constantine, how miserable its face under Julian the Apostate, how nothing was flourishing then in the Catholic Church, the most grievous persecutions of that Apostate and of the Arians testify, where almost the whole Christian world had need to groan. Interpreters, however, easily agree that it concerns the happiness of the heavenly Jerusalem, not of the militant Church, to which nothing is less proper than to enjoy earthly or temporal happiness. For wars are never lacking to the pious, nor are struggles, 2 Tim. 3.12. There will be no pain in that heavenly city, no mourning. Nor will there be any place there for tears anymore, nor for death itself. But who in this mortal life, in this dregs of a malignant world, in this state of the last times, 1 Tim. 4.1 seqq., Apoc. 12.12, in which Satan rages extremely because he knows that little time remains for him, would expect such things? A clearly different prognosis was left to the Church, John 16.2, 20. There are no golden promised times in this age. Nor does the light of perpetual joy have a place in this vicissitude of things. And how could perfect holiness be found before ἔλθῃ τὸ τέλειον, τὸ δὲ ἐκ μέρους καταργηθήσεται, 1 Cor. 13.10. How could there be nothing unclean, when infidels and hypocrites are still mixed with the faithful? For concerning the heavenly Jerusalem St. John says c. 22.3, 15. Πᾶν κατάναθεμα ὐκ ἔσαι ἔτι, ἔξω δὲ οἱ κύνες &c. Finally, where on earth are gems and pearls of such magnitude, where is a gem-like gate, or walls? And how do such splendid things, even if spoken metaphorically, befit an afflicted Church, into which all the tempests, all the storms of persecutions are thrown? Where is its glory and magnificence so illustrious? Furthermore, a new heaven and a new earth is not a renovated heaven. For to what good would the earth be renovated, if indeed there is no one who ought to inhabit it? How does Andreas say that there will be no use for the sea anymore, because the other age will not need ships to seek goods from afar, where there will be an affluence of all good things. And it is entirely different to be new, and to be renovated. Everything renovated can be called new in a certain respect and κατά τι; but that which is properly new can never have been old, and therefore could not have admitted of renovation. Add that it is said that the former heaven and the former earth have passed away, and that the sea IS NO MORE, which we have noted elsewhere to imply substantial destruction and cessation: to have fled from the face of God, chap. 20. v. 11. Conf. Is. 65.17, c. 66.22, 2 Pet. 3.13. In this earth, justice does not so much dwell as injustice rules, Ps. 14.2 seqq., Ps. 52.3, Rom. 3.10 seqq. In that one, however, nothing but justice will flourish. From this earth, pain, labor, and death do not go into exile: but in that new one there will be no place for them, Apoc. 21.4.

Moreover, Seraphinus de Fermo, as also Ubertinus de Cassalis in tract. 7 de stat. Eccles. c. 8, wish this vision to pertain not to the state of the future life, but partly to that, and partly to the state of the militant Church; which is also the opinion of Richard, Hortulanus, and Joachim the Abbot. But Alcafar more correctly accepts it as concerning the state of the triumphant Church, and proves that it must be so accepted by seven arguments. But that the Roman Church is the Wife of the Lamb does not fit in any way. For she is rather a brothel, and the great harlot, the mother of fornications, drunk with the blood of the Martyrs, the great Babylon, the habitation of Demons, and the cage of every unclean Spirit.

ὁ γὰρ πρῶτος οὐρανὸς) That heaven, which had sent famine and pestilence, above 16.2, 8.

And the first earth passed away) The third does not drink the blood of the innocent any further, as I said. In the Manuscript ἀπῆλθεν, as below 7.

And the sea is no more) That huge multitude of idolaters did not remain. Only the rivers and fountains remained. And these too are gradually to dry up. See above VIII. 10. XIV. 7. XVI. 4. In the Manuscript: And I saw the sea no more.

A new heaven is not to be explained as the eternal reward itself, just as a new earth is not to be explained as an impassible and immortal body, nor is the absence of the sea to be explained as the absence of the danger of shipwreck with Alcazar, nor does the sea properly denote here a stormy and turbulent age: for one must not depart to figurative senses where no necessity compels it, nor is the sea said to be changed into another form, as Cornelius explains, but the sea IS NOT any more, as the Arabic has it, not by fiction, as Bede wishes, but by an all-encompassing cessation. Nor is the city of new Jerusalem the empyrean heaven, seeing that scripture is entirely ignorant of that; but that most blessed state of the Saints, in which they are exhilarated by the beatific vision of God.

Latin:

VISIO SEPTIMA CAPUT XXI. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

VIdet novum cœlum & novam terram, uti vetera transierant, tabernaculum Dei & hominum sponsam Agni, novam Hierosolymam, cujus splendor aureus & gemmeus depingitur, cum fundamentis, portis, muris, plateis, templo & civibus.

Partes duæ sunt. I. Novæ Hierosolymæ ostensio ab Angelo facta ad v. 10. II. Ejusdem splendida descriptio ad v. 27.

PARS I. NOVÆ HIEROSOLYMÆ OSTENSIO.

V. 1. Καὶ εἶδον ὀυρανὸν καινὸν, καὶ γῆν καινήν ) Est aliud visum, sed quod occasionem sumpsit ex viso priore. Quo magis credatis summam illam felicitatem seculi futuri, aliquam ejus imaginem Deus nobis dedit in florentissimo Ecclesiæ statu, qui fuit a temporibus Constantini ad tempora usque Justiniani. Fuit quidem Christianorum tribus primis seculis magna pietas, sanctitas, constantia. Sed multorum virtutes tegebantur iis ipsis latebris, quibus ipsa Ecclesia tegebatur. Postquam vero secundum vetera vaticinia accessit Ecclesiæ tutela Principum, illustres admodum & conspicuæ fuere Christianorum virtutes: ad pietatem accessit eruditio & eloquentia multorum Episcoporum: constituta est certior regiminis & consonansium rituum forma decretis Conciliorum Universalium. Denique tanta facta est mutatio, ut ea prophetico more cœli novi & terræ novæ nomine recte nuncupari posset. Nam & Esaias eadem verba usurpaverat ad describendum statum illum felicem populi Judaici post debellatas Antiochi copias LXV. 17. quod clarius patet collato loco Prophetæ ejusdem LXVI. 22. Cœlum ipsum favit humano generi ob Ecclesiam florentem, sicut de Theodosio Magno dictum est: O nimium dilecte Deo, cui militat æther, Et conjurati veniunt ad classica venti. Terra non ultra impurata fuit innocentium & piorum sanguine. Sæpe scriptura res principales & rerum principalium præsagia paribus insignit nominibus.

De Ecclesiæ statu florentissimo sermonem esse, nullo constat documento. Contrarium potius dictitat Apocalypseos συνέχεια. Nam prædixerat jam persecutionem testium veritatis. Et nunc in eorum, omniumque fidelium præmiis depingendis occupatur. Neque consonat Historia. A tempore nempe Constantini M. florentissimum Ecclesiæ fuisse statum usque ad Justinianum. Quam tristis enim fors Ecclesiæ sub ipsis Constantini filiis, quam misera facies sub Juliano Apostata, quam nihil floridi tum fuerit in Catholica Ecclesia, gravissimæ Parabatis istius, & Arianorum persecutiones testantur, ubi totus fere orbis Christianus ingemiscere opus habuit. Facile autem consentiunt Interpretes, de cœlestis Hierosolymæ felicitate agi, non militantis Ecclesiæ, cui nihil minus proprium, quam terrena vel temporali felicitate frui. Nunquam enim bella piis, nunquam certamina desunt, 2. Tim. III. 12. Nullus in illa civitate cælesti erit dolor, luctus nullus. Nec lacrymis ibi amplius locus futurus, neq; morti ipsi. At quis in hac mortali vita, in hac mundi maligni fece, in hoc statu novissimorum temporum, 1. Tim. IV. 1. seqq. Apoc. XII. 12. quibus Satanas extreme furit, quod parum temporis sibi superesse norit, talia expectet? Prognosticon plane aliud relictum Ecclesiæ, Joh. XVI. 2. 20. Nulla in hoc seculo aurea promissa tempora. Neq; lux gaudii perpetua in hac rerum vicissitudine locum habet. Et quomodo perfecta sanctitas inveniretur, antequam ἔλθῃ τὸ τέλειον, τὸ δὲ ἐκ μέρους καταργηθήσεται, 1. Cor. XIII. 10. Quomodo nihil immundi, quando fidelibus adhuc infideles & hypocritæ admixti? Nam de Hierosolyma cælesti S. Johannes c. XXII. 3. 15. Πᾶν κατάναθεμα ὐκ ἔσαι ἔτι, ἔξω δὲ οἱ κύνες &c. Denique ubi terra- rum gemmæ & margaritæ tantæ magnitudinis, ubi gemmæa porta, aut muri? Et qui tam splendida, et- jam si metaphorice dicta, Ecclesiæ afflictæ, in quam omnes tempestates, omnes procellæ persecutio- num jactantur, competunt? Ubi tam illustris ejus gloria, & magnificentia? Porro cœlum novum & ter- ra nova non est cœlum renovatum. Nam terra cui bono renovaretur, siquidem nullus sit, qui eam in- colere debeat? quomodo Andreas nullum maris usum fore amplius dicit, quia navibus ad merces longe petendas non indigebit alterum seculum, ubi omnium bonorum erit affluentia. Et differunt omnino, novum esse, & renovatum. Omne renova- tum certo respectu & κατά τι novum dici potest; quod autem novum proprie est, nunquam potest fuisse vetus, ideoque nec renovationem admisisse. Adde quod transiisse dicatur prius cœlum & prior terra, & mare NON ESSE amplius, quæ sub- stantialem interitum & desitionem inferre alias no- tavimus: fugisse a facie Dei, cap. XX. v. 11. Conf. Es. LXV. 27. c. LXVI. 21. 2. Petr. III. 13. In hac ter- ra non tam justitia habitat, quam injustitia domina- tur, Ps. XIV. 2. seqq. Ps. LII. 3. Rom. III. 10. seqq. In illa vero non nisi justitia vigebit. Ab hac terra non exulat dolor, labor, & mors: quibus vero in illa nova nullus erit locus, Apoc. XXI. 4.

Cæterum Seraphinus de Fermo, ut & Ubertinus de Cassalis tract. 7. de stat. Eccles. c. 8. volunt hanc visionem non ad statum futuræ vitæ, sed partim ad illum, partim ad Ecclesiæ militantis statum perti- nere; quæ etiam Richardi, Hortulani, Joachimi Ab- batis est sententia. Rectius autem Alcafar de statu Ecclesiæ triumphantis eandem accipit, & accipien- dam esse septem argumentis probat. Quod vero Ecclesia Romana Agni Uxor sit, nullo pacto con- venit. Illa enim prostibulum potius est, & meretrix magna, mater scortationum, ebria de sanguine Martyrum, Babylon magna, habitatio Dæmonio- rum, & custodia omnis Spiritus immundi.

ὁ γὰρ πρῶτος οὐρανὸς) Cœlum illud, quod famem pe- stilentiamque immiserat, supra XVI. 2. 8.

Καὶ ἡ πρώτη γῆ παρῆλθεν) Tertia non ultra bibit inno- centum, ut dixi, sanguinem. In Manuscripto ἀπῆλθεν, ut infra 7.

Καὶ ἡ θάλασσα οὐκ ἔστιν ἔτι) Ingens illa idololatrarum mul- titudo non mansit. Mansere tantum flumina & fontes. Et hæc quoque paulatim exaritura. Vide supra VIII. 10. XIV. 7. XVI. 4. In Manuscripto: Καὶ τὴν θάλασσαν οὐκ εἶδον ἔτι.

Cœlum novum non de ipso præmio æterno, uti nec terra nova de corpore impassibili & immortali, nec maris ἀπουσία de periculi naufragii absentia cum Alcafare declaranda, neque mare seculum pro- cellosum & turbulentum hic notat proprie: nam non est ad figuratos sensus discedendum, ubi nulla cogit necessitas, neq; mare in aliam formam com- mutandum dicitur, ut explicat Cornelius, sed mare NON EST ultra, ut Arabicus habet, non per fic- cationem, ut Beda vult, sed per omnimodam de- sitionem. Nec civitas Jerusalem nova est cœlum empyræum, utpote quod plane ignorat scriptura; sed πῷ illud Sanctorum beatissimum, in quo beati- fica Dei visione ipsi exhilarantur.

## 21:2
V. 2. And I saw the holy city Jerusalem coming down from God out of heaven) In the Manuscript: new Jerusalem, just as the Latin also reads. The holy city עיר הקדש ירושלם Is. LII. 1. Those things which happen on earth by the great benefit of God are said to descend from God, John III. 13. In this book above X. 1. XVIII. 1. Mention of this vision was made by anticipation above III. 12. See what we have said regarding all those places. Do not mourn, Christians, for Jerusalem destroyed, then restored to a form smaller than the old. You shall have a new Jerusalem, that is, a mystical one. For thus the word new is taken in Matt. XXVI. 29, where we treated of it and similar expressions. Paul also in Gal. IV. 26 calls the Christian Church the Jerusalem which is above. But here she proceeds with a new adornment, widely conspicuous and dazzling the sight of her enemies with her brilliance: bearing the name of her origin, which is the vision of peace, in a twofold way, by the tranquility of conscience, and furthermore by the singular protection of God through Princes who provide all things safe for her, according to that which the Church had already long ago asked of God, 1 Tim. 2, 2. But it was reserved for these times.

The Caesarean [Eusebius] does not seem to have read the name of John, which the Royal Exemplar also does not have. Jerusalem is called holy in this life, Ap. 20, 9. But more so in the other, which is looked to in this place. For here holiness is only begun, there it will be consummated: Hence also the heavenly Jerusalem is truly called the vision of peace, which no conflict or battle disturbs, said Sap. 3, 3. It is indeed the same Jerusalem of travelers and the blessed, of those fighting and those triumphing: yet this one is new because of the perfect and consummated renewal of the Elect, 1 Cor. 13, 10. To descend from heaven is not to descend into the valley of Jehoshaphat, as Maldonatus wishes, because according to Cornelius the judgment will then already have been completed, which the order of the Apocalypse also indicates. But this is hinted at by that phrase, either because on the last day a great part of the Elect will descend from heaven with Christ in reality, though not locally, and will accompany him in the clouds: or because it is ἄνωθεν by reason of its origin from GOD, Matt. 21, 25. Jas. 1, 17. Augustine, book 20 de C. D. ch. 17. It is said to descend from heaven, because it is of heavenly grace, by which God made it. And in the sentences of Prosper, no. 31. None ascend to the fellowship of the heavenly Jerusalem, except those who confess with their whole heart that it is not of their own work, but of a Divine gift, that they ascend. It can also be applied to any faithful soul, as it is a part of the heavenly Jerusalem: of which Bernard, sermon 27 in Cant. I think every holy soul is not only heavenly because of its origin; but also heaven itself because of imitation. And then it clearly shows that its origin is truly from the heavens, when its conversation is in the heavens. Heaven is therefore some holy soul, having the sun as intellect, the moon as faith, the stars as mighty works, which shine forth especially in the night, that is, in adversities.

Ἡτοιμασμένην ὡς νύμφην κεκοσμημένην τῷ ἀνδρὶ αὐτῆς.) What had been seen before concerning the Church, which was in the family and retinue of Constantine, above 19, 17, appeared further as the care of Princes progressed in that whole body of the Church diffused throughout the Roman empire. She proceeded into public adorned, as new brides are wont to be, showing the power of her husband to all the wicked. Τῷ ἀνδρὶ, that is, in honor of the husband. There is an allusion to Isaiah 54 and following.

It is thus distinguished from the camps of the saints, which are on earth. Prepared, as a bride adorned, that is, magnificently, as Arethas has it: for then brides adorn themselves most, when they are led into the bridal chamber. Therefore, that he calls her a bride is of dignity, love, joy, and desire: That he calls her adorned is of splendor, glory, Majesty, and perfection. She is brought to the bridegroom, her future husband, so that a perpetual and indissoluble bond may be hinted at, Rom. 8, last; therefore mention is made of nuptials, v. 9.

Latin:

V. 2. Καὶ εἶδον τὴν πόλιν τὴν ἁγίαν Ἱερουσαλὴμ καταβαί- νουσαν ἀπὸ τῦ Θεῦ ἐκ τῦ ὁυρανῦ) In Manuscripto: Ἱερου- σαλὴμ καινὴν, quomodo legit & Latinus. Τὴν ἁγίαν עיר הקדש ירושלם Es. LII. 1. A Deo dicuntur de- scendere ea quæ in terris magno Dei beneficio eveniunt, Joh. III. 13. Hoc libro supra X. 1. XVIII. 1. Hujus visi mentio κατὰ πρόληψιν facta supra III. 12. Vide quæ ad omnia illa loca diximus. Nolite Christiani lugere Hiero- solyma excisa, deinde restituta in formam veteri mino- rem. Habebitis Hierosolyma nova, id est, mystica. Ita enim vox καινῇ sumitur Matth. XXVI. 29. ubi de ea & similibus loquutionibus egimus. Etiam Paulus Gal. IV. 6. Ecclesiam Christianam vocat Ἱερουσαλὴμ τὴν ἄνω. Verum hic ea cum novo cultu procedit late conspicua & fulgore suo hostibus aciem oculorum praestinguens : nomen originis suae, quae est pacis visio, duplici modo praeferens conscientiae tran- quillitate, ac praeterea singulari Dei tutela per Principes omnia ei tuta praestantes, secundum id, quod jam olim Ec- clesia Deum rogaverat, 1. Tim. 2, 2. Sed his temporibus erat reservatum.

Nomen Johannis non legisse videtur Caesariensis, quod nec Exemplar Regium habet. Sancta dicitur Hierosolyma in hac vita Ap. XX, 9. Magis autem in altera, quae hoc loco respicitur. Hic enim sanctitas est tantum inchoata, ibi erit consummata : Inde & Hierosolyma caelestis vere visio pacis, quam nulla turbat conventio vel pugna, dicitur Sap. 3, 3. Eadem quidem Hierosolyma viatorum & beatorum, pu- gnantium & triumphantium: haec tamen nova ob perfectam & consummatam Electorum renovationem 1. Cor. 13, 10. Descendere de caelo non est descendere in vallem Josaphat, ut Maldonatus vult, quia secun- dum Cornelium peractum tum jam erit judicium, quod & ordo Apocalypsios indicat. Sed hoc innui- tur illa phrasi, vel quod in novissimo die magnam partem de caelo cum Christo realiter, licet non locali- ter, descensuri Electi, eumque in nubibus stipaturi sint: vel quod ἄνωθεν ratione originis à DEO sit, Matth. 21, 25. Jac. 1, 17. Augustinus l. XX. de C. D. c. 17. De caelo dicitur descendere, quia caelestis gratiae est, qua Deus eam fecit. Et in sentent. Prosper. n. 31. Ad caelestis Jerusalem non ascendunt consortium, nisi qui toto corde profitentur, non proprii operis, sed Di- vini esse muneris, quod adscendunt. Applicari etiam potest ad quamvis fidelem animam, utpote quae pars est caelestis Hierosolymae: de qua Bernh. serm. XXVII. in Cant. Ego puto omnem animam sanctam non modo caelestem esse propter originem; sed & caelum ipsum propter imitationem. Et tunc liquido ostendit, quia vere origo ipsius de caelis est, cum conversatio ejus in caelis est. Est ergo caelum sancta aliqua anima, habens solem intellectum, lunam fidem, astra vir- tutes, quae maxime in nocte, id est, adversis emi- cant.

Ἡτοιμασμένην ὡς νύμφην κεκοσμημένην τῷ ἀνδρὶ αὐτῆς.) Quod ante de Ecclesia, quae erat in familia & comitatu Constantini, conspectum fuerat supra XIX, 17. id longius procedente Prin- cipum cura in toto illo Ecclesiae per Romanum imperium diffusae corpore apparuit. Processit in publicum ornata, ut novae nuptae solent, mariti sui potentiam omnibus malis ostendens. Τῷ ἀνδρὶ, id est, in honorem mariti. Alluditur ad Esaiae 54. & seqq.

Distinguitur ita à castris sanctorum, quae in terra sunt. Parata, sicut sponsa ornata, id est, magnifice, ut Arethas habet: tum enim sponsae maxime sese or- nant, cum in thalamum ducuntur. Quod ergo spon- sam vocat, dignitatis, amoris, laetitiae, desiderii est: Quod ornatam, splendoris, gloriae, Majestatis, perfe- ctionis. Adducitur sponso jam futuro marito suo, ut vinculum perpetuum & indissolubile innuatur, Ro- man. 8. ult. ideo nuptiarum fit mentio, v. 9.

## 21:3
Vers. 3. Καὶ ἤκουσα φωνῆς μεγάλης ἐκ τῦ ὐρανῦ.) From the highest heaven, that is, from Christ. In the Manuscript ἐκ τῦ θρόνε. That great voice was either of the Lamb the Bridegroom, or of the living creatures or the Elders, because it was heard from the throne.

Λεγόσης· ἰδὺ ἡ σκηνὴ τῦ Θεῦ μετὰ τῦν ἀνθρώπων, καὶ σκηνώ σει μετ’ αὐτῶν.) That is, ἐν ᾗ σκηνώσει. See above 13, 6. Magnificent was the habitation of God in the Tabernacle built by Moses, Lev. 26, 11. But this is much more magnificent, John 1, 10. These and the following are taken from Ezek. 37, 27. Cities are wont to be expressed under the name of tents, as Isa. 32, 20. 54, 2.

Καὶ αὐτοὶ λαοὶ αὐτῦ ἔσονται.) Those who will be in the Church will serve God openly and plainly.

Καὶ αὐτὸς ὁ Θεὸς ἔσαι μετ’ αὐτῶν.) The sense is: God will protect them. Concerning this locution see Luke 1, 28. Matt. 28, 28. The Caesarean [Eusebius] observed that the tabernacle of Moses was a prefiguration of the Church, and the Church a type of that eternal tabernacle which we await in heaven. Conf. 2 Cor. 5, 6. 7. 8. John 14, 3. 17, 24. Phil. 1, 23. 1 Thess. 4, 17. In that most blessed tabernacle are promised those things which are desired for perfect happiness, ἀφαίρεσις τὲ κακῶν, the deprivation and absence of all evils, and θέσις τὲ καλῶν, the placement and presence of all goods. Which we shall have primarily in one GOD: because He will be all in all to us, 1 Cor. 15, 28. In the embraces of the most sweet and blessed Christ, the bride, in the school of this Teacher, finds the consummated fullness of all love, all honor, all wealth, all wisdom. We are also here the people of the Lord, Lev. 26, 11. 12. temples of God, 2 Cor. 6, 16. And it has not yet appeared what we shall be, 1 John 3, 2. But from this place primarily, as well as from the disputation of Christ concerning the resurrection of the dead, Matt. 22, it is clear that the formula of the covenant of circumcision, and the name of the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, the God of Jacob, implies not only protection in this, but also in the other life.

Latin:

Vers. 3. Καὶ ἤκουσα φωνῆς μεγάλης ἐκ τῦ ὐρανῦ.) Ex summo caelo, id est, a Christo. In Manuscripto ἐκ τῦ θρόνε. Vox illa magna vel Agni Sponsi, vel animalium aut Seniorum fuit, quia de throno audita.

Λεγόσης· ἰδὺ ἡ σκηνὴ τῦ Θεῦ μετὰ τῦν ἀνθρώπων, καὶ σκηνώ σει μετ’ αὐτῶν.) Id est, ἐν ᾗ σκηνώσει. Vide supra 13, 6. Magnifica fuit Dei habitatio in Tabernaculo per Mosem structo, Levit. 26, 11. At multo haec magnificentior Joh. 1, 10. Sumta haec & se- quentia ex Ezech. 37, 27. Solent urbes sub nomine tentorio- rum exprimi, ut Esa. 32, 20. 54, 2.

Καὶ αὐτοὶ λαοὶ αὐτῦ ἔσονται.) Illi qui in Ecclesia erunt pa- lam & aperte Deo servient.

Καὶ αὐτὸς ὁ Θεὸς ἔσαι μετ’ αὐτῶν.) Sensus est : Deus eos tu- tabitur. De hac loquutione vide Luc. 1, 28. Matth. 28, 28. Re- te Caesariensis observavit tabernaculum Mosis προτύπωσιν Ec- clesiae, Ecclesiam typum istius aeterni tabernaculi, quod in coelo expectamus, esse. Conf. 2. Cor. 5, 6. 7. 8. Joh. 14, 3. 17, 24. Phil. 1, 23. 1. Thess. 4, 17. In illo beatissimo tabernacu- lo promittuntur, quae ad perfectam felicitatem desideran- tur, ἀφαίρεσις τὲ κακῶν, omnium malorum privatio & absen- tia, & θέσις τὲ καλῶν, omnium bonorum positio & præsentia. Quæ in uno DEO imprimis habebimus: quia erit nobis omnia in omnibus, 1. Cor. 15, 28. In Christi suavissimi & beatissimi amplexibus sponsa, in hujus Doctoris schola, omnis amoris, omnis honoris, omnis opulentiæ, omnis sapientiæ consum- matam invenimus plenitudinem. Sumus & hic populus Domini, Lev. 26, 11. 12. templa Dei, 2. Cor. 6, 16. Et nondum ap- paruit, quid futuri simus, 1. Joh. 3, 2. Ex hoc autem imprimis loco, necnon e disputatione Christi de resurrectione mortuo- rum, Matth. 22. liquet, quod formula fœderis circumcisionis, & nomen Dei Abrahæ, Dei Isaaci, Dei Jacobi inferat non tantum protectionem in hac, sed etiam in altera vita.

## 21:4
V. 4. And he will wipe away every tear from their eyes.) See above VII, 17. That happiness easily abolished the memory of the old things. In the manuscript ἐκ τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν, as also above.

And death shall be no more.) Pestilence and diseases sent in because of public idolatry will cease. See above VI, 8. and XVI, 2. A similar expression is in Isaiah 25, 8. concerning the times of Hezekiah, from where also those words which immediately preceded are taken. There was a great similarity both of mighty works and of events between Hezekiah and Theodosius the Great.

Neither mourning.) No mourning of Christians for their brothers killed through the cruelty of judges, such as there had been over Stephen, Acts 7, 2.

Neither crying out.) No sedition of the people against the Christians. In this sense you have κραυγάζειν in John 18, 40. 19, 6. They will no longer shout: The Christians to the lion: and how long the third race? An application of the passage of Isaiah 65, 23.

Neither pain shall be any more.) Christians will no longer be driven into prison, into mines, into stone quarries. We have had πόνον for trouble or pain also above XVI, 10. and 11. So also in Isaiah 66, 7. and elsewhere.

For the first things have passed away.) In the manuscript ὅτι is missing. But these things were before: now they are stored away, He sits in quiet. Those times of the dragon inspiring the beast have passed. So we have had ἀπῆλθεν also above XVIII, 14. עָבַר.

More vehement movements of the heart express tears, sin brings about death, a notable or any long-lasting evil brings about mourning, a sudden and vehement disturbance brings about crying out; by labor, hardships and troubles are noted, Heb. 5, 7. Job 3, 18. All those things will be absent, because they do not consist with blessedness, Isaiah 25, 7. 8. ch. 54, 11. ch. 66, 12. 20. 21. Matt. 5, 4. ch. 9, 15. 1 Cor. 15, 54.

Latin:

V. 4. Καὶ ἐξαλείψει πᾶν δάκρυον ἀπὸ τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν αὐτῶν.) Vide supra VII, 17. Felicitas illa facile abolevit veterum me- moriam. In manuscripto ἐκ τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν, quomodo & supra.

Καὶ ὁ θάνατος οὐκ ἔσται ἔτι.) Pestilentia & morbi ob ido- latriam publicam immissi cessabunt. Vide supra VI, 8. & XVI, 2. Par locutio apud Esaiam 25, 8. de temporibus Eze- chiæ, unde & illa verba petita, quæ proxime præcessere. Ma- gna fuit & virtutum & rerum similitudo inter Ezechiam & Theodosium Magnum.

Οὔτε πένθος.) Nullus luctus Christianorum ob fratres eo- rum per judicum sævitiam interfectos, qualis fuerat super Stephano, Act. 7, 2.

Οὔτε κραυγὴ.) Nulla seditio populi contra Christianos. Hoc sensu κραυγάζειν habes Joh. 18, 40. 19, 6. Non ultra cla- mabunt: Christianos ad leonem: & usque quo genus ter- tium? Applicatio loci Esaiæ 65, 23.

Οὔτε πόνος οὐκ ἔσται ἔτι.) Non amplius agentur Christiani in carcerem, in metalla, in latomias. Πόνον pro molestia aut dolore habuimus & supra XVI, 10. & 11. Sic & Esaiæ 66, 7. & alibi.

Ὅτι τὰ πρῶτα ἀπῆλθον.) In Manuscripto deest ὅτι. Sed hæc prius fuere: nunc recondita Sedet quiete. Transiere illa tempora draconis feram inspirantis. Sic ἀπῆλ- θεν habuimus & supra XVIII, 14. עָבַר.

Lacrimas exprimunt vehementiores cordis motus, mortem conciliant peccatum, luctum insigne aut diuturnum quodvis malum, clamorem subita & vehemens perturbatio; per labo- rem ærumna & molestie notantur, Ebr. 5, 7. Job. 3, 18. Ea omnia aberunt, quia cum beatitudine non consistunt, Esaiæ 25, 7. 8. cap. 54, 11. cap. 66, 12. 20. 21. Matth. 5, 4. c. 9, 15. 1. Cor. 15, 54.

## 21:5
Verf. 5. And he who sat on the throne said.) On the first throne, that is, God. See above IV, 2. 9. 10. V, 1. and elsewhere often in this book.

Behold, I make all things new.) Isaiah 43, 19 has these words, where it treats of the people returning from Babylon.

And he says to me. Write.) As above XIX, 9. It is a great thing and well to be remembered.

For these words are true and faithful.] So also in the cited place 19, 9. The things which you have now heard from Christ are truly wonderful, but they will come to pass in this way. So also below XXII, 6. These things are said with sincere faith. Nor will power be lacking to give effect to these things.

The first things have departed, as if to say according to Cornelius: The former life, not vital but mortal, which was death rather than life, with its countless miseries, has now passed. Henceforth there will not be a time of labors and hardships: that first storm of warfare and labors has departed: what will follow henceforth for all eternity will be a time of peace, joy, and triumph.

By the name of new creatures come the reborn, because renewal begins here, it will be perfected there: as regards the beginning, the faithful are said to have righteousness here, as regards the completion, to expect righteousness in the future παλιγγενεσίᾳ, Matt. 19, 28. Gal. 5, 5. 2 Pet. 3, 13. in the full ἀποκαταστάσει of all things, Acts 3, 21. Furthermore, the word γράψον repeated for the twelfth time teaches that the divine scriptures were not adorned without a command, and that they are therefore to be valued most highly, and ought to be most commended to us, and not once, but more often read and reread: especially it enjoins upon us the scrutiny of the Apocalypse, lest any doubt should arise concerning its truth (for the Spirit foresaw that there would not be lacking those who would deny it) it is added, that these are true and faithful, so that, to wit, we may be rendered indubitable of their certain completion: Conf. c. 19, 9. c. 22, 6. 1 Tim. 1, 15. 2 Tim. 2, 11. c. 3, 1. Tit. 3, 8. For they are so true (thus Arethas paraphrases) that I also command you to commit these things to writing, lest they fall into any oblivion, because they are certain to come to pass.

Latin:

Verf. 5. Καὶ εἶπεν ὁ καθήμενος ἐπὶ τῷ θρόνῳ.) In primo so- lio, id est, Deus. Vide supra IV, 2. 9. 10. V, 1. & alibi hoc li- bro sæpe.

Ἰδοὺ, καινὰ ποιῶ πάντα.) Habet hæc verba Esaias 43, 19. ubi de populo agitur reduce ex Babylonia.

Καὶ λέγει μοι. Γράψον.) Ut supra XIX, 9. Res magna est & bene retinenda.

Ὅτι οὗτοι λόγοι ἀληθινοὶ καὶ πιστοί εἰσι.] Sic & dicto loco 19, 9. Mira sane sunt, quæ jam a Christo audisti, sed ita evenient. Sic & infra XXII, 6. Dicuntur hæc sincera fide. Nec poten- tia deerit ad hæc effecta danda.

Prima abierunt, q. d. secundum Cornelium: Prior vita non vitalis, sed mortalis, quæ potius mors fuit, quam vita, cum suis miseriis innumeris jam transiit. Deinceps non erit laborum & ærumnarum tempus: prima illa militiæ ac laborum tempestas abiit: quod deinceps sequetur in omne ævum, tempus erit pacis, lætitiæ & triumphi.

Novæ creaturæ nomine veniunt & renati, quia renova- tio hic incipit, ibi perficietur: quoad initium justitiam hic habere, quoad complementum expectare justitiam dicuntur fideles in παλιγγενεσίᾳ futura, Matth. 19, 28. Gal. 5, 5. 2. Petr. 3, 13. in plena ἀποκαταστάσει omnium, Act. 3, 21. Cæterum vox γράψον duodecima vice repetita docet, non absque mandato scripturas divinas adornatas, easque maximi ideo faciendas, nobisque esse debere quam commendatissimas, nec semel, sed sæpius legendas & relegendas: imprimis etiam Apocaly- pseos nobis injungit scrutinium, de cujus veritate ne scrupu- lus suboriatur (prævidit enim Spiritus, non defuturos, qui eam negaturi sunt) additur, vera hæc esse, ac fidelia, ut scil. de certo eorum complemento reddamur indubitati: Conf. c. 19, 9. c. 22, 6. 1. Tim. 1, 15. 2. Tim. 2, 11. c. 3, 1. Tit. 3, 8. Adeo nam- que vera sunt, (sic παραφράζει Arethas) ut & scripturæ man- dare te jubeam ista, ne in ullam oblivionem veniant, quod certa sint futura.

## 21:6
Verse 6. And he said to me, I have become the A and the Ω, the beginning and the end.) He repeats what was said above at 1, 1. Arethas has I have become. And it is I have become for all time, in the Hebrew manner.

I will give to the one who thirsts from the fountain of the water of life-

δωρεὰν) In the Manuscript, τῆς πηγῆς is not present. If I have been faithful in these temporal promises, I shall be also in the eternal ones, of which these are the image and pledge. Living water, מֵי הַחַיִּים, signifies the Spirit elsewhere, but here it signifies eternal life itself, because it never ends, just as water in its own way flows perpetually. I will give, he says, to the thirsty, that is, to the one who avidly desires eternal life. See Matt. 5:6 and what is said there. But why is 'freely' added? Because when he gives eternal life, he will stipulate nothing in return for it. But the honor of eternal life is also called a reward. So it is. But the reward is immensely greater than the works. For an eternal good, God could have stipulated eternal works: He was content with works of no long time. For the actions of eternal life are rewards, not works.

Arethas reads wrongly [if he reads] γέγονα ἐγὼ τὸ Α· καὶ τὸ Ω. I have become A & O. For the other Codices with great consensus have γέγονε: And the context shows that it concerns the consummation of things, which that word expresses, c. XVI. 13. c. I. 8. 11. Is. 43:10, 44:6, c. 48:13. These things, says Primasius, ought to be believed, not explained: especially because it says it has been done in the past in such a way that it does not allow anyone to doubt about the future. Διψῶντι let there be a promise, TO THE THIRSTY, as Matt. 5:6, c. 11:27, John 7:36. The fountain of living water is the Holy Spirit, and his grace, John 7:38, c. 4:14, Rev. XXI. 1, Is. 41:17, c. 44:3, c. 55:1, Ez. 47:1, Joel 3:18. Add also Jer. 2:36, Ps. 36:10. Lest strangers, says Primasius, fail from thirst in this desert, they are rained upon, so that, having been made citizens, they may be continually inebriated from the torrent of God's delights. But both are freely, because eternal life is the grace of God, Rom. 6:23. Cf. below c. XXII. 17. The title of inheritance implies the same. For what son earns an inheritance? But we are all heirs, sons of God, and each one indeed an heir in full: because to each one God will be all in all, 1 Cor. 15:28. When one comes through hope to the reality, God himself, as Primasius says again, will be the reward of eternal blessedness for the elect, which, having been possessed by him, they may possess forever. As if he were saying, says Cornelius à Lapide, Now they are finished, now they are brought to completion, whatever God had most wisely ordained from eternity concerning the world, concerning the Elect, concerning the reprobate. Now it is done; whatever had to be done in the mortal life of men: Now it is done, whatever had to be given and done for them pertaining to the glory and happiness of the saints: Now it is done, whatever will be done throughout all eternity.

Latin:

Verf. 6. Καὶ εἶπέ μοι, γέγονα τὸ Α καὶ τὸ Ω, ἀρχὴ καὶ τέ- λος.) Repetit dicta supra I, 1. Arethas habet γέγονα ἐγώ. Et est γέγονα pro omni tempore, more Hebræo.

Ἐγὼ τῷ διψῶντι δώσω ἐκ τῆς πηγῆς τοῦ ὕδατος τῆς ζωῆς-

δωρεὰν) In Manuscripto non est τῆς πηγῆς. Si in his pro- missis temporalibus fidus fui, ero & in æternis, quorum hæc imago & arra sunt. Aqua viva, מֵי הַחַיִּים alibi spiritum significat, hic vero vitam ipsam æternam, quia nunquam definit, sicut aqua suo modo perpetuum fluit. Dabo, ait, sitienti, id est, avide vitam æternam cupienti. Vide Matth. 5,6. & ibi dicta. At cur additur gratis? Quia cum vitam æternam dabit, nihil pro ea stipulabitur. At vitæ æternæ honos etiam merces dicitur. Sic est. Sed merces im- mensum major opera. Pro æterno bono Deus potuisset æter- nas operas stipulari: Contentus fuit operis non longi tempo- ris. Nam vitæ æternæ actiones præmia sunt, non opera.

Malè Arethas legit [si legit] γέγονα ἐγὼ τὸ Α· καὶ τὸ Ω. factus ego sum A & O. Cæteri enim Codi- ces magno consensu habent γέγονε: Et συνέχεια docet de rerum consummatione, quam vox illa ex- primit, agi, c. XVI. 13. c. I. 8.11. Es. 43,10.44,6. c. 48, 13. Hæc, inquit Primasius, credi oportet, non expo- ni: præsertim quia sic dicit factum esse de præteri- to, ut dubitare quenquam non sinat de futuro. Δι- ψῶντι sit promissio, SITIENTI, ut Matth. 5, 6. c. 11, 27. Joh. 7, 36. Fons aquæ vivæ Spiritus sanctus est, ejusque gratia, Joh. 7,38.c.4,14. Ap. XXI. 1. Es. 41, 17. c. 44, 3. c. 55, 1. Ez. 47,1. Joël. 3,18. Adde & Jerem. 2, 36. Ps. 36,10. Ne peregrini, inquit Primasius, in hac eremo siti deficiant, compluuntur, ut cives facti ex torrente deliciarum Dei jugiter inebrientur. U- trumque autem gratis, quia gratia Dei vita æter- na Rom. 6, 23. Conf. infra c. XXII. 17. Idem infert hæreditatis titulus. Ecquis enim filius meretur hæ- reditatem? Sumus autem hæredes omnes Dei filii, & singuli quidem hæredes ex asse: quia singulis De- us erit omnia in omnibus, 1. Cor. 15, 28. Cum per spem venitur ad rem, ipse Deus dicente iterum Pri- masio erit electis æternæ beatitudinis præmium, quod ab eo possessi possideant in æternum. Quasi dicat, inquit Cornelius à Lapide, Jam finita sunt, jam perducta sunt ad complementum, quæcunq; Deus de mundo, de Electis, de reprobis ab æterno disposuerat sapientissime. Jam factum est; quicquid in vita homi- num mortali faciendum erat: Jam factum est, quic- quid ad gloriam & felicitatem sanctorum pertinens eis dandum & faciendum erat: Jam factum est, quic- quid fiet per omnem æternitatem.

## 21:7
V. 7. Ὁ νικῶν) He who will allow himself to be overcome neither by fear nor by pleasure. See above II.7, 11, 17, 26, III. 7, 12, 21, XV. 2.

Κληρονομήσει ταῦτα) Thus also the Manuscript κληρονομήσει, that is, he will possess by perpetual right, in the way that landed property was held among the Hebrews. Ταῦτα is a construction looking more to the thing than to the words, because in that living water, that is, in eternal life, many goods are understood equally.

Καὶ ἔσομαι αὐτῷ Θεὸς) That is, I will benefit him perpetually. See Matt. 22:32. For the same it is said: I will be a Father to him.

Καὶ αὐτὸς ἔσται μοι ὑὸς) That is, he will be like me in eternal blessedness. See this of ours in the Gospel 1:12 and in the epistle chapter III, 2, Paul in Rom. 8:23, Luke 20:36, Matt. 19:28.

Just as a King conspicuous on a Royal throne is equally in the eyes of individuals and of all who are standing by: for individuals see the King as perfectly, and feed themselves on him, as do all, just as if individuals alone had the King, that is, the appearance and image of the King, in their eyes: So also God, as an immense sun seen by the blessed, and blessing them with his vision, that is, possessing and possessed, so fills the minds of individuals and of all, that individuals say to him with the Psalmist: You are my God; and with St. Thomas: My Lord and my God. Again, just as the same music fills, feeds, and delights the ears of individual listeners equally as it does all: so also God will fill, feed, and inebriate individual Blessed ones with himself and all his delights and goods, equally as he does all. O thrice and four times blessed are they, whose lot, portion, honor, pleasure, glory, will be nothing other than God the Best and Greatest, as Cornelius has it here.

Latin:

V. 7. Ὁ νικῶν) Qui nec metu nec voluptate vinci se pa- tietur. Vide supra II.7. 11. 17. 26. III. 7. 12. 21. XV. 2.

Κληρονομήσει ταῦτα) Sic & Manuscriptus κληρονομήσει, id est, perpetuo jure possidebit, quomodo res soli teneban- tur apud Ebræos. Ταῦτα est constructio rem magis respi- ciens, quam verba, quia in illa aqua viva, id est, in vita æterna, multa pariter intelliguntur bona.

Καὶ ἔσομαι αὐτῷ Θεὸς) Id est perpetuo ei benefaciam. Vid. Matth, 22, 32. Pro eodem dicitur: Ero illi Pater.

Καὶ αὐτὸς ἔσται μοι ὑὸς) Id est, mei similis erit æterna beatitudine. Vide hunc nostrum in Evangelio I.12. & in epi- stola capite III, 2. Paulum Rom.8,23. Luc. 20,36. Matth. 19,28.

Sicut Rex in throno Regali conspicuus, æque est in oculis singulorum, ac omnium adstantium: singuli e- nim tam perfecte Regem vident, eoque se pascunt ac o- mnes, perinde ac si singuli soli Regem, id est Regis spe- ciem & effigiem haberent in oculis suis: Sic & Deus quasi sol immensus visus a beatis, eosq́; sua visione beans, hoc est possidens & possessus, ita implet mentes singulorum atq́; omnium, ut singuli dicant ei cum Psal- te: Deus meus es tu; & cum S. Thoma: Dominus meus & Deus meus. Rursum sicut musica eadem sin- gulorum audientium aures implet, pascit & oblectat, æque ac omnium: ita & Deus singulos Beatos seipso omnibusq́; suis deliciis & bonis implebit, pascet & ine- briabit, æque ac omnes. O terque quaterque beati, quorum sors, pars, honor, voluptas, gloria, non erit alia, quam Deus Optimus Maximus, ut hic habet Cornelius.

## 21:8
V. 8. Τοῖς δὲ δειλοῖς) That is, those who have deserted the Christian profession out of fear of inconveniences.

Καὶ ἀπίστοις) Those who have refused to receive the Gospel will be in an equal case.

Καὶ ἁμαρτωλοῖς) This is absent in the best books.

Καὶ ἐβδελυγμένοις) Under this name are signified those who are ἀρσενοκοῖται & μαλακοὶ, 1 Cor. 6:10. That crime is called תועבה Lev. 18:22. In Greek βδέλυγμα. But here it is a participle for the plural in the Hebrew manner. The same word is in a similar sense in the Greek Hos. 9:10.

Καὶ φονεῦσι) You have this word in 1 Peter 4:15. Likewise also φόνοι among the crimes excluding one from the kingdom of heaven, Galatians 5:21.

Καὶ πόρνοις) Take as in 1 Corinthians 5:9, 10; chapter 6:9; Ephesians 5:5; 1 Timothy 1:10. Adulterers are here also especially included.

Καὶ φαρμακοῖς) So also in the Manuscript in this place and below XXII. 15. It is a word taken from the LXX Interpreters, Exodus 7:11; chapter 9:10; chapter 22:17; Deuteronomy 18:10; Jeremiah 27:7; Daniel 1:2; Malachi 3:5. Moreover, they are usually called this, not only poisoners, but also those who use evil arts of magic. Φαρμακεῖα is mentioned among the crimes in the aforementioned place, Galatians 5:20.

Καὶ εἰδωλολάτραις) For even some who wished to be called Christians contaminated themselves by offering incense or by eating of things sacrificed. Compare 1 Corinthians 6:9; Ephesians 5:5; 1 Timothy 1:9, 10; and the aforementioned place in Galatians.

Καὶ πᾶσι τοῖς ψεύδεσι) In the Manuscript καὶ πᾶσι τοῖς ψεύσταις) So also in the aforementioned place in Timothy, among those who are wretched, ψεῦσται are placed, by which name we have said are understood those who violate pacts or contracts, Isaiah 58:6.

Τὸ μέρος αὐτῶν) The verb στηρίσεται is understood, which is placed in 2 Peter 2:17, or τίθεται, which you have with the noun μέρος, Matthew 24:51, where see the remarks.

Ἐν τῇ λίμνῃ τῇ καιομένῃ πυρὶ καὶ θείῳ) That is, which burns with sulfurous fire. See above XIX. 20.

Ὅ ἐστιν ὁ θάνατος ὁ δεύτερος.) See above XXI. 14.

They are listed almost according to the precepts of the Decalogue; for to the first commandment are to be referred both the δειλοὶ, the timid and delicate, who spare their own life, honors, resources, family, and pleasure, and prefer to save their soul than to lay it down for the glory of Christ, but who in truth lose it entirely, Matthew 10:28, 33; chapter 16:25; and the ἄπιστοι, understood both negatively and privatively, 2 Thessalonians 1:8; and the idolaters, Exodus 20:3; Deuteronomy 6:3. To the second, the sorcerers, Revelation IX. 21; Exodus 22:18; Deuteronomy 18:10. To the third, the ἐβδελυγμένοι can be reduced. To the fifth and sixth belong the murderers and fornicators, Exodus 20:5, 6. To the eighth, the liars, Proverbs 12:12. Whose naming, however, is not an exclusion of others. For all sins are βδελύγματα before the Lord; and consequently those who are subject to them can be said to be expressed by the word ἐβδελυγμένοι. Thus you may refer the rabid dogs no less to the fourth than to the fifth and sixth commandments; those who transgress against the seventh commandment of the Decalogue are also counted among the idolaters, Colossians 3:5. But concerning the sin of concupiscence, which wanders through all the commandments, Romans 7:7; James 1:14. Primasius aptly says here: These are not to be set forth so that they may be understood, whether they are vices of crimes or scourges of punishments, but rather to be thought upon, how they may be avoided through the grace of God. Compare chapter XXII. 15.

Latin:

V. 8. Τοῖς δὲ δειλοῖς) Id est, qui incommodorum metu Christianam, professionem deseruerint.

Καὶ ἀπίστοις) Pari in causa erunt, qui Evangelium reci- pere noluerint.

Καὶ ἁμαρτωλοῖς) Hoc abest in optimis libris.

Καὶ ἐβδελυγμένοις) Sub hoc nomine significantur, qui ἀρσενοκοῖται & μαλακοὶ, 1. Cor. 6, 10. Vocatur id facinus תועבה Levit. 18, 22. Graece βδέλυγμα. Est autem hic more Ebraeo participium pro plurali. Eadem vox pari sensu in Graeco Os. 9, 10.

Καὶ φονεῦσι) Habes hanc vocem 1. Petr. 4, 15. Sic & φόνοι inter crimina a regno caelorum arcentia, Gal. 5, 21.

Καὶ πόρνοις) Sume ut 1. Cor. 5, 9. 10. c. 6, 9. Eph. 5, 5. 1.Tim. 1, 10. Adulteri hic vel praecipue comprehenduntur.

Καὶ φαρμακοῖς) Sic & Manuscriptus hoc loco & infra XXII. 15. Est vox sumpta ab Interpretib. LXX. Exod. 7, 11. c. 9, 10. c. 22, 17. Deut. 18, 10. Jer. 27, 7. Dan. 1, 2. Mal. 3, 5. Vocari autem sic solent, non tantum venefici, sed & qui ma- lis magiae artibus utuntur. Φαρμακεῖα inter crimina memo- rata dicto loco Gal. 5, 20.

Καὶ εἰδωλολάτραις) Nam & quidam, qui Christiani dici volebant, contaminabant se thurificando, aut edendo de im- molatitiis. Conf. 1. Cor. 6, 9. Eph. 5, 5. 1. Tim. 1, 9. 10. & dictum ad Galatas locum.

Καὶ πᾶσι τοῖς ψεύδεσι) In Manuscripto καὶ πᾶσι τοῖς ψεύ- σταις) Sic & dicto ad Timotheum loco inter eos, qui de- plorati sunt, ponuntur ψεῦσται, quo nomine diximus intelli- gi eos, qui pacta contractusve violant Ef. 58, 6.

Τὸ μέρος αὐτῶν) Subauditur verbum στηρίσεται, quod po- nitur 2. Petr. 2, 17. aut τίθεται, quod cum nomine μέρος ha- bes, Matth. 24, 51. ubi dicta vide.

Ἐν τῇ λίμνῃ τῇ καιομένῃ πυρὶ καὶ θείῳ) Id est, quae ardet igne sulfurato. Vide supra XIX. 20.

Ὅ ἐστιν ὁ θάνατος ὁ δεύτερος.) Vide supra XXI. 14.

Recensentur fere secundum praecepta Decalogi, ad primum enim praeceptum referendi sunt tum δειλοὶ, timidi & delicatuli, qui suae vitae, honoribus, facultatibus, familiae, voluptati parcunt, animamque servare, quam pro Christi gloria ponere malunt, quam vero omnino perdunt, Matth. 10, 28.33. c. 16, 25. tum ἄπιστοι, & negative, & privative intellecti 2. Thess. 1, 8. tum idololatræ, Exod. 20, 3. Deut. 6, 3. ad secundum venefici, Apoc. IX. 21. Exod. 22, 18. Deut. 18, 10. ad tertium reduci possunt ἐβδελυγμέ- νοι : ad quintum & sextum homicidae pertinent & scortatores, Exod. 20, 5. 6. ad octavum mendaces Prov. 12, 12. Quorum vero nominatio non est aliorum exclusio. Omnia enim peccata sunt βδελύγμα- τα coram Domino: ac proinde qui illis obnoxii vo- ce ἐβδελυγμένοι expressi dici possunt. Sic canes rabidos non minus ad quartum, quam ad quintum & sextum praeceptum referas: idololatris accensen- tur etiam, qui contra septimum praeceptum Deca- logi praevaricantur, Col. 3, 5. De peccato vero con- cupiscentiae, quod per omnia praecepta vagatur, Rom. 7, 7. Jac. 1, 14. Opportune hic Primasius: Haec vel vitia criminum vel flagella poenarum non expo- nenda sunt ut intelligantur, sed cogitanda potius, quomodo per Dei gratiam devitentur. Conf. c. XXII. 15.

## 21:9
V. 9. Καὶ ἦλθεν εἷς ἐκ τῶν ἑπτὰ Ἀγγέλων, τῶν ἐχόντων τὰς ἑπτὰ φιάλας, γεμούσας τῶν ἑπτὰ πληγῶν τῶν ἐσχάτων) The sixth Angel, who had announced the victory of Constantine. Which was the beginning of this greatest change.

Καὶ ἐλάλησε μετ' ἐμοῦ, λέγων, δεῦρο) So above XVII. 1.

Δείξω σοι τὴν γυναῖκα τὴν νύμφην τοῦ ἀρνίου) That is, the Catholic Church, which was just shown in the guise of a new bride, I will show you more expressly under the form of a city placed upon a mountain, from where it may be seen far and wide. See Matt. 5, 14. Ezek. 11, 2. to which place there is a special reference here. Γυναῖκα here is a noun of sex. For the best books place this word before that τὴν νύμφην.

Et venit unus : Alcafar: One, he says, that is, the first. As the harlot's attire was exhibited above in ch. XVII, with an Angel pointing it out: so now the attire of the Bride, who is also called a woman because of the certainty of the consummation of the marriage, and because she is considered as girded who is to be girded, just as she is called mother in Gal. 4, 26. because of the principal end of marriage. Compare Heb. 12, 22.

PART II. A SPLENDID DESCRIPTION OF THE NEW JERUSALEM.

Latin:

V. 9. Καὶ ἦλθεν εἷς ἐκ τῶν ἑπτὰ Ἀγγέλων, τῶν ἐχόντων τὰς ἑπτὰ φιάλας, γεμούσας τῶν ἑπτὰ πληγῶν τῶν ἐσχάτων) Sextus Ange- lus, qui Constantini victoriam nuntiaverat. Quod initium fuit maximae hujus mutationis.

Καὶ ἐλάλησε μετ' ἐμοῦ, λέγων, δεῦρο) Sic supra XVII. 1.

Δείξω σοι τὴν γυναῖκα τὴν νύμφην τοῦ ἀρνίου) Id est Ecclesiam Catholicam, quae modo ostensa fuit in specie novae nuptae, ostendam tibi expressius sub forma urbis monti impositae, unde longe lateque conspici possit. Vide Matth. 5, 14. Ezech. 11, 2. ad quem locum maxime hic respicitur. Γυναῖκα hic est nomen sexus. Nam libri optimi hanc vocem ponunt ante illud τὴν νύμφην.

Et venit unus : Alcafar: Unus, inquit, id est, pri- mus. Ut meretricius ornatus supra c. XVII. exhibe- batur, monstrante Angelo: ita nunc ornatus Spon- sae, quae mulier etiam vocatur ob certitudinem consummandi matrimonii, & quia cingenda habe- tur pro cincta, uti mater dicitur Gal. 4, 26. ob con- jugii praecipuum finem. Confer Ebr. 12, 22.

PARS II. NOVAE HIEROSOLYMAE SPLENDIDA DESCRIPTIO.

## 21:10
Ver. 10. And he carried me away in the Spirit.] The same expression as above, XVII, 3. To a great and high mountain.] Namely, so that John might see the city not from afar but near, and not only from the outside, but also from the inside, and at the same time might be reminded of the place. Isa. 2, 2. This city was seen situated on an even plain of the mountain. Thus concerning the way to virtue, Hesiod: -- -- But when one reaches the summit, it is easy thereafter, though it be difficult. And he showed me the city.] It is so called the Church, because it is a body associated by a common government. The great.] He rightly calls it great, which extended as widely as the Roman Empire. But 'great' is absent in the Manuscript, as also in the Latin. The holy Jerusalem.] One holy Church, as it is in more than one creed.
