The Church which was shown here was holy, both by the precepts of Christ and by discipline. Descending out of heaven from God.] Above 2.

First, we are accustomed to look at the exterior things in cities: then to scrutinize and investigate the interior, and finally, having known the rest of the state, to inquire into its axioms and privileges along with its laws. Here, therefore, first the walls and streets, etc., then the size, after that the temple, further the citizens and the King, or governor, and also the glory and advantages of the heavenly Jerusalem, and likewise the laws, to which the worship of God alone especially pertains, are described.

Latin:

Vers. 10. Καὶ ἀπήνεγκέ με ἐν Πνεύματι.] Eadem loquutio, quae supra XVII, 3. Ἐπ' ὄρος μέγα καὶ ὑψηλὸν.] Nempe ut Johannes urbem non eminus sed prope, nec extra tantum, sed & intus conspiceret simulq; reminisceretur loci. Esa. 2, 2. Conspiciebatur haec urbs sita in aequali montis planitie. Sic de via ad virtutem Hesiod9: -- -- Ἐπὴν δ' εἰς ἄκρον ἵκηται Ῥηϊδίη δ' ἤπειτα πέλει, χαλεπή περ' ἐοῦσα Καὶ ἔδειξέ μοι τὴν πόλιν.] Ita vocatur Ecclesia, quia est cor- pus quoddam communi regimine sociatum. Τὴν μεγάλην.] Recte magnam vocat, quae tam late se ex- tendebat quam Imperium Romanum. Sed μεγάλην abest in Manuscripto, ut & in Latino. Ἁγίαν Ἱερουσαλὴμ.] Unam Ecclesiam sanctam, ut est in sym- bolo non uno. Sancta erat quae hic monstrabatur Ecclesia, & per praecepta Christi & per disciplinam. Καταβαίνουσαν ἐκ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ ἀπὸ τοῦ Θεοῦ.] Supra 2.

Primum exteriora solemus in civitatibus aspi- cere: tum interiora scrutari & indagare, & postre- mo cognito reliquo statu cum legibus axiomata & privilegia ejusdem inquirere. Hic ergo primum muri & plateae &c. dehinc magnitudo, post templum, porro cives & Rex, vel gubernator, nec non gloria & commoda caelestis Hierosolymae, leges item, ad quas imprimis spectat solius Dei adoratio, describuntur.

## 21:11
Ver. 11. Having the glory of God.] Endowed with that splendor which God had procured for it. For the Genitive here designates the efficient cause. Concerning the word 'glory' we have often spoken already. He will describe the whole city as much more beautiful than Solomon's temple. Its light-bearer.] i.e., in place of the Sun. For the Sun and Moon are 'light-bearers', Gen. 1, 14. 16. Wisd. 13, 2. Among these two stars, since the light of the Sun is more powerful, the name of 'light-bearer' is deservedly given to it singularly. Like a most precious stone, as a jasper stone, crystallizing.] i.e., God himself, who shines in the Church, after the manner of a most precious stone, namely a Jasper, and not just any Jasper, but one that is 'crystallizing', concerning which Dioscorides is to be consulted III, 43. That God himself is described here is apparent from the fact that it is below 24. He, however, is compared to a Jasper also above IV, 3, namely because of his invincible power, as we said there: But here it is added that this Jasper was like crystal, so that we may understand that both strength and purity are conferred upon the Church by God. Jasper is of both kinds. Therefore it can be called 'crystallizing' (masculine) or 'crystallizing' (feminine), just as another Jasper is called 'air-colored'. That 'wc' here means 'namely'.

Latin:

Vers. 11. Ἔχουσαν τὴν δόξαν τοῦ Θεοῦ.] Praeditam eo splendore, quem Deus ei procuraverat. Nam Genitivus hic causam effi- cientem designat. De voce δόξης saepe jam diximus. Describet urbem totam multo pulchriorem Salomonis templo. Ὁ φωστὴρ αὐτῆς.] i. e. vice Solis. Nam Sol & Luna φωστῆρες, Gen. I, 14. 16. Sap. 13, 2. Inter haec duo astra cum potior sit lux Solis, merito ei nomen φωστῆρος singulariter datur. Ὁμοῖον λίθῳ τιμιωτάτῳ ὡς λίθῳ ἰάσπιδι κρυσταλλίζοντι.] i. e. Deus ipse, qui in Ecclesia fulget, ad modum pretiosissimi la- pidis, nempe Jaspidis, nec cujusvis Jaspidis, sed κρυσταλλίζοντος, de quo Dioscorides videndus III, 43. Deum ipsum hic descri- bi apparet ex eo, quod infra 24. Is autem Jaspidi comparatur etiam supra IV, 3. nempe ob vim invictam, ut ibi diximus: Sed hic additur, Jaspidem istam crystallo fuisse similem, ut in- telligamus a Deo Ecclesiae conferri & robur & puritatem. Ja- spis utriusq; est generis. Itaq; dici potest κρυσταλλίζων vel κρυ- σταλλίζουσα, sicut alia Jaspis ἀερίζουσα dicitur. Illudwc hic va- let nempe.

## 21:12
Ver. 12. Having a wall great and high.] Walls exclude the enemy, they keep the citizens safe, Job 1, 10. Isa. XXVI, 1. 2. Zech. II, 5. Such is the doctrine of the Gospel in this matter, great and sublime. In the Manuscript here and in the following it is 'having' (participle), so that it is again nominative instead of oblique. Having twelve gates.] Access to this doctrine through the promises once made to the Fathers concerning Christ. Gates, 'pethachim'. And at the gates twelve Angels.] Namely those Angels who appeared to the Fathers. And names written, which are those of the twelve tribes of the sons of Israel.] In the Manuscript: 'Which are the names of the twelve', etc., i.e., the names of the Patriarchs, from whom the tribes take their name. Wherefore Joseph is to be taken here for Ephraim and Manasseh, as in Ezek. 48, 31. and following.

Latin:

Vers. 12. Ἔχουσαν τεῖχος μέγα καὶ ὑψηλὸν.] Moenia exclu- dunt hostem, cives tutos servant, Job. I, 10. Esa. XXVI, 1. 2. Zach. II, 5. Talis est in hac re doctrina Evangelii magna & sublimis. In Manuscripto hic & in sequenti ἴχουσα, ut rursum sit rectus pro obliquo. Ἔχουσαν πυλῶνας δώδεκα.] Aditus ad hanc doctrinam per promissa olim Patribus facta de Christo. Πυλῶνες, פתחים Καὶ ἐπὶ τοῖς πυλῶσιν Ἀγγέλους δώδεκα.] Nempe eos Ange- los, qui Patribus apparuere. Καὶ ὀνόματα ἐπιγεγραμμένα, ἅ ἐστι τῶν δώδεκα φυλῶν τῶν υἱῶν Ἰσραήλ.] In Manuscripto: Ἅ ἐστι τὰ ὀνόματα τῶν δώδεκα, &c. i. e. nomina Patriarcharum, unde tribus nomen ducunt. Quare Josephus sumendus hic pro Ephraim & Manasse, ut Ezech. 48, 31. & seqq.

## 21:13
Ver. 13. From the east three gates, and from the north three gates, and from the south three gates, and from the west three gates.] So that access may be open to it from every side, just as once to the cities of refuge. Those four cardinal points signify the whole world, as can be seen in Luke 13, 29. Here above 7, 1. c. 20, 8. But there are three gates at each cardinal point, because of the profession of faith in the Father, Son, and Spirit, the sponsors of salvation.

Latin:

Vers. 13. Ἀπὸ ἀνατολῶν πυλῶνες τρεῖς, καὶ ἀπὸ βοῤῥᾶ πυλῶνες τρεῖς, καὶ ἀπὸ νότου πυλῶνες τρεῖς, καὶ ἀπὸ δυσμῶν πυλῶνες τρεῖς.] Ut ab omni parte eo pateat aditus, sicut olim ad urbes confu- gii. Quatuor isti Cardines totum orbem significant, ut vide- re est Luc. 13, 29. Hic supra 7, 1. c. 20, 8. Ternae autem portae in quoque cardine, ob professionem fidei in Patrem, Filium & Spiritum, sponsores salutis.

## 21:14
Ver. 14. And the wall of the city, having twelve foundations.] Just as a structure rests upon a foundation: so the Christian faith rests upon the testimony of the Apostles, who, having received it from Christ, handed it down to the world: all fulfilling with their mouth, and some with their writings, mystically the words of Isa. 58, 12. And on them the twelve names of the twelve Apostles.] That is, by the foundations are signified those twelve Apostles, of whom it is treated in Acts I. Thus John. He acknowledged himself also to be mixed with the Princes among the Achaeans, just as Aeneas acknowledged himself in the painting of Dido; we have said that Paul and Barnabas are held as supernumeraries above XII, 1.

Latin:

Vers. 14. Καὶ τὸ τεῖχος τῆς πόλεως, ἔχον θεμελίους δώδεκα.[ Sicut fundamento innititur structura: Ita fides Christiana te- stimonio Apostolorum, qui a Christo accepta orbi tradide- runt: ore omnes, quidam & scriptis implentes μυσικῶς verba Esa. 58, 12. Καὶ ἐπ' αὐτῶν δώδεκα ὀνόματα τῶν δώδεκα Ἀποστόλων.] Id est, per fundamenta significantur duodecim illi Apostoli, de quibus agitur Act. I. Ita Johannes. Se quoque Principibus permixtum agnovit Achivis, ut se Aeneas agnovit in tabula Didonis, Paulum & Barnabam diximus haberi velut supernumerarios supra XII, 1.

## 21:15
Ver. 15. And he who was speaking with me.] The Angel. He had a golden reed as a measure.] It is an apposition of sense: He had a golden rod, which was a measuring instrument. See above 11, 1. Ez. 40, 3. There is furthermore a catachresis. For that rod is called a reed, because rods were for the most part made of reed. Thus we say a golden box, when 'pyxis' is properly made of boxwood. But that rod was golden, so that it might correspond to the building. All things excellent.

That he might measure the city.] Above 11, 2. John was forbidden to measure the city of Jerusalem, as one that would be of no good use. Now the mystical Jerusalem, as being of the highest and perpetual use, the Angel himself measures, as in Zechariah II, 2.

Latin:

Vers. 15. Καὶ ὁ λαλῶν μετ' ἐμοῦ.) Angelus. - Εἶχε μέτρον κάλαμον χρυσοῦν.) Est appositio sensus: Habe- bat perticam auream, quae erat mensorium instrumentum. Vi- de supra 11, 1. Ez. 40, 3. Est praeterea κατάχρησις. Pertica enim illa calamus dicitur, quia plerumq; perticae erant ex arundine. Sic pyxida auream dicimus, cum πυξίς sit proprie e buxo. Au- rea autem erat illa pertica, ut congrueret ædificio. Omnia præstantia.

Ἵνα μετρήσῃ τὴν πόλιν.) Supra 11, 2. Johannes vetitus erat urbem Hierosolyma metiri, ut quæ futura esset nulli bono usui. Nunc mystica Hiorosolyma, ut summi ac perpetui usus metitur ipse Angelus, ut apud Zachariam II, 2.

## 21:16
Ver. 16. And the city lies foursquare.] Thus Rome, founded by Romulus, was square. That figure signifies perfection. Thus Simonides calls a man exact to the rule: 'foursquare in hands and feet and mind', interpreting the same as 'fashioned without blame'. Plato, Protagoras, and Aristotle in the Rhetoric and in the Nicomachean Ethics make mention of this. Thus in the structure of Ezekiel there are many squares XLI, 21. XLII, 20. XLIII, 16. 17. XLV, 32. XLVII, 16. 17. 20. Add Josephus concerning the Altar, Jewish War V, 14.

And the length of it is as the breadth.) Breadth signifies capacity, length signifies duration. This city contains all men, and will endure forever. See Eph. 3, 18. This was prefigured in the building in Ezekiel 48, 16.

And he measured the city with the reed at twelve thousand stadia.) That twelve is not found in the best books, just as it is not in the Latin. That city extends as far as the twelve Apostles were able to run. A stadium is a measure of a race, 1 Cor. 9, 24. A thousand stadia, that is, an immense course. For a thousand is put for an infinite number.

The length and the breadth and the height of it are equal.) He does not say the same thing that he said just now when he was explaining the square form, but something else, namely that wherever one went, the height of both the walls and the buildings was equal: just as had been said concerning the length and the breadth. This equality signifies that all Christians are equal in dignity in the business of religion. For we said that dignity is signified by height at that place in Eph. 3, 8.

Latin:

Vers. 16. Καὶ ἡ πόλις τετράγωνος κεῖται.) Sic Roma à Ro- mulo condita quadrata. Ea figura perfectionem significat. Ita Simonides virum ad regulam exactum vocat: χερσί τε κὴ πο- σὶ νόῳ τε τετράγωνον, idipsum interpretans ἄνευ ψόγω τετυ- γμένον. Meminere Plato, Protagoras, Aristoteles in Rhetoricis & in Nicomachiis. Sic in Ezechielis structura multa quadra- ta XLI, 21. XLII, 20. XLIII, 16.17. XLV, 32. XLVII, 16.17.20. Ad- de Josephum de Altari, belli Judaici V, 14.

Καὶ τὸ μῆκος αὐτῆς ὅσον τὸ πλάτος.) Latitudo capacitatem, longitudo durationem significat. Hæc urbs omnes capit ho- mines, & semper durabit. Vide Eph. 3, 18. Figuratum hoc in ædificio apud Ezechielem 48, 16.

Καὶ ἐμέτρησε πόλιν τῷ καλάμῳ ἐπὶ σαδίως δώδεκα χιλιά- δων δώδεκα.) Illud δώδεκα non reperitur in libris optimis, ut nec in Latino. Eo usque se extendit illa urbs, quousque duo- decim Apostoli currere potuerunt. Stadium est mensura cur- fus, 1. Cor. 9, 24. Mille stadia, id est, cursus immensus. Nam mille ponitur pro infinito.

Τὸ μῆκος κὴ τὸ πλάτος κὴ τὸ ὕψος αὐτῆς ἴσά ἐσι.) Non idem dicit, quod modo cum quadratam formam explicaret, sed ali- ud, nempe quaqua iret, altitudinem & murorum & ædificiorũ suisse æqualem: sicut de longitudine & latitudine dictum fue- rat. Hæc æqualitas significat omnes Christianos in negotio religionis dignitate esse pares. Nam per altitudinem signifi- cari dignitatem diximus ad illum locum Ephes. 3, 8.

## 21:17
V. 17. And he measured the wall of it.) The height of the wall, one hundred and forty-four cubits.) That is, twelve times twelve. Great was the dignity of the Apostles here. But it will be immensely greater in the other age for all Christians whatsoever. They already possess it in their minds as if it were present.

The measure of a man, which is of an Angel.) The sense is: That rod was as great as the stature of the human form in which the Angel appeared: and consequently the cubits were also according to that measure. By that it was signified that men would one day be equal to the angels, Luke 20, 36. Angels are called men when they appear in a manly form, Gen. 18, 2. Jud. 13, 18.

The jasper is called the most precious of gems, therefore it is compared to the light, because God himself, the Sun of the city, was sufficient, on account of its remarkable splendor, to which God himself was also compared, ch. IV. 3. By the epithet crystal-like, perhaps a light is hinted at that is not superficial, but most penetrating, by which even interior counsels are manifested. The heavenly Jerusalem is surrounded by only one wall, not like the earthly one by three, see divine, Angelic, and human; but that wall is not made of brick, as in Jer. XLIII. 9, or of clay, ch. XLVIII. 31, but consists of jasper, by which (wall) Ludov. ab Alcafar ineptly wishes the mass-priests to be figured. For what kind of mass-priests would the walls be? The ramparts signify security, Is. XXVI, 1, gold signifies majesty, the Angels signify protection, the inscription of names signifies possession, the book of life signifies the register of the heavenly citizens, and they shadow them forth. The Apostles are like the foundations of the Church of the N. T., Eph. II. 20, who founded the Church by their living voice and the monuments of the Holy Scriptures, upon whose doctrine and writings it rests as upon an immovable base, Matth. XVI. v. 17. 18. The number twelve is considered perfect, as being cubic. Angels are added to the gates to designate the communion of men and Angels, Heb. XII. 28, and the Angelic joys when the elect enter through the gates, Luke XV. The regions of the world denote the catholicity of the Church, Matth. VIII. 11, ch. XXIV. 31, Luke XIII. 29, Ezech. XLVIII. Architects inscribe their names on the works built by them. But as to the fact that in 1 Cor. III. 11 only one foundation is established, Primasius reconciles it thus: In Christ the Apostles merited to be the foundations of the Church: Christ is the illuminating light, the Apostles are the illuminated light. The quadrangular figure, the square, insinuates constancy and perfection, Eph. III. 18. The capacity of the whole city is estimated at 5,306,250,000 German miles, that is, fifty times thirty-six hundred and twenty-five million thousand miles. Concerning the measure, Primasius not incongruously says: Since the Church gathered from men consists, and exalted by the promises of Christ, hopes for the equality of the Angels, and its every intention sighs for their society; therefore it says the measure of a man, which is of an Angel, or that that city consists partly of Angels already remaining there in perpetual happiness, partly of pilgrims, i.e., men, who are to reign more fully. Perhaps, however, you might not incorrectly refer here that saying of Christ in Luke 20:36, so that ἰσαγγελότης (equality to angels) may also be considered to regard the measure of a man, because we shall be like the Angels not only in quantity of mass, which does not befit Angels, but in any other intelligible likeness, which may be like a stature. Corn. à Lapide praises Gabr. Vasquez, who in part 1, q. 120, c. 1. The measure, he says, of a man, which is of an Angel, as if he were saying, although this measure seemed to be of a man, in reality, however, it was of an Angel, who, under the appearance of a man measuring that city, did not measure with a spiritual and intellectual measure, but with a human one, which is of reeds and cubits. And gathering from thence the magnitude of the heavenly Jerusalem, he exclaims from Baruch 3:24: O Israel! how great is the house of God, and how huge is the place of his possession. Concerning its inhabitants, however, we doubt that it is true what Chrysostom has in Homily 2 to the people of Antioch: How many do you think there are in our city who may be saved? It is indeed a hateful thing that I shall say, yet I will say it: There cannot be found in so many thousands a hundred who may be saved; nay, I even doubt of these. For how great, I ask, is the malice in the young: how great the sluggishness in the old? Whatever Cornelius may also oppose to Chrysostom concerning the innumerable throngs of his religious and Virgins, Priests and Prelates, and Clerics, Martyrs and Anchorites, Confessors, etc., for all of whom, insofar as they adhere to the Antichrist, a place is prepared in the infernal lake, not in heaven. But we, lest we be excluded from that beatitude, should immediately stir up the warning of St. Jerome directed to Eustochium: As often as the vain ambition of the world shall delight you, as often as you shall see anything glorious, pass over in your mind to paradise. Ansbertus, Haymo, Pannonius among Cornelius: The Church, they say, is recorded as being placed in a square, because it is robust through faith, long-suffering through hope, ample through charity, effective through operation. For individual believers have faith, by which they believe what cannot be seen, namely, God triune in persons, and one in majesty. They also have hope, because they hope that they can attain to another thing, which they do not yet see. They also have charity, i.e., the love of God and neighbor. To which virtues, so that their life may be perfect, operation is joined, without which faith is dead.

Latin:

V. 17. Καὶ ἐμέτρησε τὸ τεῖχος αὐτῆς.) Muri altitudinem, Ἑκατὸν τεσσαράκοντα τεσσάρων πηχῶν.) Id est, duodecies duodecim. Magna hic fuit Apostolorum dignitas. At immen- so major erit in altero seculo quorumvis Christianorum. Eam illi jam velut præsentem animo possident.

Μέτρον ἀνθρώπκ, ὅ ἐστιν Ἀγγέλου.) Sensus est: Illa pertica tanta erat, quanta erat statura formæ humanæ, in quaAngelus apparebat: ac proinde ad eum modũ etiam cubiti. Ea significa- batur homines aliquando fore ἰσαγγέλες, Luc. 20, 36. Angeli viri vocantur, ubi virili specie apparent, Gen. 18, 2. Jud. 13, 18.

Jaspis gemmarum dicitur τιμιωτάτος, ideo lu- mini, quod Deus ipse Sol civitatis sufficiebat, com- paratur ob insignem splendorem, cui etiam Deus ipse comparatus fuit, c. IV. 3. Epithetov κρυςαλ- λίζοντι forte innuitur lux non superficiaria, sed pe- netrantissima, qua interiora quoque consilia mani- festantur. Unico tantum muro cincta est cælestis Hierosolyma, non ut terrestris tribus, vid. divino, Angelico & humano; non autem murus ille lateri- tius est, ut Jer. XLIII. 9. vel fictilis, c. XLVIII. 31. sed e Jaspide constans, quo (muro) Ludov. ab Alcafar inepte vult sacrificulos figurari. Quales enim Mis- sifices muri forent? Mœnia securitatem Ef. XXVI, 1. aurum majestatem, Angeli protectionem, nominum inscriptio possessionem, liber vitæ matriculam civium supernorum inserunt, & adumbrant. Fundamento- rum Ecclesiæ N. T. instar sunt Apostoli, Eph. II. 20. qui viva voce & S. literarum monumentis Ecclesiam fundarunt, quorum doctrinæ & scriptis eadem tan- quam immotæ basi innititur, Matth. XVI. v. 17. 18. Numerus duodenarius perfectus censetur, utpote cubicus. Portis Angeli adjiciuntur, ad designan- dam hominum & Angelorum communionem, Ebr. XII. 28. & gaudia Angelica, cum ingrediuntur electi per portas, Luc. XV. Plagæ mundi Catholici- smum Ecclesiæ notant, Matth. VIII. 11. c. XXIV. 31. Luc. XIII. 29. Ezech. XLVIII. Architecti nomina sua inscribunt operibus abs se extructis. Quod au- tem 1. Cor. III. 11. unicum tantum fundamentum con- stituitur, Primasius ita conciliat: In Christo Apostoli meruerunt esse fundamenta Ecclesiæ: Christus lux illu- minans, Apostoli lux illuminata. Quadrangularis fi- gura τὸ τετράγωνον constantiam insinuat & perfe- ctionem, Eph. III.18. Capacitas totius civitatis mil- liarium Germanicorum æstimatur 5306250000. h. e. quinquagies tricies sexcenties viginti quinque millio- num millia milliaria. De mensura non incongrue Primasius: Quoniam ex hominibus conquisita con- stat Ecclesia, & Christi promissionibus sublimata, An- gelorum æqualitatem sperat, omnisque intentio eorum societatem suspirat, propterea dicit mensura hominis, quæ est Angeli, vel quod illa civitas partim ex Angelis ibi jam perpetua felicitate manentibq, partim ex pere- grinis, i. e. hominibus constat plenius regnatura. For- san tamen non inrecte huc referas illud Christi Luc. XX, 36. ut ἰσαγγελότης etiam mensuram hominis spe- ctare censeatur, quod eadem non tantum quanti- tate molis quæ Angelis non convenit: sed alia qua- cunq; intelligibili similitudine gemini Angelis fu- turi simus, quæ instar staturæ sit. Corn. à Lapide lau- dat Gabr. Vasquez, qui 1. part. q. 120. c. 1. Mensura, ait, hominis, quæ est Angeli, quasi dicat, licet hæc mensura videretur esse hominis, revera tamen erat Angeli, qui sub specie hominis metientis civitatem illam non men- sura spirituali & intellectuali, sed humana, quæ est ca- lamorum & cubitorum dimensus est. Colligensq; in- de magnitudinem cœlestis Hierosolymæ, exclamat à Baruch c. III, 24. O Israël! quam magna est domus Dei, & ingens locus possessionis ejus. De incolis tamen ejus verum esse ambigimus, quod habet Chrysost. homil. II. ad popul. Antioch. Quot esse putatis in ci- vitate nostra, qui salvi fiant? Infestum quidem est, quod dicam, dicam tamen: Non possunt in tot millibus cen- tum inveniri, qui salventur: quin & de his dubito. Quanta enim in juvenibus, quæso, malitia: quantus in senibus torpor? Quicquid etiam Cornelius de suorum religiosorum & Virginum, Sacerdotum & Prælatorũ, & Clericorum, Martyrum & Anachoretarum, Con- fessorum &c. innumeris examinibus Chrysostomo op- ponat, quibus omnibus, qua Antichristo adhærent, paratus est locus in infernali lacu, non in cœlo. Nos vero ne excludamur ista beatitudine, subinde S. Hieronymi excitet monitum ad Eustoch. directum: Quotiescunque te vana seculi delectabit ambitio, quo- tiescunq́; aliquid videris gloriosum, ad paradisum mente transgredere. Ansbertus, Haymo, Pannonius apud Cornelium: Ecclesia, inquiunt, in quadro po- sita esse memoratur, quia est robusta per fidem, longa- nimis per spem, ampla per charitatem, efficax per ope- rationem. Habent enim singuli fidelium fidem, qua cre- dunt, quæ videri non possunt, Deum scil. trinum in per- sonis, & unum in majestate. Habent & spem, quia spe- rant se posse contingere ad aliud, quod necdum vident. Habent quoq́; charitatem, i. e. Dei & proximi dilectio- nem. Quibus virtutibus, ut perfecta sit vita illorum, adjungitur operatio, sine qua fides mortua est.

## 21:18
V. 18. And the building of its wall was jasper. That is, an invincible work. See above 2 and 4:3. In the Orphic poems concerning the Jasper: But if a rival force lies against you. There is also here a catachresis, a translation made from a house to a city: such as that: -- They build a horse by the divine art of Pallas.

And the city was pure gold like to pure glass. The color indeed of gold, but the material itself transparent after the manner of glass. That signifies the excellence of the Church perfectly known to God alone. See above 4:6, 15:2, and add Maimonides in the Guide for the Perplexed 2:30.

Latin:

V. 18. Καὶ ἦν ἡ ἐνδόμησις τοῦ τείχους αὐτῆς ἴασπις.] Id est, in- victum opus. Vide supra II. & IV, 3. In Orphicis de Jaspide. Ἐι δέ σοι ἀντίπαλον κεῖται μένος. Est & hic κατάχρησις translatio facta à domo ad urbem: ta- lis illa: -- Equum divina Palladis arte Ædificant.

Καὶ ἡ πόλις χρυσίον καθαρὸν ὅμοιον ὑελῷ καθαρῷ.] Color quidem auri, sed ipsa materia transparens ad modum vitri. Id significat excellentiam Ecclesiæ Deo soli perfecte cognitæ. Vide supra IV, 6. XV, 2. & adde Maimonidem Ductore dubi- tantium II, 30.

## 21:19
V. 19. And the foundations of the wall of the city were adorned with every precious stone. That 'every' is to be explained from what follows, so that the most precious kinds of stones are understood. There is no doubt that it has happened in certain temples and palaces that the foundations were of very precious stone. See Isaiah 28:16, ch. 54:11, where see the sayings, and to Tobit 13:21. This is applied here mystically to signify the excellent virtues of the Apostles. Thus Plato in the Phaedo places precious stones in the heavenly earth.

The first foundation jasper. You have most of these names of stones in Exodus 28:17, 18 and 39:10 and following, and in Josephus 3:8, in the Pontifical breastplate: Some also in Ezekiel 28:13, in the ornaments of the King of Tyre. Jasper is yashpeh in Exodus 28:19, ch. 39:9. In Ezekiel there are more names in the Greek than in the Hebrew, nor is the order the same, so that it cannot be known from that which name corresponds to which. Among the Chaldean Interpreter on Canticles 5:14, the names of the twelve gems are applied to the twelve tribes, the same as here, except that there agate is put for chrysoprase, and ligyrius for hyacinth.

The second, sapphire. The same name in Hebrew is sappir, which we also have in Job 28:6, 16, Canticles 5:15, Isaiah 54:11, Lamentations 4:7, Ezekiel 1:16, ch. 9:2, ch. 10:1, ch. 28:13. Sapphire, of the same color as the sky, signifies that all the thoughts of the Apostles were heavenly. Jerome and Theodoret say the sapphire is of the same color as the sky: for that reason the priests of the Egyptians wore it.

The third, chalcedony. It corresponds to the carbuncle in Exodus. For it is a species of carbuncle, which used to be found near Chalcedon: whence the Latin here called it chalcedonium. Nor does the word kadkod, Isaiah 54:12 and Exodus 28:18, differ from Chalcedon. In the Hebrew of Exodus it is: nophek. This stone signified the burning zeal of the Apostles for the house of God. See John 2:17.

The fourth, emerald. Barak from flashing to the Hebrews. This signifies the sweetness of manners. For the emerald is most pleasant to the sight. See above 4:3.

Latin:

V. 19. Καὶ οἱ θεμέλιοι τοῦ τείχους πόλεως παντὶ λίθῳ τιμίῳ κε- κοσμημένοι.] Illud παντὶ explicandū ex sequentibus, ut intel- ligantur genera lapidum pretiosissima. Non dubium est, quin in templis quibusdam & palatiis evenerit, ut ex lapide admo- dum pretioso essent fundamenta. Vide Esa. 28, 16. c. 54, 11. ubi dicta vide, & ad Tob. 13, 21. Id hic applicatur μυσικῶς ad signi- ficandas Apostolorum virtutes eximias. Sic lapides pretiosos in terra cœlesti ponit Plato in Phædone.

Ὁ θεμέλιος ὁ πρῶτος ἴασπις.] Pleraque hæc lapidum no- mina habes Exod. 28, 17. 18. & 39, 10. & seqq. & apud Josephum 3, 8. in pectorali Pontificio: Quædam & Ezech. 28, 13. in orna- mentis Regis Tyrii. Jaspis est ישפה Exod. 28, 19. c. 39, 9. In E- zechiele plura sunt nomina in Græco, quam in Ebræo, nec or- do idem, ita, ut inde sciri non possit, quod nomē cui respon- deat. Apud Chaldæum Interpretem Cant. V, 14. duodecim gemmarum nomina duodecim tribubus aprantur, eadem quæ hic, nisi quod ibi pro Chrysopraso Achates ponitur, pro Hya- cintho Ligyrius.

ὁ δεύτερος, Σάπφειρος.) Nomen idem in Ebræo ספיר quod habemus & Job. 28, 6. 16. Cant. 5, 15. Es. 54, 11. Lam. 4, 7. Ezech. 1, 16. c. 9, 2. c. 10, 1. c. 28, 13. Sapphirus cœlo concolor significat omnes cogitationes Apostolorum fuisse cœlestes. Cœlo concolorem Sapphirum dicunt Hieron. & Theodoretius: ideo eum gestabant Ægyptiorum sacerdotes.

ὁ τρίτος, Χαλκηδών.) Respondet ἄνθρακι in Exodo. Est enim species ἄνθρακος, quæ reperiri solebat apud Chalcedonem: unde Chalcedonium hic dixit Latinus. Nec abludit à Chalcedone vox כדכד, Es. 54, 12. & Ex. 28, 18. In Ebræo Exodi est: נפך. Significabat hic lapis ardentem zelum Apostolorum pro domo Dei. Vide Joh. 2, 17.

ὁ τέταρτος Σμάραγδος.) ברק à coruscando Ebræis. Is suavitatem morum significat. Smaragdus enim aspectu jucundissimus. Vide supra IV, 3.

## 21:20
V. 20. The fifth, sardonyx. It is a species of onyx, whence it corresponds to the onyx in Exodus, where in the Hebrew it is yashpeh, although the sound of this Hebrew word approaches more closely to jasper. Sardonyx has a triple color. Thus the Apostles exhibited various colors of speech for the souls of the hearers, 1 Cor. 3:1, Heb. 5:13, 1 John 2:13 and following.

The sixth, Sardius.) אדם in Hebrew [is derived] from the color of blood: Pliny says that this gem is red in India. It signifies the readiness of the Apostles to seal their testimony with their blood.

The seventh, Chrysolite.) In Hebrew תרשיש because it was sought from Spain across the Ocean, as Pliny teaches us. It signifies that nothing would be impassable to the Apostles.

The eighth, Beryl.) Thus it is translated in Exodus as שוהם where also the Rabbis [add] אל־כרול with the Arabic article. But שוהם signifies boldness to the Arabs, and the Beryl is believed to add courage to those who wear it. Therefore, the ever-upright spirit of the Apostles is signified.

The ninth, Topaz.) פטדה not only in Exodus, but also in Job 28:19. The color was like that of fresh oil, as Alexander Polyhistor and Agatharchides have reported. That signifies a healing power in the Apostles. It is said specifically that this gem heals the eyes, and the Apostles brought a remedy to the darkness of souls.

The tenth, Chrysoprase.) This name is not found in the Greek of the Old Testament. It is of a somber color, and therefore signifies the severity of the Apostles against sinners.

The eleventh, Hyacinth.) Nor is this name in the Greek Interpreters. There are those who think it corresponds to לשם. But that is translated as Ligyrium. And therefore Jerome, in epistle 129, thinks that Hyacinth and Ligyrium are the same. Hyacinths of the best quality are of an airy color, as Arethas notes here, and Philo explains the hyacinthine color as airy. Wherefore it rightly signifies the spirit of the Apostles, patient of all the storms which the world stirred up against them.

The twelfth, Amethyst.) By the name itself it signifies sobriety, and from its likeness, every kind of temperance. Heb. אחלמה. To the significations which we have mentioned, it is not absurd to add that by these stones and gems is simultaneously shadowed forth the diversity of the lands from which those stones come, and where the Apostles gave a specimen of their virtues. But they err who think that individual articles were contributed to the creed by individual Apostles. For in the most ancient creeds there are not so many articles.

O the admirable magnitude of a single gem, because the entire wall consists of 375 miles in height and 144 cubits in thickness, not to mention the unnamed length! O most precious structure! For what is dearer than gold, gems, and pearls? But indeed this city is entirely golden, its walls all gem-like, all its gates consisting of pearls. Cf. Is. LIV, 11, 12. Tob. XIII. Of the gems, eight are held to be in the breastplate of Aaron, Exod. 28, 19: Sardius, Topaz, Emerald, Jasper, Amethyst, Beryl, Chrysolite. But four here vary: Chalcedony, Sardonyx, Chrysoprase, Hyacinth: yet they say that Onyx and Sardonyx do not differ much. But Junius makes the Carbuncle the Chrysoprase. And what Tremellius translates as Cyanus, they think is Hyacinth; and some judge the Achates to be Chalcedony, and the Jasper to be Adamant: which we leave in the middle. For the Rabbis and other lexicographers will never agree about these. Moreover, they generally wish the virtues of the Apostles to be designated, which it is extremely difficult to apply to individuals. For they even vary in order, Matt. 10:2, Mark 3:18, Luke 6:14. By the Jasper, the most precious of all, they understand the faith of Peter which did not fail, 1 Pet. 1, Luke 22. By the Sapphire, of an azure color shining with golden dots, [they understand] the heavenly conversation and migration of James, who was reddened by blood: By the Chalcedony, resisting those who carve, [they understand] St. John, who could be killed by no one: By the emerald [they understand] Andrew, who flourished before all others, John 1:41. The sardonyx is celebrated for its whiteness and redness, and is considered to express the red martyrdom of Philip. The sardius of a red color is fitted to Bartholomew who was flayed. The clear beryl refers to St. Thomas, having sharp eyes after Christ's resurrection: the chrysolite, the color of gold, to Matthew, his Apostle, because of his birth in India and Ethiopia: the topaz to James of Alphaeus, brother of the Lord, referring to Christ in life and countenance because of the brightness of his doctrine: the chrysoprase to Jude because of his golden confession of Christ among the Edessenes: the fiery hyacinth to James, brother of John, burning with love: concerning which let the writers of gems, Rucus, and others be consulted.

Latin:

V. 20. Ὁ πέμπτος, Σαρδόνυξ.) Est Onycbii species, unde respondet Ὀνυχίῳ in Exod. ubi in Ebræo est ישפה quanquam hujus vocis Ebrææ sonus propius ad Jaspidem accedit. Sardonyx triplicem habet colorem. Sic Apostoli varios exhibebant sermonum colores pro audientium animis, 1. Cor. 3, 1. Ebr. 5, 13. 1. Joh. 2, 13. & seqq.

ὁ ἕκτος, Σάρδιος.) אדם Ebræis à sanguinis colore: rubram esse in India gemmam hanc, dicit Plinius. Significat promptitudinem Apostoloru ad testimoniū suum sanguine obsignandū.

ὁ ἕβδομος, Χρυσόλιθος.) Ebraice תרשיש quia trans Oceanum petebatur ab Hispania, ut Plinius nos docet. Significat is, nihil Apostolis invium fore.

ὁ ὄγδοος, Βήρυλλος.) Sic in Exodo vertitur שוהם ubi & Rabbini אל־כרול cum Arabico artic. At שוהם Arabibus audacia significat, crediturq; Beryllus gestantibus animos addere. Significatur ergo Apostolorum erectus semper animus.

ὁ ἔννατος, Τοπάζιον.) פטדה non in Exodo tantum, sed & Jobi 28, 19. Color erat quasi recentis olei, ut Alexander Polyhistor, & Agatharchides prodidere. Id significat vim sanatricem in Apostolis. Dicitur specialiter ea gemma mederi oculis, & Apostoli animarum caligini remedium attulere.

ὁ δέκατος, Χρυσόπρασος.) Non reperitur hoc nomen in Græcis Vet. Testamenti. Est austeri coloris, ac proinde severitatem Apostolorum contra peccatores significat.

ὁ ἑνδέκατος, Ὑάκινθος.) Nec hoc quidem nomen est in Græcis Interpretibus. Sunt qui לשם ei putant respondere. Id vero Λιγύριον vertitur. Ideoque Hyacinthum & Ligyrium idem putat esse Hieronym. epist. 129. Sunt Hyacinthi optimi coloris aërii, ut hic notat Arethas, & Philo hyacinthinum colorem exponit aërium. Quare recte is significat Apostolorum animum patientem omnium tempestatum, quas mundus in eos excitabat.

ὁ δωδέκατος, Ἀμέθυστος.) Nomine ipso significat sobrietatem & ex simili omne temperantiæ genus. Ebr. אחלמה. Significationibus, quas diximus, non absurdum est addere, per hos lapides & gemmas simul adumbrari diversitatem terrarū, unde isti lapides veniunt, & ubi Apostoli virtutum suarum dedere specimen. Errant vero, qui à singulis Apostolis singulos articulos ad symbolum collatos putant. In symbolis enim vetustissimis non sunt tot articuli.

O admirandam gemmæ unius magnitudinem, quia murus integer 375. milliaria altus & 144. cubita spissus constat, ne de longitudine innominata dicam! O structuram pretiosissimam! Quid enim auro, gemmis & margaritis charius? At vero hæc civitas tota aurea, muri ejus omnes gemmei, portæ omnes ex margaritis constantes. Conf. Es. LIV, 11. 12. Tob. XIII. E gemmis octo habentur in pectorali Aaronis, Exod. 28, 19. Sardius, Topazius, Smaragdus, Jaspis, Amethystus, Beryllus, Chrysolithus. Quator vero hic variant Chalcedonius, Sardonyches, Chrysoprasus, Hyacinthus: Onychen tamen & Sardonychen non multum differre ajunt. Carbunculum vero Junius facit Chrysoprasum. Quam vero Tremell. Cyanon vertit, Hyacinthum putant; & Achatem Chalcedonium, Jaspidem nonnulli Adamantem esse censent: quæ in medio relinquimus. Nunquā enim convenient de his Rabbini, alii Lexicographi. Virtutes autem Apostolorum designari communiter volunt, quas singulis applicare perquam difficile est. Nam & ordine ipsi variant, Matth. 10, 2. Marc. 3, 18. Luc. 6, 14. Per Jaspidem omnium pretiosissimam fidem Petri non deficientem, 1. Petr. 1. Luc. 22. intelligunt. Per Sapphirum cærulei coloris aureis punctis collucentem cœlestem Jacobi sanguine rutilantis conversationem & migrationem: Per Chalcedonem scalpenti bus resistentem S. Johan. qui à nemine occidi potuit: Per Sma- ragdum Andream, qui ante omnes viruit, Joh. 1,41. Sardonyx à candore & rubore celebratur, ac marty- rium rubeum Philippi exprimere censetur. Sardius rubri coloris Bartholomæo excoriato aptatur. Be- ryllus clarus S. Thomam refert, post Christi resur- rectionem oculos perspicaces habentem: Chrysoli- thus auri color ob Indiæ & Æthiopiæ natalem Mat- thæo, ejus Apostolo: Topazius Jacobo Alphæi fratrẽ Domini, Christum vita & vultu referentem ob do- ctrinæ fulgorem: Chrysoprasus Judæ ob aureã Chri- sti confessionem apud Edessenos: Hyacinthus igneus Jacobũ fratrem Johannis amore ardentem: de qui- bus gemmarum Scriptores, Rucus, aliiq; conferantur.

## 21:21
V. 21. And the twelve gates were twelve pearls, each one of the gates was of one pearl.] Pearls are properly unions born in shells. But it is not to be doubted that here, by catachresis, a marble is understood that is shining like pearls, which is אקדח in Isaiah 54:12. Nor do I think that מרגלית is taken otherwise by the Rabbis at Psalm 87:1. Thus black stones are called by the name of Stibium, Isaiah 54:11. Mention of Parian marble, 1 Chronicles 29:2. See also Isaiah 54:12. It is signified here that there was a certain purity in the Old Testament, but not that splendor of virtues which is in the New. See above 12. Ἀνὰ εἷς, each one. For ἀνὰ is distributive, as Matthew 20:9, 10; Mark 6:40, 7:31; Luke 9:3, 14.

And the street of the city was pure gold.] He calls the forum of the city the street here and below 22:2, as in 2 Chronicles 32:6, Job 29:7, and elsewhere. By the forum, however, the assemblies of Christians are to be understood: those assemblies were incorrupt, like purified gold.

As transparent glass.] A second comparison. They live always as in the sight of God. See above 18.

The whole dowry of pearls is in their whiteness: the pearl is of eternal possession: the round one is held more precious. See Pliny. Which things befit the dignity of eternal life and the angelic whiteness of the elect.

Latin:

V. 21. Καὶ οἱ δώδεκα πυλῶνες δώδεκα μαργαρῖται, ἀνὰ εἷς ἕκαστος ή πυλώνων ἦν ἐξ ἑνὸς μαργαρίτε.] Margarita propriè sunt unio- nes in conchis nascentes. Sed non dubitandum, quin hic per κατάχρησιν marmor intelligatur candens admodῦ margaritarũ, quod אקדח Es. 54, 12. Nec aliter puto sumi מרגלית à Rab- binis ad Ps. 87, 1. Sic lapides nigri vocantur sub Stibii nomine, Es. 54, 11. Marmoris Parii mentio, 1. Par. 29, 2. Vide & Es. 54, 12. Significatur hic puritas quædam fuisse in V. T. at non is virtu- tum splendor, qui in N. Vide supra 12. Ἀνὰ εἷς singuli. Est enim ἀνὰ distributivum, ut Mat. 20, 9. 10 Marc. 6, 40. 7, 31. Luc. 9, 3. 14.

Καὶ ἡ πλατέια έ πόλεως χρυσίον καθαρόν.] Πλατέιαν hic & infra 22, 2. vocat forum urbis, ut 2. Par. 32, 6. Job. 29, 7. & alibi. Per forum autem intelligendi conventus Christianorum: Ii conventus erant incorrupti, ut aurum depuratum.

Ὡς ὕελος διαυγής.] Altera comparatio. Vivunt semper, ut in Dei conspectu. Vide supra 18.

Margaritæ omnis dos in candore: margarita æ- ternæ possessionis est: rotunda pretiosior habetur. Vid. Plin. Quæ vitæ æternæ dignitati, & Angelico Electorum candori conveniunt.

## 21:22
Vers. 22. And I saw no temple in it.] I saw no one place destined for prayers, as in the ancient Jerusalems, no shedding of blood. Christians did not call the places of their assemblies temples. See what was said at Acts 7:48.

For the Lord God Almighty is its temple and the Lamb.] Wherever God and Christ are, there is the spiritual temple, John 4:23, 1 Corinthians 1:2, chapter 4:17, Philippians 4:6.

And the city has no need of the sun nor of the moon.] Naturally, because its light is not external, but internal: it pertains to the inner man. It has no need, namely for its worship. It always serves God, not according to equinoxes or new moons.

Latin:

Vers. 22. Καὶ ναὸν ὐκ εἶδον ἐν αὐτῇ.] Non unum vidi locum orationibus destinatum, ut in veteribus Hierosolymis, nullam sanguinis effusionem. Christiani loca suorum conventuum non vocabant templa. Vide quæ dicta ad Act. 7, 48.

Ὁ γὰρ κύριος ὁ παντοκράτωρ ναὸς αὐτῆς ἐστι κὶ τὸ ἀρνίον.] U- bicunque est Deus & Christus, ibi templum spirituale, Joh. 4, 23. 1. Cor. 1, 2. c. 4, 17. Phil. 4, 6.

Καὶ ἡ πόλις ὐ χρείαν ἔχει ἡλίο ὐδὲ τῆς σελήνης.] Nimirum, quia lux ejus non externa, sed interna est: Pertinet ad τὸν ἔσω ἄνθρωπον. Non opus habet, nempe ad suum cultum. Semper Deo servit non ad æquinoctia aut novas lunas.

## 21:23
That they may shine in it.] So that either the sun or the moon may indicate the times of worship. In the Manuscript: that they may shine upon it.

V. 23. For the glory of God enlightened it.] Aorist for all time. Enlightened for enlightens. The glory of God is the intelligible light and all-radiance to Philo concerning the fabrication of the world. See above 11 and what was said there. The words are taken from Isaiah 60:14. But here in a more sublime sense. God will teach the Church through Athanasius, Basil, Nazianzen, Ambrose, Jerome, and others. And there is an allusion to the first creation, where light served in place of the sun.

and its lamp is the Lamb.] i.e., Christ will be in place of the moon, as God is in place of the sun. The moon is called light, נור, Isaiah 60:19, as also the stars. That is less than אור, Habakkuk 3:3. A lamp shines with light received from elsewhere. These two lights, one for the sun, the other for the moon, were seen in John to proceed from the Royal leaves, which were in the middle of the city.

Latin:

Ἴνα φαίνωσιν ἐν αὐτῇ.] Ut aut sol, aut luna tempora cultus indicant. In Manuscripto: ἵνα φαίνωσιν αὐτῇ.

V. 23. Ἡ γὰρ δόξα Θεῦ ἐφώτισεν αὐτήν.] Ἀόριστον pro omni tempore. Ἐφώτισε pro φωτίζει. Δόξα Θεῦ כבוד τὸ νοητὸν φῶς & παναύγεσια Philoni de mundi fabrica. Vide supra 11. & ibi dicta. Sumpta verba ex Es. 60, 14. Sed hic in sensu sublimiore. Deus Ecclesiam docebit per Athanasium, Basilium, Nazianze- num, Ambrosium, Hieronymum & alios. Et allusio est ad primam creationem, ubi lux fuit pro sole.

κὶ ὁ λύχνος αὐτῆς τὸ ἀρνίον.] i. e. Christus erit vice lunæ, ut Deus vice solis. Luna lux dicitur נור Es. 60, 19. ut & stellarũ. Id minus est, quã אור Abac. 3, 3. Lucerna lucet lumine aliunde accepto. Duæ hæ luces, altera pro sole, altera pro luna Joh. vi- sæ sunt procedere ex foliis Regalib9, quæ erant in media urbe.

## 21:24
V. 24. And the nations shall walk by its light.] From Isaiah 60:3, where in the former sense it treats of the happy state of Jerusalem after the return from Babylon. But that which is described more openly here is shadowed forth. By its light is the same as in Isaiah in the Greek, by thy light; very many nations from that Church which was in the Roman empire will be taught directly, such as the Indians, Ethiopians, Persians, Abasgi, Colchi, and Iberians.

And the kings of the earth bring their glory and honor into it. Excellently said. The sense is drawn from Is. 49:23, 60:10, 16. It treats there of the help which kings brought to the Jews, and of the gifts which they sent into the second temple: But how much more magnificently were these fulfilled, when the Roman Emperors not only came into the Church with all their Majesty, but also submitted themselves to its discipline, as Theodosius the Great.

Latin:

V. 24. κὶ περιπατήσουσι τὰ ἔθνη διὰ τῦ φωτὸς αὐτῆς.] Ex Es. 60, 3. ubi priore sensu agitur de statu Hierosol. felice post reditum ex Babylonia. Sed adumbratur id, quod hic apertius descri- tur. Διὰ τῦ φωτὸς idem quod apud Esaiam in Græco τῷ φωτί σε, Gentes plurimæ ab Ecclesia eâ, quæ erat in imperio Rom. recta edocebuntur, ut Indi, Æthiopes, Persæ, Abasgi, Colchi, Iberi.

Καὶ οἱ βασιλεῖς τῆς γῆς φέρουσι τὴν δόξαν κὶ τὴν τιμὴν αὑτῶν εἰς αὐτήν,.] Egregie dictum. Sensus depromptus ex Es. 49, 23. 60, 10. 16. Agitur ibi de auxilio, quod Reges tulere Judæis, & de do- nis, quæ miserunt in templum secundum: At quanto hæc im- pleta magnificentius, cum Imperatores Romani non modo in Ecclesiam venere cum omnia sua Majestate, sed & disciplinæ ejus se submifere, ut Theodosius Magnus.

## 21:25
V. 25. And its gates shall not be shut by day. Take day here for the space of twenty-four hours. Access will always be open to it. For the same, Isaiah said, day and night, LX, 11.

For there shall be no night there. City gates are usually shut at night. In this city there is never night. For the light is perpetual from God and Christ. Philo, speaking of heaven in the life of Joseph: He made heaven an eternal day, devoid of night and every shadow, as it is illuminated by unquenchable and pure, indivisible lights.

Latin:

V. 25. Καὶ οἱ πυλῶνες αὐτῆς ὐ μὴ κλεισθῶσιν ἡμέρας.] Diem hic sume pro spatio horarum viginti & quatuor. Semper eo pate- bit aditus. Pro eodem Esaias dixit, die & nocte, LX, 11.

Νὺξ γὰρ ὐκ ἔσαι ἐκεῖ.] Nocte solent claudi urbium portæ. In hac urbe nunquam nox est. Lux enim est perpetua à Deo & Christo. Philo de cœlo loquens in vita Josephi: Ἐνέφησε τὸν ὐρανὸν ἡμέραν αἰώνιον νυκτὸς κὶ πάσης σκιᾶς ἀμέτοχον, ἅτε περι- λαμπόμενον ἀσβέσοις κὶ ἀκράτοις ἀδιαστάτοις φέγγεσι.

## 21:27
V. 27. And there shall in no wise enter into it anything common and that worketh abomination and a lie. That there shall in no wise enter is of the potential mood. Wicked men cannot enter, who, that is, remain such. For they are barred by the stipulations of baptism. This is a mystical application of the words of Is. 52:1 and 60:18, seqq. Origen, to Celsus objecting that men of evil life are admitted to the rites of the Christians, replies that such are led to repentance, and when they testify to repentance, to the rites. Furthermore, common and that worketh are neuters for masculines or common genders. This is frequent in John, as in the Gospel VI, 36, 38, compared with the passage there 40. So also 1 Cor. 2:27, 28, when he says the foolish things, he explains that which lies hidden under the legal prohibition concerning unclean animals. For the pig denotes those living filthily, birds of prey denote robbers, as can be known from the epistle of Barnabas and those things which we said at Acts X, 14. That worketh abomination denotes those who practice idolatry. For abomination is sometimes an idol, sometimes an idolatrous act. By that worketh a lie, understand those who are unjust in covenants and contracts. See above 21:8 and what is said there. You have to work a lie also below 22:15 and Jer. 3:10. That is to work a lie, Hosea 7:1.

Except. It is not of an exception in this place, but of an opposition, as above 9:4.

They who are written in the book of life of the Lamb, who are inscribed into that life which the Lamb now lives. See above 3:5, ch. 13:8, ch. 17:8, ch. 20:12, 14.

Alcasar calls Christ the holy man: the God of holy things. The light of the sun and moon denotes the perpetual brightness, without the vicissitude of night: the glory of the nations denotes the honor of the Elect in the other life, Is. LX, 3, 11. There are eternal joys of the eternal city, says Aug. in sent. n. 37, and the infinite perpetuity of standing days will neither be varied nor will it slip away. We are the temple of God, 1 Cor. III, 16, and God is our temple: In the temple God was present, and filled it with His Majesty, 1 Kings 8; in the mercy seat He manifested Himself by divine grace, and God returned answers or oracles: in the temple a lamp shone perpetually, by the care of the Priest, and the heavenly fire always burned. The showbread was set forth, and sacrifices were offered for a sweet-smelling savor: by which, as the highest mysteries were once shadowed forth, and thus the propitiatory sacrifices of Christ, the offering of the High Priest of the N.T., and His intercession for us were prefigured, so God wills to be present with us, and to dwell in us by grace, and that the temples of our heart be filled with all His fullness, Eph. III, 17, and to manifest Himself to us, John XIV, 21, and to make us certain of His grace, Rom. VIII, 16, to shine in us with the light of the Word, until the Daystar arises in our heart, 2 Pet. I, 19, to irradiate with the fiery splendor of love, and to graciously receive the sacrifices of prayers and praises, and also the propitiatory sacrifice of Christ offered by true faith, Heb. XI, 4, 6. Again, God is our temple, because we are in God, we stand and move, Acts XVII, 28, both corporally and spiritually. God is called place in Pirke Avoth, our dwelling, because as God dwells in us, so also we are in GOD because of the perichoresis and mutual indwelling, and that heavenly and glorious one: In God we exult, in God we sing, in GOD we glorify God, in GOD Himself we see the divine face, we love Him whom we see, we celebrate Him whom we love, in the light of divine illumination we see the light of grace and divine Majesty, and we are inebriated with the torrent of glorious pleasure, Ps. 36:9, 10. All of which can also be said of the Lamb of God: therefore the Lamb is also called our temple. Into the temple of the Lord no uncircumcised person, no profane and unclean person entered, Is. 60:21, ch. 52:1. So neither is anything defiled admitted into that heavenly temple, in a word, no curse, Rev. XXII, 3.

Latin:

V. 27. Καὶ ὀυ μὴ ἐισέλθῃ ἐις ἀυτὸν πᾶν κοινὸν κὶ ποιο͂υν βδέλυγμα κὶ ψεῦδος.] Illud ὀυ μὴ ἐισέλθῃ est modi δυνητικῶ. Non possunt intrare flagitiosi, qui nempe tales manent. Arcentur enim per stipulationes baptismi. Est hic applicatio mystica verborum Es. 52, 1. & 60, 18. seqq. Origenes Celfo objicienti ad Christianorum τελετὰς admitti malæ vitæ homines, respondet tales adduci ad pœnitentiam, ubi pœnitentiam testantur, ad τελετὰς. Deinde κοινὸν & ποιο͂υν sunt neutra pro masculinis sive communibus. Frequens hoc Johanni, ut in Evang. VI, 36. 38. collato loco ibidem 40. Sic & 1. Cor. 2, 27. 28. cum dicit τὰ μωρὰ explicat id, quod latet sub interdicto legali de animalibus immundis. Nam sus denotat fœde viventes, aves carnovoræ raptores, ut cognosci potest ex Barnabæ epistola & iis, quæ diximus ad Act. X, 14. Ποιο͂υν βδέλυγμα eos denotat, qui idololatriam exercent. Nam βδέλυγμα שקץ modo est idolum, modo actus idololatrici. Per ποιο͂υν ψεῦδος intellige eos, qui in pactis & contractibus injusti sunt. Vide supra 21, 8. & ibi dicta. Ποιε͂ιν ψεῦδος habes & infra 22, 15. & Jer. 3, 10. Id ἐγγάσασθαι ψεῦδος Osex 7, 1.

Εἰ μὴ.] Non est excipientis hoc loco, sed adversantis, ut supra 9, 4.

Οἱ γεγραμμένοι ἐν τῷ βιβλίῳ τῆς ζωῆς τῶ ἀρνίω, qui ei vitæ adscripti sunt, quam jam vivit Agnus. Vide supra 3, 5. c. 13, 8. c. 17, 8. c. 20, 12. 14.

Alcasar Christum hominem sanctum: Deum sanctum sanctorum dicit. Lumen solis & lunæ perpetuam claritatem, sine vicissitudine noctis: gloria gentium honorem Electorum in altera vita notat, Es. LX. 3. 11. Æternæ civitatis æterna gaudia sunt, ait Aug. in sent. n. 37. & stantium dierum perpetuitas infinita nec variabitur, nec labetur. Nos sumus templum Dei, 1. Cor. III, 16. & Deus est templum nostrum: In templo Deus præsens erat, & replebat id Majestate sua, 1. Reg. 8. in propitiatorio manifestabat se divina gratia, & reddebat Deus responsa vel oracula: in templo lucebat perpetuo lampas, cura Sacerdotis, & ardebat semper ignis cælestis. Sistebantur panes propositionis, & offerebantur sacrificia in odorem quietis: quibus ut adumbrata sunt quondam mysteria summa, adeoque præfigurata Christi sacrificia propitiatoria, Pontificis N. T. oblatio, ejusdemq; pro nobis intercessio, ita nobis præsto esse, & in nobis habitare vult Deus gratia & cordis nostri templa impleri omni plenitudine sua, Eph. III, 17. nobisque sese manifestare, Joh. XIV, 21. nosque de gratia sua certos reddere, Rom. IIX, 16. lucere in nobis Verbi lumine, donec oriatur Phosphorus in corde nostro, 2. Petr. I, 19. irradiare igneo amoris splendore, & sacrificia precum & laudum, nec non sacrificium propitiatorium Christi vera fide oblatum gratiose suscipere, Ebr. XI, 4. 6. Rursus Deus est nostrum templum, quia nos in Deo sumus, stamus & movemur, Act. XVII, 28. cum corporaliter, tum spiritualiter. Deus in Pirke Avoth מקום locus dicitur, מְוֹן nostrum, quia ut Deus in nobis habitat, ita & nos in DEO sumus ob περιχώρησιν & circumincefsionem mutuam eamque cælestem & gloriosam: In Deo exultamus, in Deo cantamus, in DEO glorificamus Deum, in DEO ipso videmus faciem divinam, amamus, quem videmus, celebramus, quem amamus, in lumine divinæ illuminationis videmus lumen gratiæ & Majestatis divinæ, & inebriamur torrente voluptatis gloriosæ, Ps. 36, 9. 10. Quæ omnia etiam de Agno Dei dici possunt: ideo & Agnus vocatur templum nostrum. In templum Domini nullus incircumcisus, nullus profanus & immundus ingrediebatur, Esa. 60, 21. c. 52, 1. Ita nec in templum illud cælesfe aliquid coinquinatū admittitur, uno Verbo, nullum κατανάθεμα, Apoc. XXII, 3.

## 22:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXII.

ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

The river of living water, the tree of life, and the light and blessedness of the servants of God seen by John, who, about to worship the Angel, is forbidden; the coming of the Lord is promised, those to whom He is about to render reward are proclaimed blessed, keeping His commandments, the reprobate are excluded from the heavenly city, a most grave final adjuration concerning adding nothing or taking nothing away, a vow concerning the coming of the Lord, and the desire of His bride, with the final vow of the book or Epistle.

There are two parts: I. The designation of the remaining excellencies of the heavenly city, with certain things pertaining thereto, to verse 15. II. The conclusion of the book to verse 21, or if a τριχοτομία does not displease, let the middle part be in place from verse 6 to 16.

PART I. The representation of the remaining excellencies of the heavenly City.

Vers. 1. And he showed me a pure river of water of life.) These things ought not to have been torn away from the preceding ones. For they cohere. By this, however, the baptistery is signified, which in those times that are designated here, used to be in the area before the basilicas, as we have said from Eusebius in the life of Constantine, and others. It is called a river, because a perennial fountain flowed into the baptistery. Moreover, every flowing water is a river to the Hebrews speaking Greek, Ez. 47, 5. Prov. 18, 4. See what we have said at Gen. 2, 10. and at Job 7, 38. Thus also the Jurisconsults use the word for rivers. This river is called pure, because he who is to be baptized promises purity of life, 1 Pet. 3, 21. Living waters, because it leads to eternal life, Mark 16, 16. Hermas 3, 9. It is water into which men descend bound to death, but ascend assigned to life. Moreover, there is an allusion in the river, as well as in the tree, to the first creation, to which the second is preferred.

Bright as crystal.) See above IV, 6.

Proceeding out of the throne of God and of the Lamb.) These two royal seats appeared in the middle of the city, and signified the Church ruled by God and Christ. These are perpetual thrones, not that one which was said to be in the holy of holies. Moreover, the water of baptism is said to flow from thence, because its institution is from God through Christ. A similar thought is in Sirach 1, 6. 7. 8.

By the river of living water proceeding from the throne of God and the Lamb, we understand the Holy Spirit, whose characteristic property, as they call it, is procession, John 15, 26. from the Son no less than the Father from the throne of Majesty, or metonymically, of God sitting on the throne, whose glory and divine essence are the same: to whom it properly belongs to irrigate us here with the grace and His Word flowing for our sanctification, formerly full with the river of glory and heavenly pleasure, Psalm 36, 9. for our eternal glorification: To whom therefore are attributed the living waters, with which we are sprinkled for eternal recreation, and the extinction, or rather the incessant excitation, of holy thirst, John IV. Sir. XXIV, 40. Finally, that mystical water is crystalline on account of its splendor, and light, and density, and perpetuity. All of which things belong to the Holy Spirit in an exceptional manner and in a way peculiar to him. Therefore Richard and Joachim take these things concerning the grace of the Holy Spirit, Richard concerning the Holy Spirit himself. Haymo and Ansbert understand them concerning the preaching of the Gospel among the nations: But that pertains to the Church militant, not to the triumphant, with which these things deal. They do not say it badly who hold that there is an allusion here to the earthly Paradise, knowing that it refers to the heavenly Paradise from Luke 23. This is indeed the river, says Ambrose in book III de S. S. c. 21, proceeding from the seat of God, it is the Holy Spirit whom he drinks who believes in Christ, just as He Himself says: If any man thirst, let him come unto me and drink. He that believeth on me, as the scripture saith, out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water. But this he spoke of the Spirit. Therefore the river is the Spirit. Compare Isa. 66, 12. Ez. 47, 1. 5. Dan. 7, 14. and what we have said at that place.

Latin:

CAPUT XXII.

ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Fluvius aquæ vivæ, lignum vitæ, & servorum Dei lux & beatitudo à Johanne visa, qui Angelum adoraturus, prohibetur, adventus Domini promittitur, mercedem reddituri cuiq; prædicantur beati, præcepta ejus custodientes, reprobi excluduntur è civitate cælesti, finalis obtestatio de nil addendo vel demendo gravissima, votum de adventu Domini, & desiderium ejus sponsæ, cum voto libri vel Epistolæ finali.

Partes duæ sunt I. Reliquarum civitatis cælestis excellentiarū designatio, cum quibusdam eo pertinentib9 ad v. 15. II. Libri conclusio ad v. 21. vel si τριχοτομία non displiceat, mediæ partis loco sit à v. 6. ad 16.

PARS I. Reliquarum Civitatis cælestis excellentiarum repræsentatio.

Vers. 1. Καὶ ἔδειξέ μοι ποταμὸν καθαρὸν ὕδατος ζωῆς.) Hæc avelli à superioribus non debuere. Cohærent enim. Signifi- catur autem hic baptisteriū, quod eis temporibus, quæ hic de- signantur, esse solebat in area ante basilicas, ut ex Eusebio in vita Constantini, & aliis diximus. Vocatur ποταμὸς, quia fons perennis influebat in baptisterium. Omnis autem aqua profluens ποταμὸς Ebræis Græce loquentibus, Ez. 47, 5. Prov. 18, 4. Vide quæ diximus ad Gen. 2, 10. & ad Job. 7, 38. Sic & fluminum vocem usurpant Jurisconsulti. Purum dicitur hoc flumen, quia puritatem vitæ promittit is, qui baptizandus est, 1. Petr. 3, 21. Aquæ vivæ, quia ducit ad vitam æternam, Marc. 16, 16. Hermas 3, 9. Aqua est in quam descendunt homines mor- ti obligati, ascendunt vero vitæ assignati. Tam autem in flumi- ne, quam in arbore allusio est ad primam creationem, cui se- cunda præfertur.

Λαμπρὸν ὡς κρύσταλλον.) Vide supra IV, 6.

Ἐκπορευόμενον ἐκ τοῦ θρόνου τοῦ Θεοῦ κὶ τοῦ ἀρνίου.) Hæ sedes Regiæ duæ apparebant in media urbe, & significabant Eccle- siam à Deo & Christo regi. Hæc solia sunt perpetua, non il- lud, quod dicebatur esse in sancto sanctorum. Fluere autem inde dicitur aqua baptismi, quia institutio ejus est à Deo per Christum. Similis ἔννοια Sirach. I, 6. 7. 8.

Per fluvium aquæ vivæ ἐκπορευόμενον de throno Dei & Agni Spiritum S. intelligimus, cujus proprie- tas characteristica, ut vocant, est ἐκπόρευσις, Joh. 15, 26. à Filio non minus quam Patre à throno Majesta- tis, vel Metonymice, Dei sedentis in throno, cujus gloria & essentia divina idem sunt: cui convenit proprie nos irrigare hic gratiæ & Verbi sui fluentis ad nostri sanctificationem, olim plenę flumine glo- riæ & voluptatis cœlestis, Psalm. 36, 9. ad nostri æternam glorificationem : Cui proinde tribuun- tur aquæ vivæ, quibus perfundimur ad æternam re- creationem, sitisq; sanctæ non tam exstinctionem, quam indesinentem excitationem, Joh. IV. Sir. XXIV, 40. Crystallina denique est aqua illa mysti- ca ob splendorem, & lucem ac densitatem & perpetui- tatem. Quæ omnia κατ᾽ ἐξαίρετον λόγον κὶ ἰδιολέκ- τως Spiritui S. competunt. Ideo Richardus, & Joa- chimus de Spiritus S. gratia, Richardus de ipsomet Spiritu S. hæc accipiunt. Haymo & Ansbertus de prædicatione Evangelii inter gentes intelligunt : Sed illa ad Ecclesiam militantem pertinet, non ad triumphantem, qua de hæc agunt. Allusionem ad Paradisum terrestrem hîc haberi non male ajunt, qui illum referre cœlestem Paradisum è Luc. 23. norunt. Hic est utique fluvius, inquit Ambrosius libr. III. de S. S. c. 21. de Dei sede procedens, is est Spiritus S. quem bibit, qui credit in Christum, sicut ipse ait : Qui sitit, veniat ad me & bibat. Qui credit in me, sicut dicit scriptura, flumina de ventre ejus fluent aquæ vivæ. Hoc autem dicebat de Spiritu. Ergo flumen est Spiritus. Conf. Esa. 66, 12. Ez. 47, 1. 5. Dan. 7, 14. & quæ nos ad illum locum.

## 22:2
Vers. 2. In the midst of the street of it.) That is, in the middle place of the assembly, as we have said above XI, 8. XXI, 21.

And of the river on this side and on that side.) These things are to be connected in that way, and both banks of the baptistery are signified. In the Manuscript it is on this side and on that side, not badly. But that other expression is found in this Apostle's Gospel XIX, 18. Moreover, there is in these and the following things an allusion to the first Psalm.

Tree of life.) The Cross of Christ, the cause for us of the best actions. Thus Plato places trees in the heavenly earth. And Philo in the creation of the world explains the tree of life as piety.

Bearing twelve fruits, yielding its fruit every month.) The cross is fruitful, not like other trees at a certain time of the year, but always. This and the following are taken from Ezech. 47, 12. But there are many trees there: Here one in many places: because all those figures refer to one cross. It can be said here: Their fruit never perishes, nor does it fail in winter, nor in summer.

From this place it seems to have happened that certain names of virtues were added in the Latin, Gal. V, 22. so that the duodenary number of fruits might be fulfilled.

Ticonius hom. XIX. The wood, he says, by the river is the cross, which throughout the whole world, not only every month, but also every day, in those who are baptized, exhibits fruit to God. There is no wood that bears fruit at all times, except the Cross of Christ, which the faithful carry, who are watered by the water of the ecclesiastical river, and render perpetual fruit at all times. These things do not please Cornelius: But these trees, he says, were seen in the heavenly Paradise; the cross, however, is on earth and in the Church militant. Who nevertheless afterwards does not hesitate to admit that the cross of Christ and of the saints also will be in heaven for a trophy and eternal triumph, nay, he proves that from the wooden cross of the Sibyl: O happy wood, on which God Himself hung, Nor does the earth contain thee, but thou shalt see the roofs of heaven. But both are without scripture. He also adds: that there will be there flourishing, odoriferous, pleasant things, which may feast the sight, the smell, and other senses, and fill them with wonderful pleasure. And he proves this from the vision of Gregory the Great, Laurentius Justinianus, Sebastian Barradius, nay even Ambrose, Basil, Damascene, Thomas, Soto, Richard, Henry, Major, with Suarez and John Salas: This river, the trees and the fruits can be taken literally, as they sound. For what stands in the way? For if Adam enjoyed these in the earthly Paradise: much more will the Blessed enjoy the same in the heavenly Paradise: for the earthly was a specimen and image of this. But here you may rightly ask: To what purpose? For God and nature do nothing in vain. And who does not know that the scriptures use these words to explain the things of the future age. Finally, how much more convenient is the explanation of Bede, Rupert, Ansbert, Ribera, and others, not disapproved by Cornelius himself, who understand by the tree of life Christ the Lord, who by the vision and enjoyment of Himself gives immortal life to the blessed, just as the tree of life gave to Adam in Paradise. This tree bears twelve fruits for twelve months, that is, it perpetually supplies the blessed with its fruit for food and fresh pleasure, and without any weariness, indeed with always new eagerness. The leaves of the tree are the words of Christ, by which he himself will soothe and console the blessed of all nations. Whence Peter said to him: Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life. And Alcazar, whom he prefers: Divine wisdom or the beatific vision is represented here by two symbols, namely by the river of the water of life, and by the tree of life. For it is called the river of the water of life itself, because it satisfies the thirst and all the desires of the Saints, and inebriates them with the highest pleasure. The same is called the tree of life, because like it, it confers immortality upon the blessed. For the beatific vision (which is the most perfect act of wisdom) necessarily follows the highest pleasure, and also immortality. And yet these two are most aptly figured by the drink of life and the food of life: because of drink and food, drink seems more apt for indicating pleasure, but food for the sustenance of life. For in drink there is found greater pleasure, in food more robust nourishment. Furthermore, that these trees bring forth new fruits in individual months signifies that in the blessed there is a constant renewal of immortality and beatitude, and that it is always new, complete, and perfect: so much so that in individual months, days, and hours, the vision and enjoyment of God is as new, savory, and pleasant to them as it was on the first day on which they began to enjoy it: for never, not even after a thousand millions of years, will any trace of age, weariness, or satiety creep upon them. Thirdly, its leaves are for the health of the nations, not to be restored and cured: for this cannot happen, since there are no diseases there, no defect of strength; but to be preserved and prolonged for all eternity. Add that these leaves heal all the diseases and infirmities of body and soul, with which the Saints labored in this life; they therefore heal them as soon as anyone enters heaven, and then they preserve the same healed for all ages. Furthermore, these leaves signify the accidental gifts of the beatific vision, which adorn it, as leaves do a tree, such as are in the soul the highest delight, enjoyment, comprehension of the highest good: in the body full health, vigor, strength, likewise agility, clarity, subtlety, impassibility. With these agree those words of Bernard, sermon 1 on diverse subjects: In the reward there is a torrent of pleasure, and the force of a river, a torrent flooding with joy, a river of glory and a river of peace. It is clearly a river, but one that flows toward, not one that flows or flows away. It is called a river not because it passes by or passes through, but because it abounds. They compare the palm tree to the tree of life, which at each rising of the moon produces also a single branch, so that with the production of twelve branches the year is completed. Whence the Egyptians, indicating the year, used to paint a palm, as Horus Apollo has it in Hieroglyph. c. 3.

Twelve fruits of the tree of life are counted, as Bonaventure teaches in diaet. Sal. tit. 10. c. 4. 1. Health without infirmity. 2. Youth without old age. 3. Satiety without disgust. 4. Liberty without servitude. 5. Beauty without deformity. 6. Impassibility without pain. 7. Abundance without indigence. 8. Peace without perturbation. 9. Security without fear. 10. Knowledge without ignorance. 11. Glory without ignominy. 12. Joy without sadness.

And every curse shall be no more there.) The Manuscript also has κατάθεμα: and the writer of the responses to the Orthodox says: The sense is, that in the Church those who have fallen into such crimes as are mentioned above at XXI. 8 are not tolerated. It is an abstract for a concrete, in the Hebrew manner: Those who depart from the discipline cease to be ours, says Tertullian.

And the throne of God and of the Lamb shall be in it.) Always, that is, it shall not be taken away like other empires. The mystical sense of the passage Dan. 2, 44.

And his servants shall serve him.) Namely in that city, that is, the Church.

And they shall see his face.) They are friends of God, and indeed of intimate admission, whom God makes a participant in his counsels. The future for any time. Concerning this friendship see the things said at Jas. 2, 23. John 15, 14. 15.

Latin:

Vers. 2. Ἐν μέσῳ τῆς πλατείας αὐτῆς.) Id est, in medio loco conventus, ut supra diximus XI, 8. XXI, 21.

Καὶ τοῦ ποταμοῦ ἐντεῦθεν κὶ ἐντεῦθεν.) Hæc eo modo conne- ctenda sunt, & significatur utraq; margo baptisterii. In Manu- scripto est ἐντεῦθεν κὶ ἐκεῖθεν, non male. Sed altera illa loquutio reperitur in hujus Apostoli Evangelio XIX, 18. Est autem in his & sequentibus allusio ad Psalmum primum.

Ξύλον ζωῆς.) Crux Christi, causa nobis optimarum actio- num. Sic Plato in terra cœlesti arbores ponit. Et Philo in mundi creatione arborem vitæ exponit ϑεοσέβειαν.

Ποιοῦν καρποὺς δώδεκα κατὰ μῆνα ἕκαστον ἀποδιδοῦς τὸν καρπὸν αὑτοῦ.) Fructifera est crux, non ut aliæ arbores certo anni tem- pore, sed semper. Sumpta hæc & sequentia ex Ezech. 47, 12. Sed ibi plures arbores : Hic una pluribus in locis : quia omnes illæ figuræ unam crucem referunt. Dici hic potest : Τάων ὔποτε καρπὸς ἀπόλλυται, ὐδέτ᾽ ἐπιλείπει Χείματος, ὐδὲ ϑέρους.

Ex hoc loco factum videtur, ut virtutium nomina quædam ad- dita sint in Latino, Gal. V, 22. ut duodenarius fructuum nume- rus impleretur.

Ticonius hom. XIX. Lignum, inquit, juxta fluvi- um crux est, quæ per totum mundum non solum omni- bus mensibus, sed etiam omnibus diebus, in his, qui ba- ptizantur, exhibet fructum Deo. Nullum est li- gnum, quod omni tempore fructificet, nisi Crux Christi, quam gestant fideles, qui rigantur aqua Ecclesiastici fluminis, & reddunt fructum perpe- tuum omni tempore. Non placent hæc Cornelio: Verum hæ arbores, inquit, visæ sunt in Paradiso cæ- lesti; crux autem est in terra & Ecclesia militante. Qui tamen postea non dubitat admittere crucem Christi & sanctorum quoq; in cælo fore ad trophæum & tri- umphum æternum, imo de cruce lignea Sibyllæ illud probat: O lignum felix, in quo Deus ipse pependit, Nec te terra capit, sed cæli tecta videbis. Sed utrumq; ἄτερ γραφῆς. Addit etiam: fore ibi res floridas, odoriferas, amœnas, quæ visum, odoratum, aliosq; sensus pascant, & mira voluptate perfundant. Idque ex visione Gregorii M. Laurent. Just. Sebast. Barrad. quin & Ambros. Basil. Damasc. Thomæ, Soto, Richardo, Henrico, Majore, cum Schuarez & Joh. Salas probat: Fluvius hic, arbores & poma ad literam, uti sonant, accipi possunt. Quid enim obstat? Nam si his in Paradiso terrestri fruitus est Adam: mul- to magis iisdem fruentur Beati in Paradiso cælesti: hu- jus enim specimen & imago fuit terrestris. Sed hic merito quæras: Cui bono? Deus enim & natura ni- hil faciunt frustra. Et quis nescit scripturas verbis hujus uti ad explicandas res futuri seculi. Denique quanto convenientior est Bedæ, Ruperti, Ansberti, Riberæ, aliorum explicatio, nec ipsi Cornelio im- probata, per lignum vitæ intelligentium Christum Dominum, qui sui visione & fruitione dat beatis vitam immortalem, sicut lignum vitæ dabat Adamo in Para- diso. Lignum hoc fert duodecim fructus per duodecim menses, hoc est perpetuo beatis fructum suum in cibum & voluptatem recentem, ac sine ullo fastidio, imo cum nova semper aviditate suppeditat. Folia ligni sunt ver- ba Christi, quibus ipse beatos omnium gentium mulce- bit & consolabitur. Unde ad eum dixit Petrus: Do- mine, quo ibimus, verba vitæ æternæ habes? Et Alca- saris, quam is præfert: Sapientiam divinam sive vi- sionem beatificam hic repræsentari per duo symbola scilicet per fluvium aquæ vitæ, & per lignum vitæ. Di- citur enim ipsa fluvius aquæ vitæ, quia Sanctorum si- tim & vota omnia satiat, eosq; voluptate summa ine- briat. Eadem dicitur lignum vitæ, quia ejus adinstar beatis confert immortalitatem. Nam visionem bea- tificam, (quæ perfectissimus est sapientiæ actus) necessa- rio consequitur summa voluptas, nec non immortali- tas. Atqui hæc duo aptissime per potum vitæ & cibum vitæ figurantur: quia ex potu & cibo potus aptior vi- detur ad voluptatem indicandam, cibus autem ad vitæ sustentationem. Nam in potu major voluptas, in victu robustior alimonia reperitur. Porro quod hæ arbores singulis mensibus novos proferant fructus, significat in beatis jugem esse immortalitatis & beatitudinis reno- vationem, eamq; novam semper, completam & perfe- ctam: adeo, ut in singulis mensibus, diebus & horis ita eis nova, sapida & jucunda sit visio Dei & fruitio, ac fuit primo die, quo frui illa cœperunt: nunquam enim, ne quidem post mille milliones annorum obrepet illis ullum vetustatis, fastidii aut satietatis vestigium. Tertio folia ejus sunt ad sanitatem gentium non in- staurandam & curandam: Hoc enim fieri nequit, cum ibi nulli sint morbi, nullus virium defectus; sed conser- vandam & prorogandam in omne ævum. Adde folia hæc sanare omnes morbos & infirmitates corporis & animæ, quibus Sancti laborarunt in hac vita; eas ergo sanant mox ut cælum quis ingreditur, ac deinde sa- nas easdem conservant in omnia secula. Porro folia hæc significant dotes accidentales visionis beatificæ, quæ eam condecorant, uti folia arborem, quales sunt in anima summa delectatio, fruitio, comprehensio sum- mi boni: In corpore plena sanitas, vigor, robur, item agilitas, claritas, subtilitas, impassibilitas. Quibus consonant illa Bernhardi serm. I. de divers. In remuneratione torrens est voluptatis, & fluminis impetus, torrens inundans lætitiæ, flu- men gloriæ & flumen pacis. Flumen plane est, sed quod af- fluat, non quod fluat vel effluat. Flumen vocatur non quod transeat vel pertranseat, sed quod abundet, Arbori vitæ com- parant palmam, quæ ad singulos lunæ ortus singulos etiam ramos procreat, ita ut duodecim ramorum productione annus expleatur. Unde Ægyptii annum indicantes pinge- bant palmam, ut habet Horus Apollo in Hieroglyph. c. 3.

Duodecim numerantur ligni vitæ fructus, docente Bona- ventura in dixt. Sal. tit. 10. c. 4. 1. Sanitas absque infirmi- tate. 2. juventus sine senectute. 3. satietas sine fastidio. 4. libertas sine servitute. 5. pulchritudo absque deformita- te. 6. impassibilitas sine dolore. 7. abundantia sine indi- gentia. 8. pax sine perturbatione. 9. securitas absque ti- more. 10. cognitio absque ignorantia. 11. gloria sine igno- minia. 12. gaudium sine tristitia.

Καὶ πᾶν κατάθεμα ὐκ ἔσαι ἐκεῖ.) Κατάθεμα habet & Ma- nuscriptus: & ait Scriptor responsionum ad Orthodoxos: Sensus est, in Ecclesia non tolerari prolapsos in facinora ta- lia, qualia supra memorantur XXI. 8. Est abstractum pro concreto, more Ebræo: Qui de disciplina recedunt, desinunt esse nostri, ait Tertullianus.

Καὶ ὁ θρόνος τῶ Θεῶ καὶ τῶ ἀρνίς ἐν ἀυτῇ ἔσαι.) Semper scil. non auferetur ut alia imperia. Sensus mysticus loci Dan. 2, 44.

Καὶ οἱ δῦλοι ἀυτῶ λατρεύσυσιν ἀυτῷ.) Nempe in illa urbe, id est, Ecclesia.

Καὶ ὄψονται τὸ πρόσωπον ἀυτῶ.) Sunt amici Dei, & qui- dem intimæ admissionis, quos Deus consiliorum suorum particeps facit. Futurum pro quovis tempore. De hac amicitia vide dicta ad Jac. 2, 23. Joh. 15, 14. 15.

## 22:4
And his name shall be on their foreheads.) They acknowledge God as their Lord as openly as servants who bear their master's name written on their forehead. They shall all be like Aaron, see above 14, 1.

In the words, and his name on their foreheads, it is undoubtedly alluded to the plate of the High Priest; to whom the inscription was given, Holiness of the Lord, Exod. 28, 26. For Christ has made us all Priests Rev. 1, 5. c. 5, 10.

Latin:

Καὶ τὸ ὄνομα ἀυτῶ ἐπὶ τῶν μετώπων ἀυτῶν.) Tam aperte Deum agnoscunt Dominum suum, quam servi, qui nomen herile in fronte scriptum gerant. Erunt omnes Aaroni similes, vide supra 14, 1.

In verbis, & nomen ejus in frontibus eorum indubie allu- ditur ad laminam Pontificis; cui inscriptio data Sanctitas Domini, Exod. 28, 26. Fecit enim Christus nos omnes Sa- cerdotes Apoc. 1, 5. c. 5, 10.

## 22:5
V. 5. And night shall be no more there.) He repeats what he had said above 21, 25. Thus the Prophets often. In the Manuscript for ἐκεῖ is ἔτι, which is how the Latin reads. See Rom. 13, 12. 1 Thess. 5, 5.

And they have no need of lamp and light of sun.) Καὶ here means therefore. They have no need, namely those serving God. And understand by lamp the moon, or where the moon is silent, something else that takes its place, just as a lighthouse rivaling the moon removes the night-wandering lights. In the Manuscript: And they have no need of the light of a lamp and the light of the sun, constructed differently with the same noun. For both are correctly said: I have need of this thing, and I have need of this thing.

For the Lord God shall enlighten them.) Above 21, 24. Φωτιεῖ יאיר shall give them illustrious teachers in those times. See Is. 60, 1.

And they shall reign for ever and ever.) They have promises of future glory, and of an eternal kingdom 2 Tim. 2, 2. Rom. 5, 17.

Concerning which Gregory the Great in the end of the 7th Penitential Psalm. There is light without defect, joy without groaning, desire without pain, love without sadness, satiety without loathing, life without death, health without languor.

Latin:

V. 5. Καὶ νὺξ ὐκ ἔσαι ἐκεῖ.) Repetit quod dixerat supra 21, 25. Sic Prophetæ sæpe. In Manuscripto pro ἐκεῖ est ἔτι quomodo legit Latinus. Vide Rom. 13, 12. 1. Thess. 5, 5.

Καὶ χρείαν ὐκ ἔχουσι λύχνε καὶ φωτὸς ἡλίου.) Καὶ hic valet ideo. Opus non habent, nempe illi Θεῶ λατρεύοντες. Et λύχνον intellige lunam, aut ubi luna silet, aliud quod ejus sit vice, sicut Lumina noctivaga tollit pharus æmula lunæ. In Manuscripto: Καὶ ὐκ ἔχουσι χρείαν φωτὸς λύχνου καὶ φῶς ἡλίου eodem nomine diverse constructo. Utrumque enim re- cte dicitur: opus habeo hac re, & opus habeo hanc rem.

Ὅτι Κύριος ὁ Θεὸς φωτιεῖ ἀυτούς.) Supra 21, 24. Φωτιεῖ יאיר præclaros illis temporib. Doctores dabit. Vid. Es. 60, 1.

Καὶ βασιλέυσυσιν εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων.) Promissa ha- bent futuræ gloriæ, regnique æterni 2. Tim. 2, 2. Rom. 5, 17.

De quo Greg. M. in fine 7. Ps. Pæn. Ibi est lux sine defectu, gaudium sine gemitu, desiderium sine pœna, amor sine tristitia, satietas sine fastidio, vita sine morte, salus sine languore.

## 22:6
V. 6. And he says to me. These words are faithful and true.) Namely, those things which were said concerning the splendor of the Church under Christian Princes. A similar affirmation above 19, 9. he says to me, namely the Angel. Here a new section should have begun.

And the Lord God of the spirits of the prophets.) From whom all Prophetic gifts have their origin. See Heb. 12, 9. Lord here signifies יהוה

He sent his angel.) Namely to you, John, as above.
